profileDesc.creation:
Initially created: 2025-12-06T12:09:00.392+09:00 by chris Translate the following text from Classical Chinese into English.
Requirements: 1. The text contains page numbers in square brackets, such as [01], [02], etc. - These must be passed through unchanged. - Each page number must appear in exactly the same position in the translation as in the source. - The number of page markers in the output must match the input exactly.
2. Personal names, place names, titles, and other proper nouns should be rendered in Hànyǔ Pīnyīn with tone marks.
3. Do NOT transcribe the full Classical Chinese text into Pinyin.
4. Do NOT include explanatory notes, annotations, or commentary — output only the English translation.
5. The target language is English.
Input text:

p.seg: Sīmǎ Guāng
compiled by imperial decree.
Later Learning Tiān Tái
The Sīmǎ clan
were from Wēn Xiàn in Hénèi.
King Xuān Yì obtained power in Wèi;
this was passed to King Jǐng Shī,
and when it reached King Wén Zhāo,
he was first enfeoffed as the Duke of Jìn.
As Wēn Xiàn was originally Jìn territory,
it was made the name of the state.
Shìzǔ, Emperor Wǔ, the first of the upper class,
whose taboo name was Yán,
courtesy name Ānshì,
surname Sīmǎ.
He was the grandson of King Xuān Yì
and the eldest son of King Wén Zhāo.
King Wén's temple name was Tàizǔ,
hence the emperor's temple name was Shìzǔ.
According to the rules for posthumous titles: "One who brings order to chaos is called Wǔ."
In the first year of Tàishǐ
(Yǐyǒu, 265), in the twelfth month of this year,
he was about to receive the abdication and change the reign title.
This was still the second year of Xiánxī of Wèi.
1 Spring,
third month.
The ruler of Wú sent Grand Master of Splendid Happiness Jǐ Zhì and Gentleman of the Five Offices Hóng Qiú
along with Xú Shào and Sūn Yù to return the visit.
Shào and Yù's visit to Wú was mentioned in the previous year of the upper volume.
There were some who said Shào praised the beauty of the Middle Kingdom.
The ruler of Wú was enraged,
recalled them,
and killed them.
2 Summer,
fourth month.
Wú changed its reign title to Gānlù.
At this time, because of a report of auspicious dew descending at Jiǎnglín, the reign title was changed.
3 Fifth month.
The Wèi emperor granted King Wén special rites,
meaning that his banners, chariots, musical dances, and ceremonial robes
were all to be like those of an emperor.
The heir apparent was called the crown prince.
4 On the day Guǐwèi,
a general amnesty was proclaimed.
5 Autumn,
seventh month.
The ruler of Wú forced King Jǐng's empress to commit suicide
and moved King Jǐng's four sons to Wú;
soon after, he killed the two eldest among them.
The ruler of Wú demoted Empress Jǐng
and enfeoffed her four younger brothers;
this matter is mentioned in the previous year of the upper volume.
Zhǎng
is pronounced as 'zhī' or 'liǎng'.
6 Eighth month.
On the day Xīnmǎo,
King Wén died.
The crown prince succeeded him as Chancellor of State and King of Jìn.
7 Ninth month.
On the day Yǐwèi,
a general amnesty was proclaimed.
8 On the day Wùzǐ,
Hé Céng, Minister of Works of Wèi, was appointed Chancellor of Jìn;
on the day Guǐhài,
Cavalry General Sīmǎ Wàng was appointed Minister of Works.
9 On the day Yǐhài,
King Wén was buried at Chóngyáng Líng.
A textual critique states: The "Biography of Wén" in the Jìn Shū records it as
"Guǐyǒu",
but we follow the "Annals of King Chénliú" in the Wèi Zhì.
10Winter.
Bù Chǎn, Commander of Xīlíng for Wú,
Xīlíng
is Yílíng.
In the first year of Huángwǔ, the ruler of Wú, Quán, changed Yílíng to Xīlíng,
where the commandery seat of Yídū was located.
The ruler of Wú agreed,
sending Grand Master Censor Dīng Gù and Right General Zhūgě Jìng to guard Jiànyè.
Chǎn
was the son of Zhì.
During the time of the ruler of Wú, Quán,
Zhì was the Commander of Xīlíng.
Zhì,
pronounced as 'zhī' or 'rì'.
11Twelfth
month.
On the day Rénxū,
the Wèi emperor abdicated in favor of Jìn.
Emperor Yuán of Wèi was twenty years old at this time.
Kùndūn's memorial.
Emperor Wén of Wèi first received the abdication from Hàn,
and after five generations,
it perished after forty-six years.
On the day Jiǎzǐ,
he moved out of the palace to Jīnyǒng Chéng.
Jīnyǒng Chéng was in the northwest corner of Luòyáng city.
Holding the emperor's hand,
he wept and sighed uncontrollably,
saying:
"The day I die,
I will truly be a loyal minister of the Great Wèi."
On the day Bǐngyín,
the King ascended the imperial throne,
proclaimed a general amnesty,
and changed the reign title.
It was only then that the reign title was changed to Tàishǐ.
On the day Dīngmǎo,
the Wèi emperor was honored as the King of Chénliú,
and he was immediately settled in Yè.
Jí
means 'to settle'.
All followed the precedents of early Wèi.
See volume 69, the first year of Huángchū under Emperor Wén of Wèi.
King Xuān was posthumously honored as Emperor Xuān;
King Jǐng as Emperor Jǐng;
and King Wén as Emperor Wén;
the King's mother, the Grand Empress Dowager, was honored as the Empress Dowager.
His imperial grand-uncle Fú was enfeoffed as the King of Ānpíng;
his uncles Gàn as the King of Píngyuán, Liàng as the King of Fúfēng, Zhòu as the King of Dōngguǎn, Jùn as the King of Rǔyīn, Róng as the King of Liáng;
Lún as the King of Lángyá;
his younger brothers Yōu as the King of Qí, Jiàn as the King of Lè'ān, Jī as the King of Yān;
and also seventeen collateral relatives, including Minister of Works Wàng, were all enfeoffed as kings.
Wàng
was the son of Fú.
The emperor enfeoffed the various kings
by making commanderies their states.
A state of twenty thousand households was a large state,
with three armies (upper, middle, lower),
totaling five thousand soldiers;
ten thousand households was a secondary state,
with an upper and lower army,
totaling three thousand soldiers;
five thousand households was a small state,
with one army,
totaling five hundred soldiers.
Kings did not reside in their states
but held office in the capital.
Zhòu
is pronounced 'zhòu'.
Cóng
is pronounced 'cái yòng'.
Guǎn
is pronounced 'guān'.
Róng
is pronounced 'yú zhōng'.
Yān
is pronounced 'yú xián'.
Zhèng Chōng was appointed Grand Tutor;
Wáng Xiáng as Grand Guardian;
Hé Céng as Grand Commandant;
Jiǎ Chōng as General of Chariots and Cavalry;
Wáng Shěn as General of Agile Cavalry;
the rest of the civil and military officials received various promotions and advancements in rank.
On the day Yǐhài,
King Ānpíng Fú was appointed Grand Preceptor,
overseeing all military affairs at home and abroad.
The Jìn Zhì says: Grand Preceptor, Grand Tutor, Grand Guardian
were the three ducal offices of Zhōu.
In early Jìn, due to the taboo name of Emperor Jǐng,
and also adopting official titles from the Zhōu Guān,
a Grand Preceptor was established to replace the role of Grand Master,
with a rank higher than the Three Ministers,
and along with the Grand Tutor and Grand Guardian, all became High Dukes.
Grand Marshal
was an ancient office.
The Hàn system placed it above the Grand General and General of Agile Cavalry,
to replace the position of Grand Commandant,
thus it was always alternated with the Grand Commandant
and not held concurrently.
By Wèi, there was a Grand Commandant,
while Grand Marshal and Grand General were separate offices,
ranking above the Three Ministers.
Jìn followed this system,
making Grand Preceptor, Grand Tutor, Grand Guardian, Minister of the Masses, and Minister of Works civil ducal officials.
The Left and Right Grand Master of Splendid Happiness and Grand Master of Splendid Happiness who established their own offices
ranked as ducal subordinates,
wearing jìnxián caps with three cross-beams
and black jǐezé headscarves.
Grand Marshal, Grand General, Grand Commandant were military ducal officials.

Generals of Agile Cavalry, Chariots and Cavalry, Guards, Fúbō, Fǔjūn, Dūhù, Zhènjūn, Zhōngjūn, the Four Expeditions, the Four Garrisons, Lóngxiáng, Diǎnjūn, Shàngjūn, Fǔguó, and others who established their own offices
ranked as ducal subordinates,
all wearing military caps
and flat-topped black headscarves.
General of Chariots and Cavalry Chén Qiān was also appointed Grand General,
along with Minister of the Masses, King Yíyáng Wàng, and Minister of Works Xún Yǐ,
making a total of eight dukes,
all appointed at the same time.
The emperor, admonished by the weakness of the isolated Wèi clan,
therefore greatly enfeoffed his imperial clan
and entrusted them with official duties.
He also decreed that all kings could personally select the chief officials within their states;
only General of Guards, King Qí Yōu, dared not do so,
instead requesting imperial approval for all appointments.
12 An imperial edict lifted the ban on the imperial clan of Wèi
and abolished the practice of generals of *bùqǔ* and chief officials leaving hostages as sureties.
Wèi's restrictions on the imperial clan were very strict,
even prohibiting them from holding office.
Now this was abolished.
Also, when generals went on campaigns or garrison duty, and chief officials served in provinces or commanderies,
they all left hostages in the capital.
This, too, was now abolished.
*Jiāng* [將]
is pronounced *liàng* (亮).
*Zhì* [質]
is pronounced *zhì* (致).
13 The Emperor, following the harsh and extravagant era of the Wèi clan,
corrected it with benevolence and frugality.
Tàicháng丞 Xǔ Qí [許奇]
was the son of Yǔn [允].

In Jìn, the Tàicháng [太常], Guānglùxūn [光祿勳], Wèiwèi [衞尉], Tàipú [太僕], Tíngwèi [廷尉], Dàhónglú [大鴻臚], Zōngzhèng [宗正], Dàsīnóng [大司農], Shǎofǔ [少府], Jiàngzuò Dàjiàng [將作大匠], the three ministers of the Empress Dowager, and Dàchángqiū [大長秋]
were all considered high-ranking ministers (*lièqīng*),
each with a Cheng [丞], Gōngcáo [功曹], Zhǔbù [主簿], Wǔguān [五官], and other staff.
The court deliberated that since Qí's father was executed,
Qí's father, Yǔn, was executed.
The details can be found in Volume 76, under Gāoguì Xiānggōng Zhèngyuán First Year.
*Cháo* [朝]
is pronounced *zháoyáo* (直遙).
and requested that he be appointed to an external office;
the Emperor then recalled Yǔn's long-standing reputation
and praised Qí's talent,
promoting him to Cíbù Láng [祠部郎].
The Wèi Shàngshū Cáo [尚書曹] had a Cíbù Láng,
and Jìn followed this.
An edict ordered the use of green hemp to replace it.
14 Initially, censorial officials (*jiànguān*) were established,
with Sànqí Chángshì Fù Xuán [傅玄] and Huángfǔ Táo [皇甫陶] appointed to them.
From Qín and Hàn onwards, there were *jiàn dàfū* [諫大夫],
which Zhèng Chāng [鄭昌] referred to as
"an office named for remonstrance."
In the Eastern Hàn, there were *jiànyì dàfū* [諫議大夫].
Wèi did not re-establish it.
Jìn used Sànqí Chángshì [散騎常侍], *shíyí* [拾遺], and *bǔquē* [補闕],
which were the duties of censorial officials.
He was the son of Gàn [幹].
Fù Gàn [傅幹]
was the son of Hàn Fù Xiè [傅燮].
He submitted a memorial saying:
"Your servant has heard that when the former kings governed the world,
education and moral transformation flourished above,
and pure discourse prevailed below.
Recently, Wèi Wǔ [魏武] favored legalism, and the world valued legal names (*xíngmíng*);
Wèi Wén [魏文] admired open-mindedness, and the world disparaged upholding integrity.
Afterwards, the guiding principles were not controlled.
*Shè* [攝]
means to govern.
This refers to Hè Yàn [何晏], Ruǎn Jí [阮籍], and their ilk.
*Cháo* [朝]
is pronounced *zháoyáo* (直遙).
Your Majesty ascended to power and received the abdication,
promoting the transformation of Yáo [堯] and Shùn [舜].
However, you have not yet appointed pure, far-sighted, and courteous officials to strengthen integrity and moral standards,
nor have you dismissed superficial and vulgar individuals to punish disrespect.
Therefore, your servant still dares to speak."
The Emperor commended and accepted his words,
instructing Xuán to draft an edict and submit it.
However, he was unable to reform it.
15 Originally,
Hàn Zhēngxī Jiāngjūn Sīmǎ Jūn [司馬鈞]
Details of Jūn are in Volume 50, Hàn Āndì Yuánchū First Year.
begat Yǐngchuān Tàishǒu Jùn [雋],
Jùn begat Jīngzhàoyǐn Fáng [防],
and Fáng begat Xuāndì [宣帝].
This outlines the lineage of the Sīmǎ clan
to lay the groundwork for establishing temples below.
1 In spring,
the first month,
on the *dìnghài* day,
the Wèi temple was used to sacrifice to the Zhēngxī Fǔjūn [征西府君] and those below him,
including Jǐngdì [景帝], for a total of seven chambers.
Shěn Yuē's [沈約] monograph states: At the beginning of Jìn, sacrifices were made to Zhēngxī Jiāngjūn, Yùzhāng Fǔjūn [豫章府君], Yǐngchuān Fǔjūn [潁川府君], Jīngzhào Fǔjūn [京兆府君],
with Xuānhuáng [宣皇], Jǐnghuángdì [景皇帝], and Wénhuángdì [文皇帝] forming the three *zhāo* and three *mù*.
At this time,
Xuānhuáng had not yet ascended, and Tàizǔ's [太祖] position was vacant,
so six generations were sacrificed, making seven temples with Jǐngdì.
The rites were based on Wáng Sù's [王肅] teachings.
2 The
Lady Yáng [羊氏], wife of Jǐngdì, was honored as Jǐng Huánghòu [景皇后]
and resided in Hóngxùn Gōng [弘訓宮].
3 On the *bǐngwǔ* day,
Empress Yáng [楊氏] of Hóngnóng [弘農] was established;
the Empress was the daughter of Wénzōng [文宗], a Wèi tōngshì láng [通事郎].
In the early years of Wèi Huángchū,
after the Zhōngshū [中書] established a supervisor and director,
it also established a tōngshì láng.
4 *Jǐnchén* [襜臣] submitted a memorial:
"The Five Thearchs [五帝]
are the Celestial Thearchs.
The imperial *qì* varies with the times,
hence there are five names and titles.
From now on, the seats of the Five Thearchs should be removed from the Míngtáng [明堂] and the Southern Suburb."
This was followed.
Dì [帝] was Wáng Sù's [王肅] maternal grandson,
so in the rites of suburban sacrifice,
officials often followed Sù's recommendations.
The *Zhōulǐ* says: When sacrificing to Hào Tiān Shàngdì [昊天上帝], one wears a large fur coat and a crown;
the same applies to sacrificing to the Five Thearchs.
Zhèng Xuán [鄭玄] believed that Hào Tiān Shàngdì was
the Tiānhuáng Dàdì [天皇大帝], the shining *pòbǎo* [耀魄寶] of the Northern Dipper.
The Five Thearchs [五帝] were
the spirits of the refined *qì* of the Five Phases,
namely Qīngdì Língwēiyǎng [青帝靈威仰],
Chìdì Chìbiāonù [赤帝赤熛怒],
Huángdì Hánshūniǔ [黃帝含樞紐],
Báidì Báizhāojǔ [白帝白招矩],
and Hēidì Zhīguāngjì [黑帝汁光紀].
From this came the theory of Six Heavens.
The Six Heavens
refer to their supreme, pure, and void essence,
which is actually one;
considering their merit in bringing forth life during the five seasons,
there are five distinctions,
hence the Six Heavens.
Based on their essence being above,
they are called Heaven (*tiān*);
Heaven is a term for substance,
so it is said of Heaven,
*Tiān* [天]
means the summit (*diān*).
Due to their merit in bringing forth life,
they are called Thearch (*dì*);
Thearch is a term for virtue,
so the *Máoshī Zhuàn* says: "To scrutinize and discern like Thearch."
Wáng Sù [王肅] refuted this,
believing that the Five Thearchs were not Heaven,
only using the text of the *Jiāyǔ* [家語],
referring to Tàihào [太皡], Yándì [炎帝], Huángdì [黃帝], Shàohào [少皡], and Zhuānxū [顓頊] as the Five Thearchs,
as five human emperors.
Jìn *jǐnchén* [襜臣] adopted Sù's [肅] view,
believing that the Five Thearchs were the Celestial Thearchs,
and though the imperial *qì* varied with the times,
distinguishing their titles as five,
they were actually one deity.
The seats of the Five Thearchs should be removed from the Míngtáng [明堂] and Southern Suburb,
and the names of the Five Essences at the Five Suburbs should be changed
to be uniformly called Hào Tiān Shàngdì [昊天上帝].
This was followed.
*Wáng* [王]
is pronounced *yúkuàng* (于況).
5 In the second month,
the ban on the Hàn imperial clan was lifted.
After Wèi supplanted Hàn,
it prohibited the various Liú [劉] clans;
this was now abolished.
6 In the third month,
Wú [吳] sent Dàhónglú Zhāng Yǎn [張儼] and Wǔguān Zhōnglángjiàng Dīng Zhōng [丁忠] to offer condolences and sacrifices.
This was for Wénwáng's [文王] funeral.
*Lú* [臚]
is pronounced *língrú* (陵如).
7 Wú [吳] Sànqí Chángshì Wáng
Fān [蕃],
was of a lofty and clear character,
unable to flatter or comply with the Wú ruler's wishes,
and the Wú ruler was displeased.
Sànqí Chángshì Wàn Yù [萬彧] and Zhōngshū Chéng Chén Shēng [陳聲] then slandered him.
When Dīng Zhōng [丁忠] returned from his mission,
the Wú ruler convened a grand assembly of ministers.
Fān was deeply drunk and prostrated himself.
The Wú ruler suspected him of feigning,
and had Fān carried out.
After a moment,
he was summoned back.
Fān enjoyed cultivating dignified manners and acted with self-possession.
The Wú ruler was furious,
ordered his attendants to behead him below the hall,
then went out,
ascended Lái Shān [來山].
The *Shuǐjīng Zhù* states: South of Wǔchāng [武昌] city is Lái Shān,
which is Fán Shān [樊山].
Wú Sūn Hào [孫晧] ascended it and
had his close attendants throw Wáng Fān's head, which they fought over like tigers.
They made it like tigers leaping and wolves fighting to bite and gnaw, and the head was completely shattered.
Dīng Zhōng said to the Lord of Wú:
"The north has no preparations for defense or battle.
Yìyáng can be attacked and taken."
Yìyáng County
belonged to Rǔnán Commandery during the Hàn dynasty.
Emperor Wén of Wèi divided it to establish Yìyáng Commandery.
The character 說 (shuō)
is pronounced shūrúi.
Grand General of the Western Expedition Lù Kǎi said:
"The north has recently annexed Bā and Shǔ.
They sent envoys to seek peace,
not to seek aid from us,
but to conserve their strength and await their moment.
The enemy's power is now strong,
and to seek a lucky victory
is not something I see as beneficial."
Although the Lord of Wú did not dispatch troops,
he nevertheless severed ties with Jìn.
Kǎi
was a cousin of Xùn.
8. In the summer,
in the fifth month,
on the day Rénzǐ,
Wáng Shěn, Duke Yuán of Bólíng, died.
9. In the sixth month,
on the day Bǐngwǔ huì,
there was a solar eclipse.
10. During the mourning period for Emperor Wén,
his officials and people all followed the expedient decree,
removing their mourning attire after three days.
After the burial,
the Emperor also removed his;
yet he still wore plain caps and ate plain food,
grieving and emaciated as one in mourning.
In the autumn,
in the eighth month,
the Emperor was about to visit Chóngyáng Líng.
All the officials memorialized, saying,
"The autumn heat has not yet subsided.
We fear Your Majesty's grief might cause damage to your health."
The Emperor said:
"When I am able to behold the imperial tomb,
my health will naturally improve."
He further issued an edict:
"Emperor Wén of Hàn did not require the whole empire to fully mourn,
which also reflected the utmost humility of an emperor.
Emperor Wén of Hàn's dying edict is found in volume fifteen, seven years later."
Zhēn Déxiù said: "This edict of Emperor Wén
was the beginning of shortened mourning.
However, the original text was presumably intended for officials and commoners.
Could Emperor Jǐng, as the heir,
shorten his mourning based on this?
How could one have no mourning attire!"
The proposal was to wear mourning sashes when accompanying the Emperor.
The assembled officials, however, followed the old system.
Shàngshū Lìng Péi Xiù memorialized:
"Since Your Majesty has removed your mourning attire and now wishes to don it again,
the righteousness has no basis.
If the ruler wears mourning and the subjects do not,
it would also be unsettling."
The Emperor issued an edict:
"My concern is that my feelings cannot reach the desired extent,
what do clothes matter!
It means that his concern was that his feelings of grief and longing were not profound enough,
it was not about the clothes.
The character 跂 (qǐ)
is pronounced qùzhì,
meaning 'to stand on tiptoe.'
How could I deliberately go against you?"
Thereupon, he stopped.
General of the Central Army Yáng Hù said to Fù Xuán:
"Three years of mourning,
even the noble observe it;
this is ritual.
Three years of mourning,
from the Son of Heaven down to commoners—
meaning, even with the Son of Heaven's nobility,
it is still appropriate to fulfill filial piety by observing three years of mourning.
The sovereign is most filial;
although he was compelled to remove his attire,
he truly observed the mourning rites.
If we could thus restore the law of the former kings,
would it not be excellent?"
Xuán said:
"Replacing months with days
has already been practiced for several hundred years.
Replacing months with days
was a mistaken theory of Hàn Confucians;
the note is found in volume fifteen, seven years after Emperor Wén of Hàn.
It is difficult to implement."
Hù said:
"If we cannot make the whole empire conform to the rites,
then at least to allow the sovereign to complete his mourning,
would that not be better?"
Xuán said:
"If the sovereign does not remove his mourning but the empire does,
this would mean there are only father and son,
with no longer ruler and subjects."
Thereupon, it was stopped.
On the day Wùchén,
all officials memorialized requesting the Emperor to change his attire and resume normal meals.
The Emperor issued an edict:
"Each time I remember the departed in the gloom,
and I was unable to complete the ritual of coarse mourning attire
(The Zuǒ Zhuàn states: When Yàn Huánzǐ of Qí died,
Yàn Yīng wore coarse sackcloth and coarse hemp mourning attire.
Dù Yù's commentary says: Jū [苴]
refers to hemp with seeds,
taken for its coarseness.
The character 苴 [jū]
is pronounced qīyú.)
how much less should I eat polished rice and wear brocade!
That would only intensify my feelings,
not alleviate them.
I was originally from a scholar's family,
and the transmission of rites has been long-standing.
How could I suddenly change this feeling towards my heaven?
You have already conceded much.
You may try to examine Confucius's reply to Zǎi Wǒ.
The Lún Yǔ states: Zǎi Wǒ asked:
'Three years of mourning
is already too long.
If a gentleman does not perform rites for three years,
the rites will surely decay;
if he does not make music for three years,
the music will surely collapse.
The old grain has been consumed,
and new grain has ripened;
one year should be enough.'
Confucius said:
'Eating polished rice
and wearing brocade,
would you feel at ease?'
He replied:
'At ease.'
Confucius said:
'If you feel at ease,
then do it.'
When Zǎi Wǒ left,
Confucius said:
'Yǔ is truly unfeeling!
A child is born, and only after three years
is he able to leave his parents' embrace.
Three years of mourning
is a universal mourning custom throughout the world.'
The Yí Lǐ states: 'The father
is the child's heaven.'
The character 省 (xǐng)
is pronounced xǐjǐng."

Referring to their merits and demerits.
After six years of this,
the presiding officials would compile all reports,
and scrutinize their words.
Those with six excellences would be exceptionally promoted,
those with six deficiencies would be dismissed,
six excellences,
means excellent for all six years.
Six deficiencies,
means deficient for all six years.
Those with more deficiencies than excellences would be demoted.
If the assessments in between are not balanced,
and the categories have varying difficulty,
the presiding officials should certainly weigh the severity,
and make slight adjustments in rank,
without needing to meticulously follow the law.
If there are cases where merits or demerits are judged based on personal feelings,
not aligning with public opinion,
the censorial authorities should be entrusted to investigate and impeach them.
If superiors and subordinates mutually tolerate each other's faults,
this would lead to a great decline in public integrity,
and even with laws for assessment,
it would be of no benefit.”
This matter was ultimately not implemented.
the Emperor plowed the sacrificial field north of the Luò River.
a general amnesty was proclaimed.
the Lord of Wú appointed Zuǒ Yùshǐ Dàfū Dīng Gù as Sītú,
and Yòu Yùshǐ Dàfū Mèng Rén as Sīkōng.
Wú Lù states: Mèng Rén’s original name was Zōng,
changed to avoid the character Hào.
on the day of Wùzǐ,
Empress Dowager Wáng died.
The Emperor's mourning rites
entirely followed ancient protocols.
6 In summer,
in the fourth month,
on the day Wùxū,
Wáng Xiáng, the Grand Duke of Suīlíng, died.
There were no miscellaneous guests offering condolences at his gate.
His kinsman Wáng Róng sighed, saying:
“Grand Mentor Wáng Xiáng lived during the Zhèngshǐ reign era,
but he was not among those known for their eloquence.
Yet, when I occasionally conversed with him,
his reasoning and insights were clear and profound.
Could it be that his virtue overshadowed his words? ”
The so-called eloquent people of the Zhèngshǐ era
were Hè Píngshū and a few others.
When the Wèi dynasty turned into the Jìn dynasty,
what benefit did they bring to the world?
The reason Wáng Xiáng is admirable
is because of his filial piety towards his stepmother and his refusal to bow to the King of Jìn.
Yet, a gentleman would still say that he was employing others as pillars and foundations while toppling their beams and rafters.
Clear and profound reasoning —
was it from his words,
or his virtue?
The calamity of pure conversation,
reaching the Yǒngjiā era,
and spreading to the Jiangzǒ,
had not yet ceased.
7 On the day Jǐhài,
Empress Wénmíng was buried.
The officials in charge again memorialized:
“After the Yú sacrifice,
the mourning garments should be removed.”
The Yú sacrifice was performed on the day of burial,
a second Yú sacrifice on a soft day,
and the third Yú sacrifice on a strong day.
The three Yú sacrifices must be performed by turning back.
Zhèng Shì said: The Yú sacrifice
is a ritual to pacify the spirit.
The bones and flesh return to the earth,
but the soul and breath can go anywhere.
Filial children, fearing its wandering,
therefore perform three sacrifices to pacify it.
“To receive lifelong love and not repay it for many years
is something the heart cannot bear.”
The officials in charge insisted,
and the imperial edict stated:
“The trouble lies in not being able to be truly filial;
do not worry about physical harm.
The rites and ceremonies of previous generations
differ in their simplicity and refinement.
Why must we be limited by recent regulations,
causing the completion of mourning to be incomplete? ”
Dásàng
is the same as tōngsàng.
So, permission was granted;
however, they still wore plain caps and ate coarse food for the entire three years,
like during the mourning for Emperor Wén.
8 In autumn,
in the seventh month,
many stars flowed westward like rain and fell.
9 On the day Jǐmǎo,
the Emperor paid respects at the Chóngyáng Mausoleum.
10 In the ninth month,
there were great floods in the four provinces of Qīng, Xú, Yǎn, and Yù.
Qīng Province governed Qí Commandery, Jǐnán, Lè'ān, Chéngyáng, and Dōnglái.
Xú Province governed Péngchéng, Xiàpī, Dōnghǎi, Lángxié, Guǎnglíng, and Lín’huái.
Yǎn Province governed Chénliú, Púyáng, Jìyīn, Gāopíng, Rènchéng, Dōngpíng, Jìběi, and Tàishān.
Yù Province governed Yǐngchuān, Rǔnán, Xiāngchéng, Rǔyīn, Liáng State, Pèi, Qiáo, Lǔ, Yìyáng, and Ānfēng.
The Jìn Records state: Qīng Province takes its name from its location in the lesser yang, its color being blue.
Xú Province takes its meaning from “leisurely and slow.”
Yǎn
means upright
and trustworthy;
it is also said to be named after the Yǎn River.
Yù
means leisurely,
referring to its endowment with the qi of central harmony,
and its nature and principles being calm and comfortable.
11 Grand Marshal Shí Bāo had been in Huaínán for a long time,
and his prestige and benevolence were very evident.
In the third year of Gānlù under Emperor Gāoguìxiāng of Wèi,
Zhūgě Dàn was pacified,
and Bāo took his place to guard Huaínán. By this time, it had been eleven years in total.
A secret memorial accused Bāo of communicating with the Wú people.
At a time when the Wú people were about to invade,
Bāo built fortifications and dammed water to secure himself,
and the Emperor became suspicious of him.
Yáng Hù earnestly spoke to the Emperor, saying:
“Bāo would certainly not do that.”
The Emperor did not believe him,
and thus issued an edict stating that Bāo had not estimated the enemy's strength,
built fortifications, and dammed water,
disturbing the people.
He was dismissed from his office.
Kǎoyì states: Neither the Jìn Shū Wǔ Jì nor Bāo's biography contain the year and month of Bāo's dismissal.
Xiāo Fāngděng's Sānshí Guó Chūnqiū and Dù Yányè's Jìn Chūnqiū place it here,
which is followed now.
Bāo's biography also says:
“An imperial order commanded Wáng Zhòu of Lángxié to rendezvous at Shòuchūn from Xiàpī.”
According to the Wǔ Jì,
Zhòu only garrisoned Xiàpī in the second month of the following year.
This biography might be erroneous.
Xiāo Fāngděng was the son of Emperor Yuán of Liáng.
Bāo appointed Sūn Shuò of Hénèi as his aide.
Shuò had previously been good friends with Wáng Jùn of Rǔyīn,
who was then garrisoned at Xǔchāng.
Shuò visited him on his way.
Jùn knew that the court had already sent troops to attack Bāo,
and secretly told him:
“Do not get involved in the calamity!”
Shuò, upon leaving,
raced to Shòuchūn,
advised Bāo to release his troops,
and await his punishment on foot at the Dūtíng.
Shòuchūn was a Dūtíng.
When the Emperor heard of it,
his suspicions were cleared.
Bāo went to the imperial court
and returned to his residence as the Duke of Lèlíng.
12 The ruler of Wú marched out of Dōngguān;
in winter,
in the tenth month,
he sent his generals Shī Jì to enter Jiāngxià,
and Wàn Yù to attack Xiāngyáng.
An edict ordered Wáng Wàng of Yìyáng to command 20,000 central army infantry and cavalry and garrison Lóngpí.
Lóngpí
was formerly Mópí, renamed,
as seen in volume 72, Wèi Emperor Míng, Qīnglóng first year.
At that time, Hú Liè, the Inspector of Jīng Province, resisted Jì,
defeated him,
and Wàng withdrew his troops.
13 Liú Jùn, the Inspector of Jiāozhōu of Wú, and Grand Commander Xiū Zé,
Xìngpǔ says: Among the assistants of Yuánmíng was Xiū Shì.
In the Hàn dynasty, there was Commander of Cavalry Xiū Bǐng.
and Yáng Jì, the Administrator of Jiāozhǐ, all resisted and defeated them;
Yùlín and Jiǔzhēn both submitted to Jì.
Jì sent generals Máo Jiǒng and Dǒng Yuán to attack Hépǔ,
and they fought at Gǔchéng.
Gǔchéng
was probably the old city of Hépǔ Commandery.
Jiǒng,
pronounced gǔjiǒng,
and also gǔhuì.
They killed Liú Jùn and Xiū Zé,
and the remaining soldiers dispersed and returned to Hépǔ.
Jì memorialized that Jiǒng be made Administrator of Yùlín,
and Yuán be made Administrator of Jiǔzhēn.
14 In the eleventh month,
Dīng Fèng and Zhūgě Jìng of Wú came out from Sháopí
and attacked Héfēi;
General Āndōng Wáng Jùn of Rǔyīn resisted and repelled them.
15 Wáng Wàng of Yìyáng was appointed Grand Marshal,
Xún Yǐ as Grand Commandant,
and Shí Bāo as Minister of Works.
1 In spring,
in the first month,
the ruler of Wú appointed his son Jǐn as Crown Prince.
2 In the second month,
Qín Province was established by dividing Yōng, Liáng, and Liáng Provinces.
The Jìn Records state: Yōng Province was named Yōng because it was a land of four mountains;
it was also said to be the northwest position,
where the yang qi could not reach, and yin and yang qi were blocked and restrained.
It governed Jīngzhào, Féngyì, Fúfēng, Āndìng, Běidì, Xīnpíng, and Shǐpíng.
Liáng Province was named for its location in the west,
where it was cold and cool.
It governed Jīnchéng, Xīpíng, Wǔwēi, Zhāngyè,
Xī Commandery, Dūnhuáng, Jiǔquán, and Xīhǎi.
Liáng Province was named for the strong and unyielding qi of metal and hardness in the west.
It governed Hànzhōng, Zǐtóng, Guǎnghàn, Xīndū, Fúlíng, Bāxī, and Bādōng.
Qín Province governed Lǒngxī, Nán'ān, Tiānshuǐ, Lüèyáng, Wǔdū, and Yīnpíng Commandery.
Previously,
Dèng Ài had settled tens of thousands of surrendering Xiānbēi
between Yōng and Liáng,
mixed with the common people.
The court feared that this would become a problem in the long run.
As Hú Liè was known in the west,
he was therefore sent to garrison and pacify them.
These were the Hexī Xiānbēi.
3 There were great floods in the three provinces of Qīng, Xú, and Yǎn.
4 The Emperor had the ambition to conquer Wú.
On the day Rén'yín,
Yáng Hù, Minister of the Left of the Department of State Affairs, was appointed Commander-in-chief of all military affairs in Jīng Province,
garrisoning Xiāngyáng;
Wèi Guàn, General of the Expedition to the East, was appointed Commander-in-chief of all military affairs in Qīng Province,
garrisoning Línzī;
and Wáng Zhòu of Dōngguǎn, General of the Pacification of the East, was appointed Commander-in-chief of all military affairs in Xú Province,
garrisoning Xiàpī.
Hù Suí (祜綏) embraced the near and far,
greatly winning the hearts of the Jiāng (江) and Hàn (漢) regions.
He established great trust with the Wú (吳) people.
When defectors wished to leave,
he always allowed it.
He reduced the soldiers on guard and patrol,
using them to cultivate over eight hundred qǐng (頃) of land.
When he first arrived,
the army had less than a hundred days' provisions;
but by his later years,
he had a ten-year supply.
While Hù (祜) was in the army,
he often wore light furs and a loose belt,
his body unarmored.
Below his command tent (Líng Gé (鈴閤)),
his personal guards numbered no more than ten.
“Líng Xià Zú (鈴下卒)” and “Gé Xià Wēiyí (閤下威儀)” are terms for his attendants.
“Líng Xià (鈴下)” refers to those
whom he summoned by pulling a bell when he had an order,
hence the name.
“Gé Xià Wēiyí (閤下威儀)”
were in charge of managing entrances and exits, acting as guides, and receiving petitions and taking charge of affairs.
Jìyīn (濟陰) Grand Administrator Bāxī (巴西) Wén Lì (文立)
memorialized:
“The descendants of former Shǔ (蜀) famous ministers who have been relocated to the Central Plains
should be appointed to office according to their talents,
to comfort the hearts of Bā (巴) and Shǔ (蜀),
and to sway the hopes of the Wú (吳) people.”
The Emperor followed this.
A textual critique states: Lì’s (立) biography records this memorial as occurring after his transfer to Crown Prince Zhong Shùzi (中庶子).
However, in the seventh year of Tàishǐ (泰始),
when Lì (立) recommended Xì Shēn (郤詵),
he was still the Grand Administrator of Jìyīn (濟陰),
and had not yet become a Shùzi (庶子).
If Zhūgě Jīng (諸葛京) was appointed an official
not due to Lì’s (立) memorial,
then Jīng (京) must have already been appointed an official,
and Lì (立) would not have again said “should be appointed to office according to their talents.”
On the Jǐwèi (己未) day,
an edict said:
“Zhūgě Liàng (諸葛亮) in Shǔ (蜀)
exhausted his heart and strength,
and his son Zhān (瞻) died righteously in the face of calamity.”
This event is recorded in Volume 78, in the fourth year of Jǐngyuán (景元) of Emperor Yuán (元) of Wèi (魏).
Nàn (難) is pronounced dàn.
Another edict said:
“The Shǔ (蜀) generals Fù Qiān (傅僉) and his father
died for their lord.”
Fù Róng’s (傅肜) death is recorded in Volume 69, in the third year of Huángchū (黃初) of Emperor Wén (文) of Wèi (魏).
Fù Qiān (傅僉) died in the same year as Zhūgě Zhān (諸葛瞻).
How can there be a difference just because of their respective sides!
Qiān’s (僉) sons Zhù (著) and Mù (募) were enslaved into the Xīguān (奚官).
Xī (息) means
son.
Zhù (著) and Mù (募)
are the names of the two sons.
The Shàofǔ (少府) had a Xīguān Lìng (奚官令),
to whom all enslaved men and women belonged.
Since Wèi (魏),
the capital Yè (鄴) also had a Xīguān Dū (奚官督).
The Emperor appointed Wén Lì (文立) as Sànqí Chángshì (散騎常侍).
Hàn’s (漢) former Shàngshū (尚書) of Jiànwéi (犍為), Chéng Qióng (程瓊),
was truly virtuous and accomplished.
He had a deep friendship with Lì (立).
The Emperor heard of his name
and asked Lì (立) about him,
who replied:
“Your subject knows the man well,
but he is nearly eighty,
and by nature humble and reserved,
no longer having the aspirations of his younger days.”
Meaning that he had no desire for fame or advancement at that time.
When Qióng (瓊) heard this,
he said:
“Guǎngxiū (廣休) can truly be said not to be partisan.”
Wén Lì’s (文立) courtesy name was Guǎngxiū (廣休).
The Analects say: A junzi (君子) is not partisan.
In autumn,
in the ninth month,
a comet appeared in the Purple Palace constellation.
In winter,
in the tenth month,
Wú (吳) granted a general amnesty
and changed its era name to Jiànhéng (建衡).
The Imperial son Jǐngdù (景度) was enfeoffed as Chéngyáng (城陽) King.
Previously,
Hé Dìng (何定) of Rǔnán (汝南) had once been an attendant to Emperor Dà (大) of Wú (吳).
When the Lord of Wú (吳) ascended the throne,
he memorialized, stating he was an old retainer of the former emperor,
and requested to return to internal service.
The Lord of Wú (吳) made him Lóuxià Dūwèi (樓下都尉),
in charge of affairs concerning brewing and grain,
and he thus monopolized power and influence.
The Lord of Wú (吳) trusted him and entrusted him with many matters.
Left Chancellor Lù Kǎi (陸凱) rebuked Dìng (定) to his face, saying:
“Have you seen any who were disloyal to their lord and
disrupted the state’s governance
ever die a natural death!
Why do you exclusively commit treachery!
You pollute the emperor’s ears;
you should reform yourself.
Otherwise,
you will certainly face unforeseen disaster.”
Dìng (定) greatly resented him.
Kǎi (凱) dedicated his heart to public service,
his loyalty and sincerity coming from within.
His memorials and petitions all addressed facts without embellishment.
They all pointed to actual facts,
without rhetorical adornment.
The Lord of Wú (吳) sent Central Secretariat Director Dǒng Cháo (董朝) to ask what he wished to say.
Kǎi (凱) stated:
“Hé Dìng (何定) cannot be trusted;
he should be given an external appointment.
Xī Xī (奚熙), a petty official,
proposes building Pǔlǐ (浦里) Pond,
which should also not be approved.”
When Lord Xiū (休) of Wú (吳) was in power,
Yán Mì (嚴密) had once made this proposal;
Xī (熙) likely adopted his idea.
“Xuē Yíng (薛瑩), Téng Xiū (滕脩), and my kinsmen Xǐ (喜) and Kàng (抗),
some are pure and diligent,
others are talented and outstanding.
They are all good assistants to the state.
I wish Your Majesty would give them serious thought,
consult them on current affairs,
and allow each to fully express their loyalty,
to make up for any oversight.”
Shào (卲) was
the grandson of Qí (齊);
Hé Qí (賀齊) was a general under Lord Quán (權) of Wú (吳).
Zōng (綜) was his son.
Xuán (玄) was
a person from Pèi (沛).
Xiū (脩) was
a person from Nányáng (南陽).
Kǎi (凱) soon died.
The Lord of Wú (吳) had long harbored resentment towards his directness,
having hidden anger
that he kept to himself without expressing it, hence "hán" (銜).
After a long time,
he eventually exiled Kǎi’s (凱) family to Jiàn’ān (建安).
The Lord of Wú (吳) dispatched Supervisor of the Army Yú Sì (虞汜),
General Who Awe the South Xuē Xǔ (薛珝),
and Cāngwú (蒼梧) Grand Administrator Dānyáng (丹陽) Táo Huáng (陶璜) via the Jīngzhōu (荊州) route;
and Supervisor of the Army Lǐ Xù (李勗) and Army Overseer Xú Cún (徐存) via the Jiàn’ān (建安) sea route.
The Jīngzhōu (荊州) route
was to cross the mountains and enter Jiāo (交) and Guǎng (廣).
The Jiàn’ān (建安) sea route
was to sail south by sea.
Shěn Yuē (沈約) said: Jiàn’ān (建安) was originally Mǐnyuè (閩越).
Qín (秦) established it as Mǐnzhōng (閩中) Commandery.
Hàn (漢) depopulated the area,
later establishing it as Yě (冶) County,
subordinate to Huìjī (會稽) Commandery.
Later, the land of Yě (冶) was divided into the Eastern and Southern Departments of Huìjī (會稽) Commandant.
The Eastern Department
was Línhǎi (臨海).
The Southern Department
was Jiàn’ān (建安).
In the third year of Yǒng’ān (永安) under Lord Xiū (休) of Wú (吳),
the Southern Department was separated and established as Jiàn’ān (建安) Commandery.
Sòng Bái (宋白) said: In the twelfth year of Jiàn’ān (建安), Sūn Cè (孫策)
divided the land of Dōnghòu Guān (東候官) to establish Jiàn’ān (建安) County,
naming it after the era name.
In the twelfth month,
officials memorialized that the Eastern Palace’s respect for the two Tutors
differed in protocol.
The Jìn (晉) system: the Crown Prince’s Grand Tutor was of the rank of Zhōng Èrqiān Shí (中二千石),
the Junior Tutor was of the rank of Èrqiān Shí (二千石).
The Crown Prince bowed first,
and then the Tutors responded.
At that time, the Zhànshì (詹事) had not yet been established,
so all matters, great and small, of the Palace
were handled by the two Tutors.
“To highly respect tutors
is to honor the Way and value teaching.
Why speak of subjects and non-subjects!”
“Subjects and non-subjects” are the words presented by the officials in their memorial.
In spring,
in the first month,
Dīng Fèng (丁奉) of Wú (吳) entered Wōkǒu (渦口).
The Water Classic states: The Wō (渦) River originates from the Làngdàng (蒗蕩) Canal in Yángwǔ (陽武) County, Hénán (河南),
flows southeast to Xiàpéi (下邳), Huáilíng (淮陵) County, and enters the Huái (淮),
where it is called Wōkǒu (渦口).
Wō (渦) is pronounced Gē (戈).
A textual critique states: Dīng Fèng’s (丁奉) biography in the Wú Zhì (吳志) says:
“In the first year of Jiànhéng (建衡),
he attacked Jìn (晉) Gǔyáng (穀陽).”
The Jìn Dì Jì (晉帝紀) does not record this.
Fèng’s (奉) biography does not mention entering Wōkǒu (渦口).
It is suspected to be the same event.
Wú (吳) Wàn Yù (萬彧) returned to Jiànyè (建業) from Bāqiū (巴丘).
3 In summer,
in the fourth month,
Shī Jì, the Grand Marshal of the Left in Wú, died.
Lù Kàng, the General-in-Chief who Guards the Army, was appointed Area Commander of the armies of Xìnlíng, Xīlíng, Yídào, Yuèxiāng, and Gōng'ān,
and was stationed in Yuèxiāng.
The Shǔi Jīng Zhù states: Yuèxiāng city is in Chánlíng county, Nánpíng Commandery.
The Jiāng river flows north of it,
and then east, north of Gōng'ān county.
Sòng Bái said: Yuèxiāng
was the land of the State of Ruò in the Spring and Autumn period.
Its city was built by Lù Kàng
and is located within Sōngzī county.
The Jìn Dìlǐ Zhì states: Xìnlíng county belonged to Jiànpíng Commandery.
Shěn Yuē said: I suspect it was established by Wú.
The Shǔi Jīng Zhù states: The Jiāng river flows east from Kuí city,
past the south of Xìnlíng county,
and then east past the south of Yílíng county.
Yílíng
is Xīlíng.
Yuèxiāng city is located east of Sōngzī county, Jiānglíng Prefecture today.
North of Yuèxiāng city,
there is a sandbar in the river.
One can cross to the opposite bank by wading shallowly.
It is a strategically vital area along the river.
Kàng, considering that the Wú ruler's governance was severely lacking,
submitted a memorial, saying:
“I have heard that if virtue is equal, the many overcome the few;
if strength is equal, the secure control the precarious.
This is why the Six States were unified by Qín,
and why Western Chǔ submitted to Hàn.
Today, the territory held by the enemy
is not merely the land west of the pass;
it extends west of Hónggōu.
Yet, our state lacks external allies for horizontal alliance,
and internally is not as strong as Western Chǔ.
Public administration is lax,
and the common people are not yet settled.
Those who deliberate rely
merely on the Yangtze River and the steep mountains to delimit our territory.
This is merely a minor aspect of defending the state,
not what the wise prioritize.
Whenever I ponder this,
I pace my pillow in the middle of the night,
and forget to eat at meals.
The duty of serving a lord
is to remonstrate and not to deceive.
I respectfully present seventeen articles on current exigencies for your consideration.”
Kàng's biography states that the seventeen articles are lost and not recorded.
Lǐ Xù, finding the route to Jiàn'ān unfavorable,
killed the guiding general Féng Fěi
and led his army back.
Initially,
Hé Dìng had sought a marriage alliance for his son with Xù,
but Xù refused.
Therefore, Dìng reported that Xù had wrongly killed Féng Fěi,
[Lǐ Xù] withdrew the troops and returned,
and executed Xù and Xú Cún along with their families,
then burned Xù's corpse.
Dìng also ordered all generals to present imperial dogs.
The presentation
is pronounced shí zhǎng fān.
A leash and collar alone cost ten thousand coins,
for catching rabbits to supply the kitchen.
The people of Wú all blamed Dìng,
but the Wú ruler considered him loyal and diligent,
and bestowed upon him the title of marquis.
Lù Kàng submitted a memorial, saying:
“Petty people do not understand reason and morality.
Their insights are shallow,
and even if they were to exhaust their feelings and devotion,
they would still be insufficient for the task,
let alone when their treacherous hearts are deeply rooted and their likes and dislikes easily shift!”
The Wú ruler did not heed him.
4 In the sixth month,
on the day Wùwǔ,
Hú Liè attacked the Xiānbēi Tūfà Shùjīnéng at Wànhúduī.
When Shùjīnéng's ancestor Shòutián was in pregnancy,
his mother, the Xiāngyè clan,
gave birth to him in bed during sleep.
The Xiānbēi called a quilt "tūfà,"
and thus he adopted it as his clan name.
Tūfà Wūgū of Southern Liáng
was Shùjīnéng's fifth-generation descendant.
Wànhúduī is northeast of Wēnwéi River, within Gāopíng county, Āndìng Commandery.
[Hú Liè] was killed.
Fúfēng Prince Liàng, the Area Commander of Yōng and Liáng Provinces, dispatched general Liú Qí to rescue him,
but Qí observed from a distance and did not advance.
Liàng was demoted to General of the Pacifying West for this,
and Qí was to be executed.
Liàng submitted a petition, saying:
“The fault for the command and control
originated from me.
I beg for his life.”
The imperial decree said:
“If the fault is not with Qí,
then it must lie elsewhere.”
Thus, Liàng's office was revoked.
Shàngshū Lèlíng Shí Jiàn was dispatched to serve as General of the Pacifying West
and Area Commander of Qín Province.
Lèlíng county
belonged to Píngyuán Commandery in the Hàn dynasty,
and was later divided to belong to the State of Lèlíng.
Shùjīnéng's forces were strong.
Jiàn ordered Qín Province Inspector Dù Yù to deploy troops to attack him.
Yù believed that the barbarians, riding on their victory, had fat horses,
while the government troops were severely lacking.
It would be advisable to combine efforts to transport fodder and grain on a large scale
and then launch a punitive expedition in spring.
Jiàn memorialized that Yù was delaying military operations due to a lack of supplies,
and he was summoned in a cage cart to the Court of Judicial Review
and condemned to赎论 (redeem his punishment).
At that time, Yù, having married an imperial princess,
was among the Eight Deliberations,
and was condemned to redeem his punishment with the title of marquis.
Ultimately, they could not prevail.
5 In autumn,
in the seventh month,
on the day Yǐsì,
Chéngyáng Prince Jǐngdù died.
6 On the day Dīngwèi,
Rǔyīn Prince Jùn was appointed General-in-Chief who Guards the West,
Area Commander of Yōng, Liáng, and other provinces,
and stationed in Guānzhōng.
7 In winter,
in the eleventh month,
the imperial prince Dōng
was enfeoffed as Rǔnán Prince.
8 Xiù, the former General and younger paternal cousin of the Wú ruler, was the Commander of Xiàkǒu.
The Wú ruler disliked him,
and people in the populace all said that Xiù was about to be plotted against.
Xiù was the grandson of Kuāng, the Wú ruler Qúan's younger paternal brother.
Cóng
is pronounced cái yòng fān.
È
is pronounced wū lù fān.
Xiù was alarmed
and fled that night with his wife, children, and several hundred personal guards.
In the twelfth month,
Xiù was appointed General of Cavalry, opened his own administration with the ceremonial honor of the Three Ducal Ministers,
and enfeoffed as Marquis of Kuàijī.
His rewards and emoluments were made generous to attract the people of Wú.
Piào
is pronounced pǐ miào fān.
Kuàijī
is pronounced gōng wài fān.
9 In this year,
Wú granted a general amnesty.
10Initially,
the people of Wèi settled the five divisions of the Southern Xiōngnú in various commanderies of Bìng Province,
where they lived mixed with the common people of Zhōngguó.
Since the Eastern Hàn, the Southern Xiōngnú had been divided and settled in various commanderies of Bìng Province;
Wèi merely divided their population into five divisions.
Details can be found in Volume 67, the 21st year of Jiàn'ān, Emperor Xiàn of Hàn.
At that time, the Left Division commanded over ten thousand households
and resided in the old Zīshì county of Tàiyuán;
the Right Division commanded over six thousand households
and resided in Qí county;
the Southern Division commanded over three thousand households
and resided in Púzǐ county;
the Northern Division commanded over four thousand households
and resided in Xīnxīng county;
the Central Division commanded over six thousand households
and resided in Dàlíng county.
They subsequently adopted the surname Liú.
Initially,
Emperor Gāo of Hàn gave a daughter in marriage to the Chányú,
so they called themselves grandsons of the Hàn imperial clan
and adopted the surname Liú.
1 In spring,
in the first month,
Liú Měng, the Right Worthy King of the Xiōngnú, rebelled and left the frontier.
2 Yù Province Inspector Shí Jiàn was dismissed for falsely inflating the number of enemy heads in his report of defeating the Wú army.
The imperial decree said:
“Jiàn holds a high position as a minister,
and I trusted him.
How could he stoop to practicing deceit
as his subordinates do?
Yěr
means 'like this.'
He shall never again be employed for the rest of his life.”
3. The Wú man Diāo Xuán (刁玄) falsely augmented a prophecy text, saying:
"A yellow banner and purple canopy
appearing in the southeast,
the one who will eventually possess all under Heaven
is the lord of Jīng (荊) and Yáng (揚)."
The Xìngpǔ (姓譜) states: The surname Diāo (刁)
is descended from Qí (齊) grandee Shù Diāo (豎刁).
I (Sīmǎ Guāng 司馬光) comment: How could Shù Diāo (豎刁) have descendants?
The Hànshū Hòuzhí Zhuàn (漢書貨殖傳) mentions Diāo Jiān (刁間).
The Jiāngbiǎo Zhuàn (江表傳) states: Xuán (玄) went on a mission to Shǔ (蜀),
and obtained Sīmǎ Huī's (司馬徽) writings on fate and calendrical calculations.
He then falsely augmented the text to deceive the Wú (吳) people.
The character "見" (jiàn)
is pronounced like "xián" (賢) in its entirety.
On the last day of this month,
(Wú) largely dispatched troops and marched out of Huálǐ (華里).
Huálǐ (華里) is west of Jiànyè (建業).
(They marched) west from Niúzhǔ (牛渚).
The Shuǐjīng Zhù (水經註) states: Niúzhǔ (牛渚) is between Gūshú (姑孰) and Wūjiāng (烏江) counties.
Today, thirty *lǐ* (里) north of Dāngtú (當塗) County in Tàipíng (太平) Prefecture, there is Niúzhǔ Shān (牛渚山).
Below the mountain is Niúzhǔ Jī (牛渚磯),
which faces Hézhōu Héngjiāng Dù (和州橫江渡).
Dù Yòu (杜佑) says: Niúzhǔ Qí (牛渚圻) is present-day Cǎishí (采石) in Dāngtú (當塗) County.
(Emperor Wǔ of Jìn 晉武帝) did not listen.
Dōngguān Lìng (東觀令) was an official
responsible for compiling and editing books and records.
The character "觀" (guàn)
is pronounced like "gǔwán" (古玩) in its entirety.
The character "華" (huà)
is pronounced like "hùhuà" (戶化) in its entirety.
The character "覈" (hé)
is pronounced like "hùgé" (戶革) in its entirety.
The roads were ruined and broken,
soldiers, armored and bearing weapons,
a hundred men together pulled one cart,
nearly dying from cold,
all saying:
"If we meet the enemy,
we should immediately turn our spears."
(King) Zhòu (紂) dispatched troops to meet King Wǔ (武王) of Zhōu (周) in battle at Mùyě (牧野).
The vanguard turned their spears and attacked their rear,
thereby fleeing north.
(Wú) then returned.
The Emperor sent Yìyáng (義陽) Prince Wàng (望) to command the central army of 20,000 men and 3,000 cavalry, garrisoning Shòuchūn (壽春) to guard against them.
Hearing that the Wú (吳) army had retreated,
(the Jìn 晉 army) was then disbanded.
4. In the third month,
on the day Bǐngxū (丙戌),
Jùlù Yuángōng (鉅鹿元公) Péi Xiù (裴秀) died.
5. In summer,
fourth month,
Wú (吳) Jiāozhōu (交州) Inspector Táo Huáng (陶璜) attacked Jǐuzhēn (九真) Administrator Dǒng Yuán (董元),
killing him;
Yáng Jì (楊稷) replaced him with his general Wáng Sù (王素).
The Kǎoyì (考異) says: Huáng's (璜) biography states:
"He attacked unexpectedly,
going directly to Jiāozhǐ (交趾)."
I (Sīmǎ Guāng 司馬光) note that Yuán (元) was the Administrator of Jǐuzhēn (九真),
not Jiāozhǐ (交趾).
The Huáyáng Guózhì (華陽國志) states:
"Yuán (元) died of illness.
Yáng Jì (楊稷) then replaced him with Wáng Sù (王素)."
I (Sīmǎ Guāng 司馬光) note the Wǔdì Jì (武帝紀):
"In the fourth month,
Jǐuzhēn (九真) Administrator Dǒng Yuán (董元) was attacked by the Wú (吳) general Yú Sì (虞汜),
his army was defeated,
and he died."
Thus Yuán (元) did not die of illness.
Presumably, although Jì (稷) replaced Yuán (元) with Sù (素),
Yuán (元) died before Sù (素) arrived at the commandery.
6. The Hú (胡) barbarians of Běidì (北地) raided Jīnchéng (金城).
Liángzhōu (涼州) Inspector Qiān Hóng (牽弘) led an expedition against them.
All the Hú (胡) internally rebelled
and, together with Shùjīnéng (樹機能), besieged Hóng (弘) at Qīngshān (青山).
The Xù Hàn Zhì (續漢志) states: Qīngshān (青山) is in Cānluán (參䜌) County, Běidì (北地) Commandery.
Xián (賢) says: Qīngshān (青山) is in present-day Qìngzhōu (慶州),
and has the Qīngshān Shuǐ (青山水).
The Kǎoyì (考異) says: Cuī Hóng's (崔鴻) Shíliù Guó Chūnqiū Tūfà Wūgū Zhuàn (十六國春秋禿髮烏孤傳) states:
"His ancestor Shùjīnéng (樹機能) was originally a Xiānbēi (鮮卑) from Héxī (河西).
In the Tàishǐ (泰始) era,
he killed Qínzhōu (秦州) Inspector Hú Liè (胡烈)
and decapitated Liángzhōu (涼州) Inspector Qiān Hóng (牽弘)."
The Jìn Dì Jì (晉帝紀) states:
"Rebel captives killed Hú Liè (胡烈);
Běidì (北地) Hú (胡) killed Qiān Hóng (牽弘)."
Neither mentions Xiānbēi (鮮卑).
Presumably, speaking of "rebel captives internally rebelling"
implies that the Xiānbēi (鮮卑) were also among them.
Or perhaps the Běidì (北地) Hú (胡) were precisely Shùjīnéng (樹機能).
Earlier,
Grand Marshal Chén Qiān (陳騫) said to the Emperor:
"Hú Liè (胡烈) and Qiān Hóng (牽弘) are both brave but lack strategy,
overly reliant on their own judgment,
and are not talents for pacifying the frontier.
They will become a national disgrace."
At that time, Hóng (弘) was the Inspector of Yángzhōu (揚州),
and often did not comply with Qiān's (騫) orders.
At that time, Qiān (騫), as Grand Marshal, was the Grand Commander of all armies in Yángzhōu (揚州),
garrisoned at Shòuchūn (壽春).
Therefore, Hóng (弘) was summoned.
After his arrival,
he was soon again appointed as Inspector of Liángzhōu (涼州).
Qiān (騫) secretly sighed,
believing he would surely be defeated.
The two indeed failed to maintain harmony with the Qiāng (羌) and Róng (戎),
their armies were defeated and they themselves perished.
Expeditions continued for years,
only barely achieving stability.
The Emperor then regretted it.
7. In the fifth month,
Imperial Prince Xiàn (憲) was made Prince of Chéngyáng (城陽).
8. On the day Xīnchǒu (辛丑),
Yìyáng Chéngwáng (義陽成王) Wàng (望) died.
9. Court Attendant, Minister of the Imperial Secretariat, and General of Chariots and Cavalry Jiǎ Chōng (賈充),
had been favored, entrusted, and wielded power since the time of Emperor Wén (文帝).
When the Emperor was crown prince,
Chōng (充) was quite instrumental.
Details can be found in volumes 77 and 78 of the Wèi Jì (魏紀).
Chōng (充) was cunning and sycophantic.
Together with Grand Commandant and acting Grand Tutor to the Crown Prince Xún Yǐ (荀顗),
The Jìn Zhì (晉志) states: The Emperor, considering the dignity of the heir apparent,
ordered the dukes to hold the positions of the two tutors.
Because their original ranks were high,
they were either "acting" (行) or "leading" (領).
The character "顗" (yǐ)
is pronounced like "yúqǐ" (魚豈) in its entirety.
Ānpíng (安平) County,
in the Former Hàn (漢) belonged to Zhuō (涿) Commandery,
in the Later Hàn (漢) belonged to Ānpíng (安平) Kingdom,
in Jìn (晉) belonged to Bólíng (博陵) Commandery.
The character "紞" (dǎn)
is pronounced like "dūgǎn" (都感) in its entirety.
The court disliked him.
The Emperor asked Court Attendant Péi Kǎi (裴楷) about the gains and losses of the present time.
He replied:
"Your Majesty received the Mandate,
and all within the Four Seas submitted to your influence.
The reason you have not yet equaled Yáo (堯) and Shùn (舜) in virtue
is simply because people like Jiǎ Chōng (賈充) are still in court.
It is appropriate to invite wise men from all under Heaven
to promote the Way of governance,
and not to show favoritism to people."
Court Attendant Rèn Kǎi (任愷) of Lè'ān (樂安) and Hénán (河南) Administrator Yǔ Chún (庾純) of Yǐngchuān (潁川) were both at odds with Chōng (充).
Chōng (充) wished to relieve them of their close positions.
"Close positions"
refers to Court Attendant.
The character "任" (rèn)
is pronounced like "rén" (壬).
(He thought) Kǎi (愷) should be in the Eastern Palace.
The Emperor appointed Kǎi (愷) as Junior Tutor to the Crown Prince,
but his position as Court Attendant remained unchanged.
The Jìn Zhì (晉志) states: Court Attendant Rèn Kǎi (任愷) was respected and close to the Emperor.
Making him also lead as Junior Tutor was presumably a temporary arrangement.
Observing this,
then Chōng (充) intended to alienate Kǎi (愷) by a stratagem.
The Emperor was concerned.
Kǎi (愷) said:
"One should obtain a revered and influential minister with wisdom and strategy to pacify and settle them."
The Emperor said:
"Who would be suitable?"
Kǎi (愷) then recommended Chōng (充),
and Chún (純) also spoke highly of him.
In autumn,
seventh month,
on the day Guǐyǒu (癸酉),
Chōng (充) was appointed Grand Commander of all armies in Qín (秦) and Liáng (涼) two prefectures,
his positions as Court Attendant and General of Chariots and Cavalry remaining unchanged.
The Kǎoyì (考異) says: The Sānshí Guó Chūnqiū (三十國春秋) and Jìn Chūnqiū (晉春秋) both place Chōng's (充) departure in the second month of the eighth year.
I (Sīmǎ Guāng 司馬光) note the Wǔdì Jì (武帝紀) places Chōng's (充) departure in this month.
Presumably, the two Chūnqiū (春秋) texts mistakenly dated this because the Crown Prince's marriage occurred in the second month of the eighth year.
10 Wú’s Grand Commander Xuē Xǔ
and Táo Huáng, along with a force of one hundred thousand soldiers,
together attacked Jiāozhǐ.
Inside the city, provisions were exhausted and aid was cut off.
It was captured by Wú,
who took Yáng Jì, Máo Jiǒng, and others captive.
Huáng admired Jiǒng’s bravery and vigor,
and wished to spare his life;
Jiǒng plotted to kill Huáng,
so Huáng killed him.
Xiū Zé’s son, Yǔn,
disemboweled him alive,
and cut out his liver,
saying:
“Can you still commit treason now?”
Jiǒng still cursed, saying:
“I regret not killing your lord, Sūn Hào.
What kind of a dead dog was your father?!”
Yǔn’s father Zé had been killed by Jiǒng,
as seen four years prior.
The Kǎo Yì says: The Hàn Jìn Chūnqiū says:
“Initially,
Huò Yì sent Yáng Jì, Máo Jiǒng, and others to garrison Jiāozhǐ,
swearing to them: ‘If the enemy besieges the city for less than one hundred days and you surrender,
your families will be executed;
if more than one hundred days pass,
and no relief troops arrive and the city falls,
I will bear the blame.’
Jì and the others held out for less than one hundred days.
Their provisions were exhausted,
and they sought surrender from Huáng,
who did not permit it,
but instead supplied them with provisions and bade them continue to defend.
All the generals advised Huáng, saying: ‘Huò Yì is dead;
he certainly cannot rescue Jì and the others.
It would be appropriate to wait until the stipulated days are complete,
and then accept their surrender,
so that they may be without guilt,
and we may acquire righteousness,
educating our own people internally
and winning over neighboring states externally.
Would this not be acceptable?!’
When Jì and the others’ term expired and their provisions were exhausted,
and no relief troops arrived,
Huáng then accepted their surrender.”
The Huáyáng Guózhì, however, says:
“Jì and the others’ city was broken and they were imprisoned.
Jì vomited blood and died;
Jiǒng cursed the rebels and died.”
These two accounts contradict each other,
and cannot be reconciled.
However, Jìn Táo Huáng Zhuàn records both.
Upon consideration, Sūn Hào was suspicious and cruel,
so it is unlikely that Huáng would dare to supply provisions to the enemy.
We now follow the Huáyáng Guózhì.
The Wú people captured them,
and Jiǔzhēn and Rìnán all surrendered to Wú.
Wú granted a general amnesty,
and appointed Táo Huáng as Inspector of Jiāozhōu.
Huáng suppressed and brought to submission the various barbarians and tribal groups,
and the entire province was pacified.
11 In the eighth month,
on the day Bǐngshēn,
Prince Chéngyáng Xiàn passed away.
12 Yìzhōu and the four commanderies of Nánzhōng were divided to establish Níngzhōu.
Níngzhōu was named after the Jiànníng Commandery,
and governed the four commanderies of Jiànníng, Xīnggǔ, Yúnnán, and Yǒngchāng.
13 In the ninth month,
Wú’s Minister of Works Mèng Rén passed away.
14 In winter,
in the tenth month,
on the day Dīngchǒu, which was the first day of the lunar month,
there was a solar eclipse.
The Kǎo Yì says: The Sòng Shū Wǔxíng Zhì records an eclipse on the day Gēngchén in the fifth month,
but no eclipse on the day Dīngchǒu in the tenth month.
The Jìn Shū Jì and Tiānwén Zhì record an eclipse on the day Dīngchǒu in the tenth month,
but no eclipse on the day Gēngchén in the fifth month.
We now follow the Jìn Shū.
15 In the eleventh month,
Liú Měng raided Bìngzhōu,
and Bìngzhōu Inspector Liú Qīn attacked and defeated him.
The Jìn Zhì states: Bìngzhōu is not named after the Wèishuǐ,
nor is it called Héng,
but is called Bìng [“Conjoined”]
because it is situated between two valleys.
It governed Tàiyuán, Shàngdǎng, Xīhé, Lèpíng, Yànmén, and Xīnxīng.
According to what the Jìn Zhì says,
the Zhōu Lǐ states that the Bìngzhōu garrison was Héngshān.
The Chūnqiū Yuánmìng Bāo says: Yíngshì (constellation) flowed to become Bìngzhōu,
and was divided to form the state of Wèi.
16 Jiǎ Chōng was about to depart for his post,
and the high officials saw him off at Xīyáng Tíng.
Xián says: Xīyáng Tíng is west of Hénán City.
Xù said:
“You are the Prime Minister,
yet you are controlled by a single man – is this not contemptible?
However, this departure
is truly difficult to decline.
Only by marrying the Crown Prince
can you remain without having to decline.”
Chōng said:
“In that case, to whom can I entrust my thoughts?”
Xù said:
“I ask to speak of it.”
Thereupon, he said to Féng Dǎn:
“Duke Jiǎ is going far away,
and we will lose our influence.
The Crown Prince’s marriage is not yet settled;
why not persuade the Emperor to accept Duke Jiǎ’s daughter as his consort?!”
Dǎn agreed.
Previously,
the Emperor was planning to marry Wèi Guàn’s daughter to the Crown Prince.
Chōng’s wife, Guō Huái, bribed Empress Yáng’s attendants
to have the Empress persuade the Emperor to seek to marry her (Jiǎ Chōng’s) daughter.
The Emperor said:
“Duke Wèi’s daughter has five merits,
and Duke Jiǎ’s daughter has five demerits. Wèi’s lineage is virtuous and she is likely to have many children;
she is beautiful, tall, and fair-skinned.
The five merits are: virtuous lineage,
one;
likely to have many children,
two;
beautiful,
three;
tall,
four;
fair-skinned,
five.
The five demerits
can be inferred by analogy.
The character ‘shuō’
is pronounced ‘shū ruì’.
The character ‘zhǒng’
is pronounced ‘zhāng yǒng’;
similarly below.
(Jiǎ Chōng’s daughter is) ugly, short, and dark-skinned.”
The Empress, however, insisted on her request.
Xún Yǐ, Xún Xù, and Féng Dǎn all praised Chōng’s daughter as being exceptionally beautiful,
and moreover possessing talent and virtue.
The Emperor eventually complied.
Chōng was retained and reinstated to his former position.
This laid the foundation for the Jǐa clan’s disruption of the Jìn dynasty.
17 In the twelfth month,
Zhèng Mào, Grand Master of Glorious Happiness, was appointed Minister of Works,
but Mào firmly declined the offer.
18 In this year,
Liú Chán, Duke Sī of Ānlè, passed away.
19 Wú appointed Fàn Shèn of Guǎnglín, Military Governor of Wǔchāng, as Grand Commandant.
The Right General Sīmǎ Dīng Fèng passed away.
According to the Dīng Fèng Zhuàn,
for his merit in rescuing Shòuchūn, he was appointed Left General;
upon executing Sūn Chēn,
he was appointed Grand General,
with the added titles of Left and Right Protectors;
when he jointly welcomed Wú Lord Hào,
he was promoted to Right Grand Commander and Left Military Advisor.
It should be written as Right Grand Commander and Left Military Advisor.
20 Wú changed the next year’s reign title to Fènghuáng.
The reign title was changed because a phoenix gathered in the Western Garden.
1 In spring,
in the first month,
Inspector of the Army Hé Zhēn attacked Liú Měng,
defeating him repeatedly.
He secretly enticed his Left Division Commander Lǐ Kè with promises of profit.
The Left Division
was one of the five divisions.
The character ‘shuài’
is pronounced ‘suǒ lèi’.
2 In the second month,
on the day Xīnmǎo,
the Crown Prince married Jiǎ.
She was fifteen years old,
two years older than the Crown Prince.
She was jealous, cunning, and manipulative,
and the Crown Prince doted on her yet feared her.
3 Rénchén,
Ānpíng Xiàn Wáng Fú passed away,
aged ninety-three.
Fú was by nature loyal and cautious.
When Xuāndì was in power,
Fú always humbled himself.
Later, during the changes of succession,
he never participated in any conspiracy;
Jǐngdì and Wéndì, recognizing Fú as an elder of noble lineage,
also dared not pressure him.
At the time of the changes in succession,
Fú was gentle yet upright.
Details can be found in Volume 76, Zhèngyuán first year, and Volume 77, Jǐngyuán first year.
His treatment and honors were exceptionally grand.
At the New Year's court assembly,
an edict commanded Fú to ride in an imperial carriage up to the main hall,
where the Emperor personally greeted and bowed to him from the eastern steps.
The eastern steps
are the main steps
of the host.
*Shàng*
is pronounced *shí zhǎng fān*;
the same applies below.
The Emperor personally offered him a cup of wine for a long life,
in a manner befitting family etiquette.
Each time the Emperor bowed,
Fú would kneel to stop him.
Although Fú was held in high esteem and favor,
he did not regard it as an honor,
and always had a look of worry.
On his deathbed,
he left a will saying:
"Sīmǎ Fú, courtesy name Shúdá, a virtuous scholar from Hénèi of Wèi,
was neither like Yī nor Zhōu,
neither like Yí nor Huì.
He established himself and practiced the Way,
consistent from beginning to end.
He should be clothed in everyday attire
and interred in a plain coffin."
An edict bestowed upon him the Wēnmíng Mìqì from the East Garden.
Fú Qián said: The Wēnmíng of the East Garden
is shaped like a square lacquered bucket,
with one side open,
lacquered and painted.
A mirror is placed inside,
hung above the body,
and covered when the coffin is sealed.
Shīgǔ said: East Garden
is the name of an office
belonging to the Shǎofǔ,
which was in charge of making such items.
Mìqì
refers to a catalpa wood coffin,
and because it was a funerary object,
it was kept secret.
All were in accordance with the precedent of Hàn Ānpíng Xiàn Wáng;
seen in Volume 46, Hàn Zhāngdì, Jiànchū eighth year.
Of the items provided,
not a single one was used.
4 The Emperor discussed matters with the Right General Huángfǔ Táo.
In Tàishǐ fifth year,

were under Hù's command.
Hú Fèn was the General Who Pacifies the South;
Wáng Róng was the Inspector of Yùzhōu.
Xià,
pronounced as hù and yǎ.
Xú and Yáng
were under Wáng Hún's command;
Qīng and Yǎn
were under Lángyá Wáng Zhòu's command.
Their forces are scattered and their formations dispersed,
and all their defenses are critical.
When our surprise troops from Bā and Hàn exploit their weak points,
if one place collapses,
then the upper and lower regions will be shaken,
and even a wise man would not be able to strategize for Wú.
Subsequently, the pacification of Wú was all as Hù planned.
Thousands of *lǐ* from east to west,
the enemy is great,
with no respite.
Sūn Hào indulges his passions and acts arbitrarily,
and is suspicious of his subordinates.
Generals are distrusted at court,
soldiers are distressed in the field.
They have no plans for lasting security,
no fixed determination.
In peaceful times,
they still contemplate leaving or staying;
when troops approach,
there will certainly be those who respond [to us],
and they will ultimately be unable to unite their strength to fight to the death.
This is already clear.
Their customs are impulsive and they cannot endure for long;
their bows, crossbows, halberds, and shields are inferior to those of the Central Plains.
Only naval warfare is advantageous for them;
once we enter their territory,
the Long River will no longer be a safeguard for them.
They will retreat to cities and towns,
abandoning their strength and exposing their weakness,
and will not be our match.
When the government forces advance,
people will have the will to fight to the death;
the Wú people, looking inward,
will each have thoughts of defection and dispersion.
If this is the case,
our army will not take long,
and victory can be guaranteed."
The Emperor deeply accepted this.
However, the court discussion at the time was concerned about Qín and Liáng,
meaning that Shùjīné had not yet been pacified.
Cháo,
pronounced as zhí and yáo.
"When Wú is pacified, the Hú will settle themselves;
we should just quickly accomplish this great deed."
Many of the discussants differed,
Jiǎ Chōng, Xún Xù, and Féng Dǎn especially deemed attacking Wú to be unfeasible.
Hù sighed and said:
"Seven or eight out of ten things in the world do not go as desired.
If Heaven gives, and we do not take it,
will not those who deal with events regret it later?"
Only Minister of the Imperial Treasury Dù Yù
(Wèi established the Minister of the Imperial Treasury position.)
Dù,
pronounced as tú and luò.
supported his plan.
7 On the day Dīngmǎo,
Empress Yáng was established,
and a great amnesty was granted.
The Empress
was a cousin of the former Empress.
She was beautiful and possessed feminine virtues.
When the Emperor first engaged the Empress,
her paternal uncle Yáo
submitted a memorial saying:
"Since ancient times, when a single family produced two empresses,
none have been able to preserve their clan intact.
I beg that this memorial be stored in the ancestral temple,
so that in the future, if my words prove true,
I may be spared misfortune."
The Emperor agreed.
Although Yáo had this memorial,
he ultimately could not escape misfortune.
In the twelfth month,
Shǐ Jùn, the Empress's father and General of the Garrison Army, was made General of Chariots and Cavalry.
He was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Línjìn.
The state was named Jìn, yet the Empress's father was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Línjìn.
This was an inauspicious omen.
Shǐ
cannot be entrusted with the weight of the state.
The Emperor did not heed this.
Shǐ Jùn became arrogant and conceited.
Hú Fèn said to Jùn:
"My lord relies on your daughter to become even more arrogant, eh!
Looking back at past generations,
those who married into the imperial family
have never failed to have their households destroyed.
It's merely a matter of sooner or later."
Jùn replied:
"Isn't your daughter also in the imperial family?"
The Son of Heaven, as the supreme one, has no second.
Hence it is called the "imperial family" (tiānjiā),
meaning its尊 (dignity) is like heaven.
"My daughter and your daughter are just maids.
How can they cause harm or benefit?"
1 In spring,
in the first month,
on the day bǐngzǐ, the first day of the month,
there was a solar eclipse.
2 The imperial prince Yù was established as the Prince of Shǐpíng;
on the day gēngyín,
Yù died.
3 In the third month,
Wén Yāng, Protector of the Pacified Barbarians, led the armies of Liáng, Qín, and Yōng provinces to attack Shùjīnéng.
He defeated them,
and two hundred thousand Hú people surrendered.
4 In summer,
in the fifth month,
Wú generals Shào Yǐ
and Xià Xiáng led over seven thousand troops to surrender.
5 In autumn,
in the seventh month,
Mù, Prince of Zhōngshān, was demoted to Marquis of Dānshuǐ County
for enticing and harboring fugitives.
6 There was a comet in the Purple Palace constellation.
7 General of the Guards Yáng Yáo and others proposed,
thinking that
"in ancient times, enfeoffing vassals
was for the purpose of protecting the royal house;
now all the princes and dukes are in the capital,
which is not in line with the principle of defending the ramparts.
Furthermore,
as generals of other surnames reside on the borders,
it is appropriate to include imperial relatives among them."
The Study of Differences states: The Record of Official Posts holds that Yáo and Xún Xù, seeing Qí Wáng Yōu had prestige at the time,
feared difficulties for the Crown Prince later,
and therefore put forward this proposal
to send the princes to their states.
The Emperor did not initially discern this,
and then issued an edict to discuss its regulations.
According to Xù's biography, there was a different view,
and
at that time, Qí Wáng did not go to his state.
It is doubted that this account is factual.
It is not adopted here.
Large states were to establish three armies totaling five thousand men;
intermediate states, two armies totaling three thousand men;
and small states, one army totaling eleven hundred men.
At that time, Píngyuán, Rǔnán, Lángyá, Fúfēng, and Qí were designated large states;
Liáng, Zhào, Lè'ān, Yān, Ānpíng, and Yìyáng were intermediate states;
and the remaining states were small states.
Each was moved to a location closer to each other.
In the eighth month,
on the day guǐhài,
Liàng, Prince of Fúfēng, was moved to become Prince of Rǔnán,
and sent out as General-in-Chief Who Guards the South,
supervising all military affairs of Yù Province;
Lún, Prince of Lángyá, became Prince of Zhào,
overseeing the defense of Yèchéng;
Fǔ, Prince of Bóhǎi, became Prince of Tàiyuán,
supervising all military affairs of Bīng Province;
since Zhòu, Prince of Dōngguǎn, was in Xú Province,
he was moved and enfeoffed as Prince of Lángyá;
Jùn, Prince of Rǔyīn, was in Guānzhōng,
and was moved and enfeoffed as Prince of Fúfēng;
Yǒng, Prince of Tàiyuán, was moved to become Prince of Héjiān;
Jiǎn, Prince of Rǔnán, became Prince of Nányáng.
Fǔ
was the son of Fú;
Yǒng
was the grandson of Fú.
Those without official posts
were all sent to their respective states.
All the princes and dukes, reluctant to leave the capital,
departed in tears.
Furthermore, imperial prince Wěi was enfeoffed as the Prince of Shǐpíng,
Yǔn as the Prince of Púyáng,
Gāi as the Prince of Xīndū,
and Xiá as the Prince of Qīnghé.
Those ministers of other surnames who had rendered great service
were all enfeoffed as dukes or marquises of commanderies.
Jiǎ Chōng was enfeoffed as the Duke of Lǔ Commandery.
Wáng Shěn was posthumously enfeoffed as the Duke of Bólíng Commandery.
Yáng Hù, Marquis of Jùpíng, was moved and enfeoffed as the Marquis of Nánchéng Commandery.
At that time, an imperial edict designated five counties south of Mount Tài—Wǔyáng, Móu, Nánchéng, Liángfù, and Píngyáng—as Nánchéng Commandery.
Yáng Hù was originally from Nánchéng, Tàishān.
The Emperor decreed that dukes and marquises with ten thousand households or more were large states,
five thousand households or more were intermediate states,
and less than five thousand households were small states.
Hù always declined and yielded honors whenever he was appointed to office or granted a peerage.
His sincere character was well-known,
so he was specially allowed beyond the usual divisions.
"Allowed" (jiàn shēn)
means he was permitted to decline the title, and his wish was granted.
"Divisions" (fēnliè)
refers to the system of enfeoffment and ranking of titles.
This refers to his service to Emperor Wén and the Emperor.
All his proposals for improvement or reduction
were burned in draft,
so the world never heard of them;
those whom he recommended
never knew how they rose.
This means that people advanced through Hù's recommendation and promotion,
but did not know the origin of their advancement.
"To accept an official post in the public court
and then express gratitude in a private household
is something I dare not do."
8 The seven provinces of Yǎn, Yù, Xú, Qīng, Jīng, Yì, and Liáng suffered great floods.
9 In winter,
in the twelfth month,
Sūn Shèn, Grand Inspector of Xiàkǒu of Wú, invaded Jiāngxià and Rǔnán.
Jiāngxià Commandery belonged to Jīng Province,
and Rǔnán Commandery belonged to Yù Province,
which are very far apart.
Shěn Yuè's Sòng Zhì states: The Administrator of Jiāngxià governed Rǔnán County,
originally the land of Shāxiàn.
In the late Jìn period, the people of Rǔnán Commandery migrated to Xiàkǒu
and established Rǔnán there.
Thus, this Jiāngxià Commandery did not yet have a Rǔnán County.
Perhaps it was a later historical addition!
Xià
is pronounced "hù yǎ fān."
An edict was issued, sending an attendant to question Yáng Hù about his reasons for not pursuing the invaders,
and also intending to move Jīng Province.
Hù said:
"Jiāngxià is eight hundred lǐ from Xiāngyáng.
By the time news of the bandits reached us,
the bandits had already departed days ago.
How could infantry possibly pursue them?
To exhaust the army merely to avoid blame
is not my intention.
In the past, when Emperor Wèi Wǔ established Grand Inspectors,
they were generally located close to their provinces,
like the Inspector of Yáng Province governing Shòuchūn, and the Grand Inspector of military affairs of Yáng Province also governing Shòuchūn, and so on.
Jìn
is pronounced "jīn fān."
On the frontiers,
sometimes one side prevails, sometimes the other;
one should simply guard carefully.
The Zǔzhuàn says Lǔ Huángōng said:
'On the frontiers,
one should carefully guard one's territory
and prepare for the unexpected.'
The bandits appear unpredictably,
and it is also uncertain where the province should be based."
10 In this year,
Grand Marshal Chén Qiān returned to court from Yáng Province
and was dismissed as Duke of Gāopíng.
11 The Wú ruler, seeing Zhāng Chù of Kuàijī frequently slandered others,
highly favored and trusted him.
He was repeatedly promoted to Sīzhí Zhōnglángjiàng
and enfeoffed as a marquis.
His father was a lowly yamen runner in Shānyīn County;
Shānyīn County belonged to Kuàijī Commandery.
He submitted a memorial stating:
"If Chù is appointed Sīzhí,
I beg that if he commits a crime, I not be implicated."
The Wú ruler granted this.
Chù proposed establishing twenty Còuqū officials
to specialize in investigating unlawful acts.
Consequently, officials and common people accused each other based on their likes and dislikes,
prisons overflowed,
and there was widespread clamor from top to bottom.
Chù greatly engaged in corrupt profiteering,
becoming arrogant, extravagant, and tyrannical.
When his crimes were exposed,
both father and son were torn apart by chariots.
12 Wèi Guàn sent Tuòbá Shāmòhàn back to his country.
The previous year, Guàn had memorialized to keep Shāmòhàn,
but after the slanderous schemes took effect,
he sent him back.
"Entering as a hostage is seen in volume 77, under the second year of Jǐngyuán of Emperor Yuán of Wèi."
Zhì
is pronounced 'zhì'.
When Shāmòhàn returned,
the chieftains of the various tribes together slandered him and had him killed.
Soon after, Lìwēi became gravely ill.
Kùxián, King of Wūhuán, who was close to Lìwēi and in a position of power,
accepted bribes from Wèi Guàn,
intending to stir up trouble among the various tribes.
He sharpened an axe in the courtyard
and said to the chieftains:
"The Khagan resents you for slandering and killing the Crown Prince."
(At this time, the Xīanběi rulers already used the title "Khagan").
'Kè'
is now read with a 'rù' tone, like 'kān'.
'Hán'
is pronounced 'hán'.
The chieftains were afraid
and all scattered and fled.
Lìwēi died of grief
at the age of one hundred.
His fourth son, Xīlù, ascended.
"Xīlù"
is written "Xīlù"
in Wèi Shōu's *Wèi Shū*.
Initially,
Yōu and Bīng two prefectures both bordered the Xīanběi.
To the east there was Wùhuán,
and to the west, Lìwēi,
often causing border troubles.
Wèi Guàn secretly used schemes to sow discord among them:
Wùhuán surrendered and Lìwēi died.
The *Kǎoyì* says: *Hòu Wèi Shū* by Wèi Shōu:
"Tiěfú Líu Hǔ,
grandson of Xiōngnú Qū Bēi,
died in the fourth year of Zhāochéng,

According to this, the fourth year of Zhāochéng
