so Wùhuán should not have been contemporary with Guàn.
Perhaps both individuals were named Wùhuán.
His younger brother was enfeoffed as a Tínghóu.
1 In spring,
the first month,
on the day Gēngwǔ,
there was a solar eclipse.
2 Sīmǎ Dū of Dōngpíng, Mǎ Lóng,
(Jìn regulations: the two guards, Qiánqū, Yóují, and Qiángnǔ, formed three sections of sīmǎ,
each with a dū.)
Shěn Yuē says: "Diànzhōng Sīmǎ Dū" referred to the palace guards during Emperor Wǔ of Jìn's time,
called the "three sections of sīmǎ",
who were assigned to the left and right two guards along with the "Diànzhōng Jiāngjūn".
"Yáng Xīn, Inspector of Líangzhōu, has lost the harmony of the Qiāng and Róng,
he will certainly be defeated."
Lóng saying Xīn would certainly be defeated

Empress Jǐng
resided in Hóngxùn Palace.
4 Yáng Hù, due to illness, requested to enter the court.
Upon his arrival,
the emperor ordered him to enter the palace in a palanquin,
to sit without bowing.
Hù personally presented his strategy for attacking Wú,
and the emperor approved of it.
Because of Hù's illness,
it was not advisable for him to enter frequently,
so Zhang Huá was sent instead to inquire about his plans.
Hù said:
"Sūn Hào's tyranny is already excessive;
it is now possible to conquer Wú without fighting.
If Hào unfortunately dies,
and the Wú people install another capable ruler,
even with a million troops,
the Yangtze River cannot be easily crossed,
and it will become a future problem!"
Huá deeply agreed.
Hù said:
"The one who will fulfill my ambition,
is you."
The emperor wanted Hù to oversee the generals from his sickbed,
but Hù said:
"Conquering Wú does not necessarily require my personal involvement,

Your Majesty will be troubled.
As for fame and merit,
I dare not claim them;
if the matter is concluded,
there will be responsibilities to be entrusted,
and I hope you will carefully select the right person."
As the southeastern border territories were vast,
a person would be needed to guard and pacify them.
5 In autumn,
the seventh month,
on the day Jǐchǒu,
Empress Jǐngxiàn was buried at Jùnpíng Mausoleum.
This was Empress Hóngxùn.

(Sīzhōu was the area administered by the Hàn Sīlì Xiàowèi.

governing Hénán,
Xíngyáng,
Hóngnóng, Shàngluò, Píngyáng, Hédōng, Jí Commandery, Hénèi, Guǎngpíng, Yángpíng, Wèi Commandery, and Dùnqīu.
Jìzhōu: if there is chaos, Jì hopes for peace;

Míng [locusts]
are insects that eat the heart of seedlings.
"How can we assist the common people?"
The officials in charge
referred to the two bureaus of Zuǒmín and Dùzhī.
They believed:

repair them to store water,
and drain the rest,
so that the hungry can fully benefit from the abundance of fish, vegetables, snails, and clams.
This is an immediate daily benefit.
After the water recedes,
the muddy fields
will yield several *zhōng* per *mǔ*,
which is another benefit for the coming year.
The imperial stud has over forty-five thousand breeding cattle.
(The *Jìn Zhì* states that the Diǎnmù Lìng belonged to the Tàipú.)
Zhòng
is pronounced 'zhāng yǒng' in the 'fān' tone.
Some are so old they haven't been bridled.
These can be distributed to the people
so they can engage in spring plowing and planting.
After the harvest,
collect their rent and taxes.
This will be a benefit several years from now."
The emperor followed this,
and the people benefited from it.
The *Kǎoyì* says: The *Shíhuò Zhì* states "third year of Xiánníng",
while Dù Yù's biography states "fourth year".
According to the *Wǔxíng Zhì*,
there was a great flood in the third year but no insect plague,
and in the fourth year, there were locusts.
We now follow Yù's biography.
In the sixth year of Tàishǐ,
Yù returned after being disgraced as the Inspector of Qínzhōu,
and was appointed Dùzhī Shàngshū.
Seven years had passed since then.
(It was beyond counting,
people at the time called him
"Dù Wǔkù"
meaning he had everything.)
7 In the ninth month,
Hé Zēng was appointed Tàizǎi;
on the day Xīnsì,
Lǐ Yìn, the Shìzhōng Shàngshū Lìng, was appointed Sītú.
8 The Lord of Wú [Wú Zhǔ] was jealous of those who surpassed him.
Shìzhōng, Zhōngshūlìng Zhāng Shàng,
was the grandson of Hóng.
Zhāng Hóng served Sūn Cè and Sūn Quán.
See the Hàn Xiàndì Jì.
His discussions always went beyond the expected,
and the Lord of Wú gradually harbored resentment because of this.
Later, he asked:
"With whom can I compare myself when it comes to drinking wine?"
Fāng [方],
means to compare.
"Your Majesty has the capacity for a hundred gū [觚] (goblets)."
The Lord of Wú said:
"Shàng knows that Kǒng Qiū [孔丘] did not become king,
yet he compares me to him."
Kǒng Cóngzi says: Zhào Píngyuánjūn and Kǒng Zǐgāo [孔子高] were drinking together,
and Zhào Píngyuánjūn urged Zǐgāo to drink,
saying:
"The proverb says,
Yáo [堯] drank a thousand zhōng [鍾],
Kǒngzǐ [孔子] a hundred gū [觚],
Zǐlù [子路] chattered away,
and Shàng drank ten kē [榼].
The sages and worthies of antiquity
none could not drink;
why do you decline?"
Gū [觚]
is a drinking vessel,
holding two shēng [升] (liters).
Wáng [王],
pronounced yú kuàng.
Zhāng Shàng was arrested.
More than a hundred officials, from the Gōngqīng [公卿] down,
went to the palace and kowtowed,
pleading for Shàng's offense.
His death sentence was commuted,
and he was sent to Jiàn'ān [建安] to build ships,
but he was soon executed.
Kǎoyì [考異] states: The Sānshí Guó Chūnqiū [三十國春秋] says:
"Cén Hūn [岑昏] and others, with mud on their heads, pleaded to die in Shàng's place.
Shàng was thus exempted from death,
and exiled to Guǎngzhōu [廣州]."
We now follow the Shàng Zhuàn [尚傳],
with reference to Huán Shì's Wú Jì [環氏吳紀].
I observe Zhāng Shàng's character;
he probably gained closeness to Sūn Hào [孫晧] through his eloquence and quick wit,
but also incurred wrath through his eloquence and quick wit.
Those who sought his death were certainly Cén Hūn's [岑昏] ilk.
What is recorded in the Sānshí Guó Chūnqiū [三十國春秋]
probably gets at the truth of the matter.
9 In winter,
in the tenth month,
Wèi Guàn [衛瓘], General Who Conquers the North [Zhēng Běi Dàjiāngjūn], was summoned to be Shàngshūlìng [尚書令].
At this time,
the court and the common people all knew that the Crown Prince was dull-witted,
and unfit to be heir. Wèi Guàn
always wanted to present a memorial but had not dared to speak;
he happened to be feasting at the Língyún Tái [陵雲臺].
The Língyún Tái [陵雲臺]
was built by Emperor Wèi Wén [魏文帝].
He knelt before the Emperor's bed and said:
"Your subject wishes to present something."
The Emperor said:
"What is it that you wish to say, sir?"
Wèi Guàn [衛瓘] tried to speak but stopped three times,
then patted the bed with his hand and said:
"This seat is a pity!"
The Emperor understood his intention,
and then falsely said:
"Are you truly very drunk, sir?"
Wèi Guàn [衛瓘] said nothing more after this.
The Emperor summoned all the officials of the Eastern Palace [Dōng Gōng]
and held a banquet for them,
then sealed some difficult matters from the Shàngshū [尚書]
and ordered the Crown Prince to decide them.
Jiǎ [賈] was greatly afraid,
and secretly asked an outsider to answer for him,
frequently quoting ancient maxims.
The attendant Zhāng Hóng [張泓] said:
"The Crown Prince is unlearned,
as Your Majesty knows.
If the answers to the edicts frequently quote ancient maxims,
the person who drafted them will surely be questioned.
It means the name of the person who drafted the answers will be questioned.
It is better to answer directly from your own mind."
Jiǎ [賈] was greatly pleased,
and said to Zhāng Hóng [張泓]:
"Please give me a good answer,
and we shall share wealth and honor."
Gǐishǐ [給使]
means an attendant serving in the Eastern Palace.
Zhāng Hóng [張泓] was probably a standout among ordinary people.
The person who later resisted Qí Wáng Jǒng [齊王冏] for Zhào Wáng Lún [趙王倫] at Yángdí [陽翟]
must be this same person.
Now the Crown Prince wrote the answers himself,
and the Emperor was very pleased after reviewing them.
He first showed them to Wèi Guàn [衛瓘],
who was greatly embarrassed,
and then everyone knew that Wèi Guàn [衛瓘] had previously spoken.
Jiǎ Chōng [賈充] secretly sent someone to say:
"Wèi Guàn [衛瓘], that old slave,
almost ruined your family!"
This set the stage for Jiǎ's [賈] resentment towards Wèi Guàn [衛瓘].
Yǔ [語],
pronounced niú jù.
Kǎoyì [考異] states: Sānshí Guó Chūnqiū [三十國春秋] places this in Tàishǐ [泰始] year eight.
According to Wèi Guàn Zhuàn [衛瓘傳],
"In the early Tàishǐ [泰始] period, he was Governor of Qīngzhōu [青州],
then transferred to Yōuzhōu [幽州];
in the eighth year, he was not in the capital."
This event in Wèi Guàn Zhuàn [衛瓘傳] occurs after his transfer to Sīkōng [司空].
According to the Dì Jì [帝紀]:
"In the third year of Tàikāng [太康],
Jiǎ Chōng [賈充] died.
In the twelfth month,
Wèi Guàn [衛瓘] became Sīkōng [司空]."
Therefore, it is moved to after his appointment as Shàngshūlìng [尚書令].
10 The people of Wú [Wú] extensively cultivated farmland in Wǎncéng [皖城],
intending to plan an invasion.
Wáng Hún [王渾], Grand Administrator of All Military Affairs in Yángzhōu [Dūdū Yángzhōu Zhūjūnshì], sent Yángzhōu Cìshǐ Yìng Chuò [揚州刺史應綽] to attack and defeat them,
beheading five thousand people,
burning over one million eight hundred thousand hú [斛] of their accumulated grain,
trampling over four thousand or more qǐng [頃] of rice fields,
and destroying over six hundred ships.

It is simply that the plan did not originate from themselves,
and the merit will not accrue to them.
Each is ashamed of their previous mistaken words and so stubbornly adheres to their views."
(These words pointed directly at the core intentions of Jiǎ Chōng (賈充), Xún Xù (荀勗), Fēng Dǎn (馮紞), and others.
Dissenting opinions flared up.
Although people's minds differ,
it is also because they rely on imperial favor and do not consider future troubles,
thus they lightly agree or disagree.)
"Since autumn,
the plan to attack the bandits has become somewhat apparent.
If we stop now,
Sūn Hào (孫晧) might become frightened and devise counter-measures,
relocating his capital to Wǔchāng (武昌),
and further repairing and strengthening the cities south of the Jiāng (江).
He might move his residents far away.
Then the cities will be unassailable,
and there will be nothing to plunder in the countryside.
In that case, next year's plan might be beyond reach!"
The Emperor was then playing *wéiqí* (圍碁) with Zhāng Huá (張華).
(*Bówù Zhì* (博物志) says: Yáo (堯) invented *wéiqí*
to teach his son Dān Zhū (丹朱).
Some say: Shùn (舜) made *wéiqí* to teach his son Shāng Jūn (商均),
because he was foolish.
The method is such that only the wise can master it.)
Huá (華) pushed the board and cupped his hands, saying:
"Your Majesty possesses sagely martial power.
The state is rich and the army is strong.
The ruler of Wú (吳) is licentious and cruel,
executing the virtuous and capable.
If we attack him now,
we can pacify the realm without much effort.
I beg Your Majesty not to harbor doubts!"
The Emperor then agreed.
He appointed Huá (華) as Dùzhī Shàngshū (度支尚書)
to manage and calculate transportation and supplies.
Jiǎ Chōng (賈充), Xún Xù (荀勗), and Fēng Dǎn (馮紞) stubbornly argued against it.
The Emperor was greatly enraged.
Chōng (充) removed his cap and apologized.
The Púyè (僕射) Shān Tāo (山濤) retired and told others:
"Other than a sage,
external peace will surely bring internal worries."
(*Zuǒ Zhuàn* (左傳) records this as the words of Jìn (晉) grandee Fàn Wénzǐ (范文子).)
"Is this not true wisdom!"
(Shān Tāo (山濤), being a high official,
did not speak boldly in court but retired and told others,
likely seeking to ally himself with Jiǎ Chōng (賈充).)
In winter,
the eleventh month,
a grand expedition was launched to attack Wú (吳).
Zhèn Jūn Jiāngjūn (鎮軍將軍) Lángyá Wáng Zhòu (琅邪王伷) was dispatched to Túzōng (涂中).
Āndōng Jiāngjūn (安東將軍) Wáng Hún (王渾) was dispatched to Jiāngxī (江西).
(Now Hézhōu (和州) is at the crossing of Héngjiāng (橫江).)
Píngnán Jiāngjūn (平南將軍) Hú Fèn (胡奮) was dispatched to Xiàkǒu (夏口).
Zhènnán Dàjiāngjūn (鎮南大將軍) Dù Yù (杜預) was dispatched to Jiānglíng (江陵).
Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn (龍驤將軍) Wáng Jùn (王濬) and Bādōng Jiānjūn (巴東監軍) from Lǔ (魯) Táng Bīn (唐彬) went down through Bā (巴) and Shǔ (蜀).
In total, there were over two hundred thousand troops from east and west.
Jiǎ Chōng (賈充) was appointed as Shǐ Chíjié (使持節), Jiǎ Huángyuè (假黃鉞), Dà Dūdū (大都督).
(Emperor Wén (文) of Wèi (魏) appointed Cáo Zhēn (曹真) as Dūdū Zhōngwài Zhūjūn Shì (都督中外諸軍事)
and Jiǎ Huángyuè (假黃鉞).
In the fourth year of Dàhé (大和) under Emperor Míng (明),
Sīmǎ Yì (司馬懿) campaigned against Shǔ (蜀)
and was granted the title Dà Dūdū (大都督).
This was still based on the Wèi (魏) system.)
(When King Wǔ (武) attacked Zhòu (紂),
he carried a yellow *yuè* (鉞) in his left hand.
The yellow *yuè*
was an imperial implement,
not for exclusive use by subjects,
hence the term 'jiǎ' (假 - provisional/borrowed).)
('Shǐ' (使)
is read as 'shū lì' (疏吏).)
Chōng (充) adamantly argued that attacking Wú (吳) was disadvantageous,
and furthermore claimed he was old and infirm,
unfit for the role of commander-in-chief.
An imperial edict stated:
"If you do not go,
I will go myself."
Chōng (充) had no choice
but to accept the *jié yuè* (節鉞)
and lead the central army to station at Xiāngyáng (襄陽)
to regulate all the armies.
Mǎ Lóng (馬隆) crossed the Wēnshuǐ (溫水) to the west.
(East of Wǔwēi (武威) is the Wēn Wéi Shuǐ (溫圍水).)
Lóng (隆), finding the mountain paths narrow,
constructed 'biǎnxiāngchē' (扁箱車).
('Xiá' (陿)
is interchangeable with 'xiá' (狹 - narrow).)
(If the cart's box is flat,
it can travel on narrow roads.)
('Biǎn' (扁)
is read as 'bǔ diǎn' (補典).)
He put wooden structures on the carts,
(These wooden shelters
were to block wind and rain
and defend against arrows and stones.)
and traveled over a thousand *lǐ*,
killing and wounding many.
(*Kǎoyì* (考異) says: Lóng's (隆) biography states:
"Sometimes magnets were piled up along the road.
The bandits, wearing iron armor,
could not advance.
Lóng's (隆) soldiers all wore rhinoceros-hide armor
and were unhindered.
The bandits thought it divine.")
(This account seems too outlandish
and probably not credible.
I believe that magnets attracting iron armor
is indeed a real possibility.)
Communication was cut off,
and the court worried,
with some saying he was already lost.
Later, Lóng's (隆) messenger arrived at night.
The Emperor clapped his hands and laughed joyfully.
The next morning,
he summoned his ministers and said:
"If I had followed your words,
there would be no Liángzhōu (涼州) now."
He then issued an edict granting Lóng (隆) provisional *jié* (節)
and appointing him Xuānwēi Jiāngjūn (宣威將軍).
(Shěn Yuè's (沈約) treatise states: Wèi (魏) established forty general titles,
with Xuānwēi (宣威) being the second.)
The Xiānbēi (鮮卑) chieftain Cùbá Hán Qiě Wànnéng (猝跋韓且萬能) led over ten thousand households to surrender.
In the twelfth month,
Lóng (隆) engaged in a great battle with Shùjīnéng (樹機能) and
beheaded him.
Liángzhōu (涼州) was thus pacified.
8 An imperial edict inquired of court officials about the gains and losses of governance.
Sītú (司徒) Zuǒ Chángshǐ (左長史) Fù Xián (傅咸) submitted a memorial.
*Jìn Zhì* (晉志) states: The Sītú (司徒) office was augmented with one Zuǒ Chángshǐ (左長史) and one Yòu Chángshǐ (右長史).
Cháo (朝),
read zhí yáo.
"Public and private sectors are insufficient
due to too many officials being established.
Formerly, there were four Dūdū (都督);
now, including Jiānjūn (監軍), they number over ten.
In the early Wèi (魏) dynasty, Dūdū zhū jūn (都督諸軍) were established,
in the southeast to guard against Wú (吳),
in the west to guard against Shǔ (蜀),
in the north to guard against the Hú (胡).
Depending on their qualifications and importance, they were granted the titles of Zhēng (征), Zhèn (鎮), Ān (安), or Píng (平),
and there were only four of them.
Afterwards, more were added,
including Dūdū Yèchéng Shǒuzhūjūn (都督鄴城守諸軍),
Dūdū Qín Yōng Liáng Zhūjūn (都督秦雍涼諸軍),
Dūdū Liáng Yì Zhūjūn (都督梁益諸軍),
Dūdū Jīngzhōu Zhūjūn (都督荊州諸軍),
Dūdū Yángzhōu Zhūjūn (都督揚州諸軍),
Dūdū Xúzhōu Zhūjūn (都督徐州諸軍),
Dūdū Huáiběi Zhūjūn (都督淮北諸軍),
Dūdū Yùzhōu Zhūjūn (都督豫州諸軍),
Dūdū Yōuzhōu Zhūjūn (都督幽州諸軍),
Dūdū Bìngzhōu Zhūjūn (都督幷州諸軍),
making ten in total.
Those with lesser qualifications
served as Jiānjūn (監軍).
The current Cìshǐ (刺史) are almost double;

at that time, there were Cìshǐ (刺史) for the eighteen zhōus (州) of Sī (司), Yù (豫), Xú (徐), Yǎn (兗), Jīng (荊), Yáng (揚), Liáng (梁), Yì (益), Níng (寧), Jiāo (交), Qín (秦), Yōng (雍), Liáng (涼), Jì (冀), Yōu (幽), Bìng (幷), and Qīng (青).
Jī (幾),
read jū xī.
At the beginning of the Yuánshǐ (元始) reign of Hàn (漢),
there were 13,233,612 households
and 59,194,978 mouths.
This was the peak of the Hàn (漢) dynasty.
At the beginning of Emperor Huán's (桓帝) reign,
there were 2,607,906 households
and 50,066,856 mouths.
After Wèi (魏) annexed Shǔ (蜀),
in the fourth year of Jǐngyuán (景元),
counting with Shǔ (蜀),
there were 943,423 households
and 5,372,891 mouths.
The population was still about one-tenth of Hàn's (漢),
but the number of households was barely that.
Fantastically established military headquarters,
numbering in the hundreds,
were useless for guarding the palace;
five-rank feudal lords
were given officials while doing nothing.

Jūnfǔ (軍府) refers to Piàojí (驃騎), Chējí (車騎), Wèi (衞), Fúbō (伏波), Fǔjūn (撫軍), Dūhù (都護), Zhènjūn (鎮軍), Zhōngjūn (中軍), Diǎnjūn (典軍), Shàngjūn (上軍), Fǔguó (撫國), Lǐngjūn (領軍), Hùjūn (護軍), Zuǒ (左) and Yòu Wèi (右衞), Xiāojí (驍騎), Yóujī (游擊), Zuǒ (左), Yòu (右), Qián (前), Hòu Jūn (後軍), and various miscellaneous generals.

The officials for the five-rank feudal lords: kings had Fù (傅), Yǒu (友), Wénxué (文學), Lángzhōnglìng (郎中令), Zhōngwèi (中尉), Dànóng (大農), Zuǒ (左) and Yòu Chángshì (右常侍), Shìláng (侍郎), and various Lìngs (令) such as Diǎnshū (典書), Diǎncí (典祠), Diǎnwèi (典衞), Xuéguān (學官); Diǎnshū Céng (典書丞), Zhìshū (治書), Zhōngwèi (中尉), Sīmǎ (司馬), Shìzǐ (世子), Shùzǐ (庶子), Língmiào Mùzhǎng (陵廟牧長), Yèzhě (謁者), Zhōng Dàfū (中大夫), Shèrén (舍人), Diǎnfǔ (典府).
Dukes, marquises, and below had officials,
varying according to the size of their state,
without a fixed system.
All these come from the common people,
which is why they are in distress and impoverished.
The current urgency
lies in consolidating offices and reducing corvée labor,
with all, from top to bottom, dedicated to agriculture. "
Xián (咸) was the son of Xuán (玄).
At that time, there was also a discussion about reducing half of the officials in zhōus (州), jùns (郡), and xiàns (縣) to dedicate to agricultural labor.
Zhōngshū Jiān (中書監) Xún Xù (荀勗) believed,
"Reducing officials is not as good as reducing offices;
reducing offices is not as good as reducing affairs;
reducing affairs is not as good as purifying the mind.
In the past, Xiāo (蕭) and Cáo (曹) served as prime ministers for Hàn (漢),
and their pure tranquility
brought peace and unity to the people.
This matter is found in volume twelve, second year of Hàn Huìdì (漢惠帝).
Suppressing frivolous theories,
simplifying documents,
omitting minor strictures,
forgiving small errors,
and for those who like to change the normal in pursuit of profit,
their punishment must be carried out —
this is what is called 'reducing affairs.'
Consolidating the Nine Temples into the Shàngshū (尚書),
and assigning Lántái (蘭臺) to the Three Ducal Offices —
this is what is called 'reducing offices.'
The Nine Temples
refer to the nine qíng (卿) temples.
In early Hàn (漢), each of the nine qíng (卿) had specific duties;
after the Eastern capital,
the various departments of the Shàngshū (尚書) distributed and managed various affairs,
and the nine qíng (卿) became almost titular officials.
Thus, the desire was to consolidate them into the Shàngshū (尚書).
Lántái (蘭臺) was the Yùshǐ Tái (御史臺).
The Three Ducal Offices
were the Three Gōng (公) offices.
The Hàn (漢) prime minister had a Chángshǐ (長史) and a Sīzhí (司直);
the Yùshǐ Dàfū (御史大夫) had a Zhōngchéng (中丞) and a Shìyùshǐ (侍御史),
who were in charge of investigating illegal activities.
Therefore, Xù (勗) wanted to assign Lántái (蘭臺) to the Three Ducal Offices.
If all officials in the empire are reduced by half,
I fear that among the numerous civil and military officials,
and the duties in jùns (郡) and states,
some are arduous and some are easy,
so it cannot be applied uniformly.
If there are vacancies,
all will need to be re-established,
which might provoke an increase in complexity.
This cannot be taken lightly."
Collated by Wáng Chóngwǔ (王崇武), Róng Zhàozǔ (容肇祖), Niè Chóngqí (聶崇岐).

first month,
Wú (吳) granted a general amnesty.

Wáng Hún 出 Héngjiāng,

二月，
戊午,
Wáng Jùn, Táng Bīn 擊破 Dānyáng 監 Shèng Jì。
Dānyáng 城在 Zǐguī 縣東八里，
昔 Zhōu Wǔwáng 封 Xióng Yì 於 Jīng Dānyáng 之地，
即此，
今謂之 Qūtuó Chǔwáng Chéng。
並以鐵鎖橫截之；
又作鐵錐，
長丈餘，
暗置江中，
以逆拒舟艦。
Jùn 作大筏數十，
方百餘步，
縛草為人，
被甲持仗，
令善水者以筏先行，
遇鐵錐，
錐輒著筏而去。
又作大炬，
長十餘丈，
大數十圍，
灌以麻油，
在船前，
遇鎖，
然炬燒之，
須臾，
融液斷絕，
於是船無所礙。
以人力設險，
而不以人力守之，
無益也。
庚申
Jùn 克 Xīlíng，
殺吳都督 Liú Xiàn 等。
壬戌,
克 Jīngmén、Yídào 二城，
Jīngmén,
在 Xīlíng 之東，
Yídào 之西。
Dù Yù 遣牙門 Zhōu Zhǐ 等帥奇兵八百汎舟夜渡江，
襲 Lèxiāng，
帥。
讀曰率。
起火巴山。
Bāshān 在今 Jiānglíng Fǔ Sōngzī Xiàn，

幟，
昌志翻。
與 Jiānglíng 都督 Wǔ Yán 書曰：
「北來諸軍，
乃飛渡江也。」
Zhǐ 等伏兵 Lèxiāng 城外，
Xīn 遣軍出拒 Wáng Jùn，
大敗而還。
Zhǐ 等發伏兵隨 Xīn 軍而入，
Xīn 不覺，
直至帳下，
虜 Xīn 而還。
乙丑,
Wáng Jùn 擊殺吳水軍都督 Lù Jǐng。
考異曰：武紀：
「 壬戌,
Jùn 克 Yídào、Lèxiāng 城，
殺 Lù Jǐng。」
Lù Kàng 傳：

殺 Yàn；

Wáng Jùn 傳：

克 Yídào，

乙丑,
克 Lèxiāng，

今從 Jùn 傳。
甲戌,
克之，
斬 Wǔ Yán。
於是 Yuán, Xiāng 以南，
接于 Jiāo, Guǎng，
州郡皆望風送印綬。
水經：Yuán Shuǐ 出 Zāngkē Qiělán Xiàn 東北，
過 Lín Yuán Xiàn，
又東至 Chángshā Xiàjùn Xiàn 西北入于江。

東北過 Táoyáng, Quánlíng, Zhòng'ān, Én, Yīnshān, Lǐlíng, Línxiāng, Luó, Xiàjùn 等縣，
又北至 Bāqiū Shān，
入于江。
沅,
音元。
凡所斬獲吳都督、監軍十四，
牙門、郡守百二十餘人。
Hú Fèn 克 Jiāng'ān。
Jiāng'ān,
即 Gōng'ān,
吳 Nánjùn 治焉。
Dù Yù 既定 Jiāngnán，
改曰 Jiāng'ān Xiàn，

乙亥,
詔：
「Wáng Jùn, Táng Bīn 既定 Bāqiū，
與 Hú Fèn, Wáng Róng 共平 Xiàkǒu, Wǔchāng，
順流長騖，
直造 Mòlíng。
Dù Yù 當鎮靜 Líng, Guì，
懷輯 Héngyáng。
Línglíng, Guìyáng,
漢古郡。
Héngyáng,
吳主 Liàng Tàipíng 二年分 Chángshā 西部都尉立。
Jīngzhōu 南境，
固當傳檄而定。
謂重鎮既破，
其餘當望風而靡也。
太尉 Chōng 移屯 Xiàng。」
以 Jīngzhōu 已定，
不復使 Jiǎ Chōng 南屯 Xiāngyáng，
移屯 Xiàng 為諸軍節度。
Wáng Róng 遣參軍 Xiāngyáng Luó Shàng, Nányáng Liú Qiáo 將兵與 Wáng Jùn 合攻 Wǔchāng，
吳 Jiāngxià 太守 Liú Lǎng, 督 Wǔchāng 諸軍 Yú Bǐng 皆降。
Bǐng,
翻之子也。
Dù Yù 與衆軍會議，
或曰：
「百年之寇，
未可盡克，
方春水生，
難於久駐，
考異曰：Dù Yù 傳曰：
「今向暑，
水潦方降，
疾疫將起」 。
按時未暑，
今依三十國春秋。
更為大舉。」
Yù 曰：
「昔 Yuè Yì 藉 Jìxī 一戰以幷強 Qí，
事見四卷 Zhōu Nǎnwáng 三十一年。
譬如破竹，
數節之後，
皆迎刃而解，
無復著手處也。」
遂指授㣥帥方略，
徑造 Jiànyè。
The ruler of Wú, hearing that Wáng Hún was descending south,

dispatched Chancellor Zhāng Tì to oversee the Grand Administrator of Dānyáng, Shěn Yíng, the Protector of the Army, Sūn Zhèn, and the Deputy Military Advisor, Zhūgě Jìng, to lead an army of thirty thousand across the Jiāng to meet the enemy.
Upon reaching Niúzhǔ,
Shěn Yíng said:
"Jìn has been building its navy in Shǔ for a long time.
Our armies upstream
have always been unprepared.
All the famous generals are dead,
and young men are in charge.
This refers to Lù Yàn, Lù Jǐng, Liú Xiàn, Sūn Xīn, and others.
Jìn's navy will certainly reach here.
It would be advisable to conserve our strength and await their arrival,
then engage them in battle.
If we are fortunate enough to win,
Jiāngxī will be cleared.
The great river flows northward.
Speaking from Jiànyè's perspective,
Lìyáng and Wǎnchéng are both considered Jiāngxī.
If we are unfortunate enough to lose,
then the great cause will be lost!"
Zhāng Tì said:
"Wú's impending doom
is known to both the wise and the foolish;
it is not a matter of today.
I fear that when the Shǔ forces arrive here,
the hearts of the multitude will be struck with terror,
and they will be beyond reorganization.
By crossing the Jiāng now,
we can still engage in a decisive battle.
If we are defeated,
we will die with the altars of soil and grain,
and there will be nothing left to regret.
If we achieve victory,
and the northern enemy flees,
our military might will be tenfold,
and we should then advance south, capitalizing on our victory,
intercepting them midway.
There will be no worry of not defeating them.
If we follow your plan,
I fear that the soldiers will scatter completely,
and we will sit idly awaiting the enemy's arrival,
with ruler and ministers alike surrendering,
not a single person dying for the nation.
Would that not be a disgrace!"
As Zhāng Tì said,
for the Wú people at this point,
their strategies were exhausted.
However, Zhāng Tì's resolve and integrity
are also regrettable.
Nàn (難),
is pronounced as Dàn.
In the third month,
Zhāng Tì and others crossed the Jiāng and
besieged Chéngyáng Commandant Zhāng Qiáo, a general under Wáng Hún, at Yánghé;
The Shuǐ Jīng Zhù states: The Huái River flows north from Píngchūn County, Jiāngxià,
then northeast, passing south of the old city of Chéngyáng County, Rǔnán.
In the twelfth year of Emperor Gāo of Hàn,
Dìng Hóu Xī Jìng was enfeoffed as a marquisate.
During Wáng Mǎng's Xīn dynasty, it was called Xīnlì.
Wèi established Chéngyáng Commandery.
According to Gān Bǎo's Jìn Jì,
Yánghé
was the name of a bridge.

According to the perpetual calendar,
last year had an intercalary seventh month,
and this year's second month began on *Wùwǔ*,
the third month on *Wùzǐ*,
the fourth month on *Dīngsì*,
the fifth month on *Dīnghài*,

heading directly for the enemy city,
and there was no way to turn the ships around to pass Hún.
Your servant arrived at Mòlíng at noon,
and only in the evening received Hún's tally of command, which he was supposed to accept,
ordering Your servant to bring all his forces back to besiege Shítou on the sixteenth.
'The sixteenth'
means the day after the fifteenth,
hence 'the sixteenth.'
'Jiāng' [to bring],
is pronounced liàng.
The armies of Zhènnán [General who Guards the South],
those under Dù Yù's command,
were probably detached to follow Jùn eastward.
'Dìngjiàn' [fixed number]
refers to the fixed number of soldiers in the army.
'Suǒ' [to search],
Xīnkè Xiàn.
There was no way to besiege Shítou in vain;
moreover,
the fixed number of soldiers
cannot be hastily organized,
all of which were not the urgent matters of the moment,
and thus could not be adopted.
I dared not disregard the clear imperial decree.
Hào's forces abandoned him and his relatives deserted him;
he sat alone like a common man,
and like sparrows and rats clinging to life,
he merely begged for survival.
However, the armies north of the Jiāng did not know the true situation,
and failed to capture him early,
thus making a small mistake themselves.
When Your servant arrived and immediately captured him,
he instead received resentment and anger,
with all saying that they had guarded the rebel for a hundred days,
only for someone else to obtain him.
Your servant, in his humble opinion, believes that the way to serve one's sovereign
is to commit oneself to it with life and death if it benefits the state.
If one considers suspicions to avoid blame and responsibility,
this is the benefit of a disloyal minister,
and truly not a blessing for the enlightened ruler and the state!”
Hún then circulated Zhōu Jùn's letter, saying:
“Jùn's army obtained treasures from Wú.”
He circulated the letter,
and had it presented to the emperor.
“Jùn's Yámén general Lǐ Gāo set fire to Hào's false palace.”
Jùn again memorialized, saying:
“Your servant, with solitary roots, stands alone,
and has incurred the hatred of powerful clans.
Indeed, to offend a superior and defy the ruler,
the crime can be pardoned;
but to displease powerful ministers,
disaster is unforeseen.
The false Zhōngláng Jiāng Kǒng Chū said: 'In the second month, Wǔchāng fell,
and the naval forces arrived.'
The second month had already passed,
hence 'in the second month.'
'Xíngzhì' [arrived]
is like saying 'about to arrive.'
'Chū' [Chū's name]
is pronounced chōujū fān.
People around him all drew their swords and shouted loudly,
saying: 'We must fight to the death for Your Majesty to decide this!'
Hào was greatly pleased,
thinking it would certainly be so,
and then gave all his gold and treasures to them.
These scoundrels, without proper conduct,
fled as soon as they received them.
Hào, terrified,
then planned to surrender.
As soon as the surrender envoy left,
those around him plundered his valuables,
seized his wives and concubines,
and set fire to the palace.
Hào fled and hid himself,
fearing he might not escape death.
When Your servant arrived,
he dispatched an aide to rescue and extinguish the fire.
Zhōu Jùn entered Hào's palace first,
and Hún also boarded Hào's boat first;
Your servant's entry and observation
were all after them.
Inside Hào's palace,
there was not even a mat to sit on.
If there were any remaining treasures,
then Jùn and Hún would have obtained them first.
Jùn and others said that Your servant gathered the people of Shǔ,
did not send Hào in time,
and intended to rebel.
They also tried to incite the people of Wú,
saying that Your servant would execute them all,
and seize their wives and children,
hoping they would rebel,
so they could vent their private resentments.
Even the great crime of plotting rebellion
has been ascribed to me;
other slanders
are naturally to be expected.
This year's pacification of Wú
is indeed a great celebration;
but for Your servant personally,
it has brought further blame and entanglement.”
When Jùn arrived at the capital,
the officials memorialized,
“Jùn defied the imperial edict,
a great disrespect,
and request he be handed over to the Grand Judge for punishment.”
The Emperor did not permit it.
'Kē' [punish]
means to decide.
Instead, he ordered him to be handed over to the Grand Judge for investigation and detention;
all of this was arranged by Wáng Hún's partisans.
'Sōu' [boat]
is pronounced sūdāo fān.
Hún and Jùn's contention for merit did not cease,
so the Emperor ordered the Grand Judge, Liú Sòng of Guǎnglíng, to review the matter.
He designated Hún's achievement as superior,
and Jùn's as medium.
The Emperor believed that Sòng had distorted the law and erred in reasoning,
'zhéfǎ' [distort the law]
is like 'zhéyù' [adjudicate cases].
'Zhé' [distort]
means to decide.
When Emperor Wèi Wén Dì received the abdication,
he changed the Jīngzhào Yǐn to Tàishǒu, making it equal to an ordinary commandery.
On the day Gēng-chén,
Jiǎ Chōng’s household allotment was increased by 8,000 households;
Wáng Jùn was appointed Fǔguó Dàjiāngjūn,
and ennobled as Xiāngyáng Xiàn Hóu;
Dù Yù was ennobled as Dāngyáng Xiàn Hóu;
Wáng Róng was ennobled as Ānfēng Xiàn Hóu;
the two sons of Lángyá Wáng Zhòu were ennobled as Tínghóu;
Jīnglíng Hóu Wáng Hún’s household allotment was increased by 8,000 households,
and his noble rank advanced to Gōng;
Shàngshū Guānní Hóu Zhāng Huà was promoted to Guǎngwǔ Xiàn Hóu,
and his household allotment increased by 10,000 households;
Wáng Hún, in addition to his original Jīnglíng allotted households,
had 8,000 more added,
while Zhāng Huà’s Guǎngwǔ Hóu allotment was increased to 10,000 households.
One of his sons was ennobled as a Tínghóu;
Xù was made Zhōngshū Jiàn,
solely in charge of imperial edicts.
Rewards and gifts were granted with distinctions.
The emperor, for the merit of subduing Wú,
issued an imperial proclamation to Yáng Hù’s ancestral temple,
and then ennobled his wife, Lady Xiàhóu, as Wànsuì Xiāngjūn,
with an allotment of 5,000 households.
Wáng Jùn, considering his great achievements,
yet being thwarted and suppressed by Wáng Hún and his son and their faction,
whenever he had an audience,
would enumerate his military exploits and the injustices he suffered,
sometimes unable to contain his indignation,
and would leave abruptly without taking his leave;
the emperor always tolerated and forgave him.
The magnanimity of Jìn Wǔ [Dì]
was greater than that of Suí Wén [Dì].
Shèng,
pronounced shēng.
"Your merits are indeed excellent,
but I regret that the manner in which you present these merits is not entirely satisfactory.
On the day you returned with your troops,
you should have worn a horned cap in your private residence.
The Jìn Zhì says: A cap made of ge [kudzu] fabric,
shaped like a turban and worn horizontally.
In ancient times, both the noble and the humble wore it.
I say that a fú jīn is made of a horizontal piece of fabric,
while a jiǎo jīn is a cap with horns.
Guō Línzōng encountered rain,
and one corner of his cap was soaked,
that was a jiǎo jīn.
If anyone asked,
you should have said: 'The sagacious ruler's
virtue,
the generals' efforts,
what power do I, an old man, possess!'
This is how Lìn [Xiāngrú] humbled Lián Pō,
the incident is found in volume four, under Zhōu Nán Wáng, thirty-sixth year.
Shuài,
pronounced suǒ lèi.
Jùn said:
'I was initially deterred by the affair of Dèng Ài.
Dèng Ài's death
was due to Zhōng Huì's concealment,
preventing Ài's situation from reaching the top.
I could not remain silent;
that I ultimately could not put it out of my mind
shows my narrow-mindedness.'
He knew that repeatedly presenting his merits and the injustices he suffered from Wáng Hún was narrow-minded.
Biǎn,
pronounced bǔ biàn.
He was indignant about it;
Dr. Qín Xiù and others jointly submitted memorials advocating for Jùn's grievances,
whereupon the emperor transferred Jùn to Zhèn jūn Dàjiāngjūn.
The Kǎo Yì states: Jùn's biography says:
'He held the position of Bùbīng Xiàowèi.
Originally there were only five commandants;
the establishment of this camp began with Jùn.'
According to the Zhígūan Zhì:
'Túnqí, Bùbīng, Chángshuǐ, Yuèqí, and Shèshēng Xiàowèi
are the five commandants,
all Hàn dynasty officials.'
Therefore, the name Bùbīng did not originate with Jùn.
The Wǔ Dì Jì states:
'In the sixth month of this year,
on the day Dīng-chǒu,
the office of Yìjūn Xiàowèi was first established.'
It is suspected that what Jùn commanded was the Yìjūn.
Jùn strictly prepared guards and defenses
before meeting them.
When Zhōu Bó went to his feud,
whenever officials from Jiàng and Hédōng arrived,
he would always order his family members to wear armor and carry weapons to meet them,
similar to Wáng Jùn's strict preparation of guards and defenses to meet Wáng Hún.
These two men,
whose strength was sufficient to settle the troubles of the world,
and whose wisdom was sufficient to conquer a state,
yet their methods of self-protection were such—
how laughable!
Dù Yù returned to Xiāngyáng,
believing that although the world was at peace,
forgetting war would certainly lead to danger.
So he diligently practiced military arts
and strictly reinforced the garrisons.
He also drew water from the Zhì and Yù rivers to irrigate over ten thousand qǐng of fields.
The Shuǐ Jīng Zhù says: The Zhì River originates from Yáo Shān, west of Lǔshān Xiàn, Nányáng,
flows east past Chōu Xiàn,
then southeast past Kūnyáng Xiàn,
then northeast past Dìnglíng Xiàn, Yǐngchuān,
and enters the Rǔ River to the east.
The Yù River originates from Gōnglí Shān, Lúshì Xiàn, Hóngnóng,
flows southeast past Xī'è Xiàn and Wǎn Xiàn in Nányáng, then bends,
passes Yùyáng Xiàn to the south,
then passes Xīnyě Xiàn to the south,
passes Dèng Xiàn to the west,
and enters the Miǎn River to the south.
Zhì,
pronounced zhàng jǐ.
Yù,
pronounced yù.
The Shuǐ Jīng Zhù says: The Yáng River originates from Chì Hú, Jiānglíng Xiàn,
flows northeast past the south of Yǐng Chéng,
and then joins the Sānhú River to the northeast.
The Sānhú [lakes]
combine into one river,
flowing east through Huāng Gǔ.
On the east bank is Yěfù Chéng.
The Chūnqiū Zhuàn says:
"Mò'áo was strangled in Huāng Gǔ,
and the generals were imprisoned in Yěfù."
This refers to this place.
When the water is high in spring and summer,
it flows south to the great Jiāng [Yangtze River];
otherwise, it extends south to the Jiāng dykes.
The Yáng River then enters Huáróng Xiàn to the east,
and then joins the Zuòxī River to the northeast;
then flows north past Jìnglíng Xiàn,
and then flows north into the Miǎn River,
known as Yángkǒu.
Yù's biography says: The old waterway only consisted of the Miǎn and Hàn rivers reaching Jiānglíng over a thousand li,
with no northern passage.
Yù then opened Yángkǒu,
started the Xià River,
reaching Bālíng over a thousand li,
internally draining the dangers of the Cháng Jiāng,
and externally connecting the transport routes of Líng and Guì.
Dù Yòu says: The Xià River and Yángkǒu
are in present-day Jiānglíng Xiàn, Jiānglíng Jùn.
Yù did not ride horses himself,
nor could he shoot through armor plates.
Zhá,
refers to armor plates.
The Zuǒ Zhuàn: Pān Wēng's faction and Yǎng Yóujī shot at squatting armored men,
piercing seven plates.
None of the generals could match him.
When Yù was in command,
he frequently sent gifts to powerful figures in Luòyáng.
Someone asked him the reason,
and Yù replied:
"I only fear harm,
not seeking benefit."
Wáng Hún was transferred to Zhēngdōng Dàjiāngjūn,
and returned to guard Shòuyáng.
Zhūgě Jìng remained hidden and did not come out.
Jìng's visit to Wú is found in volume seventy-seven, under Wèi Gāoguì Xiāng Gōng, Gānlù second year.
Jìng's elder sister was the Lángyá Wáng,
Lángyá Wáng Zhòu.
So he went to see him.
Jìng hid in the latrine,
but the emperor compelled him to meet,
and said to him:
"I did not expect to meet you again today!"
Jìng wept and said:
"Your servant is unable to lacquer his body and peel his skin,"
meaning he could not be like Yù Ràng or Niè Zhèng.
"I am truly ashamed and regretful!"
An imperial edict appointed him Shìzhōng;
he firmly declined to accept the position,
returned to his hometown,
and for the rest of his life, never sat facing the imperial court.
All sons of the Zhūgě clan possessed integrity and principles.
3. In the sixth month,
Dānshuǐ Hóu Mù was again ennobled as Gāoyáng Wáng.
Mù's demotion in rank is found in the previous volume, Xiánníng third year.
4. In autumn,
the eighth month,
on the day Jǐ-wèi,
the imperial younger brother Yánzuò was ennobled as Lèpíng Wáng,
but passed away soon after.
5. In the ninth month,
on the day Gēng-yín,
Jiǎ Chōng and others, seeing the unification of the empire,
repeatedly requested the Fēng and Shàn sacrifices;
the emperor did not permit it.
6 In winter,
tenth month,
the former general, Inspector of Qīngzhōu and Prince of Huáinán, Hú Wēi, passed away.
The Emperor considered the four generals—Left, Right, Front, and Rear—to be the four armies.
He once admonished the Emperor for the leniency of current governance.
The Emperor said:
"Below the rank of Secretarial Court Gentleman,
I show no partiality."
Wēi replied:
"What I am referring to
is certainly not about assistant clerks or administrative officers,
but precisely about those of my own rank and above,
who are the ones who can truly enforce order and clarify the law!"
Wēi
was the son of Hú Zhì.
7 In this year,
the commanderies administered by the Director of Retainers were established as Sīzhōu.
In total there were nineteen provinces.
Kǎoyì says: The Sòngshū's Treatise on Provinces and Commanderies states:
"In the first year of Tàikāng (280 CE),
the whole country was unified,
with sixteen provinces in total.
Later, Yōng and Liáng were divided to form Qín,
Jīng and Yáng were divided to form Jiāng,
Yì was divided to form Níng,
and Yōu was divided to form Píng,
making a total of twenty."
According to Dù Yòu's Tōngdiǎn:
"After the pacification of Wú,
nineteen provinces were divided: Sī, Yǎn, Yù, Jì, Bīng, Qīng, Xú, Jīng, Yáng, Liáng, Yōng, Qín, Yì, Liáng, Níng, Yōu, Píng, Jiāo, Guǎng."
We follow this account now.
Dù Yòu said: The seat of Sīzhōu was Luòyáng.
Yǎnzhōu's seat was Lǐnqīu,
now Léizé County in Púyáng Commandery.
Yùzhōu's seat was Xiàng,
now Xiàngchéng County in Huáinán Commandery.
Jìzhōu's seat was Fángzǐ,
now Zhàojùn County.
Bīngzhōu's seat was Jìnyáng.
Qīngzhōu's seat was Línzī.
Xúzhōu's seat was Péngchéng.
Jīngzhōu's seat was initially Xiāngyáng,
later Jiānglíng.
Yángzhōu's seat was Shòuchūn,
later Jiànyè.
Liángzhōu's seat was Wǔwēi.
The three Fǔ regions were divided to form Yōngzhōu,
with its seat at Jīngzhào.
The area west of Mount Lǒng was divided to form Qínzhōu,
with its seat at Shàngguī.
Yìzhōu's seat was Chéngdū.
The lands of Bā and Hàn were divided to form Liángzhōu,
with its seat at Nánzhèng.
Yúnnán was divided to form Níngzhōu,
with its seat at Yúnnán.
Yōuzhōu's seat was Zhuō.
Liáodōng was divided to form Píngzhōu,
with its seat at Chānglí.
Jiāozhōu's seat was Lóngbiān.
The area north of Hépǔ was divided to form Guǎngzhōu,
with its seat at Pānyú.
The population was two million four hundred fifty-nine thousand eight hundred forty households.
8 An imperial edict stated:
"Since the end of the Hàn dynasty,
the four seas were fragmented.
Inspectors handled civil affairs internally
and commanded troops externally.
Now that the empire is unified,
weapons should be sheathed.
The duties of Inspectors
shall all revert to the old Hàn system,
only observing and recommending competent county magistrates.
Large commanderies shall have one hundred armed officials,
small commanderies fifty."
Táo Huáng, the Grand Administrator of Jiāozhōu, memorialized, saying:
"Jiāo and Guǎng stretch for thousands of *lǐ* east and west.
Jiāozhōu governs Hépǔ, Jiāozhǐ, Xīnchāng, Wǔpíng, Jiǔzhēn, Jiǔdé, and Rìnán.
Guǎngzhōu governs Nánhǎi, Línhè, Shǐ'ān, Shǐxīng, Cāngwú, Yùlín, Guìlín, Gāoliáng, Gāoxīng, and Níngpǔ Commanderies.
In the past,
the Qiāng and Lǚ tribes rebelled;
the characters *xià* and *yí* should be removed from the text here.
As for those who obey official duties,
there are barely over five thousand households.
The two provinces are like lips and teeth,
only defended by military force.
Furthermore,
the various barbarians of Níngzhōu
occupy the upper reaches,
with both water and land routes open.
The Púshǔi, Yèyúshuǐ, Láoshuǐ, and Qiáoshuǐ rivers all originate in Níngzhōu
and enter Jiāo and Guǎng.
Moreover, Huò Yì sent Yáng Jì and others from Níngzhōu to campaign in Jiāo and Guǎng,
which proves that both water and land routes are open.
This shows their vulnerability."
Shān Tāo, the Grand Astrologer, also stated
"that it is not advisable to remove military defenses from provinces and commanderies."
Kǎoyì says: Tāo's biography states
"he discussed it with Lú Qīn."
However, Qīn
had already died in the third month of the fourth year of Xiánníng (278 CE).
And after Yǒngníng (301-302 CE),
bandits rose everywhere,
provinces and commanderies had no defenses,
and were unable to suppress them.
The empire then fell into great chaos,
just as Tāo had predicted.
However, after that, Inspectors again concurrently managed both military and civil administration,
and the importance of provincial garrisons increased even further.
9 Since the Hàn and Wèi dynasties,
many Qiāng, Hú, and Xiānbēi who surrendered
were settled in commanderies within the frontier.
Later, they often rebelled out of resentment,
killing local officials,
gradually becoming a menace to the people.
Guō Qīn of Xīhé, a Censor, submitted a memorial, stating:
"The powerful and fierce Róng and Dí have historically been a problem.
In the early Wèi, the population was small,
and the northwestern commanderies
were all inhabited by barbarians.
Internally, even Jīngzhào, Wèijùn, and Hóngnóng
had scattered populations of them.
Although they are now submissive,
if after a hundred years there is a warning of war,
Hú cavalry from Píngyáng
and Shàngdǎng would reach Mèngjīn in less than three days.
Běidì, Xīhé, Tàiyúan, Fényì, Āndìng, and Shàngjùn
would all become Dí territory.
It is advisable, while the might from the pacification of Wú is still strong,
and with the strategies of wise counselors and fierce generals,
to gradually resettle the various Hú within the inner commanderies to the border regions,
to strengthen the defenses against the coming and going of the four barbarian tribes,
and to clarify the ancient system of frontier territories established by the former kings.
The Yǔgòng states: The five zones are five thousand *lǐ* apart in square area,
and the wilderness zone is two thousand *lǐ* from the royal domain.
The Emperor did not heed him.
This laid the groundwork for the later chaos caused by the various Hú in China.
1 In spring,
third month,
an edict ordered five thousand palace women of Sūn Hào to be selected and brought into the palace.
After the Emperor pacified Wú,
he indulged in banquets and excursions,
neglecting state affairs.
The imperial harem almost reached ten thousand people. He often rode a sheep carriage.
The Jìnshū says: A sheep carriage
is also called a *niǎn* carriage,
its upper part resembling a light chariot,
with a 'crouching rabbit' box,
and lacquered wheels and yoke.
It would reach wherever he wished to rest;
palace women competed by inserting bamboo leaves into their doors
and sprinkling salt water on the ground
to attract the Emperor's carriage.
Sheep are fond of bamboo leaves and like salt,
so these two were used to attract the Emperor's carriage.
Bribery and solicitations were rampant,
wielding great influence both inside and outside the court.
People at the time called them the "Three Yángs."
Many old officials were alienated and dismissed.
Shān Tāo repeatedly offered remonstrances,
but though the Emperor knew better, he could not change.
2 Initially,
the Xiānbēi Mòhùbá first entered from beyond the frontier and resided north of Jíchéng in Liáoxī.
Jíchéng was within Chānglí County's borders.
Later, the Mùróng clan established Jíchéng County.
In the eighth year of Zhēnjūn during Tàiwǔ's reign of the Tuòbá Wèi,
Jíchéng was merged into Lóngchéng County of Chānglí Commandery.
The Zàijì states: Mòhùbá accompanied Xuāndì in a campaign against the Gōngsūn clan and rendered meritorious service,
for which he was appointed Shuài Yì Wáng.
He first established his state north of Jíchéng.
The Wèishū states: During the reign of Hàn Huándì,
Tánshíkuài of the Xiānbēi divided their territory into three parts: Eastern, Central, and Western.
The chieftains of the Central part were Kēzuì, Quējū, Mùróng, and others.
They served as grand commanders.
This was the beginning of the Mùróng tribe.
The Zàijì states: Mòhùbá established his state north of Jíchéng.
At that time, many people in Yān and Dài wore bùyáo crowns.
Mòhùbá saw them and liked them,
so he tied up his hair and donned a crown.
The various tribes then called him
"Bùyáo."
Later, the pronunciation changed,
becoming Mùróng.
Some say: "Admiring the virtue of the Two Powers (Heaven and Earth),
and inheriting the countenance of the Three Luminaries (sun, moon, stars),"
they therefore took Mùróng as their clan name.
I consider the "Bùyáo" theory far-fetched;
as for the "some say" theory,
after the Mùróng clan gained control of the Central Plains,
their officials and sons subsequently coined this explanation.
Mùyán begot Shèguī,
who moved north of Liáodōng.
For generations, they submitted to the Central Plains,
and on numerous occasions, they participated in punitive expeditions and rendered meritorious service,
for which Shèguī was appointed Dàchányú.
In the winter, tenth month,
Shèguī first raided Chānglí.
Chānglí
was Hàn's Jiāolí County,
which belonged to Liáoxī Commandery.
In the Eastern Hàn, it belonged to the Liáodōng Subordinate State Commandant.
In the fifth year of Zhèngshǐ of Wèi,
the Xiānbēi submitted internally,
and the Liáodōng Subordinate State was re-established.
Chānglí County was established to house them.
Later, Chānglí Commandery was established.
This was the beginning of the Mùróng clan.
The Kǎoyì states: The Dìjì mentions
"Mùróng Huī."
According to Fàn Hēng's Yānshū Wǔxuānjì:
"Huī
was born in the fifth year of Tàishǐ.
At the age of fifteen,
his father, Chányú Shèguī, passed away,"
which was the fourth year of Tàikāng.
This year's raid
must have been by Shèguī.
3 In the eleventh month,
on the day Rén Yín,
Chén Qiān, Duke Wǔ of Gāopíng, passed away.
The Kǎoyì states: The Dìjì mentions
"Dàsīmǎ."
According to Qiān's biography, he resigned his position in the third year of Xiánníng
and returned to his residence as the Duke of Gāopíng.
4 This year,
Zhōu Jùn, the Inspector of Yángzhōu, relocated his garrison to Mòlíng.
Wèi Yángzhōu's seat of government was Shòuchūn.
When Jìn pacified Wú,
it was then moved to Mòlíng.
The "Yáng"
refers to the restless and energetic qi of the south of the river,
whose nature is light and uplifted.
It also means: the provincial border has many waterways,
and their waters ripple and rise.
It encompassed Dānyáng, Xuānchéng, Huáinán, Lúlíng, Lújiāng, Pílíng, Wú, Wúxīng, Kuàijī, Dōngyáng, Xīn'ān, Línhǎi, Jiàn'ān, Jìn'ān, Yùzhāng, Línchuān, Póyáng, and Nánkāng,
a total of eighteen commanderies.
Repeatedly afflicted by banditry and rebellion,
Jùn pacified them all.
He treated the elders with respect,
sought out talented individuals,
and exercised both authority and benevolence,
causing the Wú people to be pleased and submit.
1 In spring,
the first month,
on the first day Dīng Chǒu,
the Emperor personally offered sacrifice in the southern suburb.
After the ceremony,
he sighed and asked Liú Yì, the Sīlì Xiàowèi:
"To which Emperor of Hàn can I be compared?"
Yì replied:

how can their governance be discussed on the same day as that of Zhōu (周) and Shào (召)!
This means that although the Five Hegemons rose to uphold the Zhōu (周) house,
their governance cannot be discussed on the same day as the assistance provided by Zhōu (周) and Shào (召).
Zhì (治),
pronounced 'zhí lì' in the fanqiè system.
How can one surname monopolize it!
One must exercise a perfectly impartial heart,
and share its benefits and harms with all under heaven,
only then can the state enjoy long-lasting prosperity.
Therefore, Qín (秦) and Wèi (魏) desired to monopolize their power, and barely survived until their deaths;
Zhōu (周) and Hàn (漢) were able to share their benefits, and both close and distant relatives were utilized.
These are clear examples from past events.
Zhì (志) believed that it should be as proposed by the Bóshì (博士) and others."
The Emperor read it
and was greatly enraged, saying:
"Cáo Zhì (曹志) still does not understand my heart,
how much less the four seas!"
This refers to Cáo Zhì (曹志) being the son of Wèi (魏)'s Chénsī Wáng (陳思王) Zhí (植),
and Zhí (植) was the brother
of Wèi Wéndì (魏文帝).
How Wéndì (文帝) restricted Zhí (植), and now he still cannot understand my heart!
"The Bóshì (博士) did not answer what was asked, but answered what was not asked.
What was asked
was merely to bestow gifts upon Qí Wáng (齊王),
not whether Qí Wáng (齊王) should leave or not."
He ordered the authorities to dismiss Zhèng Mò (鄭默) from his post.
Thereupon, Shàngshū (尚書) Zhū Zhěng (朱整) and Chǔ Zhì (褚⿱⿰丰刀石) memorialized:
"Zhì (志) and others have encroached upon official duties, abandoned their positions,
confused and misled the imperial court,
embellished evil words,
and feigned openness without reserve.
We request that Zhì (志) and others be arrested and handed over to the Tíngwèi (廷尉) for sentencing."
An imperial edict dismissed Zhì (志) from his office,
allowing him to return to his residence as a Gōng (公).
Zhì (志) had inherited the title of Chén Wáng (陳王) in Wèi (魏).
When Jìn (晉) received the abdication,
he was demoted to Jùnchéng Xiàn Gōng (鄄城縣公).
Yǔ Chún (庾純) went to the Tíngwèi (廷尉) to confess:
"Fū (旉) showed me the draft,
and being foolish and shallow, I listened."
An imperial edict pardoned Chún (純).
Tíngwèi (廷尉) Liú Sòng (劉頌) memorialized that Fū (旉) and others committed a great disrespect,
and should be executed in the market.
The Shàngshū (尚書) requested permission to allow the Tíngwèi (廷尉) to carry out the execution.
Shàngshū (尚書) Xiàhóu Jùn (夏侯駿) said:
"The Eight Bureaus were established
precisely for this kind of situation."
The Six Cáo Shàngshū (六曹尚書), along with the Lìng (令) and Pú (僕), constituted the Eight Bureaus.
Wèi (為),
pronounced 'yú wěi' in the fanqiè system.
Zuǒ Púshè (左僕射), Xiàpí Wáng Huǎng (下邳王晃), also agreed with Jùn (駿)'s proposal.
The memorial was kept in the palace for seven days,
then an imperial edict was issued:
"Fū (旉) is the principal author of the memorial,
and should be executed;
however, as Fū (旉)'s family members have confessed,
Fū (旉) and the seven others including Guǎng (廣) should all be pardoned from the death penalty."
Gài (丐),
means 'dài' (貸).
In the second month,
an edict added Jìnán Jùn (濟南郡) to Qí Guó (齊國).
On the Jǐchǒu (己丑) day,
Yōu (攸)'s son, Chánglè Tíng Hóu Shí (長樂亭侯寔), was established as Běihǎi Wáng (北海王).
Yōu (攸) was ordered to prepare all the ceremonial items and edicts,
and to set up the Xuānxiàn (軒縣) music.
Yuè (樂),
for the Son of Heaven, it's Gōngxiàn (宮縣),
for feudal lords, it's Xuānxiàn (軒縣).
Xuānxiàn (軒縣) means
missing one side.
Xuán (縣),
pronounced 'xuán'.
Yellow axes and court carriages,
as a deputy escort for the imperial carriage.
4 In the third month,
on the Xīnchǒu (辛丑) day, the first day of the month,

5 Qí Xiàn Wáng Yōu (齊獻王攸), overcome with indignation and resentment, fell ill.
He begged to guard the imperial tombs.
Xiānhòu (先后) refers to Empresses Wénmíng (文明皇后).
Imperial physicians were dispatched to examine him,
but the physicians, trying to please the Emperor,
all reported that he had no illness.
Hé Nán Yǐn (河南尹) Xiàng Xióng (向雄) admonished:
"Although Your Majesty has many sons and younger brothers,
few possess virtue and reputation.
Qí Wáng (齊王) residing in the capital is indeed of great benefit;
this must be considered."
The Emperor did not accept his advice,
and Xióng (雄) died in vexation and anger.
Yōu (攸)'s illness worsened,
but the Emperor still urged him to depart.
Yōu (攸), forcing himself, entered to bid farewell.
He had always maintained a dignified bearing,
and even though his illness was severe,
he still composed himself,
behaving as usual.
The Emperor grew more suspicious that he was not ill.
A few days after bidding farewell and leaving,
he vomited blood and died.
The Emperor went to attend the funeral.
Yōu (攸)'s son, Jiǒng (冏), wailed and jumped,
accusing the physicians of falsely reporting his father's illness.
An imperial edict immediately executed the physicians,
and made Jiǒng (冏) his successor.
Previously,
the Emperor loved Yōu (攸) very deeply,
but was persuaded by Xún Xù (荀勗), Féng Dǎn (馮紞), and others,
who wished to consider the succession after his death,
hence he sent him away.
When he died,
the Emperor grieved inconsolably.
Féng Dǎn (馮紞), who was attending him,
said:
"Qí Wáng (齊王)'s reputation exceeded his actual merits,
and the world gravitated towards him.
Now that he has died,
it is a blessing for the state.
Why does Your Majesty grieve so excessively!"
The Emperor wiped away his tears and stopped.
An imperial edict ordered Yōu (攸)'s funeral rites to follow the precedent of Ānpíng Xiàn Wáng (安平獻王).
This matter is recorded in volume 79, Tàishǐ (泰始) 8th year.
Yōu (攸)'s actions were always in accordance with propriety,
and he rarely made mistakes.
Even the Emperor respected and feared him.
Whenever he invited him to sit together,
he would always choose his words carefully before speaking.
Xiǎn (鮮),
pronounced 'xī shàn' in the fanqiè system.
Chǔ (處),
pronounced 'chāng lǚ' in the fanqiè system.
6 Summer,
fifth month,
on the Jǐhài (己亥) day,
Lángyá Wǔ Wáng Zhóu (琅邪武王伷) died.
7 Winter,
eleventh month,
Shàngshū Zuǒ Púshè (尚書左僕射) Wèi Shū (魏舒) was made Sītú (司徒).
8 Hénán (河南) and the six states of Jīng (荊), Yáng (揚), etc., suffered great floods.
Jīng (荊),
means 'qiáng' (強),
referring to its violent and strong disposition;
also said to mean 'jǐng' (警),
referring to the frequent invasions by the southern barbarians,
whose people would submit to the Dao (道) later,
but rebel first without the Dao (道),
thus constant vigilance was necessary;
also said,
it takes its name from Jīng Shān (荊山).

It governs Jiāngxià (江夏), Nánjùn (南郡), Xiāngyáng (襄陽), Nányáng (南陽), Shùnyáng (順陽), Yìyáng (義陽), Xīnchéng (新城), Wèixīng (魏興), Shàngyōng (上庸), Jiànpíng (建平), Yídū (宜都), Nánpíng (南平), Wǔlíng (武陵), Tiānmén (天門), Chángshā (長沙), Héngyáng (衡陽), Xiāngdōng (湘東), Línglíng (零陵), Shàolíng (邵陵), Guìyáng (桂陽), Wǔchāng (武昌), and Ānchéng (安成).
9 Guīmìng Hóu Sūn Hào (歸命侯孫晧) died.
10 In this year,
Xiānbēi Mùróng Shèguī (鮮卑慕容涉歸) died.
His younger brother, Shān (刪), usurped the throne.
Kǎoyì (考異) says: In Zàijì (載記),
'Shān' (刪)
is written as
'Nài' (耐).
We now follow the Yān Shū (燕書).
Kuī (廆) hid in Xú Yù (徐郁)'s house in Liáodōng (遼東).
1 In spring,
the first month,
on the Jǐhài day,
two green dragons
were seen in the well of the Wǔkù.
The Dì observed them,
and showed a joyful expression.
All officials were about to offer congratulations,
when Shàngshū Zuǒ Púshè Liú Yì memorialized, saying:
"In the past, when dragons descended upon the court of Xià,
they eventually brought calamity upon Zhōu.
The Guóyǔ says: 'When Xià was in decline,
the spirit of the Bāorén transformed into two dragons and settled in the Xià court.
The Xià Hòu divined whether to kill them, drive them away, or let them remain,
but none was auspicious;
he divined whether to request their spittle and store it,
and that was auspicious.
Thereupon, he offered silks and announced it to them with an oracle.
The dragons vanished, but their spittle remained,
and it was placed in a casket and stored away.
Throughout the Yīn and Zhōu dynasties,
no one opened it.
At the end of Lì Wáng's reign,
he opened it and looked at it;
the spittle flowed into the courtyard,
and could not be removed.
The Wáng ordered women to strip and shout at it,
whereupon it transformed into a black lizard and entered the royal palace.
A young maidservant in the palace, who had not yet lost her baby teeth, encountered it;
when she reached adulthood, she became pregnant,
and gave birth during Xuān Wáng's reign.
She conceived without a husband,
so, out of fear, she abandoned it.
A woman who sold crossbow-cases took it,
and fled with it to Bāo.
The Bāorén had a legal dispute,
and presented the child to Yōu Wáng.
The Wáng then doted on her,
made her his queen,
and she gave birth to Bófú.
(He) wished to kill the Tàizǐ
to establish Bófú.
The Tàizǐ fled to Shēn.
The Shēn Hóu, together with the Quǎnrong, attacked the Wáng,
and killed him at the foot of Lí Shān.'
There is no ritual for congratulating on dragons."
The Dì complied with this.
2 Initially,
Chén Qún, seeing that the Ministry of Personnel was unable to thoroughly vet all the scholars in the empire,
therefore ordered each commandery and state to establish a Zhōngzhèng,
and each province to establish a Dà Zhōngzhèng.
All were to be filled by natives of the locality who held positions at court and possessed abundant virtue and talent, to serve as their agents.
They would rank and grade individuals into nine ranks (jiǔ pǐn).
This matter is detailed in volume 69, during the first year of Huángchū of Emperor Wén of Wèi.
If their principles and integrity were found wanting, they would be demoted.
The Ministry of Personnel relied on these rankings to appoint officials to various posts.
As this system was implemented for a long time,
some Zhōngzhèng were not the right people for the job,
and corruption and malpractices proliferated daily.
Liú Yì submitted a memorial, saying:
"Now, with the establishment of Zhōngzhèngs
and the determination of nine ranks,
their decisions on high and low status are arbitrary,
honor and disgrace are in their hands.
They wield the awe and blessings of the sovereign,
seizing the power and authority of the imperial court.
Publicly, they bear no responsibility for inadequate verification;
privately, they have no scruples about making accusations.
This means that if there are any improprieties in the ranking of individuals,
publicly they are not held accountable for failed verifications,
and privately, in exposing hidden faults,
they stop at nothing,
without any hesitation about making accusations.
With myriad schemes and manipulations,
the spirit of integrity and humility is extinguished,
and the custom of contention and litigation is formed.
Your servant is secretly ashamed of this for the sacred dynasty!
The establishment of the Zhōngzhèng system
has eight detriments to good governance: High and low status follow strength and weakness;
right and wrong follow prosperity and decline.
A single person's circumstances
can change dramatically in ten days.
The upper ranks have no impoverished families;
the lower ranks have no influential clans.
This is the first.
The purpose of establishing Zhōu Dū,
Zhōu Dū
refers to the Zhōngzhèngs,
was to suppress dissent
and unify opinions.
Now, their responsibility is made heavy, but the people themselves are regarded lightly,
allowing conflicting opinions to run rampant in the provinces and villages,
and grudges and animosities to form among high officials.
This is the second.
The original intent of establishing the ranking system
for the nine ranks
was to categorize talent and virtue according to superiority and inferiority,
and to order individuals according to their sequence.
Now, superior and inferior switch places,
and sequences are inverted.
This is the third.
Your Majesty rewards good and punishes evil,
always judging by law.
Yet, you uniquely established the Zhōngzhèngs,
entrusting them with a heavy responsibility for the entire nation,
without any provisions for reward or punishment.
Furthermore, people are forbidden from suing,
allowing them to act arbitrarily
without any restraints or fears.
All those who are wronged,
accumulating grievances and injustices,
cannot make them heard by the imperial court.
This is the fourth.
The scholars of a nation
number in the thousands.
Some migrate to foreign lands,
some seek their livelihood in different places—
meaning those who lack sufficient food and clothing
travel to different places to make a living.
How can all their talents be fully known?
Yet, the Zhōngzhèngs, whether they know or not,
must all evaluate and rank them.
They gather praise from official bureaus
and accept slander from rumors.
If they rely solely on themselves, they suffer from the defect of ignorance;
if they listen to others, they are prone to favoritism.
This is the fifth.
The purpose of seeking talented people
is to govern the populace.
Now, those who demonstrate effectiveness in office are sometimes assigned to lower ranks,
while those without achievements in office are given higher appointments.
This is suppressing actual merit and elevating empty reputation,
encouraging superficiality and neglecting performance evaluation.
This is the sixth.
Offices require different individuals,
and tasks require different abilities.
Now, instead of describing the suitability of their talents, they are merely graded into nine ranks.
If people are selected by rank,
it may not match their strengths and talents.
If people are selected by description,
they are limited by their original rank.
This only produces 'white discussions'—
'white'
means 'plain'.
Those who 'eat plain food' are considered 'eating empty food'.
'White discussions'
are like 'empty words'.
This is the seventh.
For those demoted by the nine ranks, their faults are not clearly stated;
for those promoted, their virtues are not listed.
Each acts on their likes and dislikes
to cultivate their private interests.
How can the people of the empire not relax their moral conduct and sharpen their personal relationships?
This is the eighth.
From this discussion,
the office named Zhōngzhèng
is in reality a den of corruption;
the system named Nine Ranks
has eight detriments.
No past or present error
is greater than this!
Your foolish servant believes that the Zhōngzhèngs should be abolished,
the Nine Ranks eliminated,
the corrupt laws of the Wèi dynasty discarded,
and a beautiful system for this generation established instead."
The Grand Commandant, Ruǎnán Wáng Liàng, and the Minister of Works, Wèi Guàn, also submitted a memorial, saying:
"The Wèi dynasty, following a period of chaos and upheaval,
saw scholars displaced and migrating,
making it impossible to conduct thorough investigations.
Thus, the nine-rank system was established,
merely serving as a provisional basis for temporary selection.
Now, the nine regions are unified,
and a great transformation is just beginning.
Your servants believe that all these lesser laws should be abolished,
and the 'local settlement' (tǔ duàn) system should be universally adopted.
'Local settlement' means using local residence as the determinant.
'Duàn' (斷)
is pronounced Dīng-Luàn.
One's current place of residence would be considered their true home,
with no more 'county guests'
whose distant affiliations lie in other lands.
Completely abolish the Zhōngzhèng and nine-rank systems,
so that the promotion of the good and the advancement of talent
are each determined by local public opinion.
Then, superficial competition will naturally cease,
and everyone will seek improvement within themselves."
The Shǐpíng Wáng Wénxué, Lǐ Chóng of Jiāngxià, submitted a memorial:
"Since Wèi,
each kingdom has appointed one master-friend and one scholar-official.
Xià,
pronounced Hù Yǎ.
Shàng,
pronounced Shí Zhǎng.
"Once the nine ranks are abolished,
it would be appropriate to first open up migration,
allowing people to settle together.
Then the reality of 'local settlement' will be achieved."
Although the Emperor approved of their words, he ultimately could not make the change.

in the twelfth month,

1 In spring,
in the first month,
Shàngshū Zuǒ Púyè Liú Yì retired from office,

The 'Kǎoyì' states: "The 'Jìn Chūnqiū' places this in the tenth month of the seventh year,
but this account follows his official biography."
2 On the day *wùchén*
Wáng Hún (Wáng Hún) was appointed Shàngshū Zuǒ Púyè (Shàngshū Zuǒ Púyè),
and his son, Jì (Jì), became Shìzhōng (Shìzhōng).
Hún’s (Hún) subordinates handled matters improperly,
as did the Shàngshū’s (Shàngshū) subordinates.
處 (Chǔ),
pronounced *chāng-lǚ* (chāng-lǚ).
當 (Dāng),
pronounced *dīng-làng* (dīng-làng).
A Shìzhōng (Shìzhōng) manages all affairs of the Ménxià (Ménxià),
hence he can be disciplined by law.
(Jì (Jì)) had long been at odds with (the Emperor),
so (the Emperor) disparaged Jì (Jì) for being unable to tolerate his father.
The Emperor therefore became estranged from Jì (Jì),
who was later dismissed from office for some transgression.
Jì (Jì) was extravagant by nature.
The Emperor said to Shìzhōng (Shìzhōng) Hé Qiáo (Hé Qiáo):
“I will scold Jì (Jì) before granting him office.
What do you think?”
Qiáo (Qiáo) replied:
“Jì (Jì) is brilliant and quick-witted,
I fear he cannot be coerced.”
The Emperor summoned Jì (Jì),
severely reprimanded him,
and then said:
“Are you quite ashamed?”
Jì (Jì) replied:
“The ballad of ‘a foot of cloth, a *dòu* of millet,’
I am always ashamed of it for Your Majesty.”
This refers to the Emperor’s inability to tolerate Qí Wáng Yōu (Qí Wáng Yōu).
為 (Wèi),
pronounced *yú-wěi* (yú-wěi).
“Your servant cannot make relatives亲 (qīn) to each other,”
meaning that his remonstrances were not heeded.
The Emperor was silent.
Qiáo (Qiáo)
was the grandson of Qiáo (Qiáo).
See Hé Qiáo (Hé Qiáo) in volume sixty-six, fourteenth year of Jiàn’ān (Jiàn’ān) during the reign of Hàn Xiàndì (Hàn Xiàndì).
3 The provinces of Qīng (Qīng), Liáng (Liáng), Yōu (Yōu), and Jì (Jì) suffered from drought.
4 Autumn,
Eighth month.
On the day *bǐngxū* (bǐngxū), the first day of the month,

5 Winter,
Twelfth month.
On the day *gēngzǐ* (gēngzǐ),
Xiāngyáng Wǔ Hóu (Xiāngyáng Wǔ Hóu) Wáng Jùn (Wáng Jùn) died.
6 This year,
Mùróng Shān (Mùróng Shān) was killed by his subordinates,
and his people again welcomed Shèguī’s (Shèguī) son, Kuì (Kuì), and enthroned him.
Shèguī (Shèguī) had long been at odds with the Yǔwén (Yǔwén) tribe.
The Yǔwén (Yǔwén) tribe was also a Xiānbēi (Xiānbēi) branch.
Their ancestor had a chieftain named Púhuí (Púhuí),
who, while hunting, found three jade seals,
inscribed with the characters
“Huángdì Xǐ (Huángdì Xǐ).”
Púhuí (Púhuí) believed it was bestowed by Heaven.
Their custom was to call the Son of Heaven
“Yǔwén (Yǔwén),”
hence their state was named Yǔwén (Yǔwén),
and they adopted it as their clan name.
The Hé Shì Xìng Yuàn (Hé Shì Xìng Yuàn) states: The Yǔwén (Yǔwén) clan originated from Yándì (Yándì).
Their descendants, due to their achievement of tasting herbs,
were called *sìfén* (sìfén) by the Xiānbēi (Xiānbēi) for grass,
and thus they were named the Sìfén (Sìfén) clan.
Later generations commonly called them Sìfén (Sìfén),
which was probably a phonetic corruption.
(Kuì (Kuì)) was to be appointed Chányú (Chányú) of the Xiānbēi (Xiānbēi) for generations.
The imperial court did not permit it.
Kuì (Kuì) was enraged,
invaded Liáoxī (Liáoxī),
killing and plundering many people.
The Emperor dispatched the Yōuzhōu (Yōuzhōu) army to attack Kuì (Kuì),
and they fought at Féirú (Féirú).
Féirú (Féirú) county belonged to Liáoxī (Liáoxī) commandery.
Yìng Shào (Yìng Shào) said: “Féi Zǐ (Féi Zǐ) fled to Yān (Yān), and Yān (Yān) was enfeoffed here.”
Xián (Xián) said: “Féirú (Féirú)
is now Píngzhōu (Píngzhōu).”
From then on, (Kuì (Kuì)) violated the border every year,
and also attacked Fúyú (Fúyú) to the east.
King Yīlǜ (Yīlǜ) of Fúyú (Fúyú) committed suicide,
and his sons and brothers fled to Wòjú (Wòjú) for protection.
Kuì (Kuì) razed their capital city,
and drove over ten thousand people away before returning.
1 Spring,
First month.
On the day *jiǎyín* (jiǎyín), the first day of the month,
there was a solar eclipse.
Wèi Shū (Wèi Shū) feigned illness,
and earnestly requested to resign his position,
retiring as Jùyángzǐ (Jùyángzǐ).
Wèi Shū (Wèi Shū) always acted first and then spoke.
At the time of his resignation,
no one knew about it.
The Kǎo Yì (Kǎo Yì) states: “There is no date for Wèi Shū’s (Wèi Shū) resignation in either the chronicles or biographies.”
His biography states:
“He resigned due to celestial anomalies,
but the Emperor did not permit it;
later, after the morning court on New Year’s Day, he returned to his residence
and submitted his seal and ribbon.”
Furthermore, the biography also says:
“At the time of his resignation,
no one knew about it.”
If he resigned on New Year’s Day this year due to the solar eclipse,
and only submitted his seal and ribbon on New Year’s Day in a later year,
then it cannot be said that
“no one knew about it.”
It is probable that he resigned due to celestial anomalies precisely on New Year’s Day after the morning court,
and simply did not rise again.
“Every time I discuss this matter with you,
it remains unresolved day after day.
Guàn (Guàn) also wanted to resign,
and we discussed this matter together,
day after day,
but it remained unresolved, as he said.
Suddenly, (I was)
‘behind’
him.”
This uses the words of Yán Yuān (Yán Yuān) from the Lúnyǔ (Lúnyǔ).
2 Summer,
Mùróng Kuì (Mùróng Kuì) raided Liáodōng (Liáodōng).
Yīluó (Yīluó), son of the former Fúyú (Fúyú) King Yīlǜ (Yīlǜ), sought to lead his existing people back to their old country,
and requested aid from Dōngyí Xiàowèi (Dōngyí Xiàowèi) Hé Kǎn (Hé Kǎn).
Kǎn (Kǎn) dispatched Dūhù (Dūhù) Jiǎ Shěn (Jiǎ Shěn) to lead troops to escort him.
Between the Wèi (Wèi) and Jìn (Jìn) dynasties,
each regional commander established a Dūhù (Dūhù),
who was an officer in charge of troops.
沈 (Shěn),
pronounced *chí-lín* (chí-lín).
Shěn (Shěn) fought bravely,
beheaded Dīng (Dīng),
and thus restored Fúyú (Fúyú).
3 Autumn,
The Xiongnú (Xiongnú) Húdū Dà Bó (Húdū Dà Bó) and Wěisuō Hú (Wěisuō Hú), each leading their tribes, over one hundred thousand people, surrendered at Yōngzhōu (Yōngzhōu).
4 Ninth month.
On the day *wùyín* (wùyín),
Fúfēng Wǔ Wáng (Fúfēng Wǔ Wáng) Jùn (Jùn) died.
5 Winter,
Eleventh month.
On the day *rénzǐ* (rénzǐ),
Tà (Tà), King of Lǒngxī (Lǒngxī), was appointed Dūdū Guānzhōng Zhū Jūnshì (Dūdū Guānzhōng Zhū Jūnshì).
Tà (Tà)
was the son of Xuāndì’s (Xuāndì) younger brother Kuí (Kuí).
6 This year,
Xiānbēi (Xiānbēi) Tuòbá Xīlù (Tuòbá Xīlù) died.
鹿 (Lù)
is also written as
祿 (Lù).
Since Tàishǐ (Tàishǐ),
the Mùróng (Mùróng) and Tuòbá (Tuòbá) branches of the Xiānbēi (Xiānbēi) had grown stronger day by day,
so historians recorded their generations.
1 Spring,
First month.
On the day *wùshēn* (wùshēn), the first day of the month,
there was a solar eclipse.
2 The hall of the Tàimiào (Tàimiào) collapsed.
Ninth
month,
the Tàimiào (Tàimiào) was rebuilt,
with sixty thousand workers.
3 This year,
the Xiongnú (Xiongnú) Dūdū (Dūdū) Dàdòudé Yī Yùjú (Dàdòudé Yī Yùjú) and others again led their tribes, eleven thousand five hundred people, to surrender.
The Wèi (Wèi) had already divided the Xiongnú (Xiongnú) within the frontier into five tribes.
Since last year,
Xiongnú (Xiongnú) leaders bringing their tribes to surrender numbered over one hundred thousand people.
The history does not state where they were settled,
these must have come from beyond the frontier,
they were tribes of the Northern Xiongnú (Xiongnú).
復 (Fù),
pronounced *fú-yòu* (fú-yòu).
1 Spring,
First month.
On the day *rénshēn* (rénshēn), the first day of the month,
there was a solar eclipse.
Comparing the solar eclipses on New Year’s Day for three consecutive years,
the Emperor soon passed away,
and the Jìn (Jìn) fell into great chaos;
Heaven’s warning
was indeed clear.
2 Summer,
Sixth month.
On the day *gēngzǐ* (gēngzǐ), the first day of the month,
there was a solar eclipse.
3 Thirty-three commanderies and states suffered from severe drought.
4 Autumn,
Eighth month.
On the day *rénzǐ* (rénzǐ),
stars fell like rain.
5 Earthquake.
