In the tenth year of Tàikāng
(Jǐyǒu, 289 CE):
1. Summer,
the fourth month.
The Tàimiào was completed.
On the day Yǐsì,
the xiá祭 was performed.
Xiá
is a grand combined sacrifice.
The Gōngyáng Zhuàn says: "What is a grand xiá?"
"It is a combined sacrifice."
"How is it a combined sacrifice?"
"The spirit tablets of the dismantled ancestral temples are arrayed before the Tàizǔ;
the spirit tablets of the temples not yet dismantled are all brought up,
and they partake of the sacrifice together with the Tàizǔ."
The character xiá
is pronounced Hú Jiá.
2. Mùróng Kuì sent an envoy to request submission.
In the fifth month,
an imperial edict appointed Kuì as Xiānbēi Dūdū.
When Kuì sought an audience with Hé Kān,
he arrived at the gate in the attire of a scholar-official,
wearing a scarf and a simple gown, in accordance with the禮 for scholar-officials.
Between the Wèi and Jìn dynasties,
when scholar-officials sought an audience with someone of high status,
they wore a scarf and a simple gown as a matter of礼.
Chě,
means a single garment.
Kān
is pronounced Kǒu Hán.
Kuì then changed into military attire and entered.
When people asked him why,
Kuì said:
"If the host does not treat the guest with ritual propriety,
what is the guest to do!"
When Kān heard this,
he was greatly ashamed
and deeply respected and admired him.
Receiving a surrender as if receiving an enemy,
a commander on the frontier
should display armed might when meeting guests from the Four Barbarians;
this is not excessive,
so why should one be ashamed of it!
The Duàn clan
were the eastern Xiānbēi.
Dù Yòu said: "Yǔwén Mòhuái originated from beyond the border of Liáodōng,
and for generations served as the Dàrén of the eastern Xiānbēi.
Duàn Jílìujiù of Túhé came from Liáoxī,
and during a time of chaos,
was sold as a slave to Kùnú, the Dàrén of the Wūhuán in Yúyáng.
Kùnú, seeing his strength,
sent him to lead a multitude of people
to Liáoxī to seek sustenance,
whereupon he attracted and enticed fugitives and rebels,
and thus became strong and prosperous."
I (the compiler) note from the biography of Wáng Jùn in the Jìnshū: "Duàn Jílìujiù
was the crown prince of Wùwùchén."
The Duàn clan had been strong and prosperous
for a long time since Wùwùchén's era;
that Jílìujiù was seized during chaos
is perhaps possible;
but since Wùwùchén was able to be the commander of the tribe,
it is probably not the case that their strength depended on his son's enticement.
Kuì humbly spoke and offered generous gifts to serve them.
Duàn Guó Shányú Jiē married his daughter to Kuì,
and they had Huǎng, Rén, and Zhāo.
The Mùróng and Duàn clans thus became nations linked by marriage.
The character shǔ
is pronounced Suǒ Jiǎo.
The character chán
is pronounced chán.
The character qī
is pronounced Qī Xì.
They moved their residence to Qīngshān in Túhé.
Túhé County,
in the Former Hàn, belonged to Liáoxī;
in the Later Hàn, it belonged to the Protectorate of Liáodōng;
during Wèi and Jìn, it was abolished
and merged into the jurisdiction of Chānglí Commandery.
Later, the Mùróng clan re-established Túhé County;
in the eighth year of Zhēnjūn during Tàiwǔ of the Tuòbá Wèi dynasty,
Túhé was merged into Guǎngxīng County of Chānglí Commandery.
Dù Yòu said: "Qīngshān in Túhé
is one hundred ninety lǐ east of the administrative city of Yíngzhōu Commandery."
3. Winter,
the tenth month.
The Míngtáng and the Five Emperors' altars in the Southern Suburbs were restored.
The Míngtáng and Southern Suburbs had eliminated the altars of the Five Emperors;
see volume seventy-nine, Tàishǐ second year.
4. In the eleventh month,
on the day Bǐngchén,
Xún Xù, the Shàngshū Lìng and Jìběi Chéng Hóu, died.
Xù was talented and resourceful,
and good at discerning the emperor's intentions,
thereby maintaining his favor.
He spent a long time in the Zhōngshū,
exclusively managing important affairs.
When he was promoted to Shàngshū,
he was very disheartened.
Wǎng
is the same as wǎng.
Wǎng describes a disheartened appearance.
Chàng
also describes a regretful, disappointed, and disheartened appearance.
Xù said:
"They have taken my Fènghuángchí from me,
why do you gentlemen congratulate me!"
5. The Emperor indulged excessively in sensual pleasures,
which led to illness.
Yáng Jùn feared Rǔnán Wáng Liàng,
and consequently had him sent away.
On the day Jiǎshēn,
Liàng was appointed Shìzhōng, Dà Sīmǎ, Jiǎ Huángyuè, Dà Dūdū, and Dū Yùzhōu Zhū Jūnshì,
stationed at
Xǔchāng;
Nányáng Wáng Jiǎn was transferred to become Qín Wáng,
Dūdū Guānzhōng Zhū Jūnshì;
Shǐpíng Wáng Wěi became Chǔ Wáng,
Dūdū Jīngzhōu Zhū Jūnshì;
Púyáng Wáng Yǔn became Huáinán Wáng,
Dūdū Yáng, Jiāng Èr Zhōu Zhū Jūnshì.
According to the Yuánkāng first year of Huì Dì,
the officials memorialized that Jīng and Yáng provinces
had vast territories and were particularly difficult to govern,
whereupon Yùzhāng, Póyáng, Lúlíng, Línchuān, Nánkāng, Jiàn'ān, Jìn'ān from Yáng Province, and Guìyáng, Ānchéng, Wǔchāng from Jīng Province,
a total of ten commanderies,
were carved out to establish Jiāng Province.
Thus, at this time, Jiāng Province did not yet exist.
It is suspected
that the characters "Jiāng Èr"
are superfluous;
further extensive research is needed.
The character pú
is pronounced Bó Mù.
The Jìn system: among those designated Dūdū Zhū Jūnshì, there were those with Shǐ Chíjié,
those with Chíjié,
and those with Jiǎjié;
a Shǐ Chíjié could execute officials of two thousand shí rank and below;
a Chíjié could execute commoners, and in military matters, had the same authority as a Shǐ Chíjié;
a Jiǎjié could only execute those who violated military orders in military matters.
Yǐng became Chéngdū Wáng,
Yàn became Wú Wáng,
Chì became Yùzhāng Wáng,
Yǎn became Dài Wáng;
the imperial grandson Yù became Guǎnglíng Wáng.
Furthermore, Dí, the son of Huáinán Wáng, was enfeoffed as Hàn Wáng;
Yí, the son of Chǔ Wáng, was enfeoffed as Pílíng Wáng;
Fúfēng Wáng Chàng was transferred to become Shùnyáng Wáng;
Chàng's younger brother Xīn was enfeoffed as Xīnyě Gōng.
Chàng
was Jùn's son.
Chàng inherited Jùn's title,
but did not hold the post in Guānzhōng,
hence the transfer of his enfeoffment.
Yáo became Dōng'ān Gōng.
Jìn
was Zhòu's son.
The Jìn system: imperial clan members enfeoffed as Jùn Gōng
had regulations similar to those of minor kings.
The character dàn
is pronounced Tú Lǎn,
and also Tú Làn.
The character zhòu
is pronounced zhòu.
At first,
the Emperor bestowed the talented woman Xiè Jiǔ upon the Crown Prince.
A cáirén
(talented woman) ranked below a měirén
(beauty). Lǐ Yánshòu said: "Emperor Wǔ of Jìn adopted the systems of Hàn and Wèi.
Below the Sān Fūrén and Jiǔ Pín
were měirén, cáirén, and zhōngcáirén,
whose rank was equivalent to officials of one thousand shí (dan) or less."
Jiǔ,
the character is reversed.
One night, there was a fire in the palace.
The Emperor ascended a tower to watch it.
Yù, who was five years old,
tugged at the Emperor's robes and led him into the darkness, saying:
"At night, in a sudden crisis,
one should be prepared for the unexpected;
the sovereign should not be exposed to the light."
The Emperor thus marveled at him.
He once praised Yù to his attendants, saying Yù resembled Emperor Xuān,
hence all under heaven looked up to him.
The Emperor knew the Crown Prince was not talented,
yet he relied on Yù's intelligence and wisdom,
and thus had no intention of deposing or establishing a new heir.
He again employed the counsel of Wáng Yòu.
Yòu
was Wáng Jì's elder cousin.
He served Emperor Wén along with Yáng Hù and others,
and the Emperor favored and trusted him.
Fù,
read fú yòu fān;
the character fù below is the same.
Yàohài
refers to the regions of Yōng, Jīng, and Yáng.
The Emperor again appointed Yòu as Běijūn Zhōnghòu
to command the imperial guard.
The Emperor carefully selected assistants for the Imperial Grandson Yù.
As Sànqí Chángshì Liú Shí's conduct was pure and simple,
he was appointed Guǎnglíng Wángfù.
Since the Wèi dynasty,
kingdoms had a shī (teacher) and yòu (friend).
Jìn, to avoid the taboo name of Emperor Jǐng,
changed shī to fù.
Xíng,
read xià mèng fān.
Shí believed that the current customs encouraged seeking advancement,
and few showed modesty and humility.
He wished
that those who were newly appointed to office and wished to submit their letter of thanks
must first promote the worthy and yield to the capable,
only then could their letter be accepted.
If an office became vacant, the person who had been yielded to the most would be chosen.
He believed:
"In human nature, when people contend, they desire to disparage those inferior to themselves;
when they yield, they eagerly promote those superior to themselves.
Therefore, when the world contends, it is difficult to distinguish superiority from inferiority;
when the era yields, the wise and intelligent are revealed.
At such a time,
if one can withdraw and cultivate oneself,
then many will yield to them;
even if one wishes to remain poor and humble,
it will not be possible.
To eagerly rush forward and yet expect others to yield,
is like walking backward and seeking to advance."
Liú Sòng, the Xiāng of Huáinán
(Kingdoms had a xiāng,
a system from the Hàn dynasty;
Jìn later changed it to Nèishǐ):
"Your Majesty, because legal prohibitions are lenient,
accumulated over time,
it is not possible to suddenly govern the subordinates with a straight rule.
This is truly appropriate for the current times.
However, as for correcting the age and remedying its defects,
it is proper to gradually move towards purity and solemnity;
it is like navigating a boat,
although one does not cross a swift current directly,
one must gradually move with the flow,
slowly heading towards the desired direction,
and then one can cross.
This draws an analogy to crossing a river.
One who crosses a great river,
although it is said to be crossing the great river directly,
navigating through chaotic currents,
must nevertheless follow the water's momentum and gradually move,
guiding the boat towards its desired direction,
to reach the shore,
only then can one successfully cross.
Otherwise, one will be controlled by the water's force,
unable to steer the boat towards the desired direction,
and will not be able to land."
"Since Tàishǐ,
almost thirty years have passed.
The Emperor received the abdication and
changed the reign title to Tàishǐ,
which was twenty-five years ago.
There has been no significant improvement compared to the past.
It means that in establishing undertakings and creating enterprises,
there has been no greater prosperity than in former times.
If we have not yet reversed the decline of this decadent age
to achieve the glory of the beginning,
and it is transmitted to later generations,
will there not be cause for concern?
Should the great enterprise of a different era
someday become unstable,
the worry and responsibility will still rest with Your Majesty."
"Your servant has heard that for the sake of the altars of soil and grain,
nothing is better than enfeoffing relatives and the worthy.
However, one should carefully assess the situation,
so that when the feudal lords act righteously,
their power is sufficient to support the imperial capital;
but if they harbor malicious intentions,
their power is insufficient to act alone.
Achieving this balance is very difficult.
Your Majesty should discuss it deeply with scholars who understand ancient and modern times."
The Emperor's deployment of the various princes to regional garrisons while lacking the means to control them internally,
this is what Liú Sòng deeply worried about.
If one is guilty, their person may be executed or banished,
but the state's sovereignty is not extinguished;
such as Zhōu cooking Qí Āigōng and enthroning his younger brother Jìng,
or King Xuān executing Lǔ Hóu Bóyù and enthroning Duke Xiào.
If a guilty person has no heir,
the state perishes with them.
See the records of the Former and Later Hàn.
Following the old system of Zhōu,
the lower ranks would be stable and the upper ranks secure.
I (the commentator) believe that the way Jìn treated its feudal princes
should not be like this.
"The world is vast,
and matters are exceedingly numerous,
but the ruler is alone,
like the sun in the sky.
Therefore, the transformation wrought by a sagely king
involves grasping the essentials oneself
and entrusting tasks to subordinates.
This is not because one dislikes labor and prefers ease,
but truly because the form of governance should be so.
To judge ability from the start of an undertaking
is very difficult to discern;
to assign merit and blame based on success and failure
is very easy to recognize.
Now, Your Majesty is always meticulous at the beginning of tasks
but overlooks the evaluation at the end.
This is why the effectiveness of governance is not yet good.
If the ruler can truly remain calm, grasp the essentials,
and assess merits and faults after success or failure,
then none of the subordinates will be able to escape their due punishment or reward."
"In ancient times, the six ministers divided their duties,
with the Zhǒngzǎi serving as their leader.
The Rítuals of Zhōu state: the Tiānguān Zhǒngzǎi,
Dìguān Sītú,
Chūnguān Zōngbó,
Xiàguān Sīmǎ,
Qiūguān Sīkòu,
and Dōngguān Sīkōng,
these were the six ministers,
and the Zhǒngzǎi oversaw them all.
The nine ranks held specific responsibilities,
with the Chéngxiàng (Chancellor) overseeing them all.
This was the system before the Western Capital.
The various ministers merely carried out their duties.
Since Emperor Guāngwǔ of Hàn,
the Shàngshū (Secretariat) was held responsible for administrative affairs,
matters were submitted to the imperial chancellery,
and the various ministers merely executed orders.
Duàn,
read dīng luàn fān.
Many matters could be delegated to the outer bureaus,
outer bureaus
refers to the bureaus of the various ministers.
The Shàngshū would oversee the general framework,
like the Chéngxiàng,
and at the end of the year, evaluate performance,
check records, and dispense rewards and punishments.
This would also be acceptable.
Now, every action receives approval from above,
and if the superior makes a mistake,
it cannot be blamed on the subordinate.
At the end of the year, if no accomplishments are made,
there is no one to hold accountable."
Now, minor faults and mistakes
are inevitable in human nature,
but if every one is corrected by law,
then no one in court or country will be able to stand.
In recent generations, those who have served as jiān sī (inspectors),
generally fail to uphold the main principles but always highlight minor faults.
Yùshǐ Tái (Censorate) officials and zhōu cìshǐ (provincial governors),
are all jiān sī.
Cháo,
pronounced as zhí yáo fān (zhāo).
Jiān,
pronounced as gōng hán fān (gān).
They diligently weave a tight net to ensnare minor offenses,
causing impeachments to follow one after another.
This appears to be selfless,
but corrupting the law is hidden within it.
This is why sagely kings do not value overly meticulous cases,
but rather demand impeachments of fierce and cunning individuals;
then the villains who harm governance
will naturally be captured.
Indeed, the merit of founding a dynasty
lies in establishing teachings and fixing regulations,
so that the lingering influence binds people's hearts,
and the remaining achievements guide the young and weak.
If later generations rely on them,
though they may be ignorant, they will still seem wise;
though they may be foolish, they will seem intelligent;
only then is it truly worthy of esteem.
This means that if the laws and regulations are well established and clear,
even if later successors are ignorant and foolish,
with something to rely on,
their rule will still be like that of the wise and intelligent.
This statement probably refers to the crown prince's inability to succeed in building the grand edifice,
and the emperor having no exemplary rules to bequeath to his descendants.
However, if one does not have the right person,
the Way cannot be put into practice in vain.
With Liú Chán's mediocrity, but supported by Zhūgě Liàng,
then even if Zhāoliè died,
he was as if not dead.
When Kǒngmíng died,
although Kǒngmíng's laws and regulations for governing Shǔ remained,
Chán could not uphold them.
As for renovating official residences,
all such construction projects
are often excessively extravagant.
There is no worry that they will not be undertaken;
this is something that Your Majesty will not need to do in the future, as it will happen on its own.
Now, by diligently doing what is not needed, you harm what you rely on,
which I secretly consider a fault."
The Emperor was unable to use any of these suggestions.
6. An edict appointed Liú Yuān as the Northern Dūwèi (Commander) of the Xiōngnú.
At this time, the five bù shuài (chieftains) of the Xiōngnú were changed to the five bù dūwèi.
He won people's hearts and engaged with others;
many prominent figures from the five bù (tribes)
and renowned scholars from Yōu and Jì provinces
went and submitted to him.
This was the basis for Liú Yuān to gather followers and eventually usurp the Jìn dynasty's throne.
7. Xi Kē's ten thousand men and women came to surrender.
Xi Kē was also an Yí (barbarian) tribe.
Emperor Xiàohuì Shàngzhīshàng,
whose taboo name was Zhōng,
courtesy name Zhèngdù,
was the second son of Emperor Wǔ.
The posthumous title law says: "Gentle in nature and benevolent to the people is called Huì."
Yǒngxī first year
(gēngxū, 290 CE)
1. In spring,
first month,
on the xīnyǒu (28th) day,
the reign title was changed to Tàixī.
Tàixī was the name changed by Emperor Wǔ.
Until the jìyǒu (46th) day of the fourth month,
the crown prince ascended the throne
and changed the reign title to Yǒngxī.
Changing the reign title before a year had passed
was still an impropriety;
how could it be that immediately after the former emperor had just passed away,
and the crown prince ascended the throne,
the reign title was changed on that very day?
2. On the jǐsì (6th) day,
Wáng Hún was appointed Sītú (Minister of Works).
3. Wèi Xuān, son of Sīkōng (Minister of Education), Shìzhōng (Palace Attendant), and Shàngshū Lìng (Director of the Imperial Secretariat) Wèi Guàn,
was married to Princess Fánchāng.
Xuān was fond of wine and
committed many transgressions.
Yáng Jùn disliked Guàn
and wanted to oust him.
So, he conspired with huángmén (eunuchs) to jointly slander Xuān
and advised Emperor Wǔ to take away the princess.
Guàn was ashamed and fearful,
so he announced his old age and humbly resigned.
An edict promoted Guàn to Tàibǎo (Grand Guardian),
allowing him to retire at home as a Duke.
Guàn was enfeoffed as Zīyáng Gōng (Duke of Zīyáng).
4. Jùyáng Kāngzǐ Wèi Shū passed away.
5. In the third month,
on the jiǎzǐ (1st) day,
Shí Jiàn, Right Guānglù Dàfū (Grandee of Splendid Happiness), was appointed Sīkōng.
Jìn records: Left and Right Guānglù Dàfū holding golden seals and purple cords, and Guānglù Dàfū with additional golden seals and purple cords,
were of the second rank.
6. The Emperor was gravely ill
and had not yet issued a deathbed edict.
Most of the veteran ministers had already passed away.
Shìzhōng (Palace Attendant) and Chējì Jiāngjūn (General of Chariots and Cavalry) Yáng Jùn alone attended to the sick Emperor within the Forbidden Palace.
Other high officials were not allowed to be near the Emperor.
Jùn thereupon arbitrarily changed crucial close officials according to his private wishes,
planting his confidants.
Just then, the Emperor had a slight remission.
Jiàn,
as written.
Jiàn means
the illness slightly improves.
The Emperor, with a serious expression, said to Jùn:
"How can you do this!"
At this time, Rǔnán Wáng Liàng had not yet departed.
Last year,
Liàng was sent out to oversee Yùzhōu (Yù Province).
The intention was for Liàng to assist in governing alongside Jùn,
and also to select several court officials with good reputation to assist him.
Jùn borrowed the edict from the Zhōngshū (Imperial Secretariat) to examine it,
and upon getting it, immediately hid it away.
Zhōngshū Jiān Huá Yì was fearful,
and personally went to demand it,
but Jùn never returned it.
The Emperor then became confused again.
The Empress proposed that Jùn assist in governing,
and the Emperor nodded his assent.
In summer,
fourth month,
on the xīncǒu (38th) day,
the Empress summoned Huá Yì and Zhōngshū Lìng Hé Shào,
and orally declared the Emperor's command to draft an edict,

appointing Jùn as Tàiwèi (Grand Commandant), Tàizǐ Tàifù (Grand Tutor to the Crown Prince), Dūdū Zhōngwài Zhūjūn Shì (Supervisor of All Military Affairs Inside and Outside), Shìzhōng (Palace Attendant), and Lù Shàngshū Shì (Manager of the Affairs of the Imperial Secretariat).
When the edict was complete,
the Empress presented it to the Emperor in the presence of Yì and Shào.
The Emperor looked at it and said nothing.
Yì was
Xīn's grandson;
Shào was
Zēng's son.
Huá Xīn served during the Hàn and Wèi dynasties,
Hé Zēng served during the Wèi and Jìn dynasties.
Both reached the rank of Gōng (Duke/Grandee),
and their personal reputations were similar.
The Emperor soon had a slight remission again
and asked:
"Has Rǔnán Wáng arrived yet?"
Those around him said he had not arrived,
and the Emperor then fell into a critical condition.
On the jǐyǒu (46th) day,
he passed away at Hánzhāng Diàn.
He was fifty-five years old.
The sixth line of the third trigram of Kūn says: "Hánzhāng may be firm."
Kūn takes encompassing magnanimity as its virtue;
it is the way of the empress.
Hánzhāng Diàn must have been in the empress's palace.
The Spring and Autumn Annals writes,
"The Duke passed away in the small sleeping chamber,"
which means he passed away peacefully.
He was intelligent and good at strategizing,
accepting honest counsel,
and never showed displeasure to anyone.

"Beating the Drum of Appeal to Higher Authority" (撾登聞鼓):
In ancient times,

The Rites of Zhōu (周禮) states that

'qióng' (窮) refers to those who are poor, wronged, or have lost their positions,
who would come and beat this drum
to convey their message to the king,
similar to how people today strike a drum to report serious matters.
This was the beginning of the "Drum of Appeal to Higher Authority."
The name "Drum of Appeal to Higher Authority"
likely originated during the period between Wèi (魏) and Jìn (晉).

Yīn and Yáng rely on it for their transformation and generation;

Thus, the function of nothingness (無),

their words cannot prevail,

Examining this letter, not only is there no corroborating evidence from Zǔ,

After the Crown Prince was deposed,

Sīmǎ Yǎ, Supervisor of the Right Guard (Yòuwèi Dū), and Xǔ Chāo, Supervisor of the Standing Retinue (Chángcóng Dū),

in charge of the Diànzhōng (殿中) bureau.
He was the son of Xù (勗).
Xù (勗) was a minister who aided in the founding of the Jìn (晉) dynasty.
Xún Yù (荀彧) was an official who aided in the founding of the Wèi (魏) dynasty.
He declined due to illness,
but Lún (倫) pressed him relentlessly.
Overwhelmed with anxiety, he fell ill,
accepted the appointment while being supported,
and died a few days later.
On *dīngyǒu* (丁酉),
the Prince of Liáng (梁), Róng (肜), was appointed Tài​zǎi (太宰);
the Zuo Guānglù Dàfū (左光祿大夫), Hé Shào (何劭), was appointed Sītú (司徒);
and the Yòu Guānglù Dàfū (右光祿大夫), Liú Shí (劉寔), was appointed Sīkōng (司空).
The *Jìn Zhì* (晉志) states: The Zuo and Yòu Guānglù Dàfū (左、右光祿大夫)
were granted golden seals and purple sashes,
ranked second grade.
Their emoluments, official positions, caps, carriages, clothing, and jade pendants
were accompanied by clerks, soldiers, and feathered guards.
The later Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū (金紫光祿大夫)
was likely the Zuo and Yòu Guānglù Dàfū (左、右光祿大夫) of the Wèi (魏) and Jìn (晉) dynasties.
However, the Dàfū (大夫) of Wèi (魏) and Jìn (晉) were all dedicated officials,
whereas in later generations, they were merely titular officials.
Dù Yòu (杜佑) stated: Since the Wèi (魏) and Jìn (晉) dynasties,
the Zuo and Yòu Guānglù Sān Dàfū (左右光祿三大夫) all held silver seals and green sashes.
For those of greater importance,
if an imperial edict added golden seals and purple sashes,
they were then called Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū (金紫光祿大夫).
Since the important ones had the title of Jīnzǐ (金紫),
the original Guānglù (光祿) was called Yínqīng Guānglù Dàfū (銀青光祿大夫).
When Crown Prince Yù (遹) was deposed,
there was a plan to establish the Prince of Huáinán (淮南), Yǔn (允), as the Imperial Younger Brother,
but the deliberators did not agree.
It means there were those who held differing opinions.
So, Yǔn (允) was appointed Píqi Jiàngjūn (驃騎將軍) with the privilege of establishing an administration equal to the Sān Sī (三司),
and concurrently held the position of Zhōnghùjūn (中護軍).
On *jǐhài* (己亥),
the Xiàngguó Lún (倫) falsely issued an imperial edict, sending Shàngshū Liú Hóng (劉弘) with "gold dust wine" to bestow death upon Empress Jiǎ (賈) in Jīnyōngchéng (金墉城).
In the fifth month,
on *jǐsì* (己巳),
an imperial edict established the Prince of Línhǎi (臨海),
Zāng (臧), as the Imperial Grandson.
Wáng (王) was returned to her mother's family;
when the Crown Prince was deposed,
Wáng (王) was sent back to her parents' home.
The Xiàngguó Lún (倫) acted as the Imperial Grandson's Grand Tutor.
On *jǐmǎo* (己卯),
the late Crown Prince was posthumously named Mǐnhuái (愍懷).
In the sixth month,
on *rén​yín* (壬寅),
he was buried in Xiǎnpíng Líng (顯平陵).
The Prince Kāng (康) of Qīnghé (清河), Xiá (遐), passed away.
The Zhōnghùjūn (中護軍), the Prince of Huáinán (淮南), Yǔn (允),
was resolute and firm by nature,
and the palace guards and soldiers all feared and respected him.
Yǔn (允) knew that the Xiàngguó Lún (倫) and Sūn Xiù (孫秀) harbored ulterior motives,
so he secretly trained commandos
and plotted to attack them.
Lún (倫) and Xiù (秀) greatly dreaded him.
In autumn,
in the eighth month,
Yǔn (允) was transferred to the position of Tàiwèi (太尉),
outwardly showing great honor,
but actually stripping him of his military authority.
The Zhōnghùjūn (中護軍) commanded troops;
being transferred to Tàiwèi (太尉) meant his military authority was gone.
Xiù (秀) sent the Yùshǐ (御史) Liú Jī (劉機) to pressure Yǔn (允),
arresting his subordinate officials and below,
and impeaching him for resisting an imperial edict,
an act of great treason and disrespect.
Yǔn (允) looked at the edict and
realized it was written by Xiù (秀)'s own hand.
Enraged,
he arrested the Yùshǐ (御史)
and was about to execute him, but
the Yùshǐ (御史) escaped.
Yǔn (允) executed two of his clerks.
These were clerks from the Lántái (蘭臺).
"The Prince of Zhào (趙) wishes to destroy my family!"
He then led the princely troops and seven hundred men from his personal retinue straight out.
Princely troops
were the troops of Huáinán (淮南) Commandery.
Personal retinue
refers to the retinue of the Zhōnghùjūn (中護軍).
Shuài (帥)
is read as Lǜ (率).
"The Prince of Zhào (趙) has rebelled;
I am going to punish him.
Those who follow me should bare their left arm!"
Consequently, many joined him.
As Yǔn (允) was about to head to the palace,
the Shàngshū Zuo Chéng Wáng Yú (王輿) closed the Yèmén (掖門).
To the left of the Dānmén (端門), the palace gate, was called the Zuo Yèmén (左掖門),
and to the right, the Yòu Yèmén (右掖門).
He then surrounded the Xiàngfǔ (相府).
At this time, Lún (倫) used the Eastern Palace as the Xiàngfǔ (相府).
Lún (倫) repeatedly lost battles,
and over a thousand people died.
The Crown Prince's Zuo Lǜ (左率) Chén Huī (陳徽) led the Eastern Palace troops, shouting and drumming inside to respond to Yǔn (允).
Zuo Lǜ (左率)
was the Zuo Wèi Lǜ (左衞率).
Bows and crossbows fired in unison,
shooting at Lún (倫),
and arrows fell like rain.
The Zhǔshū Sīmǎ Suī Mì (司馬眭祕) used his body to shield Lún (倫).
The *Xù Hàn Zhì* (續漢志): Among the thirty-six bureaux of the Shàngshū (尚書),
each bureau had three Zhǔshū (主書).
This Zhǔshū Sīmǎ (主書司馬)
was probably an official of the Xiàngguófǔ (相國府),
appointed by Lún (倫) himself.
Suī (眭),
pronounced *xī suí*,
is a surname.
Lún (倫)'s officials all hid behind trees,
each tree being hit by several hundred arrows,
from *chén* (辰) to *wèi* (未) hours.
The Zhōngshū Lìng Chén Huái (陳淮)
— previously there was Zhōngshū Lìng Chén Zhǔn (陳準) —
"Huái" (淮)
is probably
a mistaken character for "Zhǔn" (準).
Desiring to respond to Yǔn (允),
he spoke to the Emperor, saying:
"It would be advisable to send out the white tiger banner to resolve the conflict."
The white tiger banner was used to command troops forward in battle,
not to resolve conflict.
Chén Zhǔn (陳準) probably, seeing the Emperor was foolish and dim-witted,
requested to use the white tiger banner to command the army.
He wanted Lún (倫)'s troops to see it,
thinking that Yǔn (允)'s attack on Lún (倫)
originated from an imperial command,
and they would then disperse themselves.
Otherwise, how could he respond to Yǔn (允)?
The Sīmǎ Dūhù (司馬督護)
was also a military officer of the Diànzhōng (殿中),
subordinate to the two guards.
He secretly swore to Yìn (胤):
"We shall share wealth and honor."
Yìn (胤) then took out an empty tablet
(an empty tablet was a tablet with no imperial edict written on it; originally there was no imperial edict, but he secretly took an empty tablet with him when he came out).
Yǔn (允) did not notice it,
opened the formation and let him in.
Yǔn (允) dismounted to receive the edict,
whereupon Yìn (胤) killed him,
and also killed Yǔn (允)'s sons, Qín Wáng Yù (秦王郁) and Hàn Wáng Dí (漢王迪).
Thousands were implicated in Yǔn (允)'s (允) downfall and executed.
Luòyáng (洛陽) was pardoned partially.
It means the general amnesty was not extended to the entire realm,
but only to Luòyáng (洛陽),
hence "partial pardon."
Initially,
Sūn Xiù had once served as a minor official,
attending to the Palace Attendant Pān Yuè.
Pān Yuè frequently flogged him.
Sūn Xiù
was from Lángyá.
When Pān Yuè was the Administrator of Lángyá,
Sūn Xiù was a minor official
assigned to Pān Yuè,
being cunning and self-satisfied.
Pān Yuè disliked his character
and repeatedly flogged and humiliated him.
Jiàn's memorial on Lún's crimes
can be seen in the previous volume, Yuánkāng 6th year.
Lǜ Zhū was skilled at playing the flute.
Tàipíng Guǎngjì says: Below the Shuāngjiǎo Mountain in Bái Prefecture, there is now Lǜ Zhū's Well.
In the past, a daughter of the Liáng family was very beautiful.
Shí Chóng sent someone to Jiāozhōu
and bought her with three *hú* of pearls.
At the Liáng family's residence,
the old well still existed,
and those who drew water from it for drinking were sure to give birth to beautiful daughters.
The villagers, thinking that beautiful daughters were of no benefit,
eventually filled it with stones.
Shí Chóng refused to hand her over.
When Huáinán Wáng Yǔn was defeated,
Sūn Xiù then claimed that Shí Chóng, Pān Yuè, and Ōuyáng Jiàn had supported Yǔn in rebellion,
and arrested them.
Kǎoyì says: Shí Chóng's biography states:
"Shí Chóng and Ōuyáng Jiàn secretly knew of his plot
and secretly encouraged Huáinán Wáng Yǔn and Qí Wáng Jiǒng to scheme against Zhào Wáng Lún."
If Shí Chóng had indeed conspired with Yǔn,
when Yǔn was defeated,
Shí Chóng should have been fearful,
and should not have been
feasting in a tower when he was arrested.
It was probably Lún and Sūn Xiù who fabricated charges based on old grudges and killed them.
Now, according to the biography of Shí Chóng:
"Sūn Xiù demanded Lǜ Zhū,
but Shí Chóng refused.
Sūn Xiù became angry
and then advised Lún to execute Shí Chóng.
Shí Chóng was having a feast in his tower
when armed guards arrived at the gate.
Shí Chóng said to Lǜ Zhū: 'I am now in trouble because of you.'
Lǜ Zhū wept and said: 'I shall die for you, my lord.'
Thereupon, she threw herself from the tower and died."
"These slaves are just after my wealth!"
The arresting officer said:
"Knowing that wealth brings disaster,
why did you not distribute it earlier?"
Shí Chóng could not answer.
Initially,
Pān Yuè's mother often rebuked Pān Yuè, saying:
"You should know contentment,
why do you still endlessly pursue gain?"
This was to warn Pān Yuè against seizing the opportunity to seek profit
without knowing when to stop.
Fú Qián said: *gānmò* means to speculate on success or failure.
Rú Chún said: Gaining profit is *gān*,
losing profit is *mò*.
*Gān*
is pronounced *gān*.
Another explanation: using water as a metaphor,
it means that one pursues profit relentlessly,
even if it means being stranded on dry land
or drowning,
none of which is considered.
Pān Yuè apologized to his mother, saying:
"I have failed, Mother."
has the entering tone of *ān*.
Shí Chóng's household was confiscated.
Prime Minister Lún arrested Wú Wáng Yàn, younger brother of the Huáinán Wáng's mother,
intending to kill him.
Grand Master of Brightness Fù Zhī contended for him in the court,
and all the officials advised against it,
so Lún demoted Yàn to the rank of Prince of Bīntú County.
Bīntú County
belonged to Liáoxī Commandery in the Former Hàn dynasty,
to the Liaodong Dependent State Commandant in the Later Hàn dynasty,
and to Chānglí Commandery in the Jìn dynasty.
Qí Wáng Jiǒng was promoted to Cavalry General of Striking Enemies for his merits.
Jìn Zhì says: The Swift Cavalry General and Cavalry General of Striking Enemies
were both miscellaneous generals in the Hàn dynasty,
and were made central army positions in the Wèi dynasty.
In the Jìn dynasty,
the commanders of the guards, protectors, left and right guards, swift cavalry, and cavalry of striking enemies constituted the six armies.
He showed signs of resentment.
Sūn Xiù noticed this,
and also feared his presence within the capital,
so he had him sent out as General Who Pacifies the East,
garrisoned at Xǔchāng.
This laid the groundwork for Jiǒng to raise troops from Xǔchāng to attack Lún.
15 He appointed Grand Master of Brightness Chén Zhǔn as Grand Commandant,
overseeing the affairs of the Department of State Affairs;
not long after,
he passed away.
16 Sūn Xiù proposed granting the Nine Bestowments to Prime Minister Lún,
and no official dared to disagree.
Minister of Personnel Liú Sòng said:
"In the past, the Hàn bestowed them upon Wèi,
and Wèi bestowed them upon Jìn;
these were all expedient measures of their time,
not to be universally applied."
He meant that the Nine Bestowments only occurred before abdication,
not being a regular institution.
Their achievements were immense,
yet there was no mention of the Nine Bestowments being granted.
He meant that Zhōu Bó and Huò Guāng established policies to secure the Hàn imperial house,
yet there was no mention of them receiving the Nine Bestowments,
which was to thwart Lún,
and Sūn Xiù's treacherous scheme.
They considered Sòng to be a partisan of Zhāng Huá
and intended to kill him.
Sūn Xiù said:
"Killing Zhāng and Péi has already damaged public esteem;
we cannot kill Sòng again."
So they stopped.
They appointed Sòng as Grand Master of Brightness.
Jìn Zhì says: Grand Master of Brightness was equivalent to a minister,
with a salary of two thousand *shí* of grain,
wearing a *jìnxián* two-ribboned cap,
a black *jièzé*,
court robes for the five seasons,
and an aquamarine jade pendant.
Kǎoyì says: The Shísānguó Chūnqiū states:
"Lún's faction was furious
and plotted to harm Sòng.
Sòng, in fear,
committed suicide."
Sòng's biography states:
"Sòng served as Grand Master of Brightness,
and soon after died of illness."
We follow the biography here.
They further appointed his son, Fú, as General Who Guards the Army.
The position of General Who Guards the Army
was given by Emperor Wén to Emperor Wǔ,
and subsequently used to replace the Wèi dynasty.
Lún bestowed it upon his heir apparent;
what was his intention?
When Emperor Wǔ accepted the abdication,
he established the General of the Central Army,
who commanded the seven armies of the imperial guard.
This position was soon abolished,
and later re-established.
They also appointed Sūn Xiù as Palace Attendant, General Who Assists the State, and Prime Minister's Military Advisor,
with his position as Right Commander remaining unchanged.
Right Commander
refers to the Right Imperial Guard Commander.
He did not understand this official position,
but wished to control the Eastern Palace's troops.
The Prime Minister's residence troops were increased to 20,000,
the same as the imperial guards.
Including the hidden troops,
the number exceeded 30,000.
In the ninth month,
the Grand Minister of Works was changed to Chancellor,
and Liáng Wáng Róng was appointed to it,
but Róng firmly declined.
Lún and all his sons were dull, vulgar, and ignorant.
Sūn Xiù was cunning, greedy, and lewd.
Those who worked with them
were all wicked and obsequious men,
who only competed for glory and profit,
without foresight or deep strategies.
Their aspirations and interests were divergent,
and they hated each other.
Sūn Xiù's son, Huì, was Colonel of the Archers.
His appearance was short and ugly,
like a lowly servant.
Sūn Xiù had him marry the emperor's daughter, Princess Hédōng.
The histories say that Lún and Sūn Xiù's power was already at its peak,
yet they still plotted for things beyond their reach.
17 In winter,
the eleventh month,
on the *jiǎzǐ* day,
Empress Yáng was enthroned,
and a general amnesty was granted.
The Empress
was the daughter of the Secretariat Gentleman Tàishān Yáng Xuánzhī.
Her maternal grandfather, General Who Pacifies the South Lè'ān Sūn Qí,
was on good terms with Sūn Xiù,
so Sūn Xiù enthroned her.
Yáng Xuánzhī was appointed Grand Master of Brightness, Special Advance, and Palace Regular Attendant,
and enfeoffed as Marquis of Xīngjìn.
Jìn Zhì says: Grand Master of Brightness,
if granted a silver seal and a green ribbon,
was third in rank;
with the addition of Special Advance,
the rank became equivalent to the Left and Right Grand Masters of Brightness.
The Jìn established Xīngjìn Commandery
in the area of Tánghé Prefecture.
18. An imperial edict summoned the Inspector of Yìzhōu, Zhào Xīn, to be Grand Chief Guardian [Dà Chángqiū],
and appointed Gěng Téng of Zhōngshān, Administrator of Chéngdū, as Inspector of Yìzhōu.
In the Jìn dynasty, the kingdoms of the princes established Administrators [Nèishǐ],

In the ninth year of Tàikāng of Emperor Wǔ,
the chancellors of the various princely kingdoms were changed to Administrators.
*Kǎoyì* says: The Imperial Annals [Dìjì] write
"Gěng Shèng",
while the *Zàijì* and *Huáyáng Guózhì* write

We follow the latter now.
[Zhào Xīn] was a relative by marriage of Empress Jiǎ.
When he heard of the summons,
he was very afraid,
fearing that he would be implicated as a relative and partisan of Empress Jiǎ.
He secretly harbored the ambition to seize Shu,
so he opened his granaries,
and distributed relief to the displaced people,
to win the hearts of the masses.
As for Lǐ Tè and his brothers, they were brave and martial,
and their partisans were all people from Bāxī,
the same commandery as Xīn.
Lǐ Tè's partisans were originally Bā Dǐ,
and Zhào Xīn was also from Bāxī.
Lǐ Tè and his group, relying on Xīn's influence,
gathered people and became bandits,
causing trouble for the people of Shǔ.
The matter of Lǐ Tè and his group entering Shǔ
began in the eighth year of Yuánkāng, in the previous volume.
"The displaced people are fierce and aggressive,
while the people of Shǔ are timid and weak.
The hosts cannot control the guests,
which will inevitably lead to disorder.
They should be sent back to their original homes.
If they are kept in a treacherous land,"
Shǔ is a rugged and treacherous land.
The displaced people's original homes were in Qín and Yōng.
Yōng,
is pronounced 'yú yòng'.
The province received the imperial edict,
and sent over a thousand civil and military officials to welcome Téng.
At this time,
the Chéngdū commandery seat was in the Lesser City [Shǎochéng],
and the Yìzhōu provincial seat was in the Greater City [Tàichéng].
Both cities were built by Qín's Zhāng Yí.
After Zhāng Yí built the Greater City,
he built the Lesser City a year later.
The Greater City is today's Chéngdū government's inner city [zǐchéng],
while the Lesser City only has three walls: west, north, and south;
its east is the western wall of the Greater City.
Shǎo,
is pronounced 'shī zhào'.
[Zhào Xīn] had not yet left.
As Téng was about to enter the province, his Administrator of Merit [Gōngcáo], Chén Xún, advised:
"Now the animosity between the province and the commandery
is deepening day by day.
Province refers to Yìzhōu;
Commandery refers to Chéngdū.
This refers to the animosity between Xīn and Téng.
It would be better to remain in the Lesser City to observe the situation,
and issue notices to the various counties to form village strongholds to guard against the Qín Dǐ."
Lǐ Tè and his group were originally Bā Dǐ.
The people of Shǔ, because they migrated to the Qínzhōu border,
called them Qín Dǐ.
"Chén Xīyí [Chén Zǒng],
is about to arrive."
This means Zǒng is coming to take up the post of Commandant of Xīyí,
and is about to reach Chéngdū.
Jìn established the Commandant of Xīyí [Xīyí Xiàowèi] in Wènshān,
the General of Pacifying Yue [Píngyuè Zhōnglángjiàng] in Guǎngzhōu,
the Commandant of the Southern Man [Nánmán Xiàowèi] in Xiāngyáng,
and the Commandant of the Southern Yi [Nányí Xiàowèi] in Níngzhōu.
"Otherwise,"
he continued, "retreat and take refuge in Qiánwéi,
cross the Jiāngyuán river to the west,
to guard against unforeseen events."
Jiāngyuán County,
in Han times, belonged to Shǔ Commandery.
Later, Lǐ Xióng divided it to establish Jiāngyuán Commandery.
Jìn changed it to Duōróng County,
and then to Jìnyuán County.
The three counties of Jìnyuán, Qīngchéng, and Táng'ān in the Tang dynasty's Shǔ Prefecture [Shǔzhōu]
were all territories of the Han dynasty's Jiāngyuán County.
Qián,
is pronounced 'jū yán'.
That day, [Téng] led his forces into the provincial capital.
Xīn sent troops to intercept them,
and they fought at the West Gate.
Téng was defeated and killed.
*Kǎoyì* says: *Huáyáng Guózhì* says:
"They fought at Xuānhuà Pavilion in Guǎnghàn,
and killed the imperial envoy."

Moreover, if Zhào Xīn had already fought with Téng,

We follow the *Zàijì* now.
Only Chén Xún, with his hands bound, went to Xīn,
requesting Téng's burial;

Xīn also sent troops to intercept the Commandant of Xīyí, Chén Zǒng.
When Zǒng reached Jiāngyáng,
Jiāngyáng County,
in Han times, belonged to Qiánwéi Commandery.
Liú Zhāng divided it to establish Jiāngyáng Commandery.
The two counties of Lúchuān and Miánshuǐ in the Tang dynasty's Lú Prefecture [Lúzhōu]
were the territory of the Han dynasty's Jiāngyáng.
His Chief Clerk [Zhǔbù], Zhào Mó of Shǔ Commandery, said:
"Now the province and commandery are not in harmony,

We should rush there quickly.
Your headquarters is a military essential,

This means that Zǒng's Xīyí headquarters was crucial for the Shǔ military.
Righteous refers to Gěng Téng,
and rebellious refers to Zhào Xīn,

Zǒng, however, lingered along the way,
by the time he reached Nán'ān's Yúfú Crossing,
Nán'ān County,
belonged to Qiánwéi Commandery,
and had the Yúfú Crossing.
The Tang dynasty's Qīngshén County in Méi Prefecture [Méizhōu]
was the territory of the Han dynasty's Nán'ān County.
Sòng Bái said: Yìnglíng County and Zīguān County of Róng Prefecture [Róngzhōu], and Lóngyóu of Jiā Prefecture [Jiāzhōu],

Bǐ,
is pronounced 'bì mèi'.
Fú,
has the sound 'fú'.
Mó said to Zǒng:
"Scatter wealth and recruit soldiers to resist the battle.
If we defeat the provincial army,
then the province can be secured."
This means if Xīn's army is defeated, Yìzhōu can be taken,
"and the guilty person will be captured.
If we retreat downstream,
there will certainly be no harm."
This means if they retreat downstream,
Xīn's army would be unable to pursue them,
and there would certainly be no harm.
"[Zhào Xīn], the Inspector of Yìzhōu, resented Lord Gěng,
and therefore killed him.
He has no grievance with us,
why should we act like this!"
With the enemy troops right before him,
he still uttered these words.
Chén Zǒng was truly a mediocre man.
"[Now that the province has started this affair,
they will certainly kill you to establish their authority.
Even if you do not fight,
it will be useless."
His words brought tears to his eyes,
but Zǒng did not listen,
and the troops consequently dispersed.
Zǒng fled into the weeds,
while Mó put on Zǒng's clothes and fought to the death.
Xīn's soldiers killed Mó,
and seeing that it was not Zǒng,

Sōu,
means 'search'.
*Kǎoyì* says: Imperial Annals:
"Xīn also killed the Administrator of Qiánwéi, Lǐ Mì, and the Administrator of Wènshān, Huò Gù."
However, according to *Huáyáng Guózhì*,
the Administrator of Qiánwéi was Lǐ Bì, and the Administrator of Wènshān was Yáng Bīn,
not Mì and Gù.
The *Zàijì* also writes
"Lǐ Bì".
The Annals are likely mistaken.
Xīn (廞) styled himself Grand Chief Controller, Grand General, and Inspector of Yìzhōu (益州).
The Kǎoyì (考異) says: The Jìn Chūnqiū (晉春秋) records
"He adopted the reign title Tàipíng Yuánnián (太平元年),"
but this is not found in other books,
so it is not accepted here.
He replaced the prefects and magistrates.
When royal officials were summoned,
none dared not to go.
"Royal officials"
refers to those appointed by the Jìn (晉) dynasty.
"Bèi (被)"
is pronounced Píyì (皮義).
Four thousand Qíang (氐) cavalrymen, including Fú Chéng (苻成) and Wěi Bó (隗伯), surrendered to Xīn (廞).
Xīn (廞) appointed Xiáng (庠) as General Who Awed the Bandits.
Shěn Yuè’s (沈約) Zhì (志) states: General Who Awed the Bandits
is the seventh of the forty titles.
He entrusted him with vital responsibilities,
and ordered him to recruit brave and strong men from the Six Commanderies, numbering over ten thousand,
to block the northern route.
The "Six Commanderies"
refers to Tianshuǐ (天水), Lüèyáng (略陽), and the other six commanderies.
"Zhuàngyǒng (壯勇)"
refers to the strong and brave among the displaced people.
The "northern route"
is the route from Guānzhōng (關中) into Shǔ (蜀).
"Duàn (斷)"
is pronounced Dīngguǎn (丁管).
Punctuation by Wáng Chóngwǔ (王崇武), re-collated by Róng Zhàozǔ (容肇祖) and Niè Chóngqí (聶崇岐).
Sīmǎ Guāng (司馬光)
compiled it by imperial decree.
Hòu Xué Tiāntái (後學天台)
Xiàohuì Huángdì (孝惠皇帝) Zhōng zhī Shàng (中之上)
Yǒngníng Yuánnián (永寧元年)
(Xīnyǒu (辛酉), 301) This was still Yǒngkāng Èrnián (永康二年);
In the first month, on the day Yǐchǒu (乙丑),
Zhào Wáng Lún (趙王倫) changed the reign title to Jiànshǐ (建始);
In the fourth month,
the Emperor was restored to power,
and then changed the reign title to Yǒngníng (永寧).
1. Spring,
First month.
Zhāng Guǐ (張軌) of Āndìng (安定), a Mounted Regular Attendant, was appointed Inspector of Liángzhōu (涼州).
Guǐ (軌), seeing that the times were full of difficulties,
secretly harbored the ambition to secure Héxī (河西),
and thus requested to be Inspector of Liángzhōu (涼州).
At that time, the provincial borders were plagued by rampant bandits,
and the Xiānbēi (鮮卑) were raiding;
When Guǐ (軌) arrived,
he appointed Sòng Pèi (宋配) and Fàn Yuàn (氾瑗) as strategists,
and thoroughly suppressed and defeated them all,
establishing his prestige in the western lands.
This was the beginning of the Zhāng (張) clan's hold on Liángtǔ (涼土).
Alas!
When the world is in chaos, people think of preserving themselves,
but many who seek self-preservation fail to achieve it.
Dòu Róng (竇融) and Zhāng Guǐ (張軌) seeking to move to Héxī (河西)
are examples of those who sought and achieved self-preservation.
Xiè Huì (謝晦) and Yuán Yǐ (袁顗) seeking to govern Jīng (荊) and Xiāng (襄)
are examples of those who sought but failed to achieve self-preservation.
This is because Dòu Róng (竇融) and Zhāng Guǐ (張軌),
from beginning to end, were single-mindedly loyal to Hàn (漢) and Jìn (晉);
thus, they were indeed destined to enjoy lasting fortune and blessings and pass them down to their descendants.
Xiè Huì (謝晦) and Yuán Yǐ (袁顗),
whose ambition was to occupy strategic territories to preserve themselves,
had the wrong intentions,
and Heaven did not grant them success.
However, Liú Yān (劉焉) seeking to be Inspector of Yìzhōu (益州),
Yuán Shào (袁紹) aiming to control the Jìbù (冀部),
and Shí Jìngtáng (石敬瑭) desiring Hédōng (河東),
all harbored secret, unwarranted ambitions;
as for the eventual success or failure, and the speed thereof,
that was beyond human wisdom and foresight.
2. Grand Chancellor Lún (倫) and Sūn Xiù (孫秀) had the Household Commander Zhào Fèng (趙奉) falsely transmit a divine message from Xuāndì (宣帝), saying:
"Lún (倫) should enter the Western Palace early."
Sīmǎ Yì (司馬懿) was posthumously honored as Emperor Xuān (宣).
At that time, Lún (倫) used the Eastern Palace as his Grand Chancellor's residence,
referring to the Forbidden City as the Western Palace.
He was Sūn Xiù’s (孫秀) grandson,
and had always flattered Lún (倫).
Lún (倫) used Wēi (威) to concurrently serve as a Palace Attendant,
ordering Wēi (威) to threaten and seize the imperial seals and ribbons,
and compose an abdication edict.
He also ordered the President of the Department of State Affairs, Mǎn Fèn (滿奮), to carry the credentials and present the imperial seals and ribbons
for the abdication of the throne to Lún (倫).
The Left Guard General, Wáng Yú (王輿), and the Former Army General, Sīmǎ Yǎ (司馬雅), and others led armored soldiers into the palace hall,
explaining the situation to the three sectional commanders,
showing them the rewards and punishments,
and none dared to disobey.
Zhāng Lín (張林) and others guarded the various gates.
They guarded the various gates of the palace city.
On Yǐchǒu (乙丑),
Lún (倫), fully equipped with the imperial carriage, entered the palace,
and ascended the imperial throne.
The Kǎoyì (考異) says: The Sānshí Guó Chūnqiū (三十國春秋) records:
"When Lún (倫) was about to usurp the throne,
Yìyáng Wáng Wēi (義陽王威) held the edict and showed it to Jī Shào (嵇紹), saying:
'The Sage Emperor is following the example of Yáo (堯) and Shùn (舜),
will you comply?'
Shào (紹) said in a stern voice: 'There is only death,
I will never serve two!'
Wēi (威) was enraged,
drew his sword and left.
When Huìdì (惠帝) was moved to Jīnyǒng Chéng (金墉城),
only Shào (紹) firmly refused to follow,
going straight to Jīnyǒng (金墉),
absolutely refusing to communicate with Lún (倫).
Everyone at the time feared for him."
The Jìn Shū (晉書) 'Biography of the Loyal and Righteous' states:
"When Lún (倫) usurped the throne,
Shào (紹) was a Palace Attendant.
When Huìdì (惠帝) was restored to the throne,
he resumed his post."
These two accounts differ,
so neither is adopted here.
The character
"zuò (祚)" in
"Fùzuò (復祚)"
should be
"zòu (阼)".
The reign title was changed to Jiànshǐ (建始).
The Emperor departed from the Western Gate of Huálín (華林) to reside in Jīnyǒng Chéng (金墉城).
The Western Gate of Huálín (華林)
is the Western Gate of Huálín Yuán (華林園).
On the day *bǐng-yín*,
the Emperor was honored as *Tàishàng Huáng* (Retired Emperor).
Jīnyǒng was renamed Yǒngchāng Palace.
The Imperial Grandson was demoted to King of Púyáng.
The heir apparent, Huá, was made Crown Prince.
His son Fù was enfeoffed as King of Jīngzhào.
Qián was enfeoffed as King of Guǎngpíng.
Xǔ was enfeoffed as King of Bàchéng.
All served as *Shìzhōng* and commanded troops.
Liáng Wáng Róng was appointed *Zǎihéng*.
Hé Shào was appointed *Tàizǎi*.
Sūn Xiù was appointed *Shìzhōng*, *Zhōngshū Jiān*, *Piàojì Jiāngjūn*, and *Yítóng Sānsī*.
Yìyáng Wáng Wēi was appointed *Zhōngshū Lìng*.
Zhāng Lín was appointed *Wèijiāngjūn*.
The rest of their faction and associates
were all appointed *Qīng* and *Jiàng*.
*Qīng* and *Jiàng*
refers to the *Lièqīng* and various *Zhōnglángjiàng*.
*Jiàng*
is pronounced *liàng*.
They were too numerous to count;
even slaves and common soldiers
were granted titles and ranks.
At every court assembly,
*diāochán* (sable cicada decorations) filled the seats.
*Wǔguān* (military cap),
also called *Wǔbiàn*,
was worn by all military officials.
*Shìzhōng* and *Zhōngchángshì* also wore golden pendants.
Attached cicadas were used as ornamentation,
and sable tails as decoration.
This was called
the "Zhào Huìwén Crown."
Hú Guǎng explained: Zhào Wǔlíng Wáng adopted Hú attire,
adorned his head with golden pendants,
and inserted a sable tail at the front,
signifying a high-ranking position.
Qín extinguished Zhào
and bestowed this crown upon its close ministers.
Yīng Shào's *Hàn Guān* says: Interpreters believe that gold represents strength and hardness,
unconsumed by a hundred refinements;
the cicada dwells high and drinks pure (dew),
with its mouth under its armpit;
the sable is fierce and strong internally yet warm and soft externally.
These are meanings derived from the objects themselves.
Xú Guǎng said: Zhào Wǔlíng Wáng's Hú attire included this,
and Qín and Hàn adopted and used it.
Interpreters took the cicada for its lofty purity, drinking dew without eating,
and the sable for its purple-blue luster and unobtrusive fur color.
Hence, it was chosen for its symbolism.
Hú Guǎng further said: It is thought that because the north was cold,
sable fur was originally used to warm the forehead,
attached to the cap,
and thus gradually transformed into a head ornament.
Shěn Yuē said: The explanation of the *diāochán*
derives meaning from objects,
but this is not its true origin.
Its true origin is that Zhào Wǔlíng Wáng adopted Hú attire;
when Qín extinguished Zhào,
it bestowed the ruler's crown upon its *shìchén*.
Therefore, since Qín and Hàn,
*shìchén* have worn *diāochán*.
*Cháo*
is pronounced *zhí-yáo*.
"If sable is insufficient,
a dog's tail will serve to continue it."
The *Shǐjì* says: Although a fox fur robe is worn out,
it cannot be patched with yellow dog skin.
This expresses the same meaning.
All *xiánliáng*, *xiùcái*, and *xiàolián* nominated from throughout the empire were appointed without examination.
The old system stipulated that
*xiánliáng*, *xiùcái*, and *xiàolián* all had to undergo policy examinations before being appointed to office.
All *shǒulìng* who were in office on the day of the amnesty were enfeoffed as *Hóu*.
The *gāngjì* of the commanderies were all made *xiàolián*,
and the *gāngjì* of the counties were all made *liánlì*.
*Jùn gāngjì*
refers to the *Gōngcáo* and their subordinates;
*xiàn gāngjì*
refers to the *Zhǔbù*, *Lùshìshǐ* and their subordinates.
*Liánlì*
was also one of the categories for selection.
The historian states that Lún and Xiù sought to win public support through indiscriminate favors.
There was not enough to provide for gifts.
So many people were to be enfeoffed as *Hóu*
that there weren't enough seals to cast,
and some were enfeoffed with plain wooden tablets.
Originally,
the sons Bì, and nephews Máo, Fǔ, and Yǎn of the *Píngnán Jiāngjūn* Sūn Qí, all attached themselves to Sūn Xiù,
intermarrying with his clan,
and within a month, achieved prominent positions.
When Lún proclaimed himself Emperor,
the four sons all became generals
and were enfeoffed as commandery *Hóu*.
Qí was appointed *Chēqí Jiāngjūn* and granted *kāifǔ* status.
Qí believed that Bì and the others receiving Lún's official titles excessively
would surely bring disaster to the family.
He sent his youngest son, Huí, to reprimand them,
but Bì and the others did not comply.
Qí could not control them
and only wept bitterly.
According to the *Jìn Shū*,
Sūn Qí's four sons
were all known in their time for their administrative talent.
Attaching themselves to the wrong person
led to the extermination of their clan.
It is indeed difficult to choose wisely.
However, Sūn Qí had previously been close to Sūn Xiù,
which is why his sons followed and attached themselves to him.
If one does not choose one's friends carefully,
how can one properly guide one's sons!
Although he wept bitterly,
it was of no avail.
Qí was indeed responsible for the calamity of the Sūn clan.
On the day *guǐ-yǒu*,
Púyáng Āi Wáng Zāng was killed.
Sūn Xiù monopolized court affairs.
Lún's issued edicts
were often altered, granted, or revoked by Xiù.
He personally wrote edicts on green paper.
Sometimes, they were issued in the morning and changed in the evening,
and officials were replaced as swiftly as flowing water.
Zhāng Lín had always been incompatible with Xiù,
and also resented not being granted *kāifǔ* status.
He secretly sent a memorial to Crown Prince Huá,
saying:
"Xiù's monopolization of power does not align with the public sentiment,
and the meritorious officials are all petty men
who are disrupting the court.
They should all be executed."
Huá showed the letter to Lún.
Lún showed it to Xiù.
Xiù advised Lún to arrest Lín,
kill him,
and exterminate his three clans.
Xiù was wary of Qí Wáng Jiǒng, Chéngdū Wáng Yǐng, and Héjiān Wáng Yǒng,
each commanding strong armies
and holding sway over their respective regions.
Jiǒng was garrisoned at Xǔchāng,
Yǐng at Yè,
and Yǒng at Guānzhōng.
is pronounced *wū-lù*.
*Yǒng*
is pronounced *yú-róng*.
He promoted Jiǒng to *Zhèndōng Dàjiāngjūn* and Yǐng to *Zhēngběi Dàjiāngjūn*,
all with *kāifǔ yítóng sānsī* status,
to appease and pacify them with favor.
Lǐ Xiáng was valiant and courageous and had won the hearts of the people.
Zhào Xīn gradually grew jealous of him but had not yet spoken of it.
The *Chángshǐ* Dù Shú and Zhāng Càn of Shǔjùn advised Xīn, saying:
"The general has only just raised troops,
and already you have sent Lǐ Xiáng to command strong forces outside.
This refers to Xīn sending Xiáng to recruit brave men to cut off the northern road.
*Shuō*
is pronounced *shū-ruì*.
His intentions will surely be different.
This is turning weapons against oneself and handing them over to others.
You should deal with him early."
Just then, Xiáng urged Xīn to assume the imperial title.
Shú and Càn then informed Xīn that Xiáng was committing great treason and was unrighteous.
They had him brought out and executed,
along with over ten of his sons and nephews.
*Kǎoyì* says: The *Zàijì* states:
"And his sons, nephews, and clan members, over thirty people."
We now follow the *Huáyáng Guózhì*.
Also, the *Guózhì* states that
Xiáng died in the winter of last year,
while the *Jìn Chūnqiū* states it was in the spring of this year.
We now follow the latter.
Xīn sent someone to console them, saying:
"Xiáng said what he should not have said,
and his crime deserved death.
The brothers' crimes are not connected to each other."
He then appointed Tè and Liú as *Dūjiàng*.
Tè and Liú resented Xīn
and led their troops back to [text missing].
Xīn's *Yámén Jiāng*, Xǔ Yǎn of Fúlíng, requested to be *Bādōng Jiānjūn*.
Fúlíng County
belonged to Bā Commandery during the Hàn dynasty;
Shǔ divided it into Fúlíng Commandery.
*Fú*
is pronounced *fú*.
*Jiān*
is pronounced *gōng-xián*.
Yǎn, enraged,
personally killed Shú and Càn below Xīn's chambers.
Shú and Càn's attendants then killed Yǎn.
These three
were all Xīn's trusted confidants.
Xīn's power consequently declined.
With his trusted confidants dead,
Xīn had no one to rely on,
and thus his influence waned.
Zhào Xīn sent his Grand Secretary, Fèi Yuǎn of Qiánwéi,
the Administrator of Shǔjùn, Lǐ Bì, and the Supervising Commandant, Cháng Jùn, leading over ten thousand men to block the northern road,
encamping at Shízhuíting.
Lǐ Tè secretly gathered over seven thousand men,
and at night attacked Yuǎn's army,
burning it.
Eight or nine tenths of them died.
Then he advanced to attack Chéngdū.
Fèi Yuǎn, Lǐ Bì, and the army's
Libationer, Zhāng Wēi,
broke through the gate and fled during the night.
All the civil and military officials dispersed.
Xīn alone, with his wife,
escaped on a small boat.
When they reached Guǎngdū,
they were killed by their followers.
Tè entered Chéngdū,
letting his soldiers loot extensively.
He sent envoys to Luòyáng
to report Xīn's crimes.
Earlier,
the Inspector of Liángzhōu, Luó Shàng,
hearing that Zhào Xīn had rebelled,
submitted a memorial stating:
"Xīn is not a heroic talent,
and the people of Shǔ do not support him.
His defeat and demise can be counted day by day and awaited."
An imperial edict appointed Shàng as General Who Pacifies the West and Inspector of Yìzhōu,
supervising the Gate Commandant Wáng Dūn.
(This is a different Wáng Dūn.)
Tè and others, hearing of Shàng's arrival,
were very afraid.
They sent his younger brother Xiáng to greet him on the road,
and offered him treasures.
Shàng was pleased
and made Xiáng a Cavalry Commandant.
Tè and the migrants again offered wine and cattle to entertain Shàng at Shízhuí.
Wáng Dūn and Xīn Rǎn advised Shàng, saying:
"Tè and his group are pure bandits.
We should take advantage of this meeting to execute them;
otherwise,
they will surely become a future problem."
Shàng did not comply.
Rǎn had an old acquaintance with Tè
and said to Tè:
"Old friends meeting under these circumstances, it is not auspicious but rather ill-omened."
Tè became deeply suspicious and fearful.
In the third month,
Shàng arrived in Chéngdū.
The Qiāng of Wénshān rebelled.
Shàng sent Wáng Dūn to suppress them,
but he was killed by the Qiāng.
5 Qí Wáng Jiǒng planned to attack Zhào Wáng Lún.
Before he acted,
Líhú Wáng Shèng
(Líhú county,
in the Former Hàn belonged to Dōngjùn,
in the Later Hàn and Jìn belonged to Jìyīn Commandery.
In the first year of Tiānbǎo of the Táng dynasty,
it was renamed Nánhuá county,
belonging to Yùnzhōu.)
The Jìn Shū records
"Wáng Chǔmù."
[Chapter: In the Kǒng edition,
above "Chǔ"
there is exactly the character
"Wáng";
Zhāng's collation agrees.]
Zhuózé was in Chángshè county of Yǐngchuān.
The daily count was in the tens of thousands.
Lún appointed his general Guǎn Xí as the Qí Wáng's Army Administrator
to attack Shèng and Mù,
and executed them.
Jiǒng then arrested Xí
and killed him.
(The Kǎo Yì says: The biography of Qí Wáng Jiǒng states:
"Jiǒng secretly plotted with Shèng and Mù to raise troops to execute Lún.
Before they acted,
fearing the matter would be leaked,
he and Xí killed Mù
and sent his head to Lún
to appease him.")
(We now follow the Sānshí Guó Chūnqiū.)
He sent envoys to inform Chéngdū Wáng Yǐng, Héjiān Wáng Yóng, Chángshān Wáng Yì, and the Southern Central Leader, Xīnyě Gōng Xīn.
(The Jìn Zhì says: The Four Central Leaders
were all established in the Later Hàn;
since Wǔ Dì,
the Four Central Leaders sometimes also held the position of Inspector
or were appointed with a Staff of Authority.)
(Xīn
was the son of Fúfēng Wáng Jùn.)
He issued a proclamation to the expeditionary and garrison generals
(the Four Expeditionary and Four Garrison Generals,
those who held positions in various regions),
saying: "The rebellious minister Sūn Xiù
has misled Zhào Wáng.
We should jointly punish him.
Anyone who disobeys
will have their three familial relations exterminated."
The envoy arrived in Yè.
Chéngdū Wáng Yǐng summoned the Prefect of Yè, Lú Zhì, to consult.
Zhì said:
"Zhào Wáng has usurped the throne,
and both gods and men are indignant.
If Your Highness gathers heroes to meet the people's aspirations,
and relies on the great righteousness to punish him,
the common people will certainly come without being summoned,
rolling up their sleeves and eagerly advancing.
There will be nothing you cannot achieve."
("Miè"
means "without.")
Yǐng appointed Zhì as Consultative Army Administrator.
(Consultative Army Administrators were established in all Jìn Ducal residences,
presumably to consult on military matters;
their rank was above other Army Administrators.)
(Zhì
was the grandson of Yù.)
(Lú Yù is mentioned in Volume 73, during the first year of Jǐngchū of Wèi Míng Dì.)
Distant and near responded.
When he reached Cháogē,
(Cháogē county,
in the Former Hàn belonged to Hénèi Commandery,
in the Jìn it was separated and belonged to Jí Commandery.
In the second year of Dàyè of the Suí dynasty,
Cháogē county was renamed Wèi county,
belonging to Wèizhōu.
There was Cháogē city, the capital of Zhòu,
west of the county seat.)
Chāo
was the grandson of Bāo.
Shí Bāo served Wén Dì and Wǔ Dì,
and his achievements were comparable to those who assisted in founding the dynasty.
Chángshān Wáng Yì was in his state.
He and the Grand Administrator of Tàiyuán, Liú Tūn, each led their forces to support Yǐng.
Xīnyě Gōng Xīn received Jiǒng's檄文,
but did not know which side to take.
His favored attendant Wáng Suí said:
"Zhào is close and strong,
while Qí is distant and weak."
(Xīn's father, Fúfēng Wáng Jùn,
and Zhào Wáng Lún were both sons of Xuān Dì.
Xīn was Lún's nephew,
making him a close relative.
Jiǒng was Xīn's cousin,
making him a distant relative compared to Lún.)
("Bì"
is pronounced bēi yì,
also bó jì.)
Army Administrator Sūn Xún loudly declared to the multitude:
"Zhào Wáng is a凶逆,
and the world should jointly punish him.
What does closeness, distance, strength, or weakness have to do with it!"
Xīn then sided with Jiǒng.
The former Anxi Army Administrator Xiàhóu Shì was in Shǐpíng.
He gathered several thousand men to support Jiǒng,
and sent an envoy to invite Héjiān Wáng Yóng.
Yóng followed the advice of his Grand Secretary Lǐ
Hán
and sent General Who Manifests Martial Might Zhāng Fāng of Héjiān to attack and capture Shì and his partisans,
cutting them in half at the waist.
(Shěn Yuè Zhì says: The title General Who Manifests Martial Might
began at the end of the Western Hàn,
when Wáng Mǎng bestowed it upon Wáng Kuàng.)
Yóng arrested Jiǒng's envoy and sent him to Lún,
and dispatched Zhāng Fāng to lead troops to assist Lún.
When Fāng reached Huáyīn,
Yóng heard that the armies of the Two Kings were strong,
so he recalled Fāng
and changed his allegiance to the Two Kings.
(The Two Kings refer to Qí Wáng Jiǒng
and Chéngdū Wáng Yǐng.)
When Jǐǒng’s
summons reached Yángzhōu, everyone in the province wished to respond to Jǐǒng.
The Inspector, Xī Lóng,
a great-grandson of Lǜ,
because his elder brother’s son Jiàn and all his own sons were in Luòyáng,
was hesitant and undecided.
He summoned all his subordinates to deliberate.
Zhǔbù Zhào Yòu of Huáinán and former Xiùcái Yú Tán both said:
“King Zhào has usurped the throne in rebellion,
which the whole realm detests.
Now righteous armies are rising everywhere,
and his defeat is certain.
For the sake of a clear plan for you, our Lord Inspector,
there is no better course than to personally lead elite troops
directly to Xǔchāng.
This is the best strategy.
King Qí Jǐǒng was at that time stationed in Xǔchāng.
The middle strategy
is to dispatch a small force
to adapt to the situation and assist in victory.
The lowest strategy is to do nothing.”
Lóng withdrew
and secretly consulted with Biéjià Gù Yàn.
Yàn said:
“What Yòu and others call the lowest strategy
is in fact the best plan.”
Zhìzhōng Liú Bǎo, Zhǔbù Zhāng Bāo, and Xīcáo Liú Chéng heard of this
and requested an audience,
saying:
“We are unsure what our discerning Lord Inspector intends to do now.”
Lóng said:
“I have received the favor of two emperors.
The two emperors
refer to Emperor Xuān and Emperor Wǔ.
Some say: The two emperors
refer to Emperor Huì and King Zhào Lún,
which is incorrect.
I only wish to defend the province.”
