we follow the biography of Qí Wáng Jiǒng here.
Chéngdū Wáng Yǐng reached Yè.
An imperial edict dispatched an envoy to repeat the previous command.
Yǐng accepted the title of Dà Jiāngjūn [Grand General],
but declined the exceptional honors of the Jiǔ Xí [Nine Bestowals].
He submitted a memorial discussing meritorious officials who had initiated the righteous cause,
all of whom were enfeoffed as dukes or marquises.
Yǐng also memorialized to enfeoff Lú Zhì, Hé Yǎn, Dǒng Hóng, Wáng Yàn, Zhào Xiāng, and others.
"The Dà Sīmǎ [Grand Marshal] was previously in Yángdí,
facing the bandits for a long time.
The common people are exhausted and impoverished.
We request the transfer of 150,000 hù of rice from the storehouses north of the river,
to relieve the starving people of Yángdí."
He had over 8,000 coffins made,
used the salary of the state of Chéngdū for clothing,
collected and sacrificed to the warriors who died at Huángqiáo,
glorified their families,
and added two extra ranks to the regular deceased in battle.
He also ordered the burial of over 14,000 warriors who died in Zhào Wáng Lún's battle in Wēn Xiàn.
This was the Battle of Jùshuǐ.
Wēn Xiàn belonged to Hénèi Jùn.
It was the state of Zhōu Sīkòu Sū Fènshēng.
Yì,
sounds like "yú jì fān."
Yǐng was beautiful in appearance but dull in spirit,
and unlearned.
However, his character was earnest and generous.
He entrusted affairs to Zhì,
and thus achieved his success.
An imperial edict again dispatched an envoy to inform Yǐng to enter and assist the government,
and to also accept the Jiǔ Xí.
Yǐng's favorite, Mèng Jiǔ, did not wish to return to Luò,
and
Chéng Tài was overly attached to Yè Dū,
so Yǐng ultimately declined and did not accept.
Earlier, Dà Sīmǎ Jiǒng suspected Zhōngshū Láng Lù Jī of drafting the abdication edict for Zhào Wáng Lún.
He arrested him,
intending to kill him.
Dà Jiāngjūn Yǐng defended him,
allowing him to escape death.
Consequently, he memorialized to appoint him Píngyuán Nèishǐ [Administrator of Píngyuán],
and his younger brother Yún as Qīnghé Nèishǐ [Administrator of Qīnghé].
Jī's friends Gù Róng and Guǎnglíng Dài Yuān,
seeing that Zhōngguó was beset by many difficulties,
advised Jī to return to Wú.
Jī, however, felt indebted to Yǐng for saving his life,
and also believed Yǐng possessed influence and prestige
with whom he could achieve great deeds,
so he remained and did not leave.
This set the stage for Lù Jī and Lù Yún to be killed by Yǐng.
13 In autumn,
in the seventh month,
Chángshān Wáng Yì was again enfeoffed as Chángshā Wáng.
In the tenth year of Tàikāng of Wǔ Dì,
Yì was enfeoffed as Chángshā Wáng.
When Chǔ Wáng Wěi was executed,
Yì was demoted to Chángshān Wáng for being of the same mother.
Now, his former enfeoffment was restored.
14 Dōnglái Wáng Ruí
was violent and fond of drinking,
repeatedly insulting Dà Sīmǎ Jiǒng.
He also resented Jiǒng for denying his request to establish a government office.
He secretly memorialized that Jiǒng was monopolizing power
and conspired with Zuǒ Wèi Jiāngjūn Wáng Yú to depose Jiǒng.
The plot was discovered.
In the eighth month,
an imperial edict deposed Ruí as a commoner,
executed Yú and his three clans,
and exiled Ruí to Shàngyōng.
Shàngyōng Nèishǐ Chén Zhōng secretly killed him under Jiǒng's instruction.
Kǎo Yì says: In Dì Jì:
"In the sixth month, on the day Gēngwǔ,
Ruí conspired with Wáng Yú to depose Jiǒng.
The plot was discovered, and he was punished.
On the day Jiǎxū,
Jiǒng became Dà Sīmǎ."
According to the edict executing Yú, Jiǒng was already referred to as Dà Sīmǎ.
Therefore, the discovery of Yú's plot should not have occurred before Jiǒng became Dà Sīmǎ.
We now follow the Sānshí Guó Chūnqiū, placing it in the eighth month.
15 A general amnesty was proclaimed throughout the empire.
16 Dōngwǔ Gōng Dàn was exiled to Liáodōng for filial impiety.
In the ninth month,
his younger brother Dōng'ān Wáng Yáo was summoned back and his former noble title restored.
Yáo's deposition and exile can be seen in volume 82, Yuánkāng first year.
Yáo recommended Dōngpíng Wáng Máo as
Dūdū Xúzhōu Zhū Jūnshì [Supervisor of Military Affairs of Xú Province],
stationed in Xiàpī.
Kǎo Yì says: In Dì Jì:
"In the eighth month,
Máo was appointed Píngdōng [General who Pacifies the East] and supervised Xú Province.
In the ninth month,
Yáo's title was restored."
According to Máo's biography,
"Yáo was Púyè [Director of the Imperial Secretariat] and recommended Máo as Píngdōng."
Therefore, it is moved to after Yáo's return.
17 Initially,
the imperial court issued a decree to Qín and Yōng Provinces,
ordering the recall of refugees who had entered Shǔ,
and also dispatched imperial censors Féng Gāi and Zhāng Chāng to supervise this.
Lǐ Tè's elder brother, Fǔ, arrived in Shǔ from Luèyáng,
saying that Zhōngguó was about to fall into chaos
and it was not worthwhile to return.
Tè agreed with this,
and repeatedly sent Yán Shì of Tiānshuǐ to Luó Shàng to request a temporary halt.
By autumn,
he also bribed Shàng and Féng Gāi.
Shàng and Gāi assented.
The imperial court discussed the merits of suppressing Zhào Yìn,
appointing Tè as Xuānwēi Jiāngjūn [General who Spreads Awe],
and his younger brother Liú as Fènwǔ Jiāngjūn [General who Excites Martial Prowess],
all enfeoffed as marquises.
A sealed imperial edict was sent to Yì Province,
listing the refugees from the six commanderies who had joined Tè in suppressing Yìn,
intending to bestow titles and rewards upon them.
Guǎnghàn Tàishǒu Xīn Rǎn wanted to claim the credit for suppressing Yìn as his own achievement,
so he suppressed the imperial order,
suppressing the order to enfeoff Tè and Liú.
Xià,
sounds like "xiá jià fān."
Cháo,
sounds like "zhí yáo fān."
Those listed
were not truthfully reported.
Shàng,
sounds like "shí zhǎng fān";
the same below.
They were the multitudes from the six commanderies.
Luó Shàng sent an aide to supervise the dispatch of the refugees,
setting a deadline of the seventh month to set off.
At that time, the refugees were scattered across Liáng and Yì,
working as hired labor.
Hearing that the provinces and commanderies were pressing them to leave,
everyone was distressed and resentful,
not knowing what to do.
Moreover, the floods were rampant,
the harvest had not yet come in,
and they had no funds for travel.
Tè again sent Yán Shì to Shàng,
requesting a halt until winter.
Xīn Rǎn and Jiànwéi Tàishǒu Lǐ Bì deemed this unacceptable.
Shàng appointed Bìejià Dù
Tāo as Xiùcái [Filial and Incorrupt].
Shì explained to Tāo the benefits and harms of forced relocation.
Tāo also wanted to grant the refugees a year of respite.
Shàng, however, followed Rǎn and Bì's counsel
and did not agree.
Tāo then resigned his Xiùcái position
and returned home.
Sòng zhì wèi zhì.
Desiring to kill the refugee leaders
and seize their wealth,
Rǎn then reported to Shàng with Bì,
saying:
"The refugees, due to Zhào Yìn's rebellion,
engaged in much plundering.
It is advisable to set up checkpoints during their relocation to seize their possessions."
Shàng wrote to Zìtóng Tàishǒu Zhāng Yǎn,
to set up checkpoints at all important passes
to search for treasures.
The Liú clan of Shǔ divided Guǎnghàn to establish Zìtóng Commandery.
Zhū yào zhě means
all places through which roads passed, which were critical hubs for movement.
Shī guān zhě means
no checkpoints had been established before, but now they were specially set up.
Tè repeatedly pleaded for the refugees to stay.
The refugees all felt grateful and relied on him,
many rallying to him.
Tè then established a large camp at Miánzhú to house the refugees,
and sent a message to Xīn Rǎn to request clemency for himself.
Rǎn was furious
and sent people to post notices on main streets,
offering rewards for Tè and his brothers,
promising lavish prizes.
Tè saw these,
collected them all,
and with his brother Xiāng, altered the rewards to say:
"For delivering one head of any chieftain
among the Háo Lǐ, Rèn, Yán, Zhào, Shàngguān
of the six commanderies, or a Di or Sǒu king,
a reward of 100 bolts of silk will be given."
The Shǔ Sǒu were a distinct group.
Qiú,
sounds like "cí yóu fān."
Rèn,
sounds like "rén."
Those who rallied to Tè became even more numerous,
exceeding 20,000 within ten days to a month.
Liú also gathered several thousand people.
Tè (李特) again sent Yán Shì (閻式) to go to Luó Shàng (羅尚) to request an extension of the deadline.
"Shēn" (申)
means "double" or "repeated."
He sought a repeated establishment of the deadline,
so that the displaced people could relax themselves.
(Yán Shì (閻式)) plotted to conceal the displaced people,
and sighed, saying:
"The people's hearts are currently in danger;
if we rush them now,
rebellion will arise."
He also knew that the intentions of Xīn Rǎn (辛冉) and Lǐ Bì (李苾) could not be changed,
so he declined Shàng (尚) and returned to Bó (帛).
Shàng (尚) said to Shì (式):
"You should tell my intention to all the displaced people:
now, permission for extension has been granted."
Shì (式) said:
"My Lord (Mínggōng 明公) is deluded by treacherous words;
I fear there will be no actual extension.
The weak who cannot be underestimated are the people.
Now, to rush them without reason,
the anger of the multitude is difficult to offend."
(This is) a quote from Zhèng Zǐchǎn (鄭子產) in the Zuǒzhuàn (左傳).
Shàng (尚) said:
"Indeed.
I will not deceive you.
You may go!"
Shì (式) arrived at Bó (帛)
and said to Tè (特):
"Although Shàng (尚) said so,
it is not yet credible.
Why?
Shàng's (尚) authority and punishments are not established;
Rǎn (冉) and others each command strong armies.
If they suddenly turn treacherous,
it will not be within Shàng's (尚) control.
It is deeply advisable to prepare."
Tè (特) followed his advice.
Yán Shì (閻式) had already secretly observed the situation of Rǎn (冉) and the others.
In the tenth month,
Tè (特) divided his forces into two camps:
Tè (特) resided in the northern camp,
Liú (流) in the eastern camp.
They repaired their armor, sharpened their weapons,
and prepared for battle to await them.
Rǎn (冉) and Bì (苾) consulted with each other, saying:
"Lord Luó (Luó Hóu 羅侯) is greedy and indecisive.
Day after day,
he allows the displaced people to develop their treacherous schemes.
Lǐ Tè (李特) and his brothers all possess heroic talent;
we will soon be captured by them!
It is appropriate to make a decisive plan."
They wanted to settle it with a single battle.
So they dispatched Guǎnghàn (廣漢) Commander Zēng Yuán (曾元), Colonel (Yámén 牙門) Zhāng Xiǎn (張顯), Liú Bìng (劉並), and others to secretly lead thirty thousand infantry and cavalry to attack Tè's (特) camp.
Luó Shàng (羅尚), hearing of this,
also sent Supervisor Tián Zuǒ (田佐) to assist Yuán (元).
When Yuán (元) and the others arrived,
Tè (特) lay peacefully and did not move.
He waited until half of their forces had entered,
then launched his ambush to strike them,
and the dead were very numerous.
They killed Tián Zuǒ (田佐), Zēng Yuán (曾元), and Zhāng Xiǎn (張顯),
and sent their heads to show Shàng (尚) and Rǎn (冉).
Shàng (尚) said to his generals and staff:
"These barbarians have now departed!"
(This means) that although Tè (特) requested an extension of the deadline,
his plan to leave had already been made.
Xīn Rǎn (辛冉) was the Administrator (Tàishǒu 太守) of Guǎnghàn (廣漢),
hence he is referred to as such.
Shàng (尚) meant that Rǎn (冉) had recklessly used his troops,
and was defeated by Tè (特),
causing Tè's (特) power to increase even more.
Zhāng (張)
is pronounced as "zhī liàng" (知亮).
Thereupon, the displaced people of the six commanderies
jointly acclaimed Tè (特) as Acting General-in-chief Who Guards the North (Xíng Zhènběi Dàjiāngjūn 行鎮北大將軍),
and he was granted the authority to confer titles and appointments.
He appointed his younger brother Liú (流) as Acting General-in-chief Who Guards the East (Xíng Zhèndōng Dàjiāngjūn 行鎮東大將軍),
styling him as Eastern Supervisor (Dōng Dūhù 東督護),
to oversee and command.
He also appointed his elder brother Fǔ (輔) as General of Agile Cavalry (Piàojì Jiāngjūn 驃騎將軍),
and his younger brother Xiāng (驤) as General of Valiant Cavalry (Xiāojì Jiāngjūn 驍騎將軍).
They advanced their troops to attack Rǎn (冉) in Guǎnghàn (廣漢).
Guǎnghàn (廣漢) Commandery (Jùn 郡) had its seat in Guǎnghàn (廣漢) County (Xiàn 縣).
Later, during the Sòng (宋) dynasty, Suìníng (遂寧) Commandery was established.
During the Qí (齊) and Liáng (梁) dynasties,
the character
"Dōng" (東) was added.
Later, the Wèi (魏) dynasty changed Guǎnghàn (廣漢) County to Fāngyì (方義) County.
Later, the Zhōu (周) dynasty changed Dōngsuìníng (東遂寧) to Suìzhōu (遂州),
and Fāngyì (方義) became the seat of Suìzhōu (遂州).
(Rǎn (冉)), fearing Tè (特),
dared not advance.
Rǎn (冉) engaged in battle repeatedly and was defeated.
He broke through the encirclement and fled to Déyáng (德陽).
Déyáng (德陽) County
was established during the Later Hàn (後漢) dynasty,
belonging to Guǎnghàn (廣漢) Commandery.
By the Táng (唐) dynasty,
it belonged to Jiànzhōu (劍州).
(Tè (特)) appointed Lǐ Chāo (李超) as Administrator (Tàishǒu 太守),
and advanced his troops to attack Shàng (尚) in Chéngdū (成都).
Shàng (尚) sent a letter to Yán Shì (閻式),
and Shì (式) replied:
"Xīn Rǎn (辛冉) is cunning and sly;
Zēng Yuán (曾元) is a petty fellow;
Lǐ Shūpíng (李叔平) is not a talent for a general or commander.
Lǐ Bì (李苾),
courtesy name Shūpíng (叔平).
Jiàng (將)
is pronounced as "jí liàng" (即亮).
Shuài (帥)
is pronounced as "suǒ lèi" (所類).
Jin (晉) people referred to a general or commander who exclusively governed a region as 'Jiéxià' (節下).
Dù Tāo (杜弢),
courtesy name Jǐngwén (景文).
Wéi (為)
is pronounced as "yú wěi" (于偽).
Sāngzǐ (桑梓) refers to the mulberry and catalpa trees planted by grandparents for their descendants;
therefore,
those who cherish their homeland are said to 'cherish their sāngzǐ (桑梓)'.
However, in earlier days when we first arrived,
we worked for hire to find food.
This refers to the time when the displaced people first arrived in Shǔ (蜀),
unable to support themselves,
they went wherever there was food,
working for others as hired labor.
Lìn (賃)
is pronounced as "nǚ jìn" (女禁),
also meaning 'to hire'.
Then, coinciding with the autumn floods,
we begged for an extension until the winter harvest,
but were ultimately not heard.
The coercion was too excessive,
a desperate deer will turn and fight a tiger.
The displaced people were unwilling to extend their necks for the blade,
thus leading to this change.
If (you had) listened to Shì's (式) words,
and granted them an extension to prepare their provisions,
Jí (即)
means "accomplished" or "completed".
Zhìyán (治嚴)
means "to prepare one's luggage".
Zhì (治)
is pronounced as "zhí zhī" (直之).
That which has passed is 'qù' (去).
And let them reach their hometowns,
how could things have come to this!"

Tè (特) appointed his elder brother Fǔ (輔), younger brother Xiāng (驤), sons Shǐ (始), Dàng (蕩), Xióng (雄), as well as Lǐ Hán (李含), Hán's (含) sons Guó (國) and Lí (離), Rèn Huí (任回), Lǐ Pān (李攀), Pān's (攀) younger brother Gōng (恭), Shàngguān Jīng (上官晶), Rèn Zàng (任臧), Yáng Bāo (楊褒), Shàngguān Dūn (上官惇), and others as his generals and commanders;
Yán Shì (閻式), Lǐ Yuǎn (李遠), and others as his staff and assistants.
Luó Shàng (羅尚) was habitually greedy and cruel,
causing suffering to the common people.
Tè (特) established three chapters of law with the people of Shǔ (蜀),
granting favors and relief,
Dù Yù (杜預) said: "Bestowing kindness and benefits,
and exempting from forced labor."
His military administration was solemn and orderly,
and the people of Shǔ (蜀) were greatly pleased.
Shàng (尚) was repeatedly defeated by Tè (特),
so he built a long siege wall,
establishing camps along the Píshǔi (郫水),
extending seven hundred *lǐ*.
Shuǐjīngzhù (水經註) says: "The Miánshuǐ (綿水) flows west out of Miánzhú (綿竹) County,
then merges with the Jiānshuǐ (湔水),
also called the Píjiāng (郫江)."
Zàijì (載記) says: "Shàng (尚) built camps along the river,
from Dū'ān (都安) to Jiānwéi (犍為), seven hundred *lǐ*."
Shīgǔ (師古) says: "Pí (郫)
is pronounced 'pí' (疲)."
He sought aid from Liángzhōu (梁州) and the Southern Yi Colonel (Nányí Xiàowèi 南夷校尉).
The Southern Yi Colonel commanded the commanderies of Nánzhōng (南中).
In the twelfth month,
Hé Shào (何卲), Duke Kāng (康公) of Yǐngchāng (潁昌), died.
Jiǒng's (冏) sons Bīng (冰) was enfeoffed as King of Lè'ān (Lè'ān Wáng 樂安王),
Yīng (英) as King of Jìyáng (Jìyáng Wáng 濟陽王),
and Chāo (超) as King of Huáinán (Huáinán Wáng 淮南王).
In the first year of Tàiyán (太安)
(Rénxū 壬戌, 302 CE). In this year, the twelfth month,
King Qí (Qí Wáng 齊王) Jiǒng (冏) died.
Only then was the reign name changed to Tàiyán (太安);
this was still the second year of Yǒngníng (永寧).
In the spring,
third month,
Chōng (沖), the Grandson of the Crown Prince (Tàisūn 太孫), died.
Chōng (沖) is a posthumous title.
In the summer,
fifth month,
on the day Jǐyǒu (己酉),
Liáng Xiàowáng (梁孝王) Róng (肜) died.
Liú Shí (劉寔), Grand Master of Splendid Happiness of the Right (Yòuguānglù Dàfū 右光祿大夫), was appointed Grand Tutor (Tàifù 太傅),
but was soon dismissed due to old age and illness.
4 Héjiān Wáng Yǒng dispatched Dūhù Yá Bó to attack Lǐ Tè.
According to the Family Genealogies: Prince of Qín Mù took his fief at Yá,
and thus adopted it as his clan name.
Yá County,
during the Hàn dynasty, belonged to Fēngyì Commandery.
Zǐtóng County,
during the Hàn dynasty, belonged to Guǎnghàn Commandery;
Liú Shǔ divided Guǎnghàn to establish Zǐtóng Commandery.
During the Táng dynasty, Zǐtóng, Pǔ'ān, Huáng'ān, Yǒngguī, Wǔlián, Línjīn, and Jiànmén of Jiàn Prefecture were all part of Hàn Zǐtóng County.
Tóng,
pronounced the same as "tóng".
He camped at Déyáng;
Luó Shàng dispatched Dūhù Zhāng Guī to camp at Fánchéng.
Fán County,
belonged to Shǔ Commandery.

was the land of Hàn Fán County.
Sòng Bái said: Yì Prefecture's Xīnfán County,
was originally Hàn Fán County.
Then he personally attacked Guī,
and defeated him.
Dàng routed Bó's troops at Yángmiǎn,
Zǐtóng Tàishǒu Zhāng Yǎn abandoned the city and fled,

During the Táng dynasty, it was the land of Lì Prefecture's Bì and Jiāmēng Counties.
All his troops surrendered.
Héjiān Wáng Yǒng further appointed Xǔ Xióng as Liángzhōu Cìshǐ.
Tè proclaimed himself Dàjiāngjūn, Yìzhōu Mù, and Dūdū Liáng-Yì Èrzhōu Zhūjūnsì.
5 Dàsīmǎ Jiǒng, wishing to long monopolize the government,
considering that the emperor's sons and grandsons were all gone—
Crown Prince Yù had died,
the emperor had no sons;
Pú, Zāng, and Shàng had died,
the emperor had no grandsons.
Yǐng, in the order of the emperor's younger brothers, was next in line.

On the day Guǐmǎo,
Tán was established as the Crown Prince,
with Jiǒng as the Crown Prince Tàishī,

6 In autumn,
eighth month,
Lǐ Tè attacked Zhāng Wēi.
Wēi defeated him,
and then advanced to attack Tè's camp.
Lǐ Dàng led troops to rescue him.
The mountain path was steep and narrow,
"xiá" [narrow],
is the same as "xiá" [narrow].

but Dàng and Sīmǎ Wáng Xìng advised him, saying:

Tè ordered his general Jiān Shuò to guard Déyáng.
Lǐ Xiāng camped at Píqiáo.
Today, northwest of Huái'ān Garrison, there is Zhōngjiāng,

Huái'ān Garrison,
was the land of Hàn Guǎnghàn Xīndū County.
He was repeatedly defeated by Xiāng.

Jùn.

Zhūtí County,

roasted him, and killed him.
Fāng’s soldiers also shed tears for him.
The gōngqīng all went to Yè to apologize for their offenses.
Dàjiāngjūn Yǐng entered the capital
and then returned to his post in Yè.
An imperial edict appointed Yǐng as Chéngxiàng,
and Dōnghǎi Wáng Yuè was appointed to Shǒushàngshū Lìng.
Yǐng dispatched Fènwǔ Jiāngjūn Shí Chāo and others to lead fifty thousand troops to garrison the twelve city gates.
Luòyáng had three gates on the east: Jiànchūn, Dōngyáng, and Qīngmíng;
four on the south: Kāiyáng, Jīnyáng, Píngchāng, and Xuānyáng;
three on the west: Guǎngyáng, Xīmíng, and Chānghé;
and two on the north: Dàxià and Guǎngmò.
In total, twelve gates.
Shuài
is read as lǜ.
Yǐng had them all killed
and completely replaced the palace guards.
He nominated Lú Zhì as Zhōngshū Jiān,
to stay in Yè
and participate in the affairs of the Chéngxiàng’s office.
Héjiān Wáng Yǒng had stationed his army in Zhèng.
Zhèng County
belonged to Jīngzhào Commandery and was the fief of Zhōu Xuān Wáng’s younger brother, Zhèng Huán Gōng;
in the Táng dynasty, it belonged to Huázhōu.
Hearing that Liú Shěn’s troops had risen,
he returned to garrison Wèichéng.
Wèichéng County
was the old Qín Xiányáng;
in the Former Hàn, it belonged to Fúfēng,
in the Later Hàn, it was abolished,
but the place name remained;
Shí Lè established Shí’ān County;
in the Táng dynasty, it was again Xiányáng County
and belonged to Jīngzhào.
Hàoshì County
belonged to Fúfēng in the Former Hàn,
and was abolished in the Later Hàn and Jìn;
in the second year of Wǔdé of the Táng dynasty,
Hàoshì County was again established by dividing Lǐquán
and belonged to Jīngzhào.
Yǒng was afraid
and retreated into Cháng’ān,
urgently summoning Zhāng Fāng.
Fāng plundered over ten thousand official and private slaves and maids in Luòyáng and moved west.
Food was scarce in the army;
they killed people and mixed their flesh with beef and horsemeat to eat.
Liú Shěn crossed the Wèi River and encamped.
He fought with Yǒng,
and Yǒng was repeatedly defeated.
Shěn sent the Tàishǒu of Āndìng, Yá
Bó, and the Gōngcáo Huángfǔ Dàn with five thousand elite armored soldiers to attack Cháng’ān.
They entered its gates
and fought fiercely, reaching Yǒng’s tent.
Shěn’s main army arrived late;
Fēngyì Tàishǒu Zhāng Fǔ, seeing that they had no reinforcements,
led his troops to strike them from the flank,
killing Bó and Dàn.
Shěn’s troops
were then defeated,
gathered their remaining soldiers, and retreated.
Zhāng Fāng dispatched his general Dūn Wěi to attack them at night.
Shěn’s army panicked and dispersed.
Shěn fled south with his subordinates
and was pursued and captured.
Shěn said to Yǒng:
“The kindness of knowing oneself is light.”
Yǒng kept Shěn as his military advisor
and then made him the Cìshǐ of Yōngzhōu.
Shěn said: “I cannot defy the emperor’s decree
or gauge strength and weakness to preserve myself.
On the day I threw up my sleeves,
I expected to die,
the Zuǒzhuàn says: Sòng killed a Chǔ envoy,
and the Chǔ King, hearing of it,
threw up his sleeves and rose.
My death will be as sweet as water caltrops.”
Yǒng was enraged,
whipped him, and then had him cut in half at the waist.
Xīnpíng Tàishǒu Jiāngxià Zhāng Guāng had repeatedly advised Shěn on strategy.
Yǒng seized him and interrogated him.
Guāng said:
“If Liú Yōngzhōu had not used my humble schemes,
then Your Highness would have had today!”
Yǒng admired his bravery,
invited him to a joyful banquet,
and recommended him as Yòuwèi Sīmǎ.
3 Luó Shàng fled to Jiāngyáng.
The Huáyáng Guózhì says: Lúzhōu Lúchuān County
was originally Hàn Jiāngyáng County.
Also, Jiāng’ān County
was also Hàn Jiāngyáng County.
An imperial edict ordered Shàng to temporarily govern Bādōng, Bājùn, and Fúlíng to supply military provisions.
These three commanderies
originally belonged to Liángzhōu;
Shàng temporarily governed them.
Fú
is pronounced fú.
Hóng, organizing the administration, knew the transportation routes were blocked and distant.
Gāngjì
refers to Hóng’s subordinates who managed the administration of the prefecture.
He wanted to give Shàng five thousand hú of rice from Línglíng.
Hóng said:
“The world is one family;
there is no difference between us.
If I provide for him now,
then there will be no worries from the west.”
This meant that with Shàng in Bā and Fú,
he would be a shield for Jīngzhōu,
so there would be no worries from the west.
Shàng relied on this to survive.
Lǐ Xìng wished to stay and serve as Hóng’s Cānjūn.
Hóng took his hand tablet and sent him away.
A hand tablet
was an ancient hù.
Subordinates held hand tablets when showing respect to their lord.
Now, by taking Xìng’s hand tablet and sending him away,
Hóng refused to allow him to leave Shàng and serve himself.
At that time, there were over ten thousand households of displaced people in Jīngzhōu.
They were wandering and impoverished,
many becoming bandits.
Hóng largely provided them with land, seeds, and grain,
promoted their talented individuals,
and assigned them positions according to their abilities.
The displaced people then became settled.
4 In the third
month,
on the day yǐyǒu,
Chéngxiàng Yǐng submitted a memorial to depose Empress Yáng
and imprison her in Jīnyǒng Chéng;
Crown Prince Tán was deposed and made King of Qīnghé.
The establishment of Empress Yáng is found in volume 83, first year of Yǒngkāng.
The establishment of Tán is found in the previous volume, first year of Tài’ān.
5 Chén Mǐn (陳敏) battled Shí Bīng (石冰) for dozens of rounds.
Bīng's (冰) forces outnumbered Mǐn's (敏) tenfold,
but Mǐn (敏) attacked them,
and wherever he went, he was victorious.
He then joined Zhōu Kàng (周⿰王巳) in a combined assault on Bīng (冰) at Jiànkāng (建康).
In the third month,
Bīng (冰) fled north,
seeking refuge with Fēng Yún (封雲).
Fēng Yún (封雲)
was a bandit from Xúzhōu (徐州) who had responded to Bīng's (冰) call.
With Yángzhōu (揚州) and Xúzhōu (徐州) pacified, Zhōu Kàng (周⿰王巳) and Hè Xún (賀循) disbanded their armies and returned home,
not speaking of their merits or rewards.
The imperial court appointed Chén Mǐn (陳敏) as the Grand Administrator of Guǎnglíng (廣陵).
6 The Prince of Héjiān (河間), Sīmǎ Yōng (司馬顒), submitted a memorial requesting the establishment of Chancellor Sīmǎ Yǐng (司馬穎) as the Imperial Younger Brother.
On the day Wùshēn (戊申),
an imperial edict appointed Sīmǎ Yǐng (司馬穎) as the Imperial Younger Brother,
General-in-Chief of all military affairs both inside and outside the capital,
with his position as Chancellor remaining unchanged.
A general amnesty was declared.
The imperial carriage, clothing, and regalia were all moved to Yè (鄴),
and the regulations were all to follow the precedents of Emperor Wǔ of Wèi (魏武帝).
Sīmǎ Yōng (司馬顒) was appointed Grand Tutor and Grand Commander, and Governor of Yǒngzhōu (雍州);
the former Grand Mentor, Liú Shí (劉寔), was made Grand Commandant.
Shí (寔), citing old age,
firmly declined the appointment.
7 The Imperial Younger Brother Sīmǎ Yǐng (司馬穎) became increasingly extravagant and arrogant,
and his favorites held power,
greatly disappointing the people.
At that time, people hoped that Sīmǎ Yǐng (司馬穎) would assist and support the imperial house,
but now he was like this,
hence he greatly disappointed the people.
The character 嬖 (bì)
is pronounced with the meanings of bēi yì fān (卑義翻)
and also bó jì fān (博計翻).
He conspired with the Right General of the Guards, Chén Zhěn (陳眕),
and the former general of Chángshā (長沙), Shàngguān Sì (上官巳), among others, to launch a punitive expedition against him.
In autumn,
the seventh month,
on the first day of the month, Bǐngshēn (丙申),
Chén Zhěn (陳眕) led his troops into Yúnlóngmén (雲龍門),
and by imperial edict summoned the Three Dukes, all officials, and the Palace Guards.
The Palace Guards
were the generals of the three divisions.
Shí Chāo (石超) fled to Yè (鄴).
On the day Wùxū (戊戌),
a general amnesty was declared,
and Empress Yáng (羊氏) and Crown Prince Sīmǎ Tán (司馬覃) were reinstated.
On the day Jǐhài (己亥),
Sīmǎ Yuè (司馬越) escorted the Emperor on a northern expedition.
Sīmǎ Yuè (司馬越) was appointed Grand Commander.
Former Attendant Ji Shào (嵇紹) was summoned to the imperial encampment.
When the Prince of Chángshā (長沙), Sīmǎ Yì (司馬乂), was in power,
Ji Shào (嵇紹) had been appointed Attendant;
after Sīmǎ Yì's (司馬乂) death,
Ji Shào (嵇紹) was demoted and dismissed as a commoner.
Now, in the expedition against Sīmǎ Yǐng (司馬穎),
he was again summoned to the imperial encampment.
"Going now,
safety and danger are unpredictable.
Do you have a good horse, sir?"
Ji Shào (嵇紹) replied with a stern expression,
"As a subject and son, I guard the imperial carriage;
life and death are as one for this purpose.
What need is there for a good horse!"
Sīmǎ Yuè (司馬越) issued a proclamation summoning troops from all directions,
and they gathered like clouds.
By the time they reached Ānyáng (安陽),
the "Jìn Zhì" (晉志) states: Ānyáng County
belongs to Wèijùn (魏郡).
The "Wèi Tǔdì Jì" (魏土地記) states: Forty li south of Yè (鄴) city is Ānyáng (安陽) city.
The character 乘 (chéng)
is pronounced as shéng zhèng fān (繩證翻).
The character 比 (bǐ)
is pronounced as bì mèi fān (必寐翻).
Yè (鄴) was shaken with fear.
Sīmǎ Yǐng (司馬穎) convened his officials to ask for advice.
The Prince of Dōng'ān (東安), Sīmǎ Yáo (司馬繇), said,
"The Son of Heaven is personally leading an expedition; it would be appropriate to shed armor, wear plain white, go out to welcome him, and beg for forgiveness."
Sīmǎ Yǐng (司馬穎) did not follow this advice and dispatched Shí Chāo (石超) to lead fifty thousand troops to resist the attack.
The General Who Breaks the Enemy, Qiáo Zhìmíng (喬智明), advised Sīmǎ Yǐng (司馬穎) to welcome the imperial carriage.
Sīmǎ Yǐng (司馬穎) angrily said,
"You are known to be knowledgeable, and you have cast your lot with me;
now the Emperor is being pressured by petty individuals,
how can you wish me to stand by and be executed!"
Chén Zhěn's (陳眕) two younger brothers, Chén Kuāng (陳匡) and Chén Guī (陳規), came from Yè (鄴) to the imperial encampment,
saying that everyone in Yè (鄴) had already dispersed.
Because of this, little preparation was made.
On the day Jǐwèi (己未),
Shí Chāo's (石超) army suddenly arrived,
and the imperial carriage suffered a crushing defeat at Dàngyīn (蕩陰).
Dàngyīn County
belonged to Hénèi Commandery in the Hàn dynasty,
to Wèijùn Commandery in the Jìn dynasty,
and was Dàngyīn County of Xiāngzhōu in the Táng dynasty.
According to "Shuǐjīng Zhù" (水經註): Tāngyīn County was named after the Tāng River.
Sòng Bái (宋白) said: Ancient Tāngyīn County was south of the Tāng River;
in early Hàn, Ānyáng County was abolished and merged into Tāngyīn;
in the Suí dynasty, Tāngyīn was again abolished and merged into Ānyáng.
Thus, Ānyáng and Tāngyīn counties were adjacent.
Shīgǔ (師古) said: 蕩 (dàng)
is pronounced tāng (湯).
The Emperor was struck by three arrows,
and all the officials and attendants dispersed.
Ji Shào (嵇紹), in his court robes,
dismounted and boarded the imperial carriage,
shielding the Emperor with his body.
The soldiers pulled Ji Shào (嵇紹) from inside the shafts of the carriage and hacked him.
轅 (yuán)
means the shafts of a carriage.
The "Fāngyán" (方言) states: Chǔ (楚) and Wèi (衞) call them zhōu (輈).
朝 (cháo)
is pronounced zhí yáo fān (直遙翻).
"He is a loyal minister,
do not kill him!"
They replied,
"We are acting on the Imperial Younger Brother's orders;
we are only forbidden to harm His Majesty himself."
They then killed Ji Shào (嵇紹),
and his blood spattered the Emperor's robe.
The Emperor fell into the grass,
and the six imperial seals were lost.
Shí Chāo (石超) escorted the Emperor to his camp.
The Emperor was very hungry.
Shí Chāo (石超) offered water,
and his attendants presented autumn peaches.
Peaches that ripened in summer were presented to the Emperor;
autumn peaches were not suitable for presentation to the Most Exalted,
yet they were presented,
out of lack of other provisions.
On the day Gēngshēn (庚申),
they entered Yè (鄴).
A general amnesty was declared,
and the era name was changed to Jiànwǔ (建武).
The Emperor's attendants wanted to wash his robe,
but the Emperor said,
"That is the blood of Attendant Ji (嵇),
do not wash it!"
Who would say the Emperor was foolish and dim-witted then!
Chén Zhěn (陳眕), Shàngguān Sì (上官巳), and others escorted Crown Prince Sīmǎ Tán (司馬覃) to guard Luòyáng (洛陽).
Grand Commandant Sīmǎ Yuè (司馬越) fled to Xiàpī (下邳),
but the Grand Administrator of Xúzhōu (徐州), the Prince of Dōngpíng (東平), Sīmǎ Máo (司馬楙), did not admit him.
Sīmǎ Yuè (司馬越) went directly back to Dōnghǎi (東海).
The Imperial Younger Brother Sīmǎ Yǐng (司馬穎), seeing Sīmǎ Yuè (司馬越) and his brothers as eminent members of the imperial clan,
Sīmǎ Yuè (司馬越), Sīmǎ Téng (司馬騰), Sīmǎ Lüè (司馬略), and Sīmǎ Mó (司馬模) all had good reputations among the imperial clan.
Sīmǎ Yuè (司馬越) did not respond to the summons.
Former General Fènwēi (奮威), Sūn Huì (孫惠), submitted a memorial advising Sīmǎ Yuè (司馬越) to form alliances with the feudal states
and jointly assist the imperial house.
Sīmǎ Yuè (司馬越) appointed Sūn Huì (孫惠) as his Registrar and Army Advisor,
and consulted him on strategy.
The Central Supervisor of the Northern Army, Gǒu Xī (茍晞), fled to the Prince of Fányáng (范陽), Sīmǎ Xiāo (司馬虓).
Sīmǎ Xiāo (司馬虓), acting on imperial authority, appointed Gǒu Xī (茍晞) as Acting Inspector of Yǎnzhōu (兗州).
The Prince of Fányáng (范陽), Sīmǎ Xiāo (司馬虓), was at that time stationed in Xǔchāng (許昌).
The character 虓 (xiāo)
is pronounced xǔ jiāo fān (許交翻).
8 Previously,
when the three princes raised troops to suppress the Prince of Zhào (趙), Sīmǎ Lún (司馬倫),
the details are in the previous volume, under Yǒngníng (永寧) first year.
He forbade the commoners and soldiers under his command from responding to the three princes' recruitment calls.
The Imperial Younger Brother Sīmǎ Yǐng (司馬穎) wanted to attack him but was unable to.
If Sīmǎ Yǐng (司馬穎) and his brothers did not scheme against each other internally,
and instead denounced Sīmǎ Jùn's (司馬浚) crimes and attacked him,
he would certainly have had surplus strength;
why would he be unable to?
Sīmǎ Yǐng (司馬穎) appointed Right Grand Administrator Hé Yǎn (和演) as Inspector of Yōuzhōu (幽州).
Hé Yǎn (和演) had conspired with Sīmǎ Yǐng (司馬穎) to raise troops to suppress the Prince of Zhào (趙), Sīmǎ Lún (司馬倫);
he was Sīmǎ Yǐng's (司馬穎) confidant.
Hé Yǎn (和演) plotted with the Wūhuán (烏桓) Chányú (單于), Shěn Dēng (審登), to lead Sīmǎ Jùn (司馬浚) on an outing to Qīngquán (清泉) south of Jìchéng (薊城),
and then to ambush him.
However, there was a sudden heavy rain,
and their weapons became wet,
so they failed and returned.
Shěn Dēng (審登) believed that Sīmǎ Jùn (司馬浚) had divine assistance,
and so he revealed Hé Yǎn's (和演) plot to Sīmǎ Jùn (司馬浚).
Sīmǎ Jùn (司馬浚) and Shěn Dēng (審登) secretly prepared their troops
and arranged with the Inspector of Bīngzhōu (幷州), Duke Dōngyíng (東嬴), Sīmǎ Téng (司馬騰), to jointly surround and
kill Hé Yǎn (和演).
He then took charge of the Yōuzhōu (幽州) camp troops himself.
These were the Yōuzhōu (幽州) Inspector's camp troops.
Sīmǎ Téng (司馬騰) was Sīmǎ Yuè's (司馬越) younger brother.
The Imperial Younger Brother Sīmǎ Yǐng (司馬穎) issued an imperial edict summoning Sīmǎ Jùn (司馬浚).

Sīmǎ Jùn (司馬浚), together with the Xiānbēi (鮮卑) leader Duàn Wùwùchén (段務勿塵) and the Wūhuán (烏桓) leader Jié Zhū (羯朱), and Duke Dōngyíng (東嬴) Sīmǎ Téng (司馬騰), jointly raised troops to attack Sīmǎ Yǐng (司馬穎).
Sīmǎ Yǐng (司馬穎) dispatched Northern Central Inspector Wáng Bīn (王斌) and Shí Chāo (石超) to strike them.
9 Tài-dì Yǐng resented Dōng'ān-wáng Yáo's previous proposal,
and resented him for making him wear plain white to welcome the emperor and plead guilty.
On the day Wùchén,
Yáo was arrested
and killed.
Previously,
Yáo's elder brother Lángyá Gōng-wáng Jìn had died,
and his son Ruì succeeded him.
Ruì was astute, perceptive, and magnanimous.
He served as Zuǒ Jiāngjūn
and was close to Dōnghǎi Cānjūn Wáng Dǎo.
Dǎo served as a military advisor to Dōnghǎi-wáng Yuè.
Dǎo was Dūn's paternal cousin.
He had clear and far-sighted discernment.
Seeing the many troubles in the imperial court,
he often urged Ruì to return to his fief.
When Yáo died,
Ruì was with the emperor in Yè,
fearing he would be implicated in the disaster,
and prepared to flee back to his fief.
Yǐng had previously ordered the passes and ferries
not to allow any nobles to leave.
Passes were set up at crucial junctions of major roads,
to inspect those passing through the ferries,
and at places essential for crossing rivers.
He was stopped by a ferry official.
His attendant Sòng Diǎn came from behind,
brushed Ruì with a whip and laughed, saying:
"Shèzhǎng,
shèzhǎng (head of a hostel),
the head of a lodging house.
Zhǎng,
pronounced Dīng Zhàng.
Now known to have two pronunciations.
Are you also being detained?"
The official then allowed them to pass.
When they reached Luòyáng,
they welcomed Tài-xià Hóu-shì and returned together to their fief.
The restoration of Yuán-dì began here.
Xià,
pronounced Hù Yǎ.
10 The Cénɡxiànɡ Cónɡshì Zhōnglánɡ Wáng Chénɡ exposed Mèng Jiǔ's corrupt practices and illicit gains,
urging Tài-dì Yǐng to execute him.
Yǐng agreed.
11 Shàngguān Sì was in Luòyáng,
behaving cruelly and recklessly.
Zhōu Fù, the Shǒu Hénán Yǐn,
was Jùn's paternal cousin.
Zhōu Jùn had military achievements when he joined Wáng Hún in attacking Wú.
When the matter was exposed,
Fèn and others died,
but Fù fled
and escaped.
When Sīkōnɡ Yuè campaigned against Tài-dì Yǐng,
Tàizǎi Yónɡ dispatched Yòu Jiāngjūn, Fénɡyì Tàishǒu Zhānɡ Fānɡ with twenty thousand troops to rescue him.
Hearing that the emperor had already entered Yè,
he then ordered Fānɡ to garrison Luòyáng.
Sì, with another general Miáo Yuàn, resisted him
but were soundly defeated and returned.
Tài Zǐ Tán launched a night attack on Sì and Yuàn.
Sì and Yuàn fled.
Fānɡ entered Luòyáng.
Tán welcomed Fānɡ at Guǎngyángmén and bowed.
The first gate on the south side of the west face of Luòchéng was called Guǎngyángmén.
Tán and Empress Yáng were again deposed.
12 Earlier,
Tài-dì Yǐng had memorialized to appoint the Xiōnɡnú Zuǒ Xiánwáng Liú Yuān as Guànjūn Jiāngjūn,
supervising the military affairs of the Five Tribes.
When Yánɡ Jùn was regent,
he appointed Liú Yuān as Dà Dūdū of the Five Tribes.
At the end of Yuánkāng's reign,
he was dismissed from office for his tribesmen rebelling and leaving the frontier.
When Yǐng garrisoned Yè,
he memorialized to appoint him to supervise the military affairs of the Five Tribes.
Guàn,
pronounced Gǔ Wán.
Jiān,
pronounced Gōnɡ Xián.
Yuān's son Cōnɡ was
extraordinarily brave and skilled,
widely read in classics and history,
good at writing,
and could draw a bow of three hundred catties.
At the age of twenty, he traveled to the capital.
The Lǐjì's Qūlǐ says: A person aged ten is called Yòuxué,
and twenty is called Ruòguān.
Guān,
pronounced Gǔ Wán.
Yǐng appointed Cōnɡ as Jīnú Jiāngjūn.
Yuān's paternal grand-cousin, the Yòu Xiánwáng Xuān, said to his clansmen:
"Since the fall of Hàn,
our Chányú has merely held an empty title
and possessed not an inch of land.
The matter is seen in Volume 67, Jiàn'ān 21st year of Emperor Xiàn of Hàn.
Cónɡ,
pronounced Cái Yònɡ.
Chányú,
pronounced Chán.
We are reduced to common households.
Biān means to be linked in sequence.
People call them Biānmín or Biānhù,
meaning that their houses are linked in sequence,
and they are registered in the common census,
without distinction of high or low status.
We are still no less than twenty thousand people,
yet how can we bow our heads and submit to
labor,
suddenly for over a hundred years!
Yǎn means suddenly,
or abruptly.
If Heaven truly does not wish to revive the Xiōnɡnú,
it would surely not have allowed this person (referring to Liú Yuān) to be born in vain.
Now the Sīmǎ clan are slaughtering each other,
the Four Seas are in turmoil,
restoring the enterprise of Hū Hánxié –
this is the time!"
During Emperor Xuān of Hàn's time,
Jī Hóu Jiē (稽侯狦) came to court
and was called Hū Hánxié Chányú.
During Guānɡwǔ's time, Rìzhú-wáng Bǐ submitted
and was also called Hū Hánxié Chányú.
They acclaimed Yuān as Dà Chányú,
and sent his associate Hūyán Yōu to Yè to inform him.
Shīgǔ said: In the Hànshū, among the noble families of the Xiōnɡnú was the Hūyǎn clan,
which is the current Hūyán clan.
Yuān reported to Yǐng,
requesting to return for the funeral,
but Yǐng refused.
Yuān ordered Yōu to return first,
to instruct Xuān and others to gather the Five Tribes and various Hu people,
ostensibly to assist Yǐng,
but actually intending to rebel.
When Wánɡ Jùn and Dōnɡyínɡ Gōnɡ Ténɡ raised armies,
Yuān persuaded Yǐng, saying:
"Now these two regional commanders are unruly,
with a force of over one hundred thousand.
The two regional commanders refer to Yōu and Bīnɡ provinces.
Shuō,
pronounced Shū Ruì;
same below.
I request to return and persuade the Five Tribes to join His Highness in facing the national crisis."
Yǐng said:
"Can the forces of the Five Tribes
truly be mobilized or not?
Even if they can be mobilized,
the Xiānbēi and Wūhuán are not easily confronted.
I wish to escort the emperor back to Luòyáng to avoid their vanguard,
and then slowly issue a proclamation throughout the realm,
to control them through the principle of right and wrong."
He meant that he felt he lacked the strength to control the two regional commanders
and wished to summon armies from across the realm,
using righteousness to subdue rebellion.
Yuān said:
"Your Highness is a son of Emperor Wǔ,
who performed great services for the royal house.
Your might and benevolence are widely renowned.
Within the Four Seas,
who would not wish to die for Your Highness with all their strength?
What difficulty is there in mobilizing them?
Wánɡ Jùn is a mere youth,
Dōnɡyínɡ is a distant relative.
Dōnɡyínɡ Gōnɡ Ténɡ was the grandson of Xuān-dì's younger brother Dōnɡwǔ-hóu Kuí,
hence called a distant relative.
If Your Highness leaves Yè palace,
showing weakness to others,
you will not be able to reach Luòyáng.
Even if you reach Luòyáng,
your authority will no longer be with Your Highness.
Yǐng fled in defeat and lost power,
exactly as Yuān had predicted.
To settle it with peace,
Yuān requested to use two tribes for Your Highness to crush Dōnɡyínɡ,
and three tribes to behead Wánɡ Jùn.
The heads of these two scoundrels
can be hung up in a matter of days."
Yǐng was pleased
and appointed Yuān as Běi Chányú and Cān Cénɡxiànɡ Jūnjì.
Yuān arrived at Zuǒguó Chéng.
Zuǒguó Chéng
was probably the city where the Left Division of the Xiōngnú resided.
According to the biography section of the Jìn Shū,
at the beginning of Guāngwǔ's Jiànwǔ reign,
the Southern Chányú moved into Měijì of Xīhé.
The present Lìshí Zuǒguó Chéng
was the court where the Chányú was relocated.
The Shuǐjīng Zhù says: Zuǒguó Chéng is to the right of Fénzhōu,
southwest of Jièxiū Xiàn.
Dù Yòu said: Zuǒguó Chéng is in Lìshí Xiàn, Shízhōu.
Sòng Bái said: Northeast of Lìshí Xiàn is Lìshí Shuǐ,
thus it was named after it.
Within two *xún* (twenty days),
he gathered a host of fifty thousand,
establishing his capital at Lìshí.
Lìshí Xiàn had belonged to Xīhé Jùn since the Hàn dynasty.
He dispatched Zuǒ Yú Lù Wáng Hóng, commanding five thousand elite cavalry,
to meet Yǐng's general Wáng Cuì to resist Dōngyíng Gōng Téng.
Cuì had already been defeated by Téng,
so Hóng returned without reaching them.
Wáng Jùn and Dōngyíng Gōng Téng combined their forces to attack Wáng Bīn,
utterly defeating him.
Jùn made his aide Qí Hóng the vanguard.
The Xìngpǔ says: The Qí surname
is one of the twenty-five sons of the Yellow Emperor;
furthermore, Xī, the great-great-grandson of Jìn Xiànhóu, was granted a fief at Qí,
and was called Qí Xī.
Píngjí Xiàn,
belonged to Chángshān Jùn in the Hàn dynasty,
and to Zhào Guó in the Jìn dynasty.
Liú Xùn said: Hàn Píngjí Xiàn was south of the present Zhàozhōu Píngjí Xiàn.
Cavalry scouts reached Yè,
causing a great tremor in Yè.
Officials fled,
and soldiers dispersed.
Lú Zhì advised Yǐng to escort the Emperor back to Luòyáng.
At that time, there were still fifteen thousand armored soldiers.
Zhì made his arrangements by night;
by dawn, they were about to depart,
but Chéng Tài was too attached to Yè and did not want to leave,
and Yǐng was hesitant and undecided.
Suddenly, the troops scattered,
and Yǐng, with a few dozen horsemen from his personal guard, escorted the Emperor in an ox-drawn cart.
Jìn system: A black-wheeled ox-drawn cart
was for the use of dukes.
In their haste, they left with nothing.
A middle *huángmén* carried three thousand private coins in his bag.
An imperial edict granted him permission to lend them.
They bought food on the road,
slept under the middle *huángmén*'s cotton quilt at night,
and ate from clay basins.
Upon reaching Wēn,
they were about to visit the imperial tombs.
The Emperor's ancestors were
from Xiàojìng Lǐ, Wēn Xiàn, Hénèi.
From Jīngzhàoyǐn Fáng upwards,
all were buried in Wēn.
He put on the shoes of a follower,
prostrated himself, and wept.
After crossing the Hé,
Zhāng Fāng sent his son Zhāng Pí from Luòyáng, leading three thousand cavalry,
to escort the Emperor with his own carriage.
Upon reaching the foot of Mángshān,
Fāng himself, leading over ten thousand cavalry, welcomed the Emperor.
As Fāng was about to prostrate himself,
the Emperor got out of his carriage and stopped him personally.
This was even more courteous than Yí Wáng descending the hall to meet the vassals.
Those who had fled gradually returned,
and the various officials were roughly assembled.
On the *xīnsì* day,
a general amnesty was declared.
Wáng Jùn entered Yè.
His soldiers plundered violently,
and many died.
He sent Wūhuán Jié Zhū to pursue Grand Younger Brother Yǐng.
Upon reaching Cháogē,
he failed to catch him.
Jùn returned to Jì.
As the Xiānbēi had plundered many women,
he commanded:
"Anyone daring to hide them will be executed!"
Consequently, eight thousand people were drowned in the Yì Shuǐ.
Wáng Jùn failed to assist the Emperor,
and instead allowed the Xiānbēi and Wūhuán to rampage and cause chaos in Huá.
His death at the hands of Shí Lè
was too late.
Shěn,
read *chí lín fān*.
13 Dōngyíng Gōng Téng requested troops from Tuòbá Yī É to attack Liú Yuān.
Yī É and his younger brother Yī Lú combined their forces and attacked Yuān at Xīhé,
defeating him,
then made an alliance with Téng east of Fén and returned.
From then on, the Tuòbá clan frequently assisted Bìngzhōu with troops.
É,
read *tú hé fān*.
Huán,
read *cóng xuān fān*.
Also, read as is.
Liú Yuān heard that Grand Younger Brother Yǐng had left Yè,
and sighed:
"He did not heed my words,
and instead self-destructed and fled.
Truly a good-for-nothing!
However, I made a promise to him,
so I cannot fail to rescue him."
He was about to dispatch troops to attack the Xiānbēi and Wūhuán.
Liú Xuān and others remonstrated, saying:
"The Jìn people enslaved and controlled us.
Now their own flesh and blood are fighting each other.
This is Heaven abandoning them and enabling us to restore the enterprise of Hū Hánxié.
The Xiānbēi and Wūhuán are of our kind.
The Xiānbēi and Wūhuán
are descendants of Dōnghú,
sharing the same vigorous and strong spirit of the north as the Xiōngnú,
and are also of the same race.
How can we attack them!"
Yuān said:
"Excellent!
A true man should emulate Hàn Gāo
and Wèi Wǔ.
Hū Hánxié is not worth imitating!"
Xuān and others bowed their heads and said:
"We are not worthy of such a comparison!"
14 The Jīngzhōu army captured and executed Zhāng Chāng.
All his confederates had their three kindreds exterminated.
Last year, Chāng fled to Xiàjùn Shān;
only now was he captured and eliminated.
15 Lǐ Xióng, seeing Fàn Chángshēng's renowned virtue,
and that he was respected by the people of Shǔ,
wished to welcome him as ruler and serve him as a subject,
but Chángshēng refused.
The generals earnestly requested Xióng to assume the imperial throne.
In winter,
tenth month,
Xióng ascended to the throne as King of Chéngdū,
declared a general amnesty,
and changed the reign title to Jiànxīng.
He abolished Jìn laws,
and enacted a simplified code of seven chapters.
He appointed his uncle Xiāng as Tàifù,
his elder brother Shǐ as Tàibǎo,
Lǐ Lí as Tàiwèi,
Lǐ Yún as Sītú,
Lǐ Huáng as Sīkōng,
Lǐ Guó as Tàizǎi,
Yán Shì as Shàngshū Lìng,
and Yáng Bāo as Púshè.
He honored his mother, Lady Luó, as Queen Dowager,
and posthumously honored his father, Tè, as King Jǐng of Chéngdū.
Xióng valued Lǐ Guó and Lǐ Lí for their wisdom and resourcefulness,
and always consulted them before acting.
However, Guó and Lí served Xióng with even greater caution.
Historians say that the various Lǐ family members maintained the distinction between ruler and subject to preserve and solidify their position;
as the saying goes, even thieves have their own code of conduct.
16 Liú Yuān (劉淵) moved his capital to Zuǒguó Chéng (左國城).
The Kǎoyì (考異) says: The text below states,
"There was a great famine in Líshí (離石),
and he moved to Lítíng (黎亭),"
which means Yuān (淵) was still in Líshí (離石).
According to Dù Yòu's (杜佑) Tōngdiǎn (通典): Líshí (離石) had the Zuǒguó Chéng (左國城) of the Southern Chányú's (單于) court.
Therefore, although Yuān (淵) moved to Zuǒguó (左國),
he was still within Líshí (離石) County.
Yuān (淵) said to his ministers:
"In the past, the Hàn (漢) possessed the empire for a long time,
and their benevolence was ingrained in the people.
I,
being the maternal nephew of the Hàn (漢) clan,
entered into a brotherhood with them;
when the elder brother dies, the younger brother succeeds –
is this not permissible!"
Thereupon, he established the state and named it Hàn (漢).
Liú Xuān (劉宣) and others requested that he be granted an honorable title.
Yuān (淵) said:
"Currently, the four directions are not settled.
For now, it is appropriate to follow Gāozǔ (高祖) and be called King of Hàn (漢王)."
Thereupon, he ascended to the position of King of Hàn (漢王).
Liú Yuān's (劉淵)
courtesy name was Yuánhǎi (元海).
The Kǎoyì (考異) says: In the Dìjì (帝紀),
Lǐ Xióng (李雄) and Liú Yuān (劉淵) proclaimed themselves kings
both after Emperor Huì (惠帝) entered Cháng'ān (長安) in the eleventh month.
The Huáyáng Guózhì (華陽國志) states
Lǐ Xióng (李雄) proclaimed himself king in the tenth month,
one version says the twelfth month.
The Sānshí Guó (三十國), Jìn Chūnqiū (晉春秋), and Shíliù Guó Chāo (十六國鈔) all place it in the tenth month.
We follow this.
The era name was changed to Yuánxī (元熙).
He posthumously honored Ānlè Gōng (安樂公) Chán (禪) as Xiàohuái Huángdì (孝懷皇帝),
and made spirit tablets for the Three Progenitors and Five Ancestors of Hàn (漢) to sacrifice to them.
Yuān (淵) took Hàn Gāozǔ (漢高祖), Shìzǔ (世祖), and Zhāoliè (昭烈) as the Three Progenitors,
and Tàizōng (太宗), Shìzōng (世宗), Zhōngzōng (中宗), Xiǎnzōng (顯宗), and Sùzōng (肅宗) as the Five Ancestors.
He appointed Right Xiánwáng (賢王) Xuān (宣) as Prime Minister (丞相),
Cuī Yóu (崔游) as Grand Censor (御史大夫),
Left Yúlù Wáng (於陸王) Hóng (宏) as Grand Commandant (太尉),
Fàn Lóng (范隆) as Grand Usher (大鴻臚),
Zhū Jì (朱紀) as Grand Master of Ceremonies (太常),
Cuī Yìzhī (崔懿之) from Shàngdǎng (上黨) and Chén Yuándá (陳元達), a man from Hòubù (後部), both as Palace Attendants (黃門郎).
Liú Yuān (劉淵) used the Hàn (漢) official system for all appointments.
Hòubù (後部)
was the Northern Xiongnú (匈奴) tribe,
residing in Xīnxīng (新興).
Yóu (游) firmly declined the appointment.
Cuī Yóu (崔游) was Yuān's (淵) teacher;
Fàn Lóng (范隆) and Zhū Jì (朱紀)
were fellow students.
Cuī Yóu (崔游) was not only able to avoid bowing to Yuān (淵) in his capacity as a teacher,
but also upheld the principle of not changing due to the barbarians.
Shěn Yuè's (沈約) Zhì (志) states:
Wèi (魏) established the General Who Establishes Martial Power (建武將軍).
Yuándá (元達) had lofty aspirations and integrity since childhood.
Yuān (淵) once invited him,
but Yuándá (元達) did not respond.
When Yuān (淵) became King of Hàn (漢),
someone said to Yuándá (元達):
"Are you afraid?"
Yuándá (元達) laughed and said:
"I have known that man for a long time,
and he also understands my heart;
I only fear that in no more than two or three days,
an urgent dispatch will surely arrive."
That evening,
Yuān (淵) indeed summoned Yuándá (元達).
Yuándá (元達) served Yuān (淵) and repeatedly offered loyal advice,
but would destroy the drafts afterwards,
so even his children and younger brothers could not know about it.
Cǎo (草) refers to
the drafts of memorials.
Yào (曜) was born with white eyebrows
and red light in his eyes.
As a child, he was intelligent
and courageous. He was orphaned young
and raised by Yuān (淵).
When he grew up,
his appearance was imposing and grand,
and his nature was broad-minded and brilliant.
Tuò (拓) means
broad.
Luò (落) means
open and candid.
Cháng (長) is pronounced
'zhī liǎng fān'.
Guān (觀) is pronounced
'gǔ wán fān'.
He loved to read,
and was skilled at writing.
He could shoot through an iron plate an inch thick.
He often compared himself to Yuè Yì (樂毅) and Xiāo (蕭) and Cáo (曹) [Xiāo Hé (蕭何) and Cáo Shēn (曹參)];
at the time, people did not approve of him;
only Liú Cōng (劉聰) valued him greatly,
saying:
"Yǒngmíng (永明) is of the caliber of the Hàn (漢) Shìzǔ (世祖) and Wèi Wǔ (魏武);
those few gentlemen are not worth mentioning!"
Liú Yào's (劉曜)
courtesy name was Yǒngmíng (永明).
Those few gentlemen
refer to Yuè Yì (樂毅), Xiāo (蕭), and Cáo (曹).
17 After the Emperor returned to Luòyáng (洛陽),
Zhāng Fāng (張方) wielded military power and monopolized court affairs,
and the Imperial Younger Brother Yǐng (穎) was no longer allowed to participate in state matters.
The Governor of Yùzhōu (豫州), Fányáng Wáng (范陽王) Xiāo (虓), the Governor of Xúzhōu (徐州), Dōngpíng Wáng (東平王) Máo (楙), and others memorialized:
"Yǐng (穎) is incapable of bearing the burden,
and should be demoted to a fief of one city,
and his life specially spared.
The Grand Tutor should be entrusted with the responsibilities in Guān Yòu (關右),
Hějiān Wáng (河間王) Yóng (顒) was then Grand Tutor,
hence the title.
The selection and appointment of officials
should all await his approval;
for major state affairs,
such as abolitions, promotions, losses, and gains,
he should always be consulted.
This means the prefectures and commanderies in Guān Yòu (關右)
should be subject to Yóng's (顒) selection,
and court affairs should also be carried out only after consulting him.
Yǎng (仰) is pronounced
'niú xiàng fān'.
Kǒng Ānguó (孔安國) said: Chóu (疇)
means 'who'.
Yán Shīgǔ (顏師古) said: Chóu (疇)
means 'who'.
Zī (咨)
means 'to consult'.
It means consulting with the multitude,
as to who can undertake affairs.
I, however, believe that what is called chóu zī (疇咨) here
is probably not the meaning annotated by Kǒng (孔) and Yán (顏).
Indeed, chóu (疇)
means 'category' or 'kind'.
Zī (咨)
means 'to inquire'.
It means that for major state affairs,
they are categorized and inquired about with Yóng (顒).
Cháo (朝) is pronounced
'zhí yáo fān'.
As for Zhāng Fāng (張方), who did not understand adaptability
and had not immediately returned west,
he should be sent back to his commandery.
Fāng (方) was originally the Administrator of Féngyì (馮翊).
Wèi (為) is pronounced
'yú wěi fān'.
We request that all revert to the old system.
The Minister of Works (司徒) Róng (戎) and the Grand Minister of Agriculture (司空) Yuè (越)
are both loyal to the state and cautious;
they should be entrusted with pivotal matters
and the governance of the court.
Wáng Jùn (王浚) has the merit of stabilizing the state.
This refers to raising an army to attack Yǐng (穎).
He should then pacify Yōu (幽) and Shuò (朔),
and long serve as a northern bulwark.
If your subjects exhaust their strength to defend the cities
and protect the imperial house,
then Your Majesty can rule by merely folding your hands,
and the four seas will naturally be set right."
Zhāng Fāng (張方) had been in Luòyáng (洛陽) for a long time.
His soldiers' plundering had exhausted almost everything.
The populace was restless and agitated,
no longer intent on staying.
They discussed escorting the Emperor to move the capital to Cháng'ān (長安).
Fearing that the Emperor and the high officials would not comply,
they intended to wait for the Emperor to come out and then coerce him.
Xū (須)
means to wait.
The Emperor did not consent.
In the eleventh month,
on the Yǐwèi (乙未) day,
Fāng (方) led his troops into the palace.
He used his personal carriage to welcome the Emperor,
but the Emperor fled to the bamboo grove in the rear garden.
The soldiers brought the Emperor out,
forcing him to board the carriage,
and the Emperor, weeping, complied.
Fāng (方), from horseback, bowed his head to the ground and said:
"Currently, bandits roam freely,
and the imperial guards are few and scattered.
I wish Your Majesty would take refuge in your servant's encampment.
Your servant will exert his utmost strength to guard against unforeseen dangers."
At that time, all the imperial officials had fled and hidden,
only the Central Secretariat Supervisor, Lú Zhì (盧志), attended at his side,
and said:
"Your Majesty's matter today
should entirely follow the Right General."
Zhāng Fāng (張方) was then the Right General.
Fāng (方) was ordered to prepare carriages to load palace women and treasures.
The soldiers then seized and plundered the imperial concubines,
divided and contested the government treasuries,
and cut off tassels and military tents to make horse blankets.
Máo Huàng (毛晃) said: "Tassels (liú sū, 流蘇)
are embroidered balls made of twisted threads,
woven with five colors,
those that hang down concentrically.
Sū (蘇)
is like xū (鬚, beard);
it also describes a scattered appearance.
Because its stamens hang down,
it is called sū (蘇).
Today, people call the stamen at the end of a cord 'sū' (蘇)."
Mèng Kāng (孟康) said: "Today, military tents (wǔ zhàng, 武帳) are where soldiers are stationed,
placing five weapons inside the tent."
Qián (帴)
is pronounced qián (將先翻, 'jiāng xiān fān'),
it is a horse blanket.
They swept the ground clean, leaving nothing.
Fāng (方) intended to burn the ancestral temples and palaces to sever people's will to return,
but Lú Zhì (盧志) said:
"Dǒng Zhuó (董卓) was lawless,
burning Luòyáng (洛陽).
This event is recorded in volume fifty-nine, Han Xiàndì (漢獻帝), Chūpíng (初平) first year.
Its traces still remain after a hundred years,
why repeat it?"
Fāng (方) then stopped.
The Emperor stayed in Fāng's (方) encampment for three days.
Fāng (方) escorted the Emperor, along with Crown Prince Yǐng (穎) and Yùzhāng (豫章) Prince Chì (熾), to Cháng'ān (長安).
Wáng Róng (王戎) fled to Jiá (郟).
Jiá (郟) county,
in the Former Han, belonged to Yǐngchuān (潁川) Commandery.
In the Later Han, it was abolished.
In the Jìn (晉), it belonged to Xiāngchéng (襄城) Commandery.
During the Suí (隋) and Táng (唐), it was Jiáchéng (郟城) county of Rǔzhōu (汝州).
Jiá (郟)
is pronounced jiá.
Yóng (顒) came forward to pay respects.
The Emperor dismounted to stop him.
Upon entering Cháng'ān (長安),
the Emperor used the Headquarters of the General Who Conquers the West as his palace.
The Headquarters of the General Who Conquers the West was
the residence of the General Who Conquers the West,
where Yóng (顒) resided.
He acted according to imperial prerogative,
designating the Eastern and Western Courts.
Luòyáng (洛陽) was the Eastern Court,
and Cháng'ān (長安) was the Western Court.
Tūn (暾)
is pronounced tuō kūn (他昆翻, 'tuō kūn fān').
He was Xù's (勗) son.
Xún Xù (荀勗) colluded with Jiǎ Chōng (賈充),
and gained prominence in the early Jìn (晉) dynasty.
On the Bǐngwǔ (丙午) day,
the temporary court granted a general amnesty,
and the era name was changed back to Yǒng'ān (永安).
On the Xīnchǒu (辛丑) day,
Empress Yáng (羊) was reinstated.
18 Luó Shàng (羅尚) moved his garrison to Bā Jùn (巴郡),
sending troops to plunder Shǔ (蜀) territory,
capturing Lǐ Xiāng's (李驤) wife, Lady Zǎn (昝), and their son Shòu (壽).
19 In the twelfth month,
on the Dīnghài (丁亥) day,
an imperial edict ordered Crown Prince Yǐng (穎) to return to his residence as the Prince of Chéngdū (成都);
and Yùzhāng (豫章) Prince Chì (熾) was newly established as the Imperial Crown Prince.
Of the Emperor's twenty-five brothers,
only Yǐng (穎), Chì (熾), and Prince Yàn (晏) of Wú (吳) were still alive.
Yàn (晏) was mediocre in talent,
while Chì (熾) was gentle and fond of learning,
hence Grand Tutor Yóng (顒) established him.
The edict also appointed Minister of Works Yuè (越) as Grand Tutor,
to assist the imperial house with Yóng (顒);
Wáng Róng (王戎) participated in supervising court affairs.
Furthermore, Guānglù Dàfū (光祿大夫) Wáng Yǎn (王衍) was appointed Shàngshū Zuǒ Púshè (尚書左僕射).
Gāomì (高密) Prince Lüè (略) was appointed General Who Guards the South,
concurrently holding the position of Commandant of the Capital,
with authority to garrison Luòyáng (洛陽).
The *Kǎoyì* (考異) states: The *Huì Jì* (惠紀) records
"Gāomì (高密) Prince Jiǎn (簡)."
According to the *Zōngshì Zhuàn* (宗室傳),
Gāomì (高密) King Xiào (孝) Lüè (略),
courtesy name Yuánjiǎn (元簡),
was then overseeing the military affairs of Qīngzhōu (青州),
later moving to oversee Jīngzhōu (荊州),
and never garrisoned Luòyáng (洛陽).
Perhaps Jiǎn (簡) was the same as Lüè (略),
and although there was an imperial order at the time, Lüè (略) did not arrive,
or perhaps he did once garrison Luòyáng (洛陽) but the main biography omits it.
In my opinion,
at that time, imperial decrees were not effective in the regional commands,
so Lüè (略) probably never went to Luòyáng (洛陽).
He was appointed Supervisor of All Military Affairs in Jìzhōu (冀州),
garrisoning Yè (鄴).
The *Jìnshū Dìjì* (晉書帝紀) records
"General of the Eastern Central Army,"
while Mú's (模) biography records
"General of the Northern Central Army."
Furthermore, according to the Jìn (晉) system,
regional appointments
included the Four Conquerors, Four Guardians, Four Tranquilizers, and Four Pacifiers,
but no Four Stabilizers.
"Níng" (寧, Stabilizer)
should probably be
"ān" (安, Tranquilizer).
An order was issued to the provinces and commanderies to abolish harsh policies,
cherish the people, and focus on fundamental matters.
After peace and stability were restored,
they should return to Dōngjīng (東京).
This meant after those who took up arms laid down their weapons,
and the roads were clear and safe.
The Emperor was then in Cháng'ān (長安),
so Luòyáng (洛陽) was called Dōngjīng (東京).
The era name was changed.
The era name was changed to Yǒngxīng (永興).
All of them were Yuè's (越) brothers.
After Wáng Jùn (王浚) left Yè (鄴),
Yuè (越) sent Mú (模) to garrison it.
Yóng (顒), seeing the four quarters in disarray
and troubles unending,
therefore issued this edict to reconcile them,
hoping to achieve a little peace.
Yóng (顒) wanted to reconcile his brothers
at the time of the rift between Yì (乂) and Yǐng (穎).
When the situation became unmanageable,
Yóng (顒) himself could not escape.
Nán (難)
is pronounced nài dàn (乃旦翻, 'nǎi dàn fān').
Another edict appointed Grand Tutor Yóng (顒) as Supervisor of All Military Affairs Inside and Outside the Capital.
Zhāng Fāng (張方) was appointed Central Leader of the Army and Recorder of Affairs of the Imperial Secretariat,
concurrently serving as Prefect of Jīngzhào (京兆).
At that time, the Emperor was in Cháng'ān (長安),
so the Prefect of Jīngzhào (京兆) effectively managed the imperial capital.
Zhāng Fāng (張方) held military power,
and was trusted and relied upon by Yóng (顒),
hence he was made Prefect of Jīngzhào (京兆).
20 Dōngyíng (東嬴) Duke Téng (騰) sent his general Niè Xuán (聶玄) to attack Han (漢) King Yuān (淵),
battling at Dàlíng (大陵).
Dàlíng (大陵) county,
since the Han (漢) dynasty, belonged to Tàiyuán (太原) Commandery.
Wèi Shōu's (魏收) *Dìxíng Zhì* (地形志) states: "Within Tàiyuán (太原) Commandery, Shòuyáng (受陽) county has Dàlíng (大陵) city,
its territory is probably on the border between Táng (唐), Liáo (遼), and Bìng (幷) prefectures."
Dù Yòu (杜佑) said: "Wénshuǐ (文水) county was Dàlíng (大陵) county in the Han (漢)."
Niè (聶)
is pronounced nī zhé (尼輒翻, 'nī zhé fān').
Yuān (淵) sent Liú Yào (劉曜) to raid Tàiyuán (太原),
taking Xuánshì (泫氏), Túliú (屯留), Chángzǐ (長子), and Zhōngdū (中都).
Xuánshì (泫氏), Túliú (屯留), and Chángzǐ (長子) belonged to Shàngdǎng Jùn (上黨郡);
Zhōngdū (中都) belonged to Tàiyuán Jùn (太原郡).
Xián (賢) said: “Xuánshì (泫氏)
is today's Gāopíng Xiàn (高平縣) in Zézhōu (澤州).”
Liú Xùn (劉㫬) said: “Língchuān Xiàn (陵川縣) in Zézhōu (澤州)
was the Hàn (漢) Xuánshì Xiàn (泫氏縣).
Gāopíng (高平)
was the territory of Hàn's (漢) Xuánshì Xiàn (泫氏縣).”
Túliú (屯留) and Chángzǐ (長子)
both belonged to Lùzhōu (潞州) during the Táng (唐) dynasty.
Shīgǔ (師古) said: “Xuán (泫)
has the pronunciation of 'gōng xuán fān'.
Tún (屯)
has the pronunciation of 'chún'.
Cháng (長)
is read as in 'length' (長短之長);
Lù Démíng (陸德明) read it as in 'elder' (長幼之長).”
[They] took Jièxiū (介休).
Jièxiū (介休) magistrate Jiǎ Hún (賈渾) did not surrender,
so Xī (晞) killed him.
Jièxiū Xiàn (介休縣)
belonged to Tàiyuán Jùn (太原郡) during the Hàn (漢) dynasty,
to Xīhé Jùn (西河郡) during the Jìn (晉) dynasty,
and to Fénzhōu (汾州) during the Táng (唐) dynasty.
Guān (冠)
has the pronunciation of 'gǔ wán fān'.
Jiàng (降)
has the pronunciation of 'hù jiāng fān'.
His clan (Zōng Shì 宗氏) cursed Xī (晞) and wept,
so Xī (晞) killed them as well.
When Yuān (淵) heard of this,
he was greatly enraged and said:
“If the Way of Heaven has knowledge,
will Qiáo Xī (喬晞) have descendants?!”
He recalled him,
demoted him four ranks,
collected Hún's (渾) corpse,
and buried him.
Punctuation by Wáng Chóngwǔ (王崇武), re-checked by Róng Zhàozǔ (容肇祖) and Niè Chóngqí (聶崇岐).
Compiled by
Sīmǎ Guāng (司馬光)
by imperial decree.
Later
Emperor Xiàohuì (孝惠皇帝) Volume Two
Yǒngxīng (永興) Second Year
(Yǐchǒu, 305)
1. Summer,
Fourth month,
Zhāng Fāng (張方) deposed Empress Yáng (羊后).
2. Yóu Kǎi (游楷) and others attacked Huángfǔ Chóng (皇甫重)
for several years but could not conquer him.
Yóu Kǎi (游楷) and others attacked Huángfǔ Chóng (皇甫重) starting from Tàiiān (太安) Second Year,
and by this time,
it had been three full years.
Chāng (昌) went to Sīkōng (司空) Yuè (越).
Yuè (越) believed that Tàizǎi (太宰) Yóng (顒) had recently made peace with Shāndōng (山東).
The matter is found in the previous volume, previous year.
Chāng (昌) then, with the former Dìanzhōng Rén (殿中人) Yáng Piān (楊篇),
"Former Dìanzhōng Rén (故殿中人)"
refers to those formerly belonging to the Erwèi Bùqǔ (二衞部曲).
welcomed Empress Yáng (羊后) to Jīnyǒng Chéng (金墉城).
Entering the palace,
they used the Empress's (后) order to dispatch troops to attack Zhāng Fāng (張方)
and welcome the Imperial Carriage (Dàjià 大駕).
In the fourth month of this year,
Zhāng Fāng (張方) deposed Empress Yáng (羊后).
At that time, Fāng (方) had already escorted the Emperor into the Pass,
presumably using his authority to remotely threaten the hundred officials at Liútái (留臺),
forcing them to depose Empress Yáng (羊后).
Now, Huángfǔ Chāng (皇甫昌) welcomed the Empress into the palace,
intending to raise troops to attack Fāng (方).
This was merely the pretext for raising troops,
not because Fāng (方) was in Luòyáng (洛陽) and being attacked there.
At first, all the officials followed him;
but soon realizing his deception,
they jointly executed Chāng (昌).
Yóng (顒) requested to send an Imperial Censor (Yùshǐ 御史) to promulgate an imperial edict, instructing Chóng (重) to surrender.
Chóng (重) did not obey the edict.
Previously, the people in the city did not know that Chángshā Lìwáng (長沙厲王) and Huángfǔ Shāng (皇甫商) had died.
The death of Chángshā Lìwáng (長沙厲王)
is found in the previous volume, previous year.
The death of Huángfǔ Shāng (皇甫商)
is found in the previous volume, Tàiiān (太安) Second Year.
Xiān (先)
has the pronunciation of 'xī jiàn fān'.
When the Imperial Censor (Yùshǐ 御史) came to promulgate the edict,
they captured his attendants (zōu rén 騶人).
Zōu (騶)
has the pronunciation of 'cè jiū fān',
meaning 'one who drives a carriage'.
According to the Jìn (晉) regulations,
all dukes were allotted eight attendants (zōu 騶),
and down to the Imperial Censors (Yùshǐ 御史),
each had a different number.
Qíwáng Róng (齊王融) said:
“If there are no eight attendants (zōu 騶) in front of the carriage,
how can one be called a man of substance?!”
Thus, attendants (zōu 騶) were presumably soldiers who cleared the way for carriages.
“Is my younger brother leading troops here,
and has he arrived yet?”
The attendant (zōu rén 騶人) replied:
“He has already been killed by Héjiānwáng (河間王).”
Chóng (重) changed color and
immediately killed the attendant (zōu rén 騶人).
Thereupon, the people in the city knew there was no outside help,
so they jointly killed Chóng (重) and surrendered to Yóng (顒).
Zhāng Fǔ (張輔), the Administrator of Fēngyì (馮翊), was made Inspector of Qínzhōu (秦州).
Yóng (顒) appointed Zhāng Fǔ (張輔) for his achievement in defeating Liú Shěn (劉沈).
3. Sixth month,
Jiǎzǐ (甲子),
Wáng Róng (王戎), the Yuánhóu (元侯) of Ānfēng (安豐), died in Jiá (郟).
Wáng Róng (王戎) fleeing to Jiá (郟)
is found in the previous volume, previous year.
Jiá (郟)
has the pronunciation of 'jiá'.
4. Zhāng Fǔ (張輔) arrived in Qínzhōu (秦州)
and killed Fēng Shàng (封尚), the Administrator of Tiānshuǐ (天水),
intending to establish his authority.
He also summoned Hán Zhì (韓稚), the Administrator of Lǒngxī (隴西).
Zhì's (稚) son, Pǔ (朴), raised troops to attack Fǔ (輔).
Fǔ's (輔) army was defeated,
and he died.
Yáng Yìn (楊胤), the Sīmǎ (司馬) of Liángzhōu (涼州), said to Zhāng Guǐ (張軌):
“Hán Zhì (韓稚) murdered the Inspector (Cìshǐ 刺史).
You, Illustrious Duke (Mínggōng 明公), wield a battle-axe in this region,
and must not fail to punish him.”
Guǐ (軌) agreed and
sent Zhōng Dūhù (中督護) Fàn Yuàn (氾瑗) to lead twenty thousand men to attack Zhì (稚).
Zhì (稚) went to Guǐ (軌) and surrendered.
Zhōng Dūhù (中督護)
is Zhōngjūn Dūhù (中軍督護).
Fàn (氾)
has the pronunciation of 'fán'.
Yuàn (瑗)
has the pronunciation of 'yú juàn fān'.
Shuài (帥)
is read as 'lǜ' (率);
same below.
The Xiānbēi (鮮卑) Ruòluóbá Nànéng (若羅拔能) raided Liángzhōu (涼州).
Guǐ (軌) sent Sīmǎ (司馬) Sòng Pèi (宋配) to attack him,
beheaded Bá Nànéng (拔能),
captured over one hundred thousand people,
and his renown greatly spread.
Historians say that Zhāng Guǐ (張軌) was able to honor the sovereign and repel barbarians, thus achieving strength and prosperity.
5. Hànwáng Yuān (漢王淵) attacked Dōngyínggōng Téng (東嬴公騰).
Téng (騰) again sought aid from Tuòbá Yītuō (拓跋猗㐌).
Wèi Cāo (衞操) persuaded Yītuō (猗㐌) to assist him.
Yītuō (猗㐌) led several thousand light cavalry to rescue Téng (騰),
and beheaded the Hàn (漢) general Qímú Tún (綦毋豚).
An imperial edict granted Yītuō (猗㐌) the title of Dà Chányú (大單于)
and made Cāo (操) the Right General (Yòujiāngjūn 右將軍).
Jiǎshēn (甲申),
Yītuō (猗㐌) died.
His son, Pǔgēn (普根), succeeded him.
6. Liú Qià (劉洽), the Zhōngwèi (中尉) of Dōnghǎi (東海), considered that Zhāng Fāng (張方) had forcefully moved the imperial carriage.
In Jìn (晉) princely states, the Lángzhōnglìng (郎中令), Zhōngwèi (中尉), and Dànóng (大農) were the three ministers (Sānqīng 三卿).
The matter of Zhāng Fāng (張方) forcefully moving the imperial carriage is found in the previous volume, previous year.
Autumn,
Seventh month,
Yuè (越) sent a circular to the generals (Zhēng, Zhèn 征、鎮), provinces (Zhōu 州), and commanderies (Jùn 郡) east of the mountains, saying:
“I wish to gather righteous armies,
welcome the Son of Heaven,
and restore the old capital.”
The old capital (Jiùdū 舊都)
refers to Luòyáng (洛陽).
Máo (楙) was afraid.
His Chief Clerk (Chángshǐ 長史) Wáng Xiū (王脩) persuaded Máo (楙), saying:
“Dōnghǎi (東海) is a prominent and respected member of the imperial clan;
now that he is raising a righteous army,
you, Duke, should offer Xúzhōu (徐州) to him.
This will save you from disaster,
and you will also gain the merit of yielding.”
Máo (楙) followed this advice.
Yuè (越) then made the Sīkōng (司空) concurrently serve as the Dūdū (都督) of Xúzhōu (徐州).
Máo (楙) appointed himself Inspector (Cìshǐ 刺史) of Yǎnzhōu (兗州).
An edict immediately dispatched the envoy Liú Qián (劉虔) to grant this.
Máo (楙) was appointed Dūdū (都督) of Xúzhōu (徐州)
starting from volume 84, Yǒngníng (永寧) First Year.
Last year,
Fànyángwáng Xiāo (范陽王虓) had made Gǒu Xī (苟晞) acting governor of Yǎnzhōu (兗州).
Xī (晞) remained in Xǔchāng (許昌)
and had not yet reached the province,
so Máo (楙) took charge himself.
Yuè's (越) brothers also held important positions.
Yuè's (越) younger brother Lüè (略) was Dūdū (都督) of Qīngzhōu (青州),
and Mó (模) was Dūdū (都督) of Jìzhōu (冀州).
When Wáng Jùn (王浚) and others jointly proclaimed Yuè (越) as their alliance leader,
Yuè (越) took it upon himself to appoint Inspectors (Cìshǐ 刺史) and other officials.
Zhé (輒)
means 'exclusively' (專).
The court officials who went to Yuè (越)
were those who did not follow the Emperor to Cháng'ān (長安).
Cháo (朝)
has the pronunciation of 'zhí yáo fān'.
7 Chéngdū Wáng Yǐng had been deposed.
The deposition of Yǐng is described in the previous volume, last year.
Yǐng garrisoned Yè,
and at first had a good reputation;
later, although his arrogance and extravagance led to disaster,
the people of Hébĕi, weary of chaos and remembering the past,
mostly pitied him.
He raised troops in Zhào and Wèi,
their numbers reaching several tens of thousands.
Initially,
Shí Lè (a Jié man from Wǔxiāng in Shàngdǎng),
possessed courage and strength,
and was skilled in horsemanship and archery.
Wǔxiāng county
was established by the Jìn and
belonged to Shàngdǎng commandery;
later Shí Lè partitioned it to establish Wǔxiāng commandery.
Liú Xù said: The Wǔxiāng county of Táng Lùzhōu
was the Yuán county of Hàn Hédōng.
Táng Liáozhōu Yúshè county
was partitioned from Jìn Wǔxiāng county.
The Zàijì states: Lè
was a descendant of Qiāngqú, a separate branch of the Xiōngnú.
The Xiōngnú Zhuàn also says: Among the Northern Dí who moved into the area within the passes,
there were nineteen types,
and the Jié were one of them.
Jié
is read as 'juē'.
Jiànwēi Jiāngjūn Yán Suì advised Dōngyíng Gōng Téng
to seize the various Hú people in Shāndōng
and sell them to augment military supplies.
Lè was also seized,
and sold as a slave to Shī Huān of Chí píng.
Chípíng county
belonged to Dōngjùn in the Former Hàn,
to Jìbĕi Guó in the Later Hàn,
and to Píngyuán Guó in the Jìn.
Yīng Shào said: It is on the flat land of Mount Chí.
It is thought that its location should be on the border of Táng Qízhōu and Bózhōu.
Liú Xù said: Chípíng county was incorporated into Táng Bózhōu Liáochéng county.
Bèi
is read as 'píyì'.
Shīgǔ said: Chí
is pronounced 'shìyí'.
Huān's family was near a horse pasture,
so Lè and the pasture chief Jí Sāng gathered strong men to form a band of robbers.
When Gōng Shīfān rose,
Sāng and Lè led several hundred cavalry to join him.
Sāng first ordered Lè to take Shí as his surname,
and Lè as his given name.
Shí Lè began here.
They killed officials of two thousand dàns and magistrates,
advanced,
and attacked Yè.
Píngchāng Gōng Mó was greatly alarmed;
Fányáng Wáng Xiāo sent his general Gǒu Xī to relieve Yè,
and together with Guǎngpíng Tàishǒu Qiáoguó Dīng Shào, they attacked Fān,
who fled.
Hàn Wǔdì established Pínggān Guó,
which Xuāndì renamed Guǎngpíng Guó;
Hàn Guāngwǔ later abolished it and made it part of Jùlù commandery;
Wèi Wéndì in Huángchū second year re-established Guǎngpíng commandery;
in the Táng it was the land of Míngzhōu.
8 In the eighth month,
on the day Xīnchǒu,
a general amnesty was proclaimed.
9 Sīkōng Yuè appointed Lángyé Wáng Ruì as Píngdōng Jiāngjūn,
supervising all military affairs of Xúzhōu,
and to remain garrisoned at Xiàpéi.
Ruì requested Wáng Dǎo to be his Sīmǎ,
and entrusted military affairs to him.
The Kǎoyì states: Dǎo's biography says:
"Yuándì, when garrisoned at Xiàpéi,
requested Dǎo to be Ándōng Sīmǎ."
However, Yuándì was Píngdōng at that time,
and only became Ándōng when he moved to Yángzhōu.
Perhaps the character
"Píng"
was mistakenly written as
"Ān",
or he later became Ándōng Sīmǎ,
so it just says Sīmǎ.
He moved his garrison west to Xiāoxiàn;
Xiāoxiàn
belonged to Pèijùn from the Hàn dynasty onwards,
and to Xúzhōu in the Táng.
Xǔ
is Xǔchāng.
He appointed Fányáng Wáng Xiāo to lead as Yùzhōu Cìshǐ;
Qíao, asserting that Xiāo was not appointed by the Son of Heaven,
dispatched troops to resist him.
Xiāo appointed Liú Kūn as Sīmǎ,
and Yuè appointed Liú Fān as Huáibĕi Hùjūn,
and Liú Yú as Yǐngchuān Tàishǒu.
Yú and Kūn
were Fān's sons.
He listed the crimes of the Yú brothers,
and then led his army to attack Xǔ,
while the Yùzhōu Cìshǐ at that time governed Xiàng.
Shàng
is read as 'shípáng'.
Yuè's forces could not advance.
Dōngpíng Wáng Máo, in Yǎnzhōu,
made incessant demands,
which the commanderies and counties could not bear.
Fányáng Wáng Xiāo sent Gǒu Xī back to Yǎnzhōu;
Xiāo had appointed Gǒu Xī as Yǎnzhōu Cìshǐ,
as mentioned in the previous volume, last year.
Máo did not accept the order,
turned against the various lords of Shāndōng,
and allied with Liú Qiáo.
10 Tàizǎi Yǒng heard that troops had risen in Shāndōng
and was greatly alarmed.
Because Gōng Shīfān had raised troops for Chéngdū Wáng Yǐng,
on the day Rénwǔ,
he memorialized to appoint Yǐng as Zhèn Jūn Dà Jiāngjūn, Dūdu Hébĕi Zhū Jūnshì,
and granted him a thousand soldiers;
he appointed Lú Zhì as Wèijùn Tàishǒu,
to accompany Yǐng in garrisoning Yè,
hoping to pacify him.
He also sent Jiànwǔ Jiāngjūn Lǚ Láng to garrison Luòyáng.
Yǒng issued an edict
ordering Dōnghǎi Wáng Yuè and others to return to their states,
but Yuè and others did not comply.
It so happened that he received Liú Qiáo's report.
The report
concerned Dōnghǎi Wáng Yuè and others raising troops, and Qiáo attacking Xǔ to resist Yuè.
Shàng
is read as 'shípáng'.
In the tenth month,
on the day Bǐngzǐ,
an edict was issued stating:
"Liú Yú coerced Fányáng Wáng Xiāo
and concocted a heinous rebellion.
Therefore, order Zhènnán Dà Jiāngjūn Liú Hóng,
Liú Hóng supervised Jīngzhōu.
Péngchéng Wáng Shì (replacing Yáng Yī) to garrison Wǎn.
Liú Zhǔn to supervise Yángzhōu.
To combine forces with Liú Qiáo;
appoint Zhāng Fāng as Dà Dūdu,
to command a hundred thousand elite soldiers,
and together with Lǚ Láng, assemble at Xǔchāng,
to execute the Yú brothers."
Shì
was the grandson of Mù Wáng Quán, a nephew of Xuāndì.
Quán
was the son of Dōngwǔchéng Hóu Kuí, Xuāndì's brother.
The Kǎoyì states: In Liú Qiáo's biography,
"Shì"
is written as
"Yì".
The Dìjì and Zōngshì Zhuàn all write
"Shì",
so the Qiáo biography is likely mistaken.
The Dìjì states:
"In the eighth month,
Chēqí Dà Jiāngjūn Liú Hóng drove Píngnán Jiāngjūn Péngchéng Wáng Shì from Wǎn."
The biographies of Hóng, Shì, and other books do not contain this.
Hóng's biography only says that Péngchéng previously fled east and made unfavorable remarks.
However, Hóng was a loyal minister of the Jìn court;
when Liú Qiáo and Fányáng were in conflict,
Hóng still tried to reconcile them through letters
to stabilize the realm
and honor the imperial house.
Shì received the royal command to garrison Wǎn,
so would Hóng really drive him out?
Based on this,
the edict ordered Hóng and Shì to jointly suppress Liú Yú,
so it is doubtful that Hóng drove Shì out.
The Dìjì must be mistaken.
On the day Dīngchǒu,
Yǒng dispatched Chéngdū Wáng Yǐng to lead Jiāngjūn Liú
Bāo and others,
and former Chēqí Jiāngjūn Shí Chāo to lead Běi Zhōngláng Jiāng Wáng Chǎn and others to occupy Héquiáo,
to provide reinforcements for Liú Qiáo;
he promoted Qiáo to Zhèndōng Jiāngjūn
and granted him imperial authority.
Liú Hóng (劉弘) sent a letter to Qíao (喬) and Sīkōng Yuè (司空越),
wishing for them to reconcile their grievances and cease hostilities,
and together assist the imperial court.
Both refused to listen.
Hóng (弘) then submitted a memorial, saying:
"Since the recent times of chaotic warfare,
suspicion and calamity have arisen,
doubts and rifts have been formed among the princes,
and disasters have extended to the imperial clan.
Today one is loyal,
tomorrow one is rebellious.
How quickly things turn around!
It is said that right and wrong change easily.
The affairs of Jiǒng (冏), Yì (乂), Yǐng (穎), and Yóng (顒) are indeed like this.
It is said that they successively became the instigators of war.
There has never been such a calamity among kin as there is today.
I secretly grieve over this!
Now the borders lack preparedness and reserves,
and the central plains suffer from the difficulty of empty looms.
The *Shī* (詩) says: 'The Lesser East, the Greater East,
their shuttles and axles are empty.'
Zhù (杼)
is the device that holds the weft.
'Zhóu' (軸)
is also written as
'Yóu' (柚);
both are weaving tools.

People say you know about it.
If the King asks you,
how will you respond?"
Fǔ was startled and said:
"I truly have not heard that Fāng is rebelling.
What should I do?"
Yuán said:
"If the King asks you,
just say 'yes, yes';
'yes, yes'
means 'it is so, it is so'.
Otherwise, you will not escape disaster."
Fǔ entered,
and Yǒng asked him:
"Zhāng Fāng is rebelling,
do you know about it?"
Fǔ said:
"Yes."
Yǒng said:
"If I send you to apprehend him,
is that possible?"
He again said:
"Yes."
Yǒng then had Fǔ deliver a letter to Fāng,
and consequently kill him.
As Fǔ was close to Fāng,
he entered with a knife,
and the guards did not suspect him.
Fāng opened the letter under a lamp,
and Fǔ chopped off his head.
Upon his return and report,
Yǒng appointed Fǔ as Administrator of Āndìng.
He sent Fāng's head to
Yuè to request peace;
Yuè did not agree.
Sòng Zhòu attacked Héquiáo,

Píngchāng Gōng Mó dispatched Front-line Inspector Féng Sōng to join Sòng Zhòu in pressing towards Luòyáng.
Chéngdū Wáng Yǐng fled west to Cháng'ān,
and upon reaching Huáyīn,
Huáyīn county
belonged to Jīngzhào in the Former Hàn,

Huá is pronounced as Hùhuà fān.
He halted and dared not advance.
Lǚ Láng was garrisoned at Xíngyáng.
