4 Níngzhōu suffered from famine and plague for several consecutive years,

The Wǔlíng Yí were strong and prosperous,

The Wǔlíng Yí rebelled;
this matter began in the previous volume, in the second year of Tàiyán.
Líng
is pronounced lìdīng.
The Yí then besieged the provincial capital.
Lǐ Yì fell ill,

He then submitted a memorial

"I cannot contain the tyrannical bandits

If you do not show compassion,

While I am still alive,

If I am already dead,

The imperial court did not respond.
After several years,
his son Zhāo traveled from Luò to visit him.
Before he arrived,
Yì died.
Yì's daughter Xiù
was intelligent and had her father's demeanor.
The populace elected Xiù to lead the affairs of Níngzhōu.
Xiù encouraged her warriors

When food ran out in the city,
they roasted rats and ate pulled grass.
When they observed the Yí becoming slightly negligent,
they would sally forth to raid and attack,
defeating them.
5 Fàn Chángshēng went to Chéngdū;

Holding a tablet,

6 Summer,
fourth month,
jǐsì,
Sīkōng Yuè led his troops to garrison Wēn.
Initially,
Grand Tutor Yóng believed that with Zhāng Fāng's death,

Yóng regretted this,

Fifth month,
rénchén,

Yóng fled alone on horseback into Tàibái Mountain.
The Sānqín Jì states: Tàibái Mountain

"Wǔgōng Tàibái,
three hundred *lǐ* from heaven."
The Xīn Táng Shū Dìlǐ Zhì states: Tàibái Mountain is in Méi County, Fèngxiáng Prefecture.
His subordinate Xiānbēi greatly plundered,

All officials scattered and fled

Jǐhài,
Hóng and others escorted the Emperor, riding in an ox-cart, back east.
The Jìn Zhì states: In ancient times, the noble did not ride in ox-carts.
After Emperor Wǔ of Hàn extended favors,
the feudal lords became weak and few,
even riding in ox-carts.
Thereafter, they gradually became highly valued.
From Emperor Líng onwards,
from the Son of Heaven to the scholars,
it became a common mode of transport.
Indeed, when the Son of Heaven went out, there were the grand imperial retinue, the ceremonial retinue, and the imperial guard.
When the Emperor fled from Yè to Luò,
he rode in a calf-cart.
When he returned from Cháng'ān to Luò,
he rode in an ox-cart.
There was no longer the system of escort and clearing the way for departure and entry.
They held Guānzhōng.
Sixth month,
bǐngchén *shuò*,

According to Fāng's biography, his head had arrived long ago,

Xīnwèi
there was a great amnesty

Xióng (雄),
courtesy name Zhòngjùn (仲雋),

An examination of discrepancies states: The Jìn Dìjì (晉帝紀) and Sānshí Guó Jìn Chūnqiū (三十國晉春秋)
both say:
“In the sixth month of Yǒngxīng (永興) second year,

Huáyáng Guózhì (華陽國志):
“In Guāngxī (光熙) first year,
Xióng (雄) ascended the imperial throne.”
The Hòu Wèishū Xùjì (後魏書序紀) and Lǐ Xióng Zhuàn (李雄傳)
both say
“in Zhāodì (昭帝) twelfth year,
Xióng (雄) proclaimed himself emperor,”
which is Guāngxī (光熙) first year.
Shíliù Guó Chūnqiū Chāo (十六國春秋鈔):
“In the sixth month of Yànpíng (晏平) first year,
Xióng (雄) ascended the imperial throne.”
Shíliù Guó Chūnqiū Mùlù (十六國春秋目錄),
regarding Xióng’s (雄) era names,
lists Jiànxīng (建興) for two years
and Yànpíng (晏平) for five years,
which is consistent with Huáyáng Guózhì (華陽國志);
we follow this now.
Various texts
state that Xióng (雄) changed his era name to Yànpíng (晏平),
without a Dàwǔ (大武) era name;
only the Jìn Zàijì (晉載記) lists the era name Dàwǔ (大武),
without Yànpíng (晏平).
According to Xióng’s (雄) dynastic title Dàchéng (大成).
The Wèishū Xióng Zhuàn (魏書雄傳) states:
“Xióng (雄) proclaimed himself emperor,
titled his dynasty Dàchéng (大成),
and changed the era name to Yànpíng (晏平).”
Therefore, the Sānshí Guó Chūnqiū (三十國春秋) mistakenly says
“changed the year to Dàchéng (大成),”
and in the transcription of the Zàijì (載記),
it was mistakenly written as
“Dàwǔ (大武).”
Now, following various texts, we remove
the title of
“Dàwǔ (大武).”
His temple name was Shǐzǔ (始祖);

Xióng’s (雄) mother, Lady Luó (羅),

That a Grand Tutor would claim the title of Heaven and Earth,

All were exempt from taxes.

Piào (驃),

13In winter,
in the tenth month,

Chángshǐ Liú Yú (長史劉輿), knowing

At night,
he granted Yǐng (穎) death,

Yǐng’s (穎) officials had all fled and dispersed beforehand,

Tàifù Yuè (太傅越) summoned Zhì (志) to be Jūnzī Jìjiǔ (軍諮祭酒).
Yuè (越) was about to summon Liú Yú (劉輿),

“Yú (輿) is like grease;

When he arrived,
Yuè (越) kept him at a distance.
Yú (輿) secretly examined the national military registers, as well as the warehouses, cattle, horses, weaponry, and the topography of land and water,
and memorized them all.
At that time, military and state affairs were numerous,
and every time a meeting was held,
from Chángshǐ Pān Tāo (長史潘滔) downwards,

Yú (輿) was quick to analyze and strategize,
“biàn” (辨) refers to analyzing matters;
“huà” (畫) refers to planning for them.
He was immediately appointed Zuǒ Chángshǐ (左長史),

Yú (輿) persuaded Yuè (越) to send his younger brother Kūn (琨) to garrison Bīngzhōu (并州),

at night,

On the day Gēngwǔ,

Fearing she would not become Empress Dowager,

pronounced hù huà.)

Emperor Huái initially followed the old system,
holding court in the Eastern Hall.

was the Eastern Hall of the Tàijí Palace.)
He regularly discussed all affairs with the officials,

Huángmén Shìláng Fù Xuān sighed, saying:

15 In the twelfth month,
on the day Rénwǔ shūo,

strangled him,

was Yuè's younger brother.)

(Xīn'ān County,

19 Liú Kūn arrived at Shàngdǎng,

refers to Liú Yuān's faction.)
(Shù,
pronounced suǒ jué.)
The provincial generals Tián Zhēn, Zhēn's younger brother Lán, Rèn Zhǐ, Qí Jì, Lǐ Yùn, Báo Shèng, and others
(Provincial generals
refers to the various generals of Bīngzhōu.)
(Jiāng,
pronounced jì liàng.)
(Zhēn,
pronounced jī yán.)
(Rèn,
pronounced rén.)
(Yùn,
pronounced yú fěn.)
all followed Téng to seek provisions in Jìzhōu,

Yǒngjiā First Year
(Dīngmǎo, 307)
1 Spring,
first month,
on the day Guǐchǒu,
a general amnesty was issued,
and the reign era was changed.
2 Lìbù Láng Zhōu Mù,
who was the nephew of Grand Tutor Yuè's aunt,
together with his brother-in-law Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng Zhūgě Méi
advised Yuè, saying:
"The present sovereign's being Imperial Younger Brother
was Zhāng Fāng's intention.
(After Chéngdū Wáng Yǐng was deposed,
Héjiān Wáng Yóng established the Emperor as Imperial Younger Brother,
thus it was considered Zhāng Fāng's intention.)
Qīnghé Wáng
was established as Crown Prince by Qí Wáng Jiǒng,
and has been deposed several times."
Yuè did not agree.
When they repeated it,
Yuè became angry
and had them executed.
3 In the second month,
Wáng Mí raided Qīng and Xú two provinces,
proclaimed himself Commander-in-Chief of the Expedition to the East,
and attacked and killed two thousand-picul officials.
Grand Tutor Yuè appointed Gōngchē Lìng Jū Xiàn of Dōnglái as the Administrator of his home commandery.
(Jìn Zhì:
Gōngchē Lìng
belonged to the Wèiwèi.)
Mí attacked and killed him.
4 Chén Mǐn's administration was without order,
and he was not supported by the heroes;
his sons and nephews were violent,
causing trouble everywhere;
Gù Róng, Zhōu Děng, and others worried about this.
Lújiāng Nèishǐ Huá Tán sent a letter to Róng and others, saying:
"Chén Mǐn has seized Wú and Kuàijī,
his life is as precarious as morning dew.
(This means his life is like morning dew clinging to grass,
which dries up as soon as the sun appears,
and cannot last long.)
(Huá,
pronounced hù huà.)
(Yí,
pronounced yú jì.)
Or are you arrayed as close ministers,
yet debase yourselves in the court of a treacherous man,
lowering your status to join a rebellious faction?
Is this not shameful!
The father and son of Wú Wǔliè all possessed heroic talent,
inheriting the great enterprise.
(Wú posthumously titled Sūn Jiān as Wǔliè Emperor.)
A stubborn boy,
wishes to follow the lofty path of King Huán,
and tread the unparalleled track of the Great Emperor.
(Sūn Cè was posthumously titled King Huán of Chángshā,
Sūn Quán was posthumously titled Great Emperor.)
(Yǐ,
pronounced ér lǒng.)
(Niè,
pronounced ní zhé.)
Even so, it should not be permitted.
The imperial chariot has returned east,
(meaning from Cháng'ān back to Luòyáng.)
(Talent exceeding a thousand people is called Jùn.)
(Yàn,
a handsome gentleman.)
How will you worthies face the scholars of the Central Plains again!"
Róng and others had long harbored thoughts of overthrowing Mǐn,
and upon receiving the letter,
felt deeply ashamed.
They secretly sent an envoy to inform Zhēngdōng Dàjiāngjūn Liú Zhǔn,
asking him to send troops to the river,
and they would act as an internal confederate,
cutting their hair as a token of sincerity.
Zhǔn sent Yángzhōu Cìshǐ Liú Jī and others to Lìyáng to attack Mǐn.
Mǐn ordered his younger brother, Guǎngwǔ Jiāngjūn Chǎng, to lead tens of thousands of soldiers to garrison Wūjiāng.
(Shěn Yuē Zhì: Guǎngwǔ Jiāngjūn,
was established by the Jìn south of the Yangtze.
It likely began at this time.)
(The Jìn dynasty established Wūjiāng County,
which belonged to Huáinán Commandery,
named after the place where the Wūjiāng Pavilion chief moored a boat awaiting Xiàng Yǔ.)
(Sòng Bái says: Wūjiāng County,
was the territory of Hàn Dōngchéng County.
In the sixth year of Jìn Tàikāng
it was first established as Wūjiāng County within Dōngchéng's borders.)
(Chǎng,
pronounced chǒu liǎng.)
Mǐn's younger brother Chǔ knew that Gù Róng and others had disloyal intentions,
and advised Mǐn to kill them,
but Mǐn did not follow.
(Kǎoyì says: Mǐn's biography states:
"His younger brother Chǎng advised killing Róng.")
(However, Jìn Chūnqiū states:
"When Mǐn was about to die, he said to Chǔ: 'I have failed you!'")
(At that time, Chǎng had already died.)
(Now we follow Jìn Chūnqiū.)
Chǎng’s Sīmǎ, Qián Guǎng,
was from Zhōu’s home commandery.
Mì secretly ordered Guǎng to kill Chǎng,
and declared throughout the prefecture that Mǐn had already been killed.
The Yángzhōu Cìshǐ governed from Jiànyè,
so Jiànyè was called “the prefecture.”
Guǎng assembled troops south of Zhūquèqiáo;
Zhūquèqiáo was south of the palace city in Jiànyè,
spanning the Qínhuái River.
It is traditionally said that Jìn Xiàowǔ built Zhūquè Mén,
which had two bronze sparrows on it,
hence the bridge also got its name from this.
I believe Zhūquèqiáo existed since the Wú dynasty,
probably deriving its meaning from “front Vermilion Bird,”
and that this name did not originate during the time of Jìn Xiàowǔ.
Zhūquèqiáo
was also called Dàhéng.
All heavily armored and elite soldiers were entrusted to him.
Gù Róng, fearing Mǐn’s suspicion,
therefore went to Mǐn.
Mǐn said:
“You should go out to the four directions to guard,”
meaning to pacify the hearts of the people,
which is how he would protect Mǐn.
Róng then left
and, with Zhōu, persuaded Gān Zhuó, saying:
“If the affair in Jiāngdōng can succeed,
we should work together to achieve it.
However, looking at the current situation,
can it possibly succeed?
Mǐn is but an ordinary talent,
his political orders are erratic and contradictory,
and his plans are undecided.
His sons and younger brothers are already arrogant and presumptuous;
his defeat is certain.
If we merely sit idly and accept his official stipends,
on the day the affair fails,
we will cause the various armies of Jiāngxī to send our heads in boxes to Luòyáng.
The various armies of Jiāngxī refer to those sent by Liú Zhǔn to oversee the Jiāng River.
This would be a disgrace for ten thousand generations!”
Zhuó then feigned illness,
welcomed his daughter,
broke the bridge,
and collected boats on the south bank.
The bridge
was Zhūquèqiáo.
Jiànyè city was north of the Qínhuái River,
so Zhuó collected boats along the south bank.
Duàn (斷)
is pronounced Dīng Guǎn.
Sōngzī County,
belonged to Lújiāng Commandery,
and was abolished in the Late Hàn;
in the Jìn, it belonged to Ānfēng Commandery.
Liú Xù said: Táng’s Shòuzhōu Huòshān County
was the land of Hàn’s Sōngzī County.
The current Jiānglíngfǔ Sōngzī County
is the land of Wú’s Lèxiāng.
After the Jìn clan moved south,
they established Sōngzī County by relocating Sōngzī refugees;
it is not the ancient Sōngzī.
Mǐn himself led over ten thousand men to attack Zhuó.
The soldiers across the water spoke to Mǐn’s troops, saying:
“The reason we initially exerted ourselves for Chén Gōng
was precisely because of Gù Dānyáng and Zhōu Ānfēng!
Mǐn appointed Gù Róng as Dānyáng Tàishǒu and Zhōu as Ānfēng Tàishǒu,
hence they are referred to as such.
Shuài (帥)
is read as Shuài.
Yǔ (語)
is pronounced Niú Jù.
What are you doing?!”
Mǐn’s troops were hesitant and undecided.
Róng waved a white feather fan,
a white feather fan
was made by weaving white feathers.
Mǐn fled north alone on horseback,
was pursued and captured at Jiāngchéng,
and sighed, saying:
“These men misled me,
bringing me to this day!”
He said to his younger brother, Chǔ:
“I have wronged you;
you have not wronged me!”
This meant he did not follow Chǔ’s advice to kill Gù Róng and others.
His three clans were exterminated.
Thereupon, the commanderies of Kuàijī and others
all killed Mǐn’s younger brothers.
At this time, Píngdōng Jiāngjūn Zhōu Fù replaced Liú Zhǔn in guarding Shòuchūn.
In the third month,
on the first day of Jǐwèi,
Fù sent Mǐn’s head to the capital.
An imperial edict summoned Gù Róng as Shìzhōng,
and Jì Zhān as Shàngshū Láng.
Tàifù Yuè appointed Zhōu as Cānjūn
and Lù Wán as Yuàn.
Wán
was Jī’s cousin.
Róng and others reached Xúzhōu,
heard that the north was becoming more chaotic,
and hesitated to proceed.
Yuè wrote to Xúzhōu Cìshǐ Péi Dùn, saying:
“If Róng and others look around indecisively,
dispatch them with military ceremony!”
Róng and others, fearing,
escaped back.
Dùn
was Kǎi’s nephew
and Yuè’s brother.
Xīyáng barbarians attacked Jiāngxià.
Xīyáng County,
in the Spring and Autumn period, was the state of Xiánzǐ,
in the Hàn, it was a county
belonging to Jiāngxià Commandery,
in the Jìn, it belonged to Yìyáng Commandery.
At the end of Hàn Hédì’s Yǒngyuán era,
the Wū barbarians rebelled,
were suppressed and surrendered,
and then relocated to Jiāngxià;
these were the Xīyáng various barbarians.
Shěn Yuē said: Jìn Huìdì divided Yìyáng to establish Xīyáng State.
Liú Xù said: Wú divided Jiāngxià
and established Qīchūn Commandery;
Jìn changed it to Xīyáng Commandery,
and Táng’s Qīzhōu was its territory.
Sòng Bái said: Guāngzhōu Guāngshān County
was originally Hàn’s Xīyáng County.
Xià (夏)
is pronounced Hù Yǎ.
All the generals vied to present strategies,
but the cavalry commander, Zhū Sī, alone remained silent.
Mín asked:
“Why does General Zhū not speak?”
Sī replied:
“Others attack the bandits with their tongues;
I only use strength.”
Mín further asked:
“General, why have you always been victorious in your previous battles against bandits?”
Sī replied:
“When two enemies confront each other,
one must simply endure;
if they cannot endure,
and I can endure,
that is how I win.”
Mín praised him.
In all battles, if one does not use wisdom and ingenuity to achieve victory through surprise,
but instead contends with strength against strength,
there is no better approach than Zhū Sī’s advice.
An imperial edict restored the honorary title of Empress Dowager Yáng;
on Dīngmǎo,
she was reburied
and posthumously titled Wǔdào.
Empress Yáng suffered misfortune,
as seen in Volume 82, Yuánkāng first year of Emperor Huì.
On Gēngwǔ,
Quán, Prince of Yùzhāng, younger brother of Tán, Prince of Qīnghé, was established as Crown Prince.
On Xīnwèi,
a general amnesty was declared.
The Emperor
observed
and managed major state affairs,
paying close attention to various matters;
Tàifù Yuè was displeased
and insisted on being dispatched to a regional command.
On Gēngchén,
Yuè was dispatched to guard Xǔchāng.
This laid the groundwork for Yuè to kill Miù Bō and others.
Luè, Prince of Gāomì, was appointed Zhēngnán Dàjiāngjūn,
Grand Governor of military affairs in Jīngzhōu,
and stationed in Xiāngyáng;
Mó, Prince of Nányáng, was appointed Zhēngxī Dàjiāngjūn,
Grand Governor of military affairs in Qín, Yōng, Liáng, and Yì,
and stationed in Cháng'ān;
Téng, Prince of Dōngyàn, was made Prince of Xīncài,
Grand Governor of military affairs in Sī and Jì prefectures,
and remained stationed in Yè.
Last year, Téng moved from Bīngzhōu to guard Yè.
When Gōng Shī-Fān was already dead,
Jí Sāng fled back to the imperial stables in Yuàn-zhōng.
Chíf-píng was a pasture for the imperial stables.
Sāng had raised troops here to assist Gōng Shī-Fān.
After Fān died,
he fled back.
He proclaimed himself Grand General (Dà Jiāngjūn),
declaring he would avenge Chéngdū-wáng.
He made Shí Lè his vanguard,
conquering everywhere he went.
He appointed Lè as General
Who Quells Barbarians (Tǎolǔ Jiāngjūn),
and then advanced to attack Yè.
At that time, the treasuries in Yè were empty,
but Xīncài Wǔ'āi-wáng Téng had ample resources.
Téng was parsimonious,
offering no generosity or charity.
In a moment of crisis,
he only bestowed a few sheng of rice
and a zhang and chi of silk to each soldier,
which is why people would not serve him.
In summer,
the fifth month,
Sāng greatly defeated Fēng Sōng, the Administrator of Wèi-jùn,
and advanced directly into Yè.
Téng fled with light cavalry,
and was killed by Sāng's general Lǐ Fēng.
Sāng brought out the coffin of Chéngdū-wáng Yǐng.
When Yǐng died,
Lú Zhì had collected and interred him.
Now Sāng brought it out and loaded it onto a carriage.
He would consult the coffin before undertaking every matter.
He then burned the Yè palace,
the fire raging for ten days without extinguishing.
Yuán Shào, who occupied Yè,
had first begun building palaces and residences.
Wèi Wǔ-dì further expanded them.
By this time, they were all reduced to ashes.
He plundered extensively and then left.
He crossed the Jì River from Yán-jīn,
and attacked Yǎn-zhōu in the south.
The Grand Tutor (Tàifù) Yuè was greatly alarmed,
and sent Gǒu Xī and General (Jiāngjūn) Wáng Zàn to attack him.
The Qín-zhōu refugees Dèng Dìng and Hōng Dǐ and others occupied Chéng-gù,
and plundered Hàn-zhōng.
The Inspector (Cìshǐ) of Liáng-zhōu, Zhāng Yīn, sent the Administrator of Bāxī, Zhāng Yàn, to attack them.
Dèng Dìng and others, being in desperate straits,
feigned surrender to Yàn,
and also bribed him.
Yàn consequently delayed his forces.
Dìng secretly sent Hōng Dǐ to seek aid from Chéng.
The lord of Chéng, Xióng, sent Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi) Lí, Minister of Works (Sītú) Yún, and Minister of Education (Sīkōng) Huáng with twenty thousand troops to rescue Dìng.
They fought with Yàn,
and severely defeated him.
Zhāng Yīn and Dù Mèng-zhì, the Administrator of Hàn-zhōng, abandoned the city and fled.
After more than ten days,
Lí and others withdrew,
relocating all the people of Hàn-zhōng to Shǔ.
The Hàn-zhōng natives Jù Fāng and Bái Luò led officials and people back to guard Nánzhèng.
Shí Lè and Gǒu Xī and others were locked in a stalemate between Píngyuán and Yángpíng for several months,
engaging in over thirty battles, large and small,
with alternating victories and defeats.
In autumn,
the seventh month,
on the day Jǐ-yǒu (the first day of the month),
Grand Tutor (Tàifù) Yuè garrisoned Guāndù,
to provide support for Xī.
On the day Jǐ-wèi,

Lángxié-wáng Ruì was appointed General Who Pacifies the East (Āndōng Jiāngjūn), Overseer of All Military Affairs in Yáng-zhōu and Jiangnán (Dūdū Yángzhōu Jiāngnán Zhū Jūnshì), and Acting Imperial Envoy (Jiǎjié),
to be stationed at Jiànyè.
At this time, Zhōu Fù was stationed at Shòuchūn,
overseeing the areas north of the Yangtze in Yáng-zhōu.
Therefore, Ruì oversaw the areas south of the Yangtze in Yáng-zhōu.
A textual variant states: The Chronicle of Yuán-dì says:
"When Dōnghǎi-wáng Yuè moved his troops to Xiàpī,
he made the Emperor (Ruì) Overseer of Yáng-zhōu.
When Yuè went west to welcome the imperial carriage,
he left the Emperor to guard the area.
In early Yǒngjiā,
following Wáng Dǎo's plan,
he first garrisoned Jiànyè."
However, having been Overseer of Yáng-zhōu,
he should not still have been stationed at Xiàpī.
Moreover, the Chronicle of Huái-dì clearly states
"In the seventh month, on the day Jǐ-wèi,
Ruì was made Overseer of Yáng-zhōu,
and stationed at Jiànyè."
We follow this account.
In the eighth month,
on the day Jǐ-mǎo (the first day of the month),
Gǒu Xī attacked Jí Sāng at Dōngwǔyáng.
Dōngwǔyáng County
belonged to Dōng-jùn in the Hàn dynasty,
and to Yángpíng-jùn in the Wèi and Jìn dynasties.
Later, in the Wèi dynasty,
the character
"Dōng"
was removed, becoming Wǔyáng County.
In early Zhēngguān of the Táng dynasty,
Wǔyáng was abolished and merged into Xīn County of Wèi-zhōu.
In the seventh year of Kāiyuán,
it was re-established
and renamed Cháochéng County.
Dù Yòu said: To the south of Xīn County in Wèi-jùn lies Dōngwǔyáng city.
Sāng retreated and took refuge in Qīngyuān.
Qīngyuān County
belonged to Wèi-jùn in the Hàn dynasty.
Yīng Shào said: The Qīng-hé River is to the northwest of the county.
In the Jìn dynasty, it belonged to Yángpíng-jùn.
Later, in the Wèi dynasty, Línqīng County was established by division.
Later, in the Qí dynasty, Línqīng County was abolished and merged into Qīngyuān.
In the Táng dynasty, to avoid the given name of Gāo-zǔ,
Qīngyuān was renamed Línqīng,
and belonged to Bèi-zhōu.
Eight commanderies from Jīng-zhōu and Jiāng-zhōu were partitioned to form Xiāng-zhōu.

The Jìn Geographical Treatise states: The Emperor partitioned Hēngyáng, Chángshā, Xiāngdōng, Línglíng, Shàoyáng, Guìyáng from Jīng-zhōu, and Shǐ'ān, Shǐxīng, Línhè from Guǎng-zhōu, nine commanderies in total,
to establish Xiāng-zhōu.
The Imperial Chronicle states: Eight commanderies from Jīng and Jiāng were partitioned to form Xiāng-zhōu.
The Chronicle and Treatise contradict each other.
This account follows the Chronicle.
Shěn Yuè also said: Chángshā, Hēngyáng, Xiāngdōng, Shàolíng, Línglíng, Yíngyáng, Jiànchāng from Jīng-zhōu,
and Guìyáng from Jiāng-zhōu, a total of eight commanderies,
were established as Xiāng-zhōu.
In the ninth month,
on the day Wù-shēn,
Lángxié-wáng Ruì arrived in Jiànyè.
Ruì regarded Wáng Dǎo, the Chief Clerk (Sīmǎ) for the General Who Pacifies the East (Āndōng Jiāngjūn), as his chief strategist,
trusting him completely and consulting him on every matter.
Ruì's reputation had always been rather slight,
and the people of Wú did not attach themselves to him.
After he had resided there for a long time,
no gentry (shìdàfū) came to him.
Dǎo was concerned by this.
It happened that Ruì went out to observe the lustration ritual (xì).
Dǎo had Ruì ride in a sedan chair (jiānyú)
with full ceremonial regalia.
Dǎo and all the notable figures rode behind him.
Jì Zhān, Gù Róng, and others saw this and were greatly surprised.
They led others in bowing by the roadside.
Dǎo then persuaded Ruì, saying:
"Gù Róng and Hè Xún are the leading figures of this region.
You should attract them to win the hearts of the people.
Once these two men arrive,
there will be no one who does not come."
Ruì then had Dǎo personally visit Xún and Róng.
Both men answered the summons and came.
Xún was appointed Administrator of Wú-jùn (Wú-jùn Nèishǐ).
Róng was appointed Military Advisor (Jūnsī).
Jūnsī
is the same as Jūnsīmǎ.
The position was Jūnsī;
this was an additional appointment.
Both were consulted on military matters.
He also appointed Jì Zhān as Military
Libationer (Jìjiǔ),
Biàn Kǔn as Attendant Officer (Cóngshì Zhōngláng),
Zhōu as Master of Records for Granaries (Cāngcáo Shǔ),
and Liú Chāo of Lángxié as Imperial Attendant (Shèrén).
In the Jìn dynasty, each princely state had four Censors (Yèzhě),
six Grand Masters (Zhōngdàfū),
and ten Imperial Attendants (Shèrén).
Kǔn
was the son of Cuì.
Biàn Cuì can be found in the previous volume, under Emperor Huì's Tài'ān second year.
He was the great-grandson of Zhāo.
Zhāng Zhāo assisted Wú as a foundational minister.
"He treated scholars with humility,
used frugality to suffice for needs,
governed with clarity and tranquility,
and pacified both new and old people."
"New"
refers to those who came from the Central Plains;
"old"
refers to the people of Jiāngdōng.
Shuō (說) is pronounced "shū ruì."
When Ruì first arrived,
he somewhat neglected affairs due to wine.
Dǎo spoke to him about it.
Ruì ordered a drink poured,
and then overturned the cup.
From then on, he abstained.
Historians say that Emperor Yuán's ability to employ Wáng Dǎo was why he flourished in Jiāngzuǒ.
17 Gǒu Xī (苟晞) pursued Jí Sāng (汲桑),
destroying eight of his strongholds.
More than ten thousand people died.
Sāng (桑) and Shí Lè (石勒) gathered their remaining troops,
and were about to flee to Hàn (漢).
Dīng Shào (丁紹) of Qiáo (譙) Commandery, the Inspector of Jìzhōu (冀州), intercepted them at Chìqiáo (赤橋),
and defeated them again.
Sāng (桑) fled to Mǎmù (馬牧).
Mǎmù (馬牧) is in Chípíng (茌平).
The Jìn Zhì (晉志) states:
Yángpíng (陽平) Commandery has Lèpíng (樂平) County,
which was Qīng (清) County of Dōngjùn (東郡) during the Former Hàn (漢).
In the Later Hàn (漢), Emperor Zhāng (章) renamed it Lèpíng (樂平).
However, as Shí Lè (石勒) intended to flee to Hàn (漢),
this is not that Lèpíng (樂平).
Also, Bìngzhōu (幷州) has Lèpíng (樂平) Commandery,
established during the Tàishǐ (泰始) era of Emperor Wǔ (武).
It was Liáozhōu (遼州) in the Táng (唐) dynasty;
Lè (勒) fled here.
Gǒu Xī (苟晞) was promoted to General of the Army Protecting the State and Supervisor of All Military Affairs of Qīng (青) and Yǎn (兗) Provinces.
Dīng Shào (丁紹) was made General Who Pacifies the North and Superintendent of All Military Affairs of Jìzhōu (冀州).
Both were granted imperial credentials.
Xī (晞) repeatedly defeated strong bandits,
and his prestige was immense.
He was skilled at managing complex affairs
and was strict in applying the law.
His maternal cousin (from his mother's sister) relied on him,
and Xī (晞) provided for her very generously.
Her son asked to be a general,
but Xī (晞) refused,
saying:
"I do not exempt anyone from the royal law.
Won't you regret becoming a general!"
He insisted,
so Xī (晞) made him a Commandant.
Later, he broke the law,
and Xī (晞), holding his imperial credentials, beheaded him.
His maternal cousin kowtowed and begged for his life,
but Xī (晞) did not listen.
Afterward, he wore plain clothes and wept for him, saying:
"The one who killed you
is the Inspector of Yǎnzhōu (兗州);
the one who weeps for his younger brother
is Gǒu Dàojiàng (苟道將)."
Gǒu Xī (苟晞),
courtesy name Dàojiàng (道將).
18 Hú (胡) tribal leaders Dà Zhāng Bèi Dū (大張㔨督) and Féng Mòtú (馮莫突) and others,
a Hú (胡) tribal chief
called Bù Dà (部大).
Yáng Zhènghéng (楊正衡) said: Bèi (㔨),
pronounced bèi.
garrisoned at Shàngdǎng (上黨).
Shí Lè (石勒) went to them,
and persuaded Bèi Dū (㔨督) and others, saying:
"Chányú (單于) Liú (劉) raised troops to attack Jìn (晉).
Chányú (單于) Liú (劉) refers to Liú Yuān (劉淵).
说 (說),
pronounced suì.
单 (單),
pronounced chán.
Do you think you can ultimately stand alone?"
They replied:
"No, we cannot."
Lè (勒) said:
"Then how can you not align yourselves early?
Now all the tribes have already received rewards and inducements from the Chányú (單于),
and are often meeting to discuss
rebelling against the tribal leaders and returning to the Chányú (單于)."
Bèi Dū (㔨督) and the others thought this was true.
In winter,
tenth month,
Bèi Dū (㔨督) and others, following Lè (勒), rode alone to Hàn (漢).
Hàn (漢) King Yuān (淵) appointed Bèi Dū (㔨督) as Qīnhàn Wáng (親漢王),
Mòtú (莫突) as Dūdū Bù Dà (都督部大),
and Lè (勒) as Fǔhàn Jiāngjūn (輔漢將軍) and Píngjìn Wáng (平晉王),
to command them.
Wūhuán (烏桓) Zhāng Fúlìdù (張伏利度) had two thousand troops,
garrisoned at Lèpíng (樂平).
Yuān (淵) repeatedly tried to recruit him,
but failed to secure his allegiance.
Lè (勒) pretended to have committed a crime against Yuān (淵)
and fled to Fúlìdù (伏利度).
Fúlìdù (伏利度) was pleased
and became sworn brothers with him.
He ordered Lè (勒) to lead various Hú (胡) tribes to plunder,

On the Rén Yín day [of the 14th year],
Bìngzhōu Cìshǐ Liú Kūn sent Shàngdǎng Tàishǒu Liú Dūn to lead the Xiānbēi to attack Húguān.
Dù Yòu said: Táng's Lúzhōu governed Shàngdǎng.
Hàn's Húguān County
was moved by the Later Wèi to the strategic point of Yángchángbǎn's Yángtóu.
Shuài [帥],
is read "shuài".
The same applies below.
On the Bǐngwǔ day [of the 15th year],
Hàn's Dūdū Zhōngwài Zhūjūnfú,
who concurrently held the titles of Chéngxiàng and Yòuxiánwáng Xuān, passed away.
Shí Lè and Liú Líng led an army of thirty thousand to invade Wèijùn, Jíjùn, and Dūnqiū.
Jí County
belonged to Hénèi Commandery under Hàn.
In the second year of Emperor Wǔ's Tàishǐ era,
Jí Commandery was established.
Táng's Wèizhōu was located in this area.
They all granted seals and ribbons to the stockade leaders, generals, and commandants,
selected fifty thousand strong men as soldiers,
while the old and weak remained peacefully as before.
On the Jǐyǒu day,
Lè captured Wèijùn Tàishǒu Wáng Cuì at Sāntái,
and killed him.
The note for Sāntái is found later in volume 88, under Yǒngjiā 6th year.
In the twelfth month [of the 17th year],
on the Xīnwèi *shuò* (first day of the month),
a general amnesty was granted.
On the Yǐhài day [of the 18th year],
Hàn Lord Yuān appointed Dàjiāngjūn Hé as Dàsīmǎ,
and enfeoffed him as King of Liáng.
Shàngshūlìng Huānlè was appointed Dàsītú,
and enfeoffed as King of Chénliú.
The empress's father, Yùshǐ Dàfū Hūyán Yì, was appointed Dàsīkōng,
and enfeoffed as Duke of Yànmén Commandery.
All members of the imperial clan were enfeoffed as kings of commanderies and counties according to their proximity in kinship.
Those of different surnames were all enfeoffed as dukes and marquises of commanderies and counties based on their merits and achievements.
Chéng's Shàngshūlìng Yáng Bāo passed away.
The *Kǎoyì* says: The *Zàijì* states "Chéngxiàng Yáng Bāo".
We follow the *Jìn Chūnqiū* here.
When Chéng Lord Xióng first gained Shu,
resources were insufficient.
Some generals obtained official positions by offering gold and silver.
Bāo admonished him, saying:
"Your Majesty establishes official ranks
to gather the heroes of the realm.
How can one buy offices with gold?"
Xióng apologized.
Once, Xióng was drunk
and used a staff to beat the Zhōngshūlìng Tàiguānlìng.
Bāo stepped forward and said:
"The Son of Heaven is serene and dignified;
the feudal lords are grand and imposing."
This is from the *Lǐjì Qūlǐ*.
Xióng was ashamed and stopped.
In the 20th year, the Commander who Pacified the Rebels, Lǐ Fèng (李鳳), garrisoned Jìnshòu (晉壽).
Jiāmēng (葭萌) County,
under the Hàn (漢) dynasty, belonged to Guǎnghàn (廣漢) Commandery;
under the Shǔ (蜀) dynasty, it was renamed Hànshòu (漢壽) County
and belonged to Zǐtóng (梓潼) Commandery;
under the Jìn (晉) dynasty, Hànshòu was again renamed Jìnshòu.
The people of Hànzhōng (漢中) fled east to Jīngmiǎn (荊沔).
Miǎn (沔) River, flowing from Liángzhōu (梁州) into the territory of Jīngzhōu (荊州), was called Jīngmiǎn.
As banditry in Jīngzhōu was not suppressed,
an imperial edict appointed Liú Fán (劉璠) as the Administrator of Shùnyáng (順陽).
People between the Jiāng (江) and Hàn (漢) rivers rallied to him.
Fán's father, Hóng (弘), had not yet completed his mourning period,
but he was called to service from his humble mourning hut.
The people of Jīngzhōu cherished his father,
and thus rallied to his son.
Fán,
pronounced fú yuán fān.
Punctuation by Wáng Chóngwǔ (王崇武), collated by Róng Zhàozǔ (容肇祖) and Niè Chóngqí (聶崇岐).
Sīmǎ Guāng (司馬光)
compiled by imperial command.
Post-Academia Tiāntái (天台).
Emperor Xiàohuái (孝懷)
Yǒngjiā (永嘉) 3rd year
(Jǐsì, 309 CE)
1. Spring,
1st month,
on the Xīnchǒu (辛丑) day, the new moon,
Yínghuò (熒惑) trespassed into Zǐwēi (紫微).
Zǐwēi
is the Zǐgōng (紫宮).
The Kāoyì (考異) states: Jìn Chūnqiū (晉春秋) records it as
"Xiānyú Xiūzhī" (鮮于脩之).
We now follow the Zàijì (載記) and Shíliù Guó Chūnqiū (十六國春秋).
I note that among various books on surnames,
there is Xiānyú but no Xuānyú (宣于).
"Within three years,
Luòyáng (洛陽) will certainly be captured.
Púzi (蒲子) is rugged and difficult to hold for long;
the auspicious omens of Píngyáng (平陽) are flourishing,
so I request to move the capital there."
Yuān (淵) agreed.
A general amnesty was declared,
and the reign title was changed to Héruì (河瑞).
At this time, a jade seal was found in the Fén (汾) River,
so Yuān changed the reign title to Héruì.
2. 3rd month,
on the Wùshēn (戊申) day,
Gāomì Xiàowáng Lüè (高密孝王略) passed away.

Shān Jiǎn (山簡), the Left Assistant of the Department of State Affairs, was appointed General who Conquers the South and Grand Supervisor of Military Affairs of Jīng (荊), Xiāng (湘), Jiāo (交), and Guǎng (廣) four provinces,
garrisoning Xiāngyáng (襄陽).
He replaced Lüè.
He was Táo's (濤) son,
fond of wine,
and did not attend to governmental affairs.
He submitted a memorial stating,
"Liú Fán, the Administrator of Shùnyáng, has gained the hearts of the people,
and I fear the populace might force Fán to become their lord."
An imperial edict summoned Fán to be the Colonel of Elite Cavalry.
The Southern province thereupon fell into chaos,
and all the elders missed Liú Hóng (劉弘).
The historian states that Liú Hóng and his son gained the hearts of the people between the Jiāng and Hàn rivers.
3. On the Dīngsì (丁巳) day,
the Grand Tutor Yuè (越) entered the capital from Xíngyáng (滎陽).
Yuè had moved his garrison to Xíngyáng last year.
"The Grand Tutor holds all power,
but when he selects and appoints people through memorials, the Department of State Affairs still checks them according to old regulations.
His arrival today
must be to punish someone."
When the Emperor was the Imperial Younger Brother,
he was close to the Palace Aide Miù Bō (繆播).
Upon his enthronement,
he appointed Bō as Supervisor of the Central Secretariat,
and Miù Yìn (繆胤) as Grand Steward.
The Grand Steward
was one of the Nine Ministers;
but in Jìn official titles, the character
"Qīng" (卿)
was not yet used,
so the character "Qīng"
is superfluous here.
The Emperor's maternal uncle, the Imperial Household Grandee Wáng Yán (王延), the Minister Hē Suí (何綏), and the Grand Astrologer Gāo Tángchōng (高堂沖)
all participated in confidential matters.
Yuè suspected that the court officials were disloyal to him.
Liú Yú (劉輿) and Pān Tāo (潘滔) advised Yuè to execute Bō and others.
Yuè then falsely accused Bō and others of plotting rebellion.
On the Yǐchǒu (乙丑) day,
he dispatched the General who Pacifies the East, Wáng Bǐng (王秉),
leading three thousand armored soldiers into the palace.
He seized Bō and more than ten others from the Emperor's side,
handed them over to the Minister of Justice,
and had them executed.
The Emperor merely sighed and shed tears.
Suí
was the great-grandson of Zēng (曾).
Earlier,
when Hē Zēng (何曾) attended an imperial banquet with Emperor Wǔ (武帝),
upon his return,
he told his sons:
"His Majesty has founded a great enterprise,
but whenever I attend a banquet and see him, I never hear of grand plans for governing the state in the long term;
he only talks about mundane daily affairs.
This is not the way to plan for one's descendants;
it will last only through his own lifetime,
and his successors will be in peril!
You all may still escape;
pointing to his grandsons, he said:
"These ones will certainly encounter disaster."
When Suí died,
his elder brother Sōng (嵩) wept and said:
"Was our ancestor perhaps a sage?"
Zēng spent ten thousand coins a day on food,
yet still complained there was no place to set his chopsticks.
His son, Shào (劭),
spent twenty thousand a day.
Suí and his younger brothers Jī (機) and Xiàn (羨)
were even more extravagant and arrogant.
In their letters to others,
their tone and manners were dismissive and haughty.
Wáng Ní (王尼), King of Hénèi (河內), saw Suí's letter
and told others:
"Bówèi (伯蔚) lives in a chaotic world yet is so arrogant and proud;
how can he escape disaster?"
Someone said:
"If Bówèi hears your words,
he will certainly harm you."
Ní replied:
"By the time Bówèi hears my words,
he will already be dead!"
Hē Suí's
courtesy name was Bówèi.
Bǐ (比),
pronounced bì mèi fān,
means "by the time."
Wèi (蔚),
pronounced yū wù fān.
The Hē (何) clan left no descendants.
Your subject Guāng (光) says: Hē Zēng criticized
Emperor Wǔ for being lazy and indulgent,
only considering the present,
not planning for the long term;
he knew that the world would fall into chaos,
and his descendants would certainly suffer from it.
How insightful he was!
Yet he himself was extravagant and arrogant,
allowing his sons and grandsons to follow suit,
ultimately leading to their family's destruction through pride and luxury.
Where then was his insight?
Moreover, as a Prime Minister,
knowing his ruler's faults yet not reporting them but privately speaking to his family,
he was not a loyal minister.
4. Grand Tutor Yuè appointed Wáng Dūn (王敦) as the Inspector of Yángzhōu (楊州).
This laid the groundwork for Dūn's disruption of the Eastern Jìn.
5. Liú Shí (劉寔) repeatedly requested retirement for several years,
but the imperial court did not permit it.
The Left Aide of the Department of State Affairs, Liú Tǎn (劉坦), submitted a memorial stating:
"In ancient times, providing for the aged
meant excusing them from duties.
Not engaging in affairs means not being given responsibilities.
It is proper to allow Shí to retain his position."
On the Dīngmǎo (丁卯) day,
an imperial edict allowed Shí to return to his residence as a marquis.
Wáng Yǎn (王衍) was appointed Grand Commandant.
Grand Tutor Yuè relinquished the Governorship of Yǎnzhōu (兗州)
and assumed the position of Minister of Works.
Yuè believed that the troubles that arose recently
largely originated from within the palace,
referring to the execution of Yáng Jùn (楊駿),
the deposition of Empress Jiǎ (賈后),
the execution of Prince Lún (倫) of Zhào (趙) and Prince Jiǒng (冏) of Qí (齊), the suppression of Prince Yǐng (穎) of Chéngdū (成都),
and the repeated depositions and reinstatements of Empress Yáng (羊后) and Crown Prince Tán (覃).
All these were orchestrated by people in the palace.
At that time, military officers in the palace were all enfeoffed as marquises.
Consequently, those who departed were almost all of them,
leaving in tears.
Instead, the Right General of the Guards, Hē Lún (何倫), and the Left General of the Guards, Wáng Bǐng, were ordered to lead several hundred soldiers from the State of Dōnghǎi (東海) to guard the palace.
From then on, all the Emperor's close attendants were Yuè's private men.
6 Zuǒjīnǔ Jiāngjūn Zhū Dàn (朱誕) defected to Hàn.
In the fourth year of Tàishǐ (泰始) of Emperor Wǔ,
the Zhènwēi (振威) and Yángwēi (揚威) Protector-Generals were abolished,
and Zuǒyòu Jīnǔ Jiāngjūn (左右積弩將軍) were established.
He advised Hàn lord Yuān (淵) to attack them.
Yuān appointed Dàn (誕) as Qiánfēng Dūdū (前鋒都督),
and Dàmièjìn Dàjiàngjūn Liú Jǐng (劉景) as Dà Dūdū (大都督),
leading troops to attack Líyáng (黎陽),
and captured it.
They also defeated Wáng Kān (王堪) at Yánjīn (延津),
and drowned over thirty thousand men and women in the river.
Yuān (淵) heard of this
and angrily said,
"How can Jǐng (景) have the face to see Me again!
Moreover, how can the Way of Heaven tolerate this!
What I wish to eliminate
are only the Sīmǎ (司馬) clan;
what crime have the common people committed!"
He demoted Jǐng (景) to Pínglǔ Jiāngjūn (平虜將軍).
Liú Yuān’s (劉淵) insight and strategy
were beyond what Cōng (聰) and Yào (曜) could achieve.
7 In summer,
there was a great drought.
The Jiāng (江), Hàn (漢), Hé (河), and Luò (洛) rivers all dried up,
becoming fordable.
The drying up of rivers
is a sign of a state’s demise.
8 Hàn Āndōng Dàjiàngjūn Shí Lè (石勒) plundered Jùlù (鉅鹿) and Chángshān (常山).
His forces numbered over a hundred thousand.
He gathered literati and prominent figures
and formed a separate Jūnzǐ Yíng (君子營, Gentlemen's Camp).
Shí Lè (石勒) rose from a Hú Jié (胡羯) enslaved person, yet could achieve this;
this is why he could dominate the Central Plains.
Diāo Yīng (刁膺) served as his confidant,
and Kuí Ān (夔安), Kǒng Cháng (孔萇), Zhī Xióng (支雄), Táo Bào (桃豹), and Lù Míng (逯明) as his close associates.
The Xìngpǔ (姓譜) states: Descendants of Kuí (夔) used the state as their surname.
The Hòuzhào Zhī Xióng Zhuàn (後趙支雄傳) states that
his ancestors
were from the Yuèzhī (月支) Hú (胡) people.
Táo (桃)
was a state in Lǔ (魯) during the Spring and Autumn period,
and the town was used as a surname.
One theory is that they were descendants of the ancient recluse Zuǒ Bó Táo (左伯桃).
Lù (逯),
read as lú gǔ.
Initially,
Zhāng Bīn (張賓) loved to read,
was broad-minded and had great ambitions,
often comparing himself to Zhāng Zǐfáng (張子房).
When Shí Lè (石勒) swept through Shāndōng (山東),
Bīn (賓) said to his intimates,
"I have observed all the generals,
and none are like this Hú (胡) general."
Lè (勒) was
originally a Hú (胡),
hence he was called the Hú (胡) general.
He then went to the army gate with a sword,
shouting to be seen.
Lè (勒) did not find him remarkable at first.
Bīn (賓) repeatedly offered strategies to Lè (勒),
and afterward, they all turned out as he had predicted.
Lè (勒) consequently found him remarkable
and appointed him Jūngōng Cáo (軍功曹),
consulting him on all actions.
9 Hàn lord Yuān (淵) appointed Wáng Mí (王彌) as Shìzhōng (侍中), Dūdū Qīng, Xú, Yǎn, Yù, Jīng, Yáng Liùzhōu Zhūjūnshì (都督青‧徐‧兗‧豫‧荊‧揚六州諸軍事), Zhēngdōng Dàjiàngjūn (征東大將軍), and Qīngzhōu Mù (青州牧),
and together with Chǔ Wáng Cōng (楚王聰), attacked Húguān (壺關),
appointing Shí Lè (石勒) as Qiánfēng Dūdū (前鋒都督).
Liú Kūn (劉琨) sent Hùjūn Huáng Sù (護軍黃肅) and Hán Shù (韓述) to relieve them.
Cōng (聰) defeated Shù (述) at Xījiàn (西澗),
and Lè (勒) defeated Sù (肅) at Fēngtián (封田),
killing both of them.
Xījiàn (西澗) and Fēngtián (封田)
should both be southeast of Húguān (壺關).
Bài (敗),
read as bǔ mài.
The Kǎoyì (考異) states: In the Shí Lè Zàijì (石勒載記),
"Sù" (肅)
is written
as "Xiù" (秀),
and "Fēng" (封)
is written
as "Bái" (白).
We now follow the Shíliùguó Chūnqiū (十六國春秋) and Liú Kūn Jí (劉琨集).
Tàifù Yuè (太傅越) sent Huáinán Nèishǐ Wáng Kuàng (淮南內史王曠).
The Kǎoyì (考異) states: Shíliùguó Chūnqiū (十六國春秋) writes
"Wáng Guǎng" (王廣),
we now follow the Dìjì (帝紀).
Kuàng (曠) crossed the Hé (河),
intending to march straight forward.
Róng (融) said,
"They are emerging from dangerous terrain.
Although we have tens of thousands of troops,
it is still one army facing the enemy alone.
We should first rely on the water as a defense to assess the situation,
and then plan our strategy."
Kuàng (曠) angrily said,
"Are you trying to demoralize the troops!"
Róng (融) retreated and said,
"They are skilled in warfare,
and Kuàng (曠) is ignorant of the situation.
We are surely going to die today!"
Kuàng (曠) and his forces
encountered Cōng (聰)
at Tàiháng (太行),
fighting between Chángpíng (長平).
Kuàng’s (曠) army was greatly defeated,
and Róng (融) and Chāo (超) both died.
Cōng (聰) then captured Túnliú (屯留) and Chángzǐ (長子),
beheading and capturing a total of nineteen thousand heads.
Shàngdǎng Tàishǒu Páng Chún (上黨太守龐淳) surrendered Húguān (壺關) to Hàn.
Liú Kūn (劉琨) appointed Dūwèi Zhāng Yǐ (都尉張倚) as Shàngdǎng Tàishǒu (上黨太守),
occupying Xiāngyuán (襄垣).
Xiāngyuán Xiàn (襄垣縣)
belonged to Shàngdǎng Jùn (上黨郡).
Sòng Bái (宋白) said: Xiāngyuán (襄垣)
was built by Zhào Xiāngzǐ (趙襄子),
and named after it.
Initially,
Xiōngnú Liú Měng (匈奴劉猛) died.
See Volume 79, Tàishǐ (泰始) eighth year of Emperor Wǔ.
Gàoshēng Yuán (誥升爰) died,
and his son Hǔ (虎) succeeded him,
residing in Xīnxīng (新興),
and was known as the Tiěfú (鐵弗) clan.
The descendants of the Tiěfú (鐵弗) clan became Hèlián Bóbó (赫連勃勃).
The Kǎoyì (考異) states: Liú Kūn Jí (劉琨集) writes
"Bǎibù" (百部),
we now follow the Hòuwèi Shū (後魏書) and Jìn Shū (晉書).
Liú Cōng (劉聰) sent troops to attack Jìnyáng (晉陽),
but failed.
10 In the fifth month,
Hàn lord Yuān (淵) enfeoffed his son Yù (裕) as Qí Wáng (齊王)
and Lóng (隆) as Lǔ Wáng (魯王).
11 In autumn,
eighth month,
Hàn lord Yuān (淵) ordered Chǔ Wáng Cōng (楚王聰) and others to advance and attack Luòyáng (洛陽).
He issued an imperial edict for Píngběi Jiāngjūn Cáo Wǔ (平北將軍曹武) and others to resist them,
but they were all defeated by Cōng (聰).
Cōng (聰) marched straight to Yíyáng (宜陽).
Relying on his repeated victories,
he became negligent and unprepared.
In the ninth month,
Hóngnóng Tàishǒu Yuán Yán (弘農太守垣延) feigned surrender.
Yuán (垣)
is the surname;
Yán (延)
is the given name.
Jiàng (降),
read as hù jiāng.
Cōng (聰) was greatly defeated and returned.
Wáng Jùn (王浚) sent Qí Hóng (祁弘) with the Xiānbēi (鮮卑) Duàn Wùwùchén (段務勿塵) to attack Shí Lè (石勒) at Fēilóng Shān (飛龍山).
The Suí Dìlǐ Zhì (隋地理志) states that
in Shíyì Xiàn (石邑縣) of Héngshān Jùn (恆山郡), there is Fēilóng Shān (飛龍山).
The Kuòdì Zhì (括地志) states: Fēnglóng Shān (封龍山),
also known as Fēilóng Shān (飛龍山),
is forty-five lǐ (里) south of Lùquán Xiàn (鹿泉縣) in Héngshān (恆山).
Lè (勒) retreated and garrisoned Líyáng (黎陽).
In the 12th year, winter,
10th month,
the Han lord Yuān again dispatched Chǔ Wáng Cōng, Wáng Mí, Shǐ'ān Wáng Yào, and Rǔyīn Wáng Jǐng, leading fifty thousand elite cavalry, to invade Luòyáng.
Dà Sīkōng Yànmén Gāngmùgōng Hūyán Yì led infantry to follow them.
According to Běi Dí Zhuàn,
among the four prominent Xiongnú clans,
there were the Hūyán, Bǔ, Lán, and Qiáo clans,
with the Hūyán clan being the noblest.
On the day Bǐngchén,
Cōng and others arrived at Yíyáng.
The imperial court, as the Han forces had recently been defeated,
did not expect them to return,
and was greatly alarmed.
On the day Xīnyǒu,
Cōng encamped at Xīmíngmén.
Xīmíngmén
was the second gate from the south on the western side of Luòchéng.
They beheaded their Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn Hūyán Hào.
On the day Rénxū,
Cōng encamped south of the Luòshuǐ.
The Luòshuǐ
flowed south of Luòchéng.
On the day Yǐchǒu,
Hūyán Yì was killed by his subordinates,
and his troops dispersed and returned from Dàyáng.
Yuān ordered Cōng and others to withdraw their army;
Cōng memorialized, stating that Jìn forces were weak,
and they should not withdraw because of the deaths of Yì and Hào,
steadfastly requesting to remain and attack Luòyáng.
Yuān granted his request.
Tàifù Yuè fortified the city and defended himself.
On the day Wùyín,
Cōng personally prayed at Sōngshān.
Sōngshān
is in Yángchéng Xiàn, Hénán.
Tàifù Cānjūn Sūn Xún persuaded Yuè to take advantage of the opportunity to sally out and attack Lǎng,
beheading him.
Lì plunged into the water and died.
Wáng Mí said to Cōng:
"Now that our army has suffered a setback,
Luòyáng's defenses are still strong,
and our supply wagons are in Shǎn,
our provisions will not last for several days.
Cōng, from Yíyáng eastward,
and then moving south,
encamped at the Luòshuǐ,
has already been defeated by Jìn.
Our supply wagons are in Shǎn,
and the grain supply route is cut off.
Shǎn,
pronounced like *shì rǎn*.
Yuān appointed his kinsman Yào as Lóngxiáng Dàjiāngjūn.
Xiáng,
pronounced like *sī jiāng*.
We should prepare for a future campaign;
I, your subordinate, will also gather troops and grain,
awaiting orders in Yǎn and Yù.
Would this not be acceptable?"
Cōng, having himself requested to stay,
did not dare to return.
Xuānyú Xiū conveyed his words to Yuān, saying:
"The year is Xīnwèi;
only then can Luòyáng be taken.
Now the Jìn's morale is still high,
and if the main army does not return,
it will surely be defeated."
Yuān then summoned Cōng and others to return.
The people of Tiānshuǐ, Hōng Qí and others,

Previously,

Dàng,
pronounced like *tú làng*.
He ate their livers.
At this time, Zǐtóng surrendered,

In the 14th year, 11th month,
on the day Jiǎshēn,

Wáng Mí went south out of Huányuán,

Xiāngyáng Xiàn,
under Yǐngchuān Jùn in Han times,

all burned down cities and towns,

Xìndū Xiàn,

same in Jìn.

he persuaded Zhēn to raise troops to attack Jùn.

Shuō,

1st year, spring,
1st month,

Shàn,
pronounced like *shàn*.

Wú established Wúxìng Commandery by dividing Wú Commandery and Dānyáng,

Zèng,

6. Cáo Yí led his troops eastward from Dàliáng.

fourth month,

seventh month,

A small walled city is called a wǔ.

Since there was no imperial appointment,

Jiāng,

Yuān valued his loyalty and sincerity,

On Dīngchǒu,

On Jǐmǎo,

According to the perpetual calendar,
the first day of the seventh month was Rénxū,
the sixteenth day was Dīngchǒu,

The first day of the eighth month was Xīnmǎo.
There were no Dīngchǒu, Jǐmǎo, or Xīnwèi.

Therefore, Yuān died in the seventh month
and was buried in the ninth month.
The Shíliùguó Chūnqiū is mistaken.
Hé,
courtesy name Xuántài,

Hé’s nature was suspicious and unkind.
The Imperial Clan Court Grandee, Hūyán Yōu,

means ‘to think’.

Zuò,

was Yōu’s maternal nephew.

The four kings have not shown any rebellious tendencies.

was Yuān’s fourth son,

What will the world say about Your Majesty?
Moreover, the great enterprise has just begun.
Your Majesty, do not believe the words of slanderers and doubt your brothers.
If even brothers cannot be trusted,
who else is worthy of trust?”
Yōu and Ruì, enraged, said:

allows for no dissent.

After Shèng was killed,

On Rénwǔ,
Ruì led Mǎ Jǐng to attack Chǔ Wáng Cōng at Dānyútái.
Yōu led Yǒng'ān Wáng Ānguó to attack Qí Wáng Yù at Sītúfǔ.
Chéng led Ānyì Wáng Qīn to attack Lǔ Wáng Lóng.
He sent the Minister of Personnel, Tián Mì, and the General of Martial Guard, Liú Xuán, to attack Běihǎi Wáng Yì.
Mì and Xuán, taking Yì with them, broke through the gate and returned to Cōng.
Cōng ordered his men to don armor and await them.
Guànjiǎ
means to put on armor.
Shuài
is pronounced ‘lǜ’.
They quickly returned
and, with Yōu and Chéng, jointly attacked Lóng and Yù.
Yōu and Chéng suspected Ānguó and Qīn of having different intentions,
and killed them.
On that day,
Yù was killed.
On Guǐwèi,
Lóng was killed.
On Jiǎshēn,
Cōng attacked the Xīmíng Gate
and captured it.
Liú Yuān made Píngyáng his capital,
and all city gates used names of the Luòyáng city gates.
The vanguard followed him.
On Yǐyǒu,
Hé was killed in the western chamber of Guāngjí.
Liú Yuān built Guāngjídian in Píngyáng.
His head was impaled in the public thoroughfare.
All officials requested Cōng to ascend the throne.
Cōng, considering Běihǎi Wáng Yì to be
the son of Dān Hòu,
yielded the position to him.

According to the Shíliùguó Chūnqiū, it is written
which we now follow.
After a long while, Cōng agreed,
saying:
“Yì and all officials are merely saying that the disasters are still abundant,
and they covet my old age.
This is a matter of family and state;
how can I decline?
When Yì is older,
I will return the great enterprise to him.”
Thereupon, he ascended the throne.
Cōng’s
courtesy name was Xuánmíng,
Yuān’s fourth son.
He changed the era name to Guāngxīng.
He honored Dān Shì as the Empress Dowager,
and his mother Zhāng Shì as the Imperial Empress Dowager.
He made Yì the Imperial Younger Brother (Heir Apparent), Grand Chányú, and Grand Minister of Works.
