Hūyán Shì
was the paternal cousin of Yuān’s empress.
He enfeoffed his son Càn as Hénei Wáng,
Yì as Héjiān Wáng,
Yì as Péngchéng Wáng,
and Kuī as Gāopíng Wáng.
He also appointed Càn as Commander-in-Chief of All Armies, overseeing all military affairs, domestic and foreign.
He made Shí Lè Inspector of Bīngzhōu
and enfeoffed him as Jǐjùn Gōng.
Lǜeyáng Línwèi Dī chieftain Pú Hóng
was brave and resourceful.
All Dī were awed and submitted to him.
Jìn Zhì states: Lǜeyáng Commandery had Línwèi County,
probably established by Wèi.
Zàijì says: The ancestors of the Dī
were descendants of Yǒuhù Shì,
and were hereditary chieftains of the Western Róng.
Reeds grew in Hóng’s family pond,
five zhàng and five chǐ long,
with nodes like bamboo.
People at the time called him
“Pú Jiā,”
and thus it became his surname.
Later,
Hóng, based on a prophecy that said
“cǎo fù should be king,”
and also because his grandson Jiān had the characters
“艸付”
on his back,
changed his surname to Fú Shì.
Hóng did not accept,
but called himself Protector of the Dī, Inspector of Qínzhōu, and Duke of Lǜeyáng.
The matter of Pú Hóng begins here.
September,
Xīnwèi,
Emperor Yuān of Hàn was buried at Yǒngguānglíng.
His posthumous title was Guāngwén Huángdì,
and his temple name was Gāozǔ.
Many displaced people from Yōngzhōu were in Nányáng.
An imperial edict ordered them to return to their hometowns.
The displaced people, due to the desolation of Guānzhōng,
all refused to return.
The General who Conquers the South, Shān Jiǎn, and the Central Commander of Nánzhōng, Dù Ruí, each dispatched troops to escort them,
urging them to depart by a set date.
Jīngzhào Wáng Rú Suì secretly gathered brave men
and attacked the two armies at night,
defeating them.
The two armies
were those dispatched by Shān Jiǎn and Dù Ruí.
Jīngzhào Hóu Tuō Gè gathered followers to attack cities and towns,
killing magistrates to respond to him.
Before long,
his followers numbered forty to fifty thousand.
He styled himself Grand General, concurrently overseeing the two prefectures of Sī and Yōng,
and declared vassalage to Hàn.
Winter,
October,
Hàn’s Hénei Wáng Càn, Shǐ’ān Wáng Yào, and Wáng Mí led a force of forty thousand to raid Luòyáng.
Shí Lè led twenty thousand cavalry to meet Càn at Dàyáng.
They defeated Supervisor of the Army Péi Miǎo at Miǎnchí,
then drove straight into the Luòchuān.
Càn exited Huányuán,
plundering the areas of Liáng, Chén, Rǔ, and Yǐng.
Lè exited Chénggāo Pass.
Jìn Zhì states: Hénán’s Chénggāo County has a pass.
On Rén’yín,
he besieged Chénliú Governor Wáng Zàn at Cāngyuán,
but was defeated by Zàn
and retreated to camp at Wénshíjīn.
According to the Imperial Annals,
Wénshíjīn is north of the Yellow River.
Also, according to Yǒngjiā Year 6,
Lè traveled north from Gépí
to Dōngyàn,
and sent Kǒng Cháng to secretly cross Fāngtóu from Wénshíjīn
and take boats from Xiàngshuǐ.
This places Wénshíjīn to the northeast of Dōngyàn
and southeast of Fāngtóu.
Liú Kūn (劉琨) personally led an expedition to attack Liú Hǔ (劉虎) and the Báibù (白部)
Báibù (白部)
were Xiānbēi (鮮卑).
Kūn (琨) attacked them because Liú Hǔ (劉虎) and the Báibù (白部) had both submitted to Hàn (漢).
Yīlú (猗盧) sent his younger brother Fú (弗)’s son Yùlǜ (鬱律) to command twenty thousand cavalry to assist him.
They subsequently defeated Liú Hǔ (劉虎) and the Báibù (白部),
slaughtering their camps.
Kūn (琨) and Yīlú (猗盧) became sworn brothers.
Kūn (琨) memorialized to appoint Yīlú (猗盧) as Grand Chányú (大單于),
and enfeoffed him with Dàijùn (代郡) as Duke of Dài (代公).
At that time, Dàijùn (代郡) belonged to Yōuzhōu (幽州),
so Wáng Jùn (王浚) did not permit it.
He dispatched troops to attack Yīlú (猗盧).
Yīlú (猗盧) resisted and defeated them.
Jùn (浚) thereby developed a rift with Kūn (琨).
Yīlú (猗盧) considered that his enfeoffed territory was far from his state,
and his people did not interact with its inhabitants.
So he led more than ten thousand households from Yúnzhōng (雲中) into Yànmén (鴈門),
requesting the land north of Xíng (陘) from Kūn (琨).
Xíngběi (陘北)
is north of Shíxíngguān (石陘關).
Xíng (陘),
pronounced xíng.
Furthermore, wishing to rely on Kūn (琨) for support,
he moved the people of the five counties of Lóufán (樓煩), Mǎyì (馬邑), Yīnguǎn (陰館), Fánzhì (繁畤), and Guō (崞) to south of Xíng (陘).
Lóufán (樓煩)
was where the Xiōngnú (匈奴) resided,
its land being south of Běihé (北河);
today’s Lánzhōu (嵐州)’s Lóufánjùn (樓煩郡)
is not the ancient Lóufán (樓煩).
The Hàn (漢) Mǎyì (馬邑) county,
the land of the Táng (唐)’s Dàtóngjūn (大同軍) is that place.
The Hàn (漢) Yīnguǎn (陰館) county
was northwest of Gōuzhù (句注).
Fánzhì (繁畤) county
was in Wǔzhōuchuān (武州川).
Guō (崞) county
became Běiqí (北齊)’s Běixiǎnzhōu (北顯州)’s Píngkòuxiàn (平寇縣).
Although the five counties still exist today,
none are in the same locations as the ancient counties.
Xíng (陘)
refers to Xínglǐng (陘嶺).
Xíng (陘),
pronounced xíng.
The *Kǎoyì* (考異) states: *Huáidì Jì* (懷帝紀):
“In the fifth year of Yǒngjiā (永嘉)
(311 CE), in the eleventh month,
Yīlú (猗盧) plundered Tàiyuán (太原).
Liú Kūn (劉琨) moved the five counties to reside there.
In the sixth year
(312 CE), in the eighth month,
on the day Xīnhài (辛亥),
Liú Kūn (劉琨) requested troops from Yīlú (猗盧)
and memorialized to make Lú (盧) the Duke of Dài (代公).”
The *Sòngshū Suǒlǔ Zhuàn* (宋書索虜傳) places this in the third year of Yǒngjiā (永嘉) (309 CE).
The *Jìn Chūnqiū* (晉春秋) places it in the fourth year of Yǒngjiā (永嘉) (310 CE),
and also says:
“Yīlú (猗盧) led over ten thousand households to avoid calamity,
entering Yànmén (鴈門) from Yúnzhōng (雲中).”
The *Hòuwèi Xùjì* (後魏序紀) places it in the third year of Mùdì (穆帝) (310 CE),
which is the fourth year of Yǒngjiā (永嘉).
Kūn (琨)’s collected works,
in the fourth year of Yǒngjiā (永嘉) (310 CE),
in the sixth month,
on the day Guǐsì (癸巳),
submitted a memorial to the Grand Tutor’s (太傅) residence,
stating
that “Lú (盧) was moved by the grace of his enfeoffment as Duke of Dài (代公),”
therefore it is known to have occurred before the sixth month of the fourth year.
Also, Kūn (琨)’s memorial to the Chancellor (丞相) says:
“Formerly, the General of Chariots and Cavalry (車騎) was moved by Yītuō (猗㐌)’s meritorious service in saving the province,
and memorialized to enfeoff Yītuō (猗㐌) with Dàijùn (代郡) as Duke of Dài (代公),
which was approved.
At that time, the Emperor’s carriage was in Cháng’ān (長安),
and coincided with military affairs,
so the roads were impassable,
and it was ultimately not implemented.
Lú (盧) entrusted me with the matter of his enfeoffment,
and I, Kūn (琨), truly memorialized it,
reiterating the former intention of the General of Chariots and Cavalry (車騎),
and immediately received approval.
An Assistant Minister (謁者僕射) was dispatched to enthrone Lú (盧)
and bestow upon him a seal, tally, and credentials.
Jùn (浚) blamed me for this.
For a Rong (戎) or Dí (狄) to be enfeoffed with a Huá (華) commandery is indeed a breach of etiquette;
however, it was done to alleviate the crisis,
just as Jùn (浚) had previously enfeoffed Wùwùchén (務勿塵) with Liáoxī (遼西).
This breach of etiquette
was actually initiated by Jùn (浚).
Jùn (浚) then contended with Lú (盧) over Dàijùn (代郡),
raised troops to attack Lú (盧),
and was defeated by him.
The origin of this confusion
began here.
The Yànmén (鴈門) Commandery had five counties north of Xíng (陘).
Lú (盧) had newly annexed Guān (官),
and his state was very strong and prosperous.
He requested the land north of Xíng (陘) from Kūn (琨),
and had moved over thirty thousand households,
scattered among the five counties,
which were no longer under his control;
furthermore, for Kūn (琨)’s weakened state,
it allowed them to gather,
which was not inappropriate.
So, the five counties north of Xíng (陘) were moved to south of Xíng (陘).
Lú (盧), taking advantage of the move,
somewhat encroached upon Jùn (浚)’s western border, encircling the various military camps.
Jùn (浚) no longer forgave his precarious weakness but blamed him instead.”
From this perspective,
Lú (盧) did not come to avoid calamity.
Kūn (琨) sent an envoy to the Grand Tutor (太傅) Yuè (越),
requesting to dispatch troops to jointly attack Liú Cōng (劉聰) and Shí Lè (石勒);
Yuè (越) was wary of Gǒu Xī (苟晞) and Yùzhōucǐshǐ (豫州刺史) Féng Sōng (馮嵩).
There was a rift between Yuè (越) and Xī (晞),
details seen in the previous scroll, year two.
Sōng (嵩) probably also did not sincerely support Yuè (越).
Yuè (越) did not permit it.
Kūn (琨) then thanked Yīlú (猗盧)’s troops,
and sent them back to their country.
The *Kǎoyì* (考異) states: The *Hòuwèi Xùjì* (後魏序紀) says:
“Liú Kūn (劉琨) requested troops to save Luò (洛),
and Emperor Mù (穆帝) sent twenty thousand infantry and cavalry to assist him,
but Wáng Yuè (王越) of Dōnghǎi (東海) did not permit it,
due to the famine in Luòyáng (洛陽).”
According to Kūn (琨)’s memorial to the Chancellor (丞相):
“I, Kūn (琨), devoted myself and exhausted my words,
aligning with Yīlú (猗盧) in the north,
and then led the large multitude,
personally commencing military action.
I immediately reported fully to the Grand Tutor (太傅),
earnestly presenting my humble opinion,
concerning the strategy for capturing the bandits:
Cōng (聰) should be attacked immediately,
and Lè (勒) must not be indulged.
However, the Prime Minister (宰相)’s intentions differed,
and their concerns were not the same;
they were more worried about Gǒu Xī (苟晞) and Féng Sōng (馮嵩) and their ilk, thus delaying the punishment of the two bandits.
They sent envoys to suppress and
dampen my morale.
I immediately removed my armor
and sent Lú (盧)’s troops back to their country.”
If Yīlú (猗盧) had indeed sent troops to Luò (洛),
how could Kūn (琨)’s memorial not have mentioned it!
Liú Hǔ (劉虎) gathered his remaining troops,
crossed the river westward,
and resided in Shuòfāng (朔方)’s Sìlúchuān (肆盧川).
Sìlúchuān (肆盧川)
was within the Shuòfāng (朔方) frontier.
Later, the Tuòbá (拓跋) clan established Sìlújùn (肆盧郡) in that area.
In the seventh year of Zhēnjūn (真君) (446 CE),
it was merged into Xiùróngjùn (秀容郡).
Wèi Shōu (魏收)’s *Dìxíngzhì* (地形志) states that Xiùróngjùn (秀容郡)’s Xiùróngxiàn (秀容縣) had Sìlúchéng (肆盧城).
He was enfeoffed as Duke of Lóufán (樓煩公).
On the day Rénzǐ (壬子),
Liú Kūn (劉琨) was appointed General Who Pacifies the North (平北大將軍),
Wáng Jùn (王浚) was appointed Minister of Works (司空),
and the Xiānbēi (鮮卑) Duàn Wùwùchén (段務勿塵) was promoted to Grand Chányú (大單于).
The capital's famine and hardship worsened daily.
Grand Tutor (太傅) Yuè (越) sent envoys with urgent military dispatches to summon troops from across the empire,
to enter and reinforce the capital.
The Emperor said to the envoy:
“Tell all the Generals and Regional Governors (征、鎮) for me:
today it can still be saved;
later it will be too late!”
But in the end, none arrived.
General Who Attacks the South (征南將軍) Shān Jiǎn (山簡) sent Supervisor (督護) Wáng Wàn (王萬) to lead troops to reinforce,
encamping at Nièyáng (涅陽).
Nièyáng (涅陽) county
belonged to Nányángjùn (南陽郡).
Yīng Shào (應劭) said: It is on the sunny side of the Niè (涅) River.
Shī Gǔ (師古) said: Niè (涅),
pronounced nǎi jié fān.
Wàn (萬) then plundered Miǎn (沔) and Hàn (漢) extensively,
advancing to pressure Xiāngyáng (襄陽),
causing Jiǎn (簡) to fortify the city and defend himself.
Jīngzhōucǐshǐ (荊州刺史) Wáng Chéng (王澄)
Chéng (澄) was governing Jiānglíng (江陵) at the time.
wanted to reinforce the capital,
but when he reached Yíkǒu (沶口),
the *Shuǐjīng Zhù* (水經註) states: The Líng (零) River upstream connects to Liángzhōu (梁州)’s Miǎnyángxiàn (沔陽縣),
flowing east past Xīnchéngjùn (新城郡)’s Yíxiāngxiàn (沶鄉縣),
called the Yí (沶) River;
then east past Yíchéng (宜城)’s western mountain,
called the Yí (沶) Stream;
flowing east to join the Yí (夷) River,
called Yíkǒu (沶口).
Yáng Zhènghéng (楊正衡) said: Yí (沶),
pronounced yí.
his troops dispersed and returned.
The court council largely wished to move the capital to avoid calamity.
Wáng Yǎn (王衍) thought it was impermissible,
and sold his chariots and oxen to calm the populace.
Shān Jiǎn (山簡) was pressured by Yán Ní (嚴嶷) and moved his garrison from Xiāngyáng (襄陽) to Xiàkǒu (夏口).
20 Shí Lè 引兵濟河 (crossed the river with his troops),
將趣南陽 (intending to proceed to Nányáng).
Wáng Rú, Hóu Tuō, Yán Yí, etc., heard of this
and dispatched more than ten thousand troops to station at Xiāngchéng to resist Lè.
Lè attacked them,
captured all their forces,
and advanced to station north of Wǎn.
At this time,
Hóu Tuō occupied Wǎn,
and Wáng Rú occupied Ráng.
Ráng county,
during the Hàn dynasty, belonged to Nányáng Commandery;
during the Jìn dynasty, it belonged to Yìyáng Commandery.
Wáng Rú sent envoys to heavily bribe Lè,
formed a sworn brotherhood with him,
and persuaded Lè to attack Tuō.
Lè attacked Wǎn
and captured it.
Yán Yí led troops to rescue Wǎn,
but arrived too late and surrendered.
Lè beheaded Tuō;
imprisoned Yí
and sent him to Píngyáng,
absorbing all his forces.
He then plundered Xiāngyáng to the south
and attacked and captured more than thirty forts and strongholds west of the Jiāng River.
After Lè plundered Xiāngyáng to the south,
he followed the Hàn River downstream
and attacked and plundered west of the Jiāng River.
When he approached Xiāngchéng,
Wáng Rú sent his brother Lí to attack Lè.
Lè met and attacked him,
annihilating his forces,
and then re-stationed west of the Jiāng River.
21 Tài Fù Yuè, having already killed Wáng Yán and others,
which was seen in the third year of Yǒngjiā (of Emperor Huì).
Also, seeing that the Hu barbarian incursions were increasing
and feeling unsafe internally,
he entered the court in military attire
to request permission to suppress Shí Lè
and also to stabilize and gather forces in Yǎn and Yù.
The Emperor said:
“Now the Hu barbarians are pressing upon the imperial capital,
and people have no firm resolve.
The court and the state
rely on you, sir.
How can you go far away and leave the foundation isolated!”
He replied:
“If I go out
and fortunately defeat the bandits,
then the national prestige can be boosted,
which is still better than sitting idly and waiting for destitution.”
In the eleventh month,
on the Jiǎxū day,
Yuè led forty thousand armored soldiers towards Xǔchāng,
leaving Péi Shì, the heir apparent Pí, as well as Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn Lǐ Yùn, and Yòuwèi Jiāngjūn Hé Lún to guard the capital
and observe the palace.
He appointed Pān Tāo as Hénán Yǐn
to manage remaining affairs.
Yuè memorialized to have a travelling court with him,
appointed Tàiwèi Yǎn as Jūnsī,
and all prominent and respected court officials
were made his aides.
Renowned generals and strong soldiers
were all brought into his command.
Consequently, the palace had no guards left,
famine worsened daily,
and dead bodies lay across the palace halls.
Robbers acted openly,
and all government offices and camps
dug trenches to defend themselves.
Yuè stationed in Xiàng to the east,
appointed Féng Sōng as Zuǒsīmǎ,
and personally assumed the title of Yùzhōu Mù.
Jìnglíng Wáng Máo reported to the Emperor, who dispatched troops to attack Hé Lún,
but they did not succeed.
The Emperor blamed Máo,
who then fled
and escaped.
Máo
was the same as Dōngpíng Wáng Máo;
when the Emperor ascended the throne,
he was enfeoffed as Jìnglíng Wáng.
22 Yángzhōu Dūdū Zhōu Fù, considering Luòyáng to be isolated and precarious,
submitted a memorial requesting to move the capital to Shòuchūn.
Tài Fù Yuè was greatly angered because Fù did not first inform him but directly submitted the memorial,
and he summoned Fù and Huáinán Tàishǒu Péi Shuò.
Fù refused to go,
ordering Shuò to lead his troops first.
Shuò falsely claimed to have received a secret imperial edict from Yuè
to attack Fù,
but was defeated by Fù
and retreated to defend Dōngchéng.
Dōngchéng county,
during the Hàn dynasty, belonged to Jiǔjiāng Commandery;
in the Later Hàn, it belonged to Xiàpéi Kingdom;
during the Jìn dynasty, it belonged to Huáinán Commandery.
Sòng Bái said: Huáizhōu Dìngyuǎn county
is the land of Hàn Dōngchéng county.
23 An imperial edict appointed Zhāng Guǐ as Zhènxī Jiāngjūn and Dūdū Lǒngyòu Zhūjūnsì.
Kǎoyì says: The Imperial Annals state
“Ānxī”.
According to Emperor Huì’s Yǒngxīng second year,
Guǐ had already been appointed Ānxī Jiāngjūn.
Here we follow the main biography.
He was informed of the capital's hunger and scarcity.
Guǐ sent Cānjūn Dù Xūn to present five hundred horses
and thirty thousand bolts of felt cloth.
Felt cloth
is woven from fine wool.
Tǎn
is pronounced tuō gǎn.
24 Chéng Tài Fù Xiāng attacked Qiáo Dēng at Fúchéng.
Luó Shàng’s son Yǔ and his subordinates had long disliked Dēng
and did not supply him with grain.
Yìzhōu Cìshǐ Pí Sù was enraged
and intended to punish them.
In the twelfth month,
when Sù arrived at Bājùn,
Luó Yǔ sent someone to kill Sù by night.
Jiànpíng Dūwèi Bào Zhòng then killed Yǔ,
and Bājùn fell into chaos.
Xiāng knew that Dēng’s food was exhausted and his aid cut off,
so he attacked Fú more urgently.
All the soldiers and civilians smoked rats to eat them,
and many died of starvation,
yet not one person defected.
Xiāng’s son Shòu had been with Dēng,
and Dēng now returned him.
In the first year of Yǒngxīng,
Luó Shàng had plundered Xiāng’s wife and his son Shòu,
who had since been with Dēng.
The three offices
were Píngxī Jiāngjūn Fǔ, Yìzhōu Cìshǐ Fǔ, and Xīróng Xiàowèi Fǔ,
all concurrently held by Luó Shàng.
Jiān
is pronounced gǔ xián.
25 Originally,
the Emperor, because Wáng Mí and Shí Lè were pressing upon the capital region,
issued an edict for Gǒu Xī to supervise and lead the various commanderies and prefectures to suppress them.
At that time, Cáo Yí had defeated Lángxié
and brought Qí territory under his control in the north,
and his military power was very strong.
Gǒu Chún closed the city gates and defended himself.
Xī returned to rescue Qīngzhōu,
fought continuously with Yí,
and defeated him.
In the first year of Yǒngjiā,
Gǒu Xī attacked Wèi Zhí,
leaving his brother Chún to guard Qīngzhōu.
26 In this year,
Níngzhōu Cìshǐ Wáng Xùn arrived at his post
and memorialized to appoint Lǐ Zhāo as Zhūtí Tàishǒu.
At that time, Níngzhōu was externally pressed by Chéng
and internally plagued by Yi barbarians,
with cities and towns in ruins.
Xùn wore coarse clothes and ate simple food,
gathered the scattered people,
and tirelessly toiled,
so that within a few years,
the province became peaceful again.
He executed more than ten powerful families who did not abide by the law;
he dealt with the Wǔlíng Yi, who had previously caused rebellion,
as seen in Volume 85, Emperor Huì’s Tàipíng second year.
Líng
is pronounced lì dīng.
Both internal and external forces were awed and submitted.
27 Hàn Zhǔ Cōng, believing himself to have ascended out of order,
was jealous of his legitimate elder brother Gōng.
While Gōng was sleeping,
he made a hole in his wall
and stabbed him to death.
The Hán Empress Dowager Shàn passed away.
The Hán ruler, Liú Cōng, honored his mother, Zhāng Shì, as the Empress Dowager.
Shàn Shì was young and beautiful,
and Cōng had an incestuous relationship with her.
Incest committed by a subordinate with a superior is called zhēng;
incest committed by a superior with a subordinate is called bào.
Shào,
read as 'zhào' in Shī.
Shàn Shì died of shame and resentment.
Liú Yì's favor consequently gradually declined,
but due to Shàn Shì,
he had not yet been deposed.
Hūyán Hòu said to Cōng:
"When a father dies, his son succeeds;
this is the constant path of ancient and modern times.
Your Majesty inherited the enterprise of Gāozǔ (Liú Yuān,
whose temple name was Gāozǔ).
After Your Majesty's hundred years,
Càn and his brothers will surely have no descendants."
Cōng said:
"Yes,
I must think about this slowly."
Hūyán Shì said:
"Delaying affairs invites change.
As the Grand Younger Brother (Liú Yì) sees Càn and his brothers growing up,
he will surely harbor feelings of unease.
If by chance some scoundrel causes discord between them,
disaster might very well erupt today."
(This implies Liú Yì intended to kill Cōng.)
(This lays the groundwork for Cōng killing Liú Yì in the first year of Jiànwǔ of Emperor Yuán.)
"Strangers should not meddle between close kin.
The Lord has intentions for the King of Hénèi;
why does Your Highness not avoid him!"
Yì said:
"At the end of Héruì,
the Lord considered the distinction between嫡(dí, direct lineage) and 庶(shù, secondary lineage)
and offered the great position to Yì.
Because the Lord was older,
I respectfully yielded to him.
The empire
is Gāozǔ's empire;
if the elder brother dies and the younger brother succeeds,
why should it be unacceptable!
Càn and his brothers are already grown,
just like today.
Moreover, between sons and younger brothers,
how much difference is there in closeness?
How could the Lord possibly have such an intention!"
(Cōng's yielding to Yì is mentioned above.)
(Yì's words here were certainly not spoken in this year.
The Zīzhì Tōngjiàn, prompted by Hūyán Shì's words,
recorded them consecutively.)
Jī,
read as 'qǐ' in Jū.
1. In spring,
in the first month,
on the day Rénshēn,
Gǒu Xī was defeated by Cáo Nì,
abandoned his city, and fled to Gāopíng.
(Gāopíng County,
formerly belonged to Liángguó;
in Jìn it became Gāopíngguó.
The Sīshǔi river flows to its west,
and there is Gāopíng Mountain.
The mountain is ten lǐ from east to west,
five lǐ from north to south,
and four lǐ high.
It is the highest mountain,
with a flat top,
hence it is called Gāopíng Mountain,
and the county also took its name from it.)
2. Shí Lè planned to hold and secure the Jiāng and Hàn rivers,
but his Military Advisor Dūwèi Zhāng Bīn thought it was not feasible.
As the army was suffering from famine and plague,
and more than half had died,
they then crossed the Miǎn river,
attacked Jiāngxià,
and on the day Guǐyǒu,
captured it.
3. On the day Yǐhài,
Chéng Grand Tutor Lǐ Xiāng captured Fúchéng
and captured Qiáo Dēng;
Grand Protector Lǐ Shǐ captured Bāxī
and killed Wén Shí.
Thereupon, Chéng ruler Lǐ Xióng granted a great amnesty
and changed the era name to Yùhéng.
When Qiáo Dēng arrived in Chéngdū,
Xióng wanted to pardon him;
but Dēng's words and demeanor were unyielding,
so Xióng killed him.
4. Refugees from Bā and Shǔ were scattered between Jīng and Xiāng,
and were often harassed by the local populace.
A Shǔ man, Lǐ Xiāng, gathered a multitude and rebelled from Yuèxiāng.
(This is another Lǐ Xiāng,
not Chéng Grand Tutor Lǐ Xiāng.)
(Lǐlíng County
belonged to Chángshā Commandery.
Tāo,
read as 'tāo' in Tǔdāo.
During Emperor Huì's time, Shǔ was in chaos;
Huáróng, Zhōulíng, and Jiānlì three counties of Nánjùn were separated
to establish a separate Fēngdū County,
and Chéngdū Commandery was set up as the domain of the King of Chéngdū, Sīmǎ Yǐng.)
Chéng Wǔ feigned agreement but then ambushed and killed him,
awarding his wife and children as a prize,
and drowning over eight thousand people in the river;
the refugees grew even more resentful.
Shǔ people Dù Chóu and others rebelled again.
The Xiāng Province Military Advisor Féng Sù had a grudge against a Shǔ man, Rǔ Bān.
(Rǔ,
is a surname.
In Shāng there were Rǔ Jiū and Rǔ Fāng,
in Jìn there were Rǔ Kuān and Rǔ Qí.)
(Féng Sù said): "The Bā and Shǔ refugees all want to rebel."
Wǔ Diào believed this
and intended to execute all the refugees.
The refugees were greatly alarmed,
and forty to fifty thousand households rebelled simultaneously,
collectively electing Dù Tāo, who had high regard in his locality, as their leader.
Tāo proclaimed himself Governor of Liáng and Yì Provinces,
and concurrently Inspector of Xiāng Province.
5. Péi Shuò sought help from Lángyá King Sīmǎ Ruì.
Ruì sent the General Who Manifests Awe, Gān Zhuó, and others to attack Zhōu Fù in Shòuchūn.
Fù's forces disintegrated,
and he fled to Xiàng.
(The Kǎoyì says:
"Emperor's Annals:
On the day Wùyín,
Ruì sent Zhuó to attack Fù in Shòuchūn,
and Fù's forces disintegrated."
It is not known whether it was the day Zhuó was ordered,
the day of attack, or the day of disintegration,
thus it is left blank.)
Fù died of worry and indignation.
(Què was Tíngzhī's son.)
6. The Inspector of Yáng Province, Liú Táo, passed away.
Lángyá King Sīmǎ Ruì again appointed Wáng Dūn, the Libationer of the Peace-East Army, as the Inspector of Yáng Province,
and soon added him as Dūdū of All Military Affairs for Expeditions.
(Last year Dūn fled to Jiànyè.)
7. On the day Gēngchén,
King of Píngyuán, Sīmǎ Gàn, passed away.
8. In the second month,
Shí Lè attacked Xīncài,
killing Sīmǎ Què, the Prince Zhuāng of Xīncài, in Nándùn;
he advanced and captured Xǔchāng,
killing the General Who Pacifies the East, Wáng Kāng.
9. The Dī people Fú Chéng and Kuí Wén rebelled again.
10 The King Xiàoxiàn of Dōnghǎi, Sīmǎ Yuè, already had a rift with Gǒu Xī.
The matter began in the previous fascicle, in Yǒngjiā 2nd year.
Xī was enraged,
and memorialized, requesting the heads of Pān Tāo and others,
exclaiming:
“Sīmǎ Yuánchāo acts as Chancellor unfairly!
King of Dōnghǎi, Yuè,
courtesy name Yuánchāo.
How can Gǒu Dàojiāng be made to act unjustly!”
Thereupon, he sent a proclamation to all the prefectures,
boasting of his achievements,
and listing Yuè’s crimes.
The Emperor also disliked Yuè’s monopolization of power
and frequent disregard of imperial decrees.
The generals and officers he left behind, such as Hé Lún,
plundered public officials and nobles,
and sexually assaulted princesses.
The Emperor secretly bestowed upon Xī a handwritten edict,
ordering him to suppress Yuè.
Xī often exchanged letters with the Emperor,
which aroused Yuè's suspicion.
He sent cavalry scouts to patrol between Chénggāo,
and they indeed captured Xī’s envoy and the imperial edict.
Thereupon, Yuè issued a proclamation listing Xī’s crimes,
appointed Yáng Mào, the Central Provisional Aide-de-camp, as Inspector of Yǎnzhōu,
and ordered him and Pèi Dùn, the Inspector of Xúzhōu, to jointly suppress Xī.
Xī sent cavalry to arrest Pān Tāo;
Tāo fled during the night
and escaped.
He apprehended Liú Céng, the Minister, and Chéng Yán, the Palace Attendant,
and executed them.
Yuè fell ill from worry and indignation.
He entrusted future affairs to Wáng Yǎn.
In the third month,
on the bǐngzǐ day,
he died in Xiàng.
Kǎoyì says: In the Dìjì:
“In the first month of the 5th year,
the Emperor secretly ordered Gǒu Xī to suppress Yuè.
On the yǐwèi day,
Yuè sent Yáng Mào and Pèi Dùn to jointly attack Xī.
In the third month,
on the wùwǔ day,
an edict was issued detailing Yuè’s crimes,
announcing to the regional commanders to suppress him,
and appointing Xī as Grand General.
On the bǐngzǐ day,
Yuè died.”
In Xī’s biography:
“Xī issued a proclamation to all prefectures,
listing Yuè’s crimes.
The Emperor disliked Yuè’s monopolization of power,
and thus ordered Xī to issue a proclamation to the six prefectures,
to jointly launch a major campaign.
Xī sent messages to various commanders.
The Emperor again secretly ordered Xī to suppress Yuè.
Xī again memorialized, stating that Lǐ Chū had arrived,
bearing a handwritten edict,
and that he had marched swiftly with his army
to Cāngyuán.
In the 5th year,
the Emperor again ordered Xī,
detailing Yuè’s wickedness,
and that on the day the edict arrived,
it should be announced to all under heaven,
and a full-scale campaign launched.
Xī memorialized, stating that
he had already dispatched Wáng Zàn with troops to Xiàng.
Yuè sent cavalry who captured Xī’s envoy between Chénggāo,
and thus a major rift developed.”
In the Jìn Chūnqiū:
“In the 5th year,
first month,
the Emperor sent Lǐ Chū with an edict for Xī to suppress Yuè.”
Comment: If Yuè had already captured Xī’s envoy,
then the Emperor would not have been able to remain secure,
and Pān Tāo, Hé Lún, and others would not have been able to remain peacefully in Luò.
Moreover, if Tāo and others had not yet left,
then the Emperor would not have dared to openly order Xī to suppress Yuè.
Since the dates and events differ so much,
they are now all placed at the time of Yuè’s death,
which should be no mistake.
The multitude jointly nominated Wáng Yǎn as Grand Marshal,
but Yǎn dared not accept;
he yielded to the King of Xiāngyáng, Sīmǎ Fàn,
who also refused.
Fàn
was Wěi’s son.
Thereupon, Yǎn and others together escorted Yuè’s coffin back to be buried in Dōnghǎi.
Hé Lún, Lǐ Yùn, and others, hearing of Yuè’s death,
escorted Pèi and the heir apparent Sīmǎ Pí from Luòyáng eastwards,
and the city’s soldiers and populace vied to follow them.
The Emperor posthumously demoted Yuè to County King,
and appointed Gǒu Xī as Grand General and Grand Commander-in-Chief,
overseeing military affairs of Qīng, Xú, Yǎn, Yù, Jīng, and Yáng six prefectures.
11 The generals and officials of Yìzhōu together killed Bào Zhòng,
and memorialized, appointing Zhāng Luó, the Grand Administrator of Bājùn, to act as head of the three offices.
Luó and Wěi Wén and others died in battle;
Wén and others plundered officials and common people,
and surrendered westwards to Chéng.
The civil and military officials of the three offices jointly memorialized, appointing Wáng Yì of Shǔjùn, the Pacificator of the West, to act as head of the three offices.
The remaining troops in Yìzhōu were insufficient for advancing and taking territory,
and within less than a year, the leadership changed five times,
merely serving as resources for Qín and Dī to annex.
12 Previously, Zhāng Guāng, the Inspector of Liángzhōu, had met with the grand administrators of various commanderies in Wèixìng,
to jointly plan an advance.
Zhāng Yàn proclaimed:
“Hànzhōng is desolate and ruined,
close to major bandits.
The matter of restoration
should await a hero.”
Guāng believed Yàn had accepted bribes from Dèng Dìng,
leading to the loss of Hànzhōng;
the matter is seen in the previous fascicle, Yǒngjiā 1st year.
He reprimanded him and drove him out,
then executed him.
He mustered his forces and advanced,
and after several years, finally reached Hànzhōng,
pacified the desolate and ravaged areas,
and the people were pleased and submitted.
Guāng was Inspector of Liángzhōu,
seen in the previous fascicle, 2nd year.
13 Summer,
fourth month,
Shí Lè led light cavalry to pursue the funeral procession of Grand Tutor Yuè,
reaching Níngpíngchéng in Kǔxiàn.
Kǔxiàn
belonged to Chénjùn.
Shuǐ Jīng Zhù: Níngpíngchéng is north of the Shā River,
originally Níngpíng County of the Huáiyáng Kingdom in the Former Hàn;
in the Later Hàn, Huáiyáng was changed to Chén Kingdom.
The Jìn abolished Níngpíng County,
but the old city still remained.
Xián says: The old city of Níngpíng
is in the southwest of modern Bózhōu Gǔyáng County.
Qí,
read Qí Jì fān;
same below.
He let his cavalry surround them and shoot,
and more than ten thousand officers and soldiers trampled each other like a mountain,
not one escaping.
He captured Grand Commandant Wáng Yǎn, the King of Xiāngyáng Sīmǎ Fàn, the King of Rènchéng Sīmǎ Jì, the King Zhuāng of Wǔlíng Sīmǎ Dàn,
the King of Xīhé Sīmǎ Xǐ, the King Huái of Liáng Sīmǎ Xǐ, and the King of Qí Sīmǎ Chāo.
Sīmǎ Xǐ, King of Xīhé,
was a descendant of Sīmǎ Bīn, King Miù of Xīhé, brother of Emperor Xuān.
Chāo,
was the son of Sīmǎ Jiǒng, King of Qí.
He seated them under his tent,
and questioned them about the reasons for the Jin’s predicament.
Yǎn fully explained the causes of the disaster,
saying the plans were not his;
and furthermore, he claimed that he had no ambition for office since he was young
and did not participate in worldly affairs.
He then urged Lè to assume an imperial title,
hoping to save himself.
Lè said:
“You rose to court in your youth,
your fame covered the four seas,
and you held heavy responsibilities.
How can you say you had no ambition for office!
Who but you destroyed all under heaven!”
He ordered his attendants to escort him out.
The others, fearing death,
mostly presented their own explanations.
Only the King of Xiāngyáng, Sīmǎ Fàn, maintained a solemn expression,
and looking back, scolded them:
“In today’s situation,
why are you still babbling on!”
Lè said to Kǒng Cháng:
“I have traveled widely,
but I have never seen such people.
Should they be spared?”
Lè wanted to spare them,
because of their clear and refined appearance.
“They are all princes and dukes of Jin,
and will never serve us.”
Lè said:
“Even so,
they should not be killed by the sword.”
At night,
he sent men to push down a wall and kill them.
Sīmǎ Jì
was the son of Sīmǎ Líng, King Jǐng, younger brother of Emperor Xuān;
Sīmǎ Xǐ
was Dàn’s son.
He split open Yuè’s coffin,
and burned his corpse,
saying:
“This man brought chaos to the world;
I avenge the world,
and thus burn his bones to inform Heaven and Earth.”
Hé Lún (何倫) and others arrived at Wěicāng (洧倉).
The Commentary on the Waterways says:
The Wěi (洧) River
flows southeast past Chángshè (長社) County in Yǐngchuān (潁川) Commandery,
where a branch splits off and flows east past Xǔchāng (許昌) County,
then further east into the city of Wèncāng (汶倉).
People commonly regarded this as the Wèn (汶) River,
hence the name Wèncāng (汶倉).
It was merely a storehouse by the Wěi (洧) River.
After the defeat,
the Heir Apparent of Dōnghǎi (東海) and forty-eight princes of the imperial clan all perished at Lè's (勒) hands.
Kǎo Yì (考異) states: The biography of King Dōnghǎi Yuè (東海越) says
"thirty-six kings."
We now follow Dì Jì (帝紀).
Lǐ Yùn (李惲) fled to Guǎngzōng (廣宗).
Péi (裴) was plundered and sold by someone.
After a long time,
he crossed the river.
Originally,
when Lángxié (琅邪) King Ruì (睿) garrisoned Jiànyè (建業),
it was Péi's (裴) idea.
Therefore, Ruì (睿) appreciated him,
greatly showing him kindness and support,
and made his son Chōng (冲) the successor to Yuè (越).
14. Zhào Gù (趙固) and Wáng Sāng (王桑) of Hàn (漢) attacked Péi Dùn (裴盾)
and killed him.
Dùn (盾) was then in Péngchéng (彭城).
Dùn (盾),
pronounced tú sǔn.
15. Dù Tāo (杜弢) attacked Chángshā (長沙).
In the fifth month,
Xún Tiào (荀眺) abandoned the city and fled to Guǎngzhōu (廣州).
Tāo (弢) pursued and captured him.
Thereupon, Tāo (弢) defeated Líng (零) and Guì (桂) in the south,
and plundered Wǔchāng (武昌) in the east,
killing many officials, including those of the two-thousand-dàn rank and chief administrators.
16. Fù Zhī (傅祗), Grand Tutor to the Crown Prince, was appointed Sītú (司徒);
Xún Fán (荀藩), Director of the Imperial Secretariat, was appointed Sīkōng (司空);
Wáng Jùn (王浚) was granted the titles of Dà Sīmǎ (大司馬), Shìzhōng (侍中), and Dà Dūdū (大都督),
overseeing military affairs in Yōu (幽) and Jì (冀) provinces;
Nányáng (南陽) King Mó (模) was appointed Tàiwèi (太尉) and Dà Dūdū (大都督);
Zhāng Guǐ (張軌) was appointed Chējì Dà Jiàngjūn (車騎大將軍);
Lángxié (琅邪) King Ruì (睿) was appointed Zhèndōng Dà Jiàngjūn (鎮東大將軍),
also overseeing military affairs in the five provinces of Yáng (揚), Jiāng (江), Xiāng (湘), Jiāo (交), and Guǎng (廣).
Earlier,
Grand Tutor Yuè (越) believed that Nányáng (南陽) King Mó (模) was unable to pacify Guānzhōng (關中).
At that time, Guānzhōng (關中) suffered from famine and epidemics,
and bandits roamed openly,
which Mó (模) could not control.
General Chúnyú Dìng (淳于定) persuaded Mó (模) not to answer the summons,
and Mó (模) followed him.
He memorialized to send his heir apparent, Bǎo (保), as Píngxī Zhōnglángjiàng (平西中郎將),
to garrison Shàngguī (上邽).
However, Péi Bāo (裴苞), Inspector of Qín (秦) Province, resisted him.
Mó (模) sent Chén Ān (陳安), a Duwèi (都尉) under his command, to attack Bāo (苞).
Bāo (苞) fled to Āndìng (安定),
where Administrator Jiǎ Pǐ (賈疋) received him.
17. Gǒu Xī (苟晞) memorialized to request moving the capital to Cāngyuán (倉垣),
and sent Liú Huì (劉會), a Zhōngláng (中郎) of the Grand Secretariat, with dozens of boats,
five hundred imperial guards, and a thousand hù (斛) of grain to welcome the emperor.
The emperor was about to comply,
but the high officials hesitated,
and those around him were reluctant to part with their wealth,
so the journey was not carried out.
Afterwards, Luòyáng (洛陽) was gripped by famine and distress,
with people resorting to cannibalism,
and eight or nine tenths of the officials had fled.
The emperor summoned the high officials to deliberate,
intending to depart, but his escort was not ready.
The emperor clasped his hands and sighed, saying,
"How can there be no carriages!"
So he sent Fù Zhī (傅祗) to Héyīn (河陰)
to prepare boats and oars.
Héyīn (河陰)
was originally Píngyīn (平陰) County during the Hàn (漢) dynasty.
Emperor Wén (文) of Wèi (魏) renamed it Héyīn (河陰).
It is northeast of Luòyáng (洛陽)
and belonged to Hénán (河南) Commandery.
Zhì (治),
pronounced zhí zhī.
The emperor walked out of the Xīyè (西掖) Gate,
and reached Tóngtuó (銅駝) Street.
The Commentary on the Waterways says: Between the Tàiwèi (太尉) and Sītú (司徒) residential areas in Luòyáng (洛陽) city
was called Tóngtuó (銅駝) Street.
Emperor Míng (明) of Wèi (魏) placed bronze camels south of Chānghé (閶闔) Gate Street,
which is this.
Lù Jī's (陸機) Luòyáng Jì (洛陽記) says: Luòyáng (洛陽) has Tóngtuó (銅駝) Street,
where the Hàn (漢) dynasty cast two bronze camels,
which faced each other at the four-way intersection south of the palace.
A common saying goes:
"Outside Jīnmǎ (金馬) Gate, the wise gather;
on Tóngtuó (銅駝) Street, the youths assemble."
He could not proceed and returned.
Even if the emperor had reached Cāngyuán (倉垣),
he would still have been captured by Shí Lè (石勒).
The Commentary on the Waterways says: East of Xīn'ān (新安) County in Hénán (河南) there is Qiānqiū (千秋) Pavilion.
East of the pavilion is Yōnggǔ (雍谷) Stream,
with winding and circuitous mountain peaks,
and a stone path through a constricted gorge,
hence it is also called Xiáshí (峽石).
Xiànzhī (獻之).
The emperor appointed him Yángwēi Jiàngjūn (揚威將軍) and Píngyáng Tàishǒu (平陽太守),
with his duties as Dùzhī (度支) remaining unchanged.
18. Hàn (漢) ruler Cōng (聰) sent Hūyán Yàn (呼延晏), Commander of the Vanguard Army, with twenty-seven thousand troops to attack Luòyáng (洛陽).
By the time they reached Hénán (河南),
Hénán (河南) County
belonged to the Hénán (河南) Administrator.
It was the royal city of Jiápá (郟鄏) in the eastern capital of Zhōu (周).
Bǐ (比),
pronounced bì mèi.
More than thirty thousand people died.
Shǐ'ān (始安) King Yào (曜), Wáng Mí (王彌), and Shí Lè (石勒) all led their troops to converge,
but before they arrived,
Yàn (晏) left his baggage train at Zhāng Fāng's (張方) old encampment.
Zhāng Fāng's (張方) old encampment was seven lǐ (里) west of Luòyáng (洛陽).
Zhòng (重),
pronounced zhí yòng.
On Guǐwèi (癸未)
he arrived first at Luòyáng (洛陽).
On Jiǎshēn (甲申),
he attacked Píngchāng (平昌) Gate.
Píngchāng (平昌) Gate
was the first gate on the east end of the south side of Luò (洛) city.
On Bǐngxū (丙戌)
he captured it,
and then burned the Dōngyáng (東陽) Gate and all government offices.
In the sixth month,
on Dīnghài (丁亥) (the first day of the month),
Yàn (晏), as external reinforcements had not arrived,
took captives and plunder and departed.
The emperor had boats prepared on the Luò (洛) River,
intending to flee east,
but Yàn (晏) burned them all.
On Gēngyín (庚寅),
Xún Fán (荀藩) and his brother Gānglù Dàfū (光祿大夫) Zǔ (組) fled to Huányuán (轘轅).
On Xīnmǎo (辛卯),
Wáng Mí (王彌) arrived at Xuānyáng (宣陽) Gate.
Xuānyáng (宣陽) Gate
was the fourth gate from the east on the south side of Luò (洛) city,
also called Yí (謻) Gate.
On Rénchén (壬辰)
Shǐ'ān (始安) King Yào (曜) arrived at Xīmíng (西明) Gate.
On Dīngyǒu (丁酉),
Wáng Mí (王彌) and Hūyán Yàn (呼延晏) captured Xuānyáng (宣陽) Gate,
entered the Southern Palace,
ascended the Tàijí Qiándiàn (太極前殿),
unleashed their soldiers to plunder extensively,
and seized all palace women and treasures.
The emperor exited the Huálín (華林) Garden Gate,
intending to flee to Cháng'ān (長安),
but Hàn (漢) soldiers pursued and seized him,
imprisoning him at Duānmén (端門).
Yào (曜) entered through Xīmíng (西明) Gate and garrisoned the Imperial Armory.
On Wùxū (戊戌),

Yào (曜) killed Crown Prince Quán (詮), Wúxiào (吳孝) King Yàn (晏), Jìnglíng (竟陵) King Máo (楙), Right Imperial Secretary Cáo Fù (曹馥), Director of the Imperial Secretariat Lǘqiū Chōng (閭丘沖), Hénán (河南) Administrator Liú Mò (劉默), and others.
More than thirty thousand soldiers and civilians died.
He then excavated all the imperial tombs,
and burned down all the palace temples and government offices.
Yào (曜) took Empress Yáng (羊), wife of Emperor Huì (惠),
and moved the emperor and the six imperial seals to Píngyáng (平陽).
Shí Lè (石勒) led his troops out of Huányuán (轘轅)
and garrisoned Xǔchāng (許昌).
Guānglù Dàfū (光祿大夫) Liú Fān (劉蕃) and Shàngshū (尚書) Lú Zhì (盧志) fled to Bīngzhōu (幷州).
They followed Liú Kūn (劉琨).
Fān (蕃)
was Kūn's (琨) father.
On Dīngwèi (丁未),
Hàn (漢) ruler Cōng (聰) declared a general amnesty
and changed the era name to Jiāpíng (嘉平).
He appointed the emperor as Tèjìn Zuǒ Guānglù Dàfū (特進左光祿大夫)
and enfeoffed him as Píng'ā Gōng (平阿公).
Kǎo Yì (考異) states: Dì Jì (帝紀) says:
"Cōng (聰) enfeoffed the emperor as Kuàijī Gōng (會稽公)."
Zàijì (載記) and Sānshí Guó Chūnqiū (三十國春秋) say
"Píng'ā Gōng (平阿公)."
Jìn Chūnqiū (晉春秋) says
"Pínghé Gōng (平河公)."
The character hé (河)
is likely an error.
Shíliù Guó (十六國), Sānshí Guó (三十國), and Jìn Chūnqiū (晉春秋) say:
"In the second month of the following year,
the emperor was then enfeoffed as Kuàijī Gōng (會稽公)."
It is likely that he was first enfeoffed as Píng'ā (平阿),
and later promoted to Kuàijī (會稽).
Dì Jì (帝紀) is abbreviated.
We now follow the various books.
He was the elder brother of Hè (敳).
At first,
Shǐ'ān Wáng Yào was resentful that Wáng Mí had not waited for him to arrive
before entering Luòyáng.
Mí persuaded Yào, saying:
"Luòyáng is the center of All-Under-Heaven.
Its mountains and rivers form a natural barrier on all four sides.
Its city walls and palaces require no renovation.
It would be appropriate to report to the sovereign that he should move the capital here from Píngyáng."
Yào believed that All-Under-Heaven was not yet settled,
and Luòyáng was vulnerable to attack from all four directions,
making it indefensible.
He did not adopt Mí's strategy and instead burned it.
Mí cursed, saying:
"You Túcāozi,
do you have any imperial ambition?!"
The Jìn Shū states: "The Northern Dí tribes were categorized by their tribal groups.
Among those who moved into the area within the passes,
there were nineteen kinds, including the Túcāo.
All had their own tribal groups
and were not intermingled.
The Túcāo were the most powerful and noble,
hence they were able to become Chányú
and govern the other tribes."
Tú,
pronounced like "zhí yú fān."
Dù Yòu said: "Tóumàn and Mòdú are
indeed Túcāo tribes."
(He) led his troops eastward to garrison Xiàngguān.
Xiàngguān is in Xiàngxiàn, Chénjùn.
"Now the Nine Provinces are in turmoil,
and all heroes are contending.
You, General, have established an unparalleled功 (achievement) for the Hàn,
but you have also fallen out with Shǐ'ān Wáng.
How will you accommodate yourself?
It is better to occupy your home province in the east.
Mí was from Dōnglái, Qīngzhōu.
Above, you can unify the Four Seas;
below, you will not lose the enterprise of a tripod's stand.
This is the best strategy."
Mí inwardly agreed.
Sītú Fù Zhī established a traveling secretariat at Héyīn.
Sīkōng Xún Fān was in Yángchéng.
Yángchéngxiàn
belonged to Yǐngchuān Jùn during the Hàn dynasty,
and to Hénán Jùn during the Jìn dynasty.
Rǔyīn Tàishǒu Lǐ Jǔ of Píngyáng built houses for them
and transported grain to supply them.
Huì
was Xīn's great-grandson.
Fān, along with his younger brother Zǔ and his cousin Zhōnghùjūn Sōng,
and Huì, along with his younger brother Zhōnglǐngjūn Héng, established a traveling secretariat at Mì.
Mìxiàn
belonged to Hénán Jùn during the Hàn dynasty,
and to Xíngyáng Jùn during the Jìn dynasty.
They acclaimed Lángyé Wáng Ruì as their盟主 (leader of the alliance).
Fān, acting on imperial authority, appointed Sōng as Xiāngchéng Tàishǒu,
Jǔ as Xíngyáng Tàishǒu,
and former Qián Guānjūn Jiāngjūn Chǔ Jiá of Hénán as Liángguó Nèishǐ.
Yángwēi Jiāngjūn Wèi Jùn was garrisoned at Shíliángwù north of Luò.
Liú Kūn, acting on imperial authority, provisionally appointed Jùn as Hénán Yǐn.
Jùn went to Xún Fān to consult on military matters.
Fān invited Lǐ Jǔ to join the meeting.
Jǔ went at night.
All of Jǔ's subordinates said:
"Jùn cannot be trusted;
you should not go at night."
Jǔ said:
"Loyal ministers share the same heart;
what is there to doubt?"
So he went,
and they established a friendly bond before parting.
Jùn's cousin, Gāi,
gathered a crowd and occupied Yīquánwù.
The Shuǐ Jīng Zhù says: "The Luò River passes south of Lúqiūxiàn,
then flows eastward past the south of Yīhéwù.
The city is on the northern plateau of the river,
twenty zhàng high,
with north, south, and east sides,
a precipitous natural barrier.
Only the west side needs to be fortified
to make it completely secure.
The name 'Yīhé'
arose from this."
When Liú Yào attacked Hénán,
Jìn General Wèi Gāi fled here.
Gāi's biography states that
Yīquánwù is in Yíyáng.
Shěn Yuē's Zhì states that
Wèi established forty general titles,
with Wēiwǔ as the tenth,
but there was no Wǔwēi.
Yùzhāng Wáng Duān,
younger brother of Tàizǐ Quán,
fled eastward to Cāngyuán.
Gǒu Xī, leading all officials, proclaimed him Tàizǐ (Crown Prince)
and established a traveling secretariat.
Duān, acting on imperial authority, appointed Xī as Lǐng Tàizǐ Tàifù, Dūdū Zhōngwài Zhūjūn, Lù Shàngshū Shì,
and moved the garrison from Cāngyuán to Méngchéng.
Méngxiàn
belonged to Liángguó.
Fǔjūn Jiāngjūn Qín Wáng Yè,
son of Wú Xiàowáng,
and nephew of Xún Fān,
at the age of twelve,
fled south to Mì.
The Kǎo Yì says: "The Jìn Shū states
that Mǐn Dì's given name was Yè,
and Jiànyè was also changed to Jiànkāng.
However, according to the Sānshí Guó and Jìn Chūnqiū,
Mǐn Dì's
given name was Zǐyè,
sometimes written as
'Yè.'
Also, the Wú Zhì states
that Sūn Quán changed Mòlíng to Jiànyè,
taking its name from 'establishing a foundation and enterprise,'
none of which uses
the character 'Yè.'
We follow this now."
(He then) headed south to Xǔchāng.
Former Yùzhōu Cìshǐ Yán Dǐng of Tiānshuǐ
gathered several thousand displaced people from Xīzhōu at Mì,
intending to return to their hometowns.
Xún Fān, seeing that Dǐng had talent and commanded a crowd,
appointed Dǐng as Yùzhōu Cìshǐ.
He appointed Zhōngshūlìng Lǐ Gěn,
Sītú Zuǒchángshǐ Liú Chóu of Péngchéng, Zhènjūn Chángshǐ Zhōu Yǐ,
and Pí, son of Dōnghǎi Wáng Yuè,
as Zhènjūn Jiāngjūn.
He appointed Yǐ as Chángshǐ.
Yǐ,
pronounced "yú qǐ fān."
Yǐ
was Jùn's son.
At that time, All-Under-Heaven was in great chaos,

1. Spring,
first month.
Hùyán Hòu of Hàn died,
posthumously named Wǔyuán.
2. Hàn Zhèn Běi Jiāngjūn Jìn Chōng and Píng Běi Jiāngjūn Bǔ Xǔ raided Bìngzhōu;
on Xīnwèi,
they besieged Jìnyáng.
3. On Jiǎxū,
Hàn Lord Cōng appointed Sīkōng Wáng Yù’s daughter and Shàngshū Lìng Rèn Yǐ’s daughter as Zuǒ and Yòu Zhāoyí,
Zhōngjūn Dà Jiāngjūn Wáng Zhāng’s daughter, Zhōngshū Jiān Fàn Lóng’s daughter, and Zuǒ Púyè Mǎ Jǐng’s daughter were all made Fūrén,
and Yòu Púyè Zhū Jì’s daughter was made Guì,
all with gold seals and purple ribbons.
Cōng was about to take Taìbǎo Liú Yīn’s daughters as consorts.
Taìdì Yì strongly remonstrated.
Cōng asked Taìzǎi Yánnián and Taìfù Jǐng about it.
Both said,
“Taìbǎo himself says he is a descendant of Liú Kānggōng,
and thus of a different origin than Your Majesty.”
Liú Kānggōng
was a minister of Zhōu,
who held the fief of Liú.
His descendants subsequently adopted Liú as their surname.
Liú Cōng
was a descendant of the Xiōngnú,
who assumed the surname Liú as an external relative of Hàn.
Therefore, it is said they were of different origins.
Cōng was pleased,
and appointed Yīn’s two daughters, Yīng and É, as Zuǒ and Yòu Guìpín,
their rank being above Zhāoyí;
he also took four of Yīn’s granddaughters as Guìrén,
their rank being below Guì.
Thereupon, the favor shown to the six Liú women overshadowed the entire harem.
Cōng rarely went out again,
and all matters were decided by reports from the Zhōnghuángmén.
4. The former Xīnyě Wáng Xīn and Yámén Jiāng Hú Kàng gathered a multitude in Jìnglíng,
proclaimed themselves Chǔ Gōng,
and plundered the Jīng region.
They appointed Xīn’s Nánmán Sīmǎ, Dù Zēng of Xīnyě, as Jìnglíng Taìshǒu.
Zēng’s bravery surpassed that of three armies,
and he could swim in water while wearing armor.
This laid the groundwork for Zēng’s rebellion in Jīngzhōu.
Guàn
from ‘gǔ wán fān.’
Bèi
from ‘pí yì fān.’
5. Second month,
on Rénzǐ the first day,
there was a solar eclipse.
6. Shí Lè built a fortress at Gěpí.
Huáng Lǎn said: There is Gěpí in Tóngyáng Xiàn, Rúnán Jùn.
Xián said: Gěpí
is in the northwest of present-day Xīncài Xiàn, Yùzhōu.
He intended to attack Jiànyè.
Lángyá Wáng Ruì gathered a large army from the south of the Yangtze at Shòuchūn,
appointing Zhèn Dōng Chángshǐ Jì Zhān as Yángwēi Jiāngjūn,
to command all armies in order to suppress him.
Ruì was Zhèn Dōng Dà Jiāngjūn,
and appointed Zhān as Chángshǐ.
It happened that there was heavy rain,
which did not stop for three months.
Shí Lè’s army suffered from hunger and pestilence.
More than half the men died.
When he heard that the Jìn army was approaching,
he gathered his generals and aides to discuss the matter.
The Right Chief Clerk, Diāo Yīng, requested that they first send an offer of surrender to Ruì,
and seek to redeem themselves by pacifying Héshuò.
Once the Jìn army had withdrawn,
they could then slowly plan their next move.
Shí Lè looked grim and gave a long whistle.
The Zhongjiān Jiāngjūn, Kuí Ān, requested that they ascend to high ground to avoid the water.
Zhongjiān Jiāngjūn [General of the Central Army],
was a title established by Shí Lè.
The Xìngpǔ [Genealogical Records] states: The Kuí surname,
is descended from Kuí Zǐ of the Spring and Autumn period.
“General, why are you so timid!”

cut off the heads of the Wú generals,
occupy their city,
and consume their grain.
They vowed to break Dānyáng
and pacify Jiāngnán this year.
Shí Lè laughed and said:
“This is the plan of a brave general!”
Meaning that they did not consider victory or defeat,
but were merely brave in facing the enemy.
Jiāng [將],

He turned to Zhāng Bīn and said:

Zhāng Bīn said:
“General, you have captured the capital,

Even if all your hair were plucked out,

Zhuó [擢],
means to pluck.
Plucking out his hair to count his crimes is still not enough,

Shǔ [數],
is pronounced suǒ jù.

Yè has the fortifications of the Sāntái [Three Terraces].
The Shuǐjīngzhù [Commentary on the Classic of Waters] states: Northwest of Yè City are three terraces,
all built upon the city’s foundation.
They were constructed by Wèi Wǔ in the 15th year of Jiàn'ān of the Hàn dynasty.
The central one is called Tóngtái [Bronze Terrace],
ten zhàng high,
later Shí Hǔ increased it by two zhàng.
The southern one is Jīnquè Tái [Golden Sparrow Terrace],
eight zhàng high.
The northern one is Bīngjǐng Tái [Ice Well Terrace],
also eight zhàng high.
It is close to the Hàn capital,
and can strengthen our support.
It would be advisable to move north and occupy it,
to govern Héběi.
Once Héběi is settled,
there will be no one in the world superior to the General.
The Jìn’s defense of Shòuchūn
is merely because they fear the General will attack it.
When they hear we are leaving,
they will be happy to secure themselves.
How could they have time to pursue and attack our rear,
to our disadvantage!
From ancient times, states established in the southeast
have mostly pursued policies of self-preservation,
also assessing their own lack of strength to advance.”
Zhāng Bīn’s assessment was accurate.
“The General should lead a large army towards Shòuchūn.
Once the supplies are far away,
the main army can slowly return.
Why worry about having no ground for advance or retreat!”
Shí Lè rolled up his sleeves and stroked his beard, saying:
“Master Zhāng’s plan is correct!”
He reprimanded Diāo Yīng, saying:
“Since you are assisting me,
you should help achieve great success.
How can you so hastily advise me to surrender!
This strategy deserves execution!
However, I have always known you to be timid,
so I will pardon you specially.”
Thereupon, he demoted Diāo Yīng to general,
and promoted Zhāng Bīn to Right Chief Clerk,
giving him the title
“Right Marquis.”
Shí Lè led his troops from Gěpí,

They encountered Jìn transport boats,

Jì Zhān pursued them for a hundred li,
and reached Shí Lè’s army.
Shí Lè formed his lines and waited for him.
Jì Zhān did not dare to attack,
and retreated back to Shòuchūn.

Lín Shēn (臨深), Móu Mù (牟穆) and others again led their troops to surrender to Lè (勒).
The generals wanted to attack Sāntái (三臺).
Zhāng Bīn (張賓) said:
"Although Yǎn (演) is weak,
he still has several thousand men.
Sāntái (三臺) is strong and dangerous,
so it will not be easy to capture it quickly.
If we abandon it and leave,
they will collapse on their own.
At present, Wáng Péngzǔ (王彭祖) and Liú Yuèshí (劉越石)
are the Lord's great enemies.
Wáng Jùn (王浚),
courtesy name Péngzǔ (彭祖);
Liú Kūn (劉琨),
courtesy name Yuèshí (越石).
Yǎn (演) is not worth bothering with.
Moreover, the world is in famine and chaos.
Although the Lord commands a large army,
moving about as a transient,
people have no fixed resolve.
This is not the way to ensure complete safety
or control the four directions.
It would be better to choose a suitable place and occupy it,
gather extensive grain stores,
and obtain provisions from Píngyáng (平陽) to plan for Yōu (幽) and Bīng (幷).
Yōu (幽) refers to
Wáng Jùn (王浚);
Bīng (幷) refers to
Liú Kūn (劉琨).
Hándān (邯鄲) and Xiāngguó (襄國)
are strategically advantageous places.
Hándān (邯鄲) county,
belonged to Zhào (趙) kingdom in the Hàn (漢) dynasty,
and to Guǎngpíng (廣平) in the Jìn (晉) dynasty.
Xiāngguó (襄國) county,
was Xìndū (信都) during the Qín (秦) dynasty,
Xiàng Yǔ (項羽) renamed it Xiāngguó (襄國).
It belonged to Zhào (趙) kingdom in the Hàn (漢) dynasty,
and to Guǎngpíng (廣平) in the Jìn (晉) dynasty.
Xìndū (信都) was a separate county,
belonging to Xìndū (信都) kingdom in the Former Hàn (漢),
and to Ānpíng (安平) kingdom in the Later Hàn (漢).
Hándān (邯鄲),
pronounced *hándān*.
Sòng Bái (宋白) says: The Suí (隋) dynasty changed Xiāngguó (襄國) to Lónggāng (龍岡) county,
and in the Táng (唐) dynasty it was the seat of Xíngzhōu (邢州).
Lè (勒) said:
"The plan of the Right Marquis is correct!"
So he advanced and occupied Xiāngguó (襄國).
Bīn (賓) again said to Lè (勒):
"Now that we are here,
Péngzǔ (彭祖) and Yuèshí (越石) deeply fear this.
I am afraid that our city walls and moats are not yet strong, and our provisions are not yet extensive,
and the two enemies will arrive together.
We should quickly gather grain from the fields,
and also send an envoy to Píngyáng (平陽)
to fully explain our intention to secure this place."
Lè (勒) followed his advice.
He then ordered his generals to attack Jìzhōu (冀州).
Many commanderies, counties, and walled strongholds surrendered,
and their grain was transported to Xiāngguó (襄國).
He also presented a memorial to the Hàn (漢) lord Cōng (聰).
Cōng (聰) appointed Lè (勒) as the Commander-in-Chief of military affairs for the four provinces of Jì (冀), Yōu (幽), Bīng (幷), and Yíng (營).
Yíngzhōu (營州) is not among the nineteen provinces listed in Jìn (晉) Tàikāng (太康) *Dìzhì* (地志).
The *Jìn Dìlǐ Zhì* (晉地理志) states: In the second year of Xiánníng (咸寧) (276 CE),
the five commanderies and kingdoms of Chānglí (昌黎), Liáodōng (遼東), Xuántú (玄菟), Dàifāng (帶方), and Lèlàng (樂浪) were separated
to establish Píngzhōu (平州).
When Mùróng Xī (慕容熙) occupied Hélóng (和龍),
Yíngzhōu (營州) was first established at Sùjūn (宿軍),
with a governor to command it.
The Tuòbá Wèi (拓跋魏) established Yíngzhōu (營州) at Hélóng (和龍).
Lè (勒) did not have Yíngzhōu (營州) at that time.
The *Jùn Guó Zhì* (郡國志) states: The land of Yíngzhōu (營州) corresponds to the Yíngshì (營室) constellation division,
hence it is called Yíngzhōu (營州).
He was further enfeoffed as the Duke of Shàngdǎng (上黨).
21 Liú Kūn (劉琨) issued a proclamation to the commanderies and provinces,
setting a date in the tenth month for a meeting at Píngyáng (平陽)
to attack Hàn (漢).
Kūn (琨) was always extravagant and fond of music and women.
Xú Rùn (徐潤) from Hénán (河南) gained Kūn's (琨) favor through his musical talent,
and Kūn (琨) made him the magistrate of Jìnyáng (晉陽).
Rùn (潤) became arrogant and presumptuous,
interfering in government affairs.
The Protector of the Army, Línghú Shèng (令狐盛), repeatedly spoke about this,
and also urged Kūn (琨) to kill him.
Kūn (琨) did not comply.
Rùn (潤) slandered Shèng (盛) to Kūn (琨).
Kūn (琨) arrested Shèng (盛)
and killed him.
Kūn's (琨) mother said:
"You are unable to control heroes to expand your distant strategies,
but instead only eliminate those superior to yourself.
Disaster will surely befall us."
Shèng's (盛) son, Ní (泥), fled to Hàn (漢),
and fully reported the strengths and weaknesses.
The Hàn (漢) lord Cōng (聰) was greatly pleased
and sent Kàn (粲), the King of Hénèi (河內), and Yào (曜), the King of Zhōngshān (中山), to lead troops to invade Bīngzhōu (幷州),
with Línghú Ní (令狐泥) as their guide.
When Kūn (琨) heard of it,
he went east
to gather troops in Chángshān (常山) and Zhōngshān (中山).
He sent his generals Hǎo Shēn (郝詵) and Zhāng Qiáo (張喬) to lead troops to resist Kàn (粲),
and also sent envoys to seek help from Yī Lú (猗盧), the Duke of Dài (代).
Shēn (詵) and Qiáo (喬) were both defeated and killed.
Kàn (粲) and Yào (曜) took advantage of the emptiness to attack Jìnyáng (晉陽).
Gāo Qiáo (高喬), the Administrator of Tàiyuán (太原), and Hǎo Yù (郝聿), the Bìejià (別駕) of Bīngzhōu (幷州), surrendered Jìnyáng (晉陽) to Hàn (漢).
The *Kǎoyì* (考異) states: Liú Kūn's (劉琨) biography says:
"At that time, Páng Chún (龐醇) surrendered to Cōng (聰),
and the Wūhuán (烏丸) of Yànmén (鴈門) rebelled again.
Kūn (琨) personally went out to resist them,
and Kàn (粲) took advantage of the emptiness to attack and capture Jìnyáng (晉陽)."
According to
Kūn's (琨) memorial to the Crown Prince:
"On the sixteenth day of the seventh month, Cōng (聰) again decided to send troops to their death.
Your servant immediately went east,
leading the troops from Zhōngshān (中山) and Chángshān (常山),
and combining them with the armies from Lèpíng (樂平) and Shàngdǎng (上黨).
Before I could return,
Jìnyáng (晉陽) had fallen."
The *Shíliù Guó Chūnqiū* (十六國春秋) also says:
"Kūn (琨) gathered troops in Chángshān (常山)."
The main biography is mistaken.
On *gēngxū* (庚戌) (September 1, 310 CE),
Kūn (琨) returned to save Jìnyáng (晉陽),
but was too late.
He led several tens of his attendants on horseback and fled to Chángshān (常山).
On *xīnhài* (辛亥) (September 2, 310 CE),
Kàn (粲) and Yào (曜) entered Jìnyáng (晉陽).
On *rénzǐ* (壬子) (September 3, 310 CE),
Línghú Ní (令狐泥) killed Kūn's (琨) parents.
Càn and Yào escorted Shàngshū Lú Zhì, Shìzhōng Xǔ Xiá, and Tàizǐ Yòuwèi Lǜ Cuī Wěi to Píngyáng.
Cōng again appointed Yào as Chēqí Dàjiàngjūn,
and former general Liú Fēng as Bīngzhōu Cìshǐ,
to garrison Jìnyáng.
In the ninth month,
Cōng appointed Lú Zhì as Tàidì Tàishī,
Cuī Wěi as Tàifù,
Xǔ Xiá as Tàibǎo,
and Gāo Qiáo and Línghú Ní both as Wǔwèi Jiāngjūn.
On the 22nd, Jǐmǎo day,
Hàn Wèiwèi Liáng Fēn fled to Cháng'ān.
On the 23rd, Xīnsì day,
Jiǎ Yǎ and others enthroned Qínwáng Yè as Huáng Tàizǐ.
Kǎoyì says: Huáidì Jì records:
"Jiǎ Yǎ attacked Liú Càn in Sānfǔ,
and drove him away.
The Guānzhōng area was slightly pacified,
and Qínwáng was enthroned as Tàizǐ."
According to records: Jiǎ Yǎ and others attacked Liú Càn at Xīnfēng in the fifth year of Yǒngjiā,
Càn was defeated,
and returned to Píngyáng;
Qínwáng was escorted into Yōngchéng.
In the third month of the sixth year,
Liú Yào abandoned Cháng'ān and fled,
Qínwáng entered Cháng'ān,
and the Hàn forces had all retreated.
When Qínwáng became Tàizǐ,
Liú Càn was still in Jìnyáng.
The Huái Jì is mistaken.
A platform was ascended to make a "gàolèi" (announcement ceremony).
Gàolèi refers to
the ritual of offering sacrifices to Heaven
when one acts as regent
or formally ascends the throne.
When Shùn acted as regent,
he performed the sìlèi to the Shàngdì.
Kǒng Ānguó noted: "Lèi
refers to the acts of the regency,
thus announcing to Heaven and the Five Emperors.
Tāng deposed the Xià dynasty's mandate,
and openly announced it to the spirits of Heaven and the empresses,
all of which are examples of this ritual."
A general amnesty was declared.
Yán Dǐng was appointed Tàizǐ Zhānshì,
to oversee all governmental affairs;
The Tàizǐ Zhānshì supervises the palace officials.
At this time, the Tàizǐ established a mobile administrative office (Xíngtái),
thus the Zhānshì oversaw all governmental affairs;
though the specific title had not been formally rectified,
it was effectively the role of a Chéngxiàng.
Qínzhōu Cìshǐ and Nányángwáng Bǎo was appointed Dàsīmǎ.
Sīkōng Xún Fān was ordered to supervise affairs near and far,
and Guānglù Dàfū Xún Zǔ was made Lǐng Sīlì Xiàowèi and Xíng Yùzhōu Cìshǐ,
to jointly defend Kāifēng with Fān.
Kāifēng county
belonged to Hénán Jùn during the Hàn dynasty,
and to Xíngyáng Jùn during the Jìn dynasty.
On the 24th, Qínzhōu Cìshǐ Péi Bāo occupied a strategic position to resist the Liángzhōu forces.
Zhāng Shí, Sòng Pèi, and others attacked and defeated him.
Bāo fled to Róuxiōng Wù.
In the winter,
tenth month,
Hàn ruler Cōng enfeoffed his son Héng as Dàiwáng,
Chěng as Wúwáng,
Lǎng as Yǐngchuānwáng,
Gāo as Línglíngwáng,
Xù as Dānyángwáng,
Jīng as Shǔwáng,
Tǎn as Jiǔjiāngwáng,
and Huǎng as Línchuānwáng;
he appointed Wáng Yù as Tàibǎo,
Wáng Zhāng as Tàiwèi,
Rèn Yǐ as Sītú,
Mǎ Jǐng as Sīkōng,
Zhū Jì as Shàngshū Lìng,
Fàn Lóng as Zuǒ Púyè,
and Hūyán Yàn as Yòu Púyè.
On the 26th, Dàigōng Yīlú dispatched his son Liùxiū and his nephew Pǔgēn, along with generals Wèi Xióng, Fàn Bān, and Jī Dàn, leading tens of thousands of troops as a vanguard to attack Jìnyáng.
Yīlú himself led 200,000 troops to follow.
Liú Kūn gathered several thousand scattered soldiers to serve as guides.
Liùxiū battled Hàn Zhōngshānwáng Yào at Féndōng.
Yào's army was defeated,
he fell from his horse,
and sustained seven wounds.
Tǎolú Jiāngjūn Fù Hǔ offered his horse to Yào,
but Yào refused,
saying:
"You should ride it to save yourself.
My wounds are already severe;
I am prepared to die here."
Hǔ wept, saying:
"I, Hǔ, have been recognized and promoted by Your Majesty to this position;
I have always wished to repay you with my life,
and now is the time.
Moreover, the Hàn dynasty has just begun its foundation;
the world can do without Hǔ,
but not without Your Majesty!"
He then helped Yào onto the horse,
and urged him to cross the Fén River,
while he himself returned to battle and died.
Yào entered Jìnyáng.
That night,
he and Dàjiàngjūn Càn and Zhènběi Dàjiàngjūn Fēng plundered the people of Jìnyáng,
and returned by crossing Móngshān.
Wǔdài Zhì states that
Tàiyuán Jùn's Shí'ài county has Móngshān.
Wèi Shōu said: "Shí'ài county
is the Xià and Jìn dynasty's Shàng'ài county."
Jìn Zhì states that
Shàng'ài county
belonged to Lèpíng Jùn.
Also, according to Wǔdài Zhì,
Jìnyáng county has Móngshān.
This suggests that Móngshān spans the border between Jìnyáng and Shí'ài counties.
Yīlú pursued them,
and battled at Lángǔ.
Lángǔ
is southwest of Móngshān.
He captured Liú Fēng,
and beheaded Xíng Yán and over three thousand others.
Xíng Yán betrayed Kūn,
as seen in volume 5 above.
Yīlú then held a grand hunt on Shòuyángshān.
Shòuyángshān
is in Lèpíng's Shòuyáng county.
Wèi Shōu's Dìxíng Zhì writes it as
"Shòuyáng county."
This county was probably established by the Jìn.
Sòng Bái said: "Shòuyáng county
was originally part of Hàn Yúcì county,
and the Jìn established Shòuyáng county."
The mountain turned red from the hunt.
Liú Kūn walked from his camp to bow and express thanks,
and earnestly requested to advance the army.
Yīlú said:
"I am truly ashamed that I did not come sooner,
which resulted in your parents being harmed.
Now you have recovered your provincial territory.
I have come a long way,
and my soldiers and horses are weary.
Let's wait for a later campaign;
Liú Cōng cannot be annihilated yet."
He gifted Kūn over a thousand horses, cattle, and sheep each,
and a hundred chariots, then returned,
leaving his generals Jī Dàn and Duàn Fán to guard Jìnyáng.
Kūn moved to Yángqǔ.
Yángqǔ county
belonged to Tàiyuán Jùn
and was north of Jìnyáng.
Lú Chén was Liú Càn's Cānjūn,
but fled back to Kūn.
The Hàn people killed his father, Zhì.
Kǎoyì says: Liú Cōng Zàijì records:
"Zhì incited Tàidì Yì to rebel,
and was executed."
However, Zhì advised Chéngdūwáng Yǐng to raise an army of righteousness,
and cautioned Yǐng against attacking Chángshāwáng Yì;
he was loyal and steadfast,
and remained unblemished from beginning to end,
not one who incited rebellion.
Therefore, we follow the biography of Lú Chén.
Fù Hǔ was posthumously granted Yōuzhōu Cìshǐ.
In the twelfth month,
Hàn ruler Cōng established Empress Zhāng,
and appointed her father Shí as Zuǒ Guānglù Dàfū.
On the 28th, Péng Zhòngdàng's son Tiānhù, leading the Wúhú, attacked Jiǎ Yǎ.
Tiānhù feigned defeat and fled,
Yǎ pursued him,
and fell into a ravine at night.
Tiānhù seized and killed him.
The Hàn appointed Tiānhù as Liángzhōu Cìshǐ.
The people then promoted Shǐpíng Tàishǒu Qū Yǔn to lead as Yōngzhōu Cìshǐ.
Yán Dǐng contended for power with Jīngzhào Tàishǒu Liáng Zǒng.
Dǐng consequently killed Zǒng.
Qū Yǔn, along with Fǔyí Hùjūn Suǒ Lín and Féngyì Tàishǒu Liáng Sù, combined their forces to attack Dǐng.
Dǐng fled to Yōng,
and was killed by the Di chieftain Dòu Shǒu.
When the Hú and Jié were strong,
Jiǎ, Yán, Qū, and Suǒ lowered their pride and cooperated,
working together to support the Jìn dynasty,
still fearing they could not ensure its survival.
How much more so when they slaughtered each other!
The omen of Cháng'ān's defeat
is evident here.
Yōng,
pronounced "yòng".
29 Yóu Lún (游綸) and Zhāng Chái (張豺) from Guǎngpíng (廣平) gathered tens of thousands of troops
and occupied Yuànxiāng (苑鄉).
The Surname Register states: Yóu (游)
is a prominent surname from Guǎngpíng (廣平).
Gōngzǐ Yǎn (公子偃) of Zhèng (鄭),
whose courtesy name was Zǐyóu (子游),
had descendants who adopted his courtesy name as their surname.
According to Wèi Shōu’s (魏收) treatise,
Yuànxiāng City (苑鄉城) was in Rèn County (任縣) of Guǎngpíng Commandery (廣平郡).
Sòng Bái (宋白) said: Rèn County (任縣)
was the territory of Nánluán County (南䜌縣) during the Later Hàn (後漢).
The Shí (石) clan of the Later Zhào (後趙) established Yuànxiāng County (苑鄉縣) here.
During the Táng (唐), it was Rèn County (任縣)
and belonged to Xíng Prefecture (邢州).
Jiǎshǔ (假署) means
to provisionally appoint someone to a position based on expediency and authority,
lending them a title.
Their outer camp was broken.
Wáng Jùn (王浚) sent the supervising officer Wáng Chāng (王昌) to lead all the armies, along with the Duke of Liáoxī (遼西) Duàn Jílùjuàn (段疾陸眷)
The *Kǎoyì* (考異) states: The *Shí Lè Zàijì* (石勒載記) and *Hòu Wèi Shū* (後魏書) write
“Jiùlùjuàn (就陸眷).”
We follow the biography of Wáng Jùn (王浚) here.
and their fifty thousand troops to attack Lè (勒) at Xiāngguó (襄國).
Jílùjuàn (疾陸眷) encamped at Zhǔyáng (渚陽).
Bān Gù’s (班固) *Dìlǐ Zhì* (地理志) states:
In the *Yǔ Gòng* (禹貢), the Jiàng River (絳水) flows into the sea at Xìndū (信都).
The *Shuǐ Jīng Zhù* (水經註) says: The Jiàng Dú (絳瀆) flows north past the east of Xìndū City (信都城),
disperses into marshes and islets,
then goes west to the east of Xìndū City (信都城),
connecting with the old canal of Zhāng Jiǎ (張甲) in Guǎngchuān County (廣川縣),
all flowing into the sea.
Jílùjuàn (疾陸眷) likely encamped on the south bank of these islets.
All were defeated by Jílùjuàn (疾陸眷).
Jílùjuàn (疾陸眷) constructed many siege engines
and was about to attack the city.
Lè’s (勒) forces were very afraid.
Lè (勒) summoned his generals and advisors to deliberate, saying:
“Now our city defenses are not yet solid,
and our provisions are not abundant.
They are numerous, we are few,
and there is no outside relief.
I wish to commit all our forces to a decisive battle with them.
What do you think?”
All the generals said:
“It is better to stand firm and wear out the enemy,
then strike them when they retreat.”
Zhāng Bīn (張賓) and Kǒng Cháng (孔萇) said:
“Among the Xiānbēi (鮮卑) tribes,
the Duàn (段) clan is the most courageous and fierce,
and Mòpēi (末柸) is particularly so.
Their elite troops are all with Mòpēi (末柸).
Now we hear that Jílùjuàn (疾陸眷) has set a date to attack the north wall.
Their large army has come from afar,
and they have been fighting for days.
They believe we are isolated and weak,
and dare not sally forth to fight,
so their vigilance must be lax.
We should not sally forth for now,
showing them our timidity.
We should dig over twenty sally ports in the north wall.
*Mòzǐ Bèi Tū Piān* (墨子備突篇) states: For a city,
there should be one sally port every hundred paces.
A sally port
uses two cart wheels,
bound together with wood,
plastered over,
and placed within the sally port by means of ropes.
Adjust the width of the door,
so that people can enter within four feet of the door,
and place a concealed pit-trap.
Beside the door, make a bellows-like structure,
shaped like a stove;
also place mugwort.
If the bandits enter,
lower the wheels to block it,
and use the bellows to smoke them.
Dù Yòu (杜佑) said: A sally port
is a secret door dug within the city.
The number depends on the situation,
leaving five or six inches unpenetrated.
Perhaps in the middle of the night,
when the enemy first arrives
and their formation is not yet settled,
elite cavalry can leap out from the sally ports
to strike them unawares,
taking them by surprise.
While their formation is unsettled,
we can take them by surprise,
directly charging Mòpēi’s (末柸) camp.
They will surely be terrified
and have no time to formulate a plan.
We will certainly defeat them.
If Mòpēi (末柸) is defeated,
then the rest will collapse without being attacked.”
Lè (勒) adopted the plan and
secretly made sally ports.
Soon after, Jílùjuàn (疾陸眷) attacked the north wall.
Lè (勒) climbed the wall to observe
and saw that some of their generals and soldiers had laid down their weapons and were sleeping.
He then ordered Kǒng Cháng (孔萇) to lead elite troops to sally forth from the sally ports and attack them.
Seeing them resting with their weapons laid down,
he knew they were lax,
and so ordered Cháng (萇) to fight.
This is what is meant by discerning the military situation.
Cháng (萇) attacked Mòpēi’s (末柸) camp
but could not overcome it and retreated.
Mòpēi (末柸) pursued him
and entered his camp gate,
where he was captured by Lè’s (勒) forces.
Jílùjuàn’s (疾陸眷) army and others all retreated.
Cháng (萇) pressed the advantage and pursued,
leaving corpses strewn for over thirty *lǐ*,
and capturing five thousand armored horses.
Jílùjuàn (疾陸眷) gathered his remaining troops
and returned to encamp at Zhǔyáng (渚陽).
Lè (勒) held Mòpēi (末柸) as a hostage
and sent an envoy to seek peace with Jílùjuàn (疾陸眷).
Jílùjuàn (疾陸眷) agreed.
Wén Yāng (文鴦) remonstrated, saying:
“Now, for the sake of one Mòpēi (末柸), you release a doomed captive.
Will this not incur the resentment of Wáng Péngzǔ (王彭祖)
and invite future trouble?”
Jílùjuàn (疾陸眷) did not heed him.
He further bribed Lè (勒) with armored horses, gold, and silver,
and offered Mòpēi’s (末柸) three younger brothers as hostages in exchange for Mòpēi (末柸).
All the generals urged Lè (勒) to kill Mòpēi (末柸).
Lè (勒) said:
“The Liáoxī Xiānbēi (遼西鮮卑) are a strong nation,
