Kūn recalled him.
However, the people and resources within the province
were very unsettled by Shù's governance.
Officials of two thousand *shí* and prominent civil and military families
repeatedly sent envoys requesting an Inspector.
Therefore, I sent my elder brother's son Yǎn to replace Qí in leading the affairs of Yǎnzhōu.
In the first month of spring last year,
I sent him to Yè.
By now, he has beheaded Wáng Sāng and driven away Zhào Gù,'
etc.
'Now Lè occupies Xiāngguó,
pressing close to Yè Chéng,
so I ordered Yǎn to move south.
Yǎn is now governing from Lǐnqīu.
However, Lǐ Shù and Xī Jiàn both wish to contend for Yǎnzhōu,
some say they are supported by Grandee Xún,
others say by Your Excellency.
The great bandits are not yet eliminated, yet they are stirring up internal strife among themselves;
this is also a great collapse.
I have instructed Yǎn to merely defend himself cautiously.'
According to records, the defeat of Wáng Sāng and Zhào Gù and Shí Lè's attack on Yè
all occurred in Yǒngjiā sixth year.
Kūn's memorial also states:
'News from Cháng'ān reports that
the current emperor is the King of Qín.'
Also, the first day of the eleventh month, bǐngshēn, of Jiànxīng second year,
the first day of the eleventh month, rénshēn, of the first year,
the first day of the twelfth month, rén'yín.
Thus, the day Kūn sent the memorial
was the first day of the twelfth month, rén'yín, of Jiànxīng first year;
it was a copying error.
The officials and people of Yǎnzhōu did not know whom to follow."
9 Wáng Ruì, Prince of Lángxié, appointed Huá Tán, former Grand Administrator of Lújiāng, as Military Counselor Libationer.
Tán had once stayed in Shòuchūn under Zhōu Fù.
Ruì asked Tán:
"Why did Zhōu Zǔxuān rebel?"
Zhōu Fù, courtesy name Zǔxuān.
"Although Zhōu Fù is dead,
there are still honest men in the world.
Fù saw the spread of bandits and wished to relocate the capital to alleviate national difficulties.
The governing authorities were displeased
and raised troops to attack him.
Fù died not long after, and the capital Luò was lost.
If one calls this a rebellion,
is it not a calumny!"
This event is recorded in the previous volume, Yǒngjiā fourth and fifth years.
"Fù, holding the position of a provincial commander,
commanded strong troops.
When summoned, he did not come;
when danger arose, he did not support.
He is also a sinner against the world."
Tán said:
"Indeed,
not supporting during danger,
he should share the responsibility with the world;
it is not only Fù."
Ruì’s (睿) assistant officials mostly shirked duties and sought ease.
The Registrar-Recorder, Chén Yūn (陳頵),
was the Registrar-Recorder.
He was in charge of supervising all the offices,
managing their documents.
From the chief assistants downwards,
those who transgressed or erred were corrected by law.
He oversaw all matters of inspection.
Bái Shì Liù Tiē (白氏六帖) says: "The Registrar of a prefecture (zhōu zhǔ bù) and the Inspector of a commandery (jùn dū yóu)
are both now the position of Registrar-Recorder (lù shì cān jūn)."
I argue that since Ruì (睿) appointed Yūn (頵) as Registrar-Recorder,
there must have been a separate Registrar (zhǔ bù).
For details, see Biàn Wù (辨誤).
"During the peaceful times in Luòzhōng (洛中),
court officials regarded carefulness and reverence as vulgar,
and considered arrogance and haughtiness as elegant.
This trend spread and infected others,
eventually leading to the downfall of the state.
Now, our subordinates all inherit the lingering弊 of Xītái (西臺)
(the people of Jiāngdōng (江東) called Luòdū (洛都) Xītái (西臺)).
This is like the previous carriage having overturned, and the one behind is about to follow it.
I request that from now on,
those who claim illness when sent on a mission
should all be dismissed from office."
Ruì (睿) did not comply.
The execution of Zhào Wáng Lún (趙王倫) by the Three Kings
is mentioned in Chapter 84, Huì Dì Yǒngníng (惠帝永寧) first year.
On the jǐhài (己亥) day,
he continued to follow and use it.
Yūn (頵) memorialized:
"In the past, when Zhào Wáng (趙王) usurped the throne,
Huì Huáng (惠皇) lost his position,
the Three Kings raised an army to suppress him,
and therefore lavish rewards were given to win over those who leaned towards righteousness.
Now, regardless of the size of their achievements,
all are rewarded according to fixed rules,
even to the extent that gold and purple insignia are worn by soldiers,
and official tallies and documents are left at the gates of servants.
This is not the way to value prestigious titles
and rectify the state's discipline.
I request that all such practices be abolished!"
Yūn (頵) came from humble origins
and frequently offered righteous opinions.
Many in the government disliked him,
and he was sent out to be the Administrator of Qiáo Jùn (譙郡 Tàishǒu).
10 The Administrator of Wúxìng (吳興 Tàishǒu), Zhōu (周),
had a strong and flourishing clan.
Lángxié Wáng Ruì (琅邪王睿) was somewhat suspicious and fearful of him.
Ruì's (睿) favored attendants
were mostly officials who had lost their posts and territories in Zhōngzhōu (中州),
and they lorded over the Wú (吳) people,
who harbored considerable resentment.
Feeling that he had lost his position and was further belittled by Diāo Xié (刁協),
his shame and anger grew even more intense.
So, he secretly plotted with his partisans to execute the powerful officials
and replace them with various southern gentry.
The plot was revealed,
and he died of grief and indignation.
Before his death,
he said to his son Xié (勰):
"Those who killed me
are these Cāngzǐ (傖子) [northern barbarians];
if you can avenge me,
then you are truly my son."
11 Shí Lè (石勒) attacked Lǐ Yùn (李惲) at Shàngbái (上白)
and beheaded him.
Wáng Jùn (王浚) again appointed Báo Shèng (薄盛) as the Inspector of Qīngzhōu (青州 Cìshǐ).
Shàngbái (上白) city
was in Ānpíng (安平) Guǎngzōng (廣宗) County.
Lǐ Yùn (李惲) and Báo Shèng (薄盛) were both leaders of the Qǐhuó (乞活) group.
Fù (復)
is pronounced fú yòu fān.
12 Wáng Jùn (王浚) sent Zǎo Sōng (棗嵩) to oversee the various armies garrisoned at Yìshuǐ (易水).
He summoned Duàn Jílùjuàn (段疾陸眷),
intending to jointly attack Shí Lè (石勒) with him,
but Jílùjuàn (疾陸眷) did not come.
Because his younger brother Mòbēi (末柸) was allied with Shí Lè (石勒),
he was unwilling to join Jùn's (浚) forces.
Jùn (浚) heavily bribed Tuòbá Yīlú (拓跋猗盧),
and also issued a proclamation to Mùróng Guī (慕容廆) and others, calling for a joint attack on Jílùjuàn (疾陸眷).
Yīlú (猗盧) sent the Right Worthy King Liùxiū (六脩) to lead troops to join,
but they were defeated by Jílùjuàn (疾陸眷).
Guī (廆) sent Mùróng Hàn (慕容翰) to attack the Duàn (段) clan,
taking Túhé (徒河) and Xīnchéng (新城),
and reaching Yánglè (陽樂).
Yánglè (陽樂) County
belonged to Liáoxī (遼西) Commandery.
Xián (賢) said: Yánglè (陽樂)
is in modern-day Píngzhōu (平州) to the east.
Hàn (翰) then stayed to garrison Túhé (徒河),
fortifying Qīngshān (青山).
At first,
many gentry and commoners from Zhōngguó (中國) who fled the chaos
sought refuge with Wáng Jùn (王浚).
Jùn (浚) was unable to protect and comfort them,
and his governance and laws were not established,
so gentry and commoners often left him again.
The Duàn (段) brothers solely valued military bravery
and did not treat scholar-officials with courtesy.
Only Mùróng Guī (慕容廆) had clear and effective governance
and valued talented individuals,
so many gentry and commoners came to him.
Guī (廆) promoted the outstanding among them,
assigning them positions according to their talents.
He appointed Péi Yì (裴嶷) from Hédōng (河東),
Yáng Dān (陽躭) from Běipíng (北平), Huáng Hóng (黃泓) from Lújiāng (廬江),
and Lǔ Chāng (魯昌) from Dàijùn (代郡) as strategists.
Yóu Suì (游邃) from Guǎngpíng (廣平), Péng Xiàn (逄羨) from Běihǎi (北海),
Xīfāng Qián (西方虔) from Běipíng (北平)
(Hé Shì Xìng Yuàn (何氏姓苑) says: Shàohào Jīntiān Shì (少昊金天氏),
whose position was master of the West,
had descendants who took his position as their surname).
Sòng Gāi (宋該) from Píngyuán (平原), Huángfǔ Jí (皇甫岌) from Āndìng (安定), Jí's (岌) younger brother Zhēn (真), Miào Kǎi (繆愷) from Lánlíng (蘭陵),
Liú Bīn (劉斌) from Chānglí (昌黎), as well as Fēng Yì (封奕) and Fēng Yù (封裕) managed key affairs.
Yù (裕)
was the son of Chōu (抽).
Péi Yì was upright, astute, and capable.
He served as the Administrator of Chānglí Commandery,
and his elder brother, Wǔ, was the Administrator of Xuántú Commandery.
When Wǔ died,
Yì and Wǔ's son, Kāi, returned with the funeral procession.
They passed by Kuài.
Returning west from Xuántú,
they passed through Jíchéng.
Tù,
same as "Dū" (都).
When they left,
Kuài provided them generously with provisions for their journey.
As they traveled to Liáoxī,
the road became impassable.
Yì wanted to return and seek refuge with Kuài.
Kāi said:
"Our homeland is in the south.
Why go north?
Moreover, we are all displaced people.
The Duàn氏 are strong,
and the Mùróng氏 are weak.
Why must we leave here and go there?"
Yì said:
"The Central Plains are in chaos and turmoil.
To go there now
would be to lead one another into a tiger's mouth.
Furthermore, the journey is long,
how could we possibly reach it?
This refers to Chānglí being far from Hédōng,
and the roads being blocked,
making it impossible to reach.
Moreover, it is not something that can be hoped for in a few months or years.
This means that the world is in turmoil,
and there will be no time when the roads are clear and unobstructed.
How can we not carefully choose our patron?
Look at all the Duàn氏;
do they have long-term vision,
or can they treat worthy men of the state well?
Mùróng Gōng practices benevolence and righteousness,
and has the ambition of a hegemon and king.
Furthermore, his state is prosperous and his people are secure.
If we go to him now,
at best we can establish meritorious achievements and reputation,
at worst we can protect our clan.
Why do you hesitate?"
Kāi then followed his advice.
When they arrived,
Kuài was greatly pleased.
Yáng Dān was upright, honest, profound, and astute.
He served as the Administrator of Liáoxī Commandery.
Mùróng Hàn defeated the Duàn氏 at Yánglè,
capturing him.
Kuài treated him with courtesy and employed him.
Yóu Suì, Páng Xiàn, and Sòng Shì
had all served as Administrators of Chānglí Commandery.
Along with Huáng Hóng, they all sought refuge in Jì,
and later returned to Kuài.
Wáng Jùn repeatedly sent handwritten letters summoning Suì's elder brother, Chàng.
Chàng wanted to go to him,
but Suì said:
"Péngzǔ's administration is not in order,
and both Chinese and non-Chinese are rebelling.
In my estimation,
he will not last long.
Brother, you should wait and hesitate."
The first nine line of the Zhūn hexagram in the Yìjīng says: "Hesitation,
beneficial to abide in righteousness."
Wáng Bì said: "One cannot advance,
hence hesitation."
Mǎ said: "Pánhuán (磐桓) means to circle."
Dù,
same as "Tuó Luò" (徒洛).
"Péngzǔ is cruel and suspicious.
Recently, when refugees came from the north,
he ordered them to be pursued and killed wherever they were found.
Now, with his cordial handwritten letter,
if I delay and do not go,
it will likely implicate you.
Moreover, in times of chaos, clans should separate,
to preserve a remnant."
Suì followed his advice,
and ultimately perished together with Jùn.
Sòng Gāi, together with Dù Cōng of Píngyuán and Liú Xiáng, first depended on Wáng Jùn,
and then on the Duàn氏.
They all considered them unreliable,
and led all the displaced people to return to Kuài.
Cuī Bì, the Commandant of Dōngyí, invited Huángfǔ Jí to be his Chief Clerk.
He used humble words to persuade him,
but ultimately could not obtain him.
Kuài summoned him,
and Jí, along with his younger brother Zhēn, immediately arrived.
There is an ancient saying: "Birds choose trees,
how can trees choose birds?"
Shuài,
read as "Lǜ" (率).
Shuō,
same as "Shū Ruì" (輸芮).
He fought with Gāogōulì King Yǐfúlì,
and the conflict continued for years without resolution.
Lèliáng King Zūn persuaded Tǒngshuài and his more than one thousand households to return to Kuài.
Kuài established Lèliáng Commandery for them,
made Tǒngshuài the Administrator,
and Zūn the Administrator's Aide.
The remaining adherents of Wáng Rú, such as Lǐ Yùn of Fúlíng and Wáng Jiàn of Bāxī, led over three thousand households from Xiāngyáng into Hànzhōng.
Zhāng Guāng, the Inspector of Liángzhōu, dispatched his Aide, Jìn Miǎo, with troops to resist them.
Miǎo accepted bribes from Yùn and Jiàn,
and persuaded Guāng to accept their surrender.
Guāng agreed,
and settled them in Chénggù.
Afterwards, Miǎo saw that Yùn, Jiàn, and their followers possessed many treasures,
and wished to take them all.
He again persuaded Guāng, saying:
"Yùn and Jiàn's followers
do not engage in agriculture,
but specialize in crafting weapons.
Their intentions are hard to fathom.
It would be better to ambush and kill them all;
otherwise,
they will surely cause trouble."
Guāng again followed his advice.
The general was greedy below,
and the commander was unenlightened above.
The disaster of Liángzhōu
again began from this point.
Zhì,
same as "Zhí Zhī" (直之).
Miǎo led troops to attack Yùn and Jiàn,
and killed them.
Jiàn's son-in-law, Yáng Hǔ, gathered the remaining followers and attacked Guāng,
encamping at Èshuǐ.
Guāng sent his son, Mèngcháng, to attack him,
but could not defeat him.
On the day Rénchén, Wáng Ruì, Prince of Lángxié, was appointed Left Chancellor and Grand Commander,
overseeing all military affairs east of Shǎn.
Wáng Bǎo, Prince of Nányáng, was appointed Right Chancellor and Grand Commander,
overseeing all military affairs west of Shǎn.
This is what is called
"dividing Shǎn."
Shǎn,
same as "Shī Rǎn" (失冉).
"Now we should sweep away the whales and leviathans."
Whales and leviathans,
large fish
that cannot be controlled by hooks or nets,
are compared to the chief and outstanding enemies.
Jīng,
same as "Jù Jīng" (巨京).
Ní,
same as "Wǔ Xī" (五兮).
This refers to Emperor Huái being murdered in Píngyáng,
and his coffin not yet having returned.
"The Right Chancellor should lead the thirty thousand troops of Qín, Liáng, Liáng, and Yōng directly to Cháng'ān;
the Left Chancellor should lead the twenty thousand elite troops under his command directly to Luòyáng.
Together, they will meet the great opportunity
and achieve the paramount meritorious service."
Liú Yào, King Zhōngshān of Hàn, encamped at Púbǎn.
Shí Lè sent Kǒng Cháng to attack Dìnglíng,
killing Tián Huī.
Dìnglíng County,
in the Hàn dynasty belonged to Yǐngchuān Commandery,
in the Jìn dynasty belonged to Xiāngchéng Commandery.
Tián Huī
was appointed Inspector of Yǎnzhōu by Wáng Jùn.
The commanderies and counties east of the mountains
were successively captured by Lè.
Hàn Lord Cōng appointed Lè as Grandee Secretary and General Who Conquers the East.
The Wūhuán also rebelled against Wáng Jùn,
secretly defecting to Lè.
The history states that Wáng Jùn's power gradually became isolated and weak.
In the sixth month, Liú Kūn and Dài Duke Yīlú met north of Xíng to plan an attack on Hàn.
In the autumn,
seventh month, Kūn advanced and occupied Lánggǔ.
Yīlú dispatched Tuòbá Pǔgēn to encamp at Běiqū.
Běiqū County,
in the Hàn dynasty belonged to Hédōng Commandery,
in the Jìn dynasty belonged to Píngyáng Commandery.
It was the town where the Jìn prince Yíwú resided during the Spring and Autumn period.
Sòng Bái said: "Cízhōu Jiāchéng County
was originally the land of Hàn's Běiqū County."
Shīgǔ said: "Qū (屈)
is pronounced as 'Jū Wù' (居勿)."
They were about to attack Xīpíng.
Xīpíng City,
located west of Píngyáng,
was built by Hàn Lord Cōng for his son Jìnán King Jì to reside in.
General of Agile Cavalry Yì and others resisted Pǔgēn.
General Who Quells Jìn Lányáng and others helped defend Xīpíng.
Kūn and others heard this
and withdrew their troops.
Cōng ordered his various armies to remain stationed in their respective locations,
making plans for further advances.
The emperor dispatched Diànzhōng Dūwèi Liú Shǔ to summon Zuǒ Chéngxiàng Ruì by imperial edict to advance the army in due course.
Diànzhōng Dūwèi
belonged to the two guards.
In the eighth month,
on the guǐhài day,
Shǔ arrived at Jiànkāng.
Ruì declined, stating that he was still in the process of pacifying Jiāngdōng,
and had no time for a northern expedition.
He appointed Zhèndōng Zhǎngshǐ Diāo Xié as Chéngxiàng Zuǒ Zhǎngshǐ,
Cóngshì Zhōngláng Liú Wèi of Péngchéng as Sīzhí,
Shàolíng Nèishǐ Dài Miǎo of Guǎnglíng as Jūnzī Jìjiǔ.
In Bǎodǐng first year of Sūn Hào of Wú,
the northern Dūwèi of Línglíng was partitioned to establish Shàolíng Jùn.
Sòng Bái said: Shàolíng
was Zhāolíng Xiàn in the Hàn dynasty.
Wú established Shàolíng Jùn.
In the Táng dynasty, it was Shàozhōu.
Shàngshū Láng Zhōng Yǎ of Yǐngchuān was appointed Jìshì Cānjūn,
Huán Xuān of Qiáoguó as Shèrén,
Xióng Yuǎn of Yùzhāng as Zhǔbù,
and Kǒng Yú of Kuàijī as Yuàn.
Liú Wèi was thoroughly familiar with literature and history,
and adept at discerning Ruì’s intentions.
Therefore, Ruì was especially fond of him.
This laid the groundwork for the conflict between Diāo and Liú and Wáng Dūn's brothers.
Sī
is pronounced like "xiàng lì" (相吏).
Xióng Yuǎn submitted a memorial,
thinking:
"Since the outbreak of military action,
affairs have not been conducted according to laws and decrees.
Instead, new ideas are constantly being devised,
regulations are established on the spot,
made in the morning and changed in the evening.
Consequently, those in charge dare not rely on the law,
but invariably report and consult.
Guān
means 'bái' (白, to report).
I believe that all those who offer counter-arguments
should cite laws, decrees, classics, and commentaries,
and not merely speak from personal feeling,
without any basis,
thereby undermining established institutions.
If opening and closing follow expediency,
and strategic methods control things,
this is what a monarch may do,
not something that ministers and sons should exclusively employ."
Ruì, considering the many affairs of the time,
could not follow it.
Initially,
Zǔ Tì of Fányáng
had great ambition from a young age.
It was Zhuōjùn of Hàn.
Wèi Wéndì renamed it Fányáng Jùn.
Shào
is pronounced like "shī zhào" (詩照).
(He and Liú Kūn) slept together.
In the middle of the night, hearing a rooster crow,
he kicked Kūn awake, saying:
"This is not an inauspicious sound!"
He then rose and practiced swordplay.
When he crossed the Jiāng,
Zuǒ Chéngxiàng Ruì appointed him Jūnzī Jìjiǔ.
Tì resided in Jīngkǒu.
Sūn Quán of Wú moved from Wú to Dāntú,
calling it Jīngchéng.
Jīngxiàn Shān was to its east.
The city used the mountain as a rampart,
overlooking the Jiāngjīn,
hence it was called Jīngkǒu.
Three ropes combined make a "jiū" (糾);
jiū
means 'three combined into one'.
Xiāo
is pronounced like "jiān yáo" (堅堯);
same below.
"The chaos of the Jìn court
was not due to the ruler being without dao and the people resenting and rebelling,
but arose from the imperial clansmen struggling for power,
preying on each other,
which allowed the Róng Dí to seize the opportunity,
spreading their poison throughout the central lands.
Now, the surviving people have suffered devastation,
and everyone desires to exert themselves.
If Your Majesty could sincerely commission generals and dispatch armies,
and appoint someone like Tì to command them to recover the central plains,
the heroes of the commanderies and states
will surely respond to the call!"
Ruì had always lacked the ambition for a northern expedition,
so he appointed Tì as Fènwēi Jiāngjūn, Yùzhōu Cìshǐ,
granted provisions for a thousand men,
and three thousand rolls of cloth.
(This means) provisions for a thousand men and three thousand rolls of cloth, and nothing more.
He was to recruit his own forces.
Tì led his contingent of over a hundred families across the Jiāng.
In mid-stream,
he struck his oar and swore:
"If Zǔ Tì cannot clear the central plains and cross back,
may it be like this great river!"
He then garrisoned at Huáiīn.
Huáiīn Xiàn
belonged to Línhuái Jùn in the Former Hàn,
to Xiàpī Guó in the Later Hàn,
and to Guǎnglíng Jùn in the Jìn.
He recruited over two thousand men before advancing.
Hú Kàng was suspicious by nature,
and killed several of his valiant generals.
Dù Zēng, fearing for his life,
secretly enticed Wáng Chōng's troops to attack Kàng.
Wáng Chōng
was a bandit from Jīngzhōu.
The city being empty,
Zēng then killed Kàng and absorbed his followers.
Zhōu Yǐ garrisoned at Xúnshuǐ Chéng.
Lúshān Jì says: Xúnyáng Xiàn
is north of the Great River,
and on the sunny side of Xúnshuǐ.
Xúnshuǐ Chéng,
perhaps it is the ancient Xúnyáng Chéng!
Táo Kǎn sent Míngwēi Jiāngjūn Zhū Sī to rescue him.
Táo retreated to Lěngkǒu.
Shěn Yuē Zhì: Wèi established forty general titles,
Míngwēi was the third.
Tāo
is pronounced like "tǔ dāo" (吐刀).
Shuǐjīng Zhù: Lěngshuǐ flows south out of Jiǔyí Shān,
flows north past the southwest of Lěngdào Xiàn,
then flows north into Dūxī Shuǐ,
then northwest into Yíngshuǐ,
which is what is called Lěngkǒu.
Yáng Zhènghéng said: Lěng
is pronounced like "láng dīng" (郎丁).
I have investigated and this Lěngkǒu is very far from Wǔchāng.
Also, Shuǐjīng Zhù says,
the Jiāngshuǐ flows east from south of Qīchūn's old city
to get to Tónglíngkǒu.
Perhaps this is it!
"(Táo) will surely march towards Wǔchāng."
So he returned to the commandery by a shortcut to await him.
Jìngdào
is a shortcut.
Kǎn sent Zhū Sī to intercept and attack,
greatly defeating him.
Táo fled back to Chángshā.
Zhōu Yǐ left Xúnshuǐ and went to Wáng Dūn in Yùzhāng,
and Dūn kept him there.
Táo Kǎn sent Cānjūn Wáng Gòng to report the victory to Dūn.
Dūn said:
"Without Lord Táo,
Jīngzhōu would have been lost!"
He then memorialized to appoint Kǎn as Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ,
garrisoning at Miǎnjiāng.
Shuǐjīng Zhù: Dùnshuǐ flows from Báihú of Miǎnyáng,
flows southeast,
passes south of Miǎnyáng Xiàn and flows into the Jiāng,
called Dùnkǒu.
Lù Yóu said: Jiànníng Zhèn of Jiānglíng
is likely Dùnkǒu.
Wáng Dūn appointed Táo Kǎn as Jīngzhōu,
garrisoning here,
and the following year moved to Línzhàng.
Kǎn Chuán says: He first garrisoned at Dùnkǒu,
then moved into Miǎnjiāng.
Shuǐjīng Zhù: Línzhàng Gùchéng
is in Miǎnnán.
Miǎnjiāng
refers to Línzhàng.
He was again appointed Jūnzī Jìjiǔ.
At first,
the son of the Dī king Yáng Móusōu, Nándí,
sent his adopted son to trade in Liángzhōu.
He privately sold one good person's child,
and Zhāng Guāng flogged him to death.
Nándí resented this and said,
"When the administrator first arrived,
after the great famine,
the lives of the soldiers and common people depended on us Dī to survive.
If the Dī commit a small offense,
they cannot be pardoned."
When Guāng and Yáng Hǔ attacked each other,
each sought aid from Móusōu.
Móusōu sent Nándí to assist Guāng.
Nándí sought goods from Guāng,
but Guāng did not give them.
Yáng Hǔ heavily bribed Nándí
and said,
"The valuable goods of the refugees
are all with Guāng.
These are what Jìn Miǎo was said to have killed and seized.
It would be better to attack Guāng."
Nándí was greatly pleased.
Guāng fought with Hǔ,
sending Zhāng Mèngcháng to the front,
with Nándí following.
Nándí and Hǔ jointly attacked Mèngcháng,
severely defeating him.
Mèngcháng and his younger brother Yuán both died.
Guāng barricaded himself within the city walls.
In the ninth month,
Guāng, angered and agitated, fell ill.
His subordinates advised Guāng to retreat and hold Wèixīng.
Guāng pressed his sword and said,
"I have received a heavy responsibility from the state;
if I cannot suppress the rebels,
to die now would be like ascending to immortality.
Why speak of retreating!"
His voice failed, and he died.
Although Zhāng Guāng, by trusting Jìn Miǎo, brought about the disaster,
his fierce spirit is still commendable.
After he died in battle with the Dī,
the multitude acclaimed Hú Zixù, the Administrator of Shǐpíng, to lead Liángzhōu.
Xún Fān died in Kāifēng.
Xún Fān and Fù Zhī died one after another;
of the two traveling chancellery offices east of Shǎnxī,
only Xún Zǔ remained.
The "Kǎoyì" states: The "Dìjì" says
"died in Xíngyáng."
Now we follow the biography of Fān.
Yǔn was defeated in every battle;
an imperial edict appointed Suǒ Chén as General-in-chief Who Conquers the East,
leading troops to assist Yǔn.
and upon reaching Jìnglíng,
he falsely issued Táo Kǎn's order
to appoint Dù Zēng as Grand Commander of the Vanguard
to attack Wáng Chōng,
whom he beheaded,
and whose forces he completely absorbed.
Kǎn summoned Zēng,
but Zēng did not come.
Gòng, fearing punishment for falsifying orders,
then joined Zēng in attacking Kǎn.
In winter,
the tenth month,
Kǎn's army was greatly defeated,
and he barely escaped with his life.
Dūn memorialized that Kǎn should serve in his office as a commoner.
Kǎn then led Zhōu Fǎng and others to attack Dù Tāo,
greatly defeating him.
Dūn then memorialized to reinstate Kǎn's official position.
"Qū Yǔn is leading a large army outside;
Cháng'ān is empty
and can be attacked."
Yào sent Rǎn to lead five thousand elite cavalry to attack Cháng'ān.
On the night of Gēngyín,
they entered the outer city.
The Emperor fled to Shèyànlóu.
Rǎn burned Lóngwěi and the various camps.
Lóngwěi was
a road built along the city,
gradually ascending along a slope,
which was the path used to climb the battlements.
Also, the "Shuǐ Jīng" says: During the Qín dynasty, there was a black dragon
that emerged from Nánshān
and drank from the Wèishuǐ.
Its path formed a trail along the mountains,
over sixty *lǐ* long,
with its head facing the Wèishuǐ and its tail reaching Fánchuān.
When Xiāo Hé of Hàn built the Wèiyáng Palace,
he cut off the head of Lóngshǒushān to construct it.
The head was twenty *zhàng* high,
and the tail gradually sloped down,
being five or six *zhàng* high.
What is called Lóngwěi
is the tail of this mountain.
On the morning of Xīnmǎo,
they retreated and camped at Xiāoyáoyuán.
The "Shuǐ Jīng Zhù" says: The Shěnshuǐ
originates from Huángzǐpō in Fánchuān,
flows north past the west of Cháng'ān city,
and joins the water of Kūnmíngchí.
The Shěnshuǐ then flows northeast,
past the south of Dèng Ài's shrine,
and then splits into two streams to the east.
One stream enters Xiāoyáoyuán to the east.
On Rénchén,
General Qū Jiàn led five thousand men from Āchéng to relieve Cháng'ān.
Āchéng is
the city of the Qín Afánggōng.
On Guǐsì,
Rǎn withdrew.
Jiàn pursued him,
and encountered Yào at Língwǔ.
Jiàn's army was greatly defeated.
In the Former Hàn, Běidì Commandery had Língwǔ County,
which was abolished in the Later Hàn and Jìn.
By the time of the Later Wèi, Xiányáng Commandery was established,
and Chíyáng and Língwǔ counties both belonged to it.
Huángbáichéng was in Chíyáng.
Thus, this Língwǔ is clearly the Língwǔ of the Former Hàn Běidì Commandery and the Wèi Xiányáng Commandery.
Hú Zixù abandoned the city and fled.
Nándí declared himself Inspector.
In the eleventh month,
Qū Yǔn led troops to attack him.
The Hàn army was greatly defeated,
and their General Who Commands the Army, Qiáo Zhìmíng, was killed.
Yào withdrew to Píngyáng.
believed himself to be the one who fulfilled
the prophecy of "Dāngtú Gāo"
and plotted to claim the imperial title.
Wáng Jùn
was another Yuán Shù.
Gāo Róu, a subordinate of the Minister of Works, earnestly remonstrated,
but Jùn killed all of them.
Huò Yuán of Yàn State
had noble aspirations and high integrity,
and repeatedly declined recruitment.
Jùn asked him about the imperial title,
but Yuán did not reply.
Jùn falsely accused Yuán of colluding with bandits,
killed him, and displayed his head.
Thereupon, the gentry and common people were shocked and resentful,
but Jùn grew increasingly arrogant and extravagant,
not attending to government affairs.
Those he appointed were all harsh and petty individuals;
Zǎo Sōng and Zhū Shuò
were especially greedy and tyrannical.
A northern song went:
"In the residence, resplendent,
is Lord Zhū Qiū.
Ten sacks, five sacks,
go to Lord Zǎo."
Zhū Qiūbó was
Zhū Shuò's courtesy name.
Sōng was Jùn's son-in-law,
hence "Lord Zǎo."
The lower classes could not endure the oppression
and many rebelled, joining the Xiānbēi.
Hán Xián, the supervisor of Liǔchéng,
(Liǔchéng County,
in the Former Hàn, belonged to Liáoxī Commandery;
it was abolished in the Later Hàn and Jìn.)
(The character "jiān" here is pronounced as *gōng hán fān*.)
wished to admonish Jùn indirectly;
Jùn was enraged
and killed him.
Jùn initially relied solely on the Xiānbēi and Wūhuán for strength,
but later they all rebelled against him.
Moreover, locust plagues and droughts occurred for years,
weakening his military power.
Shí Lè wanted to attack him,
but not knowing the actual situation,
intended to send envoys to scout.
His aides requested to follow the precedents of Yáng Hù and Lù Kàng,
by sending a letter to Jùn.
This was to employ the courtesy of neighboring states.
Bīn said:
"Jùn is nominally a Jìn minister,
but in reality, he wishes to abolish Jìn and establish himself,
only troubled that heroes throughout the land do not follow him;
his desire to acquire the general [meaning you, Shí Lè],
is like Xiàng Yǔ's desire to acquire Hán Xìn.
The general's might shakes the world,
yet if you humble your words and offer generous gifts,
bending your will to serve him,
he would still fear you are insincere,
let alone confronting him as an equal like Yáng and Lù!
Indeed, to scheme against someone yet let them perceive your intentions,
it is difficult to achieve your aim."
Lè said:
"Excellent!"
In the twelfth month,
Lè dispatched his attendants Wáng Zǐchūn and Dǒng Zhào, carrying many precious treasures,
to present a memorial to Jùn, saying:
"Lè was originally a minor barbarian,
encountering a world of famine and chaos,
wandering and suffering hardship,
taking refuge in Jìzhōu,
secretly gathering people to preserve our lives.
Now the Jìn dynasty has declined,
and the Central Plains are without a master;
Your Highness, being of noble lineage from this region [Jùn was from Tàiyuán Commandery, Shí Lè from Shàngdǎng Commandery, both within Jìzhōu province],
Lè,
a native of Wǔxiāng in Shàngdǎng,
and Jùn was a native of Tàiyuán,
hence it says 'region'.
As for who should be emperor,
if not you, then who?
The reason Lè has sacrificed himself to raise an army,
to punish and suppress the rebellious,
is precisely to clear the way for Your Highness.
We humbly pray that Your
[Highness]
will ascend to the imperial throne soon.
Lè will revere Your Highness as heaven, earth, and parents.
If Your Highness examines Lè's humble heart,
you will also treat him as a son."
He also sent a letter to Zǎo Sōng,
bribing him heavily.
Jùn, seeing that Duàn Jílùjuàn had recently rebelled,
and many of his soldiers and common people had abandoned him,
was very pleased to hear that Lè intended to submit to him,
and said to Zǐchūn:
"Shí Gōng is a hero of his time,
holding Zhào and Wèi,
yet he wants to declare himself a vassal to me.
Can this be believed?"
Zǐchūn replied:
"General Shí's talent and strength are indeed formidable,
as Your Sagely Will suggests.
However, with Your Highness's noble reputation in the Central Plains,
whose prestige extends over barbarians and Huá (Chinese),
from ancient times, there have been Hu people who served as respected officials and aides,
but none who became emperors.
General Shí is not unwilling to be emperor but cedes it to Your Highness;
rather, he considers that the imperial position has its own destiny,
not to be seized by intellect or strength.
Even if one forcibly takes it,
it will not be granted by heaven and man.
Although Xiàng Yǔ was mighty,
he ultimately fell to Hàn.
General Shí's relation to Your Highness
is like the moon to the sun.
Therefore, he draws lessons from past events
and commits himself to Your Highness.
This is precisely where General Shí's clear discernment far surpasses others.
Why then should Your Highness be surprised?"
Jùn was greatly pleased,
enfeoffed Zǐchūn and Zhào both as Liehóu,
and sent envoys in return,
compensating them with generous gifts.
Yóu Lún's elder brother Tǒng,
who was Jùn's Sīmǎ,
stationed at Fányáng,
privately sent envoys to submit to Lè;
Yóu Lún held Yuànxiāng,
and feigned surrender to Lè,
but Lè had already attacked and captured him.
Although Jùn did not punish Tǒng,
he increasingly believed Lè was loyal and sincere,
no longer having any doubts.
29 In this year,
Left Chancellor Ruì dispatched his heir Shào to garrison Guǎnglíng,
appointing the Chancellor's clerk Cài Mó as參軍 (Cānjūn, Military Advisor).
Mó
was the son of Kè.
30 Yáo, Prince of Zhōngshān of Hàn, besieged Wèi Jùn, the Prefect of Hénán, at Shíliáng.
Shíliáng Wù
was north of the Luòshǔi.
Yáo divided his forces to engage in battle north of the river,
and defeated them;
Hépíng
[Běi]
was north of the Yellow River,
specifically north of Fùpíngjīn.
Bài
pronounced as 'bǔ mài'.
Jùn fled by night,
but was captured and killed.
The 31st generation Duke, Yīlú, built Shènglè as the Northern Capital,
and governed the old Píngchéng as the Southern Capital.
He also constructed a new Píngchéng south of the Lěi River,
and stationed the Right Worthy King Liùxiū there to govern it,
commanding the southern region.
Shènglè County
belonged to Dìngxiāng Commandery in the Former Hàn dynasty,
and to Yúnzhōng Commandery in the Later Hàn dynasty.
Píngchéng
belonged to Yànmén Commandery in the Hàn dynasty.
The Kuòdì Zhì states: Shuòzhōu's Dìngxiāng County
was originally Hàn dynasty's Píngchéng County.
When Tuòbá Wèi was flourishing,
Shuòzhōu was established in Shènglè,
and Héngzhōu was established in Píngchéng;
Píngchéng
was called the Dài Capital.
After Gāozǔ moved to Luòyáng,
and subsequently Pòliùhán Bálíng rebelled,
the old capital became ruins.
Héngzhōu was temporarily administered from Sìzhōu's Xiùróng Commandery city,
and Yúnzhōu was temporarily administered within the borders of Bìngzhōu.
Wèi Shōu's Dìxíng Zhì,
for the area north of Jǐngjǐng Ridge,
provides a brief record.
When the Suí dynasty was flourishing,
it drove the Tujue north,
restored the old Hàn garrisons,
and merged the commanderies and counties established by the Later Wèi.
Shènglè was probably within the borders of Dìngxiāng Commandery's Dàlì County,
and Píngchéng was within the borders of Mǎyì Commandery's Yúnnèi County.
When the Táng dynasty defeated the Tujue,
it completely adopted the strategies of the Wèi and Suí dynasties for the north: Shuòzhōu's Shànyáng County
was the land of Hàn's Dìngxiāng and Wèi's Sānggān;
the Chányú Dūhùfǔ's Jīnhé County
was where the Later Wèi Emperor Dàowǔ had his capital;
Yúnzhōu's Yúnzhōng County
was the Píngchéng where the Later Wèi had its capital.
However, from the Chányú Dūhùfǔ northeast to Shuòzhōu is three hundred fifty-seven *lǐ*,
so the distance from Shènglè to Píngchéng
can be known.
Dù Yòu said: Yúnzhōng
is now north of Mǎyì Commandery;
Píngchéng
is the present-day commandery,
Suí dynasty's Yúnnèi County's Héng'ān Garrison.
The Wèi Shū's Dìjì states: Yīlú repaired the old Píngchéng to make it the Southern Capital,
and a hundred *lǐ* further south,
built a new Píngchéng on the sunny side of the Lěi River at Huángguāduī.
Jìn people called it Xiǎopíngchéng.
Dù Yòu also said: Shuòzhōu's Mǎyì Commandery,
where Wèi had its capital in Píngchéng,
established Huáisuò Garrison north of the commandery;
and after moving to Luòyáng,
established Shuòzhōu.
In the early Later Wèi,
Yúnzhōng was more than three hundred *lǐ* north of the present commandery, north of the old Dìngxiāng city;
Northern Qí established Shuòzhōu
in a new city southwest of the old capital,
also named Píngchéng;
later it was moved to Mǎyì,
which is the present commandery city.
The commandery seat is Shànyáng County,
also the land of Hàn's Dìngxiāng County.
It has the Qín Mǎyì city, Wǔ Zhōu passes,
and the Zǐ Hé originates here.
Sòng Bái said: Táng's Zhènwǔ Army,
the former Chányú Dūhùfǔ,
is Hàn's Dìngxiāng Commandery's Shènglè County.
It is on the sunny side of Yīnshān,
north of the Yellow River,
and is the Shènglè where the Later Wèi had its capital.
After the Táng pacified the Tujue,
they established the Yúnzhōng Dūdūfǔ here,
later renamed Chányú Fǔ.
Bān Gù's Dìlǐ Zhì: Yòuběipíng's Jùnmí County,
the Lěi River flows south to Wúzhōng,
and east into Gēng.
Shīgǔ said: Lěi
is pronounced *lì shuǐ*;
also *láng huì*.
Lì Dàoyuán's Shuǐjīng Zhù: The Gēng River merges with the Bàojiū River.
Jùnmí is to the east,
very far from Píngchéng.
Thus, the new Píngchéng is not south of this Lěi River.
According to the Wèi Shū,
Emperor Dàowǔ traveled west to Mǎyì
to observe the source of the Lěi River;
therefore, the Lěi River likely originates in Mǎyì
and flows northeast past the south of Píngchéng.
Lì Dàoyuán,
a Wèi person,
his commentary on the Shuǐjīng should detail the matters of the Dài Capital,
but he initially does not mention a Lěi River in Píngchéng,
only stating that the Shī River flows south of Píngchéng.
The commentary states: The Shī River
originates from Shītóu Mountain in Yànmén's Yīnguǎn County,
also called Zhì River,
flowing northeast,
emerging from the mountain,
passing west of the old city of Yīnguǎn County,
which was the old Lóufán Township.
There is also the Mǎyì Chuān River,
which joins the Sānggān River and flows into the Shī River.
The Shī River flows east past the south of Píngchéng,
then flows further east past the south of Guǎngníng's Xiàluò County,
east to Yúyáng,
and enters Gōugōu.
Further examining Bān Gù's Dìlǐ Zhì,
Yànmén's Yīnguǎn County's Lóufán Township's Lěitóu Mountain
is where the Zhì River originates,
flowing east to Quánzhōu and into the sea.
Shīgǔ said: Lěi
is pronounced *lì zhuī*;
Zhì
is pronounced *yì zhī*.
I surmise that since the water originates from Lěitóu Mountain,
perhaps at that time it was also named Lěi River.
Shīgǔ's pronunciation is in the level tone,
which is similar.
I believe that what Dàoyuán called the Shī River
is the Lěi River.
Furthermore, examining Dīng Dù's Jíyùn,
the three characters "漯,"
and "㶟"
all have the same note:
"water originates from Yànmén,"
so this also appears here.
Lěi
is pronounced *lǔ shuǐ* in the Lèipiān.
Punctuation by Hé Zīquán, collated by Róng Zhàozǔ and Niè Chóngqí.
Sīmǎ Guāng
Compiled by Imperial Edict
Hòuxué Tiāntái
Emperor Xiàomǐn, Part Two
Jiànxīng Second Year
(Jiǎxū, 314 CE)
1. Spring,
First month,
Xīnwèi day.
There was something like a sun falling to the ground;
also three suns appeared in succession,
rising from the west and moving east.
Astronomical divination said: "If three, four, five, or six suns
appear together and contend,
there will be war under Heaven";
it also said: "If three suns appear together,
within three tens of days,
the feudal lords will contend to be emperor."
2. Dīngchǒu day.
A general amnesty was proclaimed.
3. A shooting star appeared in Qiānniú,
and entered Zǐwēi.
The Jìn Astronomical Treatise states: "The six stars of Qiānniú
are south of Hégǔ."
It fell north of Píngyáng,
turning into flesh,
thirty *bù* long
and twenty-seven *bù* wide.
The Hàn ruler Cōng was displeased by this,
and asked his high officials about it.
Chén Yuándá believed that
"excessive favor for female consorts
is an omen of national doom."
The Kǎoyì states: "The Zàijì says,
'Yuándá and others said:
"Your servants fear there will be an affair of three empresses in the rear palace." ' "
Setting up three empresses
occurred in the following year,
not at this time.
"This is the principle of Yin and Yang;
what does it have to do with human affairs!"
Cōng's empress Liú Shì was wise and intelligent,
and often corrected Cōng's unrighteous actions.
Jǐchǒu day,
Empress Liú Shì died,
posthumously named Wǔxuān.
From then on, favored concubines competed for advancement,
and the imperial harem became disorderly.
4 Shí Cōng (石聰) appointed the Cchéngxiàng (丞相) and seven Gōng (公).
The seven Gōng (公) are detailed below,
ranging from Jìn Wáng Càn (晉王粲) to Zhōngshān Wáng Yào (中山王曜).

Grand Generals such as Fǔhàn (輔漢), Dūhù (都護), Zhōngjūn (中軍), Shàngjūn (上軍), Fǔjūn (撫軍), Zhèn (鎮), Wèi (衞), Jīng (京), Qián-Hòu-Zuǒ-Yòu-Shàng-Xiàjūn (前‧後‧左‧右‧上‧下軍), Fǔguó (輔國), Guànjūn (冠軍), Lóngxiáng (龍驤), and Hǔyá (虎牙).
He appointed his various sons to these positions.
He also established Zuǒ Sīlì (左司隸) and Yòu Sīlì (右司隸),
each overseeing over 200,000 households.
For every 10,000 households, one Nèishǐ (內史) was appointed.
The Chányú (單于) had a Zuǒ Fǔ (左輔) and a Yòu Fǔ (右輔),
each commanding 100,000 settlements of the Six Yí (六夷).
The Six Yí (六夷)
were probably Hú (胡), Jié (羯), Xiānbēi (鮮卑), Dī (氐), Qiāng (羌), and Bāmán (巴蠻).
Some say Wūwán (烏丸),
not Bāmán (巴蠻).
Chányú (單于),
pronounced chán.
The Zuǒ Xuǎncáo Shàngshū (左選曹尚書) and Yòu Xuǎncáo Shàngshū (右選曹尚書)
both managed elections.
The six officials from the Sīlì (司隸) downwards
all ranked below a Púyè (僕射).
He appointed his son Càn (粲) as Cchéngxiàng (丞相), concurrently Grand General, and Supervisor of the Affairs of the Department of State Affairs (錄尚書事),
and promoted him to Prince of Jìn (晉王).
Jiāngdū Wáng Yánnián (江都王延年) oversaw the six affairs of the Department of State Affairs (錄尚書六條事).
The mention of "overseeing the six affairs of the Department of State Affairs" first appears here.
Shěn Yuè's (沈約) monograph states: In the era of Jìn Kāngdì (晉康帝),
Hé Chōng (何充) declined the appointment as supervisor, stating in his memorial:
"During the Xiánkāng (咸康) period,
three supervisors were appointed.
Wáng Dǎo (王導) oversaw one,
and Xún Sōng (荀崧) and Lù Yè (陸曄) each oversaw six affairs."
If so, it would seem there were twenty-four affairs.
If there were only twelve affairs,
then Xún (荀) and Lù (陸) each oversaw six affairs,
but what then did Dǎo (導) oversee?
If Dǎo (導) oversaw all,
and Xún (荀) and Lù (陸) managed parts,
then it could not be said that Dǎo (導) oversaw one of them.
Later, whenever two supervisors were appointed,
it was always said that each oversaw six affairs,
which again suggests there were only twelve affairs.
As for what these twelve affairs were,
it is not known.
Zhāng Huá (張華) on the east side of the Jiāng (江) and Yǔ Liàng (庾亮) on the west side
were both involved in seven affairs of the Department of State Affairs.
Likewise, it is not known what these affairs were.
I (the compiler) observe: After the Yuánjiā (元嘉) period of Sòng (宋),
Jiāngxià Wáng Yìgōng (江夏王義恭), Shǐxīng Wáng Jùn (始興王濬), and Nánqiáo Wáng Yìxuān (南譙王義宣) all oversaw the six affairs of the Department of State Affairs.
Shěn (沈) family members served in high positions on the east side of the Jiāng (江) for generations,
holding prominent offices,
yet even they did not know what these affairs were.
How then can later generations verify them?
Dù Yòu (杜佑) said: Hé Chōng (何充), in his memorial declining the appointment as supervisor, stated:
"During the Xiánkāng (咸康) period,
three supervisors were appointed.
Wáng Dǎo (王導) oversaw one,
and Xún Sōng (荀崧) and Lù Yè (陸曄) each oversaw two affairs."
When the Jìn (晉) clan crossed the Jiāng (江),
there were the five Ministers (Shàngshū) of Personnel (Lìbù), Sacrifices (Cíbù), Left Civil Affairs (Zuǒmín), Five Militaries (Wǔbīng), and Finance (Dùzhī).
These were the five affairs.
In the early Jìn (晉) there were six bureaux (Cáo) of Personnel (Lìbù), Three Gōng (Sāngōng), Guest Affairs (Kècáo), Imperial Carriages (Jiàbù), Military Colonies (Túntián), and Finance (Dùzhī).

During the Tàikāng (太康) period, there were six bureaux (Cáo) of Personnel (Lìbù), Palace (Diànzhōng), Five Militaries (Wǔbīng), Agriculture (Tiáncáo), Finance (Dùzhī), and Left Civil Affairs (Zuǒmín).
These were probably the six affairs.
According to Dù Yòu (杜佑),
the six affairs were probably the six bureaux (Cáo).
Shěn Yuè (沈約) misread Hé Chōng's (何充) memorial,
changing "each oversaw two affairs"
to "each oversaw six affairs,"
leading to this error.
Wáng Yù (王育) was appointed Grand Tutor (Tàifù),
Rèn Yǐ (任顗) as Grand Guardian (Tàibǎo),
Mǎ Jǐng (馬景) as Grand Minister of Works (Dà Sītú),
Zhū Jǐ (朱紀) as Grand Minister of Education (Dà Sīkōng),
and Zhōngshān Wáng Yào (中山王曜) as Grand Commander (Dà Sīmǎ).
5 On the day Rénchén (壬辰),
Wáng Zǐchūn (王子春) and other envoys from Wáng Jùn (王浚) arrived at Xiāngguó (襄國).
Shí Lè (石勒) hid his elite troops and fine armor,
and displayed his weak forces and empty treasury to them.
He bowed facing north to the envoys and received the letters.
Jùn (浚) sent Lè (勒) a chowry.
Lè (勒) pretended not to dare hold it,
hung it on the wall,
and bowed to it morning and evening,
saying:
"I am unable to see Lord Wáng (王公),
but seeing his gift
is like seeing the Lord."
He then dispatched Dǒng Zhào (董肇) to present a memorial to Jùn (浚),
promising to personally visit Yōuzhōu (幽州) in mid-third month to present the esteemed title.
He also wrote a letter to Zǎo Sōng (棗嵩),
requesting the position of Governor of Bīngzhōu (幷州) and Duke of Guǎngpíng (廣平).
Lè (勒) questioned Wáng Zǐchūn (王子春) about Jùn's (浚) governance.
Zǐchūn (子春) replied:
"Last year, Yōuzhōu (幽州) suffered a great flood,
and the people had no grain to eat.
The five grains failed to ripen,
hence no grain to eat.
He (Jùn) was unable to provide relief,
his penal policies were harsh and cruel,
and taxes and corvée were burdensome.
Loyal and worthy officials were estranged internally,
and barbarian tribes rebelled externally.
Everyone knew he was about to fall,
yet Jùn (浚) remained composed and confident,
showing no fear.
Instead, he continued to establish ministries and offices,
appointing numerous officials,
believing that Hàn Gāo (漢高) and Wèi Wǔ (魏武) were not worthy of comparison."
Lè (勒) patted the table and laughed, saying:
"Wáng Péngzǔ (王彭祖) can truly be captured!"
Jùn's (浚) envoys returned to Jì (薊),
and reported in detail
that "Shí Lè's (石勒) forces are weak,
and his loyalty is unwavering."
Jùn (浚) was greatly pleased,
becoming even more arrogant and lax,
and no longer took precautions.
6 Yáng Hǔ (楊虎) plundered officials and people in Hànzhōng (漢中) and fled to Chéng (成).
Zhāng Xián (張咸) and others from Liángzhōu (梁州) raised troops to drive out Yáng Nándí (楊難敵).
The attack on Hànzhōng (漢中) by Yáng Hǔ (楊虎) and Yáng Nándí (楊難敵) began in the previous year (detailed in the previous volume).
Xián (咸) returned his territory to Chéng (成).
Consequently, the territories of Hànjiā (漢嘉), Fúlíng (涪陵), and Hànzhōng (漢中)
Hànjiā (漢嘉) was originally Qīngyī (青衣) county in the Former Hàn (前漢),
belonging to Shǔjùn (蜀郡).
In the second year of Yángjiā (陽嘉) of Emperor Shùn (順帝) of the Later Hàn (後漢),
it was renamed Hànjiā (漢嘉).
Shǔ (蜀) established Hànjiā Jùn (漢嘉郡).
Chéng (成) ruler Xióng (雄) appointed Lǐ Fèng (李鳳) as Inspector of Liángzhōu (梁州 Cìshǐ),
Rèn Huí (任回) as Inspector of Níngzhōu (寧州 Cìshǐ),
and Lǐ Gōng (李恭) as Inspector of Jīngzhōu (荊州 Cìshǐ).
Xióng (雄) was modest and fond of worthy men,
appointing them according to their talents.
He ordered Grand Tutor Xiáng (太傅驤) to nurture the people domestically,
and Lǐ Fèng (李鳳) and others to attract and appease people externally.
Penalties and governance were lenient and simple,
and there were no lingering prisoners in jails.
He established schools
and set up official historians.
His taxes were:
three *hú* (斛) of grain per year for male adults,
half for female adults,
and half again for the sick.
Households paid no more than several *zhàng* (丈) of silk and
several *liǎng* (兩) of cotton.
Tasks were few and corvée rare,
so the people were mostly prosperous.
New adherents were all granted tax exemptions and relief.
At this time, the world was in great chaos,
but Shǔ (蜀) alone was at peace.
Crops ripened repeatedly,
to the extent that village gates were left open,
and valuables were not picked up from the roads.
The barbarian kings of Hànjiā (漢嘉), Chōng Guī (沖歸), Zhūtí (朱提), Shěn Zhào (審炤), and Jiànníng (建寧), Cuàn Jiāng (爨畺), all submitted to him.
Bājùn (巴郡) once sent an urgent message,
reporting the presence of Jìn (晉) troops.
Xióng (雄) said:
"I have always worried that Lángxié (琅邪) was weak
and would be destroyed by Shí Lè (石勒),
which deeply concerned me.
I did not expect them to be able to raise an army.
This makes me joyful."
However, Xióng's (雄) court lacked proper decorum and standards;
ranks and titles were excessively abundant.
Officials had no salaries,
taking their provisions from the people.
The army lacked proper formations,
and commands were not strictly enforced.
These were his shortcomings.
7 In the second month, on the day Rén Yín (壬寅),
Zhāng Guǐ (張軌) was appointed Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi) and Governor of Liángzhōu (涼州 Mù),
and enfeoffed as Duke of Xīpíng Commandery (西平郡公).
Wáng Jùn (王浚) was appointed Grand Commander (Dà Sīmǎ) and Supervisor of All Military Affairs in Yōu (幽) and Jì (冀) Provinces (Dūdū Yōu-Jì Zhū Jūnshì).
Xún Zǔ (荀組) was appointed Minister of Works (Sīkōng), concurrently Left Assistant (Púyè) in the Department of State Affairs, and Inspector of the Imperial Secretariat (Sīlì Xiàowèi),
acting as supervisor of the provisional court (Xíng Liútái Shì).
Liú Kūn (劉琨) was appointed Grand General (Dà Jiāngjūn) and Supervisor of All Military Affairs in Bīngzhōu (幷州) (Dūdū Bīngzhōu Zhū Jūnshì).
The imperial court, considering Zhāng Guǐ (張軌) old and ill,
appointed his son Shí (寔) as Vice Inspector (Fù Cìshǐ).
The position of Vice Inspector (Fù Cìshǐ)
had not existed before this.
8 Shí Lè
prepared to attack Wáng Jùn
but hesitated to act.
Zhāng Bīn said:
"When attacking someone,
one must take them by surprise.
Now, the army has been prepared for days but has not moved.
Is it not because you fear Liú Kūn, the Xiānbēi, and the Wūhuán becoming a problem for us from behind?"
Lè said:
"Indeed.
What should be done?"
Bīn said:
"Among those three parties, none are as wise and brave as the general.
Even if the general marches far,
they will surely not dare to move.
Moreover, they do not expect the general to be able to lead an isolated army a thousand *lǐ* to seize Yōuzhōu.
With a light army going and returning,
it will not take more than twenty days.
Even if they had the intention,
by the time they plan and dispatch their army,
we would have already returned.
Furthermore, Liú Kūn and Wáng Jùn,
though nominally both Jìn subjects,
are actually enemies.
If we send a memorial to Kūn,
offering a hostage and seeking peace,
Kūn will surely be pleased by our submission and delighted by Jùn's demise,
and will ultimately not save Jùn or attack us.
The key to using troops is speed;
do not let the opportunity pass."
Lè said:
"What I had not understood,
the Right Marquis has already understood for me."
"Liǎo" (了)
means "to decide."
Thereupon, he marched by night with torches.
When he reached Bǎirén,
Bǎirén County
belonged to the state of Zhào.
In the Táng dynasty, it was Yáoshān County of Xíngzhōu.
This was because his elder brother Tǒng was in Fànyáng,
and he feared his military plans would be leaked.
He dispatched an envoy to present a memorial and send a hostage to Liú Kūn,
confessing his crimes
and asking to attack Jùn to prove his loyalty.
Kūn was greatly pleased,
and issued a proclamation to the prefectures and commanderies,
stating:
"I was just discussing with Yīlú how to attack Lè.
Lè fled with nowhere to hide,
seeking to seize Yōudū to atone for his sins.
Now, I should immediately dispatch Liù Xiū south to attack Píngyáng,
to eliminate the rebellious usurpers
and bring down the desperado Jié barbarians."
"Rebellious usurpers"
refers to Liú Cōng.
"Desperado Jié barbarians"
refers to Shí Lè.
"Jiàng" (降)
is pronounced *hù jiāng fān*.
"Jié" (羯)
is pronounced *jū è fān*.
"To assist the imperial house
is truly the result of accumulated sincerity and divine blessings from previous years!"
Jùn
was toyed with by Kūn and did not realize it,
which explains why they both subsequently perished.
The *Kǎoyì* says: Kūn's collection
states at the beginning of the proclamation,
"The *gēngwǔ* day of the third month's first quarter,
the *jiǎxū* day of the fifth."
According to the fact that Shí Lè conquered Yōuzhōu on the *rénshēn* day,
it seems Jìnyáng was not yet aware at that time.
To finish narrating Kūn's affairs
before narrating Lè's affairs,
it is placed here.
In the third month,
Lè's army reached Yìshuǐ.
Wáng Jùn's overseer Sūn Wěi swiftly sent a messenger to inform Jùn,
asking to lead Lè's troops to resist him,
but Yóu Tǒng forbade it.
Jùn's generals and aides all said:
"The Hú are greedy and faithless;
they must have a cunning plot.
Please attack them."
Jùn angrily said:
"Lord Shí is coming
precisely to support me!
Anyone who dares to speak of attacking will be executed!"
The multitude dared not speak further.
Jùn prepared a banquet to await him.
On the *rénshēn* day,
Lè arrived at Jì in the morning.
He yelled at the gatekeepers to open the gates.
Still suspecting an ambush,
he sent several thousand cattle and sheep as a vanguard,
claiming they were an offering for a ritual.
He meant he wanted to offer the cattle and sheep to Jùn as a courtesy.
"Shàng" (上)
is pronounced *shí zhǎng fān*.
Jùn finally became afraid,
alternately sitting and standing.
Once Lè entered the city,
he unleashed his troops to plunder greatly.
Jùn's attendants requested to resist them,
but Jùn still refused.
Lè ascended his main hall.
The central courtyard was called *tīngshì*,
meaning that affairs were received and lawsuits judged there.
In Hán and Jìn, both were written as
"聽事" (tīngshì).
Since the Six Dynasties, the radical
"厂" (hán) was added
to form
"廳" (tīng).
Both are pronounced *tā jīng fān*.
A hall without four walls is called *huáng*.
Lè summoned Jùn's wife
and sat her beside him,
holding Jùn standing before them.
Jùn cursed, saying:
"Hú slave, you abuse your father!
How can you be so ferocious and rebellious!"
Lè said:
"You, sir, hold the highest official position,
wielding powerful armies,
yet you sat by and watched the collapse of the imperial court
without ever providing aid.
Instead, you desired to exalt yourself as the Son of Heaven.
Is this not ferocious and rebellious!
Moreover, you entrusted corrupt and greedy officials,
brutalized the common people,
harmed loyal and good individuals,
and spread poison throughout Yān territory.
Whose fault is this!"
He ordered his general Wáng Luòshēng to escort Jùn with five hundred cavalry to Xiāngguó.
Jùn threw himself into the water,
but was pulled out tied up
and executed in the market of Xiāngguó.
Lè killed ten thousand of Jùn's elite troops.
Jùn's generals and aides rushed to the military gate to apologize,
offering bribes profusely.
However, the former Grand Secretariat Péi Xiàn and Attendant Censor Xún Chuò alone did not come.
Lè summoned them and reproached them, saying:
"Wáng Jùn was tyrannical,
and I attacked and executed him.
Everyone else came to congratulate and express gratitude.
You two alone share his wickedness.
How will you escape execution!"
They replied:
"We, Xiàn and others, have served the Jìn dynasty for generations,
enjoying its honors and emoluments.
Though Jùn was fierce and coarse,
he was still a vassal of Jìn.
Therefore, we followed him."
Péi Xiàn fled to Yōuzhōu.
See volume 87, Emperor Huái, Yǒngjiā fifth year.
"If Your Illustrious Highness does not cultivate virtue and righteousness,
but solely relies on terror and punishment,
then our death is simply our due.
Why should we flee!
We ask to die."
They departed without bowing.
Lè summoned them and apologized,
treating them with the courtesy due to guests.
Chuò
was the grandson of Xù.
Lè denounced Zhū Shuò, Zǎo Sōng, and others for accepting bribes and disrupting governance,
becoming a scourge to Yōuzhōu.
The events are described in the previous volume, previous year.
"Shù" (數)
is pronounced *suǒ jù fān*.
He executed all of them.
This was because Tǒng wanted to secretly attach Fànyáng to him.
Only Péi Xiàn and Xún Chuò had just over a hundred bundles of books
and ten-odd *hú* each of salt and rice, no more.
Lè said:
"I am not pleased to have gained Yōuzhōu;
I am pleased to have gained these two men."
He appointed Xiàn as Attendant Censor
and Chuò as Army Supervisor.
He dispersed the displaced people,
sending each back to their hometowns.
Lè stayed in Jì for two days,
burned Jùn's palaces,
appointed the former Grand Secretariat Liú Hàn of Yānguó as acting Inspector of Yōuzhōu,
garrisoned Jì,
installed magistrates, and then returned.
Sūn Wěi ambushed him,
and Lè barely escaped.
When Lè arrived at Xiāngguó,
he dispatched an envoy to present Wáng Jùn's head and offer the victory report to Hàn.
Hàn appointed Lè as Grand Commander, Inspector of all military affairs east of Shǎn.
This "east of Shǎn"
also takes the meaning of "dividing the Shǎn" and grants it to him.
He was granted an additional twelve commanderies.
Lè firmly declined, accepting only two commanderies.
Liú Kūn (劉琨) requested troops from Tuòbá Yīlú (拓跋猗盧) to attack Hàn (漢),
but Yīlú’s (猗盧) various nomadic tribes, over ten thousand households, planned to join Shí Lè (石勒).
Yīlú (猗盧) executed them all,
and thus could not fulfill his agreement with Kūn (琨).
Kūn (琨), realizing Shí Lè (石勒) had no intention of surrendering,
became greatly alarmed,
and submitted a memorial, saying:
“Of the eight prefectures in the northeast,
Lè (勒) has annihilated seven.
Lè (勒) entered Yè (鄴),
killed Dūdū Dōngyànwáng Téng (都督東燕王騰);
attacked Xìndū (信都),
killed Jìzhōu Cìshǐ Wáng Bīn (冀州刺史王斌);
ambushed Juànchéng (鄄城),
killed Yǎnzhōu Cìshǐ Yuán Fú (兗州刺史袁孚);
attacked Xīncài (新蔡),
killed Yùzhōu Cìshǐ Xīncàiwáng Què (豫州刺史新蔡王確);
ambushed Méngchéng (蒙城),
captured Qīngzhōu Dūdū Gǒu Xī (青州都督苟晞);
conquered Shàngbái (上白),
beheaded Qīngzhōu Cìshǐ Lǐ Yùn (李惲);
attacked Xìndū (信都),
killed Jìzhōu Cìshǐ Wáng Xiàng (冀州刺史王象);
attacked Dìnglíng (定陵),
killed Yǎnzhōu Cìshǐ Tián Huī (田徽);
ambushed Yōuzhōu (幽州),
captured Wáng Jùn (王浚).
Excluding Lǐ Yùn (李惲) and Tián Huī (田徽),
who were appointed by Wáng Jùn (王浚) acting on imperial authority,
he has indeed annihilated seven.
Only I remain.
Lè (勒) holds Xiāngguó (襄國),
separated from me by mountains.
The mountains,
from Tàiháng (太行) and Héngshān (恆山) extending to Yōu (幽) and Jié (碣),
are continuous.
Xiāngguó (襄國) is east of the mountains,
Jìnyáng (晉陽) is west of the mountains.
The cities and strongholds are terrified.
Although they harbor loyalty and indignation,
their strength does not match their wishes!”
Liú Hàn (劉翰) did not want to follow Shí Lè (石勒),
so he returned to Duàn Pǐdī (段匹磾),
and Pǐdī (匹磾) then occupied Jìchéng (薊城).
Wáng Jùn’s (王浚) Cóngshì Zhōngláng Yáng Yù (從事中郎陽裕),
who was Tān (躭)’s nephew,
fled to Lìngzhī (令支).
Lìngzhī (令支) county,
which belonged to Liáoxī (遼西) in the Hàn (漢) dynasty,
was formerly the state of Gūzhú Jūn (孤竹君).
It was abolished in the Jìn (晉) dynasty.
The Duàn (段) clan occupied it and made it their capital.
Yì Shào (應劭) said: Lìng (令)
is pronounced líng (鈴).
Péi Sōngzhī (裴松之) said: Zhī (支)
is pronounced with the sound of ‘qí ér’.
Shī Gǔ (師古) said: Lìng (令)
is also pronounced with the sound of ‘láng dìng’.
Dù Yòu (杜佑) said: Lìngzhī (令支) is
the modern Lúlóng (盧龍) county in Běipíng (北平) commandery.
Zhū Zuǒchē (朱左車) of Kuàijī (會稽), Kǒng Zuǎn (孔纂) of Lǔguó (魯國), Húmǔ Yì (胡母翼) of Tàishān (泰山) fled from Jì (薊) to Chānglí (昌黎),
relying on Mùróng Huī (慕容廆).
At this time, tens of thousands of households of Chinese refugees came to Huī (廆).
Huī (廆) established Jìyáng (冀陽) commandery for the people of Jìzhōu (冀州).
According to Wèi Shōu’s (魏收) Dìxíng Zhì (地形志),
Jìyáng (冀陽) commandery should have been established within the boundaries of Húnpíng Gāng (漢北平平剛) county in Běipíng (北平) of Hàn (漢).
Chéngzhōu (成周) belonged to Yùzhōu (豫州),
hence it was used as the commandery name.
The Qiánhàn Zhì (前漢志) says: Línchú (臨渝) county in Liáoxī (遼西)
has the Yú (渝) river,
which originates from the Báiláng (白狼) river,
flows south past the west of Yíngqiū (營丘) city.
This was a commandery established by Huī (廆).
Bīngzhōu (幷州)
was ancient Táng (唐) state.
Huī (廆) accordingly used it to name a commandery.
The locations where the two commanderies, Chéngzhōu (成周) and Tángguó (唐國), were established are missing.
Initially,
Wáng Jùn (王浚) appointed Shào Xù (邵續) as the Administrator of Lèlíng (樂陵),
garrisoned at Yàncì (厭次).
Yàncì (厭次)
was originally Fùpíng (富平) county of Píngyuán (平原) commandery in the Former Hàn (前漢).
Emperor Míng (明帝) of the Later Hàn (後漢) renamed it Yàncì (厭次).
Jìn (晉) divided it and made it belong to Lèlíng (樂陵),
as its administrative seat.
Dīng Dù’s (丁度) Jíyùn (集韻) says: Yàn (厭)
is pronounced with the sound of ‘yú yǎn’.
The Jiǔyù Zhì (九域志) says: Tradition has it that Qín Shǐhuáng (秦始皇) toured the East,
tired of the qi (氣) of Jiéshí (碣石),
and made his temporary residence here,
hence the name.
Wèi Shōu (魏收) said: Yàncì (厭次) county in Lèlíng (樂陵) commandery has Fùchéng (富城),
where Shào Xù (邵續) resided.
Xù (續) attached himself to Shí Lè (石勒),
and Lè (勒) appointed Xù’s (續) son, Yì (乂), as Dūhù (督護).
Liú Yìn (劉胤) of Dōnglái (東萊), who was the Administrator of Bóhǎi (勃海) appointed by Jùn (浚), abandoned his commandery and joined Xù (續).
He said to Xù (續):
“To achieve great deeds,
one must rely on great righteousness.
My lord,
you are a loyal subject of Jìn (晉).
How can you follow a rebel and stain yourself?”
At that time, Duàn Pǐdī (段匹磾) invited Xù (續) by letter to return together to Zuǒ Chéngxiàng Ruì (左丞相睿).
Xù (續) agreed.
His men all said:
“Now if we abandon Lè (勒) and return to Pǐdī (匹磾),
what about Yì (乂)?”
Xù (續) wept and said:
“How can I consider my son and become a traitorous minister?”
He killed several dissenters.
When Lè (勒) heard of this,
he killed Yì (乂).
Xù (續) sent Liú Yìn (劉胤) as an envoy to Jiāngdōng (江東).
Ruì (睿) appointed Yìn (胤) as Cānjūn (參軍) and
Xù (續) as Administrator of Píngyuán (平原).
Shí Lè (石勒) sent troops to besiege Xù (續).
Pǐdī (匹dī) sent his younger brother, Wén Yāng (文鴦), to relieve him.
Lè (勒) then withdrew.
There was a great famine in Xiāngguó (襄國).
Two *shēng* of grain were worth one *jīn* of silver,
and one *jīn* of meat was worth one *liǎng* of silver.
Dù Tāo’s (杜弢) general Wáng Zhēn (王真) attacked Táo Kǎn (陶侃) at Línzhàng (林障).
The Shuǐjīng Zhù (水經註) says: Línzhàng (林障) is in Dùnyáng (沌陽) county, Jiāngxià (江夏).
The Miǎn (沔) river flows north of Dùnyáng (沌陽) county,
and then east past the north of the old city of Línzhàng (林障).
Sòng Bái (宋白) said: Jìn (晉) Jiāngxià (江夏) commandery was administered from Línzhàng (林障).
In the first year of Yìxī (義熙), it was moved to Xiàkǒu (夏口).
Zhōu Fǎng (周訪) rescued Kǎn (侃),
attacked Tāo’s (弢) forces,
and defeated them.
In summer,
in the fifth month,
Zhāng Guǐ (張軌), the Wǔmù Gōng (武穆公) of Xīpíng (西平), fell gravely ill.
He left a will, saying:
“All military and civil officers
must secure the common people,
above, contemplate repaying the nation,
below, bring peace to the family.”
On the *jǐchǒu* (己丑) day,
Guǐ (軌) died.
Kǎoyì (考異) says: Dìjì (帝紀) records
“rénchén (壬辰).”
We now follow Qiánliáng Lùchāo (前涼錄鈔).

Yáo Yào (姚曜), Prince of Zhōngshān (中山), and Zhào Rǎn (趙染) of Hàn (漢) plundered Cháng’ān (長安).

*Ruì* (汭)

Suǒ Qín (索綝) led troops out to resist them.

Lā (拉)

How can I dirty my horse’s hooves and sword blade?”
In the morning,

An imperial edict added the title Pàoyì Dàjiāngjūn (驃騎大將軍) to Suǒ Qín (索綝), and appointed him Shàngshū Zuǒ Púyè (尚書左僕射) and Lù Shàngshū (錄尚書),

Yuè and Rǎn again led tens of thousands of troops with General Yīn Kǎi towards Cháng'ān.
Kǎo Yì says: Jìn Chūnqiū writes

We now follow the biography of Qū Yǔn.
After Yǔn was defeated,

at night,

Mò wanted to join Lǐ Jù at Xīnzhèng,
Xīnzhèng county was
under Hénán Commandery in the Hàn dynasty.
It was abolished in the Jìn dynasty,

Zhōu Xuānwáng's younger brother, Zhèng Huángōng, was originally enfeoffed in Zhèng County of Jīngzhào;

Zuǒzhuàn records Zhèng Zhuānggōng saying

With few soldiers,

14. In the autumn,

Qū Yǔn resisted him,

15. Shí Lè first ordered the provinces and commanderies to review the actual households and population.
Each household was to provide two bolts of silk

16. In the winter,
in the tenth month,

17. In the eleventh month,
the Hàn ruler Cōng appointed Jìn Wáng Càn as Chancellor (Xiàngguó) and Grand Chányú,
to oversee all governmental affairs.
Càn was talented in his youth,
but after becoming Chancellor,
he became arrogant, extravagant, and authoritarian.
He alienated the virtuous and favored the sycophantic,
being severe and stubborn against remonstrance,
which made the people of the state begin to detest him.
This laid the groundwork for Càn later being assassinated by Jìn Zhǔn.
Shǎo,

Yuǎn,

È,

18. Zhōu Xié, following his father's dying words,

Xié,
pronounced "xié".
plotted rebellion;

1. In the spring,
in the first month,
Xú Fù killed Yuán Xiù, the Administrator of Wúxìng,

When Zhā heard of this,
he was greatly alarmed

Xié, knowing Zhā's intentions were different,

Fù's followers, in fear,
attacked Fù

Sūn Bì also died.
Zhā's son Xù also gathered followers to respond to Fù.
The Left Chancellor Ruì debated sending troops to suppress him.
Wáng Dǎo said:
"If we send too few troops now, it will not be enough to quell the rebels;
if we send too many, our base will be empty.
Xù's cousin, the Palace Attendant Yán,

I request that Yán alone be sent;
that will be sufficient to execute Xù."
Ruì agreed.
Yán traveled day and night,
arriving at the commandery.
As he was about to enter,
he encountered Xù at the gate,
and said to Xù:
"You and I should go together to Magistrate Kǒng's residence;
there is something to discuss."
Xù refused to enter,
but Yán forcibly pulled him along.
Once seated,
Yán said to Kǒng Kǎn:
"Magistrate, why do you allow a bandit to sit here?"
Xù always carried a knife in his clothes,
and immediately grabbed the knife to threaten Yán.
Yán shouted at the commandery messenger Wú Céng to kill him.
A messenger
was a commandery official;
one who propagated orders.
Zhā did not listen,
but blamed his cousin Shào and executed him.
Yán did not return home to see his mother,

Ruì appointed Zhā as Administrator of Wúxìng,
and Yán as Commander of the Crown Prince's Right Guard.
Because the Zhōu clan was a prominent family in Wú,
no exhaustive investigation was conducted,
and Xié was treated as before.
Shuài,
as is.
Zhì,
pronounced like "zhí zhī".

Huáyīn County
belonged to Jīngzhào in the Former Hàn dynasty,

Huá,
pronounced like "hù huà".

on the day Bǐngzǐ,

Wáng Bǎo, Prince of Nányáng, was appointed Chancellor (Xiàngguó).

靳,
jū xīn fān.

Cōng then reinstated Yuándá as Grand Master of Remonstrance,
with the ceremonial rank equivalent to the Three Ducal Ministers.
Yuèguāng engaged in immoral conduct,
and Yuándá reported it in a memorial.
Cōng had no choice but to depose her.
Yuèguāng, filled with shame and resentment, committed suicide.

11 Summer,
fourth month,

a general amnesty was granted.

"Cháng'ān (長安) is not yet pacified,

We now follow the Imperial Annals.
Chángshā (長沙)
was Dù Tāo's (杜弢) lair.
Prime Minister Ruì (睿) acted on imperial authority,

Dūn (敦) began to personally select and appoint officials from the Cìshǐ (刺史) downwards,

Initially,
when Wáng Rú (王如) surrendered,

he requested Dūn (敦) to assign him to his command.
Dūn (敦) said:
"These men are dangerous and fierce, difficult to control.
Your nature is impetuous and irritable,

Líng (稜) insisted,
so Dūn (敦) gave them to him.
Líng (稜) placed Rú (如) on his left and right,

Rú (如) frequently competed and fought in archery with Dūn's (敦) various generals.

When Dūn (敦) secretly harbored rebellious intentions,

Dūn (敦) was angry at his opposition,

Rú (如) seized an opportunity during a relaxed banquet,
requesting to perform a sword dance for entertainment.
Líng (稜) granted it.
As Rú (如) danced, he gradually moved forward.
Líng (稜) grew uneasy and reprimanded him,
but Rú (如) went straight forward and killed Líng (稜).
When Dūn (敦) heard of this,
he feigned surprise,
and also apprehended and executed Rú (如).
Initially,
the imperial court heard of Zhāng Guāng's (張光) death.
Guāng's (光) death
can be found in the first year of the previous volume.
The *Kǎoyì* (考異) states: Zhōu Fǎng's (周訪) biography says
"Zhēngnán Dàjiāngjūn (征南大將軍)";
we now follow Dù Zēng's (杜曾) biography.
He exited through Wǔguān (武關).
Dù Zēng (杜曾) welcomed Yī (猗) at Xiāngyáng (襄陽),

Táo Kǎn (陶侃), having defeated Dù Tāo (杜弢),

with an intention to slight Zēng (曾).
Sīmǎ Lǔ Tián (司馬魯恬) advised, saying:

Currently, among Your Excellency's generals,
none are equal to Zēng (曾),

Kǎn (侃) did not heed him,
and advanced to besiege Zēng (曾) at Shíchéng (石城).
*Shuǐjīngzhù* (水經註) states: The Miǎn (沔) River flows south past the west of Shíchéng (石城);

Yáng Hù (羊祜) of Jìn (晉) was stationed in Jīngzhōu (荊州)
and established it.
In the ninth year of Yuánkāng (元康) of Jìn Huìdì (晉惠帝),
the western Dūwèi (都尉) of Jiāngxià (江夏) was divided to establish Jìnglíng (竟陵) Commandery,
with its seat at Shíchéng (石城).
Today's Chángshòu (長壽) county in Yǐngzhōu (郢州) is that place.
Zēng (曾) secretly opened the gate and charged into Kǎn's (侃) formation,
coming out from behind them,
and counter-attacked.
Hundreds of Kǎn's (侃) soldiers died.
Zēng (曾) then headed towards Shùnyáng (順陽),
