Yīlú fled in disguise among the common people.
A common woman recognized him,
and he was then assassinated by Liùxiū.
Tuòbá Pǔgēn, who had been guarding the frontier,
heard of the trouble and came to assist.
He attacked Liùxiū
and eliminated him.
Pǔgēn succeeded to the throne,
and there was great chaos in the state.
The old and new factions were suspicious of each other
and alternately annihilated each other.
The Left General Wèi Xióng and the General of Trust and Righteousness Jī Dàn,
who had long served Yīlú
and were supported by the populace,
conspired to return to Liú Kūn.
They then said to the people:
"We hear that the old people resent the new people's fierce fighting.
'Old people' refers to the Suǒtóu tribe;
'new people' refers to the Jìn people and the Wūhuán people.
Hàn
is pronounced hóu gàn fān,
also xià hǎn fān.
What should we do?"
The Jìn people and the Wūhuán were all alarmed and fearful,
and said:
"We will live or die with the two generals!"
So, with Kūn's hostage son, Zūn, they led three thousand families of Jìn people and Wūhuán, and one hundred thousand head of horses, cattle, and sheep, to surrender to Kūn.
Kūn was overjoyed
and personally went to Píngchéng to appease and accept them.
Kūn's military power thus revived.
In summer,
in the fourth month,
Pǔgēn died.
His son was newly born,
so Pǔgēn's mother, Lady Wéi, enthroned him.
Lady Wéi
was Yī'é's wife.
4 Zhāng Shí 下令：
「My subordinates, officials, and common people, if anyone can point out my faults,
I will reward them with cloth, silk, sheep, and rice.」
The Assistant to the Inspector of Rogues, Gāo Chāng Wěi Jǐn, said:
「Since the Hàn dynasty,
in the various offices of the ducal administrations, provincial prefectures, and commanderies,
there have been aides,
there have been attachés,
and there have been assistant scribes.
In the 'Western Regions' chapter of the Former Hàn History,
the state of Chē Shī had the Gāo Chāng fortress.
The Táng History states: The state of Gāo Chāng
was the former royal court of Chē Shī of Hàn.
Later, after Gāo Chāng was conquered,
Xī Zhōu was established.
Observing this,
the Zhāng clan of Hé Xī must have established commanderies and counties in the land of Gāo Chāng,
and it only became the state of Gāo Chāng during the Later Wèi dynasty.
隗,
pronounced wěi.
Now, your enlightened lord governs,
and everything, whether big or small,
you decide yourself.
Sometimes you raise an army or issue orders,
and the administration does not know;
'administration' refers to the place where officials gather.
朝,
pronounced zhāo.
The blame has nowhere to be divided.
Your subordinates fear your might,
and merely accept what is presented.
If it is like this,
even if you reward them with a thousand pieces of gold,
they will ultimately not dare to speak.
I suggest that you should moderate your intelligence a little,
and for all matters of governance,
you should invite and consult your subordinates,
allowing each to fully express their thoughts,
and then adopt and implement them.
Then good advice will come naturally,
why must there be rewards?」
Shí was pleased,
and followed his advice;
he promoted Jǐn three ranks.
Shí dispatched General Wáng Gāi to lead five thousand infantry and cavalry to reinforce Cháng'ān,
and also to deliver the tribute and accounts from the various commanderies.
'Tribute' refers to local products;
'accounts' refers to account books.
He appointed Shí's brother, Mào, as the Inspector of Qín Zhōu.
5 Shí Lè sent Shí Hǔ to attack Liú Yǎn in Lǐnqiū.
The Inspector of Yōu Zhōu, Duàn Pǐdī, sent his brother Wén Yāng to rescue him.
Hǔ captured Lǐnqiū,
and Yǎn fled to Wén Yāng's army.
Hǔ captured Yǎn's brother Qǐ and returned.
6 The Inspector of Níng Zhōu, Wáng Xùn,
was severe, fierce, and fond of executions.
In the fifth month,
the Administrator of Píngyí, Léi Zhào,
in the fifth year of Yǒngjiā of Emperor Huái,
Xùn petitioned to divide Zāngkē, Zhūtí, and Jiànníng,
and established the Píngyí Commandery,
which was the land of the two Hàn counties of Píngyí and Bí.
鄨,
Méng Kāng pronounced it bí.
Pínglè Commandery,
as evidenced by the Suí Records,
was probably established in Qióngbù Chuān of Yuècuī Commandery,
but it is unknown who established it.
樂,
pronounced luò.
surrendered to Chéng.
7 In the sixth month,
on the first day of Dīngsì,
there was a solar eclipse.
8 In autumn,
seventh month,
the Grand Marshal of Hàn, Yào, besieged Qū Chāng, the Administrator of Běidì.
The Jìn Běidì Commandery
only governed the two counties of Níyáng and Fùpíng.
Yào surrounded the city and set it on fire,
the smoke rose and covered the sky.
He sent a double agent to deceive Yǔn, saying:
「The commandery city has already fallen,
it is too late to go now!」
The troops were terrified and routed.
Yào pursued and defeated Yǔn in Pánshí Gǔ.
Yǔn fled back to Língwǔ,
and Yào then captured Běidì.
Yǔn was benevolent and generous by nature,
but lacked authority and decisiveness,
and liked to please people with titles and ranks.
Zhú Huī, Administrator of Xīnpíng; Yáng Xiàng, Administrator of Shǐpíng; Zhú Shuǎng, Administrator of Fúfēng; and Jiāo Sōng, Administrator of Āndìng,
all held the titles of 'General Who Conquers' and 'General Who Guards',
carried imperial credentials, and were granted the titles of Attendant Official and Palace Attendant.
Even the smallest chiefs of villages and fortresses
were granted the title of 'General of Silver and Green'.
'General Who Conquers' and 'General Who Guards' refer to the titles of the Four Generals Who Conquering and Four Generals Who Guarding.
'General of Silver and Green' means a general who is granted this title and also given a silver seal and a green sash.
帥,
pronounced shuài.
Therefore, the various generals became arrogant and wanton, and the soldiers and common people were resentful.
When Guān Zhōng was in peril and chaos,
Yǔn sent an urgent message to Jiāo Sōng.
Sōng had always despised Yǔn,
and said:
「I will rescue him when Yǔn is in distress.」
Yào advanced to Jīngyáng,
and all the cities north of the Wèi River collapsed.
Jīngyáng County
belonged to Āndìng Commandery in the Former Hàn.
Bān Zhì says: Jiāntóu Shān is west of the county.
The Jīng River, as mentioned in the Tribute of Yǔ, originates there,
flows northeast to Yánglíng and enters the Wèi River,
passing through three commanderies,
travelling one thousand sixty li.
This statement that Yào reached Jīngyáng and all the cities north of the Wèi River collapsed
means his troops were already between Chíyáng and Yánglíng counties,
referring to the south bank of the Jīng River,
not Jīngyáng County of Āndìng.
Yào had long heard of Chōng's virtuousness
and offered a reward to capture him alive.
Upon seeing him,
he offered him wine and said:
「If I have you,
settling the world will not be difficult!」
Chōng said:
「As a Jìn general,
with the state in ruin,
I dare not seek life.
If I receive your grace,
a quick death would be fortunate.」
Yào said:
「He is a righteous man.」
He granted him a sword
and ordered him to commit suicide.
Liáng Wěi's wife, Lady Xīn,
was beautiful.
Yào summoned her
and intended to make her his wife.
妻,
pronounced qī.
She said: 「My husband is already dead.
It is unrighteous for me to live alone.
Moreover, how could a single woman serve two husbands?
Why would an enlightened lord like you use her!」
Yào said:
「She is a chaste woman.」
He also allowed her to commit suicide
and buried them both with proper rites.
9 The Hàn ruler Cōng elevated Lady Fán, a former maidservant of Empress Zhāng, to the rank of Supreme Empress.
In addition to the three empresses,
there were seven other women who wore the empress's seals and sashes.
Favored concubines wielded power,
and rewards and punishments were chaotic.
Grand General Fū repeatedly wept and earnestly remonstrated.
Cōng angrily said:
「Do you want your father to die quickly,
why do you come crying every morning and evening!」
Fū was grieved and indignant,
fell ill, and died.
In Hédōng Píngyáng, there was a great locust plague.
Five or six out of ten people became refugees and starved.
Shí Lè sent his general Shí Yuè to lead twenty thousand cavalry to garrison Bìng Zhōu,
to attract and accept refugees.
Two hundred thousand households returned to him.
Cōng sent an envoy to reprimand Lè,
but Lè did not accept the order,
and secretly allied with Cáo Yì.
10 In the eighth month,
the Grand Marshal of Hàn, Yào, pressed on Cháng'ān.
11 In the ninth month,
the Hàn ruler hosted a banquet for his subordinates in Guāngjí Diàn
and summoned the Imperial Younger Brother Yì.
Yì appeared emaciated,
with graying temples and hair.
He wept and apologized,
and Cōng also wept for him.
Then they drank heavily and had great fun,
treating him as before.
12 Jiāo Sōng, Zhú Huī, Sòng Zhé all led troops to rescue Cháng'ān.
The Palace Attendant Counselor, Huá Jí, supervised the armies of the four commanderies: Jīngzhào, Féngyì, Hóngnóng, and Shàngluò.
They encamped at Bàshàng.
All feared the strength of the Hàn army
and dared not advance.
Xiàngguó Bǎo sent Hú Sōng with troops to reinforce,
attacking Hàn's Grand Marshal, Yào, at Língtái,
and defeated him.
The Sānfǔ Huángtú states: King Wén of Zhōu's Língtái
is forty lǐ west of Cháng'ān,
two zhàng high,
with a circumference of 120 paces.
Qū Yǔn
was also Suǒ Chén.
Suǒ
is pronounced like "xí gè".
Then they returned to Huáilǐ.
Huáilǐ County
belonged to Fúfēng in the Hàn dynasty,
and to Shǐpíng Commandery in the Jìn dynasty.
Yào attacked and captured the outer city of Cháng'ān.
Qū Yǔn and Suǒ Chén retreated to defend the small city to secure themselves.
Inside and outside were cut off,
and there was severe famine in the city.
A dou of rice cost two liǎng of gold.
People resorted to cannibalism.
More than half died.
The desertions were uncontrollable.
Only a thousand righteous people from Liángzhōu
held their ground, defending to the death.
The righteous people of Liángzhōu
were the soldiers sent by Zhāng Guǐ and his son.
They milled wheat
and Qū Yǔn ground it into porridge to provide for the emperor.
Soon after, that too ran out.
In winter,
the eleventh month,
the Emperor tearfully said to Yǔn:
"Now we are in such dire straits,
with no outside rescue.
We must endure the shame and surrender
to save the officials and people."
Then he sighed, saying:
"Those who ruined my affairs
are the two dukes, Qū and Suǒ!"
He sent the Palace Attendant, Zōng Chǎng, to deliver the letter of surrender to Yào.
Kǎoyì says: The Imperial Annals record "Sòng Chǎng,"
but we follow Jìn Chūnqiū here.
He sent his son to persuade Yào, saying:
"The food in the city is still enough to last a year;
it is not easy to conquer.
If you promise Chén
the title of Yítóng and Marquis of a Ten-Thousand-Household Commandery,
we will surrender the city."
Yào beheaded him and sent back his head,
saying:
"The army of a sovereign
acts with righteousness.
I have led troops for fifteen years
and have never defeated anyone with cunning schemes.
I must exhaust my forces and reach the limit of my power
before taking it.
What Suǒ Chén said is thus;
the evil in the world is one and the same.
I will readily execute him for you.
If the soldiers and food are indeed not exhausted,
then you can force yourselves to hold out;
but if your provisions are depleted and your army weak,
you should also quickly recognize the mandate of Heaven."
On the jiǎwǔ day,
Zōng Chǎng arrived at Yào's camp.
On the yǐwèi day,
the Emperor rode in a lamb cart,
bare-chested, holding a jade disk in his mouth, and carrying a coffin, he exited the east gate to surrender.
His retainers cried out in lament,
clinging to the cart and grasping the Emperor's hand.
The Emperor too was overwhelmed with sorrow.
Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng, Jí Lǎng of Féngyì, sighed and said:
"My wisdom cannot strategize,
my courage cannot die.
How can I bear for sovereign and subject to follow each other,
and serve the enemy from the north!"
Then he committed suicide.
Yào burned the coffin and accepted the jade disk,
and ordered Zōng Chǎng to escort the Emperor back to the palace.
On the dīngyǒu day,
the Emperor, dukes, ministers, and others were moved to his camp.
On the xīncǒu day,
they were sent to Píngyáng.
On the rén'yín day,
the Hàn lord, Cōng, ascended the Guāngjí Diàn.
The Emperor kowtowed before him.
Qū Yǔn prostrated on the ground, weeping uncontrollably,
and could not be helped up.
Cōng was angered
and imprisoned him.
Yǔn committed suicide.
Cōng appointed the Emperor as Guānglù Dàfū
and enfeoffed him as Huái'ān Hóu.
He made Grand Marshal Yào provisional Yellow Axe-bearer, Grand Commander, Supervisor of all military affairs west of the Shǎn Pass, and Grand Tutor,
enfeoffing him as Qín Wáng.
A general amnesty was declared,
and the era name was changed to Línjiā.
Because Qū Yǔn was loyal and brave,
he was posthumously appointed Chējì Jiāngjūn
and given the posthumous title Jié Mǐn Hóu.
Yǔn was indeed loyal,
but still after Jí Lǎng!
He was executed in the marketplace.
Píngyáng had a marketplace.
Huá Jí fled to Nánshān.
Gān Bǎo's commentary says: In the past, Emperor Gāozǔ Xuān,
with his heroic talent and great capacity,
arose in response to the times.
His nature was deep and formidable, like a city's defenses,
yet he was broad-minded enough to accommodate;
he used numerology and tactics to govern things,
yet was skilled at judging people and selecting the capable.
It is said that those with "city defenses in their chest" often cannot be tolerant,
and those who rely on numerology and tactics often cannot employ people,
yet Emperor Xuān was able to do so.
It means that everyone recognized his ability,
and no one could contend with him.
Liú Liáng said: "Xiàng" (象) means "fǎ" (法, law);
it means the rise and establishment of the Jìn dynasty,
the great law began to be established from this.
Tàizǔ continued the legacy,
discarding all deviant plans,
and expanding on former achievements.
This refers to the internal execution of Lǐ Fēng and Xiàhóu Xuán,
and the external pacification of Guànqiū Jiǎn, Wén Qīn, and Zhūgě Dàn.
Thus, he enjoyed the Imperial Zenith.
Lǚ Yánjì said: "Xiǎng" (享) here means "dāng" (當, fitting);
"Huángjí" (皇極) means the position of the Son of Heaven.
He was frugal in his expenses,
harmonious but not lax,
generous yet decisive,
encompassing the old territories of Táng and Yú,
and distributing the proper calendar to the Eight Desolations.
The Eight Desolations
refer to the regions beyond the eight directions,
the wild lands of the barbarians.
The proverb "There are no poor people in the world"
Lǚ Xiàng said: meaning that the common people were all prosperous.
is also sufficient to show that the people enjoyed their lives.
After Emperor Wǔ passed away,
before the imperial tomb was dry, chaos and difficulties arose one after another.
The imperial relatives had no support like a defensive wall,
the grand tutors and ministers had no revered status for all to behold.
The Odes say: "Majestic are the Grand Tutors and ministers,
the people all look up to you."
They became like Jié and Zhí overnight;
this refers to Yáng Jùn, Wèi Guàn, Zhāng Huá, and others.
The imperial guards were scattered to the four directions,
the regional governors had no heavy, stone-like stability,
the passes had no "grass-knot" solidity.
Thirty jīn is a jūn,
four jūn is a shí.
The Zuǒ Zhuàn says: When Qín attacked Jìn,
Jìn's Wèi Kē defeated the Qín army
and captured Dù Huí.
Kē dreamed of an old man tying grass to impede Dù Huí.
Dù Huí stumbled and fell,
thus he was captured.
Why did the two emperors lose their dignity?
The establishment of successors lacked proper authority,
the entrustment was to untalented individuals,
the Four Pillars were not upheld, and expedient governance was abundant.
Jiǎ Yì's memorial says: "Propriety, righteousness, integrity, and shame
are called the Four Pillars.
If the Four Pillars are not upheld,
the state will perish."
Indeed, when the foundation is broad, it is difficult to overturn;
when the roots are deep, it is difficult to pull up;
when principles are ordered, there is no disorder;
when bound firmly, there is no displacement.
Lǐ Zhōuhàn said: "Principles ordered"
means that governance and education have order and measure.
"Bound firmly"
means to be solid.
It means that if the ruler lays a deep and broad foundation of benevolence and kindness,
and does not lose order and measure,
then the people's hearts will be firmly bound and not be displaced.
This is the way to achieve it.
The Zhōu (dynasty), from Hòujì's love for the people,
had sixteen kings until Wǔ became its first ruler.
Hòujì's son was Bùchù,
Bùchù's son was Jū,
Jū's son was Gōngliú,
Gōngliú's son was Qìngjié,
Qìngjié's son was Huángpú,
Huángpú's son was Chāfú,
Chāfú's son was Huǐyú,
Huǐyú's son was Gōngfēi,
Gōngfēi's son was Gāoyǔ,
Gāoyǔ's son was Yàyǔ,
Yàyǔ's son was Gōngshū Zǔlèi,
Gōngshū Zǔlèi's son was Gǔgōng Dànfù,
Gǔgōng Dànfù's son was Jìlì,
Jìlì's son was Wénwáng,
Wénwáng's son was Wǔwáng.
In total, sixteen kings.
Thus was its solidity.
Now, with the rise of Jìn,
its founding and establishment of roots
are certainly different from previous generations.
Furthermore, the court lacks people of pure virtue,
and the countryside lacks elders who are unwavering.
The Zhōu officials included "country elders" (xiānglǎo);
"unwavering" (bù'èr)
means not repeating mistakes.
Cháo,
read zhí yáo fān.
The things esteemed and things considered shameful have lost their proper place.
It means that what is considered shameful is not truly shameful,
and what is esteemed is not truly estimable.
Those who engage in discussion consider empty grandiloquence to be eloquence and disparage adherence to principles.
Those who conduct themselves consider wanton depravity to be broad-mindedness and disdain integrity and trustworthiness.
Those who seek official positions consider opportunistic gain to be valuable and despise upright conduct.
Those in office consider idleness to be lofty and scoff at diligence and conscientiousness.
Lǚ Yánjì said: "Idleness" (wàngkōng)
means not distinguishing right from wrong,
but merely signing names without thought.
Fù Xián frequently corrected both the virtuous and the corrupt.
The affairs of Sòng and Xián are both found in the records of Wǔ and Huì.
Zhì,
read zhí lì fān.
Those who relied on emptiness and detachment,
and those who followed others without their own convictions,
all gained widespread renown within the realm.
As for Wénwáng, who had no leisure to eat even at sunset,
and Zhòng Shānfǔ, who was diligent day and night,
they are now surely scorned and dismissed as dust!
Wénwáng, from morning till mid-afternoon,
had no time to eat,
devoting himself to harmonizing all the people.
Zhòng Shānfǔ was diligent day and night to serve one person.
Base desires rush along the path of greed;
selectors choose offices for people,
and officials choose benefits for themselves.
Lǚ Yánjì said: This means that selectors no longer choose the worthy for office,
and those in office only choose what benefits them.
Yù,
sound yú.
Wèi,
sound yú wěi fān.
They aggressively surpass and overstep,
without adhering to qualifications or sequence.
Everywhere in this chaotic world,
are ambitious and competitive individuals;
hundreds of officials are appointed,
yet there is no act of deferring to the worthy.
Zǐzhēn wrote "Chóngràng" (崇讓), but no one heeded it.
Liú Shí,
courtesy name Zǐzhēn;
the "Chóngràng Lùn" (崇讓論) is found in Volume 82, in the tenth year of Tàikāng of Emperor Wǔ.
Shěng,
read xī jǐng fān.
Liú Sòng,
courtesy name Zǐyǎ.
The system of nine ranks is found in the same place as above.
Acting on impulse,
some defied their parents-in-law,
some killed their concubines.
These two incidents were both initiated by Empress Jiǎ.
No one in the world condemned them.
Ritual, law, punishment, and government
were greatly damaged by this.
"When a state is about to perish,
its foundation must first collapse,"
is this not what is referred to?
The Zuǒzhuàn says: When a state is about to perish,
its foundation must first collapse,
and only then will its branches and leaves follow.
Therefore, observing Ruǎn Jí's conduct, one realizes the origins of the collapse of ritual education.
The incident is found in Volume 78, in the third year of Jǐngyuán of Emperor Yuán of Wèi.
Xíng,
read xià mèng fān.
The incidents are found in Volume 79, in the seventh and eighth years of Tàishǐ of Emperor Wǔ.
Considering Guō Qīn's strategy, one realizes the opportunity for the Róng and Dí.
The dispute over merit in the conquest of Wú and Guō Qīn's memorial are both found in Volume 81, in the first year of Tàikāng of Emperor Wǔ.
Fù Xuán and Liú Yì,
during the reign of Emperor Wǔ, served as Sīlì,
and repeatedly investigated and rectified,
not shying away from the nobility.
Through their words,
the corruption of all officials was exposed.
Fù Xián's memorial is found in Volume 82, in the fourth year of Yuánkāng of Emperor Huì;
the "Qiánshén Lùn" (錢神論) is found in Volume 83, in the ninth year of Yuánkāng.
Since things have come to this,
even if a ruler of mediocre talent and one who merely maintained existing order were to govern it,
Liú Liáng said: "Mediocre" (zhōngyōng)
refers to talent that is neither virtuous nor foolish;
"maintained existing order" (shǒuwén)
refers to a ruler who maintains normal, peaceful times.
Zhì,
read zhí zhī fān.
how much more so when our Emperor Huì rules with a profligate nature!
Emperor Huái ascended the throne amidst chaos,
restrained by powerful ministers;
after Emperor Mǐn was displaced and wandered,
he merely held an empty title.
The power of the empire was already lost,
and without a heroic talent destined for the age,
it cannot be recovered!
Shí Lè besieged Hán Jù, the Administrator of Lèpíng, at Diànchéng.
Hán Jù requested aid from Liú Kūn.
Liú Kūn had recently acquired the troops of Tuòbá Yīlú,
and intended to use their銳氣 (sharp morale) to attack Shí Lè.
Jī Dàn and Wèi Xióng advised,
"Although these are Jìn people,
they have long been subjugated in a foreign land,
and are not accustomed to your benevolence and trustworthiness,
so we fear they will be difficult to use.
It would be better to first gather the remaining grain of the Xiānbēi,
Tuòbá,
are Xiānbēi.
Hú,
refers to Liú and Shí.
Chāo,
read jìn jiāo fān.
devote ourselves to agriculture, and cease military operations.
Wait until they are transformed and moved by righteousness,
and then use them;
then no endeavor will fail."
Liú Kūn did not comply,
and dispatched all his troops,
ordering Jī Dàn to lead two myriad cavalry and infantry as the vanguard.
Liú Kūn encamped at Guǎngmù,
providing backup.
Guǎngmù County,
belonged to Shuòfāng Commandery in the Hàn dynasty;
at the end of Hàn, Shuòfāng was abolished,
and Guǎngmù County was established south of Xíng,
belonging to Xīnxīng Commandery,
not the old site of Guǎngmù County.
Shuài,
read as shuài.
Shí Lè (石勒) heard that Dàn (澹) was approaching,
and was about to go and attack him.
Someone said:
"Dàn's (澹) soldiers and horses are elite and strong,
their momentum cannot be resisted.
It would be better to withdraw our troops for now and avoid them,
digging deep moats and building high ramparts to blunt their锐锋 (ruì fēng).
This will surely guarantee complete safety."
Lè (勒) said:
"Although Dàn's (澹) army is numerous,
they are exhausted from their long journey.
Their commands are not unified.
How can they be elite and strong!
Now that the enemy is almost upon us,
how can we abandon our position and leave!
Once a large army is moved,
how can it easily return midway!
If Dàn (澹) takes advantage of our retreat and presses on us,
we will not even have time to flee and disperse,
how can we then dig deep moats and build high ramparts!
This is the path to self-destruction."
He immediately beheaded the speaker.
He appointed Kǒng Cháng (孔萇) as the Front Generalissimo (qián fēng dū dù),
and commanded the three armies:
"Those who are slow to advance will be executed!"
Lè (勒) occupied a strategic stronghold,
set up deceptive troops on the mountain,
placed two ambushes in front,
sent out light cavalry to engage Dàn (澹) in battle,
feigning defeat and retreating.
Dàn (澹) unleashed his troops to pursue them,
and entered the ambush.
Lè (勒) attacked Dàn's (澹) army from both front and rear,

"The Crown Prince is about to rebel,
and has already donned armor!"
Cōng 聰 was greatly alarmed and said:
"How could this be true!"
Wáng Shěn 王沈 and others all said:
"Your subjects have heard this for a long time,
and have repeatedly spoken of it,
but Your Majesty did not believe it."
Cōng 聰 ordered Càn 粲 to surround the Eastern Palace with troops.
Càn 粲 ordered Zhǔn 準 and Shěn 沈 to arrest over ten Dī 氐 and Qiāng 羌 chieftains,
and interrogated them thoroughly.
Yì 義 was the Grand Chányú 大單于,
and the Dī 氐 and Qiāng 羌 chieftains were subservient to him,
hence they all served the Eastern Palace.
Qiú 酋,
pronounced as Cí Yóu 慈由.
Zhǎng 長,
pronounced as Zhī Liǎng 知兩.
Gé 格,
made of wood.
The "Niú Rén 牛人" chapter in the Rites of Zhōu 周禮 states: For sacrifices,
they supply the wooden racks for the sacrificial oxen.
Zhèng Xuán 鄭玄 said: Hù 互 are
like the racks butchers now use to hang meat.
Zuǒ Sī's 左思 "Wú Dū Fù 吳都賦" states: Sharp racks are set up all around.
Lǚ Xiàng 呂向 said: Gé 格
is a wooden frame for hanging nets.
The chieftains falsely confessed to plotting rebellion with Yì 義.
Cōng 聰 said to Shěn 沈 and others:
"From now on, I know your loyalty!
You must remember to speak everything you know,
and not resent that your past words were not heeded!"
Thereupon, he executed the officials and retainers of the Eastern Palace, and those close to Yì 義,
as well as dozens of high-ranking officials whom Zhǔn 準, Shěn 沈 and others had long hated and resented.
He buried alive over 15,000 soldiers.
Those buried alive were
the soldiers of the four guards of the Eastern Palace.
In the fourth month,
Yì 義 was deposed and made the King of Běibù 北部.
Běibù 北部
was the rear division of the Xiōngnú 匈奴,
residing in Xīnxīng 新興.
Yì's 義 appearance and spirit were outstanding and bright,
and he was lenient, benevolent, and had a great capacity,
so many soldiers' hearts were attached to him.
When Cōng 聰 heard of his death,
he wept bitterly,
saying:
"Only two of us brothers remain, and yet we cannot tolerate each other."
Among the sons of the Hàn ruler Yuān 淵,
only Cōng 聰 and Yì 義 were alive at this time.
A great number of Dī 氐 and Qiāng 羌 rebelled.
Jìn Zhǔn 靳準 was appointed General of Chariots and Cavalry (Chēqí Dàjiāngjūn 車騎大將軍),
and he quelled them.
7 In the fifth month,
on the day Rénwǔ 壬午,
there was a solar eclipse.
The "Kǎo Yì 考異" states: The "Dì Jì 帝紀" and "Tiānwén Zhì 天文志" both say
"In the fifth month, on the day Bǐngzǐ 丙子,
there was a solar eclipse."
According to the "Cháng Lì 長曆," the first day of this month was Rénwǔ 壬午,
and there was no Bǐngzǐ 丙子.
We now take the calendar as reference.
8 In the sixth month,
on the day Bǐngyín 丙寅,
Wēn Jiào 溫嶠 and others arrived in Jiànkāng 建康.
Wáng Dǎo 王導, Zhōu Yǐ 周顗, Yú Liàng 庾亮 and others all admired Jiào's 嶠 talent,
and competed to associate with him.
At this time,

Grand Commandant and Governor of Yùzhōu 豫州 Xún Zǔ 荀組, Inspector of Jìzhōu 冀州 Shào Xù 邵續, Inspector of Qīngzhōu 青州 Cáo Yì 曹嶷, Inspector of Níngzhōu 寧州 Wáng Xùn 王遜, and Commandant of Eastern Barbarians Cuī Bì 崔毖, among others, all submitted memorials urging the Jin Prince to ascend the throne.
The Prince did not permit it.
9 Earlier,
the refugees Zhāng Píng 張平 and Fán Yǎ 樊雅 each gathered several thousand people in Qiáo 譙,
becoming leaders of fortified villages.
When the Jin Prince became Prime Minister,
he sent the Acting Military Advisor Huán Xuān 桓宣 of Qiáoguó 譙國 to persuade Píng 平 and Yǎ 雅.
Píng 平 and Yǎ 雅 both offered to surrender.
When Zǔ Tì 祖逖, Inspector of Yùzhōu 豫州, went to garrison Lúzhōu 蘆洲,
he sent Military Advisor Yīn Yì 殷乂 to Píng 平 and Yǎ 雅.
Yì 乂 had a low opinion of Píng 平,
and looking at his house,
said:
"It can be made into a horse stable."
Seeing a large cauldron,
he said:
"It can be melted down to cast ironware."
Píng 平 said:
"This is an emperor's cauldron,
to be used only when the world is peaceful.
How can it be destroyed!"
Yì 乂 said:
"You can't even guarantee your own head,
yet you cherish a cauldron!"
Píng 平 was greatly enraged,
and beheaded Yì 乂 on the spot,
then marshaled his troops and held firm in defense.
Tì 逖 attacked him,
but could not take it for over a year.
He then enticed Píng's 平 subordinate general Xiè Fú 謝浮,
and had him kill Píng 平.
Tì 逖 then advanced and occupied Tàiqiū 太丘.
Tàiqiū County 太丘縣,
belonged to Pèijùn 沛郡 in the Later Hàn 後漢;
it was abolished in the Jìn 晉.
Xián 賢 said: The old city of Tàiqiū 太丘
is in the northwest of Yongchéng County 永城縣, Bózhōu 亳州 today.
They faced off against Tì 逖.
Tì 逖 attacked but could not conquer them,
so he requested troops from the General of the Central Army Wáng Hán 王含.
Huán Xuān 桓宣 was then Hán's 含 Military Advisor,
and Hán 含 sent Xuān 宣 with five hundred soldiers to assist Tì 逖.
Tì 逖 said to Xuān 宣:
"Your trustworthiness and integrity are already known there;
now, please persuade Yǎ 雅 for me again."
Xuān 宣 then rode a single horse with two attendants to Yǎ 雅 and said:
"Governor Zǔ 祖 is planning to pacify Liú 劉 and Shí 石,
and relies on you for support;
previously Yīn Yì 殷乂 was disrespectful,
but that was not the Governor's intention."
Yǎ 雅 immediately went to Tì 逖 and surrendered.
After Tì 逖 entered Qiáochéng 譙城,
Shí Lè 石勒 sent Shí Hǔ 石虎 to besiege Qiáo 譙.
Wáng Hán 王含 again sent Huán Xuān 桓宣 to relieve it,
and Hǔ 虎 withdrew.
Tì 逖 memorialized to appoint Xuān 宣 as Intendant of Qiáoguó 譙國.
On the day Jǐsì 己巳,
the Jin Prince transmitted a manifesto to all under Heaven,
stating that
"Shí Hǔ 石虎 dared to lead dogs and sheep,
cross the river and spread poison.
Now, I send Wáng Póu 王裒, Prince of Lángxié 琅邪, and others with nine armies,
thirty thousand elite soldiers,
by four routes, land and water,
directly to the bandit territory,
under the command of Zǔ Tì 祖逖."
Soon after, Póu 裒 was recalled to Jiànkāng 建康.
10 In autumn,
the seventh month,
there was a great drought.
There was a severe locust plague in Sīzhōu 司州, Jìzhōu 冀州, Bīngzhōu 幷州, Qīngzhōu 青州, and Yōngzhōu 雍州.
The Hé 河 and Fén 汾 rivers overflowed,
sweeping away over a thousand homes.
All were within Hàn territory.
Yōng 雍,
pronounced as Yū Yòng 于用.
11 The Hàn ruler Cōng 聰 established Jìn Wáng Càn 靳王粲 as Crown Prince,
who held the titles of Prime Minister and Grand Chányú 大單于,
and managed all court affairs as before.
A general amnesty was proclaimed.
12 Duàn Pǐdī 段匹磾 nominated Liú Kūn 劉琨 as Grand Commander,
and sent a summons to his elder brother, the Duke of Liáoxī 遼西, Jílù Juàn 疾陸眷, and his uncle, Shèfù Chén 涉復辰, and his younger brother, Mòbēi 末柸, among others, to assemble at Gù'ān 固安.
Gù'ān County 固安縣,
belonged to Zhuōjùn 涿郡 in the Hàn 漢;
the Wèi 魏 and Jìn 晉 changed Zhuōjùn 涿郡 to Fányáng 范陽,
and Gù'ān 固安 to Gù'ān 故安.
Liú Xù 劉昫 said: Yì County 易縣 of Yìzhōu 易州 in the Táng 唐,
was the ancient land of Gù'ān County 故安縣.
Mòbēi 末柸 persuaded Jílù Juàn 疾陸眷 and Shèfù Chén 涉復辰, saying:
"For fathers and elder brothers to follow their younger relatives is a disgrace;
moreover, even if we are fortunate enough to achieve success, Pǐdī 匹磾 alone will claim it,
what will become of us?"
They each led their troops back.
Kūn 琨 and Pǐdī 匹磾 could not remain alone,
so they also returned to Jì 薊.
13 Xún Zǔ 荀組 was appointed Minister of Works (Sītú 司徒).
14 In the eighth month,
Zhào Gù 趙固 of Hàn attacked General Wèi Huá Huì 衛華薈 at Línyǐng 臨潁,
and killed him.
Línyǐng County 臨潁縣,
belonged to Yǐngchuānjùn 潁川郡.
Huá 華,
pronounced as Hù Huà 戶化.
Huì 薈,
pronounced as Wū Wài 烏外.
At first,
Zhào Gù and his Chief Clerk, Zhōu Zhèn, had a grudge against each other.
Zhèn secretly slandered Gù to the Hàn ruler Cōng.
When Lǐ Jǔ defeated Liú Chàng,
he found Cōng's imperial edict in Chàng's tent.
It ordered that after Chàng had conquered Jǔ,
he should return via Luòyáng,
arrest Gù and execute him,
replacing Gù with Zhèn.
Jǔ sent the edict to Gù to show him.
Gù executed Zhèn and his son,
and led a thousand cavalry to surrender.
Jǔ then ordered Gù to guard Luòyáng.
Zhèng Pān and others together resisted Wáng Yì,
but their forces were not united,
and they scattered back to Héngsāngkǒu.
The Shuǐ Jīng says: "The Miǎn River flows southeast past Yúndù County in Jiāngxià,
then east past Zuǒsāng,
which is where King Zhāo of Zhōu drowned."
Village elders say: "The common people assisted King Zhāo's funeral rites here,
hence it was called Zuǒsāng (佐喪);
Zuǒsāng (左桑)
is a misspelling."
Further east,
it is called Héngsāng,
meaning the place where King Zhāo's body was found.
Wáng Dūn dispatched the Administrator of Wǔchāng, Zhào Yòu, and the Administrator of Xiāngyáng, Zhū Guǐ, to attack them.
Pān and the others were afraid
and requested to surrender.
Dù Zēng also requested to attack Dìwǔ Yī in Xiāngyáng to redeem himself.
Yì was about to proceed to Jīngzhōu,
leaving his Chief Clerk Liú Jùn to garrison the Yángkǒulěi fortress.
The Shuǐ Jīng Zhù says: "The Lóngpí water flows past Yǐngchéng,
then northeast,
where it is called Yángshuǐ.
North of the water, it passes west of Jìnglín County,
then flows north into the Miǎn River,
where it is called Yángkǒu,
which is the middle Jiàngkǒu."
"Zēng
is a treacherous bandit;
he feigns submission
to lure the government forces west,
then will make a forced march to raid Yángkǒu.
It is advisable to make ample preparations
(meaning, one should make extensive deployments
to guard against Zēng's surprise attack).
Fēn (分) is pronounced Fúwèn."
Yì was arrogant and self-willed by nature,
deeming Sī to be old and cowardly,
so he proceeded west.
Zēng and his men indeed turned back and rushed towards Yángkǒu.
Yì then sent Sī back.
No sooner had he reached the fortress
than he was besieged by Zēng.
Liú Jùn defended the north gate himself,
and made Sī guard the south gate.
Mǎ Jùn came with Zēng to attack the fortress.
Jùn's wife and children were already inside the fortress.
Mǎ Jùn had originally joined Zhèng Pān in resisting Wáng Yì.
Pímian (皮面) means to peel off the facial skin.
"Killing his wife and children
will not lift the siege,
but only increase his rage."
So he stopped.
Zēng captured the north gate.
Sī was wounded
and retreated into a boat.
He opened the bottom of the boat to escape,
sinking and moving fifty paces,
and thus managed to get away.
Zēng sent someone to persuade Sī, saying:
"Mǎ Jùn is grateful to you for saving his wife and children.
Now, I have entrusted all hundred members of your household, inside and out, to Jùn.
Jùn has done his utmost to look after them.
You can come back now."
Sī replied:
"I am over sixty years old,
and can no longer be a bandit with you.
Even if I die, I will go south.
My wife and children are yours to decide."
He then went to Wáng Yì at Zèngshān,
where he died of his wounds.
Zèngshān is within Jìnglín's borders.
During the Suí dynasty, Zèngshān County was established,
belonging to Miǎnyáng Commandery.
Chuāng (創) is pronounced Chūliáng.
On the day Wùyín,
Zhào Yòu, Zhū Guǐ, and General of Língjiāng, Huáng Jùn, fought Zēng at Nǚguānhú.
The Shuǐ Jīng Zhù says: "The Zuòxī water originates north of Jiānglíng County,
flows east into Chuánguānhú,
the lake water then flows northeast into Nǚguānhú,
and the lake water then flows east into Yángshuǐ."
Zēng, riding on his victory, advanced directly to Miǎnkǒu,
his prestige shaking Jiāng and Miǎn.
The King sent Zhōu Fǎng, the Administrator of Yùzhāng, to attack him.
Fǎng had eight thousand troops
and advanced to Dùnyáng.
Shěn Yuè says: "Dùnyáng County
was established east of the river,
belonging to Jiāngxià Commandery."
The Shuǐ Jīng says: "The Miǎn River flows north of Dùnyáng County,
then east past the north of the old city of Línzhàng."
Dùnyáng means "south of the Dùn River."
Shěn (沈) is pronounced Chílíng.
Fǎng made General Lǐ Héng oversee the left division
and Xǔ Cháo oversee the right division;
Fǎng himself commanded the central army.
Zēng first attacked the left and right divisions.
Fǎng shot pheasants behind the lines to reassure his troops.
He ordered his troops:
"If one division is defeated,
beat the drum three times.
If both divisions are defeated,
beat the drum six times."
Zhào Yòu's son Yìn,
leading his father's remaining troops attached to the left division,
fought fiercely,
was defeated but reassembled,
and galloped to inform Fǎng.
Fǎng was angry
and roared at him to advance again.
Yìn cried out and returned to battle.
From dawn until shēn (3-5 PM),
both divisions were defeated.
Fǎng selected eight hundred elite soldiers,
personally poured wine for them,
and ordered them not to move rashly,
but to advance only upon hearing the drum.
Before Zēng's troops were thirty paces away,
Fǎng personally beat the drum.
The officers and soldiers all leapt up and rushed forward.
Zēng was then routed,
with over a thousand killed.
Fǎng pursued them at night.
His generals requested to wait until tomorrow,
but Fǎng said:
"Zēng is brave and skilled in battle.
Just now, they were tired and we were fresh,
which is why we defeated them.
We should seize the opportunity while they are weak;
then we can destroy them."
So he advanced with drums beating,
and thus pacified Hàn and Miǎn.
Zēng fled to secure Wǔdāng.
Wǔdāng County belonged to Nányáng Commandery during the Hàn,
to Shùnyáng Commandery during the Jìn.
The county was named after Wǔdāng Mountain.
During the Táng, it was Wǔdāng Commandery of Jūnzōu.
Dù Yòu says: "The commandery city
was built by Yán Cén."
Fǎng was promoted to Inspector of Liángzhōu for his achievements,
and garrisoned Xiāngyáng.
Due to Hú Zǐxù's defeat,
Liángzhōu had fallen,
hence Fǎng was appointed to govern Liángzhōu but stationed in Xiāngyáng.
In winter,
in the tenth month,
on the day Dīngwèi,
Wáng Póu, the King of Lángxié, passed away.
In the eleventh month,
on the first day Jǐyǒu,
there was a solar eclipse.
The Kǎo Yì states: "Both the Dì Jì and Tiānwén Zhì say
'solar eclipse on the day Bǐngzǐ in the eleventh month.'"
According to the Cháng Lì,
both the tenth and twelfth months began on Jǐmǎo.
This month began on Jǐyǒu,
and the twenty-eighth day was Bǐngzǐ.
In the Jìn Shū Yuándì Jì,
the eleventh month has Jiǎzǐ and Dīngmǎo.
If Bǐngzǐ were the first day of the month,
then Jiǎzǐ and Dīngmǎo would fall in the tenth month.
Also, in Liú Kūn Jí,
the third month of this year began on Guǐwèi,
and the eighth month on Gēngchén,
both consistent with the Cháng Lì,
which we now take as our basis.
On the day Dīngmǎo,
Liú Kūn was appointed as Shìzhōng and Tàiwèi.
19 Dài Miǎo (戴邈), the Commander of the Southern Expeditionary Army, submitted a memorial,
stating:
"Since the chaos and calamities began,
schools have fallen into disuse.
Some commentators say that in times of peace, culture is valued,
while in times of turmoil, martial prowess is valued.
This statement seems plausible,
but it is not true.
Indeed, the Way of the Ru (儒) is profound and abstruse,
and cannot be mastered hastily;
if one waits until the world is peaceful and stable
to cultivate it,
then it will have already been neglected for too long.
Moreover,
the sons of the nobility
may not necessarily possess the talent to capture generals and seize banners.
To employ them in military campaigns and garrisons
instead of letting them study ethics and principles in their prime,
is truly a great pity.
The world's Way has long been lost,
and customs and rituals are daily deteriorating,
like fire consuming oil,
yet no one realizes it.
Now that the royal enterprise has just begun,
and all things are in their nascent stage,
the Éryǎ (爾雅) says: 'Quányú (權輿) means
beginning.'
Let us therefore promote moral transformation."
The King followed his advice
and for the first time established the Tàixué (太學).
20 Hàn (漢) Lord Cōng (聰) went out hunting,
and made Emperor Mǐn (愍) act as Chēqí Jiāngjūn (車騎將軍),
dressed in military attire, holding a halberd and leading the way.
Those who saw him pointed and said:
"This is the former Son of Heaven from Cháng'ān (長安)."
People gathered to watch him,
and some old folks wept.
Crown Prince Càn (粲) said to Cōng:
"Did King Wǔ (武) of Zhōu (周) really enjoy killing Zhòu (紂)?
He simply feared that those with similar evil intentions would conspire,
causing trouble.
Now, all those who raise armies and gather crowds
do so in the name of your son Yè (業) [referring to Emperor Mǐn];
it would be better to eliminate him early!"
Cōng replied:
"I previously killed Yǔ Mín (庾珉) and his ilk;
[The incident of killing Yǔ Mín (庾珉) is found in Volume 88, Jiànxīng (建興) First Year.]
I cannot bear to kill again,
let's observe for a little while."
In the twelfth month,
Cōng hosted a banquet for his ministers in the Guāngjí Diàn (光極殿),
and made Emperor Mǐn (愍) serve wine and wash cups;
afterwards, he changed clothes,
and again made him hold the parasol.
Many Jìn (晉) officials shed tears,
some even cried out loud.
Shàngshū Láng (尚書郎) Xīn Bīn (辛賓) from Lǒngxī (隴西) rose,
embraced the Emperor and wailed loudly.
Cōng ordered him to be led out
and executed.
Making him hold a halberd and lead the way,
making him serve wine and wash cups,
making him hold the parasol,
the extent of his humiliation
had reached its peak!
The cunning plan of the Róngdí (戎狄) [Barbarians]
was precisely to observe the hearts of the old Jìn (晉) officials and the surviving populace through this.
[Gēng (更), pronounced Gōnghéng (工衡) fan.]
Zhào Gù (趙固) and the Prefect of Hénèi (河內), Guō Mò (郭默), invaded Hàn (漢)'s Hédōng (河東),
reaching Jiàng (絳).
[Jiàng (絳) County
was formerly the capital of Jìn (晉);
under Hàn (漢) it belonged to Hédōng (河東) Commandery,
under Jìn (晉) it belonged to Píngyáng (平陽) Commandery.
Liú Xù (劉昫) says: Táng (唐)'s Jiàngzhōu Qǔwò (絳州曲沃) County
was the territory of Hàn (漢)'s Jiàng (絳) County.]
Cōng (聰) divided the Sīlì (司隸) into left and right.
They killed over ten thousand people,
then Gù (固) and Mò (默) withdrew.
Crown Prince Càn (粲) led General Liú Yǎshēng (劉雅生) and others with 100,000 infantry and cavalry to encamp at Xiǎopíngjīn (小平津).
Gù (固) publicly declared:
"We must capture Liú Càn (劉粲) alive to ransom the Son of Heaven."
Càn (粲) memorialized Cōng (聰) saying:
"If your son Yè (業) [Emperor Mǐn] dies,
the people will have no hope,
and thus will not be used by Lǐ Jǔ (李矩) and Zhào Gù (趙固),
they will collapse without being attacked."
On the day Wùxū (戊戌),
Emperor Mǐn (愍) was killed in Píngyáng (平陽).
He was eighteen years old.
Gù (固) fled to Yángchéng Shān (陽城山).
[Hénán (河南)'s Yángchéng (陽城) County
has Yángchéng Shān (陽城山).]
21 That year,
the King ordered the supervision of agricultural work,
and officials of the rank of Èrqiānshí (二千石) and chief magistrates were judged on the amount of grain they collected,
while the various armies cultivated their own fields,
and used the produce as their provisions.
22 The Dī (氐) King Yáng Màosōu (楊茂搜) died.
His eldest son Nándí (難敵) succeeded him,
and divided the tribal forces with his younger son Jiāntóu (堅頭);
Nándí (難敵) was styled Zuǒxián Wáng (左賢王) and
garrisoned Xiàbiàn (下辨),
while Jiāntóu (堅頭) was styled Yòuxián Wáng (右賢王) and
garrisoned Héchí (河池).
[The two counties of Xiàbiàn (下辨) and Héchí (河池)
both belonged to Wǔdū (武都) Commandery.
Shīgǔ (師古) says: Biàn (辨),
pronounced Píxiàn (皮莧) fan.
Liú Xù (劉昫) says: Biàn (辨),
pronounced Bùxiàn (步莧) fan.
Xiàbiàn (下辨)
was Táng (唐)'s Chéngzhōu Tónggǔ (成州同谷) County.
Héchí (河池)
was Táng (唐)'s Wǔzhōu Pándī (武州盤隄) County.]
23 Hénán Wáng (河南王) Tǔyùhún (吐谷渾) died.
Tǔyùhún (吐谷渾)
was Mùróng Guī (慕容廆)'s illegitimate elder brother.
Their father, Shèguī (涉歸),
had separated 1,700 households to be under Tǔyùhún (吐谷渾).
When Guī (廆) succeeded to the throne,
horses from the two divisions fought.
Guī (廆) sent an envoy to rebuke Tǔyùhún (吐谷渾) saying:
"Our late father established us separately,
why are we not keeping our distance?"
[Yuǎnyì (遠異) means to go far away to be separate.]
Tǔyùhún (吐谷渾) angrily replied:
"Horses are among the six domestic animals;
[The six animals: horse, ox, sheep, dog, pig, chicken.
Xù (畜), pronounced Xǔyòu (許又) fan.]
How can this anger extend to people!
It is very easy to separate far away,
but I fear meeting again later will be difficult!
I shall now depart to a place ten thousand *lǐ* (里) away from you."
Thereupon, he led his followers west.
Guī (廆) regretted it
and sent his Chángshǐ (長史) Yǐnàlóu Féng (乙郍婁馮) to pursue him and apologize.
[Nà (郍) is the same as nà (那).
Yǐnàlóu (乙郍婁) is a three-character barbarian surname.] [He said:]
"Our late father once quoted a divination saying,
'My two sons shall both become strong and prosperous,
and their fortune will flow to later generations.'
I am
an illegitimate son;
it is unreasonable for both of us to be equally great.
Now, parting due to horses,
perhaps it is the will of Heaven!"
So he did not return,
but moved west and settled against the Yīnshān (陰山).
During the chaos of Yǒngjiā (永嘉),
he then crossed the Lǒng (隴) Mountains to the west,
occupied the west of the Táoshuǐ (洮水),
extending to Báilán (白蘭),
a territory of several thousand *lǐ* (里) in area.
[Shāzhōu Jì (沙州記) says: The Táoshuǐ (洮水) originates from Jiǎngtái (嵹臺) Mountain,
flows northeast,
passes through the midst of Tǔyùhún (吐谷渾),
then flows northeast into the pass.
This Táoxī (洮西) [west of Tao]
is west of the Táoshuǐ (洮水) outside the pass,
which is the land of Shāqiángtà (沙漒沓).
Báilán (白蘭)
is a mountain name,
where the Qiāng (羌) resided;
by the Táng (唐) dynasty,
the Dīnglíng Qiāng (丁零羌) dwelled there,
to its left belonged to the Dǎngxiàng (党項),
to its right it bordered Duōmí (多彌).
Dù Yòu (杜佑) says: Báilán (白蘭)
is a separate branch of the Qiāng (羌),
bordering Tǔyùhún (吐谷渾) to the northeast,
extending to Chìlìmótú (叱利模徒) in the west,
and bordering Jùn'è (郡鄂) to the south;
its customs and products are the same as Dàngchāng (宕昌).]
Guī (廆) remembered him fondly
and composed the "Āgān zhī Gē" (阿干之歌) for him.
Tǔyùhún (吐谷渾) had sixty sons;
his eldest son Tǔyán (吐延) succeeded him.
Tǔyán (吐延) grew up to be brave and strong,
and both the Qiāng (羌) and Hú (胡) feared him.
[The affairs of Tǔyùhún (吐谷渾) begin here.]
The first year of Dàxīng (大興)
(Wùyín (戊寅), 318 CE)
The reign era was changed in the third month of this year.
1 In spring,
the first month,
Liáoxī Gōng Jí Lùjuàn died of illness.
As his son was young,
his uncle Shèfù Chén established himself.
Duàn Pǐdī went from Jì to attend the funeral.
Duàn Mòbēi declared,
"Pǐdī's arrival
is to usurp the position."
When Pǐdī reached Yòuběipíng,
Liú Xù said: Táng's Jìzhōu Yúyáng County,
was the ancient seat of Yòuběipíng Commandery.
Dī,
read as dīngxī.
Mòbēi took advantage of the vulnerability to attack Shèfù Chén,
killed him,
and also his sons, younger brothers, and partisans,
proclaiming himself Chányú.
He engaged Pǐdī in battle,
defeated him,
and Pǐdī fled back to Jì.
2 In the third month,
on Guǐchǒu,
the news of Mǐndì's death reached Jiànkāng.
The King wore mourning clothes and lived in a hut.
The officials requested him to accept the imperial title,
but the King refused.
Jì Zhān said,
"The line of the Jìn has been broken
for two years now.
Your Majesty should succeed to the great enterprise.
Looking around at the imperial clan,
who else is there to yield to?
If you promptly ascend the great throne,
then gods and people will have something to rely on.
If you act against the heavenly timing
and violate human affairs,
the great momentum, once lost,
cannot be recovered.
Now both capitals are burned and ravaged,
the ancestral temples are without a master.
Liú Cōng usurps the title in the northwest,
while Your Majesty humbly declines in the southeast.
This is like bowing and yielding while trying to put out a fire."
The King still refused.
He ordered the Palace General Hán Jì to remove the imperial seat.
Palace General,
belonging to the two guards,
established in the early Jìn,
during court assemblies and banquets,
they wore military attire and stood directly to the left and right;
at night, when opening the city gates,
they held the White Tiger Banner to supervise.
Zuò,
read as cúwò;
the same applies to Dìzuò below.
"The Emperor's seat corresponds to the constellations."
According to the Astronomical Treatise,
the Emperor's seat is in the Purple Palace.
The King changed his countenance because of this.
Zhōu Sōng, a奉朝請 (Fèng Cháoqǐng), submitted a memorial, saying,
When the King was Prime Minister,
he made Sōng a參軍 (Cānjūn).
When he became King of Jìn,
he appointed him Fèng Cháoqǐng.
The Jìn Records say: A Fèng Cháoqǐng
is merely to attend court assemblies and await summons.
"Ancient kings
only took the throne after righteousness was complete,
and only obtained it after humility was fulfilled.
This is why their reigns lasted long
and their glory shone for ten thousand years.
Now the imperial coffin has not yet returned,
the old capital has not yet been cleared.
Righteous men weep blood,
and common folk are anxious.
It is fitting to open channels for good counsel,
train soldiers, and sharpen weapons.
First avenge the great shame of the altars of soil and grain;
fulfill the hopes of the four seas;
then where else could the divine artifacts go?"
Because of this, he displeased the emperor,
and was sent out as the Administrator of Xīn'ān.
Sūn Quán divided Dānyáng to establish Xīndū Commandery,
which Emperor Wǔ changed to Xīn'ān Commandery in the first year of Tàikāng.
Liú Xù said: Xīn'ān Commandery
was Táng's Shèzhōu.
Wǔ,
read as wǔgù.
Sōng
was Yǐ's younger brother.
On Bǐngchén,
the King ascended the imperial throne.
All officials were arranged in attendance.
The Emperor ordered Wáng Dǎo to ascend the imperial bed and sit with him.
Dǎo firmly declined, saying,
"If the sun were to descend and be the same as all things,
how could the common people look up to its light?"
The Emperor then stopped.
A general amnesty was declared,
the reign title was changed,
and all civil and military officials were promoted two ranks.
The Emperor wanted to grant an additional rank to all officials who had submitted name slips to urge his ascension,
and all commoners who had submitted name slips were to be appointed officials,
totaling over two hundred thousand people.
Máo Huàng said: Writing one's name on a memorial or report is called a cì.
"Your Majesty, responding to Heaven, has succeeded to the line,
and all within the realm have pledged allegiance.
How can it be that the feelings of those nearby are strong,
while the feelings of those far away are light?
It would be better to follow the Han method and universally bestow titles upon all under Heaven,
making the benevolence widespread.
Since Emperor Huì succeeded to the throne in Han,
he granted commoners one rank of nobility;
those with official positions or salaries were differentiated by the number of years.
Later, when various emperors first ascended,
they generally granted commoners one rank of nobility.
This would block the source of cunning and deceit."
The Emperor did not follow this.
On Gēngwǔ,
Wáng Tàizǐ Sháo was established as the Crown Prince.
The Crown Prince was benevolent and filial,
loved literature,
was skilled in martial arts,
esteemed worthy men and treated scholars with courtesy,
and accepted admonitions.
He had a commoner's friendship with Yǔ Liàng, Wēn Qiáo, and others.
Yǔ Liàng's character was lofty and upright,
and he was skilled in discussing Lǎozi and Zhuāngzi.
The Emperor highly regarded him
and sought to marry Liàng's sister to the Crown Prince.
The Emperor appointed Hè Xún as acting Grand Tutor of the Crown Prince,
Zhōu Yǐ as Junior Tutor,
and Yǔ Liàng as a Palace Secretariat Attendant serving as lecturer in the Eastern Palace.
The Emperor favored the School of Names and Laws
and bestowed Hán Fēi's book upon the Crown Prince.
Yǔ Liàng remonstrated, saying,
"Shēn and Hán are harsh and harmful to civilization,
and are not worth retaining in Your Sacred Mind."
The Crown Prince accepted this.
3 The Emperor again sent an envoy to confer upon Mùróng Huì the titles of Dragon-soaring General, Grand Chányú, and Duke of Chānglí.
Huì declined the ducal title.
Huì declined the ducal title,
outwardly showing humility,
but his ambition was not content with merely Chānglí.
Fù,
read as fúyòu.
Shǐ,
read as shūlì.
Xiáng,
read as sījiāng.
He appointed Liú Xiáng as his Chief Clerk,
and ordered Suì to establish the court rituals and regulations for the administration.
Péi Ní said to Huì,
"The Jìn dynasty is in decline,
isolated beyond the Jiāng.
Jiè,
means alone.
Ní,
read as yúlì.
The chaos in the Central Plains
cannot be remedied by anyone other than you, Illustrious Duke.
Zhěng,
means to rescue.
However, they are all ignorant and foolish gatherings.
You should gradually annex them
to serve as resources for a western campaign."
Western campaign
refers to advancing troops from Liáodōng,
entering the Central Plains to the west.
"Your words are grand,
beyond my reach.
However, you are a man of fame and virtue from the Central Court,
and you do not consider my humble and rustic nature in teaching and instructing me.
This means Heaven has bestowed you upon me to bless my state."
He then appointed Ní as Chief Clerk,
entrusting him with military and state strategies.
The weaker and smaller tribes,
he gradually attacked and seized.
4 Lǐ Jǔ (李矩) sent Guō Mò (郭默) and Guō Sòng (郭誦) to rescue Zhào Gù (趙固).
They encamped at Luòruì (洛汭).
The Shuǐ Jīng (水經) says: The Luò (洛) River flows northeast past the east of Gǒng (鞏) County,
then north into the Hé (河) River.
The five sons of Xi (傒) made Tài Kāng (太康) encamp at Luòruì (洛汭) in the summer,
which is that same place.
According to the biography of Lǐ Jǔ (李矩),
at that time Càn (粲) was encamped on the north bank of Mèngjīn (孟津).
He reported this to Prince Càn (粲),
requesting preparations be made.
Càn (粲) said:
“They heard of Zhào Gù’s (趙固) defeat,
and can barely protect themselves,
how dare they come here!
Do not alarm the officers and soldiers!”
Soon after, Zhì (稚) and the others arrived suddenly,
attacking from ten directions.
Càn’s (粲) forces were startled and collapsed,
more than half were killed or wounded.
Càn (粲) fled to protect Yángxiāng (陽鄉).
Yángxiāng (陽鄉)
was probably the land of Yángfán (陽樊) during the Spring and Autumn period,
located within the borders of Xiūwǔ (脩武) County in Jí (汲) Commandery.
They captured countless
weapons and military supplies.
At dawn,
Càn (粲) saw that Zhì (稚) and the others had few soldiers,
and together with Liú Yǎshēng (劉雅生), he gathered the remaining troops and attacked them.
The Hàn (漢) lord Cōng (聰) sent Grand Commandant Fàn Lóng (范隆) to lead cavalry to assist him.
They were in a standoff with Zhì (稚) and the others,
fighting bitterly for over twenty days,
but could not overcome them.
Lǐ Jǔ (李矩) advanced his troops to rescue them,
but the Hàn (漢) army held their ground along the river,
preventing Lǐ Jǔ’s (李矩) troops from crossing.
Zhì (稚) and the others slaughtered the cattle and horses they had captured,
burned their military supplies,
broke through the encirclement, and fled to Hǔláo (虎牢).
Chénggāo (成皋) County in Hénán (河南)
was the Hǔláo (虎牢) of Zhèng (鄭).
The Mù Tiānzǐ Zhuàn (穆天子傳) states: The elite soldiers of the seven contingents
captured a tiger alive,
and presented it to the Son of Heaven.
The Son of Heaven kept it in Dōng Guó (東虢),
and it was called Hǔláo (虎牢).
Later, when Liú Yù (劉裕) recovered the Central Plains,
he established four garrisons in Hénán (河南),
and Hǔláo (虎牢) was one of them.
The three commanderies
were Hénán (河南), Xíngyáng (滎陽), and Hóngnóng (弘農).
5 At the Hàn (漢) Zhōngsī Zébǎi Táng (螽斯則百堂), there was a disaster.
The Zhōngsī Zébǎi Táng (螽斯則百堂)
takes its meaning from the idea of grasshoppers (zhōngsī) having numerous descendants (zǐsūn zhòngduō),
and the aspiration of "thinking of Qi (齊) will bring a hundred sons" (Sī Qí Zébǎi Sī Nán zhī Yì 斯齊則百斯男之義).

6 Cōng (聰) appointed his son, Jìnán (濟南) Prince Jì (驥), as Grand General (Dà Jiāngjūn 大將軍), Supervisor of All Military Affairs Inside and Outside the Court (Dūdū Zhōngwài Zhūjūnsì 都督中外諸軍事), and Director of the Department of State Affairs (Lù Shàngshū 錄尚書),
and Qí (齊) Prince Mài (勱) as Grand Minister of Works (Dà Sītú 大司徒).
7 Jiāo Sōng (焦嵩) and Chén Ān (陳安) raised an army and pressured Shàngguī (上邽).
Prime Minister Bǎo (保) sent an envoy to report the emergency to Zhāng Shí (張寔).
Shí (寔) sent Dòu Táo (竇濤), the Administrator of Jīnchéng (金城), to lead twenty thousand infantry and cavalry to respond.
When the army reached Xīnyáng (新陽),
the Jìn Zhì (晉志) states
that Xīnyáng (新陽) County belonged to Tiānshuǐ (天水) Commandery.
Hé Chéngtiān (何承天) said: Wèi (魏) established it.
The Shuǐ Jīng Zhù (水經註) says: The Wèi (渭) River passes through Jì (冀) County,
then exits Cén Xiá (岑峽) to the east,
and enters Xīnyáng (新陽) Valley.
Xīnyáng (新陽) County was probably established here.
Bǎo (保) plotted to claim the imperial title.
Pòqiāng (破羌) Commandant Zhāng Shēn (張詵) said to Shí (寔):
“The Prince of Nányáng (南陽) is a distant relative of the state,
who forgets his great shame and urgently desires to exalt himself.
His lord and father both died at the hands of the bandits;
this is Bǎo’s (保) great shame.
The Jìn (晉) Emperor is a close relative
and moreover possesses renowned virtue.
He should lead the world to serve him.”
Bǎo (保)
was the great-great-grandson of Emperor Xuān (宣),
hence called a distant relative;
the Emperor
was the great-grandson of Emperor Xuān (宣),
hence called a close relative.
The character “帥”
is read as “率” (shuài).
He sent Yámén (牙門) Cài Zhōng (蔡忠) to present a memorial at Jiànkāng (建康).
By the time he arrived,
the Emperor had already ascended the throne.
Shí (寔) did not use the era name of Jiāngdōng (江東),
still calling it Jiànxīng (建興).
The Zhāng (張) clan in Héxī (河西) used the Jiànxīng (建興) era name
for nine generations and forty-nine years,
until the fifth year of Xiàozōng’s (孝宗) Shēngpíng (升平) era,
when Zhāng Tiānxī (張天錫) then adopted the Shēngpíng (升平) era name.
8 Summer,
Fourth month.
On the Dīngchǒu (丁丑) day, the first day of the month,
there was a solar eclipse.
9 Wáng Dùn (王敦) was appointed Governor of Jiāngzhōu (江州),
Wáng Dǎo (王導) was appointed Grand General of Agile Cavalry (Piàojì Dàjiāngjūn 驃騎大將軍) and granted the privilege of establishing an open-door office (Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī 開府儀同三司).
Dǎo (導) dispatched eight departmental officials (bù cóngshì 部從事) to inspect the commanderies and states of Yángzhōu (揚州).
Yángzhōu (揚州) at that time governed eight commanderies: Dānyáng (丹陽), Kuàijī (會稽), Wú (吳), Wúxìng (吳興), Xuānchéng (宣城), Dōngyáng (東陽), Línhǎi (臨海), and Xīn’ān (新安).
Therefore, eight departmental officials (bù cóngshì 部從事) were dispatched separately.
The character “行”
is read as “xià mèng fān” (下孟翻).
They all appeared simultaneously.
Each official reported the merits and demerits of the officials holding salaries of two thousand bushels (èr qiān shí 二千石),
but only Gù Hé (顧和) remained silent.
Dǎo (導) asked him about it,
and Hé (和) said:
“Your Excellency (mínggōng 明公) acts as chief minister.
Would you rather let the net be so loose that a fish that can swallow a boat escapes,
The Hàn Shū (漢書), treatise on criminal law, says: At the beginning of the Hàn (漢) dynasty,
although there were three simple laws,
the net was so loose that a fish that could swallow a boat escaped.
Shī Gǔ (師古) noted: It means lax;
swallowing a boat
refers to a big fish.
or govern with excessive scrutiny?”
Dǎo (導) sighed in admiration and praised him.
Hé (和)
was a kinsman (zúzǐ 族子) of Róng (榮).
10 The Chéng (成) Prime Minister Fàn Chángshēng (范長生) died.
The Chéng (成) lord Xióng (雄) appointed Chángshēng’s (長生) son, Attendant Official (Shìzhōng 侍中) Bēn (賁), as Prime Minister.
Chángshēng (長生) was widely learned
and skilled in many arts.
He was nearly a hundred years old,
and the people of Shǔ (蜀) revered him like a god.
11 The Hàn (漢) Central Regular Attendant (Zhōng Chángshì 中常侍) Wáng Shěn (王沈) had an adopted daughter of great beauty.
The Hàn (漢) lord Cōng (聰) established her as Left Empress (Zuǒ Huánghòu 左皇后).

Minister of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Lìng 尚書令) Wáng Jiàn (王鑒), Supervisor of the Central Secretariat (Zhōngshū Jiān 中書監) Cuī Yìzhī (崔懿之), and Director of the Central Secretariat (Zhōngshū Lìng 中書令) Cáo Xún (曹恂) admonished him, saying:
“We have heard that when a king establishes an empress,
she should be compared in virtue to Heaven and Earth.
Qián (乾)
represents the way of the father,
to which the ruler’s virtue is compared;
Kūn (坤)
represents the way of the mother,
to which the empress’s virtue is compared.
When she passes away, she will be matched with the Queen of Earth (Hòutǔ 后土).
One must choose from families of established virtue and distinguished lineage,
who are quiet and virtuous.
The Shī (詩) Guānju (關雎) says: 'Yǎotiǎo shūnǚ (窈窕淑女).'
Máo (毛) annotation says: Yǎotiǎo (窈窕)
means quiet and serene;
shú (淑)
means good.
Lìng (令)
also means good.
This aligns with the will of the gods.
Emperor Xiàochéng (孝成) made Zhào Fēiyàn (趙飛燕) empress,

and the ruin of the altars of soil and grain;
this is a past lesson.
The event is recorded in Volume 32, the first year of Hàn (漢) Emperor Āi’s (哀) Jiànpíng (建平) era.
This is the fourth year of Mǐn (愍) Emperor’s Jiànxīng (建興) era,
and the first year of Hàn (漢) Língjiā (麟嘉) era.
She was not chosen for her virtue.
Even if she were Shěn’s (沈) younger sister or daughter,

All the concubines in the six palaces
