How can a slave suddenly be made their mistress!
We fear this is not a blessing for the state.”
Cōng (聰) was greatly enraged and
ordered Central Regular Attendant (Zhōng Chángshì 中常侍) Xuān Huái (宣懷) to tell Prince Càn (粲):
“Jiàn (鑒) and the others are mere youths,
uttering wild and insolent words,
utterly lacking the etiquette between sovereign and subject, superior and inferior.
Quickly investigate and verify this!”
Thereupon, Jiàn (鑒) and the others were arrested and sent to the marketplace,
where they were all beheaded.
The Grand Master of Gold and Purple with Glorious Happiness (Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū 金紫光祿大夫) Wáng Yánchí (王延馳) intended to enter and admonish him,
but the gatekeepers would not allow him entry.
When Jiàn and others were about to be executed,
Wáng Shěn struck them with a staff and said:
"You lowly slaves,
can you still commit evil?
How is your father involved in your affairs!"
Jiàn glared and shouted at him:
"You punk!
The one who destroyed the great Hàn
is precisely you rat-like scoundrels, and the beheading of Zhǔn!
I will surely accuse you before the former emperor,
and seek you out underground to punish you."
Zhǔn said to Jiàn:
"I received an imperial edict to arrest you.
What evil have I done
that you say Hàn was destroyed because of me?"
Jiàn said:
"You killed the Imperial Younger Brother,
causing the emperor to gain a reputation for unfriendliness.
The state nurtured you scoundrels,
how could it not be destroyed!"
Yīzhī said to Zhǔn:
"Your heart is like an owl and a broken mirror.
An owl
eats its mother;
a broken mirror
eats its father.
A broken mirror
is like a biao but with a tiger's body.
"Body"
is also written as
"eye".
Since you devour people,
people will also devour you."
Cōng also established Xuānhuái's adopted daughter as the Central Empress.
The Siztú Xún Zǔ, in Xǔchāng,
pressured by Shí Lè,
led his hundreds of subordinates across the river.
An imperial edict appointed Zǔ, along with the Tàibǎo, Xīyáng Wáng Róng, to jointly manage the affairs of the Shàngshū.
When Duàn Pǐdī fled due to the death of Lù Juàn,
Liú Kūn sent his heir, Jiē, to escort him.
Pǐdī was defeated,
and Jiē was captured by Duàn Mòbēi.
Mòbēi treated him generously,
promised Kūn the position of Yōuzhōu Cìshǐ,
and wanted to join forces with Kūn to attack Pǐdī.
He secretly sent an envoy with a letter from Jiē,
requesting Kūn to be an internal ally.
This was intercepted by Pǐdī's scouting cavalry.
At that time, Kūn was separately garrisoned in Xiǎochéng of the Zhēngběi commandery,
and did not know about it.
Xiǎochéng of Zhēngběi
was likely where the Zhēngběi Jiāngjūn resided.
Pǐdī showed Jiē's letter to Kūn and said:
"I do not doubt you,
which is why I inform you."
Kūn said:
"I am allied with you,
hoping to wipe away the shame of the state.
If my son's letter had reached you secretly,
I would ultimately not betray you and forget righteousness for the sake of one son."
Pǐdī greatly respected Kūn,
Yǎ
means "always".
and was about to allow him to return to his garrison.
His younger brother Shūjūn said to Pǐdī:
"We
are just Húyí;
the reason we can subjugate the Jìn people
is because they fear our numbers.
Now our own kin are separated,
meaning we are fighting Mòbēi.
If someone supports Kūn and rises up,
our clan will be annihilated."
Pǐdī therefore detained Kūn.
Kūn's eldest illegitimate son, Zūn, fearing execution,
along with Kūn's Zuǒ Chángshǐ Yáng Qiáo and others, shut themselves in and defended.
Pǐdī attacked and captured them.
The Dàijùn Tàishǒu Pìlǘ Sōng,
The Xìngpǔ says: a collateral descendant of Wèi Wéngōng resided in Chǔqiū,
established Pìlǘ village,
and thus became the Pìlǘ clan.
When the matter was revealed,
Pǐdī seized Sōng, Jù, and their associates,
and executed them all.
In the fifth month,
on the day Guǐchǒu,
Pǐdī claimed an imperial edict to arrest Kūn,
strangled him to death,
and also killed four of his sons and nephews.
Kūn's Cóngshì Zhōngláng Lú Chén, Cuī Yuè and others led Kūn's remaining forces to Liáoxī,
sought refuge with Duàn Mòbēi,
and enthroned Liú Jiē as their leader.
Many of Kūn's generals and advisors fled to Shí Lè.
Yuè
was Lín's great-grandson.
Cuī Lín served Wèi,
reaching the position of Sīkōng.
Hoping he could pacify Héshuò,
they did not mourn Kūn.
Wēn Qiáo submitted a memorial, stating:
"Kūn was utterly loyal to the imperial house,
his family destroyed and he himself dead.
He should be commended and consoled."
Lú Chén and Cuī Yuè, through Mòbēi's envoy,
also submitted a memorial appealing for Kūn's injustice.
Several years later,
Kūn was posthumously granted the titles of Tàiwèi and Shìzhōng,
with the posthumous epithet Mǐn.
Thereupon, both the Yi and Jìn people, due to Kūn's death,
no longer attached themselves to Pǐdī.
Mòbēi sent his younger brother to attack Pǐdī.
Pǐdī led his several thousand troops, intending to flee to Shào Xù.
Lè's general Shí Yuè intercepted him at Yánshān.
Yánshān
is in the Bóhǎi Gāochéng county;
during the Suí dynasty, Gāochéng was renamed Yánshān County.
Sòng Bái says: Yánshān is eighty lǐ southeast of the county.
Pǐdī had formed an alliance with Kūn
to jointly support the Jìn imperial house.
After killing Kūn,
Pǐdī's power also declined,
and he was eventually captured by Shí Lè.
Pǐdī returned to garrison Jì.
Mòbēi declared himself Yōuzhōu Cìshǐ.
Earlier,
Wēn Qiáo had carried a memorial for Liú Kūn to Jiànkāng.
His mother, Lady Cuī, firmly stopped him,
but Qiáo tore his robes and left.
Upon arriving,
he repeatedly requested to return with a reply,
but the imperial court did not permit it.
When Kūn died,
he was appointed Sànqí Shìláng.
Qiáo heard of his mother's death,
but due to chaos could not attend the mourning or burial.
He firmly declined the appointment,
and earnestly pleaded to return north.
An imperial edict stated:
"Whoever performs rites
should do so in a way that is logically consistent.
Jīng
means "constant".
All the armies escorting the imperial coffin have not yet been able to advance.
How can Qiáo, as an individual,
overcome his personal difficulties
and not obey the king's command!"
Qiáo had no choice but to accept the appointment.
Earlier,
Cáo Yí, having occupied Qīngzhōu,
rebelled against Hàn and surrendered [to Jìn].
This means he sent an envoy to Jiànkāng to present a memorial encouraging the emperor's advancement.
Yí,
read Yú Lì Fān.
His forces were not connected,
so he allied again with Shí Lè.
Lè appointed Yí as Dōngzhōu Dàjiāngjūn and Qīngzhōu Mù,
and enfeoffed him as Lángxié Gōng.
Cáo Yí wavered between the two states,
and ultimately was captured by others.
Fù,
read Fú Yòu Fān.
In the sixth month,
on the day Jiǎshēn,
Diāo Xié was appointed Shàngshū Lìng,
and Xún Sōng was appointed Zuǒ Púshè.
Xié's nature was resolute and fierce,
often conflicting with others.
He and Shìzhōng Liú Wèi were both favored and trusted by the emperor.
Wishing to correct the maladies of the time,
he always exalted the superior and suppressed the inferior,
rejecting and obstructing powerful families.
Therefore, he was detested by the Wáng clan.
All the harsh and severe policies
were said to have been instituted by Wèi and Xié.
Xié also indulged in drinking and acted unrestrainedly,
offending and disparaging high officials.
Those who saw him were all apprehensive and feared him.
This sets the stage for Diāo Xié's later murder.
On the day Wùxū,
the imperial prince Xī was enfeoffed as Wǔlíng Wáng.
In the 17th year, Liú Hǔ 劉虎 from Shuòfāng 朔方 invaded Tuòbá Yùlǜ 拓跋鬱律’s western territory.
Hǔ 虎 moved to Shuòfāng 朔方.
See Volume 87, Emperor Huái’s 懷帝 Yǒngjiā 永嘉 fourth year.
In the seventh month,
Yùlǜ 鬱律 attacked Hǔ 虎,
utterly defeating him.
Hǔ 虎 fled outside the pass.
His cousin Lù Gū 路孤 led his tribe to surrender to Yùlǜ 鬱律.
Thereupon, Yùlǜ 鬱律 took the former territory of Wūsūn 烏孫 in the west,
and in the east, he incorporated the lands west of Wùjí 勿吉.
The “Northern Di Barbarians” section of the Táng Shū 唐書 states:
The Hēishuǐ Mòhé 黑水靺鞨
lived in the lands of Sùshèn 肅慎,
also called Yìlóu 挹婁.
During the Yuán Wèi 元魏, they were called Wùjí 勿吉.
The Tōngjiàn 通鑑 probably followed Wèi Shōu 魏收’s Wèi Shū 魏書.
What Yùlǜ 鬱律 took
was the land west of Wùjí 勿吉,
and he was not yet able to incorporate Wùjí 勿吉 itself.
The Tújī Hù Mùróng 徒河慕容, Lìngzhī Duàn Shì 令支段氏, Yǔwén Bù 宇文部, and Gāogōulì 高句麗
were also not subject to Yùlǜ 鬱律’s control.
He was mighty in the north.
In the 18th year, Hàn Zhǔ Cōng 漢主聰 became seriously ill.
He summoned Dàsīmǎ Yào 大司馬曜 to be Chéngxiàng 丞相,
and Shí Lè 石勒 to be Dàjiàngjūn 大將軍.
Both were to supervise the affairs of the Shàngshū 尚書,
receiving the dying emperor’s edict to assist in governance.
Yào 曜 and Lè 勒 firmly declined.
So Yào 曜 was made Chéngxiàng 丞相 and concurrently Yōngzhōu Mù 雍州牧,
and Lè 勒 was made Dàjiàngjūn 大將軍 and concurrently Yōu 幽 and Jì 冀 Èrzhōu Mù 二州牧.
Lè 勒 declined to accept.
Shàngluò Wáng Jǐng 上洛王景 was made Tàizǎi 太宰,
Jìnán Wáng Jì 濟南王驥 Dàsīmǎ 大司馬,
Chāngguó Gōng Yǐ 昌國公顗 Tàishī 太師,
Zhū Jì 朱紀 Tàifù 太傅,
Hūyán Yàn 呼延晏 Tàibǎo 太保.
All were to supervise the affairs of the Shàngshū 尚書.
Fàn Lóng 范隆 was to oversee Shàngshū Lìng 尚書令 and Yídóng Sānsī 儀同三司.
Jìn Zhǔn 靳準 was made Dàsīkōng 大司空 and concurrently Sīlì Xiàowèi 司隸校尉.
They were all to take turns deciding on memorials to the Shàngshū 尚書.
On the Guǐhài 癸亥 day,
Cōng 聰 died.
On the Jiǎzǐ 甲子 day,
Crown Prince Càn 粲 ascended the throne.
Càn 粲’s courtesy name was Shìguāng 士光.
Concubine Fán 樊氏 was titled Hóngdào Huánghòu 弘道皇后,
Concubine Wǔ 武氏 Hóngdé Huánghòu 弘德皇后,
Concubine Wáng 王氏 Hóngxiào Huánghòu 弘孝皇后.
His wife Jìn Shì 靳氏 was established as Empress,
and his son Yuángōng 元公 as Crown Prince.
A general amnesty was declared,
and the reign era was changed to Hànchāng 漢昌.
Cōng 聰 was buried at Xuānguāng Líng 宣光陵,
posthumously titled Zhāowǔ Huángdì 昭武皇帝,
with the temple name Lièzōng 烈宗.
Empress Dowager Jìn 靳太后 and others were all under twenty years of age.
Càn 粲 often behaved improperly,
showing no signs of grief or sorrow.
Jìn Zhǔn 靳準 secretly harbored ulterior motives.
He privately said to Càn 粲:
“I hear that the various lords wish to carry out the deeds of Yī 伊 and Huò 霍,
first executing the Tàibǎo 太保 and your servant,
so that the Dàsīmǎ 大司馬 can oversee all affairs.
Your Majesty should act quickly!”
Càn 粲 did not follow his advice.
Zhǔn 準, fearing,
again had the two Jìn Shì 靳氏 speak of it.
The two Jìn Shì 靳氏 were
Cōng’s 聰 Empress and Càn’s 粲 Empress.
Jìn 靳,
pronounced Jīn.
Fù 復,
pronounced Fù.
He arrested Tàizǎi Jǐng 太宰景, Dàsīmǎ Jì 大司馬驥, Jì’s 驥 maternal younger brother, Chējì Dàjiàngjūn Wú Wáng Chěng 車騎大將軍吳王逞, Tàishī Yǐ 太師顗, and Dàsītú Qí Wáng Mài 大司徒齊王勱.
All were killed.
Zhū Jì 朱紀 and Fàn Lóng 范隆 fled to Cháng’ān 長安.
They fled to Liú Yào 劉曜.
Càn 粲 arrayed his troops at Shànglín 上林,
planning to attack Shí Lè 石勒.
This refers to the construction of the Shànglín Yuàn 上林苑 in Píngyáng 平陽.
Zhì 治,
pronounced Zhì.
He then garrisoned Cháng’ān 長an.
Jìn Zhǔn 靳準 was made Dàjiàngjūn 大將軍 and supervised the affairs of the Shàngshū 尚書.
Càn 粲 frequently indulged in banquets in the inner palace,
and all military and state affairs
were decided by Zhǔn 準.
Zhǔn 準 forged an imperial edict to make his cousin Míng 明 Chējì Jiāngjūn 車騎將軍,
and Kāng 康 Wèijiāngjūn 衞將軍.
Zhǔn 準 was about to revolt,
and consulted Wáng Yán 王延.
Yán 延 did not agree.
He galloped off,
intending to report it.
He intended to report Zhǔn’s 準謀 plot to Càn 粲.
Zhǔn 準 seized Yán 延 and brought him back.
Zhǔn 準 then led his troops up to Guāngjí Diàn 光極殿,
ordering armored soldiers to seize Càn 粲,
enumerate his crimes, and kill him.
He was posthumously titled Yǐndì 隱帝.
All Liú Shì 劉氏 males and females,
young and old, were beheaded in the eastern marketplace.
He unearthed the two mausoleums of Yǒngguāng 永光 and Xuānguāng 宣光.
Yuān’s 淵 tomb was called Yǒngguāng Líng 永光陵.
He burned their ancestral temple.
Zhǔn 準 proclaimed himself Dàjiàngjūn 大將軍 and Hàn Tiānwáng 漢天王,
claiming imperial authority
and establishing officials.
He said to Hú Sōng 胡嵩 of Āndìng 安定:
“Since ancient times, no Hú 胡 person has been Son of Heaven.
Now I entrust the Heirloom Seal of the Realm to you,
so that it may return to the Jìn Jiā 晉家.”
When Luòyáng 洛陽 fell,
the Heirloom Seal of the Realm was moved to Píngyáng 平陽.
Rú 如,
means “to go.”
Xǐ 璽,
pronounced Xǐ.
Zhǔn 準 was enraged
and killed him.
He sent an envoy to inform Sīzhōu Cìshǐ Lǐ Jǔ 司州刺史李矩, saying:
“Liú Yuān 劉淵, a petty scoundrel of the Túcá 屠各,
took advantage of the Jìn’s 晉 chaos
to falsely claim the mandate of heaven,
causing the two emperors to be trapped and perish.
I have promptly led the masses to escort the imperial coffin,
and request to report this to the emperor.”
Jǔ 矩 swiftly memorialized the Emperor,
and the Emperor dispatched Tàicháng Hán Yìn 太常韓胤 and others to escort the imperial coffin.
Hàn Shàngshū Běigōng Chún 漢尚書北宮純 and others gathered Jìn 晉 people,
forming a fort in the Eastern Palace.
Jìn Kāng 靳康 attacked and annihilated them.
Běigōng Chún 北宮純 surrendered to Hàn 漢.
See Volume 87, Emperor Huái’s 懷帝 Yǒngjiā 永嘉 fifth year.
Yán 延 cursed, saying:
“You rebellious slave of the Túcá 屠各,
why do you not kill me quickly,
and place my left eye at the Xīyáng Mén 西陽門,
so I may witness the Xìangguó’s 相國 entry!”
This refers to Liú Yào 劉曜 advancing his troops from the west.
“And witness the Dàjiàngjūn’s 大將軍 entry!”
This refers to Shí Lè 石勒 advancing his troops from the east.
When Xiāngguó Yào 相國曜 heard of the chaos,
he rushed there from Cháng’ān 長安.
Shí Lè 石勒 led fifty thousand elite troops to attack Zhǔn 準,
occupying the northern ridge of Xiānglíng 襄陵.
Zhǔn 準 repeatedly challenged him to battle,
but Lè 勒 strengthened his fortifications to frustrate him.
In winter,
the tenth month,
Yào 曜 arrived at Chìbì 赤壁.
The Shuǐjīngzhù 水經註 notes: Northwest of Píshì Xiàn 皮氏縣, Hédōng 河東,
there is Chìshíchuān 赤石川.
Together with Tàifù Zhū Jì 太傅朱紀 and others, he presented a venerated title.
Yào 曜 ascended the imperial throne.
Yào 曜’s courtesy name was Yǒngmíng 永明.
He was a clansman of Yuān 淵.
Only Jìn Zhǔn 靳準’s family was not included in the amnesty.
The reign era was changed to Guāngchū 光初.
Zhū Jì 朱紀 was made concurrently Sītú 司徒,
Hūyán Yàn 呼延晏 concurrently Sīkōng 司空.
Tàiwèi Fàn Lóng 太尉范隆 and all below him were restored to their original positions.
Shí Lè 石勒 was made Dàsīmǎ 大司馬 and Dàjiàngjūn 大將軍,
bestowed with the Jiǔ Xí 九錫 (nine distinctions),
granted an additional ten commanderies,
and advanced in peerage to Zhào Gōng 趙公.
Lè 勒 advanced to attack Zhǔn 準 in Píngyáng 平陽.
Over a hundred thousand households of Bá 巴, Qiāng 羌, and Jié 羯 who surrendered.
Bá 巴 refers to
Bá Dī 巴氐.
When Wèi Wǔ 魏武 pacified Hànzhōng 漢中,
he moved the Bá Dī 巴氐 to Guānzhōng 關中.
Later, their kind spread,
and there were Bá Dī 巴氐 in Hédōng 河東 and Píngyáng 平陽.
Jié 羯,
pronounced Jié.
Hàn Zhǔ Yào 漢主曜 sent Zhēngběi Jiāngjūn Liú Yǎ 征北將軍劉雅 and Zhènběi Jiāngjūn Liú Cè 鎮北將軍劉策 to garrison Fényīn 汾陰.
Fényīn Xiàn 汾陰縣
belonged to Hédōng Jùn 河東郡 during the Hàn 漢,
and was abolished during the Jìn 晉.
In the 19th year, the eleventh month,
on the Yǐmǎo 乙卯 day,
the sun appeared at night,
three zhàng 丈 high.
In the 20th year, an edict appointed Wáng Dūn 王敦 as Jīngzhōu Mù 荊州牧,
and added Táo Kǎn 陶侃 as Dūdū Jiāozhōu Zhūjūnsì 都督交州諸軍事.
Dūn 敦 firmly declined the position of Zhōumù 州牧,
so he was allowed to serve as Cìshǐ 刺史.
On the 21st day, *gēngshēn*,
an imperial edict commanded all the *gōngqīng* and *shì* to present their views on gains and losses.
The Imperial Censor-in-Chief, Xióng Yuǎn (熊遠), submitted a memorial,
stating:
"The Hú (胡) bandits are disturbing *Huáxià* (華夏),
Kǒng Ānguó (孔安國) said: 'disturbing'
means 'causing chaos'.
*Xià* (夏)
refers to *Huáxià* (華夏).
*Xià* (夏),
pronunciation *hùyǎ* (戶雅).
Yet we are unable to dispatch troops to attack them;
this is the first failing.
All officials do not feel ashamed that the enemy has not been avenged,
but are preoccupied with jesting and feasting;
this is the second failing.
They amuse themselves by jesting with each other.
They do not assess true virtue,
but only look at superficial appearances;
they do not seek talent and ability,
but only engage in solicitation;
those in office regard handling affairs as being a 'vulgar official,'
upholding the law as 'being harsh,'
fulfilling rituals as 'flattery,'
being at ease as 'profoundly excellent,'
being unrestrained as 'a free spirit,'
and being arrogant and difficult as 'simple and refined';
this is the third failing.
Those whom the world dislikes
are submerged in mud and mire;
those whom the times favor
soar among the clouds.
Consequently, the myriad affairs are not in order,
and customs are false and shallow.
The various departments of the court
consider compliance as good,
and disagreement is met with demotion.
How can the court have ministers who dare to speak out,
and how can scholars not harbor the ambition of obtaining office through flattery!
In ancient times, when selecting officials,
they were 'to present their views in speech';
the *Shùn Diǎn* (舜典) says: 'to present their views in speech.'
Kǒng Ānguó (孔安國) noted: 'Fū' (敷)
means 'to set forth';
'zòu' (奏)
means 'to advance'.
Each was to present and advance their views on governance.
This greatly deviates from the ancient meaning.
This refers to *xiù* (秀) and *xiào* (孝) not being tested but being appointed as officials.
The law does not apply to the powerful and noble,
thus talent does not serve the tasks,
and villainy goes unpunished.
If this way is not changed,
to seek to save the chaos,
it will be difficult!"
Earlier,
the emperor, in a time of chaos and separation,
wished to comfort and please the people.
The *xiù* (秀) and *xiào* (孝) from the *zhōu* (州) and *jùn* (郡),
when they arrived, were not tested,
but were all universally appointed as officials.
*Xiù* (秀) and *xiào* (孝)
refer to the *xiùcái* (秀才) and *xiàolián* (孝廉) recommended by the *zhōu* (州) and *jùn* (郡).
The character *xiān* (先),
pronunciation *xījiàn* (悉薦).
"It is fitting to gradually follow the old system,
and test them with classics and policy essays."
In the early Jìn (晉) dynasty, those *xiù* (秀) and *xiào* (孝) who passed the classics and policy essays,
like Huá Tán (華譚) and his ilk, were of this kind.
The character *yún* (頵),
pronunciation *yúlún* (於倫),
also *jūyún* (居筠).
An edict also stated:
"Those who fail the examination,
the *cìshǐ* (刺史) and *tàishǒu* (太守) shall be removed from office."
This was to punish those who made the recommendation.
The character *zhōng* (中),
pronunciation *zhúzhòng* (竹仲).
Those who had arrived [at the capital] also all feigned illness,
so for three years, none came for the examination.
The emperor wished to specially appoint the *xiàolián* (孝廉) who had already arrived,
but the Director of the Imperial Secretariat, Kǒng Tǎn (孔坦), submitted a memorial,
stating:
"The nearby commanderies feared implicating their lords and fathers,
and thus dared not send anyone;
the distant commanderies hoped for exemption from testing,
and thus ventured to come.
If we now grant partial appointments,
this would mean that those who diligently uphold the law lose out,
and those who are lucky and take chances obtain office.
The corrupting of customs and harming of teachings
may begin from this.
It is better to dismiss them all
and postpone the deadline for them,
allowing them to attend school.
Then the law will be fair and the decree trustworthy."
The emperor followed his advice,
allowing *xiàolián* (孝廉) to delay their examination until seven years had passed since their arrival.
*Shēn* (申),
means 'to extend'.
He was Yú (愉)'s cousin.
On the 22nd day, Jìn Zhǔn (靳準) sent his chamberlain, Bǔ Tài (卜泰), to deliver the imperial carriage and ceremonial attire, requesting peace from Shí Lè (石勒);
Shí Lè (石勒) imprisoned Bǔ Tài (卜泰)
and sent him to the Hàn (漢) lord, Yào (曜).
Yào (曜) said to Bǔ Tài (卜泰):
"In the last years of the former emperor,
there was truly a great disturbance in human relations.
'Former emperor'
refers to Càn (粲);
'disturbance in human relations'
refers to his cohabiting with his stepmothers.
That I reached this point,
his achievement was great!
If you had welcomed the imperial entourage earlier,
I would have entrusted all governmental affairs to you,
let alone sparing your life!
You, for me, enter the city,
and fully convey this intention."
Bǔ Tài (卜泰) returned to Píngyáng (平陽).
Zhǔn (準), considering that he had killed Yào (曜)'s mother and brother,
hesitated and did not comply.
Yào (曜)'s mother, Lady Hú (胡),
was killed by Zhǔn (準);
his brother's name is lost to history.
*Shěnyín* (沈吟)
means 'hesitating and indecisive'.
*Shěn* (沈),
pronunciation *chílín* (持林).
The Left and Right Generals of Chariots and Cavalry, Qiáo Tài (喬泰) and Wáng Téng (王騰), and the General of the Guard, Jìn Kāng (靳康), among others,
together killed Zhǔn (準)
and enthroned the Director of the Imperial Secretariat, Jìn Míng (靳明), as their leader.
They sent Bǔ Tài (卜泰) to present the six imperial seals of state to surrender to Hàn (漢).
Shí Lè (石勒) was greatly enraged,
advanced his army to attack Míng (明),
who came out to fight,
and was utterly defeated.
He then barricaded himself within the city and held fast.
On the 23rd day, *dīngchǒu*,
the imperial son Huàn (煥) was enfeoffed as the Prince of Lángxié (琅邪).
Huàn (煥),
the son of Lady Zhèng (鄭夫人),
was two years old.
The emperor loved him
and, because his illness was critical,
he therefore made him a prince.
On the day *jǐmǎo*,
he died.
The emperor buried him with the rites for an adult,
preparing both auspicious and inauspicious ceremonial garments,
and constructing a tomb and a mausoleum,
at great expense and effort.
Sūn Xiāo (孫霄) of Kuàijī (會稽), the Right Courtier of Lángxié (琅邪) Kingdom,
*Jìn Zhì* (晉志) states: 'A kingdom establishes one Left and one Right Courtier.'
said:
"In ancient times, during times of disaster and famine, rituals were curtailed.
How much more so now, when the whole country is in chaos and turmoil,
even if we followed old regulations,
it would still be appropriate to economize.
Yet, [to follow practices] that are not found in the ritual canons,
and to lavishly adorn as such!
To bury a child who died prematurely and for whom there are no mourning rites with the rites of an adult,
is something not found in ancient canons.
To engage in useless projects,
to exhaust already distressed finances,
and to incur unnecessary expenses,
this is what your subject finds unsettling."
The emperor did not comply.
On the 24th day, Zhōu Fǔ (周撫), the Administrator of Péngchéng (彭城), killed Zhōu Mò (周默), the Administrator of Pèijùn (沛郡),
and surrendered with his forces to Shí Lè (石勒).
An imperial edict ordered Liú Xiá (劉遐), the Administrator of Xiàpī (下邳), to take charge of Péngchéng (彭城) as Administrator,
and together with Cài Bào (蔡豹), the Inspector of Xúzhōu (徐州), and Xú Kān (徐龕), the Grand Administrator of Tàishān (泰山), to jointly attack Zhōu Fǔ (周撫).
Bào (豹)
was the great-great-grandson of Zhì (質).
Cài Zhì (蔡質)
was a man of Hàn (漢),
the paternal uncle of Cài Yōng (蔡邕).
The character *kān* (龕),
pronunciation *kǒuhán* (口含).
On the 25th day, Shí Hǔ (石虎) led troops from Yōu (幽) and Jì (冀) provinces to join Shí Lè (石勒) in attacking Píngyáng (平陽).
Jìn Míng (靳明) suffered repeated defeats
and sent an envoy to request aid from Hàn (漢).
The Hàn (漢) lord, Yào (曜), sent Liú Yǎ (劉雅) and Liú Cè (劉策) to receive him.
Míng (明) led fifteen thousand men and women from Píngyáng (平陽) to flee to Hàn (漢).
Yào (曜) moved his forces west to Cùyì (粟邑),
Cùyì (粟邑) County
belonged to Fēngyì (馮翊) Commandery.
He massacred everyone, regardless of age.
Yào (曜) brought his mother, Lady Hú (胡)'s coffin, from Píngyáng (平陽)
and buried her in Cùyì (粟邑).
The tomb was named Yánglíng (陽陵),
and she was posthumously honored as Empress Dowager Xuānmíng (宣明皇太后).
Shí Lè (石勒) burned down the palaces in Píngyáng (平陽),
and ordered Péi Xiàn (裴憲) and Shí Huì (石會) to restore the two mausoleums of Yǒngguāng (永光) and Xuānguāng (宣光).
He gathered over a hundred individuals, including the Hàn (漢) lord Càn (粲), and buried them,
then stationed a garrison and returned.
Chéng Liángzhōu Cìshǐ Lǐ Fèng, who had repeatedly distinguished himself,
Chéng Zhǔ Xióng's nephew, Zhì, in Jìnshòu,
was jealous of him.
Jìnshòu County belonged to Zìtóng Commandery.
Hé Chéngtiān said: Emperor Huì of Jìn established Jìnshòu County.
Shěn Yuè said: According to the Jìn Qǐjū Zhù,
in the first year of Tàikāng (280 CE) of Emperor Wǔ,
Hànshòu in Zìtóng was renamed Jìnshòu.
The name Hànshòu,
was probably established by Shǔ;
to say Emperor Huì established it,
is incorrect.
Xióng personally went to Fú,
and sent Tàifù Xiāng to attack Fèng,
and beheaded him;
he appointed Lǐ Shòu as Qián Jiāngjūn,
supervising military affairs in Bāxī.
Collated by Hé Zīquán, Wáng Chóngwǔ, and Niè Chóngqí
Compiled by Sīmǎ Guāng
by Imperial Edict
Hòu Xué Tiāntái
Zhōngzōng Yuán Huángdì Zhōng
Second year of Tàixīng
(Jǐmǎo, 319 CE)
1 In spring,
the second month,
Liú Xiá and Xú Kān attacked Zhōu Fǔ at Hánshān,
defeated and beheaded him.
Wèi Shōu's Dìxíng Zhì says,
Péngchéng County in Péngchéng Commandery has Hánshān.
Kān,
read as kǔ hán.
Yè native Sū Jùn led several thousand families from his hometown to build a stronghold to protect themselves,
and many from near and far attached themselves to him.
Yè County,
belonged to Dōnglái Commandery.
Sū Jùn Zhuàn says,
a native of Yè in Chángguǎng.
According to the Zhì,
Chángguǎng Commandery had Tǐng County,
but no Yè County.
Shuài,
read as lǜ.
About to attack him,
Jùn led his followers and came by sea to surrender.
The emperor appointed Jùn as Yīngyáng Jiāngjūn.
Shěn Yuè's Zhì: Yīngyáng Jiāngjūn,
in the Jiàn'ān period,
Cáo Gōng bestowed this upon Cáo Hóng.
An edict appointed Xiá as Línchuái Tàishǒu,
and Jùn as Huáilíng Nèishǐ.
In the seventh year of Yuánkāng (297 CE) of Emperor Huì,
Huáilíng Commandery was established by dividing Línchuái;
its territory should be in the area of Línyí County, Yízhōu, in the Táng dynasty.
Sòng Bái said: Zhāoxìn County in Sìzhōu,
was originally Hàn Huáilíng County.
2 Shí Lè sent his Zuǒ Chángshǐ Wáng Xiū to present a victory report to Hàn,
Hàn Zhǔ Yào sent Jiān Sītú Guō Sì to bestow upon Lè the titles of Tàizǎi and Lǐng Dàjiāngjūn,
advanced his peerage to Zhào Wáng,
and granted him special courtesies,
with an escort for departure and a clear path for entry,
as in the precedent of Cáo Gōng assisting Hàn;
he appointed Wáng Xiū and his deputy Liú Mào both as generals,
and enfeoffed them as lièhóu.
Xiū's retainer Cáo Pínglè followed Xiū to Sùyì,
and then stayed to serve Hàn,
saying to Yào:
"The Dà Sīmǎ sent Xiū and others here,
Yào had just ascended the throne,
and had appointed Lè as Dà Sīmǎ,
hence the designation.
to secretly observe the strength and weakness of the imperial carriage,
awaiting their return,
they will attack your Majesty."
At that time, the Hàn army was indeed weak and fatigued,
and Yào believed him.
So he recalled Sì,
and beheaded Xiū in the marketplace.
In the third month,
Lè returned to Xiāngguó.
Liú Mào escaped and returned,
recounting Xiū's death.
Lè was furious and said:
"I have served the Liú clan,
fulfilling the duties of a minister beyond expectation.
Their foundation and enterprise,
were all established by me;
now that they have achieved their ambition,
they want to plot against me.
Zhào Wáng or Zhào Dì,
I will claim for myself,
why should I wait for them!"
So he executed Cáo Pínglè's three clans.
This laid the groundwork for the mutual attacks between Liú and Shí.
3 The emperor ordered his ministers to discuss the suburban sacrifices,
Shàngshū Lìng Diāo Xié and others believed that it should wait until they returned to Luòyáng to perform them.
Sītú Xún Zǔ and others said:
"Emperor Xiàn of Hàn, when he established his capital at Xǔ,
immediately performed the suburban sacrifices."
Fàn Shū says,
in the first year of Jiàn'ān (196 CE) of Emperor Xiàn of Hàn,
he performed the suburban sacrifices to the Supreme Deity in Ānyì;
in the seventh month of that year,
he arrived in Luòyáng,
and again performed the suburban sacrifices to the Supreme Deity;
in the eighth month,
he moved to Xǔ,
and there was no mention of suburban sacrifices.
Perhaps this is seen in another book.
Jìn Shū Lǐ Zhì records Zǔ's deliberation, saying: Emperor Xiàn moved to Xǔ,
and immediately established the suburban altars.
Perhaps the suburban sacrifices did not occur in the year of his relocation to Xǔ.
The emperor followed this advice,
and established the suburban altars at Sìdì in Jiànkāng city.
On the day Xīnmǎo,
the emperor personally performed sacrifices at the Southern Suburb.
As there was no Northern Suburb yet,
Note: In the eighth year of Xiánhé (333 CE) of Emperor Chéng,
the Northern Suburb was first established south of Fùzhōushān.
The edict stated:
"Lángyé Gōngwáng should be referred to as Huángkǎo,"
Hè Xún said:
"According to ritual,
a son dares not apply his own title to his father."
This refers to the previous statement by Hàn Shī Dān citing ritual,
the event is found in volume 33, in the first year of Jiànpíng (6 BCE) of Emperor Āi of Hàn.
4 In the beginning,
Péngpí Wù Zhǔ Chén Chuān,
Péngpí,
is the Péngzé of the Zuǒ Zhuàn,
in Jùnyí County.
When Zǔ Tì attacked Fán Yǎ,
Chuān sent his general Lǐ Tóu to assist him.
Tóu fought bravely and distinguished himself,
and Tì treated him generously.
Tóu often sighed and said:
"To have such a man as my lord,
I would have no regrets even if I died."
Chuān heard this and killed him.
Tóu's confederate Féng Chǒng led his followers to surrender to Tì,
Chuān became even angrier,
and extensively plundered the various commanderies of Yùzhōu;
Tì sent troops to attack and defeat him.
In summer,
the fourth month,
Chuān rebelled with Jùnyí,
and surrendered to Shí Lè.
Jùnyí County,
belonged to Chénliú Commandery,
and was formerly Dàliáng.
Shuài,
read as lǜ.
Jiàng,
read as hù jiāng;
same below.
5 When Zhōu Fǔ was defeated and fled,
Xú Kān's subordinate Yú Yào pursued and beheaded him;
but when the court discussed merits,
Liú Xiá was given precedence.
Kān was angry,
rebelled with Tàishān,
surrendered to Shí Lè,
and proclaimed himself Yǎnzhōu Cìshǐ.
6 Hàn Zhǔ Yào returned,
making Cháng'ān his capital.
He returned from Sùyì to Cháng'ān,
thus establishing his capital there.
This refers to Empress Yáng of Emperor Huì.
Yào married Empress Yáng,
see volume 87, Yǒngjiā fifth year of Emperor Huái.
He enfeoffed his son Xí as Chánglè Wáng,
Chǎn as Tàiyuán Wáng,
Chōng as Huáinán Wáng,
Chǎng as Qí Wáng,
Gāo as Lǔ Wáng,
Huī as Chǔ Wáng;
all imperial relatives were advanced to the title of Jùn Wáng.
Lady Yáng,
was the former Empress of Emperor Huì.
Yào once asked her:
"How do I compare to the children of the Sīmǎ family?"
Lady Yáng replied:
"Your Majesty,
is a sagely ruler who founded a dynasty;
they,
were foolish men who lost their country;
how can they be spoken of in the same breath!
They, though exalted as emperors and kings,
could not even protect their one wife, one son, and themselves.
They could not even protect them.
At that time, I
truly wished not to live,
thinking all men in the world were like that.
Since I began serving your Majesty,
I have truly come to know that there are real men in the world."
Yào greatly favored her,
and she often interfered in state affairs.
7 Nányáng Wáng Bǎo 南陽王保 proclaimed himself Jìn Wáng 晉王,
changed the era name to Jiànkāng 建康,
and established a bureaucracy.
He appointed Zhāng Shí 張寔 as Zhēngxī Dàjiāngjūn 征西大將軍 and Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī 開府儀同三司.
Chén Ān 陳安 proclaimed himself Qínzhōu Cìshǐ 秦州刺史,
surrendered to Hàn 漢,
and then surrendered to Chéng 成.
Shàngguī 上邽 suffered a great famine.
The officers and masses were in distress and forced to flee.
Zhāng Chūn 張春 escorted Bǎo 保 to Nán'ān Qíshān 南安祁山.
Zhī 之 means
'to go.'
Chén Ān 陳安 retreated to protect Zhuōgǔ 斫崝.
Zhuōgǔ 斫崝 is a place name.
In the Former Hàn 漢 dynasty, it belonged to Tiānshuǐ Jùn 天水郡.
In the Later Hàn 漢 and Jìn 晉 dynasties, it was abolished.
The commentary on the Shuǐjīng 水經 says: The Zhuōgǔ Shuǐ 斫崝水
flows north past the old Zhuōgǔ 斫崝 road,
then southeast into the Qīngshuǐ 清水,
and the Qīngshuǐ 清水 then flows southeast into the Wèi 渭 river.
Before long,
Bǎo 保 was again threatened by Ān 安.
Shí 寔 dispatched his general Sòng Yì 宋毅 to rescue him,
and Ān 安 then retreated.
8 Jiāngdōng 江東 suffered a great famine.
An imperial edict ordered all officials to submit memorials.
Yìzhōu Cìshǐ 益州刺史 Yīng Zhàn 應詹 submitted a memorial saying:
Zhàn 詹 had returned to Jiànkāng 建康 from his post as Yìzhōu Cìshǐ 益州刺史.
"Since Yuánkāng 元康 [291-300 CE],
the classics and the Way have been undervalued,
and recondite emptiness and unrestrainedness have been considered broad-mindedness.
Yí 夷 means
'expansive.'
It is fitting to greatly promote Confucian officials
to reform the customs."
9 Zǔ Tì 祖逖 attacked Chén Chuān 陳川 at Péngguān 蓬關.
Shí Lè 石勒 dispatched Shí Hǔ 石虎 with fifty thousand troops to rescue him.
They fought at Jùnyí 浚儀.
Tì's 逖 troops were defeated,
and he retreated to station them in Liángguó 梁國.
Lè 石勒 again dispatched Táo Bào 桃豹 with troops to Péngguān 蓬關.
Tì 逖 retreated to station his troops in Huáinán 淮南.
This refers to Huáinán Jùn 淮南郡,
whose seat was Shòuchūn 壽春.
Bào 豹 was left to guard Chuān's 川 former city.
10 Shí Lè 石勒 dispatched Shí Hǔ 石虎 to attack Xiānbēi Rìliù Yán 鮮卑日六延 in Shuòfāng 朔方.
They severely defeated him,
beheading twenty thousand,
and capturing over thirty thousand.
Kǒng Cháng 孔萇 attacked the various commanderies of Yōuzhōu 幽州,
taking them all.
Duàn Pǐdī's 段匹磾 officers and masses were starving and scattered, and he wished to move to protect Shànggǔ 上谷.
The Jìn Zhì 晉志 states: Shànggǔ Jùn 上谷郡,
whose seat was Jǔyáng Xiàn 沮陽縣;
Qín 秦 established the commandery,
located at the top of a valley,
hence its name.
Pǐdī 匹磾 abandoned his wife and children and fled to Lèlíng 樂陵,
relying on Shào Xù 邵續.
Lèlíng Jùn 樂陵郡,
whose seat was Yàncì 厭次.
Xù 續 protected it to serve Jìn 晉.
11 Cáo Yì 曹嶷 sent an envoy to bribe Shí Lè 石勒,
requesting to make the Hé 河 (Yellow River) their border.
Lè 石勒 agreed.
Yì 嶷 had already established garrisons along the river.
Now, bribing Lè 石勒 to request the Hé 河 as the border
was due to his fear of Lè's 石勒 invasion.
12 Liángzhōu Cìshǐ 梁州刺史 Zhōu Fǎng 周訪 attacked Dù Zēng 杜曾,
severely defeating him.
Mǎ Jùn 馬雋 and others captured Zēng 曾 and surrendered.
Fǎng 訪 executed him.
He also captured Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ 荊州刺史 Dìwǔ Yī 第五猗,
and sent him to Wǔchāng 武昌.
Fǎng 訪 believed that Yī 猗 had originally been appointed by the central court,
and moreover possessed contemporary prestige,
so he petitioned Wáng Dūn 王敦 that he should not be killed.
Dūn 敦 did not listen and executed him.
Yī 猗 had joined Dù Zēng 杜曾.
This begins in volume 89, Mǐndì's Jiànxīng 愍帝建興 fourth year.
Dūn 敦 was troubled by Dù Zēng's 杜曾 difficult-to-control nature.
He said to Fǎng 訪:
"If Zēng 曾 is captured,
I will discuss appointing you as Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ 荊州刺史."
But after Zēng 曾 died, Dūn 敦 did not do so.
Wáng Yì 王廙, while in Jīngzhōu 荊州,
killed many of Táo Kǎn's 陶侃 officers and aides.
Because Huángfǔ Fānghuí 皇甫方回 was respected by Kǎn 侃,
Yì 廙 reprimanded him for not coming to him,
arrested, and executed him.
The officials and common people were resentful and angry,
and there was unrest from top to bottom.
The Emperor, hearing of this,
summoned Yì 廙 to be Sànqí Chángshì 散騎常侍,
and appointed Zhōu Fǎng 周訪 to replace Yì 廙 as Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ 荊州刺史.
Wáng Dūn 王敦 was wary of Fǎng's 周訪 prestige and renown,
finding him difficult.
His Aide-de-camp Guō Shū 郭舒 advised Dūn 敦:
"Although our prefecture is desolate and impoverished,
it is a strategic region for warfare.
It should not be entrusted to others;
you should personally lead it."
Guō Shū 郭舒
was formerly in Jīngzhōu 荊州,
serving Liú Hóng 劉弘 and Wáng Chéng 王澄 successively.
Shuì 說 is pronounced
'shuì'.
Dūn 敦 followed his advice.
In the sixth month,
on the day Bǐngzǐ 丙子,
an edict was issued promoting Fǎng 訪 to Ānnán Jiāngjūn 安南將軍,
with his other titles remaining as before.
Fǎng 訪 was furious.
Dūn 敦 wrote a letter to placate and explain,
and also sent a jade ring and a jade bowl to express his sincere regard.
Fǎng 訪 threw them to the ground,
saying:
"Am I a mere peddler
to be pleased by treasures!"
While in Xiāngyáng 襄陽, Fǎng 訪 diligently promoted agriculture and trained troops,
secretly plotting to control Dūn's 敦 territory.
Whenever a position for a prefect or magistrate became vacant, he would fill it,
and then report it to the court.
Dūn 敦 was troubled by this but could not control him.
Wèi Gāi 魏該, being pressed by the Hú 胡 invaders,
led his forces south from Yíyáng 宜陽 to Xīnyě 新野.
Wèi Gāi 魏該 had been stationed in Yīquán Wù 一泉塢, on the border of Yíyáng 宜陽 County, since the end of Huáidì's 懷帝 reign.
Yíyáng Xiàn 宜陽縣
belonged to Hóngnóng Jùn 弘農郡.
Xīnyě Xiàn 新野縣,
in Hàn 漢, belonged to Nányáng Jùn 南陽郡;
in Jìn 晉, it belonged to Yìyáng Jùn 義陽郡.
He was appointed Shùnyáng Tàishǒu 順陽太守.
Zhào Gù 趙固 died.
Guō Sòng 郭誦 remained stationed in Yángzhái 陽翟,
Yángzhái Xiàn 陽翟縣,
in Hàn 漢, belonged to Yǐngchuān Jùn 潁川郡;
in Jìn 晉, it belonged to Hénán Jùn 河南郡.
He could not conquer it.
13 Hàn 主 Yào 漢主曜 established ancestral temples, altars for the deities of land and grain, and northern and southern suburban altars in Cháng'ān 長安.
He issued an edict saying:
"My ancestors
rose in the north.
Guāngwén 光文 established the Hàn 漢 ancestral temples to satisfy the people's wishes.
See volume 85, Huìdì's Yǒngxīng 惠帝永興 first year.
He took the Chányú 單于 as his ancestor.
Deliberate quickly and report to me!"
The court officials memorialized:
"Guāngwén 光文 was first enfeoffed as Lúnú Bó 盧奴伯.
Jìn Chéngdū Wáng Yǐng 晉成都王穎 enfeoffed Liú Yuān 劉淵 as Lúnú Bó 盧奴伯.
Zhōngshān 中山
is a division of Zhào 趙.
We request to change the dynastic title to Zhào 趙."
He agreed.
They offered Màodún 冒頓 to match Heaven,
and Guāngwén 光文 to match the Supreme Deity.
14 Xú Kān 徐龕 plundered Jǐ 濟 and Dài 岱.
Dài 岱 is
Tài Shān 泰山.
Kān 龕 plundered the area between Jǐ 濟 and Dài 岱.
Jǐ 濟 is pronounced
'jǐ'.
Shěn Yuè Zhì 沈約志 states: In the first year of Wǔdì Tàikāng 武帝太康 [280 CE],
Dōngguǎn Jùn 東莞郡 was established by separating it from Lángxié 琅邪.
The Jìn Zhì 晉志 states: Dōngguǎn 東莞
was formerly the Yùn 鄆邑 settlement of Lǔ 魯.
Liú Xù 劉昫 says: Táng 唐 Yízhōu Yíshuǐ Xiàn 沂州沂水縣 was the territory of Hàn Dōngguǎn Xiàn 漢東莞縣.
Sòng Bái 宋白 says: In the Spring and Autumn period, Jǔ 莒 and Lǔ 魯 contended over Yùn 鄆.
Dù Yù's 杜預 commentary says: South of Chéngyáng Gūmù Xiàn 城陽姑幕縣
is Yuántíng 員亭,
which is Yùn 鄆.
The characters were simply changed by common usage.
The Shísānzhōu Zhì 十三州志 says: There were two Yùn 鄆, East and West.
The one where Lǔ Zhāogōng 魯昭公 resided was West Yùn 鄆,
which is Yǎnzhōu Dōngpíng Jùn 兗州東平郡;
the one contended over by Jǔ 莒 and Lǔ 魯 was East Yùn 鄆,
which is Hàn Dōngguǎn Xiàn 漢東莞縣.
Guǎn 莞 is pronounced
'guǎn'.
Dǎo 導 believed that Yáng Jiàn 羊鑒 of Tàishān 泰山, who was the Tàizǐ Zuǒwèi Shuài 太子左衞率,
was a prominent family from Kān's 龕 hometown,
and would surely be able to control him.
Jiàn 鑒 deeply declined, saying his talent was not for generalship.
Xī Jiàn 郗鑒 also memorialized that Jiàn 鑒 lacked talent
and should not be used.
Dǎo 導 did not comply.
In autumn,
the eighth month,
Yáng Jiàn 羊鑒 was appointed Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn 征虜將軍 and Zhēngtǎo Dūdū 征討都督,
supervising Xúzhōu Cìshǐ 徐州刺史 Cài Bào 蔡豹, Línhuái Tàishǒu 臨淮太守 Liú Xiá 劉遐, Xiānbēi Duàn Wényāng 鮮卑段文鴦, and others to attack him.
Duàn Wényāng 段文鴦 was then with his elder brother Pǐdī 匹磾 in Yàncì 厭次.
In the winter of the 15th year,
Shí Lè’s Left and Right Chief Clerks, Zhāng Jìng and Zhāng Bīn,
and Left and Right Sīmǎs Zhāng Qūliù and Chéng Xiá, among others, urged Lè to assume an imperial title,
but Lè refused.
In the eleventh month,
his generals and subordinates again requested Lè to assume the titles of Grand General, Grand Chányú, Inspector of Jìzhōu, and Prince of Zhào,
following the precedents of the Han Emperor Zhāoliè in Shǔ and Wèi Wǔ in Yè.
They proposed to establish the twenty-four commanderies including Hénèi as the State of Zhào,
with all Grand Administrators serving as Grand Mentors (nèi shǐ).
Following the model of the Yǔ Gòng,
the borders of Jìzhōu were restored.

At this time, the twenty-four commanderies of Hénèi, Wèi, Jí, Dùnqiū, Píngyuán, Qīnghé, Jùlù, Chángshān, Zhōngshān, Chánglè, Lèpíng, Zhàoguó, Guǎngpíng, Yángpíng, Zhāngwǔ, Bóhǎi, Héjiān, Shàngdǎng, Dìngxiāng, Fányáng, Yúyáng, Wǔyì, Yānguó, and Lèlíng constituted the State of Zhào.
According to the Yǔ Gòng,
Wèi Wǔ restored the borders of Jìzhōu,
extending south to Mèngjīn,
west to Lóngmén,
east to the Yellow River,
and north to Sāiyuán.
The three provinces of Bīng, Shuò, and Sī were abolished.
The Jìn dynasty never established Shuòzhōu;
the abolition of Shuòzhōu here,
it is unknown who established it.
Lè consented.
On the day Wùyín,
he ascended to the position of Prince of Zhào.
Shí Lè,
courtesy name Shìlóng.
He designated the year as the "First Year" (yuánnián), in imitation of the states during the Spring and Autumn period.
At first,
Lè, seeing the chaos of the age,
and the excessiveness of laws and regulations,
ordered the Law Clerk Guàn Zhì
(Guàn
is the surname;
Zhì
is the given name)
to compile the "Xīnhài System" (Xīnhài Zhì) in five thousand characters.
After it had been in use for more than ten years,
formal laws and regulations (lǜlìng) were adopted.

When in court, he offered his fullest counsel;

felt resentful.

The three states combined their forces to attack Guī.

(When a flock of crows sees food,

"Although the two states have withdrawn,

The Yǔwén clan's soldiers numbered several tens of thousands,

"The Yǔwén chief has brought his entire nation as invaders;

preparation.)

Hán Shòu of Liáodōng said to Guī:

Guī then allowed Hàn to remain in Túhé.
Xī Dúguān heard of this and said:

Hàn knew of this,

The Yǔwén clan's cavalry, upon seeing the envoy,

The troops were all panicked and confused,

Huī captured all of their troops,

The imperial seal

Héng

Lóngxiáng Chief Clerk Sòng Gāi,

Huī advanced his title to General Lóngxiáng,

"Shí knew of their plot
and arrested Liú Hóng and killed him."
According to the Jìn Chūnqiū,
it records
"Yán Shè, Zhào Áng";
and Hóng died after Shí was killed.
We follow this account.
[Hóng] said:
"The lord has already died,
why kill me!"
Chū, enraged,
cut off his tongue and imprisoned him,
then had him torn apart by chariots in the Gūzāng marketplace,
and executed several hundred of his confederates.
Zuǒ Sīmǎ Yīn Yuán and others, seeing that Shí's son Zhāng Jùn was still young,
acclaimed Zhāng Mào as Governor (Cǐshǐ) of Liángzhōu and Duke of Xīpíng,
pardoned the people within his territory,
and appointed Jùn as General Fǔjūn.
10 On the day Bǐngchén,
Zhào generals Xiè Hǔ and Chángshuǐ Xiàowèi Yǐn Chē conspired to rebel,
associating with Bā chieftains Jù Xú, Kù Péng, and others.
When the plot was discovered,
Hǔ and Chē were both executed.
Zhào Zhǔ Yào imprisoned Xú, Péng, and fifty others in Āfáng
and was about to kill them.
Āfáng
was the old site of the Qín Āfánggōng,
also called Āchéng.
"When a sage king employs punishments,
he only executes the chief evildoers;
it is not appropriate to kill many people."
[He] argued,
kowtowing until his head bled.
Yào was furious
and, considering him to be aiding the rebels, imprisoned him.
He killed all of Xú, Péng, and the others,
displayed their corpses in the marketplace for ten days,
then threw them into the water.
Thereupon, all the Bā people revolted,
acclaiming Bā chieftain Jù Qúzhī as their lord.
He styled himself Dà Qín
and changed the era name to Píngzhào.
More than 300,000 Dī, Qiāng, Bā, and Jié from the four mountains responded to him.
Guānzhōng fell into great chaos,
and the city gates were closed during the day.
Zǐyuǎn again submitted a memorial from prison, remonstrating.
Yào tore up his memorial with his own hand and said:
"Dàlì slave,
Dàlì
is the name of a Rong tribe;
Zǐyuǎn was probably of Rong origin.
Still daring to act like this,
do you wish to die later rather than sooner!"
He shouted at his attendants to kill him quickly.
Zhōngshān Wáng Yǎ, Guō Sì, Zhū Jì, Hūyán Yàn, and others remonstrated, saying:
"Zǐyuǎn is imprisoned,
his fate uncertain,
yet he does not forget to remonstrate;
this is the utmost loyalty.
Even if Your Majesty cannot adopt his advice,
why kill him?
If Zǐyuǎn is executed this morning,
we, your ministers, will also die by evening,
to highlight Your Majesty's fault.
The world will abandon Your Majesty and depart.
With whom will Your Majesty reside?"
Yào's anger subsided,
and he pardoned him.
Yào commanded his internal and external forces to be on high alert,
intending to personally lead an expedition against Qúzhī.
Zǐyuǎn again remonstrated, saying:
"If Your Majesty can truly use my strategy,
it can be settled in one month,
and the imperial carriage need not personally go on campaign."
Yào said:
"You may try to explain it."
Zǐyuǎn said:
"They do not have great ambitions,
nor do they seek to achieve what is beyond their hopes.
They believe the affairs of emperors and kings
are not what ordinary people aspire to.
They only wish to escape death.
Your Majesty might as well issue a grand amnesty,
and let them start anew.
As for those whose families, old and young, were previously enslaved in Xīguān due to their involvement with Hǔ, Chē, and other matters,
release them all
and let them recruit each other,
allowing them to return to their occupations.
Since they have been given a path to life,
why would they not surrender?
If any among them know their crimes are serious
and remain fortified without dispersing,
I request that you lend me 5,000 weak soldiers,
and I will certainly behead them for Your Majesty.
Xiāo
refers to the unfilial owl.
The Shuō Wén states:
On the summer solstice,
owls are caught,
dismembered,
and their heads hung on a tree.
Hence, hanging a head is now called xiāoshǒu (beheading).
The character 'wèi'
is pronounced yú-wěi.
The character 'xiāo'
is pronounced jiān-yáo.
Now, the rebels cover the mountains and valleys;
Mí
means 'full'.
Bèi
is pronounced pí-yì.
I fear they cannot be eliminated in just months or years."
Yào was greatly pleased,
and immediately issued a grand amnesty that day,
appointing Zǐyuǎn as Chējì Dà Jiāngjūn, Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī, and Dūdū Yōng-Qín Zhēngtǎo Zhū Jūnsì.
Zǐyuǎn garrisoned at Yōngchéng,
and over 100,000 people surrendered.
He moved his army to Āndìng,
and all the rebels surrendered.
Only more than 5,000 families of the Jù clan and its relatives held out in Yīnmì.
Zǐyuǎn advanced and attacked them,
annihilating them.
He then led his troops to patrol Lǒngyòu.
Previously, over 100,000 Dī and Qiāng settlements
occupied strategic strongholds and refused to submit.
Their chieftain, Xūchú Quánqú, styled himself King of Qín.
Zǐyuǎn advanced to his stronghold,
and Quánqú led his troops out to resist,
but was defeated in all five battles.
Quánqú wished to surrender,
but his son, Yīyú, spoke loudly to the multitude, saying:
"Previously, when Liú Yào himself came,
he could do nothing against us,
much less this detached force.
Why speak of surrender!"
He led 50,000 elite soldiers
to press against Zǐyuǎn's camp gate at dawn.
The generals wanted to attack him,
but Zǐyuǎn said:
"Yīyú is brave and fierce,
unrivaled at present.
The soldiers he leads
are even more elite than ours.
Moreover, his father has just been defeated,
so his anger is currently at its peak.
His momentum cannot be withstood.
It is better to let him be,
and attack him after his spirit is exhausted."
So he fortified his camp and did not engage in battle.
Yīyú showed signs of arrogance.
Zǐyuǎn observed his lack of preparation,
and at night,
ordered his troops to eat a meal in their armor.
At dawn,
just as a great wind made the dust obscure the vision,
Zǐyuǎn led all his forces out to ambush him,
capturing Yīyú alive
and seizing all his troops.
Quánqú was greatly terrified,
disheveled his hair and lacerated his face, requesting to surrender.
Zǐyuǎn reported to Yào,
appointing Quánqú as Zhēngxī Jiāngjūn and Xīróng Gōng.
Qǐ
means 'to open' (to report).
To openly state one's affairs to report to a superior is called qǐ.
Yào appointed Zǐyuǎn as Dà Sītú and Lù Shàngshū Shì.
Yào established a grand academy [Tàixué],
selecting one thousand five hundred people from the populace who were intelligent and teachable,
and chose Confucian officials to instruct them.
He built the Fēngmíng Guàn
and the West Palace,
and erected the Língxiāo Tái at Hàochí.
Sīmǎ Biāo said: "Hào is within the Shànglín Yuàn."
Méng Kāng said: "Southwest of Cháng'ān there is Hàochí."
The *Gǔ Shǐ Kǎo* says: "King Wǔ moved to Hào;
it is the Hàochí in Fēngtíng, Cháng'ān."
"Hào" and "Hào" are cognate.
*[Pronounced] Hài, according to the dictionary.*
Court attendants Qiao Yù and Hé Bāo submitted a memorial,
arguing:
"Lord Wén of Wèi, succeeding after a period of chaos and ruin,
conserved resources and loved the people,
and when building palaces and residences,
did so at the appropriate time and with suitable restraint,
thus he was able to revive the legacy of Kāngshú
and extend the dynasty for nine hundred years.
Wèi was destroyed by the Dí people,
and Lord Wén moved to Qǔqiū.
Wearing clothes of coarse cloth
and caps of large silk,
he devoted himself to cultivating talent and training farmers,
facilitating commerce and benefiting artisans.
He first established cities and built palaces
at the opportune moment and with appropriate regulations.
The common people were pleased,
the state became prosperous and wealthy,
and Wèi was thereby revived.
From Kāngshú's initial enfeoffment in Wèi
until Qin finally destroyed it,
the dynasty lasted for over nine hundred years.
Common folk in the marketplaces all criticized his extravagance, saying: 'The cost of one observatory
would be enough to pacify Liángzhōu!'
This means the effort and resources to erect one observatory
would be enough to pacify the Zhāng clan west of the Yellow River.
By imitating the Qióngtái and building the Língxiāo Tái,
the labor and expense involved
would be tens of millions [compared to] Fēngmíng Guàn;
if these resources were used for the military,
then Wú and Shǔ could be conquered, and Qí and Wèi unified!
Wú
refers to Jìn;
Shǔ
refers to Lǐ Tè;
Qí
refers to Cáo Yì;
Wèi
refers to Shí Lè.
It would be four *lǐ* in circumference,
thirty-five *zhàng* deep,
with a coffin of copper,
adorned with gold.
Such an expenditure of resources
is surely beyond what the nation can afford.
Qín Shǐhuáng sealed off three springs,
but before the earth was dry, it was damaged.
*See Liú Xiàng's memorial in the thirty-first scroll, in the first year of Yǒngshǐ during Emperor Chéng of Hàn's reign.*
*[The character] gān [means] dry.*
A tomb that is not excavated
is why the sage kings practiced economical burials;
this is a deep and far-reaching consideration.
How can Your Majesty, in this era of restoration,
Yào quelled the disturbance of the Jìn clan and established himself;
hence his ministers referred to it as a restoration.
Yào issued an edict saying:
'The two court attendants are earnest and possess the spirit of the ancients;
they can be called ministers of the state.
All construction projects for palaces and residences are to be ceased;
the regulations for my tomb [shòulíng]
shall entirely follow the methods of Bālíng.
Yù is enfeoffed as the Lord of Ānchāng,
and Bāo as the Lord of Píngyú,
both holding the title of Grand Master of Remonstrance.
Moreover, this shall be proclaimed throughout the realm,
so that everyone knows that this humble court
desires to hear of its faults.'
He also abolished the Fēngshuǐ Yòu and distributed it to the poor.
Fēngshuǐ originates from the Southern Mountains of Jīngzhào,
flows northeast and empties into the Wèi River.
Yào established a park on both sides of the Fēngshuǐ.
Zǔ Tì's general Hán Qián and Hòu Zhào's general Táo Bào were separately occupying the former city of Chénchuān.
Bào occupied the west tower,
and Qián occupied the east tower.
Bào exited through the south gate,
and Qián through the east gate,
confronting each other for forty days.
Tì filled cloth sacks with earth to resemble rice,
and sent over a thousand men to transport them up the tower.
He also sent several men to carry actual rice,
resting by the road.
Bào's soldiers pursued them,
abandoning their loads and fleeing.
Bào's soldiers, long hungry,
upon obtaining the rice,
believed that Tì's troops were well-fed and abundant,
and became even more fearful.
First, he transported sacks filled with earth to make Qián suspicious;
then he had men carry rice to lure Bào's soldiers,
showing them the truth.
Tì sent Hán Qián and another general, Féng Tiě, to ambush them at the Biànshuǐ.
*The Shuǐ Jīng Zhù says: The Làngdàngqú River
flows east from Zhōngmóu,
and upon reaching Jùnyí county,
divides into two rivers.
The southern branch is called the Shāshuǐ;
the eastern branch is called the Biànshuǐ.
The Biànshuǐ flows east into Liángjùn.*
Bào fled under cover of night
and encamped at Dōngyàn Chéng.
*This is the Yàn county of the Hàn Dynasty's Dōngjùn.
Later Wèi established Dōngyàn county,
belonging to Chénliújùn.
Suí changed it to Zuòchéng county,
belonging to Dōngjùn.
Táng assigned it to Huázhōu.*
Bào's soldiers were already fearful,
and their provisions were captured by Tì,
hence they fled during the night.
Féng Tiě occupied the two towers,
and Tì garrisoned Yōngqiū.
*Fēngqiū and Yōngqiū counties
both belonged to Chénliújùn.
The *Chūnqiū Zhuàn* mentions the defeat of the Dí at Chángqiū,
which is within Fēngqiū's borders.
Yōngqiū
was an ancient state.*
Many of Hòu Zhào's garrisons and settlements defected to Tì,
and Hòu Zhào's territory gradually shrunk.
Before this,
Zhào Gù, Shàngguān Sì, Lǐ Jù, and Guō Mò had been attacking each other.
Tì swiftly sent envoys to mediate and reconcile them,
showing them the consequences of their actions,
and consequently they all submitted to Tì's command.
In autumn,
seventh month,
an imperial edict added the title of General Pacifying the West [Zhènxī Jiāngjūn] to Tì.
In the army,
Tì shared hardships with his officers and soldiers,
restrained himself and was generous,
encouraged and supervised agriculture and sericulture,
and welcomed and settled new adherents.
Even the humble and lowly were bound by his kindness and courtesy.
Regarding the various forts along the Yellow River,
those who had hostages [rènzǐ] in Hòu Zhào
were allowed to be affiliated with both sides.
*Those residing on the border of both territories
were allowed to be affiliated with both sides,
using this as a stratagem.*
*This indicates they had not yet submitted.*
The fort commanders were all grateful,
and whenever Hòu Zhào had a different plan,
they would secretly report it.
From this, many victories were achieved,
and south of the Yellow River,
many rebelled against Hòu Zhào and returned to Jìn.
Tì trained his troops and accumulated grain
in preparation for taking the territory north of the Yellow River.
King Lè of Hòu Zhào was troubled by this,
so he issued an edict to Yōuzhōu to repair Tì's ancestral tombs,
and assigned two families to guard the tombs.
*Tì was from Fànyáng,
where his ancestral tombs were located.*
*[The character] xià [is pronounced] xiá jià fān.*
He sought to establish diplomatic relations and mutual markets.
Tì did not reply to the letter,
but allowed the mutual markets,
thereby gaining tenfold profit.
Tì's gate commandant, Tóng Jiàn, killed Zhōu Mì, the Administrator of Xīncài,
and surrendered to Hòu Zhào.
*The Xìng Pǔ says: Descendants of Zhuānxù's son Lǎo Tóng adopted this as their surname.*
He sent Mì's head to Tì, saying:
"Rebel ministers and fleeing officials
are my deep enemies.
The evil [they commit against] the general
is also my evil."
Tì greatly appreciated this,
and from then on, if people from Hòu Zhào rebelled and sought to return to Tì,
Tì would not accept them.
He forbade his generals from invading or harming the people of Hòu Zhào,
and the border region
gradually found peace.
Tì allowed the various forts along the Yellow River to be affiliated with both sides;
this was the wisdom of using spies.
However, Shí Lè repaired Tì's ancestral tombs
and beheaded Tóng Jiàn, sending his head,
which was also a way to weaken Tì's ambition to push across the Yellow River.
In the 12th month of autumn,
on the day Xīnwèi,
Zhōu Fǎng, the Inspector of Liángzhōu, passed away.
Fǎng was skilled in comforting
his soldiers,
and all were willing to die for him.
He knew that Wáng Dūn harbored disloyal intentions,
and privately often ground his teeth in anger.
Grinding teeth
means rubbing the upper and lower teeth together.
He dared not yet rebel.
Dūn dispatched Guō Shū, a Gentleman of the Interior and Attendant Official, to supervise the army in Xiāngyáng.
The Emperor appointed Gān Zhuó, the Inspector of Xiāngzhōu, as Inspector of Liángzhōu,
to oversee all military affairs north of the Miǎn River,
and garrison Xiāngyáng.
Wáng Dūn feared Zhōu Fǎng and dared not rebel,
but when he raised his army,
he did not consider Gān Zhuó a threat;
he can indeed be called a cunning hero!
The Emperor summoned him to be Right Censor;
Dūn detained him and did not send him.
In the 13th month, Shí Lè, the King of Hòuzhào, dispatched Hǔ, the Duke of Zhōngshān, leading 40,000 infantry and cavalry to attack Xú Kān.
Kān sent his wife and children as hostages,
begging to surrender,
and Lè granted it.
Lè allowed Kān to surrender
because he was not yet able to capture Kān;
observing his subsequent killing of Kān
is enough to understand his intentions.
質 (zhì),
pronounced zhì.
Biànxiàn
belonged to Lǔguó.
Liú Xù said: During the Suí dynasty, Sǐshuǐxiàn was established in the old city of Biànxiàn,
and during the Táng dynasty, it belonged to Yǎnzhōu.
Bào retreated to defend Xiàpī,
but was defeated by Xú Kān.
Hǔ led his troops to fortify Fēngqiū and then returned,
relocating three hundred aristocratic families to Chóngrénlǐ in Xiāngguó.
Chóngrénlǐ
was named by Lè,
to house families of officials and gentry.
In the 14th month, Shí Lè, the King of Hòuzhào, was very strict in his application of the law,
especially severe in tabooing
the character "Hú".
Lè himself was a Hú person,
so he made it a taboo.
Initially there was a prohibition against entering the palace gates.
A drunken Hú man, riding a horse,
burst into the carriage gate.
Lè was furious
and reprimanded Fēng Zhù, the minor Judicial Officer of the palace gate.
The Judicial Officer
was an official like the Imperial Censor.
The two stars in the middle of the southern border of the Purple Palace are called the Left and Right Judicial Officers.
The former officials of Jìn set up the official system for Lè,
taking this name to establish the Judicial Officer of the palace gate,
with Zhāng Bīn as the Grand Judicial Officer,
overseeing all court affairs,
hence the minor Judicial Officer was placed at the palace gate.
翥 (zhù),
pronounced zhāng shù fān.
Zhù replied:
"Just now there was a drunken Hú,
riding a horse and charging in.
I severely admonished and tried to stop him,
but he could not be reasoned with."
Lè laughed and said:
"Hú people are indeed difficult to reason with."
He pardoned him and did not punish him.
Lè ordered Zhāng Bīn to lead the selection process,
initially establishing five ranks,
and later revising it to nine ranks.

He commanded dukes, ministers, and commanders of provinces and commanderies to annually recommend one person each who was a Xiućai (talented scholar), Zhìxiào (extremely filial), Liánqīng (incorruptible), Xiánliáng (virtuous and good), Zhíyán (frank in speech), or Wǔyǒng (brave in battle).
In the 15th month, Zhāng Mào, Duke of Xīpíng, established his nephew Jùn as heir apparent.
After Cài Bào's defeat,
he intended to go to Jiànkāng to confess his guilt,
but Wáng Shū, the Northern Commander of the Interior, stopped him.
The Emperor heard of Bào's retreat
and sent an envoy to arrest him.
Shū surrounded Bào with soldiers at night.
Bào thought it was another bandit,
and led his subordinates to attack them.
When he heard it was an imperial edict,
he stopped.
Shū seized Bào and sent him to Jiànkāng.
In winter,
the 10th month,
on the day Bǐngchén,
he was executed.
In the 17th month, Wáng Dūn killed Xiàng Shuò, the Grand Administrator of Wǔlíng.
The historical record notes Wáng Dūn's unauthorized executions
to highlight his crime of disrespecting the sovereign.
When the Emperor first took command of Jiāngdōng,
Dūn and his cousin Dǎo wholeheartedly supported him.
The Emperor also trusted and relied on them.
Dūn commanded all punitive expeditions.
In the 5th year of Yǒngjiā of Emperor Huái,
the Emperor appointed Dūn as Inspector of Yángzhōu
and added him as Supervisor of all military affairs for punitive expeditions.
His campaigns against Huá Yì, Dù Tāo, Wáng Jī, and Dù Zēng
were all his accomplishments.
從 (cóng),
pronounced cái yòng fān.
The Department of State Affairs was the foundation of all governance.
Dǎo served as Recorder of the Affairs of the Department of State Affairs,
meaning he controlled all political affairs.
People at the time had a saying about them:
"The Wángs and the Sǐmǎs
share the world."
Later, Dūn, relying on his achievements
and the powerful might of his clan,
gradually became more arrogant and unrestrained.
The Emperor feared and detested him,
so he brought in Liú Wǎi, Diāo Xié, and others as his confidants,
gradually curbing the power of the Wáng clan.
Dǎo also gradually became estranged.
Kǒng Yú, a Gentleman of the Central Secretariat, reported Dǎo's loyalty and wisdom,
stating he had rendered meritorious service in founding the dynasty
and should be given more trust and responsibility.
The Emperor sent Yú out as Chief Clerk to the Minister of Works.
Dǎo was able to act with sincerity and knew his place,
remaining calm and indifferent.
All discerning people praised his skill in handling success and failure.
But Dūn became increasingly resentful.
History says Dǎo's descendants enjoyed blessings and prosperity
because of this, while Dūn's life and head were lost,
and disaster befell Wáng Hán and his son.
處 (chǔ),
pronounced chāng lǚ fān.
Previously,
Dūn invited Shěn Chōng of Wúxīng to be his staff officer.
Chōng recommended Qián Fèng of the same commandery to Dūn,
and Dūn made him Staff Officer of the Armory.
Both men were cunning flatterers and treacherous villains.
Knowing Dūn had rebellious intentions,
they secretly helped him achieve them
and devised strategies for him.
Dūn favored and trusted them,
and their influence extended both inside and outside the court.
Dūn submitted a memorial appealing for Dǎo,
and his words were full of resentment and complaint.
Dǎo sealed it and returned it to Dūn.
Dǎo was Recorder of the Affairs of the Department of State Affairs,
so he saw Dūn's memorial first
and thus sealed it and returned it.
為 (wèi),
pronounced yú wěi fān;
the same applies to the wēi below.
Wáng Chéng, Prince of Qiáo, Left General,
was loyal, honest, and had noble conduct.
The Emperor personally trusted him.
One night,
he summoned Chéng,
showed him Dūn's memorial,
and said:
"Wáng Dūn's achievements of recent years
have earned him sufficient position and responsibility.
Yet his demands are unending,
and his words have come to this point.
What shall we do?"
Chéng replied:
"Your Majesty, if you do not deal with this earlier,
it will come to this day.
Dūn will surely become a disaster."
Liú Wèi 劉隗 made plans for the emperor,
sending trusted confidants to guard the various regions.
It happened that Dūn 敦 submitted a memorial requesting Shěn Chōng 沈充, the Internal Scribe of Xuānchéng 宣城, to replace Gān Zhuó 甘卓 as the Inspector of Xiāngzhōu 湘州.
The emperor said to Chéng 氶:
"Wáng Dūn's 王敦 treacherous rebellion is already manifest.
I fear I will become like Emperor Huì 惠帝,
the situation is not far off."
This means he would be controlled by powerful ministers, like Emperor Huì 惠帝.
"To control the junction of the three prefectures –"
The three prefectures
refer to Jīngzhōu 荊州, Jiāozhōu 交州, and Guǎngzhōu 廣州.
"How about it?"
In ancient times, the Son of Heaven called feudal lords of the same surname "paternal uncles" (bófù 伯父) or "maternal uncles" (shúfù 叔父).
Chéng 氶
was a grand-nephew of Emperor Xuān 宣帝;
and the emperor
was a great-grandson of Emperor Xuān 宣帝,
so according to their relations, Chéng 氶 was also an uncle.
"I shall obey your imperial command.
I will do as much as my strength allows,
how dare I refuse!
However, Xiāngzhōu 湘州 has suffered from the aftermath of the Shǔ 蜀 bandits."
The Shǔ 蜀 bandits
refer to the rebellion of Dù Tāo 杜弢.
"If it is obtained,
it would take about three years
before it can be used for military purposes."
This references Rǎn Yǒu's 冉有 reply to Kǒngzǐ 孔子 in the Analects.
Jí 即
means "to follow."
Zhū Xī 朱熹 said: Jí 即
means "to approach."
Róng 戎
means "military."
Bǐ 比 is pronounced bì-mèi.
"Even if I were to sacrifice my life,
it would be of no avail."
In the twelfth month,
an imperial edict stated:
"Since the Jìn 晉 dynasty was founded,
the appointment of regional commanders
has involved both close relatives and worthy individuals.
Therefore, let the Prince of Qiáo 譙, Chéng 氶, be appointed Inspector of Xiāngzhōu 湘zhōu."
Dèng Qiān 鄧騫 of Chángshā 長沙 heard of this
and sighed, saying:
"The calamity of Xiāngzhōu 湘zhōu
will come from this!"
Chéng 氶 traveled to Wǔchāng 武昌.
Dūn 敦 hosted a banquet for him,
and said to Chéng 氶:
"Your Highness has always been a refined and excellent scholar."
Yǎsù 雅素
means "ordinarily" or "usually."
Chéng 氶 replied:
"The Duke has not yet recognized me;
how can a lead knife be without any cutting use!"
This is a saying of Bān Chāo 班超 of the Later Hàn 漢.
[Dūn 敦 said:] "He knows not fear yet speaks boastfully;
this is enough to know that he is not martial
and can accomplish nothing."
So he allowed him to proceed to his post.
Although Chéng 氶 was loyal, he lacked talent.
Dūn 敦 observed him and knew he was incapable of achieving anything.
Both public and private affairs were in dire straits.
Chéng 氶 himself lived frugally,
and wholeheartedly worked to pacify and comfort the people,
earning a very good reputation for his abilities.
18 Gāogōulí 高句麗 raided Liáodōng 遼東.
Mùróng Rén 慕容仁 fought them,

After this, they dared not invade Rén's 仁 territory again.
1 In spring,
the second month,
Xú Kān 徐龕 again offered to surrender.

should probably be

4 Hòu Zhào's 後趙 Prince of Zhōngshān 中山, Hǔ 虎, attacked Duàn Pǐdī 段匹磾, the Inspector of Yōuzhōu 幽州, at Yàncì 厭次.

Wényāng 文鴦 cursed him, saying:

the incident is found in Volume 78, Yǒngjiā 永嘉 6th year of Emperor Huái 懷帝.
"I would rather die fighting

Mǎluópī 馬羅披

Tái shǐ 臺使

[Pǐdī 匹磾 said:] "You are unable to follow your brother's will,

Thus, the three prefectures of Yōu 幽, Jì 冀, and Bīng 并 all fell to Hòu Zhào 後趙.
Pǐdī 匹磾 did not treat Lè 勒 with courtesy,

After a long time,

Pǐdī's 匹磾 brothers and Shào Xù 邵續 were all killed,

to pacify the realm together.

To have previously relied on Wáng Dǎo but now to estrange and suspect him,

and lacking broad vision and foresight;

Huǎng,

Yǔ,

For a long time,
he did not cry,

1. In the spring,
the first month,
Guō Pú again submitted a memorial,
requesting an imperial pardon to be issued due to the birth of the imperial grandson.
Pú had already submitted a memorial last year requesting a general pardon;
the imperial grandson was born in the eleventh month of last year.
Fù,
pronounced Fúyòu.
On the day Yǐmǎo,
a general amnesty was granted,

Wáng Dūn appointed Pú as Jìshì Cānjūn (Secretarial Adjutant).

and knew that Dūn would surely rebel,
and that he himself would be implicated in the disaster.
He was greatly worried by this.
The Dà Jiāngjūn Yuàn (Adjutant to the Grand General) Chén Shù from Yǐngchuān died.
Pú mourned him with extreme sorrow,
saying:
"Sìzǔ,
how do you know this is not a blessing?"

was also a colleague in Dūn's administration.
Yān,
pronounced Yúqián.
As Dūn had already become estranged from the imperial court,
he detained and recorded prominent gentry members who had contemporary prestige to serve in his staff.
He appointed Yáng Màn and Xiè Kūn of Chén State as Zhǎngshǐ.
Màn was the elder brother's grandson of Hù.
Màn and Kūn were drunk all day,
so Dūn did not entrust them with affairs.
Dūn's gathering of prestigious figures was merely employing the old strategy of the princes of the Western Capital.
Hān,
pronounced Hùgān.
Dūn said to Kūn:
"Liú Wěi is treacherous and wicked,

I wish to eliminate the evil at the sovereign's side,
what do you think?"
Kūn replied:
"Wěi is indeed the instigator of calamity,

Yú Yán of the Later Hàn dynasty said: "City foxes and shrine rats
do not fear fumigation or burning."
This means they have something to rely on.
Also,
Wáng Shèng of Zhōngshān said: "Shrine rats are not flooded,
house rats are not smoked,
because of what they rely on."
The Éryǎ Yì states: Guǎn Zhòng said that a shrine is made by binding wood and plastering it.
Rats then take refuge there.
If one smokes them, one fears burning the wood;
if one floods them, one fears ruining the plaster.
This is why these rats cannot be killed:
because of the shrine.
This metaphor refers to those around the ruler.
"You are a mediocre talent,
how can you grasp the greater scheme of things!"
Kūn was sent out to be Yùzhāng Tàishǒu (Administrator of Yùzhāng),
but then detained and not allowed to leave.
On the day Wùchén,
Dūn raised troops in Wǔchāng,
and submitted a memorial listing Liú Wěi's crimes,
stating:
"Wěi is flattering, wicked, slanderous, and treacherous,
wielding power and bestowing favors at will,

exhausting and disturbing the gentry and common people,

Your subject, occupying the position of a prime minister,
cannot sit idly by and watch success or failure.
I shall advance my army to punish him.
If Wěi's head hangs in the court in the morning,
all armies will retreat in the evening.
In ancient times, Tài Jiǎ overturned his principles,
but fortunately accepted Yī Yǐn's loyal advice,
and the Yīn dao flourished again.
After Tāng died,
Tài Jiǎ overturned Tāng's laws and punishments.
Yī Yǐn banished him to Tóng.
After three years,
Tài Jiǎ repented his wrongdoing and blamed himself at Tóng.
Yī Yǐn, with ceremonial robes, escorted Tài Jiǎ back to Bó.
Relying on Yī Yǐn's instruction
to achieve his final goal.
Such events did happen in antiquity,
but they are not what a subject should do.
Then the four seas will be pacified,
and the state will be eternally secure."
Shěn Chōng also raised troops in Wúxìng to respond to Dūn.
Dūn appointed Chōng as Dà Dūdū, Dūhù Dōng Wú Zhū Jūnshì (Grand Commandant, Protector-General of all military affairs in East Wú).
When Dūn reached Wúhú,
he again submitted a memorial listing Diāo Xié's crimes.
The Emperor was greatly enraged.
On the day Yǐhài,
an edict stated:
"Wáng Dūn, relying on his favored status and divine protection,
dares to act with mad rebellion,
comparing Me to Tài Jiǎ,
wishing to see Me imprisoned.
How can this be tolerated?
What cannot be tolerated!
I shall now personally lead the six armies to punish this great rebel.
Whoever kills Dūn shall be enfeoffed as a marquis of five thousand households."
Dūn's elder brother, Hán, who was Guānglù Xūn (Minister of the Imperial Household), boarded a light boat and fled back to Dūn.
Tàizǐ Zhōngshùzǐ Wēn Jiǎo said to Púyè Zhōu Yǐ:

surely there will be no unwarranted acts?"
Yǐ said:
"Not so.
If a ruler is not Yáo or Shùn,
how can he be without fault?
How can a subject raise an army to threaten him!
Moving in such a way,
how can one say it is not rebellion!
Chǔzhòng is like a wolf, defiant and rebellious;
how can his intentions be limited!"
Wáng Dūn's
courtesy name was Chǔzhòng.
A wolf resembles a dog,
with a pointed head and white cheeks,
high in the front and broad in the back,
greedy and daring to defy people,
hence used as a metaphor.
Chǔ,
read Chāng-Lǚ fan.
Dūn initially raised an army,
sending an envoy to inform Liángzhōu Cìshǐ Gān Zhuó,

Zhuó agreed.
But when Dūn boarded his boat,
Zhuó did not come,
instead sending his Cānjūn Sūn Shuāng to Wǔchāng to remonstrate with Dūn and stop him.
Dūn was surprised and said:
"What did Lord Gān say to me before,

He must be worried that I pose a danger to the imperial court!
I am merely eliminating villains;
if the matter succeeds,
I will make Lord Gān a Gōng."
Promising Zhuó to make him a Gōng,
he tempted him with benefits,
wishing to make him join the rebellion.
Zhuó's intentions were hesitant.
Someone advised Zhuó:
"Provisionally agree with Dūn,
and wait until Dūn reaches the capital to attack him."
Zhuó said:
"In the past, during the chaos of Chén Mǐn,
I first followed him and then plotted against him (this event is described in volume 86, during Huìdì's Yǒngxīng second year and Huáidì's Yǒngjiā first year).
I have always been ashamed of that;
if I were to do the same again now,

Zhuó sent someone to inform Shùnyáng Tàishǒu Wèi Gāi of Dūn's intentions.
Gāi said:
"The reason I raised an army to resist the Hú bandits

Now Wáng Gōng raises an army against the Son of Heaven;

The historian says Gān Zhuó was not as loyal and resolute as Wèi Gāi.
Dūn sent Cānjūn Huán Pí to persuade Qiáowáng Chéng

Chéng sighed:
"I am probably going to die!

Yet, to die for loyalty and righteousness,

Chéng issued a proclamation appointing Chángshā Yú Kuī as Chángshǐ.
It so happened that Kuī was in mourning for his mother,

saying:

5. The Emperor summoned Dài Yuān (戴淵) and Liú Kuí (劉隗) to guard Jiànkāng (建康).
When Liú Kuí arrived,

Upon being admitted to the imperial presence,

The Emperor did not consent,

Sīkōng Wáng Dǎo (王導) led his younger cousin, Zhōnglǐngjūn (中領軍) Wáng Suì (王邃), Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn (左衞將軍) Wáng Yì (王廙), Shìzhōng (侍中) Wáng Kǎn (王侃), Wáng Bīn (王彬), and over twenty other clan members.

When the Emperor first governed Yángzhōu (揚州),

As Wáng Dūn was approaching,

Jīnchéng

Wáng Dūn arrived at Shítou (石頭),

Wáng Dūn followed this advice,
