Zhōu Zhá indeed opened the gates and admitted Dù Hóng.
Wáng Dūn occupied Shítou
and sighed, saying:
"I will no longer be able to perform deeds of great virtue!"
Wáng Dūn's disloyal intentions
were revealed in his words.
Fù (復),
read fúyòu.
"Why is that so?
Just let it be that from now on,
I forget and dismiss things day by day."
He meant that day by day,
he would gradually forget past events,
and thus the traces of suspicion between ruler and minister would also disappear day by day.
The emperor ordered Diāo Xié, Liú Wěi, and Dài Yuān to lead their forces to attack Shítóu.
Wáng Dǎo, Zhōu Yǐ, Guō Yì, Yú Tán, and others engaged in battle from three routes.
Xié's forces and the others were all greatly defeated.
The Crown Prince, Shào, heard of this
and wanted to personally lead the officers and soldiers to a decisive battle.
As he ascended his chariot, about to depart,
the Central Steward Wēn Qiáo seized the reins and admonished him, saying:
"Your Highness is the heir apparent of the state.
How can you so lightly risk your person for the realm!"
He drew his sword and cut the harness,
and the prince stopped.
Dùn, holding his troops, did not come to court.
He allowed his soldiers to plunder,
and the palace and government offices scattered in a rout.
Only the General of An’dōng, Liú Chāo, held his troops and directly guarded,
along with two Palace Attendants who remained by the emperor's side.
The emperor took off his military attire,
put on court robes,
and looked around, saying:
"If you want my position,
you should have said so earlier!
Why go so far as to harm the people like this!"
He also sent an envoy to tell Dùn:
"If you do not forget your original loyalty to the court,
and cease hostilities here,
then the realm can still be at peace together;
if not,
I shall return to Lángxié to make way for the worthy."
Diāo Xié and Liú Wěi, having been defeated,
both entered the palace
and saw the emperor in the eastern courtyard of the Tàijí Palace.
"Chú" (除)
refers to the palace steps.
Weeping and sobbing,
they advised him to avoid disaster.
Xié said:
"I ought to hold fast until death,
and dare not have second thoughts."
The emperor said:
"The situation is pressing now;
how can we not act!"
He then ordered horses and men to be given to Xié and Wěi,
so they could make their own plans.
Xié was old
and unable to ride a horse.
He had always been without favor or discipline,
and when he sought followers,
they all abandoned him.
He traveled to Jiāngchéng,
where he was killed by someone,
and his head was sent to Dùn.
Wěi fled to the Later Zhào,
where he became Grand Tutor to the Crown Prince and then died.
In the eighth year of Xiánhé of Emperor Chéng,
Liú Wěi died fighting Shí Hǔ at Tóngguān.
Could this be the same Liú Wěi?
The emperor ordered the dukes, ministers, and all officials to go to Shítóu to see Dùn.
Dùn said to Dài Yuān:
"In the battle the other day,
did you have any strength left?"
Yuān replied:
"How could I have had strength left to attack?
I simply lacked strength!"
Dùn said:
"What does the world think of my current undertaking?"
Yuān replied:
"Those who see the outward form call it rebellion;
those who grasp the true intent call it loyalty."
Dùn laughed and said:
"You can be called articulate."
He then said to Zhōu Yǐ:
"Bórén,
you have wronged me!"
In the first year of Jiànxīng of Emperor Mǐn,
Yǐ was besieged by Dù Tāo
and went to Dùn in Yùzhāng,
which Dùn considered a kindness.
"When you, Sir, with your war chariots, violated the order of the state,
your humble servant personally led the Six Armies,
but was unable to accomplish the task,
causing the imperial forces to flee and be defeated.
This is how I have wronged you!"
On the day Xīnwèi,
a general amnesty was declared.
Dùn was made Chancellor, Overall Supervisor of all internal and external military affairs, Director of the Imperial Secretariat, and Governor of Jiāngzhōu,
and enfeoffed as Duke of Wǔchāng Commandery.
He declined all these appointments and did not accept them.
Earlier,
when the Western Capital fell,
all four quarters urged the emperor to ascend the throne.
(See volume 90, Jiànwǔ first year.)
Fearing that the emperor's age would make him difficult to control,
they wished to deliberate on establishing someone else,
but Wáng Dǎo did not agree.
When Dùn conquered Jiànkāng,
he said to Dǎo:
"If you had not disregarded my words,
you would have almost brought about the ruin of your clan."
Dùn, seeing that the Crown Prince had courage and strategy
and was favored by the court and the populace,
wanted to falsely accuse him of unfilial conduct and depose him.
He convened a great assembly of officials
and asked Wēn Qiáo:
"By what virtue is the Crown Prince known?"
His voice and demeanor were both stern.
Qiáo replied:
"To plumb the depths and reach afar
is indeed beyond the measure of a shallow perspective;
viewed by rites,
he can be called filial."
(Meaning the Crown Prince possessed the talent to plumb the depths and reach afar,
and moreover fulfilled the rites of serving his parents,
thus dispelling Dùn's false accusation of unfilial conduct.)
Dùn's plot was thus thwarted.
The Emperor summoned Zhōu Yǐ to the Guǎngshì.
Guǎngshì
is the name of a hall.
"Recently, regarding important matters,
the two palaces are unharmed,
everyone is safe,
and the Grand General indeed lives up to expectations, does he not?"
Yǐ replied:
"The two palaces are as stated in the clear edict;
as for us officials, we cannot yet know."
Hùjūn Zhǎngshǐ Hǎo Gǔ and others urged Yǐ to avoid Dūn.
Yǐ replaced Dài Yuān as Hùjūn Jiāngjūn,
and appointed Hǎo Gǔ as Zhǎngshǐ.
"I hold the position of a great minister;
with the court suffering defeat,
how can I seek survival hiding in the grass,
and flee to the Hú and Yuè barbarians?"
Dūn's Cānjūn Lǚ Yī
had once served as a Táiláng.
The Jìn referred to Shàngshūláng as Táiláng.
Dài Yuān was a Shàngshū
and disliked him.
Yī said to Dūn:
"Zhōu Yǐ and Dài Yuān
both have high reputations,
sufficient to mislead the multitude.
Their recent words
showed no shame.
This refers to the two men's answers to Dūn's questions.
Zuò,
pronounced cái gè fān.
I fear there will certainly be concern for a repeat incident."
Dūn had long been jealous of the talents of the two men,
and his heart rather agreed with this.
He leisurely asked Wáng Dǎo:
"Zhōu and Dài
are the hopes of the north and south.
Zhōu Yǐ
was from Rǔnán;
Dài Yuān
was from Guǎnglíng.
When the Jìn clan moved south,
their names were foremost at the time.
Cóng,
pronounced qiān róng fān.
Dǎo did not answer.
He asked again:
"If not the Sānsī,
should they only be Lìngpú?"
Sānsī
are the Tàiwèi, Sītú, and Sīkōng;
Lìngpú
are the Shàngshūlìng and the Left and Right Púyè.
Dūn said:
"If not,
then they should simply be executed!"
Dǎo again did not answer.
On the day of bǐngzǐ,
Dūn sent his subordinate Jiāng Chénjùn Dèng Yuè to arrest Yǐ and Yuān.
Previously,
Dūn had said to Xiè Kūn:
"I shall make Zhōu Bórén Shàngshūlìng,
and Dài Ruòsī Púyè."
Dài Yuān's
courtesy name was Ruòsī.
He also asked Kūn:
"How are people's sentiments lately?"
Kūn replied:
"Although Your Excellency's actions
are intended to greatly preserve the altars of soil and grain,
the common talk indeed does not comprehend your lofty righteousness.
This means that people discussed Dūn's raising troops and advancing on the capital, saying it was not a righteous act.
Then people's feelings will be calm and settled!"
Dūn angrily said:
"Are you foolish?
The two men are not worthy,
I have already arrested them!"
Kūn was shocked and lost self-control.
Cānjūn Wáng Jiāo said:
" 'Many, many are the gentlemen,
through whom King Wén was at peace.'
This is a poem from the 'Wénwáng' section of the Dàyǎ of the Shī.
Jǐ,
pronounced zǐ lǐ fān.
Dūn was furious,
wishing to execute Jiāo,
and no one dared to speak.
Kūn said:
"Your Excellency has undertaken a great enterprise,
not killing a single person.
If Jiāo, by offering advice, offends your will,
and is immediately used to smear the drums with blood,
(If you say something is good, but there is something bad in it,
your servant presents the bad to perfect the good;
if you say something is bad, but there is something good in it,
your servant presents the good to replace the bad.)
Xìngǔ means killing a person and smearing blood on the drum.
Wǔ,
pronounced wǔ gù fān.
Dūn then released him,
demoting him to Lǐngjūn Zhǎngshǐ.
That a Grand General's office Cānjūn was demoted to Lǐngjūn Zhǎngshǐ
is enough to show that Dūn's residence was more important than other residences.
He was Hún's clan grandson.
When Yǐ was arrested,
he passed by the Imperial Ancestral Temple,
and loudly declared:
"The treacherous minister Wáng Dūn
overthrows the altars of soil and grain,
and unjustly kills loyal ministers!
If the gods have spirits,
they should quickly kill him!"
The arresting officer wounded his mouth with a halberd,
and blood flowed to his heels,
but his demeanor remained composed,
and all who watched shed tears.
He and Dài Yuān were executed outside the southern gate of Shítóu.
The Emperor sent Shìzhōng Wáng Bīn to comfort Dūn.
Bīn had always been friendly with Yǐ,
and first went to mourn Yǐ,
then saw Dūn.
Dūn was surprised by his sorrowful expression
and asked him.
Bīn said:
"I just cried for Bórén,
and my feelings could not be restrained."
Dūn angrily said:
"Bórén brought the execution upon himself;
furthermore, any ordinary person encountering you
(Considering Wáng Bīn's character,
that Yǐ treated him as an ordinary person
also shows his integrity.)"
Bīn said:
"Bórén was a noble man,
your elder brother's close friend.
Although he showed no bluntness or outspokenness at court,
should be
Cháo,
pronounced zhí yáo fān.
yet after a pardon, he was subjected to capital punishment,
which is why I am grieved and saddened."
Thereupon, he indignantly rebuked Dūn, saying:
"You have raised your banner and defied the rightful order,
killing loyal and good people,
plotting rebellion,
and disaster will reach your household!"
His words were fervent and impassioned,
and tears flowed down with his voice.
Dūn was greatly enraged,
and said in a stern voice:
"You are so mad and perverse!
Do you think I cannot kill you?"
At that time, Wáng Dǎo was present,
and feared for him,
urging Bīn to stand up and apologize.
Bīn said:
"My feet hurt, so I cannot bow;
besides, what is there to apologize for?"
Dūn said:
"Which is worse, foot pain or neck pain?"
Bīn showed no fear
and ultimately refused to bow.
Later, Wáng Dǎo reviewed the official documents of the Zhōngshū
and found Yǐ's memorial appealing on his behalf.
He held it and wept, saying:
"Although I did not kill Bórén,
Bórén died because of me."
He blamed himself for not answering Dūn's three questions.
"I have failed this good friend!"
Shěn Chōng captured Wúguó
and killed its Nèishǐ Zhāng Mào.
Initially,
Wáng Dūn (王敦) heard that Gān Zhuó (甘卓) had raised an army,
and was greatly alarmed.
Zhuó's (卓) nephew, Gān Áng (甘卬), was a staff officer for Dūn (敦).
Dūn (敦) sent Áng (卬) back
to persuade Zhuó (卓), saying:
"Your action is indeed a loyal act of a subject,
and I will not blame you for it.
My family's situation is dire,
so I had no choice but to do this.
I imagine you will immediately return your army to Xiāngyáng (襄陽),
and we shall then renew our good relations."
Although Zhuó (卓) admired loyalty and righteousness,
he was by nature prone to doubt and indecisiveness.
His army was stationed at Zhūkoǔ (豬口).
The Commentary on the Waterways states: "The Miǎn River (沔水) flows southeast past the east of Yúndù (雲杜) County in Jiāngxià (江夏) Commandery.
The Xià River (夏水) comes from the west to join it."
The note says: "This is also called Zhākǒu (⿰月者口)."
Zhākǒu (⿰月者),
is the same as Zhū (豬).
The army lingered,
not advancing for several weeks.
After Dūn (敦) had captured Jiànkāng (建康),
he dispatched an envoy from the court with a Zōuyú (騶虞) banner to halt Zhuó's (卓) army.
Zhū Fāng (諸方),
means waiting for various regional governors (fāng zhèn 方鎮) to mobilize their armies together.
Zōuyú (騶虞)
is a benevolent beast;
therefore, a Zōuyú (騶虞) banner was used to halt the army.
Shǐ (使)
is pronounced suō lì.
Zhuó (卓) wept and said to Áng (卬):
"What I am worried about
is precisely today.
Furthermore, if His Majesty is well,
and the Crown Prince is safe,
even if I were upstream from Dūn (敦),
I would not immediately endanger the state.
If I were to directly occupy Wǔchāng (武昌),
Dūn's (敦) power would be pressured,
and he would certainly seize the Son of Heaven to sever the hopes of the empire.
It is better to return to Xiāngyáng (襄陽)
and reconsider our future plans."
He immediately ordered the army to turn back.
Commandant Qín Kāng (秦康) and Yuè Dàoróng (樂道融) persuaded Zhuó (卓), saying:
"If we divide our troops to cut off Péngzé (彭澤) –
Péngzé (彭澤) County
belongs to Yùzhāng (豫章) Commandery.
Pénglǐ (彭蠡) Lake flows into the Great River from here.
If we divide our troops to cut off the mouth of Péngzé (彭澤) Lake,
we can prevent Dūn (敦)'s forces from communicating up and downriver.
Duàn (斷)
is pronounced dīng guǎn.
His troops will naturally disperse,
and he can be captured in one battle.
For a general to raise an army of righteousness and then stop halfway,
I secretly believe this is not acceptable for you.
Moreover, among your subordinates,
the officers and soldiers each seek their own advantage.
If they wish to return west,
I fear it may not be possible."
Zhuó (卓) did not agree.
Dàoróng (道融) wept and remonstrated day and night,
but Zhuó (卓) would not listen;
Dàoróng (道融) died of sorrow and indignation.
Zhuó (卓) was originally gentle and mild,
but suddenly became stubborn and unyielding.
This qiáng (強)
refers to violence.
Sè (塞)
refers to obstruction and lack of clear passage.
Sè (塞)
is pronounced xī zé.
His demeanor became disturbed,
and his actions were abnormal.
Those who recognized this knew he was about to die.
Wáng Dūn (王敦) appointed Xīyáng (西陽) Prince Yáng (羕) as Grand Tutor,
added Wáng Dǎo (王導) as Minister of Personnel,
and Wáng Yì (王廙) as Inspector of Jīngzhōu (荊州).
He replaced numerous officials and military commanders in various garrisons,
with hundreds being transferred, demoted, or dismissed;
some appointments made in the morning were changed in the evening,
entirely according to his whim.
When Dūn (敦) was about to return to Wǔchāng (武昌),
Xiè Kūn (謝鯤) spoke to Dūn (敦), saying:
"Since Your Excellency arrived in the capital,
you have claimed illness and not attended court.
Therefore, although you have achieved great merit, people's hearts are not yet truly convinced.
If you were to attend court today,
and ease the minds of both ruler and minister,
then everyone would be pleased and submit."
Dūn (敦) said:
"Can you guarantee there will be no trouble?"
Kūn (鯤) replied:
"I recently had an audience,
and the Emperor cleared a seat (sīxí 側席),
eager to see Your Excellency.
(Wángzhě sīxí dài xián 王者側席待賢, A king clears a seat for a worthy man).
Kūn (鯤) used this phrase.
Chí (遲)
is pronounced zhí èr,
meaning 'to await.'
There will certainly be no danger.
Mùrán (穆然)
means with respect and harmony.
I request to accompany you."
Dūn (敦) became enraged and said:
"Even if I kill a few hundred people like you,
what harm would it do to the times!"
In the end, he left without attending court.
In summer,
the fourth month,
Dūn (敦) returned to Wǔchāng (武昌).
Initially,
Zhōu Jí (周級), the Prefect of Yídū (宜都) and Tiānmén (天門) —
In the sixth year of Yǒng'ān (永安) of Sūn Hào (孫晧) of Wú (吳),
Tiānmén (天門) Commandery was established by partitioning Wǔlíng (武陵).
Chōng (充) County has Sōngliáng (松梁) Mountain.
The mountain has a rock,
where the opening is dozens of *zhàng* high.
Its height
is such that shooting upwards with a crossbow
does not reach its top.
It is named Tiānmén (天門),
and the commandery was named after it.
Sòng Bái (宋白) says: "The Shímén (石門) County of Lǐzhōu (澧州).
Wú (吳) established Tiānmén (天門) Commandery.
Suí (隋) abolished the commandery and made it Shímén (石門) County."
He sent his nephew, Zhōu Gāi (周該), to secretly go to Chángshā (長沙)
to express allegiance to Yù (乂).
Shēn (申)
means "to make clear";
kuǎn (款)
means "sincerity."
Yù (乂) sent Gāi (該) and Assistant Zhōu Qí (周崎) of Shàolíng (邵陵) to covertly seek help.
This is not Shàolíng (邵陵) of Yǐngchuān (潁川).
In the first year of Bǎodǐng (寶鼎) of Sūn Hào (孫晧) of Wú (吳),
Shàolíng (邵陵) Commandery was established by partitioning the Northern Commandant of Línglíng (零陵).
Qí (崎)
is pronounced qiū qí.
Jiān (間)
is pronounced gǔ xiàn.
Yù (乂) also told Qí (崎) to tell the people in the city
that the Grand General had already captured Jiànkāng (建康),
and Gān Zhuó (甘卓) had returned to Xiāngyáng (襄陽),
so external aid was naturally cut off.
This means, judging from the circumstances,
external aid was already severed.
Luó (邏)
is pronounced láng zuǒ.
Yǔ (語)
is pronounced niú jù.
When he reached the city walls,
he shouted loudly:
"Reinforcements are coming soon,
hold fast!"
Yù (乂) killed him.
Yù (乂) interrogated Gāi (該) to death,
but he never revealed his purpose,
and Zhōu Jí (周級) thus escaped punishment.
As Yù (乂) and others' attacks intensified daily,
Dūn (敦) again sent letters and memorials obtained from the court,
ordering Yù (乂) to shoot them into the city to show Yù (乂).
When the people in the city learned that the imperial court had not held,
none were without sorrow and regret.
The siege lasted nearly a hundred days,
Liú Yì (劉翼) died in battle,
and the dead and wounded soldiers piled up.
On the day of Guǐsì (癸巳),
Yù (乂) captured Chángshā (長沙),
and Yù (乂) and others were all captured.
When Yù (乂) was about to kill Yú Kuī (虞悝),
his children and disciples wept aloud before him.
Kuī (悝) said:
"Everyone will eventually die in life.
Now that our whole family becomes spirits of loyalty and righteousness,
what more is there to regret!"
Yì loaded Chéng and Yì Xióng onto a cage cart and sent them to Wǔchāng.
All the subordinate officials fled and dispersed.
Only the Chief Clerk, Huán Xióng, and the Registrar of the Western Bureau, Hán Jiē,
as well as the registrars of various bureaus in the administration,
ruined their clothes and became servants following Chéng,
not leaving his side.
"Ruined their clothes" means
they ruined their normal attire
and wore the clothes of servants.
Lǐ,
read as lì zhì fān.
(Dùn) feared them and killed them.
Hán Jiē and Wǔ Yán held their resolve even more firmly.
The Inspector of Jīngzhōu, Wáng Yì, acting on Wáng Dùn's order,
killed Chéng on the way.
Jiē and Yán escorted Chéng's coffin to the capital,
buried him, and then left.
Yì Xióng reached Wǔchāng,
his spirit resolute and passionate,
without any sign of fear.
Dùn sent someone to show Xióng a declaration and enumerate his crimes.
Xióng said:
"These are indeed true.
It's a pity that Xióng's position was humble and his strength weak,
so he could not save the nation from its difficulties.
To die today
is precisely what I desire."
Dùn, fearing his righteous words,
released him
and sent him to his lodging.
Everyone congratulated him.
Xióng smiled and said:
"How could I possibly live!"
Soon after, Dùn sent someone to secretly kill him.
Wèi Yì was very urgent in his search for Dèng Qiān.
All the villagers feared for him.
Qiān smiled and said:
"He wants to use me, that's all.
He has just gained control of the province
and has killed many loyal and good people,
so he seeks me to satisfy public expectations."
Thereupon, he went to see Yì.
Yì happily said:
"You are
the Jiě Yáng of antiquity."
The Zuǒ Zhuàn states: Duke Chǔ besieged Sòng;
Jìn sent Jiě Yáng to Sòng
to prevent them from surrendering to Chǔ;
the people of Zhèng captured him and presented him to Chǔ.
Duke Chǔ heavily bribed him
to reverse his message,
but he refused;
after the third time,
he agreed.
He was placed on a tower chariot
and ordered to call out to the people of Sòng and inform them;
he then delivered his lord's message (as originally intended).
Duke Chǔ was about to kill him
and sent someone to speak with him, saying:
"You already promised me (bù gǔ) and then went back on it,
why?
Hasten to your execution!"
He replied:
"Having received my orders and set out,
I would rather die than betray them.
How could I be bribed?
My agreement with you, my lord,
was to fulfill my mission;
to die and fulfill my mission
is my good fortune."
Duke Chǔ spared him and sent him home.
Jiě,
read as hù mǎi fān.
An imperial edict appointed Táo Kǎn as Inspector of Xiāngzhōu.
Wáng Dùn memorialized that Kǎn should return to Guǎngzhōu
and be granted the additional title of Sanqí Chángshì.
On the jiǎwǔ day of the 6th month,
Empress Yáng of Former Zhào died.
Her posthumous title was Xiànwén.
The family of Gān Zhuó all advised Zhuó to prepare for Wáng Dùn,
but Zhuó did not comply.
He completely dispersed his troops for farming,
and whenever he heard advice,
he would get angry.
The Administrator of Xiāngyáng, Zhōu Lǜ, secretly received Wáng Dùn's instruction
and falsely claimed that there were many fish in the lake,
persuading Zhuó to send out all his attendants to catch fish.
In the 5th month,
on the yǐhài day,
Lǜ led his troops to attack Zhuó in his sleeping quarters,
killed him,
and sent his head to Dùn,
also killing all of Zhuó's sons.
Dùn appointed Zhōu Fǔ, a Central Supervisor of Affairs, to oversee all military affairs north of the Miǎn River,
replacing Zhuó to garrison Miǎnzhōng.
From Nánzhèng to Xiāngyáng,
is where the Miǎn River flows,
hence it is called Miǎnzhōng.
(Zhōu Fǔ) was the son of (Zhōu) Fǎng.
Once Dùn had achieved his ambition,
his arrogance and insolence grew excessively.
Most of the tributes from all directions entered his mansion,
and generals, ministers, and provincial governors all came from his circle.
Shùn had the Four Peaks (sìyuè) and Twelve Pastors (shí'èrmù),
hence later those who governed regions
were called Yuèmù.
He only listened to the words of two people,
and those whom they slandered invariably died.
He appointed Zhūgě Yáo, Dèng Yuè, Zhōu Fǔ, Lǐ Héng, and Xiè Yōng as his claws and teeth.
Chōng and others were all cruel, dangerous, arrogant, and indulgent,
greatly establishing military camps and mansions,
encroaching upon fields and residences,
and plundering markets and roads.
Those with discernment all knew that their downfall was imminent.
In the autumn,
7th month,
Hǔ, Duke of Zhōngshān of Later Zhào, captured Tàishān,
and seized Xú Kān, sending him to Xiāngguó.
King Lè of Later Zhào put him in a sack
and smashed him to death from the top of a hundred-foot tower,
ordering Wáng Fúdū and others' wives and children to disembowel and eat him.
Kān had killed Wáng Fúdū,
as seen in the previous scroll, Dàxīng 3rd year.
The Inspector of Yǎnzhōu, Xī Jiàn, had been in Zōushān for three years,
having tens of thousands of followers.
In the first year of Mǐn Dì's Jiànxīng era,
the Emperor appointed Jiàn to garrison Zōushān,
and now several years had passed.
The phrase "three years, having tens of thousands of followers"
means that after Jiàn was garrisoned in Zōushān,
within three years,
the number of people who rallied to him reached this figure.
Xī,
read as chǒu zhī fān.
The common people suffered from famine,
digging up wild rats and hibernating swallows to eat them.
Swallows
hibernate after autumn.
(Xī Jiàn) withdrew and garrisoned at Héféi.
The Right Assistant of the Department of State Affairs, Jì Zhān,
believing Jiàn to possess esteemed reputation and pure virtue,
and that he should calmly serve in the central government,
submitted a memorial requesting his recall.
Thereupon, he was recalled and appointed Shàngshū.
Many fortified villages between Xú and Yǎn surrendered to Later Zhào,
and Later Zhào established prefects and magistrates to pacify them.
Wáng Dùn personally assumed the governorships of Níng and Yì provinces.
This was not by imperial decree,
hence the historian recorded it as "personally assumed."
In winter,
10th month,
on the jǐchǒu day,
Wáng Yì, the Marquis Kāng of Wǔlíng and Inspector of Jīngzhōu, died.
Wáng Dùn appointed Wáng Suì, the Grand Administrator of Xiàpī, as Governor-General of all military affairs in Qīng, Xú, Yōu, and Píng provinces,
garrisoning at Huáin.
He appointed Grand General Wèi Wáng Hán as Governor-General of all military affairs south of the Miǎn River,
concurrently serving as Inspector of Jīngzhōu.
Wáng Liàng of Dānyáng, Grand Administrator of Wǔchāng, was made Inspector of Jiāozhōu.
The "Textual Variations" states: Liàng's biography:
"In the 3rd year of Yǒngxīng,
Dùn appointed Liàng as Inspector of Jiāozhōu."
Commentary: The 3rd year of Yǒngxīng
was the 1st year of Emperor Huì's Guāngxī era,
so Liàng's biography is mistaken.
(He was) killed.
In the 3rd year of Jiànhéng of Sūn Hào of Wú,
Jiāozhǐ was divided to establish Xīnxīng Commandery.
In the 3rd year of Tàikāng of Emperor Wǔ,
its name was changed to Xīnchāng Commandery.
(He was) beheaded.
Shuò raised an army and besieged Liàng at Lóngbiān.
Lóngbiān County
belonged to Jiāozhǐ Commandery,
and both the province and commandery administrations were located there.
After Zǔ Tì died,
Later Zhào repeatedly raided Hénán,
capturing Xiāngchéng and Chéngfù.
Chéngfù County
belonged to Pèi Commandery in Former Hàn,
to Rǔnán Commandery in Later Hàn,
and to Qiáoguó in Wèi and Jìn.
This "Hénán" generally refers to the area south of the Yellow River,
not specifically Hénán Commandery.
Fù,
read as fǔ.
Zǔ Yuē, Inspector of Yùzhōu, was unable to resist
and withdrew to garrison at Shòuchūn.
Later Zhào then seized Chénliú,
and the area between Liáng and Zhèng became unsettled again.
In 11th month,
Xún Zǔ, Duke Yuán of Línyǐng, was appointed Grand Commandant.
On the xīnyǒu day,
he died.
13 Wáng Dūn 王敦 罷 (was dismissed from the post of) Sītú 司徒,
and amalgamated it with the Chéngxiàng Fǔ 丞相府 (Chancellery).
Wáng Dūn 王敦 made the officials of the Sītú 司徒 department a liú fǔ 留府 (resident office).
When Dūn 敦 returned to Wǔchāng 武昌,
he remotely controlled court politics,
hence the liú fǔ 留府 existed in Jiànkāng 建康.
14 The Emperor, troubled and indignant, fell ill.
In the intercalary month,
on the jǐchǒu 己丑 day,
he passed away;
aged forty-seven.
The Emperor was overly modest and frugal but lacked foresight and decisiveness,
thus the great enterprise was not restored, and internal strife arose.
On the gēngyín 庚寅 day,
the Crown Prince ascended the imperial throne,
declared a great amnesty,
and honored his birth mother, Lady Xún 荀氏, as Jiàn'ān Jūn 建安君.
15 In the twelfth month,
Zhào Zhǔ Yào 趙主曜 buried his parents in Sùyì 粟邑,
and declared a great amnesty.
The tomb measured two li 周 (circumference) at its base,
and was one hundred chi 尺 high at the top.
It was estimated to have employed sixty thousand laborers,
and took one hundred days to complete.
The laborers worked at night,
illuminated by fat and candles,
which caused the people great suffering.
Yóu Zǐyuǎn 游子遠 remonstrated,
but was not heeded.
16 Hòu Zhào 后赵 Púyáng Jǐnghóu 張賓 Zhāng Bīn died.
Hòu Zhào Wáng Lè 后赵王勒 cried mournfully for him,
saying:
"Does Heaven not wish to accomplish my affairs?
Why did it take my Yòuhóu 右侯 (Right Marquis) so early!"
Chéng Xiá 程遐 replaced him as Yòu Chángshǐ 右長史 (Right Chief Clerk).
Xiá 遐 was the uncle of the heir apparent, Hóng 弘.
Whenever Lè 勒 discussed matters with Xiá 遐,
and they disagreed,
he would often sigh and say:
"The Right Marquis has left me,
and now makes me work with these people!
Is this not cruel!"
Kù 酷 means
cǎn 慘 (miserable)
and nüè 虐 (tyrannical),
meaning Heaven took Zhāng Bīn's 張賓's life,
how cruel and miserable it is to me.
17 Zhāng Mào 張茂 sent his general Hán Pú 韓璞 to lead troops to take the lands of Lǒngxī 隴西 and Nán'ān 南安,
and established Qín Zhōu 秦州 (Qin Province).
After Nányáng Wáng Bǎo 南陽王保 died,
Chén Ān 陳安 could not hold onto them,
so Mào 茂 subsequently took them.
Shuài 帥
is read as lǜ 率.
18 Mùróng Guī 慕容廆 sent his heir apparent, Huǎng 皝, to attack Duàn Mòpèi 段末柸,
entered Lìngzhī 令支,
plundered over a thousand households of its residents, and returned.
Sùzōng Míng Huángdì Shàng 肅宗明皇帝上
His taboo name was Shào 紹,
his courtesy name Dàojī 道畿.
He was the eldest son of Yuán Dì 元帝.
The criteria for posthumous titles states: "One whose thoughts are far-reaching and resolute is called Míng 明."
Tàiníng Yuánnián 太寧元年
(guǐwèi 癸未, 323 CE)
1 In spring,
the first month,
Chéng Lǐ Xiāng 成李驤 and Rèn Huí 任回 raided Táidēng 臺登.
Táidēng Xiàn 臺登縣
belonged to Yuèsuī Jùn 越巂郡.
Jiǔzhōu Yàojì 九州要記 states: "Táidēng Xiàn 臺登縣 has Nuòchuān 奴諾川,
between Yīngwǔ Shān 鸚鵡山 and Hēishuǐ 黑水.
The Ruòshuǐ 若水 flows from beneath it;
the Yellow Emperor's son Chāngyì 昌意 descended to reside by the Ruòshuǐ 若水,
which is this place."
Yuèsuī Tàishǒu Lǐ Zhāo 越巂太守李釗 and Hànjiā Tàishǒu Wáng Zài 漢嘉太守王載.
Hànjiā 漢嘉 was originally the Qián Hàn 前漢 (Former Han) Qīngyī Xiàn 青衣縣,
belonging to Shǔjùn 蜀郡.
In the Hòu Hàn 后汉 (Later Han) Shùn Dì's 順帝 Yángjiā Èrnián 陽嘉二年 (133 CE),
it was renamed Hànjiā 漢嘉.
Shǔ 蜀 was divided to form Hànjiā Jùn 漢嘉郡.
Zhāo 釗
is pronounced Zhāo 昭.
2 In the second month,
on the gēngxū 庚戌 day,
Yuán Dì 元帝 was buried in Jiànpíng Líng 建平陵.
3 In the third month,
on the wùyín 戊寅 day, the first day of the month,
the reign title was changed.
4 Ráo'ān 饒安, Dōngguāng 東光, and Ānlíng 安陵 three counties suffered a disaster.
All three counties belonged to Bóhǎi Jùn 渤海郡,
only Dōngguāng 東光 was an old county from the Hàn 汉;
Ráo'ān Xiàn 饒安縣 was the Qián Hàn 前漢's Qiāntóng Xiàn 千童縣.
Hòu Hàn Líng Dì 后汉灵帝 renamed it Ráo'ān 饒安.
Ānlíng Xiàn 安陵縣 was established by Jìn 晋.
At the time, all were lands of Hòu Zhào 后赵.
Fifteen thousand people died.
5 Hòu Zhào 后赵 raided Péngchéng 彭城 and Xiàpī 下邳.
Xúzhōu Cìshǐ Biàn Dūn 徐州刺史卞敦 and Zhēngběi Jiāngjūn Wáng Suì 征北將軍王邃 retreated to defend Xūyí 盱眙.
Dūn 敦 was
Hú's 壼's paternal cousin.
6 Wáng Dūn 王敦 plotted to usurp the throne,
and subtly urged the court to summon him;
the Emperor issued a personal imperial edict summoning him.
In summer,
the fourth month,
Dūn 敦 was granted huángyuè 黃鉞 (yellow battle-ax) and bānjiàn 班劍.
Liú Liáng's 劉良's commentary on Wénxuǎn 文選 states: Bānjiàn 班劍
refers to those who hold swords and walk in procession.
Lǚ Xiàng 呂向 said: Bān 班
means liè 列 (rank, array),
meaning to have brave warriors arrayed holding swords as an honor guard.
Lǐ Zhōuhàn 李周翰 said: Bānjiàn 班劍
is a wooden sword without an edge,
made to resemble a sword,
and painted with patterns,
hence it is called bān 班.
Jìn Zhì 晋志 (Records of Jin) states,
civil and military officials of high rank
were provided twenty hǔbēn 虎賁 (Imperial Guards)
holding bānjiàn 班劍.
He entered court without hurrying,
and wore his sword and shoes into the hall.
Dūn 敦 moved his garrison to Gūshú 姑孰,
and encamped at Yúhú 于湖.
Gūshú 姑孰 was
the land of Qián Hàn Dānyáng Chūngǔ Xiàn 前漢丹楊春穀縣.
Today's Tàipíng Zhōu Dāngtú Xiàn 太平州當塗縣
is the land of Gūshú 姑孰.
Three li south of the county,
there is Gūshú Xī 姑孰溪,
which flows west into the Great River (Yangtze).
Yúhú Xiàn 于湖縣
was originally where the Wú 吳 Dūnóng Xiàowèi 督農校尉 (Colonel Overseeing Agriculture) governed.
In Wǔ Dì's 武帝 Tàikāng Èrnián 太康二年 (281 CE),
Dānyáng Xiàn 丹楊縣 was divided to establish Yúhú Xiàn 于湖縣.
Dù Yòu 杜佑 said: "Xuānzhōu Dāngtú Xiàn Chéng 宣州當塗縣城
is the Jìn Gūshú Chéng 晋姑孰城.
The old city of Yúhú 于湖 is south of the county."
Zhāng Shùnmín 張舜民 said: "Today's Tàipíng Zhōu 太平州 spans Gūshú Xī 姑孰溪."
Lù Yóu 陸游 said: "Gūshú Chéng 姑孰城 is north of Dāngtú 當塗.
Today's prefectural city is situated precisely on Gūshú Xī 姑孰溪.
To the southeast of the stream, several peaks are like dark eyebrows,
probably Qīngshān 青山.
From Gūshú Xī 姑孰溪, travel along the middle,
thirty li to Dàxìn Kǒu 大信口.
Exiting the mouth,
ascend the river past Dà Hè Shān Jī 大褐山磯 and Xiǎo Hè Shān Jī 小褐山磯,
and then past Xiāo Jī 蟂磯.
Wúhú 蕪湖,
which is Yúhú 于湖,
has Wáng Dūn Chéng 王敦城 along the Great River,
with a grand and open appearance."
Bìng 並 is pronounced pòlàng 步浪.
Kǎoyì 考異 states: Jìn Chūnqiū 晉春秋 and Hòu Wèi Shū Jiàn Jìn Zhuàn 后魏書僭晉傳 say
"encamped at Wúhú 蕪湖."
Jìn Shū Míng Dì Jì 晋書明帝紀 says
"descended to encamp at Yúhú 于湖."
We follow the latter now.
Dūn 敦 personally assumed the post of Yángzhōu Mù 揚州牧 (Governor of Yangzhou).
Dūn 敦 desired to rebel,
and Wáng Bīn 王彬 remonstrated with him bitterly.
Dūn 敦's expression changed,
he signaled to his attendants,
intending to arrest Bīn 彬.
Bīn 彬, with a stern expression, said:
"Last year you killed your elder brother,
and now you want to kill your younger brother too!"
Jìn Shū Wáng Bīn Zhuàn 晋書王彬傳 considers
that Bīn's 彬's paternal cousin, Léng 稜, was killed by Dūn 敦,
hence the statement.
I believe that the one who killed Léng 稜 was Wáng Rú 王如;
although it was at Dūn's 敦's instigation,
it was still through Rú's 如's hand.
Moreover, Léng 稜 was Dūn's 敦's paternal cousin.
This statement "killed his elder brother"
likely refers to Dūn's 敦's killing of Wáng Chéng 王澄,
which is recorded in volume 80, Huái Dì Yǒngjiā Liùnián 懷帝永嘉六年.
Bīn 彬 was made Yùzhāng Tàishǒu 豫章太守.
7 Hòu Zhào Wáng Lè 后赵王勒 sent envoys to establish good relations with Mùróng Guī 慕容廆,
but Guī 廆 seized them and sent them to Jiànkāng 建康.
8 Chéng Lǐ Xiáng and others attacked Níngzhōu.
The Inspector, Bāozhōng Zhuàng Gōng Wáng Xùn, dispatched General Yáo Yuè and others to resist them.
They fought at Tángláng.
According to the Commentary on the Water Classic, Tángláng
is the same as the county of Tángláng.
In the Former Hàn dynasty, it belonged to Jiānwéi Commandery.
In the Later Hàn dynasty, it was abolished.
The Records of Commanderies and Kingdoms states: The Zhūtí County, belonging to Jiānwéi Tributary State, has Tángláng Mountain.
The mountain is full of poisonous plants.
In the height of summer,
flying birds passing over it cannot leave.
Shǔ established Zhūtí Commandery,
and Tángláng County belonged to it.
Yuè pursued them to Lúshuǐ.
Chéng's soldiers scrambled to cross,
and over a thousand people drowned.
Yuè, judging the distance too great,
dared not cross and returned.
Xùn was furious that Yuè had not pursued them to the end,
and in a great rage,
he whipped him.
His rage was so intense
that his cap split, and he died.
Xùn had been in the province for fourteen years.
In the fourth year of Huái Dì's Yǒngjiā era,
Xùn arrived at Níngzhōu,
and by this time, exactly fourteen years had passed.
The people of the province established his son Jiān to administer the provincial government affairs.
"Province" refers to Níngzhōu;
"government" refers to the Southern Barbarian Commander's office.
9 Táo Kǎn, the Inspector of Guǎngzhōu, dispatched troops to rescue Jiāozhōu.
Before they arrived,
Liáng Shuò captured Lóngbiān
and seized the inspector Wáng Liàng's credentials.
Liàng refused to yield them,
so Shuò severed his right arm.
Liàng said:
"I do not even fear death; what is a severed arm!"
He died more than ten days later.
10 In the sixth month,
on the day Rénzǐ,
Yǔ Shì was made empress.
Her elder brother, Zhōnglǐngjūn Liàng, was appointed Zhōngshū Jiān.
11 Liáng Shuò occupied Jiāozhōu,
but his cruelty alienated the people.
Táo Kǎn sent Staff Officer Gāo Bǎo to attack Shuò
and beheaded him.
An imperial edict appointed Kǎn as Inspector of Jiāozhōu,
promoting him to Zhēngnán Dàjiāngjūn and Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī.
Not long after,
Rúǎn Fàng, the Secretary of the Ministry of Personnel, requested to be appointed Inspector of Jiāozhōu,
which was granted.
Fàng traveled to Níngpǔ.
The Guǎngzhōu Chronicle states: In the twenty-third year of Emperor Xiàn of Hàn's Jiàn'ān era,
Wú divided Yùlín Commandery to establish Níngpǔ Commandery.
The Jìn Tàikāng Geographic Records states: In the seventh year of Emperor Wǔ's Tàikāng era,
the Dūwèi of Hépǔ Tributary State was reformed to establish Níngpǔ Commandery.
In the Táng dynasty, it was Níngpǔ County of Héngzhōu.
Pǔ is pronounced pángwǔ fān.
Fàng prepared a feast for Bǎo,
and with hidden soldiers, killed him.
Bǎo's soldiers attacked Fàng,
and Fàng fled,
escaping.
He arrived at the province but died of illness a short time later.
Fàng was a cousin of Xián.
Rúǎn Xián was famous between the Wèi and Jìn dynasties.
12 Chén Ān besieged Zhào's Zhēngxī Jiāngjūn Liú Gòng at Nán'ān.
Xiūtú Wáng Shí Wǔ led his troops from Sāngchéng towards Shàngguī to rescue him.
He joined Gòng in a combined attack on Ān,
greatly defeating him.
Ān gathered his remaining eight thousand cavalry
and fled to garrison Lǒngchéng.
In autumn,
in the seventh month,
Zhào's ruler Yào personally led a siege of Lǒngchéng,
and separately dispatched troops to besiege Shàngguī.
Ān frequently sallied out to fight,
but was always defeated.
The Right Army General Liú Gàn attacked Píngxiāng
and captured it.
Píngxiāng County,
in the Hàn dynasty, belonged to Tiānshuǐ Commandery;
in the Jìn dynasty, it belonged to Lüèyáng Commandery.
Ān left his generals Yáng Bózhī and Jiāng Chōng'ér to defend Lǒngchéng,
and personally led his elite cavalry to break through the encirclement
and flee to Shǎnzhōng.
Shǎnzhōng is south of Lǒngchéng.
Shǎn is the same as Xiá,
pronounced hùjiá fān.
Ān wielded a seven-chi broadsword in his left hand
and an eighteen-chi serpent spear in his right.
At close range, both sword and spear struck,
often killing five or six men.
From a distance, he would ride around shooting arrows and fleeing.
He was also swift and agile like a bird.
Fighting Ān,
after three engagements,
he managed to seize his serpent spear.
"Three engagements" means three rounds of battle.
Ān abandoned his horse and hid with his attendants in the mountains.
Zhào's soldiers searched for him
but could not find his whereabouts.
The next day,
Ān sent his general Shí Róng to scout Zhào's forces.
Zhào's Fǔwēi Jiāngjūn Hūyán Qīngrén captured him.
He interrogated Róng about Ān's location,
but Róng steadfastly refused to speak,
so Qīngrén killed him.
When the rain cleared,
Qīngrén followed the tracks
and captured Ān in a mountain ravine,
beheading him.
Ān was good at caring for his officers and soldiers,
sharing their hardships.
Upon his death,
the people of Lǒngshàng remembered him
and composed the "Song of the Brave Warrior" for him.
The song goes:
"On Lǒngshàng, there was a brave warrior, Chén Ān,
though small in stature, his heart was vast.
He loved and cared for his officers and soldiers as if they were his own flesh and blood,
with dappled horses and iron-inlaid saddles.
His seven-chi broadsword surged like a torrent,
his eighteen-chi serpent spear circled left and right,
ten charges, ten decisive blows, none could stand before him.
After just three engagements, he lost his serpent spear,
abandoning his dappled horse, he hid in a secluded ravine,
for our foreign aid, his head was suspended.
The westbound water, the eastbound river,
once gone, it never returns, what can we do, my child!"
Wéi is pronounced yúwěi fān.
Lǒngchéng surrendered.
Another general, Sòng Tíng, beheaded Zhào Mù
and surrendered Shàngguī.
Yào moved over two thousand households of the great clans Yáng and Jiāng from Qínzhōu to Cháng'ān.
The Dī and Qiāng all sent hostages requesting to surrender.
"Rèn" refers to hostages.
He was enfeoffed as Píngxiāng Gōng.
13 The emperor, fearing the pressure from Wáng Dūn,
wanted Xī Jiàn as an external ally.
He appointed Jiàn as Inspector of Yǎnzhōu
and Supervisor of all military affairs west of the Jiāng in Yángzhōu,
stationing him at Héfèi.
Wáng Dūn, wary of this,
submitted a memorial appointing Jiàn as Shàngshū Lìng.
In the eighth month,
an edict recalled Jiàn.
On his way, he passed through Gūshú.
Dūn discussed the prominent figures of the Western Court with him,
saying:
"Yuè Yànfǔ was merely a man of limited talent.
If we examine his true merits,
how could he surpass Mǎn Wǔqiū?"
At that time, the area east of the Jiāng referred to Luòyáng as the Western Court.
Yuè Guǎng's courtesy name was Yànfǔ.
Mǎn Fèn's courtesy name was Wǔqiū.
Cháo is pronounced zhíyáo fān.
Jiàn replied:
"Yànfǔ's demeanor was calm and impartial.
During the downfall of Mǐnhuái, he was gentle yet able to uphold righteousness.
Mǎn Wǔqiū was a man who lost his integrity.
How can he be compared?"
This event is found in volume 83, in the first year of Emperor Huì's Yǒngkāng era.
Mǎn Fèn had collected the resignations of the Crown Prince's palace officials,
and during Zhào Wáng Lún's usurpation,
Fèn also offered the imperial seals and cords,
which is why he was said to have lost his integrity.
Jiàn added:
"At that time, the crisis was critical and urgent."
Dūn disliked his words
and did not meet him again,
detaining him for a long time without dispatching him.
Dūn's partisans all urged him to kill Jiàn,
but Dūn did not comply.
Jiàn returned to the court
and immediately conspired with the emperor to suppress Dūn.
14 Hòu Zhào's Zhōngshān Gōng, Hǔ, led 40,000 infantry and cavalry to attack Āndōng Jiāngjūn Cáo Yì.
Many commanderies and counties in Qīngzhōu surrendered to him.
He then besieged Guǎnggù.
The Shuǐjīng Zhù states: Guǎnggù City
was four *li* northwest of Guǎng County in Hàn's Qí Commandery.
It was surrounded by steep ravines,
protected by deep moats and water.
It was built by Cáo Yì.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: Guǎnggù City
was ancient Lè'ān City.
We now observe that there is Guǎnggù City forty *li* west of Yìdū County in Qīngzhōu.
Dù Yòu said: There is a very wide great ravine,
hence it is called Guǎnggù.
[The character] 降,
is pronounced *hù jiāng fān*.
[Cáo Yì] was sent to Xiāngguó and killed there,
and 30,000 of his followers were buried alive.
Hǔ wanted to kill all of Yì's followers.
Qīngzhōu Cìshǐ Liú Zhēng said:
"If I am kept now,
it is to govern the people;
if there are no people to govern,
I will return!"
Hǔ then left 700 men and women to be assigned to Zhēng,
making him garrison Guǎnggù.
15 Zhào Zhǔ Yào campaigned westward from Lǒngshàng to attack Liángzhōu.
He dispatched his general Liú Xián to attack Hán Pú at Jìchéng,
and Húyán Yàn to attack Níngqiāng Hùjūn Yīn Jiàn at Sāngbì.
Sāngbì
was likely within the territory of Nán'ān.
Camps were arrayed for over a hundred *li*.
The sound of gongs and drums shook the earth,
and the waters of the Hé River boiled.
Zhāng Mào's various garrisons along the river
all fled at the mere sight of them.
Yào announced his intention to cross by a hundred routes simultaneously,
heading directly for Gūzāng.
Liángzhōu was greatly alarmed.
Cānjūn Mǎ Jí urged Mào to personally go out and resist.
Chángshǐ Fàn Huī was enraged
and requested to execute him.
Jí said:
"Fàn Gōng is a worthless scholar,
a minor talent at impeachment and recommendation,
who does not consider the great plans for the family and state.
Your father and you, my lord, have wished to punish Liú Yào for the imperial court for many years.
Now Yào has come himself.
The sentiments of those far and near
are all observing your actions, my lord.
You must establish a testament of trustworthiness and courage to meet the expectations of Qín and Lǒng.
Although our strength may not be a match,
the situation does not permit us not to go out."
Mào said:
"Excellent!"
He then went out to garrison Shítou.
Shítou
was east of Gūzāng City.
"Liú Yào has raised the armies of the Sānqín,
sweeping in with his victorious momentum.
It is said that he recently defeated Chén Ān,
and comes with victorious momentum.
[The character] 卷
is read *juǎn*.
Zhēn said:
"Although Yào's army is numerous,
his elite soldiers are few.
They are mostly a motley collection of Dī and Qiāng tribesmen,
whose loyalty and trust are not yet firm.
Furthermore, he has worries from Shāndōng,"
meaning that he was planning against Shí Lè.
"If this drags on for a long time,
how will he contend with us for the lands west of the Hé River?
If he does not retreat within two *xún* (twenty days),
I request to lead a few thousand worn-out soldiers
to capture him for you, my lord."
Mào was pleased,
and ordered Zhēn to lead troops to rescue Hán Pú.
Zhào's generals eagerly wanted to cross the river.
Zhào Zhǔ Yào said:
"Although the momentum of our army is strong,
two-thirds of those who came did so out of fear of our might.
The central army is weary and exhausted;
in reality, it is difficult to use.
This indeed matched Chén Zhēn's prediction.
If I awe them with my prestige,
and if Zhāng Mào's memorial does not arrive within the middle *xún*,
then I will have failed you, my lord."
Mào soon sent an envoy to declare himself a vassal,
presenting an countless number of horses, cattle, sheep, and precious treasures.
Yào appointed Mào as Shìzhōng, Dūdū Liáng Nán Běi Qín Liáng Yì Bā Hàn Lǒngyòu Xīyù Zá Yí Xiōngnú Zhū Jūnshì, Tàishī, Liángzhōu Mù,
enfeoffed him as Liáng Wáng,
and bestowed the Jiǔxī upon him.
16 Yáng Nándí heard of Chén Ān's death,
and was greatly alarmed.
He fled south with his younger brother, Jiāntóu, to Hànzhōng.
Zhào's Zhèn Xī Jiāngjūn Liú Hòu pursued and attacked them,
obtaining great spoils before returning.
Zhào Zhǔ Yào appointed Dà Hónglú Tián Sōng as Zhèn Nán Dà Jiāngjūn and Yìzhōu Cìshǐ,
to garrison Qiúchí.
Nándí sent an envoy to request surrender to Chéng.
Chéng's Ān Běi Jiāngjūn Lǐ Zhì received a bribe from Nándí
and did not send Nándí to Chéngdū.
When the Zhào forces retreated,
he immediately sent Nándí back to Wǔdū,
and Nándí then occupied the strategic terrain and refused to submit.
Zhì regretted his miscalculation
and urgently requested to attack him.
Xióng sent Zhì's elder brother, Shìzhōng and Zhōng Lǐngjūn Hán, with Zhì to advance from Báishuǐ;

The Kǎoyì (考異) states: The Jìn Chūnqiū (晉春秋) says:
"Lè (勒) ascended the imperial throne and changed the era name to Tàihé."
However: Lè first ascended the imperial throne in Jiànpíng (建平) first year.
Now we follow Lè Zàijì (勒載記).
3 In the third month,
on *Bǐngzǐ* (丙子) day,
Empress Dowager Yǔ (庾太后) died of grief.
4 Sū Jùn (蘇峻) moved his southern camp to Yúhú (于湖).
5 In summer,
fourth month,
Hòuzhào general Shí Kān (石堪) attacked Wǎn (宛).
Nányáng Tàishǒu Wáng Guó (南陽太守王國) surrendered to him.
He then advanced to attack Zǔ Yuē's (祖約) army on the Huái (淮) River.
Zǔ Yuē's general Chén Guāng (陳光) raised troops to attack Zǔ Yuē.
Zǔ Yuē's attendant Yán Tū (閻禿)
resembled Zǔ Yuē in appearance.
Chén Guāng took him for Zǔ Yuē and captured him.
Zǔ Yuē climbed over a wall and escaped.
Chén Guāng fled to Hòuzhào.
6 On *Rénshēn* (壬申) day,
Empress Míngmù (明穆皇后) was buried at Wǔpíng Líng (武平陵).
7 Yǔ Liàng (庾亮) and Wēn Qiáo (溫嶠) were about to raise troops to suppress Sū Jùn (蘇峻),
but the roads were cut off,
and they knew nothing of the situation in Jiànkāng (建康).
At this time, Fàn Wāng (范汪) from Nányáng (南陽) arrived in Xúnyáng (尋陽),
and said:
"Sū Jùn's (峻) governance is inconsistent,
he is greedy, cruel, and rampant.
The signs of his downfall are already evident;
though strong, he is easily weakened.
The court is in extreme peril,
and an immediate punitive expedition is appropriate."
Qiáo deeply accepted this advice.
Liàng appointed Wāng (汪) as Cānhù Jūnjì (參護軍事).
Liàng and Qiáo mutually deferred to each other as the盟主 (méngzhǔ, alliance leader).
Qiáo's younger cousin, Chōng, said:
"Táo Zhēngxī (Táo, General of the Western Expedition) holds a weighty position and strong military power.
Kǎn was then the征西大將軍 (Zhēngxī Dàjiāngjūn, General-in-Chief of the Western Expedition) and都督荊、湘、雍、梁 (Dūdū Jīng, Xiāng, Yōng, Liáng, Grand Administrator of Jīng, Xiāng, Yōng, and Liáng provinces),
with sole control over the upper reaches of the river."
Qiáo then dispatched his督護 (dūhù, supervising assistant), Wáng Qiānqī, to Jīngzhōu,
inviting Táo Kǎn to join them in confronting the national crisis.
Kǎn was still resentful about not being consulted for the dying emperor's testament.
This matter is detailed in the previous volume, Xiánhé (咸和) first year.
"I am a frontier general,
and dare not overstep my bounds."
This means that internal support and external defense
each have their designated roles,
which one dare not exceed.
將 (Jiāng)
is a reversal of Liàng.
Unable to dissuade him,
Qiáo therefore acceded to Kǎn's wishes,
sending an envoy to say to him:
"Benevolent Sir, please hold your position.
Since the Hàn and Wèi dynasties,
it has been customary to address prime ministers and regional governors as 'Mínggōng' (明公, Illustrious Sir).
Now Qiáo addresses Kǎn as 'Rén'gōng' (仁公, Benevolent Sir),
likely drawing from the meaning of 'all under heaven returning to benevolence,'
implying that all Jìn (晉) generals and governors defer greatly to Kǎn."
使 (Shǐ)
is a reversal of shū lì (疏吏);
the same below.
Two days after the envoy departed,
Píngnán (平南)參軍 (cānjūn, military advisor) Máo Bǎo (毛寶) of Xíngyáng,
Qiáo was the Píngnán Jiāngjūn (平南將軍, General Who Pacifies the South),
and appointed Bǎo as his cānjūn.
heard of it and
advised Qiáo, saying:
"Whenever great undertakings are launched,
they should be shared with all under heaven.
Victory in battle depends on harmony,
and discord is inappropriate.
The Zǔochuán (左傳) states: Chǔ (楚) Dòulián (鬬廉) said, 'Victory in battle depends on harmony,
not on numbers.'
One should still outwardly feign ignorance,
let alone deliberately create division!
You should immediately recall the messenger and amend the letter.
信 (Xìn)
refers to the messenger.
If you cannot overtake the previous letter,
you should send another envoy."
Qiáo understood,
and immediately recalled the messenger to amend the letter.
Kǎn indeed agreed,
sending his dūhù, Gōng Dēng (龔登), to lead troops to Qiáo.
Qiáo had seven thousand troops.
Thereupon, he memorialized the Shàngshū (尚書, Imperial Secretariat),
appointing Kǎn as the盟主 (méngzhǔ, alliance leader),
and listed his and Liàng's names in the memorial to the Shàngshū.
上 (Shàng)
is a reversal of shí zhǎng (時掌).
He issued proclamations to the generals and governors,
shedding tears as he boarded his boat.
Táo Kǎn then recalled Gōng Dēng.
Qiáo sent a letter to Kǎn, saying:
"An army must advance, not retreat;
it can be augmented, but not diminished.
Recently, proclamations have been sent far and wide,
announcing to the alliance headquarters—
'alliance headquarters'
refers to Kǎn's headquarters;
Kǎn was the盟主 (méngzhǔ),
hence it was called the 'alliance headquarters.'
復 (Fù)
is a reversal of fú yòu (扶又).
遺 (Yí)
is a reversal of yú jì (于季).
All the commanderies' troops are already on the way.
We only await the arrival of your army, Benevolent Sir,
and then we shall advance together.
Now, Benevolent Sir, by recalling your army,
you create doubt among those far and near.
The success or failure
will likely depend on this.
My talent is slight, but my responsibility is heavy.
I truly rely on your deep affection, Benevolent Sir,
and await your established plans from afar.
As for being the first to engage in battle,
I dare not refuse.
My relationship with you, Benevolent Sir,
is like head and tail protecting each other,
or lips and teeth dependent on each other.
I fear that some may not grasp your noble intention
and will say that you, Benevolent Sir, are slow in suppressing the rebels.
Such a reputation is difficult to dispel.
You and I, Benevolent Sir, both bear the responsibility of governing a region.
Our safety and distress
are naturally intertwined.
Moreover, in our recent interactions,
our ties have been close and frequent.
Our feelings are deep, and our righteousness weighty.
Should an emergency arise,
I would expect you, Benevolent Sir, to come with all your forces to save me,
let alone a crisis for the nation!
The worries of today
are not just for my single province.
All civil and military officials are eagerly awaiting you.
This means they are craning their necks and standing on tiptoes, hoping for Kǎn's army to arrive.
難 (Nán)
is a reversal of nǎi dàn (乃旦).
Yuē and Jùn (約、峻) have established officials here.
'Here'
refers to Jiāngzhōu (江州).
長 (Zhǎng)
is a reversal of zhī liǎng (知兩).
To the east, we border the rebels,
and compounded by famine,
the coming danger
will be far worse than what this province faces today.
Benevolent Sir, advancing will make you a loyal minister of the Great Jìn,
sharing the achievements of Huán (桓) and Wén (文).
Retreating will mean abandoning a loving father's sentiment
to avenge the pain of a beloved son.
This refers to Kǎn's son Zhān (瞻) who was killed by Jùn.
The pain moves heaven and earth,
and people are united in purpose,
all gnashing their teeth.
The current advance to suppress them
is like throwing a stone at an egg.
If you recall your troops again,
it would be to fail when success is almost achieved.
I hope you will deeply consider what I have stated!"
Wáng Qiānqī said to Kǎn:
"Sū Jùn (蘇峻) is a jackal and a wolf.
If he succeeds in his ambition,
although the four seas are vast,
where will you, Duke, have a place to stand?"
Kǎn was deeply moved and understood.
He immediately donned his military attire and boarded his boat.
He did not attend Zhān's funeral when it arrived,
but advanced day and night without stopping.
Xī Jiàn (郗鑒) was in Guǎnglíng (廣陵).
The city was isolated, provisions were scarce,
and it was close to the Hú (胡) barbarians.
The people had no firm resolve.
Upon receiving the imperial edict,
he immediately shed tears and vowed to his troops
to go to the aid of the nation in crisis,
and his officers and soldiers eagerly braced themselves.
He dispatched General Xiàhóu Cháng (夏侯長) and others to travel covertly to Wēn Qiáo and say:
"We have heard that the rebels intend to seize the Son of Heaven and move east into Kuàijī (會稽).
We should first establish camps and fortifications,
occupying strategic points,
both to prevent their escape
and to cut off their grain supplies.
Then, clear the fields and strengthen the walls to await the rebels.
If the rebels attack cities but fail to capture them,
and find nothing to plunder in the fields,
and their eastern route is cut off,
their grain supplies will naturally be exhausted,
and they will certainly collapse."
Qiáo thought this was deeply correct.
The Jìn (晉) capital, Jiànkāng (建康),
relied on the Sān Wú (三吳) region for all its grain supplies,
hence the desire to first cut off the eastern route.
In the rebellions of Wáng Dūn (王敦) and Sū Jùn (蘇峻),
Xī Jiàn (郗鑒) contributed greatly to the plans for restoration.
In the fifth month,
Táo Kǎn led his troops to Xúnyáng (尋陽).
The strategists all believed Kǎn intended to execute Yǔ Liàng (庾亮) to appease the empire.
Liàng was very frightened
and, following Wēn Qiáo's plan,
went to Kǎn to prostrate himself in apology.
Kǎn was surprised
and stopped him, saying:
"Yǔ Yuánkuī (庾元規) bows to Táo Shìxíng (陶士行)?"
Táo Kǎn's
courtesy name was Shìxíng.
His demeanor was admirable,
and Kǎn unconsciously felt relieved,
saying:
"You, Marquis, fortified Shítóu (石頭) to contend with this old man."
See the previous volume, Xiánhé (咸和) first year.
He then conversed and feasted with him all day,
and subsequently proceeded with Liàng and Qiáo to Jiànkāng.
His army numbered forty thousand,
with banners and flags stretching over seven hundred lǐ,
and the sound of gongs and drums
reverberated far and near.
Sū Jùn, hearing that troops were rising in the west,
followed the advice of his cānjūn (參軍), Jiǎ Níng (賈寧),
and returned from Gūshú (姑孰) to occupy Shítóu,
dividing his forces to resist Kǎn and the others.
On the *yǐwèi* day,
Sū Jùn forced the Emperor to move to Shítóu.
Sītú Wáng Dǎo strongly opposed this,
but was not obeyed.
The Emperor wept sorrowfully as he ascended the carriage,
and cries of grief filled the palace.
At that time, there was heavy rain,
and the roads were muddy.
Liú Chāo and Zhōng Yǎ walked beside the Emperor as attendants.
Sū Jùn offered them horses,
but they refused to ride,
instead displaying sorrow and indignation.
Sū Jùn heard of this and disliked it,
but did not yet dare to kill them.
He appointed his trusted associates Xǔ Fāng and others as Sīmǎdū and Diànzhōngjiān.
Ostensibly, they were for imperial guard duty,
but internally they were meant to monitor Liú Chāo and others.
Sū Jùn used a granary as the Emperor's palace,
and came before the Emperor daily to speak foul words.
Liú Chāo, Zhōng Yǎ, Yòuguānglùdàfū Xún Sōng, and Jīnzǐguānglùdàfū Huà Héng
(Zuǒ- and Yòuguānglùdàfū
wore golden seals and purple ribbons;
Guānglùdàfū
wore silver seals and green ribbons;
those who were additionally granted golden seals and purple ribbons
were called Jīnzǐguānglùdàfū.
Huà
is pronounced *hù huà* fān.
Héng
is pronounced *hù dēng* fān)
did not leave the Emperor's side.
At that time, there was famine and rice was expensive.
Sū Jùn sent gifts,
but Liú Chāo refused to accept anything.
They attended closely day and night,
and their loyalty as subjects grew even more respectful.
Though in dire straits,
Liú Chāo still advised the Emperor
and taught him the *Xiàojīng* and *Lúnyǔ*.
Sū Jùn sent Zuǒguānglùdàfū Lù Yè to guard the Liútái.
He forced residents
to all gather in the Hòuyuàn.
He sent Kuāng Shù to guard the Yuànchéng.
Shàngshūzuǒchéng Kǒng Tǎn fled to Táo Kǎn.
Táo Kǎn appointed him Chángshǐ.
Previously,
Sū Jùn had dispatched Shàngshū Zhāng Kǎi to provisionally command the eastern army.
Sītú Wáng Dǎo secretly ordered him to convey the Empress Dowager's edict to the officials and soldiers of Sānwú.
(The Hàn dynasty established Wújùn.
Wú divided Wújùn to establish Wúxīngjùn.
Jìn further divided Wúxīng and Dānyáng to establish Yìxīngjùn.
These were called the Sānwú.
Lì Dàoyuán said: "The world refers to Wújùn, Wúxīng, and Kuàijījùn as the Sānwú."
Dù Yòu said: "Between Jìn and Sòng,
Wújùn, Wúxīng, and Dānyáng were considered the Sānwú.")
Kuàijī Nèishǐ Wáng Shū appointed Yǔ Bīng as Xíng Fènwǔjiāngjūn,
and sent him with an army of ten thousand
to cross the Zhèjiāng River westward.
Thereupon, Wúxīng Tàishǒu Yú Tán, Wúguónèishǐ Cài Mó, former Yìxīng Tàishǒu Gù Zhòng, and others all raised armies to answer the call.
Yú Tán's mother, Lady Sūn, said to Yú Tán:
"You must sacrifice your life for righteousness.
Do not let my old age be a burden!"
She sent all her household servants to join the army,
and sold her rings and pendants to provide military funds.
Cài Mó, considering that Yǔ Bīng would return to his old post,
immediately left the commandery to yield it to Yǔ Bīng.
Sū Jùn, hearing that troops had risen in the east,
sent his generals Guǎn Shāng, Zhāng Jiàn, Hóng Huī, and others to resist them.
Yú Tán and his forces fought them,
with alternating victories and defeats,
and were unable to advance.
Táo Kǎn and Wēn Qiáo's armies encamped at Qiézipǔ.
Wēn Qiáo, noting that the southern soldiers were skilled in naval warfare
while Sū Jùn's soldiers were adept at land combat,
(Southern soldiers
refers to Táo Kǎn and Wēn Qiáo's troops.
Adept at land combat
means skilled in infantry battles.)
declared, "Any officer or soldier who lands on shore shall die!"
At that time, Sū Jùn sent ten thousand *hú* of rice to provision Zǔ Yuē.
Zǔ Yuē dispatched Sīmǎ Huán Fǔ and others to receive it.
Máo Bǎo led a thousand men as Wēn Qiáo's vanguard.
He told his troops:
"Military strategy states,
'There are instances where military orders are not followed.'
How can we see the enemy as vulnerable to attack
and not go ashore to strike them?!"
He then led his men to attack Huán Fǔ,
captured all their rice,
and killed or captured tens of thousands.
Zǔ Yuē was consequently hungry and destitute.
Wēn Qiáo memorialized to have Máo Bǎo appointed Lújiāng Tàishǒu.
Táo Kǎn memorialized to have Wáng Shū supervise military affairs in Zhèdōng,
Yú Tán supervise military affairs in Zhèxī,
and Xī Jiàn be Dūdū of the armies of the eight commanderies of Yángzhōu.
He ordered Wáng Shū and Yú Tán to both follow Xī Jiàn's command.
Xī Jiàn led his forces across the river
and rendezvoused with Táo Kǎn and others at Qiézipǔ.
Yōngzhōu Cìshǐ Wèi Gāi also brought troops to join them.
On the *bǐngchén* day,
Táo Kǎn and others' naval forces sailed directly towards Shítóu,
reaching Càizhōu.
Táo Kǎn encamped at Chápǔ.
(Càizhōu
is on the western bank of Shítóu.
Chápǔ
is on the southern bank of the great river,
directly opposite the mouth of the Qínhuái River.)
Sū Jùn ascended the beacon tower,
and seeing the might of the assembled troops,
showed fear,
saying to his attendants,
"I originally knew that Wēn Qiáo could gather such a multitude."
Yǔ Liàng dispatched Dūhù Wáng Zhāng to attack Sū Jùn's partisan Zhāng Yào,
but Wáng Zhāng was defeated instead.
Yǔ Liàng sent his *jiéchuán* to Táo Kǎn as an apology.
Táo Kǎn replied,
"The ancients spoke of three defeats,
referring to the Lǔ general Cáo Mèi.
Given the urgency of the present situation,
such repeated occurrences are inappropriate."
(It means such frequent occurrences are inappropriate.
*Shù*
is pronounced *suǒ jiǎo* fān.)
"That the general does this
is not for me to judge."
Wáng Zhāng arrived and said,
"I did it myself;
the general did not know."
Táo Kǎn said,
"In the past, Yīn Róng was a gentleman,
and Wáng Zhāng was a petty man;
now Wáng Zhāng is a gentleman,
and Yīn Róng is a petty man."
Xuānchéng Nèishǐ Huán Yí,
upon hearing that the capital was undefended,
sighed with indignation and shed tears,
then advanced and encamped at Jīngxiàn.
(Huán Yí advanced from Guǎngdé to encamp at Jīngxiàn.)
Pí Huì again advised Huán Yí that he should communicate with Sū Jùn for the time being
to alleviate the danger of being besieged from all sides.
(*Shū*
means to relax.
The danger of being besieged from all sides
means that many commanderies and provinces had surrendered,
and Sū Jùn's troops would converge from all four directions.
*Fù*
is pronounced *fú yòu* fān.)
"I have received profound grace from the state;
my duty lies in giving my life.
How can I bear the shame of communicating with a rebellious minister?!
If it does not succeed,
then this is fate."
Huán Yí sent General Yú Zòng to guard Lánshí.
(Lánshí
is northeast of Jīngxiàn.)
Yú Zòng was about to be defeated,
and his attendants advised him to retreat.
Yú Zòng said,
"I have received profound grace from Marquis Huán;
I ought to repay it with my death.
That I cannot betray Marquis Huán
is just as Marquis Huán does not betray the state."
He then fought with all his might and died.
Su Zǐhuáng advanced his army and attacked Huán Yí.
In the sixth month,
the city fell,
and Huán Yí was captured
and killed.
When the various armies first arrived at Shítou,
they immediately wanted to engage in a decisive battle.
Táo Kǎn said:
"The bandit forces are currently at their peak,
it is difficult to contend with them directly.
We should take our time,
and defeat them with strategy."
After repeated battles proved fruitless,
the supervising general Lǐ Gēn requested to build the Báishí Bulwark.
At this time, none of the allied generals held the position of supervising general;
it is privately thought that Lǐ Gēn was probably a general under Xī Jiàn's command.
Since earlier histories omitted the character
later generations therefore changed
"Jiàn" (鑒)
to
"Jiān" (監).
The Báishí Bulwark
was northeast of Shítou,
extremely steep and fortified.
Dù Yòu said: Báishí Lǐ
was west of Táichéng,
and in the fourth year of Dàmíng under Emperor Wǔ of Sòng, it was used as a silkworm farm,
with a great hall built there.
At night,
the bulwark was built,
completed by dawn.
They heard Sū Jùn's army's strict sound,
referring to the sound of Sū Jùn's army beating drums and forming ranks.
Kǒng Tǎn said:
"That's not right.
If Sū Jùn were to attack the bulwark,
there would need to be a strong northeast wind,
preventing our navy from coming to assist;
today the sky is clear and quiet,
so the bandits will surely not come.
The reason for their strictness
must be to send troops out to Jiāngchéng,
to plunder east of Jīngkǒu."
It turned out to be so.
Táo Kǎn sent Yǔ Liàng with two thousand men to guard Báishí,
and Sū Jùn led over ten thousand infantry and cavalry to attack it from all four sides,
but failed.
Wáng Shū, Yú Tán,
and others repeatedly fought Sū Jùn's forces,
but were unsuccessful.
Kǒng Tǎn said:
"We shouldn't have summoned Duke Xī in the first place,
which led to no limits on the eastern gate.
Now we should send him back;
though late,
it is still better than not doing so."
He meant that even if sending him back was late,
it was still better than not sending him back.
Three bulwarks were established at Dàyè, Qǔ'ā, and Chǒutíng to divide Sū Jùn's military might.
Qǔ'ā was Qín's Yúnyáng County,
in the Former Hàn it belonged to Kuàijī Commandery,
in the Later Hàn it belonged to Wú Commandery,
and in the Jìn it belonged to Pílíng Commandery.
Dàyè
was a village name,
north of Qǔ'ā.
Dīng Dù said: Chǒutíng
was in Wúxīng.
The character 'chǒu' (庱)
is pronounced "chǒu shēng" (丑升翻).
Péi Sōngzhī said: 'Chǒutíng' (庱)
is pronounced "shū líng" (攄陵翻).
On the day Rénchén,
Wèi Gāi died.
Zǔ Yuē sent Zǔ Huàn and Huán Fǔ to raid Pénkǒu;
Pénkǒu
was in Xúnyáng,
and today, one *lǐ* west of Déhuà County in Jiāngzhōu there is Pénpǔ.
He was about to attack it himself.
Máo Bǎo said:
"The righteous army relies on you,
so you must not move.
I request to lead the punitive expedition."
Táo Kǎn agreed.
Zǔ Huàn and Huán Fǔ passed Wǎn,
and then attacked Huán Xuān, the Administrator of Qiáoguó.
Huán Xuān was then stationed at Mǎtóushān in Wǎn County.
Wǎn
is pronounced "hù bǎn" (戶版翻).
They were defeated by Zǔ Huàn and Huán Fǔ.
An arrow pierced Máo Bǎo's thigh,
passing through his saddle.
Máo Bǎo had someone step on the saddle to pull out the arrow,
and blood filled his boots.
He returned to attack Zǔ Huàn and Huán Fǔ,
defeating and routing them.
Huán Xuān was then able to escape,
returning to Wēn Jiào.
Máo Bǎo advanced to attack Zǔ Yuē's army at Dōngguān,
capturing the Heféi garrison;
then Wēn Jiào summoned him,
and he returned to Shítou.
Zǔ Yuē's generals secretly conspired with the Later Zhào,
promising to act as an internal contact.
The Later Zhào generals Shí Cōng and Shí Kān led troops across the Huái River,
attacking Shòuchūn.
In autumn,
the seventh month,
Zǔ Yuē's forces disintegrated,
fleeing to Lìyáng. Shí Cōng and others captured over twenty thousand households from Shòuchūn and returned.
8 Hǔ, Duke of Zhōngshān of the Later Zhào, led forty thousand troops and entered from Zhǐguān to the west,
attacking Héhédōng of Zhào.
Zhǐguān
was in Zhǐ County, Hénèi.
Shuài (帥)
is read as Shuài (率).
Then they advanced to attack Púbǎn.
Zhào's ruler Yào sent Wáng Shù of Héjiān to mobilize the Dī and Qiāng peoples to garrison Qínzhōu to defend against Zhāng Jùn and Yáng Nándí.
He personally led his elite central and external forces, land and water armies, to rescue Púbǎn,
crossing north of Wèiguān.
The *Jìn Shū Geography Monograph* states that Jí County in Jí Commandery has Wèiguān.
Shí Hǔ retreated.
Liú Yào pursued him,
and in the eighth month,
caught up with him at Gāohòu.
Dù Yòu said: Today, north of Wénxǐ County in Jiàngzhōu, there is Gāohòuyuán.
He thoroughly defeated them,
beheading Shí Zhān,
with corpses piled over two hundred *lǐ*,
and capturing countless supplies and weapons.
Shí Hǔ fled to Cháogē.
Dù Yòu said: Wèi County in Wèizhōu was Hàn's Cháogē County.
Zhòu's capital Cháogē
was west of the present county.
Dàyáng belonged to Hédōng Commandery.
Yīng Shào said: It was on the sunny side of the Great River,
hence called Dàyáng.
The Táng Gazetteer states that Shǎnzhōu's Shǎn County had the old pass of Dàyáng,
which was Máojīn in the Spring and Autumn period.
He breached the Qiānjīn Dyke to flood it.
He separately dispatched his generals to attack Jí Commandery and Hénèi.
The Later Zhào Administrator of Xíngyáng, Yǐn Jǔ, and Administrator of Yěwáng, Zhāng Jìn,
