Generals Jiǎng Yīng and Xīn Shù gathered several hundred thousand people and occupied Cháng'ān.
They sent envoys to surrender to the Later Zhào,
who sent Shí Shēng to lead the troops from Luòyáng to assist them.
The second month.
On the day Bǐngxū,
the various armies attacked Shítóu.
Army Supervisor Jiànwēi Téng Hán attacked Sū Yì,
and greatly defeated him.
Téng Hán advanced from Army Supervisor Jiāngē Qīngchē to Army Supervisor Jiànwēi.
They crossed the Huái River and fought.
The Huái here refers to the Qínhuái River.
"Xiāo"
is pronounced "jiān yáo."
Hán Huǎng and others were terrified,
and joined their forces with Zhāng Jiàn at Qǔ'ā.
The gate was too narrow for them to exit,
so they trampled each other,
and tens of thousands died.
The Western Army captured Sū Yì
and beheaded him.
Téng Hán's subordinate general Cáo Jù carried the Emperor to Wēn Jiǎo's boat.
All the officials saw the Emperor,
bowed their heads to the ground, and wept, asking for punishment.
The King of Xīyáng, Yáng, was killed,
along with his two sons Bō and Chōng, his grandson Sōng, and the King of Péngchéng, Xióng.
Yáng had sided with Sū Jùn as seen in the previous [volume], third year of Xiánhé,
and Xióng had fled to Jùn as seen in the previous volume, second year.
They asked for their deaths.
The Emperor said:
"These are the ones who killed my Palace Attendant and Right Guard;
they cannot be pardoned."
So they were killed.
Minister of Works Dǎo entered Shítóu,
and ordered someone to retrieve the old staff of authority.
Dǎo had been granted a staff of authority when he attacked Wáng Dūn;
when he fled Shítóu,
he abandoned it.
"Sū Wǔ's staff was not like this."
Dǎo showed a look of shame.
Dǎo was mocked by Kǎn,
and felt ashamed of his lapse in duty.
On the day Dīnghài,
a general amnesty was declared.
Zhāng Jiàn suspected Hóng, Huī, and others of being disloyal to him,
and killed them all.
He led his naval forces from Yánlíng, intending to enter Wúxīng.
Pílíng County
belonged to Kuàijī Commandery in the Former Hàn dynasty;
in the Later Hàn, it was divided and belonged to Wú Commandery;
in the Jìn, it was divided and belonged to Pílíng Commandery.
Shīgǔ said: Pílíng
was formerly Yánlíng,
which the Hàn renamed.
The Jìn divided Pílíng and Yánlíng into two counties.
Pílíng is the area of today’s Chángzhōu Jìnlíng County,
and Yánlíng is the area of today’s Rùnzhōu Dāntú and Jīntán.
Sòng Bái said: Yánlíng County
was originally the land of Hàn Qǔ'ā County.
In the second year of Tàikāng of the Jìn dynasty (281 CE),
it was established by dividing Yánlíng Township from Qǔ'ā.
帥 (shuài)
is read as 率 (shuài).
On the *yǐwèi* day
(day 2 of the 3rd month of the 3rd year of Xiánhé, 328 CE), Yángliè Jiāngjūn Wáng Yǔnzhī fought him,
thoroughly defeating him
and capturing over ten thousand men and women.
Jiàn then, with Hán Huǎng, Mǎ Xióng, and others, moved west towards Gùzhāng.
Gùzhāng County
belonged to Dānyáng Commandery in the Hàn dynasty;
the Wú dynasty established Wúxīng Commandery by dividing Dānyáng from Wú Commandery,
and Gùzhāng belonged to it.
Its land was originally the seat of Qín Zhāng Commandery,
hence it was called Gùzhāng.
Today’s Húzhōu Ānjí County
is the southern district of Gùzhāng;
today’s Guǎngdé Military Prefecture
is the land of Hàn Gùzhāng County.
Dù Yòu said: Eighty *lǐ* west of Húzhōu Chángchéng County is the old city of Zhāng Commandery,
which was the county seat of Qín Zhāng Commandery.
復 (fù)
is pronounced *fúyòu*.
趨 (qū)
is pronounced *qīyù*.
They reached Pínglíng Shān
and were all executed.
The biography of Sū Jùn records it as
"Yán Shān."
According to the Imperial Annals, Pínglíng Shān should be within Lìyáng's borders.
Shěn Yuē said: The Wú divided Lìyáng to establish Yǒngpíng County,
which Emperor Wǔ of Jìn renamed Yǒngshì.
Dǒng Lǎn’s *Wú Dì Zhì* states: The Jìn divided Yǒngshì to establish Pínglíng County.
In the ninth year of Yuánjiā of Emperor Wén of Sòng (432 CE),
it was merged into Yǒngshì and Lìyáng counties.
At this time, the palace had been reduced to ashes,
so Jiànpíng Yuán was used as the palace.
Wēn Jiào wanted to move the capital to Yùzhāng,
but the magnates of Sān Wú requested to make Kuàijī the capital.
The two opinions were hotly debated and unresolved.
Sītú Dǎo said:
"Sūn Zhòngmóu and Liú Xuándé both said, 'Jiànkāng is the residence of kings.'
(See volume 66, Hàn Xiàndì, Jiàn'ān 17th year.)
There is no need to move the capital based on abundance or scarcity.
If we genuinely focus on fundamentals and economize,
why worry about decay and ruin!
If agricultural affairs are not cultivated,
then even fertile land will become a wasteland.
Furthermore, the northern invaders, like wandering spirits,
await our weakness.
If we once show weakness
and flee to the barbarian Yue,
considering its perceived and actual implications,
I fear it is not a good plan.
'Perceived' (wàng)
refers to what is seen externally;
'actual' (shí)
refers to what exists internally.
Let the populace settle themselves."
Because of this, the capital was not moved.
Chǔ Jiá was made Dānyáng Yǐn.
At that time, after the ravages of war,
the people and resources were devastated.
Jiá collected the scattered and lost,
and the capital then became peaceful.
6. On the *rén'yín* day (day 29 of the 2nd month of the 3rd year of Xiánhé, 328 CE),
Xiāngzhōu was merged with Jīngzhōu.
(The division of Xiāngzhōu is seen in volume 86, Huáidì, Yǒngjiā 1st year.)
7. In the third month,
on the *rénzǐ* day (day 28 of the 3rd month of the 3rd year of Xiánhé, 328 CE),
rewards for quelling Sū Jùn were discussed.
Táo Kǎn was appointed Shìzhōng and Tàiwèi,
enfeoffed as Chángshā Jùn Gōng,
and additionally made Dūdū of the military affairs of Jiāo, Guǎng, and Níngzhōu.
Kǎn had previously overseen Jīng, Xiāng, Yōng, and Liáng four *zhōu*,
and now three more *zhōu* were added to his supervision.
Wēn Jiào was appointed Piàojì Jiāngjūn, Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī,
and additionally Sànqí Chángshì and Shǐ'ān Jùn Gōng.
According to the Jìn system,
the rank of Piàojì Jiāngjūn was equivalent to that of a Duke.
驃 (piào)
is pronounced *pǐmiào*.
Many others were granted titles of Hóu, Bó, Zǐ, and Nán.
Biàn Hú and his two sons Zhěn and Xū, Huán Yí, Liú Chāo, Zhōng Yǎ, Yáng Màn, and Táo Zhān
were all posthumously honored and given諡 (shì) titles.
Lù Yǒng, Kuāng Shù, and Jiǎ Níng were
all members of Sū Jùn's faction.
Before Jùn's defeat,
Yǒng and others abandoned Jùn and returned to the imperial court.
Wáng Dǎo wanted to reward them with official posts and noble ranks.
Wēn Jiào said:
"Yǒng and the others were Jùn's close confidants
and initiated the rebellion;
their crime is unsurpassed.
Although they later repented,
it is not enough to atone for their previous crimes.
To have preserved their lives
is already great fortune;
how can they be further honored and favored!"
Dǎo then ceased.
Táo Kǎn, considering Jiānglíng remote,
moved his garrison to Bālíng.
Jiānglíng was situated on the north side of the river,
and also far from Jiànkāng.
In the first year of Tàikāng of Emperor Wǔ (280 CE),
Bālíng County was established,
belonging to Chángshā Commandery;
later, Jiànchāng Commandery was established.
The *Shuǐ Jīng Zhù* states: The Xiāng River flows north to Bāqiū Shān
and enters the Jiāng.
On the right bank is the old city of Bālíng,
which was originally the Bāqiū Dǐgé of Wú.
Bāqiū Shān
is also known as Tiānyuè Shān,
and also Mùfù.
In front of it are small mounds
called the Bāshé Zhǒng.
The court deliberated on keeping Wēn Jiào to assist in governance,
but Jiào, considering Wáng Dǎo to have been appointed by the previous emperor,
firmly declined and requested to return to his fief.
Furthermore, as the capital was desolate and ruined,
and supplies were insufficient,
he left his accumulated resources and equipment behind before returning to Wǔchāng.
When the Emperor left Shítou,
Yú Liàng met the Emperor,
prostrating and choking with sobs.
The Emperor decreed that Liàng and the other ministers should ascend the throne together.
The next day,
Liàng again prostrated himself to apologize,
requesting to retire,
wishing to close his doors and flee to the mountains and seas.
The Emperor sent Shàngshū and Shìzhōng with a personal handwritten edict to console him, saying:
"This is a calamity for the state,
not the responsibility of my uncle."
Liàng submitted a memorial explaining his position:
"Zǔ Yuē and Sū Jùn's rampant violence
originated from my actions (the matter is seen in the previous volume, first year).
This is not enough to apologize to the spirits of the Seven Ancestral Temples,
nor to quell the censure of the Four Seas.
What reason does the court have to still count me among others,
and what face do I have to count myself among others!
I wish Your Majesty, though extending clemency
to preserve my life,
would still cast me aside,
allowing me to live or die on my own,
then the world will roughly know the principles of encouragement and warning."
A gracious edict did not permit it.
Liàng again wished to flee to the mountains and seas,
heading east from Jìyáng.
In the second year of Tàikāng of Emperor Wǔ (281 CE),
Jìyáng County was established by dividing Pílíng and Wúxī,
belonging to Pílíng Commandery;
its land is now within the boundaries of Píngjiāng Fǔ Chángshú County.
Dù Yòu said: Jiāngyīn
was called Jìyáng in the Jìn.
Note: Jìyáng
is now the territory of Jiāngyīn Military Prefecture;
in the Qín and Hàn dynasties, it was Jìyáng Township;
the Jìn established Jìyáng County city;
there is also Jìyáng Hú.
錄 (lù)
means to detain (jū)
or to collect (shōu).
He was appointed Dūdū of the military affairs of Yùzhōu, the western part of Yángzhōu, and Xuānchéng.
Yùzhōu and the western part of Yángzhōu included
the commanderies of Huáinán, Lújiāng, Yìyáng, Ānfēng, and Lìyáng.
Xuānchéng Commandery
belonged to Yángzhōu.
He held the post of Xuānchéng Nèishǐ
and was garrisoned at Wúhú.
When Táo Kǎn and Wēn Jiào were suppressing Sū Jùn,
they issued a proclamation to the regional governors and commanders,
ordering each to bring their troops to provide aid.
Biàn Dūn, the Marquis of Yìyáng and Inspector of Xiāngzhōu, withheld his troops and did not respond,
nor did he provide military provisions.
He merely sent a督護 (dūhù) with a few hundred men to join the main army.
No one in court or country was not surprised and sighed.
They were surprised because they did not expect him to be like this, yet he was;
thus they were surprised.
They also sighed because they considered what kind of person he had been in the past, yet he was now doing this;
thus they sighed.
Táo Kǎn memorialized that Dūn had undermined the army,
hesitated and failed to answer the national crisis,
requesting he be arrested in a cage-cart and handed over to the Grand Judge.
Táo Kǎn was the leader
of the army that was diligently working for the emperor.
Xiāngzhōu was also under Kǎn’s supervision,
so Kǎn memorialized for Dūn’s arrest.
沮 (jǔ),
is pronounced Lǚ Fān.
難 (nán),
is pronounced Nǎi Dàn Fān.
He should be given leniency,
and Dūn was transferred to General of the Pacified South and Inspector of Guǎngzhōu.
He did not go due to illness,
and was summoned to be Grand Master of Bright Happiness, concurrently holding the position of Minor Prefect.
Dūn died of worry and shame.
He was posthumously restored to his former official position,
additionally granted the title of Attendant Censor,
and given the posthumous name Jìng.
The rules for posthumous names state: "Diligent day and night in warning" is Jìng;
"Harmonizing with good principles and laws" is Jìng.
How could Biàn Dūn possibly deserve this!
Your servant Guāng says: Yǔ Liàng, as an imperial in-law, assisted in governance,
but first triggered calamity,
leading to the state's ruin and the sovereign's peril,
and then fled to barely save himself.
Biàn Dūn held the position of a regional commander,
with abundant troops and provisions.
When the imperial court was overthrown,
he sat idly and watched the outcome.
Among the crimes of officials,
what is greater than these!
Not only were they unable to enforce the laws justly,
but they were rewarded with favor and emoluments.
It is thus clear that the Jìn dynasty lacked sound governance.
Who else but Wáng Dǎo
was responsible for this?
8. Gāo Mì Wáng Hóng was transferred to be Péng Chéng Wáng.
Hóng
was Xióng’s younger brother.
9. In summer,
the fourth month,
on the Yǐwèi day,
Wēn Jiào, Duke Zhōngwǔ of Shǐ'ān, passed away.
He was buried in Yùzhāng.
The court wished to build a grand tomb for him north of the mausoleums of Emperors Yuán and Míng.
Grand Commandant Kǎn submitted a memorial saying:
"Jiào’s loyalty and integrity were manifest in this sage era,
and his meritorious deeds and righteousness moved both men and gods.
If the deceased have knowledge,
how could he be pleased by today's efforts and expenses!
I implore Your Majesty’s benevolent grace
to halt his reburial."
The imperial edict complied.
Liú Yìn, the Army Supervisor of Píngnán, was appointed Inspector of Jiāngzhōu.
Yìn had originally been Wēn Jiào’s Army Supervisor.
Grand Minister of Works Dǎo did not agree.
Someone said to Dǎo’s son Yuè:
"Now, after this great calamity,
the discipline is lax and broken.
From Jiānglíng to Jiànkāng, over three thousand *lǐ*,
countless refugees,
are scattered throughout Jiāngzhōu.
Jiāngzhōu
is the southern bulwark of the state,
a strategic and vital region.
Yet Yìn, with his extravagant and indulgent nature,
will simply lie down and face it.
忲 (tài),
means extravagance;
忲 (tài)
is pronounced *tài*,
also *dà*.
There will surely be internal troubles."
Yuè said:
"This is the intention of Wēn Píngnán."
Wēn Jiào was the General of the Pacified South.
10. In autumn,
the eighth month,
Zhào Nányáng Wáng Yìn led tens of thousands of troops from Shàngguī towards Cháng'ān.
The Róng and Xià people in the various commanderies of Lǒngdōng, Wǔdū, Āndìng, Xīnpíng, Běidì, Fúfēng, and Shǐpíng all rose in arms to respond to him.
Wèi Shōu’s *Dìxíng Zhì* mentions Lǒngdōng Commandery,
which administered the three counties of Jīngyáng, Zǔlì, and Fǔyí.
This was probably established by the Later Zhào by dividing Āndìng.
Yīng Shào said: 祖 (zǔ),
is pronounced *jū*.
Shī Gǔ said: 厲 (lì),
is pronounced *lài*.
夏 (xià),
is pronounced Hù Yǎ Fān.
The Zhèngguó Canal passed by Zhòngshān.
There was a bridge over the canal,
called Zhòngqiáo,
east of Jiǔzōngshān.
Sòng Bái said: The city of Lǐquán County in Yōngzhōu
is the Zhòngqiáo City.
Hòu Zhào Zhōngshān Gōng Hǔ led twenty thousand cavalry to relieve them.
In the ninth month,
Hǔ greatly defeated the Zhào army at Yìqú.
Yìqú
was the land of the Yìqú Róng during the Warring States period.
In the Former Hàn, it was Yìqú County;
in the Later Hàn and Jìn, it was abolished.
Hǔ pursued the fleeing enemy,
with corpses piled for a thousand *lǐ*.
Shàngguī collapsed.
Hǔ captured Zhào Crown Prince Xī, Nányáng Wáng Yìn, and their generals, dukes, ministers, and military officers, over three thousand people,
and killed them all.
The *Zàijì* says: From Liú Yuān to Yào,
three generations and twenty-seven years, and then it perished.
將 (jiāng),
is pronounced Jí Liàng Fān.
校 (jiào),
is pronounced Hù Jiāo Fān.
He also buried alive five thousand *Túgē* from five commanderies at Luòyáng.
He advanced to attack the Jímùqiě Qiāng west of the Yellow River,
conquered them,
The *Túgē* were a Hūngnú tribe,
a clan of the Former Zhào;
the *Túgē* of five commanderies
were the masses of the five Hūngnú divisions.
Jímùqiě
was the name of a Qiāng tribal settlement.
屠 (tú),
is pronounced Zhí Yú Fān.
且 (jū),
is pronounced Zǐ Yú Fān.
Qín and Lǒng were all pacified.
The Dī king Pú Hóng and the Qiāng chieftain Yáo Gēzhòng both surrendered to Hǔ.
Hǔ memorialized to appoint Hóng as Supervisor of Military Affairs of the Six Barbarians,
and Yìzhòng as Left Commander-in-Chief of the Six Barbarians.
One hundred fifty thousand Dī and Qiāng households were relocated to Sī and Jìzhōu.
11. Initially,
the Xiānbēi Qǐfú Shùyán of Lǒngxī resided in Yuànchuān.
Qǐfú
was the name of a Xiānbēi tribe,
later adopted as a surname.
The Yuànchuān River
originates from the southern mountain of Zǐchéng in Yǒngshì County, Tiānshuǐ.
It flows eastward through Zǐchéngchuān,
then northward past Mùshīyuàn,
which was the site of the Hàn imperial pastures.
There were East and West Yuànchéng,
seven *lǐ* apart.
The West City was where Qǐfú made his capital.
Dù Yòu said: Yuànchuān
is within the borders of Wǔquán County, Lánzhōu.
Their soldiers and horses were strong and prosperous.
When Zhào fell,
Shùyán was afraid and
moved to Màitián.
After Shùyán died,
his son Nǔdàhán succeeded him.
After Nǔdàhán died,
his son Sīfán succeeded him.
The *Shuǐjīng Zhù* says: Màitián Mountain
is in the northern border of Āndìng;
northeast of the mountain
is Màitián City,
and further north is Màitián Spring.
傉 (nǔ),
is pronounced Nú Wò Fān.
Qǐfú is first mentioned here.
12 The Inspector of Jiāngzhōu, Liú Yìn, became increasingly arrogant and overbearing.
He focused solely on commerce,
accumulating millions in wealth.
He indulged in wine and pleasure,
neglecting government affairs.
In winter,
the twelfth month,
an imperial edict summoned the Posterior General, Guō Mò, to become the Right Army General.
Guō Mò enjoyed being a frontier general
and did not wish to be a palace guard.
He expressed his feelings to Liú Yìn.
Guō Mò was indeed summoned after pacifying Sū Jùn,
upon his return to Xúnyáng.
The Jìn Zhì states:
"According to the time of Emperor Míng of Wèi, there was a Left Army,
so the Left Army
was a Wèi official title.
During the time of Emperor Wǔ,
a Front Army and a Right Army were also established.
In the eighth year of Tàishǐ (272 CE),
a Rear Army was also established.
These were the Four Armies,
all palace guard troops."
The character 樂
is pronounced Luò.
邊將 (biān jiàng),
pronounced like "liàng" (亮);
same below.
"This is not something that commoners can achieve."
After the Jìn dynasty,
both civil and military officials were often referred to as xiǎorén (小人, commoners).
This is still the case among people in the northwest today.
Guō Mò sought funds from Liú Yìn,
but Liú Yìn did not provide them.
Guō Mò therefore resented Liú Yìn.
Liú Yìn's Chief Clerk, Zhāng Mǎn, and others had always looked down on Guō Mò,
sometimes even appearing naked before him.
Guō Mò often gritted his teeth in anger.
On the Là Day (winter solstice sacrifice),
Liú Yìn sent Guō Mò pork and wine.
Guō Mò, in front of the messenger, threw them into the water.
信 (xìn)
means "messenger."
"The imperial court is now empty and exhausted,
and all officials are without salary.
It relies solely on Jiāngzhōu for transport and provisions.
Yet Liú Yìn's commercial caravans constantly block the roads,
prioritizing private gain over public interest.
I request that Liú Yìn be removed from office."
When the memorial arrived,
Liú Yìn did not immediately admit guilt,
but instead tried to justify himself.
A sojourner, Gài Zhūn, abducted a woman and took her as his wife.
Those who temporarily lodged were called sojourners (qiáorén).
蓋 (gài)
is pronounced like "gǔ hé" (古盍).
肫 (zhūn)
is pronounced like "tú kūn" (徒昆).
Gài Zhūn refused to comply
and said to Guō Mò:
"Liú Jiāngzhōu will not accept his dismissal."
This means Liú Yìn did not accept the order to be dismissed from office.
"He is conspiring day and night with Zhāng Mǎn and others,
only fearing you, Guō Hóu (Marquis Guō).
They wish to eliminate you first."
Guō Mò believed this to be true,
and led his followers to wait until dawn for the gate to open to attack Liú Yìn.
Liú Yìn's generals and officers wished to resist Guō Mò,
but Guō Mò yelled at them:
"I have been commanded by edict to carry out an execution.
Those who move will have their three familial generations exterminated!"
He then entered the inner chambers,
dragged Liú Yìn down,
and beheaded him.
He went out
and seized Liú Yìn's subordinates, Zhāng Mǎn and others,
falsely accusing them of high treason,
and executed them all.
He sent Liú Yìn's head to the capital
and forged an imperial edict,
announcing it inside and outside the court.
He abducted Liú Yìn's daughters and concubines.
Kǒng Yǐngdá said: "The word 妾 (qiè, concubine) implies 'joining.'
Hearing that he was courteous,
she hurried to join and be seen by the gentleman."
Initially, it was said they were sent to the lower capital, but then they were held at Liú Yìn's former residence.
Guō Mò tried to win over Huán Xuān, the Administrator of Qiáoguó,
but Huán Xuān firmly held his ground and refused to comply.
Huán Xuān had returned to Wēn Jiǎo last year
and was garrisoned in Wǔchāng.
13 This year,
the Hèlán tribe and various tribal leaders jointly enthroned Tuòbá Yìhuái as King of Dài.
The Hèlán tribe supported Yìhuái;
see the previous volume, Xiánhé second year.
The Hòu Zhōu Shū states that the ancestors of the Yǔwén originated from Yán Dì.
Yán Dì was defeated by Huáng Dì,
and his descendants fled to the northern wilderness.
Later, there was a great man named Pǔhuí,
who, while hunting, found a jade seal
inscribed with the characters
"Huángdì Xǐ" (Emperor's Seal).
Pǔhuí believed it to be a divine bestowal.
Their custom was to call the Son of Heaven
"Yǔwén,"
so the state was named Yǔwén,
and they adopted it as their surname.
I believe this was probably an embellishment made by Yǔwén's ministers and sons after the Yǔwén clan rose to prominence in Guānxī.
Lǐ Yánshòu said: The Yǔwén tribe originated beyond the frontier of Liáodōng.
Their ancestors were distant relatives of the Southern Chányú,
and for generations were great men of the Eastern tribes.
This statement is closer to the truth.
14 The King of Hénán, Tùyán,
was brave and fierce but very suspicious.
The Qiāng chieftain, Jiāng Cōng, assassinated him.
Tùyán did not draw his sword.
He summoned his general, Gēniēní,
and instructed him to assist his son, Yèyán,
and to take refuge in Báilán.
Báilán
is southwest of Tǔyùhún.
Its terrain is rugged and remote.
A different branch of the Qiāng lived there.
It bordered Lìmótú to the northwest,
and Nà'è to the south.
Its customs and products were generally similar to those of Dàngchāng.
Yèyán was filial and fond of learning.
He believed that according to the rites,
"the son of a gōngsūn (grandson of a lord) may take his paternal grandfather's courtesy name as his surname."
So he named his state Tǔyùhún.
In the Zuǒ Zhuàn,
Rǔ Zhòngzhòng said:
"The Son of Heaven establishes virtue,
grants surnames based on birth,
bestows territory, and assigns clan names.
Lords use their courtesy names."
Dù Yù's commentary states: The son of a lord is called gōngzǐ (prince).
The son of a gōngzǐ is called gōngsūn (grandson of a lord).
The son of a gōngsūn takes his paternal grandfather's courtesy name as his surname.
1 In spring,
the first month,
Liú Yìn's head arrived at Jiànkāng.
The Grand Chancellor, Dǎo, considered Guō Mò to be brave and difficult to control.
On the day Jǐhài,
a general amnesty was declared.
Liú Yìn's head was impaled on the Great Ferry,
and Guō Mò was appointed Inspector of Jiāngzhōu.
The Grand Commandant, Kǎn, heard of this
and, throwing up his sleeves, rose and said:
"This must be a fraud!"
He immediately led troops to punish him.
Guō Mò sent envoys with entertainers, concubines, and silk,
and also presented a copy of the alleged imperial edict to Kǎn.
Many of Kǎn's staff advised him, saying:
"If Guō Mò did not receive an edict,
how would he dare to do this?
If you wish to advance with the army,
it would be advisable to await the imperial reply."
Kǎn sternly said:
"The state is young,
and edicts and orders do not come from its true intent.
Liú Yìn was treated with courtesy by the court.
Although his appointment may not have been due to his talent,
how could he have been so recklessly given the ultimate punishment?
Guō Mò relies on his bravery
and is greedy and tyrannical wherever he goes.
Believing that a great disaster has just been removed—
meaning Sū Jùn had just been pacified.
The character 難 (nán)
is pronounced like "nǎi dàn" (乃旦).
He wishes to take advantage of this opportunity to act unrestrainedly!"
He dispatched an envoy to present a memorial stating the situation,
and also wrote to Dǎo, saying:
"Guō Mò kills a regional inspector and is then appointed a regional inspector?
If he harms a prime minister, will he then become a prime minister?"
Dǎo then collected Liú Yìn's head
and replied to Kǎn's letter, saying:
"Guō Mò holds the strategic advantage of the upper reaches [of the river],
and moreover possesses a ready supply of ships.
Therefore, we must tolerate and endure him,
allowing him to hold that territory,
so that the court can secretly prepare."
潛 (qián)
means "secretly";
潛嚴 (qiányán) means "secretly ordering all armies to prepare."
"Then we will strike like the wind and converge."
風發 (fēngfā)
indicates speed.
Kǎn laughed and said:
"This is simply raising a seasonal bandit!"
Yùzhōu Inspector Yǔ Liàng also requested to suppress Guō Mò.
An edict appointed Yǔ Liàng as the Grand General for the Punitive Expedition,
leading twenty thousand infantry and cavalry to meet with Kǎn.
Xīyáng Tàishǒu Dèng Yuè and Wǔchāng Tàishǒu Liú Xǔ both suspected that Huán Xuān was allied with Mò.
Yùzhōu Xīcáo Wáng Suí said:
"Xuān still hasn't attached himself to Zǔ Yuē.
This matter is found in the previous volume, Xiánhé Èrnián."
Yuè and Xǔ sent Suí to go to Xuān to observe him.
Suí said to Xuān:
"Though your esteemed self does not feel that way,
不爾 (bù ěr),
meaning 'not like this'.
說 (shuō),
read as shū ruì fān.
The only thing you can do is entrust your worthy son to me!"
Xuān then sent his son Róng to accompany Suí to welcome Táo Kǎn.
Kǎn appointed Róng as a clerk,
and recommended Xuān as Wǔchāng Tàishǒu.
2 In the second month,
the officials of Hòuzhào entreated Hòuzhào Wáng Lè to ascend the throne as emperor.
Lè then proclaimed himself Dàzhào Tiānwáng,
and acted as emperor.
Lè,
courtesy name Shìlóng,
originally named Bú,
was a Jié person from Wǔxiāng, Shàngdǎng.
His ancestors were descendants of Qiāngqú, a separate branch of the Xiōngnú.
His grandfather was Yēyìqiān,
his father Zhōuhézhu,
also named Qǐyìjiā,
and both were minor tribal chieftains.
His heir apparent, Hóng, was made Crown Prince.
He appointed his son Hóng as Piàojì Dàjiāngjūn, Dūdū Zhōngwài Zhū Jūnshì, and Dàchányú,
and enfeoffed him as Qín Wáng.
Bīn was made Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn,
and enfeoffed as Tàiyuán Wáng.
Huī was made Fǔguó Jiāngjūn,
and enfeoffed as Nányáng Wáng.
He appointed Zhōngshān Gōng Hǔ as Tàiwèi and Shàngshūlìng,
and advanced his peerage to king.
Hǔ's son Suì was made Jìzhōu Cìshǐ,
and enfeoffed as Qí Wáng.
Xuān was made Zuǒ Jiāngjūn.
Tǐng was made Shìzhōng and enfeoffed as Liáng Wáng.
He also enfeoffed Shí Shēng as Hédōng Wáng,
and Shí Kān as Péngchéng Wáng.
He appointed Zuǒ Chángshǐ Guō Áo as Shàngshū Zuǒ Púshè.
Yòu Chángshǐ Chéng Xiá was made Yòu Púshè and concurrently Lǐbù Shàngshū.
Zuǒ Sīmǎ Kuí Ān, Yòu Sīmǎ Guō Yīn, Cóngshì Zhōngláng Lǐ Fèng, and former Lángzhōnglìng Péi Xiàn
were all made Shàngshū.
Cānjūnshì Xú Guāng was made Zhōngshūlìng and concurrently Mìshūjiān.
As for the remaining civil and military officials,
their enfeoffments and appointments varied.
Zhōngshān Wáng Hǔ was enraged
and privately said to Qí Wáng Suì:
"Since the sovereign moved the capital to Xiāngguó,
Huái Dì Yǒngjiā Liùnián,
Lè occupied Xiāngguó.
I have personally endured arrows and stones
for over twenty years,
captured Liú Yuè in the south,
seen in the previous volume, Míng Dì Dàníng Sānnián.
Seen in the previous volume, Xiánhé Èrnián.
索 (suǒ),
read as xī gè fān.
Pacified Qín and Yōng in the west,
pacified Qí and Lǔ,
referring to the destruction of Xú Kān and Cáo Yì,
seen in volume ninety-two, Yuán Dì Yǒngchāng Yuánnián and Míng Dì Tàiníng Yuánnián.
Pacifying Qín and Yōng
refers to destroying the Liú family
and subduing Fú and Yáo.
The one who established the great enterprise of Zhào
is I!
The Dàchányú should have been conferred upon me,
but now it is given to a yellow-mouthed child of a slave!
Thinking of it makes me choked with anger,
I cannot eat or sleep!
After the sovereign passes away,
there will be no need to keep his descendants."
Chéng Xiá spoke to Lè, saying:
"The empire is roughly settled.
We should clearly distinguish between loyalty and rebellion.
Hence, Gāozǔ of Hàn pardoned Jì Bù and
executed Dīng Gōng.
This matter is found in volume eleven, Gāozǔ Wǔnián.
Those loyal to their lord should be praised,
and those who betray and are disloyal should be executed.
This is why the world returns to great virtue.
Now Zǔ Yuē is still alive.
Your subject is perplexed by this."
Ānxī Jiāngjūn Yáo Yìzhòng also spoke similarly.
Lè then arrested Yuē,
and executed him along with over a hundred of his relatives, both close and distant.
His wives, concubines, sons, and daughters were distributed among the various Hú tribes.
In the beginning,
Zǔ Tì had a Hú servant named Wáng Ān,
whom Tì loved dearly.
In Yōngqiū,
Tì said to Ān:
"Shí Lè is of your kind.
I have no need for you alone."
He generously provided for him and sent him away.
Ān, being brave and capable,
served Zhào as Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn.
When Yuē was executed,
Ān sighed and said:
"How can Zǔ Shìzhì be without descendants?"
Zǔ Tì,
courtesy name Shìzhì.
Tì's illegitimate son Dào Zhòng,
who was then ten years old,
Ān secretly took and brought back with him,
hid him,
and disguised him as a Buddhist monk.
When the Shí clan fell,
Dào Zhòng returned to Jiāngnán.
3 Guō Mò wanted to occupy Yùzhāng in the south.
He intended to go south from Xúnyáng to occupy it.
Mò went out to battle but was unsuccessful.
He entered the city and held it firmly,
piling up rice to form ramparts,
to show that he had plenty.
Kǎn built earthen mounds overlooking it.
In the third month,
Yú Liàng's troops arrived at Pénkǒu.
Pénkǒu,
also Pénpǔkǒu.
湓 (pén),
read as pú bēn fān.
In summer,
the fifth month,
on the day Yǐmǎo,
Mò's general Sòng Hóu bound Mò and his son and surrendered them.
Kǎn executed Mò at the army gate,
sent his head to Jiànkāng,
and forty of his confederates were killed.
An imperial edict appointed Kǎn as Dūdū Jiāngzhōu
and concurrently Cìshǐ.
By this time, Kǎn was Dūdū of eight prefectures.
He concurrently held the position of Guǎngzhōu Cìshǐ.
Kǎn returned to Bālíng,
and then moved his garrison to Wǔchāng.
Yú Liàng returned to Wúhú,
declining his titles and rewards.
4 Zhào general Liú Zhēng led several thousand men,
sailed by sea, raided the southeastern counties,
and killed Nánshā Dūwèi Xǔ Rú.
Shěn Yuē's records state that
the Jìnlíng Tàishǒu had a Nánshā Lìng,
originally the Salt Commissioner's office in Wúxiàn.
During the Wú period, it was called Shāzhōng.
After Wú was pacified,
Jìyáng was established
and a portion was ceded to it.
In Jìn Chéng Dì Xiánkāng Qīnián,
the salt office was abolished,
and it was established as Nánshā Xiàn.
This is the area of Chángshú Xiàn in Píngjiāng Fǔ today.
帥 (shuài),
read as shuài.
抄 (chāo),
read as chǔ jiāo fān.
5 Zhāng Jùn, taking advantage of the fall of the former Zhào,
re-occupied the territory south of the Yellow River,
reaching Dídào.
He established five Túnhùjūn,
thus dividing the border with Zhào.
Zhāng Jùn's loss of the territory south of the Yellow River is seen in the previous volume, Xiánhé Èrnián.
The five Túnhùjūn were Wǔjiē, Shímén, Hóuhé, Qiāngchuān, and Gānsōng.
Zhào sent Hónglú Mèng Yì to appoint Jùn as Zhēngxī Dàjiāngjūn and Liángzhōu Mù,
and granted him the Jiǔxī.
Jùn was ashamed to be a subject of Zhào
and refused the appointment,
detaining Yì and not sending him back.
6 In the beginning,
Dīnglíng Zhái Bīn,
whose family had long resided in Kāngjū,
later moved to Zhōngguó.
By this time, he came to pay homage to Zhào.
Zhào appointed Bīn as Gōudīng Wáng.
7. Zhào Jǐn Chén (趙㣥臣) persistently requested the rectification of the imperial title.
In autumn,
in the ninth month,
Zhào Wáng Lè (趙王勒) ascended the imperial throne.
The Research into Differences states: The Accounts record:
"From Xiāngguó (襄國) the capital moved to Línzhāng (臨漳),
which is Yè (鄴)."
Lè (勒) went to Yè (鄴),
and discussed building a new palace.
Three years later,
Lè (勒) went to Yè (鄴),
and visited Shí Hǔ's (石虎) residence.
When Lè (勒) was ill,
Hǔ (虎) fraudulently summoned Shí Hóng (石宏) back to Xiāngguó (襄國).
It was not until the ninth month of the first year of Hǔ's (虎) Jiànwǔ (建武) era
that the capital was first moved to Yè (鄴).
Thus, Lè (勒) never made Yè (鄴) his capital.
A general amnesty was granted,
and the era name was changed to Jiànpíng (建平).
Civil and military officials were ennobled and promoted according to their ranks.
His wife, Lady Liú (劉氏), was established as empress,
and Crown Prince Hóng (弘) as Imperial Crown Prince.
Hóng (弘) was fond of composing writings,
and respected Confucian plainness.
Lè (勒) said to Xú Guāng (徐光):
"Dàyǎ (大雅) is gentle and harmonious."
Hóng (弘)
had the courtesy name Dàyǎ (大雅).
Yīnyīn (愔愔)
means peaceful and harmonious in appearance.
(Pronunciation note for 愔愔).
Guāng (光) replied:
"Hàn Zǔ (漢祖) conquered the empire from horseback;
Xiàowén (孝文) preserved it with profound quietude.
The descendants of a sage
are destined to be those who overcome cruelty and eliminate killing.
This is the Way of Heaven."
The Analects state: Kǒngzǐ (孔子) said, "If good men govern a country for a hundred years,
they may also overcome cruelty and eliminate killing."
Wáng Shì's (王氏) commentary states: "Overcoming cruelty"
means being able to make cruel and violent people desist from evil;
"eliminating killing"
means abolishing executions and killings.
Shèng (勝)
(pronunciation note).
Qù (去)
(pronunciation note).
Guāng (光) then said:
"The Imperial Crown Prince is benevolent, filial, gentle, and respectful.
Zhōngshān Wáng Xióng (中山王雄) is brutal and full of stratagems.
Should Your Majesty one day pass away,
your servant fears the altars of soil and grain (the state) will not belong to the Crown Prince.
It is advisable to gradually strip Zhōngshān Wáng's (中山王) power
and let the Crown Prince participate in court affairs early."
Lè (勒) assented in his heart,
but could not act on it.
8. Guō Jìng (郭敬), Inspector of Jīngzhōu (荊州) for Zhào (趙), raided Xiāngyáng (襄陽).
Zhōu Fǔ (周撫), General of the Southern Gentlemen, supervised military affairs north of the Miǎn River,
garrisoned in Xiāngyáng (襄陽).
Zhào Zhǔ Lè (趙主勒) sent an express letter ordering Jìng (敬) to retreat and garrison in Fánchéng (樊城),
instructing him to furl and conceal his banners and flags,
to appear as if there were no one there.
He said:
"If they send someone to observe,
then tell them: 'You should protect yourselves and hold fast.
In seven or eight days,
a large cavalry force will arrive.
Plan accordingly,
plan accordingly!' "
This means to plan and respond to each other.
Dù Yòu's (杜佑) Tōngdiǎn (通典) writes it as
"mutually forbid."
One interpretation says:
"Xiāng Cè" (相策)
belongs to the next sentence;
cè (策)
means "to scheme" or "calculate,"
similar to saying, "I calculate you will no longer be able to run away."
Jìng (敬) had men bathe horses at the ford,
repeatedly,
without ceasing day or night.
The scouts returned and reported this to Zhōu Fǔ (周撫).
Fǔ (撫) thought a large Zhào (趙) army had arrived.
Frightened,
he fled to Wǔchāng (武昌).
Jìng (敬) entered Xiāngyáng (襄陽).
All the displaced people from Zhōngzhōu (中州) surrendered to Zhào (趙).
Wèi Gāi's (魏該) younger brother, Xiá (遐), led his followers from Shíchéng (石城) and surrendered to Jìng (敬).
Jìng (敬) destroyed the city walls of Xiāngyáng (襄陽),
moved its people to Miǎnběi (沔北),
and fortified Fánchéng (樊城) to garrison them.
Zhào (趙) appointed Jìng (敬) as Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ (荊州刺史).
Zhōu Fǔ (周撫) was dismissed from office due to this.
9. Xiūtú Wáng Qiāng (休屠王羌) rebelled against Zhào (趙).
Xiūtú Wáng Qiāng (休屠王羌)
was a tribe of Shí Wǔ (石武).
Tú (屠)
(pronunciation note).
Qiāng (羌) fled to Liángzhōu (涼州).
Xīpíng Gōng Jùn (西平公駿) was afraid,
sent Mèng Yì (孟毅) back,
and had his Chief Clerk Mǎ Shēn (馬詵) declare submission and present tribute to Zhào (趙).
10. (The imperial court) built new palaces again.
During Sū Jùn's (蘇峻) rebellion,
the palaces were burned and destroyed,
hence they were rebuilt.
Gēng (更)
(pronunciation note).
11. On the Jiǎchén (甲辰) day, Lèchéng Wáng Qīn (樂成王欽) was transferred and enfeoffed as Héjiān Wáng (河間王).
Upon the death of Héjiān Wáng Yǒng (河間王顒),
an imperial edict designated Róng (融), son of Péngchéng Wáng Zhí (彭城王植), as Yǒng's (顒) heir.
He was re-enfeoffed as Lèchéng Xiàn Wáng (樂成縣王).
When he died,
he had no son.
Yuán Dì (元帝) then designated Qīn (欽), son of Péngchéng Wáng Shì (彭城王釋), as Róng's (融) heir.
Now, his old enfeoffment as Héjiān (河間) was restored.
Previously,
Yuán Dì (元帝) had made Hóng (紘) heir to Gāomì Wáng Jù (高密王據).
When Péngchéng Wáng Xióng (彭城王雄) was executed for his involvement with Sū Jùn (蘇峻),
Hóng (紘) returned to inherit his original lineage.
Jùn (俊) was then designated heir to Gāomì Wáng (高密王).
The Research into Differences states: The Biographies of Imperial Clan Members write "Jùn" (浚).
We now follow the Imperial Annals.
12. In winter,
in the tenth month,
Chéng (成)'s Dàjiàngjūn Shòu (大將軍壽), overseeing Zhēngnán Jiāngjūn Fèi Hēi (征南將軍費黑) and others, attacked Bādōng (巴東) and Jiànpíng (建平).
They captured them.
Yáng Qiān (楊謙), Administrator of Bādōng (巴東), and Guànqiū Ào (毌丘奧), Inspector-General, retreated to defend Yídū (宜都).
1. In spring,
in the first month,
Liú Zhēng (劉徵) of Zhào (趙) again raided Lóuxiàn (婁縣),
and plundered Wǔjìn (武進).
Lóuxiàn (婁縣),
during the Former Hàn (漢), belonged to Kuàijī Jùn (會稽郡).
During the Later Hàn (漢) and Jìn (晉), it belonged to Wú Jùn (吳郡).
In the third year of Jiāhé (嘉禾) of Sūn Quán (孫權) of Wú (吳),
Dāntú (丹徒) was renamed Wǔjìn (武進).
In the third year of Tàikāng (太康) of Jìn Wǔdì (晉武帝),
it was again called Dāntú (丹徒),
and Wǔjìn Xiàn (武進縣) was established by dividing Dāntú (丹徒) and Qǔ'ē (曲阿).
It belonged to Pílíng Jùn (毗陵郡).
Jìn (晉) renamed Pílíng (毗陵) to Jìnlíng (晉陵).
Liú Xù (劉昫) said: "Táng (唐)'s Kūnshān Xiàn (崑山縣) in Sūzhōu (Sūzhōu)
was the territory of Hàn (漢)'s Lóuxiàn (婁縣)."
Fù (復)
(pronunciation note);
same below.
2. In the third month,
on the first day of Rénxū (壬戌),
there was a solar eclipse.
3. In summer,
Zhào Zhǔ Lè (趙主勒) went to Yè (鄴),
intending to build new palaces.
The Tíngwèi (廷尉) Xù Xián (續咸) of Shàngdǎng (上黨) remonstrated bitterly.
Lè (勒) was enraged,
and wanted to execute him.
Zhōngshū Lìng Xú Guāng (中書令徐光) said:
"Although Xián's (咸) words cannot be used,
he should still be tolerated.
How can you suddenly execute a high minister for speaking frankly?"
Lè (勒) sighed, saying:
"As a ruler,
must I not be able to act on my own like this?
Even a common man with a fortune of a hundred bolts of silk
still wishes to buy a house,
let alone one who possesses the four seas!
These palaces will eventually be built.
For now, I will order the construction to stop
to preserve the spirit of my upright minister."
Thereupon, he bestowed upon Xián (咸) a hundred bolts of silk
and a hundred hu (斛) of rice.
He also issued an edict for officials from the ducal ministers down to annually recommend worthy and upright individuals.
He further allowed those recommended to recommend others,
to broaden the path for seeking talent.
He built a Míngtáng (明堂), Bìyōng (辟雍), and Língtái (靈臺) west of the city of Xiāngguó (襄國).
Historians say that Shí Lè (石勒) was able to rectify his fierce and violent habits and cultivate culture.
4. In autumn,
in the seventh month,
Chéng (成)'s Dàjiàngjūn Shòu (大將軍壽) attacked Yīnpíng (陰平) and Wǔdū (武都).
Yáng Nándí (楊難敵) surrendered to him.
5. In the ninth month,
Zhào Zhǔ Lè (趙主勒) again began building palaces in Yè (鄴).
He designated Luòyáng (洛陽) as the Nándū (南都) and established an executive office there.
6. In winter,
a *zhēng*-sacrifice was offered at the Grand Ancestral Temple.
An imperial edict granted the sacrificial meat (*zuò*) to Sītú Dǎo.
The *Lǐjì* (Book of Rites) states that
winter sacrifices are called
“*zhēng*.”
The *Shǐjì* and *Hànshū* also write it as
“*zhēngjì*” (蒸祭).
The remaining meat is called *zuò*;
today it is known as sacrificial blessed meat.
The Jìn treated Wáng Dǎo with the same rites that the Zhōu applied to Qí Huán Gōng.
At first,
when the emperor ascended the throne, he was young and immature.
Each time he saw Dǎo, he would bow.
When giving Dǎo a handwritten edict, he would say,
“I am filled with trepidation to speak.”
When the Central Secretariat drafted an edict, it would say,
“With respectful inquiry.”
The relevant officials debated:
“On the day of the grand New Year’s assembly,
should the emperor show reverence to Dǎo or not?”
The Doctors Guō Xī and Dù Yuán argued,
believing that:
“The rites contain no text regarding a ruler bowing to a subject.
It is appropriate to abolish this reverence.”
Attendant Counselor Féng Huái argued,
believing that:
“The Son of Heaven attends the *Bìyōng* and
bows to the Three Elders,
let alone the instructor of the late emperor.
It is appropriate to show utmost reverence.”
Attendant Counselor Xún Yì argued,
believing that:
“On the first of the Three Dawns (New Year’s Day is the first of the Three Dawns),
the Three Dawns refer to the dawn of the year, the dawn of the month, and the dawn of the day.
*Cháo* (朝) means dawn.
If it refers to dawn
(as the character indicates),
then reverence should not be shown.
If it is a smaller assembly on another day,
then it is certainly acceptable to observe full rites.”
For a ruler to bow to a subject
and call it observing full rites,
is this acceptable?
Yì
was the son of Zǔ.
7. Mùróng Huī sent an envoy with a memorial to Grand Marshal Táo Kǎn,
encouraging him to raise troops for a northern expedition
and jointly pacify the Central Plains.
His subordinates, Sòng Gāi and others, jointly debated,
believing that
“Huī has achieved merit in one corner,
but his rank is low while his responsibility is great,
and there is no distinction in his status.
He is insufficient to pacify the Chinese and barbarians.
It is advisable to memorialize requesting the advancement of Huī’s official rank and peerage.”
Staff Officer Hán Héng retorted, saying:
“Those who establish merit worry about their trustworthiness and integrity not being evident,
not about their fame and position not being high.
Huán and Wén had the merit of restoring order,
but they did not first seek official appointments and imperial commands to lead the feudal lords.
It is advisable to repair armor and weapons,
eliminate the brutal and wicked.
After success is achieved,
the Nine Bestowals will naturally arrive.
Compared to inviting the ruler to seek favor,
is this not more glorious!”
Huī was displeased
and dismissed Héng as Magistrate of Xīnchāng.
Xīnchāng County
belonged to Liáodōng Commandery.
He requested that Huī be enfeoffed as King of Yān
and act as Grand General.
Kǎn replied, saying:
“Advancing in rank upon achieving merit
is an ancient established system.
Although the General of Cavalry has not yet been able to crush and subdue for the court,
Huī was promoted to General of Cavalry.
Therefore, Kǎn referred to him as such.
*Guān* (官)
refers to the Son of Heaven;
*Lè* (勒)
refers to Shí Lè.

(Rénchén, 332)
1. In spring,
the first month,
on the *Xīnwèi* day,
a general amnesty was granted.
2. Zhào Lord Lè held a grand banquet for all his subjects.
*Kǎoyì* says: The *Jìn Chūnqiū* states:
“Táo Kǎn sent an envoy to pay respects to Later Zhào,
and Zhào King Lè hosted him with a banquet.”
However, there is certainly no reason for Kǎn and Lè to have communicated through envoys,
so this account is not taken.
*Zàijì* states:
“Lè hosted envoys from Gāogōulí and Yǔwén Wūgū.”
Now it merely says he hosted all his subjects.
“To what kind of ancient ruler can I compare myself?”
*Fāng* (方)
means compare.
“Your Majesty’s divine prowess and strategy surpass those of Hàn Gāo.
There is no one in later generations who can compare.”
Lè laughed, saying:
“How can a person not know himself!
Your words are too exaggerated.
If I had met Hàn Gāozǔ,
I would have served him facing north,
standing shoulder to shoulder with Hán and Péng.
Dài Xī said: How could Lè truly understand Emperor Gāo?
He merely regarded himself as inferior to Hán and Péng.
If we were to contend for the Central Plains,
who knows whose hands the deer would fall into.
A true man’s actions
should be clear and straightforward,
as bright as the sun and moon.
I would never imitate Cáo Mèngdé or Sīmǎ Zhòngdá, who deceived orphaned children and widows,
using cunning flattery to seize the empire.”
*Hú* (狐)
refers to a mythical fox,
which can bewitch people with flattery.
Shí Lè used this to comment on Cáo and Mǎ.
If the deceased had consciousness,
Mèngdé and Zhòngdá
would surely feel ashamed in the underworld!
Although Lè was unlearned,
he liked to have scholars read books to him and would listen,
occasionally commenting on the successes and failures of ancient and modern times according to his own thoughts,
and those who heard him were all pleased and convinced.
He once had someone read the *Hànshū* to him.
Upon hearing that Lì Yìjī advised establishing the descendants of the Six States,
the event is found in Volume 10, Emperor Gāo of Hàn, Year 3.
“This method ought to have failed,
how then did he manage to gain the empire?”
When he then heard of Liú Hóu’s remonstrance,
he said:
“It relied on this indeed.”
3. Guō Jìng had retreated from garrisoning Fánchéng.
The event is found in the previous volume, Year 5.
In summer,
the fourth month,
Jìng attacked and recaptured it, leaving a garrison before returning.
4 Zhào’s Right Minister, Chéng Xiá, spoke to Zhào Lord Lè, saying:
“The King of Zhōngshān, Hǔ, is brave, fierce, and strategically shrewd;
among your subjects, none can match him.
Observing his ambition,
besides Your Majesty,
he views all others as nothing.
‘Miè’ [蔑]
means ‘nothing’ [無],
indicating that he sees others as if they do not exist.
Mencius said: ‘He who injures others is called a 'thief' (賊);
he who injures righteousness is called a 'tyrant' (殘).’
In the ‘Zuǒ Zhuàn,’
Zhòng Zhòng said: ‘One who is cruel and ruthless has no kin.’
His prestige shakes both internal and external circles,
and his elder sons
all hold military power.
Hǔ’s sons, Suì and Xuān,
Lè had both of them command troops.
Jiàng [將],
pronounce as ‘liàng.’
Shuài [帥],
pronounce as ‘suǒ lèi.’
Zhǎng [長],
pronounce as ‘zhī liǎng.’
While he himself may have no other intentions,
I fear he is not a minister for the young lord.
It is advisable to eliminate him early,
to facilitate the grand plan.”
Lè said:
“Currently, the world is not yet settled,
and Dàyǎ is young and immature;
he needs strong support.
The King of Zhōngshān is a close relative by blood,
and has the merit of assisting in establishing the dynasty.
He should be entrusted with the responsibilities of Yī and Huò;
how can it be as you say?
You are merely afraid of not gaining the power of an imperial uncle;
I will also consult you on my dying instructions,
so do not worry too much.”
Xiá wept and said:
“What I worry about is the state;
Your Majesty rejects it with private considerations.
How can loyal words ever enter?
Although the King of Zhōngshān was raised by the Empress Dowager,
he is not Your Majesty's blood relative.
The ‘Zài Jì’ states: Hǔ [虎]
is Lè’s cousin.
His grandfather was Yìxié [㔨邪],
and his father was Kòumì [寇覓].
Lè’s father, Zhū, adopted Hǔ when he was young,
which is why some refer to Hǔ as Lè’s younger brother.
Your Majesty’s repayment of his father and son’s kindness and honor is already sufficient,
yet his ambitions are boundless,
meaning Hǔ has the ambition to covet the throne.
If he is not eliminated,
I foresee that the ancestral temple will cease to receive blood sacrifices.”
Lè did not listen.
Xiá withdrew
and told Xú Guāng,
who said:
“The King of Zhōngshān often grinds his teeth at us two;
I fear it is not just a danger to the state,
but will also become a family disaster.”
Another day,
Guāng, seizing an opportunity, spoke to Lè, saying:
“Now the country is at peace,
yet Your Majesty’s complexion seems displeased;
why is this?”
Yí [怡]
means ‘joy’ [悅]. “The states of
Wú and Shǔ are not yet pacified,
and I fear that later generations will not consider me a king who received the mandate.”
Guāng said:
“Wèi inherited the Hàn dynasty’s destiny.
Although Liú Bèi rose in Shǔ,
how could Hàn be considered not fallen?
This is an analogy to Jìn.
It is like today’s Lí clan.
Your Majesty has encompassed the two capitals
and pacified the eight provinces.
The two capitals
are Cháng’ān and Luòyáng.
The eight provinces
are Jì, Yōu, Bīng, Qīng, Yǎn, Yù, Sī, and Yōng.
Who else could possess them?
Moreover, Your Majesty does not worry about the illness of the heart and abdomen,
but instead worries about the four limbs?
The King of Zhōngshān relies on Your Majesty's might and strategy,
conquering wherever he goes,
and everyone in the realm says his martial prowess is second only to Your Majesty.
Furthermore, his nature is unkind,
he forgets righteousness for profit.
Father and son both hold positions of power,
their influence tilting the royal court.
Yet, he constantly harbors dissatisfaction.
Recently, while feasting at the Eastern Palace,
he showed disrespect towards the Crown Prince.
I fear that after Your Majesty’s ten thousand years,
he will no longer be controllable.”
Lè was silent.
He then ordered the Crown Prince to examine and approve memorials,
and also assigned the Palace Regular Attendant Yán Zhèn to participate in reviewing their approval or rejection.
Only major decisions concerning military campaigns, executions, and other crucial matters were to be presented to him.
Consequently, Yán Zhèn’s power surpassed that of the prime ministers,
and the gate of Zhōngshān King Hǔ could be spread with a birdnet.
The ‘Hàn Shū’ states: “When Zhái Gōng was Grand Judge,

Yàng [怏],

Sometimes he carried a hoe and a plough handle in his light carriage.
Chú [鉏]
is a farm tool used for weeding.
Lěi [耒],

“Bottom” [底]

Lǐ Shòu wanted to resist Huò Biāo,

"Food in the city is scarce.
It is advisable to allow Huò Biāo to enter the city,

Lǐ Shòu agreed.
The city did not fall for a long time,
and Lǐ Shòu wanted to attack it urgently.
Hēi said:
"The Nánzhōng region is rugged and difficult to subdue.
One should control it with the passage of days and months,
waiting until their wisdom and courage are both exhausted,
and only then take it.
What is the hurry for
such trivial matters?"
Lǐ Shòu did not agree,

He then entrusted all military affairs to Hēi.

Shuài,
read as shuài.
Jì,

He meant that they should assist the young orphan like Zhōu Gōng and Huò Guāng.

Yì,

Zhào general Shí Cōng and Qiáo Jùn Administrator Péng Biāo,

then turns past Liàojiǎo to Dēngzhōu Dàyáng;
traveling northeast,
one passes Dàxiè Island, Guīxīn Island, Yū Island, and Wūhú Island, a distance of three hundred *lǐ*.
Crossing Wūhú Sea north,
one arrives at Dūlǐ Zhèn, east of Mǎshí Shān.
Mǎshí Jīn
is this very place.
14 In the ninth month,
on the *wùyín* day,
Protector General, Duke Mù of Jiānglíng, Lù Yè, died.
15 Chéng Lord Xióng's son, General of Chariots and Cavalry, Yuè (李越), garrisoned Jiāngyáng,
and rushed to Chéngdū for the funeral.
As Crown Prince Bān (李班) was not born to Xióng (李雄) himself,
Yuè (李越) was discontent
and conspired with his younger brother, General of Pacifying the East Qí (李期), to rebel.
Bān's (李班) younger brother Wǔ (李玝) advised Bān (李班) to send Yuè (李越) back to Jiāngyáng,
and appoint Qí (李期) as the Inspector of Liángzhōu,

Jiāmáng
was the land of Jìnshòu.
Wǔ,
pronounced Ruǎngǔ.
Bān (李班) could not bear to send him away,
and treated him with sincerity,
without any suspicion or estrangement,
instead sending Wǔ (李玝) to garrison Fú.
In winter,
tenth month,
on the first day of Guǐhài,
Yuè (李越) took advantage of Bān's (李班) nocturnal weeping
and assassinated him in the mourning palace.
It turned out exactly as Lǐ Xiāng (李驤) had predicted.
Zōutú refers to the mourning period;
when preparing for reburial,
the deceased is treated as a guest.
Yuè (李越) forged the order of Empress Dowager Rèn (任氏),

Initially,
Qí's (李期) mother, Lady Rǎn (冉氏), was of low status,

Qí (李期) was talented and skilled,

after Bān's (李班) death,
the multitude wished to enthrone Yuè (李越),
but Yuè (李越) supported Qí (李期) and established him.
On Jiǎzǐ,
Qí (李期) ascended the imperial throne.
Qí (李期),
courtesy name Shìyùn,
was Xióng's (李雄) fourth son.
He appointed Yuè (李越) as Chancellor,
enfeoffed him as King of Jiànníng;
Shòu (李壽) was given the additional title of Grand General and Grand Chief Controller,
and his enfeoffment changed to King of Hàn;

His elder brother Bà (李霸) was made Central Leader of the Army and Grand General Pacifying the South;
his younger brother Bǎo (李保) was made Grand General Pacifying the West and Administrator of Wénshān;
his cousin Shǐ (李始) was made Grand General Conquering the East,
replacing Yuè (李越) to garrison Jiāngyáng.
According to the Records of States: Shǐ (李始) was the eldest son of Tè (李特),
making him Qí's (李期) paternal uncle,
and Shòu's (李壽) cousin.
Cóng,
pronounced cáiyòng.
On Bǐngyín,
Xióng (李雄) was buried at Āndū Mausoleum,
with the posthumous title Emperor Wǔ (武皇帝),
and temple name Tàizōng (太宗).
Shǐ (李始) wanted to join Shòu (李壽) in attacking Qí (李期),
but Shòu (李壽) dared not act.
Shǐ (李始) was enraged,
and instead slandered Shòu (李壽) to Qí (李期),
requesting his execution.
Qí (李期) wished to rely on Shòu (李壽) to suppress Lǐ Wǔ (李玝),
so he did not consent,
instead sending Shòu (李壽) to lead troops towards Fú.
Shòu (李壽) first sent an envoy to inform Wǔ (李玝) of the advantages and disadvantages of his choices,

An imperial edict appointed Wǔ (李玝) as Administrator of Bājùn.
Qí (李期) appointed Shòu (李壽) as Inspector of Liángzhōu,
garrisoning Fú.
This laid the groundwork for Lǐ Shòu (李壽) to raise an army from Fú and depose Lǐ Qí (李期).
16 Zhào (趙) Lord Hóng (石弘) personally brought the imperial seal and sash to the Wèi (魏) Palace.
Shí Hǔ (石虎) was the King of Wèi,

Xǐ,
pronounced sīshì.
Shòu,
pronounced shòu.
Hǔ (石虎) said:

Thereupon, the Secretariat presented a memorial:
"The Wèi (魏) Office requests that, in accordance with the precedent of the Tang and Yu (唐虞) abdication, "

Hóng (石弘) walked calmly to his carriage,

None of his attendants failed to weep,

Hǔ (石虎) said:

The Examination of Differences states: The Thirty Kingdoms and Jin Chunqiu:
"When Hǔ (石虎) ascended the throne,
he changed the reign title to Yǒngxī (永熙)";
Chén Hóng's (陳鴻) Dàtǒng Calendar states:
"Shí Hǔ (石虎) ascended the throne,
and changed the fifth year of Jiànpíng to Yánxīng (延興),
and the next year to Jiànwǔ (建武)."
According to this,
the Thirty Kingdoms and Jin Chunqiu do not record Hóng's (石弘) change of reign title to Yánxī (延熙),
and Hǔ's (石虎) ascension was indeed the first year of Yánxī (延熙).
Therefore, it mistakenly says Yǒngxī (永熙).
Since Hóng (石弘) used the reign title Yánxī (延熙),
how could Hǔ (石虎) claim Yǒngxī (永熙)?
Chén Hóng (陳鴻) said:
"Hǔ (石虎) changed the fifth year of Jiànpíng to Yánxīng (延興),
which means Hóng (石弘) did not change the reign title for over a year."
I fear Chén Hóng's (陳鴻) explanation is mistaken.
Soon, he killed them all.
Hǔ (石虎) renamed the Crown Prince's Palace to Chóngxùn Palace.
Hóng (石弘) was twenty-one at the time.
The Grand Chief Controller of the Western Qiāng (西羌), Yáo Yìzhòng (姚弋仲), feigned illness and did not offer congratulations.
Hǔ (石虎) repeatedly summoned him

With a stern expression, he said to Hǔ (石虎):

Hǔ (石虎) said:

Though displeased,

Hǔ (石虎) appointed Kuí Ān (夔安) as Attendant-in-Chief, Grand Commandant, and Overseer of the Secretariat,

Shēn Zhōng (申鐘) of Wèijùn as Attendant-in-Chief,

Jiàng,
pronounced hùjiāng;

In the first year of Xiánkāng (咸康)
(Yǐwèi, 335)
1. In spring,
in the first month,
on the first day (gēngwǔ),
the Emperor underwent the capping ceremony.
Shěn Yuē (沈約)'s Lǐ Zhì (禮志) states: In ancient times, there was no capping ceremony for the Son of Heaven.
Therefore, the day and guest were divined, and the capping took place in the eastern steps,
symbolizing that the host exchanged toasts with the guest.
The three additions of caps signified increasing reverence,
all being rituals for a scholar.
Emperor Shùn (順) of Hàn (漢) underwent the capping ceremony,
incorporating Cáo Bāo (曹褒)'s new rites.
Bāo (褒)'s new rites are no longer extant.

all at the Gāomiào (高廟).

"In this propitious month and fortunate day,
the primary capping is first performed.
The Emperor, reverent and solemn,
contemplates extending his imperial duties.
He reveres and conforms to August Heaven,
making the Six Harmonies his model.
He follows and observes his ancestors,
forever without end.
May his life be without limit,
and may he receive this great blessing."
After the miǎn (冕) cap was added,
the Shìzhōng (侍中) fastened the xuándǎn (玄紞) tassel.

After the capping ceremony was completed,

Shào (少),

Rèn (任),

"Dǒu (斗)

During the Tàihé (太和) period of Emperor Míng (明) of Wèi (魏),
an edict established the position of Zhuòzuò Láng (著作郎),
and it was then that this office first existed,
subordinate to the Zhōngshū Shěng (中書省).
When Jìn (晉) received the mandate,
it was decreed:
"Zhuòzuò (著作) was formerly subordinate to the Zhōngshū (中書),
but since the Bìmì Shū (祕書) already manages literary records,
we now change the Zhōngshū Shěng Zhuòzuò (中書省著作) to Bìmì Shū Zhuòzuò (祕書著作)."
Thereupon, it was subordinated to the Bìmì Shū Shěng (祕書省);
later, a separate department was established,
but it was still subordinate to the Bìmì Shū (祕書).
"For kings, sacrificial rites
and ceremonial practices are all in place.
The Buddha,
a god from a foreign country,
is not to be worshipped by the Son of Heaven and the various Huá (華) peoples.
The Hàn (漢) dynasty first introduced its teachings,
as seen in Volume 45, the eighth year of Yǒngpíng (永平) of Emperor Míng (明) of Hàn (漢).
Hàn (漢) people initially referred to government offices as sì (寺).
Later, when the Hàn (漢) dynasty received sutras from the Western Regions carried by a white horse,
they first stopped at Hónglú Sì (鴻臚寺),
and thus took the name sì (寺)
to establish Bámǎ Sì (白馬寺).
The Wèi (魏) era was also like this.
Now, it is fitting to prohibit officials below the rank of Gōngqīng (公卿) from going to temples to burn incense and bow;
as for the people of Zhào (趙) who have become Shāmén (沙門),
they shall all return to their original attire."
This means making them return to wearing the clothes of the Huá (華) people.
"I, born in the border regions,
am unworthily the ruler of the various Xià (夏) peoples.
When it comes to sacrifices and offerings,
I should follow my native customs.
However, if the Yí (夷) and Zhào (趙) common people wish to practice Buddhism,
they are specifically permitted to do so."
13 Zhào Zhāngwǔ Wáng Bīn (趙章武王斌) led twenty thousand elite cavalry and troops from Qín (秦) and Yōng (雍) two prefectures to attack Báo Jù Dà (薄句大),
and pacified him.
Last year, Bīn (斌) and others were defeated by Báo Jù Dà (薄句大).
Bīn (斌) is pronounced
Bīn.
Shuài (帥) is
read as Shuài.

Jù (句) is pronounced

14 Luó Yǎn (羅演), maternal uncle of Chéng Tàizǐ Bān (成太子班),
conspired with Hàn Wáng Xiàng (漢王相) Tiānshuǐ Shàngguān Dàn (天水上官澹)
Lǐ Shòu (李壽) was enfeoffed as King of Hàn (漢).
Xiàng (相) is pronounced
Xī liàng fān.
Dàn (澹) is pronounced
Tú lǎn fān.
to enthrone Bān's (班) son.
When the plot was discovered,
Qí (期) killed Yǎn (演), Dàn (澹), and Bān's (班) mother, Lady Luó (羅氏).
Qí (期), believing himself to be successful,
slighted the old officials,
trusting Shàngshū Lìng (尚書令) Jǐng Qiān (景騫), Shàngshū (尚書) Yáo Huá (姚華), Tián Bāo (田褒), Zhōngchángshì (中常侍) Xǔ Fú (許涪), and others.
Major policies of reward and punishment
were all decided by these few people,
rarely involving the Gōngqīng (公卿).
Bāo (褒) had no other talent;
he had once advised Chéng Zhǔ Xióng (成主雄) to establish Qí (期) as Crown Prince,
which is why he was favored.
As a result, the discipline and order became chaotic,
and Xióng's (雄) enterprise began to decline.
15 In winter,
the tenth month,
on the day Yǐwèi (乙未), the first day of the lunar month,
there was a solar eclipse.
16 Mùróng Rén (慕容仁) sent Wáng Qí (王齊) and others back south.
Last year, Qí (齊) and others were detained by Mùróng Rén (慕容仁).
Qí (齊) was caught in a storm and did not arrive.
In the twelfth month,
Xú Mèng (徐孟) and others arrived at Jíchéng (棘城),
and Mùróng Huǎng (慕容皝) first accepted the imperial mandate.
The Duàn (段) clan and the Yǔwén (宇文) clan each sent envoys to Mùróng Rén (慕容仁),
who housed them outside Píngguō (平郭) city.
Huǎng's (皝) zhàngxiàdū (帳下督) Zhāng Yīng (張英) led over a hundred cavalrymen along a secret path, advanced swiftly, and ambushed them,
beheading over ten envoys of the Yǔwén (宇文) clan
and capturing the Duàn (段) clan's envoys alive to bring back.
17 In this year,
Emperor Míng's (明帝) mother, Jiàn'ān Jūn Xún Shì (建安君荀氏), passed away.
Xún Shì (荀氏) was in the forbidden palace,
respected equally with the Empress Dowager;
an edict posthumously granted her the title Yùzhāng Jùn Jūn (豫章郡君).
Xún Shì (荀氏) was
a palace woman of Emperor Yuán (元帝),
and gave birth to Emperor Míng (明帝).
Due to her low status,
she often harbored resentment,
and was rebuked by the emperor,
gradually becoming estranged.
When Emperor Míng (明帝) ascended the throne,
she was enfeoffed as Jiàn'ān Jūn (建安君),
and a separate residence was established for her.
In the first year of Tàiníng (太寧),
she was welcomed back to the palace,
and received generous offerings.
After the emperor ascended,
she was respected equally with the Empress Dowager.
18 Dài Wáng Yìhuái (代王翳槐) found Hèlán Àitóu (賀蘭藹頭) disrespectful.
Àitóu (藹頭) was
Yìhuái's (翳槐) maternal uncle,
and had rendered services in supporting him,
as seen in Volume 93, the second year of Xiánhé (咸和).
By the fourth year,
he expelled Hénà (紇那)
and enthroned Yìhuái (翳槐).
He was also from the Hèlán (賀蘭) tribe,
and relying on kinship and merit, hence his disrespect.
All the other tribes rebelled.
Dài Wáng Hénà (代王紇那) entered from the Yǔwén (宇文) tribe,
and the tribes once again supported him.
Hénà (紇那) had fled as seen in the previous volume, the fourth year of Xiánhé (咸和).
Fù (復) is pronounced
Fú yòu fān.
The people of Zhào (趙) treated him generously.
19 Previously,
Zhāng Guǐ (張軌) and his two sons Shí (寔) and Mào (茂),
although they held the region west of the Yellow River,
were constantly engaged in military campaigns every year.
When Zhāng Jùn (張駿) succeeded to the position,
the internal territory gradually became peaceful.
Jùn (駿) diligently managed all government affairs,
overseeing both civil and military officials,
all of whom were put to good use.
The people were prosperous and the army was strong,
and he was praised by those near and far as a virtuous ruler.
Jùn (駿) sent general Yáng Xuān (楊宣) to attack Qiūcí (龜茲) and Shànshàn (鄯善),
and consequently, the various kingdoms of the Western Regions, such as Yānqí (焉耆) and Yútián (于窴),
all came to Gūzāng (姑臧) to pay tribute.
Jùn (駿) built five halls south of Gūzāng (姑臧).
Jùn (駿) built the Qiānguāng Diàn (謙光殿),
and on each of its four sides, he built a hall: the east was called Yíyáng Qīngdiàn (宜陽青殿),
where he resided for the three months of spring;
the south was called Zhūyáng Chìdiàn (朱陽赤殿),
where he resided for the three months of summer;
the west was called Zhèngxíng Báidiàn (政刑白殿),
where he resided for the three months of autumn;
the north was called Xuánwǔ Hēidiàn (玄武黑殿),
where he resided for the three months of winter.
The robes, ornaments, and utensils
all corresponded to the directional colors.
Jùn had the ambition to annex Qín and Yōng,
and sent his Cānjūn, Qū Hù, to present a memorial,
which stated:
"Since Lè and Xióng are dead,
Hǔ and Qī have successively rebelled.
The common people have been separated from their ruler,
gradually enduring through the ages;
the old have faded away,
and the new generation does not know,
so the longing heart
grows more distant and forgets day by day.
I beg you to order Sīkōng Jiàn and Zhēngxī Liàng, among others, to sail boats on the Jiāng and Miǎn,
launching a coordinated attack from both ends."
Xī Jiàn was then garrisoned at Jīngkǒu,
and Yǔ Liàng was garrisoned at Wǔchāng.
Miǎn,
pronounced 'mǐ yǎn' in the Fanqie system.
The second
spring,
in the first month,
on the Xīnsì day,
a comet was seen in Kuí and Lóu.
The sixteen stars of Kuí in the west
are the arsenal of heaven,
presiding over the use of soldiers to suppress violence,
and also over canals and ditches.
The three stars of Lóu
form the celestial prison,
presiding over parks, pastures, and sacrifices,
and supplying offerings for suburban sacrifices.
Kuí, Lóu, and Zhòu
correspond to the divisions of Lǔ and Xúzhōu.
Huì,
pronounced 'xiáng suì' in the Fanqie system,
also 'xuán ruì' in the Fanqie system,
and also 'xú zuì' in the Fanqie system.
Jiàn,
pronounced 'xián biàn' in the Fanqie system.
Mùróng Huàng was about to attack Mùróng Rén,
and Sīmǎ Gāo Xǔ said:
"Rén has rebelled against his lord and kin;
gods and men alike are angry.
Before this, the sea had never frozen,
but since Rén's rebellion,
it has frozen three years in a row.
Moreover, Rén is exclusively prepared for a land route;
perhaps Heaven intends for us to use the sea ice to attack him."
Huàng followed this advice.
All the officials said that crossing the ice was dangerous,
and that it was better to take the land route.
Huàng said:
"My plan is already decided.
Whoever dares to obstruct it will be beheaded!"
On the Rénwǔ day,
Huàng led his younger brother Jūnshī Jiāngjūn Píng and others from Chānglí eastward,
advancing across the ice
for over three hundred *lǐ*.
They reached Lìlínkǒu.
Lìlínkǒu
is the mouth of a sea inlet.
Light troops hastened towards Píngguō.
When they were seven *lǐ* from the city,
a scout reported to Rén,
and Rén hastily went out to battle.
(The incident of Zhāng Yīng capturing the two envoys
is mentioned in the previous year.)
Shǐ,
pronounced 'shū lì' in the Fanqie system.
When Huàng arrived,
Rén thought that Huàng had again sent a detached force for a light raid and plunder,
unaware that Huàng himself had come.
He said to his左右:
"This time, we will not let a single horse return!"
On the Yǐwèi day,
Rén arrayed all his forces northwest of the city.
Mùróng Jūn led his division and surrendered to Huàng.
(In Xiánhé eighth year,
Jūn was captured by Rén.)
Chén,
read as zhèn.
Jiàng,
pronounced 'hù jiāng' in the Fanqie system.
Huàng then launched a frontal assault,
crushing them.
Rén fled,

and he was subsequently captured.
Huàng first executed those of Rén's retainers who had rebelled,
and then granted Rén death.
Dīng Héng, Yóu Yì, Sūn Jī, and others,

were seized and executed by Huàng;

Mùróng Yòu, Mùróng Zhì, Tóng Shòu, Guō Chōng, Zhái Kǎi, Páng Jiàn,

Yòu returned midway;
Huàng's troops pursued and caught Kǎi and Jiàn,

As for the remaining officials and common people who had been misled by Rén,

Gāo Xǔ was enfeoffed as Rǔyáng Hóu.
In the second month,
Shàngshū Púyè Wáng Bīn died.
On the Xīnhài day,
the Emperor presided over the court,
and sent envoys with the six rites to welcome Dù Yì's daughter, Língyáng, who was formerly Dāngyáng Hóu, as Empress.
(There are six rites for marriage: first is Nàcǎi,
meaning that for a marriage,
a matchmaker must first convey the message,
and then someone is sent to present the selected gift,
using wild geese as a token,
representing the coming and going of Yin and Yang;
second is Wènmíng,
asking for the name to divine auspiciousness or inauspiciousness;
third is Nàjí,
when an auspicious omen is obtained by divination at the ancestral temple, an envoy is sent again to announce the marriage;
fourth is Nàzhēng,
using black and crimson silks,
not wild geese;
fifth is Qǐngqī,
when the groom's family divines an auspicious day, an envoy is sent to announce it;
sixth is Qīnyíng,
the groom goes to the bride's home,
drives the carriage three times around the wheel,
then the driver takes over,
and the groom rides his own carriage ahead,
to guide the bride home.)
All the officials offered their congratulations.
In summer,
in the sixth month,
Duàn Liáo sent his Zhōngjūn Jiāngjūn, Lǐ Yǒng, to attack Mùróng Huàng.
Yǒng hastened to Wǔxīng.
Wǔxīng City
is east of Lìngzhī.
Liáo separately sent Duàn Lán to lead tens of thousands of infantry and cavalry to camp at Huíshuǐ west of Liǔchéng.
"Huíshuǐ"

flows northeast,
passes through Nǚqí County,

Also, the Rúrì River comes from outside the frontier,

then northeast past the south of Gūshān,
then southeast,
and its winding course

Also, according to the Zàijì,
Qūshuǐ should be northwest of Hǎochéng.
Jiāng,
pronounced 'jí liàng' in the Fanqie system.
Qí,
pronounced 'qí jì' in the Fanqie system.
Huàng led fifty thousand infantry and cavalry towards Liǔchéng.
Lán fled without fighting.
Huàng led his troops north towards Ānjìn.
(In Xián'ān eighth year,
Huàng built Ānjìn City.)
Qù,
pronounced 'qī yù' in the Fanqie system.
Huàng sent Sīmǎ Fēng Yì to lead light cavalry in pursuit and attack,

"The two barbarians will be ashamed of their failure

We should set up ambushes around Liǔchéng to await them."
Thereupon, he sent Fēng Yì to lead several thousand cavalry to lie in ambush at Mǎdōu Shān.
In the third month,
Duàn Liáo indeed led several thousand cavalry to raid and plunder.
Yì launched an attack,

Qián Tíngwèi Kǒng Tǎn died.

Yǔ Bīng visited him

Tǎn said with emotion:
"A great man, when approaching his end,

not be wept over like a child!"
Bīng deeply apologized to him.
In the ninth month,
Mùróng Huàng sent Chángshǐ Liú Bīn and the concurrently serving Lángzhōnglìng of Liáodōng, Yáng Jǐng, to escort Xú Mèng and others back to Jiànkāng.
(According to Jìn regulations,
only kingdoms had Lángzhōnglìng.
Huàng usurped this office before becoming a king.)
Bīn,
pronounced 'bīn'.
8 In winter,
the tenth month,
Dèng Yuè (鄧岳), the Cìshǐ (刺史) of Guǎngzhōu (廣州), sent Dūhù (督護) Wáng Suí (王隨) and others to attack Yèláng (夜郎) and Xīnggǔ (興古),

In the fifth year of Yǒngjiā (永嘉) of Emperor Huái (懷帝),

9 Chéng (成) Lord Qī (期), seeing that his cousin, Shàngshū Púyè (尚書僕射) Wǔlíng Gōng (武陵公) Zài (載), possessed outstanding talent,

falsely accused him of rebellion,

10 In the eleventh month,
an imperial edict ordered Jiànwēi Jiāngjūn (建威將軍) Sīmǎ Xūn (司馬勳) to lead troops to pacify Hànzhōng (漢中);

Shòu (壽) then appointed governors and magistrates for Hànzhōng (漢中),
garrisoned Nánzhèng (南鄭), and returned.
11 Suǒtóu Yùjú (索頭郁鞠) led three myriad people to surrender to Zhào (趙).
Suǒtóu (索頭)
are a branch of Xiānbēi (鮮卑).
They are called Suǒtóu (索頭)
to distinguish them from Hēinì Yùjú (黑匿郁鞠);
they are called Suǒtóu (索頭) because they braid their hair.
索 (Suǒ),
read as xí gè fān.
帥 (Shuài),
read as shuài.
降 (Jiàng),
read as hù jiāng fān.
Their multitudes were dispersed among the six prefectures of Jì (冀), Qīng (青), and others.
12 Zhào (趙) King Hǔ (虎) constructed the Tàiwǔ Diàn (太武殿) in Xiāngguó (襄國),

The East Palace

paved with patterned stones.
Below, a hidden chamber was dug,

being a cave chamber.
Tiles were lacquered,
with golden dāng (璫),
and silver yíng (楹).
Sīmǎ Xiāngrú’s (司馬相如) "Yǔliè Fù" (羽獵賦) says: "Huácuī Bìdāng (華榱璧璫)."

The Sānfǔ Huángtú (三輔黃圖) commentary states: "It means decorating the dāng (璫) of the tiles with jade."
Also, lángdāng (琅璫)
is a bell.
Dù Fǔ’s (杜甫) poem

presumably refers to decorating the dāng (璫) of the tiles with gold.
Yíng (楹)

Dāng (璫),
pronounced dāng.
Jade walls,
reaching the utmost in craftsmanship.

"Same as outside the palace" means
teaching court ladies to perform duties like men.
伎 (Jì),
read as qú qǐ fān.

騎 (Qí),
read as qí jì fān.
Well-worn brocade trousers,
gold and silver inlaid belts,
and five-patterned woven boots.
Five-patterned
means patterns formed by five colors.
The Guǎngyǎ (廣雅) states: "Tiānzhú Guó (天竺國) produces fine woven fabrics."
The Wèilüè (魏略) states: "Dàqín Guó (大秦國) uses water sheep wool, tree bark, and wild silkworm silk to make woven fabrics,

Here, five-colored woven fabric is used for boots.
鞾 (Xuē),
read as xǔ gē fān.
Yǔyí (羽儀),

Gǔchuī (鼓吹),

吹 (Chuī),
read as chǐ ruì fān.
At this time, Zhào (趙) suffered a great drought;
one jīn (斤) of gold was worth two dòu (斗) of grain,
and the common people cried out in misery.
Yet Hǔ (虎) continued his military campaigns without cease,

He ordered Yámén (牙門) Zhāng Mí (張彌) to move the bells and stands (zhōngjù 鍾虡), Nine Dragons (jiǔlóng 九龍), Wēngzhòng (翁仲) statues, bronze camels (tóngtuó 銅駝), and Fēilián (飛廉) statues from Luòyáng (洛陽) to Yè (鄴).
The bells and stands (zhōngjù 鍾虡), Nine Dragons (jiǔlóng 九龍), Wēngzhòng (翁仲) statues, bronze camels (tóngtuó 銅駝), and Fēilián (飛廉) statues
were all cast by Emperor Míng (明帝) of Wèi (魏).
虡 (Jù),
pronounced jù.

廣 (Guǎng),

He recruited three hundred "float-and-sink" men,

Jiě (解)
is the surname;

is the given name.
解 (Jiě),

to construct a flying bridge.

He ordered county magistrates and chiefs to lead the people into mountains and marshes to gather acorns and fish to supplement their food,

13 Earlier,
in Rìnnán, the barbarian chieftain, Fàn Zhì,
had a slave named Fàn Wén,
who often traveled to the Central Plains with merchants.
Later, he went to Línyì,
and taught the King of Línyì, Fàn Yì, how to build city walls, palaces, and weapons.
Yì loved and trusted him.
The kingdom of Línyì
was originally the Xiànglín County of the Hàn dynasty,
where Mǎ Yuán cast the bronze pillars.
At the end of the Hàn dynasty,
Qū Lián, a meritorious officer of the county,
killed the magistrate
and established himself as king.
His descendants succeeded him.
After his line had no heir,
his maternal grandson, Fàn Xióng, succeeded to the throne.
Yì
was Xióng's son.
Wén then slandered Yì's sons,
some were exiled, some fled.
In this year,
Yì died.
Wén fraudulently invited Yì's sons from other countries,
put poison in coconut wine, and killed them.
Coconut trees grow in Jiāozhǐ,
reaching tens of zhàng in height,
their leaves are similar on both sides.
The Qióngtái Zhì says: Coconuts grow at no specific season.
The tree resembles a betel nut tree,
its leaves are like phoenix tails.
The fruit is as large as a melon.
When cut open,
there is wine inside.
Its husk can be used as a drinking vessel.
The Jiāozhōu Jì says: Coconuts grow in the South Sea,
shaped like a sea palm.
The fruit is as large as a bowl,
with a coarse outer skin,
similar to large areca nuts or cardamom.
Inside, there is a liquid resembling wine,
drinking it can cause intoxication.
The Ěryǎ Yì says: The coconut tree resembles a betel nut tree,
with no branches,
standing over ten xún tall.
Its leaves are at the very top,
like a bundle of rushes.
The fruit is as large as a gourd,
hanging from the treetop.
The fruit has an outer skin
like a walnut.
Inside the kernel, there is flesh,
white as snow,
half an inch thick,
like a crab's fat,
tasting as delicious as a walnut.
Inside the flesh, there is more than a sheng of juice,
clear as water,
sweet as honey,
drinking it can quench thirst.
The kernel can be made into a drinking vessel.
Yē
is pronounced Yī Jiē.
Thereupon, he dispatched troops to attack the kingdoms of Dàqíjiè, Xiǎoqíjiè, Shìpú, Xúláng, Qūdū, Gānlǔ, and Fúdān.

14 Zhào’s Left Overseer, Chénggōng Duàn, created a courtyard brazier at the top of a pole.
The Xìngpǔ states: The descendants of Wèi Chéng Gōng took Chénggōng as their surname.
I note that during the Spring and Autumn period,
both Lǔ and Jìn had Chéng Gōngs,
so why should only the descendants of Wèi Chéng Gōng exclusively take it as their surname?
Gàng
is pronounced Gǔ Shuāng.
A tray was placed on top for the brazier.
In ancient times, rulers
held court at dawn,
hence courtyard braziers were set up.
Zhèng Shì said: On the ground, it's called liáo;
held in hand, it's called zhú.
He also said: Set up outside the gate, it's called dàzhú;
inside, it's called tíngliáo.
All are for illuminating the multitude.
Now Chénggōng Duàn hung a tray on a pole to place the brazier;
this was his own creative idea,
not an ancient method.
Liáo
is pronounced Lì Zhào;
Xú also pronounces it Lì Shāo.
Gāo
is pronounced Jū Ào.
King Hǔ of Zhào tested it and was pleased.
1 In spring,
in the first month,
on the day Gēngchén,
Zhào’s Grand Protector Kuí Ān and over five hundred civil and military officials presented a memorial to confer an honorable title.
Oil from the courtyard brazier poured onto the lower tray,
killing over twenty people.
The Kǎoyì states: The Zàijì says
“seven people”,
here we follow the Sānshí Guó Chūnqiū.
Chénggōng Duàn was cut in half at the waist.
On the day Xīnsì,
Hǔ, following the systems of the Yīn and Zhōu dynasties,
proclaimed himself Great Zhào Tiānwáng.
He ascended the throne in the southern suburbs and
issued a general amnesty.
He established his empress, Madame Zhèng, as Tiānwáng Huánghòu.
In ancient times, when one was called king,
the consort was called queen;
when one was called emperor,
the consort was called empress.
There was no title of Tiānwáng Huánghòu.
Among ancient kings,
the legitimate eldest son was called Shìzǐ;
Qín and Hàn called themselves emperors,
establishing Huáng Tàizǐ.
There was no title of Tiānwáng Huáng Tàizǐ.
Imperial kinsmen who were kings were demoted to county marquises.
Officials of all ranks were granted seals and appointments with differing statuses.
2 The Director of the Imperial Academy, Yuán Huái,

The emperor assented.
On the day Xīnmǎo,
the Imperial Academy was established,
and students were recruited.
However, the gentry favored Lǎo and Zhuāng,
and Confucianism never flourished.
Yuán Huái
was the great-grandson of Yuán Huàn.
At the end of the Hàn dynasty,

Yǐliánchéng

in the fourth month,
Duàn Liáo transported several thousand carts of grain to Yǐlián.

Xīngguóchéng
was presumably built by the Mùróng clan.
Cóng

Jiàng

Qí

Earlier,
Yáng Yù of Běipíng served Duàn Jílùjuàn and Liáo for five generations.
Jílùjuàn, Shèfùchén, Mòbēi, Yá, and Liáo

Liáo frequently engaged in conflict with Huàng.
Yù advised:

This is a saying of Chén Wǔfù from the Zuǒ Zhuàn.

There is no month without war,

The benefits do not outweigh the harm.
I fear that the troubles of the state will begin from this.
I wish that both sides would acknowledge past mistakes,
restore good relations as before,

Liáo did not heed him and sent Yù out to be the Chancellor of Běipíng.
4 Zhào Tàizǐ Suì (趙太子邃) was inherently brave and fierce.
Zhào Wáng Hǔ (趙王虎) loved him.
He often said to his attendants:
"The Sīmǎ (司馬) clan, father and son, brothers, annihilated each other,

Ā Tiě (阿鐵)
was Suì's (邃) nickname.
Ā (阿),
pronounced with the "an" (安) sound in the entering tone.
He enjoyed decorating beautiful concubines,

Hǔ (虎) was wildly addicted to wine and women,

Suì (邃) privately said to his Zhongshùzǐ (中庶子) Lǐ Yán (李顏) and others:
" 'Guānjiā (官家)' is difficult to interpret.
Calling the Son of Heaven 'Guānjiā (官家)'
first appeared here.
The Western Hàn (西漢) called the Son of Heaven 'Xiànguān (縣官)',
the Eastern Hàn (東漢) called the Son of Heaven 'Guójiā (國家)',
hence combining the two terms.
Some say: The Five Thearchs (Wǔ Dì 五帝) regarded the realm as 'guān' (官, public),
the Three Kings (Sān Wáng 三王) regarded the realm as 'jiā' (家, private),
hence the combined term.
Nán chēng (難稱),
read 'chǐ zhèng' (尺證) in fanqie.

Mào (冒),
read 'mò běi' (莫北) in fanqie.
Yán (顏) and others bowed down, not daring to reply.
In the autumn,
seventh month,

Thereupon he said to Yán (顏) and others:

Jìzhōu (冀州) was governed from Xìndū (信都).

His mother, Lady Zhèng (鄭氏), heard of this,

Fótúchéng (佛圖澄) said to Hǔ (虎):

So he ordered a trusted female palace official (Nǚ Shàngshū 女尚書) to investigate.
Suì (邃) called her forward to speak with her,

Hǔ (虎) was enraged,
arrested Lǐ Yán (李顏) and others for questioning,

Hǔ (虎) killed Yán (顏) and over thirty others.
He imprisoned Suì (邃) in the Eastern Palace,

The *Shuǐjīng Zhù* (水經註) states: Wèi Wǔdì (魏武帝) resided in Yè (鄴) in the Northern Palace;

Jiàn (見),
read 'xián biàn' (賢遍) in fanqie.
A moment later, Suì (邃) left.

Xiánkāng 4th year

1 Spring,
1st month.
Mùróng Huàng, the King of Yàn, sent the Commandant Zhào Pán to Zhào

Hǔ, the King of Zhào, was preparing to attack Duàn Liáo,

in Xiánkāng 2nd year,

Lǐ Mèng, the Inspector of Yōuzhōu, retreated and held Yìjīng.
Hǔ then appointed Táo Bào as the General of Hēnghǎi.
