宜立常員.
學生三年無成,
徒塞英儁之路,
皆當歸之於農.
殿下聖德寬明,
博察芻蕘,
文王詢于芻蕘.
刈草曰芻,
采薪曰蕘.
蕘,
如招翻.
主者處以大辟,
主者,
謂其時主斷憲、明之獄者.
忤,
五故翻.
處,
昌呂翻.
辟,
毗亦翻.
猶免官禁錮.
夫求諫諍而罪直言,
是猶適越而北行,
必不獲其所志矣.
右長史 Sòng Gāi 等阿媚苟容,
輕劾諫士,
己無骨鯁,
骨鯁,
以喻剛強正直者.
Máo Huàng 曰: 鯁,
魚骨;
又骨不下咽為鯁.
以其謇諤難受,
如魚骨之咈咽也.
掩蔽耳目,
不忠之甚者也. 」
Huàng 乃下令,
稱:
「覽封記室之諫,
孤實懼焉.
國以民為本,
民以穀為命,
可悉罷苑囿以給民之無田者.
實貧者,
官與之牛;
力有餘願得官牛者,
並依 Wèi, Jìn 舊法.
溝瀆各
有益者,
令以時修治.
今戎事方興,
勳伐既多,
王功曰勳;
積功曰伐.
俟中原平壹,
徐更議之.
工商、學生皆當裁擇.
夫人臣關言於人主,
至難也,
關,
白也.
Wáng Bāo Shèngzhǔ Dé Xiánchén Sòng 曰: 進退得關其忠.
當擇其善者而從之.
Wáng Xiàn, Liú Míng,
雖罪應廢黜,
亦由孤之無大量也,
可悉復本官,
仍居諫司.
Fēng Shēng 蹇蹇,
深得王臣之體,
易曰: 王臣蹇蹇,
匪躬之故.
宣示內外,
有欲陳孤過者,
不拘貴賤,
勿有所諱！ 」
Huàng 雅好文學,
常親臨庠序講授,
考校學徒至千餘人,
頗有妄濫者,
故 Fēng Yù 及之.
4 An imperial edict summoned the General of the Guards, Chǔ Póu
(褚裒), intending to make him the Inspector of Yángzhōu (揚州) and Director of the Imperial Secretariat.
Liú Xiá (劉遐), Minister of the Ministry of Personnel, and Wáng Húzhī (王胡之), Chief Clerk, persuaded Póu, saying:
“The Prince of Kuàijī (會稽王) has a virtuous character and esteemed reputation;
he is the Duke of Zhōu (周公) of our state.
Your Excellency should entrust him with the great affairs of state.”
Póu then firmly declined,
returning to his fief.
On the day Rénxū (壬戌),
Yù (昱), the Prince of Kuàijī, was appointed General Who Comforts the Army and Grand General,
overseeing six departments of the Imperial Secretariat.
Liú Cōng (劉聰) appointed his son Càn (粲) as Chancellor,
holding the title of Grand General,
and Director of the Imperial Secretariat;
Liú Yánnián (劉延年) oversaw six departments of the Imperial Secretariat.
Overseeing six departments of the Imperial Secretariat
was inferior to being Director of the Imperial Secretariat.
This must mean that this office existed first during the period between the Wèi (魏) and Jìn (晉) dynasties,
and Cōng (聰) adopted and established it.
The note also appeared earlier.
Huì (會),
pronounced like “gōng wài.”
Yù (昱) was pure, calm, and had few desires.
He was especially skilled in Xuanxue (玄學) discussions.
He often took Liú Tán (劉惔), Wáng Méng (王濛), and Hán Bó (韓伯) of Yǐngchuān (潁川) as his conversational guests.
He also appointed Xī Chāo (郗超) as an Aide to the General Who Comforts the Army
and Xiè Wàn (謝萬) as an Assistant Administrator.
Chāo (超) was
the grandson of Jiàn (鑒).
Xī Jiàn (郗鑒)
was a famous minister at the beginning of the Southern Migration.
Yuàn (掾),
pronounced like “yǐ juàn.”
His father, Yīn (愔),
was taciturn, modest, and frugal with money.
He accumulated tens of millions of coins.
He once opened his treasury and allowed Chāo (超) to take what he wanted;
Chāo (超) distributed it among his relatives and old friends,
exhausting it all in one day.
Historians say that Xī Chāo’s (郗超) talents and abilities were sufficient for governing the world,
but the Jìn (晉) court failed to use him,
regretting that he was used by Huán Wēn (桓溫).
Shī (施),
pronounced like “shì chǐ.”
(Xiè Wàn (謝萬)) was the younger brother of Ān (安),
clear, open-minded, and outstanding,
also having a reputation at the time.
5 In Yān (燕), a black dragon and a white dragon were seen on Dragon Mountain (Lóngshān).
Dragon Mountain was east of Dragon City (Lóngchéng).
Xiàn (見),
pronounced like “xián biàn.”
They shed their horns and departed.
Yān (燕) King Huáng (皝) personally offered a grand sacrifice (tàiláo) to them,
granted a general amnesty within his territory,
and named his newly built palace “Hélóng (和龍).”
6 Yǔ Yì (庾翼), the Marquis of Dūtíng Sù (都亭肅侯), developed a carbuncle on his back.
According to posthumous appellation rules: “Strong and capable in conquest is called Sù (肅)”;
“Resolute and decisive in mind is called Sù (肅).”
Jū (疽),
pronounced like “qiān yú.”
He entrusted the subsequent duties;
he appointed Zhū Táo (朱燾) of Sīmǎ Yìyáng (司馬義陽) as Southern Man (Nánmán) Commandant,
with a thousand men to guard Bālíng (巴陵).
In autumn,
on the seventh month,
on the day Gēngwǔ (庚午),
he died.
Yì’s (翼) generals Gān Zàn (干瓚) and others rebelled.
Gān (干),
a surname.
The Zuǒ Zhuàn (左傳) records
that Sòng (宋) had Gān Chōu (干犨).
Zàn (瓚),
pronounced like “zàng hàn.”
Zhū Táo (朱燾), along with Jiāng Pī (江虨), Chief Clerk of the General Who Guards the West,
Máo Mùzhī (毛穆之), Commander of the General Who Establishes Martial Might.
Yǔ Yì (庾翼) made his son Fāngzhī (方之) General Who Establishes Martial Might,
guarding Xiāngyáng (襄陽),
and made Mùzhī (穆之) his Commander.
Mùzhī (穆之) was in fact Hǔshēng (虎生).
Mùzhī (穆之),
courtesy name Xiànzǔ (憲祖),
small name Hǔshēng (虎生).
His name offended the taboo of Empress Wáng Jìng (王靖后),
so he changed his courtesy name;
later, because Huán Wēn’s (桓溫) mother’s given name was Xiàn (憲),
he then reverted to using his small name.
According to the biographies of empresses in the Jìn Shū (晉書),
Empress Āi Jìng (哀靖王皇后),
her taboo name was Mùzhī (穆之).
Pī (虨) was
the son of Tǒng (統).
7 In the eighth month,
Lù Yǒng (路永), Inspector of Yùzhōu (豫州), rebelled and defected to Zhào (趙).
King Hǔ (虎) of Zhào (趙) sent Yǒng (永) to garrison Shòuchūn (壽春).
Lù Yǒng (路永) was a surrendered general of Sū Jùn (蘇峻).
8 After Yǔ Yì (庾翼) died,
the court debated and generally agreed that the Yǔ (庾) family had generations resided in the western border regions,
which was comforting to the people.
It was proper to follow Yì’s (翼) request
and appoint Yǔ Yuánzhī (庾爰之) to replace him.
Hé Chōng (何充) said:
“Jīngchǔ (荊楚) is the western gate of the state,
with a population of a million households.
To its north are powerful Hu (胡) tribes,
and to its west are strong Shǔ (蜀) forces.
Its terrain is treacherous and difficult,
spanning ten thousand li.
If we get the right person, the Central Plains can be pacified;
if we lose the right person, the altars of soil and grain (state) will be endangered.
It is what Lù Kàng (陸抗) called ‘if it exists, Wú (吳) exists;
if it perishes, Wú (吳) perishes.’
The memorial Lù Kàng (陸抗) submitted before his death
can be found in volume eighty, Emperor Wǔ’s (武帝) Tàishǐ (泰始) tenth year.
Huán Wēn (桓溫) has extraordinary strategic talent,
possessing both literary and military prowess.
For the responsibility of the western frontier,
there is no one superior to Wēn (溫).”
The debaters again said:
“Would Yǔ Yuánzhī (庾爰之) yield to Wēn (溫)?
If he were to resist with troops,
the shame and fear would be considerable.”
Meaning, they would not be able to control Yuánzhī (爰之),
which would be a national disgrace,
and also cause fear.
This was probably referring to how Wáng Dūn (王敦) and Sū Jùn (蘇峻) treated Yuánzhī (爰之).
“Wēn (溫) is capable of controlling him;
gentlemen, do not worry.”
Liú Tán (劉惔), the Administrator of Dānyáng (丹楊), always admired Wēn’s (溫) talent,
but knew he had ambitions to usurp power.
He said to Yù (昱), the Prince of Kuàijī:
“Wēn (溫) should not be allowed to occupy strategically important places;
his rank and title should always be suppressed.”
He urged Yù (昱) to personally guard the upper reaches of the river,
and take himself as the army supervisor.
Yù (昱) did not listen;
he also requested to go himself,
but was also not listened to.
Liú Tán (劉惔) was
merely a conversational guest;
his words about Huán Wēn (桓溫) were always accurate,
as he deeply understood Wēn’s (溫) talents.
Supposing Yù (昱) guarded the upper reaches,
and Tán (惔) was his Sīmǎ (司馬),
it would still not be enough to contend with Yān (燕) and Qín (秦).
Yángzǐ (揚子) said: “It’s not just knowing it,
but truly acting upon it;
it’s not knowing that is difficult,
but acting that is difficult.”
Tán (惔),
pronounced like “tú gān.”
On the day Gēngchén (庚辰),

Huán Wēn (桓溫), Inspector of Xúzhōu (徐州), was appointed General Who Pacifies the West, Bearing the Credential, Overall Supervisor of Military Affairs for the six provinces of Jīng (荊), Sī (司), Yōng (雍), Yì (益), Liáng (梁), and Níng (寧), concurrently holding the title of Protector of the Southern Man (Nánmán) Commandant and Inspector of Jīngzhōu (荊州),
laying the groundwork for Huán Wēn’s (桓溫) exclusive control of the Jìn (晉) court.
Yōng (雍),
pronounced like “yú yòng.”
Furthermore, Liú Tán (劉惔) was appointed Supervisor of Military Affairs for Miǎnzhōng (沔中),
concurrently holding the title of Grand Administrator of Yìchéng (義成),
replacing Yǔ Fāngzhī (庾方之).
Fāngzhī (方之) and Yuánzhī (爰之) were transferred to Yùzhāng (豫章).
Huán Wēn (桓溫) once rode out in the snow, intending to hunt.
He first visited Liú Tán (劉惔).
Tán (惔) saw his very stern attire
and said to him:
“What does this old bandit intend to do with this?”
Wēn (溫) laughed and said:
“If I don’t do this,
how can you sit and talk so freely?”
Wēn (溫) used these words to answer Tán (惔),
expressing everything;
Wēn (溫) also knew that Tán (惔) fully understood his talents,
hence he spoke these words.
9 The younger brother of the Han ruler, Shì [Shì], the Grand General Guǎng [Guǎng],
seeing that Shì [Shì] had no son,
requested to be made Crown Prince;
Shì [Shì] would not allow it.
Mǎ Dāng [Mǎ Dāng] and Xiè Sīmíng [Xiè Sīmíng] remonstrated, saying:
"Your Majesty does not have many brothers.
If you again depose one,
you will become even more isolated and perilous."
They firmly requested that he assent.
Shì [Shì] suspected that they were in league with Guǎng [Guǎng],
arrested Dāng [Dāng] and Sīmíng [Sīmíng] and executed them,
exterminating their three clans.
The position of Crown Prince cannot be requested.
If Mǎ Dāng [Mǎ Dāng] and Xiè Sīmíng [Xiè Sīmíng] were acting for the good of the state,
they should have spoken leisurely,
allowing their lord to come to his own realization.
How could they make such a firm request!
Their going together to their deaths
was fitting.
Xiè [Xiè],
pronounced 'hù mǎi fān'.
Guǎng [Guǎng] was demoted to Marquis of Línqióng [Línqióng],
and Guǎng [Guǎng] committed suicide.
When Sīmíng [Sīmíng] was arrested,
he sighed, saying:
"The state has not perished
because a few people like us are here.
Now it is in danger!"
He spoke and laughed as usual and then died.
Sīmíng [Sīmíng] had wisdom and strategy,
and dared to remonstrate;
Mǎ Dāng [Mǎ Dāng] had always been popular;
when they died,
there was no scholar or commoner who did not mourn them.
10 In winter,
in the tenth month,
Yān [Yān] King Huàng [Huàng] sent Mùróng Kè [Mùróng Kè] to attack Gāogōulí [Gāogōulí],
capturing Nánsū [Nánsū].
Nánsū [Nánsū] city was east of Nánxiá [Nánxiá].
When the Táng [Táng] pacified Gāolì [Gāolì],
Nánsū [Nánsū] Prefecture was established there.
11 In the twelfth month,
Zhāng Jùn [Zhāng Jùn] attacked Yānqí [Yānqí],
and it surrendered.
In this year,
Jùn [Jùn] divided Wǔwēi [Wǔwēi] and eleven other commanderies into Liángzhōu [Liángzhōu].

Jùn [Jùn] divided Wǔwēi [Wǔwēi], Wǔxīng [Wǔxīng], Xīpíng [Xīpíng], Zhāngyè [Zhāngyè], Jiǔquán [Jiǔquán], Jiànkāng [Jiànkāng], Xījùn [Xījùn], Huánghé [Huánghé], Jìnxīng [Jìnxīng], Xūwǔ [Xūwǔ], and Āngù [Āngù], a total of eleven commanderies, into Liángzhōu [Liángzhōu].
He divided Xīngjìn [Xīngjìn] and eight other commanderies into Hézhōu [Hézhōu].

Jùn [Jùn] divided Xīngjìn [Xīngjìn], Jīnchéng [Jīnchéng], Wǔshǐ [Wǔshǐ], Nán'ān [Nán'ān], Yǒngjìn [Yǒngjìn], Dàxià [Dàxià], Wǔchéng [Wǔchéng], and Hànzhōng [Hànzhōng], eight commanderies, into Hézhōu [Hézhōu].
He divided Dūnhuáng [Dūnhuáng] and three other commanderies and the three garrisons of the Protectorate of the Western Regions into Shāzhōu [Shāzhōu].
The Jìn Zhì [Jìn Zhì] only recorded Dūnhuáng [Dūnhuáng] and Jìnchāng [Jìnchāng] two commanderies,
and the Protectorate of the Western Regions;
Zhāng Mào [Zhāng Mào] established Shāzhōu [Shāzhōu] with the command of colonel, Yùmén [Yùmén], Grand Protector-General, three commanderies, and three garrisons.
One commandery is not mentioned in the histories,
probably due to a lacuna.
Dūn [Dūn],
pronounced 'tú mén fān'.
Jùn [Jùn] proclaimed himself Grand Commander, Grand General, and acting King of Liáng [Liáng],
overseeing the three prefectures;
he began to establish officials such as Libationer, Gentlemen of the Palace, Grand Masters, Palace Attendants, and Ushers,
whose titles all imitated those of the Imperial Court
but with slight modifications to their names;
his chariots, attire, banners, and flags were styled after those of a king.
12 Zhào [Zhào] King Hǔ [Hǔ] appointed Champion General Yáo Yìzhòng [Yáo Yìzhòng] as Bearer of Credentials, Grand Commander of Ten Commanderies and Six Barbarian Tribes, and Champion Grand General.
Yìzhòng [Yìzhòng] was clean, frugal, upright, and unyielding,
not bothering with grand deportment,
and spoke without fear or evasion.
When Hǔ [Hǔ] usurped the throne,
Yìzhòng [Yìzhòng] sternly rebuked him,
which shows that his words were without fear or evasion.
Zhì [Zhì],
pronounced 'zhí zhī fān';
similarly below.
Whenever he participated in deliberations,
the dukes and ministers all feared and respected him.
The Left Commandant of Wǔchéng [Wǔchéng],
was the younger brother of Hǔ's [Hǔ's] favorite concubine.
Wǔchéng [Wǔchéng] county in Dōng [Dōng] belonged to Qīnghé [Qīnghé] Commandery,
and in the Táng [Táng] Dynasty belonged to Bèizhōu [Bèizhōu].
Yìzhòng [Yìzhòng]'s encampment was at Shèntóu [Shèntóu] in Guǎngchuān [Guǎngchuān]-Qīnghé [Qīnghé].
He harassed Yìzhòng [Yìzhòng]'s troops.
Yìzhòng [Yìzhòng] seized him and counted his offenses, saying:
"You are a禁尉 (jìn wèi, Imperial Guard),
a jìn wèi [jìn wèi] means that the duty of a commandant is to prohibit evil and wrongdoing.
Shǔ [Shǔ],
pronounced 'suǒ jù fān'.
I am a high minister,
and what I personally see
cannot be condoned."
He ordered his attendants to behead him;
the commandant kowtowed until his head bled,
and the attendants firmly remonstrated,
whereupon Yìzhòng [Yìzhòng] stopped.
13 Yān [Yān] King Huàng [Huàng] believed that in ancient times, when feudal lords ascended the throne,
each would declare his own first year.
Therefore, he began not to use the Jìn [Jìn] era name,
and proclaimed his twelfth year.
From this time on, Yān [Yān] no longer submitted to the mandate of Jìn [Jìn].
14 Zhào [Zhào] King Hǔ [Hǔ] sent General Who Conquers the East Dèng Héng [Dèng Héng] with tens of thousands of soldiers to garrison Lè'ān [Lè'ān],
to construct siege equipment,
in preparation for taking Yān [Yān].
Yān [Yān] King Huàng [Huàng] appointed Mùróng Bà [Mùróng Bà] as General Who Pacifies the Di [Dí].
The title General Who Pacifies the Di [Dí]
began with Emperor Guāngwǔ [Guāngwǔ] of Hàn [Hàn] appointing Páng Méng [Páng Méng] to it.
Héng [Héng] feared him
and dared not attack.
1 In spring,
in the first month,
on the day Bǐngyín [Bǐngyín],
a general amnesty was declared.
2 On the day Jǐmǎo [Jǐmǎo],
Hú [Hú] Xiāng [Xiāng] Wénmùgōng [Wénmùgōng]
Hé Chōng [Hé Chōng] died.
Chōng [Chōng] possessed great capacity,
governed with integrity,
took the fate of the state as his personal responsibility,
and selected and employed people based on their effectiveness,
not for personal ties or old acquaintances.
3 At first,
Fúyú [Fúyú] resided at Lùshān [Lùshān].
Fúyú [Fúyú] was over a thousand *lǐ* north of Xuántú [Xuántú].
Lùshān [Lùshān] likely corresponded to that land.
Dù Yòu [Dù Yòu] said: The state of Fúyú [Fúyú] had a seal
with the inscription
"Seal of the King of Huì [Huì]".
The state had an old city
named Huìchéng [Huìchéng],
which was originally the land of the Huì [Huì] and Mò [Mò] peoples.
Its country was north of the Great Wall,
a thousand *lǐ* from Xuántú [Xuántú],
bordering Gāolì [Gāolì] to the south, Yìlóu [Yìlóu] to the east, and Xiānbēi [Xiānbēi] to the west.
There were three Hàn [Hàn] states among the Eastern Yi [Yí]: one was Mǎhán [Mǎhán],
second was Chénhán [Chénhán],
third was Biànhán [Biànhán].
Mǎhán [Mǎhán] had fifty-four states,
and Bǎijì [Bǎijì] was one of them.
Later, it gradually grew stronger
and absorbed several smaller states;
its country was originally, like Gōulí [Gōulí], over a thousand *lǐ* east of Liáodōng [Liáodōng].
The Suí Shū [Suí Shū] states: Bǎijì [Bǎijì] originated from Dōngmíng [Dōngmíng].
Later, there was Qíutái [Qíutái],
who first established the state
and gradually became powerful.
Initially, a hundred families crossed the sea,
hence the name Bǎijì [Bǎijì].
Dù Yòu [Dù Yòu] said: Bǎijì [Bǎijì] bordered Xīnluó [Xīnluó] to the south,
resisted Gāolì [Gāolì] to the north by over a thousand *lǐ*,
was bounded by the great sea to the west,
and was situated south of the small sea.
It moved west, closer to Yān [Yān],
but made no preparations.
Yān [Yān] King Huàng [Huàng] sent Crown Prince Jùn [Jùn] to lead Generals Mùróng Jūn [Mùróng Jūn], Mùróng Kè [Mùróng Kè], and Mùyú Gēn [Mùyú Gēn] with seventeen thousand cavalry to raid Fúyú [Fúyú].
Jùn [Jùn] directed from the center,
entrusting all military matters to Kè [Kè],
and subsequently captured Fúyú [Fúyú],
taking its King Xuán [Xuán] and over fifty thousand people from his tribe captive, and returned.
Huàng [Huàng] made Xuán [Xuán] General Who Guards the Army
and married his daughter to him.
4 In the second month,
on the day Guǐchǒu [Guǐchǒu],
Left Grand Master of Glorious Happiness Cài Mó [Cài Mó] was appointed Minister of Works,
to assist in governing alongside King Yù [Yù] of Huìjī [Huìjī].
5 Chǔ Póu [Chǔ Póu] recommended former Grand Master of Glorious Happiness Gù Hé [Gù Hé] and former Left Chief Clerk to the Minister of Works Yīn Hào [Yīn Hào];
in the third month,
on the day Bǐngzǐ [Bǐngzǐ],
Hé [Hé] was appointed President of the Board of Civil Office,
and Hào [Hào] was appointed General Who Establishes Martial Might and Inspector of Yángzhōu [Yángzhōu].
Hé [Hé] was in mourning for his mother,
and firmly declined to take up the post,
saying to his close associates:
"Ancient people laid aside their mourning clothes to serve the king
because their talent was sufficient to manage the times;
someone like me
would only undermine filial piety
and damage customs."
Those who knew him praised this.
Hào [Hào] also firmly declined.
King Yù [Yù] of Huìjī [Huìjī] wrote to Hào [Hào], saying:
"We are currently facing an unfortunate destiny,
and the crisis and decay have reached their extreme.
Your profound insight and extensive experience
are sufficient to govern the state.
If you again deeply cling to withdrawal and humility,
stubbornly pursuing your original intention,
I fear that the affairs of the world will depart from this point.
Your acceptance or rejection
determines the rise or fall of the present time,
in which case the family and state are not different.
This means that if the state prospers, the family will also prosper with it;
if the state falls, the family will also fall with it.
Hào [Hào] then took up his post.
6 In summer,
in the fourth month,
on the day Jǐyǒu [Jǐyǒu], the first day of the month,
there was a solar eclipse.
7 In the fifth month,
on the day *bǐngxū*,
Zhāng Jùn (張駿), Duke Zhōngchéng (忠成) of Xīpíng (西平), passed away.

His officials and retainers enthroned his heir apparent, Zhāng Chónghuá (張重華), as Bearer of the Staff, Grand Marshal, Grand Commandant, Colonel Protector of the Qiāng, Governor of Liángzhōu, Duke of Xīpíng, and Acting King of Liáng;
they granted a general amnesty throughout his domain;
they honored his legitimate mother, Lady Yán (嚴), as Grand Queen Dowager,
and his birth mother, Lady Mǎ (馬), as Queen Dowager.
8 Yán Shēng (嚴生), a Yellow Gate official of Zhào, harbored a grudge against the Minister Zhū Guǐ (朱軌).
It happened to be raining for a long time,
so Yán Shēng slandered Zhū Guǐ, accusing him of failing to maintain the roads
and also of disparaging the court administration.
King Hǔ (虎) of Zhào imprisoned him.
Pú Hóng (蒲洪) remonstrated, saying:
"Your Majesty already possesses Xiāngguó (襄國) and Yè (鄴) Palaces,
and now you are also repairing the palaces in Cháng'ān (長安) and Luòyáng (洛陽).
What will you use them for?
You have built a thousand hunting chariots
and enclosed thousands of *lǐ* to raise wild animals,
and seized over ten myriad wives and daughters to fill the imperial harem.
These matters were all seen last year.
Is this truly the case?
Now, because the roads are not maintained,
you wish to execute a Minister.
Your Majesty's virtuous governance is not cultivated,
and Heaven has sent incessant rain,
which only cleared after seventy days.
It has only cleared for two days;
even if there were a million ghost soldiers,
they would not be able to clear the mud and puddles from the roads,
let alone mere men!
With such governance and punishments,
what will become of the four seas?
What will become of future generations?"
He meant that the world and future generations
would surely criticize his errors.
"Abolish the hunting parks,
release the palace women,
pardon Zhū Guǐ,
to satisfy the hopes of the multitude."
Though Hǔ (虎) was displeased,
he did not punish him for it.
He did stop the construction in Cháng'ān (長安) and Luòyáng (洛陽),
but he ultimately executed Zhū Guǐ (朱軌).
He also established a law against privately discussing court affairs,
allowing officials to report on their superiors
and slaves to report on their masters.
From dukes and ministers downwards,
when attending court, they would glance at each other with their eyes,
not daring to visit or speak with one another again.
9 Wáng Zhuó (王擢), a general of Zhào, attacked Zhāng Chónghuá (張重華).
He ambushed Wǔjiē (武街),
capturing the Garrison Commander Cáo Quán (曹權) and Hú Xuān (胡宣).
Zhāng Jùn (張駿) had established five garrison commanders,
and Wǔjiē (武街) was one of them,
located in Lǒngxī (隴西).
The *Shuǐjīng Zhù* (水經註) states: "To the southwest of Dídào (狄道) County is Wǔjiē (武街) City."
The *Jìn Zhì* (晉志) states that
Emperor Huì (惠) divided Lǒngxī (隴西) to establish Dídào (狄道) Commandery,
and also established Wǔjiē (武街) County, which belonged to it.
Mázhōu Cǐshǐ (麻秋刺史),
Mǎ Qiū (麻秋) of Zhào attacked Liángzhōu (涼州),
so he was appointed *Cǐshǐ*.
The Administrator Zhāng Chōng (張沖) surrendered,
and Liángzhōu (涼州) was greatly alarmed.
Zhāng Chónghuá (張重華) dispatched all the troops within his domain,
ordering General Zheng Nán (征南將軍) Péi Héng (裴恆) to lead them to resist Zhào;
Péi Héng (裴恆) encamped at Guǎngwǔ (廣武).
Zhāng Shí (張寔) divided Lìngjū (令居) and Zhīyáng (枝陽) Counties from Jīnchéng (金城),
and also established Yǒngdēng (永登) County,
combining these three counties to establish Guǎngwǔ (廣武) Commandery.
The *Shuǐjīng Zhù* (水經註) states,
"Guǎngwǔ (廣武) City is west of Zhīyáng (枝陽) County."
The *Wǔdài Zhì* (五代志) states,
"Yǔnwú (允吾) County of Wǔwēi (武威) Commandery,
established by the Later Wèi (魏),
was called Guǎngwǔ (廣武)."
Liú Xù (劉昫) states: "The Tang (唐) Guǎngwǔ (廣武) County of Lánzhōu (蘭州) was
the land of Han (漢) Zhīyáng (枝陽) County."
Héng (恆) is pronounced *hù dēng fān*.
Zhāng Dān (張耽), the Sīmǎ (司馬) of Liángzhōu (涼ōu), spoke to Zhāng Chónghuá (張重華), saying:
"The nation's survival or demise depends on its army,
and the army's victory or defeat depends on its generals.
Currently, those who recommend generals
mostly promote the old and experienced.
However, the appointment of Hán Xìn (韓信)
was not based on his old virtues.
The matter of Hán Xìn's appointment can be found in Volume 9, first year of Emperor Gāo of Han (漢高帝).
There is no fixed rule for appointing people;
whoever possesses the talent for it
should be entrusted with important affairs.
Now a powerful enemy is at our border,
our generals are not advancing,
and the people are anxious and fearful.
The Chief Clerk Xiè Ài (謝艾),
possesses both literary and military skills,
and can be used to resist Zhào."
Zhāng Chónghuá (張重華) summoned Xiè Ài (謝艾)
and asked him for a strategy;
Xiè Ài (謝艾) requested seven thousand troops,
promising to defeat Zhào in return.
Zhāng Chónghuá (張重華) appointed Xiè Ài (謝艾) as General Zhōngjiān (中堅將軍),
provided him with five thousand infantry and cavalry,
and sent him to attack Mǎ Qiū (麻秋).
Xiè Ài (謝艾) led his troops out to Zhènwǔ (振武).
That night, two owls hooted in the center of his camp.
Xiè Ài (謝艾) said:
"In *liùbó* (六博), one who gets an owl wins;
the *Ěryǎ Yì* (爾雅翼) states: 'The pieces of *bó* (博) include the owl.'
*Bó* (博) also follows evil ways,
hence the owl is used as a piece.
This is a sign of victory over the enemy."
He advanced and fought against Zhào,
thoroughly defeating them,
beheading five thousand.
Zhāng Chónghuá (張重華) enfeoffed Xiè Ài (謝艾) as Earl of Fúlù (福祿伯).
Fúlù (福祿) County
has belonged to Jiǔquán (酒泉) Commandery since the Han (漢) dynasty.
Sòng Bái (宋白) states: "Sùzhōu (肅州) Fúlù (福祿) County
was Lèguàn (樂涫) County during the Zhōu (周) and Suí (隋) dynasties;
it was renamed Fúlù (福祿) during the Wǔdé (武德) era,
adopting its old Han (漢) name."
When Mǎ Qiū (麻秋) captured Jīnchéng (金城),
the county magistrate, Chē Jì (車濟) of Dūnhuáng (敦煌), refused to surrender
and fell on his sword.
"County magistrate"
refers to the magistrate of Jīnchéng (金城) County.
Dūn (敦) is pronounced *tú mén fān*.
Dàxià (大夏) County
belonged to Lǒngxī (隴西) Commandery in the Han (漢) dynasty;
Zhāng Guǐ (張軌) reassigned it to Jìnxīng (晉興) Commandery,
and later Dàxià (大夏) Commandery was established.
The *Shuǐjīng Zhù* (水經註) states,
"The old city of Dàxià (大夏) County
is southwest of Páohǎn (枹罕) County,
bordering the Táo (洮) River to the north."
Liú Xù (劉昫) states: "Hézhōu (河州) Dàxià (大夏) County
was an ancient Han (漢) county,
named after the Dàxià (大夏) River west of the county."
He surrendered the city to Mǎ Qiū (麻秋).
Mǎ Qiū (麻秋) sent Yàn (晏) with a letter to entice Sòng Jǔ (宋矩) of Dūnhuáng (敦煌), the Commandant of Wǎnshù (宛戍);
Sòng Jǔ (宋矩) said:
"As a subject, if my efforts are unsuccessful,
the only option is to die for my principles."
He first killed his wife and children, and then committed suicide.
Mǎ Qiū (麻秋) said:
"They are all righteous gentlemen,"
and collected and buried them.
10 In winter,
Lǐ Yì (李奕), Grand Protector of Han (漢), raised an army from Jìnshòu (晉壽) to rebel.
Many people in Shǔ (蜀) followed him,
and his forces reached several tens of thousands.
Shì (勢), the ruler of Han (漢), ascended the city wall to resist the attack.
At that time, Lǐ Yì's (李奕) troops had advanced and were pressing upon Chéngdū (成都).
The gatekeepers shot and killed him,
and his forces all scattered.
Shì (勢) granted a general amnesty throughout his domain
and changed the era name to Jiāníng (嘉寧).
Shì (勢) became arrogant and indulgent,
neglecting state affairs.
He often stayed within the Forbidden Palace,
rarely meeting with high officials.
He grew distant from and suspicious of old ministers,
trusting only his close attendants.
Slander and flattery advanced together,
and punishments became harsh and arbitrary,
causing disunity both within and outside the court.
Previously, there were no *Láo* (獠) people in the land of Shǔ (蜀),
but by this time, they began to emerge from the mountains,
from Bāxī (巴西) to Jiānwéi (犍為) and Zǐtóng (梓潼),
filling the mountain valleys with over ten myriad settlements,
which could not be controlled,
becoming a great problem for the people;
moreover, with famine,
the entire domain
became desolate.
Anxī Jiāngjūn Huán Wēn was about to invade Hàn.
His officers all thought it was impossible.
Jiāngxià Xiàng Yuán Qiáo urged him, saying:
"Indeed, planning major undertakings
is certainly not within the grasp of ordinary understanding.
A wise person understands it in his mind
and does not necessarily need all opinions to agree.
Now, the scourges of the world
are merely the two bandit groups, the Hú and Shǔ.
Although Shǔ is treacherous and strong,
compared to the Hú it is weaker.
If one wishes to eliminate them,
one should first deal with the easier one.
Lǐ Shì is without proper governance;
his subjects do not support him.
Moreover, he relies on his treacherous remoteness
and has not prepared for war.
It is advisable to take ten thousand elite troops, lightly equipped, and advance rapidly.
By the time they realize it,
we will have already passed through their strategic strongholds.
'Already passed through their strategic strongholds'
means having crossed the treacherous terrain and emerged onto flat land.
Shǔ is rich and fertile,
and its population is numerous.
Zhūgě Wǔhóu used it to contend with Zhōngxià.
Zhūgě Liàng was posthumously titled Zhōngwǔhóu.
Xià
is pronounced 'hù yǎ fān'.
This is a great benefit to the state.
Some argue that if the grand army goes west,
the Hú will certainly covet and spy.
This seems plausible but is incorrect.
When the Hú hear that we are campaigning ten thousand *lǐ* away,
they will assume that we have heavy defenses within,
and will certainly not dare to move.
Even if there is an invasion,
the various armies along the river are sufficient to resist and defend;
there will certainly be no worry."
Huán Wēn followed this advice.
Qiáo
was the son of Yuán Huái.
See Yuán Huái in Volume 95, Emperor Chéngdì Xiánkāng's 3rd year.
Huái
is pronounced 'gōng huí fān'.
In the eleventh month,
on the day of Xīnwèi,
Huán Wēn, leading Yìzhōu Cìshǐ Zhōu Fǔ and Nánjùn Tàishǒu Qiáowáng Wú Jì, attacked Hàn.
He submitted his memorial and immediately set off.
He entrusted the remaining affairs to Anxī Chángshǐ Fàn Wāng,
and added Fǔ as Dūdū of the four commanderies of Liángzhōu and various military affairs.
The four commanderies of Liángzhōu
were Fúlíng, Bādōng, Bāxī, and Bājùn.
The imperial court, considering the treacherous distance of the Shǔ roads
and that Huán Wēn's forces were small but penetrating deep,
all expressed worry.
Only Liú Tán believed they would certainly succeed.
Someone asked him why, and
Tán said:
"I know it through *bó* (a game).
Huán Wēn
is skilled at *bó*;
he does not act unless he is certain of success.
My only fear is that after conquering Shǔ,
Huán Wēn will ultimately monopolize control of the court."
In spring,
in the second month,
Huán Wēn's army reached Qīngyī.
Qīngyī County,
during the Hàn dynasty, belonged to Shǔ Commandery.
In the second year of Yángjiā of Emperor Shùndì of the Later Hàn,
it was renamed Hànjiā.
Shǔ established it as Hànjiā Commandery.
Liú Xù said: Qīngshén County in Méizhōu is on the Qīngyī River;
the Western Wèi established Qīngyī County.
The Qīngyī River flows out from beyond the border of Lúshān,
flows northeast to Wǔyáng and joins the Jiāng.
Dù Yòu said: Jiāzhōu was the former Yèláng Kingdom.
Emperor Wǔ of Hàn opened and established Jiànwéi Commandery,
governing Lóngyóu County,
which was the Qīngyī Road of Hàn.
It was at the confluence of the Dàjiāng and Qīngyī rivers.
Huán Wēn dispatched his uncle, Yòuwèi Jiāngjūn Fú, his cousin, Zhènnán Jiāngjūn Quán, and Qián Jiāngjūn Zǎn Jiān, etc., to lead troops,
heading from Shānyáng towards Héshuǐ.
The area of Shānyáng
was probably north of the Mín Jiāng,
on the southern side of Mount Éméi.
The *Shuǐ Jīng Zhù* says: The Jiāng River flows southeast past Wǔyáng County in Jiànwéi.
The Qīngyī River and Mò River come from the southwest to join it.
The so-called Héshuǐ
must be this place.
Cóng
is pronounced 'cái yòng fān'.
Zǎn
is pronounced 'zǐ gǎn fān'.
Jiāng
is pronounced 'jí liàng fān'.
Qù
is pronounced 'qī yù fān'.
Zǎn Jiān did not comply.
He led his troops from Yuānyāng Qí north of the river, crossing towards Jiànwéi.
In the third month,
Huán Wēn reached Péngmó.
Péngmó was
the Péngwáng Village of Wǔyáng County in Jiànwéi Commandery of Hàn,
the place where Cén Péng died.
The *Shuǐ Jīng Zhù* says: The Jiāng River from Wǔyáng flows east to Péngwáng Village,
called the Píngmó River,
also called the Wàishuǐ.
Píngmó is two hundred *lǐ* from Chéngdū,
in present-day Péngshān County, Méizhōu.
The armies advanced by different routes
to divide the Hàn forces.
Yuán Qiáo said:
"Now our suspended army has penetrated ten thousand *lǐ* deep.
If we win, great deeds can be achieved;
if we lose, no one will be left alive.
We should combine forces and unite our strength
to achieve victory in one battle.
If we divide into two armies,
the hearts of the troops will not be unified.
If one side unfortunately suffers a defeat—
'suffers a defeat'
means that with two routes advancing in parallel,
one army is defeated by Shǔ—
it is better to advance with the entire army,
abandoning cooking pots and tripods,
carrying only three days' provisions,
to show that there is no intention of returning.
Victory can then be assured."
Huán Wēn followed this.
He left Cānjūn Sūn Shèng and Zhōu Chǔ to lead the weak troops guarding the baggage train,
while Huán Wēn personally led the infantry directly to Chéngdū.
Chǔ
was Fǔ's son.
Lǐ Fú attacked Péngmó.
Sūn Shèng and others bravely counter-attacked
and routed them.
Huán Wēn advanced and
encountered Lǐ Quán.
They fought three battles and won three victories.
The Hàn troops scattered and fled back to Chéngdū.
Zhènjūn
Jiāngjūn Lǐ Wèi Dū came to meet Huán Wēn and surrendered.
When Zǎn Jiān reached Jiànwéi,
he then realized he was on a different route from Huán Wēn.
He returned,
crossing from Shātóu Jīn.
By the time he arrived,
Huán Wēn had already encamped at Shílǐ Mò outside Chéngdū.
Zǎn Jiān's troops disintegrated on their own.
Lǐ Shì brought out all his forces to battle at Zuòqiáo in Chéngdū.
The *Shuǐ Jīng Zhù* says: West of Wànlǐ Qiáo,
the upper part is called Yíqiáo,
also called Zuòqiáo.
Zuò
is pronounced 'jí gè fān'.
Cānjūn Gōng Hù died in battle.
An arrow struck Huán Wēn's horse's head.
The troops were afraid
and wanted to retreat, but
the drum officer mistakenly beat the advance drum.
The thunder drum was used to signal advance to the troops, called the advance drum.
Consequently, they were greatly defeated.
Huán Wēn, seizing the victory, advanced rapidly to Chéngdū
and set fire to its city gates.
The Hàn people were terrified
and had no further will to fight.
Lǐ Shì opened the east gate at night and fled.
When he reached Jiāmēng,
he sent Sànqí Chángshì Wáng Yòu to deliver his surrender document to Huán Wēn.
Sàn
is pronounced 'xī dàn fān'.
Qí
is pronounced 'qí jì fān'.
"Luèyáng Lǐ Shì bows his head, guilty unto death."
The Lǐ clan
had moved from Bāxī to Luèyáng in its early days.
Huán Wēn untied his binds and burned his coffin (prepared for surrender ritual),
sending Lǐ Shì and over ten members of his imperial clan to Jiànkāng.
He appointed Hàn Sīkōng Qiáo Xiànzhī and others as his advisors,
promoting the virtuous and commending the good.
The people of Shǔ were pleased.
On the 2nd day, Xiàhóu Lǎn (夏侯覽), the Administrator of Rìnán (日南), was greedy and unrestrained.
He oppressed and exploited foreign merchants,
and also levied boat-building materials,
claiming he intended to launch an expedition.
Because of this, the various states were resentful.
Wén (文), King of Línyì (林邑), attacked and captured Rìnán,
where five to six thousand soldiers died.
He killed Lǎn (覽)
and offered his body as a sacrifice to Heaven.
He sent a proclamation to Zhū Fān (朱蕃), Inspector of Jiāozhōu (交州),
requesting to establish Hèngshān (橫山) north of the commandery as the border.
Today, the southern border of Yōngzhōu (邕州) has a Hèngshān (橫山).
This mountain traverses rivers,
and our dynasty established Hèngshānzhài (橫山寨) and a horse farm there.
According to Liú Xù's (劉昫) old Táng Records,
Emperor Wǔ of Hàn (漢武帝) opened up Bǎiyuè (百越),
and established Rìnán Commandery three thousand *lǐ* south of Jiāozhǐ (交趾) Commandery,
with its seat at Zhūwú (朱吾).
Línyì (林邑)
was originally Xiànglín (象林) County of Hàn's Rìnán Commandery,
located four hundred *lǐ* south of the commandery border.
During the Later Hàn (後漢) period, when the Central Plains were in chaos,
Qū Lián (區連), a man from Xiànglín (象林) County,
killed the county magistrate
and proclaimed himself King of Línyì (林邑),
thus establishing the state of Línyì (林邑).
Yōngzhōu (邕州) is reached by crossing the sea to Jiāozhǐ (交趾),
and Jiāozhǐ (交趾) is three thousand *lǐ* to Rìnán (日南).
This Hèngshān (橫山) was naturally at the northern border of Rìnán Commandery,
not the Hèngshān (橫山) of modern Yōngzhōu (邕州).
Fān (蕃) sent Supervising Commander Liú Xióng (劉雄) to garrison Rìnán (日南).

On the 3rd day, Wáng Shì (王誓), former Grand Minister Remonstrant; Dèng Dìng (鄧定), General Who Guards the East; Wáng Rùn (王潤), General Who Pacifies the South; and General Kuí Wén (隗文) all raised armies in rebellion,
each numbering over ten thousand.
Huán Wēn (桓溫) personally attacked Dìng (定),
and sent Yuán Qiáo (袁喬) to attack Wén (文),
defeating them all.
Wēn (溫) ordered Zhōu Fǔ (周撫), Inspector of Yìzhōu (益州), to garrison Péngmó (彭模),
and executed Wáng Shì (王誓) and Wáng Rùn (王潤).
Wēn (溫) stayed in Chéngdū (成都) for thirty days,
then returned to Jiānglíng (江陵) with his troops in formation.
The *Zhuàn* (傳) says: "Entering and shaking the troops."
Dù Yù (杜預) notes: "Zhèn (振)
means to array;
lǚ (旅)
means the multitude (troops)."
He was enfeoffed as Marquis Guīyì (歸義侯).
In summer,
fourth month,
on the *dīngsì* day,
Dèng Dìng (鄧定), Kuí Wén (隗文) and others entered and occupied Chéngdū (成都).
Yáng Qiān (楊謙), General Who Conquers Barbarians, abandoned Fúchéng (涪城)
and retreated to defend Déyáng (德陽).
On the 4th day, Má Qiū (麻秋), Administrator of Liángzhōu (涼州) for Zhào (趙), attacked Fúhǎn (枹罕).
Láng Tǎn (郎坦), Administrator of Jìnchāng (晉昌), believed the city was too large to defend.
Emperor Huì (惠帝) divided Dūnhuáng (敦煌) and Jiǔquán (酒泉) to form Jìnchāng (晉昌) Commandery.
Fúhǎn (枹罕) County,
in the Former Hàn (前漢), belonged to Jīnchéng (金城) Commandery;
in the Later Hàn (後漢), it belonged to Lǒngxī (隴西) Commandery;
Zhāng Guǐ (張軌) divided it to belong to Jìnxīng (晉興) Commandery.
The *Shuǐjīng Zhù* (水經註) says,
Jìnchāng Chuān (晉昌川) is southwest of Hàoxìn (浩舋) County in Huángzhōng (湟中).
Liú Xù (劉昫) says: Jìnchāng (晉昌) Commandery
was the land of Hàn's Zhì'ān (寘安) County;
in Táng (唐), it was Jìnchāng (晉昌) County,
the seat of Guāzhōu (瓜州).
Fú (枹) is pronounced *fū*.
Zhāng Quān (張悛), Administrator of Wǔchéng (武成), said:
Wǔchéng (武成) Commandery
was also established by the Zhāng (張) clan.
Quān (悛)
is pronounced *chǒu yuán fān*,
and also *qī lún fān*.
"If we abandon the outer city, it will alarm the people's hearts,
and the great enterprise will be lost."
Zhāng Qú (張璩), Commandant Who Pacifies Barbarians, followed Quān's (悛) advice
and firmly defended the main city.
Commandant Who Pacifies Barbarians
was also an office established by the Zhāng (張) clan.
Láng Tǎn (郎坦) and Zhāng Quān (張悛) presumably, as administrators of their respective commanderies, followed Zhāng Qú (張璩) in defending Fúhǎn (枹罕).
Qú (璩)
is pronounced *qiú yú fān*.
Scaling ladders and tunnels were used,
with attacks advancing from a hundred directions.
"Earth tunnels"
refers to digging tunnels to emerge inside the city.
Qiū's (秋) army suffered tens of thousands of casualties.
Hǔ (虎), King of Zhào (趙), again sent his generals Liú Hún (劉渾) and others to lead two thousand infantry and cavalry to join him.
Láng Tǎn (郎坦) regretted that his advice was not taken
and instructed the soldier Lǐ Jiā (李嘉) to secretly lead over a thousand Zhào (趙) soldiers to scale the city wall.
Qú (璩) rallied his generals to fight fiercely,
killing over two hundred people,
and the Zhào (趙) soldiers then retreated.
Qú (璩) burned their siege equipment,
and Qiū (秋) retreated to defend Dàxià (大夏).
Hǔ (虎) appointed Shí Níng (石寧), Director of the Imperial Secretariat, as General Who Conquers the West,
to lead over twenty thousand soldiers from Bìng (幷) and Sī (司) provinces as reinforcements for Qiū (秋) and others.
Sòng Qín (宋秦) and others, generals of Zhāng Chónghuá (張重華), led twenty thousand households to surrender to Zhào (趙).
Chónghuá (重華) appointed Xiè Ài (謝艾) as Bearer of the Imperial Credentials, Army Strategist General,
and sent him to lead thirty thousand infantry and cavalry to advance to Línhé (臨河).
Ài (艾) rode in a light cart,
wearing a white hat,
beating drums as he advanced.
Qiū (秋) saw him from afar
and angrily said:
"Ài (艾) is a young scholar,
dressed like that,
he despises me!"
He ordered three thousand men of the Black Lance Dragon Charger unit to charge and attack him.
Ài's (艾)左右 attendants were greatly alarmed.
Someone advised Ài (艾) to mount a horse,
but Ài (艾) refused,
dismounted,
and sat on a *húchuáng* (胡牀).
*Húchuáng* (胡牀) is probably similar to today's folding chair.
Kǒng Yǐngdá (孔穎達) says: Today's *jiāochuáng* (交牀)
was originally adopted from the barbarians.
During the Suí (隋) dynasty, due to a prophecy mentioning *hú* (胡),
its name was changed to *jiāochuáng* (交牀).
The Zhào (趙) people thought there was an ambush,
and feared to advance.
A separate general, Zhāng Mào (張瑁), led troops by a secret path to cut off the rear of the Zhào (趙) army.
The Zhào (趙) army retreated,
and Ài (艾) took advantage of the situation to attack,
severely defeating them,
beheading their generals Dù Xūn (杜勳) and Jí Yú (汲魚),
and capturing thirteen thousand heads of enemies.
Qiū (秋) fled alone on horseback to Dàxià (大夏).
In the fifth month,
Qiū (秋) and Shí Níng (石寧) again led twelve thousand troops to encamp south of the river.
Liú Níng (劉寧) and Wáng Zhuó (王擢) plundered Jìnxīng (晉興), Guǎngwǔ (廣武), and Wǔjiē (武街).
Zhāng Guǐ (張軌) established Jìnxīng (晉興) Commandery by dividing parts of Xīpíng (西平).
Qūliǔ (曲柳)
is a place name
north of Hóngchí Lǐng (洪池嶺).
They retreated to defend Fúhǎn (枹罕),
causing great alarm in Gūzāng (姑臧).
Chónghuá (重華) wished to personally lead troops to resist them,
but Xiè Ài (謝艾) earnestly remonstrated.
Suǒ
Xiá (遐) said:
"The ruler
is the bulwark of the state;
he must not move lightly."
Thereupon, Ài (艾) was made Bearer of the Imperial Credentials, Inspector-General of all military matters for expeditions, and Acting General of the Guards.
Xiá (遐) was made Military Censor-General.
There were Military Censors in ancient times.
The *Huángdì Fǎ* (黃帝法) says,
a Censor is not subordinate to a general,
and reports if a general commits a crime.
It was presumably an enforcer of military law.
The Zhāng (張) clan then made it a general's title.
A separate general, Yáng Kāng (楊康), defeated Liú Níng (劉寧) at Shāfù (沙阜).
Níng (寧) retreated to encamp at Jīnchéng (金城).
On the 5th day,
in the sixth month,
on the *xīnyǒu* day,
a general amnesty was granted.
On the 6th day,
in autumn,
seventh month, Línyì (林邑) again captured Rìnán (日南)
and killed Supervising Commander Liú Xióng (劉雄).
On the 7th day, Kuí Wén (隗文), Dèng Dìng (鄧定) and others established Bēn (賁), son of the former Imperial Preceptor Fàn Chángshēng (范長生), as emperor and served him.
Lǐ Xióng (李雄) had made Fàn Chángshēng (范長生) Imperial Preceptor.
Many people from Shǔ (蜀) flocked to him.
On the 8th day, Hǔ (虎), King of Zhào (趙), again sent Sūn Fúdū (孫伏都), General Who Conquers the West, and General Liú Hún (劉渾) to lead two thousand infantry and cavalry to join Má Qiū's (麻秋) army,
marching rapidly across the river to attack Suìchéng (遂城) and Chángzuì (長最),
held by Zhāng Chónghuá (張重華).
Chángzuì (長最)
is a place name
north of the Jīnchéng (金城) River.
*Kǎoyì* (考異) says: *Jìn Chūnqiū* (晉春秋) writes
"Shàngzuì (上最)".
We follow the *Chónghuá Zhuàn* (重華傳) here.
A wind blew, causing the banners and flags to point southeast.
Suǒ Xiá (索遐) said:
"Wind serves as a command.
Now the banners and flags point towards the enemy,
which is Heaven's endorsement."
The *Fēngyún Qìhòu Zázhàn* (風雲氣候雜占) says: "If the wind does not scatter sideways,
and the banners and flags flutter steadily with the wind,
or point towards the enemy,
the army will achieve success all day,
indicating victory."
Wáng Zhuó (王擢) fought with Ài's (艾) vanguard,
was defeated,
and fled back to Hénán (河南).
In the eighth month,
on the *wùwǔ* day,
Ài (艾) advanced and attacked Qiū (秋),
severely defeating him.
Qiū (秋) fled back to Jīnchéng (金城).
Hǔ (虎) heard of this
and sighed, saying:
"I used a division of my army to pacify the nine provinces,
but now with the strength of the nine provinces, I am trapped at Fúhǎn (枹罕).
They have a talented man there;
they cannot be easily conquered yet!"
Upon Ài's (艾) return,
he suppressed the rebellious barbarians, Sīgǔzhēn (斯骨真) and others, over ten thousand households,
and defeated and pacified them all.
9 Zhào Wáng Hǔ held ten *zhōu* of land:
Yōu, Bīng, Jì, Sī, Yù, Yǎn, Qīng, Xú, Yōng, and Qín.
The rare and exotic tributes from foreign lands,
and the treasures in his treasuries,
were uncountable.
Yet he still considered them insufficient,
so he unearthed the tombs of previous dynasties,
taking their gold and jewels.
The Shāmén Wú Jìn spoke to Hǔ, saying:
Yuán Hóng's *Hàn Jì* states: Shāmén
in Hàn speech means "rest,"
which is to say, resting desires to return to non-action.
"The fortune of the Hú is about to wane;
the Jìn will revive.
It is fitting to impose harsh labor on the Jìn people to suppress their spirit."
Hǔ ordered Shàngshū Zhāng Mǐn to mobilize 160,000 men and women from nearby commanderies,
and 100,000 carts,
to transport earth to build the Huálín Yuàn and a long wall north of Yè,
extending for dozens of *lǐ* in all directions.
Shēn Zhōng, Shí Pú, Zhào Lǎn, and others submitted memorials stating that the celestial phenomena were in disorder,
and the common people were suffering.
Hǔ was furious and said:
"If the wall of the garden is completed in the morning,
and I die in the evening,
I will have no regrets."
He urged Zhāng Mǐn to have them light candles and work at night;
a violent storm and heavy rain caused
tens of thousands of deaths.
The commanderies and states successively sent sixteen azure unicorns
and seven white deer.
Hǔ ordered Sī Yú Zhāng Gézhù to train them to pull the Zhīgài.
The *Jìn Zhíguān Zhì* states that
among the subordinates of the Tàipú was the Diǎnyú Dūwèi.
Zhào's Sī Yú
was this official.
Zhāng Gézhù
is a person's name.
The Zhīgài
means the canopy was shaped like a propitious *zhī*.
In the ninth month,
he ordered Crown Prince Xuān to go out to pray for blessings at mountains and rivers,
and to hunt while traveling.
Xuān rode in a grand carriage,
with feathered canopy and ornate parasol,
displaying the emperor's banners and flags.
Sixteen armies and 180,000 soldiers marched out from the Jīnmíng Mén.
The *Shuǐ Jīng Zhù* states:
Yè City had seven gates: to the south, the Fèngyáng Mén;
in the middle, the Zhōngyáng Mén;
next, the Guǎngyáng Mén;
to the east, the Jiànchūn Mén;
to the north, the Guǎngdé Mén;
next, the Jiùmén;
to the west, the Xīmíng Mén,
which was probably the Jīnmíng Mén.
He laughed and said:
"With my family, father and son, like this,
unless heaven collapses and earth sinks,
what else is there to worry about!
Just hold children and play with grandchildren,
and enjoy oneself daily."
Wherever Xuān stayed,
people were arranged to form a long encirclement,
each side a hundred *lǐ*,
driving wild animals.
By evening, all were gathered in his designated area.
He made all civil and military officials kneel and stand,
forming multiple lines of encirclement and guard,
with torches making it as bright as day.
He ordered over a hundred skilled horsemen to gallop and shoot within it.
Xuān and his concubines observed from a palanquin.
This ceased when all the animals were gone.
If an animal escaped,
the person on guard,
if an official, had his horse confiscated
and was made to walk for a day;
if not an official, was whipped one hundred times.
Over ten thousand soldiers died of hunger and cold,
and the three *zhōu* and fifteen commanderies through which they passed
had no supplies left.
This is what Tāo was sent to征 (conquer/collect) with.
The three *zhōu* Xuān passed through
were probably Sī, Yǎn, and Yù.
Hǔ then ordered
Tāo to set out in succession,
from Bīngzhōu to Qín and Yōng, doing the same.
Xuān was angry that Tāo was his equal,
and grew increasingly jealous of him.
The eunuch Zhào Shēng was favored by Xuān,
but not by Tāo.
He subtly persuaded Xuān to eliminate Tāo,
and thus the plan to kill Tāo began.
10 Zhào Máqiū again attacked Zhāng Chónghuá's general Zhāng Mào,
defeated him.
According to the *Zài Jì*,
Mào was stationed in Héshǎ at that time.
"Defeated,"
pronounced *mài*.
The Húhǎn protector Li Kuí led seven thousand people to surrender to Zhào.
South of the Yellow River,
the Dī and Qiāng all submitted to Zhào.
11 In winter,
the tenth month,
on the *Yǐchǒu* day,
the Shìyùshǐ Yú Guī was sent to Liángzhōu,
to bestow upon Zhāng Chónghuá the titles of Shìzhōng, Dà Dūdū, Dū Lǒngyòu Guānzhōng Zhū Jūnshì, Dà Jiāngjūn, Liángzhōu Cìshǐ, and Xīpíng Gōng.
When Guī arrived at Gūzāng,
Chónghuá wanted to be called the King of Liáng,
and was unwilling to accept the edict.
He had his confidant Shěn Měng privately tell Guī:
"My lord has for generations been a loyal minister of the Jìn.
*Yìshì*
means successive generations.
Why?
The imperial court enfeoffed Mùróng Huàng as the King of Yàn,
yet my lord is only a Grand General.
How can this commend and encourage the loyal and worthy!
Your Excellency should move to the west of the river
and jointly persuade the provincial lord to become the King of Liáng."
Guī was a Shìyùshǐ;
because he was carrying an imperial mission,
he was called "Your Excellency."
"Move"
refers to a written communication.
"If it benefits the state,
you may act on your own authority."
Guī replied:
"My good sir, you speak amiss!
In ancient times,
the *dàfū* of various states commonly addressed each other as 'my good sir.'
The *Yílǐ Zhù* says: 'Zǐ'
is a term of respect for men.
Saying 'Wúzǐ'
is a term of intimacy.
Among noble ranks, none is higher than the Grand Duke.
In the Three Dynasties, enfeoffment established five ranks of nobility:
namely, duke, marquis, count, viscount, and baron.
The Grand Duke, with nine distinctions, was made chief.
Wú and Chǔ first usurped the title of king,
and the feudal lords did not criticize it,
probably because they were treated as barbarians.
If Qí and Lǔ were to claim the title of king,
would the feudal lords not attack them from all four sides!
Hàn Gāozǔ enfeoffed Hán and Péng as kings,
but soon exterminated them.
This was merely a temporary expedient,
not a bestowal of special favor.
His Majesty esteems your noble lord as loyal and worthy,
thus ennobling him as a Grand Duke,
and entrusting him with the authority of a regional governor.
His honor and glory are extreme.
How can he be compared to the Xiānbēi barbarians!
Moreover, I have heard that
merits vary in size,
and rewards vary in weight.
Now your noble lord has only just succeeded to his family's position and seeks to be king."
This refers to Chónghuá having just succeeded his father's position,
and not yet having performed any meritorious service for Jìn, yet seeking to be king.
"If you were to pacify the Hú and Jié in the east,
restore the imperial tombs and temples,
and welcome the Son of Heaven back to Luòyáng,
what more could you possibly add to that?"
Chónghuá then stopped.
12 The Dī King Yáng Chū of Wǔdū sent an envoy to pledge allegiance.
An imperial edict appointed Chū as Shǐ Chíjié, Zhēngnán Jiāngjūn, Yōngzhōu Cìshǐ, and Qiúchí Gōng.
13 In the twelfth month,
Zhènwēi Hùjūn Xiāo Jìngwén killed Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn Yáng Qiān,
attacked Fúchéng,
captured it,
and proclaimed himself Yìzhōu Mù.
He then took Bāxī
and opened communication with Hànzhōng.
Zhènwēi Hùjūn
was a Jìn official.
Xiāo Jìngwén, seeing that Jìn had newly incorporated Shǔ
and that there was also the rebellion of Fàn Bēn,
also took advantage of the situation to rebel.
Fú
is pronounced *fú*.
