Xué Tiāntái
Xiàozōng Mù Huángdì Volume 1, Part 2
Yǒnghé Fourth Year
(Wùshēn, 348 CE)
1 Summer,
fourth month,
Lín Yì raided Jiǔzhēn.
Having twice broken Rì Nán,
they then advanced to raid Jiǔzhēn.
Jiǔzhēn Commandery
was Áizhōu in the Táng Dynasty.
2 Zhào Qín Gōng Tāo (趙秦公韜) was favored by Zhào Wáng Hǔ (趙王虎).
Hǔ wanted to establish him as the heir,
but as Crown Prince Xuān (宣) was older,
he hesitated and could not decide.
Xuān once displeased Hǔ,
and Hǔ angrily said:
"I regret not having established Tāo!"
Tāo therefore became even more arrogant.
He built a hall in the Grand Commandant's (Tàiwèi) (太尉) residence,
named Xuānguāng Diàn (宣光殿),
with a beam nine *zhàng* (丈) long.
When Xuān saw it,
he was furious,
beheaded the carpenter,
cut the beam, and left;
this was because it offended his name.
Tāo increased its length to ten *zhàng*.
When Xuān heard of this,
he said to his favored Yang Bēi (楊杯),
Móu Chéng (牟成), and Zhào Shēng (趙生):
"That wicked fellow is so arrogant and reckless as to dare to do such a thing!
If you can kill him,
I will enter the Western Palace."
Hǔ resided in the Western Palace.
"When Tāo dies,
His Majesty will surely attend the mourning.
I will then carry out the great matter,
and it will surely succeed."
The *Zuǒ Zhuàn* (左傳) says: Pān Chóng (潘崇) said to Chǔ Shāng Chén (楚商臣):
"Can you carry out the great matter?"
Dù Yù (杜預) noted: "Great matter"
refers to assassinating the ruler.
In autumn,
in the eighth month,
Tāo held a banquet with his subordinates at Dōngmíng Guān (東明觀) at night.
The *Shuǐ Jīng Zhù* (水經註) says: Shí Shì (石氏) erected Dōngmíng Guān (東明觀) on the eastern city wall of Yè (鄴).
A Buddhist *jīngshè* (精舍)
is a Buddhist temple.
It is a place where monks devote themselves to spiritual cultivation,
hence it is called a *jīngshè*.
The *Shìwù Jì Yuán* (事物紀原) says: Emperor Míng (明帝) of Han built a *jīngshè* outside the eastern gate of the capital
to house Shè Mó Téng (攝摩騰) and Zhú Fǎ Lán (竺法蘭).
The ladder was small but long,
people climbed it like macaques,
hence it was called the Macaque Ladder (Yuánhóu Tī) (獮猴梯).
His knife and arrows were placed there, and he left.
The next day,
Xuān reported it.
Hǔ was so shocked and grief-stricken that he fainted,
only to revive after a long time.
As he was about to go and mourn,
Sīkōng (司空) Lǐ Nóng (李農) advised:
"The person who harmed Qín Gōng (秦公) is unknown,
and the bandit is in the capital.
The imperial carriage should not venture out lightly."
Hǔ then stopped,
deployed soldiers, and expressed his grief at Tàiwǔ Diàn (太武殿).
Xuān went to mourn Tāo,
but did not cry,
instead saying
"Haha,"
and made them lift the quilt to view the corpse,
then laughed loudly and left.
A large quilt is called a *qīn* (衾).
Hǔ was about to assign him the crime.
Hǔ suspected Xuān of killing Tāo
and wanted to summon him,
but feared he would not come.
So he falsely claimed that his mother, Empress Dù (杜后), was gravely ill from excessive grief;
Xuān did not realize he was suspected,
and entered the Central Palace (Zhōnggōng) (中宮) for an audience.
He was then detained.
Shǐ Kē (史科) of Jiànxīng (建興) knew of the plot
and informed him;
The *Wèi Tǔdì Jì* (魏土地記) says: Jiànxīng Commandery's (建興郡) seat was Yáng'ā (陽阿) County;
Yáng'ā County
belonged to Shàngdǎng Commandery (上黨郡) in the Han dynasty.
The *Wèi Shōu Zhì* (魏收志) says: Mùróng Yǒng (慕容永) divided Shàngdǎng (上黨) to establish Jiànxīng Commandery (建興郡).
Thus, its territory was not the Jiànxīng Commandery established by Shí Zhào (石趙).
The *Shuǐ Jīng Zhù* (水經註) says: Tián Róng (田融) said that Zhào (趙) established Jiànxīng Commandery within Guǎngzōng (廣宗) city,
which is probably correct.
All fled;
Zhào Shēng (趙生) was captured,
interrogated,
and confessed everything.
Hǔ's grief and anger intensified.
He imprisoned Xuān in the Mat Storeroom (Xíkù) (席庫),
Xíkù (席庫)
is a place for storing mats.
He took the knife and arrows that killed Tāo and licked their blood,
his mournful wails shaking the palace.
Fótúchéng (佛圖澄) said:
"Xuān (宣) and Tāo (韜) are both Your Majesty's sons.
Now, to kill Xuān for Tāo
is to compound the disaster.
If Your Majesty shows mercy and forgiveness,
your fortune will still be long;
but if you must execute him,
Xuān will descend as a comet to sweep the Yè Palace."
Hǔ did not listen.
He piled firewood north of Yè (鄴),
erected a pole on top,
placed a *lùlú* (鹿盧) at the end of the pole,
passed a rope through it.
A *lùlú* (鹿盧) is a wooden pulley (木鹿轤).
Xuān was sent below it,
and Tāo's favored eunuchs Hǎo Zhì (郝稚) and Liú Bà (劉霸) were ordered to pull out his hair,
tear out his tongue,
and drag him up the ladder;
Hǎo Zhì (郝稚) threaded a rope through his jaw,
and the *lùlú* (鹿盧) tightened it.
Liú Bà (劉霸) cut off his hands and feet,
gouged out his eyes and disemboweled him,
just like Tāo's injuries.
Fire was set from all four sides,
and the smoke and flames reached the sky.
Hǔ, along with several thousand people including the *Zhāoyí* (昭儀) and others, ascended the Central Terrace (Zhōngtái) (中臺) to watch.
The Central Terrace (Zhōngtái) (中臺)
is the central one of the three terraces,
namely the Bronze Sparrow Terrace (Tóngjué Tái) (銅爵臺).
The ashes were divided and placed at the intersections of all roads.
*Jiāodào* (交道)
means a crossing road;
one vertical and one horizontal forms a crossing road.
Xuān's (宣) youngest son was only a few years old,
and Hǔ had always loved him.
He held him and wept,
wanting to pardon him,
but his ministers would not allow it.
They took him from his embrace and killed him;
the child tugged at Hǔ's (虎) clothes and cried out loudly,
until his sash broke.
Hǔ fell ill because of this.
He also deposed Xuān's wife, Lady Dù (杜氏), to a commoner.
Three hundred people, including his four leaders (*shuài*) and others, were executed,
and fifty eunuchs,
all dismembered by chariots and chopped into pieces,
and cast into the Zhāng Shuǐ (漳水).
The Eastern Palace (Dōnggōng) (東宮) had four *shuài* (率): Left, Right, Front, and Rear.
*Shuài* (率)
is pronounced *suǒ lǜ*.
*Zhījiě* (支解) means dismembering the four limbs;
*jiéjiě* (節解) means dismembering every joint of the bones.
The [unclear character]
over ten thousand guards of the Eastern Palace (Dōnggōng) (東宮) were all banished to garrison Liángzhōu (涼州).
As Zhào (趙) had not yet obtained Liángzhōu (涼州),
Liángzhōu (涼州) was established in Jīnchéng (金城),
and they were exiled to guard the border of Liángzhōu (涼州).
This laid the groundwork for Gāo Lì (高力) to rebel against Zhāng Běn (張本).
Zhào Lǎn (趙攬) said to Hǔ (虎):
"There will be a change in the palace,
it is advisable to prepare for it."
When Xuān (宣) killed Tāo (韜),
Hǔ suspected that Zhào Lǎn (趙攬) knew but did not report it,
and also executed him.
Historians say that Zhào Lǎn (趙攬) discussed celestial phenomena in a court of suspicion and violence, bringing disaster upon himself.
*Xiān* (先)
is pronounced *xī jiàn*.
3 The court debated the merits of pacifying Shǔ (蜀),
and wanted to enfeoff Huán Wēn (桓溫) with Yùzhāng Commandery (豫章郡).
Shàngshū Zuǒchéng (尚書左丞) Xún Ruí (荀蕤) said:
"If Wēn (溫) were to pacify Hé (河) and Luò (洛) again,
what would he be rewarded with then?"
So, Wēn (溫) was promoted to Grand General of the Western Expedition (Zhēngxī Dàjiāngjūn) (征西大將軍) and granted the privileges of a Minister with a Tribunal (Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī) (開府儀同三司),
and enfeoffed as Duke of Línhè Commandery (臨賀郡公);
King Qiáo Wú Jì (譙王無忌) was promoted to Front General (Qián Jiāngjūn) (前將軍);
Yuán Qiáo (袁喬) was appointed Dragon Galloping General (Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn) (龍驤將軍)
and enfeoffed as Count of Xiāngxī (湘西伯).
Ruí (蕤)
was the son of Sōng (崧).
Xún Sōng (荀崧) was the younger brother of Xún Pān (荀藩);
during the disaster of Yǒngjiā (永嘉),
they jointly established a traveling office (*xíngtái*) in Mì (密);
at the beginning of Jiànxīng (建興),
he also once garrisoned Wǎn (宛).
After Wēn (溫) destroyed Shǔ (蜀),
his prestige greatly increased,
and the court feared him.
Kuàijī Wáng Yù (會稽王昱), seeing that Yángzhōu (揚州) Inspector Yīn Hào (殷浩) had a great reputation
and was admired by both court and commoners,
brought him in as a trusted confidant
to participate in managing court affairs,
hoping to use him to counterbalance Wēn (溫);
from then on, he and Wēn (溫) gradually grew suspicious and estranged from each other.
This laid the groundwork for Wēn (溫) to depose Hào (浩) and coerce the court.
*Cháo* (朝)
is pronounced *zhí yáo*.
*Kuài* (會)
is pronounced *gōng wài*.
Hào appointed Xún Xiàn, the Grand Historian of the Commander-in-chief of the North, and Wáng Xīzhī, the former Inspector of Jiāngzhōu,
who both had excellent reputations.
He promoted Xiàn to be the Administrator of Wú Commandery.
Among the commanderies and states south of the Jiāng,
Wú was considered the foremost.
He took them as his wings.
Xiàn
was Ruí’s younger brother;
Wáng Xīzhī
was Dǎo’s nephew by a paternal cousin.
Wáng Xīzhī believed that only when internal and external affairs were harmonized
could the state be at peace.
He advised Hào
not to create a rift with Wēn.
Hào did not follow.
4 Yàn King Mùróng Huàng became ill.
He summoned the heir apparent, Mùróng Jùn, and entrusted him, saying:
“The Central Plains are not yet pacified,
and we still rely on talented and outstanding individuals to manage world affairs.
Mùróng Kè possesses both wisdom and courage,
and is capable of bearing heavy responsibilities.
You should entrust him,
to achieve my ambition!”
He further said:
“Yáng Shìqiū’s conduct is lofty and pure,
and his loyalty and integrity are firm.
Yáng Wù,
courtesy name Shìqiū.
‘Xíng’ [conduct],
read Xià Mèng.
Treat him well!”
In the ninth month,
on the bǐngshēn day,
he passed away.
He was fifty-two years old.
5 Zhào King Shí Hǔ discussed establishing a crown prince.
Grand Commandant Zhāng Jǔ said:
“The Duke of Yàn, Shí Bīn, possesses military prowess;
the Duke of Péngchéng, Shí Zūn, possesses literary virtue.
It is for Your Majesty to choose.”
Shí Hǔ said:
“Your words are exactly what I had in mind.”
General Róngzhāo Zhāng Chái said:
The Records of the States says: Shí Hǔ established the positions of General Róngzhāo and General Yàowǔ,
whose rank was above that of the Left and Right Guards.
“The mother of the Duke of Yàn is of low birth
and has also committed faults before.
This refers to her intention to kill Zhāng Hèdù,
the incident is found in volume 96, during Emperor Chéng’s Xiánkāng 6th year.
Shí Zūn and Shí Suì shared the same mother.
The deposition of the Zhèng clan is found in volume 95, Xiánkāng 3rd year.
I fear there may be some lingering resentment.
Your Majesty should consider this carefully!”
Previously,
when Shí Hǔ captured Shàngguī,
found in volume 94, Emperor Chéng’s Xiánhé 4th year,
he saw a woman of extraordinary beauty
and took her into his harem.
Shí Hǔ doted on her,
and she bore him the Duke of Qí, Shí Shì.
Zhāng Chái, seeing Shí Hǔ was old and ailing,
wished to establish Shí Shì as his successor,
hoping that the Liú clan would become Empress Dowager
and he himself could assist in government.
So he persuaded Shí Hǔ, saying:
“Your Majesty has twice established crown princes,
and their mothers were all of humble or entertainer origins,
hence chaos followed.
Now, you should choose one whose mother is noble and whose son is filial.”
Shí Hǔ said:
“Say no more,
I know where the crown prince is.”
Shí Hǔ again discussed with his close ministers in the Eastern Hall.
Shí Hǔ said:
“I wish to use three hu of pure ash to wash my intestines clean.
Why do I only bear wicked sons
who, once past twenty, immediately want to kill their father!
Now Shì is only ten years old.
By the time he is twenty,
I will already be old.”
Thereupon, he and Zhāng Jǔ and Lǐ Nóng settled on a plan,
ordering the high officials to submit a petition requesting the establishment of Shí Shì as Crown Prince.
Grand Minister of Agriculture Cáo Mò refused to sign.
Shí Hǔ sent Zhāng Chái to ask the reason.
Mò prostrated himself and said:
“The state is a heavy vessel;
it is not appropriate to establish a minor.
Therefore, I dare not sign.”
Shí Hǔ said:
“Mò is
a loyal subject,
but he has not grasped my intention.
Zhāng Jǔ and Lǐ Nóng understand my intention.
You may instruct them to enlighten him.”
Consequently, Shí Shì was established as Crown Prince,
and Lady Liú Zhāoyí was made Empress.
Shí Hǔ’s father-son mutual destruction,
discarding the elder and establishing the younger,
was Heaven intending to use Rǎn Mǐn to exterminate his kind.
6 In winter,
the eleventh month,
on the jiǎchén day,
Yàn Civil and Martial King was buried.
Huàng was posthumously titled Wénmíng.
Jùn,
courtesy name Xuānyīng,
was Huàng’s second son.
An envoy was sent to Jiànkāng to report the death.
His younger brother Mùróng Jiāo was made Left Worthy King,
and Left Grand Historian Yáng Wù was made Lángzhōng Lìng.
7 In the twelfth month,

Cài Mó, who was Left Grand Master of Glorious Happiness, concurrently Grand Minister over the Masses, and Recorder of Affairs of the Masters of Writing, was appointed Attendant-in-ordinary and Grand Minister over the Masses.
Mó submitted a memorial firmly declining,
and said to his intimates:
“If I were to become Grand Minister over the Masses,
I would be ridiculed by future generations.
I righteously dare not accept.”
1 In spring,
the first month,
on the xīnwèi day, the first day of the month,
a general amnesty was proclaimed.
2 Zhào King Shí Hǔ ascended the imperial throne.
Shí Hǔ had ascended the position of Heavenly King in Emperor Chéng’s Xiánkāng 3rd year.
Now he ascended the imperial throne.
He changed the era name to Tàiníng.
All his sons were advanced in noble rank to kings.
More than ten thousand “High Strength” (gāolì) troops from the former Eastern Palace
Shí Xuān selected strong men to guard the Eastern Palace,
calling them "High Strength" (Gāolì),
and appointed supervising generals to command them.
Fúfēng was the city of Yōng county.
Yōng,
read Yú Yòng;
same below.
And ordered the Inspector of Yōngzhōu, Zhāng Mào, to escort them.
Mào stripped them all of their horses,
making them push deer carts on foot
to deliver grain to the garrison.
The Gāolì commander Liáng Dú from Dìngyáng
Dìngyáng county,
belonged to Shàngjùn during the Hàn dynasty,
and was abolished during the Jìn.
The Northern Wèi established Dìngyáng Commandery during the Tài'ān era;
during the Táng, it was Línzhēn county of Yánzhōu.
conspired to revolt and return east.
When the multitude heard of it,
they all leapt up, clapped their hands, and shouted loudly.
Yǒng means
to jump.
Biàn means
to clap hands.
Hū means
Huǒ Gù.
He led his forces to attack and capture Xiàbiàn.
General Ānxī Liú Níng attacked them from Āndìng
but was defeated by Dú.
All the Gāolì were strong and skilled archers,
one could contend with more than ten men.
Although they had no armor or weapons,
they plundered axes from the common people,
affixed a ten-foot handle to them,
and fought like gods.
Kē means axe handle.
All the garrison soldiers followed him,
attacking and seizing commanderies and counties,
killing chief officials and those receiving salaries of two thousand shi,
and advanced eastward unopposed.
By the time they reached Cháng'ān,
their numbers had already reached one hundred thousand.
King Lèpíng Shí Bāo exerted all his elite forces to resist them,
but was defeated in one battle.
Dú then exited Tóngguān to the east,
advancing towards Luòyáng.
Zhào ruler Shí Hǔ appointed Lǐ Nóng as Grand Chief Controller and Acting Grand General,
commanding the Garrison Army General Zhāng Hèdù and others, with one hundred thousand infantry and cavalry, to suppress them.
They battled at Xīn'ān,
Xīn'ān county,
belonged to Hóngnóng Commandery during the Hàn dynasty,
and to Hénán Commandery from the Jìn onwards.
Qí (cavalry),
read Qí Jì;
same below.
They battled at Luòyáng,
were again defeated,
and retreated to fortify Chénggāo.
Dú then plundered eastward through the various commanderies of Xíngyáng and Chénliú.
In the second year of Tàishǐ of Emperor Wǔ,
Xíngyáng Commandery was established by dividing Hénán.
Yān Wáng Bīn was appointed Grand Commander,
overseeing all military affairs internal and external.
He was to lead Grand General Champion Yáo Yìzhòng and General of Chariots and Cavalry Pú Hóng and others to suppress Dú.
Yìzhòng led his more than eight thousand men to Yè.
From Shètóu to Yè.
Jiāng (將),
pronounced as liàng.
Hǔ was ill,
and did not see him.
He was led into the Lǐngjūn Office.
The Lǐngjūn Office
was the place where the Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn conducted his affairs.
Yìzhòng was enraged,
and refused to eat,
saying:
"The sovereign summoned me to attack the rebels,
and should personally grant me strategies.
Am I here for food!
Moreover, if the sovereign does not see me,
how am I to know whether he lives or dies?"
Hǔ, despite his illness, saw him.
Yìzhòng chided Hǔ, saying:
"Your son died,
are you grieving?
Why are you ill?
When your son was young, you did not choose good people to teach him,
leading him to become a rebel;
since he became a rebel and was executed,
what is there to grieve about?
Furthermore, you have been ill for a long time,
and the son you established is young.
Refers to Crown Prince Shì.
The world will surely be in chaos;
you should worry about this first,
not the rebels!
Dú and his ilk are desperate and wish to return home,
they gathered to become bandits.
Wherever they passed, they were cruel and violent.
How far can they get?
This old Qiāng will settle it for you in one fell swoop!"
Liǎo (了),
means to decide.
Regardless of their status, all people belonged to you.
Hǔ did not blame him either.
In his seat, Hǔ granted him the title of Commissioner with Imperial Credentials, General who Conquers
the West,
and bestowed upon him armor and a horse.
Yìzhòng said:
"Do you think this old Qiāng is capable of defeating the rebels?"
Thereupon, he donned his armor and mounted his horse in the courtyard,
then spurred his horse and galloped south,
leaving without a word of farewell.
He then, with Bīn and others, attacked Dú in Xíngyáng,
utterly defeating him,
cutting off Dú's head and returning.
They pursued his remaining partisans,
annihilating them completely.
Hǔ ordered Yìzhòng to wear his sword and shoes when entering the palace hall,
and not to rush when entering court,
and advanced his title to Duke of Xīpíng Commandery.
Pú Hóng was made Grand General of Chariots
and Cavalry, Minister of the Right and Left with powers equal to the Three Excellencies, Grand Commander of all military affairs in Yōng and Qín Provinces, and Inspector of Yōng Province,
and advanced to Duke of Lüèyáng Commandery.
3 Mǎ Xù of Shǐpíng gathered troops,
calling himself General.
Dù Yòu said: Hán's Pínglíng,
Jìn changed it to Shǐpíng,
where there is the old city of Mǎwéi.
More than three thousand households were executed.
4 In summer,
the fourth month,
Zhōu Fǔ, Inspector of Yì Province, and Zhū Táo, General of Valiant Cavalry, attacked Fàn Bēn,
and beheaded him.
Yì Province was pacified.
The Fàn Bēn rebellion began in the third year of the previous volume.
Xiāng (驤),
pronounced as jiāng.
5 An imperial edict dispatched Court Usher Chén Shěn to Yān,
to appoint Mùróng Jùn as Commissioner with Imperial Credentials, Attendant, Grand Commander, overseeing all military affairs north of the Yellow River, Governor of Yōu and Píng Provinces,
Grand General, Grand Chányú, and King of Yān.
6 Huán Wēn dispatched Supervising Commandant Téng Jùn to lead troops from Jiāo and Guǎng to attack Lín Yì Wáng Wén at Lúróng.
He was defeated by Wén,
and retreated to garrison Jiǔzhēn.
7 On the day Yǐmǎo,
Zhào Wáng Hǔ's illness worsened greatly.
He appointed Péngchéng Wáng Zūn as Grand General,
to guard Guānyòu;
Yān Wáng Bīn as Chancellor,
overseeing the affairs of the Secretariat;
Zhāng Chái as Grand General who Guards the Camp, General of the Palace Guard, and Minister of Personnel.
Liú Cōng established sixteen Grand Generals,
and Guarding the Camp was one of them.
Shí Hǔ established the General who Guards the Camp,
above the General of Chariots and Cavalry;
now making Zhāng Chái Grand General who Guards the Camp
elevates his title.
The General of the Palace Guard commanded military power,
and the Minister of Personnel managed appointments.
Thus, both civil and military powers were entirely entrusted to Chái.
Empress Liú disliked Bīn assisting in governance,
fearing it would be unfavorable to the Crown Prince,
and conspired with Zhāng Chái to remove him.
Bīn was then in Xiāngguó.
She sent an envoy to falsely tell Bīn:
"The sovereign's illness has gradually improved, and the King should go hunting.
You may stay a little longer."
Bīn had always been fond of hunting and addicted to alcohol,
so he stayed to hunt,
and indulged in drinking.
Lady Liú and Chái then forged an imperial edict stating that Bīn had no loyalty or filial piety,
stripped him of his office, and sent him back to his residence,
ordering Chái's brother Xióng to lead five hundred Longténg soldiers to guard him.
This was Shí Hǔ's old trick to confine Shí Hóng,
and Zhāng Chái followed and used it.
Was it not Hǔ who taught him?
Shí Bīn was but an ordinary man!
When his lord and father was gravely ill,
summoned to receive the will and assist in governance,
even if Hǔ's illness had slightly improved,
he should have traveled day and night.
Instead, he indulged in heavy drinking and hunting.
His lack of wisdom was thus!
Even if he had gained power,
his younger brothers would have twisted his arm and taken it away.
Zhāng Jǔ said he had military prowess;
that is false!
On the day Yǐchǒu,
Zūn arrived at Yè from Yōu Province.
He was ordered to receive his appointment in the court hall,
and was assigned thirty thousand imperial guards to dispatch him.
Zūn departed in tears.
On this day,
Hǔ's illness slightly improved.
He asked:
"Has Zūn arrived yet?"
His attendants replied:
"He left long ago."
Hǔ said:
"I regret not seeing him!"
Hǔ faced the western gate,
which was the western gate of Tàiwǔ Hall.
Hǔ asked:
"What do you seek?"
They all replied:
"Your Majesty's health is unwell,
it is advisable to let Yān Wáng enter the palace guard,
and command the military forces."
Some said:
"We beg that he be made Crown Prince."
Hǔ said:
"Is Yān Wáng not within?
Summon him!"
His attendants said:
"The King is ill from alcohol,
and cannot enter."
Hǔ said:
"Hurry and bring a palanquin to fetch him,
I should entrust him with the imperial seal and sash."
Yet, none went.
All the attendants were for Empress Liú and her son,
hence none went.
Xǐ (璽),
pronounced as sì.
Shòu (綬),
pronounced as shòu.
Hūn (惛),
means confused and forgetful.
Xuàn (眩),
means disordered vision.
They wanted to kill Bīn to unify everyone's hearts,
how could they know that there were already those inciting Shí Zūn to enter and be established?
On the day Wùchén,
Lady Liú again forged an edict to make Chái Grand Tutor, Grand Commander of all military forces internal and external,
and oversee the affairs of the Secretariat,
following the precedent of Huò Guāng.
Attendant Xú Tǒng sighed, saying:
"Chaos is about to erupt,
I will not be involved in it."
He swallowed poison and died.
On the day Jǐsì,
Hǔ died.
Crown Prince Shì ascended the throne,
and honored Lady Liú as Empress Dowager.
Lady Liú held court and issued decrees,
making Zhāng Chái Chancellor.
Chái declined to accept,
requesting that Péngchéng Wáng Zūn and Yìyáng Wáng Jiàn be made Co-Chancellors of the Left and Right,
to appease them.
Lady Liú complied.
Zhāng Chái 張豺 plotted with the Grand Commandant Zhāng Jǔ 張舉 to assassinate the Minister of Works Lǐ Nóng 李農.
Jǔ 舉 had always been on good terms with Nóng 農,
and secretly informed him;
Nóng 農 fled to Guǎngzōng 廣宗,
and led several tens of thousands of Qǐhuó 乞活 families to defend Shàngbái 上白.
The Qǐhuó 乞活
were the remnants of Lǐ Yùn 李惲 and Tián Huī 田徽's followers,
and since Yǒngjiā 永嘉,
had gathered and settled at Shàngbái 上白.
Shuài 帥
is read as lǜ 率;
the same applies below.
Chái 豺 appointed Zhāng Lí 張離 as General-in-Chief of the Garrison,
overseeing all military affairs inside and outside the capital,
making him his deputy.
Pénchéng Wáng Zūn 彭城王遵 arrived at Hénèi 河內
and heard of the death (of Shì 世).
Yáo Yìzhòng 姚弋仲, Pú Hóng 蒲洪, Liú Níng 劉寧, and the General Who Conquers Barbarians Shí Mǐn 石閔, and the General of the Imperial Guard Wáng Luán 王鸞 and others, returning from suppressing Liáng Dú 梁犢,
met Zūn 遵 at Lǐchéng 李城.
The Xù Hàn Zhì 續漢志 states
that Lǐchéng 李城 is in Píngzég 平睪 County, Hénèi 河內.
The Shǐ Jì 史記 states,
"Lǐ Tóng 李同 of Hándān 邯鄲 repelled the Qín 秦 army,"
and Zhào 趙 enfeoffed his father as Lǐ Hóu 李侯,
which is this city.
"Your Highness is grown and virtuous,
and the late emperor also intended to make Your Highness his heir;
meaning Hǔ 虎 wished to follow Zhāng Jǔ's 張舉 words.
Shuō 說,
read as shū ruì 輸芮.
Zhǎng 長,
read as zhī liǎng 知兩.
was misled by Zhāng Chái 張豺.
Now the empress rules the court,
corrupt officials are in power,
Shàngbái 上白 is still under siege and not yet subdued,
and the capital's guards are empty.
If Your Highness proclaims Zhāng Chái's 張豺 crimes,
and marches forth to punish him,
who would not open their gates and turn their weapons to welcome Your Highness!"
Zūn 遵 followed this advice.
Zūn 遵
raised an army from Lǐchéng 李城
and quickly returned to Yè 鄴.
The Inspector of Luòzhōu 洛州, Liú Guó 劉國, led the forces from Luòyáng 洛陽 to join him.
When the dispatch reached Yè 鄴,
Zhāng Chái 張豺 was greatly alarmed,
and hastily summoned the army from Shàngbái 上白.
On the day of Bǐngxū 丙戌,
Zūn's 遵 army encamped at Dàngyīn 蕩陰,
with ninety thousand soldiers.
Shí Mǐn 石閔 was the vanguard.
The elders and Jié 羯 soldiers all said:
"The Prince of Pénchéng 彭城 has come to mourn;
we should go out to welcome him.
We cannot defend the city for Zhāng Chái 張豺!"
They climbed over the city walls and left.
Chái 豺 beheaded them,
but could not stop them.
Zhāng Lí 張離 also led two thousand of the Lóngténg 龍騰,
cut open the gates, and welcomed Zūn 遵.
Liú Shì 劉氏 was afraid,
summoned Zhāng Chái 張豺,
and wept bitterly before him, saying:
"The late emperor's coffin is not yet interred,
and calamity has reached this point!
Now the heir is young and immature,
entrusted to the general.
What will the general do?
If we give Zūn 遵 a high position,
can we pacify him?"
Chái 豺 was terrified and did not know what to do,
only saying,
"Yes, yes."
So an imperial edict was issued,
appointing Zūn 遵 as Chancellor,
concurrently Grand Marshal, Grand Commander, Commander of all military forces inside and outside the capital,
and Director of the Imperial Secretariat,
with the addition of the Yellow Ax and the Nine Bestowals.
On the day of Jǐchǒu 己丑,
Zūn 遵 arrived at Ānyáng Tíng 安陽亭.
Ānyáng Xiàn 安陽縣
belonged to Wèijùn 魏郡.
This was probably the main pavilion of Ānyáng Xiàn 安陽縣.
Zūn 遵 ordered him (Zhāng Chái 張豺) to be seized.
On the day of Gēngyín 庚寅,
Zūn 遵 donned his armor and displayed his troops,
entered through the Fèngyáng Mén 鳳陽門,
ascended to the front hall of the Tàiwǔ Diàn 太武殿,
grieved with extreme sorrow,
then retired to the Eastern Pavilion.
This was the Eastern Pavilion of the Tàiwǔ Diàn 太武殿.
Yèdū 鄴都 had Pínglè Shì 平樂市.
Lè 樂,
pronounced Luò 洛.
He falsely issued an edict from Liú Shì 劉氏, saying:
"The heir is young and immature,
appointed by the late emperor's private affection.
The imperial enterprise is too weighty,
something he is unable to bear.
Therefore, Zūn 遵 shall succeed to the throne."
Thereupon, Zūn 遵 ascended the throne,
issued a general amnesty,
and lifted the siege of Shàngbái 上白.
On the day of Xīnmǎo 辛卯,
Shì 世 was enfeoffed as the King of Qiáo 譙.
The Zàijì 載記 states: Shì 世 was on the throne for a total of thirty-three days.
The Kǎoyì 考異 states: The Jìn Chūnqiū 晉春秋 and Shíliù Guó Chūnqiū Chāo 十六國春秋鈔
both say that the Empress Dowager was deposed as Zhāoyí 昭儀.
Now we follow the Zàijì 載記.
The Shíliù Guó Chūnqiū 十六國春秋 and Zàijì 載記
also say that Shì 世 was on the throne for thirty-three days.
According to calculation, from the Jǐsì 己巳 day of the fourth month to the Gēngyín 庚寅 day of the fifth month,
there are twenty-two days in total.
Lǐ Nóng 李農 came to confess his crimes,
and was reinstated to his former position.
Zūn 遵 honored his mother Zhèng Shì 鄭氏 as Empress Dowager.
Zhèng Shì 鄭氏 was indeed Suì's 邃 mother.
The deposition of Empress Zhèng 鄭 is found in volume 95, during the third year of Xiánkāng 咸康 of Emperor Chéng 成.
Yǎn 衍, son of the former King of Yān 燕 Bīn 斌, was made Crown Prince.
Jiàn 鑒, the King of Yìyáng 義陽, was appointed Attendant and Grand Tutor.
Chōng 沖, the King of Pèi 沛, was appointed Grand Guardian.
Bāo 苞, the Duke of Lèpíng 樂平,
was appointed Grand Marshal.
Kūn 琨, the King of Rǔyīn 汝陰, was appointed Grand General.
Mǐn 閔, the Duke of Wǔxīng 武興, was appointed Commander of all military forces inside and outside the capital and General Who Upholds the State.
This laid the groundwork for Shí Mǐn 石閔 to gain military power and exterminate the Hú 胡 and Jié 羯.
On the day of Jiǎwǔ 甲午,
a violent storm in Yè 鄴 uprooted trees,
with thunder and lightning,
and hail as large as bowls and sheng 升 measures.
As large as bowls and sheng 升.
Yǔ 雨,
read as yú jù 于具.
All the gates, watchtowers, and pavilions were swept away,
more than half of the imperial carriages and accoutrements
were burned,
all metal and stone items were consumed,
and the fire was not extinguished until after more than a month.
At this time, Chōng 沖, the King of Pèi 沛, was garrisoned at Jì 薊.
Chōng 沖 probably replaced Zūn 遵 in garrisoning Jì 薊.
Jì 薊,
pronounced jì 計.
He said to his subordinates:
"Shì 世 received the command of the late emperor,
but Zūn 遵 arbitrarily deposed and killed him.
There is no greater crime!
Therefore, order all inside and outside the capital to be on high alert.
I will personally lead an expedition to punish him."
So he left Níngběi Jiāngjūn 寧北將軍 Shù Jiān 沭堅 to guard Yōuzhōu 幽州,
and led fifty thousand troops southward from Jì 薊.
He sent dispatches to Yān 燕 and Zhào 趙,
and everywhere people gathered like clouds.
By the time they reached Chángshān 常山,
the army numbered over a hundred thousand,
encamping at Yuànxiāng 苑鄉.
When they encountered Zūn's 遵 amnesty decree,
Chōng 沖 said:
"They are all my brothers.
The dead cannot be brought back.
Why should we continue to harm each other!
I will return."
He intended to return to Jì 薊.
"Pénchéng 彭城 usurped and murdered to elevate himself;
his crime is great!
Although the King turns his banner northward,
your servant will head southward.
After pacifying the capital
and capturing Pénchéng 彭城,
I will then respectfully welcome the Grand Imperial Carriage."
Chōng 沖 then advanced again.
Zūn 遵 hastily sent Wáng Zhuó 王擢 with a letter to admonish Chōng 沖,
but Chōng 沖 did not listen.
Zūn 遵 ordered Wǔxīng Gōng Mǐn 武興公閔 and Lǐ Nóng 李農 to lead a hundred thousand elite soldiers to suppress him,
fighting at Píngjí 平棘.
Píngjí Xiàn 平棘縣
belonged to Chángshān Jùn 常山郡 in the Hàn 漢 dynasty,
to Zhàoguó 趙國 in the Jìn 晉 dynasty,
and was the seat of Zhàozhōu 趙州 in the Táng 唐 dynasty.
Chōng 沖 was captured at Yuánshì 元氏.
Yuánshì Xiàn 元氏縣
belonged to Chángshān Jùn 常山郡 in the Hàn 漢 dynasty,
to Zhàoguó 趙國 in the Jìn 晉 dynasty.
Kàn Yīn 闞駰 states: "It was the fief of Prince Yuán 元 of Zhào 趙,
hence called Yuánshì 元氏."
In the Táng 唐 dynasty, Yuánshì Xiàn 元氏縣 belonged to Zhàozhōu 趙州.
Liú Xù 劉昫 states: "Yuánshì 元氏 was the seat of Chángshān Jùn 常山郡 in the Hàn 漢 dynasty;
its old city is south of modern Zhàozhōu Yuánshì Xiàn 趙州元氏縣."
Over thirty thousand of his soldiers were buried alive.
Wǔxīng Gōng Mǐn (武興公閔) said to Zūn (遵):
"Pú Hóng (蒲洪)
is a hero among men.
Now if Hóng (洪) is stationed to guard Guānzhōng (關中),
I fear that the lands of Qín (秦) and Yōng (雍) will no longer belong to the state.
Although this was the late emperor's dying wish,
since Your Majesty has ascended the throne,
it is fitting to revise the plan."
Zūn (遵) agreed with this,
and relieved Hóng (洪) of his post as Dūdū (都督),
but kept his other positions as before.
Hóng (洪) was angered,
returned to Fāngtóu (枋頭),
and sent an envoy to surrender.
Hóng (洪) was encamped at Fāngtóu (枋頭),
(see volume eighty-five, during Emperor Chéng's (成帝) Xiánhé (咸和) eighth year).
Surrendered,
(Hù Jiāngfān (戶江翻)).
Yān Píngdí Jiāngjūn (燕平狄將軍) Mùróng Bà (慕容霸) submitted a memorial to Yān Wáng Jùn (燕王儁), saying:
"Shí Hǔ (石虎) was extremely cruel and violent,
abandoned by Heaven.
His remaining embers barely cling on,
and they devour each other.
Now the people of Zhōngguó (中國) are in dire straits,
looking forward to benevolent relief.
If the great army makes a move,
they will surely throw down their weapons."
Běipíng Tàishǒu (北平太守) Sūn Xìng (孫興) also presented a memorial saying:
"The Shí (石) clan is in great chaos,
it is fitting to seize the opportunity to advance and take Zhōngyuán (中原)."
Jùn (儁), having recently suffered a great loss (referring to the previous year when Huáng (皝) died),
did not agree.
(Referring to last year when Huáng (皝) passed away).
(Mùróng Bà (慕容霸)) said to Jùn (儁):
"What is hard to obtain and easy to lose
is the opportune moment.
Should the Shí (石) clan, by some chance, decline and then revive,
or should a hero seize their established assets,
(meaning that a hero in Zhōngyuán (中原) might take advantage of the chaos to seize Zhào (趙),
taking possession of its already established resources),
I fear it would become a future calamity."
Jùn (儁) said:
"Though Yèzhōng (鄴中) is in chaos,
Dèng Héng (鄧恆) occupies Ānlè (安樂).
(Referring to previous references,
'Ānlè' (安樂)
should be
'Lè'ān' (樂安)).
If we attack Zhào (趙) now,
the eastern route is impassable;
we must go via Lúlóng (盧龍).
The mountain path at Lúlóng (盧龍) is steep and narrow.
(The 'Shuǐjīng Zhù' (水經註) states: The Rúshuǐ (濡水) flows southeast past Lúlóng Sài (盧龍塞).
The pass road exits east from Wúzhōng Xiàn (無終縣),
crosses the Rúshuǐ (濡水) towards Línlán Xíng (林蘭陘),
and reaches Qīngxíng (清陘) to the east.
The peril of Lúlóng (盧龍)
lies in its winding, steep slopes,
hence its name 'Nine Precipices.'
If we are troubled from beginning to end,
what can be done?"
Bà (霸) said:
"Although Héng (恆) wishes to hold out for the Shí (石) clan,
his generals and soldiers care for their families,
and everyone yearns to return home.
If the great army approaches them,
they will naturally disintegrate.
I request to be Your Highness's vanguard,
to march east through Túhé (徒河),
secretly advance to Lìngzhī (令支),
and catch them by surprise.
When they hear of it,
they will surely be terrified.
At best, they will close their gates and defend themselves;
at worst, they will abandon the city and flee in disarray.
How will they have time to resist us?
Then Your Highness can advance at a steady pace,
without any further difficulties."
Jùn (儁) hesitated, undecided,
and consulted Wǔcái Jiāngjūn (五材將軍) Fēng Yì (封奕).
(The Yān (燕) state established the title Wǔcái Jiāngjūn (五材將軍),
presumably taking its meaning from Sòng Zǐhǎn's (宋子罕) saying,
"Heaven created the five materials, who can remove weapons?").
(Yì (奕) said): "The way of warfare is:
if the enemy is strong, use strategy;
if the enemy is weak, use force.
Therefore, to swallow the small with the great
is like a wolf eating a pig;
to replace chaos with order
is like the sun melting snow.
Your Majesty, since ancient times,
has accumulated virtue and benevolence,
and your army is strong and well-trained.
Shí Hǔ (石虎) was utterly cruel and violent;
even in death, his eyes would not close.
His descendants fight over the throne,
and there is disorder from top to bottom.
The people of Zhōngguó (中國)
have fallen into misery,
craning their necks and standing on tiptoe awaiting deliverance.
If Your Majesty raises an army and marches south,
first taking Jìchéng (薊城),
then pointing to Yèdū (鄴都),
proclaiming your might and virtue,
and comforting the remaining populace,
who would not support the elderly and carry the young to welcome Your Majesty?
The evil faction will shatter like ice at the sight of your banner;
how can they cause harm?"
Cóngshì Zhōngláng (從事中郎) Huáng Hóng (黃泓) said:
"Now Tàibái (太白) (Venus) traverses the sky,
and Suì (歲) (Jupiter) converges north of Bì (畢);
the Yīn (陰)
state is receiving the Mandate,
this is a sure sign.
(The 'Hànshū Tiānwénzhì' (漢書天文志) states: When Tàibái (太白) traverses the sky,
the world will be revolutionized, and kings will change.
Mèng Kāng (孟康) noted: This means it appears in the east and enters the west,
or appears in the west and enters the east.
Tàibái (太白) is
a Yin star;
if it appears in the east, it should hide in the east;
if it appears in the west, it should hide in the west.
To pass the meridian is 'traversing the sky.'
Jìn Zhuó (晉灼) said: The sun
is Yang;
when the sun rises, stars disappear.
To be seen in the sky at noon is 'traversing the sky.'
Where Suìxīng (歲星) (Jupiter) is located,
that state cannot be attacked,
but can attack others.
The space between Mǎo (昴) and Bì (畢) is Tiānjī (天街),
its north is the Yīn (陰) state.
When Suì (歲) converges north of Bì (畢),
it clearly indicates that the Yīn (陰) state is destined to receive the Mandate and become king.
This is to comply with Heaven's will."
Zhéjìong Jiāngjūn (折衝將軍) Mùyú Gēn (慕輿根) said:
"The people of Zhōngguó (中國) are suffering from the chaos of the Shí (石) clan,
and all wish for a change of rulers to save them from their urgent plight.
This is a once-in-a-thousand-years opportunity,
which must not be missed.
Since Wǔxuān Wáng (武宣王) (referring to Mùróng Guī (慕容廆), posthumously titled Wǔxuān Wáng (武宣王)),
we have cultivated agriculture and trained the army,
just waiting for this day.
If the time has come and we do not seize it,
but instead hesitate and worry,
is it that Heaven does not yet wish for the realm to be pacified,
or that Your Majesty does not wish to take the world?"
Jùn (儁) smiled and agreed.
He appointed Mùróng Kè (慕容恪) as Fǔguó Jiāngjūn (輔國將軍),
Mùróng Píng (慕容評) as Fǔbì Jiāngjūn (輔弼將軍),
and Zuǒ Chángshǐ (左長史) Yáng Wù (陽騖) as Fǔyì Jiāngjūn (輔義將軍),
calling them
the "Three Fǔ (輔)."
The titles of Fǔbì (輔弼) and Fǔyì (輔義) generals
were also created at this time.
(He also created the title) Jiànfēng Jiāngjūn (建鋒將軍).
(This was also newly created).
They drilled the troops and enforced a state of alert,
preparing for an offensive.
(Kǎoyì (考異) states: The 'Yān Jǐngzhāo Jì' (燕景昭紀) records the assembly of troops in the fourth month.
At that time, Shí Hǔ (石虎) had just died,
and his sons had not yet begun to contend;
the 'Shíliù Guó Chūnqiū' (十六國春秋) places it in the fifth month,
hence it is followed.
However, the 'Yānshū' (燕書) records Fēng Yì's (封奕) and Mùyú Gēn's (慕輿根) words
both referring to Rǎn Mǐn (冉閔).
Upon examination, Mǐn (閔) had not yet usurped Zhào (趙) at this time,
so the historian likely embellished it,
hence it is omitted).
8 In the sixth month,
Zhào Wáng Hǔ (趙王虎) was buried at Xiǎnyuán Líng (顯原陵),
with the temple
name Tàizǔ (太祖).
9 Huán Wēn (桓溫) heard of the chaos in Zhào (趙),
and moved his troops to garrison Ānlù (安陸).
Ānlù County (安陸縣) had belonged to Jiāngxià Commandery (江夏郡) since the Hàn (漢) dynasty.
In the Táng (唐) dynasty, it was the seat of Ān Prefecture (安州).
Wēn (溫) moved from Jiānglíng (江陵) to garrison Ānlù (安陸).
Wáng Jiá (王浹), the Inspector of Yáng Prefecture (揚州刺史) of Zhào (趙), offered Shòuchūn (壽春) in surrender;
Chén Kuí (陳逵), the General of the Central Army of the West, advanced and occupied Shòuchūn (壽春).
Chǔ Póu (褚裒), the General-in-Chief Who Conquers the North, submitted a memorial requesting an expedition against Zhào (趙).
Chǔ Póu (褚裒) was then garrisoned at Jīngkǒu (京口).
Póu (裒),
read as "pú hóu fān".
directly advanced to Sìkǒu (泗口).
The court deliberated that since Póu's (裒) responsibility was weighty and important,
it would be
advisable to first send a detachment.
Póu (裒)
was the Empress Dowager's father,
and also held a regional command,
hence it is said his responsibility was weighty and important.
"Previously, [we had already sent
the Supervising Commander Wáng Yízhī (王頤之) and others directly to Péngchéng (彭城),
and later sent the Supervising Commander Mí Yì (麋嶷) to advance and occupy Xiàpī (下邳).
Now, it is advisable to launch the expedition quickly
to build up momentum."
In the autumn,
in the seventh month,
Póu (裒) was promoted to Grand Commander of Punitive Expeditions (征討大都督),
overseeing military affairs of Xú (徐), Yǎn (兗), Qīng (青), Yáng (揚), and Yù (豫) five prefectures.
Póu (裒) led an army of thirty thousand,
directly heading to Péngchéng (彭城).
Northern scholars and commoners surrendering and defecting numbered thousands daily.
Both court and common people believed that the Central Plains could soon be recovered.
However, Cài Mó (蔡謨), the Grand Master of Guanglu, alone told his confidant,
"The destruction of the Hú (胡) barbarians would indeed be a great celebration,
but I fear it will bring further worries to the imperial court."
His confidant said,
"What do you mean?"
Mó (謨) replied,
"Indeed, only a supreme sage or a hero can align with heaven, seize the opportune moment, and rescue the people from hardship.
As for others, it is better to measure their virtue and assess their strength.
Observing today's situation,
it is likely beyond what the current worthies can achieve.
They will surely strive to expand beyond their capabilities,
exhausting the people to satisfy their ambition;
meaning they will not be able to drive straight through and pacify the Central Plains,
but will inevitably need to establish garrisons and fortifications in the territories they gain,
delineating borders and defending them,
exhausting the people to satisfy their aspirations.
Another interpretation:
Fēn (分),
pronounced as 'fú wèn fān',
refers to the inherent capacity of individuals,
implying that recovering the Central Plains was beyond the capabilities of the talent available at that time.
If one plans and operates beyond one's capacity,
then success cannot be achieved;
the able-bodied suffer from war,
the old and weak are burdened by transport,
exhausting the people to satisfy one's ambition without succeeding.
If their aspirations are not met,
their resources will be depleted and their strength exhausted,
their wisdom and courage both spent,
how can the imperial court not be worried?"
Afterwards, Yīn Hào's (殷浩) defeat
ultimately turned out exactly as Cài Mó (蔡謨) had predicted.
Over five hundred households of the people of Lǔ Commandery (魯郡)
collectively rose in arms to join the Jìn (晉) dynasty,
seeking aid from Chǔ Póu (褚裒).
Póu (裒) dispatched his generals Wáng Kān (王龕) and Lǐ Mài (李邁) with three thousand elite troops to meet them.
Lǐ Nóng (李農), the Grand Commander of Southern Expeditions of Zhào (趙), led twenty thousand cavalry and fought Kān (龕) and others at Dàipī (代陂).
Kān (龕) and others suffered a great defeat,
and were all captured by Zhào (趙).
In the eighth month,
Póu (裒) retreated and garrisoned at Guǎnglín (廣陵).
Chén Kuí (陳逵) heard of this,
burned the accumulated provisions at Shòuchūn (壽春),
destroyed the city, and fled back.
Póu (裒) submitted a memorial requesting self-demotion,
but the imperial edict did not permit it;
it ordered Póu (裒) to return to garrison Jīngkǒu (京口),
and relieved him of the title of Commander of Punitive Expeditions.
At that time, there was great chaos north of the Yellow River.
Over two hundred thousand displaced people crossed the river, intending to defect and seek refuge.
However, by the time Póu (裒) had already returned,
his authority and influence did not reach them,
so they were all unable to extricate themselves,
and nearly all died.
The 'Kǎo Yì' (考異) states: Póu's (裒) biography says:
"They were plundered by Mùróng Huǎng (慕容皝) and Fú Jiàn (苻健),
and all died."
However, by this time, Mùróng Huǎng (慕容皝) had already died over a year ago.
In the sixth year of Yǒnghé (永和),
Mùróng Jùn (慕容儁) first led his troops south;
after Shí Jiàn (石鑒) ascended the throne,
Pú Hóng (蒲洪) first had an army of one hundred thousand.
In the sixth year of Yǒnghé (永和), Hóng (洪) died,
and Jiàn (健) first succeeded him.
None of them had any interaction with Póu (裒),
so this account is not adopted here.
10 Zhào (趙) Lèpíng (樂平) Prince Bāo (苞) plotted to lead the forces from Guān Yòu (關右) to attack Yè (鄴).
Shí Guāng (石光), the Left Chief Clerk, Cáo Yào (曹曜), the Commandant, and others strongly remonstrated,
but Bāo (苞) grew angry
and killed Guāng (光) and over a hundred others.
Bāo (苞) was greedy by nature and lacked strategy.
The local heroes of Yōng Prefecture (雍州) knew he would achieve nothing,
and all sent envoys to inform the Jìn (晉) dynasty.
Sīmǎ Xūn (司馬勳), the Inspector of Liáng Prefecture (梁州), led his troops to respond.
Xūn (勳)
was the great-grandson of Sīmǎ Suì (司馬遂), the Prince of Jìnán (濟南), who was a nephew of Emperor Xuān (宣帝).
Yōng (雍),
read as 'yú yòng fān'.
Shǐ (使),
read as 'shū lì fān'.
11 Yáng Chū (楊初) attacked Zhào (趙) Xīchéng (西城);
and defeated it.
Yáng Chū (楊初)
was the Di (氐) King of Wǔdū (武都).
This Xīchéng (西城) was probably the place where Kuí Xiāo (隗囂) fled during the Hàn (漢) dynasty.
12 In the ninth month,
the officials of Liáng Prefecture (涼州) collectively petitioned to appoint Zhāng Chónghuá (張重華) as Chancellor, King of Liáng (涼王), and Governor of Yōng (雍), Qín (秦), and Liáng (涼) three prefectures.
Chónghuá (重華) frequently bestowed money and silk upon his favored courtiers;
he also enjoyed board games.
Bó (博)
refers to chūpú (樗蒲);
Yì (弈)
refers to yiqí (弈棋).
Xǐ (喜),
read as 'xǔ jì fān'.
Suǒ Zhèn (索振), the Executive Aide, remonstrated, saying:
"The former king diligently and frugally worked day and night to fill the imperial coffers,
precisely because the humiliation had not yet been avenged,
and he was determined to pacify the realm.
At the beginning of Your Highness's reign,
powerful invaders pressed in.
Zhēngshì (徵事)
was an office established by Liáng (涼).
Refers to Zhào's (趙) attack,
details found in the second and third years of the previous volume.
Suǒ (索),
read as 'xī gè fān'.
We gained the dedicated efforts of the warriors,
referring to generously rewarding warriors with money and silk,
thus gaining their utmost efforts even unto death.
Now, the accumulated reserves are empty, and the enemies are still present.
How can we lightly squander them
on those who have rendered no meritorious service?
In the past, Emperor Guāngwǔ (光武) of Hàn (漢) personally managed all state affairs.
Memorials reaching the palace
were responded to within the day,
thus he was able to achieve the great enterprise of the restoration.
Now, memorials are delayed,
often taking months.
Three months make a season,
three decades make a month.
Deep grievances languish in prison.
This is hardly the conduct of an enlightened ruler."
Chónghuá (重華) apologized.
13 Sīmǎ Xūn (司馬勳) exited Luògǔ (駱谷),
defeated Zhào's (趙) Chángchéng (長城) garrison.
The Chángchéng (長城) garrison was where Sīmǎ Wàng (司馬望) and Dèng Ài (鄧艾) of Wèi (魏) had held out against Jiāng Wéi (姜維).
It was two hundred *lǐ* (里) from Cháng'ān (長安).
He sent Liú Huàn (劉煥), the Administrator, to attack Cháng'ān (長安),
and beheaded Liú Xiùlí (劉秀離), the Grand Protector of Jīngzhào (京兆).
Liú Xiùlí (劉秀離) probably engaged in battle and was defeated and killed.
Huàn (煥) was unable to reach the city walls of Cháng'ān (長安).
Many local heroes in Sānfǔ (三輔) killed their governors and magistrates to join Xūn (勳),
totaling over thirty strongholds,
with a force of fifty thousand.
Zhào (趙) Lèpíng (樂平) Prince Bāo (苞) then abandoned his plan to attack Yè (鄴),
and ordered his generals Má Qiū (麻秋) and Yáo Guó (姚國) to lead troops to resist Xūn (勳).
Zūn (遵), the Lord of Zhào (趙), dispatched Wáng Lǎng (王朗), the General of Chariots and Cavalry, with twenty thousand elite cavalry under the pretext of suppressing Xūn (勳),
but actually to abduct Bāo (苞) and send him to Yè (鄴).
Xūn (勳) had few troops,
and fearing Lǎng (朗), dared not advance.
If Huán Wēn (桓溫) had attacked Guānzhōng (關中) at this time,
Guānzhōng (關中) could have been taken.
Shǎo (少),
read as 'shī zhǎo fān'.
In winter,
the tenth month,
he released the suspended hook,
captured Wǎnchéng (宛城),
killed Yuán Jǐng (袁景), the Grand Protector of Nányáng (南陽) of Zhào (趙),
and then returned to Liáng Prefecture (梁州).
14 At first,
when Zhào Lord Zūn set out from Lǐchéng,
he said to Wǔxīng Gōng Mǐn:
“Work hard!
If the mission succeeds,
I will make you Crown Prince.”
Later, he established Crown Prince Yǎn.
Mǐn, relying on his achievements,
wanted to monopolize the court administration,
but Zūn did not permit it.
Mǐn was naturally brave and skilled in combat,
and he repeatedly achieved military successes,
making both barbarian and Han veteran generals wary of him.
After becoming Dūdu,
and having overall command of the internal and external military power,
he then appeased and cared for the generals and officers in the palace,
all of whom he nominated as Diànzhōng Yuánwài Jiāngjūn,
and ennobled as Guānwài Hóu.
Diànzhōng Jiāngjūn
was first established in the Jìn dynasty;
Diànzhōng Yuánwài Jiāngjūn
was established later.
Guānwài Hóu
was established by Wèi Wǔ Wáng during the Jiàn'ān 20th year of Hàn Xiàndì,
what was called a nominal marquis.
I note that in Qín and Hàn, Lièhóu possessed states and cities;
Guānnéi Hóu had no states or cities,
ranked in the court,
and for those without official positions,
residing in the capital,
they were therefore called Guānnéi Hóu.
Many Lièhóu who went to their states
were outside the passes.
Later, Cáo Cāo established Guānwài Hóu below Guānnéi Hóu,
which was not the intention of the Qín and Hàn system of peerage.
And he further titled them based on good and evil to suppress them,
which caused widespread resentment and anger.
Zhōngshū Lìng Mèng Zhǔn and Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn Wáng Luán advised Zūn to gradually strip Mǐn of his military power.
Mǐn's resentment and expectations grew.
Hènwàng
is the same as Yuànwàng.
In the eleventh month,
Zūn summoned Yìyáng Wáng Jiàn, Lèpíng Wáng Bāo, Rǔyīn Wáng Kūn, and Huáinán Wáng Zhāo and others to discuss before Zhèng Tàihòu,
saying:
“Mǐn's disloyal acts are becoming apparent.
Now I wish to execute him.
What do you think?”
Jiàn and the others all replied:
“It is fitting!”
Lady Zhèng said:
“When the troops returned from Lǐchéng,
without Jínú,
how could we have reached this day?
Rǎn Mǐn's
childhood name was Jínú.
She meant that Mǐn was quite arrogant due to his achievements,
and it would be best to be lenient with him.”
Jiàn, upon leaving,
sent the eunuch Yáng Huán to quickly inform Mǐn.
Mǐn then coerced Lǐ Nóng and Yòuwèi Jiāngjūn Wáng Jī to secretly plot to depose Zūn,
and sent generals Sū Yàn and Zhōu Chéng to lead three thousand armored soldiers to seize Zūn at the Nántái.
It refers to the Nántái of the Sāntái.
The Commentary on the Water Classic states: South of the Tóngquè Tái is the Jīnquè Tái,
eight zhàng high,
with one hundred and ninety rooms.
Shuài
is read as Lǜ.
The Yìjīng says: For Tánqí,
two people play a game,
each having six white and black pieces.
First, the pieces are arranged opposite each other,
then they take turns shooting them.
The board is made of stone,
four sides are low and the middle is high.
Wèi Wéndì was good at Tánqí,
and could use the corner of a handkerchief.
At one time, a scholar could also bend his head and flick the pieces with the ramie turban he wore.
Liú Gòngfù's poem says:
“When the Hàn Emperor first tired of the toil of Cùjú,
his attendants then created the game of Tánqí.”
Tánqí probably originated in Hàn.
The Shìshuō says: Tánqí originated in Wèi,
a game of the inner palace's cosmetics boxes.
This statement is incorrect.
According to the Xījīng Zájì,
Hàn Chéngdì liked Cùjú,
but his advisors considered it too physically demanding,
unsuitable for the supreme ruler.
The emperor ordered them to choose something similar but less strenuous,
and his family members presented Tánqí,

Hóu Chǔ Póu,

"Zhào people"

Jiàng,

Shuài,

Yìn, Míng, and Yù were all made kings.
Yìn, Míng, and Yù
were Mǐn’s three sons.
He was enfeoffed as the Prince of Qí,
and all his sons were enfeoffed as county dukes.
He sent envoys, bearing credentials, to pardon the various army garrisons;
none of them complied.
The various army garrisons
refers to Zhāng Shěn and Pú Hóng, etc.
Má Qiū persuaded Fú Hóng, saying:
“Rǎn Mǐn and Shí Zhī are currently entangled in conflict,
and the chaos in the Central Plains cannot be settled yet.
It would be better to first take Guānzhōng,
and once our foundation is secure,
then contend for the world in the east.
Who would dare oppose us?”
Hóng deeply agreed with this.
Afterwards, Qiū, taking advantage of a banquet, poisoned Hóng,
intending to annex his troops;
the heir apparent, Jiàn, arrested Qiū and beheaded him.
Hóng said to Jiàn:
“The reason I have not yet entered the pass [Guānzhōng]
is because I thought the Central Plains could be pacified;
now, unfortunately, I am in distress due to this scoundrel.
The Central Plains is not something you brothers can manage.
After I die,
you must immediately enter the pass!”
With these words, he died.
Jiàn succeeded to the command of his troops,
then relinquished the titles of Grand Commander, Grand General, and King of the Three Qín,
claimed the official titles of Jìn,
and sent his uncle, Ān, to report the death [of Fú Hóng]
and also to request imperial decree.
Zhào Xīnxīng Prince Zhī ascended the imperial throne at Xiāngguó.
Kǎoyì states: The Jìn Emperor’s Chronicle
places Zhī’s ascension in the intercalary month;
the Thirty Kingdoms and Jìn Chūnqiū both place it in the third month.
According to Shíliù Guó Chūnqiū,
Zhī claimed emperorship
and appointed Yáo Yìzhòng and Fú Jiàn to official positions,
but did not mention Fú Hóng.
Hóng died in the third month,
hence the suspicion that Zhī ascended the throne in the third month.
He appointed Rǔyīn Prince Kūn as Chancellor,
and the six foreign tribes
occupying provinces and commanderies all responded to him.
The six foreign tribes
were the Hú, Jié, Dī, Qiāng, Duàn clan, and Bāmán.
He treated them with special courtesy.
Yìzhòng’s son Xiāng was
courageous, brave, and resourceful,
and many commoners loved him.
They requested Yìzhòng to make him his successor,
but Yìzhòng, because Xiāng was not his eldest son,
did not allow it;
Xiāng
was Yìzhòng’s fifth son.
Zhǎng
is pronounced zhìliǎng fān.
Yìzhòng then sent him to lead troops.
Zhī appointed Xiāng as General of Agile Cavalry, Governor of Yùzhōu, and Duke of Xīnchāng.
He also appointed Fú Jiàn as Commander of All Military Affairs in Hénán, General Who Guards the South, Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī, Governor of Yǎnzhōu, and Duke of Luèyáng Commandery.
Summer,
fourth month.
The Zhào ruler Zhī sent Rǔyīn Prince Kūn to lead an army of 100,000 to attack Wèi.
The Wèi ruler Mǐn killed Lǐ Nóng and his three sons,
along with Minister of the Secretariat Wáng Mó, Palace Attendant Wáng Yǎn, Regular Palace Attendant Yán Zhèn, and Zhào Shēng.
Mǐn sent an envoy to Jìn on the banks of the river, saying:
“The rebellious Hú have disturbed the Central Plains,
but they have now been executed;
those who can assist in suppressing them
may send troops.”
The imperial court did not respond.
Fifth month.
Lújiāng Grand Administrator Yuán Zhēn attacked Wèi Héfèi,
captured it,
took its residents captive, and returned.
Sixth month.
Zhào Rǔyīn Prince Kūn advanced to Hándān,
and General Who Guards the South Liú Guó joined him from Fányáng.
Fányáng County,
in Hàn, belonged to Wèijùn,
in Jìn, belonged to Dùnqīujùn;
during Suí, Fányáng was abolished and merged into Nèihuáng County of Xiāngzhōu.
He was greatly defeated,
with over ten thousand dead.
Liú Guó returned to Fányáng.
Earlier,
Duàn Lán died at Lìngzhī.
Duàn Lán was stationed at Lìngzhī,
as seen in the previous volume, Emperor Kāng, Jiànyuán first year.
Lìng
is pronounced líng,
also lángdìng fān.
Zhī
is pronounced qí.
Due to the chaos of the Shí clan,
he led his tribe south.
Autumn,
seventh month.
Kān led his troops east to occupy Guǎnggù.
Kān moved east from Chénliú to occupy Guǎnggù.
Eighth month.
People from Dàijùn, led by Zhào Kē, with over three hundred families, rebelled against Yān and surrendered to Zhào Bīngzhōu Governor Zhāng Píng.
Yān Prince Jùn relocated the people of Guǎngníng and Shànggǔ commanderies to Xúwú.
Xúwú County,
in Hàn and Jìn, belonged to Yòuběipíng Commandery,
abolished in Later Zhōu,
merged into Wúzhōng County.
Táng renamed Wúzhōng to Yùtián County,
belonging to Jìzhōu.
Fearing they would rebel again and return to Zhào,
he therefore relocated them.
14 When Wáng Lǎng
departed Cháng’ān, Lǎng’s Sīmǎ, Dù
Hóng, occupied Cháng’ān,
declaring himself Jìn Zhēngběi Jiāngjūn and Yōngzhōu Cìshǐ.
He appointed Zhāng Jū of Féngyì as his Sīmǎ.
The Yi and Huá peoples of Guānxī all responded to him.
Fú Jiàn wished to take it,
but fearing Hóng would know,
he accepted the official titles from Zhào.
These were bestowed by Zhào Lord Zhī.
He garrisoned Wēn,
and appointed Niú Yí as Ānjí Jiāngjūn,
garrisoning Huái.
Ānjí Jiāngjūn
was a position established by the Fú clan,
named for pacifying and gathering the people and the Yi.
Wēn Xiàn and Huái Xiàn both belonged to Hénèi Jùn.
Wēn Xiàn
belonged to Mèngzhōu in the Táng dynasty.
The old city of Huái Xiàn was west of Wǔzhì Xiàn in Huáizhōu.
He ordered the people to plant wheat,
showing no intention of moving west.
If anyone knew but did not plant,
Jiàn would kill them to make an example.
Later, he declared himself Jìn Zhēngxī Dàjiāngjūn, Dūdū Guānzhōng Zhū Jūnshì, and Yōngzhōu Cìshǐ.
He appointed Jiǎ Xuánshuò of Wǔwēi as Zuǒ Chángshǐ,
Liáng Ān of Luò
yáng as Yòu Chángshǐ,
Duàn Chún as Zuǒ Sīmǎ,
Xīn Láo as Yòu Sīmǎ,
and Wáng Yú of Jīngzhào, Chéng Gōng of Āndìng, Hú Wén, and others as Jūnzī Jìjiǔ.
He led all his troops west.
He appointed Yú Zūn as vanguard,
and upon reaching Méngjīn,
constructed a floating bridge to cross.
He dispatched his younger brother, Fǔguó Jiāngjūn Xióng, leading five thousand troops to enter through Tóngguān,
and his nephew, Yángwǔ Jiāngjūn Jīng, leading seven thousand troops to enter through Zhǐguān.
Entering Tóngguān from Hénán to Huáyīn,
and entering Zhǐguān from Héběi,
crossing the river west from Pújīn to Wèiběi,
they would combine forces to attack Cháng’ān.
Shuài
is read as Shuài;
the same below.
He held Jīng’s hand and said:
“If the mission is not successful,
you will die north of the river,
I will die south of the river,
and we will never see each other again.”
After crossing,
he burned the bridge
and personally led the main army to advance with Xióng.
When Dù Hóng heard this,
he wrote a letter to Jiàn,
insulting him.
He appointed Zhāng Jū’s younger brother Xiān as Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn,
leading thirteen thousand troops to meet and fight north of Tóngguān.
Xiān’s army was utterly defeated
and fled back to Cháng’ān.
Hóng gathered all the troops from Guānzhōng to resist Jiàn.
Hóng’s younger brother Yù advised Hóng to welcome Jiàn,
but Hóng refused.
Yù led his部曲 to surrender to Jiàn.
Jiàn sent Fú Xióng to campaign in Wèiběi.
The Dī chieftain Máo Shòu, garrisoned at Gāolíng,
Gāolíng Xiàn
belonged to Féngyì in the Hàn dynasty;
Jìn renamed it Gāolù
and it belonged to Jīngzhào.
The Qiāng chieftain Bái Dú, garrisoned at Huángbái,
which is Huángbái Chéng.
Qiú
is pronounced Cí Yóu.
Both beheaded Hóng’s envoys
and sent their sons to surrender to Jiàn.
All the cities and towns passed by Fú Jīng and Yú Zūn
surrendered without exception.
Hóng was afraid
and fortified Cháng’ān.
15 Zhāng Hèdù, Duàn Qín, Liú Guó, and Jìn Tún met at Chāngchéng.
Wèi Shōu’s Dìxíng Zhì: Wèi Jùn’s Chānglè Xiàn has Chāngchéng.
Chānglè Xiàn
was established by separating from Wèi Xiàn in the 21st year of Tàihé of the Later Wèi.
Jìn
is pronounced Jū Xìn.
Wèi Lord Mǐn personally led an attack against them,
fighting at Cāngtíng.
Cāngtíng is on the river,
sixty lǐ southwest of Dōng’ē.
Zì Jiāng
is read as Jì Liàng.
Twenty-eight thousand people died.
Jìn Tún was pursued and beheaded at Yīn’ān.
Yīn’ān Xiàn
belonged to Wèi Jùn in the Hàn dynasty,
and to Dùnqiū Jùn in the Jìn dynasty.
Liú Xù said: Yīn’ān Chéng is north of Dùnqiū Xiàn in Chánzhōu.
Mǐn had over three hundred thousand soldiers,
with banners, gongs, and drums stretching over a hundred lǐ.
Even during the peak of the Shí clan,
there was nothing that surpassed this.
Xīn Mì of Lǒngxī, former Jìn Sànqí Chángshì,
had a high reputation.
Sàn
is pronounced Xī Dǎn.
Qí
is pronounced Qí Jì.
He declined all invitations to serve.
Mǐn, with full courtesy, invited him to be Tàicháng.
Mì sent a letter to Mǐn,
believing that
“when things reach their extreme, they reverse;
when they reach their ultimate, they become dangerous.
The Zhànguó Cè says: things reverse when they reach their extreme,
like winter and summer.
They become dangerous when they reach their ultimate,
like a stack of qī.
Gāo Yòu’s commentary says: winter solstice gives birth,
summer solstice kills,
hence it is called reversal.
Zhì
means extreme.
You should take advantage of this great victory
to return yourself to the Jìn court.
You will surely have the integrity of Yóu and Yí,
and enjoy the longevity of Sōng and Qiáo.”
Yóu and Yí
are Xǔ Yóu and Bó Yí.
Sōng and Qiáo
are Chì Sōngzǐ and Wángzǐ Qiáo.
16 In the ninth month,
Yān Lord Jùn campaigned south in Jìzhōu,
taking Zhāngwǔ and Héjiān.
In the first year of Tàishǐ of Jìn Wǔdì,
Zhāngwǔ Guó was established by separating from Bóhǎi.
The Wǔdài Zhì: Later Wèi established Yíngzhōu with Héjiān.
Within its jurisdiction was Píngshū Xiàn,
where Zhāngwǔ Jùn was formerly established.
Jiǎ Jiān of Bóhǎi,
young, valued integrity.
He served Zhào as Diànzhōng Dū.
When Zhào fell,
Jiān abandoned Wèi Lord Mǐn and returned to his hometown,
leading several thousand households of部曲.
Mùróng Píng of Yān campaigned in Bóhǎi
and sent an envoy to recruit him,
but Jiān ultimately did not surrender.
Píng fought with him
and captured him.
Jùn appointed Píng as Zhāngwǔ Tàishǒu
and Fēng Yù as Héjiān Tàishǒu.
Jùn and Mùróng Kè both admired Jiǎ Jiān’s talent.
Jiān was over sixty years old at the time.
Kè, hearing of his skill in archery,
placed an ox a hundred paces away to test him.
Jiān said:
“When I was young, I could make sure not to hit.
Now that I am old,
I often hit.”
Then he shot two arrows:
one arrow brushed the spine,
one arrow grazed the belly,
both merely touched the skin and shed hair,
upper and lower equally.
Observers all admired his skill.
Jùn appointed Jiān as Lèlíng Tàishǒu,
governing Gāochéng.
Gāochéng Xiàn
had belonged to Bóhǎi Jùn since the Hàn dynasty.
Xián said: The old city of Gāochéng
is south of today’s Yánshān Xiàn in Cāngzhōu.
17 Fú Jīng fought with Zhāng Xiān north of the Wèi River
and captured him.
All the commanderies, counties, forts, and walls of Sānfǔ surrendered.
In winter,
the tenth month,
Fú Jiàn marched straight to Cháng’ān.
Dù Hóng and Zhāng Jū fled to Sīzhú.
Fúfēng’s Zhōuzhì Xiàn had Sīzhú Yuán.
Sòng Bái said: Bamboo is between Hù and Zhōuzhì.
Hàn officials had Zhú Chéng.
Wèi established officials to manage it,
and Later Wèi had Sīzhú Dūwèi.
18 Yān Lord Jùn returned to Jì,
leaving his generals to guard it.
Jùn returned to Lóngchéng
and paid respects at the ancestral temples.
In the 11th month of the 19th year,
Wèi Zhǔ Mǐn (魏主閔) led 100,000 infantry and cavalry to attack Xiāngguó (襄國).
He appointed his son, Tài Yuán Wáng Yìn (太原王胤), as Dà Chányú (大單于) and Piàojì Dà Jiāngjūn (驃騎大將軍),
and assigned 1,000 surrendered Hú (胡) people as his subordinates.
Guānglù Dàfū Wéi Suǒ (光祿大夫韋謏) remonstrated, saying:
"The Hú (胡) and Jié (羯) are all our enemies.
Now they have come to surrender and attach themselves to us,
merely to preserve their lives.
Should they perchance revolt,
what regret will be enough?
I request that we execute and expel the surrendered Hú (胡) and
abolish the title of Chányú (單于),
to prevent problems while they are still nascent."
Mǐn (閔) was just then intending to pacify and welcome the various Hú (胡) tribes,
so he was furious
and executed Suǒ (謏) and his son Bóyáng (伯陽).
This laid the groundwork for the surrendered Hú (胡) to capture Yìn (胤) and surrender him to Zhào Zhāng Běn (趙張本).
On the 20th day, a Jiǎwǔ (甲午) day,
Fú Jiàn (苻健) entered Cháng'ān (長安).
As the people's hearts inclined towards Jìn (晉),
he dispatched his参军 (cānjūn), Dù Shānbó (杜山伯), to Jiànkāng (建康) to present the victory report
and also to establish good relations with Huán Wēn (桓溫).
Thereupon, the barbarians and Chinese in Qín (秦) and Yōng (雍) all submitted to him.
The barbarians and Chinese all submitted to Jiàn (健),
because he was returning to Jìn (晉).
"Hǎo (好)"
is pronounced 'hū dào fān'.
"Yōng (雍)"
is pronounced 'yú yòng fān'.
"Xià (夏)"
is pronounced 'hù yǎ fān'.
In the 12th month,
Fú Xióng (苻雄) attacked and killed him.
Cài Mó (蔡謨) was appointed Sītú (司徒),
but did not assume office for three years.
In the fourth year,
Mó (謨) was again appointed Sītú (司徒).
The Empress Dowager sent an envoy to convey her intentions,
but Mó (謨) ultimately refused.
Thereupon, the emperor presided over court,
sending the Shìzhōng (侍中) Jì Jù (紀據) and the Huángmén Láng (黃門郎) Dīng Zuǎn (丁纂) to summon Mó (謨).
Mó (謨) pleaded severe illness,
and had his Zhǔbù (主簿) Xiè Yōu (謝攸) present his refusal.
From dawn until shēn (申) (3-5 PM),
the envoys made more than ten trips,
but Mó (謨) did not come.
At that time, the emperor was only eight years old,
and very tired.
He asked his attendants:
"Why has the person I summoned not arrived yet?
When will the court session end?"
The Empress Dowager, seeing that both ruler and minister were exhausted,
then issued an edict:
"If he absolutely will not come,
then the court should be dismissed."
The Zhōngjūn Jiāngjūn (中軍將軍) Yīn Hào (殷浩) memorialized for the dismissal of the Lìbù Shàngshū (吏部尚書) Jiāng Pīn (江虨) from office.
Kuàijī Wáng Yù (會稽王昱) issued an order to the Cáo (曹) (department), saying:
This refers to issuing an order to the Shàngshū Cáo (尚書曹).
Yù (昱) at that time oversaw the six affairs of the Shàngshū (尚書).
"Huì (會)"
is pronounced 'gōng wài fān'.
"Duke Cài (蔡公) defiantly disobeys the emperor's command,
showing no etiquette worthy of a minister.
If the ruler humbles himself before his subordinates,
and great principles are not practiced among the people,
then I do not know how to govern."
The Gōngqīng (公卿) then memorialized:
"Mó (謨) is disrespectful and arrogant towards the emperor,
his crime is tantamount to treason.
We request he be sent to the Tíngwèi (廷尉) to rectify the criminal code."
Mó (謨) was afraid,
and led his sons and disciples to the
palace gate to kowtow,
and personally went to the Tíngwèi (廷尉) to await punishment.
Yīn Hào (殷浩) wanted to impose capital punishment on Mó (謨).
Just then, Xúzhōu Cìshǐ Xún Xiàn (徐州刺史荀羨) came to court.
Xiàn (羨) came from Jīngkǒu (京口) to Jiànkāng (建康) to pay his respects.
Xiàn (羨) said:
"Duke Cài's (蔡公) situation today is perilous,"
meaning Mó (謨) would die.
He said he would raise an army to question his guilt.
An edict was issued to dismiss Mó (謨) as a commoner.

Xiàozōng Mù Huángdì (孝宗穆皇帝) Volume Zhōng zhī Shàng (中之上)
Yǒnghé (永和) 7th Year
(Xīnhài (辛亥), 351 CE)
1. Spring,
1st month,
on a Dīngyǒu (丁酉) day,
there was a solar eclipse.
2. Fú Jiàn’s (苻健) Zuǒ Chángshǐ (左長史) Jiǎ Xuánshuò (賈玄碩) and others requested that he emulate Liú Bèi (劉備) by claiming the title of Hànzhōng Wáng (漢中王).
This event is found in Volume 68, during the 24th year of Jiàn'ān (建安) of Hàn Xiàndì (漢獻帝).
Xuánshuò (玄碩) wanted to memorialize this to the Jìn (晉) court.
"Dān (單)"
is pronounced 'chán'.
"How can I be worthy of being Qín Wáng (秦王)?
Moreover, the Jìn (晉) envoy has not yet returned;
my official titles,
are not for you to know."
Soon after, he secretly sent Liáng Ān (梁安) to subtly suggest that Xuánshuò (玄碩) and others offer him the honorable title.
Jiàn (健) declined repeatedly,
and only then accepted.
On a Bǐngchén (丙辰) day,
Jiàn (健) assumed the position of Tiānwáng (天王) and Dà Chányú (大單于).
Fú Jiàn (苻健),
courtesy name Jiànyè (建業),
was the third son of Hóng (洪).
There was a general amnesty,
and the era name was changed to Huángshǐ (皇始).
His father Hóng (洪) was posthumously honored as Wǔhuì Huángdì (武惠皇帝),
with the temple name Tàizǔ (太祖).
His wife, Lady Qiáng (強氏), was established as Tiānwáng Hòu (天王后).
His son Cháng (萇) was made Tàizǐ (太子).
Jìng (靚) was made Píngyuán Gōng (平原公).
Shēng (生) was made Huáinán Gōng (淮南公).
Dí (覿) was made Chánglè Gōng (長樂公).
Fāng (方) was made Gāoyáng Gōng (高陽公).
Shuò (碩) was made Běipíng Gōng (北平公).
Téng (騰) was made Huáiyáng Gōng (淮陽公).
Liǔ (柳) was made Jìn Gōng (晉公).
Tóng (桐) was made Rǔnán Gōng (汝南公).
Sōu (廋) was made Wèi Gōng (魏公).
Wǔ (武) was made Yān Gōng (燕公).
Yòu (幼) was made Zhào Gōng (趙公).
Fú Xióng (苻雄) was appointed Dūdū Zhōngwài Zhūjūn Shì (都督中外諸軍事), Chéngxiàng (丞相), concurrently Lǐng Chējì Dà Jiāngjūn (領車騎大將軍), Yōngzhōu Mù (雍州牧), and Dōnghǎi Gōng (東海公).
Fú Jīng (苻菁) was appointed Wèi Dà Jiāngjūn (衞大將軍) and Píngchāng Gōng (平昌公),
guarding the two palaces.
The "two palaces"
refer to the residence of Jiàn (健) and that of his son Cháng (萇).
Máo Guì (毛貴) was made Sīkōng (司空).
Liàoyáng (略陽) native Jiāng Bózhōu (姜伯周) was made Shàngshū Lìng (尚書令).
Liáng Léng (梁楞) was made Zuǒ Púyè (左僕射).
Wáng Duò (王墮) was made Yòu Púyè (右僕射).
Yú Zūn (魚遵) was made Tàizǐ Tàishī (太子太師).
Qiáng Píng (強平) was made Tàifù (太傅).
Duàn Chún (段純) was made Tàibǎo (太保).
Lǚ Póloú (呂婆樓) was made Sànqí Chángshì (散騎常侍).
"Sàn (散)"
is pronounced 'xī dǎn fān'.
"Qí (騎)"
is pronounced 'qí jì fān'.
This refers to Jiàn's (健) maternal uncle.
Píng (平)
was the younger brother of the Queen.
Póloú (婆樓)
was originally a chieftain of the Dī (氐) people from Liàoyáng (略陽).
3. Duàn Kān (段龕) requested to submit Qīngzhōu (青州) to the imperial court.
In the 2nd month, on a Wùyín (戊寅) day,
Kān (龕) was appointed Zhènběi Jiāngjūn (鎮北將軍)
and enfeoffed as Qí Gōng (齊公).
Duàn Kān (段龕) occupied Guǎnggù (廣固).
This began in the previous year of the preceding volume.
"Kān (龕)"
is pronounced 'kǔ hán fān'.
4. Wèi Zhǔ Mǐn (魏主閔) besieged Xiāngguó (襄國) for over a hundred days.
In the 11th month of the previous year,
Mǐn (閔) attacked Xiāngguó (襄國).
He then relinquished the title of emperor
and called himself Zhào Wáng (趙王),
sending Tàiwèi (太尉) Zhāng Jǔ (張舉) to request aid from Yān (燕),
promising to send the imperial seal;
Zhōngjūn Jiāngjūn (中軍將軍) Zhāng Chūn (張春) requested aid from Yáo Yìzhòng (姚弋仲).
Yìzhòng (弋仲) sent his son Xiāng (襄) to lead 28,000 cavalry to rescue Zhào (趙),
cautioning him:
"Rǎn Mǐn (冉閔) abandoned benevolence and betrayed righteousness,
slaughtering and exterminating the Shí (石) clan.
This event is found in the 5th and 6th years of the preceding volume.
"Bèi (背)"
