pronounced lú gē fān.
Wèi Jǐng's (魏憬) children often traveled to and from Shòuchūn (壽春).
Xiāng (襄) grew more suspicious and fearful,
and sent his Cānjūn (參軍) Quán Yì (權翼) as an envoy to Hào (浩).
Hào (浩) said:
"I and Yáo Píngběi (姚平北) are both subjects of the King,
sharing joy and sorrow.
Píngběi (平北) always acts independently in every move,
greatly losing the principle of mutual reliance (fúchē),
which is not what I expected!"
The Zuǒ Zhuàn (左傳) says: "Fú (輔) and chē (車) depend on each other."
Dù Yù (杜預) annotated: "Fú (輔) is the cheek;
fúchē (輔車) are the upper and lower jawbones."
Chē (車),
pronounced chǐ shē fān.
"Píngběi (平北)'s heroic bearing is unparalleled.
He commands tens of thousands of troops.
His distant submission to the Jìn (晉) court
is because the court has a righteous Way
and its chief ministers are enlightened and wise.
Now, the General lightly believes slanderous words
and has a rift with Píngběi (平北).
I foolishly believe that the source of suspicion and distrust
lies here, not with him."
Hào (浩) said:
"Píngběi (平北) has a proud and unrestrained nature,
killing and sparing at will,
and moreover allowed his ruffians to plunder my horses.
Is this truly the conduct of a king's subject?"
Yì (翼) said:
"Píngběi (平北) submitted to the sacred court;
how could he kill the innocent without cause!
Treacherous and lawless individuals
are also not tolerated by the king's law.
What harm is there in killing them!"
Hào (浩) said:
"Then what about plundering the horses?"
Yì (翼) said:
"The General believes Píngběi (平北) is formidable and difficult to control,
and will eventually attack him,
so he took the horses to defend himself."
Hào (浩) laughed and said:
"How could it come to this!"
Quán Yì's (權翼) words
had captured Hào's (浩) true feelings,
hence he laughed.
The history records that Hào (浩) was unable to manage and pacify those newly submitted.
Earlier,
Hào (浩) secretly sent people to entice Liáng Ān (梁安) and Léi Ruò'ér (雷弱兒),
to kill Qín Zhǔ Jiàn (秦主健),
promising them the post of Guānyòu (關右);
Ruò'ér (弱兒) falsely agreed,
and moreover requested troops for support.
Hào (浩) heard that Zhāng Yù (張遇) had rebelled,
and that Jiàn's (健) elder brother's son, Fúguó Jiāngjūn (輔國將軍) Fú Huángméi (苻黃眉), had fled west from Luòyáng (洛陽).
He believed that Ān (安) and the others' plan had succeeded.
In winter,
in the tenth month,
Hào (浩) personally led seventy thousand troops from Shòuchūn (壽春) on a northern expedition,
intending to advance and occupy Luòyáng (洛陽),
and restore the imperial mausoleums.
Lìbù Shàngshū (吏部尚書) Wáng Biāozhī (王彪之) presented a memorial to Kuàijī Wáng (會稽王) Sīmǎ Yù (司馬昱),
believing that:
"Ruò'ér (弱兒) and others may be deceitful,
and Hào (浩) should not advance lightly."
But it was not followed.
Even if Liáng (梁) and Léi (雷) had indeed been swayed by Hào (浩)'s machinations and killed Jiàn (健),
Hào (浩) would still not have been able to cross the Guān (關) and Shǎn (陝) passes to take Cháng'ān (長an);
his desire to take advantage of Fú Huángméi's (苻黃眉) departure to occupy Luòyáng (洛陽) was merely to claim credit for restoring the imperial mausoleums.
Yù (昱) then truly believed that he could achieve merit,
and did not listen to Wáng Biāozhī's (王彪之) words,
which made it appropriate for Huán Wēn (桓溫) to use this to depose Hào (浩) and control Yù (昱).
Hào took Yáo Xiāng as his vanguard.
Xiāng led his troops north.
Anticipating Hào's arrival,
he deceptively ordered his troops to abscond by night,
while secretly ambushing with armed men.
Hào heard of this and pursued Xiāng to Shānsāng.
Shānsāng County,
during the Former Hàn dynasty, belonged to Pèi Jùn;
during the Later Hàn dynasty, it belonged to Rǔnán Jùn;
during the Jìn dynasty, it belonged to Qiáo Jùn.
According to Shānsāng,
during the military conflicts of the Six Dynasties,
it was the land of Wōyáng.
During the Táng dynasty, it was part of Méngchéng County in Bó Zhōu.
Hào was greatly defeated,
abandoned his baggage train,
and fled to defend Qiáo Chéng.
Xiāng captured and beheaded over ten thousand,
collected all their supplies and weapons,
and sent his elder brother Yì to guard Shānsāng.
Xiāng then returned to Huáinán.
Kuàijī Wáng Yù said to Wáng Biāozhī:
"Your words are never wrong.
Zhāng and Chén cannot surpass you!"
Zhāng and Chén
refer to Zhāng Liáng and Chén Píng.
14 Xīpíng Jìngliè Gōng Zhāng Chónghuá fell ill.
His son, Yàolíng, was only ten years old.
He was established as the heir apparent [shìzǐ],
and a general amnesty was declared within his territory.
Chónghuá's half-brother, Chángníng Hóu Zuò,
was courageous, strong, and capable in official duties.
Shuǐ Jīng Zhù: Forty lí northwest of Jīnchéng Xīpíng, there is Chángníng Tíng.
During the Jìn dynasty, Xīpíng Jùn had Chángníng Xiàn.
He formed sworn brotherhoods with Chónghuá's favored retainers Zhào Cháng and Wèi Jī, among others.
Wèi
is a surname.
Zuǒ Zhuàn mentions Zhèng Grandee Wèi Zhǐ.
Bì
is pronounced "bēi" or
also "bó jì."
Chónghuá said:
"I intend to make Zuò my Zhōu Gōng,
to assist my young son.
What are these words you speak?"
The difficulty of entrusting an orphan has been great since ancient times,
let alone for Zhāng Chónghuá!
Xiè Ài, by virtue of his achievement at Fúhǎn—
the details are in Volume 97, Yǒnghé third year.
Fú
is pronounced "fū"—
his associates were jealous of him
and slandered Ài,
leading to his being sent out as the Administrator of Jiǔquán.
Ài submitted a memorial saying:
"Powerful favorites are in charge,
the ducal house is in danger.
I beg to be allowed to enter and serve."
He also said,
"Chángníng Hóu Zuò and Zhào Cháng and others will cause rebellion;
it is advisable to banish them all."
In the eleventh month,
on the Jǐwèi day,
Chónghuá's illness worsened.
He personally issued an order to summon Ài as Wèi Jiāngjūn,
to supervise all military affairs internal and external,
and assist in governance.
Zuò, Cháng, and others concealed it and did not announce it.
On the Dīngmǎo day,
Chónghuá died.
The heir apparent Yàolíng was enthroned,
assuming the titles of Dà Sīmǎ, Liángzhōu Cìshǐ, and Xīpíng Gōng.
Zhào Cháng and others forged Chónghuá's dying wishes,
appointing Chángníng Hóu Zuò as Dū Dū Zhōngwài Zhū Jūn Shì, Fǔjūn Dà Jiāngjūn,
to assist in governance.
History records this as the rebellion of the Zhāng clan.
15 Yīn Hào sent his generals Liú Qǐ and Wáng Bīmzhī to attack Yáo Yì at Shānsāng.
Yáo Xiāng attacked them from Huáinán,
and Qǐ and Bīmzhī were both defeated and killed.
Qǐ
was the grandson of Liú Yú.
16 At the end of Zhào,
Zhū Tū of Lèlíng, Dù Néng of Píngyuán, Dīng Ráo of Qīnghé,
and Sūn Yuán of Yángpíng each held troops and occupied cities.
At this point, they all requested to surrender to Yān.
Yān Zhǔ Jùn appointed Tū as Qīngzhōu Cìshǐ,
Néng as Píngyuán Tàishǒu,
Ráo as Lìjié Jiāngjūn,
and Yuán as Yǎnzhōu Cìshǐ,
each remaining to govern their encampment.
17 Qín Chéngxiàng Xióng captured Chíyáng
and beheaded Kǒng Chí.
In the twelfth month,
Qīnghé Wáng Fǎ and Fú Fēi captured Hù
and beheaded Liú Zhēn and Xiàhóu Xiǎn.
18 Yáo Xiāng crossed the Huái River
and encamped at Xūyí.
He recruited and gathered refugees,
whose numbers reached seventy thousand.
He appointed officials and magistrates,
and encouraged farming and sericulture.
Yáo Xiāng's actions were merely like this,
yet the Jìn people were already terrified by them.
This was surely laughed at by cunning heroes.
He also made self-declarations and apologies.
An imperial edict appointed Xiè Shàng as Dū Dū Jiāngxī Huáinán Zhū Jūn Shì and Yùzhōu Cìshǐ,
stationing him at Lìyáng.
Since Shàng had gained Xiāng's favor,
this was both to win him over and pacify him,
and also to guard against him.
19 Liáng Yòu Chángshǐ Zhào Cháng and others proposed,
believing that
"the current difficulties are not yet pacified;
it is fitting to establish an elder ruler.
Yàolíng is young and immature.
We request to establish Chángníng Hóu Zuò."
Zhāng Zuò had previously gained favor with Chónghuá's mother, Mǎ Shì.
Mǎ Shì agreed to it,
and so Zhāng Yàolíng was deposed as Liángníng Hóu,
and Zuò was established as Dà Dū Dū, Dà Jiāngjūn, Liángzhōu Mù, and Liáng Gōng.
Having achieved his ambition, Zuò
indulged in wanton debauchery and cruelty,
killing Chónghuá's concubine Péi Shì and Xiè Ài.
The debauchery
refers to his incest with his lord's mother;
the cruelty
refers to killing Péi and Xiè Ài.
These two instances
are but remnants of his other debauchery and cruelty.
20 Yān Wèi Jiāngjūn Kè, Fǔjūn Jiāngjūn Jūn, Zuǒ Jiāngjūn Biāo
and others repeatedly recommended Gěishì Huángmén Shìláng Bà, saying he possessed talent for the age [mìngshì zhī cái]
and should be entrusted with great responsibility.
In this year,
Yān Zhǔ Jùn appointed Bà as Shǐ Chíjié, Āndōng Jiāngjūn, and Běi Jìzhōu Cìshǐ,
stationing him at Chángshān.
The Jìzhōu Cìshǐ was stationed at Xìndū;
now Běi Jìzhōu was established at Chángshān.
1 Spring,
first month.
Zhāng Zuò proclaimed himself Liáng Wáng,
changing Jiànxīng forty-second year to Hépíng first year.
The Zhāng clan of Héxī
was loyal to the Jìn dynasty,
observing the Jiànxīng reign title for over forty years.
Zhāng Zuò, being ruthless and debauched,
changed the reign title and usurped imperial prerogatives,
which his ancestors would not have countenanced.
His son Tàihé was made the crown prince [tàizǐ].
His younger brother Tiānxī was enfeoffed as Chángníng Hóu,
and his son Tíngjiān as Jiànkāng Hóu.
Jiànkāng Jùn
was presumably established by the Zhāng clan,
and Zhāng Mào assigned it to Liángzhōu.
He established all official posts,
performed suburban sacrifices to Heaven and Earth,
and used the rites and music of the Son of Heaven.
Shàngshū Mǎ Jí offered urgent remonstrance [qièjiàn]
and was dismissed from office.
Lángzhōng Dīng Qí again remonstrated, saying:
"Since our Wǔ Gōng's time—
Zhāng Guǐ's posthumous title was Wǔ Gōng.
Fù
is pronounced "fú yòu"—
we have upheld loyalty and practiced humility for over fifty years.
Lǚqiān
means never having established a state and made oneself king.
From Huì Dì's Yǒngníng first year, when Zhāng Guǐ governed Liángtǔ,
to this point is fifty-four years.
We have resisted the barbarians of the whole world;
armies have been raised annually,
but the people have not complained of weariness.
Your Highness's merits and virtues are not yet higher than those of the former Duke,
yet you hastily plan a revolution.
I do not see how this is acceptable.
The reason why the soldiers and people are obedient,
and why those from all directions turn to us,
is that we are able to uphold the Jìn dynasty.
If you now exalt yourself,
then the hearts of both internal and external people will be alienated.
How can you resist the powerful enemies of the world
with a mere corner of land?"
Zuò became greatly enraged
and had him beheaded beneath the palace gate.
Since ancient times, none who executed remonstrating ministers have avoided ruin.
2 Therefore, Zhōu Chéng (周成), a surrendered general of Wèi, rebelled.
Zhōu Chéng's surrender was seen by the Emperor seven years prior.
降 (Jiàng),
read Hù Jiāng (戶江).
將 (Jiàng),
read Jí Liàng (即亮).
Xīnyǒu (辛酉) day,
Dài Shī (戴施), Grand Administrator of Hénán, fled to Wěizhǔ.
Shuǐjīngzhù says: The Hé River passes through Gǒng Xiàn in Hénán;
to its north is a mountain overlooking the river,
called Yínyuánqiū (崟原丘);
below it is a cavern,
called Gǒngxué (鞏穴),
meaning
it reaches the river;
directly opposite the cavern is a sandbar,
called Wěizhǔ (鮪渚).
鮪 (Wěi),
read Yú Guǐ (于軌).
3 Qín Chancellor Xióng (雄) conquered Sīzhú;
Hú Yángchì (胡陽赤) fled to Bàchéng,
relying on Hūyán Dú (呼延毒).
4 Zhōngjūn Jiāngjūn and Cìshǐ of Yángzhōu, Yīn Hào (殷浩), campaigned north for successive years,
his armies were repeatedly defeated,
and all provisions and weapons were exhausted.
Zhēngxī Jiāngjūn Huán Wēn (桓溫), capitalizing on the resentment of both court and commoners,
submitted a memorial enumerating Hào's crimes,
requesting his dismissal.
The imperial court, having no alternative,
demoted Hào to a commoner,
and exiled him to Xìn'ān in Dōngyáng.
Dōngyáng Commandery was originally the western Dūwèi of Huìjī;
Sūn Hào of Wú established it as a commandery in the first year of Bǎodǐng.
Xìn'ān Xiàn,
in the third year of Chūpíng during the reign of Emperor Xiàn of Hàn,
was established as Xīn'ān Xiàn by dividing Tàimò;
in the first year of Tàikāng during the reign of Emperor Wǔ,
its name was changed to Xìn'ān.
Dōngyáng Commandery,
during the Táng dynasty, was Wùzhōu.
Xìn'ān Xiàn,
during the Táng dynasty, was the seat of Qúzhōu.
Historians say that the Jìn dynasty lost power
because it used Yīn Hào in a way that violated his talents.
Hào, in his youth, was as renowned as Wēn,
but their competitive spirits meant neither would yield to the other,
and Wēn often disparaged him.
After Hào was dismissed and degraded,
although he was distressed and resentful, it did not show in his words or expression;
he often wrote "Duō Duō Guàishì" (咄咄怪事)
in the air.
After a long time,
Wēn said to his aide Xī Chāo (郗超):
"Hào has virtue and eloquence;
if he had been made Lìngpú,
he would have been sufficient to serve as a model for all officials.
The imperial court simply used him in a way that violated his talents."
He was about to make Hào Shàngshūlìng,
and informed him by letter.
Hào gladly accepted,
and was about to reply,
but fearing a mistake,
he opened and closed the letter more than ten times,
eventually sending an empty envelope.
Wēn was furious,
and thus their relationship was severed.
Hào died at his place of exile.
Wáng Shù (王述), formerly the Grand Administrator of Huìjī,
was appointed Cìshǐ of Yángzhōu.
5 In the second month,
Yǐchǒu (乙丑) day,
Huán Wēn led 40,000 infantry and cavalry from Jiānglíng;
his navy entered Jūnkǒu from Xiāngyáng,
reaching Nánxiāng.
Shuǐjīngzhù says: In Zhúyáng Xiàn of Shùnyáng Commandery, there is Shèdū Chéng;
the Miǎn River flows northeast past it;
the Jūn River enters the Miǎn River in the county,
which is called Jūnkǒu.
Zhúyáng and Nánxiāng Xiàn
both belonged to Nányáng Commandery during the Hàn dynasty;
in the Jiàn'ān period of Hàn,
Nánxiāng Commandery was established by dividing the western part of Nányáng,
and these two counties belonged to it;
Emperor Wǔ changed its name to Shùnyáng Commandery;
in the fourth year of Xiánkāng during the reign of Emperor Chéng,
it was again called Nánxiāng Commandery.
Xī Xiàn,
in the Former Hàn, belonged to Hóngnóng Commandery,
in the Later Hàn, it belonged to Nányáng Commandery,
it was Báiyǔ in the Spring and Autumn period.
Wǔguān is to its west.
Wén Yǐng (文穎) said: Wǔguān is 170 lì from Xī Xiàn.
Xián (賢) said: Xī
is today's Nèixiāng Xiàn in Dèngzhōu.
The Later Wèi established Xīchuān Xiàn,
where the Xī River flows;
the Later Zhōu incorporated it into Nèixiāng Xiàn.
Lì Xūn (命勳) was ordered to march out from Liángzhōu.
6 Yàn Wèijiāngjūn Kè (恪) besieged Lǔkǒu;
in the third month,
he captured it.
Lǚ Hù (呂護) fled to Yěwáng,
and sent his younger brother to present a memorial apologizing to Yàn.
Yàn appointed Hù as Grand Administrator of Hénèi.
7 Yáo Xiāng (姚襄) sent an envoy to surrender to Yàn.
8 Yàn King Jùn (儁) appointed Mùróng Píng (慕容評) as Zhènnán Jiāngjūn,
Dūdū of the military affairs of the ten provinces of Qín, Yōng, Yì, Liáng, Jiāng, Yáng, Jīng, Xú, Yǎn, and Yù,
temporarily stationed at Luòshuǐ;
and Mùróng Qiáng (慕容強) as Qiánfēng Dūdū,
supervising the military affairs of Jīng and Xú provinces and along the Huái River,
advancing to occupy Hénán.
This Hénán
refers to the area south of the Dàhé (Yellow River).
9 Huán Wēn's separate detachment attacked Shàngluò,
capturing Qín Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ Guō Jìng (郭敬);
they then attacked Qīngní,
defeating it.
Qīngní Chéng is south of Lántián Xiàn.
Liáng Qínzhōu Cìshǐ Wáng Zhuó (王擢) attacked Chéncāng in response to Wēn.
After Zhào fell,
Wáng Zhuó returned to the Zhāng (張) clan,
hence he is linked to Liáng.
Chancellor Xióng, Prince of Huáinán Shēng (生), Prince of Píngchāng Jīng (菁), and Prince of Běipíng Shuò (碩) led an army of 50,000 to camp at Yáoliǔ to resist Wēn.
The Tǔdìjì says: South of Lántián Xiàn is Yáoguān,
the place is named Yáoliǔ,
the road connects to Jīngzhōu.
The Jìndìdàojì says: The pass is northwest of Shàngluò Xiàn.
帥 (Shuài),
read as Shuài;
same below.
嶢 (Yáo),
read Wǔ Liáo (五聊).
In the fourth month,
Jǐhài (己亥) day,
Wēn battled Qín forces at Lántián.
Qín Prince of Huáinán Shēng charged into the formation alone,
breaking through and retreating more than ten times,
killing and wounding many Jìn officers and soldiers.
Wēn personally directed a fierce fight,
and the Qín army was utterly defeated.
General Huán Chōng (桓沖) further defeated Qín Chancellor Xióng at Báilùyuán.
Shuǐjīngzhù says: West of Bàchuān is Báilùyuán.
Sānqínjì says: West of Lìshān is Báilùyuán.
Wèi Shōu's Dìxíngzhì says: Jīngzhào Lántián Xiàn has Báilùyuán.
又敗 (Yòu bài),
read Bǔ Mài (補邁).
He was Wēn's younger brother.
Wēn fought his way forward,
and on Rén'yín (壬寅) day,
advanced to Bàshàng.
Qín Crown Prince Cháng (萇) and others retreated to camp south of the city.
Qín ruler Jiàn (健) held the small city of Cháng'ān with 6,000 old and weak,
and dispatched all 30,000 elite troops,
sending Grand Sīmǎ Léi Ruò'ér (雷弱兒) and others to combine forces with Cháng to resist Wēn.
All commanderies and counties in Sānfǔ came to surrender.
Wēn appeased the residents,
allowing them to settle down and resume their livelihoods.
People vied to bring cattle and wine to welcome and reward them,
men and women lined the roads to watch,
and some elders shed tears,
saying:
"We never expected to see the imperial army again today!"
Qín Chancellor Xióng led 7,000 cavalry to raid Sīmǎ Xūn (司馬勳) in Zǐwǔgǔ,
defeating him.
Xūn retreated to Nǚwābǎo.
10 On Wùshēn (戊申) day,
Yàn ruler Jùn enfeoffed Fǔjūn Jiāngjūn Jūn (軍) as Prince of Xiāngyáng,
Zuǒjiāngjūn Péng (彭) as Prince of Wǔchāng;
appointed Wèijiāngjūn Kè (恪) as Dà Sīmǎ, Shìzhōng, Dà Dūdū, Lù Shàngshūshì,
and enfeoffed him as Prince of Tàiyuán;
Zhènnán Jiāngjūn Píng (評) as Sītú, Piàojì Jiāngjūn,
and enfeoffed him as Prince of Shàngyōng;
enfeoffed Āndōng Jiāngjūn Bà (霸) as Prince of Wú;
Zuǒxiánwáng Yǒu (友) as Prince of Fányáng,
Sànqí Chángshì Lì (厲) as Prince of Xiàpī,
Sànqí Chángshì Yí (宜) as Prince of Lújiāng.
散 (Sàn),
read Xī Dàn (悉亶).
He also enfeoffed his younger brother Huán (桓) as Prince of Yídū,
Dài (逮) as Prince of Línhé,
Huī (徽) as Prince of Héjiān,
Lóng (龍) as Prince of Lìyáng,
Nà (納) as Prince of Běihǎi,
Xiù (秀) as Prince of Lánlíng,
Yuè (嶽) as Prince of Ānfēng,
Dé (德) as Duke of Liáng,
Mò (默) as Duke of Shǐ'ān,
Lóu (僂) as Duke of Nánkāng;
his son Xián (咸)
as Prince of Lè'ān,
Liàng (亮) as Prince of Bóhǎi,
Wēn (溫) as Prince of Dàifāng,
Shè (涉) as Prince of Yúyáng,
Wěi (暐) as Prince of Zhōngshān;
and appointed Shàngshūlìng Yáng Wù (陽騖) as Sīkōng,
retaining his position as Shàngshūlìng.
The Grand Tutor of Jìzhōu, Wú Wáng Bà, was ordered to move his administration to Xìndū.
Last year, Bà governed Chángshān.
Yān Wáng Huàng admired Bà’s talent,
hence named him Bà,
intending to make him the heir apparent;
his retainers remonstrated, and he stopped,
yet Bà’s favor and treatment still surpassed that of the heir apparent.
Because of this, Jùn disliked him.
As Bà had once fallen from a horse and broken a tooth,
Jùn renamed him Pí.
Soon after, because he aligned with a prophecy,
Jùn renamed him Chuí.
He was promoted to Shìzhōng,
put in charge of the affairs of the Liú Tái,
and then moved to garrison Lóngchéng.
Chuí gained great harmony in the northeast,
which Jùn disliked even more,
so he recalled him.
Although Jùn was wary of Chuí,
it was Chuí who ultimately restored the Yān dynasty’s mandate.
What Heaven has established,
how can it be abolished!
In the fifth month,
Guo Chǎng and other refugees from Jiangxi
captured Liú Shì, the Grand Administrator of Chénliú,
and surrendered to Yáo Xiāng.
After the Jìn crossed south,
Chénliú Commandery was temporarily administered within the borders of Chángyuán County, Qiáojùn.
According to the Zàijì,
Liú Shì was in Tángyì at the time.
Zhōu Mǐn, the Minister of Personnel, was appointed General of the Central Army,
garrisoning Zhōngtáng.

Huán Wēn was surprised by him

Měng was likely pointing out Wēn's true intentions,

This was why Wēn had no response.
However, I observe Huán Wēn's military strategy:

In both cases, he advanced on the crest of victory,
pressing upon their capitals,

Wēn was

Advancing on the crest of victory,
pressing upon their capitals,
he hoped they would be awestruck and terrified,
leading to internal collapse.
When he pressed upon their capitals and the enemy showed no internal collapse,
he therefore adopted a cautious approach to await it.
When his intentions were revealed and his power weakened,
the enemy took advantage of it,
thus leading to defeat.
This is what Sū Zǐyóu referred to as "when wisdom meets wisdom,

Zhào Jù garrisoned Yíyáng;
this event is mentioned in the previous year of the preceding volume.
*Cóng*,
pronounced *cáiyòng* (才用翻).
He then appointed Jù as Director of the Imperial Secretariat.
Jù firmly declined due to illness,
and said to Sháo and Huì:
"You no longer consider your ancestors,
and wish to bring about the destruction of your clan!
What crime did Máo and Liáng commit
that they were executed?
What merit do I have
that I should replace them?
You two may act on your own,
but I shall surely die!"
He then died of grief.
In the 14th year of Jiànxīng, Sòng Hùn’s army was at the Great Marsh of Wǔshǐ.
Zhāng Jùn had divided Dídào county
and established Wǔshǐ Commandery.
Sòng Hùn fled west,
raising an army that would certainly not turn east towards Dídào.
The Shuǐ Jīng (Classic of Rivers) states: The Dūyě Marsh is northeast of Wǔwēi County.
A note says: It is three hundred *lǐ* north of Gūzāng city.
Dūyě is the Zhūyě of the Yǔ Gòng (Tributes of Yǔ).
Its water flows down from the Gūzāng Wǔshǐ Marsh,
which is west of Gūzāng.
In the intercalary month,
Hùn’s army reached Gūzāng.
Liáng King Zhāng Zuò captured Zhāng Guàn’s younger brother Jū and his son Sōng,
intending to kill them.
Jū and Sōng heard of this
and recruited several hundred market people,
proclaiming:
"Zhāng Zuò is without principle!
My elder brother's great army has already arrived east of the city!
Those who dare to raise a hand will have their three clans exterminated!"
Thereupon, they opened the west gate to admit Hùn’s troops.
Commander of the Palace Guard Zhào Cháng and others, fearing punishment—
Zhào Cháng
was one of those who had supported Zhāng Zuò’s enthronement,
hence his fear of punishment—
enthroned Liáng Wǔhóu Xuánjìng as ruler.
Yì Chuǎi and others led troops into the palace,
arrested Cháng and the others,
and killed them.
Zhāng Zuò clutched his sword in the palace hall,
shouted loudly,
and ordered his attendants to fight with all their might.
Zhāng Zuò had long lost the hearts of the people,
and no one was willing to fight for him.
He was then killed by the soldiers.
Hùn and others displayed his head,
showed it to the inner and outer courts,
and exposed his body by the roadside.
Everyone in the city cried "Long live!"
He was buried with the rites of a commoner,
and his two sons were also killed.
Hùn and Jū elevated Xuánjìng to Great General, Governor of Liángzhōu, and Duke of Xīpíng.
(The character "上" [shàng],
here read *shàng*).
The era name was reverted to Jiànxīng, 43rd year.
Zhāng Zuò had changed the Jiànxīng era name;
see the previous volume, previous year.
Zhāng Guàn arrived in Gūzāng,
enthroned Xuánjìng as King of Liáng,
and appointed himself Imperial Commissioner, Grand Commandant of All Military Affairs, Director of the Imperial Secretariat, Governor of Liángzhōu, and Duke of Zhāngyè Commandery.
He appointed Sòng Hùn as Assistant Director of the Imperial Secretariat.
Lǒngxī native Lǐ Yǎn occupied the commandery,
refused Zhāng Guàn’s command,
and used the era name of Jiāngdōng.
He used the Yǒnghé era name.
This established the basis for Lǐ Yǎn’s submission to Qín.
Before he arrived,
Xīpíng native Wèi Chén also seized the commandery and rebelled.
Bà Bīng’s army collapsed,
and he fled back.
Zhāng Guàn sent his younger brother Jū to attack Wèi Chén,
and defeated him.
Jiǔquán Administrator Mǎ Jī raised an army to support Wèi Chén.
Zhāng Guàn sent Commander Zhāng Yáo and Wáng Guó to attack and execute him.
In the 15th year of Jiànxīng, winter,
in the tenth month,
Xiè Shàng, Governor of Yùzhōu, was appointed Inspector of Bīng, Jì, and Yōu three prefectures.
At that time, the Eastern Jìn had established the four prefectures of Qīng, Jì, Bīng, and Yōu north of the Yangtze River.
At the beginning of the southern migration,
Zǔ Tì, as Governor of Yùzhōu, governed Qiáochéng.
In the first year of Yǒngchāng,
Zǔ Yuē retreated and garrisoned Shòuchūn.
In the fourth year of Xiánhé of Emperor Chéng,
Yú Liàng, as Governor of Yùzhōu, governed Wúhú.
In the fourth year of Xiánkāng,
Máo Bǎo, as Governor of Yùzhōu, governed Zhūchéng.
In the sixth year,
Yú Yì, as Governor of Yùzhōu, governed Wúhú.
In the first year of Yǒnghé,
Zhào Yìn, as Governor of Yùzhōu, governed Niúzhǔ.
In the second year,
Xiè Shàng, as Governor of Yùzhōu, governed Wúhú.
Now he advanced to Shòuchūn,
all of which were western barriers of Jiànkāng.
For offensive operations, they garrisoned Shòuchūn;
for defending the Yangtze, they were mostly at Lìyáng and Wúhú.
Duàn Kān, General Who Guards the North, wrote to Yàn Ruler Mùróng Jùn,
asserting the formalities of kinship.
Mùróng Jùn was a relative by marriage of the Duàn clan,
hence Duàn Kān asserted the formalities of kinship.
(Kān,
pronounced *kǔ hán*;
same below).
Mùróng Jùn was angry.
In the eleventh month,
he appointed Mùróng Kè, Prince of Tàiyuán, as Grand Commander and General Who Comforts the Army,
with Yáng Wù as his deputy,
to attack Duàn Kān.
Qín appointed Xīn Láo as Director of the Imperial Secretariat,
Zhào Sháo as Left Assistant Director of the Imperial Secretariat,
Secretariat Administrator Dǒng Róng as Right Assistant Director of the Imperial Secretariat,
and Central Protector of the Army Zhào Huì as Colonel Director of Retainers.
In the twelfth month,
Gāogōulí King Zhāo sent an envoy to Yàn to offer a hostage and present tribute,
to request the return of his mother.
Yàn Ruler Mùróng Jùn granted his request
and dispatched Palace General Diāo Kān to escort Zhāo’s mother, Lady Zhōu, back to her country.
He appointed Zhāo as General Who Conquers the East and Governor of Yíngzhōu,
enfeoffed him as Duke of Lèlàng,
and maintained his status as king.
He kept him as King of Gāogōulí as before.
Shàngdǎng native Féng Yāng drove out the Yàn Administrator Duàn Gāng,
occupied Ānmín City.
Wèi Shōu’s Dìxíng Zhì (Treatise on Geography) states: Yàn’s Administrator of Shàngdǎng governed Ānmín City.
Ānmín City is in Xiāngyuán County.
It was probably built during the Yǒngjiā era
by Liú Kūn, who sent Zhāng Yǐ
to settle the people of Shàngdǎng,
hence its name.
He sent an envoy to surrender.
Qín Chancellor Léi Ruò'ér was upright and unyielding.
Regarding Zhào Sháo and Dǒng Róng’s misgovernment,
he often spoke publicly in court,
gritting his teeth whenever he saw them.
Sháo and Róng slandered him to Qín Ruler Fú Shēng.
Fú Shēng killed Ruò'ér, along with his nine sons and twenty-seven grandsons.
At this, all the Qiāng tribes became disaffected.
Léi Ruò'ér
was a chief of the Nán'ān Qiāng.
He died without cause,
hence all the Qiāng tribes became disaffected.
Although Fú Shēng was in a period of mourning,
he indulged in drinking as usual,
displaying bows and drawn blades
when meeting court officials.
Hammers, tongs, saws, and chisels—
tools that could harm people—
were placed readily at his side.
Not long after his ascension,
he had killed over five hundred people, from queens and high officials down to servants.
There were frequent instances of severed shins, broken ribs, sawed necks, and disemboweled pregnant women.
Yàn Ruler Mùróng Jùn, considering Duàn Kān to be strong,
said to Mùróng Kè, Prince of Tàiyuán:
"If Kān sends troops to defend the river and prevents you from crossing,
you can directly take Lǚ Hù and return."
Lǚ Hù was then occupying Yěwáng.
He prepared boats and observed Duàn Kān’s intentions.
Kān’s younger brother Pí,
who was brave and resourceful,
said to Kān:
"Mùróng Kè is skilled in warfare,
and his forces are numerous.
If you allow him to cross the river and advance to the city gates,
I fear that even begging for surrender
may not be possible.
I request that you hold fast while I lead the elite troops to resist him at the river.
If we are fortunate enough to win the battle,
you can then lead the main army to follow up,
and there will certainly be great achievements.
If we do not win,
it would be better to surrender early,
and still not fail to become a Marquis of a Thousand Households."
Kān did not follow.
Pí persistently pleaded,
but Kān grew angry
and killed him.
1 In spring,
in the first month,
Yàn (燕) King Tàiyuán (太原) Kè (恪) led his troops across the Hé (河).
Before reaching Guǎnggù (廣固) by a hundred *lǐ*,
Duàn Kān (段龕) led thirty thousand troops to meet them in battle.
On the *bǐngshēn* (丙申) day,
Kè (恪) severely defeated Kān (龕) at Zīshuǐ (淄水).
According to the *Zàijì* (載記),
Kè (恪) defeated Kān (龕) south of the Jǐshuǐ (濟水).
The current text says, "before reaching Guǎnggù (廣固) by a hundred *lǐ*,"
presumably meaning they met and battled at Zīshuǐ (淄水).
The *Shuǐjīng* (水經) states that
the Zhuóshuǐ (濁水) flows west of Guǎnggù (廣固) city,
then east to Guǎngráo (廣饒),
entering Jùdiàn (巨淀),
and further north merging with Zīshuǐ (淄水).
The Right Senior Clerk Yuán Fàn (袁範) and others were beheaded.
Qí (齊) King's Companion Pìlǘ Wèi (辟閭蔚) was wounded.
Duàn Kān (段龕) called himself King of Qí (齊),
hence he established the office of King's Companion.
Wèi (蔚),
read *yú wù* (紆勿) reverse spelling.
Wounded (創),
read *chū liáng* (初良) reverse spelling.
Someone was sent to look for him,
but Wèi (蔚) was already dead.
Several thousand soldiers surrendered.
Kān (龕) escaped
and returned to the city to defend it.
Kè (恪) advanced his army and besieged it.
2 Qín (秦) Minister of Works Wáng Duò (王墮) was of a stern and upright nature.
The Right Prime Minister Dǒng Róng (董榮) and Palace Attendant Qiáng Guó (強國) had both risen through flattery and favoritism.
Duò (墮) detested them as if they were enemies.
Each time they had an audience at court,
Róng (榮) never spoke with him.
The phrase "Each time they had an audience at court" ends the sentence.
Court (朝),
read *zhí yáo* (直遙) reverse spelling.
Meet (見),
read as written.
"Lord Dǒng (董) is incomparably favored and esteemed;
you should humble yourself a little to interact with him."
Duò (墮) said:
"What kind of chicken and dog is Dǒng Lóng (董龍)?"
Lóng (龍)
was Dǒng Róng's (董榮) courtesy name.
Later, there was an omen of heavenly change.
Róng (榮) and Qiáng Guó (強國) spoke to Qín (秦) ruler Shēng (生), saying:
"Today's heavenly rebuke is very severe;
it would be appropriate to use an esteemed minister to respond to it."
Shēng (生) said:
"The only esteemed ministers are the Grand Marshal and the Minister of Works."
Róng (榮)
said:
"The Grand Marshal is a close relative of the state;
he cannot be killed."
The Grand Marshal referred to Wǔdū (武都) King Ān (安),
who was Shēng's (生) uncle.
When about to be executed,
Róng (榮) said to him:
"Do you dare compare Dǒng Lóng (董龍) to a chicken and dog again today?"
Duò (墮) glared and cursed him.
The Prefect of Luòzhōu (洛州), Dù Yù (杜郁),
was Duò's (墮) nephew.
The Left Prime Minister Zhào Sháo (趙韶) disliked him
and slandered him to Shēng (生),
accusing him of being disloyal to Jìn (晉) and having him killed.
On the *rénxū* (壬戌) day,
Shēng (生) hosted a banquet for his ministers in the Tàijí (太極) Palace.
He appointed the Director of the Department of State Affairs, Xīn Láo (辛牢), as the wine supervisor.
When the wine flowed freely,
Shēng (生) angrily said:
"Why are you not forcing people to drink, and some are still sitting down!"
He drew his bow and shot Láo (牢),
killing him.
The ministers were terrified,
and no one dared not to be drunk,
falling over and losing their caps.
Shēng (生) was then pleased.
3 The Xiōngnú (匈奴) chieftain Liú Wùhuán (劉務桓) died.
His younger brother Èntóu (閼頭) succeeded him
and was about to betray to Dài (代).
In the second month,
Dài (代) King Shíyìjiān (什翼犍) led his troops on a western tour to Lín Hé (臨河).
Èntóu (閼頭) was afraid
and requested to surrender.
4 Yàn (燕) King Tàiyuán (太原) Kè (恪) called for the submission of Duàn Kān's (段龕) various cities.
Kè (恪) was besieging Guǎnggù (廣固) but had not yet taken it,
so he first called for the submission of the various cities under his command.
On the *jǐchǒu* (己丑) day,
Wáng Téng (王騰), Duke of Yángdū (陽都) and Duàn Kān's (段龕) appointed Prefect of Xúzhōu (徐州), led his troops to surrender.
Kè (恪) ordered Téng (騰) to return to garrison Yángdū (陽都) with his former post.
Duàn Kān (段龕) established Xúzhōu (徐州) in Yángdū (陽都) County of Lángyé (琅邪).
Dù Yòu (杜佑) said: The old city of Hàn (漢) Yángdū (陽都) County is south of Yíshuǐ (沂水) County in Yízhōu (沂州).
5. The Grand General of Qin, Governor of the East, Prince of Jìn, Fú Liǔ, dispatched his staff officers Yán Fù and Liáng Shū as envoys to Liáng,
with a letter to persuade the King of Liáng, Zhāng Xuánjìng.
When Fù and Shū arrived at Gūzāng,
Zhāng Guàn met them and said:
"I
am a minister of Jìn;
a minister has no dealings outside the borders.
How do you two gentlemen condescend to come?"
Fù and Shū said:
"The Prince of Jìn is a neighboring vassal to your lord.
Although mountains and rivers separate us,
our customs and principles are the same.
The Qin envoy Fú Liǔ is stationed in Púbǎn,
not adjacent to Liángzhōu,
hence the phrase 'customs and principles are the same' is used.
Why are you surprised?"
Guàn said:
"I have served Jìn with utmost loyalty,
for six generations now.
Guǐ, Shí, Mào, Jùn, Chónghuá, Yàolíng, Zuò are seven generations,
now it says six generations,
excluding Zuò from the generational count.
This is to violate the will of our former lords above,
and to destroy the integrity of the gentry and common people below.
How can this be?"
Fù and Shū said:
"The Jìn dynasty has been in decline
and lost the Mandate of Heaven
for a long time now;
this is why the two Kings of Liáng submitted to the Two Zhào in the north,
simply because they knew the opportune moment.
Zhāng Mào declared himself a vassal to the Former Zhào,
and Zhāng Jùn declared himself a vassal to the Later Zhào.
If the King of Liáng wishes to claim emperorship of Héyòu,
then he is not an match for Qín;
if he wishes to serve the great with the small,
then why not abandon Jìn and serve Qín,
to long preserve his good fortune and emoluments?"
Guàn said:
"The Central Plains are prone to breaking promises.
Previously, Shí's envoy had just returned,
when barbarian cavalry already arrived.
I dare not trust them."
Fù and Shū said:
"Since ancient times, emperors residing in the Central Plains
have had different governments and policies.
Zhào was treacherous and deceitful,
Qín upholds faith and righteousness.
How can they be treated equally?
Gài is for leveling dou and hu,
to treat them equally
means there is no high or low.
The former emperor attacked and captured him,
'captured Zhāng' is seen in Volume 98, Year 6,
never captured Yáng Chū,
Fù and Shū merely said this.
They were honored with ranks and titles,
certainly not comparable to the Shí family."
Guàn said:
"If it is as you say,
and Qín's prestige and virtue are unrivaled,
why not first take Jiāngnán,
then the whole world would belong to Qín.
Why would the Governor of the East bother to send such a mission?"
Fù and Shū said:
"The people of Jiāngnán have the custom of tattooing their bodies,
anciently the custom of the Jīngmán,
cutting hair and tattooing bodies to avoid harm from dragons.
Fù and Shū used this to speak disparagingly of them.
At that time, garments, caps, culture and objects
were all in Jiāngnán,
and it was where the legitimate calendar was located.
Fù and Shū bark at Yáo and criticize Yóu,
knowing that each serves their own master!
The transformation is complete when they submit later.
Zhèng Xuán said: 'wū'
is like 'shā' (kill).
The Yì Jīng says: 'Gāozōng attacked Guǐfāng,
and conquered it in three years.'
The commentators of the world consider Jīng and Chǔ to be light and fierce,
their ways defiled, rebelling first,
transformation complete when they submit later,
thus Fù and Shū also used this to speak disparagingly of Jiāngnán.
Héyòu can be won by righteousness,
therefore we sent envoys first to express great goodwill.
If your lord does not comprehend the Mandate of Heaven,
then Jiāngnán may gain a few more years of life,
but Héyòu may no longer be your lord's territory."
Guàn said:
"I occupy three prefectures,
the three prefectures refer to Liáng, Hé, Shā,
established by Zhāng Mào and Zhāng Jùn.
To the west it encompasses Cōnglǐng,
to the east it reaches the Yellow River.
I have more than enough to attack others,
let alone defend myself.
Why should I fear Qín?"
Fù and Shū said:
"The fortifications of your esteemed prefecture's mountains and rivers,
how do they compare to Xiáo and Hán?
The abundance of people and resources,
how does it compare to Qín and Yōng?
Dù Hóng and Zhāng Jū,
benefiting from the Zhào family's resources,
with strong armies and abundant wealth,
had the ambition to encompass Guānzhōng and sweep across the four seas.
When the former emperor's banners pointed west,
they melted like ice and scattered like clouds.
Within a month,
they unknowingly changed masters.
The event is seen in Volume 98, Year 6.
If he were to furiously arise,
with a million archers,
marching westward with drums,
how do you think your esteemed prefecture would meet him?"
Guàn laughed and said:
"This matter must be decided by the King,
it is not for me to resolve."
Liǎo
means to decide.
"Although the King of Liáng is brilliant and wise at a young age,
he is still in his infancy;
you hold the responsibility of Yī and Huò.
The safety and danger of the state
depend on your single action."
Guàn was afraid,
so he sent an envoy, on behalf of Xuánjìng, to declare vassalage to Qín.
Qín then bestowed upon him the official titles that Xuánjìng had claimed.
6. General Liú Dù attacked Qín's Inspector of Qīngzhōu, Wáng Láng, at Lúshì;
Lúshì County,
belonged to Hóngnóng Commandery during Hàn,
Shàngluò Commandery during Jìn,
and Guózhōu during Táng.
He attacked Qín's Inspector of Yōuzhōu, Qiáng Zhé, at Péishìbǎo.
During the chaos of Yǒngjiā,
the Péi clan fortified a stronghold in a dangerous place to defend themselves.
Later generations consequently established garrisons,
hence the fort still bears the name Péishì,
probably within Hédōng territory.
Zhǎng,
read as liǎng.
Jiànjié General Dèng Qiāng resisted Cháng Qīng.
Fēi had not yet arrived when Dù retreated.
Qiāng fought with Cháng Qīng,
thoroughly defeating him,
capturing Cháng Qīng and over two thousand armored heads.
7. Huán Wēn requested to move the capital to Luòyáng,
and restore the imperial tombs,
submitting over ten memorials;
it was not granted.
Wēn was appointed Grand Commander of Campaigns,
overseeing all military affairs of Sī and Jì prefectures,
to attack Yáo Xiāng.
8. In the third month,
the ruler of Qín, Fú Shēng, conscripted people from Sānfǔ to build the Wèiqiáo bridge.
Gold and Purple Grand Master of Brilliant Rank Chéng Gōng remonstrated,
arguing that it would hinder agriculture;
Shēng killed him.
9. In summer,
fourth month,
there was a great wind in Cháng'ān,
tearing off roofs and uprooting trees.
The wind rolled up roof tiles,
lifting eaves and rafters is called 'tearing off roofs'.
Some claimed that bandits had arrived,
and the palace gates were closed during the day.
It only stopped after five days.
The ruler of Qín, Fú Shēng, sought out those who spread rumors of bandits,
and disemboweled them.
Left Grand Master of Brilliant Rank Qiáng Píng remonstrated:
"Heaven sends down calamities and anomalies.
Your Majesty should cherish the people and serve the spirits,
lighten punishments and promote virtue to respond to them,
then they can be stopped."
Mí
means to stop.
He drilled through his skull and killed him.
General of the Guards, Prince of Guǎngpíng, Fú Huángméi, Former General, Prince of Xīnxīng, Fú Fēi, and Jiànjié General Dèng Qiāng,
because Píng
was the Empress Dowager's younger brother,
prostrated themselves and strongly remonstrated;
Shēng did not listen.
He sent Huángméi out as Administrator of Zuǒfēngyì, Fēi as Administrator of Yòufúfēng, and Qiāng to act as Grand Administrator of Xiányáng.
Fúfēng and Wèichéng counties in the Former Hàn,
were Qín's Xiányáng,
abolished by Later Hàn and Jìn.
Wèi Shōu's 'Dìxíng Zhì' states: Xiányáng Commandery governed Shí'ān County,
which was Hàn's Wèichéng,
Shí Lè renamed it.
This commandery was established by the various Hú after Yǒngjiā.
Thus, none of them were killed.
In the fifth month,
Empress Dowager Qiángshì died of sorrow and resentment.
Her posthumous title was Míngdé.
10. Yáo Xiāng attacked Zhōu Chéng from Xǔchāng at Luòyáng.
Zhōu Chéng had previously seized and occupied Luòyáng,
seen in the previous volume, year 10.
In the 11th month of the 6th year,
Qín Zhǔ Shēng issued an edict saying:
"I have received the mandate of August Heaven,
to rule over all nations.
Since inheriting the succession,
what evil have I committed
that calumny and slander
should spread throughout the world!
Dù Yù said: 'Dú'
means 'to slander.'
Dú,
pronunciation 'tú mù fān'.
Yet I am called cruel and tyrannical!
Those who travel shoulder to shoulder
are not so few.
Xī
means 'few'.
What more can they do to me!"
Since last spring,
west of Tóngguān,
up to Cháng'ān,
tigers and wolves have been rampant,
by day they follow the roads,
meaning tigers and wolves are constantly seen on the roads.
"Jì"
is written as
"duàn" in the Shǔ version.
They do not eat livestock,
but are intent on eating people,
having killed over seven hundred people in total.
The people abandoned farming and sericulture,
gathering in towns and villages,
yet the harm did not cease.
In autumn,
the 7th month,
Qín Zhōngchén petitioned to ward off the disaster,
but Shēng said:
"Wild beasts eat people when hungry;
when full, they will stop naturally.
What is there to ward off!
Moreover, how could Heaven not love the people?
It is precisely because there are many criminals
that it helps me kill them!"
The historian said Fú Shēng's tyranny was worse than that of Jié and Zhòu.
On the day bǐngzǐ,
Yàn Xiànhuái Tàizǐ Yè died.
Yáo Xiāng attacked Luòyáng,
but could not conquer it for over a month.
His Chángshǐ, Wáng Liàng, admonished him:
"Your Excellency's illustrious name covers the world,
your army is strong, and the people are attached to you.
Now you have halted your army beneath a strong city,
your strength will be exhausted and your prestige diminished,
and you might be taken advantage of by other invaders.
This is the path to danger and ruin!"
Xiāng did not listen.
Huán Wēn launched a northern expedition from Jiānglíng,
sending Dūhù Gāo Wǔ to occupy Lǔyáng,
Fǔguó Jiāngjūn Dài Shī to garrison Héshàng,
while he himself led the main army to advance.
He ascended the Píngchéng Lóu with his subordinates,
Píngchéng Lóu
is a tower on a large ship.
and sighed:
"To allow the Divine Land to sink into ruin,
becoming a wasteland for a hundred years,
Wáng Yífǔ and others cannot escape their responsibility!"
He believed that Wáng Yǎn and others indulged in pure conversation and did not care about state affairs,
leading to the barbarians disrupting Huá.
All Jìn Dukes and those attached to the ducal government had Jìshì,
who were in charge of memorials, official documents, and proclamations.
"Fortune has its rise and fall;
how can it necessarily be the fault of those individuals!"
Wēn's expression changed, and he said:
"In the past, Liú Jǐngshēng had a great ox weighing a thousand catties,
which ate ten times more fodder and beans than an ordinary ox,
yet in carrying heavy loads and traveling far,
it was not even as good as a lean cow.
Wēn intended to liken Hóng to the ox,
meaning he could only consume his salary and had no practical use in governing the world.
Liú Biǎo's courtesy name was Jǐngshēng.
Dàn,
pronunciations 'tú làn fān' and 'tú lǎn fān'.
Léi,
pronunciation 'lún wéi fān'.
Zì,
pronunciation 'jí zhì fān', a female ox.
In the 13th year of Jiàn'ān during Emperor Xiàn's reign of Hàn,
Cáo Cāo entered Jīngzhōu.
In the 8th month,
on the day jǐhài,
Wēn arrived at the Yīshuǐ,
the Yīshuǐ is south of Luòyáng city.
He hid his elite troops in the woods north of the river,
and sent an envoy to tell Wēn:
"Upon learning that you, Marshal, have personally led the royal army here,
I, Xiāng, now surrender myself and pledge allegiance.
I request that you order your three armies to retreat slightly,
and I shall prostrate myself by the roadside."
Wēn said:
"I am here to restore the Central Plains,
and pay respects at the imperial tombs;
it has nothing to do with your affairs.
If you wish to come, then come forward.
We will meet soon;
there is no need to trouble an envoy."
Xiāng resisted by the water and fought,
Wēn formed his ranks and advanced,
personally donned armor and supervised the battle.
Xiāng's forces were greatly defeated,
with several thousand killed.
Xiāng led several thousand cavalry from his command to flee to the northern mountains of Luòyáng,
the northern mountains of Luòyáng are the Běimáng Shān.
Qí,
pronunciation 'qí jì fān'.
Over five thousand people abandoned their wives and children to follow Xiāng.
Xiāng was brave and loved his people;
although he was repeatedly defeated in battle,
when the people knew where Xiāng was,
they would support the elderly and carry the young,
rushing to him.
Rumors spread in Wēn's army that Xiāng had died from his wounds,
and the men and women of Xǔ and Luò who had been captured by Wēn
all looked north and wept.
The historian said Yáo Xiāng had gained the hearts of the people.
Wēn pursued but could not catch him.
Yáng Liàng of Hóngnóng fled to Wēn from Xiāng's side,
Wēn asked about Xiāng's character,
and Liàng said:
"Xiāng possesses extraordinary bearing,
a peer of Sūn Cè,
but his heroic valor surpasses him."
Chóu
means 'equal'
or 'kind'.
Zhōu Chéng led his troops and surrendered.
Wēn garrisoned in front of the old Tàijí Diàn,
and then moved his garrison to Jīnyǒng Chéng.
On the day jǐchǒu,
he paid respects at the imperial tombs,
repairing those that were damaged,
and appointed a Línglìng for each.
Hàn established Língyì,
and each Yì had a Línglìng.
Later, this system was followed,
and each imperial tomb had a Línglìng,
subordinate to the Tàicháng.
He garrisoned Luòyáng.
Since he had not yet arrived,
he left Yǐngchuān Tàishǒu Máo Mùzhī, Dūhù Chén Wǔ, and Hénán Tàishǒu Dài Shī with two thousand men to guard Luòyáng,
protect the mountains and imperial tombs,
relocated over three thousand surrendered households to the area between the Jiāng and Hàn rivers,
and returned with Zhōu Chéng captured.
Yáo Xiāng fled to Píngyáng,
and Qín Bìngzhōu Cìshǐ Yǐn Chì again surrendered his troops to Xiāng,
Yǐn Chì's rebellion against Xiāng is mentioned in the 8th year of the previous scroll.
Xiānglíng County,
belonged to Hédōng Commandery during Hàn,
and Píngyáng Commandery during Jìn;
later, Northern Wèi changed Xiānglíng to Qínchāng County,
and Suí and Táng restored it to Xiānglíng.
In the 7th year of Yǒnghé,
Zhāng Píng surrendered to Qín,
but later wavered and sided with Yàn.
The Tōngjiàn attributes the official position granted by Qín to this.
Then he made an oath of brotherhood with Píng,
and both demobilized their troops.
Duàn Kān sent his subordinate Duàn Yùn
to request aid,
and an imperial edict ordered Xúzhōu Cìshǐ Xún Xiàn to lead troops with Yùn to relieve him.
When Xiàn arrived at Lángyá,
this is ancient Lángyá.
Wáng Téng attacked Juànchéng,
Juànchéng County,
belonged to Dōng Commandery during Hàn,
and Púyáng during Jìn.
This is not the ancient Juànchéng County;
it is probably a relocated county.
Heavy rains coincided,
the city walls collapsed,
and Téng was captured
and executed.
Duàn Kān appointed Wáng Téng as Xúzhōu Cìshǐ,
garrisoning Yángdū.
He had previously surrendered to Yàn,
and came to attack for Yàn.
In winter,
the 10th month,
on the first day of the month, guǐsì,
there was a solar eclipse.
16 Qín Zhǔ Shēng 夜食棗多，
旦而有疾，
召太醫令 Chéng Yán，
使診之，
Yán 曰：
「陛下無他疾，
食棗多耳。」
Shēng 怒曰：
「汝非聖人，
安知吾食棗！」
遂斬之。
17 Yān Dàsīmǎ Kè 圍 Duàn Kān 於 Guǎnggù，
諸將請急攻之，
Kè 曰：
「用兵之勢，
有宜緩者，
有宜急者，
不可不察。
若彼我勢敵，
外有強援，
恐有腹背之患，
則攻之不可不急。
若我強彼弱，
無援於外，
力足制之者，
當羈縻守之，
以待其斃；
兵法十圍五攻，
正謂此也。
Sūnzǐ 曰：用兵之法，
十則圍之，
五則攻之。
未有離心；
濟南之戰，
即淄水之戰。
曰濟南者，
以濟水南北大界言之。
但 Kān 用之無術，
以取敗耳。
今憑阻堅城，
上下戮力，
我盡銳攻之，
計數日
可拔，
然殺吾士卒必多矣。
自有事中原，
兵不蹔息，
蹔，
與暫同。
夜而忘寐，
奈何輕用其死乎！
要在取之，
不必求功之速也！」
諸將皆曰：
「非所及也。」
軍中聞之，
人人感悅。
於是為高牆深塹以守之。
Qí rén 爭運糧以饋 Yān jūn。
Kān 嬰城自守，
樵采路絕，
城中人相食。
Kān 悉衆出戰，
Kè 破之於圍裏，
時外築長圍，
故戰於圍裏。
屯廣固城諸門也。
騎，
奇寄翻。
僅而得入，
餘兵皆沒。
於是城中氣沮，
莫有固志。
十一月，
丙子，
Kān 面縛出降，
幷執 Zhū Tū 送 Jì。
Kè 撫安新民，
悉定 Qí dì，
徙 Xiānbēi、Hú、Jié 三千餘戶于 Jì。
Yān Wáng Jùn 具 Zhū Tū 五刑，
Zhū Tū 殺 Mùróng Gōu 而奔 Kān，
見上卷十年。
Kè 留 Mùróng Chén 鎮 Guǎnggù，
以尚書左丞 Jū Yīn 為 Dōnglái Tàishǒu，
Zhāngwǔ Tàishǒu Xiānyú Liàng 為 Qíjùn Tàishǒu，
乃還。
Yīn，
Péng 之子也。
Péng 時為 Yān Dàzhǎngqiū，
以書戒 Yīn 曰：
「Wáng Mí、Cáo Yì，
必有子孫，
汝善招撫，
勿尋舊怨，
以長亂源！」
Yīn 推求，
得 Mí Cóngzǐ Lì、Yì Sūn Yán 於山中，
請與相見，
深結意分，
Péng 復遣使遺以車馬衣服，
郡民由是大和。
Jū Péng 自 Dōnglái 歸 Yān，
見九十一卷 Yuándì Dàxīng 二年。
Xún Xiàn 聞 Kān 已敗，
退還 Xiàpéi，
留將軍 Zhūgě Yōu、Gāopíng Tàishǒu Liú Zhuāng 將三千人守 Lángxié，
Cānjūn Qiáoguó Dài Duàn 等將二千人守 Tàishān。
Yáng Zhènghéng 曰： Duàn，
音遁。
Biànchéng，
即 Jùnyí Chéng。
余謂
當作
Lǔguó Biàn Xiàn Chéng 也。
Liú Xù 曰：Yǎnzhōu Sìshuǐ Xiàn，
Biàn Xiàn Gǔchéng 也。
18 詔遣兼 Sīkōng、Sànqí Chángshì Chē Guàn 等持節如 Luòyáng，
脩五陵。
Xuāndì Líng 在 Héyīn Shǒuyáng Shān；
Jǐngdì Líng 曰 Jùnpíng，
Wéndì Líng 曰 Chóngyáng，
Wǔdì Líng 曰 Jùnyáng，
Huìdì Líng 曰 Tàiyáng。
散，
悉亶翻。
騎，
奇寄翻。
車，
尺奢翻。
Gēngxū，
帝及㣥臣皆服緦，
臨於 Tàijí Diàn 三日。
緦，
十五升布，
抽去其半。
臨，
力鴆翻。
19 Sīzhōu Dūdū Xiè Shàng 以疾不行，
以 Dānyáng Yǐn Wáng Húzhī 代之。
Húzhī，
Yì 之子也。
Wáng Yì，
Wáng Dūn 之從弟，
見八十九卷 Mǐndì Jiànxīng 三年。
Yì，
羊至翻，
又逸職翻。
20 是歲，
Qiúchí Gōng Yáng Guó Cóngfù Jùn 殺 Guó 自立；
以 Jùn 為 Qiúchí Gōng。
Guó Zǐ Ān 奔 Qín。
其後 Qín 用 Yáng Ān 以取 Qiúchí，
豈即 Guó 之子邪？
Shēngpíng Yuánnián
(Dīngsì、三五七)
正月，
Rénxū Shuò，
帝加元服；
太后詔歸政，
大赦，
改元，
太后徙居 Chóngdé Gōng。
2 Yān Zhǔ Jùn 徵 Yōuzhōu Cìshǐ Yǐ Yì 為 Zuǒguānglù Dàfū。
Yì Fūfù 共載鹿車；
子 Zhāng 從數十騎，
服飾甚麗，
奉迎於道。
Yì 大怒，
閉車不與言，
到城，
深責之，
到城，
謂到 Jì Chéng 也。
Yǒnghé Bānián，
Yān Wáng Dū Jì，
於 Lóngchéng 置 liú tái，
以 Yǐ Yì lǐng liú wù，
蓋以 Yōuzhōu Cìshǐ zhèn Lóngchéng 也。
騎，
奇寄翻。
Yì 常憂其敗，
而 Zhāng 更被擢任，
歷 Zhōngshū Lìng、Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng。
Yì 乃歎曰：
「吾少自脩立，
克己守道，
僅能免罪。
Zhāng 不治節檢，
專為奢縱，
而更居清顯，
此豈惟 Zhāng 之忝幸，
實時世之陵夷也。」
3 In the second month,
on the day Guǐchǒu,
Lord Jùn of Yān established his son, Wěi, King of Zhōngshān, as Crown Prince.
There was a general amnesty,
and the era name was changed to Guāngshòu.
4 Táibái entered Dōngjǐng.
An official of Qín presented a memorial:
"Táibái is a punitive star,
and Dōngjǐng is the Qín quarter.
There will certainly be a violent uprising of troops in the capital."
Lord Shēng of Qín said:
"Táibái entering the well
is merely thirsty itself;
what is there to be alarmed about!"
5 Yáo Xiāng was planning to seize Guānzhōng.
In the summer,
in the fourth month,
he advanced from Běiqū and garrisoned Xìngchéng.
Běiqū County,
during the Hàn dynasty, belonged to Hédōng Commandery;
during the Jìn dynasty, it belonged to Píngyáng Commandery.
Shīgǔ said: Qū,
pronounced jūwù.
It was where the Jìn prince Yíwú resided.
The Bān Records state,
"Húkǒu Mountain of the Yǔ Tribute is southeast of Běiqū County."
The Commentary on the Water Classic states: "Běiqū is ten *lǐ* west of the Yellow River;
Mèngmén Mountain is on the river."
Xiāng probably crossed the Yellow River from Běiqū and garrisoned Xìngchéng.
The Five Dynasties Records state: "Fénzhōu's Chāngníng County has Húkǒu Mountain."
Sòng Bái said: "Cízhōu's Jíxiāng County
was the Hàn Běiqū County;
the ancient city twenty-one *lǐ* north of the present county
is where the Hàn administration was located."
Wèi Shōu's Geographical Monograph states,
"Chéngchéng County has Xìngchéng."
Shīgǔ said: "Chéngchéng
was the Hàn Féngyì's Zhēng County."
Zhēng,
pronounced chéng.
According to the Records of Raids,
Xìngchéng was north of Mǎlán Mountain.
Dù Yòu said: "Yáo Cháng established Xìngchéng Garrison,
seven *lǐ* west of present-day Fāngzhōu."
Fūchéng,
the Táng dynasty's Fāngzhōu Fūchéng County it is;
the Later Wèi dynasty established Fūchéng County,
the Suí dynasty changed its name to Fūchéng.
The Illustrious Martial General
was probably an appointment made by Shí of Zhào.
Lán,
Xiāng's cousin;
Yìshēng,
Xiāng's elder brother.
Five myriad households of Qiāng, Hú, and Qín people submitted to him.
Qín general Fú Fēilóng attacked Lán
and captured him.
Xiāng led his troops and advanced to occupy Huángluò;
Lord Shēng of Qín dispatched the Grand General of the Guards, Huángméi, King of Guǎngpíng, the Pacifying North General Fú Dào, the Dragon Soaring General Jiān, King of Dōnghǎi,
and the Establishing-Axe General Dèng Qiāng.
Between the Hàn and Wèi dynasties, the Establishing-Axe Colonel was established,
later made a general's title.
Xiāng firmly fortified his position and did not engage in battle.
Qiāng said to Huángméi:
"Xiāng was defeated by Huán Wēn and Zhāng Píng,
and his morale is lost.
However, he is a fierce and stubborn man.
If we beat drums, shout, and wave flags,
directly pressing against his encampment,
he will surely come out in anger,
and we can capture him in one battle."
In the fifth month,
Qiāng led three thousand cavalry to press against the gate of his encampment and arrayed them.
Xiāng, enraged,
led all his forces out to battle.
Qiāng feigned defeat and fled.
Xiāng pursued him to Sānyuán.
Sānyuán was within the borders of Hàn Féngyì's Chíyáng County.
Sòng Bái said: "Fú Jiān established the Sānyuán Military Protectorate north of Jiéyè;
the Later Zhōu dynasty established Sānyuán County."
Huángméi and the others followed with a large army,
and Xiāng's troops were greatly defeated.
The swift horse Xiāng rode was called Lí méi guā.
The horse fell,
and Qín soldiers captured and beheaded him.
His younger brother Cháng led his forces and surrendered.
Xiāng carried the coffin of his father, Yìzhòng, in his army.
Lord Shēng of Qín buried Yìzhòng with royal rites at Gūpán.
Gūpán
was in the border region of Tiānshuǐ's Jì County.
Huángméi and the others returned to Cháng'ān,
but Shēng did not reward them;
instead, he repeatedly publicly humiliated Huángméi.
Huángméi was angered,
and plotted to assassinate Shēng;
the plot was discovered,
and he was executed.
The matter implicated many princes, dukes, and relatives,
and a great number of people died.
6 On the day Wùyín,

Lord Jùn of Yān dispatched the General who Soothes the Army, Chuí, the Central Army General Qián, and the Protector Army General Píng Xī, leading eighty thousand infantry and cavalry to attack the Chìlè north of the frontier.
The New Book of Táng states: "The Chìlè,
their ancestors were Xiōngnú.
During the Northern Wèi dynasty, they were called the Gāochē tribe.
Later, the name was corrupted to
'Tiělè.'
The fifteen tribes of Tiělè in the Táng dynasty are these."
The Records of Raids state:
"Dīnglíng Chìqín
[Lè]"
They were greatly defeated,
over one hundred thousand were captured or beheaded,
and one hundred thirty thousand horses
and myriad heads of cattle and sheep were seized.
7 Hú Xiōngnú Chányú Hèlài Tóu led his tribe of thirty-five thousand people to surrender to Yān.
Since the Eastern Hàn dynasty,
the Xiōngnú who settled within the frontier totaled nineteen tribes,
and Hèlài was one of them.
Chán,
pronounced chán.
During the Hàn dynasty, Dàijùn had Píngshū County;
Bóhǎi had Dōngpíngshū County.
Dōngpíngshū,
during the Later Hàn dynasty, belonged to Héjiān Kingdom;
during the Jìn dynasty, it belonged to Zhāngwǔ Kingdom.
Píngshū of Dàijùn
never changed its affiliation;
it is recorded as Dàijùn to distinguish it from Zhāngwǔ's Píngshū.
Píngshū of Dàijùn
should be in the northern border region of Táng's Wèi.
Chǔ,
pronounced chānglǚ.
8 Lord Shēng of Qín dreamed of a large fish eating *pú* (cattails).
The Fú clan
was originally from the Pú family,
hence the dream of a fish eating *pú* was considered unusual.
"A great fish from the Eastern Sea transforms into a dragon,
all males become kings, and females become dukes."
Shēng then executed Grand Tutor, Administrator of Affairs of the Imperial Secretariat, and Duke of Guǎngníng Yú Zūn, along with his seven sons and ten grandsons.
The Gold Purple Grand Master of Emoluments, Niú Yí, fearing disaster,
requested to be assigned to Jīngzhōu.
Qín Jīngzhōu's seat of government was at Fēngyángchuān.
He was made Central Army General.
When granted an audience, Shēng teased him, saying:
"Cattle are by nature slow and heavy,
good at holding the shafts and yokes;
the shaft,
is the pole of the carriage.
The front of the shaft is called the yoke,
placed on the neck of the ox.
Yoke,
pronounced è.
It can carry a hundred *shí* of weight."
Yí said:
"Although I can pull a large carriage,
I have not yet traversed steep cliffs;
I wish to be tested with a heavy load,
only then will my merits be known."
Shēng laughed and said:
"How quick-witted you are!
Do you complain that your load is light?
I shall bestow upon you the rank and position of Duke Yú."
Yí, terrified,
returned home and committed suicide.
He indulged in drinking day and night,
sometimes not emerging for a whole month.
When memorials were presented, he was not attentive,
often dozing off,
or making decisions while drunk;
his attendants consequently took advantage to commit misdeeds,
and rewards and punishments lacked standards.
Sometimes he would not appear at court until the hours of Shēn or Yǒu (3-7 PM),
and in his drunkenness he committed many massacres.
Because he had one eye,
he forbade mentioning
words like "disabled, defective, partial, single, few, without, incomplete,"
and those who inadvertently uttered them and died
were innumerable.
He liked to flay oxen, sheep, donkeys, and horses alive,
and scald chickens, pigs, geese, and ducks,
releasing them in front of the palace,
dozens at a time.
Sometimes he would peel off a person's face,
and make them sing and dance,
watching them as entertainment.
He once asked his attendants,
"Since I ascended the throne,
what have you heard from outside?"
One replied,
"Your sagacious and enlightened rule presides over the world,
rewards and punishments are clear and just,
the world sings only of peace."
He was enraged and said,
"You flatter me!"
He had him seized and executed.
Another day he asked again,
and one replied,
"Your Majesty's punishments are slightly excessive."
Again he was enraged and said,
"You slander me!"
He also had him executed.
His meritorious old officials and close relatives
were almost all put to death,
and his attendants, if they survived for a day,
felt it was like enduring ten years.
Fú Jiān, Prince of Dōnghǎi,
had always enjoyed a good reputation;
a "good reputation"
means being praised and admired by the people of the time.
Zàn and Yì secretly advised Fú Jiān, saying,
"The emperor is suspicious, cruel, and tyrannical,
and both those within and outside the court are disaffected.
Now, who else but Your Highness
is fit to preside over the Qín sacrifices!
We hope you will make plans early,
lest another family obtains it!"
Fú Jiān consulted Shàngshū Lǚ Póluó,
who said,
"I am
a 'knife-ring man' (an insignificant person, or one who will be killed);
between the Wèi and Jìn dynasties,
people often used knife-rings to build (kill) people;
meaning, they would be killed by their own lives.
Or it is said: a knife's use is its blade,
the part above the knife-ring is useless;
Póluó uses this to describe himself.
The character 鐶,
is pronounced Hù-guān.
In my neighborhood, there is Wáng Měng,
a man whose strategic mind is 'not seen in the world' (uncommon);
'not seen in the world' means
that such a person is rarely born in the world.
Fú Jiān, through Lǚ Póluó, invited Wáng Měng,
and upon meeting him, they were like old friends;
when they discussed current affairs,
Fú Jiān was greatly pleased,
likening himself to Liú Xuándé meeting Zhūgě Kǒngmíng.
See volume sixty-five, twelfth year of Jiàn'ān of Emperor Xiàndì of Hàn.
In the sixth month,
Tàishǐlìng Kāng Quán reported to Qín Lord Shēng, saying:
The family genealogy says: Kāng,
descended from Wèi Kāngshū,
is also a Western Hú surname.
"Last night, three moons appeared together,
a comet entered Tàiwēi,
and connected to Dōngjǐng.
Since the first ten days of last month,
there has been continuous cloudy weather without rain
until now.
There will be a calamity of subordinates plotting against a superior."
This is also said according to the Hóngfàn Wǔxíng Zhuàn.
The character 沈,
is pronounced Chí-lín.
Considering this as a demonic utterance,
he had Kāng Quán beaten to death.
Tèjìn, Lǐng Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng Liáng Pínglǎo and others said to Fú Jiān,
"The emperor has lost his virtue,
and everyone, high and low, is clamoring;
'clamoring' means
the mournful voices of the masses.
Yān and Jìn, two states,
are watching for an opportunity to act,
and we fear that when calamity strikes,
both family and state will perish.
This is Your Highness's responsibility,
and you should plan for it early!"
Fú Jiān agreed in his heart,
but fearing Fú Shēng's swift bravery,
he did not dare to act.
One night, Fú Shēng said to his chambermaid,
"Even Āfǎ's brothers cannot be trusted;
I should eliminate them tomorrow."
"Tomorrow"
refers to the next morning,
meaning the next day.
Fú Fǎ, along with Liáng Pínglǎo and Tèjìn Guānglù Dàfū Qiáng Wāng, led several hundred brave men and secretly entered Yúnlóngmén.
When Emperor Míng of Wèi built the Luòyáng palace,
the main south gate of the palace city was called Yúnlóngmén.
When the Fú clan occupied Cháng'ān,
they also named the main south gate of the palace city Yúnlóngmén.
The character 帥,
is read as Shuài;
the same below.
The palace guards and officers all abandoned their weapons and went over to Fú Jiān.
Fú Shēng was still drunk and asleep.
When Fú Jiān's soldiers arrived,
Fú Shēng woke with a start and asked his attendants,
"Who are these people?"
His attendants said,
"They are rebels!"
Fú Shēng said,
"Why do you not bow to them!"
Fú Jiān's soldiers all laughed.
Fú Shēng again declared loudly,
"Why do you not quickly bow?
Those who do not bow will be executed!"
Fú Jiān's soldiers led Fú Shēng to a separate chamber,
deposed him as Prince of Yuè,
and soon after killed him,
giving him the posthumous title Lìwáng.
He was twenty-three years old.
Fú Jiān offered the throne to Fú Fǎ,
who said,
"You are the legitimate heir,
and moreover virtuous;
you should be established."
Fú Jiān's mother, Lady Gǒu,
was Fú Xióng's primary wife,
hence Fú Jiān was considered the legitimate heir.
"My elder brother is older,
he should be established."
Fú Jiān's mother, Lady Gǒu, wept and said to the attendants,
"The affairs of the state are grave,
my young son knows he is incapable;
if there is regret someday,
the fault will be with you gentlemen."
The attendants all prostrated themselves, requesting Fú Jiān be established.
Fú Jiān then relinquished the title of Emperor,
called himself Dà Qín Tiānwáng (Heavenly King of Great Qín),
and ascended the throne in the Tàijí Diàn;
Fú Jiān,
courtesy name Yǒnggù,
was the son of Fú Xióng.
He issued a general amnesty
and changed the era name to Yǒngxīng.
He posthumously honored his father Fú Xióng as Wénhuán Huángdì (Emperor Wénhuán),
his mother Lady Gǒu as Huáng Tàihòu (Empress Dowager),
Lady Gǒu (his wife) as Huánghòu (Empress),
and the heir apparent Fú Hóng as Huáng Tàizǐ (Crown Prince).
He appointed Fú Fǎ, Prince of Qīnghé, as Dūdū Zhōngwài Zhūjūnshì, Chéngxiàng, Lù Shàngshūshì, and Duke of Dōnghǎi.
All other princes were demoted to dukes.
He appointed his paternal cousin Yòu Guānglù Dàfū, Yǒng'ān Gōng Hóu as Tàiwèi,
and Jìn Gōng Liǔ as Chēqí Dàjiāngjūn and Shàngshūlìng.
He enfeoffed his brother Fú Róng as Duke of Yángpíng,
Fú Shuāng as Duke of Hénán,
his son Fú Pī as Duke of Chánglè,
Fú Huī as Duke of Píngyuán,
Fú Xī as Duke of Guǎngpíng,
and Fú Ruì as Duke of Jùlù.
He appointed Lǐ Wēi of Hànyáng as Zuǒ Púyè;
Lǐ Wēi was favored by Fú Jiān's mother as Bìyáng (a male favorite),
thus he was promoted.
Qiáng Wāng was appointed Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn,
Lǚ Póluó as Sīlì Xiàowèi,
and Wáng Měng as Zhōngshū Shìláng.
Róng was fond of literature,
discerning and surpassing others;
what he heard, he could recite,
and what he saw, he never forgot.
He could contend against a hundred men,
was skilled in horsemanship, archery, and stabbing,
and had a good reputation from a young age.
Fú Jiān valued and esteemed him greatly,
often discussing state affairs with him.
Fú Róng managed both internal and external affairs comprehensively,
ensuring that laws and administration were clear and just.
He recommended talented individuals and promoted those who were overlooked,
providing immense benefit.
Hóng
means "great."
In governing the people and judging cases,
everyone was second to Fú Róng.
The historian says that Fú Jiān had such a brother and son, yet there was no salvation from defeat and ruin,
showing that what Heaven abandons
cannot be sustained by man.
Zhì
is pronounced like zhí.
Duàn
is pronounced like dīng luàn.
Wēi
was the maternal cousin of Empress Dowager Gǒu.
He was always on good terms with Wèi Wáng Xióng.
Shēng repeatedly wanted to kill Fú Jiān,
but Wēi’s rescue saved him from death.
Wēi was favored by Empress Dowager Gǒu,
and Fú Jiān treated him like a father.
Wēi knew of Wáng Měng’s sagacity,
and often advised Fú Jiān to entrust state affairs to him.
Fú Jiān said to Wáng Měng:
“Lǐ Gōng knows you
just as Bāo Shúyá knew Guǎn Zhòng.”
When Guǎn Zhòng was young, he befriended Bāo Shúyá,
and Bāo Shúyá knew his sagacity
and treated him well.
Guǎn Zhòng said:
“When I was in distress,
I traded with Bāo Shúyá.
I took more of the profits for myself,
but Bāo Shúyá did not consider me greedy,
knowing I was poor.
I once planned affairs for Bāo Shúyá
but ended up in greater poverty,
yet Bāo Shúyá did not consider me foolish,
knowing that times have their advantages and disadvantages.
I served three times and was dismissed three times,
but Bāo Shúyá did not consider me unworthy,
knowing I had not met my time.
I fought three battles and retreated three times,
but Bāo Shúyá did not consider me cowardly,
knowing I had an elderly mother.
When Gōngzǐ Jiū was defeated,
Zhào Hū died for him,
and I was imprisoned and disgraced,
yet Bāo Shúyá did not consider me shameless,
knowing I did not feel shame for minor matters but for not achieving fame and merit throughout the world.
My parents gave me life,
but Bāo Zǐ understood me.”

Xià
is pronounced like hù yǎ.
He wanted to be an enemy state to Yān and Qín.

he wished to be an enemy state to Yān and Qín.
In the tenth month,
Píng plundered the Qín border.
Píng likely sensed Qín’s internal difficulties,
how could he know that this would lead to his defeat and ruin!
(Fú Jiān) added the title of Bìngzhōu Mù (Governor of Bìngzhōu) and stationed him at Púbǎn to defend against him.

帥 [shuài],
pronounced as 率 [shuài].

1 In spring,
the first month,

(Cháo,

His demeanor was arrogant.
At that time, Empress Dowager Kě Zúhún often interfered in external affairs.
Gēn wished to cause trouble,

"Now the emperor is young and immature,

Your Highness should guard against unexpected changes,

Moreover, the one who settled the realm

A brother succeeding a deceased brother

Kè said:

Gēn, ashamed, apologized and withdrew.
Kè told Wú Wáng Chuí,

Kè said:

Mìshū Jiān Huángfǔ Zhēn said to Kè:

and since the national mourning,

which will lead to disaster and rebellion.
Your Excellency today occupies the position of the Duke of Zhōu.
You should plan deeply for the state,
and take action early."
Kè did not listen.
Gēn again spoke to Kě Zúhún Shì and Yān Zhǔ Wěi, saying:

Kě Zúhún Shì was about to agree,

"The two dukes

The late emperor chose them

How do we know it isn't the Tàishī who wishes to cause trouble?"
Thereupon, she stopped.
Gēn also yearned for the Eastern Land,
(Lóngchéng was northeast of Yèchéng,
hence called the Eastern Land.)
and said: "Today the realm is desolate,

Kè heard of this,

They secretly submitted a memorial detailing Gēn's crimes.
They sent Yòu Wèi Jiāngjūn Fù Yán to the inner palace to execute Gēn,

A general amnesty was declared.
(After executing Gēn and his wife, children, and associates,
fearing that the hearts of the people would turn rebellious,
a general amnesty was therefore granted to pacify them.)
The extermination was disorderly,
causing fear inside and outside the court.
However, Tàizǎi Kè's demeanor was as usual;

Every time he went in or out,
only one person followed him on foot.
Some advised him to take stricter precautions,
but Kè said:
"People are currently afraid.
I should remain calm and steady to reassure them.
How can I alarm and disturb myself again?
What will the people look up to then?"
Because of this, people's hearts gradually settled.
Although Mùróng Kè
held a great responsibility,
he was scrupulous and strict
in court etiquette.
He always consulted with the Sītú on every matter
and never made a unilateral decision.
He humbly treated scholars,
sought good counsel,
and appointed people according to their abilities,
so no one overstepped their position.
If his officials or court ministers committed an offense,
he would not expose their fault,
but would expediently transfer them to another post,
not allowing them to lose their rank,
by transferring them to another official position,
not letting them lose their proper rank and status.
People at the time considered this a great shame,
and no one dared to offend.
If someone committed a minor fault,
they would reproach themselves, saying:
"Do you still hope to be promoted by Zǎigōng!"
Kè was the Tàizǎi,
hence he was called Zǎigōng.
Fù
is pronounced with the Fú-yòu tone.
Everyone thought the Central Plains could be conquered.
Huán Wēn said:

The historian states that Mùróng Kè was able to assist the young lord,

In the third month,
on the day of Jǐmǎo,

His temple name was Lièzǔ.
The soldiers levied from commanderies and states,
due to the many difficulties faced by the Yàn court,

From Yè southwards,
roads were cut off and blocked.

Tàizǎi Kè appointed Wú Wáng Mùróng Chuí as an Envoys with Imperial Credentials, General Who Attacks the South, Area Commander of all military affairs in Hénán, Inspector of Yǎnzōu, and Governor of Jīngzōu,

Sūn Xī was appointed Inspector of Bīngzōu,

the borders then became peaceful.
The historian states that Kè, in a time of great concern and public anxiety,
handled the situation skillfully.
Shuài
is pronounced as Lǜ.
Qí
is pronounced with the Qí-jì tone.
Guān
is pronounced with the Gǔ-wán tone,
meaning to show.
Guānbīng means to display military might.
He was the younger brother of Sūn Yǒng.
Sūn Yǒng resisted Zhào,
as seen in volume 96, year 4 of Xiánkāng of Emperor Chéng.
Historical records state that the descendants of Sūn Yǒng, Jú Péng, and Sòng Zhú
all became distinguished in Yàn,
which encouraged those who pledged allegiance to remain loyal unto death

In the fifth month, Xiōngnú Liú Wèichén sent an envoy to surrender to Qín,
requesting to cultivate land within the interior,

In summer,
in the fourth month,

Fú Jiān angrily said:

He dismissed Yǒng to hold office as a commoner,

Wèichén then moved to reside within the passes,

In summer,
in the sixth month,

in the seventh month,

In the sixth month, on the first day of the eighth month,
on the day of Xīnchǒu,
there was a solar eclipse,
which was total.
Xiè Ān had a great reputation in his youth,
and was repeatedly summoned to office,
but never accepted;
he lived in Kuàijī,
amusing himself with landscapes and literature.
Although he was a commoner,
people at the time all expected him to become a grand preceptor or minister,
and literati even said to each other:
"If Ānshí does not come out,
what will become of the common people!"
Xiè Ān,
courtesy name Ānshí.
The people of Jiāngdōng initially placed their hopes on Yīn Hào,
but Hào failed to meet their expectations,
and subsequently their hopes turned to Xiè Ān,
who ultimately succeeded in assisting the Jìn dynasty.
Commentators of the time
all praised Ān and disparaged Hào.
I believe that beneath a great reputation,
it is truly difficult to live up to it.
Hào's failure was precisely because he was equally famous as Huán Wēn,
and he easily despised Wēn;
and he also happened to be amidst the chaos of the Shí family,
thinking he could establish merits,
but failed due to his rashness.
Xiè Ān, during the time when Huán Wēn wielded power,
and having himself served as his subordinate,
learned from Hào's mistakes,
guarded against Wēn and prepared for him;
after Wēn's death, facing the might of Qín,
he meticulously planned for self-preservation,
always maintaining a sense of fear,
which is why he succeeded.
The historian said he was able to conceal his true feelings and calm the situation,
perhaps knowing this from the broken clog teeth and the dream of the white chicken.
Dōngshān
is forty-five lǐ southwest of present-day Shàoxīng Fǔ, Shàngyú Xiàn.
Ān's former residence is now Guóqìng Chánsì.
Sītú Yù heard this

Ān's wife,
who was Liú Dàn's sister,
seeing the prosperity and prominence of her family,
Liú Dàn was prominent for his pure conversation;
and Xiè Shàng, Xiè Yì, and Xiè Wàn were all regional governors,

Dàn
is pronounced with the Tú-gān tone.
said:
"A true man does not live like this!"
Ān covered his nose and said:

He meant he was afraid he couldn't avoid it like his brothers.
Ān first developed the ambition to enter officialdom

General Who Conquers the West Huán Wēn invited him to be his Sīmǎ,
and Ān then accepted the summons.
Wēn was greatly pleased,

In the eighth month,
in the tenth month,

Fú Jiān followed his advice.

In the first month,
in the first month,

Hù (護) has no accumulated supplies within,
and no external relief,
so I will dig deep moats and build high ramparts,
and simply guard it,
resting the troops and nourishing the soldiers,
and sowing discord among his followers.
This will not exhaust us, while the enemy's situation will worsen daily.
In no more than ten days,
we will surely take it.
Why should we kill many soldiers to achieve a temporary victory!"
So he built a long siege-wall and besieged it.
7 In summer,
in the fourth month,
Huán Wēn (桓溫) appointed his younger brother, Huángménláng Huò Dū (黃門郎豁都),
Grand Commander of military affairs of the seven prefectures in Miǎnzhōng (沔中),

Wèixīng (魏興), Xīnchéng (新城), Shàngyōng (上庸), Xiāngyáng (襄陽), Yìchéng (義成), Jìnglíng (竟陵), and Jiāngxià (江夏).

should be written as Chéng (成).
Yān (燕) general Mùróng Chén (慕容塵) was defeated.
8 Liáng (涼) Piàojì Dàjiāngjūn Sòng Hùn (驃騎大將軍宋混) fell gravely ill,
Zhāng Xuánjìng (張玄靚) and his grandmother Mǎ (馬) went to visit him,
and said:
"Should the general unfortunately perish,

Hùn (混) replied:
"My son Línzōng (林宗) is young and weak,

If Your Highness does not abandon my family,
my brother Chéng (澄) is better than I in governmental affairs,
but I fear he is too儒緩 (Rúhuǎn) and cannot adapt to circumstances in responding to tasks and achieving success.
All scholars tend to be too leisurely and relaxed,
and cannot respond to opportunities to carry out tasks and achieve success.
Chēng (稱),
pronounced chǐ zhèng.
It is acceptable."
Hùn (混) admonished Chéng (澄) and his sons, saying:
"Our family has received great favor from the state,
and should repay it with death;
do not rely on your power and position to be arrogant towards others."
He also saw the court officials
and admonished them all to be loyal and faithful.
When he died,
passersby shed tears for him.
Xuánjìng (玄靚) appointed Chéng (澄) as Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn (領軍將軍),
to assist in governance.
9 In the fifth month,
on the day Dīngsì (丁巳),
the emperor passed away,
at the age of nineteen.
The Empress Dowager issued an edict saying:
"Lángxié Wáng Pī (琅邪王丕),
the true heir of the restoration;
Yuándì (元帝), Míngdì (明帝), Chéngdì (成帝) all passed down the orthodox succession.
Lángxié Wáng Pī (琅邪王丕),
is Chéngdì's (成帝) eldest son,
hence he is called the true heir of the restoration.
None can compare with him,
let him be enthroned to lead the great succession!"
Thereupon, all officials, fully equipped with imperial carriages, welcomed him at the Lángxié (琅邪) residence.
On the day Gēngshēn (庚申),
he ascended the imperial throne,
and issued a general amnesty.
On the day Rénxū (壬戌),
Dōnghǎi Wáng Yì (東海王奕) was re-enfeoffed as Lángxié Wáng (琅邪王).
In autumn,
in the seventh month,
on the day Wùwǔ (戊午),
Mùdì (穆帝) was buried at Yǒngpínglíng (永平陵),
with the temple name Xiàozōng (孝宗).
10 The Yān (燕) people besieged Yěwáng (野王) for several months.
Lǚ Hù (呂護) sent his general Zhāng Xīng (張興) to battle,

and the city was increasingly pressed.
Huángfǔ Zhēn (皇甫真) admonished his division commanders, saying:
"Hù (護) is in a desperate situation and will flee,
he will surely choose a weak point to break through;
my soldiers are mostly weak,
and their armor is not refined,
so we must be thoroughly prepared."
He therefore ordered many shields,
and personally inspected night watchmen.
When Hù (護)'s food ran out,
he indeed led all his elite troops at night towards Zhēn (真)'s division.
Qū (趨),
pronounced qī yù.
He could not break out;
Tàizǎi Kè (太宰恪) led troops to attack him,
Hù (護)'s forces were almost entirely killed or wounded,
and he abandoned his wife and children and fled to Xíngyáng (滎陽).
Kè (恪) comforted and settled the surrendered people,
and provided them with provisions;
he relocated scholars and generals to Yè (鄴),
while the rest were allowed to go wherever they pleased;
he appointed Hù (護)'s staff officer, Liáng Chēn (梁琛) of Guǎngpíng (廣平), as Zhōngshū Zhùzuò Láng (中書著作郎).
Jìn Wǔdì (晉武帝) had combined the Secretarial Bureau with the Central Secretariat,
hence the title Zhōngshū Zhùzuò Láng (中書著作郎).
Chēn (琛),
pronounced chǒu lín.
11 In the ninth month,
on the day Wùshēn (戊申),
Lady Wáng (王氏) was enthroned as Empress.

was Móng (濛)'s daughter.

12 Liáng (涼) Yòusīmǎ Zhāng Yōng (右司馬張邕) resented Sòng Chéng (宋澄)'s monopoly on power,
raised troops to attack Chéng (澄),
killed him,
and exterminated his entire clan.
How could Sòng Chéng (宋澄) merely be unable to adapt to circumstances?
His entire clan was exterminated!
From this, one knows that managing the world is not something those who are leisurely and relaxed can do.
His paternal uncle Tiānxī (天錫) became Zhōnglǐngjūn (中領軍),
jointly assisting in governance.
13 Zhāng Píng (張平) attacked Yān (燕)'s Píngyáng (平陽),
killed Duàn Gāng (段剛) and Hán Bāo (韓苞);

Afterwards, when he was attacked by Qin (秦),

The Yān (燕) people, seeing Píng (平)'s fickleness,
did not rescue him,
so Píng (平) was then destroyed by Qin (秦).
14 On the day Yǐhài (乙亥),
Qin (秦) issued a general amnesty.
15 Xú (徐) and Yǎn (兗) prefectures' Inspector Fàn Wāng (范汪)
was always disliked by Huán Wēn (桓溫).
When Huán Wēn (桓溫) first settled the upper reaches as Ānxī Zhèn (安西鎮),
Wāng (汪) was his chief subordinate;
he disliked him probably because he was different from him.
If Wāng (汪) at this time could have established a difference,
he would surely have known Wēn (溫)'s intentions.
È (惡),
pronounced wū lù.
He ordered Wāng (汪) to lead his troops out to Liángguó (梁國).
In winter,
in the tenth month,
he was dismissed as a commoner for failing to meet the deadline,
subsequently removed from office,
and died at home.
Zǐníng
loved Ruism.
His nature was straightforward.
He often said that the crimes of Wáng Bì and Hé Yàn were deeper than those of Jié and Zhòu.
Some thought this was too harsh a condemnation,
but Níng said:
“Wáng and Hé scorned and abandoned the classic texts,
submerged benevolence and righteousness,
and with their glib words and empty theories
swept away the younger generation,
causing officials to suddenly change their ways,
leading to the collapse of rites and music,
the overthrow of the Central Plain,
and a lingering influence and customs
that remain a problem to this day.
Jié and Zhòu were tyrannical for a time,
