which was sufficient to destroy their persons and overthrow their states,
(sàng,
xī làng fān.)
but how could they turn the sight and hearing of the common people?
Therefore, I believe that the calamity of one generation is light,
while the affliction across generations is heavy;
the evil of self-destruction is small,
but the crime of misleading the masses is great!”
Lǚ Hù rebelled again
and fled to Yàn.
The Yàn people pardoned him
and appointed him as the Inspector of Guǎngzhōu.
Yàn had no Guǎngzhōu;
they merely gave Hù the title of Inspector.
Liáng's Zhāng Yōng was arrogant, self-important, and unrestrained in his immorality.
He formed factions and monopolized power,
executing many,
which the people of the state deplored.
Liú Sù of Dūnhuáng, a close confidant of Zhāng Tiānxī, said to Tiānxī:
“The affairs of the state are not yet settled!”
Tiānxī asked:
“What do you mean?”
Sù replied:
“Now, the commander of the guards (hùjūn) coming and going
resembles Chángníng.”
Chángníng Hóu was Zhāng Zuò.
“I have always suspected this,
but dared not speak out.
What plan should we adopt?”
Sù said:
“We should simply eliminate him quickly!”
Tiānxī asked:
“Where can we find such a person?”
Sù replied:
“I, Sù, am that person!”
Sù was not yet twenty years old at the time.
Tiānxī said:
“You are young;
seek others to assist you.”
Sù said:
“Zhào Báijū and I are enough.”
In the eleventh month,
Tiānxī and Yōng both entered the court.
Sù and Báijū followed Tiānxī.
Sù struck but missed.
Báijū followed,
but also failed.
The two, along with Tiānxī, entered the palace.
Yōng managed to escape
and led over three hundred armored soldiers to attack the palace gate.
Tiānxī climbed onto the roof and shouted:
“Zhāng Yōng is violent, rebellious, and without principle!
Having already destroyed the Sòng clan,
he now wishes to overthrow my family!
You, soldiers, have been subjects of Liáng for generations;
how can you bear to turn your weapons against me?
What we seek now
is only Zhāng Yōng;
we ask nothing else!”
Thereupon, Yōng's soldiers all scattered and fled.
Yōng committed suicide by slitting his throat,
and his entire clan and faction were exterminated.
Xuánjìng appointed Tiānxī as Emissary with Imperial Credentials, General-in-Chief of Champions, and Grand Administrator of All Military Affairs Inside and Outside the Capital,
to assist in governing.
After Zhāng Chónghuá's death,
Zhāng Zuò, Zhāng Guàn, Sòng Hùn, Sòng Chéng, as well as Zhāng Yōng and Zhāng Tiānxī,
successively slaughtered each other,
and Liáng gradually declined.
(shǐ,
shū lì fān.) (guān,
gǔ wán fān.)
They began to rename Jiànxīng forty-nine
and adopted the Shēngpíng reign title.
It was only at this point that Liáng adopted the Jiànkāng reign title.
Yàn issued a great amnesty.
Qín Wáng Jiān ordered his provincial governors, prefects, and magistrates to each recommend individuals who were filial, fraternal, incorruptible, upright, scholarly, and skilled in governance.
Those whose recommendations were found to be accurate were rewarded;
those whose recommendations were inaccurate were punished.
As a result, no one dared to make reckless recommendations,
and private petitions ceased to be effective.
All scholars strove to better themselves;
even members of the imperial clan and imperial in-laws
who lacked talent were dismissed and not employed.
At this time,
officials, both internal and external,
were mostly competent;
fields were cultivated and opened,
granaries were full,
and banditry ceased.
This year,
Guīyì Hóu Lǐ Shì died.
In Yǒnghé three,
Lǐ Shì surrendered,
and died at this point.
Emperor Āi's
personal name was Pī,
the eldest son of Emperor Chéng.
His courtesy name was Qiānlíng.
In Xiánkāng eight,
he was enfeoffed as Lángyé Wáng.
The posthumous title rules state: "Respectful and benevolent, but dying young, is called Āi."
Lónghé First Year (rénxū, 362)
1 In spring,
the first month,
on the day rénzǐ,
a great amnesty was declared,
and the reign title was changed.
2 On the day jiǎyín,
land tax was reduced,
with two shēng collected per mù.
In Chéngdì's Xiánhé five,
the land of the common people was first surveyed,
and one-tenth was collected per mù,
typically three shēng of rice per mù;
now it was reduced,
with two shēng collected per mù.
3 Yàn's Inspector of Yùzhōu, Sūn Xīng, requested to attack Luòyáng,
saying:
“Jìn's general Chén Yòu has only a thousand worn-out soldiers
guarding an isolated city;
it is not worth taking!”
The Yàn people followed his advice
and dispatched General Níngnán Lǚ Hù to garrison Héyīn.
4 In the second month,
on the day xīnwèi,
Yǔ Xī, the Administrator of Wú County, was appointed Northern Central Army General and Inspector of Xú and Yǎn provinces,
garrisoning Xiàpī.
Yuán Zhēn, General Lóngxiáng, was appointed Western Central Army General, Supervisor of Military Affairs of Yù, Sī, Bīng, and Jì provinces, and Inspector of Yùzhōu,
garrisoning Rǔnán.
Since Xī and Zhēn were both granted imperial credentials,
their official duties should be similar;
it is suspected that Xī should also have held the supervisory position,
but the historian omitted it.
(xiáng,
sī jiāng fān.) (jiān,
gōng xián fān.)
Xī was the son of Bīng.
Yǔ Bīng held power in Xiánkāng.
5 On the day bǐngzǐ,
Emperor's mother, Consort Zhōu Guìrén, was appointed Empress Dowager,
with ceremonial attire similar to that of an Empress Dowager.
6 Yàn's Lǚ Hù attacked Luòyáng.
In the third month,
on the day yǐyǒu,
the Administrator of Hénán, Dài Shī, fled to Wǎn.
In Yǒnghé twelve,
Huán Wēn left Dài Shī to garrison Luòyáng.
(wǎn,
yú yuán fān.)
In the fifth month,
on the day dīngsì,
Huán Wēn dispatched Yǔ Xī and the Administrator of Jìnglín, Dèng Xiá, leading three thousand naval troops to assist Yòu in defending Luòyáng.
Xiá was the son of Yuè.
Dèng Yuè was a general of Wáng Dūn.
After Dūn's defeat, he surrendered himself and made contributions in Jiāo and Guǎng.
Huán Wēn (桓溫) submitted a memorial requesting to move the capital to Luòyáng (洛陽),
and that all those who had been dispersed to the Jiāngbiǎo (江表) since the Disorder of Yǒngjiā (永嘉之亂)
should be moved north,
to populate Hénán (河南).
The imperial court feared Huán Wēn
and dared not object;
but the northern lands were desolate,
and people were suspicious and afraid.
Although all knew it was unfeasible,
none dared to be the first to remonstrate.
Sànqí Chángshì (散騎常侍) and concurrent Zuòzhù Láng (著作郎) Sūn Chuò (孫綽) submitted a memorial, stating:
"The 'Jìn Zhì' (晉志) says: 'The Zuòzhù Láng
held the responsibility of the Left Historian of Zhōu (周).'
In the Eastern Capital of Hàn (漢東京),
archives and records were in the Dōngguān (東觀),
so scholars were made to 'compose and write' in the Dōngguān,
which had the name,
but not yet the official post.
In the Tàihé (太和) era of Wèi Míngdì (魏明帝),
an edict established the Zuòzhù Láng,
at which point the official post first came into being,
subordinate to the Zhōngshū Shěng (中書省).
Jìn Huìdì (晉惠帝) established the Mìshū Jiān (祕書監),
which also governed the Zuòzhù Shěng (著作省).
Thus, although the Zuòzhù was established as a separate department,
it was still subordinate to the Mìshū (祕書).
I have noted that Bān Gù's (班固) 'Xīdū Fù' (西都賦) says: 'Chéngmíng (承明), Jīnmǎ (金馬),
the court of composition.'
If this is the case,
then although the Hàn (漢) Western Capital had not yet established the official post of composition,
Chéngmíng (承明) and Jīnmǎ (金馬) were also places of composition.
Sàn (散),
pronounced like 'xī dān' (悉亶).
Qí (騎),
pronounced like 'qí jì' (奇寄).
'When Zhōngzōng (中宗) rose to power,
Yuándì (元帝) was given the temple name Zhōngzōng (中宗).
The 'Yì Dàzhuàn' (易大傳) says: "What Heaven assists is compliance.
What man assists is trust."
Now, since the chaos of war,
over sixty years have passed.
Since the deposition of Empress Jiǎ (賈后),
and the execution of Zhào Wáng Lún (趙王倫),
followed by the warring of various princes,
and the rise of the Hú (胡) and Jié (羯),
the world fell into great chaos,
and by now it has been over sixty years.
Sàng (喪),
pronounced like 'xī làng' (息浪).
Hánxià (函夏) is desolate.
Hán (函),
means 'to contain'.
Xià (夏),
means 'great'.
It refers to the land of the Central Plains,
which contains a vast area.
Xià (夏),
pronounced like 'hù yǎ' (戶雅).
Several generations have passed;
those who remain are old people and their eldest grandchildren,
while those who perished have graves forming rows.
Although the thoughts of the north wind stir their original feelings,
the present sorrow is truly poignant.
If the day of moving the capital and turning back arrives,
Jiǎ Gōngyàn (賈公彥) said: 'Ruò' (若)
is a word indicating uncertainty.
it will once again become a distant, remote region.
The five imperial mausoleums of the restoration,
Yuándì's (元帝) Jiànpíng Líng (建平陵), Míngdì's (明帝) Wǔpíng Líng (武平陵), Chéngdì's (成帝) Xīngpíng Líng (興平陵), Kāngdì's (康帝) Chóngpíng Líng (崇平陵), Mùdì's (穆帝) Yǒngpíng Líng (永平陵),
are all in Jiāngnán (江南).
Miǎn (緬),
means 'distant'.
Xiá (遐),
also means 'distant'.
Since it is difficult to secure it by reason,
meaning, from a rational perspective,
moving the capital to Luò (洛)
makes it difficult to ensure the security of Mount Tài (泰山).
How could this not trouble the sagely heart!
Zhēngzhēng (烝烝),
means 'advancing steadily'.
It means that if the capital were moved to Luò (洛),
the heart would be troubled by the imperial tombs in Jiāngnán (江南),
and filial thoughts would advance steadily.
If there is a sincere desire to consider the beginning and end comprehensively,
and to plan for the nation in the long term;
but the common people are shocked and terrified,
all harboring feelings of danger and fear,
is it not because the joy of returning to the old ways is remote,
and the sorrow of rushing to death is imminent!
Why is this?
Roots have been planted outside the Jiāng (江) for decades.
The Central Plains referred to Jiāngnán (江南) as 'outside the Jiāng' (江外),
also called Jiāngbiǎo (江表).
Forced into
a barren wilderness;
carrying families for ten thousand *lǐ* (里),
crossing dangers and deep waters,
leaving ancestral graves,
abandoning their livelihoods.
Fields and homes cannot be sold again,
boats and carts cannot be acquired,
abandoning a land of peace and joy,
to move to a region accustomed to chaos,
they will collapse on the roads,
or drown in rivers,
with only a few reaching their destination.
This is what benevolent people should pity,
and what the state should consider deeply!
My humble opinion
is that it would be more appropriate to first send generals with prestige and substantial resources
to garrison Luòyáng (洛陽),
and pacify Liáng (梁) and Xǔ (許).
Liáng (梁)
refers to Liángguó (梁國);
Xǔ (許)
refers to Xǔchāng (許昌);
both are vital routes for entering Luò (洛) from Jiāngnán (江南).
When the transport routes are clear,
and abundant provisions from reclamation have been accumulated,
and the jackals and wolves have retreated far away,
and the Central Land enjoys a minor peace,
then we can slowly deliberate on relocation.
How can we abandon the long-term principle of a hundred victories,
and gamble the entire realm in a single throw!"
Chuò (綽)
was the grandson of Chǔ (楚).
Sūn Chǔ (孫楚) served during the reign of Wǔdì (武帝)
and had a reputation for talent.
He once wrote the 'Suíchū Fù' (遂初賦) to express his aspirations.
Huán Wēn (桓溫) saw Sūn Chuò's (孫綽) memorial
and was displeased,
saying:
"Convey my regards to Xìnggōng (興公),
Sūn Chuò's (孫綽) courtesy name was Xìnggōng (興公).
How can he know about the affairs of my family and state!"
At the time, the imperial court was anxious and fearful,
and was about to send a palace attendant to stop Huán Wēn (桓溫).
Yángzhōu Cìshǐ (揚州刺史) Wáng Shù (王述) said:
"Huán Wēn (桓溫) only wants to intimidate the imperial court with empty boasts,
it is not a practical matter;
just comply with him,
and nothing will come of it."
So an edict was issued to Huán Wēn (桓溫), saying:
"In the past chaos,
suddenly five *jì* (紀) have passed.
Kǒng Yǐngdá (孔穎達) said: 'Yán zài xī zhě' (言在昔者)
is a phrase used when speaking from a lower position upwards;
'yán xī zài zhě' (言昔在者)
is a phrase used when speaking from an upper position downwards.
Sàng (喪),
pronounced like 'xī làng' (息浪).
From the first year of Yǒngxīng (永興) under Huìdì (惠帝), when Liú Yuān (劉淵) first rebelled, until this year is fifty-nine years;
from the fifth year of Yǒngjiā (永嘉) under Huáidì (懷帝), when Luòyáng (洛陽) fell, until this year is fifty years.
Successively inheriting dire circumstances,
recalling the west
fills my heart with sorrow.
I know you wish to personally lead the three armies,
to sweep away the foulness,
and cleanse the central capital region.
Zhōngjī (中畿),
means the royal domain.
The 'Zhōu Lǐ' (周禮) describes the Nine Regions,
the royal domain was a thousand *lǐ* (里) square,
beyond it were the Hóu (侯), Diàn (甸), Nán (男), Cǎi (采), Wèi (衞), Mán (蠻), Yí (夷), Zhèn (鎮), and Fān (蕃) regions,
all described in terms of five hundred *lǐ* (里) beyond the Mán (蠻).
The royal domain was in the center of the Nine Regions,
hence it is called Zhōngjī (中畿) here.
Shuài (帥),
read as 'shuài' (率).
Were it not for those who sacrifice themselves for the nation,
who could accomplish such a feat!
All arrangements
are entrusted to your great wisdom.
However, the Hé (河) and Luò (洛) are ruins,
what needs to be established is vast,
the effort of commencing such an undertaking
would cause much anxiety."
The matter indeed did not proceed.
Huán Wēn (桓溫) also proposed moving the bells and stands (*zhōngjù*) of Luòyáng (洛陽).
Wáng Shù (王述) said:
"The weakness of Yǒngjiā (永嘉) led to a temporary capital in Jiāngzuǒ (江左).
We are still in the process of pacifying the realm,
and returning to the old capital.
If that is not to be the case,
then the imperial tombs should be relocated,
it is inappropriate to prioritize the bells and stands!"
Huán Wēn (桓溫) then stopped.
The imperial court, considering Jiāo (交) and Guǎng (廣) to be vast and distant,
while Huán Wēn (桓溫) was overseeing eight provinces: Jīng (荊), Sī (司), Yōng (雍), Yì (益), Liáng (梁), Níng (寧), Jiāo (交), and Guǎng (廣).
Huán Wēn (桓溫) submitted a memorial declining to accept the latter two.
Qín Wáng Jiān (秦王堅) personally visited the Imperial Academy (Tàixué, 太學),
tested the students' understanding of the classics,
and engaged in discussions with the erudites,
after which he visited monthly.
8 In the sixth month,
on the jiǎxū day,

Liú Bá (劉拔), Aide to the Administrator of the Eastern Expedition of Yàn (燕), assassinated Mùróng Yǒu (慕容友), General of the Eastern Expedition, Inspector of Jìzhōu (冀州), and Prince of Fànyáng (范陽), in Xìndū (信都).
9 In autumn,
in the seventh month,
Lǚ Hù (呂護) retreated to defend Xiǎopíngjīn (小平津),
because Jin (晉) reinforcements had arrived.
Yàn (燕) general Duàn Chóng (段崇) withdrew his troops and crossed north,
stationing them at Yěwáng (野王).
Dèng Xiá (鄧遐) advanced to Xīnchéng (新城);
Xīnchéng (新城)
was the state of Róngmánzǐ (戎蠻子) during the Spring and Autumn period;
since the Hàn (漢) dynasty,
it belonged to Hénán (河南);
the Suí (隋) dynasty changed it to Yīquè Xiàn (伊闕縣).
Yuán Zhēn (袁真), General of the Western Central Army, advanced to Rǔnán (汝南),
transporting 50,000 hù of rice to provision Luòyáng (洛陽).
10 In winter,
in the eleventh month,
Dài (代) Prince Shíyìjiān (什翼犍) gave his daughter in marriage to Yàn (燕),
and the Yàn (燕) people also gave their daughter in marriage to him.
11 In the twelfth month,
on the wùwǔ day, the first day of the month,
there was a solar eclipse.
12 Yú Xī (庾希) retreated from Xiàpī (下邳) to Shānyáng (山陽),
and Yuán Zhēn (袁真) retreated from Rǔnán (汝南) to Shòuyáng (壽陽).
As the Luòyáng (洛陽) troops had disbanded and retreated,
the Yàn (燕) army soon arrived again.
The 1st year of Xīngníng (興寧) (guǐhài, 363)
1 In spring,
in the second month,
on the jǐhài day,
a general amnesty was proclaimed,
and the reign era was changed.
2 In the third month,
on the rényín day,
Grand Empress Dowager Zhōu (周) of the Imperial Family passed away at her residence in Lángyé (琅邪).
On the guǐmǎo day,
the Emperor went to the residence to observe mourning rites,
and an edict was issued for Sītú (司徒) Kuaìjī Wáng Yù (會稽王昱) to oversee all internal and external affairs.
The Emperor wished to observe three years of mourning for the Grand Empress Dowager,
but Púshè (僕射) Jiāng Pìn (江虨) memorialized:
"According to the rites,
one should observe sìmá (緦麻) mourning."
He also wished to reduce the mourning to one year,
but Pìn (虨) said:
"Suppressing private feelings
is for showing reverence to ancestors."
So he observed sìmá (緦麻) mourning.
The Zhōu Lǐ (周禮) states: "The King observes sǐ (緦) for feudal lords,
wearing coarse hemp with a cap and adding a cord."
Also,
according to the rites,
one who is adopted as heir becomes a son to the adopter,
therefore one observes three years of zhǎncuaī (斬衰) mourning for the adopter,
and reduces mourning for one's birth parents to one year.
Pìn (虨) believed that sǐ (緦) mourning should be observed
because the Emperor became heir to the senior branch of the imperial clan,
thus Lady Zhōu (周) was the mother of Lángyé (琅邪),
and should be mourned with the rites for feudal lords.
Yàn (厭),
yè in pūyè fān.
Yán (嚴),
means zūn (尊).
3 In summer,
in the fourth month,
Yàn (燕) General of Tranquilizing the East Mùróng Zhōng (慕容忠) attacked Liú Yuǎn (劉遠), Administrator of Xíngyáng (滎陽),
who fled to Lǔyáng (魯陽).
4 In the fifth month,

Huán Wēn (桓溫), General-in-Chief of the Western Expedition, was additionally granted Shìzhōng (侍中), Dàsīmǎ (大司馬), Commander-in-Chief of all armies internal and external, and Recording Secretary of the Department of State Affairs,
and provisionally granted the yellow battle-axe.
Wēn (溫) appointed Wáng Tǎnzhī (王坦之), Administrator of the Pacifying Army, as his Chief Clerk.
Tǎnzhī (坦之) was
the son of Shùzhī (述之).
He also appointed Xī Chāo (郗超), clerk of the Western Expedition, as his Aide,
and Wáng Xún (王珣) as his Head Secretary,
consulting with both of them on every matter.
Within the mansion, a saying circulated:
"Bearded Aide,
short Head Secretary,"
because Chāo (超) had a long beard and Xún (珣) was short.
Yuàn (掾),
juàn in yújuàn fān.
Xī (郗),
chǐ in chǒuzhī fān.
"Capable of making the Duke angry."
Wēn (溫) had a lofty and arrogant spirit,
rarely deferring to anyone,
but when speaking with Chāo (超), he often claimed he could not fathom him,
and treated him with great respect;
Chāo (超) also deeply cultivated their relationship.
Xún (珣) was
the grandson of Dǎo (導);
he and Xiè Xuán (謝玄) were both clerks under Wēn (溫),
who valued both of them highly.
He said:
"Xiè Yuàn (謝掾) will certainly bear a general's banner and staff at forty,
and Wáng Yuàn (王掾) will become a high-ranking official
— neither are ordinary talents."
Xuán (玄) was
the son of Yì (奕).
In the second year of Shēngpíng (升平),
Xiè Yì (謝奕) died.
5 Yuán Zhēn (袁真), General of the Western Central Army, was appointed Commander of military affairs for Sī, Jì, and Bìng (司、冀、幷) three provinces,
and Yú Xī (庾希), General of the Northern Central Army, was appointed Commander of military affairs for Qīngzhōu (青州).
6 On the guǐmǎo day,
the Yàn (燕) people captured Mìchéng (密城).
Mìxiàn (密縣),
during the Former Hàn (漢), belonged to Hénán Jùn (河南郡);
during the Latter Hàn (漢) and Jìn (晉), it belonged to Xíngyáng Jùn (滎陽郡).
7 In autumn,
in the eighth month,
a comet appeared in Jiǎo (角) and Kàng (亢).
Jiǎo (角)
has two stars;
Kàng (亢)
has four stars.
The Jìn Tiānwén Zhì (晉天文志) states: "Jiǎo (角), Kàng (亢), Dǐ (氐)
correspond to Zhèng (鄭) and Yǎnzhōu (兗州)."
Bèi (孛),
nèi in pū nèi fān.
Kàng (亢),
láng in jū láng fān.
8 Zhāng Xuánjìng's (張玄靚) paternal grandmother Lady Mǎ (馬) died,
and his concubine mother Lady Guō (郭) was honored as Grand Empress Dowager.
Lady Guō (郭), seeing that Zhāng Tiānxī (張天錫) wielded dictatorial power,
conspired with minister Zhāng Qīn (張欽) and others to execute him;
the plot was revealed,
and Qīn (欽) and the others all died.
Xuánjìng (玄靚) was afraid
and offered his position to Tiānxī (天錫);
Tiānxī (天錫) did not accept.
Right General Liú Sù (劉肅) and others advised Tiānxī (天錫) to enthrone himself.
In the intercalary month,
Tiānxī (天錫) sent Sù (肅) and others to lead soldiers into the palace at night,
where they assassinated Xuánjìng (玄靚),
and publicly declared that he had died suddenly,
bestowing upon him the posthumous title Chōng Gōng (沖公).
Tiānxī (天錫) proclaimed himself Commissioner with Imperial Credentials, Grand Commander, Grand General, Administrator of Liángzhōu (涼州), and Duke of Xīpíng (西平),
being eighteen years old at the time.
He honored his mother, Lady Liú (劉) the Beautiful Consort, as Grand Empress Dowager.
He dispatched his Sīmǎ (司馬) Lún Qiān (綸騫) to present a memorial to Jiànkāng (建康) to request investiture.
Lún (綸)
is a surname.
The Xìngpǔ (姓譜) states: "Wèi Zhì (魏志): Sūn Wénduān's (孫文端) minister Lún Zhí (綸直)."
In the third year of Mùdì (穆帝)'s Yǒnghé (永和) era,
an envoy returned to Liángzhōu (涼州),
and only now returned.
9 On the guǐhài day,
a general amnesty was proclaimed.
10 In winter,
in the tenth month,
Yàn (燕) General Guarding the South Mùróng Chén (慕容塵) attacked Yuán Pī (袁披), Administrator of Chénliú (陳留), at Chángpíng (長平);
Chángpíng Xiàn (長平縣),
during the Former Hàn (漢), belonged to Rǔnán Jùn (汝南郡);
during the Latter Hàn (漢) and Jìn (晉), it belonged to Chén Jùn (陳郡).
Xián (賢) said: "The old city of Chángpíng (長平)
is now in the northwest of Wǎnqiū Xiàn (宛丘縣) in Chénzhōu (陳州)."
He conquered it.
The Kǎoyì (考異) states: The Yàn Shū (燕書) writes
"Zhū Lí (朱黎)."
This account follows the Jìn Dìjì (晉帝紀).
11 Dài (代) Prince Shíyìjiān (什翼犍) attacked Gāochē (高車),
greatly defeating them.
Gāochē (高車)
are the same as the Chìlè (敕勒);
their custom was to ride high-wheeled carts,
hence they were also called the Gāochē (高車) tribe.
Lǐ Yánshòu (李延壽) said: "Gāochē (高車)
are probably a remnant branch of the ancient Chìdí (赤狄)."
Initially called
"Dílì (狄歷),"
northerners called them Gāochē Dīnglíng (高車丁零).
Their migrations followed water and grass,
they wore furs and ate meat,
the same as the Rouran (柔然),
only their cart wheels were high and large,
with a great many spokes.
Jiān (犍),
yán in jū yán fān.
More than a million head of horses, cattle, and sheep were captured.
12 Huán Chōng (桓沖), General Subduing the Barbarians, was appointed Inspector of Jiāngzhōu (江州).
In the eleventh month,
Zhāng Jùn (張駿), a former general of Yáo Xiāng (姚襄), killed Zhào Pí (趙毗), Supervisor of Jiāngzhōu (江州),
and led his followers in rebellion to the north;
Chōng (沖) campaigned against and beheaded him.
When Huán Wēn (桓溫) defeated Yáo Xiāng (姚襄),
he captured Xiāng's (襄) generals Zhāng Jùn (張駿), Yáng Níng (楊凝), and others,
and resettled them in Xúnyáng (尋陽).
1 In spring,
in the first month,
on the bǐngchén day,
Yàn (燕) proclaimed a general amnesty.
2 In the second month,
Yàn (燕) Grand Tutor Píng (評) and General of the Dragon Soaring Lǐ Hóng (李洪) seized territory in Hénán (河南).
3 In the third month,
on the day Gēngxū (朔),
a grand census of households was conducted.
It was ordered that local land be used as the basis [for registration],
so that gentry and commoners from the northwest who had temporarily settled in the southeast
would be registered as permanent residents based on their local land.
The character 斷 (duàn) [is explained by]
丁亂 (dīngluàn) reversed.
This was called the Gēngxū Regulation.
4 The Emperor believed the words of a fangshi (方士),
abstaining from grains and taking medicine in pursuit of immortality.
Attendant-in-ordinary Gāo Sōng (高崧) admonished him, saying:
"This is not something suitable for one who commands ten thousand chariots to do;
Your Majesty's current undertaking
is truly like an eclipse of the sun or moon."
The Analects say: Zǐgòng (子貢) said: "When a jūnzi (君子) makes a mistake,
it is like an eclipse of the sun or moon."
On the day Xīnwèi,
the Emperor's illness, induced by the medicine, flared up,
making him unable to personally attend to all affairs of state.
Empress Dowager Chǔ (褚) again presided over court and assumed regency.
Emperor Mù (穆) had succeeded to the throne in his tender youth,
and Empress Dowager Chǔ had presided over court and issued decrees.
In the first year of Shēngpíng,
the Emperor underwent the capping ceremony,
and the Empress Dowager returned governance to him.
Although the Emperor was of age when he ascended the throne,
his illness prevented him from personally governing,
so the Empress Dowager again presided over court.
The character 復 (fù) [is explained by]
扶又 (fúyòu) reversed.
The character 朝 (cháo) [is explained by]
直遙 (zhíyáo) reversed.
5 In summer,
in the fourth month,
on the day Jiǎchén,
Yān's Lǐ Hóng (李洪) attacked Xǔchāng (許昌) and Rǔnán (汝南),
defeating the Jìn (晉) forces at Xuánhù (懸瓠).
The Administrator of Yǐngchuān (潁川), Lǐ Fú (李福), was killed in battle.
The Administrator of Rǔnán, Zhū Bīn (朱斌), fled to Shòuchūn (壽春).
The Administrator of Chénjùn (陳郡), Zhū Fǔ (朱輔), retreated to secure Péngchéng (彭城).
Grand Marshal Huán Wēn (桓溫) dispatched Western Central Protector-General Yuán Zhēn (袁真) and others to resist them.
In the fifth month of the previous year,
Huán Wēn was granted the titles of Dūd (督), Lù (錄), and Jiǎhuángyuè (假黃鉞).
At this point, only his official titles were recorded, not his surname,
indicating that "thick ice was approaching."
The Yān (燕) people then captured Xǔchāng, Rǔnán, and Chénjùn,
relocating over ten thousand households to Yōu (幽) and Jì (冀) provinces.
They dispatched the General Who Guards the South, Mùróng Chén (慕容塵), to garrison Xǔchāng.
6 In the fifth month,
on the day Wùchén,
Wáng Shù (王述), the Inspector of Yángzhōu (揚州), was appointed Shàngshūlìng (尚書令).
Grand Marshal Huán Wēn was further granted the titles of Yángzhōu Mù (揚州牧) and Lùshàngshūshì (錄尚書事).
On the day Rénshēn,
an attendant was sent to summon Huán Wēn to participate in court affairs;
Wēn declined and did not come.
Whenever Wáng Shù received an official position,
he would not make empty gestures of refusal;
what he truly declined, he would not accept.
When he was appointed Shàngshūlìng,
his son, Tǎnzhī (坦之), said to Shù:
"According to custom, one should decline."
Shù said:
"Do you think I am incompetent?"
Tǎnzhī said:
"Not so,
but modesty and yielding are inherently good things."
Shù said:
"Since you say I am competent,
why should I decline again!
People say you are better than me;
it seems you are definitely not."
7 In the sixth month,
Qín (秦) King Jiān (堅) dispatched the Grand Messenger to appoint Zhāng Tiānxī (張天錫) as Grand General, Inspector of Liángzhōu (涼州), and Duke of Xīpíng (西平).
8 In autumn,
in the seventh month,
on the day Dīngmǎo,
an imperial edict again summoned Grand Marshal Huán Wēn to court.
In the eighth month,
Wēn arrived at Zhěqí (赭圻).
An edict ordered Shàngshū Chē Guàn (車灌) to stop him.
Wēn then built a city at Zhěqí and resided there.
Zhěqí was within Xuānchéng (宣城) prefecture.
According to the Nánshǐ (南史),
Shěn Yōuzhī (沈攸之) advanced from Hǔlánzhōu (虎檻洲) to attack Zhěqí,
while Táo Liàng (陶亮) and others led troops from Quètou (鵲頭) to relieve it.
Liú Xù (劉昫) said: "Xuānzhōu's Nánlíng (南陵) county was the land of Hàn's Chūngǔ (春穀) county.
The Liáng (梁) dynasty established Nánlíng county, with its former seat in Zhěqí city.
In the fourth year of Táng (唐) Cháng'ān,
the seat was moved to Qīngyáng (青陽) city."
According to Wēn's memorial, "Zhěqí city in Chūngǔ county
is on the east bank of the Jiāng (江),
about twenty lǐ (里) upstream from Dāngrúxūkǒu (當濡須口),
three hundred thirty lǐ from Jiànkāng (建康) Palace.
To its south is Shēnglǐ (聲里),
and to its north is Gāo'ān Shù (高安戍)."
The character 車 (chē) [is explained by]
昌遮 (chāngzhē) reversed.
The character 圻 (qí) [is explained by]
渠希 (qúxī) reversed.
Nèilù (內錄)
refers to Lùshàngshūshì (錄尚書事).
9 Qín's Duke of Rǔnán, Téng (騰), plotted rebellion
and was executed.
Téng
was the younger brother of Qín ruler Shēng (生).
At this time,
Shēng's younger brother, Duke of Jìn (晉), Liǔ (柳), and five others still remained.
Wáng Měng (王猛) spoke to Jiān (堅), saying:
"If the five dukes are not removed,
they will eventually become a problem."
Jiān did not agree.
This laid the groundwork for Liǔ and others to rebel later.
The character 去 (qù) [is explained by]
羌呂 (qiānglǚ) reversed.
10 Yān Attendant-in-ordinary Mùyú Lóng (慕輿龍) arrived at Lóngchéng (龍城),
relocating the ancestral temples and all remaining officials to Yè (鄴).
11 Yān Grand Tutor Kè (恪) was about to capture Luòyáng (洛陽).
The Kǎoyì (考異) states: The Emperor's Annals say:
"Mùróng Wěi (慕容暐) attacked Luòyáng."
It was previously stated
that "Fú Jiān's (苻堅) separate forces invaded Hénán (河南)."
However, the following year,
Kè captured Luòyáng, while Jiān's personal generals were preparing for Tóngguān (潼關).
This means they did not dare to contend with Yān for Hénán.
The biography of Jiān in the Shíliù Guó Chūnqiū (十六國春秋) also has no record of this action;
the Emperor's Annals are probably mistaken.
All nearby fortified settlements submitted to him.
So he sent Sīmǎ Yuè Xī (司馬悅希) to garrison Méngjīn (盟津),
and Inspector of Yùzhōu (豫州) Sūn Xīng (孫興) to garrison Chénggāo (成皋).
Earlier,
Shěn Chōng's (沈充) son, Jìng (勁),
whose father died in a rebellion (see volume 93, Emperor Míng's (明) Tàiníng (太寧) second year),
was over thirty years old
and unable to enter officialdom due to his family's criminal record.
Wúxīng (吳興) Administrator Wáng Húzhī (王胡之), then Inspector of Sīzhōu (司州),
submitted a memorial praising Jìng's talent and conduct,
requesting the lifting of the prohibition on his service and his participation in the affairs of his yamen.
The court granted it.
However, Húzhī became ill
and did not take up his post.
When the Yān people threatened Luòyáng,
General of the Champion Army Chén Yòu (陳祐) defended it,
with a force of no more than two thousand.
Jìng personally requested to be assigned to Yòu to contribute his efforts.
An edict appointed Jìng as Chief Clerk to the General of the Champion Army,
ordering him to recruit brave men himself, and he obtained over a thousand to go with him.
Jìng repeatedly attacked the Yān forces with a small number,
crushing and defeating them.
However, Luòyáng ran out of provisions and aid was cut off.
Yòu, judging that he could not hold out,
then, under the pretext of relieving Xǔchāng,
in the ninth month,
left Jìng with five hundred men to defend Luòyáng,
while Yòu led his forces eastward.
Jìng rejoiced, saying:
"My ambition is to sacrifice my life."
The Analects say: Zǐzhāng (子張) said: "When one sees danger, one sacrifices one's life."
Zhūzǐ (朱子) said: "To sacrifice one's life
means to wholly commit one's life,
similar to saying to 'give one's life'."
Yòu heard that Xǔchāng had already fallen
and then fled to Xīnchéng (新城).
Yān's Yuè Xī led his troops to plunder various cities in Hénán,
taking them all.
12 Qín King Jiān ordered that each ducal state establish three ministers (Qīng, 卿).
The Jìn system: A princely state establishes a Lángzhōnglìng (郎中令), Zhōngwèi (中尉), and Dànóng (大農) as the three ministers.
Qín followed this system.
For them alone, a Lángzhōnglìng was established.
Wealthy merchants like Zhào Duō (趙掇) and others displayed extravagant carriages and clothing,
and the dukes competed to appoint them as ministers.
Yellow Gate Attendant Shìláng (侍郎) Chéng Xiàn (程憲) of Āndìng (安定)
requested that they be punished.
Jiān then issued an edict stating:
"Originally, I intended for the dukes to select outstanding scholars,
but instead, they have become so vulgar and excessive!
It is fitting for the relevant authorities to investigate and examine.
Those who have appointed the wrong people
shall all have their ranks demoted to marquis.
From now on, all state officials shall be entrusted to the Qún Héng (銓衡).
Qún Héng
refers to the Shàngshū of the Ministry of Personnel.
They are not allowed to ride in carriages or on horseback.
Within one hundred lǐ of the capital,
merchants, artisans, and servants
are not permitted to wear gold, silver, brocade, or embroidery.
Those who violate this shall be executed in the marketplace."
Thereupon, the five dukes of Píngyáng (平陽), Píngchāng (平昌), Jiǔjiāng (九江), Chénliú (陳留), and Ānlè (安樂) all had their ranks demoted to marquis.
1 In spring,
in the first month,
on the day Gēngshēn,
Empress Wáng (王) passed away.
2 Liú Wèichén (劉衞辰) again rebelled against Dài (代).
Liú Wèichén (劉衞辰) submitted to Dài (代).
See the fifth year of Shàngpíng (上升平).
Fù (復).
Read as fú yòu.
They attacked and drove him away.
Shíyìjiān (什翼犍) was generous and magnanimous.
The Lángzhōnglìng (郎中令) Xǔ Qiān (許謙) stole two bolts of silk.
Shíyìjiān (什翼犍) knew but concealed it.
According to the Běishǐ (北史),
it was the custom in the Dài (代) kingdom to have no silk or cloth.
Since Qiān (謙) stole it,
his crime was unforgivable.
However, Shíyìjiān (什翼犍) was able to tolerate it.
Therefore, the historian used this to illustrate one aspect of his generosity.
"I cannot bear to look at Qiān's (謙) face.
If Qiān (謙) feels ashamed and commits suicide,
that would be me killing a worthy man for the sake of property."
He once suppressed rebels in the west.
A stray arrow hit him in the eye.
Later, when the archer was captured,
his attendants wanted to dismember him.
Shíyìjiān (什翼犍) said:
"They were just fighting for their respective lords.
What crime have they committed?"
So, he released him.
3 The Grand Marshal Wēn (溫) moved his garrison to Gūshú (姑孰).
Wēn (溫) again moved eastward from Zhèqí (赭圻) to garrison Gūshú (姑孰).
On the day Yǐwèi (乙未),
his younger brother, the Right General Huò (豁), was made Supervisor of the Military Affairs of Jīngzhōu's (荊州) and Yángzhōu's (揚州) Yìchéng (義城) and Yōngzhōu's (雍州) Jīngzhào (京兆) areas,
and also appointed Governor of Jīngzhōu (荊州).
Yìchéng (義城) Commandery was established in Xiāngyáng (襄陽).
Xiāngyáng (襄陽) Commandery belonged to Jīngzhōu (荊州).
However, Yìchéng (義城) Commandery included Píng'ē (平阿) and Xiàcài (下蔡) in Yángzhōu's (揚州) Huáinán (淮南).
This is probably because Huán Xuān (桓宣) first retreated with Zǔ Yuē (祖約) to Huáinán (淮南),
then garrisoned Xiāngyáng (襄陽).
Táo Kǎn (陶侃) established Yìchéng (義成) Commandery in Gǔchéng (穀城) using his Huáinán (淮南) troops.
It probably means that there were people from Yángzhōu (揚州) and also Yángzhōu (揚州) provisional counties were established in Gǔchéng (穀城).
Gǔchéng (穀城)
was a place under the jurisdiction of Jīngzhōu (荊州).
Hence it is called Yìchéng (義成) of Jīngzhōu (荊州) and Yángzhōu (揚州).
The name Yìchéng (義成)
means "army formed by righteousness" (以義成軍),
and thus the commandery was named.
Later generations
added
the radical
"tǔ" (土) next to the character "chéng" (成),
thus losing the original meaning of the commandery's establishment.
Jīngzhào (京兆) Commandery belonged to Yōngzhōu (雍州) and was also temporarily established in Xiāngyáng (襄陽) at that time.
Yōng (雍).
Read as yú yòng.
Originally,
Chōng (沖) was the Governor of Jiāngzhōu (江州),
and also Administrator of Xīyáng (西陽) and Qiáo (譙) Commanderies.
Now he was additionally made Supervisor of Jiāngxià (江夏) and Suí (隨) Commanderies of Jīngzhōu (荊州), and Rǔnán (汝南), Xīyáng (西陽), Xīncài (新蔡), and Yǐngchuān (潁川) Commanderies of Yùzhōu (豫州),
a total of six commanderies,
making eight commanderies including Xúnyáng (尋陽), which he already governed.
Jiān (監).
Read as gōng xián.
The Kǎoyì (考異) says: The Dìjì (帝紀) states:
"Chōng (沖) was appointed Southern Man (蠻) Commander."
According to historical records, only Jīngzhōu (荊州) on the left bank of the Yangtze River governed the Southern Man (蠻).
There is no mention in Chōng's (沖) biography either.
Perhaps the Dìjì (帝紀) confused it with Huán Huò (桓豁).
This information is not accepted here.
Sītú Yù (司徒昱), hearing that Chén Yòu (陳祐) had abandoned Luòyáng (洛陽),
met with Grand Marshal Wēn (溫) at Lièzhōu (洌洲).
There is now Lièshān (洌山) in the Jiāng (江) River at Gūshú (姑孰),
which is that place.
On the day Bǐngshēn (丙申),
the Emperor died in the Xītáng (西堂) at the age of twenty-five.
Xītáng (西堂)
was the West Hall of the Tàijí (太極) Palace.
The Tàijí (太極) Palace in Jiànkāng (建康) had East and West Halls.
The East Hall was for meeting officials,
and the West Hall was a place for resting.
The Emperor had no heir.
On the day Dīngyǒu (丁酉),
the Empress Dowager issued an edict to enthrone the King of Lángyá (琅邪), Yì (奕), to succeed to the great lineage.
Yì (弈)
should be written as Yì (奕).
On this day,
he ascended the imperial throne and issued a general amnesty.
4 Qín (秦) issued a general amnesty and changed the era name to Jiànyuán (建元).
5 The Grand Tutor Kè (恪) of Yān (燕) and King Chuí (垂) of Wú (吳) together attacked Luòyáng (洛陽).
Kè (恪) said to his generals:
"You always complain that I do not attack.
Now Luòyáng (洛陽) has high walls but weak troops, it is easy to capture.
Do not again be fearful, timid, or lazy!"
So, they attacked it.
In the third month,
they captured it and arrested General Yángwǔ (揚武) Shěn Jìn (沈勁).
Jìn (勁) was composed and self-possessed.
Kè (恪) intended to pardon him.
The Commander of the Central Army, Mùyú Qián (慕輿虔), said:
"Although Jìn (勁) is an exceptional person,
judging by his ambition and demeanor,
he will never serve others.
If we pardon him now,
he will certainly become a future trouble."
So, they killed him.
Kè (恪) expanded his territory to Xiáo (崤) and Miǎn (澠).
Xiáo (崤) is Xiáogǔ (崤谷).
Miǎn (澠) is Miǎnchí (澠池).
Miǎn (澠).
Read as mí yǎn.
King Jiān (堅) of Qín (秦) personally led his troops to garrison Shǎnchéng (陝城) to prepare for them.
The Yān (燕) people appointed Left Central Secretariat Director Mùróng Zhù (慕容筑) as Governor of Luòzhōu (洛州),
garrisoned at Jīnyǒng (金墉).

King Chuí (垂) of Wú (吳) was appointed Supreme Commander of the Military Affairs of the ten prefectures of Jīng (荊), Yáng (揚), Luò (洛), Xú (徐), Yǎn (兗), Yù (豫), Yōng (雍), Yì (益), Liáng (涼), and Qín (秦), General Who Conquers the South, and Governor of Jīngzhōu (荊州),
with ten thousand troops, garrisoned at Lǔyáng (魯陽).
Grand Tutor Kè (恪) returned to Yè (鄴)
and said to his subordinates:
"When I pacified Guǎnggù (廣固) before,
I failed to save Pìlǘ Wèi (辟閭蔚).
See Emperor Mù's (穆) twelfth year of Yǒnghé (永和) in the previous volume.
I allowed Shěn Jìn (沈勁) to be killed.
Although neither was my original intention,
as the commander-in-chief,
I truly feel ashamed before all under Heaven."
The imperial court praised Jìn's (勁) loyalty
and posthumously appointed him Governor of Dōngyáng (東陽).
Your servant Guāng (光) says: Shěn Jìn (沈勁) can be called a filial son!
Ashamed of his father's evil deeds,
he died to cleanse them,
transforming a vicious and rebellious family into a loyal and righteous one.
The Yìjīng (易經) says:
"Rectifying the decay of the father
brings renown."
This is the hexagram Gǔ (蠱), line six-five of the Yìjīng (易經).
The Xiàng (象) says: Rectifying the father brings renown,
sustained by virtue.
"You should moreover cover up the faults of your predecessors,
with loyalty and filial piety."
See the Shàngshū (尚書).
6 As a general, Grand Tutor Kè (恪)
did not rely on strictness and authority,
but exclusively used kindness and trust.
In handling his soldiers, he focused on the main principles,
not on harsh regulations,
allowing everyone to feel at ease.
In peacetime, the camp was loose and relaxed,
seeming easily violated.
However, the defenses were strict and tight,
so when an enemy arrived, none could approach.
Therefore, he never suffered defeat.
7 On the day Rénshēn (壬申),
Emperor Āi (哀) and Empress Jìng (靜) were buried at Ānpínglíng (安平陵).
Empress Wáng (王) was posthumously named Jìng (靜).
The Jìnshū (晉書) writes
"Jìng" (靖).
8 Summer.
In the fourth month, on the day Rénwǔ (壬午),
the Grand Commandant of Yān (燕), Wǔpíngkuāng Duke Fēng Yì (武平匡公封奕), died.
The Shìfǎ (諡法) states: "One with a firm heart and great magnanimity is called Kuāng (匡)."
The Imperial Attendant and Grand Master of Glorious Happiness Huángfǔ Zhēn (皇甫真) was appointed Minister of Works
and concurrently Supervisor of the Central Secretariat.
Mù (騖) had served four courts:
Mùróng Huì (慕容廆), Mùróng Huǎng (慕容皝), Mùróng Jùn (慕容儁), and Mùróng Wěi (慕容暐).
Cháo (朝).
Read as zhí yáo.
From Grand Tutor Kè (恪) downwards, all paid homage to him.
Yet Mù (騖) was humble, respectful, and earnest,
even more so than in his youth.
He disciplined his children and grandchildren,
and though many of them held high positions (朱紫羅列),
none dared to violate his rules and standards.
Fēng Yì (封奕), serving Yān (燕),
also served four courts,
and his efforts surpassed those of Yáng Mù (陽騖), and his descendants' eminence and wealth also surpassed those of the Yáng (陽) clan.
Was Yì's (奕) humble virtue perhaps inferior to Mù's (騖)?
Or perhaps the historian wrote based on the Yáng (陽) clan's family records,
while the Fēng (封) clan's records were lacking?
Shào (少).
Read as shí zhào.
9 In the sixth month,
on the day *wùzǐ*,
Zhōu Fǔ (周撫), Governor (cìshǐ 刺史) of Yìzhōu (益州) and Duke Xiāng of Jiànchéng (建城襄公), passed away.
According to the rules for posthumous names: "One who achieves merit through their deeds is called Xiāng."
In the third year of the Yǒnghé (永和) era of Emperor Mù (穆帝) (347 CE),
Huán Wēn (桓溫) pacified Shǔ (蜀),
and left Fǔ (撫) to guard it.
Only nineteen years had passed by this time.
Before Jìn (晉) acquired Shǔ (蜀),
the office of Governor of Yìzhōu (益州) was established in Bādōng (巴東),
and Fǔ (撫) had already served as Governor;
once Wēn (溫) had conquered Shǔ (蜀),
Fǔ (撫) remained Governor of Yìzhōu (益州),
garrisoned at Péngmó (彭模).
The statement that he was in Yìzhōu (益州) for more than thirty years
is due to the historians combining the number of years he guarded Bādōng (巴東) and Péngmó (彭模).
An imperial edict appointed his son, Chǔ (楚), Prefect (tàishǒu 太守) of Qiánwéi (犍為), to succeed him.
10 In autumn,
the seventh month,
on the day *jǐyǒu*,
Yù (昱), Prince of Kuàijī (會稽), was reinstated as Prince of Lángyá (琅邪).
Emperor Yuán (元帝) had made Yù (昱) Prince of Lángyá (琅邪)
to maintain the sacrifices for Prince Gōng (恭王).
In the first year of the Xiánhé (咸和) era of Emperor Chéng (成帝) (326 CE),
the Prince's birth mother, Lady Zhèng (鄭夫人), died.
The Prince, mourning, requested to observe the mourning rites,
and was moved again to be enfeoffed as Prince of Kuàijī (會稽).
Thereafter,
Emperor Kāng (康帝), Emperor Āi (哀帝), and the current emperor
all entered to inherit the great succession from Lángyá (琅邪).
Coincidentally,
*gōng* (工) is glossed as *wài fān* (外翻).
11 On the day *rénzǐ*,
Lady Yǔ (庾氏) was established as empress.
The empress
was the daughter of Bīng (冰).
12 On the day *jiǎshēn*,
Chāngmíng (昌明), the son of Yù (昱), Prince of Lángyá (琅邪), was established as Prince of Kuàijī (會稽);
Yù (昱) firmly declined,
and still referred to himself as Prince of Kuàijī (會稽).
13 Cáogǔ (曹轂), the Right Virtuous King (yòuxiánwáng 右賢王) of the Xiōngnú (匈奴), and Líu Wèichén (劉衞辰), the Left Virtuous King (zuǒxiánwáng 左賢王), both rebelled against Qín (秦).
Gǔ (轂) led a force of twenty thousand to raid Xìngchéng (杏城).
Qín Wáng Jiān (秦王堅) personally led an expedition to suppress them.
He ordered the Grand General of the Vanguard (wèidàjiàngjūn 衞大將軍), Lǐ Wēi (李威), and the Left Grand Mentor (zuǒpúshè 左僕射), Wáng Měng (王猛), to assist Crown Prince Hóng (宏) in guarding Cháng'ān (長安).
In the eighth month,
Jiān (堅) attacked Gǔ (轂),
defeated him,
and beheaded Gǔ's (轂) younger brother Huó (活).
Gǔ (轂) requested to surrender,
and six thousand households of his prominent figures were resettled in Cháng'ān (長安).
The General Who Establishes Awe (jiànjiéjiàngjūn 建節將軍), Dèng Qiāng (鄧羌), attacked Wèichén (衞辰),
and captured him at Mùgēn Shān (木根山).
Mùgēn Shān (木根山) is in Shuòfāng (朔方).
In the ninth month,
Jiān (堅) went to Shuòfāng (朔方)
to inspect and console the various Hú (胡) tribes.
In winter,
the tenth month,
Yòu (幼), General Who Conquers the North (zhēngběijiàngjūn 征北將軍) and Duke of Huáinán (淮南公), leading the forces from Xìngchéng (杏城), took advantage of the vulnerability to attack Cháng'ān (長安).
Lǐ Wēi (李威) attacked and beheaded him.
Yòu (幼)
was also the younger brother of the Qín (秦) ruler Shēng (生).
14 Tuōfà Chuíjīn (禿髮椎斤) of the Xiānbēi (鮮卑) passed away
at the age of one hundred and ten.
His son, Sīfùjiān (思復鞬), succeeded him in governing his people.
Chuíjīn (椎斤)
was the grandson of Wùwán (務丸), a paternal cousin of Shùjīnéng (樹機能).
Shùjīnéng (樹機能) caused chaos in Liángzhōu (涼州),
as seen in the Biography of Emperor Wǔ of Jìn (晉武帝紀).
*cóng* (從) is glossed as *cáiyòng fān* (才用翻).
15 Sīmǎ Xūn (司馬勳), Governor of Liángzhōu (梁州),
governed with cruelty and violence.
If his Chief Clerk (zhìzhōng 治中), Deputy (biéjià 別駕), or the powerful gentry of the province
spoke words that displeased him,
he would immediately execute them by decapitation on the spot,
or even personally shoot them to death.
He constantly harbored ambitions to control Shǔ (蜀),
but feared Zhōu Fǔ (周撫)
and dared not act.
When Fǔ (撫) died,
Xūn (勳) then raised an army and rebelled.
Yǒng Duān (雍端), the Deputy, and Wěi Cuì (隗粹), the Western Rong (Xīróng 西戎) Commander, strongly remonstrated.
The Western Rong Commander
was a subordinate official of the Western Rong Colonel (Xīróng Xiàowèi 西戎校尉).
*Yǒng* (雍) is glossed as *yúyòng fān* (於用翻).
*Wěi* (隗) is glossed as *wǔzuì fān* (五罪翻).
He proclaimed himself Governor (mù 牧) of Liáng (梁) and Yì (益) Provinces and Prince of Chéngdū (成都王).
In the eleventh month,
Xūn (勳) led his troops into Jiàngé (劍閣)
and attacked Fú (涪).
Guànqiū Wěi (毌丘暐), the Western Yi (Xīyí 西夷) Colonel, abandoned the city and fled.
Early in the Jìn (晉) dynasty, the Western Yi Colonel (Xīyí Xiàowèi 西夷校尉) was established,
governing from Wénshān (汶山).
Now it was probably governing from Fúchéng (涪城).
*Fú* (涪)
is pronounced *fú*.
On the day *yǐmǎo*,
Zhōu Chǔ (周楚), Governor of Yìzhōu (益州), was besieged in Chéngdū (成都).

The Grand Marshal (dàsīmǎ 大司馬), Wēn (溫), memorialized to appoint Zhū Xù (朱序) of Yìyáng (義陽), Prince of Jiāngxià (江夏), and General Who Inspires Awe (yīngyángjiàngjūn 鷹揚將軍), as Commander of the Punitive Expedition (zhēngtǎodūhù 征討都護) to rescue him.
16 Qín Wáng Jiān (秦王堅) returned to Cháng'ān (長安).
He appointed Lǐ Wēi (李威) as Grand Protector (tàiwèi 太尉)
and added the title Attendant-in-ordinary (shìzhōng 侍中).
He made Cáogǔ (曹轂) Duke of Yànmén (鴈門公)
and Líu Wèichén (劉衞辰) Duke of Xiàyáng (夏陽公),
each to command his own tribe.
17 In the twelfth month,
on the day *wùxū*,
Wáng Biāozhī (王彪之), Minister (shàngshū 尚書), was appointed Grand Mentor (púshè 僕射).
The Duke of Hǎixī (海西公), the aforementioned
name Yì (奕),
courtesy name Yánlíng (延齡),
was the younger brother of Emperor Āi's (哀帝) mother.
In the eighth year of Xiánkāng (咸康) (342 CE),
he was enfeoffed as Prince of Dōnghǎi (東海王).
In the fifth year of Shēngpíng (升平) of Emperor Mù (穆帝) (361 CE),
he was re-enfeoffed as Prince of Lángyá (琅邪).
After his enthronement,
Huán Wēn (桓溫) deposed him as Duke of Hǎixī (海西公).
The first year of Tàihé (太和) (丙寅, 366 CE)
1 In spring,
the third month,
Huán Huò (桓豁), Governor of Jīngzhōu (荊州), ordered the Area Commander (dūhù 督護) Huán Pí (桓羆) to attack Nánzhèng (南鄭)
to suppress Sīmǎ Xūn (司馬勳).
2 Kè (恪), Grand Tutor (tàizǎi 太宰) and Grand Marshal (dàsīmǎ 大司馬) of Yān (燕), and Píng (評), Grand Preceptor (tàifù 太傅) and Minister of Works (sītú 司徒),
bowed their heads and returned their authority,
submitting their seals and ribbons,
requesting to return to their residences.
The ruler of Yān (燕), Wěi (暐), did not permit it.
3 In summer,
the fifth month,
on the day *wùyín*,
Empress Yǔ (庾氏) passed away.
4 Zhū Xù (朱序) and Zhōu Chǔ (周楚) attacked Sīmǎ Xūn (司imǎ Xūn),
defeated him,
captured Xūn (勳) and his followers,
and sent them to the Grand Marshal (dàsīmǎ 大司馬), Wēn (溫);
Wēn (溫) had them all beheaded
and their heads sent to Jiànkāng (建康).
5 Shíyìjiān (什翼犍), Prince of Dài (代), dispatched his Left Chief Clerk (zuǒchángshǐ 左長史), Yān Fèng (燕鳳), to present tribute at the Qín (秦) border.
6 In autumn,
the seventh month,
on the day *guǐyǒu*,
Empress Xiào (孝皇后) was buried at Jìngpíng Líng (敬平陵).
Empress Yǔ (庾后)
was given the posthumous name Xiào (孝).

7 Wáng Měng (王猛), General Who Supports the State (fǔguójiàngjūn 輔國將軍) of Qín (秦), Yáng Ān (楊安), General of the Vanguard (qiánjiàngjūn 前將軍), and Yáo Cháng (姚萇), General Who Manifests Military Might (yángwǔjiàngjūn 揚武將軍), among others, led a force of twenty thousand to raid Jīngzhōu (荊州),
attacking Nánxiāng Jùn (南鄉郡).
Huán Huò (桓豁), Governor of Jīngzhōu (荊州), went to their rescue.
In the eighth month,
he encamped at Xīnyě (新野).
The Qín (秦) army plundered over ten thousand households from Ānyáng (安陽) and returned.
Ānyáng Xiàn (安陽縣)
belonged to Hànzhōng Jùn (漢中郡) during the Hàn (漢) dynasty.
Wèi (魏) established Wèixīng Jùn (魏興郡),
and Ānyáng (安陽) belonged to it;
Jìn (晉) abolished it.
If Qín (秦) attacked Nánxiāng (南鄉) and then retreated,
how could they penetrate deep into the mountainous obstacles
and plunder the people of Ānyáng (安陽)?
The *Zàijì* (載記) states
"Hànyáng" (漢陽),
referring to the north of the Hàn (漢) river.
It should follow the *Zàijì* (載記) to be correct.
8 In the ninth month,
on the day *jiǎwǔ*,
a partial amnesty was granted to Liáng (梁) and Yì (益) Provinces.
After Sīmǎ Xūn's (司馬勳) initial suppression,
his remaining partisans and those coerced were pardoned.
9 In winter,
the tenth month,
Yù (昱), Minister of Works (sītú 司徒), was promoted to Chancellor (chéngxiàng 丞相) and Director of the Secretariat (lùshàngshūshì 錄尚書事),
allowed to enter court without hurrying,
to be addressed by his title rather than his name when acclaimed,
and to wear swords and shoes when ascending the hall.
10 Zhāng Tiānxī (張天錫) sent an envoy to the Qín (秦) border
to announce the cessation of relations with Qín (秦).
Liáng (涼) had communicated with Qín (秦),
as seen in the preceding volume, the twelfth year of Yǒnghé (永和) of Emperor Mù (穆帝).
*shǐ* (使) is glossed as *shūlì fān* (疏吏翻).
11 Lì (厲), Prince of Xiàpī (下邳王) and General of the Protecting Army (fǔjūnjiàngjūn 撫軍將軍) of Yān (燕), raided Yǎnzhōu (兗州),
capturing several commanderies including Lǔ (魯) and Gāopíng (高平),
appointing administrators and then returning.
12 Initially,
Lǒngxī Lǐ Yǎn, with his commandery, surrendered to Qín.
Soon after, he re-established communication with Zhāng Tiānxī.
Lǐ Yǎn occupied Lǒngxī.
The matter began in volume 1 of Shàng Juǎn, Yǒnghé eleventh year.
Jiàng,
hù jiāng fān.
Fù,
fú yòu fān.
Qiāng Liǎn Qí, with four thousand households from Lüèyáng, rebelled against Qín
and declared himself a vassal of Yǎn.
Zàijì records
"Liǎn Qí".
Zhāng Tiānxī Zhuàn records
"Lián Qí".
Liǎn
is a Qiāng surname.
He severed ties with Qín and Liáng.
13 Nányáng Dūhù Zhào Yì, holding Wǎnchéng, surrendered to Yān.
The Grand Administrator Huán Dàn fled to secure Xīnyě.
The Yān people sent Nán Zhōnglángjiāng Zhào Pán from Lǔyáng to garrison Wǎn.
14 Xú and Yǎn Èr Zhōu Cìshǐ Yǔ Xī,
owing to his imperial in-law status,
and his brothers' prominence,
Dà Sīmǎ Wēn was wary of him.
1 In spring,
in the first month,
Yǔ Xī was dismissed from office
for his failure to rescue Lǔ and Gāopíng.
Kǎoyì states: According to Dìjì,
in this month,
Xī committed a crime
and fled to the sea.
However, according to his biography,
after the deposition of Empress Hǎixī,
Xī first fled to Hǎilíng,
and at this time, he was merely dismissed from office.
2 In the second month,
Yān Fǔjūn Jiāngjūn Xiàpí Wáng Lì and Zhènběi Jiāngjūn Yídū Wáng Huán attacked the Chìlè.
3 Qín Fǔguó Jiāngjūn Wáng Měng, Lǒngxī Tàishǒu Jiāng Héng, Nán'ān Tàishǒu Nán'ān Shào Qiāng, Yángwǔ Jiāngjūn Yáo Cháng, and others led a force of seventeen thousand to attack Liǎn Qí.
In the third month,
Zhāng Tiānxī sent Qián Jiāngjūn Yáng Yù towards Jīnchéng
and Zhēngdōng Jiāngjūn Cháng Jù towards Zuǒnán.
Zhāng Guǐ established Zuǒnán Xiàn,
which was subordinate to Jìn Xīng Jùn.
Kàn Yīn's Shísān Zhōuzhì states: One hundred and forty lǐ west of Shíchéng
is Zuǒnán Chéng.
The Hé River passes south of it
and is called Zuǒnán Jīn.
Yù,
pronounced yù.
Jìn Zhì states that Bǎitǔ Xiàn was subordinate to Jīnchéng Jùn.
Shísān Zhōuzhì: Sixty lǐ west of Zuǒnán Jīn is Bǎitǔ Chéng.
The city is north of the Great River
and serves as a crossing point along the river.
Cāngsōng Xiàn,
since the Hàn dynasty, belonged to Wǔwēi Jùn.
Later, Lü Guang of the Later Liáng changed its name to Chāngsōng Xiàn.
Jiàng,
jí liàng fān.
Liǎn Qí's tribes had previously belonged to Yáo Yìzhòng.
Hearing of Yáo Cháng's arrival,
they all surrendered.
Wáng Měng then captured Lüèyáng,
and Liǎn Qí fled to Báimǎ.
Báimǎ
is the territory of the Báimǎ Dī in Wǔdū.
4 In summer,
in the fourth month,
Yān Mùróng Chén raided Jìnglíng.
The Grand Administrator Luó Chóng defeated him.
5 Zhāng Tiānxī attacked Lǐ Yǎn's Dàxià and Wǔshǐ commanderies
and captured them.
Sòng Bái says: In the eighteenth year of Zhāng Jùn,
Dàxià Jùn was established by dividing Wǔshǐ, Xīngjìn, and Guǎngwǔ.
In the Táng dynasty, it was Dàxià Xiàn,
subordinate to Hézhōu.
Zhāng Jùn established Wǔshǐ Jùn with Dídào Xiàn.
Today's Xīzhōu is that area.
Xià,
hù yǎ fān.
Tiānxī advanced and stationed at Zuǒnán.
Yǎn was afraid,
retreated to defend Fúhǎn,
and sent his nephew Chún to apologize to Qín
and request aid.
Qín Wáng Jiān sent Qián Jiāngjūn Yáng Ān and Jiànwēi Jiāngjūn Wáng Fǔ with twenty thousand cavalry
to join Wáng Měng in rescuing Yǎn.
Měng sent Shào Qiāng to pursue Liǎn Qí.
Wáng Fǔ guarded Hóuhé,
and Jiāng Héng guarded Báishí.
Báishí Xiàn
belonged to Jīnchéng Jùn in the Former Hàn
and to Lǒngxī Jùn in the Later Hàn.
Xián says: Báishí Shān is in present-day Lánzhōu.
Sòng Bái says: Hézhōu Fènglín Xiàn
was originally the territory of Hàn Báishí Xiàn.
In the eighth year of Zhāng Jùn,
it was renamed Yǒnggù Xiàn.
Tiānxī sent Yáng Yù to counter-attack east of Fúhǎn.
Měng utterly defeated him,
capturing and beheading seventeen thousand heads,
and was stalemated with Tiānxī beneath the city.
Beneath Fúhǎn City.
Sent him away.
Měng sent a letter to Tiānxī, saying:
"I was ordered to rescue Yǎn,
not to fight with Liángzhōu.
Now I shall build deep walls and high ramparts,
awaiting further orders.
Prolonging the conflict,
I fear both families will be exhausted.
This is not a good strategy.
'Both families'
refers to Qín and Liáng.
If I take Yǎn and go east,
and you, General, move your people west,
would that not be acceptable?"
Tiānxī said to his generals:
"Měng's letter is thus.
I originally came to punish a rebel,
not to fight with Qín."
Thereupon, he led his troops back.
Lǐ Yǎn still did not admit the Qín army.
Wáng Měng, dressed in white, rode in a carriage,
with dozens of attendants,
and requested a meeting with Yǎn.
Yǎn opened the gate and welcomed him.
Before preparations could be made,
officers and soldiers followed in,
and Yǎn was seized.
Lìzhōng Jiāngjūn Péng Yuè was appointed Píngxī Jiāngjūn and Liángzhōu Cìshǐ,
garrisoning Fúhǎn.
Lìzhōng Jiāngjūn
was a title created by Fú Qín.
When Zhāng Tiānxī returned west,
Lǐ Yǎn's general Hè Zhūn advised Yǎn, saying:
"With your Lord's divine martial prowess
and the bravery of your officers and soldiers,
how can you surrender yourself to others?
Wáng Měng's isolated army has come a long way,
his soldiers are weary.
Moreover, since we requested aid,
he will certainly not be prepared.
If we attack him while he is off guard,
we can achieve our ambition."
Yǎn said:
"To seek aid from others to escape a calamity,
and then attack them once the calamity is averted—
what will the world say of me?
It is better to hold fast and wear them out.
They will eventually retreat on their own."
Měng reproached Yǎn for not immediately coming out to welcome him.
Yǎn informed him of Hè Zhūn's plan.
Měng beheaded Zhūn
and returned with Yǎn.
Upon arrival in Cháng'ān,
Jiān appointed Yǎn as Guānglùxūn
and bestowed upon him the title of Guī'ān Hóu.
6 Yān Tàiyuán Huánwáng Kè said to Yān Zhǔ Wěi:
The posthumous title rules state: 'Opening up territory and subjugating distant peoples is called Huán.'
"Wúwáng Chuí's
talent as a general and minister is ten times mine.
The late emperor, considering the order of seniority,
allowed me to precede him.
After my death,
I wish Your Majesty to entrust the entire state to Wúwáng."
In the fifth month,
on the day of Rénchén,
Kè was gravely ill.
Wěi personally visited him
and asked about posthumous matters.
Kè said:
"I have heard that there is no greater way to repay kindness than to recommend a worthy person.
Even if a worthy person is in humble circumstances,
they can still be a prime minister.
This refers to Yīn Wáng Gāozōng raising Fù Yuè from among bricklayers
and appointing him as prime minister.
Wúwáng is endowed with both civil and military talents,
second only to Guǎn and Xiāo.
This means his talent is inferior only to Guǎn Zhòng and Xiāo Hé.
The state can be secure.
Otherwise,
Qín and Jìn will surely harbor schemes of encroachment."
He finished speaking and then died.
Qín Wáng Jiān heard of Kè's death,
and secretly harbored plans to seize Yān.
Desiring to ascertain its feasibility,
he ordered the Xiōngnú, Cáo Gǔ, to send an envoy to Yān to offer tribute.
Cáo Gǔ
was the Right Worthy King of the Xiōngnú,
and had surrendered to Qín the previous year.
Cháo,
read Zhí Yáo.
Guō Biàn served as his deputy.
Jìn Wǔ Dì established the Western Regions Commandant at Cháng'ān;
Qín apparently inherited this.
The Chief Clerk
was one of its subordinates.
Kǎoyì says: In the eighth year of Jiànxī of Yān,
Huángfǔ Zhēn became Grand Commandant.
The Yān Shū, Zàijì, and Zhēn Zhuàn
all place Guō Biàn's arrival in Yān
after Zhēn became Grand Commandant.
Jìn Chūnqiū places it in the eighth month of the tenth year of Jiànxī.
I fear neither is correct,
hence it is appended under Cáo Gǔ's surrender to Qín.
Tiǎn was Cavalry Regular Attendant.
Huángfǔ Zhēn,
originally from Āndìng,
served in Yān.
Cóng,
read Cái Yòng.
Sǎn,
read Xī Dǎn.
Qí,
read Qí Jì.
He visited all the dukes and ministers,
and said to Zhēn:
"I am originally a Qín person;
my family was executed by Qín.
Therefore, I entrusted my life to King Cáo.
Your esteemed elder brother, the Regular Attendant, and your brothers Fèn and Fù, are all old acquaintances."
Zhēn angrily replied:
"Your subject has no dealings outside the borders.
How does this statement concern me!
You seem like a treacherous person;
are you perhaps using this as a false pretense?"
He reported it to Wěi,
requesting a thorough investigation;
Grand Tutor Píng did not permit it.
Biàn returned
and said to Jiān:
"The Yān court has no discipline in its governance;
it is indeed ripe for seizure.
Only Huángfǔ Zhēn
discerns the opportune moment and recognizes change."
Jiān said:
"With the populace of six provinces,
The six provinces are Yōu, Bìng, Jì, Sī, Yǎn, Yù.
Cáo Gǔ soon died.
Qín divided his tribe into two,
and had his two sons govern them separately,
calling them Eastern and Western Cáo.
Jiān divided Gǔ's tribe.
More than twenty thousand households west of Èrchéng
were placed under the command of Gǔ's eldest son, Xǐ;
more than twenty thousand households east of Èrchéng
were placed under the command of Gǔ's younger son, Yín.
7 Jīngzhōu Inspector Huán Huò and Jìnglíng Administrator Luó Chóng attacked Wǎn,
and captured it.
Zhào Yì fled;
Zhào Pán retreated to Lǔyáng.
Huò pursued and attacked Pán at Zhìchéng,
capturing him.
Zhì County,
since the Hàn dynasty, belonged to Nányáng Commandery.
Its location should be within the present-day Xiàngchéng County, Déngzhōu, Tángzhōu.
The Xīn Táng Zhì states: eighty *lǐ* north of Xiàngchéng County is Lǔyáng Pass.
8 Autumn,
seventh month.
Yān's Xiàpí Wáng Lì and others defeated the Chìlè,
capturing tens of thousands of horses and cattle.
Initially,
Lì's army passed through Dài territory,
encroaching upon their broomcorn millet fields.
Dài Wáng Shíyìjiān was angered.
Yān's General Who Pacifies the North, Duke Wǔqiáng, Ní, garrisoned Yōuzhōu troops in Yúnzhōng.
Eighth month.
Shíyìjiān attacked Yúnzhōng,
and Ní abandoned the city and fled.
Ní,
same as Ní.
9 Ninth month.
Xī Yīn, the Internal Historian of Kuàijī, was appointed Overall Governor of military affairs of Xú, Yǎn, Qīng, Yōu, and Jìnlíng of Yángzhōu, and Inspector of Xú and Yǎn provinces,
stationed at Jīngkǒu.
10When Qín's Huáinán Gōng Yòu rebelled,
the General Who Attacks the East, Inspector of Bìngzhōu, and Duke of Jìn, Liǔ,
and the General Who Attacks the West, Inspector of Qínzhōu, and Duke of Zhào, Shuāng,
had both conspired with him.
Qín Wáng Jiān, considering Shuāng
to be his full brother and closest kin,
and Liǔ
to be Jiàn's beloved son,
concealed the matter and did not investigate.
Liǔ and Shuāng further conspired to rebel with the General Who Guards the East, Inspector of Luòzhōu, and Duke of Wèi, Sōu,
and the General Who Pacifies the West, Inspector of Yōngzhōu, and Duke of Yān, Wǔ.
The Chief Clerk of the General Who Guards the East, Yáo Tiào of Nán'ān,
remonstrated, saying:
"Your Excellency, as a close relative like Zhōu and Shào,
you hold a provincial commission.
When the state is in difficulty,
you should exert your utmost to eliminate it,
let alone create difficulties yourself!"
Sōu did not listen.
When Jiān heard of this,
he summoned Liǔ and others to Cháng'ān.
Winter,
tenth month.
Liǔ occupied Púbǎn,
Shuāng occupied Shàngguī,
Sōu occupied Shǎnxī Chéng,
and Wǔ occupied Āndìng,
all raising troops in rebellion.
It was indeed as Wáng Měng had said.
"My treatment of you all
has been most benevolent.
Why do you rebel?
I will now cease the summons.
You should dismiss your troops,
each settle in your position,
and everything will be as before."
Each of them bit into a pear as a token of sincerity.
None of them complied.
Pear flesh is brittle and easily bitten through,
symbolizing that when relatives betray each other,
the state's power becomes fragile
and will be exploited by enemies.
Therefore, he bit into a pear and gave it to the envoy
to bestow upon Liǔ and others as a token of sincerity.
Shǐ,
read Shū Lì.
Niè,
read Yú Jié.
11Dài Wáng Shíyìjiān attacked Liú Wèichén.
The river ice had not yet frozen solid.
Shíyìjiān ordered reeds to be tied with ropes to hold the floating ice.
Soon after, the ice froze solid.
He attacked Shuòfāng from Dài,
crossing the Yellow River to the west.
The ford was called Jūnzǐ Jīn.
Gěn,
read Jū Dēng.
Then reeds were scattered on top,
and the ice and grass intertwined,
resembling a floating bridge.
The Dài army crossed on it.
Wèichén did not expect the troops to arrive suddenly,
and fled west with his clan.
Shíyìjiān recovered sixty to seventy percent of his tribe and returned.
Wèichén fled to Qín.
Qín Wáng Jiān sent Wèichén back to Shuòfāng
and dispatched troops to garrison it.
12Twelfth month.
Jiǎzǐ.
Yān's Grand Commandant, Duke Jìng of Jiànníng, Yáng Wù, died.
The posthumous epithet rules: "Jìng" means conforming to benevolent laws.
"Jìng" also means being vigilant day and night.
Grand Master of Guanglu, Lǐ Hóng, became Minister of Works.
1 Spring,
first month.
Qín Wáng Jiān dispatched General of the Rear Yáng Chéngshì and General of the Left MáoSōng to divide and attack Shàngguī and Āndìng.
General Who Aids the State Wáng Měng and General Who Establishes Valor Dèng Qiāng attacked Púbǎn.
General of the Vanguard Yáng Ān and General of Guǎngwǔ Zhāng Háo attacked Shǎnxī Chéng.
Jiān ordered the armies at Pú and Shǎn to maintain a distance of thirty *lǐ* from the cities,
to fortify their positions and not engage in battle,
and to wait until Qín and Yōng were pacified,
then combine their forces to take them.
2 At first,
Yān tài zǎi Kè 燕太宰恪 fell ill.
He considered Yān zhǔ Wěi 燕主暐 to be young and weak,
and that political power was not in his own hands.
Tài fù Píng 太傅評 was often suspicious and jealous,
and he feared that the responsibility of Dà sī mǎ 大司馬 might not be given to the right person.
He said to Wěi's 暐 brother, Lè'ān Wáng Zāng 樂安王臧:
“Now, to the south there is the remaining Jìn 晉,
and to the west there is the strong Qín 秦.
These two states constantly harbor ambitions of conquest,
they are just waiting for an opportune moment for us.
The
rise and fall of a state
depends on its辅相 (ministers/regents).
The Dà sī mǎ 大司馬 commands all six armies,
and this position cannot be entrusted to an unsuitable person.
After I die,
speaking of kinship,
it should be among you and Chōng 沖.
Although you two are talented and discerning,
you are still young
and not yet capable of handling many difficulties.
Wú Wáng Chuí 吳王垂 is naturally heroic and brilliant,
and his wisdom and strategy surpass the age.
If you two can recommend the Dà sī mǎ 大司馬 position to him,
he will surely be able to unite the four seas.
What's more, external invaders
will not be a cause for fear.
Be careful not to pursue profit and forget about harm,
and not to disregard the state.”
“Pursuing profit and forgetting about harm”
means that the profit lies in gaining military power,
and recklessly taking on the responsibility of Dà sī mǎ 大司馬,
while forgetting the harm of national ruin and family destruction.
When Kè 恪 died,
Píng 評 did not follow his advice.
In the second month,
Chē qí jiāng jūn 車騎將軍, Zhōngshān Wáng Chōng 中山王沖, was made Dà sī mǎ 大司馬.
Chōng 沖
was Wěi's 暐 younger brother.
Jīngzhōu cìshǐ 荊州刺史, Wú Wáng Chuí 吳王垂, was made Shìzhōng 侍中, Chē qí dà jiāng jūn 車騎大將軍, and Yí tóng sān sī 儀同三司.
This laid the groundwork for the rift between Píng 評 and Chuí 垂.
“騎” (Qí)
is pronounced “qí” (奇寄翻).
3 Qín Wèi gōng Sōu 秦魏公廋 surrendered Shǎnchéng 陝城 to Yān 燕,
and requested troops for assistance.
The Qín 秦 people were greatly alarmed,
and heavily guarded Huàyīn 華陰.
Huàyīn xiàn 華陰縣 is west of Shǎnchéng 陝城,
and has the strategic pass of Tóngguān 潼關.
“降” (Jiàng)
is pronounced “hú jiāng fān” (戶江翻).
“華” (Huá)
is pronounced “hù huà fān” (戶化翻).
Yān Wèi yǐn Fànyáng Wáng Dé 燕魏尹范陽王德
Yè 鄴 was the capital of Yān 燕,
and the Tàishǒu 太守 of Wèijùn 魏郡 was the Wèi yǐn 魏尹.
He believed:
“The late emperor received the Mandate of Heaven,
and aimed to pacify the whole world.
Your Majesty has inherited the throne,
and should continue and complete this task.
Now Fú's 苻氏 kin are divided,
the state is split into five parts.
Púbǎn 蒲阪, Shǎnchéng 陝城, Shàngguī 上邽, Āndìng 安定, and Cháng'ān 長安 constitute the five.
These events follow one after another,
this is Heaven bestowing Qín 秦 upon Yān 燕.
If Heaven grants something and one does not take it,
one will instead suffer calamity.
The affair of Wú 吳 and Yuè 越
is enough to observe.
Guóyǔ 國語 states: Yuè Fàn Lí 越范蠡 said, ‘In the past, Heaven bestowed Yuè 越 upon Wú 吳,
but Wú 吳 dared not take it.
Now Heaven bestows Wú 吳 upon Yuè 越,
how can Yuè 越 dare to defy Heaven!’
If Wú Wáng Chuí 吳王垂 leads the troops from Xǔ 許 and Luò 洛 to quickly relieve Sōu's 廋 siege,
and the Tài fù 太傅 mobilizes the imperial capital's elite troops as a second force to follow up,
and sends proclamations to the Sān fǔ 三輔,
showing them the consequences (fortune or misfortune),
and clearly establishes rewards for surrender,
they will surely respond at once.
The time for unification
will then be at hand!”
At that time, many Yān 燕 people requested to relieve Shǎn 陝,
and then to seize Guānzhōng 關中.
Tài fù Píng 太傅評 said:
“Qín 秦
is a great state.
Although it now faces difficulties,
it is not easily conquerable.
Although the court is enlightened,
it is not like the late emperor.
The Yān 燕 people referred to their ruler as the court.
Nor is it comparable to the Tài zǎi 太宰.
It is enough simply to close the passes and protect our borders.
Conquering Qín 秦 is not our business.”
Wèi gōng Sōu 魏公廋 sent a letter to Wú Wáng Chuí 吳王垂 and Huángfǔ Zhēn 皇甫真, saying:
“Fú Jiān 苻堅 and Wáng Měng 王猛
are both exceptional men,
and their plans to harm Yān 燕 have been long-standing.
If we do not seize this opportunity to take them,
I fear that in the future, the Yān 燕 ruler and ministers will have the regret of Yǒngdōng 甬東!”
Zuǒzhuàn 左傳 states: When Wú 吳 invaded Yuè 越,
the Viscount of Yuè 越 fortified himself at Kuàijī 會稽,
and sent an envoy to make peace with Wú 吳.
The Viscount of Wú 吳 agreed.
Wǔ Zǐxū 伍子胥 remonstrated,
but was not heeded.
Later, Yuè 越 invaded Wú 吳,
and requested that the King of Wú 吳 reside in Yǒngdōng 甬東.
The King of Wú 吳 said:
“I am old,
and cannot serve a king.
I regret not heeding Zǐxū's 子胥 words,
and thus bringing myself to this plight!”
Then he hanged himself.
Jiǎ Kuí 賈逵 said: Yǒngdōng 甬東
is a border region of Yuè 越,
east of the Yǒngjiāng 甬江.
Suǒyǐn 索隱 says: Present-day Mào xiàn 鄮縣 is that place.
“甬” (Yǒng)
is pronounced “yú lǒng fān” (余隴翻).
“Currently, the one who poses a threat to us is certainly Qín 秦.
The Lord (Yān zhǔ Wěi 燕主暐) is young,
and observing the Tài fù's 太傅 (Píng's 評) discernment,
how can he contend with Fú Jiān 苻堅 and Wáng Měng 王猛?”
Zhēn 真 replied:
“Indeed,
although I know this,
what can be done if my words are not heeded!”
4 In the third month,
on the Dīngsì 丁巳 day, the first day of the month,
there was a solar eclipse.
5 On the Guǐhài 癸亥 day,
a general amnesty was declared.
6 Qín Yáng Chéngshì 秦楊成世 was defeated by Zhào gōng Shuāng's 趙公雙 general Gǒu Xìng 苟興,
and Máo Sōng 毛嵩 was also defeated by Yān gōng Wǔ 燕公武,
and they both fled back.

Qín Wáng Jiān 秦王堅 again dispatched Wǔwèi jiāng jūn 武衞將軍 Wáng Jiàn 王鑒, Níngshuò jiāng jūn 寧朔將軍 Lǚ Guāng 呂光, and generals Fēngyì Guō Jiàng 馮翊郭將 and Zhái Rǔ 翟傉, leading a force of thirty thousand to attack them.
In summer,
the fourth month,
Shuāng 雙 and Wǔ 武, emboldened by their victories, reached Yúméi 榆眉,
with Gǒu Xìng 苟興 as their vanguard.
Wáng Jiàn 王鑒 wanted a quick battle,
but Lǚ Guāng 呂光 said:
“Xìng 興 has just achieved victory,
and his morale is high.
We should maintain a strong defense and wait for him.
When his provisions are exhausted, he will surely retreat.
If we attack him then,
there will be no failure!”
After twenty days, Xìng 興 retreated.
Guāng 光 said:
“Xìng 興 can now be attacked.”
So he pursued him;
Xìng 興 was defeated.
Then they attacked Shuāng 雙 and Wǔ 武,
greatly defeating them,
and beheading or capturing fifteen thousand heads.
Wǔ 武 abandoned Āndìng 安定,
and along with Shuāng 雙, both fled to Shàngguī 上邽.
Jiàn 王鑒 and others advanced to attack them.
Jìn gōng Liǔ 晉公柳 repeatedly issued challenges,
but Wáng Měng 王猛 did not respond.
Liǔ 柳 thought Měng 猛 feared him.
In the fifth month,
he left his heir Láng 良 to guard Púbǎn 蒲阪,
and led a force of twenty thousand west towards Cháng'ān 長安.
When they were over a hundred *li* from Púbǎn 蒲阪,
Dèng Qiāng 鄧羌 led seven thousand elite cavalry in a night raid,
and defeated them.
Liǔ 柳 led his army back,
but Měng 猛 intercepted and attacked them,
capturing all their troops.
Liǔ 柳 and a few hundred cavalry entered the city,
and Měng 猛 and Qiāng 羌 advanced to attack it.
In autumn,
the seventh month,
Wáng Jiàn 王鑒 and others captured Shàngguī 上邽,
beheaded Shuāng 雙 and Wǔ 武,
and pardoned their wives and children.
Zuǒwèi jiāng jūn 左衞將軍 Fú Yǎ 苻雅 was appointed Qínzhōu cìshǐ 秦州刺史.
In the eighth month,
Chánglè gōng Pī 長樂公丕 was appointed Yōngzhōu cìshǐ 雍州刺史.
In the ninth month,
Wáng Měng 王猛 and others captured Púbǎn 蒲阪,
and beheaded Jìn gōng Liǔ 晉公柳 and his wife and children.
Měng 猛 was stationed at Púbǎn 蒲阪,
and dispatched Dèng Qiāng 鄧羌 to join Wáng Jiàn 王鑒 and others in attacking Shǎnchéng 陝城.
The princes and imperial relatives of Yān [Yān] often appropriated commoners as "shade households" (yīnhù [yīnhù]),
so the state's registered households
were fewer than those of private families.
The granaries and treasuries were empty,
and expenditures were insufficient.
Shàngshū Zuǒ Púyè [Shàngshū Zuǒ Púyè], Guǎngxìn Gōng Yuè Wǎn [Guǎngxìn Gōng Yuè Wǎn], said:
"Currently, the three powers stand in a tripartite configuration,
The three powers
refer to Yān [Yān], Jìn [Jìn], and Qín [Qín].
Yet the state's laws and governance are not established,
and the powerful and noble act wantonly.
This has led to the exhaustion of commoner households,
with no revenue coming in from taxes.
Officials' regular salaries are cut,
and soldiers' rations are stopped.
The government has to borrow grain and silk to support itself.
This is not only unacceptable to our neighboring enemies,
but also not the way to govern.
It is advisable to abolish all 'shade households' at once,
and return them all to the commanderies and counties."
Yān Zhǔ Wěi [Yān Zhǔ Wěi] agreed,
and appointed Wǎn [Wǎn] to specifically manage this affair.
He investigated and exposed hidden abuses,
and no one dared to conceal them.
Over 200,000 households were recovered,
and the entire court harbored resentment and anger.
Wǎn [Wǎn] had been ill before,
but he forced himself to meticulously inspect the household registers,
and his illness worsened rapidly.
In winter,
the eleventh month,
he died.
8 In the twelfth month,
Qín Wáng Měng [Qín Wáng Měng] and others captured Shǎntchéng [Shǎntchéng],
seizing Wèi Gōng Sōu [Wèi Gōng Sōu],
and sent him to Cháng'ān [Cháng'ān].
Qín Wáng Jiān [Qín Wáng Jiān] asked him why he rebelled.
He replied:
"Your subject originally had no intention to rebel,
but because my brothers repeatedly plotted rebellion and disorder,
I feared being implicated and dying with them,
hence I plotted rebellion."
Jiān [Jiān] wept and said:
"You are usually a virtuous person,
so I naturally know this was not your true intention.
Moreover, Gāozǔ [Gāozǔ] cannot be without an heir."
Fú Jiàn's [Fú Jiàn] temple name was Gāozǔ [Gāozǔ].
He pardoned his seven sons,
making the eldest son inherit the title of Wèi Gōng [Wèi Gōng],
and all the other sons were enfeoffed as county dukes [xiàngōng] [xiàngōng]
to succeed Yuè Lì Wáng [Yuè Lì Wáng] and those younger brothers who had no heirs.
Fú Shēng [Fú Shēng] was deposed as Yuè Wáng [Yuè Wáng],
with the posthumous title Lì [Lì].
"Sōu [Sōu] and Shuāng [Shuāng] both rebelled,
but Shuāng [Shuāng] alone was not allowed to have an heir.
Why?"
Jiān [Jiān] said:
"The empire
is Gāozǔ's [Gāozǔ] empire;
Gāozǔ's [Gāozǔ] son cannot be without an heir.
As for Zhònggāng [Zhònggāng],
he disregarded the Empress Dowager [Tàihòu] [Tàihòu]
and plotted to endanger the imperial ancestral temple.
Fú Shuāng [Fú Shuāng],
courtesy name Zhònggāng [Zhònggāng].
He cannot be shown leniency!"
He appointed Fànyáng Gōng Yì [Fànyáng Gōng Yì] as Zhēngdōng Dàjiàngjūn [Zhēngdōng Dàjiàngjūn] and Bīngzhōu Cìshǐ [Bīngzhōu Cìshǐ],
garrisoned at Púbǎn [Púbǎn];
Dèng Qiāng [Dèng Qiāng] as Jiànwǔ Jiàngjūn [Jiànwǔ Jiàngjūn] and Luòzhōu Cìshǐ [Luòzhōu Cìshǐ],
garrisoned at Shǎntchéng [Shǎntchéng].
He promoted Yáo Tiào [Yáo Tiào] to Jí Jùn Tàishǒu [Jí Jùn Tàishǒu].
9 He granted Dàsīmǎ Wēn [Dàsīmǎ Wēn] exceptional courtesy,
placing him above all the princely kings.
10 In this year,
he appointed Qiúchí Gōng Yáng Shì [Qiúchí Gōng Yáng Shì] as Qínzhōu Cìshǐ [Qínzhōu Cìshǐ],
and Shì's [Shì] younger brother Tǒng [Tǒng] as Wǔdū Tàishǒu [Wǔdū Tàishǒu].
Shì [Shì] also declared himself a subject to Qín [Qín],
and Qín [Qín] appointed Shì [Shì] as Nánqínzhōu Cìshǐ [Nánqínzhōu Cìshǐ].
Collated and punctuated by Wáng Chóngwǔ [Wáng Chóngwǔ]; reviewed by Róng Zhàozǔ [Róng Zhàozǔ] and Niè Chóngqí [Niè Chóngqí].
Sīmǎ Guāng [Sīmǎ Guāng]
Compiled by Imperial Edict
HÒU [HÒU] XUÉ [XUÉ] TIĀN [TIĀN] TÁI [TÁI]
Hàixī Gōng Xià [Hàixī Gōng Xià]
Tàihé [Tàihé] Fourth Year (Jǐsì [Jǐsì], 369 CE)
1 In spring,
the third month,

Dàsīmǎ Wēn [Dàsīmǎ Wēn] requested to attack Yān [Yān] together with Xú [Xú] and Yǎn [Yǎn] Provincial Governors Xī Yīn [Xī Yīn] and Jiāngzhōu Cìshǐ Huán Chōng [Jiāngzhōu Cìshǐ Huán Chōng], and Yùzhōu Cìshǐ Yuán Zhēn [Yùzhōu Cìshǐ Yuán Zhēn].
Initially,
Yīn [Yīn] was in the Northern Command (Běifǔ) [Běifǔ].
The capital of Jìn [Jìn] was Jiànkāng [Jiànkāng],
with Jīngkǒu [Jīngkǒu] designated as the Northern Command,
Líyáng [Líyáng] as the Western Command,
and Gūshú [Gūshú] as the Southern Province.
"The wine of Jīngkǒu [Jīngkǒu] is potable,
and its soldiers are usable."
The soldiers of Jīngkǒu [Jīngkǒu] were usable,
probably due to the local environment and customs,
not necessarily waiting until Xiè Xuán [Xiè Xuán] used them for enemies to feel awe!
However, Yīn [Yīn] was ignorant of strategic opportunities,
and thus sent a memorial to Wēn [Wēn],
wishing to jointly assist the imperial house,
requesting to lead his troops out to the area north of the river.
Yīn's [Yīn] son Chāo [Chāo], who was Wēn's [Wēn]参军 [cānjūn],
took it and read it,
then tore it to shreds inch by inch.
He then re-wrote Yīn's [Yīn] memorial,
stating that he was not a talent for command,
unfit for military campaigns,
old and ill,
requesting a quiet place to recuperate,
and urging Wēn [Wēn] to take over his command.
Wēn [Wēn] was greatly pleased upon receiving the memorial,
and immediately transferred Yīn [Yīn] to Guànjūn Jiàngjūn [Guànjūn Jiàngjūn] and Kuàijī Nèishǐ [Kuàijī Nèishǐ].
Wēn [Wēn] personally assumed the titles of Xú [Xú] and Yǎn [Yǎn] Provincial Governors.
In summer,
the fourth month,
on the gengxu [gēngxū] day,
Wēn [Wēn] led 50,000 infantry and cavalry from Gūshú [Gūshú].
2 On the jiazi [jiǎzǐ] day,
Yān Zhǔ Wěi [Yān Zhǔ Wěi] established Empress Kèzúhún Shì [Kèzúhún Shì].
She was the daughter of the Empress Dowager's younger cousin, Shàngshū Lìng Yùzhāng Gōng Yì [Shàngshū Lìng Yùzhāng Gōng Yì].
3 Dà Sīmǎ Wēn (桓溫) launched an expedition from Yǎnzhōu (兗州) to attack Yān (燕).
Xī Chāo (郗超) said:
"The route is long,
and the Biànshuǐ (汴水) is shallow.
After the disturbances of war,
the Biànshuǐ (汴水) has become silted up
and has never been dredged,
hence its shallowness.
Biàn (汴),
pronounced 'pí biàn'.
Wēn (溫) did not comply.
In the sixth month,
on the day Xīnchǒu (辛丑),
Wēn (溫) reached Jīnxiāng (金鄉).
Jīnxiāng (金鄉) County,
in the Later Hàn (漢) it belonged to Shānyáng Jùn (山陽郡),
in the Jìn (晉) it belonged to Gāopíng Jùn (高平郡),
in the Suí (隋) it belonged to Jìyīn Jùn (濟陰郡),
in the Táng (唐) it belonged to Yǎnzhōu (兗州),
and in our Sòng (宋) it belongs to Jìzhōu (濟州).
The county is ninety *lǐ* southeast of the prefecture.
The waterway was cut off.
Wēn (溫) ordered the Champion General, Máo Hǔshēng (毛虎生), to dig the Jùyě (鉅野) for three hundred *lǐ*,
to divert the Wènshuǐ (汶水) to meet the Qīngshuǐ (清水).
In Bān Gù's (班固) 'Dìlǐ Zhì' (地理志),
the Wènshuǐ (汶水) originates southwest of Láiwú (萊蕪) County in Tàishān (泰山)
and enters the Jì (濟).
'Shuǐjīng Zhù' (水經註): The Jìshuǐ (濟水) flows northeast into Jùyě (鉅野),
its former channel then turns northeast and joins the Hóngshuǐ (洪水) on the right;
the Hóngshuǐ (洪水) flows from the Xuēxùn Zhǔ (薛訓渚) of Jùyě (鉅野),
and is called Huán Gōng Dú (桓公瀆),
from there the Jì (濟) flows north.
Dù Yòu (杜佑) said: The Jìshuǐ (濟水),
due to the drying up of the canals at the end of Wáng Mǎng's (王莽) reign, no longer intersected the Yellow River;
now in the borders of Dōngpíng (東平), Jǐnán (濟南), Zīchuān (淄川), and Běihǎi (北海) there is a river flowing into the sea,
called Qīnghé (清河),
which is actually the confluence of the Hézé (菏澤) and Wènshuǐ (汶水),
also called Jìhé (濟河),
adopting the old name,
but it is not the Jìshuǐ (濟水).
Wèn (汶),
pronounced 'wèn'.
He was Bǎo's (寶) son.
Máo Bǎo (毛寶) had previously achieved merit in pacifying Sū Jùn (蘇峻).
The note is also seen before.
The ships stretched for several hundred *lǐ*.
Xī Chāo (郗超) said:
"The Qīngshuǐ (清水) flows into the Yellow River,
making transportation difficult.
From the Qīngshuǐ (清水) entering the Yellow River,
it is all upstream,
and the route is winding and distant,
hence the difficulty in transportation.
The supply route is also cut off,
relying on the enemy for resources,
but gaining nothing,
this is a dangerous path.
It would be better to lead all the existing troops directly to Yèchéng (鄴城).
They, fearing your illustrious name,
will surely flee at the mere sight of you,
and retreat north to Liáo (遼) and Jié (碣).
If they can come out to fight,
then the matter can be swiftly decided.
If you wish to besiege and hold Yè (鄴),
then in this peak summer,
it will be difficult to achieve anything.
The common people are scattered across the fields,
all becoming property of the government,
and the region south of the Yìshuǐ (易水) will surely beg for their lives with clasped hands.
But I fear that your Excellency considers this plan too risky and decisive,
with victory uncertain.
If you wish to act with caution,
then it is best to halt your troops along the Yellow River and Jì (河、濟),
control the grain transport,
wait until supplies are abundant,
and then advance your troops next summer.
Although this may seem like a delay,
*shē* (賒),
means distant.
To abandon these two strategies and march north with a continuous army,
advance will not be swift,
and retreat will surely be hampered.
