*Qiān* (愆),
means error or failure.
means lack or exhaustion.
This refers to food transport.
Gradually, as autumn and winter approach,
the water will become even more difficult to navigate.
Moreover, the northern lands experience early cold,
and few of the three armies have fur and coarse clothes.
I fear that at that time, the worries will not be limited to just a lack of food."
Wēn (溫) again did not comply.
Xī Chāo's (郗超) strategies and plans,
how could they be matched by ordinary people?
It is fitting that Huán Wēn (桓溫) valued them.
But though he valued them, he did not follow his plans,
because to directly attack Yèchéng (鄴城) and decide victory in one battle
was something Wēn (溫) dared not do;
and to halt the troops along the Yellow River and Jì (河、濟) to wait for the next year,
allowing Yān (燕) time to prepare,
Wēn (溫) would also not do.
Wēn (溫) sent Jiànwēi Jiāngjūn (建威將軍) Tán Xuán (檀玄) to attack Húlù (湖陸),
and captured it.
Húlù (湖陸) County,
in the Former Hàn (漢) was called Húlíng (湖陵),
belonged to Shānyáng Jùn (山陽郡).
Emperor Zhāng (章帝) renamed it Húlù (湖陸);
in the Jìn (晉) it was divided and belonged to Gāopíng Jùn (高平郡).
Xián (賢) said: The old city of Húlù (湖陸) is in the southeast of modern Yǎnzhōu Fāngyǔ (兗州方與) County.
Yān (燕) Lord Wěi (暐) appointed the Prince of Xiàpí (下邳) Lì (厲) as the Grand Chief Controller for Punitive Expeditions (Zhēngtǎo Dà Dūdū 征討大都督),
and led twenty thousand infantry and cavalry to meet the attack at Huángxū (黃墟).
'Shuǐjīng Zhù' (水經註): In Xiǎohuáng (小黃) County of Chénliú (陳留) there is Huángxiāng (黃鄉).
Dù Yù (杜預) said: East of Wàihuáng (外黃) County there is Huángchéng (黃城).
After the chaos of war,
the cities and towns became ruins,
hence it was called Huángxū (黃墟).
Shuài (帥),
read as *shuài*.
Qí (騎),
pronounced 'qí jì'.
He fled back on a single horse.
The Grand Administrator of Gāopíng (高平), Xú Fān (徐翻), surrendered with his entire commandery.
The vanguards Dèng Xiá (鄧遐) and Zhū Xù (朱序) defeated the Yān (燕) general Fù Yán (傅顏) at Línzhǔ (林渚).
'Shuǐjīng Zhù' (水經註): The Huáshuǐ (華水) flows east past the north of Fěichéng (棐城),
which is the Běilín (北林) pavilion.
In the Spring and Autumn (春秋) period, the feudal lords met at Fěilín (棐林) to save Zhèng (鄭),
and encountered each other at Běilín (北林).
According to this, the old city of Línxiāng (林鄉) is north of Xīnzhèng (新鄭);
there is also Báiyàn Pí (白鴈陂),
northeast of Chángshè (長社),
southwest of Línxiāng (林鄉).
Bài (敗),
pronounced 'bǔ mài'.
Zāng (臧) could not resist,
and so sent the Sànqí Chángshì (散騎常侍) Lǐ Fèng (李鳳) to seek help from Qín (秦).
Sàn (散),
pronounced 'xī dǎn'.
Qí (騎),
pronounced 'qí jì'.
Autumn,
seventh month,
Wēn (溫) encamped at Wǔyáng (武陽).
This is Dōngwǔyáng (東武陽),
in the Hàn (漢) it belonged to Dōngjùn (東郡),
in Wèi (魏) and Jìn (晉) it belonged to Yángpíng Jùn (陽平郡),
in the Táng (唐) it was renamed Cháochéng (朝城) County and belonged to Wèizhōu (魏州).
Wēn (溫) arrived at Fāngtóu (枋頭).
Wěi (暐) and the Grand Tutor Píng (評) were greatly alarmed,
and plotted to flee to Hélóng (和龍).
The Prince of Wú (吳) Chuí (垂) said:
"I ask to attack them;
if we do not succeed,
it will not be too late to flee."

Wěi (暐) then appointed Chuí (垂) to replace the Prince of Lè'ān (樂安) Zāng (臧) as bearer of imperial credentials (Shǐchíjié 使持節) and Grand Chief Controller of the Southern Expedition (Nántǎo Dà Dūdū 南討大都督),
leading fifty thousand troops including Zhēngnán Jiāngjūn (征南將軍) Fányáng Wáng Dé (范陽王德) to resist Wēn (溫).
Chuí (垂) submitted a memorial requesting Sītú Zuǒ Chángshǐ (司徒左長史) Shēn Yìn (申胤), Huángmén Shìláng (黃門侍郎) Fēng Fú (封孚), and Shàngshū Láng (尚書郎) Xīluóténg (悉羅騰) all to join the army.
Xīluóténg (悉羅騰),
was likely a barbarian,
taking his clan name from his tribe,
similar to what is recorded in the 'Wèishū Guānshì Zhì' (魏書官氏志),
such as the Chìluó (叱羅) and Rúluó (如羅) clans among the remnants of various surnames who entered during the Shényuán (神元) period.
He was Zhōng's (鍾) son;
Fú (孚)
was Fàng's (放) son.
Shēn Zhōng (申鍾) is seen in volume 95, Emperor Chéng (成帝), Xiánhé (咸和) 9th year.
Fēng Fàng (封放) is seen in volume 99, Emperor Mù (穆帝), Yǒnghé (永和) 7th year.
Wěi again sent the Cavalry Attendant-in-ordinary, Yuè Sōng, to request aid from Qín,
promising to bribe them with the land west of Hǔláo.
Qín Wáng Jiān summoned his close ministers to deliberate in the Eastern Hall.
All said:
"In the past, Huán Wēn attacked us,
reaching Bàshàng,
and saw the ninety-nine scroll-volumes of Yǒnghé's tenth year.
Now Wēn attacks Yàn,
why should we rescue them?
Moreover, Yàn does not claim vassalage to us,
so why should we rescue them?"
Wáng Měng secretly told Jiān:
"Although Yàn is powerful,
Mùróng Píng is no match for Wēn.
If Wēn takes Shāndōng,
advances and garrisons Luòyì,
gathers the troops of Yōu and Jì,
and draws provisions from Bīng and Yù,
then parades his forces at Xiáo and Miǎn,
Your Majesty's great enterprise will be lost.
It is better now to combine our forces with Yàn to repel Wēn;
once Wēn retreats,
Yàn will also be weakened.
Then we can take advantage of their weakness and conquer them.
Would this not be excellent?"
Wáng Měng's capture of Lǐ Yǎn
also stemmed from this plan.
In the eighth month,
he dispatched General Gǒu Chí and Luòzhōu Inspector Dèng Qiāng, leading twenty thousand infantry and cavalry, to rescue Yàn.
They departed from Luòyáng
and reached Yǐngchuān;
Yǐngchuān Commandery
was governed from Xǔchāng.
Wáng Měng was appointed Grand Secretariat.
The Grand Tutor of the Crown Prince, Fēng Fú, asked Shēn Yìn:
"Wēn's army is strong and well-ordered,
advancing directly with the current.
Now our great army merely lingers on the high bank,
not engaging in battle.
I do not see the principle of defeating them.
What will happen to the situation?"
Yìn replied:
"With Wēn's current prestige and power,
he seems capable of action,
yet in my view,
he will certainly not succeed.
Why?
The Jìn dynasty is weak,
and Wēn monopolizes control of the state.
Jìn's court officials may not all be of the same mind as him.
Therefore, Wēn's ambition is not desired by the multitude,
and they will certainly obstruct and ruin his enterprise.
(Guāi
means 'different';
zǔ
means 'obstructed';
bài
is pronounced bǔ mài fān.)
Wēn is arrogant and relies on his numerous forces,
but is timid in adapting to change.
His vast army has advanced deep,
and when a favorable opportunity arose,
he instead leisurely lingered in the middle of the river,
not moving to seize the advantage,
hoping for a prolonged campaign,
to achieve complete victory without effort.
This is exactly Wēn's strategy.
Shēn Yìn's assessment of it is accurate.
When his true intentions are revealed and his strength exhausted,
he will defeat himself without a battle.
This is the natural course of events."
Wēn attacked Qín but did not cross the Bàshǔi,
and attacked Yàn but hesitated at Fāngtóu.
Everyone blamed him for not advancing.
Knowing himself and knowing his enemy,
Wēn probably had this insight only when facing the enemy.
Though Wēn's wisdom was insufficient to suppress violence and establish achievements,
he was still far superior to the common people.
(Qiān
refers to the grain transport being delayed and not arriving;
xuán
means 'cut off';
jiàn
is pronounced xián biàn fān.)
Wēn used Duàn Sī, a surrendered Yàn man, as a local guide.
Xīluó Téng fought Wēn and
captured Sī alive.
Wēn sent the former Zhào general Lǐ Shù to patrol Zhào and Wèi.
Téng, along with the General of the Tiger Guards and Central Attendant, Rǎmgān Jīn, attacked and killed him.
(Rǎmgān
is also a foreign surname,
similar to Xīluó.)
Initially, Wēn sent Yùzhōu Inspector Yuán Zhēn to attack Qiáo and Liáng,
and to open Shímén to facilitate water transport.
Zhēn conquered Qiáo and Liáng but could not open Shímén.
(Qiáo and Liáng
refer to Qiáo Commandery and Liáng Kingdom.)
In the ninth month,
Yàn's Fànyáng Wáng Dé led ten thousand cavalry, and the Lántái Attendant Censor, Liú Dāng, led five thousand cavalry to garrison Shímén.
Yùzhōu Inspector Lǐ Guī led five thousand provincial troops to cut off Wēn's supply route.
(Yàn's Yùzhōu Inspector was based in Xǔchāng.
Duàn
is pronounced dīng guǎn fān.
He was Pèi's son.
Liú Pèi was a general under Mùróng Huǎng,
who repelled Shí Hǔ
and attacked Yǔwén,
achieving merits in both.
When encountering Jìn forces,
Zhòu said:
"Jìn people are light and nimble,
timid in engaging the enemy,
but brave in pursuing a retreat.
We should set a bait to lure them."
He then sent two hundred cavalry to challenge,
dividing the remaining cavalry into three ambushes.
The challengers feigned retreat before engaging,
and Jìn forces pursued them.
Zhòu led the ambush to attack them,
and many Jìn soldiers died.
Wēn had been unfavorable in several battles,
and his provisions were exhausted.
He also heard that Qín troops were approaching.
On bǐngshēn,
he burned his boats,
abandoned his baggage and armor,
and fled back by land.
He appointed Máo Hǔshēng to oversee military affairs of the four commanderies including Dōngyàn,
and to serve as Governor of Dōngyàn.
(Shěn Yuē said: Dōngyàn Commandery
was established by the Southern Dynasties by dividing Púyáng.
I note that Shí Hǔ assigned Dōngyàn Commandery to Luòzhōu,
so this commandery was probably established by Zǔ Dié when he was in Yùzhōu.
Yàn
is pronounced yú xián fān.)
Wēn exited Cāngyuán from Dōngyàn,
dug wells for water.
(The Biànshǔi and Jìdú both flow from north to south;
fearing that pursuing troops might poison their upper reaches,
he therefore dug wells for water.)
Yàn's generals all clamored to pursue him.
Wú Wáng Chuí said:
"No,
Wēn is in a state of initial panic and retreat,
he must have strictly set up defenses,
and selected elites as a rear guard.
Attacking them now may not succeed.
It's better to go slowly.
He will take advantage of our delay and certainly rush day and night.
Wait until his troops are exhausted and their morale low,
then attack them.
There will be nothing that cannot be overcome."
He then led eight thousand cavalry, slowly following in their wake.
Wēn indeed advanced day and night.
After several days,
Chuí told his generals:
"Wēn can be attacked now."
He then urgently pursued,
catching Wēn at Xiāngyì.
(Xiāngyì County
has belonged to Chénliú Commandery since the Hàn dynasty.)
He, along with Chuí, attacked Wēn from both sides,
severely defeating him,
beheading thirty thousand.
Qín's Gǒu Chí intercepted and attacked Wēn at Qiáo,
again defeating him,
with tens of thousands more dead.
Sūn Yuánsuì occupied Wǔyáng to resist Yàn.
Yàn's Left Guard General Mèng Gāo attacked and captured him.
In winter,
the tenth month,
on the Jǐsì day,
Grand Marshal Huán Wēn collected the scattered troops
and encamped at Shānyáng.
Liú Xù said: Shānyáng
was the territory of Shèyáng County in the Hàn dynasty.
During the Jìn dynasty, Shānyáng Commandery was established,
and it was renamed Shānyáng County.
In the Táng dynasty, it was the seat of Chǔzhōu.
Then, he blamed Yuán Zhēn,
holding Zhēn accountable for the Shímén pass not opening and the grain supply being cut off.
He also dismissed Dèng Xiá, the General Who Guards the Army, from office.
Zhēn believed Huán Wēn had falsely accused him,
and did not submit.
He submitted a memorial detailing Huán Wēn's crimes;
the imperial court did not respond.
Zhēn then occupied Shòuchūn, rebelled, and surrendered to Yān,
and requested aid.
He also sent an envoy to Qín.
Huán Wēn appointed Máo Hǔshēng as Administrator of Huáinán,
to guard Lìyáng.
The Administrator of Huáinán was originally based in Shòuchūn.
Since Shòuchūn had rebelled,
Hǔshēng was appointed Administrator of Huáinán and commanded to guard Lìyáng.
Lìyáng was originally a subordinate county of Huáinán.
Hǔshēng guarded it,
outwardly to prepare against Shòuchūn,
and inwardly to protect Jiāngnán.
4 As Yān and Qín had already formed a good relationship,
envoys frequently traveled between them.
Hǎo Guǐ, Gentleman of the Palace (Cavalry), and Liáng Chēn, Palace Attendant and Yellow Gate Attendant, of Yān,
successively traveled to Qín.
Guǐ had a long-standing acquaintance with Wáng Měng,
and Měng received him with familiar courtesy,
inquiring about affairs in the East.
Guǐ saw that Yān's governance was not in order while Qín was greatly prosperous,
and secretly wished to rely on Měng,
so he revealed quite a bit of the truth.
When Chēn arrived in Cháng'ān,
Qín King Fú Jiān was hunting in Wànnián.
Wànnián
was Qín's Yuèyáng,
renamed by Hàn Emperor Gāodì.
It belonged to Féngyì,
and later to Jīngzhào in the Jìn dynasty.
Chēn said:
"When Qín's envoy arrived in Yān,
the ruler and ministers of Yān donned court attire and prepared the full rites,
sweeping and cleaning the palace courts,
before daring to grant an audience.
Now the Qín King wishes to grant an audience in the wilderness;
your humble servant dares not accept this command!"
Shàngshū Láng Xīn Jìng said to Chēn:
"When a guest enters the borders,
it is solely up to the host how to treat them.
How can Your Excellency presume to dictate the rites!
Moreover, the Son of Heaven uses the term 'imperial carriage,'
and wherever he stops is called 'imperial sojourning place.'
How can there be a fixed residence!
Furthermore,
the *Chūnqiū* also mentions 'encountering rites.'
The *Chūnqiū*: in the fourth year of Yǐn,
Duke Yǐn and the Duke of Sòng encountered each other at Qīng.
The *Gōngyáng Zhuàn* says: What is 'encountering'?
It means not having an appointment.
Dù Yù noted: An encounter
is a temporary meeting in the field,
where two states each simplify their rites,
like meeting on the road.
Chēn said:
"The Jìn dynasty is not in order,
and its spiritual mandate has reverted to virtue.
Spiritual mandate
is what Bān Biāo's *Wángmìng Lùn* calls the divine mandate.
Both received the clear mandate.
But Huán Wēn, in his madness,
spied on our kingly domain.
The *Zuǒzhuàn*: invaded and damaged the kingly domain.
Dù Yù's commentary says: 'domain'
refers to management and regulations.
I believe this 'domain'
refers to demarcated territory,
as in the *Zuǒzhuàn*
'The King gave him the domain of Duke Wǔ.'
He cannot stand alone.
Therefore, the Qín ruler empathizes with the current troubles,
and seeks to form a good alliance.
The ruler and ministers of the Eastern Court
stretch their necks looking west,
ashamed of their lack of strength,
and consider it a neighbor's concern.
'Jìng'
means strength.
'Cháo'
is pronounced zháoyáo fān;
the same below.
They treat [Qín's envoys] with utmost respect.
Now that the strong invaders have retreated,
and diplomatic exchanges are just beginning,
it is appropriate to uphold rites and emphasize righteousness to solidify the goodwill between our two states.
If you treat your envoy with disdain,
this is to belittle Yān,
how can this be the meaning of cultivating good relations!
Indeed, the Son of Heaven takes the four seas as his home,
hence when he travels, it is called 'imperial carriage,'
and when he stops, it is called 'imperial sojourning place.'
Now the world is divided.
Zōu Yǎn said: There is the Red Land Divine Region within China;
within the Red Land Divine Region are the Nine Provinces,
which Yu described;
outside of it is a surrounding sea.
The saying 'sea counties'
is probably derived from this.
How can one speak of 'imperial carriage' and 'imperial sojourning place' now!
According to rites,
to meet without appointment is called an 'encounter.'
This is due to exigency and expediency,
and the rites are simplified.
How can it be for ordinary, leisurely occasions!
An envoy traveling alone
is indeed at the host's mercy;
however, if it is not in accordance with rites,
I dare not comply."
Fú Jiān then set up a temporary palace for him.
The
hundred officials attended,
and then the guest was invited in,
following the ceremony of the Yān court.
After the affair,
Fú Jiān hosted a private banquet for him,
imitating the ancient ritual of private audience.
"Who are the famous ministers of the Eastern Court?"
Chēn said:
"Grand Tutor, Prince Píng of Shàngyōng,
is of illustrious virtue and distinguished kin,
brightly assisting the imperial house;
General of Chariots and Cavalry, Prince Chuí of Wú,
possesses martial strategies that surpass the age,
thwarting and resisting insults;
the others, some advanced through literary talent,
some employed for martial prowess,
all hold their offices competently,
and no worthy men are left unnoticed in the wilderness."
Chēn's elder cousin Yì was a Shàngshū Láng in Qín.
Fú Jiān made him the Director of Guests,
and lodged Chēn in Yì's residence.
The Hàn dynasty had the office of Director of Guests,
later renamed Grand Minister of Ceremonies.
This was merely a temporary appointment as Director of Guests.
'Guǎn'
is pronounced 'guàn';
the same for 'guǒguǎn' below.
"In the past, Zhūgě Jǐn was sent by Wú as an envoy to Shǔ,
and he met Zhūgě Liàng only in public court,
with no private meetings upon retirement.
Jǐn and Liàng were brothers.
'Wéi'
is pronounced 'yúwěi fān.'
Now to make me stay in a private residence,
is something I dare not do."
Thus, he was not lodged there.
Yì frequently came to the official guest-house,
sleeping and rising with Chēn,
and secretly inquired about the affairs of the Eastern State.
Chēn said:
"Now the two sides occupy separate territories,
and both brothers enjoy honor and favor.
Regarding their original intentions,
each has his own place.
Your humble servant wishes to speak of the virtues of the Eastern State,
but fears it is not what the Western State wishes to hear;
Yān is east of the pass,
Qín is west of the pass,
the two sides occupy separate territories,
hence Yān is called the Eastern State,
and Qín the Western State.
Moreover, it is not for an envoy to discuss.
Why does my brother ask?"
Fú Jiān ordered the Crown Prince to meet Chēn.
The Qín people wished Chēn to bow to the Crown Prince,
and first prompted him, saying:
"The ruler of a neighboring state
is like one's own ruler;
how can the heir apparent of a neighboring state
be any different?"
Chēn said:
"The Son of Heaven's son is treated as a primary scholar,
wishing him to rise from a humble position to nobility.
The *Lǐjì Jiāotèsheng* says: The Son of Heaven's eldest son
is a scholar;
there is no one in the world born noble.
How much more so for a minister of another state!
If there is not complete reverence,
then rites involve reciprocity.
How could I forget respect,
but I fear that condescending and bending the knee would be troublesome."
He meant that he should return the bow.
Wáng Měng (王猛) urged Jiān (堅) to keep Chēn (琛),
but Jiān (堅) refused.

5 Yàn (燕) Lord Wěi (暐) sent the Grand Minister of the Imperial Clan, Wēn Tǒng (溫統), to confer upon Yuán Zhēn (袁真) the titles of Envoy with Imperial Credentials, Area Commander of All Military Affairs in Huáinán (淮南), General Who Conquers the South, and Inspector of Yángzhōu (揚州),
and enfeoffed him as Duke of Xuānchéng (宣城).
Tǒng (統) died before crossing the Huái (淮) River.
6 Wú (吳) King Chuí (垂) returned to Yè (鄴) from Xiāngyì (襄邑).
His prestige and reputation grew even greater,
which made Grand Tutor Píng (評) increasingly jealous of him.
Chuí (垂) submitted a memorial
stating, "The recruited officers and soldiers forgot themselves to achieve merit.
Generals Sūn Gài (孫蓋) and others thrust their vanguard into the enemy lines and broke through."
It means "achieved merit."
"Jù jué" (句絕) means "to sever."
"Chuí" (椎)
means "to pound" or "to strike,"
directly pounding with their vanguards.
Píng (評) suppressed all of these and did not act on them.
Chuí (垂) repeatedly spoke of this,
arguing with Píng (評) in court,
and their animosity deepened further.
Empress Dowager Kězúhún (可足渾) had always disliked Chuí (垂).
The details are in Volume 100, Mù Dì's (穆帝) Shēngpíng (升平) 1st year.
is pronounced ōulù fān (烏路翻).
She conspired secretly with Píng (評) to assassinate him.
Kǎi (楷), son of Grand Preceptor Kè (恪), and Lán Jiàn (蘭建), Chuí's (垂) maternal uncle, knew of this
and told Chuí (垂), saying,
"He who strikes first gains the upper hand.
The art of war says: 'He who strikes first controls others;
he who strikes last is controlled by others.'
There is nothing else we can do."
Chuí (垂) said,
"For kin to slaughter each other and initiate chaos in the state,
I would rather die
than bear to do it."
After a while,
the two told him again,
saying,
"The internal decision has been made."
"Internal decision"
refers to the intention of Empress Kězúhún (可足渾).
Chuí (垂) said,
"If it absolutely cannot be patched up,
I would rather avoid it by going abroad;
anything else is not to be discussed."
Chuí (垂) was inwardly troubled by this
but had not dared to tell his sons.
His heir, Lìng (令), asked,
"Your Excellency has recently looked troubled.
Lìng (令) addresses his father as 'Your Excellency.'
"Bǐ" (比)
is pronounced pízì fān (毗至翻).
Is it because the Grand Tutor despises the virtuous
and, with your high achievements and great prestige,
suspects you even more?"
Chuí (垂) said,
"Yes.
I exhausted my strength and risked my life to defeat powerful enemies,
originally intending to preserve our family and state.
How could I know that after achieving success,
I would instead find no place for myself?
Since you know my heart,
what plan do you have for me?"
Lìng (令) said,
"The Emperor is dim-witted and weak,
entrusting power to the Grand Tutor.
Once disaster strikes,
it will be as swift as a startled trigger.
"Jī" (機)
means the trigger of a crossbow.
It is likened to drawing a crossbow,
where the trigger fires unexpectedly,
startling people.
Hence it is called 'hài jī' (駭機), a startled trigger.
Without losing the great principle,
it would be best to flee to Lóngchéng (龍城),
offer humble words and apologize for your faults,
and await the Emperor's discernment,
like Duke of Zhōu's (周公) stay in the East.
Hopefully, he will be moved and awakened, and you will be able to return.
This is the greatest fortune."
The Shu (書) says: When King Wǔ (武王) was ill,
the Duke of Zhōu (周公) offered a prayer on behalf of King Tàizǔ (太王), King Jì (王季), and King Wén (文王),
asking to substitute himself.
After King Wǔ's (武王) death,
Guǎn Shú (管叔) and his younger brothers spread rumors, saying,
"The Duke will be unfavorable to the young prince."
The Duke of Zhōu (周公) campaigned in the East.
After the Duke of Zhōu (周公) resided in the East for two years,
the culprits were found.
He then composed a poem to present to the King,
named "Chī Xiāo" (鴟鴞).
The King still dared not reprimand the Duke.
There was a great thunderstorm with wind from Heaven.
The King opened the golden casket
and found the Duke of Zhōu's (周公) prayer to substitute for King Wǔ (武王).
He then held the document and wept,
welcoming the Duke of Zhōu (周公) back.
"Jī" (幾)
is pronounced jūxī fān (居希翻).
"Alternatively, we could internally pacify Yān (燕) and Dài (代),
externally conciliate the various Yi (夷) tribes,
and hold the strategic passes of Féirú (肥如) to protect ourselves.
This would be the next best option."
The strategic passes of Féirú (肥如)
are the Lúlóng (盧龍) pass.
"Excellent!"
In the eleventh month,
on the Xīnhài (辛亥) day (which was the first day of the month),
Chuí (垂) requested permission to hunt in Dàlù (大陸).
The Xùhànzhì (續漢志) says: Jùlù (鉅鹿),
formerly Dàlù (大鹿),
has the Dàlù (大陸) marsh,
which is also the Guǎng'ā (廣阿) marsh.
He planned to head for Lóngchéng (龍城).
When they reached Hándān (邯鄲),
his youngest son, Lín (麟),
who was never loved by Chuí (垂),
fled back to report.
Many of Chuí's (垂) entourage deserted.
Grand Tutor Píng (評) reported to Yàn (燕) Lord Wěi (暐),
who dispatched Xīpíng (西平) Duke Qiáng (強) with elite cavalry to pursue him,
overtaking him at Fànyáng (范陽).
Heir Lìng (令) covered the rear,
and Qiáng (強) dared not press closer.
As dusk fell,
Lìng (令) said to Chuí (垂),
"We originally intended to secure Dōngdū (東都) to save ourselves."
Since Yàn (燕) had its capital at Yè (鄴),
Lóngchéng (龍城) was referred to as Dōngdū (東都).
"The plan was not carried out.
Qín (秦) Lord is currently inviting heroes and talented individuals;
it would be better to go and seek refuge with him."
Chuí (垂) said,
"For today's plan,
where else can we go but there!"
So, they dispersed their cavalry, erasing their tracks,
and returned to Yè (鄴) along the southern mountains,
hiding in Xiǎnyuánlíng (顯原陵) of Zhào (趙).
Xiǎnyuánlíng (顯原陵)
was the place where Zhào (趙) Lord Shí Hǔ (石虎) held a false burial.
To resist them was impossible;
to escape was without a path;
they knew not what to do.
Just then, the hunting hawks all soared away,
and the many horsemen dispersed.
Chuí (垂) then killed a white horse to sacrifice to Heaven
and swore an oath with his followers.
Heir Lìng (令) said to Chuí (垂),
"The Grand Tutor is jealous of the virtuous and despises the capable.
Since he instigated this affair,
people have been especially resentful."
This refers to the plot to assassinate Chuí (垂).
"Not knowing Your Excellency's whereabouts,
they are like infants longing for their mother.
Both Yi (夷) and Xià (夏) feel the same.
If we follow the will of the multitude
and strike them when they are unprepared,
taking them will be as easy as pointing to one's palm.
After the matter is settled,
we will reform abuses and appoint the capable,
greatly rectify court governance,
assist the Emperor,
secure the state, and preserve the family.
This would be the greatest achievement.
Today's opportunity
truly must not be missed.
I ask for a few horsemen;
that will be enough to accomplish this."
Chuí (垂) said,
"If your plan succeeds,
it would indeed be a great blessing,
but if it fails, what regrets would suffice!
It is better to flee west;
that would ensure complete safety."
His son Mǎnúpú (馬奴) secretly plotted to escape back.
Chuí (垂) killed him and proceeded.
Upon reaching Héyáng (河陽),
they were stopped by the ferry official.
They killed him and crossed.

They then fled from Luòyáng (洛陽) to Qín (秦) with Lady Duàn (段), Heir Lìng (令), Lìng's (令) younger brothers Bǎo (寶), Nóng (農), Lóng (隆), his nephew Kǎi (楷), maternal uncle Lán Jiàn (蘭建), and Langzhong 令 Gāo Bì (高弼).
They left Lady Kězúhún (可足渾) in Yè (鄴).
Lady Duàn (段)
was Chuí's (垂) former wife's younger sister.
Kězúhún (可足渾)
was the younger sister of Empress Dowager Kězúhún (可足渾);
details are in Volume 100, Mù Dì's (穆帝) Shēngpíng (升平) 2nd year.
Gāo Bì (高弼)
was Chuí's (垂) State Minister.
Yǐquán (乙泉) garrison
was the Yǐquánwù (乙泉塢) defended by Wèi Gāi (魏該),
located southwest of Yíyáng (宜陽) County,
on the plateau north of the Luò (洛) River.
Wénxiāng (閺鄉) is in Hóngnóng (弘農) Hú (湖) County.
"Wén" (閺)
is pronounced mín (音旻).
Initially,
Qín Wáng Jiān heard that Tàizǎi Kè had died,
and secretly harbored ambitions to seize Yàn.
However, he was apprehensive of Mùróng Chuí's formidable reputation
and dared not act.
When he heard that Chuí had arrived,
he was greatly pleased,
and went out to the suburbs to welcome him.
Grasping his hand, he said:
"Heaven, in giving birth to wise and eminent heroes,
surely intends for them to work together to accomplish great deeds.
This is the natural course of events.
We must together pacify the world,
announce our success at Dàizōng,
and then I shall return you to your homeland,
granting you Yōuzhōu as an hereditary fiefdom for generations.
This way, when you leave your state, you will not lose the filial piety due to a son,
and when you return to my service, you will not lose the loyalty due to a subject.
Is this not excellent?"
Chuí bowed and replied:
"As a sojourning minister,
it is already fortunate to have escaped punishment;
the honor of my homeland
is not something I dare to aspire to!"
Jiān also admired the talents of the Heir Apparent Lìng and Mùróng Kǎi,
and treated them both with great courtesy,
bestowing upon them enormous wealth.
Every time they were granted an audience,
he would fix his gaze upon them.
The literati and common people in Guānzhōng had long heard of Chuí and his son's renown,
and all admired them.
Wáng Měng spoke to Jiān, saying:
"Mùróng Chuí and his son
are like dragons and tigers;
they are not creatures that can be tamed.
'Xún'
means to disturb,
to follow,
to obey.
To raise fierce beasts and make them disturb, be close to, and obey human will is called 'xún'.
'Xún'
is pronounced like 'xiáng zūn'.
If they cannot be controlled again
it would be better to eliminate them early."
Jiān said:
"I am currently gathering heroes to pacify the four seas;
how could I kill them?
Moreover, when they first arrived,
I already showed them my sincerity and accepted them.
Even a common man does not go back on his word,
let alone the sovereign of a myriad chariots!"
Thereupon, he appointed Chuí as Guànjūn Jiāngjūn,
and enfeoffed him as Bīntú Hóu.
Kǎi was made Jīnǔ Jiāngjūn.
Yàn Wèi Yǐn, Fányáng Wáng Dé, had always been on good terms with Chuí.
And Jùjí Cóngshì Zhōngláng Gāo Tài
were both dismissed from office.
When Chuí was Jùjí Dàjiāngjūn in Yàn,
he had appointed Tài as Cóngshì Zhōngláng.
"Now that Wú Wáng has fled,
there is much talk outside,
Shīgǔ said: 'Jíjí'
is like 'fēnfēn'.
This can roughly dispel the slander."
Píng asked:
"Who is capable of this?"
Shào replied:
"Gāo Tài is their leader."
Thereupon, Tài was appointed Shàngshū Láng.
Tài was
Zhān's grandnephew;
see Gāo Zhān, volume 91, Yuándì Tàixīng 2nd year.
"Cóng"
is pronounced like "cái yòng".
He was Yìn's son.
Qín detained Liáng Chēn for over a month
before sending him back.
Chēn traveled at an accelerated pace.
Chéng
means an inn stage.
It refers to travelers taking two inns as one stage.
If one travels four inns in one stage,
this is 'accelerated travel'.
Wú Wáng Chuí had already fled to Qín.
Chēn said to Tàifù Píng:
"The Qín people are daily reviewing their armies
and gathering much grain east of Shǎn.
In my opinion,
the peace will surely not last long.
Now Wú Wáng has gone to join them,
Qín must have designs on Yàn,
and preparations should be made early."
Píng said:
"How could Qín accept a renegade minister and ruin our good relations?"
Chēn said:
"Now the two states divide the Central Plains,
and constantly harbor ambitions to devour each other.
When Huán Wēn invaded,
they rescued us with a stratagem,
not out of love for Yàn.
If Yàn has an opening,
how could they forget their original ambition?"
Fú Jiān and Wáng Měng's strategies
were indeed already perceived by Liáng Chēn.
"What kind of person is the Qín ruler?"
Chēn replied:
"He is insightful and decisive."
When asked about Wáng Měng,
he said:
"His reputation is not unearned."
Píng did not agree with any of this.
Chēn also informed Yàn Zhǔ Wěi,
who also disagreed.
He informed Huángfǔ Zhēn,
who was deeply worried.
He submitted a memorial, stating:
"Although Fú Jiān sends envoys to visit us repeatedly,
he actually harbors intentions to spy on our great state,
not out of admiration for virtue and righteousness,
nor to uphold long-standing agreements.
Previously, when he dispatched troops to Luòchuān,
referring to Gǒu Chí and Dèng Qiāng rescuing Yàn.
The dangers, advantages, strengths, and weaknesses of our state
have all been revealed to them.
Now Wú Wáng Chuí has also gone to join them,
becoming their chief strategist.
We must guard against the disaster of Wǔ Yuán.
Wǔ Yuán left Chǔ and fled to Wú,
borrowing Wú's troops to avenge Chǔ's invasion of Yǐng;
the event is seen in Zuǒzhuàn.
Yuán
is pronounced like 'yún'.
Therefore, we should all select generals and increase our forces
to prevent what might happen."
The Qín route for attacking Yàn later
was indeed as Zhēn had predicted.
Dù Yòu said: Lùzhōu Shàngdǎng Xiàn
was Húguān Xiàn in Hàn.
Píng said:
"Qín is a small state with limited strength,
relying on us for aid.
Furthermore, Fú Jiān is almost aligned with the good path.
It means that although Fú Jiān cannot purely use good principles to interact with neighbors,
he is still close to it.
'Jī'
is pronounced like 'jū xī'.
We should not sever the good relations between our two states,
nor should we lightly alarm ourselves and provoke aggression."
In the end, no preparations were made.
Qín sent Huángmén Láng Shí Yuè as an envoy to Yàn.
Tàifù Píng showed him lavish displays,
hoping to boast of Yàn's wealth and prosperity.
Gāo Tài and Tàifù Cānjūn Hékàn Liú Jìng spoke to Píng, saying:
"Yuè's words are grand, and his gaze is far-reaching;
he is not seeking good relations,
but rather observing our vulnerabilities.
We should display our military strength to him
to thwart his plans.
Now, by showing him our extravagance,
we are only making him despise us more."
Píng did not listen.
Tài then feigned illness and returned home.
At this time, Empress Dowager Kězúhún-shì
encroached upon and disrupted the nation's governance. Grand Tutor Píng
was insatiably greedy,
offering bribes
to those above.
"Liú" means to flow.
Water flows downwards;
there is no principle for it to flow upwards.
"Huòlù shàngliú" means bribes flowing upwards,
indicating that it defies common sense.
"Shàng" is pronounced
"shí zhǎng fān";
the same applies below.
Thus, those below were resentful and angry.
Shàngshū Zuǒchéng Shēn Shào submitted a memorial,
stating:
"Governors and magistrates
are the foundation of good governance.
Current governors and magistrates
are mostly not the right people.
Some are military officers from the ranks,
others are noble relatives raised in luxury.
They are neither selected from the local communities
nor have they served in various court positions.
Furthermore, there are no regulations for demotion or promotion.
The greedy and indolent have no fear of punishment,
and the upright and diligent have no encouragement from rewards.
As a result, the common people are suffering,
bandits are rampant,
the framework is collapsing, and order is in disarray,
with no one to rectify or control it.
'Jiū' means
to supervise.
'Shè' means
to record.
'Wěn' is pronounced
'wèn'.
This surpasses previous generations.
Both public and private affairs are in chaos,
unable to bear the troubles.
The household population of Dà Yàn
is several times that of the two enemies,
referring to Jìn and Qín as the two enemies.
None in the four directions can match it;
yet recently, we have repeatedly been defeated in battles.
This is all due to the unfair levies and conscriptions by governors and magistrates,
and their endless exploitation,
which has left both those serving and those staying behind in distress,
so no one is willing to risk their lives.
There are over four thousand women in the imperial harem,
with servants and attendants even more numerous.
The daily expenses
amount to tens of thousands of gold.
Officials and commoners follow suit,
competing in extravagance.
Those of Qín and Wú are presumptuous and remote,
meaning Qín presumptuously adopted an imperial title and Wú was remote in a corner.
They harbor ambitions of annexation,
while we, both high and low, follow old practices,
losing order day by day.
Our failure to cultivate ourselves
is their wish.
Therefore, it is advisable to carefully select governors and magistrates,
merge offices and streamline positions,
provide relief for military families,
so that both public and private interests are satisfied,
curb extravagance,
cherish expenditures,
ensure rewards match achievements,
and punishments match crimes.
If this is done, Wēn and Měng can be eliminated,
referring to Huán Wēn and Wáng Měng.
'Xiāo' is pronounced
'jiān yáo fān'.
How can merely protecting our borders and pacifying our people be enough!
Furthermore,
Suǒtóu Shíyìjiān is exhausted, ill, confused, and perverse.
Xiāo Zǐxiǎn said: The Xiānbēi had their hair unbound and wore clothes with lapels opening to the left,
hence they were called Suǒtóu.
'Suǒ' is pronounced
'xī gè fān'.
'Jiān' is pronounced
'jū yán fān'.
'Bèi' is pronounced
'pú nèi fān'.
'Yù' means
to advance.
Yet we dispatch troops for distant garrisons,
which is harmful and useless.
Yàn garrisoned Yúnzhōng to guard against the Dài.
Control Xīhé,
strengthen Húguān in the south,
fortify Jìnyáng in the north.
When western invaders come, we resist and defend.
If they pass, we cut off their retreat.
This is better than garrisoning isolated cities and defending useless territories."
The memorial was presented,
but not heeded.
6 On the day Xīnchǒu,
Chancellor Yù met with Grand Marshal Wēn in Túzhōng
to plan future actions.
Wēn's heir Xī was appointed Inspector of Yùzhōu and granted the Staff of Authority.
7 Initially,
the Yàn people had promised to cede the territory west of Hǔláo to Qín.
After the Jìn forces retreated,
the Yàn people regretted it,
and told the Qín people:
"Our envoy misspoke.
Referring to the envoy promising to cede territory as misspoke.
To share hardships and rescue from calamity
is a constant principle."
Qín King Jiān was furious.
He dispatched Auxiliary General Wáng Měng, General Jiànwēi Liáng Chéng, and Inspector of Luòzhōu Dèng Qiáng, leading thirty thousand infantry and cavalry to attack Yàn.
In the twelfth month,
they advanced and attacked Luòyáng.
8 Grand Marshal Wēn conscripted people from Xú and Yǎn provinces to build Guǎnglín city,
and moved his garrison there.
At that time, conscriptions were frequent,
and an epidemic broke out,
killing four or five tenths of the people.
The common people lamented and resented.
Secretary to the Imperial Library Sūn
Shèng
Emperor Huán of Hàn established the post of Secretary to the Imperial Library;
Emperor Wǔ of Jìn merged the Secretariat with the Central Secretariat;
Emperor Huì re-established the Secretary to the Imperial Library,
with subordinates including aides and gentlemen,
also overseeing the Bureau of Literary Works.
directly recorded contemporary events.
Grand Marshal Wēn saw it,
became angry,
and said to Shèng's sons:
"Fāngtóu was indeed a defeat,
but how could it be as your father said!
Jìn people referred to a man's father as Zūnjūn or Zūngōng in front of his son.
This concerns your family's fate!"
Meaning he wished to exterminate their family.
At that time, Shèng was old and living at home,
his character was stern and upright,
with a sense of propriety.
Even his sons and grandsons with gray hair
were treated with increasing strictness.
Upon hearing this, his sons wept and prostrated,
begging him to consider the lives of their hundred family members.
Shèng was greatly angered
and refused.
His sons then secretly altered the text.
Shèng had already copied another version
and transmitted it to foreign countries.
When Emperor Xiàowǔ later sought unusual books,
he obtained one from a person in Liáodōng,
which differed from the current version,
so both were preserved.
The historian said that although Huán Wēn used coercion to alter Sūn Shèng's book,
he ultimately could not suppress the truth.
1 In spring,
the first month,
on the day Jǐhài,
Yuán Zhēn, claiming that Zhū Xiàn, the Inner Administrator of Liángguó and Pèijùn, and his younger brother Bīn, the Inner Administrator of Rǔnán, were secretly communicating with Grand Marshal Wēn,
killed them.
2 Qín King Měng sent a letter to Yàn Inspector of Jīngzhōu Wǔwēi King Zhú,
saying:
"Our state has now blocked the strategic pass of Chénggāo
and closed the road of Méngjīn.
Our grand army, a million strong,
will advance from Zhǐguān to take Yèdū.
The garrison of Jīnyǒng is isolated,
without external aid.
The army at the city walls
is under your command, General."
'Jiān' means
to see.
It means what is seen with one's own eyes.
Zhú was afraid
and surrendered Luòyáng.
'Jiàng' is pronounced
'hù jiāng fān'.
Yàn General Wèi, King of Lè'ān Zāng, built Xīnlè city
and defeated Qín forces at Shímén.
Shímén is in Xíngyáng;
Xīnlè should also be in Xíngyáng territory.
Sòng Bái said: Xīnxiāng County in Wèizhōu governs the ancient city of Xīnlè.
Xīnlè city,
during the Sixteen Kingdoms period,
was built by Yàn General King of Lè'ān Zāng.
Wáng Měng, upon setting out from Cháng'ān,
invited Mùróng Lìng to participate in his military affairs
as a local guide.
Before departing,
he visited Mùróng Chuí and drank with him.
He casually said to Chuí:
"Now we are about to part for a long time.
What will you give me
so that I may see an object and think of you?"
Chuí removed his scabbard-knife and gave it to him.
When Měng arrived in Luòyáng,
he bribed Chuí's confidant, Jīn Xī,
to falsely pretend to be Chuí's messenger
and say to Lìng:
"My father and I came here
to escape death.
Now Wáng Měng hates people as if they were enemies,
and his slanders deepen daily;
although the Qín king outwardly treats us kindly,
his true intentions are hard to know.
A man who flees death and ultimately cannot escape it
will become a laughingstock of the world.
I heard that the Eastern Court has recently begun to regret its actions,
and the Lord and Empress blame each other."
"Lord and Empress"
refers to Yān Lord Wěi and Empress Kězúhún.
"Blame each other"
means they reproached each other's faults.
"Therefore, I sent to inform you;
I have already left,
so you should depart quickly."
Lìng was suspicious,
hesitated all day,
and could not verify the message.
So he took his old cavalry,
"Old cavalry"
refers to those who followed him when he fled from Yān to Qín.
"Cavalry,"
pronounced "qí" (odd ji),
same below.
and fled to Prince Lè'ān Zāng at Shímén.
Měng reported Lìng's rebellion.
Chuí, in fear, fled,
but at Lántián,
he was captured by pursuing cavalry.
Qín King Jiān received him in the Eastern Hall
and comforted him, saying:
"Your family and state are in disharmony,
so you entrusted yourself to me.
Your worthy son does not forget his origins,
still cherishing the thought of returning to his homeland."
The Lǐjì Tángōng states: "Tàigōng was enfeoffed in Qí,
and for five generations, all were reburied in Zhōu.
The gentleman said: 'Enjoy what gives you birth,
and in ritual, do not forget your origin.'
The ancients had a saying:
'When a fox dies, it turns its head towards its den;
this is benevolence.'"
"Shǒu,"
pronounced "shì yòu fān."
"He is not to be deeply blamed.
However, Yān's impending downfall
is not something Lìng could prevent;
it is a pity he merely entered the tiger's mouth.
Furthermore, father and son, brothers,
their crimes do not implicate each other."
Jìn Jiùjì recommended Jì Quē to Duke Wén of Jìn.
The Duke said:
"His father committed a crime;
is this acceptable?"
He replied:
"Shùn's crime
was to execute Gǔn;
his promotion
was to elevate Yǔ."
The Kānggào states: "If the father is not kind,
the son is not respectful;
if the elder brother is not friendly,
the younger brother is not compliant –
they do not implicate each other."
"A wolf,
when advancing, treads on its dewlap;
when retreating, it trips over its tail."
"Bèi"
is a type of wolf.
Its offspring
lack one leg.
The two must cling to each other to move,
hence the world refers to those who cannot move forward or backward as "lángbèi."
"The Yān people, because Lìng rebelled and then returned,
and his father was highly favored by Qín,
suspected Lìng of being a double agent
and moved him to Shāchéng,"
600 *lǐ* northeast of Lóngdū.
"Shāchéng
is in the sandy plains.
Lóngdū
is Lóngchéng."
Minister Guāng said: In ancient times, Zhōu obtained Wēizǐ and changed the mandate of Shāng.
As Yīn Zhòu's tyranny grew daily,
Wēizǐ embraced the sacrificial vessels and fled to Zhōu.
King Wǔ then declared to the feudal lords:
"Yīn has committed grave crimes,
and must be attacked."
He then attacked Zhòu,
killed him,
and changed the Yīn mandate.
The Shǐjì states: The Róng sent Yóu Yú as an envoy to Qín.
Duke Mù detained Yóu Yú and sent female musicians to the Róng king.
The Róng king received them and was pleased.
Duke Mù then returned Yóu Yú.
Yóu Yú repeatedly admonished but was not listened to.
Duke Mù sent agents to secretly persuade Yóu Yú,
and Yóu Yú then surrendered to Qín.
Duke Mù questioned him about the strategy to attack the Róng,
annexed twelve states,
expanded territory by a thousand *lǐ*,
and thus became hegemon of the Western Róng.
Chǔ killed Wǔ Shē,
and his son Yuán fled to Wú.
King Hélǘ of Wú used his strategies to attack Chǔ,
defeated Chǔ, and entered Yǐng.
(This event is found in Volume 9, Hàn Gāodì Years 2 to 4.)
(This event is found in Volume 63, Hàn Xiàndì Jiàn'ān Year 5.)
To make them serve oneself
is an excellent resource for advancement and conquest.
Wáng Měng knew Mùróng Chuí's intentions were long-standing and hard to trust.
But did he not consider that Yān was not yet destroyed,
and Chuí, due to his high talent and great achievements,
was unjustly suspected without fault,
and in distress returned to Qín,
without any ulterior motives?
To hastily kill him out of suspicion and jealousy
would be to aid Yān in its unrighteousness and close the door to future comers.
How could that be acceptable?
Therefore, Qín King Jiān treated him with ceremony to attract the hopes of Yān,
befriended him to learn Yān's true situation,
favored him to sway the Yān populace,
and trusted him to win over the hearts of Yān.
This was not excessive.
Why was Měng so eager to kill Chuí,
acting like a market hawker
who begrudges another's favor and slanders them?
How could this be fitting for a gentleman of noble virtue?
3 Prince Lè'ān Zāng advanced and garrisoned Xíngyáng.
Wáng Měng dispatched General Jiànwēi Liáng Chéng and Governor of Luòzhōu Dèng Qiāng to attack and drive him away.
He left Qiāng to garrison Jīnyǒng,
and appointed Commandery Administrator of Hóngnóng Huán Yín as Sīmǎ of Fǔguó.
Měng was General Fǔguó,
and he appointed Yín as Sīmǎ.
Qín initially appointed the Governor of Luòzhōu to garrison Shǎn.
Now that Dèng Qiāng had advanced to garrison Jīnyǒng,
Huán Yín was thus appointed to replace him in guarding Shǎn.
"Shǎn,"
pronounced "shī rǎn fān."
Qín King Jiān appointed Wáng Měng as Sītú
and Lù Shàngshū Shì,
and enfeoffed him as Marquis of Píngyáng Commandery.
Měng firmly declined, saying:
"Now Yān and Wú are not yet pacified,
and the war chariots are being readied.
If I receive the reward of the Three Excellencies
after only capturing one city,
"Three Excellencies"
refers to the Sāngōng.
what will there be to add to it?"
Jiān said:
"If I do not briefly set aside my own wishes,
how can I display the beauty of your humility?
I have already ordered the relevant authorities to temporarily allow you to retain your current post;
titles and rewards are for meritorious service."
"Yōng"
means merit.
4 In the second month,
on the *guǐyǒu* day,
Yuán Zhēn died.
Administrator of Chénjùn Zhū Fǔ appointed Zhēn's son Jǐn as General Jiànwēi and Governor of Yùzhōu,
to defend Shòuchūn.
He dispatched his son Gānzhī and Sīmǎ Cuàn Liàng to Yè to request a mandate.
The Yān people appointed Jǐn as Governor of Yángzhōu,
and Fǔ as Governor of Jīngzhōu.
5 In the third month,
Qín King Jiān appointed Minister of Personnel Quán Yì as Shàngshū Yòupúyè.
In summer,
in the fourth month,
Wáng Měng was again appointed Sītú
and Lù Shàngshū Shì.
Měng firmly declined,
and so it was stopped.
6 Yān and Qín both dispatched troops to assist Yuán Jǐn.
Grand Marshal Wēn sent Director Zhú Yáo and others to defend against them.
The Yān troops arrived first.
Yáo and others fought them at Wǔqiū,
and defeated them.
Wǔqiū
is Qīutóu.
When King Wén pacified Zhūgě Dàn,
he renamed it Wǔqiū
to commend military achievements.
Dù Yòu said: Qīutóu is Shěnqiū County of Yǐngzhōu.
Emperor Huì divided Rǔnán
and established the Nándùn Commandery.
Nánchéng
is the southern city of Shòuchūn.
Wēn’s disciple.
7 King Jiān of Qín again sent Wáng Měng to supervise General Zàngnán Yáng Ān and ten other generals, with sixty thousand infantry and cavalry, to attack Yān.
8 Mùróng Lìng judged that he would ultimately not escape.
He secretly plotted to raise an army.
In Shāchéng, there were several thousand exiled soldiers,
whom Lìng treated generously.
In the fifth month,
on the day Gēngwǔ,
Lìng killed Yámén Mèng Guī.
Chéng Dà Shè Guī was afraid
and offered his loyalty.
The Book of Surnames says: Shè
is a surname.
The *Zuǒ Zhuàn* states that Jìn had a grandee named Shè Tuó.
Guī,
pronounced Jū Wéi.
He placed him at his side.
He then led the exiled soldiers eastward to raid Wēidé Chéng.
Wēidé Chéng
was the city where Yǔwén Shè Yègān resided.
King Huǎng of Yān renamed it Wēidé Chéng.
He occupied the city and made deployments,
sending people to recruit the various garrisons to the east and west.
They all responded enthusiastically.
General Zhèndōng, the King of Bóhǎi Liàng, garrisoned Lóngchéng.
Lìng intended to attack him.
His younger brother Lín informed Liàng,
and Liàng closed the city gates and held firm.
On the day Guǐyǒu,
Shè Guī, while on duty, struck Lìng.
Lìng had placed Shè Guī at his side,
which is how he was able to strike him while on duty.
His partisans all scattered.
Shè Guī pursued Lìng to Xuēlízé,
captured and killed him,
and went to Lóngchéng to report to Liàng.
Liàng executed Shè Guī
and collected Lìng’s body for burial.
9 In the sixth month,
on the day Yǐmǎo,
King Jiān of Qín sent Wáng Měng off at Bàshàng,
saying:
“Today I entrust you with the responsibility for Guāndōng.
You must first conquer Húguān
and pacify Shàngdǎng.
Wèi Shōu said: Qín established Shàngdǎng Commandery,
governing Húguān City.
The Former Hàn governed Chángzǐ City.
Dǒng Zhuó governed Húguān City.
The Mùróng clan governed Ānmín City,
and later moved to Húguān City.
As the saying goes, ‘Thunder strikes so fast there’s no time to cover your ears.’
From the *Huáinánzǐ*.
Set out with the stars,
‘set out with the stars’ means to depart while the stars are still visible.
Advancing by both land and water.
You should not worry about anything in the future.”
Měng said:
“Your servant, wielding your divine might
and following your established plan,
will sweep away the remaining barbarians
like the wind sweeping leaves.
I ask that the imperial carriage not be troubled to personally brave the dust and fog,
but only that you quickly order the relevant officials to arrange dwellings for the Xiānbēi.”
This means to prepare shelters in advance
to await their arrival.
10 In autumn,
in the seventh month,
on Guǐyǒu *shuò*,
there was a solar eclipse.
11 King Měng of Qín attacked Húguān,
and Yáng Ān attacked Jìnyáng.
In the eighth month,
Lord Wěi of Yān ordered Grand Tutor, the King of Shàngyǒng Píng, to lead three hundred thousand elite troops from both the imperial court and outside to resist Qín.
The *Kǎoyì* says: The *Zàijì* says
“four hundred thousand,”
but we follow the *Jìn Chūnqiū* here.
He summoned Cavalier Attendant-in-ordinary Lǐ Fèng,
Sǎn,
pronounced Xī Dǎn.
Qí,
pronounced Qí Jì;
the same below.
“How are the Qín troops, in terms of numbers and strength?
Now that our large army has set out,
can Qín still fight?”
Fèng replied:
“Qín is a small state with weak forces,
no match for the royal army.
Jǐnglüè is an ordinary talent,
and no match for the Grand Tutor;
there is no need to worry.”
Wáng Měng’s courtesy name was Jǐnglüè.
“Victory and defeat lie in strategy,
not in numbers.
Qín has come from afar as an invader,
how can they not fight?
Moreover, we should use strategy to seek victory,
how can we merely hope that they do not fight?”
Wěi was displeased.
Wáng Měng conquered Húguān,
captured the Grand Administrator of Shàngdǎng, the King of Nán'ān Yuè.
All commanderies and counties he passed through
surrendered at his approach.
The Yān people were greatly alarmed.
The Yellow Gate Attendant Fēng Fú asked Secretary to the Minister of Works Shēn Yìn:
“What will become of these affairs?”
Yìn sighed and said:
“Yè will surely fall,
and we will all become captives of Qín this year.
However, Yuè gained favor with the year star, and Wú attacked it,
ultimately suffering misfortune.
*Zuǒ Zhuàn*: Zhaogong 32nd year,
Wú attacked Yuè.
Shǐ Mò said:
‘Within forty years,
will Yuè possess Wú?
Yuè has gained favor with the year star, yet Wú attacked it,
Wú will surely suffer misfortune.’
Dù Yù’s commentary says: This year, the year star was in Xīngjì.
Xīngjì
is the division of Wú and Yuè.
Where the year star is located,
that state has good fortune.
Wú used military force first,
and therefore suffered misfortune in return.
Zú,
pronounced Zǐ Xù.
Good fortune was with Yān,
also meaning the year star was in Yān’s division.
This is what Fú Jiān later meant when he said,
‘In the past, when I destroyed Yān,
I also offended the year star but was victorious.’
But the re-establishment of Yān
will be no more than one *jì* (twelve years) later.”
This sets the stage for the later restoration of Yān.
Fù,
pronounced Fú Yòu,
also as is.
12 Grand Marshal Wēn led twenty thousand troops from Guǎnglíng to attack Yuán Jǐn.
He appointed Administrator of Xiāngchéng Liú Bō as Administrator of Huáinán,
leading five thousand men to garrison Shítóu.
Bō
was the grandson of Kuí.
At the end of Emperor Yuán’s reign,
Liú Kuí, to avoid Wáng Dūn’s rebellion,
fled north to the Later Zhào.
Shuài,
pronounced Lǜ.
Jiāng,
pronounced Jì Liàng;
the same below.
On Guǐchǒu,
Wēn defeated Jǐn at Shòuchūn
and then besieged him.
Yān’s Left Guard General Mèng Gāo led cavalry to rescue Jǐn.
He reached the north of the Huái River,
but before crossing,
as Qín was attacking Yān,
Yān recalled Gāo.
13 The demon bandit Lǐ Hóng of Guǎnghàn,
falsely claiming to be the son of the Han Marquis Guīyì Shì,
gathered over ten thousand people.
He proclaimed himself the Sagely King
and adopted the era name Fènghuáng.
Lǐ Gāo of Lǒngxī,
falsely claiming to be the son of King Xióng of Chéng,
attacked and broke Fúchéng
and drove out the Inspector of Liángzhōu, Yáng Liàng.
In the ninth month,
Inspector of Yìzhōu Zhōu Chǔ sent his son Qióng to attack Gāo,
and also sent Qióng’s son, Administrator of Zǐtóng Xiāo, to attack Hóng.
Both were pacified.
14 Qín’s Yáng Ān attacked Jìnyáng.
Jìnyáng’s troops were numerous and its provisions ample,
so for a long time it could not be taken.
Wáng Měng left the屯騎校尉 (Leader of the Cavalry Escort) Gǒu Cháng to guard Húguān.
“Gǒu Cháng”
should probably be
“Gǒu Cháng”.
He dug a tunnel
and sent the 虎牙將軍 (Tiger-tooth General) Zhāng Háo to lead several hundred brave men to secretly enter the city.
They shouted loudly, cut down the gates,
and let the Qín troops in.
On the day Xīnsì,
Měng and Ān entered Jìnyáng
and captured the Yān Bīngzhōu Cìshǐ (Governor of Bīng Province) Dōnghǎi Wáng Zhuāng.
The Tàifù (Grand Tutor) Mùróng Píng, fearing Měng, dared not advance
and encamped at Lùchuān.
According to the Shuǐ Jīng Zhù, Lùchuān is north of Lùxiàn in Shàngdǎng.
Kān Yīn said: Lùshuǐ
is the Zhāngshuǐ.
It floods Jìzhōu.
In the tenth month,
on the day Xīnhài,
Měng left the general Wǔdū Máo Dāng to guard Jìnyáng,
advanced his troops to Lùchuān,
and engaged Mùróng Píng in a standoff.
On the day Rénxū,
Měng dispatched General Xú Chéng to scout the key strategic points of the Yān army.
“Xíng” (形) refers to
what is visible externally;
“yào” (要) refers to
what is contained within.
Scouting their external appearance
is not sufficient to determine victory or defeat;
scouting their key points
will decide the outcome of victory or defeat.
“Chān” (覘) is pronounced Chǒu-lián,
or Chǒu-yàn.
Chéng returned at dusk,
and Měng was enraged,
intending to behead him.
Dèng Qiāng pleaded for him, saying:
“Now the enemy is numerous and we are few.
We are about to fight at dawn tomorrow;
Dù Yù said: “Jiézhāo” (詰朝)
means dawn.
“Jié” (詰) is pronounced Qù-jí.
“Zhāo” (朝) is pronounced as written.
He is a great general,
so you should spare him for now.”
Měng said:
“If Chéng is not killed,
military law will not be established.”
Qiāng insisted:
“Chéng is
Qiāng’s郡將 (commander of the commandery).
Chéng was probably the Administrator of Qiāng’s home commandery.
“Jiāng” (將) is pronounced Jì-liàng;
the same below.
Qiāng is willing to fight with Chéng to redeem him.”
“Xiàozhàn” (効戰) means to exert one’s full effort in battle.
Qiāng, angered, returned to his camp,
beat the drums to assemble his troops,
and was about to attack Měng.
Měng asked him the reason,
and Qiāng said:
“I received an imperial edict to suppress distant bandits;
now there are nearby bandits
who kill each other,
so I want to eliminate them first!”
Měng considered Qiāng righteous and brave,
and had someone tell him:
“General, stop.
I will now pardon him.”
After Chéng was spared,
Qiāng went to Měng to apologize.
Měng held his hand and said:
“I was only testing you, General.
Since you act this way for a mere commander,
how much more so for the state!
I no longer worry about the enemy!”
Tàifù Píng, seeing that Měng had advanced deeply with an isolated army,
intended to defeat him through attrition.
Píng was greedy and contemptible.
He blocked off mountain springs,
and sold firewood and water.
Mountains
are relied upon for firewood;
springs
are relied upon for water.
By blocking off mountain springs,
he prevented the soldiers from gathering firewood and water,
and instead sold firewood and water for profit.
Jiǎ Gōngyàn said: “Gāo” (高) refers to a small mound,
“dà fù” (大阜) refers to a large mound.
No one had the will to fight.
Měng heard of this and
laughed, saying:
“Mùróng Píng is truly a despicable wretch!
Even if his forces were hundreds of millions, they would not be formidable,
let alone hundreds of thousands!
I shall certainly defeat him this year.”
He then sent the Yóují Jiāngjūn (Roving General) Guō Qìng to lead five thousand cavalry
to take a secret path at night, emerging behind Píng’s camp
to burn Píng’s baggage train.
The fire was visible from Yèzhōng.
Yān Lord Wěi was fearful
and sent the Shìzhōng (Palace Attendant) Lán Yī to reproach Píng, saying:
“You, King,
are the son of Gāozǔ.
Mùróng Guī’s temple name was Gāozǔ.
How can you neglect the soldiers and monopolize the sale of firewood and water,
focusing solely on making money?
The wealth in the treasury
is shared by Us and you, King;
what is there to worry about poverty?
If the enemy troops advance further,
and the family and state are lost,
where will you, King, put your money and silk?”
He then ordered all his money and silk to be distributed among the soldiers.
Lì Dàoyuán said: Píng sold water to the soldiers;
one roll of silk
was exchanged for two shi (石) of water.
Píng was greatly alarmed
and sent an envoy to request battle from Měng.
On the day Jiǎzǐ,
Měng arrayed his forces at Wèiyuán and swore an oath.
Note that the Wèishuǐ does not originate in Lùxiàn.
The Shuǐ Jīng Zhù mentions the Nièshuǐ originating from Fùzèngshān west of Lùxiàn.
Could it be that
the character “Wèi” (渭)
is
a mistake for “Niè” (涅)?
Also, according to Wēn Gōng’s Jīgǔ Lù,
it records Wáng Měng defeating Píng at Qīngyuán.
Dù Yù said: There is Qīngyuán north of Wénxǐxiàn in Hédōng.
This place is also far from Lùchuān,
so I will leave this as a doubt to await those who know.
Dù Yòu’s Tōng Diǎn writes
“Lùyuán”.
“Chén” (陳)
is read “zhèn”;
the same below.
“Wáng Jǐnglüè has received great favor from the state,
and his responsibilities encompass both internal and external affairs.
Now, with all of you, we have penetrated deep into enemy territory.
We must exert our utmost strength to the death,
advance without retreat,
and together achieve great merits
to repay the state.
To receive titles in the court of an enlightened ruler,
and toast to one’s parents in their home,
is this not glorious!”
“Shòu jué míng jūn zhī cháo” (受爵明君之朝) means to receive rewards at court for one’s achievements.
“Chēng shāng fùmǔ zhī shì” (稱觴父母之室) means to return home after receiving rewards,
and raise a cup to toast one’s parents.
“Cháo” (朝) is pronounced Zhí-yáo.
They broke their cooking pots and discarded their provisions,
shouting and pressing forward.
Měng looked at the numerous Yàn soldiers
and said to Dèng Qiāng:
"Today's situation,
without the General, we cannot defeat this formidable enemy.
The chance of success or failure
lies in this one action.
General, strive hard!"
Qiāng said:
"If you can give me the post of Sīlì,
then you need not worry, my lord."
Měng said:
"That is beyond my authority."
He insisted on being granted the positions of Anđìng Tàishǒu and Wànhù Hóu.
The Qín Yōngzhōu Cìshǐ governed Anđìng,
and Anđìng was a large commandery in Qínzhōng.
處 (chǔ, to grant a position).
The sound is like Chānglǚ (翻 refers to Fǎnqiè, a phonetic notation method).
Soon after, the armies clashed.
Měng summoned Qiāng,
but Qiāng was sleeping and did not respond.
Měng rode quickly to him and granted his request.
Only then did Qiāng drink a great deal in his tent,
and with Zhāng Háo, Xú Chéng, and others, mounted his horse, wielded his spear,
and charged into the Yàn formation.
He went in and out several times,
as if there were no one else around him,
killing and wounding several hundred.
By midday,
the Yàn army was utterly defeated,
with over fifty thousand captured or beheaded.
Taking advantage of the victory, they pursued,
killing or accepting the surrender of another hundred thousand people.
Píng escaped alone and returned to Yè.
Cuī Hóng commented: Dèng Qiāng's request for a commandery to bend the law
was for his own private gain;
his bringing troops to attack Wáng Měng
showed insubordination;
his demanding the Sīlì position before the battle
was an act of presumption.
With these three faults,
which sin is greater?
Měng was able to tolerate his shortcomings
and utilize his strengths,
like taming a fierce tiger
or riding a wild horse,
thereby achieving great success.
The Shī Jīng says:
"When gathering fěng and fěi,
do not reject the lower parts."
This is from the "Gǔfēng" poem in the Shī Jīng.
Máo Shì said: Fěng
is xū;
fěi is
wù;
lower parts
are roots and stems.
Zhèng Shì said: These two vegetables,
the turnip and the hog-peanut,
can both be eaten whole,
yet their roots have good times
and bad times.
Those who gather them
should not discard their leaves simply because the roots are bad.
Lù Jī's Cǎomù Shū says: Fěng
is the turnip.
Fěi is xīcài.
Guō Pú said: Fěng
is the Chinese cabbage.
South of the Jiāng there is Chinese cabbage,
and north of the Jiāng there are turnips;
they are similar but different.
Fěi and
wù
are the wild cucumber.
Xīcài resembles the turnip,
with purple-red flowers,
and is edible.
Fú has
large leaves,
white flowers,
roots like fingers,
white in color and edible.
葍 (fú),
the sound is like fāngliù (翻 refers to Fǎnqiè, a phonetic notation method).
The Qín army advanced eastward,
attacking Yè from Lùchuān eastward.
On Dīngmǎo day,
Yè was besieged.
Měng submitted a memorial stating:
"On the Jiǎzǐ day,
your minister utterly annihilated the enemy.
This refers to the victory on Jiǎzǐ day, an event similar to King Wǔ of Zhōu defeating Zhòu.
殲 (jiān),
the sound is like Xīlián (翻 refers to Fǎnqiè, a phonetic notation method).
The common people of the six provinces
did not even realize the change of ruler.
Unless they stubbornly resisted and disobeyed orders,
no one was harmed."
Qín Wáng Jiān replied to him, saying:
"Your general's campaign did not exceed a season,
three months constitute a season.
Your achievements surpass those of ancient times.
I will now personally lead the six armies,
setting out at dawn and arriving with the speed of lightning.
The Shī Jīng says: 'Setting out at dawn with the stars still visible.'
This means driving early, seeing the stars and traveling.
Arriving with the speed of lightning
describes its swiftness.
帥 (shuài)
is read as 率 (shuài).
Wait for me to arrive,
and then take it."
Before Měng arrived,
robbery and plunder were rampant near Yè.
But when Měng arrived,
order was restored near and far;
his commands were strict and clear,
and the army committed no private transgressions.
This means the soldiers dared not privately harm the people of Yè.
The Yàn people each settled into their livelihoods
and said to one another:
"We never expected to see King Tàiyuán again today!"
Wáng Měng heard this
and sighed, saying:
"Mùróng Xuángōng is indeed an extraordinary man;
he can be called a 'lingering love' from antiquity!"
Mùróng Kè,
courtesy name Xuángōng,
was enfeoffed as King Tàiyuán.
In the eleventh month,
Qín Wáng Jiān left Lǐ Wēi to assist the Crown Prince in defending Cháng'ān,
and Yángpíng Gōng Róng to guard Luòyáng.
He himself led a hundred thousand elite troops to Yè,
arriving at Ānyáng in seven days.
The Jìn Zhì says: Ānyáng County belonged to Wèijùn.
Wèi Shōu's Zhì says: In the early Tiānpíng era,
Dàngyīn and Ānyáng were merged and belonged to Yè.
Also, in the northern Xiūwǔ County of Jíjjùn, there was Ānyáng City.
Fú Hóng's father and son had previously garrisoned Fāngtóu;
some old veterans were still alive,
and hearing of Jiān's arrival,
they welcomed him at Ānyáng,
so he hosted a banquet.
Jiān asked:
"Why did Zhōu Yàfū not welcome Emperor Wén of Hàn?
See volume fifteen, 'Six years after Emperor Wén of Hàn'.
What was the reason?"
Měng replied:
"Yàfū retreated from his lord to gain fame;
your minister secretly despises this.
Moreover, your minister serves under Your Majesty's divine might,
striking a dying enemy,
like fish in a pot,
what is there to worry about?
The regent is young and immature,
'Crown Prince defending' means 'regent'.
監 (jiān),
the sound is like Gōngxián (翻 refers to Fǎnqiè, a phonetic notation method).
If something unexpected were to happen,
what regret could compare?
Has Your Majesty forgotten your minister's words at Bàshàng?"
Initially,
Yàn Yídū Wáng Huán led over ten thousand troops to garrison Shātíng.
Dù Yù says: Yuánchéng County in Yángpíng has Shātíng.
Hearing of Píng's defeat,
he led his troops to garrison Nèihuáng.
Nèihuáng County had belonged to Wèijùn since the Hàn dynasty.
On Dīngchǒu day,
Huán led five thousand Xiānbēi to flee to Lóngchéng.
On Wùyín day,
Yàn Sànqí Shìláng Yú Wèi led over five hundred Fúyú, Gāogōulí, and Shàngdǎng hostages,
at night,
opened Yè's north gate to admit the Qín troops.
Yàn Zhǔ Wěi, along with Shàngyōng Wáng Píng, Lè'ān Wáng Zāng, Dìngxiāng Wáng Yuān, Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn Mèng Gāo, and Diànzhōng Jiāngjūn Ài Láng, fled to Lóngchéng.
Xìngpǔ: The Ài surname.
In Yànzǐ Chūnqiū, Qí had a Dàfū Ài Kǒng.
Fēngsú Tōng mentions Páng Jiǎn's mother, Lady Ài.
On Xīnsì day,
Qín Wáng Jiān entered the Yè palace.
Mùróng Chuí saw the dukes, ministers, grandees, and former colleagues and subordinates of Yān,
and showed resentment.
Gāo Bì said to Chuí:
"Your Royal Highness, relying on the accumulated resources of your ancestors,
possessing the strategy of an eminent hero,
encountered hardship and adversity,
and sojourned in a foreign land.
Although the state and your family are now overthrown,
how do we know this is not the beginning of a resurgence?
Your humble servant believes that for the old retainers of the state,
you should display the breadth of the rivers and seas,
so as to comfort and reconcile their hearts,
to lay the foundation of 'overturning a basket of earth'
and achieve the 'nine-rèn' accomplishment.
The saying is like building a mountain,
starting with overturning one basket of earth and progressing to achieve the nine-rèn accomplishment.
'Kuì'
is pronounced 'qiúwèi',
meaning an earth-basket.
Eight chǐ is one rèn.
Your humble servant secretly thinks that Your Royal Highness should not act in this way!"
Gāo Bì had previously followed Chuí when he fled to Qín,
hence he dared to offer this advice.
'Wéi'
is pronounced 'yúwèi'.
Mùróng Chuí followed his advice.
When Yān Lord Wěi departed from Yè,
his guards still numbered over a thousand cavalry.
Once outside the city,
they all dispersed,
with only about ten cavalrymen accompanying him.
Qín King Jiān sent the General of Campaigning, Guō Qìng, to pursue him.
At that time, the roads were difficult.
Mèng Gāo assisted and protected Wěi,
and guarded the two princes.
The two princes
referred to Prince Lè'ān Zāng and Prince Dìngxiāng Yuān.
Furthermore, they encountered bandits everywhere,
fighting as they advanced.
After several days,
they reached Fúlù.
They rested by a tomb.
"Jiěxī"
means untying saddles and resting horses.
"Zhǒng"
is pronounced "zhīlóng".
All carried bows and arrows.
Gāo held a sword and fought,
killing and wounding several people.
Gāo's strength was exhausted.
This means his strength was depleted and he was very tired.
He then directly went forward, hugged a bandit,
and slammed him to the ground,
shouting loudly:
"A man is cornered!"
The other bandits shot Gāo from the side,
killing him.
Ài Lǎng saw Gāo fighting alone,
also rushed back to confront the bandits,
and died together with him.
Wěi lost his horse and fled on foot.
Guō Qìng caught up with him at Gāoyáng.
His subordinate general Jù Wǔ was about to bind him.
The "Xìngpǔ" says: Jù
is a surname.
Wěi said: "What kind of petty person are you,
daring to bind the Son of Heaven?"
Wǔ said:
"I received an imperial edict to pursue a rebel,
what Son of Heaven are you talking about?"
He captured him and brought him to Qín King Jiān.
Jiān questioned him about his not surrendering but fleeing.
Wěi replied:
"A fox dies with its head towards its den; I wished to die by the tombs of my ancestors."
The ancestors of the Mùróng clan were all buried in Chānglí.
Jiān ordered him to return to his palace
and lead his civil and military officials to surrender.
In the eighth year of Jìn Emperor Mù's Yǒnghé era,
Yān Lord Jùn changed the era name and declared himself emperor.
The throne was passed to his son Wěi.
The state lasted for a total of nineteen years before its demise.
"Shuài"
is pronounced "lǜ".
Jiān ordered a generous burial for Mùróng Wěi
and appointed his son as a Lángzhōng.
Guō Qìng advanced to Lóngchéng.
Grand Tutor Píng fled to Gāogōulì.
Gāogōulì captured Píng
and sent him to Qín.
Prince Yídū Huán killed the General who Guards the East, Prince Bóhǎi Liàng,
incorporated his forces,
and fled to Liáodōng.
The Administrator of Liáodōng, Hán Chóu,
had already surrendered to Qín.
When Huán arrived,
he was unable to enter.
He attacked the city
but failed to conquer it.
Guō Qìng sent General Zhū Yí to attack him.
Huán abandoned his troops and fled alone.
Yí captured and killed him.
All the regional governors and administrators, as well as the chiefs of the Six Barbarian Tribes, surrendered to Qín.
In total, Qín acquired one hundred and fifty-seven commanderies,
two million four hundred and sixty thousand households,
and nine million nine hundred and ninety thousand people.
The palace women and treasures of Yān were distributed among the generals and soldiers as rewards.
An imperial edict of general amnesty was issued, which read:
"We, being of limited virtue,
have presumptuously received this glorious mandate.
Unable to pacify distant lands through virtue
and bring peace to the four cardinal directions,
The four cardinal directions:
southeast,
southwest,
northeast,
and northwest.
We have harmed these people.
Although it is the fault of the common people, it is also Our fault.
Therefore, there shall be a great amnesty throughout the realm,
and a fresh start shall be made with them."
Initially,
when Liáng Chēn was sent as an envoy to Qín,
Gǒu Chún, the Palace Attendant, was made his deputy.
The office of Palace Attendant was likely a close official position established by Yān.
Chēn did not inform Chún beforehand;
Chún resented this,
and upon returning, told Yān Lord Wěi:
"Chēn was very close to Wáng Měng in Cháng'ān;
I suspect he has ulterior motives."
Chēn also repeatedly praised Qín King Jiān and Wáng Měng,
and further stated that Qín was about to raise an army,
and preparations should be made.
Afterwards, Qín indeed attacked Yān,
and everything was as Chēn had said.
Wěi then suspected that Chēn knew the truth.
When Mùróng Píng was defeated,
Chēn was consequently arrested and imprisoned.
Qín King Jiān entered Yè and released him,
appointing him as a Zhōngshū Zhùzuò Láng.
Qín probably followed the early Jìn system
of combining the Secretarial Bureau with the Central Secretariat.
Jiān said to him:
"You once said that the Prince of Shàngyōng and the Prince of Wú were both exceptional talents as generals and ministers.
Why were they unable to plan,
allowing their state to perish?"
Chēn replied:
"The rise and fall of states are decreed by Heaven; how could those two men change it?"
Jiān said:
"You failed to 'perceive the subtle stirrings' and act accordingly,
instead falsely praising Yān's beauty.
Your loyalty did not protect you,
but rather brought disaster upon yourself.
Can this be called wisdom?"
Chēn replied:
"Your servant heard that 'subtle stirrings are the minute movements,
the first indications of good fortune.'
This is a phrase from the Great Commentary of the Yì.
'Jī'
is pronounced 'jūxī'.
'Jiàn'
is pronounced 'xiánbiàn'.
This is truly beyond my grasp.
However, as a minister, there is nothing better than loyalty;
as a son, there is nothing better than filial piety.
Unless one has a resolute heart,
one cannot maintain loyalty and filial piety from beginning to end.
Therefore, the brave men of old,
did not change in the face of danger,
and did not shy away from death,
in order to serve their ruler and parents.
Those who 'perceive the subtle stirrings' understand safety and danger in their hearts,
choose whether to stay or leave with their bodies,
and disregard their family and state.
Even if your servant knew how to do this,
I still would not bear to do it,
let alone it being beyond my grasp!"
Liáng Chēn was loyal to his duties.
Qín King Jiān could not properly recognize and utilize him.
Discerning people knew from this that the Qín dynasty would not last long.
Jiān heard of Yuè Wǎn's loyalty.
Yuè Wǎn's deeds can be found in Volume 10, Year 3.
He appointed his son as a Lángzhōng.

Jiān appointed Wáng Méng as Imperial Commissioner (使持節), Area Commander-in-Chief of Military Affairs of the Six Guāndōng Prefectures (都督關東六州諸軍事), Grand General of Chariots and Cavalry (車騎大將軍), Minister with the Privileges of the Three Ducal Ministers (開府儀同三司), and Governor of Jìzhōu (冀州牧),
to guard Yè.
His noble rank was advanced to Marquis of Qīnghé Commandery (清河郡侯).
All the possessions from Mùróng Píng’s residence were bestowed upon him.
Yáng Ān was granted the title of Marquis of Bópíng County (博平縣侯). Dèng Qiāng was appointed Imperial Commissioner (使
持節), General Who Conquers Barbarians (征虜將軍), and Administrator of Āndìng (安定太守),
and was granted the title of Marquis of Zhēndìng Commandery (真定郡侯).
Guō Qìng was appointed Imperial Commissioner (持節), Area Commander-in-Chief of Military Affairs of Yōuzhōu (都督幽州諸軍事), and Inspector of Yōuzhōu (幽州刺史),
to guard Jì,
and was granted the title of Marquis of Xiāngchéng (襄城侯).
Those who were granted titles
were granted the rank of marquis,
but did not possess a state or territory.
One account states that
they had not been previously ranked with titles,
and were now granted them for the first time.
Jiān appointed Wéi Zhōng of Jīngzhào as Administrator of Wèijùn (魏郡太守),
and Péng Bào as Administrator of Yángpíng (陽平太守).
As Yān’s capital was Yè,
the Administrator of Wèijùn served as the metropolitan prefect.
Yángpíng
was an auxiliary commandery.
Therefore, Jiān appointed Qín people to govern all of them.
He retained them based on their previous positions.
He completely replaced the governors (牧), administrators (守), magistrates (令), and chiefs (長) of the prefectures and counties.
This not only startled public opinion,
but also because human sentiment meant that new and old officials would not get along.
Therefore, he kept the old ones.
He sent Wéi Zhōng and Wéi Rú of Jīngzhào, who was a Gentleman of the Yellow Gate (散騎侍郎), together as Embroidered Uniform Envoys (繡衣使者)
to tour the prefectures and commanderies of Guāndōng,
observe local customs,
encourage agriculture and sericulture,
relieve the poor and distressed,
collect and bury the dead,
honor exemplary conduct,
and abolish any Yān policies that were inconvenient for the people.
Both Yān and Qín people were used as Embroidered Uniform Envoys.
Yān people were used
because they were familiar with Guāndōng customs;
Qín people were used
to proclaim Jiān’s virtuous intentions.
行 (Háng),
pronounced as Mèng.
In the twelfth month,
King Jiān of Qín relocated Mùróng Wěi and the empress dowager, dukes, and officials of Yān, along with over forty thousand households of the Xiānbēi, to Cháng’ān.
This laid the groundwork for the later Xiānbēi to exploit chaos and attack Qín.
Wáng Méng submitted a memorial requesting to retain Liáng Chēn as his Chief Clerk (主簿)
and concurrently as Records Officer (記室督).
The Jìn system stipulated that each ducal mansion had one Chief Clerk and one Records Officer.
Now Méng appointed Chēn to hold both positions concurrently.
Méng discussed with his subordinates and the envoys from the Yān court.
Méng said,
"People's hearts differ. Formerly, Lord Liáng, upon arriving in Cháng’ān,
exclusively praised his own court;
Lord Yuè only spoke of Huán Wēn's powerful army;
Lord Hǎo subtly mentioned the nation's failings."
Liáng Chēn, Yuè Sōng, and Hǎo Guǐ.
"His own court" (本朝) and "nation's failings" (國弊) both refer to Yān.
朝 (Cháo),
pronounced as Zhí Yáo.
使 (Shǐ),
pronounced as Shū Lì.
"Now these three men are all ministers of this country."
"This country" refers to Qín.
Méng said,
"Lord Hǎo was the first to understand the opportune moment."
Dàn said,
"In that case, Your Excellency rewarded Dīng Gōng and punished Jì Bù."
This means his method of selecting ministers
differed from that of Emperor Gāo of Hàn.
King Jiān of Qín traveled from Yè to Fāngtóu.
He feasted the elders
and renamed Fāngtóu to Yǒngchāng,
restoring it for all generations.
On the Jiǎyín day,
he arrived in Cháng’ān. He enfeoffed Mùróng Wěi as Marquis of Xīnxīng (新興侯).
Among the former officials of Yān, Mùróng Píng was appointed Attendant Official (給事中),
Huángfǔ Zhēn as Cavalry Commandant (奉車都尉),
and Lǐ Hóng as Commandant of Cavalcade (駙馬都尉),
all serving at court.
These three men
were the Three Ducal Ministers of Yān.
Fēng Héng was appointed Grand Secretary (尚書郎),
and Mùróng Dé as Administrator of Zhāngyè (張掖太守).
This laid the groundwork for Dé’s nephew Chāo to remain in Zhāngyè and later join the Yáo clan.
Xīluó Téng was appointed Administrator of the Three Bureaus (三署郎).
The Hàn dynasty had Administrators of the Five Official Bureaus (五官署郎), Administrators of the Left Bureau (左署郎), and Administrators of the Right Bureau (右署郎),
hence the name "Administrators of the Three Bureaus."
According to the old system, officials aged fifty or above
belonged to the Five Official Bureaus,
while others were distributed among the Left and Right Bureaus.
Qín then adopted "Administrators of the Three Bureaus" as an official title.
Héng was the son of Yù.
When Mùróng Guàng rose to power,
Fēng Yù distinguished himself through loyal remonstrance.
The former Grand Astrologer of Yān, Huáng Hóng, sighed and said,
"Yān will surely be revived!
Will it be through the King of Wú?
I regret that I am old
and will not live to see it!"
When Mùróng first rose,
Huáng Hóng pledged allegiance to him.
When Jùn conquered the Central Plains,
Huáng Hóng praised his decision. Hóng was knowledgeable in calculations.
"Heaven's will lies with Yān,"
referring to the Jupiter star being in the Yān constellation division.
"And in fifteen years,
Qín will again belong to Yān."
Mùróng Huán’s son Fèng,
at the age of eleven,
secretly harbored the ambition of revenge.
All Xiānbēi and Dīnglíng people with spirit and ability leaned towards him and formed connections.
This laid the groundwork for Mùróng Fèng and the Dīnglíng to later raise an army and attack Qín.
"My son is just about to distinguish himself with his talent and prestige;
do not emulate your father, who did not recognize Heaven's mandate!"
Fèng sternly replied,
"The former king wished to establish loyalty but did not succeed;
this is the principle of a minister.
How can your Lordship's words
be considered an encouragement for future righteousness?"
Yì changed his expression and apologized,
then spoke to King Jiān of Qín, saying,
"Mùróng Fèng is spirited and talented;
but he has the heart of a wolf,
and I fear he will ultimately not be used by others."
The Zǔzhuàn says: Chǔ Lingyin Zǐwén said,
"The wolf cub has a wild heart."
The historian implies that the ministers and sons of Yān would not long be subservient.
In the 16th year, Qín abolished Yōngzhōu.
Qín had established Yōngzhōu in Āndìng,
but now it was abolished and incorporated into the jurisdiction of the Director of Retainers (司隸校尉).
In the 17th year,
Duke Yáng Shì of Qiúchí died.
