His son Zuǎn succeeded him,
and immediately broke ties with Qín.
His uncle Tǒng, the Administrator of Wǔdū, contended with him for the state,
raising troops to attack each other.
This laid the groundwork for Qín to attack Qiúchí.
Punctuation by Wáng Chóngwǔ, reviewed by Róng Zhàozǔ and Niè Chóngqí.
Compiled by Sīmǎ Guāng
by imperial decree.
Later studies, by Tiāntái.
Emperor Jiǎnwén of Tàizōng
was named Yù,
courtesy name Dàowàn,
the youngest son of Emperor Yuán.
He was enfeoffed as King of Lángyá,
later transferred to King of Kuàijī.
After Emperor Hǎixī ascended the throne,
the Lángyá line became extinct,
so he was again transferred to King of Lángyá,
which he firmly declined.
Therefore, although he was enfeoffed as King of Lángyá, he did not abandon the title of Kuàijī.
The rules for posthumous titles state: "Unwavering in virtue is called Jiǎn;
profound in morality and knowledge is called Wén."
Xián'ān First Year (Xīnwèi, 371 AD).
In the eleventh month of this year,
Emperor Hǎixī was deposed,
and the Emperor ascended the throne,
beginning the new era name Xián'ān.
The Zīzhì Tōngjiàn chronicles by year,
thus associating it with the new era name.
1. Spring,
first month.
Yuán Jǐn and Zhū Fǔ sought aid from Qín.
King Jiān of Qín appointed Jǐn as Inspector of Yángzhōu (揚州刺史)
and Fǔ as Inspector of Jiāozhōu (交州刺史),
and dispatched Wǔ Wèi General Wǔdū Wáng Jiàn and Former General Zhāng Háo, leading twenty thousand infantry and cavalry, to rescue them.
Grand Marshal Huán Wēn sent Huái'nán Administrator Huán Yī and Nándùn Administrator Huán Shíqián, among others, to attack Jiàn and Háo at Shíqiáo.
According to the biography of Huán Wēn,
Shíqiáo was north of the Féishuǐ.
守 (Shǒu),
pronounced as Shì Yòu.
The Qín forces retreated and encamped at Shènchéng.
Shèn County,
during the Hàn dynasty, belonged to Rǔnán Commandery;
the Jìn dynasty separated it to belong to Rǔyīn Commandery.
The Shèn County of Táng Lúzhōu
was the Shèn County of Nánliáng Commandery during the Liáng and Wèi dynasties,
the land of Qūnjí County of Jiǔjiāng in the Hàn dynasty,
and not this Shènchéng.
He was Xuān’s son.
Huán Xuān assisted Zǔ Tì in resisting Zǔ Yuē,
and defended Xiāngyáng,
both with merit.
On the Dīnghài day,
Wēn captured Shòuchūn, seized Jǐn and Fǔ,
and sent them and their clans to Jiànkāng,
where they were executed.
2 Qín Wáng Jiān relocated 150,000 households of eminent figures from Guāndōng and various non-Hàn groups to Guānzhōng.
He settled the Wūhuán in Féngyì and Běidì,
and the Dīnglíng Zái Bīn in Xīn'ān and Miǎnchí.
This laid the groundwork for Zái Bīn to raise an army amidst Qín's chaos.
處 (chǔ)
Chānglǚ fān.
澠 (miǎn)
Mǐyǎn fān.
斌 (bīn)
Yīn Bīn.
Those who wished to return to their former professions
were all allowed to do so.
3 In the second month,
Qín appointed Wèi Jùn Tàishǒu Wéi Zhōng as Qīngzhōu Cìshǐ,
with the seat of Qīngzhōu Cìshǐ at Guǎnggù.
Shèshēng Xiàowèi Xú Chéng was made Bìngzhōu Cìshǐ,
Wǔwèi Jiāngjūn Wáng Jiàn as Yùzhōu Cìshǐ,
Zuǒ Jiāngjūn Péng Yuè as Xúzhōu Cìshǐ,
Tàiwèi Sīmǎ Huángfǔ Fù as Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ.
Jìn Zhì says: After Qín conquered Yān,
it stationed the Yǎnzhōu Cìshǐ at Cāngyuán,
the Bìngzhōu Cìshǐ at Jìnyáng,
the Yùzhōu Cìshǐ at Luòyáng,
and the Xúzhōu Cìshǐ at Péngchéng.
Qín initially stationed the Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ at Fēngyáng,
later moving it to Xiāngyáng.
I (Yú) note that Qín had not yet gained Xiāngyáng at this time,
so it probably remained at Yān's old station of Lǔyáng.
Fúfēng Nèishǐ Wáng Tǒng was made Yìzhōu Cìshǐ.
Liángzhōu belonged to Zhāng Tiānxī.
Yìzhōu
was Jìn territory.
Qín likely established Liángzhōu in the Tiānshuǐ region
and Yìzhōu in the Fúfēng region.
校 (jiào)
Hùjiào fān.
雅 (yǎ)
Fú Shì also.
Before this, there was no Jìnzhōu;

and Qín likely established Jìnzhōu here.
雍 (yōng)
Yūyòng fān.
Jiān wanted to advance and take Liáng and Yì,
hence he appointed Cìshǐ for Liáng and Yì prefectures.
After Yáng Ān captured Chóuchí,
he was first given the title of Dū Nánqínzhōu
and stationed at Chóuchí.
使 (shǐ)
Shūlì fān.
Governing Púbǎn;
Qín abolished Yōngzhōu, as seen in the previous volume, last year.
復 (fù)
Fúyòu fān.
雍 (yōng)
Yūyòng fān.
阪 (bǎn)
Yīn Bǎn.
Chéng
was Pínglǎo's son;
Tǒng
was Zhuó's son.
In Mù Dì Yǒnghé Shí Nián (355 CE),
Wáng Zhuó surrendered to Qín.
For governors and magistrates, capable people were needed,
so Wáng Měng was instructed to use his discretion to select talented individuals,
appointing them as governors and magistrates for the six prefectures.
After the appointments were made,
it was said that the imperial court formally approved them.
Presented to the Qín court,
they were formally appointed.
Alas!
Xún Qīng Zǐ said: "Conquest is easy,
consolidation is difficult."
With Fú Jiān's insight
and Wáng Měng's strategy,
they selected talented individuals from the six prefectures to appoint as governors and magistrates.
However, when the Xiānbēi rallied with a single cry amidst the chaos,
they swiftly united for Yān.
From this, one knows that the situation in the world
depends only on the inclinations of the people.
4 In the third month,
on the Rénchén day,
Yìzhōu Cìshǐ Jiànchéng Dìng Gōng Zhōu Chǔ died.
The rule for posthumous titles says: "Great foresight and pacifying the people is called Dìng."
5 Qín's Hòujiāngjūn Jīnchéng Jùnán attacked Lánlíng Tàishǒu Zhāng Mǐnzǐ at Táoshān.
俱 (jù)

Given name.

6 Qín's Xīxiàn Hóu Yǎ, Yáng Ān, Wáng Tǒng, Xú Chéng, along with Yǔlín Zuǒjiān Zhū Róng, and Yángwǔ Jiāngjūn Yáo Cháng, led 70,000 infantry and cavalry to attack Chóuchí Gōng Yáng Zuǎn.
7 Dài general Chángsūn Jīn plotted to assassinate Dài Wáng Shíyìjiān.

He then seized Jīn
and killed him.
Dài's ancestor, Tuòbá Lín,
made his second eldest brother the Bábá Shì,

將 (jiàng)
Jíliàng fān.

the fourth month,

"In the past, your esteemed ancestors called themselves vassals of Liú Yào and Shí Lè,

"There has never been a ruler bowing in front
while a minister bows behind."
At that time,
the relationship between the ruler and ministers of Jìn (晉)
can thus be understood.
This is what the meaning of "subtle yet manifest" in the Chūnqiū (春秋) refers to.
On the day Wùwǔ (戊午),
a general amnesty was granted,
and the ranks of civil and military officials were raised by two grades.
On the day Jǐwèi (己未),
Wēn (溫) went to Báishí (白石)
and submitted a memorial requesting to return to Gūshú (姑孰).
On the day Gēngshēn (庚申),
an edict appointed Wēn (溫) as Chancellor
and Grand Marshal, as before,
to remain in the capital to assist in governance.
Wēn (溫) firmly declined,
then requested to return to his garrison.
On the day Xīnyǒu (辛酉),
Wēn (溫) returned to Gūshú (姑孰) from Báishí (白石).
Qín Wáng Jiān (秦王堅), hearing of Wēn's (溫) deposition and establishment,
said to his attendants:
"Wēn (溫) previously suffered a defeat at Bàshàng (灞上),
see Vol. 99, Tàihé (太和) 10th year of Mù Dì (穆帝).
See earlier volume, Tàihé (太和) 4th year.
Now he again deposes a ruler to please himself.
A sixty-year-old man,
acting like this,
how will he be able to accommodate himself in the four seas!
The proverb says: 'Being angry with his wife, he shows his displeasure to his father.'
This refers to Huán Wēn (桓溫)."
In the 19th year [of the Jianwǔ era], Qín's Grand General of Chariots and Cavalry, Wáng Měng,
considering the heavy responsibility of the six provinces,
spoke to Qín King Jiān,
requesting that he be replaced by a trusted and worthy person;
and as for the selection of suitable officials by the府 (fǔ, household),
he had already stopped it,
instead asking for one province to prove himself.
Jiān replied,
"My relationship with you,
in terms of righteousness, is that of lord and minister,
but in intimacy, it surpasses that of flesh and blood.
Although Huán and Zhāo had Guǎn and Yuè,
Qí Huán Gōng had Guǎn Zhòng,
and Yān Zhāo Wáng had Yuè Yì.
I consider myself to surpass them.
For a ruler, it is laborious to seek talent,
but leisurely to obtain worthy men.
Wáng Bāo's 'Ode to a Sagely Lord Obtaining Worthy Men' says: 'He who governs men,
is diligent in seeking the worthy,
and leisurely in obtaining men.'
Thus, I have no worries about the east,
which is not to say that I value you highly,
but rather that I seek my own ease and comfort.
Indeed, what is difficult to obtain,
is also difficult to maintain.
If the wrong person is appointed,
trouble will arise beyond expectation.
表 (biǎo),
means 'outside'.
Kǒng Yǐngdá said: 'A rebellion outside the borders is called 表 (biǎo).'
This is also your responsibility.
Therefore, I leave the high position of the Prime Minister vacant and prioritize the division of authority.
You have not understood my heart,
which greatly deviates from my usual expectations.
New policies await talent,
so you should quickly appoint and supplement them.
When the transformation of the east is complete,
you shall return to the west in your ceremonial robes."
When Zhōu Gōng campaigned in the east,
a Grandee of Zhōu composed the poem 'Jiǔ Yù' for him,
its words saying:
"Trout and bream are fish of the nine-net,
I saw that gentleman,
in ceremonial robes and embroidered skirt."
It also says:
"Therefore, there are ceremonial robes,
do not let our lord return,
do not make my heart sorrowful."
The commentary says: "The king should greet Zhōu Gōng with the attire of a high lord."
So Měng continued to manage affairs as before.
The historians say that the relationship between Fú Jiān and Wáng Měng as lord and minister was so profound,
which allowed Měng to fully display his talents.
讜 (dǎng),
pronounced 'duo lang fan'.
In the 20th year, in the twelfth month,
Grand Marshal Huán Wēn memorialized:
"Those who have been deposed and dismissed,
should be kept far away,
and should not be allowed to oversee the common people.
The King of Dōnghǎi should follow the precedent of Chāngyì."
The Chāngyì incident is found in Volume 24, during the Yuánpíng first year of Emperor Zhāodì of Hàn.
The Empress Dowager's edict said:
"To make him a commoner,
I cannot bear it.
He may be specially enfeoffed as a king."
Wēn further memorialized:
"He may be enfeoffed as Marquis of Hǎixī County."
On the day Gēngyín,
he was enfeoffed as Duke of Hǎixī County.
The 'Kǎo Yì' says: The 'Chronicles of the Duke of Hǎixī' states:
"In the second year of Xián'ān,
in the first month,
he was degraded and enfeoffed."
We now follow the 'Chronicles of Emperor Jiǎnwén'.
Wēn's prestige shook both within and outside the court.
Although the Emperor held the esteemed position,
he merely stood silent and still,
constantly fearing deposition.
Before this,
the planet Yínghuò (Mars) had been observing the Duānmén of Tàiwēi.
The 'Astronomy Monograph' says: "The space between the two stars in the southern barrier of Tàiwēi is called Duānmén."
先 (xiān),
pronounced 'xi jie fan'.
On the day Xīnmǎo,
Yínghuò retrograded and entered Tàiwēi.
The Emperor was greatly disturbed by this.
The Imperial Secretary, Xī Chāo, was on duty,
meaning he was on duty in the imperial office.
[The Emperor said:] "The length or shortness of my life,
I originally do not consider;
but will there truly be no recent incident related to this?"
When the Emperor was Fǔjūn,
he had invited Chāo to be his staff officer,
which is why he dared to ask him frankly now.
復 (fù),
pronounced 'fu you fan'.
[Chāo replied:] "Grand Marshal, your servant Huán Wēn,
is stabilizing the state internally,
and expanding his strategies externally.
For any extraordinary event,
your servant guarantees it with a hundred lives."
When Chāo requested urgent leave to visit his father,
the Jìn regulations stated: "For urgent leave, one may take five days at a time,
with a limit of sixty days in a year."
Historical records referring to 'taking urgent leave' or 'requesting urgent leave'
all mean applying for leave.
省 (shěng),
pronounced 'xi jing fan'.
[The Emperor said:] "Convey my regards to your honorable father.
The affairs of the family and state
have reached such a point,
due to my inability to assist and protect it with integrity.
My shame and lament are so profound,
how can words express them!"
He then recited Yǔ Chǎn's poem:
"A man of resolve grieves at the court's peril,
a loyal minister mourns his lord's humiliation."
And thereupon, tears streamed down, soaking his lapel.
This was also a clear talk,
but his emotion overflowed beyond words.
朝 (cháo),
pronounced 'zhi yao fan';
same below.
[The Emperor] was good at dignified demeanor,
and devoted to classical texts,
with thick dust covering his mat,
yet he remained calm and serene.
Although his spirit and consciousness were tranquil and expansive,
he lacked grand strategies to save the world.
Xiè Ān considered him to be like Emperor Huì's caliber,
but only slightly better at clear talks.
Clear talks are of no benefit to state affairs;
that Xiè Ān, at that time,
could express this view,
can be said to be superior to the common people.
Because of Xī Chāo's connection to Wēn,
everyone in court feared and served him.
Xiè Ān once visited Chāo with General of the Left Guard Wáng Tǎnzhī.
It was late in the day, and they had not yet been granted an audience.
Tǎnzhī wanted to leave,
but Ān said:
"Can you not endure for a moment for the sake of your life?"
The historians say that Xiè Ān, amidst his elegant demeanor,
was capable of managing affairs and responding to situations.
Furthermore, although Xī Chāo's power and influence were so great,
after Huán Wēn's death,
Chāo was able to die in his own bed,
presumably through his wisdom.
為 (wèi),
pronounced 'yu wei fan'.
and return to garrison Fúhǎn.
Xīngjìn and Fúhǎn
were both established as commanderies by the Zhāng clan of Héxī.
Xīngjìn was also likely near the border of Fúhǎn.
[Lǐ Biàn] moved his administration from Tiānshuǐ to Jīnchéng.
Greatly fearing,
because Qín's shift of its garrison was pressing upon him,
hence his fear.
He sacrificed three animals,
led his officials,
and remotely swore an oath with the Three Ducal Ministers of Jìn.
He dispatched Commissioner-Secretary Hán Bó to present a memorial and the text of the alliance,
and also to send a letter to Grand Marshal Huán Wēn,
scheduling to meet
in Shàngguī in the summer of the following year.
He wanted Jìn to raise an army to attack Shǔ and then meet him in Shàngguī.
Qín's Governor of Yìzhōu, Wáng Tǒng, attacked Qǐfú Sīfán of the Lǒngxī Xiānbēi at Dùjiān Mountain.
Sīfán led 30,000 cavalry to resist Tǒng at Yuànchuān.
Tǒng secretly attacked Dùjiān Mountain.
The Qǐfú clan had first moved south from Mòběi to garrison Gāopíng Chuān,
then from Gāopíng moved southwest to Màitián Mountain,
and Sīfán further moved from Màitián to Dùjiān Mountain.
The 'Commentary on the Water Classic' says: "Yuànchuān is within the borders of Yǒngshì County, Tiānshuǐ."
Dù Yòu says: "It is within the borders of Wǔquán County, Lánzhōu."
Judging from the later mention of Qǐfú Tǔléi as Defender of Yǒngshì,
then the 'Commentary on the Water Classic' is correct.
His troops, hearing that their wives and children had surrendered to Qín,
scattered without a fight.
Sīfán had nowhere to go,
and also went to Tǒng to surrender.
Qín King Jiān made Sīfán the Southern Chányú,
keeping him in Cháng'ān;
and made Sīfán's paternal uncle, Tǔléi, Defender of Yǒngshì.
Yǒngshì,
a Hàn county,
abolished during Jìn.
This refers to the establishment of a Defender based on the name of a Hàn county.
This laid the groundwork for the later rebellion of Qǐfú Bùtuí and his Xiānbēi against Qín.
1 In spring,
in the second month,
Qín appointed Fáng Kuàng of Qīnghé as Shàngshū Zuǒchéng.
It summoned Fáng Kuàng’s elder brother Mò, along with Cuī Chěng of Qīnghé and Hán Yìn of Yān State, to be Shàngshū Láng.
Yáng Zhì, Tián Xié, and Yáng Yáo of Běipíng were made Zuòshū Zuǒ Láng.
Jìn Zhì says: There was one Zuòshū Láng,
called the Grand Zuòshū,
who solely managed historical records.
Eight Zuǒ Zuòshū Láng were also appointed.
Xié
is pronounced xié.
He was recommended by Wáng Měng.
Yáo
was Yáng Wù’s son.
Yáng Wù served Yān,
having served three courts.
Wù
is pronounced wù.
The General of Champion Wèi, Mùróng Chuí, said to Qín King Jiān:
"My uncle Píng
is one of Yān’s Èlái-types.
Èlái served Zhòu with his great strength,
and Zhòu favored him, leading to the kingdom's demise."
"Èlái-types"
is in one version written as
"Èlái Gē."
Shǐ Jì says: Èlái was skilled at slandering,
which caused the feudal lords to become increasingly distant.
"Bèi"
should be
"Gē."
"I wish Your Majesty would execute him for Yān."
Jiān then sent Píng out to be the Administrator of Fányáng,
and all the princes of Yān were appointed to border commanderies.
Your servant, Guāng, says: The ancients,
when they destroyed a country, people rejoiced.
Why?
Because they eliminated harm for people.
Only Tāng and Wǔ could truly achieve this;
below them, Gāo Dì of Hàn was still close.
Wéi
is pronounced yú wěi.
One who obscures the ruler, monopolizes power,
is jealous of the worthy, envious of achievements,
ignorant, dark, greedy, and cruel, thereby losing their country—
if the country is lost but they do not die,
they flee and are captured.
The matter is found in the previous volume, Haixigong Taihe 5th year.
Yet, they are still favored and given high positions.
Zhì
means order,
or office.
Chǒngzhì
means to favor them and order their offices,
so that they do not lose their proper sequence.
This greatly loses the hearts of the people.
Therefore, when they bestow kindness upon people, no one feels grateful to them;
when they exhaust their sincerity toward people, no one feels sincere toward them.
Ultimately, their achievements and fame are unfulfilled,
and they have no place to settle,
because they do not follow the right path.
2 In the third month,
on the day Wùyǒu,
the Palace Attendant Wáng Tǎnzhī was sent to summon the Grand Marshal Wēn to assist the court;
Wēn again declined.
3 Qín King Jiān decreed:
"Among the people east of the pass, those who have mastered one classic and developed one skill
should be
courteously sent forth.
Those in office holding a salary of one hundred shí or more,
who have not mastered one classic and have not developed one skill,
shall be dismissed and returned to commoner status."
Fú Jiān’s governance was like this, yet he still could not endure to the end;
how much more so for those who fall short of Fú Jiān!
4 In summer,
in the fourth month,
Hǎixīgōng was moved to Xīcháilǐ in Wú County.
The Administrator of Wú Commandery, Diāo Yí, was ordered to guard him,
and the Imperial Censor Gù Yǔn was sent to oversee him.
Yí
was Xié’s son.
Diāo Xié
was trusted by Yuán Dì.
5 In the sixth month,
on the day Guǐyǒu,
Qín appointed Wáng Měng as Chancellor, Central Secretariat Supervisor, Minister of Personnel, Grand Mentor of the Crown Prince, and Colonel Director of Retainers.
His titles of Special Advanced, Palace Attendant, Bearer of the Imperial Credentials, General, and Marquis remained as before.
He continued to hold the seals and sashes of Special Advanced, Mounted Palace Attendant, Bearer of the Imperial Credentials, General of Chariots and Cavalry, and Marquis of Qīnghé Commandery.
He replaced Wáng Měng in garrisoning Yè.
Shǐ
is pronounced shū lì.
6 Yú Xī and Yú Miǎo, along with Zūn, the son of the late Inspector of Qīngzhōu Wǔ Shěn, gathered a crowd and entered Jīngkǒu city by night.
The Administrator of Jìnlíng, Biàn Dān, climbed over the city wall and fled to Qǔ'ē.
Yú Xī falsely claimed to have received a secret imperial edict from Hǎixīgōng to execute Grand Marshal Wēn.
Jiànkāng was shaken and disturbed,
and martial law was declared both inside and outside the capital.
Biàn Dān dispatched two thousand soldiers from various counties to attack Xī;
Xī was defeated
and closed the city to defend himself.
Wēn sent the Administrator of Dōnghǎi, Zhōu Shàosūn, to suppress him.
Yuán Dì had separated the northern border of Hǎiyú County in Wú Commandery to form Dōnghǎi Commandery.
In the seventh month,
on the day Rénchén,
the city was taken,
and Xī, Miǎo, and their close associates were captured
and all executed.
The lineage of Yú Liàng was extinguished.
He was Hú’s son.
Biàn Hú served Emperors Yuán and Míng,
and died in the calamity of Sū Jùn.
7 On the day Jiǎyín,
the Emperor became unwell and
urgently summoned Grand Marshal Wēn to assist the court,
issuing four imperial edicts within one day and night;
Wēn declined to come.
Initially,
when the Emperor was Prince of Kuàijī,
he married Wáng Shù’s paternal cousin
and had his heir Dàoshēng and his younger brother Yúshēng.
Dàoshēng was flighty and ill-behaved,
and both mother and son died in confinement.
His other three sons,
Yù, Zhūshēng, and Tiānbèi,
all died young.
The imperial concubines had been barren for nearly ten years,
so the Prince sent a skilled physiognomist to examine them;
they all said:
"They are not the right person."
He then had the serving maids examined,
among whom was Lǐ Língróng,
who was in the weaving workshop,
dark-skinned and tall.
The palace women called her
"Kūnlún"
because she resembled a person from Kūnlún.
Kūnlún Kingdom
is south of the seas.
Lún
is pronounced lú kūn.
"This is the person!"
The Prince summoned her to attend him,
and she gave birth to Chāngmíng and Dàozǐ.
Jìn Shū says: Initially,
Emperor Jiǎnwén saw a prophecy that said:
"The fortune of Jìn ends with Chāngmíng."
When Emperor Xiàowǔ was pregnant,
Empress Dowager Lǐ dreamed that a divine being told her: "If you give birth to a boy,
let his courtesy name be Chāngmíng."
When she gave birth,
the east was just dawning,
so he was named after it.
The Emperor later realized this
and wept.
When Emperor Xiàowǔ died,
Jìn began to decline from then on.
On the day Jǐwèi,
Chāngmíng was established as Crown Prince;
he was ten years old.
Dàozǐ was made Prince of Lángxié
and given control of Kuàijī Commandery
to offer sacrifices to the Emperor's mother, Empress Zhèng.
When the Emperor was enfeoffed as Prince of Lángxié, his birth mother, Lady Zhèng, died.
He firmly requested to wear mourning clothes,
was then transferred and enfeoffed as Prince of Kuàijī,
and Lady Zhèng was posthumously honored as Empress of Kuàijī.
Kuài
is pronounced gōng wài.
"Grand Marshal Wēn followed the precedent of Duke of Zhōu acting as regent."
It also said:
"If the young son can be assisted, assist him;
if not,
you may take it yourself."
This used the words of Emperor Zhāoliè of Hàn entrusting Zhūgě Liàng.
Shào
is pronounced shī zhào.
(Wáng Tǎnzhī) slandered him before the Emperor.
The Emperor said:
"The world,
if it is a chance occurrence,
what do you dislike?"
Tǎnzhī said:
"The world
belongs to Xuān and Yuán."
Emperor Xuān laid the foundation of the imperial enterprise,
and Emperor Yuán revived it,
hence he said so.
The Emperor then had Tǎnzhī revise the edict to say:
"All matters of the state and royal household
shall be subject to the Grand Marshal,
following the precedents of Zhūgě Wǔhóu and Chancellor Wáng."
Chancellor Wáng
was Dǎo.
The Emperor passed away.
He was fifty-three years old.
The imperial ministers were in doubt,
and did not dare to immediately establish an heir.
Some said:
"We must await the Grand Marshal's (Dà Sīmǎ) decision."
The Imperial Secretariat Director (Shàngshū Púyè), Wáng Biāozhī, said with a stern expression:
"When the Son of Heaven (Tiānzǐ) dies,
the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ) succeeds him;
how can the Grand Marshal (Dà Sīmǎ) be allowed to differ!
If we were to first consult him in person,
we would surely be rebuked by him."
The court discussion was thus settled.
The Crown Prince (Tàizǐ) ascended the imperial throne,
and a general amnesty was declared.
An edict from Empress Dowager Chóngdé stated:
Empress Dowager Kāngxiàn Chǔ, having returned political power to Emperor Mù,
resided in Chóngdé Palace (Chóngdé Gōng).
During the reigns of Emperor Āi and Duke Hǎixī,
she again presided over court and issued edicts.
After Hǎixī was deposed,
Emperor Jiǎnwén ascended the throne,
honoring the Empress as Empress Dowager Chóngdé.
As he was still in the period of mourning,
an edict instructed Wēn to act as regent, following the precedent of Duke of Zhōu (Zhōugōng) in his regency.
When the matter was about to be implemented,
Wáng Biāozhī said:
"This is an extraordinarily important matter.
The Grand Marshal (Dà Sīmǎ) will certainly strongly decline,
causing all government affairs to stagnate,
and delaying the imperial burial.
We dare not comply with this order,
and respectfully return it sealed."
The matter was thus not carried out.
This incident marked the beginning of sealing and returning imperial edicts.
Wēn had hoped that Emperor Jiǎnwén, on his deathbed, would abdicate in his favor,
or else he would act as regent.
As his hopes were not fulfilled,
he was greatly indignant and resentful,
and wrote to his younger brother, Chōng, saying:
"The imperial will merely instructs me to follow the precedents of Marquis Wǔ and Duke Wáng."
Wēn suspected Wáng Tǎnlán and Xiè Ān of being responsible,
and held a grudge against them.
An edict ordered Xiè Ān to summon Wēn to assist in governance;
Wēn again declined.
8th month:
Qín Prime Minister (chéngxiàng) Méng arrived in Cháng'ān,
and was again given the additional title of Grand Supervisor of All Military Affairs Inside and Outside (Dūdū Zhōngwài Zhūjūn Shì).
Méng declined, saying:
"The heavy responsibility of the Prime Minister (Yuánxiàng),
the esteemed position of the Imperial Tutor (Chǔfù),
the numerous duties of the Imperial Secretariat (Duān Yòu),
the great charge of the Capital Governor (Jīngmù),
overall command of military affairs,
and the issuing and receiving of imperial commands—
'Yuánxiàng' refers to the Prime Minister (Chéngxiàng).
'Chǔfù' refers to the Grand Tutor of the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ Tàifù).
'Duān Yòu' refers to the Director of the Imperial Secretariat (Shàngshū Lìng).
'Jīngmù' refers to the Commandant of the Capital (Sīlì Xiàowèi).
'Overall command of military affairs' refers to the Grand Supervisor of All Military Affairs Inside and Outside (Dūdū Zhōngwài Zhūjūn Shì).
'Issuing and receiving of imperial commands' refers to the duties of the Palace Recorder (Zhōngshū Jiān) and the Imperial Attendant (Chángshì).
All matters, great and small, are involved.
Even with the wisdom of Yī, Lǚ, Xiāo, and Dèng,
they could not manage to combine them.
'Yī, Lǚ, Xiāo, and Dèng' refer to Yī Yǐn, Lǚ Wàng, Xiāo Hé, and Dèng Yǔ.
I am untalented.
'Untalented' is another way of saying 'unworthy.'
Qín King (Qín Wáng) Jiān did not permit it,
saying:
"I am about to unify the four seas,
and there is no one else I can entrust this to but you.
Your inability to decline the premiership
is like my inability to decline the world."
As Méng was Prime Minister (xiàng),
Jiān sat reverently above,
while all officials managed their own affairs below.
All matters, military and domestic, within and without the state,
were handled by him.
Méng was resolute, clear-sighted, incorruptible, and solemn.
He clearly distinguished good from evil,
dismissed incompetent officials,
'Incompetent officials' refers to those who occupy a position without performing their duties and merely consume food.
encouraged agriculture and sericulture,
and trained the army.
Officials were appointed according to their talents,
and punishments were meted out according to the crime.
Consequently, the state became wealthy and its army strong,
victorious in every battle,
and the state of Qín was greatly governed.
Jiān instructed Crown Prince (Tàizǐ) Hóng and Duke Chánglè (Chánglè Gōng) Pī, etc., saying:
"You shall serve Duke Wáng
as you serve me."
Duke Yángpíng (Yángpíng Gōng) Róng was in Jìzhōu.
He carefully selected his subordinate officials.
'Subordinate officials' refers to those who manage various affairs as staff.
Family Records: The Fáng (Fáng) surname originated from Dān Zhū.
Shùn enfeoffed him as Marquis of Fángyì (Fángyì Hóu).
His son Líng adopted his father's fief as his surname.
He oversaw the record-keeping.
Róng was young,
and in his governance, he favored novelty and originality,
valuing severity and meticulousness.
Shēn Shào repeatedly corrected him,
guiding him toward leniency and harmony.
Although Róng respected him,
he could not fully follow his advice.
Later, Shào was sent out to be the Administrator of Jìběi (Jìběi Tàishǒu).
Róng frequently heard reports of his own mistakes,
and was often reprimanded.
He then regretted not having followed Shào's words.
Róng once sat
and built a schoolhouse, for which he was impeached by the appropriate authorities.
He sent his Chief Clerk (Zhǔbù), Lǐ Zuǎn, to Cháng'ān to explain himself;
Zuǎn, consumed by worry and fear,
died on the way.
Róng asked Shēn Shào:
"Who can I send?"
Shào replied:
"The Director of the Imperial Secretariat (Shàngshū Láng) of Yān, Gāo Tài,
is clear-spoken, eloquent, courageous, and intelligent;
he can be sent."
Before this, Prime Minister (chéngxiàng) Méng and Róng had repeatedly invited Tài to serve,
but Tài had declined.
At this point,
Róng said to Tài:
"A gentleman helps those in urgent need;
you must not decline again!"
Tài then complied.
Upon arriving in Cháng'ān,
Méng saw him
and laughed, saying:
"Master Gāo Zǐbó, you have only now arrived;
why so late?"
Gāo Tài's courtesy name was Zǐbó.
"A criminal comes to face his punishment;
why ask about speed?"
Méng said:
"What do you mean by that?"
Tài replied:
"In ancient times, Duke Xī of Lǔ commemorated the Pàn Palace (Pàn Gōng) with an ode.
The ode 'Pàn Shuǐ' in the 'Odes of Lǔ' (Lǔ Sòng Pàn Shuǐ) praises Duke Xī for his ability to repair the Pàn Palace.
Historical Records (Shǐjì): King Xuān of Qí enjoyed scholars who engaged in literary discourse and persuasion.
Seventy-six people, including Zōu Yǎn, Chúnyú Kūn, Tián Pián, Shèn Dào, Jiē Zǐ, and Huán Yuān,
were all granted residences.
There were several hundreds or thousands of scholars at Jìxià.
Liú Xiàng's Other Records (Biélù) states: Qí had the Jì Gate (Jì Mén), which was a city gate.
Scholars who engaged in discourse gathered at Jìxià.

The sorrow of qīgōng 期功 (mourning for relatives under 'one year' or 'nine months' mourning)

Yìzhōu Cìshǐ Zhú Yáo 益州刺史竺瑤 and Wēiyuǎn Jiāngjūn 威遠將軍 (General who Makes Distant Regions Tremble) Huán Shíqián 桓石虔 led thirty thousand troops to attack Diànjiāng 墊江.

Huáyáng Guózhì 華陽國志 says:

Later, it was named Wǔchéng Xiàn 五城縣 accordingly,

Zhāng Yù 張育 proclaimed himself Shǔ Wáng 蜀王,

seventh month,

Ninth month,

Dèng Qiāng 鄧羌 attacked Zhāng Yù 張育 and Yáng Guāng 楊光 at Zhú 竹,
beheading both of them.
Yìzhōu 益州 once again fell under Qín 秦.
5 In winter,

“Fish” (魚) and “lamb” (羊)

After this, Mùróng rose in rebellion and attacked Qín,

Hū,

The Jìn’s Secretarial Department had Cánɡ and Láng,

Qín appointed Zhěng as Mìshū Láng,

Jiān did not listen.
Zhěng

well-read and with a strong memory,

submitting memorials and offering face-to-face remonstrances,

Mùróng Chuí’s wife was favored by Jiān,

Zhěng sang:

Below “Wèichén”

Jiān,

All of Húan’s clan and partisans considered this ill-advised,

Shī: Xiǎoyuān: anxious and careful,

Hóu;

Guǎn,

Tàiyuán元年 (丙子、三七六)
1 Spring,

工外翻。
郗，
丑之翻。

挹淫翻。

奇寄翻。
Xiè Ān wanted to appoint Wáng Yùn as Fangbo,
and therefore first relieved Chōng of Xúzhōu.
On the day Yǐmǎo,
Xiè Ān was promoted to Censor-in-chief of the Chancellery, and

替，

3 The third month,
Qín troops raided Nánxiāng,
capturing it,

From the time of the Spring and Autumn period,
south of the Yī and Luò rivers,
and north of the Bā, Wū, Hàn, and Miǎn rivers,
the great mountains and long valleys
were all inhabited by barbarians.
In the sixteenth year of Wén Gōng,
the people of Yōng led the Jīnbānmán to rebel against Chǔ.
Yōng

In the fourth year of Āi Gōng,

Liáng

Huò

Hàn Gāo Dì used the Bāyúmán to pacify the Sān Qín,

Later, Jì Zūn of the Later Hàn attacked the Xīnchéngmán and Bǎihuāmán,
destroying the Huòyáng settlement,

Thereafter there were also the Wūmán, Nánjùnmán, and Jiāngxiàmán.
West of Xiāngyáng,
and in the western mountains of Zhōnglú and Yíchéng,
all were inhabited by barbarians,
what were called the mountain barbarians.
After the Sòng and Qí dynasties,
they were called the Yōngzhōumán.
降，

"Since the time of the Róng (戎) and Dí (狄),

second month,

In the nineteenth year,
first month,

Now following the Shíliù Guó Chūnqiū (十六國春秋).

seventh month,

"Sending a beloved son as a hostage,

Tiānxī (天錫) ordered Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn (龍驤將軍) Mǎ Jiàn (馬建) to lead 20,000 men to resist Qín (秦).

Mǎ Jiàn was afraid,

south of Gūzāng.
"Zhǎng Jù"

"Cháng Jù",

They camped at Jīnchāng Chéng.

"Your servant observes human affairs by day

Zhāng Shí divided Lìngjū and Zhīyáng from Jīnchéng

"Mǎ Jiàn has come forth from the ranks,

Gǒu Cháng and Zhǎng Jù fought at Hóngchí.

The people of Hexi considered him a good general,

"This is my place of death,

bowed to the west,

The Qín soldiers killed Jūnsī Xí Lè.

Sībīng was

Chōngzhé died.
Tiān Xī sallied out of the city to fight,

Tiān Xī fled with several thousand cavalry back to Gūzāng.

In the first year of Huì Dì's Yǒngníng era (304 CE),

There were a total of nine rulers,

Chèn
is pronounced like "chū jìn".
In the ninth month,
Qín Wáng Jiān appointed Liáng Xī as Cìshǐ of Liángzhōu,

He enfeoffed Tiān Xī as Guīyì Hóu

Qín established Běibù Shàngshū

When the Qín forces set out,

He appointed Tiān Xī's Jìnxīng Tàishǒu, Lǒngxī Péng Hézhèng, as Huángmén Shìláng;
Zhāng Guǐ divided the territory of Xīpíng

Gāochāng Yáng Gàn as Gāochāng Tàishǒu.

Liáng Xī was honest, frugal, and loved the people;

Earlier,
Āi Dì reduced the land tax,
collecting two *shēng* per *mǔ*.
See Volume 101, Lónghé first year.
On the Yǐsì day,
the system of surveying land and collecting rent was abolished.
From princes and dukes downwards,
a poll tax of three *hú* of rice was levied per person,
with those in service exempted.
In winter,
in the tenth month,
people north of the Huái River were moved to south of the Huái River.

Liú Wèichén was pressured by Dài

Xiāng
is read as *xiàng*.

Huī and his men traveled through the marshlands,

According to the law, they should have been executed.

Qín Wáng Jiān said,
“Water recedes and dries up in spring and winter,

not the fault of Huī and his men.

He ordered Huī and his men to return and join the northern army,

The Dài people were originally of the Xiānbēi Suǒtóu clan,
hence they were called Suǒlǔ.
Suǒ,
is pronounced as 'xī gè fān'.
They did not respond quickly.
Jiān said,
“Huī and his men are delighted to be spared death;

Since Huī and his men returned from the west,
the army attacking Dài was called the eastern army.
In the eleventh month,
on the day of Jǐsì, which was the first day of the month,

The Dài Wáng Shíyìjiān sent the Báibù and Dúgūbù to defend against the Qín forces in the south,

Among the Xiānbēi there was a Báibù.

Línghú Défēn said: At the beginning of the Wèi dynasty,

Jiān,

Zhǒng,

Initially,

Zú,

Shí's death is seen in the previous volume, first year of Xián'ān of Emperor Jiǎnwén.

At that time, the Qín army was still at Jūnzǐjīn.

then south past the east of Chéngchéng,

The northerners called
[Hu]
and thus took it as their surname.

ensuring that his descendants will forever be non-aggressive and non-rebellious subjects."
This uses the words of Róngzǐ Jūzhī from the Zuǒ Zhuàn.
Jiān followed his advice.
He divided the Dài people into two sections:

Hè Shì returned with Guī to the Dúgūbù,

An edict was issued saying:

to the east they made tributary the Huì and Mò peoples.

should be
'濊 (huì)'.

The officials should quickly distribute rewards and grant titles.

means '次 (cì)' (order).

should be
'授 (shòu)' (grant).

constantly seeking victory without rest.
Garrisoning Yúnzhōng in the north,
and guarding Shǔ and Hàn in the south,

after the Qín people had conquered Liángzhōu,

means the western border.
"Their tribes live mixed together,

'騎 (qí)'

during Tuòbá Lìwēi's time,

[xīn]

is as written,

is pronounced *lí*.

is pronounced *shǐ*.

concurrently serving as Works Bureau Aide,
and extensively repaired boats and weapons,
decorating them with gold and silver,

Mùróng Nóng privately said to Mùróng Chuí:

was similar to Shào and Kǎi's.
Huán Huò submitted a memorial recommending Zhū Xù, the Governor of Yǎnzhōu, as Governor of Liángzhōu,

in the seventh month,
on the *dīngwèi* day,

in the tenth month,

6 Qín Wáng Jiān appointed Jiànyì Dàfū Péi Yuánlüè as Tàishǒu of the two commanderies, Bāxī and Zǐtóng,
and secretly ordered him to prepare a naval force.
He wanted to emulate Wáng Jùn’s old strategy,
to sail eastward downstream to attack Jìn.
7 In the ninth month,
Mídiān (彌窴), the King of the Former Division of Chēshī (車師), and Xiūmìtuó (休密馱), the King of Shànshàn (鄯善),
paid court to Qín (秦),
requesting to serve as guides
to attack those in the Western Regions who were not submissive,
and then, following the Hàn (漢) precedent, to establish a Protector-General (dūhù 督護) to govern them.
Qín Wáng Jiān (秦王堅) appointed Lǚ Guāng (呂光), the General of Galloping Cavalry, as Envoy with Imperial Credentials and Supervisor of the Various Armies for the Western Regions Expedition,
along with Jiāng Fēi (姜飛), the General of Lingjiang.
The title "General of Lingjiang"
was established by Jìn Wén Wáng (晉文王)
and bestowed upon Luó Xiàn (羅憲).
Dù Jìn (杜進) and Kāng Shèng (康盛) reached the rank of general,
but did not have a specific general title.
With five thousand iron-clad cavalry,
he set out to attack the Western Regions.
Yángpíng Gōng Róng (陽平公融) remonstrated, saying:
"The Western Regions are desolate and distant;
their people cannot be employed,
and their land cannot be cultivated for food.
Emperor Wǔ of Hàn (漢武) conquered them,
but the gains did not compensate for the losses.
This refers to Emperor Wǔ of Hàn's (漢武) campaign
which
greatly defeated Lóulán (樓蘭) and Gūshī (姑師),
and cultivated land in Chēshī (車師).
Now, to weary our troops thousands of miles away,
following the past error of the Hàn (漢) dynasty,
I secretly regret it."
(Jiān) did not listen.
8 Huán Chōng (桓沖) sent Zhū Chuò (朱綽), the General Who Manifests Awe, to attack Dū Guì (都貴), the Qín (秦) Governor of Jīngzhōu (荊州), at Xiāngyáng (襄陽),
burning and trampling the military farms north of the Miǎn (沔) River,
and returning after plundering over six hundred households.
9 In winter,
in the tenth month,
Qín Wáng Jiān (秦王堅) assembled his ministers at the Tàijí (太極) Palace
and deliberated, saying:
"Since I ascended to power,
almost thirty years have passed.
Jiān (堅) established himself in the first year of Shēngpíng (升平) and by this point, twenty-six years had passed.
Only in the longevity of the years
do I fear it will not last,
still hoping for it;
yet wanting to weary the people to satisfy my ambition,
it is fitting that it should perish.
The four quarters are generally settled;
only the southeastern corner
has not yet received the king's transforming influence.
Now, by a rough count, my soldiers
number ninety-seven myriad;
I wish to personally lead them to attack it.
What do you think?"
Mìshū Jiān (祕書監) Zhū Róng (朱肜) said:
"Your Majesty reverently carries out Heaven's punishment;
there will surely be an expedition but no battle.
If the Jìn (晉) ruler does not present the ceremonial jade at the camp gate,
he will flee and die in the rivers and seas.
Your Majesty will return the scholars and people of the central plains
to their native places.
This refers to the descendants who fled south to avoid chaos at the end of Yǒngjiā (永嘉).
And proclaim your achievements at Dàizōng (岱宗)."
Dù Yòu (杜佑) remarked: Dàizōng (岱宗)
is the Eastern Marchmount.
It is specifically called Dàizōng (岱宗) because
it is located in the northeast,
between Yín (寅) and Chǒu (丑),
the place where all things begin and end,
and where yin and yang alternate.
It is the宗, or patriarch, of all mountains,
hence it is called Dàizōng (岱宗).
Jiān (堅) rejoiced, saying:
"This is my ambition!"
Shàngshū Zuǒ Púyè (尚書左僕射) Quán Yì (權翼) said:
"In the past, when Zhòu (紂) was without the Way,
three benevolent men were at court,
yet King Wǔ (武) still turned back his army for him.
The Analects say: Wēizǐ (微子) left him,
Jīzǐ (箕子) became his slave,
and Bǐgān (比干) admonished him and died.
Confucius said:
'The Yīn (殷) had three benevolent men.'
The Shǐjì (史記) says: Nine years after King Wǔ (武) ascended the throne,
he marched east to observe the troops at Méngjīn (盟津),
and eight hundred feudal lords gathered without prior agreement.
They all said:
'Zhòu (紂) can be attacked!'
King Wǔ (武) said:
'Not yet.'
And so he returned his army.
Two years later,
Zhòu's (紂) tyranny became even more severe;
he killed Prince Bǐgān (比干),
imprisoned Jīzǐ (箕子),
and Wēizǐ (微子) fled to Zhōu (周).
King Wǔ (武) announced to the feudal lords:
'The Yīn (殷) has committed grave crimes,
and must be attacked!'
He then destroyed them.
朝 (cháo),
read zhí yáo fān.
猶為 (yóu wéi),
read yú wěi fān.
(The Jìn (晉)) has not yet committed a great evil.
Xiè Ān (謝安) and Huán Chōng (桓沖) are both great men south of the Jiāng (江),
and ruler and ministers are harmonious;
internal and external are of one mind.
In my opinion,
they cannot yet be plotted against!"
Jiān (堅) remained silent for a long time,
then said:
"Let each of you state his own mind."
Tàizǐ Zuǒwèishūai (太子左衞率) Shí Yuè (石越) said:
"This year the planet Zhèn (鎮) is in Dǒu (斗),
and good fortune is in Wú (吳).
Suì (歲) is Jupiter.
Zhèn (鎮) is Saturn.
Dǒu (斗), Niú (牛), Nǚ (女) are the divisions of Wú (吳), Yuè (越), and Yángzhōu (揚州).
There will surely be a heavenly calamity.
Moreover, they hold the strategic advantage of the Changjiang River,
and the people are used by them;
it is probably not yet advisable to attack!"
Jiān (堅) said:
"In the past, King Wǔ (武) attacked Zhòu (紂),
going against the year-star and disregarding divination.
Xúnzǐ (荀子) said: When King Wǔ (武) punished Zhòu (紂),
he faced east to meet the Grand Year-Star.
Yáng Jìng's (楊倞) commentary says: 'Meeting' (yíng 迎) means going against the Grand Year-Star.
Shīzǐ (尸子) says: When King Wǔ (武) attacked Zhòu (紂),
Yú Xīn (魚辛) admonished him, saying:
'The year-star is in the north,
so one cannot campaign north.'
King Wǔ (武) did not comply.
The Shǐjì Qí Shìjiā (史記齊世家) says: When King Wǔ (武) was about to attack Zhòu (紂),
he divined with tortoise shells,
and the prognostication was inauspicious.
Wind and rain suddenly came violently,
and all the dukes were afraid.
Only Tàigōng (太公) strengthened him
and encouraged King Wǔ (武),
so King Wǔ (武) proceeded.
It is not easy to know.
Fūchā (夫差) and Sūn Hào (孫晧) both held strategic positions on the rivers and lakes,
but they could not escape destruction.
Now, with my multitude,
if I throw my whip into the river,
it is enough to cut off its flow.
What strategic advantage is there to rely on?"
(Shí Yuè (石越)) replied:
"The rulers of the three kingdoms were all licentious, tyrannical, and without the Way,
The rulers of the three kingdoms refer to Zhòu (紂), Fūchā (夫差), and Sūn Hào (孫晧).
easy to pick up like lost property.
Now, although Jìn (晉) lacks virtue,
it has not committed a great crime.
I wish Your Majesty would temporarily hold back the troops and accumulate grain,
to await their vulnerability."
Thereupon, all the ministers stated their advantages and disadvantages,
and for a long time no decision was made.
Jiān (堅) said:
"This is like 'building a house by the roadside';
it will never be completed.
The Shī (詩) says: 'Like those who build a house by consulting on the road,
they fail to complete it.'"
All the other officials went out,
leaving only Yángpíng Gōng Róng.
Fú Jiān said to him:
“Since ancient times, those who accomplish great deeds
rely on no more than one or two ministers.
Now, numerous opinions are conflicting,
only disturbing people's minds.
I shall decide this with you.”
Róng replied:
“Now, there are three difficulties in attacking Jìn: Heaven's way is not favorable,
that is the first;
the state of Jìn has no weakness,
that is the second;
our army is weary from numerous battles,
and the people have a fear of the enemy,
that is the third.
All the officials who say Jìn should not be attacked
are loyal ministers.
I wish Your Majesty would listen to them.”
Fú Jiān's expression changed, and he said:
“You too are like this!
What more can I hope for?
My powerful army numbers a million,
and our armaments are like mountains.
Though I may not be a sagacious ruler,
neither am I dim-witted or inferior.
Inferior,
meaning weak.
To attack a nation on the verge of collapse,
what trouble is there in not conquering it?
How can we allow these remaining bandits to stay,
and long be a source of worry for the state!”
The chancellor of Hàn and Wèi once said: relying on the greatness of one's state,
boasting of the multitude of one's people,
and desiring to display power to the enemy,
is called an arrogant army.
An arrogant army perishes.
This must be what Fú Jiān refers to!
Fù (復),
read Fú Yòu;
the Fù in the following 'Fù Liú' is the same.
“Jìn cannot yet be destroyed,
this is clearly evident.
Now, to exhaust the army with a grand expedition,
I fear there will be no complete success.
Moreover, what your subject worries about
is not limited to this.
Your Majesty has favored and nurtured the Xiānbēi, Qiāng, and Jié,
spreading them throughout the imperial domain.
These groups are all our deep enemies.
The Crown Prince is left alone with only tens of thousands of weak soldiers to guard the capital.
Your subject fears that unforeseen changes may arise from within and around us,
which would be impossible to regret.
Your subject's stubborn foolishness
is indeed not worth adopting;
Wáng Jǐnglüè was a hero of his time,
and Your Majesty often compared him to Zhūgě Wǔhóu.
Zhūgě Liàng's posthumous title was Wǔhóu.
See volume Níngkāng 3rd year.
At this, many court officials advanced their remonstrances.
Fú Jiān said:
“For me to attack Jìn,
comparing the strength and weakness of the forces,
it is like a strong wind sweeping autumn leaves.
Yet, both within and outside the court, everyone says it cannot be done.
This is truly something I do not understand!”
Crown Prince Hóng said:
“This year is in the sector of Wú,
and moreover, the Jìn ruler is innocent. If a grand expedition is not victorious,
I fear that our prestige will be frustrated externally,
and our financial strength exhausted internally.
This is why all your subjects are doubtful!”
Fú Jiān said:
“Formerly, when I destroyed Yān,
it also violated the celestial cycles, yet I was victorious.
Heaven's way is indeed difficult to know.
When Qín destroyed the Six States,
were the rulers of the Six States all tyrannical?”
Guànjūn and Jīngzhàoyǐn Mùróng Chuí
Guànjūn,
meaning Guànjūn Jiāngjūn (General).
The biographies in the Jìn Shū record
the general's title without attaching 'Jiāngjūn';
the Zīzhì Tōngjiàn follows this.
Guàn (冠),
read Gǔ Wán.
“The weak are annexed by the strong,
the small by the great;
this is a natural principle and tendency,
not difficult to know.
With Your Majesty's divine might responding to the times,
your prestige extends overseas,
your tiger army numbers a million,
and Hán and Bái fill the court.
Hán and Bái,
referring to Hán Xìn and Bái Qǐ.
Meaning Qín had many excellent generals.
If they alone defy the king's command,
how can they be allowed to remain and be left to future generations?
The Shī (Classic of Poetry) says:
‘When counselors are too many,
nothing is achieved.’
From the poem Xiǎo Mín.
Why must we widely consult the multitude of the court?
When Jìn Wǔpacified Wú,
he relied on only two or three ministers like Zhāng and Dù.
If he had followed the words of the court multitude,
how could there have been the achievement of unification?”
Referring to Zhāng Huà and Dù Yù.
Details can be found in volume 80, Wǔ Dì Xiánníng 5th year.
Cháo (朝),
read Zhí Yáo.
“Among those who will help me pacify the world,
only you alone remain.”
He was bestowed 500 bolts of silk.
Fú Jiān was determined to take Jiāngdōng,
unable to sleep until dawn.
Yángpíng Gōng Róng remonstrated, saying:
“‘He who knows contentment suffers no disgrace;
he who knows where to stop meets no danger.’
Words from the Lǎozi Dé Jīng, ‘Lì Jiè Piān’.
There is none that has not perished.
Moreover, our state is originally from the Róng and Dí,
and the legitimate succession will not ultimately return to us.
Huì (會),
meaning 'ultimately' or 'in essence',
meaning that essentially, the legitimate succession of China
does not return to the barbarians.
However, the orthodox lineage of Huáxià,
Heaven's will will surely not cut it off.”
Fú Jiān said:
“The reigns of emperors and kings,
how can they be constant?
It is only where virtue lies!
Was Liú Shàn not a descendant of Hàn?
Yet he was ultimately destroyed by Wèi.
The reason you are not like me
is precisely this failure to adapt to change!”
Fú Jiān had always deeply trusted the Shāmén Dào'ān.
When Dào'ān was in Xiāngyáng,
Fú Jiān conquered Xiāngyáng
and had him brought there in a carriage.
In the eleventh month,
Fú Jiān rode in the same carriage as Dào'ān, touring the Eastern Park.
Fú Jiān said:
“I shall travel south with you to Wú and Yuè,
float on the Cháng Jiāng,
and overlook the boundless sea.
Is that not delightful!”
Dào'ān said:
“Your Majesty, in response to Heaven, governs the world,
residing in the Central Plains and controlling the four directions,
which is sufficient to rival Yáo and Shùn.
Why must you brave wind and rain,
and strategize for distant lands?
Moreover, the Southeast is low and humid,
where noxious energies are easily formed.
Yú Shùn traveled there but did not return,
and Dà Yǔ went but did not come back.
Yú Shùn made a southern inspection tour
and died in the wilderness of Cāngwú.
Yǔ made an eastern inspection tour
and died at Kuàijī.
Fú Jiān said:
“Heaven gives birth to the multitude of people and establishes rulers for them,
to shepherd them.
How dare I shirk labor
and allow that one region alone not to receive my bounty?
If it must be as you say,
then the ancient emperors and kings all had no punitive expeditions!”
Dào'ān said:
“If it is absolutely necessary,
Your Majesty should halt your imperial progress at Luòyáng,
send an envoy to carry a letter ahead,
and let your generals lead the grand army behind.
They will surely bow down as subjects,
and you will not need to personally cross the Jiāng and Huái rivers.”
Fú Jiān did not listen.
Fú Jiān's favored Consort Zhāng
remonstrated, saying: "Your concubine has heard that Heaven and Earth generate all things,
and sage kings govern the world,
all by following their natural course and adapting to them,
hence no undertaking is unsuccessful.
Therefore, the Yellow Emperor harnessed oxen and rode horses,
making use of their nature.
This means that by understanding the nature of oxen and horses,
they can pull heavy loads and travel far.
Draining the Nine Marshes
was done by utilizing their topography.
This means that by understanding the lay of the land,
one can clear the sources and dam the marshes.
[Agriculture] relies on the right season.
By sowing and planting according to the season,
all grains will ripen.
[Military action] relies on the will of the people.
By deploying troops in accordance with the will of the people,
the world will submit.
帥 (shuài)
is read as 率 (shuài).
Without these foundations, one will fail.
Now, everyone in the court and among the populace says that Jìn cannot be attacked,
yet Your Majesty alone has decided to proceed.
Your concubine does not know upon what Your Majesty bases this decision.
The *Shū* says: 'Heaven's discernment comes from the discernment of my people.'
This is a passage from the *Gāo Táo Mó* of the *Shū*.
How much more so should this apply to human beings!
Your concubine has also heard that when a king raises an army,
he must observe the Way of Heaven above,
and comply with the will of the people below.
Now, the will of the people is already not in favor,
please let us examine the Way of Heaven.
The proverb says: 'When chickens crow at night, it is unfavorable for military campaigns;
when dogs howl mournfully, palaces will soon be empty;
when troops move and horses are startled,
the army will be defeated and not return.'
Since autumn and winter,
many chickens have crowed at night,
and dogs have howled mournfully.
Furthermore, many horses have been startled,
and the weapons in the arsenal have moved and made sounds by themselves.
These are all not auspicious signs for raising an army."
Fú Jiān said:
"Matters of the military
are not for women to be involved in!"
Fú Jiān's youngest son, the Duke of Zhōngshān, Fú Shēn, was most favored,
and he also remonstrated, saying:
"Your servant has heard that the rise and fall of a state
depends on the employment or rejection of wise individuals.
Now, the Duke of Yángpíng, Fú Róng,
is the chief strategist of the state,
yet Your Majesty disregards him.
Jìn has Xiè Ān and Huán Chōng,
yet Your Majesty plans to attack them.
Your servant is secretly puzzled by this!"
Fú Jiān said:
"How can a mere child
understand the great affairs of the world!"
10 Qín's Liú Lán was sent to suppress locusts,
and he could not eliminate them through autumn and winter.
In the twelfth month,
the officials reported and proposed summoning Lán to the Grand Judge's office.
Qín King Fú Jiān said:
"Calamities descend from Heaven;
they cannot be removed by human effort.
This is due to my misgovernance;
what crime has Lán committed!"
That year,
Qín had a great harvest.
The best fields yielded seventy *shí* per *mǔ*,
and the poorer ones thirty *shí*.
Locusts did not leave the borders of Yōuzhōu,
and did not eat hemp or beans.
The best fields yielded one hundred *shí* per *mǔ*,
and the poorer ones fifty *shí*.
When things go against the norm, it is an omen.
Locusts as a disaster have a long history.
For locusts to be born and not eat grain
is the greatest of omens.
Farmers tilled the fields and toiled diligently,
until harvest time.
Since ancient times,
there has never been a yield of one hundred *shí* or seventy *shí* per *mǔ*.
And a yield of fifty *shí* or thirty *shí* per *mǔ*
has also never been heard of.
If it were truly so,
would it not be a great reversal of the norm?
If it were not so,
then the prefectures and counties conspired to deceive the emperor with false embellishments,
which is also a great inauspicious sign.
Qín's fall was inevitable!

Sīmǎ Guāng
Compiled by Imperial Edict
Hòu Xué Tiān Tái
Lièzōng Xiàowǔ Huángdì Shàng Zhī Xià
Tàiyuán Eighth Year (Guǐwèi, 383)
1 Spring,
first month.
Qín's Lǚ Guāng departed from Cháng'ān,
using Xiūmìtuó, King of Shànshàn, and Mǐtián, King of the Former Chēshī, as guides.
2 Third month,
on the day of Dīngsì,
a general amnesty was declared.
3 Summer,
fifth month.
Huán Chōng led an army of one hundred thousand to attack Qín,
besieging Xiāngyáng.
He dispatched Former General Liú Bō and others to attack the cities north of the Miǎnwèi River.
Auxiliary General Yáng Liàng attacked Shǔ,
capturing five cities,
and advanced to attack Fúchéng.
Soaring Eagle General Guō Quán attacked Wǔdāng.
Sixth month.
Huán Chōng's detached forces attacked Wànsùi and Zhúyáng,
capturing them.
Wànsùi is a city name,
probably near Zhúyáng.
Zhúyáng County,
during the Hàn dynasty belonged to Nányáng Commandery,
during the Jìn dynasty belonged to Shùnyáng Commandery.
In the Spring and Autumn period, it was the state of Gǔ Bó.
In the Táng dynasty, it was Gǔchéng County of Xiāngzhōu.
Shī Gǔ said: Zhú
is pronounced *zhú*.
Guān
is pronounced *wán*.
Qí
is pronounced *jì*.
Rear General Zhāng Háolè and Infantry Colonel Yáo Cháng rescued Fúchéng.
Fú Ruì's army was stationed at Xīnyě,
and Mùróng Chuí's army was stationed at Dèngchéng.
Dèngchéng County
belonged to Xiāngyáng Commandery,
probably established by Jìn.
Autumn,
seventh month.
Guō Quán and Champion General Huán Shíqián defeated Zhāng Chóng at Wǔdāng,
plundering two thousand households before returning.
The Duke of Jùlù, Fú Ruì, dispatched Mùróng Chuí as the vanguard,
advancing to the Miǎnwèi River.
At night, Mùróng Chuí ordered his soldiers, each carrying ten torches,
to tie them to tree branches.
Their light illuminated for dozens of *lǐ*.
Huán Chōng was afraid,
and retreated to Shàngmíng.
Huán Chōng's garrison at Shàngmíng is mentioned in the previous volume, second year.
Yáng Liàng withdrew his troops.
Huán Chōng memorialized that his nephew, Huán Shímín, be appointed Prefect of Xiāngchéng
and garrison Xiàkǒu.
Huán Chōng himself requested to be appointed Inspector of Jiāngzhōu.
The emperor granted the request.
4 Qín Wáng Jiān 秦王堅 issued an edict to launch a major invasion.
For every ten commoners, one soldier was conscripted;
among the sons of respectable families, those aged twenty and under
who possessed talent and bravery
were all appointed as Yǔlín Láng 羽林郎.
He further said:
"Let Sīmǎ Chāngmíng 司馬昌明 be Shàngshū Zuǒ Púyè 尚書左僕射,
Xiè Ān 謝安 be Lìbù Shàngshū 吏部尚書,
and Huán Chōng 桓沖 be Shìzhōng 侍中;
the return of the army is not far off."
This means that, judging by the situation,
the conquest of Jìn 晉
is imminent,
and the army will return soon.
"Huán" 還
is pronounced "xuán,"
or as written.
Over thirty thousand cavalry of sons from respectable families arrived,
and Zhào Shèngzhī 趙盛之, Qínzhōu Zhǔbù 秦州主簿,
was appointed Shàonián Dūtǒng 少年都統.
Dūtǒng 都統 is an official title
that originated here.
"Shǎo" 少
is pronounced "shī zhào fān";
the same applies below.
All the court officials were unwilling to have Jiān 堅 proceed,
except Mùróng Chuí 慕容垂, Yáo Cháng 姚萇, and the sons of respectable families, who urged him on.
Yángpíng Gōng Róng 陽平公融 said to Jiān 堅:
"The Xiānbēi 鮮卑 and Qiāng 羌 barbarians
are our sworn enemies.
Mùróng Chuí 慕容垂 is a Xiānbēi 鮮卑;
Yáo Cháng 姚萇 is a Qiāng 羌;
their states were all destroyed by Qín 秦.
Although they claim to submit,
they are in fact enemies.
How can their proposed strategies
be followed?
The young men from respectable families are all wealthy sons,
unfamiliar with military matters,
and merely offer flattering words to please Your Majesty.
"Huì" 會
means to accord with.
If we rashly embark on such a great undertaking,
I fear that not only will the achievement fail,
but there will also be future troubles,
and regret will be too late!"
Jiān 堅 did not listen.
In the eighth month,
on the day wùwǔ 戊午,
Jiān 堅 dispatched Yángpíng Gōng Róng 陽平公融 to command Zhāng Háo 張蚝, Mùróng Chuí 慕容垂, and others, with an army of two hundred and fifty thousand infantry and cavalry, as the vanguard.
He appointed Yǎnzhōu Cìshǐ 兗州刺史 Yáo Cháng 姚萇 as Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn 龍驤將軍 and Dūdú Yì-Liángzhōu Zhū Jūnshì 都督益‧梁州諸軍事.
Jiān 堅 said to Cháng 萇:
"Formerly, I established my enterprise with the title Lóngxiáng 龍驤."
Jiān 堅, as Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn 龍驤將軍, killed Fú Shēng 苻生
and gained the state of Qín 秦.
"Xiáng" 驤
is pronounced "sī jiāng fān."
"You must exert yourself!"
Zuǒ Jiāngjūn 左將軍 Dòu Chōng 竇衝 said:
"A king has no idle words;
this is an inauspicious omen!"
Jiān 堅 remained silent.
Mùróng Kǎi 慕容楷 and Mùróng Shào 慕容紹 said to Mùróng Chuí 慕容垂:
"The emperor's arrogance and conceit have become excessive.
Uncle, the task of restoring the dynasty
lies in this expedition!"
Chuí 垂 said:
"Indeed.
If not you,
who else can accomplish it?"
At this point,
Chuí 垂 knew that Jiān 堅 was bound to fail,
and therefore spoke about it with his nephew, Míng 明.
On the day jiǎzǐ 甲子,
Jiān 堅 departed from Cháng'ān 長安,
with over six hundred thousand soldiers
and two hundred and seventy thousand cavalry.
Their banners and drums stretched as far as the eye could see,
covering a thousand li from front to back.
In the ninth month,
Jiān 堅 arrived at Xiàngchéng 項城.
The troops from Liángzhōu 涼州 had just reached Xiányáng 咸陽;
the troops from Shǔ 蜀 and Hàn 漢 were just sailing downstream;
and the troops from Yōu 幽 and Jì 冀 had reached Péngchéng 彭城.
Covering ten thousand li from east to west,
they advanced simultaneously by water and land,
with ten thousand ships transporting supplies.
The army of Yángpíng Gōng Róng 陽平公融 and others, numbering three hundred thousand,
first reached Yǐngkǒu 潁口.
This is the mouth where the Yǐngshǔi 潁水 enters the Huái 淮.
According to the Dìlǐ Zhì 地理志: the Yǐngshǔi 潁水 originates from Yánggān Shān 陽乾山 in Yángchéng Xiàn 陽城縣,
and flows eastward to Xiàcài 下蔡 to enter the Huái 淮.
An imperial edict appointed Shàngshū Púyè 尚書僕射 Xiè Shí 謝石 as Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn 征虜將軍 and Zhēngtǎo Dà Dūdú 征討大都督.
Xú-Yǎn Èrzhōu Cìshǐ 徐、兗二州刺史 Xiè Xuán 謝玄 was appointed Qiánfēng Dūdú 前鋒都督,
and together with Fǔguó Jiāngjūn 輔國將軍 Xiè Yǎn 謝琰 and Xīzhōngláng Jiāng Huán Yī 西中郎將桓伊, commanded a total of eighty thousand troops to resist them.
Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn 龍驤將軍 Hú Bīn 胡彬 was sent with five thousand marines to reinforce Shòuyáng 壽陽.
Yǎn 琰
was the son of Ān 安.
At this time, as the Qín 秦 army was powerful,
the capital was seized with terror.
Xiè Xuán 謝玄 entered
to ask Xiè Ān 謝安 for a plan.
Ān 安 remained calm.
"Yí" 夷
means calm
and peaceful.
It means he was as calm as on any normal day.
He said, "I already have a separate instruction."
After that, there was silence.
Xuán 謝玄 dared not speak again,
so he ordered Zhāng Xuán 張玄 to ask again.
Ān 安 then ordered his carriage and went to his mountain villa to relax.
All his friends and relatives gathered,
and he played Go with Xuán 謝玄, wagering the villa.
Ān's 安棋 Go was usually inferior to Xuán's 謝玄,
but on this day,
Xuán 謝玄, being afraid,
played as an equal but still did not win.
"Díshǒu" 敵手
means to play a Go game where one fights for territory and captures pieces,
demonstrating comparable wisdom and calculation.
Xuán's 謝玄 mind was not on the game,
hence he could not defeat Ān 安.
He only returned at night.
Huán Chōng 桓沖 was deeply worried about the foundations of the state,
and dispatched three thousand elite troops to guard the capital.
Xiè Ān 謝安 firmly declined them,
saying:
"The court's arrangements are already settled,
and there is no shortage of soldiers and weapons.
The western border should keep them for defense."
Chōng 桓沖 sighed to his aides, saying:
"Zhū Fānfǔ Cānzuǒ 諸藩府參佐 are his aides.
Xiè Ānshí 謝安石 has the capacity for statecraft,
but is not skilled in military strategy.
Now that a great enemy is imminent,
he is still engrossed in idle talk.
He sends inexperienced youths to resist them,
and their forces are few and weak.
The fate of the empire is already clear;
surely we will become barbarians!"
5 Lángyé Wáng Dàozǐ 琅邪王道子 was appointed Lù Shàngshū Liù Tiáo Shì 錄尚書六條事.
The office of Lù Shàngshū Liù Tiáo Shì 錄尚書六條事
originated with Liú Cōng 劉聰.
6 In winter,
the tenth month,
Qín Yángpíng Gōng Róng (秦陽平公融) and others attacked Shòuyáng (壽陽);
on Guǐyǒu (癸酉) day,
they captured it,
and seized Pínglǔ Jiāngjūn (平虜將軍) Xú Yuánxǐ (徐元喜) and others.
Róng (融) appointed his staff officer, Guō Bāo (郭褒) of Hénán (河南), as the grand administrator of Huáinán (淮南).
Huáinán Commandery (淮南郡) was originally governed from Shòuyáng (壽陽).
When Qín (秦) had obtained it,
they appointed Guō Bāo (郭褒) as the grand administrator.
Dù Yù (杜預) said: "Southeast of Yúndù County (雲杜縣) in Jiāngxià (江夏) is Yúnchéng (鄖城)."
Yún (鄖),
pronounced "yúfēn fān".
They retreated and defended Xiáshí (硤石).
The Commentaries on the Water Classic (水經註) says: "The Huái River (淮水) flows eastward past the north of Shòuchūn County (壽春縣),
on its right, it joins the Féi River (肥水);
it then flows northward through mountain gorges,
which are called Xiáshí (峽石).
On the mountain opposite, two cities were built
to guard the vital ford."
Dù Yòu (杜佑) said: "Xiáshí (硤石) is today Xiàcài County (下蔡縣) in Rǔyīn Commandery (汝陰郡)."
Qín (秦)衛 Jiāngjūn (衞將軍) Liáng Chéng (梁成) and others led a force of fifty thousand men and encamped at Luòjiàn (洛澗),
building a stockade across the Huái River (淮) to block the eastern armies.
The Commentaries on the Water Classic (水經註) says: "Luòjiàn (洛澗) receives its upper waters from the Sǐmǎtáng River (死馬塘水),
flows north past Qín Xū (秦墟),
and empties into the Huái (淮),

Shuài (帥)
is read as "lǜ";
the same applies below.
They feared Chéng (成) and dared not advance.
Hú Bīn (胡彬) ran out of provisions,
and secretly sent an envoy to inform Shí (石) and others, saying:
"Now the enemy is strong and provisions are exhausted.
I fear I will not see the main army again!"
The Qín (秦) people captured him
and sent him to Yángpíng Gōng Róng (陽平公融).
Róng (融) urgently sent a messenger to report to Qín Wáng Jiān (秦王堅), saying:
"The enemy is few and easy to capture,

It is advisable to hasten to them!"
Jiān (堅) then left his main army at Xiàngchéng (項城),

marching rapidly to join Róng (融) at Shòuyáng (壽陽).
He sent Shàngshū Zhū Xù (尚書朱序) to persuade Xiè Shí (謝石) and others,
saying:
"The strong and the weak are in different situations,
it is better to surrender quickly."
Three years prior,
Jiān (堅) had captured Zhū Xù (朱序) at Xiāngyáng (襄陽),
and appointed him Dùzhī Shàngshū (度支尚書).
Shuō (說)
is pronounced "shū ruì fān".
Jiàng (降)
is pronounced "hù jiāng fān".
"If Qín's (秦) million troops all arrive,
it would indeed be difficult to contend with them.
Now, before all the armies have gathered,
it is advisable to attack them quickly;
if we defeat their vanguard,
then their morale will already be broken,
and they can then be completely defeated."
Shí (石) heard that Jiān (堅) was in Shòuyáng (壽陽),
and was very afraid.
He wished to avoid battle and wear out the Qín (秦) army.
Xiè Yǎn (謝琰) advised Shí (石) to follow Xù's (序) suggestion.
In the eleventh month,
Xiè Xuán (謝玄) sent Guǎnglíng Xiàng (廣陵相) Liú Láozhī (劉牢之) to lead five thousand elite soldiers towards Luòjiàn (洛澗).
Before they had reached within ten *li*,
Liáng Chéng (梁成) blocked the stream and arrayed his forces to await them.
Láozhī (牢之) advanced directly, crossed the water,
attacked Chéng (成),
and utterly routed him.
He beheaded Chéng (成) and Yìyáng Tàishǒu (弋陽太守) Wáng Yǒng (王詠).

Qín (秦) was not yet able to possess this territory,
Wáng Yǒng (王詠) merely held the title of Grand Administrator.
Yìyáng (弋陽)
was, in the Táng (唐) dynasty, the land of Guāng (光), Qí (蘄), and Huáng (黃) three prefectures.
The Qín (秦) infantry and cavalry collapsed,
scrambling to reach the Huái River (淮水).
Fifteen thousand soldiers died.
They captured Qín (秦) Yángzhōu Cìshǐ (揚州刺史) Wáng Xiǎn (王顯) and others,
and seized all their weapons and military supplies.
Thereupon, Xiè Shí (謝石) and the other armies
advanced by both land and water.
Qín Wáng Jiān (秦王堅) and Yángpíng Gōng Róng (陽平公融) ascended the Shòuyáng (壽陽) city wall to observe.
They saw the Jìn (晉) army's battle formation was strict and orderly.
They also looked at the vegetation on Bāgōng Mountain (八公山), and all of it seemed to them to be Jìn (晉) soldiers.
Bāgōng Mountain (八公山) is four *li* north of present-day Shòuchūn County (壽春縣).
It is said that in the Hàn (漢) dynasty, Huáinán Wáng Ān (淮南王安) was fond of immortals.
Suddenly, eight old men (the Bāgōng (八公)) with white hair and eyebrows
came to his gate seeking an audience.
The gatekeeper said:
"Our King is fond of longevity,
but you, sirs, have no art to stop aging.
I dare not announce you."
The Bāgōng (八公) all transformed into children.
Thus, a temple was built on the mountain.
Some say that those now worshipped in this mountain temple
are the eight individuals Zuǒ Wú (左吳), Zhū Jiāo (朱驕), Wǔ Bèi (伍被), Léi Bèi (雷被), and others,
all retainers of Huáinán Wáng (淮南王);
the world mistakenly considers the Bāgōng (八公) to be immortals.
"These are also formidable enemies,
how can they be called weak!"
He was dismayed and first showed signs of fear.
The Qín (秦) army pressed close to the Féi River (肥水) and formed their lines,
preventing the Jìn (晉) army from crossing.
Xiè Xuán (謝玄) sent an envoy to Yángpíng Gōng Róng (陽平公融), saying:
"Your lordship has advanced deep with a detached force,
and placed your lines close to the water.
This is a strategy for prolonged conflict,
not one for a quick decisive battle.
If you move your formation back a little,
allowing the Jìn (晉) army to cross,
to decide the victory or defeat,
would that not be excellent!"
All the Qín (秦) generals said:
"We are many, they are few.
It is better to block them
and prevent them from coming ashore,
which guarantees complete safety."
Jiān (堅) said:
"Just draw back the troops a little,
let them cross halfway,
and I will crush and kill them with my iron cavalry.
There will be no doubt of victory!"
Róng (融) also agreed,
and thereupon waved his army to retreat.
The Qín (秦) army then retreated
and could not be stopped.
When two formations face each other,
the one that retreats first is defeated;
this is the usual state of military affairs.
Fù (復)
is pronounced "fú yòu fān".
Róng (融) galloped his horse along the lines,
wanting to lead the retreating troops,
but his horse fell,
and he was killed by the Jìn (晉) army.
The Qín (秦) army then collapsed.
Xuán (玄) and others pursued and attacked, taking advantage of the victory,
reaching Qīnggāng (青岡).
Qīnggāng (青岡) is thirty *li* from present-day Shòuchūn County (壽春縣).
Those who trampled each other to death
covered the fields and blocked the rivers.
It means that the defeated soldiers trampled upon each other,
lying dead one upon another.
Jiè (藉)
is pronounced "cí yè fān".
Sè (塞)
is pronounced "xī zé fān".
All believed that the Jìn (晉) army was about to arrive,
and dared not rest day or night,
traveling through grass and sleeping in the open.
Traveling through grass means
walking through grass,
not daring to take mountain roads;
sleeping in the open means
sleeping in the wilderness,
not daring to enter human dwellings;
all fearing the pursuing army.
Seven or eight tenths of them died.
Initially,
when the Qín (秦) army retreated a little,
Zhū Xù (朱序) shouted from behind the lines:
"The Qín (秦) army is defeated!"
The troops then fled in a great panic.
Xù (序) then came over with Zhāng Tiānxī (張天錫) and Xú Yuánxǐ (徐元喜).
They captured Qín Wáng Jiān's (秦王堅) personal mica carriage.
They recaptured Shòuyáng (壽陽),
and seized its grand administrator, Guō Bāo (郭褒), whom Qín (秦) had appointed.
Jìn (晉) recaptured Shòuyáng (壽陽),
thus the grand administrator appointed by Qín (秦) was captured.
Jiān (堅) was struck by a stray arrow.
He fled alone on horseback to north of the Huái River (淮北),
feeling extremely hungry.
A commoner offered him a pot of cooked rice and a pork leg.
Jiān (堅) ate it,
and rewarded him with ten bolts of silk
and ten catties of cotton.
The man declined, saying:
"Your Majesty has grown weary of comfort and happiness,
and has brought yourself into peril and distress.
I am Your Majesty's son,
and Your Majesty is my father.
How can a son feed his father and seek repayment!"
He departed without looking back.
Jiān (堅) said to Zhāng Fūrén (張夫人):
"What face do I have now to govern the world!"
Tears streamed down his face.
At this time,
all the armies had collapsed.
Only the thirty thousand men led by Mùróng Chuí remained intact.
Chuí had separately attacked Yúnchéng,
and did not participate in the Battle of Féishuǐ.
Moreover, his army was disciplined and orderly,
hence, while all other armies collapsed, Chuí's army alone remained intact.
將,
read as liàng.
His heir apparent, Mùróng Bǎo, said to Chuí:
"Our home and state are ruined.
Heaven's mandate and the hearts of the people all belong to the Supreme One.
It is merely that the opportune moment has not yet arrived,
hence we have hidden our tracks and concealed ourselves.
Now the Qín ruler's army is defeated,
and he entrusts himself to us.
This is an opportune moment provided by Heaven to restore the Yàn dynasty.
This moment must not be lost.
I hope you will not forget the importance of the state for the sake of emotional loyalty and minor favors!"
Emotional loyalty and minor favors refers to Fú Jiān's generous treatment of Chuí and his son.
"What you say is correct.
However, he has offered his life to me with a sincere heart.
How can I harm him?
If Heaven truly abandons him,
I will not worry that he will not perish.
It would be better to protect him in his distress to repay his kindness,
and then gradually wait for his vulnerability to act.
This way, I will not betray my original intention,
and I can also acquire the empire righteously."
Mùróng Chuí's words here
still exhibited the demeanor of a true ruler.
"When Qín was strong, it annexed Yàn;
when Qín is weak, we should plot against it.
This is to avenge ourselves and wipe out our shame,
not to betray our original intention.
Elder brother, why would you obtain it and not take it,
releasing tens of thousands of troops to hand over to others?"
Chuí replied:
"In the past, I was not tolerated by Tàifù.
Having no place to settle,
I fled to Qín to escape death.
(See juan 102, 'Haixi Gong Taihe Sishi Nian' [Year 4 of Taihe, Duke of Haixi].)
I was received with utmost grace and courtesy.

Only the Qín ruler was able to clear me.
(See 'Taihe Wunian' [Year 5 of Taihe].)
If the Dī dynasty is truly destined to fail,

Guānxī will not be mine anyway."
Zhà Qiū, the Staff Officer of the Champion Army, said:
"Your Excellency is destined to restore the Yàn dynasty,

Now that the opportune moment has arrived,

If you kill the Qín ruler,

Many of Chuí's relatives and associates urged Chuí to kill Fú Jiān.
Chuí did not comply with any of them,

Píngnán Jiāngjūn Mùróng Wěi was stationed at Yúnchéng.
Hearing of Fú Jiān's defeat,

Upon reaching Xíngyáng,
Mùróng Dé again persuaded Wěi to raise an army to restore the Yàn dynasty.
Wěi did not comply.
Xiè Ān received an urgent dispatch,

At the time, he was playing go with a guest.
He put the letter on the bed,
showing no sign of joy.
攝 means
collect.
The guest asked him about it.
He slowly replied:
"The young fellows have indeed defeated the enemy."
After finishing,
he returned inside.
Crossing the threshold,

This signifies his extreme joy.
Historians say that Ān feigned his emotions and remained composed.
A minister who takes joy in stabilizing the state

The breaking of the clog teeth

On the day Dīnghài,
Xiè Shí and others returned to Jiànkāng.
They obtained Qín court musicians
who were skilled in the ancient music.
Thus, the ancestral temples for the first time were equipped with music from bronze bells and stone chimes.
During the chaos of Yǒngjiā,

When the Eastern Jìn was first established,
the ancestral temples lacked refined music and performers.
The Bureau of Grand Music and the drum and wind instruments were abolished.
Afterwards, some music for ceremonial singing and imperial banquets was gradually acquired,
but it was still incomplete.
At the end of Tàiníng,
Emperor Míng again consulted Ruǎn Fú and others to augment it.
During Xiánhé,
Emperor Chéng finally re-established the office of Grand Music,

When Mùróng Jùn defeated Rǎn Mǐn,

some musicians from Yè also came.
Xiè Shàng, while garrisoning Shòuyáng,

Refined music began to be quite complete.
However, when Wáng Měng pacified Yè,
the music that the Mùróng clan had obtained
again entered Guānyòu.
Now, having defeated Fú Jiān,
they captured his court musicians such as Yáng Shǔ,
who were skilled in ancient music.
Thus, bronze bells and stone chimes were finally complete.
On the day Yǐwèi,
Zhāng Tiānxī was appointed Sànqí Chángshì.
散,

騎,

7 Qín King Fú Jiān gathered the scattered remnants.
By the time he reached Luòyáng,
his forces numbered over one hundred thousand,
and his officials, ceremonial items, and military appearance were roughly restored.

It is precisely the time to carefully secure its jesses and leash,
Biāo (飊)

Tāo (絛),

"If heaven's mandate entails rise and fall,

Yì (翼) said:

He dispatched generals Lǐ Mán (李蠻), Mǐn Liàng (閔亮), and Yǐn Gù (尹固)

Quán Yì (權翼) secretly sent strongmen to intercept Chuí (垂) in an empty granary south of Héqiáo (河橋).
Chuí (垂) suspected something amiss.
From Liángmǎtái (涼馬臺), he made a grass raft to cross the river.

Tóngyī (同衣),
pronounced yú jì.
Qù (趣),
pronounced qī yù.
They galloped together and escaped.
In the twelfth month,
Qín (秦) King Jiān (堅) arrived at Cháng'ān (長安).
He mourned Gōng (公) of Yángpíng (陽平) before entering,

8 Gēngwǔ (庚午),
a great amnesty was declared.
Xiè Shí (謝石) was appointed Shàngshū Lìng (尚書令).
Xiè Xuán (謝玄) was promoted to the title of Qián Jiāngjūn (前將軍);

9 Xiè Ān's (謝安) son-in-law, Wáng Guóbǎo (王國寶),
was Tǎnzhī's (坦之) son.
Ān (安) disliked his character,
and always suppressed him, not employing him for important posts,
making him a Shàngshū Láng (尚書郎).
Guóbǎo (國寶) considered himself to be from a prominent family,
and traditionally served only in the Ministry of Personnel,
not in other departments.
Shàngshū Láng (尚書郎),
under the Jìn (晉) system, there were thirty-five bureaus,
with twenty-three *láng* (郎) who supervised each other.
When the court moved to the south of the Yangzi,
there were no *láng* for the ten bureaus of Zhíshì (直事), Yòumín (右民), Túntián (屯田), Chēbù (車部), Biébīng (別兵), Dūbīng (都兵), Qíbīng (騎兵), Zuǒ/Yòushì (左/右士), and Yùncáo (運曹).
After Kāng (康) and Mù (穆),
there were also no *láng* for Yúcáo (虞曹) and Èrqiānshí (二千石),

only the eighteen bureaus of Diànzhōng (殿中), Cíbù (祠部), Lìbù (吏部), Yícáo (儀曹), Sāngōng (三公), Bǐbù (比部), Jīnbù (金部), Cāngbù (倉部), Dùzhī (度支), Dūguān (都官), Zuǒmín (左民), Qǐbù (起部), Shuǐbù (水部), Zhǔkè (主客), Jiàbù (駕部), Kùbù (庫部), Zhōngbīng (中兵), and Wàibīng (外兵).
Later, Zhǔkè (主客), Qǐbù (起部), and Shuǐbù (水部) were abolished,
leaving fifteen bureaus,
among which Lìbù (吏部) was considered the most prestigious.
Because of this, he resented Ān (安).
Guóbǎo's (國寶) cousin was Huìjī Wáng Dàozǐ (會稽王道子).
The emperor and Dàozǐ (道子) were both fond of drinking,
and indulged in intimate flattery.
Guóbǎo (國寶) then slandered Ān (安) to Dàozǐ (道子),
causing him to alienate the emperor from Ān (安).
As Ān's (安) merits and fame grew,
those who were treacherous and sought advancement
often disparaged Ān (安),
and the emperor consequently became somewhat distant and wary of him.
10 Initially, the alcohol prohibition was lifted.
During the Jiàn'ān (建安) period of Hàn (漢),
Cáo Gōng (曹公) strictly prohibited alcohol.
The tax was five *shí* per person.
In the fifth year of Xiánhé (咸和),
Emperor Chéng (成帝) first measured the land of the common people,
taking one-tenth,
taxing three *shēng* of rice per *mǔ*.
Upon Emperor Āi's (哀帝) ascension,
the land tax was reduced,
collecting two *shēng* per *mǔ*.
In the second year of Tàiyuán (太元),
the emperor abolished the system of land measurement and rent collection.
From dukes and kings downward,
the poll tax was three *hú*,
only exempting those serving in active duty.
By this year,
the rice tax was again increased,
to five *shí* per person.
11 Qín (秦)'s Lǚ Guāng (呂光) traveled over three hundred *lǐ* across the Liúshā (流沙),
departing from Yùmén (玉門),
crossing the Liúshā (流沙),
going west to Shànshàn (鄯善),
and then north to Chēshī (車師).
Also,
the kingdom of Qiěmò (且末國) was west of Shànshàn (鄯善).
To its northwest,
there were several hundred *lǐ* of Liúshā (流沙),
with hot winds in summer,
posing a danger to travelers.
Where the wind reached,
only old camels knew in advance.
They would grow angry and gather together,
burying their mouths and noses in the sand.
People often used them as a signal,
and would immediately cover their own noses and mouths with felt.
The wind was swift,
passing quickly.
If one did not take precautions,
death was certain.
Sāng Qīn (桑欽) said: The Liúshā (流沙) region is northwest of Zhāngyè (張掖)'s Jūyán (居延) county.

eighty *lǐ* west of Dūnhuáng (敦煌) commandery.
Lì Dàoyuán (酈道元) said: The Ruòshuǐ (弱水) flows into the Liúshā (流沙).
Liúshā (流沙),
flows with water.

which is north of Xīhǎijùn (西海郡);

the Liúshā (流沙) emerges.

a kingdom had two Attendants-in-ordinary.
