Nùguān Wěi from Shàngdǎng,
drew Qǐtè Guī from Dōng'ē eastward,
and summoned Guāngliè Jiāngjūn Píng Ruì and Ruì's elder brother, Rǔyáng Tàishǒu Yòu, from Yānguó northward.
Wěi and the others all responded.
He also sent Lán Hàn to attack Dùnqīu,
and conquered it.
Dùnqīu county
belonged to Dōngjùn during the Hàn dynasty;
in the second year of Wǔdì Tàishǐ,
Dùnqīu commandery was established by division.
The army did not engage in private looting,
meaning their army dared not plunder residents and keep their belongings for themselves.
Chánglè Gōng Pī sent Shí Yuè with over ten thousand infantry and cavalry to suppress them.
Nóng said,
"Yuè has a reputation for wisdom and courage.
Now he does not resist the main army to the south but comes here;
this means he fears the king but looks down upon me."
"King" refers to Mùróng Chuí.
"We can take him by strategy."
The multitude requested to fortify Lièrén city.
Nóng said,
"Those who are skilled in warfare
bind their soldiers with hearts,
not with external objects."
"External objects"
is equivalent to "other things."
"They only seek the enemy,
and should use mountains and rivers as their fortifications.
Why bother fortifying Lièrén?"
On the day Xīnmǎo,
Yuè arrived west of Lièrén.
Nóng sent Zhào Qiū and Cānjūn Qíguàn Téng to attack Yuè's vanguard,
and defeated it.
Yuè's morale was already broken.
"Although Yuè's armor and weapons are excellent,
the hearts of his men are in dread and fear,
so they are easy to break.
We should attack them urgently."
Nóng said,
"Their armor is external,
our armor is in our hearts."
If the soldiers' hearts desire to fight,
then even without armor and helmets, they will be brave in battle,
hence "armor is in our hearts."
"If they see our outward appearance, they will be daunted.
It is better to wait until dusk to attack them;
we can surely defeat them."
He ordered his soldiers to prepare diligently and wait,
not to make any rash movements.
Yuè erected a palisade to secure himself.
Nóng laughed and said to his generals,
"Yuè's troops are elite and numerous,
yet he does not take advantage of the initial vigor upon arrival to attack us,
but instead sets up a palisade.
I know he is incapable of anything."
As dusk approached,
Nóng sounded the drums and shouts, emerging and
arraying his forces west of the city.
Yámén Liú Mù requested to be the first to attack Yuè's palisade.
Nóng laughed and said,
"When people see delicious food,
who doesn't desire it?
How can you alone request it?
However, your fierceness and courage are commendable,
so I shall grant you the vanguard."
Mù then led four hundred brave men, scaled the palisade, and entered.
The Qín soldiers scattered;
Nóng led the main army to follow,
greatly defeating the Qín forces,
beheading Yuè,
and sending his head to Chuí.
Yuè and Máo Dāng
were both valiant generals of Qín,
so Qín Wáng Jiān sent them to assist his two sons in defending.
Subsequently, they were successively defeated and perished,
and people's sentiments were agitated.
Sāo
means 'worried'
or 'disturbed'.
On the day Gēngxū,
Yān Wáng Chuí arrived in Yè.
He changed the twentieth year of Qín Jiànyuán to the first year of Yān.
The official dress and court rituals
were all restored to the old system.
He appointed the former Mínshān Gōng Kù Nùguān Wěi as Zuǒ Chángshǐ,
the former Shàngshū Duàn Chóng as Yòu Chángshǐ,
and Yíngyáng Zhèng Huò and others as Cóngshì Zhōngláng.
All those with the character "former" (前)
refer to officials appointed by the Former Yān.
Chuí then bestowed upon them the offices they had claimed.
These were the offices acclaimed by Zhāng Xiáng and others.
He enfeoffed his younger cousins, Bá and seventeen others, as well as his nephew Yǔwén Shū,
and his maternal cousin Lán Shěn, all as kings.
The remaining members of his clan and meritorious officials who were enfeoffed as dukes numbered thirty-seven,
and those as marquises, earls, viscounts, and barons numbered eighty-nine.
Kězúhún Tán gathered over twenty thousand soldiers
and attacked Yěwáng,
capturing it.
Chuí had sent Tán to gather troops at Shāchéng in Hénèi,
and subsequently he attacked and captured Yěwáng.
Píng Yòu, along with his younger brothers Ruì and Guī, also led tens of thousands of people to join Chuí in Yè.
Chánglè Gōng Pī sent Jiāng Ràng to rebuke Yàn Wáng Chuí,
and said to him:
"To correct one's mistakes,
even now it is not too late."
Chuí said:
"I have received an unprecedented favor from the sovereign,
and therefore I wish to ensure the safety of Chánglè Gōng,
so that he may lead all his people to the capital.
The capital
refers to Cháng'ān.
Live as good neighbors with Qín Yǒng.
Why are you so blind to the opportune moment
that you do not surrender Yèchéng?
If you remain confused and do not return,
I will exhaust my military power,
and I fear that even to seek survival alone
will be impossible."
Ràng sternly rebuked him, saying:
"General, you were not tolerated in your own state,
and you pledged your life to the sacred court.
How could you, General, have any share
in even an inch of Yān's land?
The sovereign and you, General, are of different customs and distinct races.
It is said that the Dī are in Guānxī,
and the Xiānbēi are in the northeast.
They are neither of the same customs
nor of the same race.
Yet you were treated as close as a clan member,
and favored beyond old meritorious officials.
Since ancient times, has there ever been a more generous encounter
between a monarch and his minister?
Suddenly, because of a minor defeat of the royal army,
you harbor disloyal intentions!
Chánglè Gōng,
the sovereign's eldest son,
has been entrusted with the duty of governing a region.
How can he stand idly by and surrender a hundred cities to you, General?
General, you wish to 'rend the crown and destroy the cap'.
The Zuǒ Zhuàn states:
Jìn led the róng and dí to attack Yǐng.
King Jǐng sent Zhān Huánbó to make a formal protest to Jìn, saying:
'For us, the elder uncle [Jìn],
is like a crown and cap for clothes,
a root and source for trees and water,
and a chief counselor for the people.
If the elder uncle 'rends the crown and destroys the cap',
'uproots the source and blocks the origin',
and unilaterally abandons the chief counselor,
even if it were the róng or dí,
how could they tolerate this sole person [i.e., the king]!'
Why say more?
I only regret that at your age of seventy, General,
your head will be hung from a white banner,
[Wǔ Wáng decapitated Zhòu and hung his head from a large white banner.]
and you will become
a rebellious ghost!"
Chuí remained silent.
Jiāng Ràng's words were direct,
and Chuí felt inwardly ashamed,
so he had no reply.
Chuí said:
"Each serves his own lord,
what crime is there!"
He treated Ràng with courtesy and sent him back,
giving Pī a letter and submitting a memorial to Qín Wáng Jiān,
detailing the advantages and disadvantages,
and requesting that Pī be sent back to Cháng'ān.
Jiān and Pī were enraged,
and wrote back severely rebuking him.
2 Yīngyáng Jiāngjūn Liú Láozhī attacked Qín's Qiáochéng
and captured it.
Huán Chōng sent Shàngyōng Tàishǒu Guō Bǎo to attack Qín's three commanderies of Wèixīng, Shàngyōng, and Xīnchéng,
and captured them.
Jiāngjūn Yáng Quánqī advanced to occupy Chénggù
and attacked Qín's Liángzhōu Cìshǐ Pān Měng,
who fled.
Quánqī
was Liàng's son.
Yáng Liàng is mentioned in the previous volume, Tàiyuán Second Year.
3 On the day of Rénzǐ,
Yàn Wáng Chuí attacked Yè
and captured its outer city wall.
Chánglè Gōng Pī retreated to defend the inner city.
Many prefectures and counties in the six eastern provinces sent envoys to surrender to Yàn.
On the day of Guǐchǒu,
Chuí appointed Chénliú Wáng Shào as acting Jìzhōu Cìshǐ,
garrisoning Guǎng'ā.
Guǎng'ā County,
during the Former Hàn, belonged to Jùlù Commandery.
During the Later Hàn, it was merged into Jùlù County.
There was Guǎng'ā Zé [Lake Guǎng'ā],
within Jùlù County,
which is Dàlù Zé.
4 Fēngchéng Xuānmù Gōng Huán Chōng, hearing of Xiè Xuán and others' achievements,
realized he had spoken wrongly,
referring to his statement
"We shall become left-collared"
of the previous year.
In the second month,
on the day of Xīnsì,
he died.
The court deliberated appointing Xiè Xuán as the Cìshǐ of Jīng and Jiāng provinces.
Xiè Ān felt that the father and son's positions were too prominent,
and also feared that the Huán clan would resent losing their posts,
so he appointed Liángjùn Tàishǒu Huán Shímín as Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ,
Hédōng Tàishǒu Huán Shíqián as Yùzhōu Cìshǐ,
and Yùzhōu Cìshǐ Huán Yī as Jiāngzhōu Cìshǐ.
5 Yàn Wáng Chuí led over two hundred thousand Dīnglíng and Wūhuán troops, using flying ladders and tunnels to attack Yè,
but failed to capture it.
So he built a long siege wall and guarded it,
and quartered the old and weak in Féixiāng.
The Jìn Zhì says
Féixiāng County belonged to Guǎngpíng Commandery.
Wèi Shōu says: in the early Tiānpíng era,
it was merged into Línzhāng County of Wèijùn.
The Suí dynasty re-established Féixiāng County,
and in the Táng dynasty, it belonged to Míngzhōu.
The character Chǔ (處)
has the pronunciation Chāng Lǚ.
6 The officials of Qín's Zhēngdōng Fǔ suspected Cānjūn Gāo Tài,
an old minister of Yàn,
of having disloyal intentions.
Fú Pī was Zhēngdōng Dàjiāngjūn.
Gāo Tài had previously served Yàn;
Mùróng Chuí had made him Cóngshì Zhōngláng.
He fled back to Bóhǎi with Wú Sháo, a Yúcáo Cóngshì of the same commandery.
Qín's Zhēngdōng Fǔ established Yúcáo Cóngshì to manage the mountains and lakes in their jurisdiction.
Tài and Sháo
were both from Bóhǎi.
"The Yàn army is near Féixiāng;
it would be appropriate to follow them."
Tài said:
"I came here only to escape calamity;
to leave one lord
and serve another,
is not something I would do!"
Shēn Shào saw this and sighed, saying:
"To act or retreat according to the Way
can be called a jūnzi!"
7 Yàn's Fànyáng Wáng Dé attacked Qín's Fāngtóu,
captured it,
stationed troops, and returned.
8 Dōnghú Wáng Yàn occupied Guǎntáo
to provide support for Yè.
Many Xiānbēi, Wūhuán, and people from commanderies and counties who held fortified villages did not submit to Yàn.
Yàn Wáng Chuí sent Tàiyuán Wáng Kǎi and Zhènnán Jiāngjūn Chénliú Wáng Shào to attack them.
Kǎi said to Shào:
"The Xiānbēi, Wūhuán, and people of Jìzhōu
were originally all subjects of Yàn.
Now that the great enterprise has just begun,
people's hearts are not yet united,
which is why there are minor differences.
It is only proper to pacify them with virtue,
not to intimidate them with might.
I will stay in one place
as the base of military prestige.
You should tour and console the barbarians and the people,
showing them the great principle,
and they will surely obey."
Kǎi then garrisoned at Pìyáng.
The Dìlǐ Fēngsú Jì says: sixty lǐ southwest of Guǎngchuān is Pìyáng Tíng,
an old county.
Hàn Gāodì enfeoffed Shěn Shíqí as a marquisate there.
Wèi Shōu's Dìxíng Zhì says: Xìndū County of Chánglè Commandery has Pìyáng Chéng.
Kǎi explained the advantages and disadvantages,
and Yàn, with Shào, went to Kǎi to surrender.
Thereupon, several hundred thousand Xiānbēi, Wūhuán, and villagers from fortified places surrendered.
Kǎi kept their old and weak,
appointed governors and magistrates to comfort them,
and dispatched over one hundred thousand of their able-bodied men
to go to Yè with Wáng Yàn.
Chuí was greatly pleased and said:
"You brothers possess both civil and military talents,
sufficient to succeed the former king!"
He meant sufficient to succeed Mùróng Kè.
9 In the third month,
Wèi Jiāngjūn Xiè Ān was appointed Tàibǎo.
10 Qín's Běidì Chángshǐ Mùróng Hóng, hearing that Yàn Wáng Chuí was attacking Yè,
fled eastward to Guāndōng,
gathered the Xiānbēi,
whose numbers reached several thousand,
and returned to garrison at Huáyīn.
He defeated Qín Jiāngjūn Qiáng Yǒng,
and his forces became strong.
He proclaimed himself Dūdū Shǎnxī Zhū Jūnjì, Dàjiāngjūn, Yōngzhōu Mù, and Jìběi Wáng,
and recognized Chuí as Céngxiàng, Dūdū Shǎndōng Zhū Jūnjì, Lǐng Dàsīmǎ, Jìzhōu Mù, and Wú Wáng.
Fú Jiān, the King of Qín, said to Quán Yì:
"I did not heed your words.
This means that Fú Jiān did not heed Yì's words and sent Mùróng Chuí away.
As for the land east of the passes,
I will no longer contend with them for it.
What shall we do about Mùróng Hóng?"
Thereupon, he appointed Gǔangpíng Gōng Xī as the Inspector of Yōngzhōu,
to guard Púbǎnr.
He summoned Yōngzhōu Mù, Jùlù Gōng Ruì, to be the Supreme Commander of All Military Affairs Inside and Outside the Capital, Grand General of the Guards, and Supervisor of the Imperial Secretariat,
assigning him 50,000 troops;
he appointed Zǔo Jiāngjūn Dòu Chōng as Chief Clerk,
and Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn Yáo Cháng as Army Supervisor,
to suppress Hóng.
Mùróng Chōng, the Administrator of Píngyáng, also raised an army in Píngyáng,
with 20,000 men.
He advanced to attack Púbǎn;
Fú Jiān sent Dòu Chōng to suppress him.
Kùrǔguān Wěi led tens of thousands of his troops to Yè.
The King of Yān, Mùróng Chuí, enfeoffed Wěi as the Prince of Āndìng.
Fú Dìng, the Marquis of Fùchéng and Inspector of Jìzhōu under Qín, guarded Xìndū.
Gāochéng Nán Shào was in his state.
Gāochéng County belonged to Bóhǎi Commandery.
In the Táng Dynasty, it was Yánshān County of Cāngzhōu.
Gù'ān Hóu Jiàn guarded Zhōngshān.
The King of Yān, Mùróng Chuí, dispatched the Former General, Prince of Lèlang, Wēn, to lead various armies to attack Xìndū,
but they did not succeed.
In summer,
in the fourth month,
on the day of bǐngchén,
he sent Fǔjūn Dàjiāngjūn Lín to reinforce them.
Dìng and Jiàn
were Fú Jiān's cousins on his father's side.
Shào and Mó
were his younger cousins on his father's side.
Liàng
was his nephew.
Wēn
was Mùróng Chuí's nephew.
Mùróng Hóng, hearing that the Qín army was approaching,
was afraid
and led his troops to flee to Guāndōng.
Fú Ruì, Duke Mǐn of Jùlù under Qín, was rough, fierce, and underestimated the enemy.
He wanted to rapidly advance his troops to intercept them.
Yáo Cháng admonished him, saying:
"All the Xiānbēi have a desire to return home,
which is why they have risen in rebellion.
It is best to drive them out of the passes;
they should not be stopped.
Even a field mouse, if its tail is held,
can still turn and bite a person.
The field mouse
is also called the gānkǒu rat.
It eats food without pain.
The Éryǎ states: some have venomous stings.
Xī,
pronounced xī.
If we push them to their deaths,
and by some chance suffer a defeat,
what regrets will avail us?
We should just beat our drums and follow them;
they will then flee in such haste that they will have no time for anything else."
If Fú Ruì had followed Yáo Cháng's advice,
Mùróng Hóng would certainly have fled east,
and Mùróng Chōng, being defeated and having nowhere to go,
would also have been captured.
They fought at Huázé.
Huázé is the marsh of Huáyīn.
Huá,
pronounced huà.
Ruì was killed by Hóng.
Cháng sent Lóngxiáng Zhǎngshǐ Zhào Dū and Cānjūn Jiāng Xié to Fú Jiān, the King of Qín, to apologize;
Fú Jiān was enraged
and killed them.
Cháng was afraid and
fled to Wèiběi Mǎmù.
Mǎmù
was a place for pasturing horses,
similar to the Han Dynasty's Mùyuàn.
He instigated the Qiāng chieftains,
and over 50,000 households returned to Cháng,
recognizing Cháng as their alliance leader.
Cháng proclaimed himself Grand General, Grand Chányú, and King of Wànnián Qín,
issued a general amnesty,
and changed the era name to Báiquè.
Zīzhì Tōngjiàn Mùlù: Yánjīngguówěi.
From this point onwards,
Yáo Cháng is referred to as Hòuqín.
Chán,
pronounced chán.
Yáo Huàng of Nán'ān and Yǐn Wěi were appointed Left and Right Army Supervisors;
Dí Bózhī of Tiānshuǐ and others were appointed Attendant Censors;
Qiāng Xùn and others were appointed Clerks;
Wáng Jù and others were appointed Army Supervisors;
Wáng Qīn, Lú Yáo, Fāng Chéng and others were appointed generals and commanders.
Qín's Dòu Chōng attacked Mùróng Chōng in Hédōng
and severely defeated him.
Chōng led 8,000 Xiānbēi cavalry to Mùróng Hóng.
Hóng's forces reached over 100,000.
He sent an envoy to Fú Jiān, the King of Qín, saying:
"The Prince of Wú has already pacified Guāndōng.
You should quickly prepare the grand carriage
and escort our elder brother, the emperor,
Wěi
is Hóng's elder brother,
back to Yèdū.
We will establish Hǔláo as the border with Qín
and be good neighbors forever."
Fú Jiān was greatly enraged.
He summoned Mùróng Wěi and rebuked him, saying:
"Now Hóng's letter is like this.
If you wish to leave,
I will provide for you.
Your clan can be said to have human faces but beastly hearts;
they cannot be considered national heroes!"
Wěi kowtowed until his head bled,
weeping and apologizing.
After a long while, Fú Jiān said:
"This is the doing of those three rascals themselves,
not your fault."
The three rascals
refer to Chuí, Hóng, and Chōng.
He treated Wěi as before.
He ordered Wěi to write letters to persuade Hóng, Chōng, and Chuí.
Wěi secretly sent an envoy to Hóng, saying:
"I am a man in a cage;
there is no hope of my return.
Moreover, I am a sinner of the Yān court."
Wěi could not protect the Yān ancestral altars;
hence he referred to himself as a sinner.
"You should strive to establish a great enterprise.
Appoint the Prince of Wú as Chancellor,
the Prince of Zhōngshān as Grand Tutor and Grand Commander,
and you can be Grand General and Grand Minister of Education.
You will act on imperial authority to bestow titles and appointments.
When you hear of my death,
you may immediately assume the imperial throne."
Hóng then advanced towards Cháng'ān
and changed the era name to Yānxīng.
The King of Yān, Mùróng Chuí, considered Yèchéng still strong.
He convened his advisors to discuss the matter.
Right Army Supervisor Fēng Héng requested to divert the Zhāng River to flood it.
This was using Cáo Cāo's old stratagem when attacking Yè.
Chuí was conducting the siege,
and was drinking in Huálínyuán.
Both Luòdū
and Yèdū had Huálínyuán;
the Huálínyuán in Yè
was built by Wèi Wǔ.
Arrows fell like rain,
and Chuí almost could not get out.
Champion General Lóng led his cavalry to charge,
and Chuí barely escaped.
Zhào Tǒng, the Administrator of Jìnglíng, attacked Xiāngyáng.
Dū Guì, the Inspector of Jīngzhōu under Qín, fled to Lúyáng.
In the fifth month,
Zhāng Wǔhǔ, the Inspector of Luòzhōu under Qín, occupied Fēngyáng and surrendered.
Yáng Liàng, the Inspector of Liángzhōu, led 50,000 troops to attack Shǔ,
sending Fèi Tǒng, the Administrator of Bāxī, with 30,000 land and naval troops as the vanguard.
Liàng garrisoned Bājùn.
Wáng Guǎng, the Inspector of Yìzhōu under Qín, sent Kāng Huí, the Administrator of Bāxī, and others to resist him.
Xìngpǔ: The Western Hú have their own Kāng surname.
Qín's Fú Dìng and Fú Shào both surrendered to Yān.
Dìng surrendered Xìndū,
and Shào surrendered Gāochéng.
Jiàng
is pronounced jiàng;
the same below.
Fú Mó guarded Chángshān.
Hòuqín King Yáo Cháng advanced to garrison Běidì.
Yáo Cháng is written as Hòuqín
to distinguish him from Fú Qín.
In the sixth month,
on guǐchǒu day, the first day of the month,
Empress Dowager Chǔ of Chóngdé passed away.
22 Qín Wáng Jiān personally led 20,000 infantry and cavalry to attack the Hòu Qín army at Zhào Shì Wū.
According to the Jìn Shū Zài Jì,
Zhào Shì Wū was in Běidì.
帥,
read as 率.
騎,
sound Qí Jì.
The Hòu Qín forces were repeatedly defeated.
They beheaded Yǐn Mǎi, the General of the Garrison Army and younger brother of Hòu Qín Wáng Cháng.
There were no wells in the Hòu Qín camp.
The Qín people blocked Ān Gōng Gǔ and dammed Tóng Guān Shuǐ to trap them.
Ān Gōng Gǔ and Tóng Guān Shuǐ are both in present-day Yàozhōu.
Wèi Shōu's Dìxíng Zhì states that
Běidì Jùn had Tóngguān Xiàn,
established in the seventh year of Zhēnjūn.
Dù Yòu said: Tóngguān was originally the land of Hàn Gūyǔ Xiàn.
During the Jìn, it was Pínyáng.
Fú Qín established Tóngguān Hùjūn in Tóngguān Chuān, north of Gūyǔ.
Later, Wèi Tàiwǔ abolished the Hùjūn
and established Tóngguān Xiàn.
Later, Zhōu Wǔdì moved it to its current location.
From Suí onwards,
it was only written as Tóngguān.
塞,
sound Sī Zé.
Some died of thirst.
Coincidentally, there was a heavy rain,
and the Hòu Qín camp had three feet of water,
but beyond a hundred paces around the camp,
there was only about an inch,
and the Hòu Qín army revived.
Qín Wáng Jiān sighed, saying:
"Does Heaven also protect these rebels?"
Heaven does not aid Qín,
it cannot be sustained any longer.
23 Mùróng Hóng's strategists Gāo Gài and others believed that Hóng's virtue and prestige were inferior to Mùróng Chōng's,
and that his enforcement of the law was harsh and severe.
So they killed Hóng
and established Chōng as the Imperial Younger Brother (Huáng Tàidì),
who then acted by imperial authority
and appointed all officials.
Gài was appointed Shàngshū Lìng.
Hòu Qín Wáng Cháng sent his son Sōng as a hostage to Chōng to request peace.
He wished to join forces to defeat Qín,
and also feared Chōng's strong army.
質,
sound Zhì.
24 General Liú Chūn attacked Lǔyáng,
and Dū Guì fled back to Cháng'ān.
25 Hòu Qín Wáng Cháng led 70,000 troops to attack Qín.
Qín Wáng Jiān sent Yáng Bì and others to resist him,
but they were defeated by Cháng.
Yáng Bì and several dozens of generals and officials, including Right General Xú Chéng and Garrison General Máo Shèng, were captured.
Cháng treated them with courtesy and sent them away.
26 Yān Mùróng Lín captured Chángshān,
and Qín's Fú Liàng and Fú Mó both surrendered.
Lín advanced to besiege Zhōngshān.
In autumn,
the seventh month,
he captured it
and seized Fú Jiàn.
All of Jìzhōu became Yān territory,
with only Fú Pī defending Yè.
He remained garrisoned in Zhōngshān.
27 Qín's Yōuzhōu Cìshǐ Wáng Yǒng and Píngzhōu Cìshǐ Fú Chōng led the forces of the two prefectures to attack Yān.
Yān Wáng Chuí sent Píng
Shuò General Píng Guī to attack Yǒng.
This Píng Guī is another Píng Guī,
younger brother of Píng Yòu,
not the Píng Guī who rebelled with Fú Luò.
Chǎng's army was defeated,
and Guī advanced to occupy Jìnán.
28 Qín's Píngyuán Gōng Huī led 70,000 troops from Luòyáng and Shǎn Chéng to return to Cháng'ān.
29 Qín
Wáng Jiān heard that Mùróng Chōng was approaching Cháng'ān,
so he withdrew his troops and returned.
He returned from Běidì Zhào Shì Wū to prevent Chōng from pressing on Cháng'ān.
Jiān was still locked in a stalemate with Cháng,
and the outcome of victory or defeat had not yet been determined.
When Chōng's army pressed close,
Jiān had no choice but to return to Cháng'ān.
Cháng was able to secure the area north of the ridge as resources.
Jiān and Chōng fought fiercely, and Cháng waited for their exhaustion.
When Jiān died, the Xiānbēi moved eastward.
Cháng effortlessly seized Guānzhōng.
This is truly a case of "the snipe and clam grapple, the fisherman profits."
He garrisoned Lìshān
and appointed Píngyuán Gōng Huī as Commander-in-Chief of All Armies Inside and Outside, General of Chariots and Cavalry, and Director of the Department of State Affairs,
assigning him 50,000 troops to resist Chōng.
Chōng fought Huī at Zhèngxī
and decisively defeated him.
Jiān again sent Former General Jiāng Yǔ and his youngest son, Hélián Gōng Lín, to lead 30,000 troops to resist Chōng at Bàshàng.
Lín and Yǔ were both defeated and killed.
Chōng then occupied Āfáng Chéng.
This is the city of Qín's Āfáng Gōng.
30 Qín Kāng's troops were repeatedly defeated
and retreated to Chéngdū.
The Governor of Zǐtóng, Lěi Xí, surrendered with Fúchéng.
This was a victory for Jìn's western army.
The Xìng Pǔ says: The Hòu Zhào Lù records Lěi Chéng,
whose original surname was Péi.
He sent the Governor of Hénán, Gāo Mào, to garrison Luòyáng in the north.
This was the Jìn army moving north from Xiāng and Miǎn.
31 On the day Jǐ Yǒu,
Empress Kāngxiàn was buried at Chóngpíng Líng.
32 Yān's Zhái Bīn, presuming on his achievements, became arrogant and unrestrained,
making insatiable demands.
Moreover, as the siege of Yè Chéng dragged on,
he secretly harbored rebellious intentions.
Crown Prince Bǎo requested to eliminate him.
Yān Wáng Chuí said:
"The covenant of Hénán cannot be betrayed.
Bīn led his troops to meet Chuí in Luòyáng, and Chuí made a covenant with him, which was probably in Hénán Xiàn.
The fault would lie with Bīn.
If we kill him now, before his intentions are manifest,
people will surely say that I am jealous of his abilities and achievements.
I am currently gathering heroes to achieve a great enterprise;
I must not show narrow-mindedness and lose the trust of all under Heaven.
Even if he has a scheme,
I will counter it with wisdom,
and he will be powerless."
Fányáng Wáng Dé, Chénliú Wáng Shào, and General of Agile Cavalry Nóng all said:
"Zhái Bīn and his brothers, presuming on their achievements, are arrogant and will surely become a national calamity."
Chuí said:
"Arrogance leads to swift defeat;
how can they become a calamity?
焉,
sound Yū Gān, meaning 'how'.
Let them bring about their own downfall."
He treated them with even greater deference.
Bīn subtly prompted the Dīnglíng and his followers to request that Bīn be appointed Shàngshū Lìng.
Chuí said:
"Zhái Wáng's achievements merit the highest advisory position.
However, since the administration has not yet been established,
this office cannot be hastily created."
Bīn grew angry
and secretly conspired with Former Qín Chánglè Gōng Pī.
The Tōngjiàn, for all matters of Fú Qín, writes "Qín";
this character "前"
is superfluous.
Yān had diverted the Zhāng Shuǐ to flood Yè,
so Bīn wanted to breach the dike to release the water.
Chuí killed Bīn and his brothers Tán and Mǐn,
but pardoned the rest.
Bīn's nephew, Zhēn,
fled north with his camp at night to Hándān,
then led his troops back towards the siege of Yè,
intending to act in concert with Pī from inside and outside.
Crown Prince Bǎo and General of Champion Army Lóng attacked and defeated him.
Zhēn retreated to Hándān.
Tàiyuán Wáng Kǎi and Chénliú Wáng Shào said to Chuí:
"The Dīnglíng do not harbor great ambitions;
they are merely causing trouble due to excessive favor.
If we press them now, they will gather and become bandits.
If we relax, they will disperse on their own.
If we attack them after they disperse,
there will be no failure."
Chuí agreed.
The King of Qūzī, Bó Chún, was in a desperate situation.
Lǚ Guāng had advanced with his army and attacked Qūzī last year.
Qūzī,
pronounced Qiūcí.
Jiǒng,
pronounced qú yǔn fān.
Kuàihú,
was probably to the west of Qūzī.
Yáng Zhènghéng said: Kuài,
pronounced gǔ mài fān.
Nà Lóng, one person,
Kuí, another person,
Hóu Jiàng,
was an official title;
in the Western Regions during the Hàn dynasty,
each state had a Fǔguó Hóu, Ānguó Hóu, Zuǒ Jiàng, and Yòu Jiàng.
Later, Gài combined Hóu and Jiàng into one office.
Nà,
pronounced nǚ liè fān,
also nǚ yù fān.
Jiàng,
pronounced jí liàng fān.
Kuí,
pronounced qú zhuī fān.
The combined forces of these various states, numbering over 700,000, came to rescue Qūzī.
Qín's Lǚ Guāng fought them west of the city
and utterly defeated them.
Bó Chún fled.
More than thirty kings and marquises surrendered.
Lǚ Guāng entered their city;
the city resembled Cháng'ān in its markets and dwellings,
and the palaces were magnificent.
Lǚ Guāng pacified the Western Regions;
his might and benevolence were greatly manifest.
Distant states,
which previous dynasties had been unable to subdue,
all came to submit,
presenting the imperial seals and tallies bestowed by the Hàn dynasty.

In the eighth month,
Zhái Zhēn fled north from Hándān.
King Yān Chuí sent the King of Tàiyuán, Kǎi, and the Pàoqí Dàjiàngjūn, Nóng, to lead cavalry to pursue him.
They caught
him at Xiàyì.
Kǎi wanted to fight,
but Nóng said:
"The soldiers are hungry and tired.
Moreover, looking at the enemy camp, we see no able-bodied men,
so there is likely an ambush."
Kǎi did not listen and advanced to battle,
and the Yān army was greatly defeated.
Zhēn hastened north to Zhōngshān
and encamped at Chéngyíng.
Those who feign weakness with an exhausted army
must have an ambush.
This is common knowledge,
yet many often fall into this trap without realizing it,
leading to the annihilation of their army.
Qū,
pronounced qī yù fān;
the same below.
In Yè, fodder was completely exhausted,
and pine wood was shaved to feed the horses.
King Yān Chuí said to his generals:
"Fú Pī is a desperate bandit,
and there is no reason for him to surrender;
it is better to withdraw and camp at Xīnchéng,
which is the Xīnxīngchéng of Féixiāng.
This is to repay the kindness of the King of Qín in the past,
and also to plan for the suppression of Zhái Zhēn."
On the night of Bǐngyín,
Chuí lifted the siege and hastened to Xīnchéng,
sending Mùróng Nóng to tour Qīnghé and Píngyuán
to collect taxes and levies.
Nóng clearly established regulations,
distributed resources fairly,
and maintained strict military discipline,
without any侵暴 (violence or depredation).
As a result, grain and silk filled the roads,
and military supplies were abundant.
On Wùyín,
Xī Yīn, Duke Wénmù of Nánchāng, passed away.
Tài Bǎo Ān submitted a memorial requesting to take advantage of Fú's decline
to expand into the Central Plains,
appointing Xiè Xuán, the Inspector of Xú and Yǎn provinces, as the vanguard commander,
and leading Huán Shíqián, the Inspector of Yù Province, to attack Qín.
When Xuán reached Xiàpī,
Qín's Inspector of Xú Province, Zhào Qiān, abandoned Péngchéng and fled.
Xuán advanced and occupied Péngchéng.
This was the Jìn army advancing north from Huái and Sì.
King Qín Jiān heard that Lǚ Guāng had pacified the Western Regions,
and appointed Lǚ Guāng as the Supervisor of all military affairs west of Yùmén,
and Western Regions Commandant.
The roads were cut off
and impassable.
Qín's Inspector of Yōuzhōu, Wáng Yǒng, sought aid from Zhènwēi Jiàngjūn Liú Kùrén.
Earlier,
Qín had appointed Liú Kùrén as Zhènwǔ Jiàngjūn.
He greatly defeated Píng Guī south of Jì
and, taking advantage of the victory, drove straight on
and occupied Tángchéng.
In the ninth month,
Xiè Xuán sent Liú Láozhī, the Inner Historian of Péngchéng, to attack Qín's Inspector of Yǎn Province, Zhāng Chóng.
On Xīnmǎo,
Zhāng Chóng abandoned Juànchéng and fled to Yān.
Liú Láozhī occupied Juànchéng,
and all the castles and fortresses in Hénán came to submit.
Tài Bǎo Ān submitted a memorial requesting to lead the northern expedition himself;
Ān was given the additional title of Supervisor of the armies of Yáng, Jiāng, and fifteen other provinces,
and granted the yellow battle-axe.
The fifteen provinces were probably Yáng, Xú, Nánxú, Yǎn, Nányǎn, Yù, Nányù, Jiāng, Qīng, Jì, Yōu, Bìng, Sī, Jīng, and Yōng.
Mùróng Chōng advanced and pressed towards Cháng'ān.
King Qín Jiān ascended the city wall to observe them
and sighed,
saying:
"Where did these barbarians come from!"
He shouted and rebuked Chōng, saying:
"Slave, why do you come to seek death!"
Chōng replied: "Slave is tired of being a slave
and wishes to take your place!"
Chōng was favored by Jiān when he was young.
Chōng had the beauty of Lóngyáng when he was young
and gained favor with Jiān.
Shào,
pronounced shī zhào fān.
Chōng sent his Chamberlain, claiming to be the Imperial Younger Brother, to reply:
"My heart is now set on the empire;
how can I care about a small favor of a single robe!
If you know your fate,
let your lord and ministers bind their hands
and promptly send the Emperor."
The Emperor referred to Mùróng Wěi.
Jiān was furious and said:
"I did not heed the words of Wáng Jǐnglǜe and the Duke of Yángpíng!"
The events are recorded in volume 103, Níngkāng 3rd year, and in the previous volume, Tàiyuán 7th year.
The Zàijì states: The Qín people generally referred to the Xiānbēi as 'White Barbarians'.
In winter,
the tenth month,
on the first day of the month, Xīnhài,
there was a solar eclipse.
On Yǐchǒu,
a general amnesty was proclaimed.
Xiè Xuán sent Gāo Sù, the Administrator of Yīnlíng, to attack Qín's Inspector of Qīngzhōu, Fú Lǎng.
Yīnlíng county
belonged to Jiǔjiāng Commandery during the Hàn dynasty.

belonged to Línhuái Commandery in the Former Hàn,

Huáilíng Commandery was established.
"Yīn"
should be written
"Huái".
Fú Lǎng came to surrender.
Fú Lǎng
was Jiān's cousin.
46 Zhái Zhēn (翟真) was at Chéngyíng (承營),

(Zhái Zhēn (翟真)) formed an alliance with (Gōngsūn Xī (公孫希) and Sòng Chǎng (宋敞)).

Wén (文), the son of Mùyú Jù (慕輿句), the Grand Tutor of the Yān (燕) Crown Prince, and Cháng (常), the son of Mùyú Qián (慕輿虔), the Duke of Línglíng (零陵) —

— knew that the troops from the three commanderies were reluctant to undertake a distant campaign,

Thus it is known that mere bravery without strategy
is useless in determining success or failure.
Háo (蚝)

(Pī (丕)) deliberated with his subordinates.

and he is setting up two alternatives,

promising that upon the arrival of the king's army,

if he does not comply,

Yīng (膺) considered himself capable of controlling Pī (丕).
Yáng Yīng (楊膺)
was Pī’s (丕) brother,

49 Xiè Xuán (謝玄) sent Téng Tiánzhī (滕恬之), the Administrator of Jìnlíng (晉陵), to cross the river and guard Líyáng (黎陽).

50 Hòuqín (後秦) King Cháng (萇) heard that Mùróng Chōng (慕容沖) was attacking Cháng’ān (長安),
and gathered his subordinates to discuss strategy.
They all said:
“Your Majesty should first take Cháng’ān (長安),
establish a base,
and then operate in the four directions.”
Cháng (萇) said:
“Not so.
The Yān (燕) people started their army because their troops wished to return home.
If they achieve their goal,
they will not stay long in Guānzhōng (關中).
I should move my camp to Lǐngběi (嶺北).
Lǐngběi (嶺北)
refers to the north of Jiǔzōng (九嵕);
all the lands of Xīnpíng (新平), Běidì (北地), and Āndìng (安定) are there.
I will wait for Qín (秦) to fall and Yān (燕) to leave,
and then I can take it easily.”
So he left his eldest son Xīng (興) to guard Běidì (北地),
ordered the General of Stabilizing the North, Yáo Mù (姚穆), to guard Tóngguān Chuān (同官川),
and personally led his forces to attack Xīnpíng (新平).
Initially,
the people of Xīnpíng killed their commandery administrator.
Qín Wáng Jiān cut off a corner of their city wall to shame them.
Towards the end of Shí Hǔ's reign,

and was killed by the people of the commandery.
Yuè's son, Yè, served Jiān
as a Shàngshū Láng.
He memorialized, stating that his father's murderers
could not coexist with him under the same heaven,
and requested to return to Jìzhōu.
Jiān commiserated with him
and banned the people of Xīnpíng,
cutting off a corner of their city wall to shame them.
将 (jiāng),
read as liàng.

降 (jiàng),

"In the past, Tián Dān used one city to preserve Qí.

Even with over a hundred connected cities,

51 Wáng Jiā, an recluse from Lǒngxī,
