The Shuǐjīng Zhù states: Dàohǔ Shān is south of Xīnfēng Xiàn.
處 (chǔ),
read as chāng lǚ.
He could foresee future events;
the Qín people regarded him as divine.
Qín Wáng Jiān, Hòu Qín Wáng Cháng, and Mùróng Chōng all sent envoys to welcome him.
In the eleventh month,
Jiā entered Cháng'ān.
When the populace heard of it,
they believed Jiān was blessed,
and thus a sage was assisting him.
Over forty thousand Dī and Qiāng from the Three Fǔ fortresses and the Four Mountains surrendered to Jiān.
Jiān placed Jiā and the Bhikkhu Dào'ān in the outer hall,
consulting them on all matters.
52 Yān Mùróng Nóng, from Xìndū, attacked Dīnglíng Zhái Liáo at Lǔkǒu to the west,
and defeated him.
Liáo retreated and garrisoned Wújí,
while Nóng garrisoned Gǎochéng to press him.
Wújí Xiàn,
in Hàn belonged to Zhōngshān,
in Jìn was abolished;
Hòu Wèi re-established Wújí Xiàn,
and in late Táng it was the administrative seat of Qízhōu.
Gǎochéng Xiàn,
in Former Hàn belonged to Zhēndìng,
in Later Hàn belonged to Jùlù,
in Jìn was abolished.
The place garrisoned now is likely the former county seat.
Táng re-established Gǎochéng Xiàn,
belonging to Héngzhōu.
This was Zhēn's cousin.
53 There were still over a thousand Xiānbēi in Cháng'ān city.
Mùróng Sù, elder brother of Mùróng Shào,
secretly conspired with Mùróng Wěi to stir up trouble among the Xiānbēi.
In the twelfth month,
Wěi informed Jiān that
his son had recently married,
and requested Jiān to visit his home,
where he would set a banquet and ambush him to kill him.
Jiān agreed,
but it happened to rain heavily,
so he did not go.
When the plot was discovered,
Jiān summoned Wěi and Sù.
Sù said:
"The matter must have leaked;
if we go in, we will both die.
Now the city is already alert,
'already alert'
refers to the Xiānbēi troops.
Once we get out,
the main force will gather."
Wěi did not comply
and went in with him.
Jiān said:
"How have I treated you,
that you harbor such intentions?"
Wěi made excuses in response.
Sù said:
"The affairs of our family and state are paramount;
why speak of personal sentiments!"
'Personal sentiments'
refers to Jiān's kind treatment.
Thereupon, he killed Wěi and his clan,
and all Xiānbēi in the city, young and old, male and female,
were killed.
Yān Wáng Chuí's youngest son, Róu,
was raised in the home of the eunuch Sòng Yá as Yá's adopted son,
and thus escaped punishment.
He, along with Crown Prince Bǎo's son Shèng, took advantage of the opportunity to escape
and fled to Mùróng Chōng.
This laid the foundation for Mùróng Shèng and others later to return to Yān from Chángzǐ.
間 (jiàn),
read as gǔ xiàn.
54 Yān Mùróng Lín and Mùróng Nóng combined their forces and attacked Zhái Liáo,
utterly defeating him.
Liáo fled alone on horseback to Zhái Zhēn.
55 Yān Wáng Chuí, because Qín Chánglè Gōng Pī was still occupying Yè and not leaving,
led his troops to besiege Yè again,
opening a path for his escape to the west.
Chuí's aim was to capture Yè,
so he opened an escape route for him,
which is what is meant by "leaving a gap when besieging a city."
Xuán wanted to summon Pī as a hostage
before dispatching troops;
Kuí steadfastly asserted Pī's sincerity and loyalty,
and also expressed Yáng Yīng's view.
Xuán then sent Liú Láozhī, Téng Tiánzhī, and others to lead a force of twenty thousand to relieve Yè.
Pī reported famine,
so Xuán transported two thousand hù of rice by water and land to provision him.
56 Qín Liángzhōu Cìshǐ Pān Měng abandoned Hànzhōng
and fled to Cháng'ān.
The territory of Liángzhōu
thereupon reverted to Jìn.
Wang Chóngwǔ punctuation, Róng Zhàozǔ and Niè Chóngqí reviewed and corrected.
Sīmǎ Guāng
Compiled by imperial command.
後學天台
Lièzōng Xiàowǔ Huángdì Zhōng Zhī Shàng
Tàiyuán Tenth Year (Yǐyǒu, 385 CE)
1 Spring,
first month.
Qín Wáng Jiān held a morning banquet for his officials.
At that time, Cháng'ān was suffering from famine,
and people resorted to cannibalism.
The generals, upon returning home,
would spit out meat to feed their wives and children.
2 Mùróng Chōng ascended the imperial throne at Éfáng,
establishing Xī Yān.
Chōng was self-satisfied
and dispensed rewards and punishments according to his whims.
Mùróng Shèng, at thirteen years old,
said to Mùróng Róu:
"Indeed, the leader of ten people
must also possess talent surpassing nine others,
only then can he be secure.
Now, Zhōngshān Wáng's talent does not surpass others,
his achievements are not yet made,
yet his arrogance and extravagance are already excessive.
It will be difficult for him to succeed!"
Chōng was enfeoffed as Zhōngshān Wáng during Former Yān.
汰 (tài),
means extravagant
or excessive.
The history states that Mùróng Shèng, though young, possessed wisdom and strategic acumen,
which is why he was able to exert himself and establish a state.
Shèng and Róu returned to Chōng,
as mentioned in the previous volume, previous year.
3 Hòu Qín Wáng Cháng left his generals to attack Xīnpíng
and personally led his troops to attack Āndìng,
capturing Qín Ānxī Jiāngjūn, Bóhǎi Gōng Zhēn.
All the cities north of the mountain range surrendered to him.
4 On the *jiǎyín* day,
Qín Wáng Jiān (秦王堅) battled with Xīyàn Zhǔ Chōng (西燕主沖) at Qiúbān Qú (仇班渠)
and greatly defeated him.
Mùróng Chuí (慕容垂) had revived his power in Shāndōng (山東),
while Chōng (沖) claimed a title in Guānzhōng (關中).
Therefore, Xīyàn (西燕) is written to distinguish it.
On the *yǐmǎo* day,
they fought at Quèsāng (雀桑),
and Chōng (沖) was again defeated.
On the *jiǎzǐ* day,
they fought at Báiqú (白渠).
Báiqú (白渠)
is the one excavated by Báigōng (白公) in the Hàn (漢) era.
The Xīyàn (西燕) army surrounded Qín Wáng Jiān (秦王堅).
Diànzhōng Jiāngjūn Dèng Mài (殿中將軍鄧邁) fought valiantly and repelled them,
allowing Jiān (堅) to escape.
On the *rénshēn* day,
Chōng (沖) sent Shàngshū Lìng Gāo Gài (尚書令高蓋) to launch a night attack on Cháng'ān (長安),
entering its southern city.
Zuǒ Jiāngjūn Dòu Chōng (左將軍竇衝) and Qián Jìn Jiāngjūn Lǐ Biàn (前禁將軍李辯) and others attacked and defeated them,
beheading eight hundred people,
and divided their corpses to eat them.
On the *yǐhài* day,
Gāo Gài (高蓋) led his troops to attack the various strongholds north of the Wèi (渭) River.
Tàizǐ Hóng (太子宏) fought them at Chéng'èrbì (成貳壁).
Chéng'èr (成貳)
is a person's name.
Guānzhōng (關中) was in great chaos,
and people built walls to protect themselves,
which then became place names.
Three thousand heads were cut off.
5 Yàn Dàifāng Wáng Zuǒ (燕帶方王佐) and Níngshuò Jiāngjūn Píng Guī (寧朔將軍平規) together attacked Jì (薊).
Wáng Yǒng's (王永) army suffered repeated defeats.
In the second month,
Yǒng (永) sent Sòng Chǎng (宋敞) to burn the palaces in Hélóng (和龍) and Jìchéng (薊城),
and led his thirty thousand troops to flee to Húguān (壺關).
Zuǒ (佐) and others entered Jì (薊).
6 Mùróng Nóng (慕容農) led his troops to join Mùróng Lín (慕容麟) at Zhōngshān (中山),
and together they attacked Zhái Zhēn (翟真).
Lín (麟) and Nóng (農) first led several thousand cavalry to Chéngyíng (承營)
to observe the situation.
When Zhái Zhēn (翟真) saw them,
he arrayed his troops and came out.
The generals wanted to retreat.
Nóng (農) said:
"The Dīnglíng (丁零) are not necessarily strong and brave,
but Zhái Zhēn (翟真) is cowardly.
Now, let's select our elite,
charge directly at Zhēn's (真) position.
If Zhēn (真) flees,
his troops will surely scatter.
Then we can block the gate and press them,
and we can kill them all."
He ordered Xiāoqí Jiāngjūn Mùróng Guó (驍騎將軍慕容國) to lead over a hundred cavalry to charge them.
Zhēn (真) fled,
and his troops scrambled for the gate,
trampling each other.
More than half died.
They then captured the outer wall of Chéngyíng (承營).
7 On the *guǐwèi* day,
Qín Wáng Jiān (秦王堅) battled Xīyàn Zhǔ Chōng (西燕主沖) west of the city.
This was west of Cháng'ān (長安) city.
He pursued the fleeing enemy to Āchéng (阿城).
Āchéng (阿城)
is the city of Āfáng Gōng (阿房宮),
Chōng's (沖) lair.
Jiān (堅) feared being ambushed by Chōng (沖),
so he withdrew his troops.
A ruler of ten thousand chariots
indeed should not take risks and seek luck in dangerous situations.
However, given the Qín's (秦) defeats like this,
taking advantage of his generals' victorious morale to achieve a slim chance of success
would have been acceptable.
Why did he withdraw his troops
and return?
The character for 'return' (還)
is pronounced like 'xuān' (宣) and 'fān' (翻).
8 On the *yǐyǒu* day,
Qín Yìzhōu Cìshǐ Wáng Guǎng (秦益州刺史王廣) appointed Lǐ Pī (李丕) of Jiāngyáng (江陽), a native of Shǔ (蜀) and a Tàishǒu (太守) of Jiāngyáng (江陽), as Yìzhōu Cìshǐ (益州刺史),
to guard Chéngdū (成都).
Shěn Yuē (沈約) said: Jiāngyáng Jùn (江陽郡)
was established by Liú Zhāng (劉璋) by dividing Jiànwéi (犍為).
The character 'shǒu' (守)
is also pronounced as 'shì' (式) and 'yòu' (又).
On the *jǐchǒu* day,
Guǎng (廣) led his department to flee back to Lǒngxī (隴西),
and over thirty thousand people from Shǔ (蜀) followed him.
9 Liú Láozhī (劉牢之) arrived at Fāngtóu (枋頭).
Yáng Yīng (楊膺) and Jiāng Ràng's (姜讓) plot was exposed.
Yīng (膺) and Ràng's (讓) plot can be seen in the previous volume, previous year.
Láozhī (牢之) heard of it,
hesitated and did not advance.
10 Qín Píngyuán Dàogōng Huī (秦平原悼公暉) was repeatedly defeated by Xīyàn Zhǔ Chōng (西燕主沖).
Qín Wáng Jiān (秦王堅) reproached him, saying:
"You
are my talented son,
yet you command a large army to fight against a 'white barbarian' little boy
and are repeatedly defeated.
What use is there in living!"
In the third month,
Huī (暉), filled with anger and indignation, committed suicide.
Qián Jìn Jiāngjūn Lǐ Biàn (前禁將軍李辯) and Dūshuǐ Shǐzhě Lǒngxī Péng Hézhèng (都水使者隴西彭和正) feared that Cháng'ān (長安) would not be held,
so they summoned people from Xīzhōu (西州).
The Jìn Shū (晉書) "Zhígān Zhì" (職官志) says: Dūshuǐ Zhǎng (都水長)
was subordinate to the Dàsīnóng (大司農).
Shěn Yuē's (沈約) "Zhì" (志) says: Dūshuǐ Shǐzhě (都水使者)
was in charge of boats and water transport.
Lǐ Biàn (李辯)
was the son of Lǐ Yǎn (李儼),
and also a native of Lǒngxī (隴西).
Jiān (堅) summoned them,
but they did not come.
This sets the stage for Jiān's (堅) later attack on Jiǔyuán (韮園).
The character 'jiǔ' (韮)
is pronounced like 'jǔ' (舉) and 'yǒu' (有).
11 Xīyàn Zhǔ Chōng (西燕主沖) attacked Qín Gāoyáng Mǐngōng Fāng (秦高陽愍公方) at Líshān (驪山),
and killed him.
Fú Fāng (苻方) garrisoned Líshān (驪山),
as seen in the previous volume, previous year, seventh month.
He appointed Fāng's (方) son, Qiān (謙), as Fēngyì Tàishǒu (馮翊太守),
and sent him to recruit the people of the Sānfǔ (三輔).
Fēngyì Lěizhǔ Shào Ānmín (馮翊壘主邵安民) and others reproached Qiān (謙), saying:
"You are from a prominent clan in Yōngzhōu (雍州),
with seven Prime Ministers and five Dukes.
The prominent clan of Yōngzhōu (雍州)
were descendants of Zhōng (鍾), Gài (蓋), Wéi (韋), and Xián (賢).
The character 'yōng' (雍)
is pronounced like 'yú' (於) and 'yòng' (用).
To commit disloyalty and injustice with him,
how can you have the face to walk among people in the world!"
Qiān (謙) reported this to Zhōng (鍾).
Zhōng (鍾) committed suicide,
and Qiān (謙) came to surrender.
Qín Zuǒ Jiāngjūn Gǒu Chí (秦左將軍苟池) and Yòu Jiāngjūn Jù Shízǐ (右將軍俱石子) battled Xīyàn Zhǔ Chōng (西燕主沖) at Líshān (驪山),
and their army was defeated.
Xīyàn Jiāngjūn Mùróng Yǒng (西燕將軍慕容永) beheaded Gǒu Chí (苟池).
Jù Shízǐ (俱石子) fled to Yè (鄴).
Yǒng (永)
was the grandson of Yùn (運), the younger brother of Huī (廆).
Shízǐ (石子)
was the younger brother of Nán (難).
Jù Nán (俱難) is seen in volume 104, Tàiyuán (太元) third year.
The character 'huī' (廆)
is pronounced like 'hù' (戶) and 'zuì' (罪).
He greatly defeated them,
captured over ten thousand Xiānbēi (鮮卑) people, and returned,
burying them all alive.
Dìng (定)
was the grandson of Fónú (佛奴).
The Běi Shǐ (北史) says: Dìng (定)
was the son of Fónú (佛奴);
Fónú (佛奴)
was the son of Sòngnú (宋奴).
12 Zhèng Xiè (鄭燮) of Xíngyáng (滎陽) surrendered with his commandery.
13 Yàn Wáng Chuí (燕王垂) attacked Yè (鄴) but could not take it for a long time.
He was about to go north to Jìzhōu (冀州),
so he ordered Fǔjūn Dàjiāngjūn Lín (撫軍大將軍麟) to garrison Xìndū (信都),
Lèlàng Wáng Wēn (樂浪王溫) to garrison Zhōngshān (中山),
and summoned Piàojí Dàjiāngjūn Nóng (驃騎大將軍農) back to Yè (鄴).
At this, people far and near heard of it
and considered Yàn (燕) to be in decline,
many harboring thoughts of leaving or joining others.
When Nóng (農) arrived at Gāoyì (高邑),
Gāoyì (高邑) was originally Gāoxiàn (鄗縣).
Hàn Guāngwǔ (漢光武) ascended the throne here
and changed its name to Gāoyì (高邑),
belonging to Chángshān (常山).
The Jìn Zhì (晉志) says it belonged to Zhàoguó (趙國).
He did not return by the appointed time.
Chángshǐ Zhāng Pān (長史張攀) said to Nóng (農):
"The subordinate officials right here
(subordinate officials right here means those close at hand).
I request to recall the army and punish them."
Nóng (農) did not respond.
He issued an order to prepare temporary appointments,
appointing Suì (邃) as Gāoyáng Tàishǒu (高陽太守),
and all subordinate officials whose families were north of Zhào (趙)
were given temporary appointments and sent home.
North of Zhào (趙)
means north of Zhàoguó (趙國).
Those given temporary appointments
were temporarily appointed to their positions with provisional documents
without first reporting to Yàn Wáng Chuí (燕王垂).
Over twenty Chángshǐ (長史)
retreated and said to Pān (攀):
"Your view is quite mistaken.
How can we now slaughter each other like fish and meat!
Wait until I return north,
and Suì (邃) and the others will naturally welcome us by the roadside.
Just watch."
This sets the stage for Suì (邃) and others welcoming Nóng (農) later.
Yuèqū Wáng Wēn was in Zhōngshān.
His military strength was very weak,
and the Dīnglíng people were scattered,
occupying various cities.
Wēn said to his generals:
"With our forces,
we are insufficient for offense,
but more than enough for defense.
The General of Agile Cavalry (Piàojì Dàjiāngjūn) and the General Who Soothes the Army (Fǔjūn Dàjiāngjūn)
are linking their forces from front to back,
and will surely annihilate the rebels.
We only need to gather provisions and sharpen our weapons to await the opportune moment."
Thereupon, he comforted the old and attracted the new,
encouraging agriculture and sericulture.
People who came to submit followed one after another,
and the commanderies and counties with their fortified settlements competed to send military provisions,
filling the granaries to overflowing.
Zhái Zhēn attacked Zhōngshān by night,
but Wēn defeated him,
and thereafter, Zhái Zhēn dared not return.
Wēn then dispatched ten thousand soldiers to transport provisions to xiǎng Chuí,
and also to build palaces and official residences in Zhōngshān.
He intended to welcome Chuí to make Zhōngshān his capital.
Liú Láozhī attacked Yàn's Administrator of Líyáng, Liú Fǔ, at Sūn Jiù's stockade.
Sūn Jiù
was a person's name.
He probably built a stockade in the Líyáng area,
and Liú Fǔ then garrisoned there.
Qín's Chánglè Gōng Pī led his own troops to relieve him.
When Qín's Chánglè Gōng Pī heard of this,
he dispatched troops to launch a surprise night attack on Yàn's camp while it was undefended.
Nóng defeated him.
Liú Láozhī fought with Chuí,
but was defeated,
and retreated to garrison at Líyáng.
Chuí then returned to Yè.
Lǚ Guāng, seeing that Qiūcí was prosperous and pleasant,
wished to remain and reside there.
The Indian Śramaṇa Kumārajīva said to Guāng:
"This is a land of doom and destruction,
not worth staying in.
According to historical records,
Kumāra
was his surname,
and Jīva
was his given name.
In the middle of your journey, there will be a blessed land suitable for dwelling."
Kumārajīva knew divination,
and knew that Lǚ Guāng would surely obtain and occupy the land of Liángzhōu.
When discussing whether to advance or stop,
everyone wished to return.
So, with over twenty thousand camels laden with exotic treasures and rare curiosities,
and driving over ten thousand swift horses, they returned.
Summer,
fourth month.
Liú Láozhī advanced his troops to Yè.
Yàn Wáng Chuí counterattacked and was defeated,
so he lifted the siege
and retreated to garrison at Xīnchéng.
On the day yǐmǎo,
he fled north from Xīnchéng.
Láozhī did not inform Qín's Chánglè Gōng Pī,
but immediately led his troops to pursue him.
Pī heard of this
and sent troops to follow.
On the day gēngshēn,
Láozhī overtook Chuí at Dǒngtáng Yuān.
Chuí said:
"Qín and Jìn are like 'tiles joined together',
relying on each other for strength.
'Tiles joined together'
means their power is not firmly consolidated.
If you touch and move them,
and one tile falls and shatters,
then all the tiles will come apart.
'Dài' (待)
should be
'shì' (恃).
Now, looking at the character 'dài',
the meaning is also self-explanatory.
If one fails, all will collapse;
they are not of one mind.
Now, their two armies are following each other,
their momentum not yet combined.
We should attack them urgently."
Láozhī's army rushed two hundred Lǐ,
reaching Wǔqiáo Zé.
Wǔqiáo Zé
is north of Línzhāng Xiàn.
The art of war says that to rush a hundred Lǐ for gain will cripple the supreme general;
how much more so at two hundred Lǐ!
Chuí ambushed and attacked them,
severely defeating them and
beheading several thousand.
Láozhī fled on a single horse,
but Qín's reinforcements arrived,
and he escaped.
Yàn's Champion General (Guànjūn Jiāngjūn) Yídū Wáng Fèng
fought fearlessly in every battle,
and in two hundred and fifty-seven battles, large and small,
never failed to achieve success.
Chuí cautioned him, saying:
"Now that the great enterprise is just completed,
you must first take care of yourself!"
He made him Deputy to Chējì Jiāngjūn Dé to curb his impetuosity,
because Dé was known for his prudence.
There was a severe famine in Yè,
so Chánglè Gōng Pī led his troops to Jìn's granaries at Fāngtóu.
Liú Láozhī entered Yèchéng,
collected the scattered survivors,
and his army somewhat recovered;
for his military defeat,
he was summoned back.
Yàn and Qín had been locked in a stalemate for a year.
In the first month of the previous year,
Chuí attacked Yè.
People resorted to cannibalism,
and settlements were desolate.
Many of Yàn's soldiers starved to death;
Yàn Wáng Chuí prohibited the people from raising silkworms,
using mulberries as military provisions.
Chuí was about to go north to Zhōngshān.
He made Piàojì Dàjiāngjūn Nóng his vanguard.
The officials he had previously appointed, such as Suī Suì, all came to greet him.
Everything was as before,
and Lǐ Pān
was then convinced of Nóng's wisdom and strategy.
Previously written as
"Zhāng Pān,"
here written as
"Lǐ Pān,"
it is unknown which is correct.
Kuàijī Wáng Dàozǐ loved to monopolize power.
He was again incited by treacherous flatterers,
and became estranged from Tàibǎo Ān.
Ān wished to avoid him.
Coincidentally, Qín Wáng Jiān came to seek help,
so Ān requested to personally lead the relief effort.
On the day rénxū,
he went out to garrison at Bùqiū in Guǎnglíng,
built a fortification called Xīnchéng, and resided there.
Today's Shàobó Zhèn in Yángzhōu
is that very place,
sixty Lǐ north of Yángzhōu City.
The Jìn history states: Ān built a dike at Bùqiū,
which later generations called Zhàobó Dài.
Xīnpíng ran out of grain and arrows.
Later Qín had been attacking Xīnpíng since the previous year.
Hòuqín Wáng Cháng sent someone to say to Gǒu Fǔ:
"I am about to gain the world by righteousness,
why would I be an enemy to loyal ministers!
You merely need to lead the people in the city back to Cháng'ān;
I just want to obtain this city."
Fǔ believed him,
and led five thousand people out of the city.
Cháng surrounded them and buried them alive,
leaving no men or women.
Only Fēng Jié's son Zhōng managed to escape
and fled to Cháng'ān.
Fēng Jié's advice to Fǔ to resist Later Qín can be seen in the previous volume, last year.
All were posthumously titled Jiémǐn Hóu,
and Zhōng was made Administrator of Xīnpíng.
Zhái Zhēn moved his camp from Chéngyíng to Xíngtáng,
which was the Nánxíngtáng Xiàn of the Hàn dynasty,
belonging to Chángshān Jùn.
Yàn Wáng Chuí pressed towards Zhōngshān,
and Zhēn was compelled by him,
hence he moved his camp.
He declared himself King of Zhào.
The camp's people collectively killed Qǐ,
and established Zhēn's cousin Chéng as their leader;
many of his followers surrendered to Yàn.
In the fifth month of the 20th year,
the ruler of Western Yàn, Mùróng Chōng, attacked Cháng'ān.
Qín King Fú Jiān personally supervised the battle,
arrows filled his body,
and blood flowed freely.
Mùróng Chōng let his troops rampage and plunder,
the gentry and commoners of Guānzhōng scattered,
roads were cut off,
and for a thousand *lǐ* there was no smoke from hearths.
There were more than thirty fortified strongholds,
which elected General Píngyuǎn Zhào Áo as their leader.
The titles Ānyuǎn and Píngyuǎn,
two general titles,
were probably all conferred at that time.
Defying difficulties, they sent troops and provisions to aid Fú Jiān,
but many were killed by Western Yàn.
Fú Jiān said to them:
"I hear that those who come often do not arrive safely.
This is indeed the loyalty of true ministers,
but now the bandit troubles are overwhelming and numerous,
not something that one person's strength can save.
You would merely follow me into the tiger's mouth,
what good would that do!
You all should cherish yourselves for the sake of the state,
store grain and sharpen weapons,
to await the opportune moment.
Perhaps good fortune will not always end in misfortune,
and there will be a time for prosperity!"
The people of Sānfǔ who had been plundered by Mùróng Chōng
secretly sent people to inform Fú Jiān,
requesting him to send troops to attack Mùróng Chōng,
and offering to set fires as an internal signal.
Fú Jiān said:
"I deeply grieve your sincerity and loyalty!
However, my valiant warriors are like tigers and leopards,
and our sharp weapons like frost and snow,
yet we are trapped by these ragtag rebels.
Is this not Heaven's will!
I fear that it would only cause you gentlemen to be annihilated without cause,
and I cannot bear that!"
The men insisted repeatedly,
so he sent seven hundred cavalry to them.
Those who set fires in Mùróng Chōng's camp
were instead burned by the wind and fire themselves;
only one or two tenths of them escaped.
Fú Jiān offered sacrifices and wept for them.
The historian says that the people of Guānzhōng
were sincerely devoted to Fú Jiān,
but their strength could not save him;
it was probably Heaven abandoning Qín.
General Wèi Yáng Dìng fought Mùróng Chōng west of the city
and was captured by Mùróng Chōng.
Yáng Dìng
was one of Qín's brave generals.
Fú Jiān was greatly alarmed.
Based on a book of prognostication that said:
"The emperor goes out to Wǔjiàng, and long stability is achieved."
According to the *Zàijì*,
this book of prognostication was referred to as *Gǔfú Zhuànjiǎ Lù*.
Qín King Fú Jiān had initially forbidden people from studying prognostication,
but when he reached the extreme of defeat and loss,
he then wished to use a book of prognostication,
fleeing to Wǔjiàngshān to seek escape.
His confusion and errors were extreme,
indicating that his death was imminent.
Chèn (谶),
pronounced *chǔ zèn fān*.
He said to them:
"Perhaps Heaven wishes to guide me to go outside.
You should guard the city well,
and do not contend for advantage with the bandits.
I will go out to Lǒng to gather troops and transport provisions to supply you."
Thereupon, he led several hundred cavalry with Fūren Zhāng and Zhōngshān Gōng Shēn, and his two daughters, Bǎo and Jǐn, and fled to Wǔjiàngshān.
*Xīntángshū Dìlǐzhì* states: Jīngzhào Lǐquán Xiàn has Wǔjiàngshān.
*Shuǐjīngzhù* states: Fúfēng Dùyáng Xiàn has Wǔjiàngshān.
Also, according to Táng Dù Yòu,
Fèngxiáng Fǔ Qíshān Xiàn has Wǔjiàngshān.
He planned to rescue Cháng'ān in the first month of winter.
Fú Jiān passed by and raided Jiǔyuán.
Lǐ Biàn fled to Yàn,
meaning to Western Yàn,
and committed suicide.
In the intercalary month of the 21st year,
Luó Yǒu, the Governor of Guǎngzhōu, was appointed Governor of Yìzhōu,
garrisoning Chéngdū.
On the *gēngxū* day of the 22nd year,
Yàn King Mùróng Chuí arrived at Chángshān
and besieged Zhái Chéng at Xíngtáng.
He ordered Dàifāng Wáng Zuǒ to garrison Lóngchéng.
In the sixth month,
Gāogōulì raided Liáodōng.
Zuǒ sent Sīmǎ Hǎo Jǐng to lead troops to relieve it,
but they were defeated by Gāogōulì.
Gāogōulì then captured Liáodōng and Xuántú.
From this point, Yàn could not defeat Gāogōulì.
Tú (菟),
pronounced *tóng dū fān*.
Qín Crown Prince Fú Hóng could not defend Cháng'ān,
and with several thousand cavalry, his mother, wife, and imperial clan members, fled west to Xiàbiàn;
the hundred officials scattered,
and Sīlì Xiàowèi Quán Yì and several hundred others fled to Later Qín.
Quán Yì was originally an official of Yáo Xiāng;
since the Fú clan was defeated,
he therefore fled to Later Qín.
[Mùróng Chōng] let his troops plunder widely,
and the dead were countless.
In the autumn of the 24th year,
in the seventh month,
there was a drought
and famine,
and all wells dried up.
Later Qín King Yáo Cháng moved from Gùxiàn to Xīnpíng.
Hàn Āndìng Jùn had Āndìng Xiàn;
it was abolished in Later Hàn and Jìn,
hence it was called Gùxiàn.
Qín King Fú Jiān arrived at Wǔjiàngshān.
Later Qín King Yáo Cháng sent General Xiāoqí Wú Zhōng to lead cavalry and besiege him.
All the Qín soldiers scattered and fled,
only about ten attendants remained by his side.
Fú Jiān's expression was calm and self-possessed;
he sat and waited for them,
summoning the cook to bring food.
Soon Wú Zhōng arrived,
seized him,
sent him to Xīnpíng,
and confined him in a separate room.
Crown Prince Fú Hóng arrived at Xiàbiàn,
but Yáng Bì, the Governor of Nánqínzhōu, resisted him.
Fú Jiān defeated Chóuchí and established Nánqínzhōu.
Yáng Bì
was of the Dī ethnicity,
served Qín and married into the imperial family,
holding an important regional post.
As Fú Hóng fled in defeat,
he resisted and did not admit him.
Mencius said:
"When assistance is utterly meager,
even relatives rebel against one."
Truly, these words are faithful!
Fú Jiān's daughter, Shùnyáng Gōngzhǔ,
abandoned her husband and followed Fú Hóng.
Fú Hóng fled to Wǔdū,
seeking refuge with the Dī magnate Qiáng Xī,
who lent him a path to come and take refuge.
An edict ordered him to be settled in Jiāngzhōu.
This is the root cause of Fú Hóng later attaching himself to Huán Xuán and being executed.
Chǔ (處),
pronounced *chāng lǚ fān*.
Chánglè Gōng Pī led thirty thousand troops from Fāngtóu, intending to return to Yèchéng.
General Lóngxiáng Tán Xuán attacked him,
fighting at Gǔkǒu.
Tán Xuán
was a Jìn general.
Gǔkǒu is west of Fāngtóu.
Fú Pī re-entered Yèchéng.
In the 28th year, Yàn General Jiànjié Yú Yán rebelled,
heading north from Wǔyì towards Yōuzhōu.
Yàn King Mùróng Chuí dispatched a messenger to order Yōuzhōu general Píng Guī, saying:
"Hold firm and do not fight;
wait until I defeat the Dīnglíng and then I will personally attack him."
Píng Guī went out to fight
and was defeated by Yú Yán.
Yú Yán entered Jì,
plundered over a thousand households, and departed,
then occupied Lìngzhī.
On the *guǐyǒu* day,
Zhái Chéng's Chángshǐ Xiānyú Dé beheaded Zhái Chéng and surrendered.
Mùróng Chuí massacred Xíngtáng,
burying all of Zhái Chéng's troops alive.
Last year the Dīnglíng rebelled against Yàn,
and by this time they were annihilated.
Jiàng (降),
pronounced *hù jiāng fān*.
In the 29th year, Tàibǎo Xiè Ān became ill and requested to return.
Xiè Ān was stationed at Bùqiū in Guǎnglíng.
In the eighth month,
Xiè Ān arrived in Jiànkāng.
On the *jiǎwǔ* day of the 30th year,
there was a general amnesty.
On the *dīngyǒu* day of the 31st year,
Jiànchāng Wénjìng Gōng Xiè Ān passed away.
Posthumous title rules state:
"Gentle in virtue and peaceful to the multitude is called Jìng;
broad-minded and joyous till the end is called Jìng."
Following the precedent of Dà Sīmǎ Huán Wēn.
Jìn thus honored and favored Xiè Ān;
but how could Xiè Ān's refined aspirations wish to be the same as Huán Wēn's!
On the *gēngzǐ* day,
Sītú Lángyá Wáng Dàozǐ was appointed Governor of Yángzhōu, Supervisor of the Department of State Affairs, and Commander-in-Chief of all military affairs at home and abroad.
Wáng Dàozǐ gained power,
and Jìn fell into chaos from this point.
The 32nd year. Hòu Qín [後秦] King Yáo Cháng [姚萇] sent an envoy to request the Imperial Seal of the transmission of the state from Qín [秦] King Fú Jiān [苻堅].
He said:
"Cháng [萇] is next in line according to the Mandate of Heaven;
you might bestow this favor."
Fú Jiān [苻堅] glared and shouted at him, saying:
"You minor Qiāng [羌] dare to press the Son of Heaven!
The succession of the Five Hú [五胡] [tribes]
does not include your Qiāng [羌] name.
Hú [胡], Jié [羯], Xiānbēi [鮮卑], Dī [氐], Qiāng [羌]—
this is the order of the Five Hú [五胡].
There is no mention of your Qiāng [羌] name.
This is what the prophetic texts say."
Yáo Cháng [姚萇] himself claimed to be next in line for the Mandate of Heaven,
so Fú Jiān [苻堅] also spoke of the prophetic texts.
Chēn [瞋] (to glare),
read Qī Rén [七人].
It cannot be obtained!"
Yáo Cháng [姚萇] again sent Right Sīmǎ [司馬] Yǐn Wěi [尹緯] to persuade Fú Jiān [苻堅],
requesting for him to abdicate and transfer the throne.
Fú Jiān [苻堅] said:
"Abdication and transfer [of the throne]
are matters for saints and sages.
Yáo Cháng [姚萇] is a rebellious brigand,
how can he do that!"
As Fú Jiān [苻堅] spoke with Yǐn Wěi [尹緯],
he asked Yǐn Wěi [尹緯]:
"What office did you hold in My court?"
Yǐn Wěi [尹緯] replied:
"Shàngshū Lìngshǐ [尚書令史]."
Since the Latter Hàn [漢], the Shàngshū [尚書] had eighteen Lìngshǐ [令史],
with a salary of two hundred dàn [石].
"You,
a peer of Wáng Jǐnglǜe [王景略],
possess the talent of a chancellor,
yet I did not know you.
No wonder I am doomed!"
Fú Jiān [苻堅] believed that he had shown great kindness to Yáo Cháng [姚萇] throughout his life,
and was particularly enraged by him.
He repeatedly cursed Yáo Cháng [姚萇], seeking death,
and said to Lady Zhāng [張夫人]:
"How can I let a Qiāng [羌] slave disgrace my sons?"
So he first killed Bǎo [寶] and Jǐn [錦].
Fú Jiān [苻堅] knew that after his death,
his daughter would surely be taken by Yáo Cháng [姚萇].
On the day of Xī丑 [辛丑],
Yáo Cháng [姚萇] sent someone to hang Fú Jiān [苻堅] in the Buddhist temple of Xīnpíng [新平].
He was forty-eight years old.
The officers and soldiers of Hòu Qín [後秦] all mourned for him with deep sorrow.
Yáo Cháng [姚萇] wished to conceal his [own] name [in connection with the murder]
and posthumously titled Fú Jiān [苻堅] Zhuàngliè Tiānwáng [壯烈天王].
Your servant Guāng [光] says: All commentators believe that Qín [秦] King Fú Jiān's [苻堅] downfall
was due to his failure to kill Mùróng Chuí [慕容垂] and Yáo Cháng [姚萇].
Your servant alone believes otherwise.
Xǔ Shào [許劭] called Wèi Wǔdì [魏武帝] a capable minister in times of peace,
and a treacherous hero in times of chaos.
This matter is found in Volume 58, Hàn [漢] Emperor Líng's [靈] Zhōngpíng [中平] First Year.
Zhì [治] (to govern),
read Zhí Lì [直吏].
If governed, then Chuí [垂] and Cháng [萇] would both have been capable ministers of Qín [秦].
How could they have caused chaos?
The reason for Fú Jiān's [苻堅] downfall
was his repeated victories leading to arrogance.
Wèi Wénhóu [魏文侯] asked Lǐ Kè [李克] [about]
the reason for Wú's [吳] downfall,
to which he replied:
"Frequent battles and frequent victories."
Wénhóu [文侯] said:
"Frequent battles and frequent victories
are a blessing to the state.
Why did it fall?"
He replied:
"Frequent battles exhaust the people,
and frequent victories make the ruler arrogant.
To command exhausted people with an arrogant ruler
has never failed to lead to downfall."
Qín [秦] King Fú Jiān [苻堅] was similar.
The 33rd year. Chánglè Gōng [長樂公] Fú Pī [苻丕] was in Yè [鄴],
intending to go west to Cháng'ān [長安].
Yōuzhōu Cìshǐ [幽州刺史] Wáng Yǒng [王永] was in Húguān [壺關].
In the spring of this year,
Wáng Yǒng [王永] fled from Yōuzhōu [幽州] to Húguān [壺關].
Fú Pī [苻丕] then led over sixty thousand men and women from Yè [鄴] westward to Lùchuān [潞川].
Piàojì Jiāngjūn [驃騎將軍] Zhāng Há [張蚝] and Bīngzhōu Cìshǐ [幷州刺史] Wáng Téng [王騰] welcomed him into Jìnyáng [晉陽].
Fú Pī [苻丕]
only then learned that Cháng'ān [長安] could not be held and
that Fú Jiān [苻堅] had died.
He then observed mourning [for Fú Jiān [苻堅]]
and ascended the imperial throne.
Fú Pī [苻丕], courtesy name Yǒngshū [永叔], was Fú Jiān's [苻堅] eldest illegitimate son.
His temple name was Shìzǔ [世祖].
He issued a general amnesty
and changed the era name to Dà'ān [大安].
The 34th year. Yàn [燕] King Mùróng Chuí [慕容垂] appointed Mùróng Hé [慕容和] (Prince of Lǔ [魯]) as Nánzhōnglángjiāng [南中郎將],
stationed at Yè [鄴].
He sent Mùróng Nóng [慕容農] out through Yē'ōng Sài [蠮螉塞],
passing through Fánchéng [凡城],
heading towards Lóngchéng [龍城],
to gather troops and attack Yú Yán [餘巖].
Mùróng Lín [慕容麟] and Mùróng Lóng [慕容隆] from Xìndū [信都] swept through Bóhǎi [勃海] and Qīnghé [清河].
Mùróng Lín [慕容麟] attacked Fēng Yì [封懿], the Administrator of Bóhǎi [勃海],
captured him,
and then garrisoned at Lìkǒu [歷口].
Shuǐjīngzhù [水經註]: Qīnghé [清河] flows northeast from Guǎngchuān [廣川],
passing south of the old city of Lìxiàn [歷縣],
which was a subordinate county of the Xìndū [信都] state in the Former Hàn [漢].
Yìng Shào [應劭] said: Thirty *lǐ* northwest of Guǎngchuān [廣川] county, there is Lìchéngtíng [歷城亭],
which was an old county.
Now the pavilion is at the crossing place east of the county,
called Lìkǒudù [歷口渡].
He was Fēng Fàng's [封放] son.
Fēng Fàng [封放] is mentioned in Volume 99, Mùdì's [穆帝] Yǒnghé [永和] Seventh Year.
The 35th year. Xiānbēi [鮮卑] Liú Tóujuàn [劉頭眷] attacked and defeated the Hèlán [賀蘭] tribe at Shànwú [善無].
Shànwú [善無] county, in the Former Hàn [漢], belonged to Yànmén [鴈門] Commandery;
in the Latter Hàn [漢], it belonged to Dìngxiāng [定襄] Commandery.
At the end of the Hàn [漢], it was abandoned to the wilderness.
Yìqīn Shān [意親山] is likely Yìxīn Shān [意辛山];
Qīn [親] and Xīn [辛] are phonetically similar.
According to the Wèishū Dìjì [魏書帝紀], in the fifth year of Dàowǔ's [道武] Déngguó [登國] reign,
in the fourth month,
he visited Yìxīn Shān [意辛山],
and together with Zhìlín [質驎], attacked the Hèlán [賀蘭], Hétūlín [紇突鄰], and Hèxī [紇奚] tribes,
greatly defeating them.
In the sixth month, he returned to Niúchuān [牛川].
Therefore, Yìxīn Shān [意辛山] is north of Niúchuān [牛川].
"Recently, when campaigning,
I have been invincible;
however, there is a serious internal problem that I wish to resolve early!"
Tóujuàn [頭眷] said:
"Who is it?"
Luó Chén [羅辰] said:
"Your cousin Xiǎn [顯]
is a ruthless man,
and will certainly cause trouble."
Tóujuàn [頭眷] did not listen.
Xiǎn [顯]
was Kùrén's [庫仁] son.
Soon after,
Xiǎn [顯] indeed killed Tóujuàn [頭眷] and established himself.
He also intended to kill Tuòbá Guī [拓跋珪].
Guī [珪] depended on Liú Kùrén [劉庫仁], as seen in Volume 104, Tàiyuán [太元] First Year.
She was Guī's [珪] aunt.
Ní [埿]
is the same as Ní [泥].
Xiǎn's [顯] chief strategist, Liáng Liùjuàn [梁六眷],
who was the nephew of Dàiwáng [代王] Shíyìjiān [什翼犍],
also had his tribesmen Mù Chóng [穆崇] and Xī Mù [奚牧] secretly inform Guī [珪],
"Wèishū Guānshìzhì [魏書官氏志]: The ancestors of the Tuòbá [拓跋] clan,
when annexing other states,
each had their own tribal group,
and within the tribal group, separate clans were considered 'inner surnames.'
The Qiūmùlíng [丘穆陵] clan was later changed to Mù [穆] clan.
Furthermore, Tuòbá Lín [拓跋鄰] changed his brother's clan to Dázī [達奚] clan,
which was later changed to Xī [奚] clan."
"If the plot is exposed,
this will serve to clear our names."
Lady Hè [賀氏] gave Xiǎn [顯] wine at night,
made him drunk,
and then secretly had Guī [珪] and his old retainers Chángsūn Jiān [長孫犍], Yuán Tuō [元他], and Luó Jié [羅結] escape with light cavalry.
Yuán Tuō [元他] and Luó Jié [羅結] were two people.
Tuō [他]
is read Táng Hé [唐何].
Lady Hè [賀氏] then startled the horses in the stables,
making Xiǎn [顯] get up to investigate.
Lady Hè [賀氏] cried, saying:
"My sons were just here;
now they are all gone!
Which of you killed them?"
Because of this, Xiǎn [顯] did not pursue them urgently.
Guī [珪] then fled to the Hèlán [賀蘭] tribe,
relying on his maternal uncle Hè Nè [賀訥].
Hè Nè [賀訥] was originally Hèlán Nè [賀蘭訥].
Later, Emperor Xiàowén [孝文] of Wèi [魏] changed the old northern surnames,
changing the Hèlán [賀蘭] clan to Hè [賀] clan.
Historians thus simplify their writing,
like Mù Chóng [穆崇] and Xī Mù [奚牧] mentioned above, all of which are examples.
"After regaining your state,
you must remember this old minister!"
Guī [珪] smiled and said:
"Indeed, as my uncle says,
I would not dare to forget."
Xiǎn [顯] suspected that Liáng Liùjuàn [梁六眷] had leaked his plot
and intended to imprison him.
Mù Chóng [穆崇] publicly declared:
"Liùjuàn [六眷] disregarded kindness and righteousness,
aiding Xiǎn [顯] in his rebellion.
I have seized his wife and horses,
which is enough to vent my anger."
Xiǎn [顯] then let him go.
Hè Shì’s (賀氏) younger paternal cousin, the Outer Court Great Official Hè Yuè (賀悅), offered his部 (bù) to Fú Guī (苻珪).
Hè Yuè (賀悅),
was an Outer Court Great Official during Shíyìjiān’s (什翼犍) time.
The Wèi Shū Guānshì Zhì (魏書官氏志) says: In the second year of Dēngguó (登國),
following the old system, Southern and Northern Great Officials were established,
who governed the two部 (bù) respectively;
also, Outer Court Great Officials were established,
without a fixed number.
They were primarily responsible for receiving imperial edicts,
serving as envoys abroad,
and traveling outside the forbidden palace.
Whenever the state had major mourning rites or grand ceremonies,
they all participated in deliberation,
each according to their responsibilities.
從 (cóng)
is pronounced Cái Yòng (才用).
When Fú Guī (苻珪) was about to kill Hè Shì (賀氏),
Hè Shì (賀氏) fled to Kàngní (亢埿) family’s home,
hiding in a divine chariot for three days.
Northern people had no permanent houses,
moving with water and grass,
they placed their deities in chariots and reverently served them,
thus calling them divine chariots.
Thus, Hè Shì (賀氏) escaped.
The former Southern Great Official Zhǎngsūn Sōng (長孫嵩), leading over seven hundred households from his部 (bù), rebelled against Liú Xiǎn (劉顯)
and fled to Wǔyuán (五原).
Sōng (嵩) relied on the Liú (劉) clan, as also seen in Volume 104, first year of Tàiyuán (太元).
Wǔyuán (五原)
was a Qín (秦) commandery.
Wèi (魏) and Jìn (晉) abandoned it to the wilderness.
帥 (shuài)
is read as 率 (shuài).
Sōng (嵩) wanted to follow Liú Xiǎn (劉顯);
Wūwò (烏渥) said to Sōng (嵩):
“The son who murdered his father
is not worth following.
Shí Jūn (寔君) murdered Shíyìjiān (什翼犍),
as seen in the first year of Tàiyuán (太元).”
Sōng (嵩) followed Wūwò (烏渥).
The historian says that Zhǎngsūn Sōng (長孫嵩) thus became an功臣 (gōngchén) who assisted Tuòbá Guī (拓跋珪) in establishing his reign,
and his good fortune extended to his descendants.
There was chaos among Liú Xiǎn’s (劉顯)部 (bù),
so the former Central Great Official Yǔ Héchén (庾和辰) brought Hè Shì (賀氏) to Fú Guī (苻珪).
Whenever “former” is mentioned,
it refers to officials previously appointed by Shíyìjiān (什翼犍).
The Wèi Shū Guānshì Zhì (魏書官氏志) states: Among the various surnames that entered from other tribes during Tuòbá Zhífén’s (拓跋詰汾) time,
there was indeed the Yǔ (庾) clan,
which was not the Yǔ (庾) clan of Central China.
Hè Nè’s (賀訥) younger brother, Rǎngān (染干), seeing that Fú Guī (苻珪) was gaining popular support,
became jealous.
He ordered his partisan Hóuyǐn Qītū (侯引七突)
to kill Fú Guī (苻珪).
Wèi Gǔzhēn (尉古真) of Dài (代) learned of this
and informed Fú Guī (苻珪), so Hóuyǐn Qītū (侯引七突) dared not act.
Hóuyǐn Qītū (侯引七突)
is not mentioned in the Guānshì Zhì (官氏志).
The Zhì (志) says: “As the years passed, some surnames were gradually altered;
their rise and fall, existence and extinction,
were interspersed.
We now list those that are ascertainable,
but there are also those that are unascertainable and therefore not listed.”
The Western Yùchí (尉遲) clan
later changed its name to Wèi (尉) clan.
尉 (wèi)
is read like 鬱 (yù).
Fú Guī (苻珪) seized and interrogated Hóuyǐn Qītū (侯引七突).
訊 (xùn)
means to question thoroughly.
His head was clamped,
and one eye was injured,
but he did not yield,
so he was released.
Rǎngān (染干) then raised troops and besieged Fú Guī (苻珪).
Hè Shì (賀氏) came out
and said to Rǎngān (染干):
“Where do you intend to place me,
if you kill my son?”
Rǎngān (染干) was ashamed and left.
The historian says that Hè Nè’s (賀訥) brothers were unable to offer their部 (bù) to Tuòbá Guī (拓跋珪),
which laid the groundwork for Tuòbá Guī (拓跋珪) to attack the Hèlán (賀蘭)部 (bù).
Fú Guī (苻珪) endured many dangers and hardships to achieve his great enterprise,
but ultimately died at the hands of the Hèlán (賀蘭) clan.
Is this perhaps the will of Heaven?
36In the ninth month,
Qín Zhǔ Pī (秦主丕) appointed Zhāng Háo (張蚝) as Shìzhōng (侍中) and Sīkōng (司空),
Wáng Yǒng (王永) as Shìzhōng (侍中), Dūdū Zhōngwài Zhūjūnshì (都督中外諸軍事), Chējì Dàjiāngjūn (車騎大將軍), and Shàngshū Lìng (尚書令),
Wáng Téng (王騰) as Zhōngjūn Dàjiāngjūn (中軍大將軍) and Sīlì Xiàowèi (司隸校尉),
Fú Chōng (苻沖) as Shàngshū Zuǒpúyè (尚書左僕射)
and enfeoffed him as Xīpíng Wáng (西平王);
he also appointed Zuǒ Chángshǐ Yáng Fǔ (左長史楊輔) as Yòupúyè (右僕射),
Yòuchángshǐ Wáng Liàng (右長史王亮) as Hùjūn Jiāngjūn (護軍將軍),
established Yáng (楊) clan as Empress,
his son Níng (寧) as Crown Prince,
Shòu (壽) as Chánglè Wáng (長樂王),
Qiāng (鏘) as Píngyuán Wáng (平原王),
Yī (懿) as Bóhǎi Wáng (勃海王),
and Chǎng (昶) as Jìběi Wáng (濟北王).
Lǚ Guāng (呂光) returned from Qiūcí (龜茲) and arrived at Yíhé (宜禾).
The Bān Zhì (班志) says: Guǎngzhì (廣至) County in Dūnhuáng (敦煌) Commandery had Kūnlún Zhàng (昆侖障),
where the Yíhé (宜禾) Dūwèi (都尉) was based.
Jìn (晉) divided it into Yíhé (宜禾) County,
belonging to Jìnchāng (晉昌) Commandery.
Liú Xù (劉昫) says: Chánglè (常樂) County in Guāzhōu (瓜州) was Hànguǎngzhì (漢廣至) County;
Wèi (魏) divided Guǎngzhì (廣至) to establish Yíhé (宜禾) County;
Lǐ Gǎo (李暠) established Liángxìng (涼興) Commandery here;
Suí (隋) abolished it
and established Chánglè (常樂) Town.
In the fifth year of Wǔdé (武德),
the town was changed to a county.
Qiūcí (龜茲)
is pronounced Qiū Cí (丘慈).
Yáng Hàn (楊翰), the Grand Administrator of Gāochāng (高昌), said to Liáng Xī (涼熙):
Lǐ Yánshòu (李延壽) says: Gāochāng (高昌)
was the former territory of the Previous King of Chēshī (車師).
In ancient times, Emperor Wǔ (武) of Hàn (漢) sent troops to campaign in the west,
and his armies became exhausted.
Those who were particularly distressed settled there.
The terrain was high and spacious,
and the people were prosperous,
hence it was named Gāochāng (高昌).
There was a Gāochāng (高昌) rampart from the Hàn (漢) period there.
Jìn (晉) made it Gāochāng (高昌) Commandery;
later, it became a state name.
“Lǚ Guāng (呂光) has recently defeated the Western Regions.
His troops are strong and morale is high.
Hearing of the chaos and disorder in the Central Plains,
he will surely have other intentions.
The Hexi (河西) region spans ten thousand里 (lǐ),
with a hundred thousand armored soldiers,
which is enough to defend ourselves.
If Lǚ Guāng (呂光) exits Liúshā (流沙),
his momentum will be difficult to resist.
The strategic pass of Gāowú (高梧) Valley Mouth is perilous;
we should first guard it and cut off his water supply.
Gāowú (高梧) Valley Mouth
should be on the western border of Gāochāng (高昌).
This way, we can control him without moving.
If that is considered too far,
Yīwúguān (伊吾關) can also be used to resist.
Yīwú (伊吾) County
was established during Jìn (晉) dynasty,
belonging to Jìnchāng (晉昌) Commandery,
and had Yīwúguān (伊吾關).
Even with Zhāng Zǐfáng’s (張子房) strategy,
it would be useless!”
Meaning that once the geographical advantage is lost,
even with Zhāng Liáng’s (張良) plan,
it would be of no use.
Jiānwéi (犍為) Zhāng Tǒng (張統), the Prefect of Měishuǐ (美水), said to Liáng Xī (涼熙):
“Now Guānzhōng (關中) is in great chaos,
and the fate of the capital is unknown.
Cháng’ān (長安) has fallen,
yet Liángzhōu (涼州) is unaware;
this is due to obstructed roads.
犍 (jiān)
is pronounced Jū Yán (居言).
His intentions are hard to fathom;
how will the General resist him?”
Liáng Xī (涼熙) said:
“I am worried,
but I don’t know what to do.”
Zhāng Tǒng (張統) said:
“Lǚ Guāng (呂光)’s wisdom and strategy surpass ordinary men.
Now he commands soldiers eager to return home
and rides on the momentum of victory.
His vanguard is not easy to oppose.
The General has received great kindness for generations,
and his loyalty has long been evident.
It is today that you should establish meritorious service for the imperial house.
Fú Luò (苻洛), the acting Duke of Táng (唐),
is the Emperor’s paternal cousin;
his courage is unmatched at this time.
My counsel for the General is no better than to support him as the盟主 (méngzhǔ) to gather popular support,
and to advocate loyalty and righteousness to lead the heroes.
Then, even if Lǚ Guāng (呂光) arrives,
he would not dare to have ulterior motives.
Using his elite forces,
we can then conquer Máo Xīng (毛興) to the east.
Máo Xīng (毛興) was then the Inspector of Hèzhōu (河州).
Wáng Tǒng (王統) was then the Inspector of Qínzhōu (秦州),
and Yáng Bì (楊璧) was then the Inspector of Nánqínzhōu (南秦州).
Sweeping away the villains
and bringing peace to the imperial court,
this would be an achievement like Huán (桓) and Wén (文).”
Liáng Xī (涼熙) again refused to listen
and killed Fú Luò (苻洛) at Xīhǎi (西海).
Fú Luò (苻洛) was moved to Xīhǎi (西海) as seen in Volume 104, fifth year of Tàiyuán (太元).
Liáng Xī (涼熙) wanted to resist Lǚ Guāng (呂光),
yet he killed Fú Luò (苻洛).
He merely wished to secure Liángzhōu (涼州),
and had no intention of supporting the fallen or sustaining the imperiled.
Guāng heard of Yáng Hàn's scheme,
and was afraid,
not daring to advance.
Dù Jìn said:
"Liáng Xī is cultured and refined,
but lacks foresight.
He will ultimately not use Hàn's scheme,
so there is no need to worry.
It is advisable to strike while his superiors and subordinates are disunited,
and quickly advance to capture him."
Guāng followed his advice.
Jìn arrived at Gāochāng,
and Yáng Hàn welcomed him by surrendering the commandery.
Xī was unable to utilize Yáng Hàn's scheme,
so Hàn consequently surrendered to Guāng.
[footnote] *To surrender*:
The character 戶 (hù) is mistakenly written as 江 (jiāng) and 翻 (fān);
the same below. [/footnote]
Xī issued a proclamation rebuking Guāng, demanding he withdraw his army,
and appointed his son Yìn as Yīngyáng General,
sending him with Zhènwēi General Nán'ān Yáo Hào and Biejia Wèi Hàn, leading a force of fifty thousand, to resist Guāng at Jiǔquán.
Dūnhuáng Administrator Yáo Jìng and Jìnchāng Administrator Lǐ Chún surrendered their commanderies to Guāng.
Guāng responded to the proclamation from Liángzhōu,
rebuking Xī for his lack of resolve to face difficulties
and for blocking the return of the imperial forces.
He dispatched Péng Huàng, Dù Jìn, and Jiāng Fēi as vanguards,
and battled Yìn at Ānmí.
[footnote] *Ānmí county has belonged to Jiǔquán Commandery since the Hàn dynasty.* [/footnote]
They captured him.
Thereupon, the Hú and Yí of the four mountains all pledged allegiance to Guāng.
Wǔwēi Administrator Péng Jì seized Xī and surrendered,
and Guāng executed him.
Guāng entered Gūzāng,
and personally assumed the title of Liángzhōu Inspector.
He memorialized to appoint Dù Jìn as Wǔwēi Administrator,
while the remaining generals and advisors
each received their respective positions.
All the commanderies and counties of Liángzhōu surrendered to Guāng,
with the exception of Jiǔquán Administrator Sòng
Hào and Xījùn Administrator Sòng Pàn.
[footnote] *The Jìn annals state: The Hàn dynasty divided Rìlè, Shāndān, and other counties of Zhāngyè to establish Xījùn,
its territory being a crucial mountain pass.* [/footnote]
Guāng attacked and captured them,
then reprimanded Pàn, saying:
"I received an imperial edict to pacify the Western Regions,
but Liáng Xī cut off my return route.
He is a criminal against the court;
why did you side with him?"
Pàn replied:
"The general received an edict to pacify the Western Regions,
not an edict to bring chaos to Liángzhōu.
What crime did Duke Liáng commit that the general should kill him?
Pàn merely laments his lack of strength
to avenge his lord and father;
how could he act like the rebellious Dī, Péng Jì?
When the lord is destroyed, the minister dies;
that is the natural order."
Guāng executed Pàn and Hào.
The Chief Clerk, Wèi Yòu,
was treacherous and cunning.
He and Péng Jì together seized Liáng Xī,
and Guāng favored and trusted him.
Yòu slandered and caused the deaths of more than ten prominent scholars, including Yáo Hào,
which caused the people of Liángzhōu to be displeased.
In the past, the people of Qí attacked Yān
and defeated it.
Mencius said:
"If taking it makes the people of Yān pleased,
then take it;
if taking it makes the people of Yān displeased,
then do not take it."
Afterwards, Yān eventually retaliated against Qí.
Lǚ Guāng, upon first acquiring the land of Liáng, failed to win the hearts of the people of Liángzhōu,
so it was natural that his reign would not be long.
When Yòu reached Yǔnwú,

Jiāng Fēi attacked and defeated him.
Yòu fled
and took refuge in Xìngchéng.

Qífú Guórén proclaimed himself Grand Commander, Grand General, Chányú, and Governor of Qín and Hé two provinces.
He changed the era name to Jiànyì,
appointed Yǐzhān Tóngní as Left Chancellor,
Wūyǐn Chūzhī as Right Chancellor,
Dúgū Pītí as Left Assistant,
and Wǔlú Yǒngshì as Right Assistant.
[footnote] *Yǐzhān, Wūyǐn, Dúgū, and Wǔlú

Ní
is the same as 泥.* [/footnote]
He divided his territory into twelve commanderies, including Wǔchéng.
[footnote] *Historical records state: He established the twelve commanderies of Wǔchéng, Wǔyáng, Āngù, Wǔshǐ, Hànyáng, Tiānshuǐ, Lüèyáng, Qiángchuān, Gānsōng, Kuāngpéng, Báimǎ, and Yuànchuān.

Qín Shangshu Ling and Wèichāng Gōng, Zuǎn, fled from Guānzhōng to Jìnyáng.
Qín Lord Pī appointed Zuǎn as Tàiwèi
and enfeoffed him as King of Dōnghǎi.
Winter.
In the tenth month,
Western Yān Lord Chōng dispatched Shàngshū Lìng Gāo Gài, leading a force of fifty thousand, to attack Later Qín.
They fought south of Xīnpíng,
and Gài was utterly defeated,
surrendering to Later Qín.
Initially,
Gài had adopted Yáng Dìng as his son.
When Gài was defeated,
Dìng fled to Lǒngyòu
and regrouped his former followers.
Fú Dìng, Fú Shào, Fú Mó, and Fú Liàng, hearing that Qín Lord Pī had ascended the throne,
all sent envoys from north of the Yellow River to apologize.
[footnote] *Dìng, Shào, Mó, and Liàng had surrendered to Yān;
see the previous year in the preceding volume.* [/footnote] They were originally Dī from Xīnpíng,
and firmly held Bólíng
to resist Yān for Qín.
In the eleventh month,
Pī appointed Yǎn as Píngzhōu Inspector,
Dìng as Jìzhōu Shepherd,
Shào as Jìzhōu Commander,
Mó as Yōuzhōu Shepherd,
and Liàng as Commander of Yōu and Píng two provinces,
all advanced to the rank of Jun Gong.
Zuǒ Jiāngjūn Dòu Chōng held Zīchuān.
[footnote] *Zīchuān
is Báchuān;
Báshuǐ was anciently called Zīshuǐ.
When Duke Mù of Qín became Hegemon,

It is now called Zīchuān,
based on the ancient name.* [/footnote]
He, along with Qínzhōu Inspector Wáng Tǒng, Hézhōu Inspector Máo Xìng, Yìzhōu Inspector Wáng Guǎng, Nánqínzhōu Inspector Yáng Bì, and Wèi Jiāngjūn Yáng Dìng, all sent envoys from Lǒngyòu to invite Pī
to jointly attack Later Qín.
Pī appointed Dìng as Yōngzhōu Shepherd,
Chōng as Liángzhōu Shepherd,
and added the titles of Zhènxi Dàjiāngjūn to Tǒng,
Chējì Dàjiāngjūn to Xìng,
and Zhēngnán Dàjiāngjūn to Bì,
all granted the privilege of establishing an administration and ranking as San Si.
Guǎng was additionally appointed Ānxī Jiāngjūn,
and all were promoted to the rank of Zhōumù.
Yáng Dìng soon moved his administration to Lìchéng
and established a supply depot at Bǎiqǐng.
[footnote] *Bǎiqǐng,
since the time of Yáng Màosōu,
had been used as a stronghold.* [/footnote]
He sent an envoy to declare himself a vassal;
an imperial edict allowed him to use the title he proclaimed.
Afterwards, he also seized the territories of Tiānshuǐ and Lüèyáng,
and proclaimed himself Qínzhōu Inspector and King of Lǒngxī.
Cài Kuāng of Yìmù rebelled against Yān by holding his city.
[footnote] *Yìmù county,
since the Hàn dynasty, belonged to Qīnghé Commandery.
It was abolished during the Suí dynasty
and merged into Dézhōu Ānlè county.* [/footnote]
Tàishān Administrator Rèn Tài secretly led his army to rescue Kuāng.
When they reached eight lǐ south of Kuāng's camp,
the Yān people realized it.
The generals were greatly worried that Kuāng had not yet been subdued and an external enemy had suddenly arrived.
Lóng said:
"Kuāng relies on outside help,
which is why he has not yet surrendered.
Now, Tài's forces number no more than a few thousand men.
Let's strike them before they can combine with Kuāng.
If Tài is defeated,
Kuāng will surrender on his own."
So, they ignored Kuāng and attacked Tài,
thoroughly defeating him and beheading over a thousand men.
Kuāng then surrendered,
but Yān King Chuí executed him
and also massacred his camp.
43 Mùróng Nóng reached Lóngchéng.
He passed through the Yānwēng Pass and all the way to Fánchéng,
then arrived at Lóngchéng.
His generals all said:
"Your Highness came
by a very swift route,
yet now you have lingered here for a long time without advancing.
Why is this?"
Nóng replied:
"The reason I came swiftly
was that I feared Yú Yán would cross the mountains to plunder and raid,
harassing the good people.
This mountain
refers to Mount Báiláng.
Chāo (鈔),
pronounced chǔ jiāo.
He enticed hungry children,
who gathered like crows,
without any discipline or order.
I have already choked his throat;
in a short while, they will disperse,
and he will be powerless.
Now, the fields are ripe,
and if we were to leave without harvesting,
it would be a needless waste.
We should wait until the harvest is complete;
then, when we go, we will easily defeat him.
It will not take more than ten days."
A short while later,
Nóng led 30,000 cavalry and infantry to Lìngzhī.
Yán's forces were greatly alarmed,
and little by little, they climbed over the city walls to surrender to Nóng.
Yán, at his wit's end, came out and surrendered.
Nóng executed him.
He then advanced to attack Gāogōulì,
recovering the two commanderies of Liáodōng and Xuántú.
After Hǎo Jǐng's defeat,
Gāogōulì had seized Liáodōng and Xuántú.
Tú (菟),
pronounced tóng dū.
He submitted a memorial requesting the repair of the imperial tombs and ancestral temples.
Since before Mùróng Huǎng, the Yàn had all been buried in Liáoxī,
so the imperial tombs and ancestral temples were there.
The King of Yàn, Chuí, appointed Nóng as Imperial Commissioner, Grand Commander of Military Affairs in Yōu and Píng Provinces and for the Northern Di, and Governor of Yōu Province,
to guard Lóngchéng.
He transferred Zuo, the King of Dàifāng and Governor of Píng Province, to guard Píngguō.
Nóng then established laws and regulations.
Affairs were handled with leniency and simplicity.
He cleared up criminal cases,
reduced taxes and corvée,
and encouraged agriculture and sericulture.
The residents became wealthy and abundant,
and tens of thousands of displaced people from all directions arrived one after another.
Previously, many displaced people from Yōu and Jì had entered Gāogōulì.
Nóng appointed Páng Yuān of Fányáng, a Cavalry Commander, as Administrator of Liáodōng,
to recruit and pacify them.
44 Mùróng Lín attacked Wáng Yǎn in Bólíng.
Within the city, food and arrows were exhausted.
Gōngcáo Zhāng Yī climbed over the city wall and left,
gathering a crowd to respond to Lín.
Yǎn, from the city wall, rebuked him, saying:
"You are a citizen of Qín,
and I am your lord.
You raise an army to respond to a bandit
and call yourselves 'righteous soldiers.'
How contrary are your name and reality!
The ancients sought loyal ministers surely from the homes of filial sons.
This is a saying by Wéi Biāo of the Later Hàn.
If you abandon and disregard your lord,
what do I have?
Today, people may accept your temporary achievements,
but how can they forget your disloyal and unfilial acts?
I did not expect that the Central Plains, a land of禮儀 (propriety and righteousness),
would produce someone like you!"
In the twelfth month,
Lín captured Bólíng,
seized Yǎn and Fú Jiàn,
and killed them.
Sòng Chǎng, the Administrator of Chānglí, led the Wūhuán and Suǒtóu forces to rescue Yǎn,
but arrived too late and returned.
Qín Lord Pī appointed Chǎng as Governor of Píng Province.
Chǎng was then with Wáng Yǒng at Húguān.
45 Yàn Lord Chuí went north to Zhōngshān,
and said to his generals:
"King Lèlàng (Wēn) gathered the displaced,
filled the granaries,
supplied provisions for the army externally,
and constructed palaces internally.
Even Xiāo Hé's achievements,
how could they surpass this!"
King Lèlàng Wēn's achievements are detailed above.
When Emperor Gāo of Hàn and Xiàng Yǔ were in a standoff,
Xiāo Hé pacified Guānzhōng,
serving as their foundation.
On the day Bǐngshēn,
Chuí first established his capital at Zhōngshān.
Dù Yǒu said: "Later Yàn's capital was Zhōngshān,
which is now the Tángchāng County in Bólíng Commandery."
46 Fú Dìng of Qín held Xìndū to resist Yàn.
King Chuí of Yàn appointed his cousin Jīng, the King of Běidì, as Governor of Jì Province,
and sent him with troops to attack it.
47 Tuòbá Guī's great-granduncle Hélú and his brother Jiàn, along with the chieftains of various tribes, collectively asked Hè Nà to support Guī as their leader.

in the first month,
on the day Wùshēn,
Tuòbá Guī held a grand assembly at Niúchuān.

North of Niúchuān
was all the vast desert.

when Kūdū came to invade,

Zhì (治),

Cháo (朝),

Chángsūn Dàoshēng, Hè Pí, and others attended on him,

If it is not permissible to replace a wife with a concubine,

Yǐn (隱) was elder and virtuous,
why should he not have been enthroned?
The heir is established by seniority, not by virtue;
a son is established by nobility (of mother), not by seniority.
Why was Huán (桓) noble?
His mother was noble.
If the mother is noble,
then why is the son noble?
The son is noble by the mother,
and the mother is noble by the son.

about a hundred *lǐ* from Cháng'ān city.
Dù Yòu said: Jīnchéng County in Jīngzhào has the old city of Mǎwéi.
Sūn Jǐng'ān's *Zhēng Tú Jì* says: Mǎwéi was built by
people of an unknown dynasty.
Jīnchéng
was called Quǎnqiū in the Zhōu dynasty,
Fèiqiū in the Qín dynasty,
and Huáilǐ in the Hàn dynasty.
Lín,
pronounced "lí zhēn".
Wéi,
pronounced "wú huí".
In summer,
fourth month,
Yáo Cháng, King of Later Qín, attacked them from Āndìng.
Lín fled to Hànzhōng.
Cháng captured Duō and advanced.
Nú was afraid
and requested to surrender.
He was appointed General who Guards the North and Grand Commander of Liùgǔ.
There are six valleys in the southern mountains of Cháng'ān.
17 On the *Guǐsì* day,
Lù Nà, the Grand Secretary of the Department of State Affairs, was appointed Left Grand Secretary,
and Tián, Prince of Qiáo, was appointed Right Grand Secretary.
The *Jìn Zhì* says: The Left and Right Grand Secretaries were sometimes not both appointed,
but simply called Grand Secretary of the Department of State Affairs.
(He) was Wán's son.
For Lù Wán,
see volume 94, Emperor Chéngdì's Xiánhé fourth year.
18 Máo Xīng attacked Wáng Guǎng,
defeated him,
and Guǎng fled to Qínzhōu.
Pǐ Lán, a Xiānbēi from Lǒngxī, captured Guǎng and sent him to Later Qín.
Xīng again wished to attack Wáng Tǒng in Shàngguī.
All the Dī people in Fúhǎn were weary of military affairs.
(As for) all the Dī people,
presumably Fú Jiān, King of Qín, had put Máo Xīng in charge of them to guard Fúhǎn.
Fù,
pronounced "fú yòu".
Fú,
pronounced "fū".
They nominated Wèi Píng as Inspector of Hézhōu,
because Wèi Píng's clan was powerful,
so they nominated him.
19 Mùróng Chuí, Lord of Yān, enfeoffed his son Nóng as Prince of Liáoxī,
Lín as Prince of Zhào,
and Lóng as Prince of Gāoyáng.
20 Tuòbá Guī, King of Dài, first changed his title to King of Wèi.
From then on, the Tuòbá clan's state name was Wèi.
21 Zhāng Dàyù advanced from Yángwù and encamped west of Gūzāng city.
Wáng Mù and Xīyú, son of Tūfà Sīfùjiàn, led thirty thousand troops and encamped south of the city.
Lǚ Guāng sallied out and attacked them,
inflicting a great defeat,
beheading more than twenty thousand, including Xīyú.
22 Qín issued a general amnesty.
Wèi Píng was appointed General who Guards the Army and Inspector of Hézhōu,
and Lǚ Guāng was appointed General of Chariots and Cavalry and Governor of Liángzhōu.
The envoys were all intercepted by Later Qín
and could not reach their destinations.
At that time, Fú Pī, Lord of Qín, was in Jìnyáng,
and Later Qín blocked his path,
so the envoys could not reach the two garrisons.
23 Mùróng Chuí, Lord of Yān, appointed Dé, Prince of Fányáng, as Minister of the Department of State Affairs;
Kǎi, Prince of Tàiyuán, as Left Grand Secretary;
and Wēn, Prince of Lèlàng, as Commandant of the Capital.
Wēn defended Zhōngshān,
and had the merit of constructing palaces and establishing a capital city,
so he was appointed Commandant of the Capital.
Lèlàng,
pronounced "luò láng".
24 Yáo Cháng, King of Later Qín, ascended the imperial throne in Cháng'ān.
Cháng's courtesy name was Jǐngmào,
and he was the twenty-fourth son of Yáo Yìzhòng.
He changed the era name to Jiànchū,
and the state name to Dà Qín.
He posthumously honored his father Yìzhòng as Emperor Jǐngyuán,
and established his wife, Lady Shé, as empress.
*Lèipiān*'s entry for Shé,
pronounced "yǐ zhě",
(says it) is a barbarian surname.
*Xìngpǔ* says: Yáo Cháng's empress, Lady Shé,
was from Nán'ān.
Shé,
pronounced "shí zhē",
also "tā".
He established all the officials.
Cháng feasted with his ministers.
When the wine was flowing freely,
he said:
"All of you, my lords, used to serve the Qín court.
Now suddenly you are my ministers.
Are you not ashamed?"
Zhào Qiān said:
"Heaven is not ashamed to take Your Majesty as its son;
what shame is there for us ministers to be your subjects?"
Cháng laughed heartily.
25 Tuòbá Guī, King of Wèi, went east to Língshí.
Língshí
is a place name,
east of Shènglè.
His generals requested to pursue them.
Guī said:
"Hóuchén and others have served for generations.
If they have committed a crime, we should endure it for now.
Our state is just beginning,
and people's hearts are not yet unified.
It is natural for the foolish to advance and retreat.
(The phrase) 'one advance, one retreat'
means their allegiance is not constant.
The historians say that Guī was able to understand the times and discern changes to pacify the wavering."
26 In the sixth month,
on the *Gēngyín* day,
Yáng Liàng, former General who Guards the State, was appointed Inspector of Yōngzhōu,
to guard the imperial tombs.
The emperor established Yōngzhōu in Xiāngyáng;
now Liàng is sent to assume Yōngzhōu,
guarding Luò.
Yōng,
pronounced "yú yòng".
(He was ordered to) descend (to the lower reaches of the Yellow River).
The *Xìngpǔ* says: The *Zuǒ Zhuàn* mentions the Yàn clan of Qí,
who were officials for generations.
Hú and Shǎn counties
both belonged to Hóngnóng.
Shǎn,
pronounced "shì rán".
27 Diāo Yún and others of Western Yān killed Zhōng, Lord of Western Yān.

They nominated Mùróng Yǒng as Bearer of Credentials, Grand Commander of All Military Affairs Inside and Outside, Grand General, Grand Chányú, Governor of the Four Provinces of Yōng, Qín, Liáng, and Liáng, Overseer of the Department of State Affairs, and Prince of Hédōng.
He declared himself a vassal to Yān.
(Meaning) he declared himself a vassal to Mùróng Chuí, Lord of Yān.
Shǐ,
pronounced "shū lì".
Yōng,
pronounced "yú yòng".
28 Mùróng Chuí, Lord of Yān, sent Kǎi, Prince of Tàiyuán, Lín, Prince of Zhào, Shào, Prince of Chénliú, and Zhōu, Prince of Zhāngwǔ, to attack Fú Dìng, Fú Shào, Fú Mó, Fú Liàng and others of Qín.
Last year,
Fú Dìng and others had betrayed Yān for Qín.
After explaining the advantages and disadvantages,
Dìng and the others all surrendered.
Chuí enfeoffed Dìng and others as marquises,
saying:
"To repay the kindness of the Lord of Qín."
29 Fú Pī, Lord of Qín, appointed Wáng Yǒng, Overseer of All Military Affairs Inside and Outside, Minister of Works, and Overseer of the Department of State Affairs, as Left Grand Chancellor;
Zuǎn, Grand Commandant and Prince of Dōnghǎi, as Grand Marshal;
Zhāng Háo, Minister of Works, as Grand Commandant;
Xú Yì of Xiányáng, Minister of the Department of State Affairs, as Minister of Works;
and Wáng Téng, Commandant of the Capital, as General of Swift Cavalry with the rank of the Three Ducal Ministers.
Yǒng issued a circular to all the marquises, governors, fortress commanders, and local magnates in the four directions,
to jointly attack Yáo Cháng and Mùróng Chuí,
ordering each to lead their forces
to assemble with the imperial carriage at Línjìn in the first ten days of the tenth month.

Thereupon Jiāng Yán of Tiānshuǐ, Kòu Míng of Féngyì, Wáng Zhāo of Hédōng, Zhāng Yàn of Xīnpíng, Dù Mǐn of Jīngzhào, Mǎ Láng of Fúfēng, and Wáng Mǐn of Fúfēng, General who Establishes Loyalty and Commander of the Pastoral Office of Gāopíng, and others,
(The title) General who Establishes Loyalty,
was probably also created by the Fú clan.
Gāopíng County,
belonged to Āndìng Commandery in the Hàn dynasty,
was abolished in the Jìn dynasty.
Liú Yào of Former Zhào made it the seat of Shuòzhōu,
and Qín established the Commander of the Pastoral Office in that area.
Each had tens of thousands of troops.
They sent envoys to Qín.
Pī appointed them all as generals and commandery governors,
and enfeoffed them as ranked marquises.
Dèng Jǐng, General of Valiant Cavalry, commanded five thousand troops and occupied Péngchí,
forming a pincer movement with Dòu Chōng
to attack Later Qín.
"Péngchí"
should probably be
"Biāochí".
Biāochí is west of Cháng'ān,
which is what the poem referred to as
"Biāochí flows north".
Dòu Chōng occupied Zīchuān,
southeast of Cháng'ān,
allowing them to form a pincer movement.
Also, according to the *Xīn Táng Shū Dìlǐ Zhì*,
Níngzhōu has Péngchí,
but it is far from Zīchuān.
Jǐng
was Qiāng's son.
Dèng Qiāng
was a famous general of Qín.
30 Yáo Cháng, King of Later Qín, moved over five thousand households from Āndìng to Cháng'ān.
In the autumn of the 31st year,
in the seventh month,
Jīn Xī, the Grand Administrator of Píngliáng, and Mòyì Gān, the Commandant of Āndìng, both of Qín, battled Yáo Fāngchéng, the Left General of Later Qín, in Sūnqiū Gǔ.
Sūnqiū Gǔ should be in Āndìng.
The Later Qín ruler, Cháng, appointed his younger brother, Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn Xù, as Sīlì Xiàowèi,
stationing him in Cháng'ān.
Cháng personally led troops to Āndìng
to attack Xī and others,
and utterly routed them.
Jīn Xī was originally of the Dōnghú stock.
Qín referred to the Xiānbēi people living in Liáojié as Dōnghú.
種,
zhāng yǒng fān.
He was the chieftain of the Duōlán tribe of the Xiānbēi.
The various Dī tribes in Fúhǎn,
considering Wèi Píng to be old and infirm,
and difficult to achieve great success with,
discussed deposing him.
However, fearing the strength of his clan,
they remained undecided for several days.
Dī Dànqīng said to the generals:
"Important matters should be settled promptly,
otherwise,
changes will arise.
Gentlemen, simply invite Duke Wèi to a meeting,
and observe what I do."
When a grand banquet for the Qīxī Festival was held,
Dànqīng drew his sword and stepped forward, saying:
"Today, the world is in great chaos.
We share common joys and sorrows.
Without a worthy lord, we cannot achieve great things.
Duke Wèi is old
and should return to his original attire to make way for a worthy path.
Wèi Píng was originally a subordinate general of Máo Xīng.
Though a distant relative of the royal house,
Fú Dēng possesses heroic aspirations and brilliant strategies.
I request that we jointly enthrone him
to respond to the imperial carriage."
He wished to act on Wáng Yǒng's manifesto to respond to Qín ruler Pī.
"Any dissent must be expressed immediately."
Then, he brandished his sword and bared his arm,
threatening to execute anyone who disagreed.
Everyone followed him,
not daring to look up.
Thereupon, they acclaimed Fú Dēng as Shǐchíjié,
Dūdū Lǒngyòu Zhū Jūnwǔ, Fǔjūn Dàjiāngjūn, Yōng Hé Èrzhōu Mù, and Lüèyáng Gōng.
Leading a force of 50,000,
he marched east down Lǒng,
attacked Nán'ān,
captured it,
and swiftly dispatched an envoy to request an appointment from Qín.
Fú Dēng
was a cousin of Qín ruler Pī.
This marks the beginning of Fú Dēng's exploits.
使,
shū lì fān.
雍,
yū yòng fān.
帥,
read as shuài;
the same below.
Mì Yí and Mòhóu Tìjuàn led their more than 30,000 households
to surrender to Qǐfú Guórén.
Guórén appointed Yí as Cìshǐ of Dōngqín Zhōu,
and Tìjuàn as Cìshǐ of Liáng Zhōu.
Mòhóu
is an夷 surname.
降,
hù jiāng fān;
the same below.
On the day of Jǐyǒu,
Wèi King Guī returned to Shènglè,
having come back from Língshí.
After more than ten days,
he again fled to Liú Xiǎn.
Guī sent his grandson, Bèijīn, to take command of his troops.
Liú Xiǎn's younger brother, Fèiní, led his troops to surrender to Wèi.
In the eighth month,
Yān ruler Chuí left Crown Prince Bǎo to guard Zhōngshān,
and appointed Zhào King Lín as Shàngshū Yòupúshè,
to oversee the imperial office in the capital.
On the day of Gēngwǔ,
Chuí personally led Fànyáng King Dé and others to campaign south,
and sent Gāoyáng King Lóng to march east through Píngyuán.
Xiānyú Qǐ of the Dīnglíng occupied the western mountains of Qǔyáng.
Qǔyáng County belonged to Chángshān Commandery.
He ventured out to encamp at Wàngdōu.
Wàngdōu County belonged to Zhōngshān Commandery.
According to the commentary on the Shuǐjīng, Yáo was enfeoffed in Táng,
with Yáoshān to the northeast and Yáo's mother, Qìngdūshān, to the south.
From Yáoshān, Dūshān could be seen,
hence Wàngdōu County was named for it.
Zhào King Lín personally went to attack him.
All the generals said:
"Your Highness, leaving the capital for a distant expedition
and returning without success, even if by chance,
would diminish your prestige.
It would be better to send the generals to attack him."
Lín said:
"Qǐ, hearing that the imperial carriage is away,
has no fears or scruples,
and will certainly not be prepared.
He can be taken in one swift strike,
nothing to worry about."
So, he publicly announced that he was going to Lǔkǒu.
At night,
he turned and rushed towards Qǐ.
By dawn,
he reached his camp,
launched a surprise attack,
and captured him.
Zháí Liáo raided Qiáo.
Zhū Xù attacked and drove him away.
Qín ruler Pī appointed Fú Dēng as Zhēngxī Dàjiāngjūn, Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī, and Nán'ān Wáng,
with the titles of Chíjié, Zhōumù, and Dūdū,
all bestowed according to his own declarations.
He also appointed Xú Yì as Yòuchéngxiàng.
He left Wáng Téng to guard Jìnyáng,
Yòupúshè Yáng Fǔ to garrison Húguān,
and personally led a force of 40,000
to advance and encamp at Píngyáng.
Earlier,
Yáo Shuòdé, the younger brother of Later Qín ruler Cháng, commanded his Qiāng tribe
living in Lǒngshàng.
Hearing that Cháng had raised an army,
he declared himself Zhēngxī Jiāngjūn
and gathered troops in Jìchéng to respond to him.
He appointed his elder brother's grandson, Yáo Xiáng, as Ānyuǎn Jiāngjūn,
to occupy Lǒngchéng,
and his grand-nephew, Yáo Xùn, as Ānxī Jiāngjūn,
to occupy Chìtíng in Nán'ān.
The various Yáo tribes were originally the Chìtíng Qiāng.
Cháng led his troops from Āndìng to meet Shuòdé and attack Tǒng.
More than 20,000 households of the Tógē in Tiānshuǐ and the Qiānghú in Lüèyáng responded to them.
Wáng Pí, the Grand Administrator of Lüèyáng for Qín, surrendered to them.
Earlier,
when Qín destroyed Dài,
it relocated Kūduō, the youngest son of Dài King Shíyìjiān, to Cháng'ān.
The event is recorded in Volume 104, Tàiyuán First Year.
窟,
kǔ gǔ fān.
咄,
dāng mò fān.
Wáng Yǒng appointed Kūduō as Xīnxīng Tàishǒu.
Liú Xiǎn sent his younger brother, Kàngní, to welcome Kūduō,
and followed him with troops,
threatening the southern border of Wèi.
Various tribes became agitated.
Yu Huán and others among Wèi King Guī's attendants, along with some tribesmen, conspired to seize Guī
and respond to Kūduō.
Mò Tí and other Dài people, who were Chuáng Jiàng, also secretly communicated with Kūduō.
According to the Guānshì Zhì of Wèi Shōu,
in the first year of Dàowǔ Dēngguó,
six Chuáng Jiàng were appointed,
who commanded the palace guards who stayed overnight in the forbidden palace,
from Shìzhōng downwards, and from Zhōngsǎn upwards, all were under their command.
During the time of Tuòbá Jiéfēn,
among the various tribes that entered,
there was the Mònàlóu clan,
which later became the Mò clan.
幢,
zhí jiāng fān.
Guī executed Huán and five others,
but Mò Tí and seven other clans were all pardoned without interrogation.
This laid the groundwork for Guī's later killing of Mò Tí.
He crossed the Yīnshān to the north
and again took refuge with the Hèlán tribe.
He sent Ān Tóng of Liáodōng, an Dàrén of the outer court,
to seek aid from Yān.
The Xìngpǔ states: a prince of Ānxī came to serve and became a Hàn person.
According to Fēngsú Tōng,
there was Ān Chéng as Grand Administrator in Hàn.
The Lúshān Jì mentions Ān Gāo, a prince of the Ānxī kingdom.
朝,
zhí yáo fān.
In the ninth month,
Wáng Tǒng surrendered Qín Zhōu to Later Qín.
Later Qín ruler Cháng appointed Yáo Shuòdé as Shǐchíjié, Dūdū Lǒngyòu Zhū Jūnwǔ, and Qínzhōu Cìshǐ,
to garrison Shàngguī.
Lǚ Guāng, upon receiving the news of Qín King Jiān's demise,
had his entire army don white mourning clothes
and posthumously honored him as Wénzhāo Huángdì.
In the winter,
tenth month,
there was a general amnesty,
and the reign era was changed to Dà'ān.
The Jìnshū Zàijì records it as
"Tài'ān."
In 42, Mùróng Yǒng of Western Yān sent an envoy to Fú Pī, the lord of Qín, to request passage to return east.
Pī refused.
He fought with Yǒng at Xiānglíng.
Xiānglíng County
belonged to Hédōng Commandery during the Hàn dynasty,
and to Píngyáng Commandery during the Jìn dynasty.
Both Zuo Chéngxiàng Wáng Yǒng and Wèi Dàjiāngjūn Jù Shízǐ died.
Earlier,
Dōnghǎi Wáng Zuǎn came from Cháng'ān.
Last year,
Zuǎn fled to Pī.
Pī was wary of him.
After his defeat,
fearing that Zuǎn would kill him,
he led several thousand cavalry south to Dōngyuán.
Dōngyuán County,
the Hàn dynasty had already changed it to Zhēndìng;
this Dōngyuán is in the vicinity of Xīn'ān County, Hénán.
Sòng Bái said: Wángwū County, Hénán Fǔ,
was Hédōng Commandery Yuán County territory during the Hàn dynasty.
Also,
Yuán County of Jiàng Zhōu
was originally a county name of Hédōng Commandery,
its land was where Zhōu and Shào divided their territory.
He also said: Hénán Fǔ,
was Hénán Commandery during the Hàn dynasty,
with its seat in Luòyáng;
the Later Hàn capital was Luòyáng,
Hénán belonged to the Sīlì Xiàowèi.
Wèi Chénliú Wáng Huàn combined Hénán and four other commanderies to establish Sī Zhōu.
Liú Cōng made it Jīng Zhōu,
Shí Hǔ made it Luò Zhōu,
Fú Jiān made it Yù Zhōu;
when Sòng Wǔ entered Luò,
he re-established Dōngyuán and Xīyuán two counties,
and still established Sī Zhōu at Hǔláo.
帥 (shuài),
read as 'shuài'.
騎 (qí),
read as 'qí' and 'jì'.
Yángwēi Jiāngjūn Féng Gāi intercepted and attacked him from Shǎn,
killing Pī,
and capturing his crown prince Níng and Chánglè Wáng Shòu,
sending them to Jiànkāng.
An imperial edict pardoned them from execution,
and entrusted them to Fú Hóng.
Fú Hóng had fled to them last year,
and was placed in Jiāng Zhōu.
The remaining princes, dukes, and officials were all captured by Yǒng.
Yǒng then advanced and occupied Chángzǐ,
ascended the imperial throne,
and changed the era name to Zhōngxīng.
He intended to make Qín's empress Yáng Shì his senior consort,
but Yáng Shì drew a sword and stabbed Yǒng,
and was killed by Yǒng.
In 43, on the jiǎshēn day,
Hǎixī Gōng Yì died in Wú.
He was forty-five years old.
In 44, Yān's palace attendant Wú Shēn rebelled at Qīnghé.
Yān Zhǔ Chuí attacked him,
but failed to overcome him.
In 45, Hòu Qín Zhǔ Cháng returned to Āndìng.
He returned to Āndìng from Shàngguī.
In 46, after Qín Nán'ān Wáng Dēng conquered Nán'ān,
three thousand households of barbarians and Han people submitted to him.
He then advanced to attack Yáo Shuòdé at Qín Zhōu.
Hòu Qín Zhǔ Cháng personally went to rescue him.
Dēng fought with Cháng at Húnú Fù.
Húnú Fù is west of Shàngguī.
He decapitated over twenty thousand,
and General Tàn Qīng shot Cháng,
wounding him.
Cháng's wound was severe,
he fled and secured Shàngguī,
and Yáo Shuòdé took over command of the troops.
In 47, Yān Zhào Wáng Lín's army had not yet reached Wèi,
Tuòbá Kūdú gradually pressed closer to Wèi Wáng Guī,
and Hè Rǎngān invaded Wèi's northern region to support him.
Wèi's forces were alarmed and disturbed.
The northern chieftain Shúsūn Pǔluò fled to Liú Wèichén.
Lín heard of this,
and urgently sent Ān Tóng and others to return.
The Wèi people knew that the Yān army was nearby,
and their morale somewhat stabilized.
Kūdú advanced and stationed at Gāoliǔ.
Gāoliǔ County,
belonged to Dài Commandery during the Hàn dynasty,
and was abolished during the Jìn dynasty.
Lì Dàoyuán said: Gāoliǔ is in central Dài,
its mountains have layered peaks and overlapping ridges,
rising high like clouds and mist.
Its mountains extend indistinctly eastward towards the Liáo frontier.
Kūdú suffered a great defeat,
and fled to Liú Wèichén.
Wèichén killed him.
Guī collected all of his troops,
and made Kùdí Gān of the Dài people the northern chieftain.
Wèi Shū Guānshì Zhì: Among the southern tribes,
there was the Kùdí clan,
later changed to Dí clan.
Liú Wèichén resided in Shuòfāng,
his soldiers and horses were very numerous.
Hòu Qín Zhǔ Cháng appointed Wèichén as Dàjiāngjūn, Dà Shànyú, Héxī Wáng, and Yōuzhōu Mù.
Xī Yān Zhǔ Yǒng appointed Wèichén as Dàjiāngjūn and Shuòzhōu Mù.
In November of 48,
Qín Shàngshū Kòu Yí, with Bóhǎi Wáng Yì and Jǐběi Wáng Chǎng, fled from Xìngchéng to Nán'ān.
Nán'ān Wáng Dēng held a funeral and wore mourning clothes,
and posthumously honored Qín Zhǔ Pī as Āipíng Huángdì.
Dēng deliberated on establishing Yì as lord,
but the衆 (zhòng) said:
“Although Bóhǎi Wáng is the son of the former emperor,
he is young and immature,
and not yet capable of handling many difficulties.
Now the three barbarians are eyeing us greedily,
The three barbarians refer to Yáo Cháng, Mùróng Chuí, and Mùróng Yǒng.
Only the Great King can deal with them.”
Dēng then built an altar in Lǒngdōng,
and ascended the imperial throne.
Dēng,
courtesy name Wéngāo,
was a grand-nephew of Jiān.
He changed the era name to Tàichū,
and established all official positions.
In 49, Mùróng Róu, Mùróng Shèng, and Shèng's younger brother Huì were all in Chángzǐ.
In the ninth year of Tàiyuán,
Róu and others escaped from Cháng'ān,
and fled to Mùróng Chōng;
after Chōng died, they followed Yǒng in his eastward migration.
“The present lord has already revived Yōu and Jì,
The present lord refers to Yān Zhǔ Chuí.
East refers to Yān Zhǔ Chuí;
West refers to Yān Zhǔ Yǒng.
Whether wise or foolish,
none will escape,
it is better to return east in due time,
and not sit idly waiting to be meat on the chopping block!”
So they fled together back to Yān.
More than a year later,
Xī Yān Zhǔ Yǒng completely executed the descendants of Yān Zhǔ Jùn and Yān Zhǔ Chuí,
leaving no male or female alive.
The historian praises Mùróng Shèng's wisdom.
In 50, Zhāng Dàyù entered Líntáo from Xī Jùn,
plundering over five thousand households,
and secured Kújù Chéng.
Kújù Chéng is within Líntáo territory.
In December of 51,
Lǚ Guāng proclaimed himself Shǐchíjié, Shìzhōng, Zhōngwài Dàdūdū, Dūd Lǒngyòu Héxī Zhū Jūnshì, Dàjiāngjūn, Liángzhōu Mù, and Jiǔquán Gōng.
In 52, Qín Zhǔ Dēng established the spirit tablet of Shìzǔ in the army.
Qín Zhǔ Jiān's temple name was Shìzǔ.
A carriage with screens on all four sides is called a zīpíng.
軿 (píng),
read as 'píng'.
He guarded it with three hundred Hǔbēn,
and whatever he wished to do,
he would first report to the spirit tablet before acting.
He led fifty thousand troops,
to attack Hòu Qín in the east.
His officers and soldiers all carved the characters
“死” (sǐ)
and “休” (xiū)
on their halberds and armor.
鉾 (máo),
a spearhead.
鎧 (kǎi),
armor.
鉾 (máo),
pronounced 'máo'.
Meaning, they would fight to the death to avenge and not rest until then.
Yáng Zhènghéng said: Zìlín: 鉾 (máo),
ancient character for 矛 (máo).
Knowing there was favoritism and unfair distribution,
he distributed rewards fairly,
so people fought for themselves,
and were invincible wherever they went.
Earlier,
when Cháng'ān was about to fall, refers to when Fú Jiān was besieged by Mùróng Chōng.
they built ramparts to protect themselves;
later they accepted official titles from Hòu Qín.
