When Dēng arrived, Sōng and Kōng surrendered to him with their troops.
Dēng appointed Sōng as Yōngzhōu Cìshǐ,
Kōng as Jīngzhào Yǐn,
and reburied Jiān with the rites of an emperor.
53 On the *yǐyǒu* day,
Yān Zhǔ Chuí attacked Wú Shēn's strongholds,
and captured them.
Wú Shēn fled alone on horseback.
Wú Shēn at that time occupied Qīnghé and rebelled against Yān.
Liáochéng County,
in the Hàn dynasty, belonged to Dōngjùn;
in the Jìn dynasty, it belonged to Píngyuánjùn.
Wēn Xiáng, the Palace Groom to the Crown Prince of Yān, came to defect.
He was appointed Administrator of Jìběi
and garrisoned at Dōng'ē.
Dōng'ē County,
in the Hàn dynasty, belonged to Dōngjùn;
in the Jìn dynasty, it belonged to Jìběijùn.
洗,
is pronounced *xǐ* (悉薦翻).
濟,
is pronounced *jǐ* (子禮翻).
Wēn Xiáng sent his younger cousin Pān to guard the south bank of the Hé,
and his son Kǎi to guard Què'áo to resist them.
54 Yān Zhǔ Chuí appointed Wèi Wáng Guī as the Western Chányú,
and enfeoffed him as Shànggǔ Wáng;
Guī refused the appointment.
Guī's refusal of the Yān enfeoffment
showed his ambition was not small.
單,
is pronounced *chán* (音蟬).

Tàiyuán twelfth year (Dinghai, 387 CE)
1 Spring,
first month,
on the *yǐsì* day,
Zhū Xù was appointed Inspector of Qīng and Yǎn prefectures,
replacing Xiè Xuán to garrison Péngchéng;
Xù requested to garrison Huáinīn,
and permission was granted.
Xù requested to garrison Huáinīn,
because Yān was strong
and would surely advance to take Hénán.
Péngchéng was far from Jiànkāng,
so support could not reach there.
Yuán was favored with an inland location.
會,
is pronounced *kuài* (工外翻).
2 On the *dīngwèi* day,
a general amnesty was declared.
3 Yān Zhǔ Chuí reviewed his troops by the river.
Wéi Zhāo said: 觀,
means "to show,"
displaying troops to demonstrate power.
觀,
is pronounced *guàn* (古玩翻).
"Wēn Xiáng and his ilk
are all pale-faced scholars,
a rabble gathered together,
merely relying on the long river to secure themselves.
If the grand army crosses the river,
they will surely be shattered at the sight of our flags,
without even needing a battle."
Chuí agreed with him.
On the *wǔwǔ* day,
he dispatched Zhènbei Jiāngjūn Lán Hàn and Hùjūn Jiāngjūn Píng Yòu to cross the river forty *lǐ* west of Què'áo,
while Lóng arrayed the main force on the north bank.
Wēn Pān and Wēn Kǎi indeed fled towards the city,
which was Dōng'ē city.
趣,
is pronounced *qù* (七喻翻).
They were greatly defeated.
That night, Wēn Xiáng took his wife and children and fled to Péngchéng.
His three myriad households and more all surrendered to Yān.
Chuí appointed Tàiyuán Wáng Kǎi as Inspector of Yǎnzhoū,
garrisoning at Dōng'ē.
Initially,
when Chuí was in Cháng'ān,
Qín Wáng Jiān once spoke with him face to face.
Róngcóng Púshè Guāng Zuò said to Jiān:
"Does Your Majesty not doubt Mùróng Chuí?
Chuí is not one to long remain subordinate to others."
Jiān told Chuí about this.
When Qín Zhǔ Pī fled from Yè to Jìnyáng,
the event is mentioned in the previous volume, tenth year.
Guāng Zuò followed Fú Pī in Yè,
mentioned in the previous volume, ninth year.
He was the son of Yì.
Fēng Yì served Yān,
and Yān rose in Chānglí,
with Yì's significant contribution.
See volume 105, ninth year.
An edict appointed Guāng Zuò and others as Administrators of various prefectures north of the Yellow River.
They all encamped in Jìběi and Púyáng.
Jìběi, Púyáng,
are two prefectures.
濟,
is pronounced *jǐ* (子禮翻).
濮,
is pronounced *pú* (博木翻).
Shī Gǔ said: It means merely nominally subject to them.
They all went to the Yān army and surrendered.
Chuí pardoned them
and treated them as before.
When Chuí saw Guāng Zuò,
tears streamed down his lapel,
and he said:
"Qín Wáng treated me deeply,
and I served him to the utmost.
However, due to the suspicion and jealousy of the two dukes,
The two dukes refer to Chánglè Gōng Pī and Píngyuán Gōng Huī.
See volume 105, ninth year.
I could not sleep through the night."
Guāng Zuò was also mournful.
Chuí bestowed gold and silk upon Guāng Zuò.
Guāng Zuò firmly declined.
Chuí said:
"Are you still suspicious?"
Guāng Zuò said:
"In the past, I only knew to be loyal to whom I served.
I did not expect Your Majesty to remember it to this day.
How would I dare escape death!"
Chuí said:
"This is indeed your loyalty,
which is what I seek.
My earlier words were just a jest."
Using Confucius's words.
He was appointed Zhōng Chángshì.
Guāng Zuò was a eunuch of Qín,
hence this official position.
4 Zhái Liáo dispatched his son Zhāo to raid Chén and Yǐng.
Zhū Xù sent General Qín Yīng to attack and repulse him.
5 Qín Zhǔ Dēng established the Máo clan as empress,
and Bóhǎi Wáng Yī as imperial younger brother and heir apparent.
The empress
was the daughter of Xīng.
He sent an envoy to appoint Dōnghǎi Wáng Zuǎn as Commissioner with Imperial Credentials, Area Commander-in-Chief of All Military Affairs, Grand Tutor, and concurrently Grand Marshal,
enfeoffing him as Lǔ Wáng.
Zuǎn's younger brother Shīnú was appointed Grand General of the Pacification Army and Governor of Bīngzhōu,
enfeoffed as Shuòfāng Gōng.
Zuǎn angrily said to the envoy:
"Bóhǎi Wáng is the son of the former emperor.
Why was Nán'ān Wáng not established but he established himself?"
The Chief Clerk Wáng Lǚ remonstrated:
"Nán'ān has already been established,
and it is logically impossible to change it now.
Now, with the invaders not yet eliminated,
we cannot create enemies among our own imperial clan."
Zuǎn then accepted the appointment.
Thereupon, Lúshuǐ Hú Péng Pèigǔ, Túgè Dǒng Chéng, Zhāng Lóngshì, Xīnpíng Qiāng Léi Èdì, and others all attached themselves to Zuǎn,
gathering a host of over ten myriad people.
Since Dēng and Zuǎn combined their forces,
their influence grew,
so they collectively submitted to them.
屠,
is pronounced *tú* (直於翻).
6 Later, Qín Zhǔ Cháng moved three myriad households of prominent people from Qínzhōu to Āndìng.
Last year, Cháng moved the people of Āndìng to populate Cháng'ān.
Now, he again moved the prominent people of Qínzhōu to populate Āndìng.
Cháng raised his army with Āndìng as his base
and wished to make Cháng'ān his capital.
Therefore, he gradually moved people based on the distance.
7 Initially,
Qí Shè (齊涉) from Āncì (安次) gathered over eight thousand families and occupied Xīnzáh (新柵).
He surrendered to Yān (燕),
becoming Āncì County (安次縣).
In the Former Hàn (漢), it belonged to Bóhǎi (勃海);
in the Later Hàn, it belonged to Guǎngyáng Guó (廣陽國);
in the Jìn (晉), it belonged to Yān Guó (燕國).
Xīnzáh was probably within Wèijùn's (魏郡) borders.
Jiàng (降) is pronounced Hù Jiāng Fān.
Soon after, he rebelled again,
uniting with Zhāng Yuàn (張願).
Yuàn personally led over ten thousand men to advance and garrison at Wèngkǒu (瓮口) in Zhù'ā (祝阿).
Zhù'ā County (祝阿縣)
belonged to Píngyuán Jùn (平原郡) in the Hàn,
and Jìnán Jùn (濟南郡) in the Jìn.
Yuàn had advanced and garrisoned there from Tàishān (泰山).
Liú Xù (劉昫) said: Qízhōu (齊州) Yǔchéng County (禹城縣)
was Hàn Zhù'ā County (祝阿縣).
In Tiānbǎo (天寶) first year,
its name was changed.
Sòng Bái (宋白) said: Zhù'ā (祝阿)
is like Dōng'ē (東阿).
It was the ancient Zhù Guó (祝國), descendants of the Yellow Emperor.
According to ancient Dōng'ē,
Qí (齊) was Dōng'ē,
Hàn (漢) was Zhù'ā County (祝阿縣).
Its old city was two *lǐ* northeast of present-day Fēngqí County (豐齊縣).
The Táng (唐) changed it to Yǔchéng (禹城).
Fù (復) is pronounced Fú Yòu Fān.
Shuài (帥)
is read as Shuài.
Wèng (瓮)
is pronounced Wū Gòng Fān.
They mutually supported Shè.
Gāoyáng Wáng Lóng (高陽王隆) spoke to Chuí (垂), saying:
"Xīnzáh (新柵) is strong and secure;
attacking it would not be easy to capture suddenly.
If we delay our troops under its walls for long,
Zhāng Yuàn (張願) will gather and lead displaced people,
drawing in the Dīnglíng (丁零) from the west.
Dīnglíng (丁零)
refers to Zhái Liáo (翟遼).
Shuài (帥)
is read as Shuài.
Although Yuàn's (願) forces are numerous,
they are all newly attached
and not yet capable of fighting with strength.
Taking advantage of his self-approach,
it is advisable to strike him first.
Yuàn (願) and his son, relying on their bravery,
will surely not be willing to avoid and flee.
We can capture them in a single battle.
If Yuàn is defeated,
then Shè (涉) will not be able to survive."
Chuí (垂) followed his advice.
In the second month,
Fànyáng Wáng Dé (范陽王德), Chénliú Wáng Shào (陳留王紹), and Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn Zhāng Chóng (龍驤將軍張崇) were dispatched
to lead twenty thousand infantry and cavalry to join Lóng (隆) in attacking Yuàn (願).
The army reached Dòuchéng (斗城),
over twenty *lǐ* from Wèngkǒu (瓮口),
where they dismounted and rested.
Yuàn (願) led his troops to arrive suddenly.
The Yān (燕) forces were alarmed and panicked.
Dé's (德) troops retreated,
but Lóng (隆) disciplined his troops and held his ground.
Yuàn's (願) son, Guī (龜), rushed out to assault the formation.
Lóng (隆) sent his retainers Wáng Mò (王末) to counterattack,
and they beheaded him.
Lóng (隆) then slowly advanced and engaged,
and Yuàn's (願) forces finally retreated.
Dé (德) marched for about one *lǐ*,
regrouped his troops,
and returned to join Lóng (隆),
saying to Lóng (隆):
"The enemy's morale is currently strong;
we should proceed cautiously for now."
Lóng (隆) replied:
"Yuàn (願) attacked when we were unprepared,
and should have achieved a great victory.
However, our soldiers are all cut off by the river ford,
and due to the urgent situation,
each man is eager to fight for himself.
This means the troops are cut off by the river ford,
with a strong enemy ahead,
and drowning if they retreat.
Therefore, they think of this and fight for themselves.
Now the enemy has gained no advantage;
their morale is exhausted and their power is waning.
They all have thoughts of advancing and retreating,
and cannot unite in their efforts.
We should attack them quickly."
Dé (德) said:
"I will simply do as you say."
Thereupon, they advanced
and fought at Wèngkǒu (瓮口),
achieving a great victory.
Seven thousand eight hundred heads were taken;
Yuàn (願) escaped and took refuge at Sānbùkǒu (三布口).
The Yān (燕) army advanced to Lìchéng (歷城).
Lìchéng County (歷城縣) had belonged to Jìnán Jùn (濟南郡) since the Hàn (漢).
Chuí (垂) appointed Chénliú Wáng Shào (陳留王紹) as Qīngzhōu Cìshǐ (青州刺史),
garrisoning Lìchéng (歷城).
Dé (德) and others returned with their army,
and Dōng Luán (冬鸞) from Xīnzáh (新柵) captured Shè (涉) and sent him to them.
It was exactly as Mùróng Lóng (慕容隆) had predicted.
Tángyùn (唐韻): Dōng (冬)
is a surname.
All others were spared.
8 In the third month,
Qín (秦) Lord Dēng (登) appointed Dòu Chōng (竇衝) as Nán Qínzhōu Mù (南秦州牧),
Yáng Dìng (楊定) as Yìzhōu Mù (益州牧),
Yáng Bì (楊壁) as Sīkōng (司空) and Liángzhōu Mù (梁州牧),
and Qífú Guórén (乞伏國仁) as Dà Jiāngjūn (大將軍), Dà Chányú (大單于), and Yuànchuān Wáng (苑川王).
Dù Yòu (杜佑) said: Yuànchuān (苑川) is in Lánzhōu (蘭州) Wǔquán County (五泉縣),

I believe Dù Yòu (杜佑) spoke from conjecture.
Dān (單)
is pronounced Chán.
9 Wáng Mǐn (王敏) from Shànggǔ (上谷) in Yān (燕) killed the Grand Administrator Fēng Jí (封戢).
Xǔ Qiān (許謙) from Dàijùn (代郡) drove away the Grand Administrator Jiǎ Rùn (賈閏).
Each, with their respective commanderies, defected to Liú Xiǎn (劉顯).
This sets the stage for Yān (燕) to attack Liú Xiǎn (劉顯).
10 Yān (燕) Lèlàng Wáng Wēn (樂浪王溫) was appointed Shàngshū Yòupúshè (尚書右僕射).
Below "Yān" (燕)
there should be
the character "yǐ" (以).
Lèlàng (樂浪)
is pronounced Luò Láng.
11 In summer,
fourth month,
on the day Wùchén (戊辰),
the Emperor's mother, Lady Lǐ (李氏), was honored as Huáng Tài (皇太),
with imperial ceremonial attire like that of an empress dowager.
12 Hòu Qín (後秦) Zhēngxī Jiāngjūn Yáo Shuòdé (征西將軍姚碩德) was pressed by Yáng Dìng (楊定)
and retreated to defend Jīngyáng (涇陽).
Jīngyáng County (涇陽縣),

Dù Yòu (杜佑) said: Hàn Jīngyáng County (漢涇陽縣) is the old city of Jīngyáng (涇陽) within the present-day Píngliáng Jùn (平涼郡) borders.
Fighting at Jīngyáng (涇陽),
Shuòdé (碩德) suffered a great defeat.
Hòu Qín (後秦) Lord Cháng (萇) personally came from Yīnmì (陰密) to rescue him.
Zuǎn (纂) retreated and garrisoned at Fūlù (敷陸).
Yīnmì County (陰密縣)
belonged to Āndìng Jùn (安定郡);

Fūlù (敷陸)
is the same place as Táng (唐) Fāngzhōu (坊州) Fūchéng County (鄜城縣).
13 Yān (燕) Lord Chuí (垂) returned to Zhōngshān (中山) from Què'áo (碻磝).
Mùróng Róu (慕容柔), Mùróng Shèng (慕容盛), and Mùróng Huì (慕容會) arrived from Chángzǐ (長子).
Róu (柔) and the others had fled from Chángzǐ (長子) last year
and only now reached Zhōngshān (中山).
On the day Gēngzǐ (庚子),
Chuí (垂) granted a general amnesty for them.
Delighted that his sons and grandsons had survived and returned east,
he therefore granted a general amnesty.
Wéi (為) is pronounced Yú Wěi Fān.
"What is the situation like among the people of Chángzǐ (長子)?
Is it possible to take it?"
Shèng (盛) replied:
"The Western army is in disarray,
and the people have thoughts of returning east.
Your Majesty only needs to cultivate benevolent governance and await them.
If the grand army once arrives,
they will surely throw down their spears and come,
like filial sons returning to their benevolent father."
Chuí (垂) was pleased.
On the day Guǐwèi (癸未),
Róu (柔) was enfeoffed as Yángpíng Wáng (陽平王),
Shèng (盛) as Chánglè Gōng (長樂公),
and Huì (會) as Qīnghé Gōng (清河公).
14. Zái Chàng, a native of Gāopíng, captured Prefect Xú Hányuǎn
and surrendered the commandery to Zái Liáo.
Yàn ruler Mùróng Chuí said to his generals,
"Liáo, with the population of a single city,
has repeatedly shifted allegiance among three states."
The three states
refer to Jìn, Yàn, and Xī Yàn.
In the fifth month,
he appointed Zhāngwǔ Wáng Zhòu as Supervisor of all military affairs, both internal and external,
and assigned him to assist Crown Prince Bǎo in guarding Zhōngshān.
Chuí himself led his generals south to attack Liáo,
with Tàiyuán Wáng Kǎi as the vanguard commander.
Liáo's troops were all people from Yàn and Zhào.
When they heard of Kǎi's arrival,
they all said,
"Prince Tàiyuán
is our father and mother!"
Kǎi's father, Mùróng Kè, had been a chancellor of Yàn,
and the people of Yàn and Zhào held him in esteem,
hence their words.
Liáo was frightened
and sent an envoy to request surrender.
Chuí appointed Liáo as Governor of Xúzhōu
and enfeoffed him as Hénán Gōng.
Chuí then advanced to Líyáng,
accepted his surrender, and returned.
Jiǎ Bào, a native of Jǐngxíng,
Jǐngxíng County belonged to Chángshān Commandery.
Xíng
is pronounced xíng.
launched a night attack on Zhōngshān
and breached its outer wall.
Zhāngwǔ Wáng Zhòu led elite troops out from the exterior,
while Crown Prince Bǎo raised a battle cry from within.
They attacked together,
inflicting a great defeat on Jiǎ Bào,
capturing all his forces.
Only Yáo and Bào escaped on single horses.
15. Liú Xiǎn was vast in territory and strong in military power,
dominating the north.
When his brothers fell into conflict,
Wèi Chancellor Zhāng Gǔn addressed Wèi Wáng Guī, saying,
"Xiǎn's ambition is to annex all.
If we do not seize this opportunity to take him while he is internally disintegrating,
Nuózhēn and Fèiní have successively come to surrender,
hence these words.
However, we cannot conquer him alone;
I request to attack him jointly with Yàn."
Guī agreed
and again sent Ān Tóng to request troops from Yàn.
Last year, Wèi sent Ān Tóng to request troops from Yàn to defeat Kūdú,
hence the word "again" here.
Fù
is pronounced fú yòu fān.
16. An imperial edict summoned Dài Kuí, a reclusive scholar from Kuàijī.
Kuí repeatedly declined,
but the commandery and county authorities pressed him incessantly.
Kuí fled and hid in Wú.
Xiè Xuán submitted a memorial, stating,
"Kuí seeks to uphold his own aspirations,"
The Analects say: "To live in retirement in order to seek one's aspirations."
"and will suffer the hardships of wind and frost.
Since Your Majesty already loves and values him,
you should also allow his person and reputation to coexist.
I request that the summons be withdrawn."
The Emperor granted it.
Xuán was the Administrator of Kuàijī,
hence he submitted the memorial for Kuí.
He was the elder brother of Dài Juàn.
See Dài Juàn in Volume 104, 4th year.
17. Qín ruler Fú Dēng appointed his elder brother Fú Tóngchéng as Sītú and Grand Secretariat,
enfeoffing him as Yǐngchuān Wáng;
his younger brother Fú Guǎng as Grand Guardian of the Central Secretariat,
enfeoffing him as Ānchéng Wáng;
and his son Fú Chóng as Left Prime Minister of the Department of State Affairs,
enfeoffing him as Dōngpíng Wáng.
18. Yàn ruler Mùróng Chuí returned to Zhōngshān from Líyáng.
19. Wú Shēn killed Dīng Guó, the Yàn Administrator of Qīnghé;
Wáng Zǔ, a man from Zhāngwǔ, killed Prefect Bái Qīn;
and Zhāng Shēn, a man from Bóhǎi, occupied Gāochéng and rebelled.
Gāochéng County belonged to Bóhǎi Commandery.
Xián says: The old city of Gāochéng
is south of modern Cāngzhōu Yánshān County.
20. Yuànchuān Wáng Guórén led thirty thousand cavalry to attack the three Xīanběi tribes of Mìguì, Yùgǒu, and Tílún at Liùquán.
Mìguì was one tribe,
Yùgǒu was one tribe,
and Tílún was one tribe.
Liùquán is in Gāopíng.
Shuài
is read as lǜ.
Qí
is pronounced qí jì fān.
In the seventh month,
he battled Mòyìgān Jīn Xī at Kěhún Chuān.
According to the records,
Guórén attacked the three tribes,
and Mòyìgān and Jīn Xī joined forces to attack Guórén,
hence the battle at Kěhún Chuān.
This place should be northeast of Tiānshuǐ Yǒngshì County.
All three tribes surrendered.
21. Qín ruler Fú Dēng camped at Wǎtíng.
Later Qín ruler Yáo Cháng attacked Péng Pèigǔ's fortress,
captured it,
and Pèigǔ fled to Xìngchéng.
Péng Pèigǔ was a Lúshuǐ Hú,
who built a fortress in Èr County.
Dù Yòu says: Xìngchéng is west of Fāngzhōu.
Yáo Cháng then stationed Crown Prince Yáo Xīng in Cháng'ān.
22. Yàn Zhào Wáng Mùróng Lín attacked Wáng Mǐn at Shànggǔ
and beheaded him.
23. Liú Wèichén offered horses to Yàn,
but Liú Xiǎn plundered them.
Yàn ruler Mùróng Chuí was enraged
and sent Tàiyuán Wáng Kǎi with troops to assist Zhào Wáng Lín in attacking Xiǎn,
inflicting a great defeat on him.
Xiǎn fled to the west mountains of Mǎyì.
Wèi Wáng Guī led troops to join Lín in attacking Xiǎn at Mízé.
According to the Wèi Shū Dì Jì,
Mízé is south of Mǎyì.
Xiǎn fled to Xī Yàn.
Lín took possession of all his forces
and captured millions of horses, cattle, and sheep.
With the destruction of Liú Xiǎn, the Tuòbá clan grew stronger.
For those who planned for the Mùróng clan,
none would suggest it was better to benefit both and keep them both in existence,
which could avoid the disaster of national demise on another day.
24. Lǚ Guāng's generals Péng Huàng and Xú Jiǒng attacked Zhāng Dàyù at Líntáo
and defeated him.
Zhāng Dàyù fled to Líntáo,
see last year in the previous volume.
Táo
is pronounced tǔ dāo fān.
Wáng Mù fled to Jiànkāng.
In the eighth month,
people from Guǎngwǔ captured Dàyù and sent him to Gūzāng,
where he was beheaded.
Mù then attacked and occupied Jiǔquán,
proclaiming himself Grand General and Governor of Liángzhōu.
25. On the day Xīnsì,
Imperial Prince Dézōng was established as Crown Prince,
and a general amnesty was granted.
26. Yàn ruler Mùróng Chuí established Liú Xiǎn's brother Kění as King of Wūhuán
to pacify his people,
and relocated over eight thousand households to Zhōngshān.
27. Qín Fèngyì Prefect Lán Dú led twenty thousand troops from Pínyáng into Héníng.
Pínyáng County
was established by Qín Lìgōng.
Since the Hàn dynasty, it belonged to Fèngyì.
Yīng Shào notes: It is on the south bank of the Pín River.
According to the records,
Héníng is southeast of Xìngchéng, north of the ridge.
Shuài
is read as lǜ.
Fú Zǎn's younger brother Fú Shīnú urged Zǎn to adopt an imperial title,
but Zǎn refused.
Shīnú then killed Zǎn and took his place.
Dú consequently broke off relations with Shīnú.
Xī Yàn ruler Fú Yǒng attacked Dú.
Dú
requested aid from Later Qín,
and Later Qín ruler Yáo Cháng wanted to go rescue him himself.
Grand Secretariat Yáo Mín and Left Prime Minister Yǐn Wěi said,
"Fú Dēng is nearby at Wǎtíng and will take advantage of our absence to attack our rear."
Cháng said,
"Fú Dēng's forces are strong,
and cannot be defeated overnight.
Dēng is slow and indecisive,
and will certainly not risk lightly penetrating deep with his army.
Within two months,
I will surely defeat the rebels and return.
Even if Dēng arrives,
he will be able to do nothing."
In the ninth month,
Cháng's army was at Níyuán.
The Hàn Shū Dì Lǐ Zhì states that Běidì Commandery had Níyáng County.
Yīng Shào's commentary notes: The Ní River originates in the northern barbarians of Yùzhì.
He suffered a great defeat
and fled to the Xiānbēi.
Later Qín captured all his forces,
and Túcá Dǒng Chéng and others all surrendered.
With the defeat of Fú Zǎn and his brothers,
Fú Dēng's power was isolated.
Tú
is pronounced zhí yú fān.
28. Qín ruler Fú Dēng advanced and occupied Húkōng Bǎo.
This fortress was built by Húkōng, the Qín Commander of Cavalry,
and is within Xīnpíng territory.
29. In winter,
tenth month,
Zái Liáo again rebelled against Yàn
and sent troops with Wáng Zǔ and Zhāng Shēn to raid Qīnghé and Píngyuán.
In 30, the Later Qín Lord Yáo Cháng advanced to attack Xīyàn King Mù Róng Yǒng at Héxī.
“Xīyàn King”
should be
“Xīyàn Lord”.
From Lóngmén to Huàyīn,
this is west of the Yellow River.
Lán Dú again marshaled his troops and resisted,
and Cháng attacked him.
In the twelfth month,
Dú was captured,
and then Cháng proceeded to Xìngchéng.
In 31, Later Qín's Yáo Fāngchéng attacked the fortress of Xú Sōng, the Qín Governor of Yōngzhōu.
He captured it,
seized Sōng, and reproached him.
Sōng cursed, saying:
"You Yáo Cháng are guilty of ten thousand deaths!
Fú Huángméi wanted to execute you,
but the Former Emperor stopped him.
This refers to the time of Yáo Xiāng's defeat in the first year of Shēngpíng of Emperor Mù.
Your favor and honor were extreme!
Yet you were not even as good as a dog or horse in recognizing the grace of your sustenance,
and personally committed great rebellion.
This refers to the killing of Qín King Fú Jiān at Xīnpíng Fósì.
Why don't you kill me quickly!"
Fāngchéng was enraged,
and cut Sōng into three pieces.
"Cut into three pieces" means
cutting off his feet,
cutting him at the waist,
and cutting off his neck.
He awarded Sōng's wife and children to the army.
The Later Qín Lord Yáo Cháng dug up the corpse of Qín Lord Fú Jiān,
whipped it countless times,
stripped off its clothes, leaving it naked,
pierced it with thorns,
and then buried it in a shallow pit.
Fú Jiān was buried between the two fortresses of Xú Sōng and Hú Kōng.
Since Xú Sōng's fortress had fallen,
Yáo Cháng was able to dig up the grave and whip the corpse to vent his anger.
Lǔo (倮)
is pronounced láng guǒ fān (郎果翻).
Jiàn (薦)
means "to spread" or "to lay out".
In 32, Liángzhōu suffered a great famine.
A *dòu* of rice cost five hundred coins,
people ate each other,
and more than half died.
In 33, Lü Gūang's Xīpíng Grand Administrator Kāng Níng declared himself Xīóngnú King,
and killed Huánghé Grand Administrator Qíang Xī in rebellion.
Xīpíng Commandery was established at the end of the Eastern Hàn dynasty by dividing Jīnchéng.
The Shànzhōu of the Táng dynasty
is its location.
Huánghé Commandery was established by the Zhāng clan of Héxī,
and it was probably also within the borders of Shànzhōu.
Qíang (強)
is pronounced qí liǎng fān (其兩翻).
Kāng Níng allied with Péng Huǎng in the east
and communicated with Wáng Mù in the west.
Gūang wanted to personally attack Huǎng,
but all his generals said:
"Now Kāng Níng is in the south,
waiting for an opportunity to act.
If Huǎng and Mù are not yet executed,
and Kāng Níng returns,
we will be in a predicament whether we advance or retreat,
and the situation will inevitably be extremely dangerous."
Gūang said:
"What you say is true.
However, if I don't go now,
it's waiting for them to come.
If the three bandits unite their forces,
The "three bandits" refer to Kāng Níng, Péng Huǎng, and Wáng Mù.
then everything outside the city will not be ours,
and the great matter will be lost.
Now Huǎng has just rebelled,
and his relationship with Níng and Mù is not yet close.
If we strike them by surprise,
it will be relatively easy to capture them."
So he personally led thirty thousand cavalry,
marching at double speed day and night.
Upon arrival,
he attacked for twenty days,
captured the city,
and executed Huǎng.
Initially,
Wáng Mù raised an army
and sent an envoy to invite the recluse Guō Yǔ of Dūnhuáng.
Yǔ sighed, saying:
"Now the common people will have their clothes folded to the left,
how can I bear not to save them!"
So he and Suǒ Gǔ of the same commandery raised an army to support Mù,
and transported thirty thousand *dàn* of grain to supply him.
Mù appointed Yǔ as Grand Steward Left Chief Clerk and Military Advisor General,
and Gǔ as Dūnhuáng Grand Administrator.
Later, Mù listened to slanderous words,
and led his troops to attack Gǔ.
Yǔ advised against it but was not heeded.
He went outside the city and wept loudly,
raising his hands to bid farewell to the city, saying:
"I will not see you again!"
He returned and pulled a quilt over his face,
spoke to no one,
and died of starvation.
When Lü Gūang heard of this, he said:
"The two bandits are attacking each other;
this is a ready catch.
One must not be deterred by the effort of repeated battles and lose the opportunity for lasting peace."
"Lasting peace in one effort" is an ancient saying.
He defeated them.
He then advanced his forces to Liángxīng.
Liángxīng Commandery was established by the Zhāng clan of Héxī,
located within the borders of Chánglè County, Guāzhōu of the Táng dynasty.
Before he arrived,
Mù's forces disintegrated,
and Mù fled alone on horseback.
Guō Wén of Xīngmǎ County beheaded him and sent his head.
Xīngmǎ County belonged to Jiǔquán Commandery,
probably established during the Wèi and Jìn periods.
Xīng (騂)
is pronounced sī róng fān (思榮翻).
After Lü Gūang newly acquired Héxī,
there were factions rebelling internally
and enemies attacking externally.
Although he won many battles,
his foundation was not solid,
and it was not sufficient to pass on to his descendants.
Thirteenth Year (Wùzǐ, 388)
1. In spring,
the first month,
Kānglè Xiànwǔ Gōng Xiè Xuán died.
2. In the second month,
Qín Lord Fú Dēng's army was at Cháonà.
Cháonà County had belonged to Āndìng Commandery since the Hàn dynasty.
This Wǔdū must also be within the borders of Āndìng.
The Five Dynasties Gazetteer states: Cháonà County.
The Western Wèi established Ānwǔ Commandery.
Ānwǔ was an old Hàn county name.
The name Wǔdū must have been named after Ānwǔ.
3. Zhái Liáo sent his Military Advisor Suī Qióng to Yān to apologize.
Yān Lord Mù Róng Chuí, seeing his frequent treachery,
executed Qióng to sever ties with him.
Liáo then declared himself Wèi Tiānwáng,
changed the era name to Jiànguāng,
and established all officials.
4. Yān's Qīngzhōu Governor, Chénliú Wáng Mù Róng Shào, was pressed by Píngyuán Grand Administrator Pìlǘ Hún,
and retreated to garrison at Huángjīn Gù.
At the end of the Hàn dynasty, the Yellow Turban rebels gathered and fortified themselves in this area,
hence the name.
The people of Qí called a fortress a "gù".
Shào retreated from Lìchéng to garrison there;
this area is north of Zhāngqiū City in Jǐnán Commandery.
Hún
was the son of Wèi.
Pìlǘ Wèi is mentioned in Volume 100, Yǒnghé twelfth year of Emperor Mù.
Wèi (蔚)
is pronounced yū hū fān (紆忽翻).
He brought the Qí territory to surrender.
Later, Pìlǘ Hún was killed by Mù Róng Dé.
Jiàng (降)
is pronounced hù jiāng fān (戶江翻).
5. In the third month,
on the day Yǐhài,
Yān Lord Mù Róng Chuí appointed Crown Prince Mù Róng Bǎo as Overseer of the Affairs of the Department of State,
entrusting him with governance,
while Chuí himself only managed the general outlines.
6. Yān's Zhào Wáng Mù Róng Lín attacked Xǔ Qiān,
defeating him.
Last year, Xǔ Qiān rebelled against Yān and joined Liú Xiǎn.
He then abolished Dàijùn,
and moved all its people to Lóngchéng.
7. When Lü Gūang stabilized Liángzhōu,
Dù Jìn contributed greatly.
Gūang appointed him as Wǔwēi Grand Administrator.
This matter is mentioned in Volume 10, ten years earlier.
None of his peers could compare.
Gūang's nephew Shí Cōng came from Guānzhōng.
Gūang asked him:
"What do people in Zhōngzhōu say about my governance?"
Cōng replied:
"I only heard of Dù Jìn,
but not of my uncle."
Guāng feasted with his subordinates.
When the conversation turned to political affairs,
Duàn Yè (段業) of Jīngzhào (京兆), who was a Cānjūn (參軍), said:
"Your Excellency's enforcement of the law is too severe."
Guāng replied:
"Wú Qǐ (吳起) lacked compassion, yet Chǔ (楚) became strong;
Shāng Yāng (商鞅) enforced strict laws, and Qín (秦) rose to power."
Yè said:
"Qǐ (起) lost his life,
and Yāng (鞅) lost his family.
These were all consequences of their cruelty.
The matter of Wú Qǐ (吳起) can be found in Volume 1, during the fifteenth year of King Ān (安) of Zhōu (周).
The matter of Shāng Yāng (商鞅) can be found in Volume 2, during the thirty-first year of King Xiǎn (顯).
喪 (sàng)
is pronounced xī làng fān.
To emulate Yáo (堯) and Shùn (舜) in their conduct,
the *Shī* (詩) says: 'High mountains are gazed upon;
bright conduct is followed.'
Máo Cháng (毛萇) said: '景 (jǐng)
means great.'
Zhèng Xuán (鄭玄) said: '景 (jǐng)
means bright.'
To aspire to be like the ancients,
if there are those with lofty virtue,
then one admires them;
if there are those with bright conduct,
then one emulates them.
行 (xíng)
is pronounced xià mèng fān.
If you were to admire Qǐ (起) and Yāng (鞅) in their governance,
how could this be what the men and women of this province expect?"
Guāng changed his expression and apologized to him.
Jǔqú Méngxùn (沮渠蒙遜) and his brothers raised an army,
and their reason for pushing Duàn Yè (段業) to a position of importance
was precisely because of these words, which earned him the respect and allegiance of the people of Liángzhōu (涼州).
8. Summer,
fourth month,
Wùwǔ (戊午):
Zhū Xù (朱序) was appointed Dūdū (都督) of the military affairs of the four provinces of Sī (司), Yōng (雍), Liáng (梁), and Qín (秦), and governor (刺史) of Yōngzhōu (雍州),
stationed in Luòyáng (洛陽).
Tián (恬), the King of Qiáo (譙), replaced Xù (序) as Dūdū (都督) of the military affairs of Yǎn (兗), Jì (冀), Yōu (幽), and Bīng (幷)
provinces, and governor (刺史) of Qīng (青) and Yǎn (兗) provinces.
9. Wànguó Rén (王國仁) of Yuànchuān (苑川) defeated the Xiānbēi (鮮卑) Yuèzhì Chìlí (越質叱黎) at Píngxiāng (平襄).
Píngxiāng (平襄) County
belonged to Tiānshuǐ (天水) Commandery during the Hàn (漢) dynasty,
and to Lüèyáng (略陽) Commandery during the Jìn (晉) dynasty.
Yuèzhì (越質) was likely the name of a Xiānbēi (鮮卑) tribe,
later adopted as a surname.
10. Dīnghài (丁亥):
The Yān (燕) ruler, Chuí (垂), established his consort, Lady Duàn (段氏), as Empress,
and appointed Crown Prince Bǎo (寶) as Dàshányú (大單于).
Lady Duàn (段氏) was the daughter of the Right Guānglù Dàfū (右光祿大夫), Yí (儀);
her younger sister married Dè (德), the King of Fányáng (范陽).
Yí (儀) was Bǎo's (寶) maternal uncle.
This lays the groundwork for Bǎo (寶) forcing the Duàn (段) Empress to commit suicide later.
The death of Lady Duàn (段氏) can be found in Volume 100, during the second year of Shēngpíng (升平) of Emperor Mù (穆).
11. Fifth month:
Qín (秦) Grand Younger Brother Yì (懿) died,
and was posthumously titled Xiàn'āi (獻哀).
12. Zhái Liáo (翟遼) moved his garrison to Huátái (滑臺).
Liáo (遼) moved his garrison from Líyáng (黎陽) to Huátái (滑臺),
having already broken ties with Yān (燕), desiring to rely on the river as a stronghold.
Huátái (滑臺) city is west of Báimǎ (白馬) County,
it was the Yányì (延邑) of Zhèng (鄭) Lǐn (廩) during the Spring and Autumn period,
and Huázhōu (滑州) during the Táng (唐) dynasty.
13. Sixth month:
Qífú Guórén (乞伏國仁), King of Yuànchuān (苑川), died,
and was posthumously titled Xuānliè (宣烈), with the temple name Lièzǔ (烈祖).
His son, Gōngfǔ (公府), was still young,
so his subordinates nominated Guórén's (國仁) younger brother, Gānkuí (乾歸), to be Dàdūdū (大都督), Dàjiāngjūn (大將軍), Dàshányú (大單于), and King of Hénán (河南).
At that time, the Qífú (乞伏) clan held territory across Liángzhōu (涼州) and Hénán (河南),
which then became the name of their state.
This lays the groundwork for Gōngfǔ (公府) killing Gānkuí (乾歸) later.
單 (shàn)
is pronounced chán (蟬).
The era name was changed to Tàichū (太初).
14. Wèi (魏) King Guī (珪) defeated the Kùmò Xī (庫莫奚) south of Ruòluò (弱落) River.
The *Xīn Tángshū* (新唐書) says: "The Xī (奚) were also of the Dōnghú (東胡) lineage,
defeated by the Xiōngnú (匈奴), and took refuge in Wūwán (烏丸) Mountain;
when Cáo Cāo (曹操) of Hàn (漢) beheaded Tàdùn (蹋頓), this was probably their descendants."
Ruòluò (弱落) River is the Ráolè (饒樂) River,
located within the Xī (奚) territory.
Seventh month:
The Kùmò Xī (庫莫奚) again attacked the Wèi (魏) camp,
and Guī (珪) again defeated them.
The Kùmò Xī (庫莫奚) originally belonged to the Yǔwén (宇文) tribe,
they are of the same category but different species as the Qìdān (契丹).
Their ancestors were all defeated by Yān (燕) King Huàng (皝),
and relocated between Sōngmò (松漠).
The Qìdān (契丹) state, from the West Tower, going forty *lǐ* (里) east,
reaches Zhēnzhū Zhài (真珠寨),
then continues east,
where the terrain gradually rises.
Looking west, the pine forest is lush,
for several tens of *lǐ* (里),
then enters a flat plain.
契 (qì)
is pronounced qī qì fān.
Hóng Mài (洪邁) said: "The pronunciation of Qìdān (契丹) is like chī,
only the *Xīn Tángshū* (新唐書) has this sound."
種 (zhǒng)
is pronounced zhāng yǒng fān.
15. Qín (秦) and Hòu Qín (後秦) had been at a standoff since spring,
with repeated battles and alternating victories and defeats,
until now they each withdrew.
The heroes and prominent figures of Guānxī (關西), seeing that Hòu Qín (後秦) had long failed to achieve success,
mostly left and joined Qín (秦).
16. Hénán (河南) King Gānkuí (乾歸) established his wife, Lady Biān (邊氏), as Queen;
he set up a bureaucracy,
imitating the Hàn (漢) system,
appointing Chūlián Qǐdū (出連乞都), the Marquis of Nánchuān (南川), as Chancellor (丞相).
Chūlián (出連) also took the name of his tribe as his surname.
Biān Ruì (邊芮) of Jīnchéng (金城) was appointed Left Chief Clerk (左長史),
Mì Yí (祕宜), the Governor (刺史) of Dōngqínzhōu (東秦州), as Right Chief Clerk (右長史).
The Qífú (乞伏) clan established Dōngqínzhōu (東秦州) in Nán'ān (南安).
Sōngshòu (松壽), the King of Lüèyáng (略陽), was appointed Chief Scribe (主簿).
His cousin, Kētán (軻彈), was appointed Shepherd (牧) of Liángzhōu (梁州);
his brother, Yìzhōu (益州), was appointed Shepherd (牧) of Qínzhōu (秦州);
and Qūjuàn (屈眷) was appointed Shepherd (牧) of Hézhōu (河州).
The Shepherds (牧) appointed by Qífú Gānkuí (乞伏乾歸)
merely divided their residences between the Hé (河) and Lǒng (隴) regions.
從 (cóng)
is pronounced cái yòng fān.
17. Eighth month:
Qín (秦) Ruler Dēng (登) established his son Chóng (崇) as Crown Prince,
Biàn (弁) as King of Nán'ān (南安),
and Shàng (尚) as King of Běihǎi (北海).
18. Yān (燕) Protector-General (護軍將軍) Píng Yòu (平幼) joined Zhāngwǔ (章武) King Zhòu (宙) in attacking Wú Shēn (吳深).
They defeated him,
and Shēn (深) fled to defend Yìmù (繹幕).
Yìmù (繹幕) County
had belonged to Qīnghé (清河) Commandery since the Hàn (漢) dynasty.
19. Wèi (魏) King Guī (珪) secretly harbored the ambition to conquer Yān (燕).
He sent Gōng Yí (公儀), the Duke of Jiǔyuán (九原), as an envoy to Zhōngshān (中山).
Yān (燕) Ruler Chuí (垂) questioned him, saying:
"Why did Wèi (魏) King not come himself?"
Yí (儀) replied:
"Our former kings and Yān (燕) both served the Jìn (晉) court and
were brothers for generations.
Wèi (魏) and Yān (燕) are both of Xiānbēi (鮮卑) stock.
Tuòbá Lìwēi (拓跋力微) and Mùróng Shèguī (慕容涉歸) both served the Jìn (晉) court.
This is not contrary to reason."
Chuí (垂) said:
"My might now extends across the four seas;
how can things be compared to former days!"
Yí (儀) replied:
"If Yān (燕) does not cultivate virtue and propriety,
but wishes to strengthen itself through military might,
this is a matter for generals,
not for an envoy like me."
Upon his return, Yí (儀) reported to Guī (珪), saying:
"The Yān (燕) ruler is old and frail,
and the Crown Prince is dim-witted and weak.
The King of Fányáng (范陽) is confident in his talent and spirit;
at this time Mùróng Dé (慕容德) among the Yān (燕) imperial clan certainly had qualities unlike others.
Once the Yān (燕) ruler dies,
internal strife is bound to erupt.
That will be the time to make plans.
Now is not the time."
Guī (珪) approved of his words.
This lays the groundwork for Wèi (魏) attacking Yān (燕) later.
Guī (珪) was the son of his maternal younger brother,
Hàn (翰).
20. Ninth month:
Hénán (河南) King Gānkuí (乾歸) moved his capital to Jīnchéng (金城).
21. Zhāng Shēn (張申) attacked Guǎngpíng (廣平),
and Wáng Zǔ (王祖) attacked Lèlíng (樂陵).
Rénwǔ (壬午):
Yān (燕) King Gāoyáng (高陽), Lóng (隆), led troops to attack them.
22. Winter,
tenth month:
Hòu Qín (後秦) Ruler Cháng (萇) returned to Āndìng (安定).
Qín (秦) Ruler Dēng (登) advanced to Xīnpíng (新平) for provisions,
leading over ten thousand men to besiege Cháng's (萇) camp.
They cried loudly from all four sides.
Cháng (萇) ordered those in his camp to cry in response,
whereupon Dēng (登) retreated.
23. Twelfth month,
Gēngzǐ (庚子):
Shàngshū Lìng (尚書令), Nánkāng Xiānggōng (南康襄公) Xiè Shí (謝石), died.
24 Yàn (燕) Tàiyuán (太原) King Kǎi (楷) and Zhào (趙) King Lín (麟) led troops to meet Gāoyáng (高陽) King Lóng (隆) at Hékǒu (合口).
The Shuǐ Jīng (水經) states: The Héngzhāng (衡漳) River passes through Chéngjiàn (建成) County in Bóhǎi (勃海),
then flows east.
On its left, it meets the old channel of the Hūtúo (呼沱) tributary.
Then it flows northeast into the Qīnghé (清河),
which is called Hékǒu (合口).
Wèi Shōu’s (魏收) Dìxíng Zhì (地形志) says: Fúyáng (浮陽) County borders the Zhāngshuǐ (漳水) to the west.
The Héngshuǐ (衡水) flows into it there,
and is now called Hékǒu (合口).
Wáng Zǔ (王祖) led all the garrisons to rescue him.
They attacked the Yàn (燕) army by night.
The Yàn (燕) people met and repelled them,
putting them to flight.
Lóng (隆) wanted to pursue them.
Kǎi (楷) and Lín (麟) said:
"Wáng Zǔ (王祖) is an old rogue.
We fear he might be feigning retreat and setting an ambush.
It's better to wait until dawn."
Lóng (隆) said:
"These are mere bandits from an open field,
who gathered like crows.
They're hoping for a lucky victory.
They don't have long-standing discipline,
nor can they unify their advance and retreat.
Now that they've suffered a loss and fled,
their forces are disunited.
If we pursue them while riding the momentum,
within just a few *lǐ* (里),
we can capture them all.
Shēn’s (申) only reliance
is on Zǔ (祖).
If Zǔ (祖) is defeated,
then Shēn (申) will surrender."
So he left Kǎi (楷) and Lín (麟) to guard Shēn’s (申) camp.
Lóng (隆) and Píng Yòu (平幼) attacked them from different directions.
By dawn,
they had gained a great victory and returned,
displaying the captured heads to Shēn (申).
On the *jiǎyín* (甲寅) day,
Shēn (申) came out and surrendered.
Zǔ (祖) also confessed his guilt.
25 Qín (秦) appointed Yǐngchuān (潁川) King Tóngchéng (同成) as Tàiwèi (太尉).
Tóngchéng (同成)
was the elder brother of Qín (秦) ruler Dēng (登).
14th Year (389 CE, *Jǐchǒu* (己丑))
1 Spring,
1st month.
Yàn (燕) appointed Yángpíng (陽平) King Róu (柔) to garrison Xiāngguó (襄國).
Liáoxī (遼西) King Nóng (農) had been in Lóngchéng (龍城) for five years.
Having managed all affairs well,
he submitted a memorial which said:
"Your servant, having been sent to the frontier in the course of a campaign,
Nóng (農) executed Yú Yán (餘巖),
and attacked Gāogōulí (高句麗),
then garrisoned Lóngchéng (龍城).
See Volume 10 of the previous scroll.
The remaining bandits in Qīng (青), Xú (徐), Jīng (荊), and Yōng (雍) are still numerous.
I wish to return for a period
and exert my humble efforts.
To have no strength left while alive,
and no regrets when dead,
that is your servant's ambition!"
On the *gēngshēn* (庚申) day,
Yàn (燕) ruler Chuí (垂) summoned Nóng (農) to be Shìzhōng (侍中) and Sīlì Xiàowèi (司隸校尉).
He appointed Gāoyáng (高陽) King Lóng (隆) as Dūdū Yōu-Píng Èrzhōu Zhūjūnshì (都督幽‧平二州諸軍事), Zhēngběi Dàjiāngjūn (征北大將軍), and Yōuzhōu Mù (幽州牧).
He established a Liútái (留臺) in Lóngchéng (龍城),
and appointed Lóng (隆) to oversee the Shàngshū matters of the Liútái (留臺).
He also appointed Hùjūn Jiāngjūn (護軍將軍) Píng Yòu (平幼) as Zhēngběi Chángshǐ (征北長史),
and Sànqí Chángshì (散騎常侍) Fēng Fú (封孚) as Sīmǎ (司馬),
both concurrently serving as Liútái Shàngshū (留臺尚書).
Lóng (隆) followed Nóng’s (農) former regulations,
improved and expanded upon them,
and thus Liáo (遼) and Jié (碣) became peaceful.
Liáo (遼) and Jié (碣)
refer to the Liáoshuǐ (遼水) and Jiéshí (碣石).
Jié (碣),
pronounced *qiè*.
2 Later Qín (秦) ruler Cháng (萇), seeing that the Qín (秦) army had repeatedly won battles,
believed he had the divine aid of Qín (秦) King Jiān (堅).
He also erected an image of Jiān (堅) in his army and prayed to it, saying:
"My elder brother Xiāng (襄) ordered me to avenge him.
In the 1st year of Mùdì’s (穆帝) Shēngpíng (升平) era,
Yáo Xiāng (姚襄)
was killed by Qín (秦).
See Volume 10 of the previous scroll.
This was not my fault.
Fú Dēng (苻登),
a distant relative of Your Majesty,
still seeks revenge.
How could I dare to forget my brother!
Moreover, Your Majesty commanded me to establish my career with the title Lóngxiáng (龍驤).
See Volume 105, 8th year.
Xiáng (驤),
pronounced *jiāng*.
Now I erect an image for Your Majesty.
May Your Majesty not hold my transgressions against me."
Qín (秦) ruler Dēng (登) ascended a tower
and remotely called out to Cháng (萇), saying:
"As a subject, to murder his lord,
and then erect an image to seek blessings—
what good will that do!"
He then shouted loudly:
"You regicidal thief Yáo Cháng (姚萇), why don't you come out yourself!
I will settle this with you!"
Cháng (萇) did not respond.
After a long time,
as the battle had not turned favorable,
and there were several scares in the army every night,
he cut off the image's head and sent it to Qín (秦).
3 Qín (秦) ruler Dēng (登) appointed Hénán (河南) King Gān’guī (乾歸) as Dàjiāngjūn (大將軍), Dà Chányú (大單于), and Jīnchéng (金城) King.
4 On the *jiǎyín* (甲寅) day,
Wèi (魏) King Guī (珪) attacked the Gāochē (高車),
and defeated them.
5 2nd month.
Lǚ Guāng (呂光) proclaimed himself Sānhé (三河) King.
Lǚ Guāng’s (呂光) courtesy name was Shìmíng (世明).
Guāng (光) at this time held the territory of Liángzhōu (涼州) and Héxī (河西),
but had not yet been able to fully possess Sānhé (三河).
He changed the era name to Línjiā (麟嘉),
and appointed civil and military officials.
Guāng’s (光) wife Shí Shì (石氏), son Shào (紹), and younger brother Déshì (德世) came from Qiúchí (仇池) to Gūzāng (姑臧).
During the chaos in Cháng’ān (長安),
Lǚ Guāng’s (呂光) family fled to Qiúchí (仇池) and relied on the Yáng (楊) family.
Shào (紹) was made Crown Prince.
6 On the *guǐsì* (癸巳) day,
Wèi (魏) King Guī (珪) attacked the Tǔtūlín (吐突鄰) tribe at Nǚshuǐ (女水).
Nǚshuǐ (女水) is west of Ruòluòshuǐ (弱落水),
over 3,000 *lǐ* (里) from Píngchéng (平城).
Later, Wèi Xiǎnzǔ (魏顯祖) renamed it Wǔchuān (武川).
He completely relocated their tribes and returned.
7 Qín (秦) ruler Dēng (登) left his baggage train at Dàjiè (大界).
Dàjiè (大界)
should be between Āndìng (安定) and Xīnpíng (新平).
Zhòng (重),
pronounced *zhòng*.
He conquered it.

Zhái Liáo (翟遼) raided Xíngyáng (滎陽),
and captured the Grand Administrator Zhāng Zhuó (張卓).
9 Yàn (燕) appointed Chánglè (長樂) Duke Shèng (盛) to garrison Jìchéng (薊城),
and repair the old palace.
Yàn (燕) ruler Jùn (儁) had initially moved his capital from Lóngchéng (龍城) to Jì (薊),
where the old palace was located.
Lè (樂),
pronounced *luò*.
Jì (薊),

Gān’guī (乾歸) bestowed official ranks and noble titles upon them all.
11 Later Qín (秦) ruler Cháng (萇) fought Qín (秦) ruler Dēng (登) and was defeated several times.
So he sent Zhōngjūn Jiāngjūn (中軍將軍) Yáo Chóng (姚崇) to raid Dàjiè (大界).
Dēng (登) ambushed him at Ānqīu (安丘).
Wèi Shōu’s (魏收) Dìxíng Zhì (地形志) states: Āncūn (安村) County in Āndìng (安定) has Ānchéng (安城).
12 Yàn (燕) Fányáng (范陽) King Dé (德) and Zhào (趙) King Lín (麟) attacked Hè Nà (賀訥).
They pursued the fleeing enemy to Wùgēn (勿根) Mountain.
Nà (訥), in desperation, requested to surrender.
He was relocated to Shànggǔ (上谷),
and his younger brother Rǎngān (染干) was held as hostage in Zhōngshān (中山).
13 Autumn,
7th month.
Pìqí Chángshǐ (驃騎長史) Wáng Chén (王忱) was appointed Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ (荊州刺史) and Dūdū Jīng-Yì-Níng Sānzhōu Zhūjūn (都督荊‧益‧寧三州諸軍).
Chén (忱)
was Guóbǎo’s (國寶) younger brother.
14 Qín Lord Dēng attacked Hòu Qín Right General Wú Zhōng and others at Píngliáng,
and captured it.
In the eighth month,
Dēng occupied Gǒutóu Yuán to press Āndìng.
The generals advised Hòu Qín Lord Cháng to fight a decisive battle,
but Cháng said:
"Competing for victory with cornered enemies
is forbidden by military strategists;
I will take them by strategy."
So, he left Grand Secretary Yáo Mín to guard Āndìng,
and at night,
led thirty thousand cavalry
to raid Qín's baggage train at Dàjiè.
He captured it,
as they valued their baggage too much and neglected their defenses;
this was why Fú Dēng was defeated.
"重" (zhòng),
pronounced as "zhí yòng fān."
Shàng (尚),
Shàng (尚),
was Qín Lord Dēng's son.
They plundered over fifty thousand men and women and returned.
Lady Máo was beautiful and courageous,
skilled in horsemanship and archery.
When the Hòu Qín army entered her camp,
Lady Máo still drew her bow and mounted her horse,
leading several hundred brave men
to fight.
Their numbers

you have already killed the Son of Heaven,
referring to the killing of Qín King Jiān.
Will August Heaven and Sovereign Earth
tolerate you?"
Cháng killed her.
The generals wanted to use the Qín army's panic and chaos to attack them,
but Cháng said:
"Although Dēng's forces are in disarray,
their anger is still fierce;
they cannot be taken lightly."
So, he stopped.
Those victorious in battle become arrogant,
and those angered in battle become ferocious.
If one meets ferocity with arrogance,
then those who are first defeated and then victorious are many.
Yáo Cháng saw the military situation
and therefore rallied his troops and stopped.
Cháng sent Yáo Shuòdé to garrison Āndìng,
moved over one thousand households from Āndìng to Yīnmì,
and dispatched his younger brother, General Zheng'nán Jìng, to garrison it.
15 In the ninth month,
on the day Gēngwǔ,
Right Grandee Secretary Lù Nà was appointed Grand Secretary.
16 When Qín Lord Dēng went east,
Hòu Qín Lord Cháng sent Yáo Shuòdé to appoint prefects and magistrates in Qínzhōu,
appointing his cousin Cháng to garrison Lǒngchéng,
Xíng Nú to garrison Jìchéng,
and Yáo Xiáng to garrison Lüèyáng.
Yáng Dìng attacked Lǒng and Jì,
captured them,
beheaded Cháng,
and captured Xíng Nú;
Xiáng abandoned Lüèyáng and
fled to Yīnmì.
Dìng proclaimed himself Governor of Qínzhōu and King of Lǒngxī;
Qín then granted him these titles as he claimed them.
17 In winter,
in the tenth month,
Qín Lord Dēng appointed Dòu Chōng as Grand Marshal, Grand Controller of all military affairs east of Lǒng, and Governor of Yōngzhōu;
and Yáng Dìng as Left Chancellor, Grand Controller of all military affairs within and without, and Governor of Qín and Liáng two prefectures.
They agreed to jointly attack Hòu Qín;

he also arranged for Supervisor of military affairs west of the Yellow River and Inspector of Bìngzhōu, Yáng Zhèng, and Controller of military affairs east of the Yellow River and Inspector of Jìzhōu, Yáng Kǎi, to each lead their forces to meet at Cháng'ān.
Zhèng and Kǎi were both from Hédōng.
After Qín Lord Pī was defeated,
Zhèng and Kǎi gathered tens of thousands of displaced households.
Zhèng occupied the area west of the Yellow River,
and Kǎi occupied the area between Hú and Shǎn,

Dēng then granted them their titles.
After Dàjiè fell, Fú Dēng's military power declined,
hence he made arrangements with Dòu Chōng and others to jointly attack Hòu Qín.
"陝" (Shǎn),
pronounced as "shì rǎn fān."
"使" (shǐ),

The Yàn Inspector of Jìzhōu governed Xìndū.
Lèlàng (樂浪),
pronounced as "luò láng."
Hé Chéngtiān's Xìngyuàn contains the old surname.
"帳" (zhàng),

Púhǎn Qiāng Péng Xīniàn pledged allegiance to Qǐfú Gān'guī,

Púhǎn was formerly the seat of Hézhōu.

appointing Qū Juàn as its governor,
hence Púhǎn was made Běihézhōu,

pronounced as "fū."
20 Initially,
the Emperor personally managed state affairs.
In the first year of Tàiyuán, Empress Dowager Chóngdé returned governance,
and the Emperor began to personally manage state affairs.
He possessed the qualities of a ruler.
However, he later indulged in wine and women,
entrusting affairs to Prince Dàozǐ of Lángyá.
Dàozǐ also loved wine,
and spent his days and nights with the Emperor in revelry and song.
He also highly esteemed Buddhism,
indulging in extreme luxury and extravagance,
and those he was intimate with were all wet nurses and Buddhist monks and nuns.
His close attendants
vied for power,
engaged in illicit influence peddling,
and bribery was rampant.
Official rewards were chaotic and disorderly,
and legal judgments were erroneous and perverse.
Grand Secretary Lù Nà looked at the palace and sighed, saying:
"What a fine household! Is this delicate child trying to smash it?"
The Left Guard Commander of the encampment, Xǔ Yíng of Kuàijī
served as Left Guard General and commanded the encampment soldiers,
hence he was called Left Guard Commander of the encampment.
Xǔ Yíng (許營),
is also written as
"Róng" (榮).
"Now, bureau officials of the central government, military officers of the imperial guard, and even servants and slave girls who take their mother's surname
(children born from private liaisons of official slave girls,
whose father cannot be clearly identified,
thus take their mother's surname as their own)
all get to become commandery governors and county magistrates.
Some hold official positions within the palace,
and monks, nuns, and wet nurses
compete to advance their relatives and factions,
and also accept bribes.
They frequently take charge of offices and lead the populace,
making governance and education unfair,
acting oppressively and lawlessly.
Prohibitions are unclear,
and robbery is rampant.
Last year, a decree was issued ordering all below to offer suggestions,
but although many opinions were gathered,
none were adopted.
I have heard that Buddha
is a pure, distant, profound, and ethereal deity.
Now, monks and nuns often rely on their religious attire,
yet they cannot even follow the rough laws of the five precepts,
let alone the subtle ones!
The Buddha has five precepts:
no illicit sexual conduct,
no stealing,
no killing,
no false speech,
and no indulging in alcohol.
Yet people compete to revere them,
and they also exploit the common people,
taking wealth as 'benevolence,'
which also does not accord with the way of giving. "
This memorial was submitted,
but it was not heeded.

"This is how King Chéng (Chéng) honored the Duke of Zhōu (Zhōu Gōng).

grew angry,

As Níng (Níng) was about to depart,
he submitted a memorial stating:
"Today, border beacons are not raised, yet granaries are empty.
In ancient times, people were employed for no more than three days a year.
(The 'Wángzhì' (Wángzhì) records: 'In ancient times, the strength of the people was used for no more than three days a year,
the work of the elderly was taken on,

and widowers and widows dare not marry.

('Placing fire on piled firewood'

"The gentry and commoners of the Central Plains (Zhōngyuán) who have drifted to the south of the Yangzi River (Jiāngzuǒ)
have grown accustomed to their livelihoods over the years.
Originally, the ancestors of all people under heaven
migrated with the times;
why should they alone be unable to do so now?
It is appropriate to rectify their territorial divisions,
and all households should be settled according to their land (tǔ duàn).
(During the Jìn (Jìn) dynasty, gentry and commoners from the Central Plains (Zhōngyuán) who moved south
were settled in newly established commanderies and counties in the Jiangzuǒ (Jiāngzuǒ) region,
not according to their actual place of residence (tǔzhù) for taxation.
Duàn (Duàn),
Ding Luan Fan (Dīng Luàn Fān).)
Human nature is boundless,
and extravagance or frugality depends on circumstances.
Now, even households that have annexed much land
often find themselves in want.
It is not that their financial resources are insufficient,
but rather that their expenditures are unrestrained,
as they compete in ostentation and luxury,
without limit.
(In Rites, a 'chángshāng' (chángshāng) is a person who dies at nineteen,

Cháng (Cháng),

At thirteen, one is considered 'half a male adult' (bàndīng).
If the tasks assigned are no longer those of children,
how can it not violate natural principles and burden the common people?
It is fitting to consider twenty as a full adult male (quándīng),
