Then people would not suffer premature death,
and the population would thrive and multiply."
The Emperor adopted much of his advice.
While Níng (Níng) was in Yùzhāng (Yùzhāng),
he dispatched fifteen Councilors (Yìcáo) to the subordinate counties.

(Yùzhāng (Yùzhāng) administered sixteen counties: Nánchāng (Nánchāng), Hǎihūn (Hǎihūn), Xīngàn (Xīngàn), Jiànchéng (Jiànchéng), Wàngcài (Wàngcài), Yǒngxiū (Yǒngxiū), Jiànchāng (Jiànchāng), Wúpíng (Wúpíng), Yùzhāng (Yùzhāng), Péngzé (Péngzé), Ài (Ài), Kānglè (Kānglè), Fēngchéng (Fēngchéng), Xīnchāng (Xīnchāng), Yífēng (Yífēng), and Zhōnglíng (Zhōnglíng).
One county was near the commandery seat,
and the other fifteen counties each had one Councilor (Yìcáo) dispatched to them.
Xià (Xià),
Xiá Jià Fān (Xiá Jià Fān).)
These, together with officials on leave,
inquired into the merits and demerits of local officials.
Xú Miǎo (Xú Miǎo) wrote to Níng (Níng), saying:
"If your administration is clear and fair,
and all matters proceed without impediment,
then officials will be cautious about their faults.
(Fù (Fù)
refers to guilt.
If officials fear guilt,
then they will be more diligent in every matter.
Duàn (Duàn),
Dīng Luàn Fān (Dīng Luàn Fān).
Rén Tīng (Rén Tīng)
means Mín Tīng (Mín Tīng).
The court historians of the Jìnshū (Jìnshū) avoided the taboo name of Emperor Tàizōng (Tàizōng) of Táng (Táng),
changing Mín (Mín) to
'Rén' (Rén),
and the Zīzhì Tōngjiàn (Zīzhì Tōngjiàn) followed suit.)
How can you adorn their idle rumors?
Not only will it bring no benefit,
but it will actually be a source of 'silkworm and fish' (cányú)."
('Silkworm and fish' (Cányú)
refers to those dispatched preying on and exploiting the people.
Zhèng Xuán (Zhèng Xuán) said: 'Shí' (Shí) and 'Shí' (Shí) (寔, 實) are homophones east of Zhào (Zhào) and Wèi (Wèi).
'Shí' (Shí) (寔)
means 'is.'
The 'Shī' (Shī) says:
'Shí yǒng shí hè,
shí mǔ shí jí.'
'Shí' (Shí) (實)
should be written as
'Shí' (Shí) (寔).
It means that the ancestors of Hán Hóu (Hán Hóu) were weak,
and many of the states they received were destroyed.
Now, their old positions are restored,
and lost lineages are continued.
Therefore, this city is built and repaired,
these ditches and wells are mended,
these fields are cultivated,
and these taxes are collected,
returning them to their former state.
Kǒng Yǐngdá (Kǒng Yǐngdá) said: 'Generally, when "shí" (實) is used, there must already be the matter before it is "shí" (實) (realized).
Now, this passage speaks of what should not be 'shí' (實) (realized),
so it is changed to 'shí' (寔),
meaning 'is.'
East of Zhào (Zhào) and Wèi (Wèi), 'shí' (寔) and 'shí' (實) are homophones;
Zhèng (Zhèng) verified this with contemporary usage.
In the sixth year of Duke Huán (Huán) in the 'Chūnqiū' (Chūnqiū),
it says: 'Zhōugōng (Zhōugōng) shí lái' (寔來).
This is because they are homophones,
so the character changed.
I observe that Xú Miǎo's (Xú Miǎo) interpretation of 'shí' (寔) as 'is'
also makes sense.)
Will there be many who come to make accusations?
Since ancient times,
those who wished to serve as 'ears and eyes'
were all petty individuals,
who first used small loyalties to achieve great disloyalty,
and first relied on small trusts to achieve great distrust,
thus allowing slander and flattery to advance together,
and good and evil to be inverted.
How can one not be cautious?
You should carefully select your 'gāngjì' (gāngjì) (subordinates).
(A commandery's 'gāngjì' (gāngjì) refers to its subordinate officials.)
If all departments have good officials to manage documents and records,
(Shè (Shè)
means 'to gather,' 'to organize.'
Àn (Àn)
means 'to base on.'
Wén'àn (Wén'àn) refers to documents from various departments kept as records.)
then clarity or turbidity, competence or incompetence,
will become apparent through their work.
You merely need to handle matters with a fair mind;
what need is there for 'ears and eyes'?
In the past, the Virtuous Empress Mǎ (Mǎ) never spoke directly with her attendants.
(Empress Mǎ (Mǎ) of Emperor Míng (Míng) of Hàn (Hàn) was posthumously honored as 'Míngdé Huánghòu' (Míngdé Huánghòu).)
How much more so should a true man be able to avoid this!"
On the 21st day of the twelfth month,
Yáo Cháng, ruler of Hòu Qín, sent his East Gate General, Rèn Péng,
the East Gate General,
whom Cháng had put in charge of guarding the East Gate of Āndìng.
Rèn,
has the sound of 'rén'.
Péng,
is the same as 盆 (pén),
pronounced 'pú bēn fān'.
to offer to open the gate and let him in.
Fú Dēng was about to follow,
when Zhēngdōng Jiāngjūn Léi Èdì, who was leading troops outside,
Jiāng,
pronounced 'jí liàng fān'.
rode swiftly to see Dēng,
and said:
"Yáo Cháng is full of tricks
and cannot be trusted!"
Dēng then stopped.
When Cháng heard that Èdì had gone to Dēng,
he said to his generals:
"This Qiāng has seen Dēng,
so the plan will not succeed!"
Dēng, considering Èdì's extraordinary courage and strategy,
secretly feared him.
Èdì, in fear,
surrendered to Hòu Qín.
Cháng appointed Èdì as Zhènjūn Jiāngjūn.
Qín appointed Ānchéng Wáng Guǎng as Sītú.
Fifteenth Year (Gēngyín, 390 CE)
1 In spring,
the first month,
on the Yǐhài day,
Qiáo Jìng Wáng Tián passed away.
2 Mùróng Yǒng, ruler of Xī Yàn, led his troops towards Luòyáng.
Zhū Xù crossed the Yellow River north from Héyīn
and defeated him.
Xù pursued him to Báishuǐ.
The Shuǐjīng Zhù states: Báishuǐ flows out from the west of the old city of Gāodū County in Shàngdǎng,
and flows east, passing through Tiānjǐng Guān.
The place Xù reached
was 160 lǐ from Chángzǐ.
Coincidentally, Zhái Liáo was planning to move towards Luòyáng,
so Xù led his troops back
and defeated him;
he left Yīngyáng Jiāngjūn Zhū Dǎng to garrison Shímén,
and ordered his son, Zhū Luè, to supervise Luòyáng,
assisted by Cānjūn Zhào Fān,
while he himself returned to Xiāngyáng.
3 Lángyá Wáng Dàozǐ, relying on imperial favor, became arrogant and indulgent, getting drunk at banquets
and sometimes violating proper etiquette.
The emperor grew increasingly displeased and wished to select esteemed figures as regional governors to secretly curb Dàozǐ.
He asked Tàizǐ Zuǒwèilǜ Wáng Yǎ:
"What do you think of my intention to appoint Wáng Gōng and Yīn Zhòngkān?"
Yǎ replied:
"Wáng Gōng has a noble demeanor and dignified spirit,
with a steadfast and solemn character;
Zhòngkān is meticulous in small details
and renowned for his literary talent.
However, both are rigid, narrow-minded, and self-righteous,
and lack outstanding strategic ability;
if entrusted with regional command,
in times of peace,
they would be sufficient to hold their positions,
but if trouble arises,
they will surely become instigators of chaos!"
The emperor did not heed him.
This laid the groundwork for Wáng and Yīn later raising troops.
He was Yùn's son;
Wáng Yùn
was the Empress's father.
He was Róng's grandson.
Yīn Róng is mentioned in volume 96, during Emperor Chéng's Xiánkāng 5th year.
On the Xīnsì day,
Wáng Gōng, the Zhōngshū Lìng, was appointed Dūdū of Qīng, Yǎn, Yōu, Bīng, and Jì five prefectures' military affairs, and Governor of Yǎn and Qīng prefectures,
garrisoned at Jīngkǒu.
4 In the third month,
on the Wùchén day,
a general amnesty was declared.
5 Yáo Cháng, ruler of Hòu Qín, attacked Qín's Fúfēng Tàishǒu Qí Yìnán at Xīnluóbǎo
and captured it.
Yìnán fled.
Fú Dēng, ruler of Qín, attacked Hòu Qín's Tiānshuǐ Tàishǒu Zhāng Yèshēng in Lǒngdōng.
Lǒngdōng
was part of Jīngyáng County in Āndìng.
Dēng then withdrew.
6 In summer,
the fourth month,
Qín's Zhèndōng Jiāngjūn Wèi Jiēfēi declared himself Chōngtiān Wáng.
The Jìnshū Zàijì records him as
"Wèi Hèfēi."
In the first year of Tàiyuán,
Qín sent Tíngzhōng Jiāngjūn Wèi Héfēi to attack the Dī and Qiāng,
presumably referring to this person.
Zhènjūn Jiāngjūn Léi Èdì rebelled and responded to him,
attacking Zhèndōng Jiāngjūn Yáo Hàn dé at Lǐrùn.
Lǐrùn
is a place name,
south of Xíngwàng.
Lǐ Yánshòu stated: East of Féngyì is Lǐrùn Town.
According to the Wèishū Zōngshì Lièzhuàn,
Āndìng Wáng Xiè's memorial upon being appointed Huázhōu Cìshǐ said:
"I humbly observe that the prefectural seat is in Lǐrùn Fort.
Although it is the old land of Shàoliáng,
and the granted territory of Jìn and Ruì,
the Hú and Yí tribes have since assimilated
and formed encampments here.
I request to move it to the ancient city of Féngyì."
All his ministers said:
"Your Majesty does not worry about Fú Dēng, who is sixty lǐ away
(at that time, Dēng was heading towards Cháng'ān
and occupying Qiānhù Gù in Xīnfēng),
why is that?"
Cháng replied:
"Dēng cannot be quickly eliminated,
and my city cannot be quickly taken by Dēng either.
Èdì's intelligence and strategy are extraordinary;
if he leads Jiēfēi south
and allies with Dǒng Chéng in the east
(Dǒng Chéng was of the Túcì tribe
and at that time occupied Běidì),
the northeast of Cháng'ān will not be ours."
Thereupon, he secretly led 1,600 elite troops to confront them.
Jiēfēi and Èdì had tens of thousands of troops,
with Dī and Hú tribesmen continuously flocking to them.
Every time Cháng saw a new army arrive,
he would rejoice.
His ministers found this strange and asked him,
Cháng said:
"Jiēfēi and others are instigating and seducing evildoers,
and their factions are very numerous.
Although I can defeat their leaders,
the remaining factions will not be easy to pacify quickly;
now they are gathering like crows,
and I will seize them in victory,
so they can be wiped out in one fell swoop."
This was Cáo Cāo's old strategy for defeating Mǎ Chāo and Hán Suì.
He led all his troops to attack them;
Cháng held his ground without fighting,
showing weakness,
and secretly sent his son, Zhōngjūn Jiāngjūn Chóng, to lead several hundred cavalry to attack their rear.
Jiēfēi's army became chaotic.
Cháng sent Zhènyuǎn Jiāngjūn Wáng Chāo and others to unleash their troops and attack them,
beheading Jiēfēi and over ten thousand of his officers and soldiers.
Èdì requested to surrender,
and Cháng treated him as before.
Èdì said to others:
"I considered myself to be outstanding in wisdom and courage for a time,
but every time I met Old Man Yáo, I was in trouble;
it is my destiny!"
Cháng ordered Yáo Dāngchéng to mark his encampment area,
planting a tree in each fence opening to commemorate the battle's achievements.
Holes were dug in the ground,
and wooden stakes were erected to form a fence,
hence "fence opening."
When asked,
Dāngchéng said:
"The camp was too small,
so I have expanded it."
Cháng said:
"Since I came of age,
when fighting against others,
I have never had such exhilaration.
With little over a thousand troops, I defeated an army of thirty thousand.
A small camp is extraordinary;
why should a large one be valued?"
7 Tùyùhùn Shìlián sent envoys to pay respects to Jīnchéng Wáng Gān Guī.
Gān Guī appointed Shìlián as Shāzhōu Mù and Báilán Wáng.

Zhāng Mào of Héxī controlled Dūnhuáng, Jìnchāng, the Protectorate of the Western Regions, the Commandant, and the Commander of Yùmén Pass, comprising three commanderies and three garrisons, as Shāzhōu;
Tùyùhùn had not yet taken control of that land.
Lǐ Yánshòu stated: This refers to the Tùyùhùn territory having yellow sands,
extending for several hundred lǐ in circumference,
where no grass or trees grew,
and thus it was named Shāzhōu.
Shǐ,
pronounced 'shū lì fān'.
Xiàn,
pronounced 'xián biàn fān'.
8 On the Bǐngyín day,
Wèi Wáng Guī met Yàn Zhào Wáng Lín at Yìxīn Shān.
Yìxīn Shān is north of Niúchuān,
where the Hèlán tribe resided.
According to the Běishǐ,
it was north of the Yīnshān Mountains,
where the Hèlán tribe was.
He defeated him,
and Gētūlín and Gēxī both surrendered to Wèi.
The histories say Yàn cleared the way for Wèi.
Jiàng,
pronounced 'hù jiāng fān'.
9 Autumn.
In the seventh month,
Guō Zhì, a man from Fēngyì, raised troops in Guǎngxiāng to respond to Qín.
Wèi Shōu’s Dìxíng Zhì states:
Zhèngxiàn has the Guǎngxiāng Yuán.
Zhèngxiàn at that time belonged to Jīngzhào.
“Yáo Cháng is cruel and oppressive,
his poison reaching even the gods and men.
We have for generations enjoyed the benevolence of the former emperors Yáo and Shùn.
‘Former emperors’
refers to Qín’s ruler Jiān.
Chángbó
is a Shìzhōng.
Nàyán
is a Shàngshū.
Rather than live in shame,
how can it compare to dying upholding the Dao?”
Thereupon, all the garrisons and fortresses in Sānfǔ responded to him;
only Gǒu Yào, a man from Zhèngxiàn,
gathered several thousand followers and attached himself to Later Qín.
Qín appointed Guō Zhì as Fēngyì Tàishǒu.
Later Qín appointed Gǒu Yào as Yùzhōu Cìshǐ.
Later, Gǒu Yào played both sides,
and was killed by Later Qín.
The details are given later.
10 Liú Wèichén sent his son Zhílìdī to attack the Hèlán tribe.
Hè Nè was in distress and difficulty,
and requested to surrender to Wèi.
On the bǐngzǐ day,
Wèi Wáng Guī led troops to rescue him.
Zhílìdī retreated.
Guī relocated Nè’s tribe,
settling them in the eastern territory.
11 In the eighth month,
Liú Láozhī attacked Zhái Zhāo at Juànchéng.
Zhāo fled north of the Yellow River;
he also defeated Zhái Liáo at Huátái.
Zhāng Yuàn came to surrender.
Zhái Liáo and Zhāng Yuàn rebelled,
as seen in volume 11 of the previous scroll.
“Zǒu”
is pronounced “zòu.”
“Bài”
is pronounced “bǔmài fān.”
“Juàn”
is pronounced “juàn.”
12 In the ninth month,
Wú Zhù, a man from Běipíng, gathered over a thousand people
and established the shāmen Fǎcháng as emperor.
They broke through Běipíng Jùn,
then invaded Guǎngdū,
and entered Báiláng Chéng.
Báiláng Xiàn,
in the Former Hàn, belonged to Yòu Běipíng Jùn.
In the Later Hàn and Jìn, it was abolished.
Wèi Shōu’s Dìxíng Zhì states: in the eighth year of Zhēnjūn of Later Wèi,
Jiàndé Jùn was established,
governed from Báiláng Chéng,
and Guǎngdū Xiàn was subordinate to it.
During the Yàn period, it should have belonged to Běipíng Jùn.
The jùnxiàn shǒuzǎi all gathered.
The populace heard that Zhù had rebelled,
and requested Lóng to return to the city,
and send a large army to suppress him.
Lóng said:
“Currently, the common people are living in peace,
and do not desire chaos.
Zhù and others have used deceitful schemes to confuse foolish people,
and lured and coerced them to gather.
They are incapable of accomplishing anything.”
So he stayed until the burial was finished,
and sent the Guǎngpíng Tàishǒu and Guǎngdū Lìng to return first.
“Guǎngpíng”
should be
“Běipíng.”
When Zhù’s followers heard this,
they all dispersed.
They were pursued and captured,
and he was executed.
13 Wáng Guóbǎo, the Shìzhōng, was made Zhōngshū Lìng,
and soon also concurrently Zhōnglǐngjūn.
This was under Dàozǐ’s patronage.
14 On the dīngwèi day,
Wáng Xún, the Wújùn Tàishǒu, was appointed Shàngshū Yòu Púyè.
15 Tǔyùhún Shìlián died.
His son Shìpī succeeded him.
Shìpī, seeing that his father and grandfather were benevolent
and thus were invaded and insulted by their neighbors—
Tǔyùhún Pìxī and Shìlián were benevolent,
as seen in volume 103, Xián'ān first year of Emperor Jiǎnwén—
desired to establish achievements.
Winter,
tenth month.
Jīnchéng Wáng Gān Guī sent an envoy to bestow upon Shìpī the title of Shāzhōu Mù and Báilán Wáng;
Shìpī did not accept.
This serves as background for the later Kǐfú Gān Guī’s attack on Tǔyùhún.
16 In the twelfth month,
Guō Zhì and Gǒu Yào battled east of Zhèng.
Guō Zhì was defeated
and fled to Luòyáng.
Zhèngdōng
is east of Zhèngxiàn.
17 Yuèzhì Jiéguī held Píngxiāng
and rebelled against Jīnchéng Wáng Gān Guī.
In the twelfth year,
Yuèzhì Jiéguī attached himself to the Kǐfú clan.
Sixteenth Year (Xīnmǎo, 391 CE)
1 Spring,
first month.
Yàn established an Xíngtái at Jì,
and bestowed upon Chánglè Gōng Shèng the title of Lù Xíngtái Shàngshū Shì.
2 Jīnchéng Wáng Gān Guī attacked Yuèzhì Jiéguī;
Jiéguī surrendered.
Gān Guī gave him a woman from his imperial clan in marriage.
3 Hè Rǎngān plotted to murder his elder brother Nè.
Nè, knowing this,
raised troops and attacked him.
Wèi Wáng Guī reported to Yàn,
requesting to act as a local guide to suppress him.
Second month,
on the jiǎxū day.
Yàn Zhǔ Chuí sent Zhào Wáng Lín to lead troops to attack Nè,
and Zhèn Běi Jiāngjūn Lán Hàn led the troops from Lóngchéng to attack Rǎngān.
Hè Rǎngān’s tribe
likely resided in the eastern part of the Hèlán tribe’s territory,
thus Yàn used the troops from Lóngchéng to attack him.
“Jiàng”
is pronounced “jíliàng fān.”
“Shuài”
is read as “shuài.”
4 Third month.
Qín Zhǔ Dēng attacked Hòu Qín Āndōng Jiāngjūn Jīn Róng from Yōng at Fànshì Bǎo.
He captured it;
then he crossed the Wèi River,
and attacked Jīngzhào Tàishǒu Wéi Fàn at Duànshì Bǎo,
but failed to capture it;
he advanced and occupied Qǔláo.
Qǔláo is northeast of Dùxiàn.
5 Summer,
fourth month.
Yàn’s Lán Hàn defeated Hè Rǎngān at Niúdū.
“Dū”
means a gathering place.
Its location should be in Niúchuān,
where barbarians grazed their livestock
and gathered,
hence the name.
6 Gǒu Yào had ten thousand followers.
He secretly summoned Qín Zhǔ Dēng,
promising to act as an inside supporter;
Dēng advanced from Qǔláo towards Fánchuān.
Fánchuān
is probably the Fánchuān of Dùlíng Xiàn.
Fifth month.
Hòu Qín Zhǔ Cháng led troops to meet and fight him.
Dēng attacked and defeated him,
beheading his Yòu Jiāngjūn Wú Zhōng.
Cháng rallied his troops and fought again.
Yáo Shuòdé said:
“Your Majesty has been cautious about engaging in light battles,
always wishing to achieve victory through strategy.
Now, after suffering a defeat in battle, you are pressing forward against the enemy again. Why is this?”
Cháng said:
“Dēng employs his army slowly
and does not understand the real and the empty.
Now he is advancing lightly with his troops,
occupying our east from afar.
The land of Mǎtóu Yuán is likely east of Cháng’ān.
One who is skilled in warfare
observes the enemy’s movements to understand their true situation,
and thus is able to achieve victory.
Therefore, before their forces are fully joined,
one should swiftly attack them to disrupt and scatter their plans.”
Then he advanced and fought,
greatly defeating them.
Dēng retreated and encamped at Méi.
7 Qín Yǎnzhōu Cìshǐ Qiáng Jīnchuí held Xīnpíng
and surrendered to Later Qín,
giving his son Kuí as a hostage.
Hòu Qín Zhǔ Cháng, with several hundred cavalry, entered Jīnchuí’s camp.
His subordinates remonstrated with him,
but Cháng said:
“If Jīnchuí were to leave,
and Fú Dēng also wanted to plot against me,
where would I find refuge?
Moreover, he has just come to submit,
so I should treat him with sincerity to bind him to me.
How can I harbor suspicion and distrust?”
Soon after, the Dǐ subordinates
wanted to seize Cháng,
but Jīnchuí refused to follow them.
Qiáng Jīnchuí
was of Dǐ ethnicity,
and a relative of Qín.
Yáo Cháng treated him with sincerity
to win over Fú Dēng’s faction.
8 In the sixth month,
on the Jiǎchén day,
Yàn Zhàowáng Lín 燕昭王麟 defeated Hè Nè 賀訥 at Chìchéng 赤城,
capturing him.
The Shuǐjīng 水經 states: "The Héshǔi 河水 flows from the south of Zhēnlíng 楨陵 County in Yúnzhōng 雲中 Commandery, passing east of Chìchéng 赤城,
then south, passing west of Tóngguò 桐過 County in Dìngxiāng 定襄."
The Wèishū Dìjì 魏書帝紀 also records that
in the third year of Dēngguó 登國,
Emperor Tàizǔ Dàowǔdì 拓跋珪 traveled to Dōngchìchéng 東赤城.
In the eighth year of Tàicháng 泰常 during the reign of Emperor Míngyuán 明元,
a great wall was built south of the Chángchuān 長川 River,
starting from Chìchéng 赤城
and extending west to Wǔyuán 五原,
for a length of over two thousand *lǐ* 里.
Yàn Zhǔ Chuí 燕主垂 ordered Lín 麟 to return Hè Nè’s 賀訥部落 tribal groups
and relocate Rǎgān 染干 to Zhōngshān 中山.
Lín 麟 returned
and said to Chuí 垂:
"I observe Tuòbá Guī’s 拓跋珪 actions;
he will ultimately become a national calamity.
It would be better to summon him back to court
and let his younger brother supervise the state affairs."
Chuí 垂 did not follow this advice.
*Shè* 攝
means to record,
to gather.
Mùróng Lín 慕容麟 was cunning and deceitful;
he knew that Tuòbá Guī 拓跋珪 would ultimately be uncontrollable.
But Mùróng Chuí 慕容垂 did not heed his words.
Heaven was about to empower Guī 珪 to destroy Yàn 燕.
Even with Chuí’s 垂 insight,
he barely noticed this.
*Jiān* 監,
pronounced like *gōng xián fān* (工銜翻).
9 The Xīyàn 西燕 ruler Yǒng 永 raided Hénán 河南.
The Grand Administrator Yáng Quánqī 楊佺期 attacked and defeated him.
10 In autumn,
the seventh month,
on the Rénshēn day,
Yàn Zhǔ Chuí 燕主垂 went to Fányáng 范陽.
Fányáng 范陽 County,
during the Hàn 漢 dynasty, belonged to Zhuójùn 涿郡.
Wèi Wéndì 魏文帝 changed Zhuójùn 涿郡 to Fányángjùn 范陽郡.
11 Wèi Wáng Guī 魏王珪 sent his younger brother Gū 觚 to present himself to Yàn 燕;
Yàn Zhǔ Chuí 燕主垂 was old and infirm,
and his sons and younger brothers were in power,
so they detained Gū 觚 to demand good horses.
Wèi Wáng Guī 魏王珪 refused to give them,
and thus broke off relations with Yàn 燕;
this laid the groundwork for the future conflict between Yàn 燕 and Wèi 魏.
Gū 觚 escaped and returned.
Yàn Tàizǐ Bǎo 燕太子寶 pursued and recaptured him,
but Chuí 垂 treated him as before.
12 Qín Zhǔ Dēng 秦主登 attacked Xīnpíng 新平.
Hòuqín Zhǔ Cháng 後秦主萇 rescued it,
and Dēng 登 withdrew.
13 Qín Piàojì Jiāngjūn Mòyì Gān 秦驃騎將軍沒弈干
offered his two sons as hostages to Jīnchéng Wáng Gān Guī 金城王乾歸,
requesting to jointly attack Xiānbēi Dàdōu 鮮卑大兜.
Gān Guī 乾歸 and Mòyì Gān 沒弈干 attacked Dàdōu 大兜 at Míngchán Bǎo 鳴蟬堡,
and conquered it.
According to the Zàijì 載記,
Dàdōu 大兜 at that time occupied Ānyáng Chéng 安陽城.
Ānyáng Chéng 安陽城 was in the area of Lǒngchéng 隴城 County, Qínzhōu 秦州, during the Táng 唐 dynasty;
Míngchán Bǎo 鳴蟬堡 also must have been in that region.
Gān Guī 乾歸 collected his tribal groups and returned,
giving back Mòyì Gān’s 沒弈干 two sons.
Mòyì Gān 沒弈干 soon rebelled,
allying with Liú Wèichén 劉衞辰 to the east.
In the eighth month,
Gān Guī 乾歸 led ten thousand cavalry to suppress Mòyì Gān 沒弈干.
Mòyì Gān 沒弈干 fled to Tālóu Chéng 他樓城.
Tālóu Chéng 他樓城 was in Gāopíng 高平.
In the sixth year of Zhēnguān 貞觀 during the reign of Táng Tàizōng 唐太宗,
the surrendered Tújué 突厥 households were settled in Yuánzhōu 緣州,
with its seat at Tālóu Chéng 他樓城 in Pínggāo 平高.
Gāozōng 高宗 established Tālóu 塔樓 County,
which was later abolished and incorporated into Xiāoguān 蕭關 County, Yuánzhōu 原州.
*Zhōng Mù* (中目).
14 In the ninth month,
on the Guǐwèi day,
Wáng Xún 王珣, Shàngshū Yòu Púyè 尚書右僕射, was appointed Zuǒ Púyè 左僕射,
and Xiè Yǎn 謝琰, Tàizǐ Zhānshì 太子詹事, was appointed Yòu Púyè 右僕射.
Tàixué Bóshì Fàn Hóngzhī 太學博士范弘之 proposed that Yīn Hào 殷浩 should be posthumously honored and given a posthumous title,
and in doing so, he recounted Huán Wēn’s 桓溫 acts of disloyalty.
At this time, the Huán 桓 clan was still powerful.
Wáng Xún 王珣
was Huán Wēn’s 桓溫 former subordinate;
Wáng Xún 王珣 had previously served as Huán Wēn’s 桓溫 Prefect of the Secretariat.
He possessed integrity and loyalty;
he demoted Fàn Hóngzhī 范弘之 to Yúháng Líng 餘杭令.
Yúháng 餘杭 County,
during the Hàn 漢 dynasty, belonged to Kuàijījùn 會稽郡.
Gù Lái 顧來 said: "The county
was established by Qín Shǐhuáng 秦始皇.
Later, the Hàn 漢 dynasty divided it to belong to Wújùn 吳郡.
The Wú 吳 state divided it to belong to Wúxīngjùn 吳興郡."
He was the grandson of Wāng 汪.
Fàn Wāng 范汪 had offended Huán Wēn 桓溫;
see Volume 101, first year of Āidì Shēngpíng 哀帝升平.
15 In winter,
the tenth month,
on the Rénchén day,
Yàn Zhǔ Chuí 燕主垂 returned to Zhōngshān 中山.
He returned from Fányáng 范陽.
16 Initially,
the Ròurán 柔然 tribal people had served Dài 代 for generations.
Wèi Shōu 魏收 wrote: "Towards the end of Shényuán 神元’s reign,
a raiding cavalry found a slave
whose hair had just reached his shoulders.
He had forgotten his original name.
His master gave him the nickname Mùgǔlǘ 木骨閭."
Mùgǔlǘ 木骨閭
means "bald head."
Mùgǔlǘ 木骨閭 and
"Yùjiǔlǘ" 郁久閭
sound similar,
so later generations adopted it as their surname.
Once Mùgǔlǘ 木骨閭 grew up,
he was released from slavery to become a cavalryman.
During Mùdì’s 穆帝 reign,
he was sentenced to death for being late.
He fled and hid in the valleys of Guǎngmò 廣漠,
gathering fugitives,
obtaining over a hundred men,
and relied on Hētūlín 紇突鄰.
After Mùgǔlǘ 木骨閭 died,
his son Chēlùhuì 車鹿會 was valiant and strong.
He began to have tribal groups
and called himself Ròurán 柔然.
The tribe was divided into two: the eldest son Pǐhòubá 匹候跋 succeeded his father and resided in the east,
while the second son Yūnhétí 縕紇提 lived separately in the west.
Qín Wáng Jiān 秦王堅 destroyed Dài 代;
the destruction of Dài 代 is mentioned in Volume 104, first year.
When Wèi Wáng Guī 魏王珪 ascended the throne,
he attacked various tribes such as Gāochē 高車,
and they all submitted,
only Ròurán 柔然 did not serve Wèi 魏.
On the Wùxū day,
Guī 珪 led his army to attack them.
The entire Ròurán 柔然 tribe fled.
Guī 珪 pursued them for six hundred *lǐ* 里.
The generals, through Zhāng Gǔn 張袞, said to Guī 珪:
"The enemy is far, and our provisions are exhausted;
it is better to return early."
Guī 珪 asked the generals: "If we kill the spare horses
for three days' food,
will it be enough?"
Generally, northerners using cavalry
each rode one horse and had another horse as a spare.
"It will be enough."
So he again doubled his pace in pursuit,
reaching them at the foot of Nánchuáng Shān 南牀山, south of the Dàqì 大磧.
At this time, Wèi 魏 was strong,
spanning Dàiběi 代北.
The Ròurán 柔然 fled west to Nánchuáng Shān 南牀山,
which was probably northwest of the Dàqì 大磧.
The *Shǐ Dìjì* (史帝紀) writes
"Nánshāng Shān" (南商山).
*Fù* 復,
pronounced like *fú yòu fān* (扶又翻).
He captured half of their tribe.
Pǐhòubá 匹候跋 and the other tribal leader Wūjī 屋擊 each gathered their remaining forces and fled.
Guī 珪 sent Zhǎngsūn Sōng 長孫嵩 and Zhǎngsūn Féi 長孫肥 to pursue them.
Guī 珪 said to his generals and advisors:
"Do you understand my previous question about three days' provisions?"
They replied:
"We do not know."
Guī 珪 said:
"The Ròurán 柔然 drove their livestock and fled for several days;
when they reach water, they will surely stop.
I pursued them with light cavalry;
calculating the distance,
we will reach them in no more than three days."
They all said:
"That is beyond our comprehension."
Sōng 嵩 pursued and beheaded Wūjī 屋擊 at Píngwàng Chuān 平望川.
Féi 肥 pursued Pǐhòubá 匹候跋 to Zhuóxié Shān 涿邪山.
Pǐhòubá 匹候跋 led his entire tribe to surrender,
capturing Hédàhàn 曷多汗, son of Yūnhétí 縕紇提,
and his nephews Shèlún 社崙 and Húlǜ 斛律,
and several hundred other members of the clan.
Yūnhétí 縕紇提 was about to flee to Liú Wèichén 劉衞辰.
Guī 珪 caught up with him,
and Yūnhétí 縕紇提 also surrendered.
Guī 珪 relocated all their tribal groups to Yúnzhōng 雲中.
This laid the groundwork for Shèlún’s 社崙 later rebellion and establishment of a state.
17 Zhái Liáo 翟遼 died,
and his son Zhāo 釗 succeeded him,
changing the era name to Dìngdǐng 定鼎.
He attacked Yàn Yèchéng 燕鄴城.
Yàn Liáoxī Wáng Nóng 燕遼西王農 attacked and repelled him.
This laid the groundwork for Yàn’s 燕 destruction of Zhái Zhāo 翟釗.
18 Sānhé Wáng Guāng 三河王光 sent troops to attack Jīnchéng Wáng Gān Guī 金城王乾歸 while he was vulnerable;
taking advantage of his vulnerability from attacking Mòyì Gān 沒弈干.
Gān Guī 乾歸 led his troops back,
and Guāng’s 光 troops also retreated.
19 Liú Wèichén (劉衞辰) sent his son Zhílìdī (直力鞮) to lead a force of eighty or ninety thousand to attack the southern part of Wèi (魏).
In the eleventh month,
on the day Jǐmǎo (己卯),
King Guī (珪) of Wèi (魏) led five or six thousand troops to resist them.
On the day Rénwǔ (壬午),
he severely defeated Zhílìdī (直力鞮) south of Tiěqíshān (鐵岐山).
Zhilìdī (直力鞮) fled on a single horse.
Taking advantage of the victory, he pursued them.
On the day Wùzǐ (戊子),
he crossed the Hé (河) south from Wǔyuán Jīnjīn (五原金津).
Jīnjīn (金津) should be between Yíliáng (宜梁) and Jiǔyuán (九原) counties of Wǔyuán (五原) Commandery.
Wèichén's (衞辰) tribes were startled and in disarray.
On the day Xīnmǎo (辛卯),
Guī (珪) directly reached Yuèbáchéng (悅跋城), where Wèichén (衞辰) resided.
According to the Zàijì (載記),
Yuèbáchéng (悅跋城) was the same as Dàiláichéng (代來城).
On the day Rénchén (壬辰),
he dispatched his generals with light cavalry to pursue them.
General Yīwèi (伊謂) captured Zhílìdī (直力鞮) at Mùgēnshān (木根山).
In the Guānshì Zhì (官氏志) of the Wèishū (魏書),
Tuòbá Lín (拓跋鄰) was the Yīlóu (伊婁) clan through his younger brother,
later changed to Yī (伊) clan.
Mùgēnshān (木根山) is west of the Hé (河) in Wǔyuán (五原).
In the twelfth month,
Guī's (珪) army camped at Yánchí (鹽池).
According to the Hàn Dìlǐ Zhì (漢地理志),
Chéngyí (成宜) county in Wǔyuán (五原) Commandery had salt officials.
Wǔyuán (五原) county in Táng (唐) Yánzhōu (鹽州) had salt from Wū (烏) and Bái (白) pools, etc.
Sòng Bái (宋白) said: The Qīng (青) and Bái (白) salt pools are north of Yánzhōu (鹽州).
All the corpses were thrown into the Hé (河),
to avenge Wèichén's (衞辰) use of Qín (秦) troops in Yuánnián (元年) to destroy Dài (代).
Over three hundred thousand horses were captured,
and over four million cattle and sheep.
The state's resources became abundant from this.
Wèichén's (衞辰) youngest son, Bóbó (勃勃), fled to the Xuēgān (薛干部) tribe.
Guī (珪) sent someone to seek him.
Tài Xīzhàng (太悉仗), the leader of the Xuēgān (薛干部) tribe,
brought out Bóbó (勃勃) and showed him to the envoy, saying:
“Bóbó (勃勃)'s state is destroyed and his family ruined.
He came to me in his desperation.
I would rather perish with him
than bear to capture him and hand him over to Wèi (魏).”
Then he sent Bóbó (勃勃) to Mòyìgān (沒弈干),
who gave Bóbó (勃勃) his daughter as wife.
This laid the groundwork for Bóbó (勃勃) to kill Mòyìgān (沒弈干) and re-establish his state.
Qī (妻)
is pronounced qī (七細翻).
20 On the day Wùshēn (戊申),
Lord Chuí (垂) of Yàn (燕) went to Lǔkǒu (魯口).
21 Lord Dēng (登) of Qín (秦) attacked Āndìng (安定).
Lord Cháng (萇) of Hòu Qín (後秦) went to Yīnmì (陰密) to resist him.
He said to Crown Prince Xīng (興):
“If Gǒu Yáo (苟曜) hears that I have gone north,
going from Cháng'ān (長安) to Yīnmì (陰密) is considered going north.
You shall execute him.”
Yáo (曜) indeed met Xīng (興) in Cháng'ān (長安).
Xīng (興) ordered Yǐn Wěi (尹緯) to reprimand and then execute him.
A skilled strategist who can defeat enemies
can achieve success by seizing opportunities.
Gǒu Yáo (苟曜) wavered repeatedly between Fú (苻) and Yáo (姚).
Cháng'ān (長安) was only three hundred *lǐ* (里) from Zhèng (鄭),
so he was a tumor in Yáo (姚)'s flank.
If Cháng (萇) had summoned him,
Yáo (曜) would certainly not have come.
If Cháng (萇) had been in Cháng'ān (長安),
Yáo (曜) would also have been afraid and not dared to come.
Cháng (萇) went out to lure him,
and Yáo (曜) was also suspicious and dared not come.
The two Qín (秦) states were at war,
and border emergencies frequently occurred.
Cháng's (萇) going north seemed unavoidable.
Gǒu Yáo (苟曜) had no suspicions or fears,
thinking that Yáo Xīng (姚興) was incapable of doing anything by guarding the capital,
so he lightly came once,
and ultimately met his death.
Yáo (姚)'s flank affliction was removed.
Was this not achieving success by seizing opportunities?
Cháng (萇) defeated Dēng (登) east of Āndìngchéng (安定城).
Dēng (登) retreated and held Lùchéngbǎo (路承堡).
Lù Chéng (路承) was a person's name.
He built a fortress to defend himself,
and at the time, it was named after him.
Cháng (萇) held a grand banquet.
All the generals said:
“If we had met King Wǔ (武) of Wèi (魏)
Yáo Cháng (姚萇) usurped the title,
and posthumously honored his elder brother Xiāng (襄) as King Wǔ (武) of Wèi (魏).
Your Majesty would be too cautious.”
Jiāngláo (將牢)
means to first secure oneself and not act rashly,
like people today say “bǎwěn (把穩)” (to be steady/reliable).
“I am inferior to my deceased elder brother in four respects: his height was eight *chǐ* (尺) and five *cùn* (寸),
his arms hung below his knees,
people feared him at first sight—this is one;
he commanded an army of one hundred thousand,
contending for supremacy with the world,
advancing at the sight of his banner,
with no obstacles before him—this is two;
he was learned in ancient times and knew the present,
discussed the Way and arts,
and gathered talented individuals—this is three;
he led the masses,
and everyone from top to bottom was pleased,
people exerted their utmost—this is four.
The reason I have been able to establish achievements
and employ all the worthy ones
is precisely that I rely on having a slight advantage in strategy and foresight.”
All the officials
cheered, “Long live!”
Punctuation by Wáng Chóngwǔ (王崇武), proofread by Róng Zhàozǔ (容肇祖) and Niè Chóngqí (聶崇岐).
Sīmǎ Guāng (司馬光)
compiled by imperial decree.
Hòuxué Tiāntái (後學天台)
Xià (下) of Lièzōng Xiàowǔ Huángdì (烈宗孝武皇帝)
Tàiyuán (太元) Seventeenth Year (Rénchén (壬辰), 392 CE)
1 Spring,
first month,
on the day Jǐsì (己巳) Sakkō (朔),
a general amnesty was proclaimed.
2 Lord Dēng (登) of Qín (秦) enthroned Lady Lǐ (李) of Lǒngxī (隴西), a Zhāoyí (昭儀), as empress.
3 In the second month,
on the day Rén'yín (壬寅),
Lord Chuí (垂) of Yàn (燕) went from Lǔkǒu (魯口) to Héjiān (河間) and Bóhǎi (渤海).
Zhái Zhāo (翟釗) of Píngyuán (平原) sent his general Zhái Dū (翟都) to invade Guǎntáo (館陶),
and garrison at Sūkānglěi (蘇康壘).
Sū Kāng (蘇康)
is a person's name.
Guǎntáo (館陶) county,
during Hàn (漢) belonged to Wèijùn (魏郡),
during Jìn (晉) belonged to Yángpíngjùn (陽平郡).
Jiàng (將)
is pronounced liàng (亮翻);
same below.
Chuí (垂) led troops south to attack Zhāo (釗).
4 Pàojì Jiāngjūn (驃騎將軍) Mòyìgān (沒弈干) of Qín (秦) led his forces and surrendered to Hòu Qín (後秦).
Hòu Qín (後秦) made him Chējì Jiāngjūn (車騎將軍)
and enfeoffed him as Gāopíng Gōng (高平公).
5 Lord Cháng (萇) of Hòu Qín (後秦) became gravely ill.
He ordered Yáo Shuòdé (姚碩德) to garrison Lǐrùn (李潤),
and Yǐn Wěi (尹緯) to guard Cháng'ān (長安).
He summoned Crown Prince Xīng (興) to the marching camp.
Cháng (萇) was garrisoned at Āndìng (安定) at the time.
Cháng (萇)
is pronounced cháng (長).
“Now the enemy has not been destroyed,
and I am gravely ill again.
Wáng Tǒng (王統) and others all have their own troops
and will eventually become a problem;
they should all be eliminated.”
Xīng (興) followed this advice,
and killed Wáng Tǒng (王統), Wáng Guǎng (王廣), Fú Yìn (苻胤), Xú Chéng (徐成), and Máozéng (毛盛).
They were all former officials of the Fú (苻) clan.
“Wáng Tǒng (王統)'s brothers
are from my hometown,
and truly have no other ambitions;
Xú Chéng (徐成) and the others are all famous generals from the previous dynasty,
I was about to use them,
how could I kill them so rashly!”
If Cháng (萇) truly considered killing Tǒng (統) and the others to be a crime,
he should have punished the initial instigators of the plot;
but he merely got angry.
Was he truly angry?
6 Lord Chuí (垂) of Yàn (燕) advanced and pressed Sūkānglěi (蘇康壘).
Summer,
fourth month,
Zhái Dū (翟都) fled south to Huátái (滑臺).
Zhái Zhāo (翟釗) sought aid from Xī Yàn (西燕).
Lord Yǒng (永) of Xī Yàn (西燕) consulted with his officials.
Shàngshū Láng (尚書郎) Bào Zūn (鮑遵) of Bóhǎi (渤海) said:
“Let the two enemies wear each other out;
we will then take advantage of their aftermath.
This is the strategy of Biàn Zhuāngzǐ (卞莊子).”
Zhōngshū Shìláng (中書侍郎) Zhāng Téng (張騰) of Tàiyuán (太原) said:
“Chuí (垂) is strong, Zhāo (釗) is weak;
what aftermath is there to take advantage of?
It is better to rescue him quickly
to form a tripartite balance of power.
Now if we lead troops towards Zhōngshān (中山),
creating many feints by day
and many torches by night,
Chuí (垂) will certainly be afraid and come to his own rescue.
We will strike him from the front,
and Zhāo (釗) will follow him from behind.
This is an opportunity granted by Heaven
that must not be missed.”
Yǒng (永) did not follow it.
If Zhái Zhāo (翟釗) is defeated,
the demise of Xī Yàn (西燕) will be a foregone conclusion.
7 Yàn (燕) proclaimed a general amnesty.
8 Fifth month,
on the day Dīngmǎo (丁卯) Sakkō (朔),
there was a solar eclipse.
9 In the sixth month,
the Yàn Lord, Mùróng Chuí, campaigned at Líyáng,
approaching the Yellow River to cross it.
Zhái Zhāo arrayed his troops on the south bank to resist him.
On the xīnhài day,
Chuí moved his camp to Xīwù,
forty *lǐ* west of Líyáng.
He built over a hundred ox-hide boats,
feigned a display of arms,
and went upstream.
Zhāo urgently led his troops towards Xīwù.
Chuí secretly dispatched Zhōnglěi Jiāngjūn Guìlín Wáng Zhèn and others to cross the river at Líyáng Ford by night,
and encamp south of the river.
By dawn, the camp was complete.
When Zhāo heard of this,
he immediately returned
and attacked Zhèn and the others' camp.
Chuí ordered Zhèn and the others to hold their fortified positions and not engage.
Zhāo's troops, fatigued and parched from their movements,
were unable to capture the camp by assault,
and were about to withdraw.
Zhèn and the others led their troops out to battle.
Piàojì Jiāngjūn Nóng crossed from Xīwù
and attacked them in a pincer movement with Zhèn and the others,
utterly defeating them.
The Yàn Lord Mùróng Chuí employed military tactics on the Yellow River twice:
against Wēn Xiáng, he led his troops directly across to take it;
against Zhái Zhāo, he displayed a feigned army in the west and secretly crossed his army in the east,
also achieving victory.
This depended on the strength or weakness of the enemy.
Piào,
pronounced pǐ miào.
Jì,
pronounced qí jì.
Nóng
was the Piàojì Dàjiāngjūn of Yàn;
the character
"dà"
is omitted here.
He took his wife and children,
gathered the remaining troops,
crossed the Yellow River northwards,
and ascended Mount Báilù.
Shuǐjīng Zhù: North of Xiūwǔ County in Hénèi Commandery is Mount Báilù.
The Yàn army could not advance.
Nóng said,
"Zhāo has no provisions;
he cannot remain in the mountains for long."
So he led his troops back,
leaving cavalry to observe.
Zhāo indeed descended the mountain.
Nóng's returning troops ambushed and attacked them,
capturing all of his forces.
Zhāo fled alone on horseback to Chángzǐ.
The Xī Yàn Lord, Mùróng Yǒng, appointed Zhāo as Chēqí Dàjiāngjūn and Yǎnlü Zhōumù,
and enfeoffed him as Dōngjùn Wáng.
After more than a year,
Zhāo plotted rebellion,
and Yǒng killed him.
At first,
Hǎo Guǐ, Cuī Chěng, and Cuī Hóng of Qīnghé, Zhāng Zhuó of Xīnxīng, Kuí Téng of Liáodōng,
Kuí
is a surname.
There was a minister of Shí Zhào named Kuí Ān.
They fled the Qin chaos and came to surrender.
An imperial edict appointed them to various commanderies in Jìzhōu,
each leading their subordinates to encamp south of the Yellow River.
Afterwards, they accepted official ranks from the Zhái clan.
When the Zhái clan was defeated,
they all surrendered to Yàn.
The Yàn Lord Mùróng Chuí used each according to their talent.
Zhāo's jurisdiction over seven commanderies and over thirty thousand households
were all settled as before.
He appointed Zhāngwǔ Wáng Zhòu as the Cìshǐ of Yǎn and Yù prefectures,
garrisoning Huátái.
He relocated over seven thousand households of Xúzhōu people to Líyáng,
and appointed Péngchéng Wáng Tuō as Xúzhōu Cìshǐ,
garrisoning Líyáng.
The people of Xúzhōu
were likely those plundered by Zhái Zhāo.
Tuō was Chuí's younger brother's son.
Chuí appointed Cuī Yīn as Zhòu's Sīmǎ.
Initially,
Chénliú Wáng Shào was Zhènnán Jiāngjūn,
Tàiyuán Wáng Kǎi was Zhēngxī Jiāngjūn,
and Lèlàng Wáng Wēn was Zhēngdōng Jiāngjūn.
Chuí appointed Yīn as their assistant in all cases.
Yīn was talented, capable, discerning, astute, strong, and upright,
and adept at offering advice and remonstrance.
All four kings held him in awe.
Wherever he went, he simplified punishments and laws,
lightened taxes and labor services.
Displaced people returned to him,
and the population grew.
In autumn,
the seventh month,
Chuí went to Yè.
He appointed Tàiyuán Wáng Kǎi as Jìzhōu Mù,
and Yòu Guānglù Dàfū Yú Wèi as Zuǒ Púyè.
10 The Qín Lord, Fú Dēng, hearing that the Hòu Qín Lord, Yáo Cháng, was seriously ill,
was greatly pleased.
Jí shèn means 'seriously ill.'
Fú Jiān's temple name was Shìzǔ.
He advanced his position by two grades,
prepared his horses and sharpened his weapons,
and advanced to threaten Āndìng,
about ninety *lǐ* from the city.
In the eighth month,
Cháng's illness slightly abated,
and he went out to resist him.
Dēng led his troops out of camp,
intending to engage in battle.
Cháng dispatched Ānnán Jiāngjūn Yáo Xīlóng to separately attack the Qín camp.
Dēng, fearful, returned.
That night, Cháng led his troops to circle around and approach from their rear.
At dawn, the scout cavalry reported,
"The enemy's camps are already empty;
their direction is unknown."
Dēng exclaimed in surprise,
"What kind of person is he,
who leaves without my knowledge,
and arrives without my awareness?
I thought he was about to die,
yet suddenly he returns.
That I, the Emperor, should live in the same era as this Qiāng,
how unfortunate!"
Fú Dēng was repeatedly frustrated by Yáo Cháng,
hence his fear of Cháng.
It was at this point that Dēng's morale declined.
Cháng also returned to Āndìng.
11 The Sānhé Wáng, Qífú Guāng, dispatched his younger brother, Yòu Jiāngjūn Bǎo, and others to attack Jīnchéng Wáng Qífú Gān’guī.
Bǎo and over ten thousand officers and soldiers died.
He then dispatched his son, Hǔbēn Zhōnglángjiàng Cuàn, to attack the Southern Qiāng Pēng Xīniàn.
Cuàn also returned defeated.
Guāng personally led an attack on Xīniàn at Báohǎn,
capturing it.
Xīniàn fled to Gānsōng.
Gānsōng Commandery
was established by Qífú Guórén.
Jí jiāng,
pronounced jí liàng.
Same below.
Bēn,
pronounced bēn.
Báo,
pronounced fú.
12 In winter,
the tenth month,
on the xīnhài day,
the Cìshǐ of Jīngzhōu, Wáng Chén, died.
13 The Cìshǐ of Yōngzhōu, Zhū Xù, requested to resign due to old age and illness.
An imperial edict appointed Tàizǐ Yòuwèilǜ Xī Huī as Yōngzhōu Cìshǐ,
replacing Xù to garrison Xiāngyáng.
Huī
was the son of Xī Tán.
Xī Tán is seen in juan 100, Mù Dì, Shēngpíng third year.
Lǜ,
pronounced suǒ lǜ.
Xī,
pronounced chǒu zhī.
Tán,
pronounced tú hán.
14 The Bā and Shǔ people in Guānzhōng all rebelled against Hòu Qín,
occupying Hóngnóng to align with Qín.
The Qín Lord, Fú Dēng, appointed Dòu Chōng as Zuǒ Chéngxiàng.
Chōng moved his garrison to Huáyīn.
Xī Huī dispatched Jiāngjūn Zhào Mù to guard Jīnyōng.
Hénán Tàishǒu Yáng Quánqí led a multitude of troops to Húchéng,
attacked Chōng,
and routed him.
15 In the eleventh month,
on the guǐyǒu day,
Yīn Zhòngkān, a Huángménláng, was appointed Dūdū Jīng‧Yì‧Níng Sānzhōu Zhū Jūnjì, and Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ,
garrisoning Jiānglíng.
Although Zhòngkān had a distinguished reputation,
his standing and prestige were still shallow,
and critics did not deem the appointment appropriate.
Upon arriving in office,
he was fond of dispensing minor favors,
and the main principles of governance were not upheld.
Huán Xuán, Duke of Nánjùn, relied on his talent and background,
considering himself a heroic and formidable figure.
He relied on his talent and his family's distinguished background.
“Chǔ” (處)
is pronounced Chāng Lǚ.
At twenty-three years old,
he was first appointed Prince's Equerry (Tàizǐ Xǐmǎ).
Huán Xuán once visited Wáng Dàozǐ, Prince of Lángxié.
Finding him in a drunken state,
Wáng Dàozǐ stared with wide eyes at his guests and said,
“Huán Wēn at the end of his career wanted to become a rebel.
What do you say?”
Huán Xuán prostrated himself, sweating,
unable to rise.
Because of this, he became even more uneasy
and constantly gnashed his teeth at Wáng Dàozǐ.
Later, he was appointed Governor (Tàishǒu) of Yìxīng,
but was disheartened and frustrated.
He sighed, saying,
“My father was the lord of the nine provinces,
and his son is merely the chief of the five lakes!”
Thereupon, he abandoned his office and returned to the capital.
Huán Xuán inherited the title of Duke of Nánjùn.
“The achievements of my late father in diligently serving the emperor and restoring the dynasty
have been forgotten by the imperial court;
I will not dwell on them further.
As for the late emperor ascending the throne
and Your Majesty continuing his brilliance—
this refers to Huán Wēn deposing Emperor Hǎixī and enthroning Emperor Jiǎnwén, and the emperor then inheriting the succession.
The Yì Jīng says: 'Two brightnesses arise from Lì;
the great person continues their brilliance to illuminate the four directions.'
Whose doing is this?”
His memorial was left unanswered.
When Huán Xuán was in Jiānglíng,
Zhòngkān greatly respected and feared him.
The Huán clan had governed Jīngzhōu for generations,
and Huán Xuán was again arrogant and oppressive.
The gentry and common people feared him
more than Zhòngkān.
He once playfully rode his horse in front of Zhòngkān's office
and pointed a spear at Zhòngkān.
Liú Mài of Péngchéng, Zhòngkān's Staff Officer of the Central Army (Zhōngbīng Cānjūn), said to Huán Xuán,
Emperor Yuán decreed that there should be thirteen bureaux of Staff Officers in Jiāngdōng,
including the Central Army, Outer Army, and Cavalry.
“Your horsemanship and spearmanship are excessive,
but your refined reason is lacking.”
Huán Xuán was displeased,
and Zhòngkān turned pale.
When Huán Xuán left,
Zhòngkān said to Mài,
“You are
a madman!
If Huán Xuán sends men to kill you tonight,
how can I save you?”
He made Mài go to the capital to avoid him.
“Dū” (都)
refers to Jiànkāng.
Mài barely escaped with his life.
Hú Fān of Yùzhāng, Staff Officer of the General Who Conquers Barbarians (Zhēnglǔ Cānjūn), passed through Jiānglíng
and met Zhòngkān.
He persuaded him, saying,
“Huán Xuán's ambitions are unpredictable,
and he is always discontented about being out of office.
Your Excellency's excessive deference and respect towards him
is probably not a good plan for the future!”
Zhòngkān was displeased.
Hú Fān's younger cousin by his father's side,
Luó Qǐshēng, was Zhòngkān's Administrator (Gōngcáo).
After Hú Fān withdrew,
he said to Qǐshēng,
“If Marquis Yīn turns his spear over to others,
disaster will surely befall him.
If you do not plan your departure early,
regret will be too late!”
This set the stage for Huán Xuán later killing Qǐshēng and Zhòngkān.
“Qǐ” (企)
is pronounced Qū Zhì.
16 In the year Gēngyín,
Imperial Prince Déwén was made Prince of Lángxié,
and Wáng Dàozǐ, Prince of Lángxié, was transferred to be Prince of Huìjī.
17 In the twelfth month,
Yān Lord Chuí returned to Zhōngshān.
He appointed Wáng Nóng, Prince of Liáoxī, as Grand Commander (Dūdū) of military affairs of Yǎn, Yù, Jīng, Xú, and Yōng provinces,
stationed in Yè.
18 Quán Qiānchéng of the Xiūguān tribe occupied Xiǎnqīn
and declared himself Governor (Mù) of Qínzhōu.
Xiūguān (休官)
is the name of a barbarian tribe.
Xiǎnqīn County (顯親縣) was established by Emperor Guāngwǔ of Hàn
and belonged to Hànyáng Commandery.
The Jìn changed Xiǎnqīn to Xiǎnxīn
and Hànyáng back to Tiānshuǐ Commandery.
In the “Yáo Xīng Zàijì” of the Jìn Shū,
“Quán Qiānchéng” (權千成)
is written
as
“Quán Gānchéng” (權干城),
a prominent family of Luèyáng.
19 Lǐ Liáo of Qīnghé submitted a memorial requesting an imperial edict for Yǎnzhōu to repair the Confucius Temple.
The Confucius Temple was in Lǔ.
Lǔ Commandery
belonged to Xúzhōu in the Former Hàn,
Yùzhōu in the Later Hàn and Jìn,
and was first assigned to Yǎnzhōu south of the Yangtze.
He also requested the establishment of schools
to recruit scholars for teaching,
saying,
“There are matters that seem distant but are actually urgent.”
“Shí” (寔) here has the same meaning as “shí” (實) in “yì yǔ xū shí zhī shí” (義與虛實之實).
The memorial was not considered.
1 Spring,
first month.
Yān Píngyáng Xiàowáng Róu passed away.
2 Quán Qiānchéng, pressed by Qín,
requested to surrender to Gān Guī, Prince of Jīnchéng.
Gān Guī appointed him Inspector (Cǐshǐ) of Dōngqínzhōu, Grand Commander (Dàdūtǒng) of Xiūguān, and Duke of Xiǎnqīn.
3 Summer,
fourth month.
On the day Gēngzǐ,
Yān Lord Chuí bestowed the title of Grand Chányú (Dà Chányú) upon太子 Bǎo.
He appointed Kùnǔguān Wěi, Prince of Āndìng, as Grand Preceptor (Tàiwèi);
Dé, Prince of Fányáng, as Minister of Works (Sītú);
Kǎi, Prince of Tàiyuán, as Minister of Education (Sīkōng);
and Shào, Prince of Chénliú, as Right Assistant Director of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Yòupúyè).
In the fifth month,
he made his son Xī Prince of Héjiān,
Láng Prince of Bóhǎi,
and Jiàn Prince of Bólíng.
4 Qín Right Chancellor (Yòuchéngxiàng) Dòu Chōng prided himself on his talent and looked down on others.
“Shàng rén” (尚人) means to despise others and rise above them.
Qín Lord Dēng did not allow it.
In the sixth month,
Dòu Chōng declared himself King of Qín
and changed the era name to Yuánguāng.
5 Gān Guī, Prince of Jīnchéng, established his son Chìpán as Crown Prince.
Chìpán was courageous, strategic, and decisive,
surpassing his father.
6 Autumn,
seventh month.
Qín Lord Dēng attacked Dòu Chōng at Yěrén Fort.
Dòu Chōng sought help from Later Qín.
Yǐn Wěi said to Later Qín Lord Cháng,
“The Crown Prince has a reputation for benevolence and generosity
known far and wide,
but his heroic strategies are not yet established.
Please let him attack Fú Dēng to establish them.”
Cháng agreed.
Crown Prince Xīng led troops to attack Húkōng Fort.
Fú Dēng lifted the siege on Dòu Chōng to go to its aid.
Xīng then raided Píngliáng
and returned with great spoils.
After his defeat at Dàjiè,
Fú Dēng had made Píngliáng his base.
7 Wèi King Guī, because Xuēgān Tàixīfú did not send Liú Bóbó (as mentioned in the sixteenth year of the previous volume),
attacked his city
and massacred it.
Tàixīfú fled to Qín.
8 The Dī chief Yáng Fósōng rebelled
and fled to Later Qín.
Yáng Quánqī and Zhào Mù pursued him,
and in the ninth month,
on the day Bǐngxū,
defeated Yáng Fósōng at Tóngguān.
Later Qín general Yáo Chóng rescued Yáng Fósōng,
defeated the Jìn forces,
and Zhào Mù died.
9 Winter,
tenth month.
Later Qín Lord Cháng became seriously ill
and returned to Cháng'ān.
10 Yān Zhǔ Chuí 議伐西燕，
諸將皆曰：
「Yǒng 未有釁，
我連年征討，
士卒疲弊，
未可也。 」
Fànyáng Wáng Dé 曰：
「Yǒng 既國之枝葉，
又僭舉位號，
惑民視聽，
宜先除之，
以壹民心。
士卒雖疲，
庸得已乎！ 」
Chuí 曰：
「Sītú 意正與吾同。
吾比老，
叩囊底智，
足以取之，
終不復留此賊以累子孫也。 」
Chuí 不欲留 Mùróng Yǒng 以累子孫，
而不知 Tuòbá Guī 已窺於代北矣。
是以有國有家者，
不恃無敵國外患，
恃吾所以傳國承家者足以待之耳。
累，
力瑞翻。
復，
扶又翻。
十一月，
Chuí 發 Zhōngshān 步騎七萬，
遣鎮西將軍‧Dānyáng Wáng Zǎn、
「Zǎn」 ，
當作
「Zàn」 。
攻西燕 Wǔxiāng Gōng Yǒu 於 Jìnyáng，
征東將軍 Píng Guī 攻鎮東將軍 Duàn Píng 於 Shātíng。
Shātíng 在 Yè 西南。
Yǒu，
Yǒng 之弟也。
十二月，
Chuí 至 Yè。
11 Jǐhài ，
Hòu Qín Zhǔ Cháng 召太尉 Yáo Mín、僕射 Yǐn Wěi、Yáo Huǎng、將軍 Yáo Dàmù、尚書 Dí Bózhī 入禁中，
受遺詔輔政。
Cháng 謂太子 Xīng 曰：
「有毀此諸公者，
慎勿受之。
汝撫骨肉以恩，
接大臣以禮，
待物以信，
遇民以仁，
四者不失，
吾無憂矣。 」
Yáo Cháng 所以詔其子者，
勝於 Fú Jiàn。
Cháng 曰：
「今大業垂成，
Xīng 才智足辦，
奚所復問！ 」
Gēngzǐ ，
Cháng 卒。
年六十四。
以其叔父 Xù 鎮 Āndìng，
Shuòdé 鎮 Yīnmì，
弟 Chóng 守 Cháng'ān。
或謂 Shuòdé 曰：
「公威名素重，
部曲最強，
今易世之際，
必為朝廷所疑，
不如且奔 Qínzhōu，
Shuòdé 本起兵 Lǒngshàng，
據 Jìchéng。
Shuòdé 曰：
「太子志度寬明，
必無他慮。
今 Fú Dēng 未滅而骨肉相攻，
是自亡也；
吾有死而已，
終不為也。 」
遂往見 Xīng，
Xīng 優禮而遣之。
Xīng 自稱大將軍，
以 Yǐn Wěi 為長史，
Dí Bózhī 為司馬，
帥衆伐 Qín。
Qín Zhǔ Dēng 聞 Hòu Qín Zhǔ Cháng 卒，
喜曰：
「Yáo Xīng 小兒，
吾折杖笞之耳。 」
乃大赦，
盡衆而東，
輕敵者敗，
宜 Fú Dēng 所以不亡於 Yáo Cháng 之時而亡於 Yáo Xīng 之初立也。
太子 Chóng 守 Húkōngbǎo；
遣使拜 Jīnchéng Wáng Gān Guī 為左丞相、Hénán Wáng、領秦‧梁‧益‧涼‧沙五州牧，
加九錫。
Tūfà Sīfùjiān 卒，
子 Wūgū 立。
Wūgū 雄勇有大志，
與大將 Fēntuó 謀取 Liángzhōu。
欲幷 Lǚ Guāng 也。
將，
即亮翻。
「公必欲得 Liángzhōu，
宜先務農講武，
禮俊賢，
修政刑，
然後可也。 」
Wūgū 從之。
Sānhé Wáng Guāng 遣使拜 Wūgū 冠軍大將軍、Héxī Xiānbēi Dà Dūtǒng。
Wūgū 與其㣥下謀之曰：
「可受乎？ 」
皆曰：
「吾士馬衆多，
何為屬人！ 」
Shízhēn Ruòliú 不對。
Wūgū 曰：
「卿畏 Lǚ Guāng 邪？ 」
Shízhēn Ruòliú 曰：
「吾根本未固，
小大非敵，
若 Guāng 致死於我，
何以待之！
不如受以驕之，
俟釁而動，
蔑不克矣。 」
Wūgū 乃受之。
Fēntuó 與 Shízhēn Ruòliú，
皆能審宜應事者也。
史言 Tūfà Wūgū 所以興。
Fēn 與 Shízhēn，
蓋皆夷姓。
3 二月，
Qín Zhǔ Dēng 攻屠各 Yáo Nú、Bó Pú 二堡，
克之。
二堡，
在 Húkōngbǎo 之東。
屠，
直於翻。
4 Yān Zhǔ Chuí 留 Qīnghé Gōng Huì 鎮 Yè，
發司、冀、青、兗兵，
遣 Tàiyuán Wáng Kǎi 出 Fúkǒu，
Liáoxī Wáng Nóng 出 Húguān，
Chuí 自出 Shātíng 以擊西燕，
「tíng」 ，
當作
「tíng」 ；
其地在 Yè 西南。
軍各就頓。
分處置兵以疑敵，
使不知所備。
趣，
七喻翻；
下同。
嚴兵分道拒守，
聚糧 Táibì，
水經註：潞縣北對故 Táibì，
漳水出其南，
本潞子所立也。
魏收地形志，
Xiāngyuán Jùn Yìlíng Xiàn，
漢、晉之 Lù Xiàn 也，
有 Táibì。
時西燕之臣有二 Yìdòuguī，
故此稱 Xiǎo Yìdòuguī。
從，
才用翻。
In the 5th month, summer,
Qín主 Fú Dēng, from Liùmò, went to Fèiqiáo.
Hòu Qín Shǐpíng 太守 Yáo Xiáng took position at Mǎwéibǎo to resist him.
Tàizǐ Yáo Xīng dispatched Yǐn Wěi to lead troops to relieve Yáo Xiáng.
Yǐn Wěi positioned himself at Fèiqiáo to await the Qín forces.
The Qín soldiers fought over water,
but could not get any.
Two or three tenths died of thirst,
and so they urgently attacked Yǐn Wěi.
Yáo Xīng swiftly sent Dí Bózhī to tell Yǐn Wěi:
"Fú Dēng is a cornered foe;
it is advisable to proceed cautiously to defeat him."
Yǐn Wěi said:
"The late emperor has ascended to the distant realm.
Zhèng Xuán said: 'Dēng'
means 'ascend';
'xiá'
means 'already.'
To 'ascend already'
is like departing to become an immortal.
'Shàng'
is pronounced shí zhǎng fān.
If we do not now seize this moment of inspired fervor to capture the enemy,
our great cause will be lost!"
Thereupon, he engaged the Qín forces in battle,
and the Qín army was utterly defeated.
That night,
the Qín host disintegrated.
Fú Dēng fled alone on horseback to Yōng.
Tàizǐ Fú Chóng and Ānchéng Wáng Fú Guǎng, hearing of the defeat,
both abandoned their cities and fled.
When Fú Dēng arrived,
having nowhere to go,
he then fled to Píngliáng,
collected his remaining troops,
and entered Mǎmáo Shān.
Píngliáng city
was within the boundaries of Hàn Āndìng Qúnyīn Xiàn.
Hòu Zhōu first established Píngliáng Jùn and Xiàn.
During the Táng, it was Yuánzhōu Xiàn.
When Hèlián Dìng was defeated,
Wèi also took position at Mǎmáo Lǐng to capture Xī Jīn.
This was indeed a strategic stronghold of Píngliáng.
In the 6th month, the 5th day of the cyclical calendar, Yàn主 Mùróng Chuí halted his army southwest of Yè
and did not advance for more than a month.
Xī Yàn主 Mùróng Yǒng was puzzled by this,
thinking that the Tàiháng road was wide
and suspecting that Mùróng Chuí intended to take it by a deceptive route.
So he gathered all his armies and garrisoned them at Zhǐguān,
blocking the entrance to Tàiháng,
leaving only one army at Táibì.
On the *jiǎxū* day,
Mùróng Chuí led his large army out of Fǔkǒu
and entered Tiānjǐngguān.
The *Qián Hàn Shū Dìlǐ Zhì* states that
in Gāodū Xiàn of Shàngdǎng Jùn, there is Tiānjǐngguān.
Cài Yōng said: "On Mount Tàiháng there is Tiānjǐngguān,
north of the well,
hence its name."
I, Yú, note that in Jìnchéng Xiàn of Zézhōu today, there is Tàihángguān,
and within the pass are three Tiānjǐngquán (Heavenly Well Springs),
which is Tiānjǐngguān.
On the *yǐyǒu* day,
the Yàn army reached Táibì.
Mùróng Yǒng sent his cousin, Tàiwèi Dà Yìdòuguī, to relieve it.
Píng Guī attacked and defeated him.
Xiǎo Yìdòuguī went out to battle.
Liáoxī Wáng Mùróng Nóng again attacked and defeated him,
beheading Lè Mǎjū
and capturing Wáng Cìduō.
Thereupon, Táibì was besieged.
Mùróng Yǒng recalled the Tàiháng army
and personally led 50,000 elite troops to resist them.
Diāo Yún and Mùróng Zhōng, struck with fear,
led their followers to surrender to Yàn.
Mùróng Yǒng executed their wives and children.
On the *jǐhài* day,
Mùróng Chuí arrayed his forces south of Táibì
and dispatched Xiāoqí Jiàngjūn Mùróng Guó to ambush a thousand cavalry in the ravine.
On the *gēngzǐ* day,
he engaged Mùróng Yǒng in battle.
Mùróng Chuí feigned retreat.
Mùróng Yǒng's forces pursued him.
After a few *lǐ*,
Mùróng Guó's cavalry emerged from the ravine,
cutting off their rear.
All armies advanced from four sides,
severely defeating them,
beheading over eight thousand.
Mùróng Yǒng fled back to Chángzǐ.
The defending general of Jìnyáng, hearing of this,
abandoned the city and fled.
Dānyáng Wáng Mùróng Zàn and others advanced and took Jìnyáng.
The 7th month, Hòu Qín Tàizǐ Yáo Xīng first held the mourning ceremony
and was enthroned as emperor at Huáilǐ.
Yáo Xīng,
courtesy name Zǐlüè,
was Yáo Cháng's eldest son.
Huáilǐ Xiàn,
during the Hàn, belonged to Fúfēng;
during the Jìn, it belonged to Shǐpíng Jùn.
Sòng Bái said that the old city of Hàn Huáilǐ Xiàn
was seven *lǐ* southeast of Táng Qízhōu Xīngpíng Xiàn.
Yáo Xīng, having defeated Fú Dēng,
first held the mourning ceremony and assumed the throne.
He changed the reign title to Huángchū;
then proceeded to Āndìng.
He posthumously honored Hòu Qín主 Yáo Cháng as Wǔzhāo Huángdì,
with the temple name Tàizǔ.
The 8th month,
on the *rénzǐ* day,
Huìjī Wáng's Tàizhèng Shì was posthumously honored as Jiǎnwén Xuāntàihòu.
The ministers suggested that Xuāntàihòu should be enshrined alongside Yuándì.
Tàizǐ Qiánshuài Xú Mò said:
"The *Jìn Zhì* states: Huìdì established the Eastern Palace,
and the position was called Zhōngwèishuài.
In the 5th year of Tàishǐ, it was divided into left and right,
each commanding one army.
During Huìdì's time,
Mǐnhuái Tàizǐ was in the Eastern Palace,
and Front and Rear Shuài were added.
South of the Jiāng, the Front and Rear Shuài were abolished,
but during Xiàowǔ's Tàiyuán era, they were re-established."
'Shuài'
is pronounced suǒ lèi fān.
"When Xuāntàihòu was alive,
she was not consorted with the late emperor.
This statement is incorrect.
'Kàng'
is pronounced kǔ làng fān,
meaning 'equal.'
'Lì'
is pronounced lì jì fān,
meaning 'paired.'
How can one establish a consort for a deceased ancestor?"
Guóxué Míngjiào Dōngguǎn Zāng Táo said:
"According to the *Jìn Shū Rúlín Zhuàn*: Yuándì inherited the cycle of Bǎilìu
and brilliantly initiated the restoration.
Although he honored Confucianism and promoted learning,
repeatedly issuing imperial edicts,
yet the 'Eastern Periphery and Western Collars' (schools)
were not known for their 'strings and chanting' (music and recitation).
Míngdì cherished scholarly pursuits,
and Jiǎnwéndì diligently delighted in the classics.
Thus, they attracted and gathered students
and encouraged excellent conduct.
The office of Guóxué Míngjiào
must have been established during the time of Míngdì and Jiǎnwéndì.
'Guǎn'
is pronounced guān.
"Now that the revered title is rectified,
the ultimate filial devotion is expressed.
By establishing a separate sleeping temple,
the significance of the revered ancestral temple is made clear.
'Yán'
means 'venerate.'
'Ní'
means 'father's temple.'
This also clarifies the source of eminence,
attributing it to the son's connection,
as Jiǎnwéndì's status is linked to Xuāntàihòu.
The *Chūnqiū Zhuàn* says: 'A mother becomes noble through her son.'
'Chēng'
is pronounced chǐ zhèng fān.
Is this not excellent?"
Thereupon, a temple was built west of the Tàimiào road.
The 9th month, Yàn主 Mùróng Chuí advanced his army and besieged Chángzǐ.
Xī Yàn主 Mùróng Yǒng wished to flee to Hòu Qín.
Shìzhōng Lán Yīng said:
"In the past, when Shí Hǔ attacked Lóngdū,
Tàizǔ (Mùróng Huǎng) held firmly and did not leave.
This event is recorded in the 96th scroll, Jìn Chéngdì Xiánkāng's 4th year.
Now, Mùróng Chuí is a seventy-year-old man,
weary and suffering from warfare.
He will ultimately be unable to maintain a siege for years to attack us.
We only need to defend the city to wear him out."
Mùróng Yǒng followed his advice.
The variations in military engagements
are infinite.
Only those who know themselves and their enemy
can fight a hundred battles without danger.
Mùróng Yǒng wished to compare himself to the events at Jíchéng,
hoping that those who shared the defense of Chángzǐ at that time
could indeed fight to the death and not leave,
like the various ministers of Mùróng Huǎng!
10 Qín zhǔ Dēng sent his son, Ruìnyáng Wáng Zōng (汝陰王宗), as a hostage to Hénán Wáng Gānɡuī (河南王乾歸) to request aid.
He conferred the title of Liáng Wáng (梁王) upon Gānɡuī,
and offered his sister to be Liáng Wáng hòu (梁王后).
Gānɡuī dispatched Qiánjūn Jiāngjūn Qǐfú Yìzhōu (前軍將軍乞伏益州) and others, leading one myriad cavalry, to rescue him.
In autumn,
the seventh month,
Dēng led his troops out to meet Gānɡuī's forces.
Hòuqín zhǔ Xīng (後秦主興) traveled from Āndìng (安定) to Jīngyáng (涇陽),
and fought Dēng at Shānnán (山南),
which is Mǎmáo shānnán (馬髦山南).
He killed him.
Dēng was fifty-two years old.
Xīng ordered the people to return to agriculture;
he relocated thirty thousand households from Yīnmì (陰密) to Cháng'ān (長安),
and bestowed Lǐ hòu (李后) upon Yáo Huǎng (姚晃).
Yìzhōu and the others, hearing of this,
withdrew their troops.
read from Xuān (宣),
also as written.)
Xīng then ascended the imperial throne,
changing the era name to Yánchū (延初);
he posthumously honored Dēng as Gāo Huángdì (高皇帝),
with the temple name Tàizōng (太宗).
11 Hòuqín Ānnán Jiāngjūn Qiáng Xī (安南將軍強熙) and Zhènyuǎn Jiāngjūn Qiáng Duō (鎮遠將軍強多) rebelled,
elevating Dòu Chōng (竇衝) as their leader.
Hòuqín zhǔ Xīng personally led an expedition to suppress them.
When his army reached Wǔgōng (武功),
Duō's elder brother's son Liángguó (良國) killed Duō and surrendered.
Xī fled to Qínzhōu (秦州),
and Chōng fled to Qiānchuān (汧川),
which is the land of Qiān xiàn (汧縣) in Fúfēng (扶風).
read kǔ jiān (苦堅).)
12 Sānhé Wáng Guāng (三河王光) appointed his son Fù (覆) as Dūdū Yùmén Yǐxī Zhūjūnshì (都督玉門以西諸軍事) and Xīyù Dàdūhù (西域大都護),
to garrison Gāochāng (高昌);
he ordered the sons and younger brothers of high officials to accompany him.
13 In the eighth month,
on the day Jǐsì (己巳),
Empress Dowager Lǐ (李氏) was honored as Huáng Tàihòu (皇太后)
and resided in Chóngxùn Gōng (崇訓宮).
14 Xīyàn zhǔ Yǒng (西燕主永), in dire straits,
sent his son, Chángshān Gōng Hóng (常山公弘), and others to seek aid from Yōngzhōu Cìshǐ Xī Huī (雍州刺史郗恢),
and also presented a jade seal.
Huī reported:
"If Chuí (垂) annexes Yǒng,
the trouble will deepen.
It is better to keep both alive,
so we can seize the opportunity to eliminate both."
The Emperor deemed this correct and
issued an edict to Qīng-Yǎn Èrzhōu Cìshǐ Wáng Gōng (青‧兗二州刺史王恭) and Yùzhōu Cìshǐ Yǔ Kǎi (豫州刺史庾楷) to rescue him.
(Kǎi
was the grandson of Liàng (亮).
The Yǔ clan was purged by Huán Wēn (桓溫),
and Kǎi was unable to revive it;
from then on, its influence waned.)
Yǒng also sent his heir apparent Liàng (亮) to serve as a hostage.
Píng Guī (平規) pursued Liàng and overtook him at Gāodū (高都),
capturing him.
(Gāodū xiàn (高都縣) belonged to Shàngdǎng Jùn (上黨郡).
During the Suí (隋) dynasty, it was Zézhōu Dānchuān xiàn (澤州丹川縣).
During the Táng (唐) dynasty, it was Jìnchéng xiàn (晉城縣).)
Wèi Wáng Guī (魏王珪) dispatched Chénliú Gōng Qián (陳留公虔) and Jiāngjūn Yǔ Yuè (將軍庾岳), leading fifty thousand cavalry, to cross the Yellow River eastward
and garrison Xiùróng (秀容) to rescue him.
(This is the northern Xiùróng,
within the boundaries of Hàn Dìngxiāng Jùn (漢定襄郡).
Later, Wèi (魏) established Xiùróng Jùn (秀容郡) and Xiùróng xiàn (秀容縣) there.
They also established the Xiùróng Hùjūn (秀容護軍) sixty li northwest of the Fénshuǐ (汾水),
relocating the Hú (胡) people from northern Xiùróng there.
This is the southern Xiùróng.
Liú Xù (劉昫) states: Xīnzhōu Xiùróng xiàn (忻州秀容縣) was the land of Hàn Fényáng xiàn (漢汾陽縣).
During the Suí (隋) dynasty, it was moved from the old city of Xiùróng to this location,
and its name was changed accordingly.)
read shuài (率).
騎,
read qí jì (奇寄).)
(He was the son of Gérɡēn (紇根).
Gérɡēn is mentioned in Juan 104, first year.
紇,
read hù ɡǔ (戶骨).)
The generals of Dàyì Dòuguī (大逸豆歸)'s部, Fáqín (伐勤) and others, opened the gates and let the Yàn (燕) troops in.
The Yàn (燕) people seized Yǒng,
beheaded him,
and also executed his high officials, grand generals Diāo Yún (刁雲) and Dàyì Dòuguī, and more than thirty others.
They obtained the eight commanderies and over seventy thousand households that Yǒng had controlled, as well as many chariots, imperial regalia, musicians, treasures, and other valuables from Qín (秦).
Yàn zhǔ Chuí (燕主垂) appointed Dānyáng Wáng Zàn (丹楊王瓚) as Bīngzhōu Cìshǐ (幷州刺史),
to garrison Jìnyáng (晉陽);
Yídū Wáng Fèng (宜都王鳳) as Yōngzhōu Cìshǐ (雍州刺史),
to garrison Chángzǐ (長子).
Yǒng's Shàngshū Púyè Chānglí Qū Zūn (尚書僕射昌黎屈遵),

Shàngshū Yángpíng Wáng Dé (尚書陽平王德), Mìshū Jiān Zhōngshān Lǐ Xiān (祕書監中山李先), Tàizǐ Zhānshì Bóhǎi Fēng Zé (太子詹事渤海封則), Huángmén Láng Tàishān Húmǔ Liàng (黃門郎太山胡母亮), Zhōngshū Láng Zhāng Téng (中書郎張騰), and Shàngshū Láng Yànjùn Gōngsūn Biǎo (尚書郎燕郡公孫表) were all promoted according to their talents.
(Lǐ Xiān and Gōngsūn Biǎo
later both served Wèi (魏)
and attained prominent positions.)
In the ninth month,
Chuí traveled from Chángzǐ to Yè (鄴).
15 In winter,
the tenth month,
Qín zhǔ Chóng (秦主崇) was driven out by Liáng Wáng Gānɡuī (梁王乾歸)
and fled to Lǒngxī Wáng Yáng Dìng (隴西王楊定).
Dìng left Sīmǎ Shào Qiáng (司馬邵彊) to guard Qínzhōu (秦州),
and personally led twenty thousand men with Chóng to attack Gānɡuī.
Gānɡuī dispatched Liángzhōu Mù Kētán (涼州牧軻彈), Qínzhōu Mù Yìzhōu (秦州牧益州), and Lìyì Jiāngjūn Jiéguī (立義將軍詰歸), leading thirty thousand cavalry, to resist them.
(Kētán, Yìzhōu, and Jiéguī were all of the Qǐfú (乞伏) clan.
The two provincial governors of Liáng and Qín were appointed by Gānɡuī,
indicating he did not truly possess that territory.
"Kētán"
is written "Kētán" (軻殫) in the Jìnshū Zàijì (晉書載記).
帥,
read shuài (率);
same below.)
They were defeated at Píngzhōu (平州).
The Zàijì (載記) writes
"Píngchuān" (平川),
which should be followed.
Kētán's Sīmǎ Zhái Wēn (司馬翟瑥) brandished his sword and angrily said:
"The Lord, with his heroic might, established his foundation,
invincible in every direction,
and his prestige shook Qín (秦) and Shǔ (蜀).
As a member of the imperial clan, you hold the position of grand marshal;
you should exert your utmost to serve the state, even to the point of death.
Though Qínzhōu is now lost,
our two armies are still intact.
How can you retreat at the mere sight of the enemy?
With what face will you meet the Lord?"
"Though I, Wēn, am unworthy,
can I not, by expediency, execute the general?"
Kētán apologized, saying:
"I did not know the hearts of the men until now.
If you can indeed be so,
how dare I cherish my life!"
Thereupon, he led his cavalry forward to battle.
Yìzhōu and Jiéguī also deployed their troops to follow,
utterly defeating Dìng's army.
Dìng and Chóng were killed,
and seventeen thousand heads were taken.
(In the seventh year of Mùdì Yǒnghé (穆帝永和),
Qín Wáng Jiàn (秦王健) changed the era name and ascended the throne,
ruling through six lords,
and perished after forty-two years.
Qǐfú (乞伏) only then gained Qínzhōu.)
Dìng had no sons.
His uncle Fóɡǒu (佛狗)'s son Shèng (盛),
who had previously guarded Chóuchí (仇池),
proclaimed himself Zhēngxī Jiāngjūn (征西將軍), Qínzhōu Cìshǐ (秦州刺史), and Chóuchí Gōng (仇池公).
He posthumously honored Dìng as Wǔ Wáng (武王);
he then sent envoys to declare himself a vassal.
Qín Tàizǐ Xuān (秦太子宣) fled to Shèng.
He divided the
Dī (氐) and Qiāng (羌) into twenty Hùjūn (護軍) units,
each serving as a garrison,
without establishing commanderies or counties.
16 Yàn zhǔ Chuí (燕主垂) made an eastern tour to Yángpíng (陽平) and Píngyuán (平原).
He ordered Liáoxī Wáng Nóng (遼西王農) to cross the Yellow River
and, with Ānnán Jiāngjūn Yǐn Guó (安南將軍尹國), seize territory in Qīng (青) and Yǎn (兗) provinces.
Nóng attacked Lǐnqīu (廩丘),
and Guó attacked Yángchéng (陽城);
both were captured.
Dōngpíng Tàishǒu Wéi Jiǎn (東平太守韋簡) was killed in battle.
The commanderies of Gāopíng (高平), Tàishān (泰山), and Lángyé (琅邪) were all abandoned by their officials who fled.
Nóng advanced his army to Línhǎi (臨海),
which is near Dōnghǎi (東海).
17 Ruòrán Gédūohàn (柔然曷多汗) abandoned his father
and, with Shèlún (社崙), led their followers westward.
(The Ruòrán submitted to Wèi (魏),
seen in Volume 16, last year.
汗,
read hán (寒).
崙,
read lú kūn (盧昆).)
They reached Bánà shān (跋那山) in Shàngjùn (上郡) and
beheaded Gédūohàn.
Shèlún gathered several hundred of the remaining followers
and fled to Hòubá (候跋).
Hòubá settled them in the southern border region.
Shèlún attacked Hòubá and
killed him;
Hòubá's sons Qǐbá (啟跋) and Wújié (吳頡) all fled to Wèi (魏).
Shèlún plundered the various tribes west of Wǔyuán (五原)
and fled across the Mòběi (漠北).
From this point, the Ruòrán became a constant threat to Wèi (魏).
(According to the Zàijì (載記),
Shèlún was a Xīanbéi (鮮卑) of Héxī (河西),
thus the Ruòrán were also of Xīanbéi (鮮卑) stock.)
18th day of the 11th month,
Yān's Liáoxī Wáng Nóng (燕遼西王農) defeated Pìlǘ Hún (辟閭渾) at Lóngshuǐ (龍水).
Guō Yuánshēng (郭緣生)'s *Shùzhēng Jì* (述征記) states: Fēngshān (逢山) is twenty *lǐ* south of Guǎnggù (廣固).
Yángshuǐ (洋水) flows past its north face and then northeast,
commonly known as Shígōu Shuǐ (石溝水).
It emerges from north of Wēisù Shān (委粟山)
and flows east into Jùyáng Shuǐ (巨洋水),
known as Shígōu Kǒu (石溝口).
However, the lower reaches of this river sometimes experience obstructions;
when its waters swell in spring and summer,
the currents flow without interruption,
and it is also sometimes called Lóngquán Shuǐ (龍泉水).
敗 (bài),
bǔ mài fān.
In the 12th month,
Yān Zhǔ Chuí (燕主垂) summoned Nóng (農) and others to return.
19th day of the month, Qín Zhǔ Xīng (秦主興) sent envoys to establish good relations with Yān,
and also sent Bǎo (寶)'s son Mǐn (敏) to Yān.
Yān enfeoffed Mǐn (敏) as Hédōng Gōng (河東公).
20th day of the month, Liáng Wáng Gānɡuī (梁王乾歸) declared himself Qín Wáng (秦王)
and issued a general amnesty.
From this point onward,
historians distinguish his state as Xī Qín (西秦).
1st day of spring,
in the 1st month,
Yān Zhǔ Chuí (燕主垂) dispatched Sànqí Chángshì Fēng Zé (散騎常侍封則) to return the diplomatic visit to Qín.
Then he hunted from Píngyuán (平原) to Guǎngchuān (廣川), Bóhǎi (勃海), and Chánglè (長樂) before returning.
Hàn Gāozǔ (漢高祖) established Xìndū Jùn (信都郡).
In the 2nd year of Jǐngdì (景帝),
it became Guǎngchuān Guó (廣川國).
Míngdì (明帝) renamed it Lèchéng (樂成).
Āndì (安帝) changed it to Ānpíng (安平).
Jìn (晉) changed it to Chánglè Jùn (長樂郡),
and also separately established Guǎngchuān Jùn (廣川郡).
樂 (lè),
音 luò.
2nd day of the month, Xī Qín Wáng Gānɡuī (西秦王乾歸) appointed Crown Prince Chìpán (熾磐) as Shàngshū Lìng (尚書令),
Zuǒ Chángshǐ Biān Ruì (左長史邊芮) as Zuǒ Púyè (左僕射),
and Yòu Chángshǐ Mì Yí (右長史祕宜) as Yòu Púyè (右僕射).
All official appointments followed the precedents of Wèi Wǔ (魏武) and Jìn Wén (晉文).
However, he still referred to himself as Dà Chányú (大單于) and Dà Jiāngjūn (大將軍).
Biān Ruì (邊芮) and others retained their positions as departmental aides.
3rd day of the month, Xuēgān Tàixífú (薛干太悉伏) fled from Cháng'ān (長安) back to Lǐngběi (嶺北).
Lǐngběi (嶺北)
refers to the north of Jiǔzōng Lǐng (九嵕嶺).
In the 18th year,
Tàixífú (太悉伏) went over to Qín (秦).
4th day of the 2nd month,
on the *Jiǎyín* day,
Shàngshū Lìng Lù Nà (尚書令陸納) passed away.
5th day of the 3rd month,
on the first day of the month, *Gēngchén*,
there was a solar eclipse.
6th day of the month, the Crown Prince moved into the Eastern Palace.
Dānyáng Yǐn Wáng Yǎ (丹楊尹王雅) was appointed acting Shàofù (少傅).
At that time, Huìjī Wáng Dàozǐ (會稽王道子) wielded exclusive power and was extravagant and indulgent.
His favored attendants Zhào Yá (趙牙), originally an actor,
and Rú Qiānqiū (茹千秋), originally a thief-catcher from Qiántáng (錢唐).
Qiántáng Xiàn (錢唐縣),
during the Former Hàn (前漢) was subordinate to Huìjī Jùn (會稽郡),
during the Later Hàn (後漢) was subordinate to Wú Jùn (吳郡).
*Qiántáng Jì* (錢唐記) says: The prefectural administrator Huá Xìn (華信) proposed building this dike to prevent seawater.
When construction began,
those who could bring one *hú* of earth were offered one thousand *qián*.
Within a month,
those who came gathered like clouds.
The dike was not yet complete when payments stopped.
Thereupon, all who carried earth and stone abandoned them and left.
The dike was completed thereby,
hence it was named Qiántáng (錢塘).
Yáng Zhènghéng (楊正衡) says: 茹 (Rú),
pronounced as rú,
also èr jù fān;
this surname existed in Zhè (浙) region in ancient times.
Dàozǐ (道子) appointed Yá (牙) as Wèijùn Tàishǒu (魏郡太守)
and Qiānqiū (千秋) as Piàojì Zīyì Cānjūn (驃騎諮議參軍).
Yá (牙) opened the Eastern Residence for Dàozǐ (道子),
built mountains and dug ponds,
incurring expenses in the tens of thousands.
The Emperor once visited his residence
and said to Dàozǐ (道子):
"There is a mountain within the palace,
which is very good;
however, the ornamentation is excessive."
Dàozǐ (道子) had no reply.
After the Emperor left,
Dàozǐ (道子) said to Yá (牙):
"If the Emperor knew the mountain was man-made,
you would surely die!"
Yá (牙) said:
"With Your Grace here,
how dare I die!"
The construction intensified.
Qiānqiū (千秋) sold offices and abused his power,
accumulating hundreds of millions in wealth.
Bópíng Lìng Wúxīng Wénrén Shì (博平令吳興聞人奭) submitted a memorial on this matter.
Bópíng Xiàn (博平縣),
during the Hàn (漢) was subordinate to Dōngjùn (東郡),
during the Jìn (晉) was subordinate to Píngyuán Jùn (平原郡);
south of the Yangtze, it was subordinate to Wèijùn (魏郡),
both the county and the prefecture were established by displaced populations.
But pressured by the Empress Dowager,
he could not bear to dismiss them.
Therefore, he promoted esteemed figures and trusted confidantes such as Wáng Gōng (王恭), Xī Huī (郗恢), Yīn Zhòngkān (殷仲堪), Wáng Xún (王珣), Wáng Yǎ (王雅), etc.,
placing them in crucial internal and external positions to guard against Dàozǐ (道子).
Dàozǐ (道子) also brought in Wáng Guóbǎo (王國寶) and Guóbǎo (國寶)'s cousin Lángyá Nèishǐ Xù (琅邪內史緒) as his confidantes.
From this, factions arose in competition,
and the former joy of brotherly affection no longer existed.
The Empress Dowager constantly mediated their disputes.
Zhōngshū Shìláng Xú Miǎo (中書侍郎徐邈) casually spoke to the Emperor, saying:
