Xián said: The former city of Jǔyáng County
is east of present-day Guīzhōu.
is pronounced *jǔ*.
Mùróng Chuí was seventy-one years old.
On the *bǐngshēn* day,
he arrived at Zhōngshān.
On the *wùxū* day,
his death was announced.
He was posthumously given the title Chéngwǔ Huángdì,
and his temple name was Shìzǔ.
On the *rénchén* day,
Tàizǐ Bǎo ascended the throne.
Bǎo,
courtesy name Dàoyòu,
was Mùróng Chuí's fourth son.
The era name was changed to Yǒngkāng.
In the fifth month,
on the *xīnhài* day,
Fànyángwáng Dé was appointed Dūdū of the military affairs of Jì, Yǎn, Qīng, Xú, Jīng, and Yù six provinces, Chēqí Dàjiàngjūn, and Jìzhōu Mù,
stationed at Yè.
Liáoxīwáng Nóng was appointed Dūdū of the military affairs of Bīng, Yōng, Yì, Liáng, Qín, and Liáng six provinces, and Bīngzhōu Mù,
stationed at Jìnyáng.
Additionally, Āndìngwáng Kùrùguān Wěi was made Tàishī,
and Fúyúwáng Wèi was made Tàifù.
Yú Wèi
was a prince of Fúyú.
Yān Wáng Huàng defeated Fúyú and obtained him.
When Yān fell,
he entered Qín.
When Qín was in chaos,
he returned to Yān.
Mùróng Chuí, Lord of Yān, enfeoffed him as Fúyúwáng.
On the *jiǎyín* day,
Zhàowáng Lín was made Lǐng Shàngshū Zuǒ Púyè,
Gāoyángwáng Lóng was made Lǐng Yòu Púyè,
Chánglègōng Shèng was made Sīlì Xiàowèi,
and Yídūwáng Fèng was made Jìzhōu Cìshǐ.
5 On the *yǐmǎo* day,
Sànqí Chángshì Liú Gāi of Péngchéng was made Xúzhōu Cìshǐ,
stationed at Juānchéng.
6 On the *jiǎzǐ* day,
Wàngcàigōng Xiè Yǎn was made Shàngshū Zuǒ Púyè.
Wàngcài County belonged to Yùzhāng Commandery.
Shěn Yuē said: During the Zhōngpíng era of Emperor Líng of Hàn,
the people of Shàngcài in Rǔnán were relocated to this city,
and a county was established named Shàngcài.
In the first year of Tàikāng of Emperor Wǔ of Jìn,
the name was changed.
Sòng Bái said: Because the people of Shàngcài longed for their homeland,
it was called Wàngcài (Longing for Cài).
7 In the beginning,
Mùróng Chuí, King of Yān, first had sons Lìng and Bǎo by Empress Duàn.
Later, Empress Duàn bore sons Lǎng and Jiàn.
He favored Lín, Nóng, Lóng, Róu, and Xī, sons of other concubines.
When Bǎo was first Crown Prince,
he had a good reputation,
but later became wild and negligent,
causing disappointment both inside and outside the court.
The latter Empress Duàn once said to Mùróng Chuí:
Mùróng Chuí, King of Yān, first married a Lady Duàn,
who died due to the slander of Empress Kězúhún.
When he later ascended the throne,
he posthumously honored her as Empress.
He then took another Lady Duàn as Empress,
hence the historical record distinguishes her as "latter Empress Duàn."
"The Crown Prince, in an era of peace and stability,
would be capable of maintaining the established order.
However, with the current difficulties of the nation,
I fear he lacks the talent to save the world.
Liáoxī and Gāoyáng, the two kings,
are your Majesty's virtuous sons.
You should choose one of them
to entrust with the great enterprise.
Zhàowáng Lín is treacherous, deceitful, headstrong, and perverse.
In the future, he will surely be a calamity for the state;
you should deal with him early."
Bǎo was skilled at serving Mùróng Chuí's attendants,
and many of the attendants praised him.
Therefore, Mùróng Chuí considered him virtuous and
said to Lady Duàn:
"Do you wish to make me another Jìn Xiàngōng!"
Jìn Xiàngōng believed the slander of Lǐ Jī and killed Crown Prince Shēnsheng.
She told her sister, Fànyángwáng,
"That the Crown Prince is untalented is known throughout the world.
I speak of it for the sake of the state,
yet the Lord takes me for Lǐ Jī.
How bitter this is!
Observing the Crown Prince, he will surely ruin the state.
Fànyángwáng possesses extraordinary temperament and capacity.
If the Yān dynasty's destiny is not yet exhausted,
perhaps it lies with the King!"
Bǎo and Lín heard this and resented her.
On the *yǐchǒu* day,
Bǎo had Lín tell Lady Duàn:
"You often said that the Lord could not maintain the great enterprise.
Now, can he indeed not?
You should commit suicide early
to preserve the Duàn clan!"
Lady Duàn angrily said:
"You brothers do not hesitate to force your own mother to her death,
how much less will you be able to preserve the ancestral enterprise!
Do I value death?
I only lament that the state will not last long."
Thereupon, she committed suicide.
Bǎo deliberated, arguing that since Empress Duàn had plotted to depose the legitimate heir,
she had not behaved as an empress mother should,
and therefore, a proper funeral should not be held.
Many officials all agreed.
However, Zhōngshūlìng Suī Suì boldly proclaimed in court:
"There is no principle for a son to abolish his mother's status.
Empress Ānsī Yán of Hàn personally deposed Emperor Shùn.
This event is recorded in volume fifty of the Hàn [history] under the third year of Yánguāng of Emperor Ān.
Moreover, the former Empress's words were vague;
whether they were true or false is unknown!"
Thus, a proper funeral was held.
8 In the sixth month,
on the day of Guǐyǒu,
Wèi Wáng Guī sent General Wáng Jiàn and others to attack Yān’s Grand Administrator of Guǎngníng, Liú Kàngní.
They beheaded him.
Guǎngníng County,
in the Hàn dynasty, belonged to Shànggǔ Commandery.
In the Tàikāng period of the Jìn dynasty,
it was separated to establish Guǎngníng Commandery.
Kàng,
pronounced as Kǔlàngfān.
Yān’s Grand Administrator of Shànggǔ and Duke of Kāifēng, Xiáng, abandoned his commandery and fled.
Xiáng
was the great-grandson of Huáng.
9 On the day of Dīnghài,
Wèi Hètài died.
She was the mother of Wèi Wáng Guī.
10 Yān Zhǔ Bǎo decided to re-evaluate the old registers of the gentry families,
distinguishing between clear and turbid (elite and commoner),
reviewing households;
he abolished the households that were sheltered and privileged by military camps,
assigning them all to commanderies and counties.
The households sheltered and privileged by military camps
were those occupied by various armies as their retainers.
This caused them to harbor disloyal sentiments.
To implement this matter
was not necessarily wrong;
however, at the beginning of Mùróng Bǎo's reign,
the national army had just suffered a defeat,
Many among the lower classes harbored rebellious thoughts,
so it was not appropriate to proceed hastily.
The Great Learning says: "Things have a root and branches,
affairs have an end and a beginning.
Knowing what comes first and what comes last
will bring one close to the Way."
11 Sānhé Wáng Lǚ Guāng ascended to the position of Heavenly King,
established the state title of Dàliáng,
issued a general amnesty,
and changed the reign title to Lóngfēi.
Lǚ Guāng,
whose courtesy name was Shìmíng,
was a Dī from Luèyáng.
His father, Póróu,
had assisted Fú Jiān.
He made his heir, Shào, the Crown Prince,
and enfeoffed twenty of his sons and younger brothers as dukes and marquises.
He appointed Zhōngshūlìng Wáng Xiáng as Shàngshū Zuǒ Púyè,
and five others, including Zuòshùláng Duàn Yè, as Shàngshū.
Guāng sent an envoy to appoint Tūfà Wūgū as Zhēngnán Dàjiāngjūn, Yìzhōumù, and Zuǒxiánwáng.
Wūgū said to the envoy:
"King Lǚ's sons are greedy and lewd.
Among Guāng's sons mentioned in history are
Zuǎn, Hóng, Shào, and Fù.
Guāng's nephew, Shí Cōng, slandered and killed Dù Jìn.
The other two should be investigated.
How can I go against the will of the people
and accept an unrighteous title!
I should be doing the work of an emperor and king."
So, he kept their drums, trumpets, and feathered ceremonial implements,
expressed his gratitude, and sent them away.
12 Píng Guī gathered his remaining partisans and occupied Gāotáng.
Gāotáng County,
since the Hàn dynasty, belonged to Píngyuán Commandery.
The people of the eastern lands,
who had long harbored a desire for generosity and benevolence,
thronged the roads to welcome him.
"Xiāng shǔ yú lù" means they were connected along the road.
Shǔ,
pronounced as Zhīyùfān.
In the seventh month,
Lóng advanced his army to the river.
Guī abandoned Gāotáng and fled.
Lóng sent Jiànwēi Jiāngjūn Mùróng Jìn and others to cross the river and pursue him.
They beheaded Guī in Jìběi.
Píng Xǐ fled to Péngchéng.
13 He took the daughter of the late Zhōngshūlìng Wáng Xiànzhī as Crown Princess.
Xiànzhī
was the son of Xīzhī.
Xīzhī
was a cousin of Wáng Dǎo.
14 Wèi's officials persuaded Wèi Wáng Guī to adopt an imperial title.
Guī then began to display the emperor's banners and flags,
using the imperial escort rituals for going out and returning,
and changed the reign title to Huángshǐ.
Guī
was the legitimate grandson of Shíyìjiān and the son of Shí.
Details can be found in Volume 104, first year.
Since Fú Jiān's defeat at Huái and Féi,
fourteen years had passed.
Between Guān and Hé,
the chiefs of the Róng and Dí
rose and fell repeatedly.
The Jìn people viewed this
with indifference, as it did not concern their hearts.
With the rise of Tuòbá Guī,
the shape of the North and South was determined.
Once the shape of the North and South was determined,
eventually the South would be annexed by the North.
Alas!
Since the Suí dynasty,
among those whose names were renowned in their time,
six or seven out of ten were descendants from north of the Daì region.
What good, then, was the distinction of clans?
Guī approved of this.
Yān Liáoxī Wáng Nóng led tens of thousands of his retainers to Bìngzhōu.
Bìngzhōu had always lacked provisions,
and that year there was an early frost,
so the people could not supply their food.
He also sent various departmental military governors to supervise the various Hú tribes.
Because of this, both the common people and the barbarians resented him
and secretly summoned the Wèi army.
In the eighth month,
on the day of Jǐhài,
Wèi Wáng Guī launched a major campaign against Yān.
Without internal support or a sure plan for victory,
a large-scale campaign should not be launched.
He marched south from Mǎyì,
crossed Jùzhù,
his banners and flags stretching over two thousand *lǐ*,
and advanced with drums beating.
Zuǒ Jiāngjūn Lǐ Lì of Yànmén led fifty thousand cavalry as the vanguard.
He separately sent General Fēng Zhēn and others to march from the eastern route through Jūndū
to attack Yān’s Yōuzhōu.
The Wèi Shū, Guānshì Zhì states:
During the time of Tuòbá Jié fén,
among the other clans who migrated inward were the Bēns,
later changed to Fēng.
Jūndū County,
in the Former Hàn, belonged to Shànggǔ Commandery;
in the Later Hàn, it belonged to Guǎngyáng Commandery;
in the Jìn, it belonged to the State of Yān.
There was Jūndū Pass.
Xián says: Today, Chāngpíng County in Yōuzhōu has Jūndū Mountain,
located to its northwest.
15 Yān Zhēngběi Dàjiāngjūn, Governor of Yōu and Píng Provinces, and Duke of Qīnghé, Huì, whose mother was of humble birth but older,
was valiant and intelligent, possessing remarkable talents. Yān Zhǔ Chuí loved him.
When Bǎo attacked Wèi,
Chuí ordered Huì to assume the affairs of the Eastern Palace and oversee all records.
He was treated with the same courtesies as the Crown Prince.
Zǒnglù
means to oversee all court affairs.
Chuí ordered Huì to garrison Lóngchéng,
entrusting him with the responsibilities of the northeast.
Officials and assistants for the state government
were all selected from the most talented and respected individuals of the time.
When Chuí was gravely ill,
he left a will instructing Bǎo to make Huì his successor.
However, Bǎo loved his youngest son, Púyáng Gōng Cè,
and his intention was not for Huì.
Chánglè Gōng Shèng was the same age as Huì
and felt ashamed to be beneath him.
So, he and Zhào Wáng Lín together persuaded Bǎo to establish Cè.
Bǎo agreed.
On the day of Yǐhài,
Lady Duàn was established as Empress,
and Cè was made Crown Prince.
Both Huì and Shèng were promoted to the rank of king.
Cè was eleven years old
and had always been foolish and weak.
When Huì heard of this,
he was resentful in his heart.
In the ninth month,
Zhāngwǔ Wáng Zhòu escorted the coffins of Yān Zhǔ Chuí and Chéng'āi Duàn Hòu for burial at Xuānpínglíng in Lóngchéng.
Chéng'āi Hòu
was the Empress Duàn, Bǎo's stepmother, whom Bǎo had killed.
The previous year, Lóng had returned to Zhōngshān from Lóngchéng.
Huì had actually replaced him,
so he was ordered to return his retainers and assistants.
He kept many retainers and did not send them away.
Zhòu was older and senior in lineage,
but Huì constantly insulted and treated him with contempt in all matters.
All who saw this knew he harbored different ambitions.
This laid the groundwork for the conflict between Bǎo and his son Huì.
16 On the day of Wùwǔ,
the Wèi army arrived at Yángqǔ.
Yángqǔ County, since the Hàn dynasty, belonged to Tàiyuán Commandery.
Sòng Bái said: The old city of Yángqǔ County
is forty-five *lǐ* north of Tàiyuán County.
It was moved at the end of the Later Hàn.
Suí Wéndì changed its name to Yángzhí,
and soon after changed it again to Fényáng County.
They approached Jìnyáng,
sent cavalry to surround the city and make a great clamor, then left.
Yān Liáoxī Wáng Nóng went out to battle,
suffered a great defeat,
and fled back to Jìnyáng.
Sīmǎ Mùyú Sōng closed the gates and refused him entry.
Previously, there was Mùyú Sōng who was executed for plotting to support Zhào Wáng Lín in a rebellion.
This is another person.
Wèi Zhōnglǐng Jiāngjūn Zhǎngsūn Féi pursued him.
Zhōnglǐng Jiāngjūn,
established by Wèi,
was equivalent to the Zhōnglǐngjūn of Wèi and Jìn.
Shuài
is pronounced as "lǜ."
He captured Nóng's wife and children.
The Yān army was completely annihilated.
Nóng was wounded,
and fled back to Zhōngshān alone with only three cavalrymen.
The King of Wèi, Tuòbá Guī, then took Bīngzhōu.
He first established the Grand Secretariat and various ministries,
appointing officials from Cìshǐ, Tàishǒu, Shàngshū Láng downwards.
All were filled by Confucian scholars.
When scholar-officials came to the military gate,
regardless of age,
all were brought in for comfort and consultation,
allowing everyone to speak freely.
Those with even a little talent or utility
were all promoted and appointed.
The historians say this is why Tuòbá Guī was able to take the Central Plains.
"Shào" (少),
pronounced "Shǎo" with a second tone.
On the day Jǐwèi,
Xi Mù, the Fǔguó Jiāngjūn, was sent to raid Fénchuān.
"Xī Shōu" (奚收)
should be
"Xī Mù" (奚牧).
Líshí Xiàn, since the Hàn dynasty, had belonged to Xīhé Jùn.
Yān established a Hùjūn to govern the Jīhú.
They pacified the scattered people
and encouraged agriculture and sericulture.
Mùróng Bǎo, the Lord of Yān, hearing that the Wèi army was about to arrive,
deliberated in the Eastern Hall.
Fú Mó, the Zhōngshān Yǐn, said:
"Now the Wèi army is strong and numerous,
fighting a thousand li away.
Riding on their victorious momentum, they are sharp;
if we allow them to enter the open plains,
they will be unstoppable.
We should block the strategic passes to resist them."
Fú Mó surrendered to Yān; see volume 106, 11th year.
"Wèi has many cavalry,
coming and going swiftly, plundering.
They carry provisions on horseback,
for no more than ten days;
we should order the prefectures and counties to gather the people,
with a thousand families forming one stronghold,
digging deep moats and raising high ramparts,
clearing the fields to await them.
When they arrive, having nothing to plunder,
in no more than sixty days,
their food will run out, and they will retreat on their own."
Fēng Yì, the Shàngshū, said:
"Now the Wèi army numbers several hundred thousand,
they are a formidable enemy under heaven.
Even if the people build strongholds,
it will not be enough to secure themselves;
this would be gathering soldiers and provisions to supply them.
Moreover, it would shake the people's morale
and show weakness.
It is better to block the passes and resist in battle;
this is the best strategy."
Mùróng Lín, the King of Zhào, said:
"Wèi is now riding on victorious momentum,
its vanguard is irresistible.
We should fully guard Zhōngshān,
and wait for them to be exhausted before striking."
Thereupon, they repaired the city walls and amassed grain,
preparing for a prolonged defense.
Not relying on strategic passes to resist in battle but rather defending the city walls;
this is why Mùróng Bǎo was defeated.
Ānxǐ,
was Ānxiǎn Xiàn in the Former Hàn dynasty.
In the Later Hàn dynasty, Emperor Zhāng changed its name to Ānxǐ,
belonging to Zhōngshān Jùn.
All matters were entrusted to Mùróng Lín.
This sets the stage for Mùróng Lín's rebellion against Mùróng Bǎo.
17 The emperor was addicted to wine,
lingering in the inner palace;
the times he governed when sober
were few.
Meaning, the times he was intoxicated were many,
and the times he was sober and handled affairs were few.
Guìrén Zhāng's favor surpassed all other consorts in the harem;
all in the harem feared her.
On the day Gēngshēn,
the emperor was feasting with his consorts,
all the courtesans and musicians attending.
At this time, Guìrén Zhāng was nearly thirty.
The emperor jested with her, saying:
"You, too, should be dismissed due to your age;
my heart now belongs to younger women."
Guìrén Zhāng was secretly enraged.
Towards evening,
the emperor, drunk, went to sleep in the Qīngshǔ Diàn,
Qīngshǔ Diàn
was built by the emperor.
She dismissed the attendants,
and ordered a maid to cover the emperor's face with a quilt,
assassinating him.
She heavily bribed those around her,
claiming
he "suddenly collapsed due to a nightmare."
At that time, the crown prince was weak-minded,
and Huìjī Wáng Dàozǐ was dissolute and confused,
so no further investigation was conducted.
Wáng Guóbǎo knocked on the Forbidden Gate at night,
wanting to enter and forge an imperial edict.
Shìzhōng Wáng Shuǎng refused him, saying:
"The Great Departed has passed away;
the Crown Prince has not yet arrived.
Anyone who dares to enter will be executed!"
Wáng Guóbǎo then stopped.
Wáng Shuǎng
was the younger brother of Wáng Gōng.
On the day Xīnyǒu,
the Crown Prince ascended the imperial throne
and declared a general amnesty.
On the day Guǐhài,
the officials proposed: Huìjī Wáng Dàozǐ should be promoted to Tàifù and Yángzhōu Mù,
and be granted the yellow yuè axe.
It was decreed that all internal and external affairs, whether active or static, should be consulted with him.
Emperor Ān was young and unintelligent;
Dù Yù said: unintelligent
is what the world calls an "idiot."
He could not even distinguish between hot and cold, or hunger and fullness;
his eating, drinking, sleeping, and waking were all not initiated by himself.
His younger maternal brother, Lángxié Wáng Déwén,
was respectful and cautious by nature.
He constantly attended to him,
adjusting things for him,
and only then did they become appropriate.
"Jiéshì" (節適)
means to adjust matters for his mouth and body.
"Wèi" (為)
pronounced "Wèi" with a fourth tone.
Originally,
Wáng Guóbǎo allied himself with Huìjī Wáng Dàozǐ.
Wáng Guóbǎo allied with Dàozǐ;
this began in volume 105, 8th year.
He was repeatedly impeached by Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng Chǔ Càn.
Wáng Guóbǎo built a private hall
that rivaled the Qīngshǔ Diàn.
Emperor Xiàowǔ greatly disliked this.
Wáng Guóbǎo, fearing,
then sought to curry favor with the emperor again and distanced himself from Dàozǐ.
The emperor again favored and cherished him.
Dàozǐ was greatly enraged.
He once confronted and rebuked Wáng Guóbǎo in the inner province,
and threw a sword at him.
Their old friendship was completely broken.
When the emperor passed away,
Wáng Guóbǎo again served Dàozǐ.
He and Wáng Xù colluded in wickedness and flattery.
Dàozǐ was further deluded by them,
relying on them as his confidants.
They then participated in managing court power,
their prestige shaking both inside and outside the court,
and were both hated by the people of the time.
Wáng Gōng arrived to attend the imperial funeral.
He always spoke with a serious expression and direct words,
which Dàozǐ deeply feared.
When Wáng Gōng finished court,
he sighed, saying:
"Although the rafters and ridgepole are new,
I already lament the 'Millet and Wheat!'"
The Grand Master of Zhōu, on official duty, passed by the old ancestral temples and palaces,
which had all become fields of millet and wheat,
and therefore composed the poem "Shǔ Lí."
Through Wáng Gōng's attendance at court,
he advised the Prince-Regent to ambush and kill him,
but Wáng Guóbǎo did not permit it.
Dàozǐ wished to reconcile internal and external affairs,
so he deeply confided in Wáng Gōng,
hoping to remove old grievances.
However, whenever Wáng Gōng spoke of current politics,
he would raise his voice and change his expression.
Dàozǐ knew Wáng Gōng could not be reconciled,
and thus conceived the intention to plot against him.
Someone advised Wáng Gōng (王恭) to take advantage of his court visit to execute Guó Bǎo (國寶) with his troops.
Wáng Gōng, however, felt that Yú Kǎi (庾楷), the Inspector of Yùzhōu (豫州), possessed numerous soldiers and horses,
and was allied with Guó Bǎo.
Fearing him,
Wáng Gōng dared not act.
Wáng Xún (王珣) said to Wáng Gōng:
"Although Guó Bǎo will ultimately bring disaster,
his crimes and rebellion have not yet been clearly exposed.
If we act hastily now,
we will surely lose the goodwill of the court and the populace.
Moreover, if you secretly unleash strong forces in the capital,
who would not call it rebellion?
If Guó Bǎo continues unchanged,
and his wickedness spreads throughout the land,
then, acting in accordance with the will of the people to eliminate him,
you will have no fear of failure."
Wáng Gōng then stopped.
Afterwards, he said to Wáng Xún:
"Lately, I've seen you as just like Hú Guǎng (胡廣)."
This meant: equivocating between powerful villains to preserve one's position and salary.
Bǐ (比)
is read as "pí zhì fān" (毗至翻),
meaning "near" (近).
"Wáng Líng (王陵) contended at court,
Chén Píng (陳平) maintained cautious silence,
but the question is what happens in the end!"
This meant: Wáng Líng lost his position due to his court contentions,
while Chén Píng, through cautious silence, was ultimately able to secure the Liú (劉) dynasty.
Zhēng (爭)
is read as "zhèng" (諍).
In winter,
the tenth month,
on the jiǎshēn (甲申) day,
Emperor Xiàowǔ (孝武帝) was buried in the Lóngpínglíng (隆平陵) mausoleum.
Wáng Gōng returned to his post.
Before leaving,
he said to Dàozǐ (道子):
"The emperor is in a period of mourning and silence.
The responsibility of the prime minister
was difficult even for Yī (伊) and Zhōu (周).
I hope Your Royal Highness will personally attend to all affairs of state,
accept frank advice,
ban profligate music,
and keep deceitful people at a distance."
Jī (幾)
is the same as jī (機).
Yuǎn (遠)
is read as "yú yuàn fān" (于願翻).
The eighteenth year (of Tàiyuán, 太元), Wèi (魏) King Guī (珪) dispatched the General of Champions, Yú Lìdī (于栗磾) of Dàirén (代人),
According to the "Official and Clan Records of the Wèi Shū" (魏書官氏志): Among the various tribes that assimilated during the time of Tuòbá Jiéfén (拓跋詰汾) were the Wùniǔyú (勿忸于) clan,
later changed to Yú (于) clan.
Guān (冠)
is read as "gǔ wán fān" (古玩翻).
Dī (磾)
is read as "dīng xī fān" (丁奚翻).
He secretly opened Hán Xìn's (韓信) old path from Jìnyáng (晉陽).
This was Hán Xìn's old path from Jǐngxíng (井陘) to attack Zhào (趙).
Shuài (帥)
is read as "lǜ" (率).
Qí (騎)
is read as "qí jì fān" (奇寄翻).
On the jǐyǒu (己酉) day,
Guī proceeded from Jǐngxíng towards Zhōngshān (中山).
Lǐ Xiān (李先) surrendered to Wèi.
The previous year,
Lǐ Xiān had returned to Yān (燕) from Xī Yān (西燕).
Qū (趨)
is read as "qī yù fān" (七喻翻).
Jiàng (降)
is read as "hù jiāng fān" (戶江翻).
The nineteenth year, Kētán (軻彈), the Minister of Lángzhōu (涼州) for Xī Qín (西秦), was at odds with Yìzhōu (益州), the Minister of Qínzhōu (秦州).
Kētán fled to Liáng (涼).
The twentieth year, Wèi King Guī attacked Chángshān (常山),
capturing it and obtaining its Grand Administrator Gǒu Yán (苟延).
All the governors and magistrates from Chángshān eastward
either fled or surrendered,
and all the commanderies and counties pledged allegiance to Wèi.
Only the three cities of Zhōngshān, Yè (鄴), and Xìndū (信都) remained under Yān's control.
Zhōngshān was the Yān capital,
Mùróng Dé (慕容德) guarded Yè,
and Mùróng Fèng (慕容鳳) guarded Xìndū,
all of which were important strongholds.
Wèi (為)
is read as "yú wěi fān" (于偽翻).
Guī ordered Gōng Yí (儀), the Duke of Dōngpíng (東平), to lead fifty thousand cavalry to attack Yè,
and General of Champions Wáng Jiàn (王建) and Left General Lǐ Lì (李栗) to attack Xìndū.
On the wùwǔ (戊午) day,
Guī advanced his army to Zhōngshān;
on the jǐwèi (己未) day,
he attacked it.
Mùróng Lóng (慕容隆), the King Gāoyáng (高陽) of Yān, defended the southern outer wall,
leading his troops in a fierce battle.
From dawn until dusk,
thousands were killed or wounded,
and the Wèi forces then retreated.
Guī said to his generals:
"Zhōngshān is a strong city,
and Bǎo (寶) will surely not be willing to fight outside.
A swift attack would wound our soldiers,
and a long siege would deplete our provisions.
It is better to first capture Yè and Xìndū,
and then plan for this."
On the dīngmǎo (丁卯) day,
Guī led his army south.
Zhāngwǔ (章武) King Zhòu (宙) returned from Lóngchéng (龍城).
Hearing of the Wèi invasion,
he rushed into Jì (薊)
and, with Zhènběi General Yángchéng (陽城) King Lán (蘭), they fortified the city and held their ground.
Lán was Chúi's (垂) younger cousin.
Wèi's detached general, Shí Hétóu (石河頭), attacked it,
but failed to overcome it.
According to the "Official and Clan Records of the Wèi Shū" (魏書官氏志): Among the various tribes that assimilated during the time of Tuòbá Jiéfén (拓跋詰汾) were the Wèishílán (嗢石蘭) clan,
later changed to Shí (石) clan.
Yúyáng (漁陽) County
belonged to Yúyáng Commandery in the Hàn (漢) dynasty;
it was abolished in the Jìn (晉) dynasty.
Guī's army encamped at Lǔkǒu (魯口).
Bólíng (博陵) Grand Administrator Shēn Yǒng (申永) fled to Hénán (河南),
and Gāoyáng (高陽) Grand Administrator Cuī Hóng (崔宏) fled to Hǎizhǔ (海渚).
Hǎizhǔ was an island in the sea.
Guī sent cavalry in pursuit,
captured them,
and appointed Cuī Hóng as a Gentleman of the Yellow Gate,
entrusting him, along with Gentleman of the Yellow Gate Attendant Zhāng Gǔn (張袞), with important strategic affairs and the establishment of new systems.
This laid the groundwork for the future eminence of Cuī Hóng and his son in Wèi.
Guī appointed Cuī Hóng as Central Secretariat Director,
responsible for issuing orders and overseeing all literary documents.
Yān's Fànyáng (范陽) King Dé dispatched Nán'ān (南安) King Qīng (青) and others to attack the Wèi army at Yè under the cover of night.
They defeated them,
and the Wèi army retreated to Xīnchéng (新城).
Xīnchéng was the city built by Yān's Lord Chúi when he attacked Yè.
Biéjià (別駕) Hán (韓) said:
"The ancients planned before they fought.
There are four reasons why the Wèi army should not be attacked: They are a detached force from afar,
whose advantage lies in open-field battle—this is one;
they have deeply penetrated our territory and are positioned in a death ground—this is two;
their vanguard has already been defeated,
but their rear formation is still solid—this is three;
their numbers are great while ours are few—this is four.
There are three reasons why our imperial army should not move: We are fighting on our own ground—this is one;
When fighting on one's own ground,
troops are easily defeated and scattered.
The morale of the troops is difficult to solidify—this is two;
Our city walls and moats are not yet repaired,
so we are unprepared for an enemy attack—this is three.
Currently, Wèi lacks provisions.
It is better to build deep fortifications and consolidate our forces to wear them out."
Dé agreed with him and recalled Qīng.
Qīng was Xiáng's (詳) elder brother.
In the twelfth month,
Hèlàilú (賀賴盧), the Duke of Liáoxī (遼西) for Wèi, led twenty thousand cavalry to join Gōng Yí (儀), the Duke of Dōngpíng, in attacking Yè.
Lailú was Nà's (訥) younger brother.
This lays the groundwork for Hèlàilú's surrender to Mùróng Dé.
According to the "Official and Clan Records of the Wèi Shū" (魏書官氏志),
among the assimilated clans were the Hèlài (賀賴) clan,
and in the north were the Hèlán (賀蘭) clan,
both later becoming the Hè (賀) clan.
Presumably, those who assimilated became the Hèlài clan,
and those who remained in the north became the Hèlán clan.
"Lán" (蘭)
and
"Lài" (賴)
were merely phonetic shifts.
Also, some Xiongnú (匈奴) tribes also had the Hèlài clan.
The great chieftain of a separate Wèi tribe, Mògēn (沒根), was brave and daring.
Wèi Wáng Guī (魏王珪) resented him.
Mògēn, fearing execution,
on the *jǐchǒu* day,
led several tens of his personal guards and surrendered to Yān.
Yān Zhǔ Bǎo (燕主寶) appointed him Zhèndōng Dàjiàngjūn (鎮東大將軍)
and enfeoffed him as Yànmén Gōng (鴈門公).
Mògēn requested to return and attack Wèi.
Bǎo found it difficult to give him heavy troops,
so he provided him with a hundred odd cavalry.
Mògēn imitated their command signals
and entered the Wèi camp at night,
reaching the central quarters.
Guī then became aware of it
and fled in panic and disarray.
Mògēn, with few followers,
was unable to rout their large force,
but he captured many heads and returned.
The historian states that Mùróng Bǎo (慕容寶) was unable to use the surrendered man as a spy to defeat Wèi.
*Shǎo* (少),
read as *shīzhǎo* (*詩沼*) reverse.
*Huài* (壞),
pronunciation *guài* (*怪*).
Yáng Shèng (楊盛) sent an envoy to request appointment;
an imperial edict appointed Shèng (盛) as Zhènnán Jiàngjūn (鎮南將軍) and Chóuchí Gōng (仇池公).
Shèng (盛) memorialized Fú Xuān (苻宣) as Píngběi Jiàngjūn (平北將軍).
This year,
Yuèzhì Jiéguī (越質詰歸) led two thousand households in rebellion against Xīqín (西秦) and surrendered to Qín (秦).
Yuèzhì Jiéguī (越質詰歸) had surrendered to Xīqín (西秦)
as seen in Volume 16 of the previous scroll.
*Shuài* (帥),
read as *lǜ* (*率*);
same below.
Chéngjì (成紀) county had belonged to Tiānshuǐ (天水) Commandery since the Hàn (漢) dynasty.
*Chù* (處),
read as *chānglǚ* (*昌呂*) reverse.
Qín Lǒngxī Wáng Shuòdé (秦隴西王碩德) attacked Jiāng Rǔ (姜乳) at Shàngguī (上邽).
Rǔ (乳) led his troops to surrender.
Qín (秦) appointed Shuòdé (碩德) as Qínzhōu Mù (秦州牧),
garrisoned at Shàngguī (上邽);
Rǔ (乳) was summoned to be Shàngshū (尚書).
Qiáng Xī (強熙) and Quán Qiānchéng (權千成) led thirty thousand troops to jointly besiege Shàngguī (上邽).
Shuòdé (碩德) defeated them.
Xī (熙) fled to Chóuchí (仇池),
and then came to surrender.
Shuòdé (碩德) attacked Qiānchéng (千成) to the west at Lüèyáng (略陽).
Qiānchéng (千成) surrendered.
After Xīyàn (西燕) was destroyed,
its appointed Hédōng Tàishǒu (河東太守) Liǔ Gōng (柳恭) and others each held troops and defended themselves.
Qín Zhǔ Xīng (秦主興) sent Jìn Wáng Xù (晉王緒) to attack them.
Gōng (恭) and others resisted at the river,
and Xù (緒) was unable to cross.
Initially,
during the Disorder of Yǒngjiā,
the Xuē (薛) clan of Fén yīn (汾陰) gathered their kinsmen
and, relying on the river, fortified themselves,
refusing to serve Liú (劉) or Shí (石).
When the Fú (苻) clan rose,
they courteously invited Xuē Qiáng (薛彊)
and appointed him Zhèndōng Jiàngjūn (鎮東將軍).
Qiáng (彊) led the Qín (秦) army to cross from Lóngmén (龍門).
The Wèi (魏) geographical record states: North of Liángshān (梁山) is Lóngménshān (龍門山),
which Dà Yǔ (大禹) excavated,
connecting to the Hé (河) estuary at Mèngjīn (孟津).
It is eighty paces wide,
with carved traces on the cliffs,
leaving his功 (gōng) still extant.
Liángshān (梁山) is northwest of Xiàyáng (夏陽) county in Féngyì (馮翊).
Gōng (恭) and others all surrendered.
Xīng (興) appointed Xù (緒) as the Mù (牧) of Bìng (幷) and Jì (冀) provinces,
garrisoned at Púbǎn (蒲阪).
Wáng Chóngwǔ (王崇武) punctuated, Róng Zhàozǔ (容肇祖) and Niè Chóngqí (聶崇岐) re-collated.
Sīmǎ Guāng (司馬光)
Compiled by Imperial Command
Later Academic Tiāntái (天臺)
Emperor Ān (安皇帝) A
His personal name was Dézōng (德宗),
courtesy name Dézōng (德宗),
the eldest son of Xiàowǔ Dì (孝武帝).
According to the posthumous naming system: "peaceful and not contentious" is called Ān (安);
also: "born with little decisiveness" is called Ān (安).
After the emperor ascended the throne,
Huán Xuán (桓玄) usurped power,
Liú Yù (劉裕) restored order,
there were southern expeditions and northern summons
[attacks]
and the Central Plains also experienced many troubles.
The *Tōngjiàn* records a total of ten volumes,
hence the number of volumes is written using the Ten Heavenly Stems.
Lóng’ān (隆安) First Year (*dīngyǒu*, 397 CE)
1 Spring,
First Month,
on the *jǐhài* day, the new moon,
the Emperor underwent the capping ceremony,
and changed the era name.
Wáng Xún (王珣), the Left Minister of the Department of State Affairs, was appointed Minister of the Department of State Affairs;
Wáng Guóbǎo (王國寶), the General of the Imperial Guards, was appointed Left Minister of the Department of State Affairs,
overseeing selections;
"overseeing selections"
means overseeing the selections of the Ministry of Personnel.
*Xuǎn* (選),
read as *xūliàn* (*須戀*) reverse.
The Prince of Kuàijī (會稽王), Dàozǐ (道子), gave all the Eastern Palace troops to Guóbǎo (國寶),
making him command them.
2 Yān Fànyáng Wáng Dé (燕范陽王德) sought help from Qín (秦).
The Qín (秦) army did not come out,
causing panic in Yè (鄴).
Hè Lài Lú (賀賴盧), considering himself Wèi Wáng Guī’s (魏王珪) maternal uncle,
refused to obey the orders of Dōngpíng Gōng Yí (東平公儀),
thereby creating a rift with Yí (儀).
Yí's (儀) Sīmǎ (司馬) Dīng Jiàn (丁建) secretly communicated with Dé (德)
and subsequently sowed discord,
shooting a letter into the city detailing the situation.
On the *jiǎchén* day,
there was a windstorm and haze,
making it dark at daytime.
There was a fire in Lài Lú's (賴盧) camp.
Jiàn (建) said to Yí (儀):
"Lài Lú (賴盧) is burning his camp to make trouble!"
Yí (儀) believed him
and withdrew his troops;
Lài Lú (賴盧), hearing of this,
also withdrew;
Jiàn (建) led his troops to Dé (德) and surrendered,
moreover stating that Yí's (儀) army was old and could be attacked.
Dé (德) sent Guìyáng Wáng Zhèn (桂陽王鎮) and Nán'ān Wáng Qīng (南安王青) to lead seven thousand cavalry to pursue and attack the Wèi (魏) army,
greatly defeating them.
Victory of an army lies in harmony;
discord among generals
is the root of defeat.
Yān Zhǔ Bǎo (燕主寶) sent Zuǒwèi Jiàngjūn (左衞將軍) Mùyú Téng (慕輿騰) to attack Bólíng (博陵),
killing Wáng Jiàn (王建) and other appointed governors and magistrates of Wèi (魏).
(He) attacked Xìndū (信都),
but could not take it for over sixty days,
and many soldiers died.
On the *gēngshēn* day,
Wèi Wáng Guī (魏王珪) himself attacked Xìndū (信都).
On the night of *rénxū*,
Yān Yídū Wáng Fèng (燕宜都王鳳) scaled the wall and fled to Zhōngshān (中山).
Fèng (鳳), knowing of Guī’s (珪) arrival,
lost his courage and fled.
On the *guǐhài* day,
Xìndū (信都) surrendered to Wèi (魏).
3 Liáng Wáng Guāng (涼王光) considered Xīqín Wáng Qián Guī (西秦王乾歸) to be repeatedly perfidious,
meaning that Qián Guī (乾歸) had previously pledged allegiance to Guāng (光) but then regretted it.
數 (shù),
read as suǒ jiǎo.
Qián Guī (乾歸) then requested to move east to Chéngjì (成紀) to avoid them, saying:
Chéngjì County (成紀縣),
since the Hàn (漢) dynasty, belonged to Tiānshuǐ Commandery (天水郡),
with its seat at Xiǎokēng Chuān (小坑川);
during the Táng (唐) dynasty, Xiǎnqīn County (顯親縣) was merged into Chéngjì County (成紀縣),
and the seat of Chéngjì County (成紀縣) was moved to Xiǎnqīn Chuān (顯親川).
"The victory or defeat of an army
lies in skill or clumsiness,
not in numbers.
Although Guāng's (光) army is numerous, it lacks discipline,
and his younger brother Yán (延), though brave, lacks strategy;
they are not worth fearing.
Moreover, all their elite troops are with Yán (延);
if Yán (延) is defeated,
Guāng (光) himself will flee."
Guāng (光) garrisoned at Chángzuì (長最),
and sent Tàiyuán Gōng Zuǎn (太原公纂) and others to lead three myriad infantry and cavalry to attack Jīnchéng (金城);
Qián Guī (乾歸) led two myriad troops to relieve it,
but before they arrived,
Zuǎn (纂) and others had captured Jīnchéng (金城).
Guāng (光) also sent his general Liáng Gōng (梁恭) and others with over one myriad armored soldiers to exit Yangwǔ Xiáxiá (陽武下峽).
Yángwǔ Xiáxiá (陽武下峽) is west of Gāopíng (高平),
where the Héshuǐ (河水) flows.
將 (jiàng),
read as jí liàng.
Tiānshuǐ Gōng Yán (天水公延) attacked Líntáo (臨洮), Wǔshǐ (武始), and Héguān (河關) with the troops from Fúhǎn (枹罕),
and captured them all.
Líntáo County (臨洮縣),
during the Hàn (漢) dynasty, belonged to Lǒngxī Commandery (隴西郡);
Huìdì (惠帝) divided it to belong to Dídao Commandery (狄道郡).
Wǔshǐ Commandery (武始郡),
was formerly the territory of Dídao County (狄道縣).
Héguān County (河關縣),
during the Former Hàn (前漢), belonged to Jīnchéng Commandery (金城郡);
during the Later Hàn (後漢), it belonged to Lǒngxī Commandery (隴西郡);
during the Jìn (晉) dynasty, it belonged to Dídao Commandery (狄道郡).
枹 (fú),
pronounced fū.
洮 (táo),
read as tǔ dāo.
"Qián Guī's (乾歸) army collapsed,
and he fled to Chéngjì (成紀)."
Yán (延) wanted to lead light cavalry to pursue him,
but Sīmǎ Gěng Zhì (司馬耿稚) advised:
"Qián Guī (乾歸) surpasses others in courage and strategy;
how could he possibly collapse at the mere sight of our army?
When he previously defeated Wáng Guǎng (王廣) and Yáng Dìng (楊定),
he always used a weak army to lure them.
For the defeat of Yáng Dìng (楊定), see the previous volume, Xiàowǔ Tàiyuán (孝武太元) nineteenth year.
In the eleventh year of Tàiyuán (太元),
Wáng Guǎng (王廣) was captured by Xiānbēi Pǐlán (鮮卑匹蘭)
and sent to Later Qín (後秦);
at this time, Qián Guī (乾歸) had not yet taken charge of state affairs.
Qián Guī's (乾歸) defeat of Guǎng (廣) should have been during Qǐfú Guórén's (乞伏國仁) time.
稚 (zhì),
read as zhí lì.
羸 (léi),
read as lún wéi.
There must be a deception;
it is advisable to array our ranks and advance,
ensuring that infantry and cavalry are connected,
and wait for all our forces to assemble.
Only then should we attack,
and there will be nothing we cannot overcome."
Yán (延) did not heed the advice,
advanced,
and encountered Qián Guī (乾歸).
Yán (延) died in battle.
Zhì (稚) and general Jiāng Xiǎn (姜顯) gathered the scattered troops
and returned to garrison at Fúhǎn (枹罕).
Guāng (光) also led his troops back to Gūzāng (姑臧).
4 Tūfà Wūgū (禿髮烏孤) proclaimed himself Grand Commander (大都督), Grand General (大將軍), Grand Chányú (大單于), and King of Xīpíng (西平王).
He issued a general amnesty
and changed the era name to Tàichū (太初).
He trained his troops at Guǎngwǔ (廣武)
and attacked Liáng (涼) Jīnchéng (金城),
capturing it.
Liáng Wáng Guāng (涼王光) sent general Dòu Gǒu (竇苟) to attack him,
and they battled at Jiētíng (街亭),
where the Liáng (涼) army suffered a great defeat.
5 Yān Zhǔ Bǎo (燕主寶), hearing that Wèi Wáng Guī (魏王珪) was attacking Xìndū (信都),
moved out to garrison at Shēnzé (深澤).
Shēnzé County (深澤縣),
during the Former Hàn (前漢), belonged to Zhuó Commandery (涿郡);
during the Later Hàn (後漢), it belonged to Ānpíng Kingdom (安平國);
during the Jìn (晉) dynasty, it belonged to Bólíng Commandery (博陵郡).
Sòng Bái (宋白) said: Shēnzé County (深澤縣) was named for the deep and wide waterways within its borders.
The Jùn Guó Zhì (郡國志) states: Púyīn County (蒲陰縣) of Zhōngshān (中山) has Yángchéng (楊城).
Bǎo (寶) brought forth all his treasures and palace women to recruit bandits from commanderies and kingdoms to attack Wèi (魏).
In the second month,
on the first day of the Jǐsì (己巳) cycle,
Guī (珪) returned to garrison at Yángchéng (楊城).
Mògēn's (沒根) nephew Chǒu Tí (醜提), who was the inspector of Bīngzhōu (幷州),
hearing that his uncle had surrendered to Yān (燕),
feared execution and
led his troops back to his country
to rebel.
Guī (珪) wanted to return north
and sent his Chancellor Shè Yán (涉延) to seek peace with Yān (燕),
and also requested to offer his younger brother as a hostage.
Bǎo (寶), hearing of Wèi's (魏) internal difficulties,
did not agree.
The Art of War (兵法) says: "If you know yourself and know your enemy, you will not be imperiled in a hundred battles."
Mùróng Bǎo (慕容寶) merely wished to take advantage of Tuòbá Guī's (拓跋珪) internal discord and trap him,
but he did not realize his own talent and strategy were insufficient to accomplish this.
難 (nàn),
read as nǎi dàn.
Bǎo (寶)
mustered all his forces, one hundred twenty thousand infantry and thirty-seven thousand cavalry, and garrisoned at Bǎisì (柏肆) in Qǔyáng (曲陽).
This is Xiàqǔyáng County (下曲陽縣) of Zhào Kingdom (趙國).
There was Bǎisì Wù (柏肆塢).
In the sixteenth year of Kāihuáng (開皇) of the Suí (隋) dynasty, Bǎisì County (柏肆縣) was established,
but was later abolished and merged into Chángshān Gǎochéng County (常山稾城縣).
The Wèi Shū Dì Jì (魏書帝紀) writes
"Bǎisì Wù (柏肆塢) of Jùlù (鉅鹿)."
According to the Dìxíng Zhì (地形志): The seat of Jùlù Commandery (鉅鹿郡) was Qǔyáng (曲陽).
On the Dīngchǒu (丁丑) day,
the Wèi (魏) army arrived
and encamped south of the river.
Bǎo (寶) secretly led his army across the river at night,
recruited over one myriad brave men to raid the Wèi (魏) camp.
Bǎo (寶) arrayed his troops north of the camp to provide support for them.
The recruited soldiers used the wind to start fires
and fiercely attacked the Wèi (魏) army.
The Wèi (魏) army fell into great disarray.
Guī (珪) was startled awake,
abandoned his camp, and fled barefoot.
The Yān (燕) general Qǐtèzhēn (乞特真), with over a hundred men, reached his tent
and obtained Guī's (珪) clothes and boots.
Soon after, the recruited soldiers were inexplicably startled themselves
and began to hack and shoot at each other.
Guī (珪), seeing this from outside the camp,
then beat the drum to rally his troops.
His attendants and the officers and soldiers of the central army gradually gathered.
He spread many torches outside the camp
and unleashed his cavalry to charge them.
The recruited soldiers suffered a great defeat.
The enemy was caught by surprise,
so they fled;
seeing the enemy's disorder, they then returned to battle;
indeed, those skilled in warfare observe changes and act accordingly.
Bǎo (寶) led his troops back across the river to the north.
On the Wùyín (戊寅) day,
Wèi (魏) organized its forces and arrived,
engaging Yān (燕) in a standoff.
The Yān (燕) army lost morale.
Bǎo (寶) retreated to Zhōngshān (中山),
and the Wèi (魏) army pursued and attacked them.
The Yān (燕) army was repeatedly defeated.
Bǎo (寶), fearing,
abandoned his main army
and led twenty thousand cavalry in a panicked retreat.
At that time, there was a great snowstorm,
and the frozen bodies piled up.
Bǎo (寶) feared being overtaken by the Wèi (魏) army
and ordered his soldiers to abandon hundreds of thousands of robes, staffs, and weapons,
not a single blade was kept.
Many Yān (燕) officials, generals, and soldiers surrendered to Wèi (魏) or were captured by Wèi (魏).
Previously,
Zhāng Gǔn (張袞) had once spoken to Wèi Wáng Guī (魏王珪) about the talent of Yān (燕) imperial secretary Cuī Chěng (崔逞).
According to the Biography of Zhāng Gǔn (張袞傳),
Gǔn (袞) had never met Chěng (逞),
but heard of his talent and praised him.
先 (xiān),
read as xī jiàn.
Guī (珪) was very pleased
and appointed Chěng (逞) as Shàngshū (尚書),
making him oversee the thirty-six bureaus (cáo).
Hàn Guāngwǔ (漢光武) divided the Shàngshū (尚書) into six bureaus (cáo)
and appointed thirty-four secretaries (láng),
totaling thirty-six including the Zǔo Cěng (左丞) and Yòu Cěng (右丞).
By the Wèi (魏) dynasty,

In the second year of Qīnglóng (青龍) of Míngdì (明帝),

Later, Yùncáo (運曹) was added,
making a total of thirty-five bureaus (cáo);
twenty-three secretaries (láng) were appointed,
who supervised each other in turn.
Now Wèi (魏) further increased them to thirty-six bureaus (cáo).
Some Wèi (魏) soldiers, having fled from Bǎisì (柏肆), returned
and reported that the main army had been defeated and scattered,
and they did not know the king's whereabouts.
Passing through Jìnyáng (晉陽),
the Jìnyáng (晉陽) defending general Fēng Zhēn (封真) consequently raised troops to attack the Bīngzhōu (幷州) inspector Qǔyáng Hóu Sùyán (曲陽侯素延).
Sùyán (素延) attacked and beheaded him.
Nán’ān Gōng Shùn, who was guarding Yúnzhōng,
heard of it,
and intended to personally take charge of the state affairs.
Zhuàng, who was about to replace a person, Mòtí, said:
"This is a major matter,
and should not be taken lightly.
It is advisable to carefully await further instructions;
otherwise,
the disaster will not be small."
Shùn then stopped.
Shùn
was the grandson of Shíyìjiān.
The chieftain of the Hèlán tribe, Fùlìjuàn, the chieftain of the Hélín tribe, Nìwùní, and the chieftain of the Héxī tribe, Chìnúgēn, all raised armies in rebellion.
Shùn attacked them,
but was unsuccessful.
Guī sent the An’yuǎn General, Yǔ Yuè, to lead ten thousand cavalry back to suppress the three tribes.
He pacified them all,
and the people of the state then felt secure.
Guī wanted to soothe and comfort the newly submitted people,
and deeply regretted the execution at Cānhé.
The details are in the previous scroll, during Emperor Xiàowǔ's Tàiyuán twentieth year.
Guī realized that the Yān people, warned by the disaster at Cānhé,
would fight desperately and not surrender,
hence his deep regret.
He dismissed officials.
He appointed Xī Mù as the Inspector of Bīngzhōu.
Mù wrote a letter to the Lord of Dōngqín, Xīng, addressing him with
"Dùnshǒu,"
treating him as an equal in etiquette.
At this time, the Qǐfú clan established a state in Lǒngxī,
calling it Qín,
hence the historical texts refer to Yáo Qín as Dōngqín to distinguish them.
When this was reported to Guī,
Guī executed Mù for it.
On the night of Jǐmǎo,
Mùyú Hào, a Shangshū Láng of Yān, plotted to assassinate the Lord of Yān, Bǎo,
and to install Zhào Wáng Lín.
He failed,
broke through the gate, and fled to Wèi.
Lín was unsettled by this.
This sets the stage for Lín fleeing to Xīshān.
6. In the third month,
Yān appointed Yítóng Sānsī Wǔxiāng Zhāng Chóng as Sīkōng.
Shí Lè divided Shàngdǎng to establish Wǔxiāng Commandery and Wǔxiāng County.
The present-day Yúshè County of Táng's Liáozhōu is that place.
7. Originally,
Yān's Qīnghé Wáng Huì, hearing that the Wèi army was advancing eastward,
submitted a memorial requesting to go to the aid.
Lord Bǎo of Yān granted his request.
Huì initially had no intention of leaving,
meaning he initially had no intention of leaving Lóngchéng.
Chóng
was the son of Sōng.
The rest of Sōng can be found in the previous scroll, Emperor Xiàowǔ's Tàiyuán twenty-first year.
Nǔ
is pronounced Núwò.
Xīnchāng County in Liáodōng has Lúlóng Mountain.
During the Táng dynasty, it was Píngzhōu's Lúlóng County.
The strategic pass of Féirú, as mentioned by Mùróng Lìng,
is that place.
This Xīnchāng in Liáodōng
was later established by people within the boundaries of Hàn's Liáoxī Commandery,
not in the old Hàn commandery or county territories.
Jìn
is pronounced Qíjìn.
Horses and cattle were almost all consumed.
Huì did not depart.
Bǎo was angry,
and repeatedly issued stern edicts.
Huì had no choice but
to use the excuse of "ordering the ranks and selecting the able"
and remained for more than a month.
At this time, the roads were impassable.
Wěi wanted to send light troops ahead to open the path,
to scout the strength of Wèi,
and also to create a display of power.
All the generals were apprehensive and unwilling to go.
Yú Chóng bravely declared:
"Now that the great bandits are rampant,
and the capital is in dire straits—
the capital
refers to Zhōngshān.
You gentlemen, who bear the state's favor and trust,
why do you still cling to your lives?
If the state should fall,
and our loyalty as subjects is not upheld,
death will bring even greater disgrace.
You gentlemen may remain here safely;
Chóng requests to take on this task."
Wěi was pleased
and assigned him five hundred infantry and cavalry.
Chóng advanced to Yúyáng,
where he encountered over a thousand Wèi cavalry.
Chóng said to his troops:
"They are many, we are few;
if we don't attack, we won't escape."
So he beat the drums, shouted, and charged straight ahead.
Chóng personally killed more than ten people.
The Wèi cavalry scattered and fled,
and Chóng also withdrew.
He took heads and captured prisoners,
and thoroughly reported the enemy's situation,
which somewhat boosted the morale of the troops.
Huì then set out slowly on the road.
In that month,
he finally reached Jìchéng.
Wèi had besieged Zhōngshān for a long time,
and the officers and soldiers within the city all wished to sally forth and fight.
The Zhēngběi Great General Lóng said to Bǎo:
"Although Shè Guī has repeatedly achieved minor successes,
he has been bogged down with his army for a year—
'Shè Suì' means 'for a year.'
Last year, in the eleventh month,
Wèi attacked Zhōngshān.
More than half of his soldiers and horses have died or been wounded,
and the people yearn to return home.
The various tribes are disintegrating—
referring to the Hèlán, Hélín, and Héxī tribes.
Furthermore, the entire city is eager to fight.
If we rely on our vigor
and exploit their decline,
there is nothing we cannot overcome.
If, however, we hold back and remain indecisive,
the morale of the generals and soldiers will be lost,
and we will be increasingly isolated and distressed.
If the situation drags on, changes will arise.
Even if we wish to act then,
it will not be possible!"
Bǎo agreed with him.
But the Wèi Great General Lín repeatedly thwarted his proposals—
Lín had other ambitions,
hence he thwarted Lóng's proposals.
This happened several times, repeatedly.
Mùróng Bǎo sent an envoy to request of Wèi Wáng Guī,
wishing to return his younger brother Mùróng Gū.
The matter of Mùróng Gū being detained in Yàn is seen in volume 107, Xiàowǔ Tàiyuán year 16.
West of Chángshān,
this was the territory of Bìngzhōu.
Afterward, Mùróng Bǎo regretted it.
On the day Jǐyǒu,
Tuòbá Guī proceeded to Lúnú.
According to the Wèi Shū Dìxíng Zhì: the seat of Zhōngshān Jùn was Lúnú.
Lì Dàoyuán said: In the northwest corner of Lúnú city,
there is water,
deep but not flowing,
a hundred paces north-south,
and over a hundred paces east-west;
the water is jet black, which is called Lú,
and not flowing is called Nú,
hence the city derived its name from this.
On the day Xīnhài,
he again besieged Zhōngshān.
Dù Yòu said: Later Yàn's capital was Zhōngshān,
which is now Tángchāng Xiàn of Bólíng Jùn.
Tángchāng was originally Kǔxíng Xiàn of the Hàn dynasty,
Emperor Zhāng renamed it Hàngchāng,
Cáo Wèi renamed it Wèichāng,
Suí renamed it Suíchāng,
and during the Wǔdé era of Táng, it was renamed Tángchāng.
Fù,
pronounced Fú Yòu.
"Now we merely sit and defend this isolated city,
eventually becoming exhausted and defeated.
Your ministers wish to sally forth and fight joyfully.
The soldiers are all willing to fight to the death, thus fighting joyfully.
This is to fight joyfully.
Lè,
pronounced Luò.
This is to bring about self-destruction.
Moreover, we have been under siege for a long time,
without any other surprising changes.
We merely hope that with time, the bandits will retreat on their own.
Now, the strength of those inside and outside [the city] is vastly disparate.

It is advisable to follow the majority and make a decisive stand."
Mùróng Bǎo agreed to it.
Mùróng Lóng withdrew and marshaled his troops,
summoning his subordinates and saying to them:
"The imperial majesty is not upheld,
and the bandits insult us from within.
As ministers and sons, we share this disgrace,
and it is our duty not to care for our lives.
If we are fortunate enough to defeat the bandits,
and return successfully, that would be excellent;
but if we are unfortunate,
it will still allow my aspirations and integrity to be displayed.
If any of you go north and see my mother,
please convey this message to her for me!"
Mùróng Lóng first garrisoned Lóngchéng,
and went north with his mother;
when Mùróng Chuí summoned Mùróng Lóng to attack Wèi,
his mother remained in Lóngchéng.
Wèi,
pronounced Yúwěi.
They waited at the gate for orders.
Mùróng Lín again firmly stopped Mùróng Bǎo,
and the masses were greatly indignant.
Mùróng Lóng returned weeping.
That night,
Mùróng Lín, with his troops, coerced the Left Guard General, Běidì Wáng Jīng,
to lead the imperial guards to assassinate Mùróng Bǎo.
Mùróng Jīng refused him on grounds of righteousness.
Mùróng Lín was enraged,
killed Mùróng Jīng,
and fled to Xīshān,
relying on the remnants of the Dīnglíng people.
Two hundred *lǐ* northwest of Zhōngshān is Lángshān.
From Lángshān westward,
it connects to Chángshān in the south.
The valleys are deep and perilous.
At the end of the Hàn dynasty, Hēishān Zhāng Yàn and in the Five Dynasties Sūn Fāngjiǎn and his brothers all relied on this terrain for defense.
The Dīnglíng remnants
Having been defeated by Yàn,
they retreated and gathered in Xīshān.
Xīshān
is the western mountain of Qǔyáng.
Mùróng Bǎo did not know where Mùróng Lín had gone.
Zhī,
meaning to go.
Fearing that Mùróng Lín would seize Huìjūn,
and first occupy Lóngchéng,
he summoned Mùróng Lóng and the General of Agile Cavalry Mùróng Nóng,
and deliberated leaving Zhōngshān
to flee and take refuge in Lóngchéng.
Mùróng Lóng said:
"The late emperor toiled arduously to establish the enterprise of revival.
Before a full year passed since his death, the world is in great chaos.
How can one not call this a betrayal!
Now, external invaders are powerful, and internal strife has arisen again.
Our kinsmen are estranged,
and the common people are suspicious and fearful.
Indeed, we cannot resist the enemy.
Moving north to the old capital
is also what the situation dictates.
Lóngchuān is narrow and its people are poor.
Lóngchuān here refers to the area of Hélóng.
To hope for great accomplishments in a short time
is certainly impossible.
If we economize and cherish the people,
focus on agriculture and train soldiers,
within a few years,
both public and private resources will be abundant.
Meanwhile, in the region between Zhào and Wèi,
the people will be weary of banditry and violence,
and long for Yàn's benevolence.
Perhaps then we can return with our banners,
and recover our former territory.
If we cannot achieve that,
then relying on the perilous terrain to secure ourselves
would still be sufficient to live in comfort and recuperate our strength."
Mùróng Bǎo said:
"Your words are entirely reasonable.
I will completely follow your will."
Mùróng Lóng's plan was indeed excellent,
but what could be done about fate?
Military strategists can turn defeat into victory,
but Mùróng Lóng's wisdom was insufficient to reach this level.
If Mùróng Bǎo had followed Mùróng Lóng's advice consistently,
he might still have avoided the disaster of Lán Hàn.
Gāo Fǔ of Liáodōng,
who was skilled in divination,
and whom Mùróng Lóng had always trusted and respected,
privately said to Mùróng Lóng:
"Your Highness, if you go north,
you will ultimately not be able to reach [your destination],
nor will you be able to see the Grand Empress Dowager.
If the Emperor goes alone,
and Your Highness secretly remains here,
you will certainly achieve great deeds."
Mùróng Lóng said:
"The state is in great difficulty,
and the Emperor is in distress.
Moreover, my old mother is in the north.
If I can die facing north,
I will have no regrets.
What are you saying!"
He then summoned all his subordinates,
and asked about their departure or stay.
Only Sīmǎ Lǔ Gōng and Cānjūn Chéng Jí wished to follow,
the rest all wanted to stay.
Mùróng Lóng allowed them all.
Gǔ Huìguī, a subordinate of Mùróng Nóng, persuaded Mùróng Nóng, saying:
"All the people in the city
are those whose fathers, elder brothers, sons, and younger brothers were killed by Tuòbá Guī at Cánhé.
They weep tears of blood and yearn [to fight Wèi], but are suppressed by the Guard Army.
Mùróng Lín was the General-in-chief of the Guards,
thus he was referred to as the Guard Army.
They all say:
'If we can take one of the Mùróng clan, enthrone him,
and fight Wèi with him,
we will have no regrets even if we die.'
If Your Royal Highness fortunately remains here,
to fulfill the hopes of the masses,
repel the Wèi army,
pacify the capital region,
and welcome the imperial carriage,
you would still be considered a loyal minister."
Mùróng Nóng wanted to kill Gǔ Huìguī but valued his talent and strength,
so he said to him:
"If you expect to live by doing this,
it is better to die!"
Both Mùróng Nóng and Mùróng Lóng were known for their wisdom and strategy,
yet their views were like this.
When Heaven wishes to abolish Yàn,
the wise lose their wisdom.
On the day Rénzǐ,
that night,
Mùróng Bǎo, along with the Crown Prince Mùróng Cè, Liáoxī Wáng Mùróng Nóng, Gāoyáng Wáng Mùróng Lóng, Chánglè Wáng Mùróng Shèng, and over ten thousand cavalry, set out to meet the army.
Héjiān Wáng Mùróng Xī, Bóhǎi Wáng Mùróng Lǎng, and Bólíng Wáng Mùróng Jiàn were all young
and unable to leave the city.
Mùróng Lóng returned to fetch them,
personally harnessing the carriage for them,
and they all managed to escape.
Yàn generals Wáng
Shěn and others surrendered to Wèi.
Lèlang Wáng Huì, Zhōngshū Shìláng Hán Fàn, Yuánwàiláng Duàn Hóng, Tàishǐ Lìng Liú Qǐ, and three hundred artisans and technicians fled to Yè.
Zhōngshān city was without a lord,
and the common people were terrified and bewildered.
The eastern gate was left open.
Wèi Wáng Guī wanted to enter the city at night.
Guānjūn Jiāngjūn Wáng Jiàn's ambition was plunder,
so he said that he feared the soldiers would steal from the government treasuries,
and requested to wait until morning.
Guī then stopped.
Yān Kāifēng Gōng Xiáng, having failed to follow Bǎo,
was made lord by the people in the city,
who then closed the gates and resisted the siege.
Guī attacked them with all his forces,
but failed to breach the city for several days.
He sent men to ascend a "nest-cart."
Dù Yù said: A nest-cart
is a cart with a turret built upon it.
Lù Démíng said: It is a war-cart as high as a nest to observe the enemy.
Dù Yòu said: An eight-wheeled cart upon which a tall pole is erected,
with a windlass at the top of the pole.
A rope is used to hoist a plank-house to the top of the pole
to peer into the city.
The plank-house is four *chǐ* square
and five *chǐ* high,
with twelve holes.
Carts are separately arranged on its four sides,
allowing it to advance and retreat.
It circles the city,
observed from a distance within the camp,
resembling a bird's nest,
hence it is also called a nest-cart.
"[Mùróng] Bǎo has already abandoned you and fled.
You common people are needlessly courting death.
For whom are you doing this?"
They all said:
"We are insignificant and ignorant.
We fear repeating the fate of the army at Cānhé.
Therefore, we are merely trying to prolong our lives for a month or so."
Guī looked at Wáng Jiàn and spat in his face.
He sent Zhōnglǐng Jiāngjūn Zhǎngsūn Féih, and Zuǒ Jiāngjūn Lǐ Lì, leading three thousand cavalry, to pursue Bǎo to Fányáng.
They did not catch him,
but destroyed his Xīnchéng outpost and returned.
The *Qian Han Zhi* states: Zhōngshān Commandery had Běixīnchéng County.
The *Jùnguó Zhì* states: Zhuó Commandery had Běixīnchéng County,

The *Shuǐjīng Zhù* states Xīnchéng County was south of Wǔsuí County,

8. On the *jiǎyín* day,
Empress Dowager Lǐ was honored as Grand Empress Dowager.
On the *wǔwǔ* day,
Empress Wáng was installed.
9. Yān Lord Bǎo left Zhōngshān
and met Zhào Wáng Lín at Jǐngchéng.
Examining character dictionaries,
there is no
character "⿰⻖开",

*Shuài* [率],

similarly below.

On the *jiǎyín* day,

Bǎo was surprised by Huì's resentful expression and demeanor.

*Yàng* [怏],
pronounced *yúliǎng*.

On the *bǐngchén* day,
Bǎo moved all the government treasuries from Jì northward to Lóngchéng.

Qīnghé Wáng Huì said:

He said to his former subordinate, Liútái Zhìshū Yáng Qiú:

*Qiú* [璆],

"In Zhōngshān city, there were tens of thousands of soldiers,

belonged to Jiǔquán Commandery in the Hàn.
Later, the Northern Zhōu abolished it and merged it into Fúlù County.
Guàn,
pronounced gū huān,
also gǔ wán.
The army was defeated,
and Chéng died.
Lěi
is the surname;
Chéng
is the given name.
Nán Chéng (男成) attacked Jiànkāng (建康),
and sent an envoy to persuade the Administrator of Jiànkāng (建康), Duàn Yè (段業), saying:
"The Lǚ (呂) clan's government is in decline,
powerful ministers abuse their authority,
punishments and executions are erratic,
and people have no place to call their own.
Within a single province,
rebels are seen everywhere,
the form of disintegration is clear before our eyes,
and the common people are wailing, having no one to rely on.
How can you, Prefect, with your world-shaking talent,
wish to establish loyalty to a dying state!
Nán Chéng (男成) and others have already proclaimed the great cause,
and wish to invite you, Prefect, to govern our humble province,
so that those who have suffered in dire straits
may receive the benefit of renewed life.
The *Shū* (書) says: 'We wait for our sovereign,
when the sovereign comes, they will revive.'
Yè (業) did not comply.
They faced each other for twenty days,
and no external relief arrived.
Gāo Kuí (高逵) and Shǐ Huì (史惠) and other people of the commandery urged Yè (業) to accept Nán Chéng's (男成) request.
Yè (業) had always been on bad terms with the Liáng (涼) Attendant-in-ordinary Fáng Guǐ (房晷) and the Palace Aide Wáng Xiáng (王詳),
and feared for his own safety,
so he agreed.
Nán Chéng (男成) and others promoted Yè (業) to Grand Commander-in-chief, General of the Dragon Stratagem, Governor of Liángzhōu (涼州), and Duke of Jiànkāng (建康),
and changed the era name to Shénxǐ (神璽).
Nán Chéng (男成) was appointed General Who Aids the State,

Méng Xùn (蒙遜) led his troops to submit to Yè (業),

Guāng (光) ordered Gōng Zuǎn (公纂), the Duke of Tàiyuán (太原), to lead troops to attack Yè (業),
but he did not succeed.
16 In the sixth month,
Qín (秦) King Gān Guī (乾歸) summoned Píng Xīniàn (彭奚念), the Inspector of Běihézhōu (北河州), as General Who Guards the Palace;

"Wū Hóng" (屋弘),
should be

Zhāng Jùn (張駿) divided Xìnjìn (興晉), Jīnchéng (金城), Wǔshǐ (武始), Nán'ān (南安), Yǒngjìn (永晉), Dàxià (大夏), Wǔchéng (武成), and Hànzhōng (漢中) into Hézhōu (河州).
Běihézhōu (北河州) was established by the Qǐfú (乞伏) clan,

He guarded Fāohǎn (枹罕).
Zhāng Mào (張茂) divided Wǔxīng (武興), Jīnchéng (金城), Xīpíng (西平), and Āngù (安故) into Dìngzhōu (定州).
Xìnjìn (興晉) Commandery was also established by the Zhāng (張) clan.
Fāohǎn (枹罕) County,
in Han times belonged to Jīnchéng (金城) Commandery,
in Later Han belonged to Lǒngxī (隴西) Commandery,
later again was divided and belonged to Xīpíng (西平) Commandery,
Zhāng Jùn (張駿) divided it to belong to Jìnxīng (晉興) Commandery,
later again Xìnjìn (興晉) Commandery was separately established.
*Wēn* (瑥),
pronounced wēn.
pronounced fū.
17 In autumn,
the seventh month,
Mùróng Xiáng (慕容詳) killed Kězhúhún Tán (可足渾潭).
Xiáng (詳) was addicted to wine and extravagant pleasures,
he did not care for his soldiers and people,
and his punishments and executions were excessive,
he executed over five hundred people, from kings and dukes downwards,
causing everyone to become disloyal.
The city was starving,
Xiáng (詳) did not allow the people to go out to gather wild grains,
and the dead lay piled upon each other.
The entire city conspired to welcome Zhào (趙) King Lín (麟).
Xiáng (詳) sent Fǔguó Jiāngjūn (輔國將軍) Zhāng Xiāng (張驤) with over five thousand men to supervise grain collection in Chángshān (常山).
Lín (麟) entered Xiāng's (驤) army from Dīnglíng (丁零),
secretly attacked Zhōngshān (中山),
the city gates were not closed,
he captured Xiáng (詳),
and beheaded him.
Lín (麟) then proclaimed his imperial title,
and allowed people to go out in all directions to gather wild grains.
Once the people were full,

Wèi (魏) King Guī's (珪) army was at Lǔkǒu (魯口),

entering its outer city wall;
Lín (麟) pursued them to the Huái (泒) River.
The Huái (泒) River
is in Xīnshì (新市) County, Zhōngshān (中山).
The *Yúdì Zhì* (輿地志) says: "The north of Lúnú (盧奴) city faces the Qī (滱) River,
and fronts the Huái (泒) River."
*Huái* (泒),
pronounced gōng hū fān (攻乎翻).
In the eighth month,
on the *bǐngyín* (丙寅) day, the first day of the lunar month,
Wèi (魏) King Guī (珪) moved his army to Jiǔmén (九門) in Chángshān (常山).
Chángshān (常山) Commandery had Jiǔmén (九門) County.
Many people and animals died,
and the generals and soldiers all wanted to return.
Guī (珪) asked his generals about the plague,
and they replied:
"Only four or five out of ten remain."
Guī (珪) said:
"This is indeed fate,
what can we do about it!
The people of the Four Seas

it depends on how I manage them,

His subordinates then dared not speak.
He sent Fǔjūn Dàjiāngjūn (撫軍大將軍) Lüèyáng (略陽) Duke Zūn (遵) to attack Zhōngshān (中山),
entered its outer city wall and returned.
18 Yàn (燕) appointed Liáoxī (遼西) King Nóng (農) as Grand Commander of All Military Affairs, Grand Marshal, and Superintendent of the Department of the Palace Secretariat.
19 Liáng (涼) Cavalier Attendant-in-ordinary and Grand Exorcist, Guō Én (郭黁) of Xīpíng (西平),
was skilled in astronomy and numerology,
and the people of the state respected and trusted him.
At that time, the planet Mars was in the constellation Dōngjǐng (東井),

"In the region corresponding to Liáng (涼),
there will be a great war.
The sovereign is old and ill,
the crown prince is ignorant and weak,
and the Duke of Tàiyuán (太原) is fierce and violent.
Should something unexpected happen,
disaster and chaos will surely arise.
We two have long held important positions within the court;
they constantly gnash their teeth at us,
and we will be the first to be executed.
Among the Tiánhú (田胡), Wáng Qǐjī's (王乞基) tribe is the strongest,
Tiánhú (田胡)
is a type of Hu (胡).
He has many old followers.
I wish to undertake a great enterprise with you,
and proclaim Qǐjī (乞基) as our lord.
The forces of the Two Parks
will all be ours.
The seat of Liángzhōu (涼州) is Gūzāng (姑臧),
which has East and West Park cities.
Let us discuss this further."
Xiáng (詳) agreed.
That night, Én (黁) used the forces of the Two Parks to set fire to Hóngfàn (洪範) Gate,
and had Xiáng (詳) act as an internal confederate;
the plot was exposed,
Xiáng (詳) was executed,
and Én (黁) then occupied the East Park and rebelled.
The common people all said that when a sage raises an army,
nothing fails,
and many followed him.
Liáng (涼) King Guāng (光) summoned Gōng Zuǎn (公纂), the Duke of Tàiyuán (太原), and ordered him to attack Én (黁).
When Zuǎn (纂) was about to return,
all the generals said:
"Duàn Yè (段業) will surely pursue our army from behind,
so we should secretly withdraw at night."
Zuǎn (纂) said:
"Yè (業) has no heroic talent;
he relies on the city walls for defense.
If we secretly withdraw at night,
it will only serve to boost his morale."
So he sent an envoy to inform Yè (業), saying:
"Guō Én (郭黁) has raised a rebellion,
I am now returning to the capital;
'capital' refers to Gūzāng (姑臧).
*Shǐ* (使),
pronounced shū lì fān.
You can come out to fight early."
Thereupon, he led his army back.
Yè (業) dared not come out.
Zuǎn sīmǎ Yáng Tǒng (楊統) said to his paternal cousin Huán (桓):
"Guō Nán (郭黁) raising troops
will surely not be in vain.
I wish to kill Zuǎn (纂),
and enthrone you, elder brother, as the lord.
We will attack Lǚ Hóng (呂弘) in the west,
occupy Zhāngyè (張掖),
and issue orders to all the commanderies.
This is a once-in-a-thousand-years opportunity."
Huán (桓) angrily said:
"I am a minister to the Lǚ (呂) clan,
peacefully enjoying their emoluments.
If I cannot save them in times of danger,
how can I further increase their difficulties!
If the Lǚ (呂) clan were to perish,
I would be like Hóng Yǎn (弘演)!"
In the Spring and Autumn period, Duke Yì (懿) of Wèi (衞) fought the Dí (狄) people at Yíngzé (熒澤),
and was killed by the Dí (狄) people.
Hóng Yǎn (弘演) offered his liver to die in loyalty to him.
Huán's (桓) daughter was married to Zuǎn (纂),
and he was treated with exceptional favor compared to other ministers,
hence he spoke thus.
Thereupon, he rebelled and returned to Nán (黁).
Fānhé (番禾) county,
in the Hàn (漢) dynasty belonged to Zhāngyè (張掖) Commandery,
in the Jìn (晉) dynasty belonged to Wǔwēi (武威) Commandery.
In the Tiānbǎo (天寶) era of the Táng (唐) dynasty,
it was renamed Tiānbǎo (天寶) county.
"Fān" (番),
pronounced "Pán" (盤).
This refers to Zuǎn's (纂) younger brother.
Zuǎn (纂) and the Administrator of Xī'ān (西安), Shí Yuánliáng (石元良), together attacked Nán (黁),
heavily defeating him,
and then were able to enter Gūzāng (姑臧).
Nán (黁) had obtained eight grandsons of Guāng (光) in the eastern garden,
and after his defeat, in his rage,
he threw them all onto spear points,
dismembering them limb by limb.
He drank their blood to swear an oath with his troops,
and all the troops covered their eyes.
The people of Liáng (涼), Zhāng Jié (張捷) and Sòng Shēng (宋生) and others, gathered three thousand Róng (戎) and Xià (夏) people,
and rebelled at Xiūtú (休屠) city.
They jointly enthroned the Latter General of Liáng (涼), Yáng Guǐ (楊軌), as their盟主 méngzhǔ (盟主).
Guǐ (軌) was a Dī (氐) from Lüèyáng (略陽).
General Chéng Zhào (程肇) admonished him, saying:
"You abandon the dragon's head and follow the serpent's tail,
which is not a wise plan."
Guǐ (軌) did not listen;
he proclaimed himself Grand General, Governor of Liángzhōu (涼州), and Duke of Xīpíng (西平).
Zuǎn (纂) attacked and defeated Nán's (黁) general Wáng Fěi (王斐) west of the city.
Nán's (黁) military strength gradually declined,
so he sent envoys to request aid from Tūfà Wūgū (禿髮烏孤).
In the ninth month,
Wūgū (烏孤) sent his younger brother, the Cavalry General Lìlùgū (利鹿孤), to lead five thousand cavalry to assist him.
The Empress Dowager Shé (虵) of Qín (秦) passed away.
The Lord of Qín (秦), Xīng (興), was excessively grief-stricken,
and did not personally attend to government affairs.
His close ministers requested that, following the precedents of Hàn (漢) and Wèi (魏),
once the burial was complete, he should resume auspicious practices.
Shàngshū Láng (尚書郎) Lǐ Sōng (李嵩) submitted a memorial, saying:
"Governing the world with filial piety
is the noble practice of the former kings.
It is fitting to follow your sagely nature to glorify the teachings of the Dao.
After the burial,
you should wear plain clothes when holding court."
Yǐn Wěi (尹緯) retorted, saying:
"Sōng (嵩) is deviating from common practice and overstepping propriety."
Yǐn Wěi (尹緯) was accustomed to what he heard and saw,
and so he contradicted Lǐ Sōng (李嵩), calling it deviating from common practice and overstepping propriety.
Alas,
ever since the system of short mourning periods was implemented,
people have long been ignorant of propriety!
pronounced "Běi Jiǎo" (北角).
Xīng (興) said:
"Sōng (嵩) is a loyal minister and a filial son.
What crime has he committed?
Let us follow Sōng's (嵩) proposal entirely."
The Xiānbēi (鮮卑) Xuē Bó (薛勃) rebelled against Qín (秦).
Xuē Bó (薛勃) occupied Èrchéng (貳城),
was attacked by Wèi (魏) and surrendered to Qín (秦).
Bó (勃) was defeated,
and fled to Mòyì Gān (沒弈干).
Mòyì Gān (沒弈干) apprehended and delivered him.
Yáo Mǎidé (姚買得), a man from Xuànshì (泫氏) in Qín (秦), plotted to assassinate the Lord of Qín (秦), Xīng (興),
but failed and died.
The Lord of Qín (秦), Xīng (興), invaded Húchéng (湖城).
The Administrator of Hóngnóng (弘農), Táo Zhòngshān (陶仲山), and the Administrator of Huáshān (華山), Dǒng Mài (董邁), both surrendered to him;
he then reached Shǎnchéng (陝城),
advanced and invaded Shàngluò (上洛),
and captured it.
He established two garrisons at Hú (湖) and Shǎn (陝),
seen in volume 106, Xiàowǔ (孝武) Tài Yuán (太元) 11th year.
Huáshān (華山) Commandery,
during the Jìn (晉) dynasty, was established by dividing Huáyīn (華陰) from Hóngnóng (弘農), Zhèng (鄭) from Jīngzhào (京兆), and Xiàyáng (夏陽) and Héyáng (郃陽) from Féngyì (馮翊).
Shàngluò (上洛) county,
in the Former Hàn (漢) dynasty belonged to Hóngnóng (弘農),
in the Latter Hàn (漢) dynasty belonged to Jīngzhào (京兆);
in the 2nd year of Tàishǐ (泰始) during Emperor Wǔ (武) of Jìn (晉),
Shàngluò (上洛) Commandery was established by dividing the southern part of Jīngzhào (京兆).
"Huá" (華),
pronounced "Hù Huà" (戶化).
"Shǎn" (陝),
pronounced "Shī Rǎn" (失冉).
The Administrator of Hénán (河南), Xiàhóu Zōngzhī (夏侯宗之), stubbornly defended Jīnyǒng (金墉).
Chóng (崇) attacked it but failed to capture it,
so he relocated over twenty thousand refugee households and returned.
The Dī (氐) of Wǔdū (武都), Tú Fēi (屠飛) and Dàn Tiě (啖鐵) and others, occupied Fāngshān (方山) and rebelled against Qín (秦).
According to the Jìnshū Zàijì (晉書載記),
at that time Fēi (飛) and Tiě (鐵) killed the Administrator of Lǒngdōng (隴東), Yáo Huí (姚迴),

Zhù Mù (祝穆) said: Fāngshān (方山) is forty *lǐ* east and west of Wǔdū (武都) Commandery.
Fēi (飛) and Tiě (鐵) were executed.
Xīng (興) was diligent in governance,
receptive to good advice.
Dù Jǐn (杜瑾) and others from Jīngzhào (京兆) were all promoted for their discussions on affairs.
Jiāng Kān (姜龕) and others from Tiānshuǐ (天水) were revered for their Confucian scholarship.
Gǔchéng Shēn (古成詵) and others, serving as Huángmén Shìláng (黃門侍郎), participated in confidential matters through their literary talents.
Gǔchéng (古成) is a surname.
"Shēn" (詵),
pronounced "Shū Zhēn" (疎臻).
He took moral education as his responsibility.
Wéi Gāo (韋高) of Jīngzhào (京兆) admired Ruǎn Jí (阮籍) and his character.
During his mother's mourning,
he played the *qín* and drank wine.
Shēn (詵) heard of this and wept,
holding a sword, he sought Gāo (高),
intending to kill him.
Gāo (高) was frightened and fled into hiding.
Zhōngshān (中山) suffered a severe famine.
Mùróng Lín (慕容麟) led over twenty thousand people out to occupy Xīnshì (新市).
Xīnshì (新市) county,
since the Hàn (漢) dynasty, belonged to Zhōngshān (中山).
Liú Xù (劉昫) said: Xīnshì (新市) was an ancient subsidiary state of Xiānyú (鮮虞),
in the Táng (唐) dynasty it became Xīnlè (新樂) county in Dìngzhōu (定州).
Dù Yòu (杜佑) said: The Táng (唐) Zhènzhōu (鎮州) was governed from Zhēndìng (真定) county,
the old city of Hàn (漢) Xīnshì (新市) county was to its northeast.
"Shuài" (帥),
read as "shuài" (率).
On the *jiǎzǐ* day,
King Guī (珪) of Wèi (魏) advanced his army to attack it.
The Grand Astrologer Cháo Chóng (鼂崇) said:
"It is inauspicious.
In the past, Zhòu (紂) perished on a *jiǎzǐ* day,
which is called a 'sick day'.
The *Zuǒ Zhuàn* says: When the celestial stem is *zǐ* or *mǎo*,
it is called a 'sick day'.
Dù Yù (杜預) annotated: 'Sick' (疾)
means 'evil'.
Zhòu (紂) perished on a *jiǎzǐ* day,
Jié (桀) perished on an *yǐmǎo* day,
hence they are considered taboo days."
"Cháo" (鼂),
pronounced "Zhí Yáo" (直遙).
Guī (珪) said:
"If Zhòu (紂) perished on a *jiǎzǐ* day,

Chóng (崇) had no reply.
In winter,
the tenth month,
on the *bǐngyín* day,
Lín (麟) retreated and held his ground at Huáishuǐ (泒水).
On the *jiǎxū* day,
Guī (珪) fought Lín (麟) at Yìtái (義臺),

According to Lǐ Yánshòu's (李延壽) *Běishǐ* (北史),

Wèi Shōu's (魏收) *Dìxíngzhì* (地形志) states that
Xīnshì (新市) county has Yìtái (義臺) city.
Lín (麟), with dozens of cavalry, rushed to take his wife and children into Xīshān (西山),
and then fled to Yè (鄴).
On the *jiǎshēn* day,
Wèi (魏) conquered Zhōngshān (中山).
The dukes, ministers, Shàngshū (尚書), generals, officials, and soldiers of Yàn (燕) who surrendered numbered over twenty thousand.
Zhāng Xiāng (張驤) and Lǐ Shěn (李沈) had previously surrendered to Wèi (魏),
but later absconded.
When Guī (珪) entered the city,
he pardoned them all.
He obtained Yàn's (燕) imperial seals, official insignia, maps, documents, state treasury, and countless treasures.

"Five clans"
refers to relatives within the five degrees of mourning.
On the *dīnghài* day,
three thousand cavalry were dispatched to Wèi Wáng Yí (衞王儀),

The Commander of Chángshuǐ (長水), Yáo Zhēn (姚珍) of Qín (秦), fled to Western Qín (西秦).
King Gān Guī (乾歸) of Western Qín (西秦) gave him his daughter in marriage.
The twelve tribal chiefs, such as Tǔmò of the Xiānbēi in Hénán,

This is south of Jīnchéng.

When Dé’s memorial arrived,

Bǎo then extensively selected soldiers and horses,
intending to retake the Central Plains.
He dispatched Hónglú Lǔ Suì to invest Dé as chéngxiàng and Jìzhōu mù,
granting that the dukes, marquises, shepherds, and governors of the southern Xià region should all receive appointments and enfeoffments by his authority.
In the eleventh month,
on the day of Guǐchǒu,
Yān granted a general amnesty.
In the twelfth month,
the levied troops were all assembled.
A state of alert was declared, and they were stationed.
General Qǐ Lún was sent south to inspect the terrain.
On the day of Yǐhài,
Mùróng Lín arrived in Yè,
again calling himself King of Zhào.
He said to Fányáng King Dé:
"Since Wèi has conquered Zhōngshān,

Although there are stockpiles in Yè,

Moreover, the people's hearts are anxious and fearful,

It is better to move south to Huátái,
block the river to await Wèi,
seize opportunities as they arise,

At that time, Lǔyáng King Hé was garrisoned at Huátái.
Hé,
who was Chuí’s younger brother’s son,

Dé agreed to it.
