Lóng'ān 2nd year (wùxū, 398 CE)
In spring,
first month,
Yān Fányáng King Dé led forty thousand households from Yè south to Huátái.
Wèi Wèi King Yí entered Yè,
seized its granaries and armories,
and pursued Dé to the river,
but did not catch him.
Zhào King Lín offered an honorable title to Dé.
Dé, following the example of his elder brother Chuí,
called himself King of Yān.
This event is recorded in volume 105, Xiàowǔ Tàiyuán 9th year.
He exercised imperial authority through the commander-in-chief's office.
The "commander-in-chief's office"
meant that all regional garrisons were under the authority of the Yān King's office;
"exercising imperial authority"
meant acting by imperial decree.
He appointed Zhào King Lín as Sīkōng and concurrently Shàngshū Lìng,
Mùróng Fǎ as Zhōngjūn Jiāngjūn,
Mùyú Bá as Shàngshū Zuǒ Púyè,
and Dīng Tōng as Yòu Púyè.
Lín again plotted rebellion,
and Dé killed him.
On the day of Gēngzǐ,
Wèi King Guī traveled south from Zhōngshān to Gāoyì,
where he found Wáng Yǒng’s son Xiàn.
He rejoiced, saying:
"He is the grandson of Wáng Jǐnglüè!"
He appointed him as Zhōngzhèng of his native prefecture.
Wáng Měng was a native of Jù County, Běihǎi Prefecture, Qīngzhōu.
During the Tàikāng era,
Jù was divided and belonged to Dōngguǎn Commandery.
During the Jìn, Dōngguǎn belonged to Xúzhōu.
The "Jìn Shū" biography records him from Jù County, Běihǎi;
probably Měng considered it a Hàn commandery.
However, his family was in Wèijùn, and he lived in seclusion in Huáyīn,
from which he submitted to Qín.
His son Yǒng garrisoned Yōuzhōu,
and died in battle with Fú Pī at Xiānglíng,
so Xiàn lived as an exile in Gāoyì.
Now Wèi appointed him Zhōngzhèng of his native prefecture,
implying that Qīng and Xú had not yet been acquired,
probably to make him classify and rank the scholars of Dōngxià.
He also managed the Ménxià.
"Xuǎncáo"
refers to the duties of the Lìbù Shàngshū;
"Ménxià"
refers to the duties of Shìzhōng, Chángshì, and Jǐshì Huángmén.
The character "選"
is pronounced "xù" (須絹翻).
He established a Xíngtái.
Zhèng Qiáo said: "Xíngtái existed since Wèi and Jìn.
When Jìn Wén King attacked Zhūgě Dàn,
Sànqí Chángshì Péi Xiù and Shàngshū Púyè Chén Tài accompanied him with a Xíngtái.
Dōnghǎi King Yuè led his troops and encamped at Xǔchāng,
taking a Xíngtái with him.
Later, Wèi called it Shàngshū Dà Xíngtái,
with separate officials.
He and Zuǒ Chéng Jiǎ Yí led five thousand officials and soldiers to garrison Yè.
Since Hàn Guāngwǔ entrusted responsibilities to the Shàngshū,
affairs were handled by the Táigé.
The Shàngshū Shěng was called Shàngshū Tái.
When Jìn Huìdì moved west to Cháng'ān,
a Liútái was established in Luòyáng
to manage remaining affairs,
thus the name Liútái arose.
When the Tuòbá clan established Xíngtái,
it was placed wherever needed
to manage the affairs of a region."
The "Wèi Shū Guānshì Zhì" states: "Among the noble families who entered the court, there was the Sùhé clan,
later changed to the Hé clan."
"Xiáng"
is pronounced "si jiāng fān."
Guī returned from Yè to Zhōngshān,
intending to return north.
He dispatched ten thousand soldiers to construct a straight road,
cutting through Mount Hénglǐng from Wàngdū to Dài, over five hundred li.
Hénglǐng
is the ridge of Mount Héngshān,
northwest of Shàngqǔyáng,
which is the road to Dàomǎ Guān.
The "Jìn Shū Dìdào Jì" calls it Hóngshàng Guān.
Shěn Kuò said: "The Northern Sacred Peak, Héngshān,
is what is now called Dàmào Shān.
The sacred shrine was formerly at the foot of the mountain.
After the Shí Jìn,
it gradually moved inland.
The place is now called Shénpéng.
The current shrine is in Qǔyáng.
North of the shrine is Wàngyuè Tíng.
On a clear day after fresh rain,
Dàmào can be seen.
The Fēihú road is west of Dàmào.
It goes north from Yínyě Zhài, passes Dàomǎ Guān,
then passes Shíménzi and Lìngshuǐ Pù,
enters between Píngxíng and Méihuí two camps,
and reaches Dàizhōu.
However, what Shěn Kuò called Dàizhōu
was Yànmén.
From there, one could also reach Wèi’s capital Dài,
but it may not be a straight road."
The "Shuǐjīng Zhù" states: "The Qíyí River flows out east of Píngshū County,
flows northeast past south of Lántíng,
then northeast past north of Shímén Guān,
the old road comes out of the old pass of Zhōngshān."
The "Wèi Tǔdì Jì" states: "Nine li west of Dàichéng is Píngshū Chéng."
This is the ancient Dàichéng.
"Héng"
is pronounced "hù dēng fān."
There was a disturbance in Shāndōng,
so a Xíngtái was again established in Zhōngshān,
and Wèi King Yí was ordered to garrison it;
Fǔjūn Dàjiāngjūn, Lüèyáng Gōng Zūn was appointed Shàngshū Zuǒ Púyè,
garrisoning Hékǒu in Bóhǎi.
Right General Yǐn Guó oversaw tax collection in Jìzhōu.
Hearing that Guī was about to return north,
he plotted to attack Xìndū.
Ānnán Jiāngjūn Zhǎngsūn Sōng apprehended Guó
and executed him.
3 Yān Qǐlún (燕啟倫) returned to Lóngchéng (龍城).
Last year, Bǎo (寶) sent Qǐlún (啟崙) south to observe the terrain.
"Lún (倫)"
should be written
"Lún (崙)",
pronounced Lú Kūn fān.
The ruler of Yān (燕), Bǎo (寶), ordered the cessation of military operations.
Liáoxī Wáng Nóng (遼西王農) spoke to Bǎo (寶), saying:
"The capital has just been relocated,
so it is not yet advisable to campaign south.
We should instead take advantage of the assembled army to attack the Kùmò Xī (庫莫奚),
seize their cattle and horses to replenish military supplies,
then further assess the true situation,
and deliberate next year."
Bǎo (寶) followed this advice.
On the Jǐwèi (己未) day,
he traveled north.
On the Gēngshēn (庚申) day,
he crossed the Jiāoluò Shuǐ (澆洛水).
The Jiāoluò Shuǐ (澆洛水)
is likely the Ràolè Shuǐ (饒樂水).
Xián (賢) said: The river is north of today's Yíngzhōu (營州).
In the time of Táng Tàizōng (唐太宗),
the Xī (奚) submitted,
and the Ràolè Dūdūfǔ (饒樂都督府) was established.
It says
"Shè Guī (涉珪) went westwards."
"Went westwards"
means returning to Yún (雲) and Dài (代) from Zhōngshān (中山) via the Hénglǐng (恆嶺) to the west.
"Shàng (上)"
pronounced Shí Zhǎng fān.
Yán (延) pursued Bǎo (寶) and caught up with him.
Bǎo (寶) was overjoyed
and immediately ordered his return.
4 On the Xīnyǒu (辛酉) day,
Wèi Wáng Guī (魏王珪) departed Zhōngshān (中山),
relocating over 100,000 officials, commoners, and various non-Hàn (漢) peoples from the six eastern prefectures to populate Dài (代).
This was the strategy of Hàn Gāodì (漢高帝) relocating the powerful families from Guāndōng (關東) to populate Guānzhōng (關中).
In Hàn (漢) times,
Zhāngwǔ Chéng (章武城) belonged to Píngshū Xiàn (平舒縣) of Bóhǎi (勃海) Commandery.
In the first year of Tàishǐ (泰始) of Jìn Wǔdì (晉武帝),
Zhāngwǔ Guó (章武國) was established,
later becoming a commandery.
It was abolished during the Suí (隋) dynasty,
belonging to Yíngzhōu (瀛州),
and incorporated into Píngshū Xiàn (平舒縣).
Guǎngchuān Tàishǒu Hèlài Lú (廣川太守賀賴盧),
whose nature was bold and robust.
Guǎngchuān Xiàn (廣川縣)
belonged to Xìndū Guó (信都國) in the Former Hàn (前漢),
to Qīnghé Jùn (清河郡) in the Later Hàn (後漢),
to Bóhǎi Jùn (勃海郡) in the Jìn (晉),
and later became Guǎngchuān Jùn (廣川郡).
"Shǒu (守)"
pronounced Shì Yòu fān.
He attacked Fǔ (輔),
killed him,
and led the defending troops,
plundering the various commanderies of Yángpíng (陽平) and Dùnqīu (頓丘),
then crossed the river south
and defected to Nán Yān (南燕).
Nán Yān Wáng Dé (南燕王德) appointed Lài Lú (賴盧) as Bìngzhōu Cìshǐ (幷州刺史)
and enfeoffed him as Guǎngníng Wáng (廣甯王).
5 Xī Qín Wáng Gān Guī (西秦王乾歸) dispatched Qífú Yìzhōu (乞伏益州) to attack the three cities of Zhīyáng (支陽), Wǔ (武), and Yǔnwú (允吾) in Liáng (涼),
conquering them.
Zhīyáng (支陽) and Yǔnwú (允吾)
were both ancient Hàn (漢) counties,
belonging to Jīnchéng Jùn (金城郡).
Wǔchéng (武城) should be between these two counties.
Zhāng Shí (張寔) assigned Zhīyáng (支陽) to Guǎngwǔ Jùn (廣武郡).
Yǔnwú (允吾) likely remained the seat of Jīnchéng Jùn (金城郡).
Liú Xù (劉昫) said: Táng (唐) Lánzhōu Guǎngwǔ Xiàn (蘭州廣武縣) was the Hàn (漢) Zhīyáng Xiàn (枝陽縣);
Shànzhōu Lóngzhī Xiàn (鄯州龍支縣) was the Hàn (漢) Yǔnwú Xiàn (允吾縣).
"Yǔnwú (允吾)"
pronounced Qiān Yá.
6 The ruler of Yān (燕), Bǎo (寶), returned to the Lóngchéng Gōng (龍城宮),
and issued an edict for all armies to take up cantonments.
"Dùn (頓)"
refers to a place where an army halts and quarters.
All civil and military officers and soldiers
had their families accompany the imperial carriage.
"Jià (駕)"
refers to the imperial carriage,
similar to what Hàn (漢) people called 'chéngyú' (乘輿).
It was believed that the troops were exhausted and weak,
and Wèi (魏) had just achieved its ambitions,
making them not yet formidable opponents.
It was advisable to rest the troops and observe the situation.
Bǎo (寶) was about to follow this advice,
when Fǔjūn Jiāngjūn Mùyú Téng (撫軍將軍慕輿騰) said:
"The common people can share in the joy of success,
but it is difficult for them to plan for beginnings.
This uses the meaning of Shāng Yāng's (商鞅) words.
"Lè (樂)"
pronounced Luò.
It is proper to make a decision solely from Your Majesty's heart,
seizing the opportunity to advance and take,
and not widely gather differing opinions to obstruct the grand plan."
Bǎo (寶) then said:
"My decision is made;
whoever dares to remonstrate shall be executed!"
In the second month,
on the Yǐhài (乙亥) day,
Bǎo (寶) went out to the cantonment,
leaving Shèng (盛) to manage later affairs.
On the Jǐmǎo (己卯) day,
the Yān (燕) army departed Lóngchéng (龍城).
Mùyú Téng (慕輿騰) led the vanguard,
Sīkōng Nóng (司空農) led the central army,
and Bǎo (寶) led the rearguard,
each separated by one cantonment.
Considering the following text which mentions "continuous camps for a hundred *lǐ* (里)",
one cantonment was probably thirty *lǐ* (里).
On the Rénwǔ (壬午) day,
Bǎo (寶) arrived at Yǐlián (乙連).
Chángshàng Duàn Sùgǔ (長上段速骨) and Sòng Chìméi (宋赤眉), etc., taking advantage of the general reluctance for military service,
then instigated a rebellion.
All palace guards rotated shifts;
"Chángshàng (長上)" meant not rotating.
According to Táng (唐) official regulations,
Huáihuà Zhíjǐ Chángshàng (懷化執戟長上) and Guīdé Zhíjǐ Chángshàng (歸德執戟長上)
were both military *sànjiē* (散階),
ninth rank.
The office of Chángshàng (長上) has a long history.
"Shàng (上)"
pronounced Shí Zhǎng fān.
Together, they compelled Lóngzǐ Gāoyáng Wáng Chóng (隆子高陽王崇) to become their leader,
killing Lèlàng Wēiwáng Zhōu (樂浪威王宙), Zhōngmóu Xī Gōng Duàn Yì (中牟熙公段誼), and various princes of the imperial clan.
Héjiān Wáng Xī (河間王熙) had always been on good terms with Chóng (崇).
Chóng (崇) protected and helped him,
so he alone escaped.
The ruler of Yān (燕), Bǎo (寶), with over ten horsemen, fled to Sīkōng Nóng's (司空農) camp.
Nóng (農) was about to go out to meet him,
but his attendants embraced his waist
and stopped him, saying:
"It's advisable to wait for things to settle a little."
This means that the multitude was in chaos,
like turbid water.
It is advisable to wait a short while for it to settle,
like water becoming clear,
and not go out rashly.
Nóng (農) drew his knife as if to strike them,
then went out to see Bǎo (寶),
and also quickly sent a messenger to pursue Mùyú Téng (慕輿騰).
On the Guǐwèi (癸未) day,
Bǎo (寶) and Nóng (農) led their troops back to the main camp.
The main camp
referred to Bǎo's (寶) camp.
Nóng's (農) camp soldiers also disliked military service
and all abandoned their weapons and fled.
When people are employed in an easy way,
even if they toil, they do not complain;
when people are killed in a way that preserves their lives,
even if they die, they do not complain about being killed.
Whoever acts contrary to this
rarely escapes defeat.
Bǎo (寶) and Nóng (農) fled back to Lóngchéng (龍城).
Chánglè Wáng Shèng (長樂王盛) heard of the rebellion
and led troops out to meet them.
Bǎo (寶) and Nóng (農) barely escaped.
7 Huìjī Wáng Dàozǐ (會稽王道子) feared the pressure from Wáng (王) and Yīn (殷).
Knowing that Qiáo Wáng Shàngzhī (譙王尚之) and his brother Xiūzhī (休之) possessed talent and strategy,
he made them his close confidants.
Shàngzhī (尚之) persuaded Dàozǐ (道子), saying:
"Currently, the regional governors are strong,
while the prime minister's power is weak.
It is advisable to secretly establish confidants externally to protect oneself."
Dàozǐ (道子) followed this advice,
appointing his Sīmǎ Wáng Yú (司馬王愉) as Jiāngzhōu Cìshǐ (江州刺史),
supervising the military affairs of Jiāngzhōu (江州) and four commanderies of Yùzhōu (豫州),
using him as a strategic support,
consulting with Shàngzhī (尚之) day and night
to look for weaknesses in all directions.
This prepared the ground for Yú Kǎi (庾楷) to persuade Wáng (王) and Yīn (殷) to again raise an army.
"Shuì (說)"
pronounced Shū Ruì fān.
"Sì (伺)"
pronounced Xiàng Lì fān.
8 Wèi Wáng Guī (魏王珪) went to Fánzhì Gōng (繁畤宮).
Fánzhì Xiàn (繁畤縣)
belonged to Yànmén Jùn (鴈門郡).
Wèi (魏) built a palace here.
In the early Tiānpíng (天平) era,
Fánzhì Jùn (繁畤郡) was established.
During the Suí (隋) dynasty, it reverted to a county.
In the Táng (唐) dynasty, it belonged to Dàizhōu (代州).
"Zhì (畤)"
pronounced Zhǐ.
Tuòbá Guī hunted at Báidēngshān.
Lì Dàoyuán said: "Seventeen *lǐ* east of Píngchéng today there is a platform,
which is the Báidēngtái.
South of the platform, facing the hills,
is Báidēngshān."
He said to the Champion General, Yú Lìdī:
"Your name means brave and strong.
Can you wrestle this (beast)?"
Yú Lìdī replied:
"Beasts are cheap, people are precious.
If I wrestle it and do not win,
would it not be a vain loss of a brave man?"
So, they drove the beast before Tuòbá Guī,
and shot and captured it entirely.
Tuòbá Guī looked back and thanked him.
Ěrzhū Yǔjiàn, the chieftain of Xiùróngchuān, followed Tuòbá Guī in attacking Jìnyáng and Zhōngshān and rendered meritorious service.
He was appointed Sànqí Chángshì.
His residence was encircled,
and three hundred *lǐ* of land were demarcated and enfeoffed to him.
This was the northern Xiùróng.
This laid the groundwork for Ěrzhū Róng's rebellion against Wèi.
The biography of Ěrzhū Róng states: "Yǔjiàn's ancestors
were chieftains of tribes for generations,
residing in Ěrzhūchuān,
and thus took the surname."
Tuòbá Guī initially thought the southern Xiùróngchuān was expansive and fertile,
and wanted him to reside there.
Yǔjiàn said:
"My family has served the state for generations,
attending to the emperor's left and right.
Northern Xiùróng is already within the *chǎn* area,
somewhat closer to the capital.
Why should I move to a distant place just because of fertile or barren land?"
Tuòbá Guī agreed.
Thus, northern Xiùróng was probably close to Píngchéng.
環,
pronunciation: huàn.
酋,
pronunciation: cí yóu fān.
長,
pronunciation: zhī liǎng fān.
散,
pronunciation: xī dǎn fān.
騎,
pronunciation: qí jì fān;
same below.
The Ròurán frequently invaded the Wèi border.
Lǐ Xiān, the Shàngshū Zhōngbīngláng, requested to attack them;
Tuòbá Guī agreed,
and they greatly defeated the Ròurán and returned.
9 Yáng Guǐ appointed his Sīmǎ, Guō Wěi, as Xīpíng Xiàng,
and led twenty thousand infantry and cavalry north to join Guō Nún.
Tūfà Wūgū dispatched his younger brother, the Chēqí Jiāngjūn Nǔtán, to lead ten thousand cavalry to assist Yáng Guǐ.
Yáng Guǐ arrived at Gūzāng
and encamped north of the city.
10 Lán Hàn, the Yàn Shàngshū and Dūnqiū Wáng, secretly conspired with Duàn Sùgǔ and others,
leading troops to encamp east of Lóngchéng.
The garrison troops in the city were few,
so Chánglè Wáng Shèng moved the people from outside into the city,
obtaining more than ten thousand able-bodied men,
and defended the city walls to resist them.
Duàn Sùgǔ and his co-conspirators numbered barely over a hundred people;
the rest were all coerced and threatened,
having no will to fight.
In the third month,
on the *Jiǎwǔ* day,
Duàn Sùgǔ and others were about to attack the city.
Mùróng Nóng, the Liáoxī Huánliè Wáng, feared he could not hold out,
and was also enticed by Lán Hàn.
At night,
he secretly slipped out to join them,
hoping to save himself.
Mùróng Nóng was known for his wisdom and strategy,
yet he wanted to surrender to Duàn Sùgǔ to save himself,
not knowing that he was merely hastening his own death.
Perhaps Heaven had deprived him of his judgment.
Duàn Sùgǔ and others attacked the city,
and the defenders on the wall resisted fiercely,
resulting in hundreds of deaths among Duàn Sùgǔ's forces.
Duàn Sùgǔ then led Mùróng Nóng along the city wall.
將,
as is,
to lead,
to hold.
The multitude in the city relied on Mùróng Nóng for strength,
but suddenly saw him below the city,
and all were astonished, demoralized,
and consequently fled and dispersed.
Duàn Sùgǔ entered the city,
unleashed his soldiers to kill and plunder,
and the dead lay strewn everywhere.
Mùróng Bǎo, Mùróng Shèng, and Mùyú Téng, Yú Chóng, Zhāng Zhēn, Lǐ Hàn, Zhào Ēn, and others rode lightly south.
Duàn Sùgǔ imprisoned Mùróng Nóng in the palace.
Ājiāluó, the Chángshàng, was Duàn Sùgǔ's chief strategist.
Thinking Gāoyáng Wáng Chóng was young and weak,
he wanted to enthrone Mùróng Nóng instead.
Zōng Ràng and Chūlì Jiàn, confidants of Mùróng Chóng, heard of this,
and on the *Dīngyǒu* day,
killed Ājiāluó and Mùróng Nóng.
Even if Duàn Sùgǔ had indeed enthroned Mùróng Nóng,
he would certainly have died by Lán Hàn's hand as well,
because the situation had already deteriorated,
and wisdom could not be applied.
Yǔwén Bá, Mùróng Nóng's former official and Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn, fled to Liáoxī.
On the *Gēngzǐ* day,
Lán Hàn attacked Duàn Sùgǔ,
and all his partisans,
killing them all.
He deposed Mùróng Chóng,
enthroned the Crown Prince Cè,
and, by imperial decree, granted a general amnesty.
He sent envoys to welcome Mùróng Bǎo,
meeting him at Jìchéng.
Mùróng Bǎo wanted to return,
but Chánglè Wáng Shèng and others all said:
"Lán Hàn's loyalty or treachery is still unknown.
If we go to him with a single rider now,
and if by any chance Lán Hàn has other intentions,
we would regret it too late.
It is better to go south to the Fányáng Wáng,
gather troops to take Jìzhōu;
if that does not succeed,
we can gather the southern forces
and slowly return to Lóngdū,
which would not be too late either."
Mùróng Bǎo followed their advice.
Lóngchéng
was the former capital of Yàn,
hence called Lóngdū.
Mùróng Shèng's wisdom and foresight far surpassed his father's.
11 Hūyán Tiě, the Hú chieftain of Líshí, and Zhāng Chóng, the Hú chieftain of Xīhé, and others were unhappy about being relocated to Dài.
They gathered crowds and rebelled against Wèi.
Yǔ Yuè, the Wèi Ānyuǎn Jiāngjūn, suppressed them.
12 Wèi Wáng Tuòbá Guī summoned Wèi Wáng Yí to assist him,
and appointed Luèyáng Gōng Zūn to replace him in guarding Zhōngshān.
In summer,
fourth month,
on the *Rénxū* day,
Mù Chóng, the Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn, was appointed Tàiwèi,
and Zhǎngsūn Sōng, the Ānnán Jiāngjūn, was appointed Sītú.
13 Yàn Zhǔ Bǎo, traveling by a side path, passed through Yè.
The people of Yè asked him to stay,
but Bǎo refused.
He went south to Líyáng
and lay in ambush on the west bank of the river.
The river then turns from Zhēhài Tíng and flows northeast,
passing south of Líyáng Xiàn.
The west bank of the river belonged to Líyáng,
and the east bank to Huátái.
“On the second month, the Emperor received the Chancellor’s memorial.”
Bǎo was given the title Sītú based on his virtue,
hence he is referred to as Chancellor.
Upon reaching Yǐlián,
he encountered a rebellion led by Chángshàng.
He lost his base and came here.
What a ruler relies on
is power.
With the multitude in revolt and kin estranged,
the great power is gone,
and he has lost his support.
Zhōng,
Dé's cousin,
was the first to urge Dé to claim the imperial title.
Upon hearing this, he abhorred it.
He seized Sī and handed him over to prison,
reporting the situation to Nányàn Wáng Dé.
Dé said to his subordinates:
“You all, for the great plan of the altars of soil and grain,
urged me to assume regency.
I, too, considering that the heir apparent has fled and wandered —
Bō
means bú or fú (flee),
and qiān (move).
Yuè
means yuǎn (far),
and zǒu (run).
— therefore temporarily acceded to your wishes to secure the loyalty of the masses.
Now Heaven has regretted the disaster,
and the heir apparent can return.
I will prepare the imperial equipage to welcome him,
apologize at the temporary palace,
what do you think? ”
The place where the Son of Heaven travels to has a temporary palace.
The palace’s front gate
is called xíngquè (temporary palace gate).
“Now the world is in great chaos.
Without a heroic talent, it is impossible to bring peace and save the people.
The heir apparent is dim-witted and weak,
unable to continue and glorify the former lineage.
If Your Majesty adheres to the integrity of a commoner,
abandoning the enterprise granted by Heaven,
once your authority is gone,
your head and body will not be safe,
how much less will the altars of soil and grain receive sacrifices! ”
Mùyú Hù said:
“The heir apparent does not understand the exigencies of the time,
abandoning the capital.
Bǎo abandoned Zhōngshān,
see volume shang, previous year.
He is incapable of facing many difficulties;
this is already clear.
In the past, Kuǎikuì fled,
but Wèi Zhé did not admit him,
which the Spring and Autumn Annals affirmed.
If a son can reject his father,
how much more can a father reject his son!
Dé was Bǎo’s paternal uncle.
Before the truth is known,
I request to rush there for Your Majesty to scout him out. ”
Dé shed tears and sent him.
Sending Hù with tears,
intending him to kill Bǎo.
Hù led several hundred brave men
with Sī to the north,
ostensibly to welcome and protect him,
but actually to scheme against him.
After Bǎo had sent Sī to Zhōng,
he later heard from a woodcutter that
Dé had already assumed the imperial title.
Fearing this, he fled north.
When Hù arrived,
he found no one,
so he seized Sī and returned.
Dé, thinking Sī was well-versed in statecraft and precedents,
wanted to keep and employ him.
Sī said:
“Even dogs and horses know to long for their master.
Although I am a condemned official,
I beg to return to my lord. ”
Huànzhě
means xíngchén (condemned official).
Shàng
refers to Bǎo.
Sī said angrily:
“When the Zhōu House moved east,
Jìn and Zhèng were its support.
King Píng of Zhōu moved east to Luòyì,
and Marquis Wén of Jìn and Wǔ of Zhèng secured the royal house.
Therefore, Duke Huán of Zhōu said:
'When our Zhōu moved east,
we relied on Jìn and Zhèng.'
Occupying the position of a senior duke,
yet unable to lead the various feudal lords to support the imperial house,
but instead delighting in the collapse of the foundation,
acting like Zhào Wáng Lún —
the matter is found in volume eighty-nine, under Emperor Huì's Yǒngníng first year.
This refers to Zhào Wáng Lún, a member of the imperial clan, who usurped the throne of Jìn.
Dé's actions are similar.
Lún was Emperor Huì's grand-uncle;
Dé was Bǎo's paternal uncle.
Shuài
is read as shuà.
When Wú defeated Chǔ and entered Yǐng,
Shēn Bāoxū begged for troops from Qín,
which then defeated the Wú army,
and King Zhāo of Chǔ restored his state.
Gōng Shèng,
courtesy name Jūnbīn,
his story is found in volume thirty-seven, under Wáng Mǎng’s Shǐjiànguó third year.
Bǎo sent Fúfēng Zhōnggōng Mùyú Téng and Chánglè Wáng Shèng to gather troops in Jìzhōu.
Shèng, knowing Téng was habitually violent and arrogant,
and resented by the people,
killed him.
He traveled to Jùlù and Chánglè,
persuading various local strongmen,
who all wished to raise troops to support Bǎo.
Bǎo, seeing Lán Hàn performing sacrifices to the Yàn ancestral temple,
which seemed to be an act of submission,
intended to return to Lóngchéng,
unwilling to stay in Jìzhōu,
so he proceeded north.
Upon reaching Jiàn'ān,
Jiàn'ān Chéng is north of Lìzhī and south of Yǐlián.
Cáo, who was historically brave and strong,
asked to gather troops for Bǎo.
Shèng also advised Bǎo that he should temporarily halt
and observe Hàn’s situation.
Bǎo then sent the eunuch attendant, Púshè Lǐ Hán, to first see Hàn,
while Bǎo stayed and camped at Shíchéng.
Shíchéng Xiàn,
in the Former Hàn, belonged to Yòuběipíng Jùn.
In the Later Hàn and Jìn, the county was abolished,
belonging to Jiàndé Jùn.
In Suí and Táng, it was merged into the territory of Yíngzhōu Liǔchéng Xiàn.
Sòng Bái said: Shíchéng Xiàn was named after the Jíshí (Stone Pillar) that stood like a city.
He was to express Hàn's loyalty.
Bǎo considered Hàn to be his maternal uncle,
the father of Shèng,
and believed there would be no treachery,
so without waiting for Hán to return,
he continued his journey.
Shèng shed tears and repeatedly remonstrated,
but Bǎo did not listen,
leaving Shèng behind.
Shèng and General Zhāng Zhēn then left the road and went into hiding.
On the *Dīnghài* day,
Bǎo reached the Suǒmòhán Pass,
forty *lǐ* from Lóngchéng.
Everyone in the city was delighted.
Hán was terrified
and wanted to go out himself to beg for forgiveness,
but his brothers jointly advised him against it.
Hán then sent his younger brother, Jiānán, to lead five hundred cavalry to welcome Bǎo;
he also sent his elder brother, Dī, to close the city gates, stop military activities,
and forbid people from going in and out.
Everyone in the city knew that he was about to make a move,
but there was nothing they could do.
Jiānán met Bǎo north of the pass.
After bowing and paying respects,
which is to say,
after the ritual of bowing and paying respects was completed,
Yǐngyīn Liè Gōng Yú Chóng secretly said to Bǎo:
"Observing Jiānán's expression,
a disaster and coup are imminent.
You should think thrice;
why proceed directly?"
Bǎo did not listen.
After traveling a few *lǐ*,
Jiānán first seized Chóng.
Chóng loudly yelled and cursed:
"Your family fortunately rose through loyal service,
receiving imperial favor and glory.
Even the destruction of your clan would not suffice to repay it.
Now you dare to plot usurpation and rebellion!
This is something that heaven and earth cannot tolerate.
I calculate that you will be slaughtered and annihilated within days or hours.
My only regret is that I cannot personally slice you all to pieces!"
*Kuài*
means to finely slice meat.
Jiānán led Bǎo into the outer residence of Lóngchéng
and assassinated him.
He was forty-four years old.
He also killed Xiàn'āi Tàizǐ Cè and over a hundred princes, dukes, ministers, and scholars.
He declared himself Dà Dūdū, Dà Jiāngjūn, Dà Dān Yú, and Chānglí Wáng,
changing the era name to Qīnglóng.
He appointed Dī as Tàiwèi
and Jiānán as Chēqí Jiāngjūn.
He enfeoffed Héjiān Wáng Xī as Liáodōng Gōng,
following the precedent of Rú and Sòng.
King Wǔ of Zhōu enfeoffed the descendants of Xià in Rú
and the descendants of Yīn in Sòng.
Chánglè Wáng Shèng heard of this
and rushed, intending to mourn;
Zhāng Zhēn stopped him.
Shèng said:
"I am now returning to Hán in destitution.
Hán is foolish and shallow by nature,
and he will surely remember our marital ties
and not bear to kill me.
Within ten days or a month,
it will be enough for me to express my feelings and aspirations."
So he went to see Hán.
Hán's wife, Lady Yǐ, and Shèng both tearfully pleaded with Hán for Shèng's life,
and Shèng again kowtowed to all the brothers.
Hán was moved and took pity on him,
so he housed Shèng in the palace
and appointed him Shìzhōng and Zuǒ Guānglù Dàfū,
treating him with intimacy as before.
Dī and Jiānán repeatedly requested to kill Shèng,
but Hán refused.
Dī was arrogant, unruly, and debauched,
often acting disrespectfully towards Hán.
Shèng thus sowed discord between them.
From then on, Hán and his brothers gradually became suspicious and resentful of each other.
This laid the groundwork for Shèng to execute Hán.
The fourteenth day. Liáng Tàiyuán Gōng Zuǎn led troops to attack Yáng Guǐ.
Guō Nún rescued him,
and Zuǎn was defeated and returned.
The fifteenth day. Duàn Yè sent Jǔqú Méngxùn to attack Xī Jùn.
This commandery was west of Wǔwēi,
occupying a strategic mountain pass.
Méngxùn took it,
so the former Jìnchāng and Dūnhuáng both surrendered.
*Jǔ*,
pronounced *zǐ yú*.
*Chún*
was a disciple of Guāng.
Thereupon, Wáng Dé, the administrator of Jìnchāng, and Zhàojùn Mèng Mǐn, the administrator of Dūnhuáng, both surrendered their commanderies to Yè.
Yè enfeoffed Méngxùn as Línchí Hóu,
appointed Dé as Jiǔquán Tàishǒu,
and Mǐn as Shāzhōu Cìshǐ.
The sixteenth day. In the sixth month,
on the *Bǐngzǐ* day,
King Guī of Wèi ordered his ministers to deliberate on the national title.
They all said:
"Before Zhōu and Qín,
all rulers ascended to Son of Heaven from being feudal lords,
thus taking their state's name as the name for the realm.
Since the Hàn dynasty,
none have had an inch of land as their base.
Our state has been passed down for a hundred generations,
establishing its foundation north of Dài,
and then pacifying and possessing the regions of the four quarters of China."
According to Kǒng Ānguó's commentary on the *Shàngshū*,
"four quarters of China"
refers to the central states of the four directions.
*Xià*,
pronounced *hù yǎ*.
Huángmén Shìláng Cuī Hóng said:
"In ancient times, the Shāng people did not always reside in one place,
hence they were called both Yīn and Shāng.
Qì was first enfeoffed in Shāng.
Huángfǔ Mì said: 'The present day Shāng in Shàngluò is it.'
Qì's grandson Xiàngtǔ resided in Shāngqiū.
From Qì to Chéngtāng,
there were eight relocations.
Tāng first resided in Bó,
following the residence of the former kings.
Later, Zhòngdīng moved to Xiāo,
Hédǎnjiǎ resided in Xiāng,
and Zǔyǐ resided in Gěng.
The *Shū* says: 'Pángēng relocated five times,
intending to settle in Bóyīn,
following the residence of the former kings.'
This refers to following the residence of Dì Kù,
residing in Bó.
'Its mandate is renewed.'
At the beginning of the reign,
it was already changed to Wèi.
This event is recorded in volume 106, Xiàowǔ Tàiyuán eleventh year.
*Gēng*,
pronounced *gōng héng*.
'Great name' refers to a superior state in Shénzhōu.
The *Zuǒ Zhuàn* states: Bǔ Yǎn said:
'Wèi
is a great name.'
During the Warring States period,
Wèi was a great state.
China is referred to as Shénzhōu."
Guī followed his advice.
The seventeenth day. Yáng Guǐ, relying on the strength of his forces,
wanted to engage King Guāng of Liáng in a decisive battle,
but Guō Nún always restrained him based on the celestial omens.
He said that the celestial omens were not favorable yet.
Guō Nún was skilled in divination,
hence his words.
*Nún*,
pronounced *nú kūn*.
Duàn Yè sent Jǔqú Nánchéng and Wáng Dé to attack him.
Guāng sent Tàiyuán Gōng Zuǎn to lead troops to meet them.
Yáng Guǐ said:
"Lǚ Hóng has ten thousand elite soldiers.
If he joins with Guāng,
then Gūzāng will become even stronger
and cannot be taken."
So he and Tūfà Lìlùgū jointly ambushed and attacked Zuǎn.
Zuǎn fought them and thoroughly defeated them;
Guǐ fled to Wáng Qǐjī.
Wáng Qǐjī
was a Tián Hú.
He was not supported by the common people.
Hearing of Guǐ's defeat and flight,
he surrendered to Xī Qín.
King Gān Guī of Xī Qín appointed him Jiànzhōng Jiāngjūn and Sànqí Chángshì.
*Sàn*,
pronounced *xī dān*.
*Qí*,
pronounced *qí jì*.
Hóng led his troops, abandoned Zhāngyè, and fled eastward.
Duàn Yè moved his seat of government to Zhāngyè,
and intended to pursue and attack Hóng.
Jǔqú Méngxùn advised him:
"Do not intercept a returning army;
do not pursue desperate bandits.
These are the words of Sūnzi."
Yè did not listen
and was severely defeated and returned,
relying on Méngxùn to escape.
Yè built a city at Xī'ān
and appointed his general Zāng Mòhái as its administrator.
Yè established the Xī'ān Commandery on the eastern border of Zhāngyè.
*Hái*,
pronounced *hé kāi*.
"Mòhái is brave but lacks strategy;
he knows how to advance but not how to retreat.
This is building a tomb for him,
not a city!"
Yè did not listen,
and Mòhái was soon defeated by Lǚ Zuǎn.
18 Yān’s (Former Yàn) Prince of Tàiyuán, Mùróng Qí,
was the son of Mùróng Kǎi,
and the maternal grandson of Lán Hàn.
Lán Hàn also did not kill him,
instead making him General of the South.
Mùróng Qí was able to gain an audience with Chánglè Wáng Mùróng Shèng.
Mùróng Shèng secretly arranged for Mùróng Qí to escape and raise an army.
Mùróng Qí raised an army at Jiàn’ān;
his forces reached several thousand.
Lán Hàn dispatched Lán Dī to suppress him.
Mùróng Shèng said to Lán Hàn:
“The young boy Shànjū
is not yet capable of managing this.
Shànjū
was Mùróng Qí’s childhood name.
Tàiwèi Lán Dī has always been arrogant
and untrustworthy.
It is not advisable to entrust him with a large army.”
Lán Hàn had made Lán Dī the Tàiwèi,
hence this appellation.
Lán Hàn then recalled Lán Dī’s troops.
Sū Shì once said,
“A tree must first be worm-eaten
before insects will breed in it;
a person must first be suspicious
before slander will enter him.”
Lán Hàn was cruel and rebellious;
his brothers naturally harbored suspicion and jealousy towards each other.
Therefore, Mùróng Shèng was able to exploit this to exert his wisdom
and avenge his sovereign and father.
Thereupon, Lóngchéng experienced no rain from summer until the seventh month of autumn.
Lán Hàn daily visited the Yān ancestral temples and the shrines of the sacred deities, prostrating himself and praying.
He attributed the blame to Lán Jiānán,
saying that Lán Jiānán was responsible for the assassination of Mùróng Bǎo.
And fearing execution,
on the Yǐsì day,
Lán Dī and Lán Jiānán, together with their subordinates, attacked the army of Qiúní Mù.
They defeated him.
Lán Hàn was greatly alarmed
and sent his太子 (Crown Prince) Lán Mù to lead troops to suppress them.
Lán Mù said to Lán Hàn:
“Mùróng Shèng is our sworn enemy;
he must be in collusion with Mùróng Qí.
This is a sickness of the heart and stomach
that cannot be allowed to grow.
It should be eliminated first.”
Lán Hàn wanted to kill Mùróng Shèng;
he first summoned him for an audience
to observe him.
Lán zhī (a woman of the Lán family, likely Lán Hàn’s wife or concubine), knowing of this,
secretly informed Mùróng Shèng.
Mùróng Shèng feigned illness and did not appear.
Lán zhī’s actions
differed from those of Yōng Jí (a woman who assisted her husband’s family against her own).
Although it is said that women prioritize their husband’s family over their parents’ family,
a person like Lán zhī,
facing a conflict between husband and wife, father and son,
gained one and lost the other.
Lǐ Hàn, Wèi Shuāng, Liú Zhōng, Zhāng Háo, and Zhāng Zhēn
were all people Mùróng Shèng had always been close to.
Lán Mù, however, had taken them as his confidants.
Lǐ Hàn and Wèi Shuāng were able to enter and exit Mùróng Shèng’s residence
and secretly conspired with Mùróng Shèng.
On the Dīngwèi day,
Lán Mù attacked Lán Dī and Lán Jiānán, etc.,
and defeated them.
On the Gēngxū day,
Lán Hàn hosted a banquet for his generals and soldiers.
Lán Hàn and Lán Mù both became drunk.
Mùróng Shèng went to the latrine at night,
then climbed over the wall into the Eastern Palace
and, with Lǐ Hàn and others, killed Lán Mù.
At that time, the army had not yet been dismissed;
all were gathered in Lán Mù’s quarters.
Hearing that Mùróng Shèng had escaped,
they cheered and vied to be first
to attack Lán Hàn,
and they beheaded him.
Lán Hàn’s sons, Lǔ Gōng Lán Hé and Chén Gōng Lán Yáng, were garrisoned separately at Lìngzhī and Báiláng.
Mùróng Shèng dispatched Lǐ Hàn and Zhāng Zhēn to attack and execute them.
Lán Dī and Lán Jiānán fled and went into hiding;
they were captured
and beheaded.
Thereupon, internal and external affairs were settled,
and men and women celebrated with each other.
Yǔwén Bá led several hundred brave warriors to come and assist.
Yǔwén Bá came from Liáoxī.
On the Xīnhài day,
Mùróng Shèng made an announcement to the Imperial Ancestral Temple,
stating:
“Thanks to the blessings of the Five Ancestors
(The Five Ancestors
refer to Mùróng Shèguī, Mùróng Kuì, Mùróng Huǎng, Mùróng Jùn, and Mùróng Chuí,
totaling five temples),
the ancestral temples and the altars of state have been restored to prominence.
Not only has this solitary one, with his humble self, been spared the responsibility of not sharing the same sky (with the enemy)
(The Lǐ Jì states: one does not share the same sky with the killer of one’s father),”
he then issued a general amnesty
and changed the era name to Jiànpíng.
Mùróng Shèng humbly dared not assume the imperial title,
and as Chánglè Wáng, temporarily governed the state.
Mùróng Shèng,
courtesy name Dàoyùn, was Mùróng Bǎo’s eldest illegitimate son.
(The character) Lè (in Chánglè)
is pronounced Luò.
He appointed Dōngyáng Gōng Gēn as Shàngshū Zuǒ Púyè,
Wèi Lún, Yáng Qiú, Lǔ Gōng, and Wáng Téng
as Shàngshū,
Yuè Zhēn as Shìzhōng,
Yáng Zhé as Zhōngshū Jiān,
and Zhāng Tōng as Zhōng Lǐngjūn.
All other civil and military officials were restored to their former positions.
Mùróng Bǎo’s posthumous title was changed to Huìmǐn Huángdì,
and his temple name was Lièzōng.
Previously,
Prince of Tàiyuán Mùróng Qí had raised an army at Jiàn’ān,
and people from both the south and north flocked to him.
“Southerners”
refers to those who came from the Central Plains;
“Northerners”
refers to the Xiānbēi.
Mùróng Qí attacked and destroyed them,
returning with not a single horse,
and advanced to garrison at Yǐlián.
After Mùróng Shèng executed Lán Hàn,
he ordered Mùróng Qí to disband his troops.
Mùróng Qí, acting on the advice of the Dīnglíng Yán Shēng and the Wūhuán Wáng Lóng,
thus refused to obey the order.
On the Jiǎyín day,
he led more than 30,000 troops and advanced to Hénggōu,
ten *li* from Lóngchéng.
Mùróng Shèng sallied out and attacked,
thoroughly defeating him.
He captured Mùróng Qí and returned,
executing over a hundred of his followers.
Mùróng Qí was granted death,
and the lineage of Huán Wáng was thus severed.
Mùróng Kè was enfeoffed as Prince of Tàiyuán
with the posthumous title Huán.
Chǔ Zhuāng Wáng exterminated the Ruò’áo clan but pardoned Zhēnyǐn Kè Huáng,
saying:
“If Zǐwén (Ruò’áo Zǐwén) has no descendants,
how can one encourage goodness?”
How could Mùróng Kè, who assisted in establishing the Yān enterprise,
be allowed to have his lineage cut off?
Mùróng Shèng did not agree (to allow Mùróng Qí to be spared for the sake of Mùróng Kè’s lineage).
19 Wèi Wáng Tuòbá Guī moved the capital to Píngchéng.
He began to build palaces,
establish ancestral temples,
and erect altars of state.
There were five annual sacrifices at the ancestral temples,
held at the solstices, equinoxes, and during the *là* festival.
The capital of Wèi was Píngchéng.
The offices of Dài Yǐn and Sī Zhōu were established in Píngchéng.
Dù Yòu said: The Later Wèi capital was Píngchéng,
which is now the seat of Yúnzhōng Jùn.
Yúnzhōng Xiàn is now Mǎyì Jùn;
Běipíngchéng is now the *jùn* (district),
and during the Suí dynasty, it was Yúnnèi Xiàn’s Héng’ān Zhèn.
The ancestral temples mentioned here
are the Eastern Temple of the Dài capital.
20 Huán Xuán sought to be appointed Governor of Guǎngzhōu.
Huìjī Wáng Sīmǎ Dàozǐ, jealous of Huán Xuán,
did not want him to reside in Jīngzhōu.
Therefore, acceding to his wish,
he appointed Huán Xuán as Supervisor of Military Affairs for Jiāo and Guǎng prefectures, and Governor of Guǎngzhōu.
Huán Xuán accepted the appointment but did not proceed to his post.
Yùzhōu Cìshǐ Yǔ Kǎi, because Sīmǎ Dàozǐ had carved out four of his commanderies and put Wáng Yú in charge of them,
submitted a memorial stating:
“Jiāngzhōu is an inland territory
(Jiāngzhōu’s seat was Xúnyáng,
south of the Yangtze,
hence called inland territory).
The Jìn dynasty made Jīngkǒu the Northern Command
and Lìyáng the Western Command.
Yùzhōu’s seat was Lìyáng,
west of the Yangtze,
hence it is said to be ‘bordering the northern bandits.’ ”
The imperial court did not permit this.
Yǔ Kǎi was enraged,
and sent his son Yǔ Hóng to speak to Wáng Gōng, saying:
“Shàngzhī’s brothers
(referring to Qiáo Wáng Sīmǎ Shàngzhī and his brother Sīmǎ Xiūzhī)
(Shuì
is pronounced with the initial of shū and the final of ruì;
the same below)
are worse than Wáng Guóbǎo.
They wish to use imperial authority to weaken the regional governors,
learn from previous mistakes,
and cause unpredictable disaster.
Now, while their plans are not yet complete,
we should act quickly against them.”
Wáng Gōng agreed,
and informed Yīn Zhòngkān and Huán Xuán.
Yīn Zhòngkān and Huán Xuán assented,
acclaimed Wáng Gōng as their盟主 (Alliance Leader),
and set a date to advance together on the capital.
At that time, suspicion and obstruction existed both internally and externally,
and patrols and checkpoints were strict.
Yīn Zhòngkān wrote a letter on a piece of slanted silk,
inserted it into an arrow shaft,
and sealed the arrowhead with lacquer.
Dí (鏑)
means arrowhead.
Wáng Gōng opened the letter,
but the silk writing was crumpled and distorted,
so he could no longer discern Zhòngkān's handwriting.
Lì (戾)
means bent,
or amiss.
The slanted silk had no selvedge,
and its warp and weft could not hold together,
hence it was crumpled and distorted at the corners.
Moreover, he believed that Zhòngkān had already failed to keep his appointment last year,
a matter detailed in the previous volume.
Thus, Wáng Gōng raised an army ahead of schedule.
The Sīmǎ, Liú Láozhī, remonstrated, saying:
"General,
you are the nation's maternal uncle;
the Prince of Kuàijī
is the Son of Heaven's paternal uncle.
The Prince of Kuàijī also controls the government,
and previously he killed your beloved Wáng Guóbǎo and Wáng Xù for you,
and also sent a letter to Wáng Yīn.
These matters are detailed in the previous volume.
Wéi (為)
is pronounced yú wěi.
The appointments recently bestowed,
though not entirely satisfactory,
were not a great loss.
What harm does it do to you, General, to cede Yǔ Kǎi's four commanderies to Wáng Yú?
How can the army of Jìnyáng
be raised so often!"
Wáng Gōng did not listen.
He submitted a memorial requesting to attack Wáng Yú and Sīmǎ Shàngzhī's brothers.
Dàozǐ sent someone to persuade Kǎi, saying:
"In the past, you and I
had an affection like flesh and blood.
Kǎi had previously allied with Wáng Guóbǎo,
and Dàozǐ was also close to him.
The pledge of brotherhood
can be said to have been close.
This must refer to the events when Yǔ Kǎi went to the rescue in Tàiyuán 21st year.
Will you form new alliances

30 Xīqín (Xīqín) King Gān Guī (Gān Guī) sent the Qínzhōu (Qínzhōu)牧 Yìzhōu (Yìzhōu) and Wǔwèi Jiāngjūn (Wǔwèi Jiāngjūn) Mù Wù (Mù Wù).
"Mù Wù" (Mù Wù),
the Jìn Shū Zàijì (Jìn Shū Zàijì) writes
"Mùróng Wù" (Mùróng Wù).
Mù Wù (Mù Wù) was likely also of the Qǐfú (Qǐfú) clan;
the Zàijì (Zàijì) is mistaken.
31 In winter,
tenth month,
on the day Guǐyǒu (Guǐyǒu),
the Yān (Yān) ministers again submitted a memorial urging the emperor to assume his title.
On the day Bǐngzǐ (Bǐngzǐ),
Chánglè (Chánglè) King Shèng (Shèng) formally ascended the imperial throne,
granted a general amnesty,
honored Empress Duàn (Duàn) as Empress Dowager,
and the former Lady Dīng (Dīng) as Xiànzhuāng Huánghòu (Xiànzhuāng Huánghòu).
Previously,
when Lán Hàn (Lán Hàn) was in power,
Shèng (Shèng) fled with Yān (Yān) Lord Bǎo (Bǎo),
while Lán (Lán) served Lady Dīng (Dīng) even more diligently.
When Hàn (Hàn) was executed,
Shèng (Shèng) was implicated and wanted to kill her;
Lady Dīng (Dīng), due to her efforts in preserving him,
staunchly argued against it,
and he was spared,
but he ultimately did not make her empress.
32 (He granted) a general amnesty.
33 Yīn Zhòngkān received the imperial edict,
and was furious.
It was an edict removing him to Guǎngzhōu.
Huán Xuán and others were pleased with the imperial decree
and intended to accept it,
but they hesitated, unable to make a decision.
When Zhòngkān heard of this,
he immediately returned south from Wúhú,
sending an envoy to inform the soldiers at Càizhōu, saying:
"If you do not disperse and return home,
when I reach Jiānglíng,
I will execute all of your remaining kin."
Yuán Quánqī's general, Liú Xì, led two thousand men and returned first.
Huán Xuán and the others were greatly afraid,
and hastily returned west,
pursuing Zhòngkān to Xúnyáng,
where they caught up with him.
Since Zhòngkān had lost his position,
he relied on Huán Xuán and the others for support,
and Huán Xuán and the others also needed Zhòngkān's troops.
Although they harbored mutual suspicion,
circumstances compelled them to unite.
They then exchanged their sons and younger brothers as hostages.
On the day Rénwǔ,
they swore an oath at Xúnyáng;
they all refused to accept the imperial decree,
and jointly submitted a memorial to vindicate Wáng Gōng,
requesting the execution of Liú Láozhī and Qiáo Wáng Shàngzhī,
and also pleading that Zhòngkān was innocent
but had been unilaterally demoted and dismissed.
The imperial court was deeply apprehensive of this,
and there was turmoil both within and without.
Consequently, they again dismissed Huán Xiū,
returned Jīngzhōu to Zhòngkān,
and issued a conciliatory edict to pacify him,
seeking reconciliation.
Zhòngkān and the others then accepted the edict.
The Imperial Censor-in-Chief, Jiāng Jì, impeached Huán Xiū, accusing him of acting solely for his own benefit
and misleading the court,
stating that he intended to divide Jiāng and Yōng prefectures to Huán Xuán and Yáng Quánqī,
while taking Jīngzhōu for himself.
劾 (hài),
is pronounced hù gài fān,
and also hù dé fān.
Previously,
when Huán Xuán was in Jīngzhōu,
his behavior was arrogant and unrestrained.
Zhòngkān's close associates all advised Zhòngkān to kill him,
but Zhòngkān did not listen.
When he was in Xúnyáng,
he relied on Huán Xuán's prestige and family background.
声 (shēng)
refers to his reputation;
地 (dì)
refers to his family background.
Huán Xuán became even more arrogant.
Yáng Quánqī was proud and fierce by nature.
Huán Xuán often treated him as a humble scholar,
which Quánqī deeply resented.
He secretly told Zhòngkān that Huán Xuán would eventually become a menace,
and asked to ambush him at the altar.
Zhòngkān feared the bravery and strength of Quánqī and his brothers,
thinking that if Huán Xuán were killed,
they would be uncontrollable.
He strenuously forbade it.
Thereupon, they each returned to their respective garrisons.
Huán Xuán also knew of Quánqī's plan,
and secretly harbored the ambition to seize Quánqī.
This laid the groundwork for Huán Xuán's later killing of Yīn and Yáng.
He appointed Biàn Fànzhī of Jìyīn, the Administrator of Shǐ'ān, as his chief clerk and principal strategist.
In the first year of Gānlù of Sūn Hào of Wú,
the southern commandery of Línglíng was separated to establish Shǐ'ān Commandery,
which belonged to Guǎngzhōu;
during Emperor Chéng of Jìn's reign, it was reassigned to Jīngzhōu;
during the Suí and Táng dynasties, it was part of Guìzhōu.
夏 (xià),
is pronounced hù yǎ fān.
濟 (jì),
is pronounced zǐ lǐ fān.
The imperial edict alone did not pardon Yǔ Kǎi.
Huán Xuán appointed Yǔ Kǎi as the Administrator of Wǔchāng.
Originally,
Xī Huī resisted the Western Army for the imperial court.
Before Huán Xuán had obtained Jiāngzhōu,
he wanted to seize Xī Huī's Yōngzhōu,
and appoint Xī Huī to Guǎngzhōu.
When Xī Huī heard of this,
he was afraid
and consulted his subordinates.
They all said:
"If Yáng Quánqī comes,
who would not strive their utmost?
But if Huán Xuán comes,
I fear it would be difficult to contend with him."
The Huán clan had resided in Xīchǔ for generations,
so the people feared them.
Xī Huī then plotted with Lǘqiū Xiàn to resist with troops.
Lǘqiū Xiàn was then the Administrator of Nányáng,
and a subordinate of Yōngzhōu.
They falsely claimed that Huán Xuán was coming to enter Miǎn,
with Yáng Quánqī as the vanguard.
Xī Huī's forces believed this
and all fled at the mere rumor.
Xī Huī requested to surrender.
Quánqī entered the administration,
executed Lǘqiū Xiàn,
and released Xī Huī to return to the capital.
When Xī Huī reached Yángkǒu,
Yīn Zhòngkān secretly sent men to kill him
and his four sons,
attributing it to bandits.
34 Qífú Yìzhōu of Western Qín fought Shìpí, King of Tǔyùhún, at Dùzhōuchuān.
Dùzhōuchuān
is west of Lónghé, outside Líntáo fortress.
吐 (tǔ),
is from tūn with the entering tone.
谷 (gǔ),
is pronounced yù.
Shìpí fled and took refuge in Báilán Shān,
sending his son Dàngqǐ as hostage to Western Qín to sue for peace.
Qífú Gānkuī, King of Western Qín, married him to a woman of his clan.
35 Lǐ Luán, the General of Jiànwǔ of Liang, surrendered Xīngchéng to Tūfà Wūgū.
Xīngchéng is east of Lóngzhībǎo, southwest of Yǔnwú County.
36 In the eleventh month,
Wáng Déwén, the Prince of Lángxié, was appointed General of the Guard, Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī.
Yuán Xiǎn, General Who Conquers Barbarians, was appointed Central Leader of the Army.
Wáng Yǎ, Leader of the Army, was appointed Left Grandee Secretary.
37 On the day Xīnhài,
Wèi Wáng Guī ordered Dèng Yuān, the Lang of the Ministry of Personnel in the Department of State Affairs, to establish official regulations,
and harmonize musical tones;
Dǒng Mì of Qīnghé, the Lang of the Ceremony Bureau, to formulate rites and ceremonies;
Wáng Dé, the Lang of the Three Dukes, to set laws and ordinances.
The Langs of the Ministry of Personnel, Ceremony Bureau, and Three Dukes
were all offices established by Cáo Wèi.
Cuī Hóng, the Minister of Personnel, oversaw and refined them,
to serve as a perpetual model.
Dèng Yuān
was the grandson of Dèng Qiāng.
Dèng Qiāng
was a famous general of Fú Qín.
38 Yáng Guǐ and Wáng Qǐjī led several thousand households to surrender to Wūgū, the King of Xīpíng.
In the twelfth month of the 39th year,
on the day Jǐchǒu,
Wèi Wáng Guī ascended the imperial throne.
A great amnesty was declared,
and the era name was changed to Tiānxīng.
He commanded that all, both in court and in the countryside, bind their hair and wear caps.
He posthumously honored twenty-seven distant ancestors, starting from Máo, as emperors;
Wèi posthumously named Máo as Chéng Huángdì.
Five generations later, to Tuīyín,
who moved south to Dàzé,
an area of over a thousand *lǐ*,
was posthumously named Xuān Huángdì.
Seven generations later, Línshǐ first emerged south,
residing in the former territory of the Xiōngnú,
and was posthumously named Xiàn Huángdì.
Xiàn Dì’s son was named Jiéfén,
and was posthumously named Shèngwǔ Huángdì.
His temple name was Shǐzǔ;
his grandfather Shíyìjiān was named Zhāochéng Huángdì,
with the temple name Gāozǔ;
his father Shí was named Xiànmíng Huángdì.
Lìwēi was posthumously named Shényuán Huángdì,
his son Shāmòhàn was named Wén Huángdì,
and Shāmòhàn’s son Fúzhèng was named Sī Huángdì.
After Fúzhèng died,
Lìwēi’s son Lùguān ascended,
and was posthumously named Zhāo Huángdì.
He divided the state into three parts.
Yīdā and Yīlú,
the two sons of Shāmòhàn,
shared the governance of the three parts with Lùguān.
Yīdā campaigned westward,
bringing various states into submission,
and was posthumously named Huán Huángdì.
Yīlú, seeing Lùguān’s death,
united the three parts into one,
and also assisted the state of Jìn, thus increasing its strength,
and was posthumously named Mù Huángdì.
After Yīlú died,
Lùguān’s son Yùlǜ succeeded him,
and was posthumously named Píngwén Huángdì.
After Yùlǜ was assassinated,
Yīdā’s son Hèlǔ ascended,
and was posthumously named Huì Huángdì.
After Hèlǔ died,
his younger brother Hénà ascended,
and was posthumously named Yáng Huángdì.
Yìwèi,
Yùlǜ’s son,
was enthroned by the people of the state, who expelled Hénà,
and was posthumously named Liè Huángdì.
In the first month of summer, sacrifices were made to Heaven and the Eastern Ancestral Temple,
the ancestral temple being in the east,
perhaps also following the principle of "left for ancestors."
In the first month of autumn, sacrifices were made to Heaven in the western suburbs.
From this time on,
they began to follow ancient systems,
establishing the rites and music for suburban sacrifices, ancestral temples, and court banquets.
However, only the sacrifices to Heaven in the first month of summer were performed personally by the emperor.
Dù Yòu said: In the second year of Tiāncì of Wèi Dàowǔ,
sacrifices were made to Heaven in the western suburbs,
on a square altar,
with two staircases on the east.
The earthen staircases had no distinct steps.
There was a surrounding wall with four gates,
each named after its directional color.
Seven wooden spirit tablets were placed on the altar.
The sacrificial animals used were one white calf, one yellow colt, and one white lamb.
On the day of the sacrifice,
the emperor, in his grand carriage, arrived at the suburban site,
standing inside the green gate,
near the south,
facing west;
the inner court officials all stood north of the altar;
the outer court officials, great personages, and foreign guests all stood outside the green gate.
The empress, leading the six palaces, entered from the black gate,
lining up inside the green gate,
near the north,
all facing west.
The superintendent of sacrificial animals was in charge of the livestock,
arranging them in front of the altar.
The female shamans held drums,
standing east of the altar,
facing west.
Seven sons from the emperor’s seven clans held wine, south of the shamans,
facing west, with the northernmost being the most senior.
The female shamans ascended the altar and shook their drums.
The emperor bowed,
the empress bowed respectfully,
and after the inner and outer officials had bowed and completed the sacrifice,
seven animals were slaughtered;
the seven wine-holders,
facing west,
sprinkled wine on Heaven and the spirit tablets,
and bowed again.
This was done three times.
After the rites were completed, they retired.
From then on, there was one sacrifice per year.
Moreover, adopting Cuī Hóng’s proposal,
they claimed to be descendants of Huángdì.
Wèi Shōu said: The ancestors of Wèi originated from Huángdì.
Huángdì’s son was named Chāngyì.
Chāngyì’s son was enfeoffed in the northern country,
where there was the Great Xiānbēi Mountain,
from which they took their name.
Their descendants were rulers for generations,
governing the north of Yōudū
and the vast wilderness.
Huángdì reigned by the virtue of earth (tǔdé),
and the northern custom called earth
"Tuò",
and empress "Bá",
hence they took Tuòbá as their clan name.
Two thousand households of prefects, magistrates, and local magnates from six *zhōu* and twenty-two *jùn* were moved to the capital of Dài,
which extended east to Dàijùn.
The Wèi capital was Píngchéng,
and Píngchéng was considered the capital of Dài,
following the name of the state established by Hàn.
Hàn’s Píngchéng County originally belonged to Yànmén Jùn,
while Dàijùn’s seat was Sānggān,
later moved to Gāoliǔ during the Later Hàn,
and to Píngshū during the Jìn.
Wèi Shōu’s *Dìxíng Zhì* states that Shànggǔ Jùn
was Jìn’s Dàijùn,
which became the territory of Wèizhōu during the Táng.
Wèi’s capital of Dài
became the territory of Yúnzhōu Yúnzhōng County during the Táng.
To the south was Yīnguǎn,
Shànwú County,
which belonged to Yànmén Jùn during the Hàn,
to Dìngxiāng Jùn during the Later Hàn,
and Shànwú Jùn was established in the second year of Tiānpíng during the Yuán Wèi.
Bān Zhì states:
Yīnguǎn County belonged to Yànmén Jùn,
originally Lóufán Township,
established in the third year after Emperor Jǐng.
Yīnguǎn County had Lěitóu Mountain,
where the Zhì River originated.
The *Wǔdài Shǐ Zhì* states:
Dàizhōu Yànmén County has Lěitóu Mountain.
Thus, Hàn’s Yīnguǎn County had already been merged into Yànmén County.
All these were within the capital region.
Outside this, in the four cardinal and four intermediate directions, eight部師 (Bābù Shī) were established
to supervise them.
*Wèi Shū* writes
"Bābù Shuài".
The Bābù Shuài encouraged farming,
assessed income,
and used this for evaluating performance.
(Jiān, read as *gōng xián fān*).
On the day Jǐhài,
Yàn Yōuzhōu Cìshǐ Mùróng Háo, Shàngshū Zuǒ Púshè Zhāng Tōng, and Chānglí Yǐn Zhāng Shùn were executed for conspiring to rebel.
Previously,
Sūn Tài, a man from Lángxié, learned demonic arts from Dù Zǐgōng of Qiántáng,
and many commoners and officials served him.
Wáng Xún disliked him
and exiled Tài to Guǎngzhōu.
Wáng Yǎ recommended Tài to Emperor Xiàowǔ,
saying he knew the method of nourishing life.
He was recalled and gradually rose in office to Xīn'ān Tàishǒu.
Tài knew that the Jìn dynasty was nearing its end.
Taking advantage of Wáng Gōng’s rebellion,
he gathered troops under the pretext of suppressing Gōng,
and amassed vast wealth.
(Yì (億) times a hundred million (yì) is Jùyì (鉅億).)
Those who understood the situation worried about his rebellion,
but since Zhonglǐngjūn Yuán Xiǎn was on good terms with him,
no one dared to speak out.
Huìjī Nèishǐ Xiè Yóu exposed his plot.
On the day Jǐyǒu,
Huìjī Wáng Dàozǐ had Yuán Xiǎn lure and execute him,
along with his six sons;
his nephew, Ēn, escaped to sea.
The ignorant people still believed that Tài had "shed his cicada skin" and was not dead.
(A cicada shedding its shell is called "tuì".)
(Immortals are said to "shed their corpse" (shījiě),
meaning they ascend to immortality by shedding their corpse like a cicada sheds its shell.)
(Tuì, read as *shū ruì fān*, also *tǔ wài fān*.)
Ēn then gathered over a hundred fugitives
to plot revenge.
This laid the groundwork for Sūn Ēn’s later rebellion.
Xīpíng Wáng Tuòfǎ Wūgū changed his title to Wǔwēi Wáng.
In this year,
Yáng Shèng sent envoys to pledge allegiance to Wèi.
Wèi appointed Shèng as the King of Chóuchí.
Punctuation by Wáng Chóngwǔ, reviewed by Róng Zhàozǔ and Niè Chóngqí
Sīmǎ Guāng
Compiled by imperial decree
Later Student Tiāntái
Emperor Ān, year Bǐng
In the third year of Lóng'ān (jǐhài, 399 CE),
1. Spring,
the first month.
On the day Xīnyǒu,
a general amnesty was proclaimed.
2. On the day Wùchén,
Liú Zhōng (留忠), the Commandant of Chānglí (昌黎) in Yàn (燕), plotted rebellion
and was executed.
The matter implicated Gēn (根), Duke of Dōngyáng (東陽) and Minister of the Secretariat, and Duàn Chéng (段成), Minister,
who were both found guilty and died.
Wèi Shuāng (衞雙), General of the Central Guard, was sent to execute Liú Zhōng’s (留忠) younger brother
Zhì (志) in Fánchéng (凡城).
Yuán Wéi (元為), Prince of Píngyuán (平原) and General of the Guard, was appointed Minister of Education and Minister of the Secretariat.
3. On the day Gēngwǔ,
Wèi (魏) ruler Guī (珪) embarked on a northern tour.
He dispatched three armies under Dàjiàngjūn (大將軍) Chángshān (常山) Prince Zūn (遵) and others to take the eastern route out of Chángchuān (長川).
Chángchuān (長川) was located northwest of the Yùyí (禦夷) garrison,
at the eastern edge of the great desert.
What follows, referred to as the western and central routes,
suggests that the routes across the desert were divided into three.
Guī (珪) personally led the main army along the central route, emerging from the Bóránhuǐ (駮髯水) river to attack the Gāochē (高車).
4. On the day Rénwǔ,
Zhāng Zhēn (張真), General of the Right in Yàn (燕), and Hé Hàn (和翰), Commandant of the City Gates, were executed for plotting rebellion.
5. On the day Guǐwèi,
Yàn (燕) proclaimed a general amnesty
and changed the era name to Chánglè (長樂).
Yàn (燕) ruler Shèng (盛) personally judged cases every ten days,
without resorting to torture,
and often uncovered the truth.
6. Wǔwēi (武威) Prince Wūgū (烏孤) moved his capital to Lèdū (樂都).
He stationed his younger brother, Xīpíng (西平) Duke Lìlùgū (利鹿孤), in Ānyí (安夷).
Ānyí (安夷) County
belonged to Jīnchéng (金城) Commandery during the Hàn (漢) Dynasty,
and was later assigned to Xīpíng (西平) Commandery during the Jìn (晉) Dynasty.
Xīpíng (西平) Commandery was governed from Lèdū (樂都) County,
which is the present-day Huángshuǐ (湟水) County of Shànzhōu (鄯州) in the Táng (唐) Dynasty.
The character 傉 is pronounced
nú wò.
He stationed Ruòliú (若留) in Jiāohé (澆河).
His cousin Tìyǐn (替引) was stationed in Lǐngnán (嶺南).
Lǐngnán (嶺南)
refers to the south of Hóngchí (洪池) Ridge.
His paternal cousin Tǔruòliú (吐若留) was stationed in Hàowěi (浩亹).
Both Hú (胡) and Xià (夏) talents
were assigned positions according to their abilities.
They occupied prominent positions within the government
and governed commanderies and counties externally,
each finding their appropriate role.
Wūgū (烏孤) said to his ministers:
"Lǒngyòu (隴右) and Héxī (河西)
were originally several commanderies.
During the Hàn (漢) Dynasty, Héxī (河西) had four commanderies: Wǔwēi (武威), Zhāngyè (張掖), Jiǔquán (酒泉), and Dūndhwáng (敦煌);
Lǒngyòu (隴右) had two commanderies: Lǒngxī (隴西) and Jīnchéng (金城).
They have since split into over ten states.
The Lǚ (呂), Qǐfú (乞伏), and Duàn (段) clans are the strongest.
Now, I wish to conquer them.
Which of the three should be targeted first?"
Yáng Tǒng (楊統) replied:
"The Qǐfú (乞伏) clan was originally one of our tribes,
and will eventually submit.
Both Qǐfú (乞伏) and Tùfā (禿髮) clans
are Xiānbēi (鮮卑).
They are incapable of causing trouble
and have even formed good relations with us;
attacking them would be unjust.
Lǚ Guāng (呂光) is old and senile,
and his heir is weak.
This refers to Guāng (光) making his son Shào (紹) his heir.
If Hàowěi (浩亹) and Liánchuān (廉川) continuously attack when they are unprepared,
they will surely be exhausted by the constant rushing to defend.
Within two years,
their soldiers will be weary and their people impoverished,
and then Gūzāng (姑臧) can be taken.
Gūzāng (姑臧)
was the capital of Lǚ Guāng (呂光).
Then, the two other enemies will submit without being attacked."
Wūgū (烏孤) said:
"Excellent!"
7. The second month.
On the day Dīnghài (丁亥) at the new moon,
the Wèi (魏) army greatly defeated over thirty Gāochē (高車) tribes,
capturing over seventy thousand people,
over three hundred thousand horses,
and over one million four hundred thousand cattle and sheep.
Wèi (衞) Prince Yí (儀), leading thirty thousand cavalry separately, crossed over a thousand lǐ of desert,
defeated seven of their tribes,
captured over twenty thousand people,
over fifty thousand horses,
and over twenty thousand cattle and sheep.
The Gāochē (高車) tribes were greatly shaken.
8. Lín Yì (林邑) King Fàn Dá (范達) seized Rìnán (日南) and Jiǔzhēn (九真),
and then raided Jiāozhǐ (交趾).
The Prefect Dù Yuàn (杜瑗) attacked and defeated them.
9. On the day Gēngxū,
Wèi (魏) General Zhēnglǔ (征虜) Yǔ Yuè (庾岳) defeated Zhāng Chāo (張超) at Bóhǎi (勃海)
and executed him.
Zhāng Chāo (張超) was based in Nánpí (南皮),
as mentioned in the previous volume, previous year.
10. Duàn Yè (段業) assumed the throne as King of Liáng (涼)
and changed the era name to Tiānxǐ (天璽);
this was the Northern Liáng (北涼).
The character 璽 is pronounced
sī shì.
Liáng Zhōngyōng (梁中庸) was made Assistant Minister of the Right.
11. Wèi (魏) ruler Guī (珪) held a great hunt south of Niúchuān (牛川),
using Gāochē (高車) people as beaters,
encompassing over seven hundred lǐ.
He then drove the wild animals
south to Píngchéng (平城),
and had the Gāochē (高車) build a deer park,
tens of lǐ wide.
The third month.
On the day Jǐwèi,
Guī (珪) returned to Píngchéng (平城).
On the day Jiǎzǐ,
Guī (珪) divided the thirty-six departments of the Secretariat and external offices,
establishing a total of three hundred sixty departments,
and appointed eight Dàfū (大夫) to oversee them.
The eight Dàfū (大夫)
should probably be
"eight Dàrén (大人)."
In the first year of Tiānxīng (天興) of Wèi (魏) King Guī (珪),
eight Dàrén (大人) were established in the Imperial City.
One person was placed in each of the four cardinal directions and four corners,
to correspond to the eight senior ministers,
and were called "eight states."
Each had subordinate officials,
with Regular Attendants and Scholars-in-Waiting directly serving on the left and right,
relaying royal commands.
This was similar to how the Minister of the Secretariat and Grand Guardian managed affairs.
Five Erudites of the Five Classics were appointed,

"According to the legal code,
if a gōng (公) or hóu (侯) commits a crime,
they may redeem themselves with gold and silk.
During the Warring States period,
Wèi Wénhóu's (魏文侯) teacher Lǐ Kuī (李悝) compiled and organized the laws of various states,
writing the Fǎjīng (法經).
He believed that in the governance of a king,
nothing was more urgent than bandits and thieves.
Bandits and thieves required investigation and capture,
hence he wrote the two chapters Wǎng (網) and Bǔ (捕).
For light cunning, scaling walls, gambling, borrowing, dishonesty, extravagance, and exceeding regulations,
he created a chapter on miscellaneous laws.
He also detailed the additions and subtractions to these laws.
Thus, the six chapters he wrote
all concerned the classification of crimes.
Hàn (漢) Xiāo Hé (蕭何) supplemented the Xing (興), Kòu (廏), and Hù (戶) chapters of the law,
making a total of nine chapters.
Wèi (魏) Chén Qún (陳㣥) and others adopted the Hàn (漢) laws,
creating eighteen new chapters of law.
The collection of criminal precedents was named Xíngmíng (刑名),
placed at the beginning of the legal code.
The Dàolǜ (盜律) [Law on Theft] contained provisions for robbery, extortion, and human trafficking;
the Kē (科) [Ordinances] contained provisions for holding hostages;
these were not matters of theft.
They were separated into the Jiélüè Lǜ (劫略律) [Law on Robbery and Plunder].
The Zéilǜ (賊律) [Law on Brigandage] contained provisions for deception, fraud, crossing borders, and counterfeiting edicts;
the Qiúlǜ (囚律) [Law on Prisoners] contained provisions for fraud, life and death;
the Lìng Bǐng (令丙) [Edict C] contained provisions for fraudulently excusing oneself;
as these matters were numerous and varied,
they were divided into the Zhàlǜ (詐律) [Law on Fraud].
The Zéilǜ (賊律) contained provisions for cutting down trees,
killing or injuring people and livestock, and various instances of lost seals;
the Jīnbù Lǜ (金布律) [Law on Gold and Silk] contained provisions for damaging or losing government property;
these were divided into the Huǐwáng Lǜ (毀亡律) [Law on Destruction and Loss].
The Qiúlǜ (囚律) contained provisions for accusation and investigation, and transmission and review;
the Yìlǜ (⿸广既律) [Law on Post Stations] contained provisions for reporting rebellion and receiving arrests;
the Kē (科) contained provisions for petitioning and appealing;
these were divided into the Gàohé Lǜ (告劾律) [Law on Accusation and Impeachment].
The Qiúlǜ (囚律) contained laws on detaining prisoners, conducting trials, and adjudicating cases;
the Xīnglǜ (興律) [Law on Levies] contained matters of appealing cases to higher courts;
the Kē (科) contained provisions for examining cases and reporting verdicts;
these should be separated into a distinct chapter
and divided into the Xìxùn Duànwù Lǜ (繫訊斷獄律) [Law on Detention, Interrogation, and Adjudication].
The Dàolǜ (盜律) contained provisions for receiving bribes by supervisors and receiving money by perverting the law;
the Zálǜ (雜律) [Miscellaneous Laws] contained provisions for borrowing and dishonesty;
the Lìng Yǐ (令乙) [Edict B] contained provisions for scolding people who accept money;
the Kē (科) contained provisions for envoys verifying bribes;
as these matters were similar,
they were divided into the Qǐngqiú Lǜ (請賕律) [Law on Soliciting and Receiving Bribes].
The Dàolǜ (盜律) contained provisions for insult and strong robbery;
the Xīnglǜ (興律) contained provisions for requisitioning and conscripting corvée labor;
the Jùlǜ (具律) [Law on Instruments] contained provisions for selling;
the Kē (科) contained provisions for construction and repair work;
these were divided into the Xīngdàn Lǜ (興⿰⺘亶律) [Law on Levies and Construction].
The Xīnglǜ (興律) contained provisions for failing corvée and delays;
the Zéilǜ (賊律) contained provisions for failing to prepare stores;
the Yìlǜ (⿸广既律) contained provisions for failing military supplies and levies, and the old statutes contained provisions for not carefully observing the law and not complying with edicts;
these were implemented by the Hàn (漢) dynasty
and are no longer suitable as law.
They were separately established as the Liúlǜ (留律) [Law on Delays].
During the Qín (秦) era, there were Yìzhì (⿸广既置) [post stations], Chéngzhuàn (乘傳) [relaying carriages], Fùchē (副車) [extra carriages], and Shíchú (食廚) [food kitchens].
The Later Hàn (漢) only established Jìzhì (騎置) [mounted post stations],
without carriages and horses,
yet the law still retained these provisions,
which were therefore nominal provisions.
Thus, the Yìlǜ (⿸广既律) was abolished,
and its useful parts were combined with the Kē (科) to form the Yóuyì Lìng (郵驛令) [Ordinance on Post and Courier Stations].

The Gàohé Lǜ (告劾律) contained provisions for reporting unusual matters, and the Lìng (令) [Ordinance] contained provisions for reporting urgent and startling matters, along with the Xīnglǜ (興律) provisions on beacon fires and the Kē Lìng (科令) [Ordinances and Edicts],
which were made into the Jīngshì Lǜ (驚事律) [Law on Alarming Matters].
The Dàolǜ (盜律) contained provisions for returning stolen goods to the owner;
the Jīnbù Lǜ (金布律) contained provisions for fines and redemptions to be applied to debts, and for using gold as a price;
the Kē (科) contained provisions for common people involved in stolen goods;
these were made into the Chángzāng Lǜ (償贓律) [Law on Compensation for Stolen Goods].
When the laws were first enacted,
there was no provision for exemption from punishment.
Zhāng Tāng (張湯) and Zhào Yǔ (趙禹) first created the precedent for supervisors and principal officers who knowingly condoned crimes;
those who knew but intentionally did not report or impeach
were punished with redemption;
those who did not see or know were not punished.
The provisions for exemption from punishment were numerous and complex,
and should be summarized into a general rule for exemption
to simplify the ordinances.
Thus, they were revised and made into the Miǎnzùo Lǜ (免坐律) [Law on Exemption from Punishment].
In the early Jìn (晉) dynasty, Jiǎ Chōng (賈充) codified the laws,
adding eleven chapters to the original nine chapters of Hàn (漢).
The old laws were revised into Xíngmíng Fǎlì (刑名法例) [Names of Punishments and Legal Precedents].
The Qiúlǜ (囚律) was divided into Gàohé (告劾), Xìxùn (繫訊), and Duànwù (斷獄).
The Dàolǜ (盜律) was divided into Qǐngqiú (請賕), Zhàwěi (詐偽), Shuǐhuǒ (水火), and Huǐwáng (毀亡).
According to the nature of the matters, Wèijìn (衞禁) [Guarding Prohibitions] and Wéizhì (違制) [Violating Regulations] were created.
The Zhōu Guān (周官) [Rites of Zhou] was compiled into the Zhūhóu Lǜ (諸侯律) [Law on Feudal Lords],
making a total of twenty chapters.
Kǒng Yǐngdá (孔穎達) said: In ancient times, redemption for crimes was all by copper.

but reduced its weight
to be equivalent to gold.
Hàn (漢) and later Wèi (魏) all used gold for redemption.
Later Wèi (魏), finding gold difficult to obtain,
made one liǎng (兩) of gold
equivalent to ten bolts of silk.
Now the law again reverts to ancient copper for redemption.
This is utterly meaningless.
From now on, all shall be permitted to redeem themselves by performing meritorious service,
and no longer be required to pay gold and silk."
