When the Qín people invaded Xiāngyáng,
Xī Huī, the Cìshǐ of Yōngzhōu, wrote a letter to Wèi Chángshān Wáng Zūn seeking aid, saying:
"My worthy elder brother strides like a tiger through the Central Plains."
Guī, finding Huī disrespectful of the lord-vassal relationship,
ordered Gǔn and Chěng to write a reply,
instructing them to surely belittle Huī's lord.
Gǔn and Chěng referred to the emperor as "Guìzhǔ."
Guī angrily said:
"I commanded you to belittle him, yet you call him 'Guìzhǔ,'
how is that different from 'worthy elder brother'?"
When Chěng surrendered to Wèi,
(See Juan 109, Lóng'ān Yuánnián),
he feared that no descendants would remain,
so he left his wife, Zhāng Shì, and four sons in Jìzhōu,
and Chěng alone, with his youngest son Zé,
went
to Píngchéng.
His left-behind wife and sons subsequently fled to Nányàn.
Guī held Chěng accountable for this as well
and bestowed death upon Chěng.
Lú Pǔ accepted titles and appointments from Yàn,
plundered Wèi commanderies and counties,
and killed Fēng Tàgān, the Cìshǐ of Wèi Yōuzhōu.
Guī believed that all those recommended by Gǔn were unsuitable
and demoted Gǔn to Shàngshū Lìshǐ.
Gǔn then shut his gate and ceased all social interaction,
dedicating himself solely to hand-editing classics and books.
He died after more than a year.
After Yàn Zhǔ Bǎo's defeat,
Fēng Yì, Zhōngshū Lìng and Mínbù Shàngshū, surrendered to Wèi.
Guī appointed Yì as Gěishì Huángmén Shìláng and Dūzuò Dàguān.
There were three Dàguān positions in Wèi: Dūzuò Dàguān, Wàidū Dàguān, and Nèidū Dàguān.
"Zuò"
is pronounced as "cuó wò fān".
Yì's responses were careless and slow,
and he was also dismissed to his home.
Guī likely felt suspicious,
believing that the literati disdained him.
Wǔwēi Wáng Tūfà Wūgū, while drunk,
was injured in the ribs by a running horse and died.
He left a dying instruction to enthrone the eldest son.
The people of the state instead enthroned his younger brother, Lìlùgū,
posthumously naming Wūgū "Wǔ Wáng" and
giving him the temple name "Lièzǔ."
Lìlùgū declared a great amnesty
and moved the capital to Xīpíng.
Nányàn Wáng Dé sent an envoy to persuade Pìlǘ Hún, the Cìshǐ of Yōuzhōu,
intending to take him.
(When the Jìn clan moved south,
they provisionally established the four zhōu of Yōu, Jì, Qīng, and Bīng north of the Jiāng;
Qín besieging Tián Luò, the Cìshǐ of Yōuzhōu, at Sān'ā
is evidence of this.
In the late Tài Yuán era of Xiàowǔ,
they recaptured the Qí region
and moved the two zhōu of Yōu and Jì to Qí.
Those who later guarded Qí
usually led the Cìshǐ of Qīng and Jì zhōu.
Hún, leading Yōuzhōu Cìshǐ,
was probably from the north moving south,
not yet purely a Jìn subject,
sent to lead Yōuzhōu and guard Guǎnggù.)
"Shuì"
is pronounced as "shū ruì fān".
Dé dispatched Běidì Wáng Zhōng, leading twenty thousand infantry and cavalry, to attack him.
Dé advanced to occupy Lángyá,
and over a hundred thousand people from Xú and Yǎn zhōu submitted to him.
Dé led his troops north from Lángyá,
appointing Nánhǎi Wáng Fǎ as Cìshǐ of Yǎnzhōu,
to guard Liángfù.
He then attacked Jǔchéng;
the defending commander Rèn Ān abandoned the city and fled.
Dé appointed Pān Cōng as Cìshǐ of Xúzhōu,
to guard Jǔchéng.
(Jǔ Xiàn
belonged to Chéngyáng Guó in the Former Hàn,
to Lángyá in the Later Hàn,
and was divided to Dōngguǎn Jùn in Jìn.)
"Jiāng"
is pronounced as "jí liàng fān".
"Rèn"
has the sound of "rén".
Fēng Fú, Yàn Lìbù Shàngshū, fled south to Pìlǘ Hún.
Hún memorialized to appoint him as Bóhǎi Tàishǒu.
When Dé arrived,
Fú surrendered.
Dé was greatly pleased and said:
"My gaining Qīngzhōu does not make me happy;
I am happy to have gained you!"
He then entrusted him with confidential matters.
Běidì Wáng Zhōng sent circulars to all commanderies in Qīngzhōu,
explaining the consequences of submission or resistance.
Pìlǘ Hún moved over eight thousand households to defend Guǎnggù,
and sent Sīmǎ Cuī Dàn to garrison Bóxún
Gù,
and Píngyuán Tàishǒu Zhāng Huò to garrison Liǔquán.
(Bóxún
was likely a person's name.
In times of chaos, he gathered people to defend this place,
which then became its name.
The people of Qí generally referred to a defended settlement as Gù.)
(Hànshū Dìlǐ Zhì: Běihǎi Jùn had Liǔquán Hóuguó,
which was abolished in the Later Hàn and Jìn.)
Hún, in fear,
took his wife and children and fled to Wèi.
Dé sent Shèshēng Xiàowèi Liú Gāng to pursue him.
He caught up with him at Jǔchéng
and killed him.
Hún's son, Dàoxiù, went to Dé himself,
requesting to die together with his father.
Dé said:
"Although your father was disloyal,"
(referring to Pìlǘ Hún's betrayal of Yàn as disloyalty)
"I will pardon you especially."
Hún's Cānjūn, Zhāng Yīng, had written the circular for Hún,
which contained many insolent phrases.
Dé seized him and reproached him.
Yīng remained composed,
and slowly said:
"Hún having me
is like Hán Xìn having Kuǎi Tōng.
Tōng met Hàn Zǔ and survived."
(The story is found in Juan 12, Gāozǔ Shíyīnián.)
"Compared to ancient people,
I am only unfortunate!"
Dé killed him.
He then established his capital at Guǎnggù.
Yàn Lǐ Hán traveled to Jiàn'ān,
and Yàn Zhǔ Shèng urgently recalled him.
The courtiers could not fathom the reason.
In the ninth month,
on the day Xīnwèi,
he was dispatched again.
Lǐ Lǎng, hearing that his family had been executed,
gathered over two thousand households to secure himself.
Upon hearing that Hán had returned,
he thought there was an internal change
and no longer maintained defenses.
He left his son Yǎng to guard Lìzhī
and went himself to welcome the Wèi army at Běipíng.
(In the Former Hàn, Běipíng Jùn was governed from Pínggāng;
in the Later Hàn, from Tǔyín;
in Jìn, from Xúwú;
in Later Wèi, from Lúlóng.)
On Rénzǐ,
Hán attacked Lìzhī,
conquered it,
and sent Guǎngwēi Jiāngjūn Mèng Guǎngpíng to pursue Lǎng to Wúzhōng
and killed him.
(Wúzhōng
was the state of Wúzhōngzǐ in the Spring and Autumn period.
Since the Hàn dynasty,
it has been a county, belonging to Yòuběipíng.)
(Liú Xù said: Táng Jìzhōu Yùtián Xiàn
was the land of Hàn Wúzhōng Xiàn.)
Qín Zhǔ Xīng,
seeing frequent appearances of disasters and anomalies,
lowered his title to "Wáng,"
and issued an edict ordering all gōng, qīng, shì, jiàng, mù, shǒu, and zǎi to each lower their rank by one grade.
He declared a general amnesty
and changed the era name to Hóngshǐ.
He inquired about and provided for the orphaned and poor,
promoted and selected the virtuous and talented,
simplified laws and regulations,
clearly investigated lawsuits,
rewarded those governors and magistrates who had political achievements,
and executed those who were greedy and cruel.
Far and near, there was solemn respect.
In the winter of the 31st year [of the reign period],
in the tenth month,
on the jiǎwǔ day,
Wèi Shuāng (衛雙), the Zhongwèi General (中衞將軍) of Yān (燕), committed a crime,
and was granted death.
Lǐ Hàn (李旱) returned,
and upon hearing of Wèi Shuāng's death,
he became afraid,
abandoned his army, and fled.
When he reached Bǎnxíng (板陘),
he returned to confess his crime.
Yān Zhǔ (燕主) Shèng (盛) restored his noble rank,
and said to Shìzhōng (侍中) Sūn Qíng (孫勍):
"Hàn (旱) abandoned his army as a general,
a crime for which there is no pardon.
However, when the late emperor suffered hardship,
and his family was estranged,
and the dukes and ministers lost their integrity,
only Hàn (旱), as a eunuch, was loyal and diligent without slackening,
consistent from beginning to end.
This event is recorded in the second year of the previous volume."
Xīn Gōngjìng (辛恭靖) held fast for over a hundred days,
but the Wèi (魏) relief force had not arrived.
The Qín (秦) army captured Luòyáng (洛陽),
and took Gōngjìng (恭靖) prisoner.
When Gōngjìng (恭靖) saw Qín Wáng Xìng (秦王興),
he did not bow,
saying:
"I will not serve a Qiāng (羌) bandit as a minister!"
Xìng (興) imprisoned him,
but Gōngjìng (恭靖) escaped and returned.
North of the Huái (淮) and Hàn (漢) rivers,
many cities requested to surrender,
and sent hostages to Qín (秦).
Wèi Zhǔ Guī (魏主珪) appointed Mù Chóng (穆崇) as Yùzhōu Cìshǐ (豫州刺史),
garrisoning Yěwáng (野王).
After Qín (秦) had conquered Luòyáng (洛陽),
Wèi (魏) established a garrison at Yěwáng (野王)
to guard against their crossing the river to invade.
Huìjī Shìzǐ (會稽世子) Yuánxiǎn (元顯)
was harsh and severe by nature,
exercising power over life and death arbitrarily.
He summoned those in the eastern territories, from various commanderies, who were "freed slaves acting as retainers" (免奴為客),
and those who were "slave households" (奴戶者),
and if they committed a crime, they were confiscated to become official slaves.

From dukes and ministers down to ninth-rank officials, as well as imperial relatives, state guests, descendants of former sages, and sons and grandsons of scholars, who occupied land and were protected (占蔭) as tenant households (客戶),
this was called "freed slaves acting as retainers" (免奴為客).
They were relocated to the capital
to fill military service,
causing widespread suffering in the eastern territories.
Sūn Ēn (孫恩), taking advantage of the people's unrest,
led his followers from the sea island and killed the magistrate of Shàngyú (上虞).
Shàngyú County (上虞縣),
since the Hàn (漢) dynasty, belonged to Huìjī Prefecture (會稽郡),
and was over a hundred lǐ northwest of the prefectural city.
帥 (shuài)
is read as 率 (shuài).
Huìjī Nèishǐ (會稽內史) Wáng Níngzhī (王凝之),
son of Xīzhī (羲之),
had for generations practiced the Tiānshīdào (天師道).
Tiānshīdào (天師道)
is what Zhāng Dàolíng (張道陵) transmitted.
會 (kuài)
is pronounced like 工外 (gōng wài).
He also made no preparations,
but daily kowtowed and chanted spells in his Daoist chamber.
A Daoist chamber (道室)
is a room dedicated to practicing Daoism.
稽 (qǐ)
is pronounced qǐ.
Níngzhī (凝之) said:
"I have already invited the Great Dao
to borrow ghost soldiers to guard the crucial crossings,
each several tens of thousands strong.
There is no need to worry about the bandits."
When Ēn (恩) gradually approached,
he then allowed troops to be dispatched,
but Ēn (恩) had already reached below the prefecture.
On the jiǎyín day,
Ēn (恩) captured Huìjī (會稽),
Níngzhī (凝之) fled,
Ēn (恩) seized and killed him,
along with all his sons.
Níngzhī's (凝之) wife, Xiè Dàoyùn (謝道蘊),
daughter of Yì (奕),
heard that the rebels were coming,
but remained composed.
She ordered a maid to carry a litter,
drew a sword, and went out the gate,
personally killing several people,
before she was captured.
Wúguó Nèishǐ (吳國內史) Huán Qiān (桓謙), Línhǎi Tàishǒu (臨海太守) Xīnqín Wáng Chóng (新秦王崇),
the Book of Jìn (晉書) writes
"Xīncài Wáng Chóng" (新蔡王崇).
Chóng (崇) was the great-grandson of Rǔnán Wáng Yòu (汝南王祐).
Since his grandfather,
he had inherited the enfeoffment of the state of Xīncài (新蔡).
"Qín" (秦)
should be
"Cài" (蔡).
Thereupon, Xiè Zhēn (謝鍼) of Huìjī (會稽), Lù Huái (陸⿰王褱) of Wújùn (吳郡), Qiū Wāng (丘尩) of Wúxīng (吳興),
Xǔ Yǔnzhī (許允之) of Yìxīng (義興), Zhōu Zhòu (周冑) of Línhǎi (臨海), Zhāng Yǒng (張永) of Yǒngjiā (永嘉), and others, as well as people from Dōngyáng (東陽) and Xīn'ān (新安), a total of eight commanderies,
all simultaneously rose in rebellion,
killing their chief officials to respond to Ēn (恩).
Within ten days,
their multitude numbered several hundred thousand.

Xiè Miǎo (謝邈), the governor of Wúxīng (吳興), Sīmǎ Yì (司馬逸), the governor of Yǒngjiā (永嘉), Gù Yìn (顧胤), Duke of Jiāxīng (嘉興), Xiè Mínghuì (謝明慧), Duke of Nánkāng (南康), Huángménláng (黃門郎) Xiè Chōng (謝沖), Zhāng Kūn (張琨), Zhōngshūláng (中書郎) Kǒng Dào (孔道), and others were all killed by Ēn's (恩) faction.
Miǎo (邈) and Chōng (沖)
were both nephews of Ānzhī (安之).
At that time, the three Wú (吳) areas had enjoyed peace for a long time,
and the people were unaccustomed to warfare.
Thus, the prefectural and county troops all collapsed at the mere sight of the enemy.
Ēn (恩) occupied Huìjī (會稽),
proclaimed himself Zhēngdōng Jiāngjūn (征東將軍),
forced scholars to become his officials,
and called his followers
"Changshēng Rén" (長生人, People of Eternal Life).
If any commoner did not join them,
they were executed down to infants,
with seven or eight out of ten dying.
He minced the magistrates of various counties
to feed to their wives and children.
Those who refused to eat
were immediately dismembered.
Dismemberment (支解)
means to cut and peel apart according to the limbs and joints,
like dismembering an ox.
They burned towns and houses,
incinerated granaries,
cut down trees,
and filled in wells.
Kǒng Ānguó (孔安國) said: Kān (刊)
means to chop down trees;
yīn (堙)
means to block up.
Women with infants who could not flee
were thrown into the water,
with the words:
"I congratulate you on being the first to ascend to the immortal hall;
I will follow you soon."
Ēn (恩) impeached Huìjī Wáng Dàozǐ (會稽王道子) and Shìzǐ Yuánxiǎn (世子元顯) for their crimes,
and requested their execution.
Since the emperor's enthronement,
there had been internal and external discord.
Everything south of Shítou (石頭) was occupied by Jīng (荊) and Jiāng (江) provinces.
Everything to the west was exclusively held by Yùzhōu (豫州).
The Jiāng (江) river, from the border of Jīng (荊) and Jiāng (江) provinces, enters the border of Yángzhōu (揚州),
all flowing northeast.
Lìyáng (歷陽) is west of the river,
Jiànkāng (建康) is east of the river.
Sūn Quán (孫權) built Shítóu City (石頭城),
which was to control the strategic crossing of the Jiāng (江).
The imperial government's authority
was exercised only over the three Wú (吳) areas.
When Sūn Ēn (孫恩) rebelled,
all eight commanderies came under Ēn's (恩) control.
The eight commanderies were Huìjī (會稽), Línhǎi (臨海), Yǒngjiā (永嘉), Dōngyáng (東陽), Xīn'ān (新安), Wú (吳), Wúxīng (吳興), and Yìxīng (義興).
Bandits rose everywhere,
and some of Ēn's (恩) followers were secretly lurking in Jiànkāng (建康).
People were fearful and apprehensive,
always worried about a sudden uprising.
Thus, a state of emergency was declared internally and externally.
Dàozǐ (道子) was granted the yellow axe (黃鉞),
Yuánxiǎn (元顯) was appointed Zhōngjūn Jiāngjūn (中軍將軍).
Xúzhōu Cìshǐ (徐州刺史) Xiè Yǎn (謝琰) was ordered to concurrently oversee military affairs in Wúxīng (吳興) and Yìxīng (義興) to suppress Ēn (恩).
Liú Láozhī (劉牢之) also dispatched troops to suppress Ēn (恩),
and immediately set out upon presenting his memorial.
Láozhī (牢之) was garrisoned at Jīngkǒu (京口).
Xī Qín (西秦) appointed Jīnchéng Tàishǒu (金城太守) Xīn Jìng (辛靜) as Yòuchéngxiàng (右丞相).
In the twelfth month,
on the jiǎwǔ day,
Gāo Hú (高湖), Yān Jùn Tàishǒu (燕郡太守) of Yān (燕), led three thousand households to surrender to Wèi (魏).
Hú (湖) was the son of Tài (泰).
This laid the groundwork for Gāo Huán's (高歡) usurpation of Wèi (魏) later.
降 (jiàng)
is pronounced like 戶江 (hù jiāng).
On the bǐngwǔ day,
Yān Zhǔ Shèng (燕主盛) enfeoffed his brother Yuān (淵) as Zhāngwǔ Gōng (章武公),
Qián (虔) as Bólíng Gōng (博陵公),
and his son Dìng (定) as Liáoxī Gōng (遼西公).
On the dīngwèi day,
Yān Tàihòu (燕太后) Duàn (段) passed away.
She was posthumously honored as Huìdé Huánghòu (惠德皇后).
Xiè Yǎn (謝琰) attacked and beheaded Xǔ Yǔnzhī (許允之),
welcomed Wèi Yǐn (魏隱) back to his prefecture,
then attacked Qiū Wāng (丘尩),
defeating him.
Together with Liú Láozhī (劉牢之), he fought his way forward,
conquering every place they went.
Yǎn (琰) remained garrisoned at Wūchéng (烏程).
Wūchéng County (烏程縣),
in the Former Hàn (前漢) dynasty, belonged to Huìjī Prefecture (會稽郡);
in the Later Hàn (後漢) dynasty, it belonged to Wújùn (吳郡);
since the Wèi (魏) and Jìn (晉) dynasties, it belonged to Wúxīng Prefecture (吳興郡).
He advanced to the Zhejiang (浙江) River.
An imperial edict appointed Láozhī (牢之) as Dūdū Wújùn Zhūjūnshì (都督吳郡諸軍事, Commander of all military affairs in Wújùn).
In the beginning,
Liú Yù of Péngchéng,
was born and his mother died.
His father, Liú Qiáo, lived in Jīngkǒu as a sojourner.
The family was poor,
and they were about to abandon him.
The mother of Liú Huáijìng from the same commandery,
who was Yù’s maternal aunt,
had given birth to Huáijìng less than a year prior.
She rushed to save him,
cutting off Huáijìng's milk and nursing Yù instead.
When he grew up,
he was brave, strong, and had great ambitions.
He barely recognized characters,
earned a living by selling shoes,
and enjoyed gambling with *chūpú*,
which made him despised by the local community.
When Liú Láozhī attacked Sūn Ēn,
he brought Yù in as a staff officer (*cānjūnshì*).
According to the system of the Jìn and Sòng dynasties,
staff officers who were not assigned to a specific department had no fixed number.
He encountered several thousand bandits,
and immediately engaged them.
All his followers died,
and Yù fell down an embankment.
The bandits approached the bank, intending to descend.
Yù bravely wielded his long saber, striking upwards and killing several people,
thus managing to climb back onto the bank.
He then let out a great shout and pursued them,
causing all the bandits to flee.
The number of bandits Yù killed and wounded was very large.
Liú Jìngxuān was surprised that Yù had not returned for a long time,
and led his troops to search for him.
He saw Yù single-handedly driving away several thousand men,
and everyone sighed in admiration.
They then advanced to attack the bandits,
thoroughly defeating them,
and capturing over a thousand heads.
Liú Yù's career began here.
At first,
Ēn heard that eight commanderies had responded,
and said to his subordinates,
"There is nothing left to do in the world.
We should all go to Jiànkāng in court robes."
He meant that he wanted to assume the throne.
Cháo
is pronounced Zhíyáo.
He said,
"Even if I only occupy the area east of the Zhèjiāng River,
I won't fail to be a Gōujiàn!"
He wanted to be like King Gōujiàn of Yuè, holding Kuàijī.
Jù
is pronounced Gōu.
On the day of Wùshēn,
Láozhī led his troops across the Jiāng River.
Ēn heard of it and said,
"I am not ashamed to flee."
The *Jiāngbiǎo Zhuàn* says: When Zhōu Yú defeated Wèi's army,
Cáo Gōng said,
"I am not ashamed to flee."
Therefore, Ēn cited this as his remark.
He abandoned many treasures and his children on the road.
The government troops eagerly scrambled to take them,
and Ēn thus managed to escape,
fleeing back into the sea islands.
Gāo Sù defeated Ēn's faction in Shānyīn.
Shānyīn County belonged to Kuàijī Commandery,
and the county's boundaries extended north of the commandery city.
Wáng Huái
was the Administrator of Wúxīng, Qiū Wǎng, and the Magistrate of Yúyáo, Shěn Mùfū of Wúxīng.
Yúyáo County belonged to Kuàijī Commandery,
and was over 200 *lǐ* east of the commandery city.
The eastern region, having suffered chaos,
eagerly awaited the arrival of the government troops.
However, Láozhī and others allowed their soldiers to loot and plunder,
disappointing the gentry and common people.
There were no longer any traces of people in the commandery and county cities.
After more than a month, some people gradually began to return.
The court worried that Ēn would return,
and appointed Xiè Yǎn as Administrator of Kuàijī and Area Commander of the five commanderies' military affairs,
to lead the civil and military officials of Xúzhōu to guard the sea coasts.
The five commanderies were
Kuàijī, Línhǎi, Dōngyáng, Yǒngjiā, and Xīn'ān.
Today, from Kānshān eastward to Lánfēng, Shíyàn, Mínghè, Sōngpú, Xièpú, and Dìnghǎi,
all are sea coasts.
Shuài
is read as Shuài.
He appointed Yuánxiǎn as Director of the Department of State Affairs (*lù shàngshūshì*).
At the time, people called Dàozǐ the "Eastern Director" (*dōnglù*),
and Yuánxiǎn the "Western Director" (*xīlù*).
The carriages at the Western Residence were numerous and crowded,
while at the Eastern Residence, one could cast a net at the gate (meaning it was deserted).
Yuánxiǎn had no good teachers or friends.
Those he trusted and relied on were mostly flattering and sycophantic people.
Some considered them temporary heroes,
others considered them refined scholars.
Due to this, Yuánxiǎn grew increasingly arrogant and extravagant.
He subtly instructed the officials of rites to propose a discussion,
arguing that because of his profound virtue and prominent reputation,
and since he was overseeing the myriad affairs of state (*lù bǎikuí*),
all officials should show him full respect.
Shùn appointed the *bǎikuí*.
Yǔ resided over the *bǎikuí*.
The *Zhōu Guān* says: Táng and Yú studied antiquity,
establishing one hundred officials.
Internally there were the *bǎikuí* and Four Peaks,
externally there were the provincial governors and feudal lords.
All referred to *bǎikuí* as an official title.
Kǒng Ānguó said: Kuí
means 'to measure' or 'to assess';
Shùn appointed the Eight Worthies,
making them measure and assess all affairs.
This explains the meaning of naming the office *bǎikuí*.
Jìn people often used *bǎikuí* to refer to 'all officials'.
Everyone who saw Yuánxiǎn bowed.
At that time, military campaigns frequently arose,
and the national treasury was depleted.
From the Minister of Works (*sītú*) downwards,
their daily ration was seven *shēng*,
yet Yuánxiǎn's accumulation of wealth never ceased,
exceeding that of the imperial household.
This laid the groundwork for Yuánxiǎn's downfall and the ruin of his family.
Shù
is pronounced Suǒjiǎo.
Liǎn
is pronounced Lìshàn.
40 Yīn Zhòngkān, fearing Huán Xuán's arrogance,
therefore allied with Yáng Quánqí through marriage for support.
Quánqí repeatedly wanted to attack Xuán,
but Zhòngkān always restrained him.
Xuán feared that he would eventually be annihilated by Yīn and Yáng.
He then reported to the regent,
requesting to expand the area under his jurisdiction.
The regent also wanted to sow discord
and cause them to split apart.
So he added Xuán as Area Commander of the four commanderies of Jīngzhōu.
The regent
refers to Yuánxiǎn.
The four commanderies of Jīngzhōu
refer to Chángshā, Héngyáng, Xiāngdōng, and Línglíng.
Quánqí was indignant and fearful.
Yáng Guǎng wanted to resist Huán Wěi,
but Zhòngkān did not allow it,
sending Guǎng out as Administrator of the two commanderies of Yídū and Jiànpíng.
Yáng Zījìng had previously been Chancellor of Jiāngxià.
Xuán attacked him with troops and kidnapped him,
making him a Consultant and Staff Officer (*zīyì cānjūn*).
Quánqí assembled his troops and established his standard,
proclaiming that he was coming to support Luòyáng,
wishing to attack Xuán together with Zhòngkān.
Although Zhòngkān outwardly allied with Quánqí, he inwardly doubted his intentions,
and sternly forbade him.
Still fearing he could not restrain him,
he sent his cousin Yù to garrison the northern border,
to block Quánqí.
Since Quánqí could not act alone,
and did not understand Zhòngkān's true intentions,
he disbanded his troops.
Zhòngkān was full of doubts and lacked decisiveness.
The Consultant and Staff Officer, Luó Qǐshēng, said to his younger brother Zūnshēng,
"Lord Yīn is benevolent but indecisive,
and will surely meet with disaster.
I have received his recognition and trust,
and it is my duty not to leave.
I will surely die for him."
That year,
Jingzhōu suffered a great flood.
The water reached three *zhàng* on flat ground,
and Zhòngkān exhausted his granaries to relieve the starving populace.
Huán Xuán wished to take advantage of this vulnerability and attack him,
so he dispatched troops westward,
also announcing that he was going to rescue Luòyáng.
He wrote a letter to Zhòngkān, saying:
"Quánqī received the grace of the state but abandoned the imperial tombs.
We should both punish him for this.
Jìn has restored Luòyáng and assigned it to the administration of Yōngzhōu,
which is why Xuán blames Quánqī for abandoning the imperial tombs.
My troops have already halted at the mouth of the river.
If you show no duplicity towards me,
*yǔ*,
means 'to permit',
'to follow',
'to be a partisan of'.
To hold two positions in one's heart is *èr* (duplicity).
If not,
then I shall lead my troops into the river."
"Into the river"
means intending to attack Jiānglíng.
*Shuài*,
pronounced *shuài*;
the same below.
Xuán first sent troops to raid and capture it.
Guō Quán, the Inspector of Liángzhōu, was on his way to his post,
passing through Xiàkǒu.
Xuán falsely claimed that the imperial court had sent Quán to be his vanguard,
and then gave him the forces of Jiāngxià,
making him supervise the advance of all the armies.
He secretly informed his elder brother Wěi to act as an inside accomplice.
Wěi was flustered and did not know what to do.
*Huáng*,
means 'urgent'.
*Jù*,
also means 'urgent'.
Zhòngkān seized Wěi as a hostage,
and made him write a letter to Xuán,
the words of which were extremely bitter and sincere.
Xuán said:
"Zhòngkān is indecisive,
always calculating success or failure,
and worrying for his sons.
My brother surely has nothing to worry about!"
Zhòngkān dispatched Yīn Yù to lead seven thousand marines to Xījiāngkǒu.
*Shuǐjīng* (Commentary on the Classic of Waters): The Jiāng River flows east to the north of Xiàjùn County in Chángshā,
where the Xiāng River flows in from the south.
The Jiāng River then flows further east, encountering the two Xiàpǔ on the left.
The note says: Xiàpǔ,
is commonly called Xījiāngkǒu.
In the tenth year of Tàiyuán of Emperor Xiàowǔ,
Fú Hóng came to defect,
and was settled in Jiāngzhōu.
Xuán then made him a general.
Xuán halted at Bālíng,
and consumed its grain.
Zhòngkān sent Yáng Guǎng and his nephew Dàohù and others to resist him,
but they were all defeated by Xuán.
Jiānglíng was struck with terror.
There was a shortage of food in the city,
so sesame was given to the soldiers.
Sesame,
now called *zhīmá*,
has grains smaller than millet,
and is black,
from which oil can be made.
It is cooked and sun-dried nine times,
to make food,
which, when eaten,
prevents hunger.
"*Lǐn*"
should be
"*bǐng*",
meaning 'to supply'.
Língkǒu,
is the mouth where the Língxī stream enters the river.
Zhòngkān urgently summoned Yáng Quánqī to save himself.
Quánqī said:
"Jiānglíng has no food,
how can it await the enemy?
You should come and join me,
and together we will defend Xiāngyáng."
Zhòngkān's ambition was to preserve his army and protect his territory,
not wishing to abandon the province and flee.
So he deceived him, saying:
"Through recent collection,
we already have stores."
Quánqī believed him,
and led eight thousand cavalry and infantry,
their gleaming armor shining in the sun,
to Jiānglíng.
Zhòngkān only provided rice to his army.
Quánqī was greatly enraged and said:
"This time we are defeated!"
He did not meet Zhòngkān,
but together with his elder brother Guǎng, attacked Xuán.
Xuán feared their ferocity
and retreated his army to Mǎtóu.
South of Jiānglíng County, there is the Jiāngjīnsù fort,
and south of the fort facing it is Mǎtóu bank.
Quánqī led his troops to fiercely attack Guō Quán,
almost capturing him.
At that moment, Xuán's troops arrived,
and Quánqī was utterly defeated,
fleeing alone on horseback to Xiāngyáng.
Zhòngkān fled to Cuózichéng.
Cuó County
is the very town enfeoffed to Xiāo Hé;
under Hàn, it belonged to Nányáng Commandery,
and Jìn divided it to belong to Shùnyáng Commandery.
*Cuó*,
pronunciation *zàn*.
Both were captured and killed,
their heads sent to Jiànkāng.
Quánqī's younger brother Sīpíng,
and his cousins Shàng Bǎo and Zījìng, fled into the barbarian territories.
When Zhòngkān heard of Quánqī's death,
he led several hundred men, intending to flee to Cháng'ān.
Upon reaching Guànjūnchéng,
Guànjūn County
is the very town enfeoffed to Huò Qùbìng;
it belonged to Nányáng Commandery,
its territory being in the southern border of Líntuān County of Táng Dèngzhōu.
*Guàn*,
pronounced *gǔwán*.
He returned to Zuòxī.
*Shuǐjīngzhù*: The Zuòxī stream originates north of Jiānglíng County,
probably from various scattered ponds,
all converging,
accumulating to form a river.
It flows east past Yìlùshuǐ,
where there is a large bridge,
the place where Zhòngkān hanged himself.
It then flows east into Chuánguānhú.
*Zuò*,
pronounced *zǐgè*,
and also *zàigè*.
Yīn Dàohù was also killed.
Zhòngkān followed the Way of the Celestial Masters,
praying to ghosts and spirits,
not sparing wealth and bribes,
but was stingy in helping those in urgent need.
He liked to do small favors to please people;
for the sick, he would personally diagnose their pulse and dispense medicine.
He used convoluted and intricate schemes,
but was short on discernment and strategy,
thus leading to his defeat.
When Zhōngkān fled,
none of his civil or military officials escorted him;
only Luó Qǐshēng followed him.
As they passed by his house,
his younger brother Zūnshēng said:
“Since we are parting like this,
how can we not clasp hands one last time!”
Qǐshēng turned his horse around and offered his hand.
Zūnshēng was strong,
and thus pulled him down,
saying:
“We have an old mother at home;
where are you going to go?”
Qǐshēng wiped away tears and said:
“Today’s events
mean I am bound to die.
If you all continue to care for [our mother],
you will not fail in your duty as sons.
Among one family,
having both loyalty and filial piety,
what more could one regret!”
Zūnshēng embraced him even more tightly.
Zhōngkān waited for him on the road,
and seeing that Qǐshēng could not get away,
he spurred his horse and left.
When Huán Xuán arrived,
there was no one from Jīngzhōu who did not go to see Xuán,
but Qǐshēng alone did not go,
instead managing Zhōngkān’s household affairs.
Someone said:
“If you do this,
disaster is sure to come!”
Qǐshēng said:
“Lord Yīn treated me as a statesman of the realm.
I was prevented by my younger brother,
unable to follow him and eliminate the wicked rebels together.
What face do I have to seek life from Huán anymore!”
Xuán heard this and was enraged,
but he had always treated Qǐshēng generously,
so he first sent someone to say:
“If you apologize to me,
I will release you.”
Qǐshēng said:
“I was an official for Yīn, the Governor of Jīngzhōu.
Jīngzhōu has fallen;
I could not save it.
What is there to apologize for now!”
Xuán then arrested him
and again sent someone to ask Qǐshēng what he wanted to say.
Qǐshēng said:
“Emperor Wén killed Jī Kāng,
but Jī Shào became a loyal official of Jìn.
[The account of] Jī Kāng’s killing can be found in Volume 78, under Jingyuán 3rd year of Emperor Yuán of Wèi.
Jī Shào’s death can be found in Volume 85, under Yǒngxīng 1st year of Emperor Huì.
Xuán then killed Qǐshēng but pardoned his younger brother.
Liáng Wáng Guāng was gravely ill,
and established Crown Prince Shào as the Heavenly King,
styling himself Grand Emperor;
he appointed the Duke of Tàiyuán, Zuǎn, as Grand Commandant,
and the Duke of Chángshān, Hóng, as Minister of Works.
He said to Shào:
“Now the state faces many difficulties,
and three neighbors are watching for opportunities.
[The] three neighbors [are] Tūfà, Qǐfú, and Duàn Yè.
Nán [is pronounced] nài dàn fān.
Let Zuǎn command the six armies,
and Hóng manage court affairs.
You should be respectful and do nothing,
entrusting heavy responsibilities to your two elder brothers.
Perhaps then we can succeed.
If you harbor mutual suspicion internally,
then the ‘calamity within the screen’
will arrive at any moment!”
He also said to Zuǎn and Hóng:
“Yǒngyè’s talent is insufficient to restore order,
Lǚ Shào’s courtesy name is Yǒngyè.
and he holds the position of sovereign undeservedly.
You [should] be the sovereign.
People’s hearts are not yet settled.
If you brothers live in harmony,
then your reign will last ten thousand generations.
‘Jī’
should be
‘jí’.
Otherwise, disaster will not be far behind!”
Zuǎn and Hóng wept and said:
“We dare not.”
He then grasped Zuǎn’s hand and cautioned him, saying:
“Your nature is rough and violent,
which deeply worries me.
Assist Yǒngyè well,
and do not listen to slanders!”
On that day,
Guāng died.
He was sixty-three years old.
Zuǎn pushed open the gate and entered to weep,
and after expressing his full grief, he exited.
Shào was afraid,
and offered his position to him,
saying:
“Elder brother’s achievements are great and his age is advanced;
he ought to succeed to the great統. ”
Zuǎn said:
“Your Majesty is the state’s primary heir.
How dare your subject usurp it!”
Shào insisted on yielding,
but Zuǎn did not permit it.
General of Agile Cavalry Lǚ Chāo said to Shào:
“Zuǎn has been a general for many years,
his might shakes inside and out.
During mourning, he shows no grief;
he walks tall and looks far,
he must have ulterior motives.
You should get rid of him early.”
Shào said:
“The late emperor’s words are still in my ears;
how can I abandon them!
I, in my young age, bear a great responsibility,
and now rely on my two elder brothers to bring peace to the family and state.
Even if he plots against me,
I view death as returning home.
I will ultimately not bear to have such an intention.”
You, sir, say no more!”
Zuǎn met Shào in the Zhànlù Hall.
Chāo stood by his side, holding a sword,
and looked at Zuǎn, requesting that he be arrested,
but Shào would not allow it.
This set the stage for Chāo eventually killing Zuǎn.
He was the son of Guāng’s younger brother Bǎo.
Hóng secretly sent Minister Jiāng Jì to tell Zuǎn:
“The sovereign is dim-witted
and not yet capable of handling many difficulties.
Your brother’s authority and benevolence are well-known.
You should act for the sake of the altars of soil and grain,
and not cling to minor principles.”
That night, Zuǎn led several hundred brave men to scale the northern wall,
and attacked the Guǎngxià Gate.
Hóng led the troops from the eastern park,
using axes on the Hóngfàn Gate.
Wáng Yǐn’s Jìn Shū says: The city of Liángzhōu was three lǐ from east to west,
and seven lǐ from north to south,
originally built by the Xiōngnú.
During the time of the Zhāng clan,
four more cities were added,
each measuring a thousand paces;
the eastern city was named Jiǎngwǔ Cháng,
the northern city was named Xuánwǔ Pǔ,
both planted with orchards and fruit trees,
and had palaces.
Guǎngxià Gate and Hóngfàn Gate
were both gates of the inner city.
‘Shuài’
is read ‘shuai’.
‘Xià’
is pronounced hù yǎ fān.
Someone asked him in reverse:
“Who are you?”
The crowd said:
“The Duke of Tàiyuán.”
The follower said:
“The state has suffered a great calamity,
the sovereign has just ascended the throne.
The Duke of Tàiyuán travels not by the proper path,
and enters the forbidden city at night.
Is he planning a rebellion?”
Then he drew his sword and rushed forward,
chopping Zuǎn on the forehead.
Zuǎn’s attendants seized him.
Zuǎn said:
“He is a righteous man,
do not kill him!”
Shào sent the Commandant of the Tiger Guards, Lǚ Kāi, to lead the imperial guards to resist battle at the Duānmén,
and Lǚ Chāo led two thousand soldiers to join them.
The troops had always feared Zuǎn,
and all fled without fighting.
Zuǎn entered through the Qīngjiǎo Gate
and ascended the Qiānguāng Hall.
The Qīngjiǎo Gate
was likely the eastern gate of the inner city of Liángzhōu.
The Qiānguāng Hall
was built by Zhāng Jùn;
he, though ruling alone west of the Yellow River,
maintained the dignity of a subject through generations,
and although modest, was still glorious,
hence the name of the hall.
Lǚ Chāo fled to Guǎngwǔ.
Zǔn, fearing Hóng’s strength,
offered his position to Hóng.
Hóng said,
“I, Hóng, succeeded to the great succession as a younger brother,
but the hearts of the multitude were not compliant.
Therefore, I disregarded the late emperor’s dying wish and deposed him,
ashamed to face the Yellow Springs!
Dù Yù said: The springs beneath the earth,
thus called Yellow Springs.
How could this be Hóng’s original intention!”
Zǔn then sent Hóng out to inform the multitude, saying,
“The late emperor received this decree at his deathbed.”
All the officials said,
“If the state has a master,
who dares to disobey!”
Zǔn then ascended the throne as Heavenly King.
Zǔn, courtesy name Yǒngxù,
was Guāng’s eldest illegitimate son.
He changed the era name to Xiánníng,
posthumously honored Guāng as Yìwǔ Huángdì,
with the temple name Tàizǔ;
and posthumously honored Shào as Yǐnwáng.

He appointed Hóng as Grand Commander, Overseer of All Military Affairs Inside and Outside the Capital, Grand Marshal, General of Chariots and Cavalry, Colonel-Director of the Retainers, and Minister of the Secretariat,
and re-enfeoffed him as Duke of Fānhé Commandery.
Zǔn said to Qí Cóng,
“You attacked me before,
how exceedingly so!”
Cóng wept and said,
“Yǐnwáng
was established by the late emperor;
although Your Majesty accords with Heaven and follows the people,
my humble intentions were not understood.
I only feared that Your Majesty would not die,
so what do you mean by ‘exceedingly so’!”
Zǔn rewarded his loyalty
and treated him well.
Zǔn’s uncle, General Who Attacks the East Fāng, was garrisoned at Guǎngwǔ.
Zǔn sent an envoy to Fāng, saying,
“Chāo is indeed a loyal minister,
whose righteousness and bravery are commendable;
but he does not understand the greater scheme of the state
and the expediency of timely change.
Fāng relies on his usefulness
to overcome the difficulties of the world,
so you can explain this meaning to him.”
Chāo submitted a memorial to express his gratitude and apology,
and Zǔn restored his titles and rank.
This set the stage for Chāo to kill Zǔn.
42 This year,
Yān ruler Shèng appointed Héjiān Gōng Xī as Overseer of All Military Affairs Inside and Outside the Capital and Left Grandee Secretary,
concurrently leading the Central Army Protector.
43 Liú Wèichén’s son, Wénchén, surrendered to Wèi;
Wèi ruler Guī married him to a woman of the imperial clan,
appointed him Grand General,
and bestowed upon him the surname Sù.
Among the Wèi’s internally integrated surnames was the Sùliùjīn clan,
which was changed to Sù;
presumably to merge Wénchén with this clan.
1 In spring,
the first month,
on the *rénzǐ* day, the first day of the month,
Yān ruler Shèng granted a general amnesty,
demoting himself to Commoner Heavenly King.
2 Wèi's military official general, Hé Bá,
attacked Lú Pǔ in Liáoxī.
On the *wǔwǔ* day,
he captured him.
Pǔ had defected to Yān,
as mentioned last year.
He was torn apart by chariots.
Yān ruler Shèng sent General Guǎngwēi Mèng Guǎngpíng to rescue Pǔ but did not reach him in time.
He executed Wèi's governor and magistrate of Liáoxī and returned.
3 On the *yǐhài* day,
a general amnesty was granted.
4 Western Qín King Gān Guī moved his capital to Yuànchuān.
The Qífú clan originally resided in Yuànchuān.
Gān Guī moved to Jīnchéng and now returned to Yuànchuān as his capital.
5 Tūfà Lìlùgū granted a general amnesty
and changed the era name to Jiànhé.
6 Gāogōulí King Ān was disrespectful in performing Yān rituals;
in the second month,
on the *bǐngshēn* day,
Yān King Shèng personally led an army of thirty thousand to attack him,
with General of Chariots and Cavalry Xī as the vanguard.
They captured Xīnchéng and Nánsū, two cities,
expanding their territory by over seven hundred *lǐ*,
resettling over five thousand households, and then returned.
Xī’s bravery surpassed all the generals.
Shèng said,
“My uncle is valiant and resolute,
possessing the demeanor of Shìzǔ.”
Mùróng Chuí's temple name was Shìzǔ.
*Guàn*,
pronounced like *gǔwán*;
similarly below.
7 Initially,
Wèi ruler Guī married the daughter of Liú Tóujuàn,
who was favored above all in the imperial harem,
and bore a son, Sì.
When he conquered Zhōngshān,
the conquest of Zhōngshān is recorded in Juan 109, Lóng'ān first year.
intending to establish an empress,
he followed the custom of his state:
casting a golden figurine to divine the outcome.
The figurine cast by Lady Liú did not form,
while that by Lady Mùróng did.
In the third month,
on the *wùwǔ* day,
Lady Mùróng was established as empress.
The *Běishǐ* states: According to Wèi custom,
when an empress was to be established,
she must personally cast a golden figurine;
if it formed, it was auspicious,
otherwise, she could not be established.
8 Huán Xuán, having conquered Jīng and Yōng,
submitted a memorial requesting to lead Jīng and Jiāng provinces.
An imperial edict appointed Xuán as Overseer of Military Affairs of seven provinces: Jīng, Sī, Yōng, Qín, Liáng, Yì, and Níng, and Inspector of Jīng Province,
and appointed Central Protector Huán Xiū as Inspector of Jiāng Province.
Xuán submitted a memorial firmly requesting Jiāng Province;
thereupon, Xuán was promoted to Overseer of Military Affairs of eight provinces and eight commanderies of Yáng and Yù,
and again concurrently led Jiāng Province as Inspector.
Xuán then appointed his elder brother Wěi as Inspector of Yōng Province,
and the court could not object.
He also appointed his nephew Zhèn as Prefect of Huáinán.
Since Xuán oversaw eight provinces and eight commanderies of Yáng and Yù,
his jurisdiction extended west to Mín and Bá,
and east to Lìyáng and Wúhú.
All were within his control.
The Huáinán Commandery of the Hàn and Jìn dynasties was originally administered from Shòuchūn.
During Emperor Chéng’s reign,
Zǔ Yuē and Sū Jùn caused unrest,
and barbarian incursions were frequent.
The number of people migrating south across the Yangtze River increased.
Thus, a Huáinán Commandery was established as a temporary settlement south of the river.
Later, Yúhú of Dānyáng was also ceded to be part of Huáinán’s territory.
Xuán sent Zhèn to guard it,
which was a gradual step towards threatening Jiànkāng.
*Cóng*,
pronounced like *cáiyòng*.
9 Liáng King Zǔn, fearing Dàsīmǎ Hóng’s high merits and proximity,
was jealous of him;
Hóng also suspected himself.
So, he used the troops from the East Park to start a rebellion,
attacking Zǔn.
Zǔn sent his general Jiāo Biàn to attack him.
Hóng’s forces collapsed,
and he fled.
Zǔn allowed his troops to plunder extensively,
distributing all the women from the East Park as rewards to the army,
Hóng’s wife and children were also among them.
Zǔn laughed and said to all the officials,
“How was today’s battle?”
Attendant-in-ordinary Fáng Guǐ replied,
“Heaven brings calamity upon the Liáng house,
and misfortunes repeatedly befall it.
The late emperor had just passed away,
and Yǐnwáng was deposed;
the imperial tomb had just been completed,
and the Dàsīmǎ raised troops;
blood flowed in the capital,
and brothers clashed weapons.
Although Hóng brought destruction upon himself,
it was also because Your Majesty lacked the kindness of the *Chángdì* [poem].
The *Zuǒ Zhuàn* states: Fù Chén said,
‘Zhào Mùgōng, reflecting on Zhōu's virtue not being uniform,
gathered his clan members in Chéngzhōu,
and composed a poem which said: "The flowers of the *chángdì*
have closely attached sepals.
Among all people today,
none are like brothers."
Its fourth stanza says: "Brothers quarrel within the wall,
but ward off insult from outside."
Thus,
even if brothers have small disagreements,
it does not sever their close kinship.'
And then you further allowed the troops to plunder extensively,
imprisoning and disgracing gentlemen and ladies!
Though the conflict originated with Hóng,
what crime have the common people committed!
Moreover, Hóng’s wife
is Your Majesty’s sister-in-law,
and Hóng’s daughters
are Your Majesty’s nieces.
How can you allow unruly commoners to disgrace them as婢妾 concubines and maids?
Heaven, Earth, and the divine spirits
could not bear to see this!”
He then sighed and shed tears.
Zǔn changed his expression and apologized to him;
he summoned Hóng’s wife and children and placed them in the Eastern Palace,
treating them generously.
Hóng intended to flee to Tūfà Lìlùgū.
On his way, he passed through Guǎngwǔ
and went to Lǚ Fāng.
Fāng saw him
and wept greatly, saying,
“The world is so vast,
why did you come here!”
He then seized Hóng and sent him to prison.
Zǔn sent strongman Kāng Lóng to strangle him to death.
He installed Yáng Shì as empress,
and made her father, Huán, Shàngshū Zuǒ Púyè and Liáng Dōuyǐn.
Liángdū was Gūzāng,
so the Grand Administrator of Wǔwēi was renamed Liáng Dōuyǐn.
10th day, Xīnmǎo.
Duàn Dēng, Prefect of Xiāngpíng of Yàn, and others plotted rebellion,
and were executed.
11th day. Liáng King Zuǎn was about to attack Wǔwēi King Lìlùgū.
Zhōngshūlìng Yáng Yǐng remonstrated, saying:
"Lìlùgū's subordinates are all loyal and obedient;
the state has no weaknesses yet,
so it cannot be attacked."
He did not listen.
Lìlùgū sent his younger brother, Nǔtán, to resist him.
In summer,
the fourth month,
Nǔtán defeated the Liáng army at Sāntuī.
Sāntuī
is south of Hàowěi River.
Bài (defeated),
is pronounced Bǔmài.
12th day. At first,
Lǒngxī Lǐ Gǎo was fond of literature
and had a good reputation.
He once lodged with Guō Nún and his half-brother from the same mother, Dūnhuáng Sòng Yáo.
Nún rose and said to Yáo:
"You will reach the highest office among officials,
and Lord Lǐ will eventually possess the state.
There is a mare that has given birth to a white-forehead colt."
Kēmǎ
means a mare.
Kē
is pronounced Kè.
The Jìn Shū writes
"Guā".
When Mèng Mǐn became Inspector of Shāzhōu,
he appointed Gǎo as Prefect of Xiàogǔ;
Xiàogǔ County,
since the Hàn dynasty,
belonged to Dūnhuáng Commandery.
Shīgǔ said: It was originally Yúzézhàng.
Sāng Qīn said: In the sixth year of Yuánfēng of Emperor Xiàowǔ,
Cuī Bùyì of Jìnán became Magistrate of Yúzé,
taught diligent farming,
and because of the hard work, obtained grain,
thus it was established as a county name.
Later, the Northern Zhōu merged it into Dūnhuáng County.
He was appointed Zhōngsàn Chángshì.
It means a Zhōngsàn Dàfū attending at the emperor's left and right.
Sàn
is pronounced Xīdǎn.
Dūnhuáng Protector of the Army Féngyì Guō Qiān, Shāzhōu Zhìzhōng Dūnhuáng Suǒ Xiān, and others
esteemed Gǎo for his gentleness, resolve, and benevolent governance,
and recommended him as Grand Administrator of Dūnhuáng.
Gǎo initially found it difficult.
Coincidentally, Sòng Yáo returned from Zhāngyè,
and said to Gǎo:
"King Duàn lacks far-sighted strategy
and will ultimately achieve nothing.
Have you forgotten Guō Nún's words, my brother?
The white-forehead colt has already been born."
Gǎo then agreed
and sent an envoy to seek appointment from Yè;
Yè then appointed Gǎo as Grand Administrator of Dūnhuáng.
The Right Guard General, Dūnhuáng Suǒ Sì, said to Yè:
"Lǐ Gǎo should not be allowed to occupy Dūnhuáng."
Yè then replaced Gǎo with Sì as Grand Administrator of Dūnhuáng,
and ordered him to lead five hundred cavalry to his post.
When Sì was less than twenty *lǐ* away,
he sent a message to Gǎo to welcome him;
When he was barely twenty *lǐ* from Dūnhuáng,
he sent a letter to Gǎo ordering him to welcome him.
Gǎo was about to go out to welcome him.
Xiàogǔ Prefect Zhāng Miǎo and Sòng Yáo stopped him, saying:
"King Duàn is dim and weak;
now is precisely the time for heroes to act.
The General possesses the resources of a state;
how can you surrender it with folded hands!
Sì relies on his home commandery,
believing that people will flock to him,
and does not expect the General to suddenly resist him.
He can be captured in one battle."
Gǎo followed their advice.
He first sent Yáo to meet Sì,
luring him with sweet words.
When Yáo returned,
he said to Gǎo:
"Sì is arrogant and his troops are weak;
he is easy to take."
Gǎo then sent Miǎo, Yáo, and his two sons Xīn and Ràng, to intercept and attack Sì.
Sì was defeated and fled,
returning to Zhāngyè.
Gǎo had always been friendly with Sì,
and particularly resented him,
so he petitioned Yè to execute Sì.
Jǔqú Nánchéng also disliked Sì
and advised Yè to eliminate him;
Yè then killed Sì.
Duàn Yè, having lost Zhāngyè,
and then killing Suǒ Sì to clip his own wings,
ultimately died at the hands of Jǔqú Méngxùn.
È (dislike),
is pronounced Wūlù.
He promoted Gǎo to Supervisor of all Military Affairs west of Liángxìng and General Who Guards the West.
Duàn Yè divided Liángxìng and Wūzé from Dūnhuáng,
and Yíhé from Jìnchāng, to form Liángxìng Commandery.
During the Yǔwén clan,
Guǎngzhì, Yí'ān, and Yuānquán of Jìn were merged
to form Liángxìng County;
Chánglè County of Guāzhōu during the Suí and Táng dynasties was that area.
13th day. Tǔyùhún Shìpí died.
The heir Shùluògān was only nine years old,
so his younger brother Wūgétí was enthroned.
He married Shùluògān's mother, Lady Niàn,
and had Mùguī and Mùyán.
Wūgétí was timid, weak, and dissolute,
unable to govern the state;
Lady Niàn exclusively controlled state affairs,
possessing courage and intelligence,
and the people of the state feared and obeyed her.
14th day. Yàn's Former General Duàn Jī,
the nephew of Empress Dowager Duàn,
was implicated by Duàn Dēng's confession.
In the fifth month,
on the Rénzǐ day,
he fled to Liáoxī.
This laid the groundwork for the later assassination of Shèng by Duàn Jī and others.
Shèng, punishing Lán Hàn,
strictly enforced severe penalties on his subordinates,
and also eventually died at the hands of others.
If a person is not benevolent,
hating it too much
leads to chaos.
15th day. On the Bǐngyín day,
Wei General Dōngtíng Xiànhóu Wáng Xún died.
16th day. On the Jǐsì day,
Wèi ruler Guī traveled east to Zhuōlù,
and west to Mǎyì,
to observe the source of the Luǐ River.
17th day. On the Wùyín day,
Yàn's Duàn Jī returned to confess his crime;
Yàn King Shèng pardoned him,
bestowed upon him the title Sīhuǐhóu,
arranged for him to marry a princess,
and had him serve directly within the palace.
18th day. Xiè Yǎn, based on his status and reputation, garrisoned at Kuàijī.
Zī
refers to his family background and accumulated resources;
Wàng
refers to his contemporary prestige.
Kuài
is pronounced Gōngwài.
He also made no military preparations.
All the generals remonstrated, saying:
"The rebels are close by the seashore,
observing opportunities.
We should open a path for them to reform themselves."
Yǎn did not listen,
saying:
"Fú Jiān's army of a million
still met their end south of the Huái River.
Yǎn and Xiè Xuán together defeated Fú Jiān,
thus he underestimated Sūn Ēn.
Having been defeated and fleeing into the sea,
how can he emerge again!
If he does indeed emerge,
it is Heaven's will to kill him."
Soon after, Ēn's bandits attacked Jiá kǒu.
Jiá kǒu
is now outside Hǔdūnshān in Dìnghǎi County, Míngzhōu.
Jiá
is pronounced Jíyè.
Dù Yòu said: Jiá kǒu is seventy *lǐ* northeast of Màoxiàn, Míngzhōu.
They captured Shàngyú
and advanced to Xíngpǔ.
The Jìn Shū says: Xíngpǔ is thirty-five *lǐ* north of Shānyīn.
Ēn retreated.
A few days later,
he again attacked Xíngpǔ.
The government forces suffered a defeat,
and Ēn advanced directly, pressing his advantage.
On the Jǐmǎo day,
he reached Kuàijī.
Yǎn had not yet eaten,
saying:
"I must first destroy this rebel before eating."
Thereupon, he mounted his horse and went out to battle.
His army was defeated,
and he was killed by Zhāng Měng, the commander under his tent.
Yǔ Huán, Grand Administrator of Wúxīng, feared that the people of the commandery would again side with Ēn,
so he killed thousands of men and women.
Ēn then turned to attack Línhǎi.
The court was greatly shaken
and dispatched General Who Exemplifies the Army Huán Bùcái,
General Who Assists the State Sūn Wúzhōng, and General Who Pacifies the North Gāo Yǎzhī to resist him.
19 Qín's Grand General of the West-Conquering Army, Lǒngxī Gōng Shuòdé, led five thousand troops
to attack Xīqín.
Five thousand [troops],
might be too few.
This should be verified.
Nán'ānxiá Gorge
is within the borders of Táng's Qínzhōu, Lǒngchéng Xiàn.
Déjiāng
is read as Liàngfān.
He encamped at Lǒngxī.
20 Yáng Guǐ and Tián Xuánmíng plotted to assassinate Wǔwēi Wáng Lìlùgū.
Lìlùgū killed them.
In Lóng'ān second year,
Yáng Guǐ surrendered to Lìlùgū.
21 In the sixth month,
on the gengchen new moon day,
there was a solar eclipse.
22 Hé Chéng, the teacher of Lángxié Wáng, was appointed Shàngshū Zuǒ Púyè.
The Jìn princes each had one teacher (shī), one friend (yǒu), and one literatus (wénxué).
Initially, to avoid the taboo on Jǐng Dì's given name,
"shī"
was changed
to
"fù".
Later, as ancestral temples did not observe this taboo,
it was restored
to "shī".
He was Zǔn's son.
See Hé Zǔn in one hundred juan, Mù Dì's Shēngpíng first year.
23 On the jiazi day,
Yàn declared a great amnesty.
24 Liáng Wáng Zuǎn was about to attack Běiliáng.
Jiāng Jì admonished him, saying:
"It is midsummer and farm work is in full swing;
it is advisable to rest the troops.
Now, to embark on a distant expedition to Lǐngxī,
marching northwest from Gūzāng to Zhāngyè,
there is a great mountain range in between.
After crossing the range to the west,
Xī Jùn holds the strategic pass.
What will you do?"
He did not listen.
He advanced and besieged Zhāngyè,
and plundered Jiànkāng to the west.
Tūfà Nǔtán heard of this
and led ten thousand cavalry to attack Gūzāng.
Zuǎn's younger brother, Lǒngxī Gōng Wěi, fortified himself by relying on the northern city wall.
Nǔtán set up a feast above the Zhūmíngmén gate,
rang bells and beat drums,
entertained his officers and soldiers,
and displayed his troops at the Qīngyángmén gate.
Zhūmíngmén
is the southern gate of Gūzāng city;
Qīngyángmén
is the eastern gate.
Nǔ
is read as Núwòfān.
When Zuǎn heard of this,
he withdrew his troops and returned.
25 In autumn,
the seventh month,
on the renzi day,
Grand Empress Dowager Lǐ Shì passed away.
26 On the dingmao day,
a great amnesty was declared.
27 Xīqín Wáng Gān Guī dispatched Wǔwèi Jiāngjūn Mùwū and others to garrison and defend.
The Qín army's supply routes for firewood and forage were cut off.
Qín Wáng Xīng secretly led troops to rescue them.
When Gān Guī heard of this,
he ordered Mùwū to lead twenty thousand central army troops to encamp at Bǎiyáng.
The Shuǐjīngzhù states: Bóyáng Shuǐ river flows out of Bóyáng Gǔ valley,
east of Dǒngtíng;
further east is Bóyáng Chéng city,
and south of the city is called Bóyáng Chuān plain.
This was probably the route Lǐ Ěr took when he went west,
so the plains, gullies, and valleys
often bear its name.
Later, it was corrupted to Bǎiyáng.
The Wǔdàizhì states: Tiānshuǐ Jùn's Qínlǐng Xiàn.
The Later Wèi established Bóyáng Xiàn.
During Suí's Kāihuáng era, it was renamed Qínlǐng.
In Táng, Qínlǐng was merged into Qīngshuǐ Xiàn.
Shuài
is read as lǜ;
the same applies below.
Gān Guī personally led several thousand light cavalry to scout for the Qín army.
Coinciding with a strong wind and dim fog,
he lost contact with the central army
and was pressed by pursuing cavalry.
He entered the outer army.
At dawn,
he fought Qín
and suffered a great defeat,
fleeing back to Yuànchuān.
His three hundred and sixty thousand followers all surrendered to Qín.
Xīng advanced his army to Báohǎn.
Gān Guī fled to Jīnchéng.
He said to his chieftains:
"I am untalented,
and have usurped this title
for over twelve years.
In Xiàowǔ Dì's Tàiyuán thirteenth year,
Gān Guī succeeded to the state;
by now, it has been thirteen years.
I have nothing to withstand the enemy,
and wish to seek refuge in Yǔnwú to the west.
Yǔnwú Xiàn,
in Hàn belonged to Jīnchéng Jùn,
Jìn records abolished it.
Liú Xù said: Táng's Shànzhōu's Lóngzhī Xiàn
was Hàn's Yǔnwú Xiàn.
Yǔnwú
is pronounced Qiányá.
If I must not be spared,
you all remain here,
and each with your followers surrender to Qín
to preserve your clans,
do not follow me."
They all said:
"We wish to follow Your Majesty in life and death."
Gān Guī said:
"I will now have to rely on others for sustenance.
If Heaven has not yet destroyed me,
perhaps one day I can recover my former enterprise
and see you all again.
To die together now
is of no benefit."
Thereupon, he wept bitterly and parted.
Gān Guī alone led several hundred cavalry to Yǔnwú
and pleaded for surrender to Wǔwēi Wáng Lìlùgū.
Lìlùgū sent Guǎngwǔ Gōng Nǔtán to welcome him
and settled him in Jìnxīng.
Zhāng Guǐ divided a part of Xīpíng's territory
to establish Jìnxīng Jùn.
Kàn Yīn said: Forty li west of Yǔnwú Xiàn
is the small Jìnxīng Chéng city.
Nǔ
is read as Núwòfān.
Zhènběi Jiāngjūn Tūfà Jùyán said to Lìlùgū:
"Gān Guī was originally our vassal state,
who elevated himself during the chaos.
Now, at the end of his tether, he surrenders his life;
this is not his true sincerity.
If he escapes to the Yáo clan,
he will surely become a national threat.
It is better to move and settle him among the Yǐfú.
Yǐfú
are also a Xiānbēi tribe,
residing in Xīhǎi.
The Běishǐ states: North of Tǔyùhún there is the Yǐfú Wùdí kingdom.
The kingdom has Qǔhǎi lake,
which is over a thousand li in circumference.
The tribe has ten thousand households,
and their customs are similar to Tǔyùhún.
The Běishǐ also states: The Yǐfú were hereditary chieftains of Tǔyùhún,
residing in Qīnghǎi,
and were called the King of Qīnghǎi.
Lìlùgū said:
"He comes to us in desperation,
yet we question his sincerity beforehand?
How will this encourage futurecomers?"
Jùyán
was Lìlùgū's younger brother.
Once the Qín army retreated,
the Southern Qiāng, Liáng Gē and others, secretly invited Gān Guī.
Gān Guī was about to respond to them.
His minister, Wūyǐn Āluò, reported this to Jìnxīng Tàishǒu Yīn Chàng.
Chàng immediately informed Lìlùgū.
Lìlùgū sent his younger brother Tǔléi to lead three thousand cavalry to encamp at Mén Tiānlǐng.
Mén Tiānlǐng
is southeast of Yǔnwú.
Gān Guī said to his heir apparent, Chìpán:
"If my sons and I remain here,
we will surely not be tolerated by Lìlùgū.
Now the Yáo clan is strong;
I will go over to them.
If we all go together,
we will surely be overtaken by pursuing cavalry.
I will use you, your brothers, and your mother as hostages;
they will surely not suspect.
When I am in Cháng'ān,
they will ultimately not dare to harm you."
Thereupon, he sent Chìpán and others to Xīpíng.
In the eighth month,
Gān Guī fled south to Báohǎn,
and subsequently surrendered to Qín.
28 On the dinghai day,
Shàngshū Yòu Púyè Wáng Yǎ passed away.
29 In the ninth month,
on the guichou day,
there was an earthquake.
30 Liáng's Lǚ Fāng surrendered to Qín.
Three thousand households of Guǎngwǔ's commoners fled to Wǔwēi Wáng Lìlùgū.
Lǚ Fāng governed Guǎngwǔ.
After he surrendered to Qín,
his people were without a master,
hence they fled to the Tūfà clan.
In the 31st winter,
the eleventh month,
Gāo Yǎzhī (高雅之) fought Sūn Ēn (孫恩) at Yúyáo (餘姚).
Yǎzhī (雅之) was defeated
and fled to Shānyīn (山陰),
where seven or eight tenths of his men died.
An imperial edict appointed Liú Láozhī (劉牢之) as Area Commander of five prefectures, including Kuàijī (會稽),
to lead his troops to attack Ēn (恩).
Ēn (恩) fled into the sea.
Láozhī (牢之) camped east at Shàngyú (上虞),
and sent Liú Yù (劉裕) to garrison Gòuzhāng (句章).
Gòuzhāng (句章) county,
since the Hàn (漢) dynasty, belonged to Kuàijī (會稽) Commandery.
Today, Yínxiàn (鄞縣) to the east, Dìnghǎi (定海), and Chāngguó (昌國)
are all its territory.
The Hùdú (滬瀆) fortress was built to defend against Ēn (恩).
Sōng (崧)
was Qiáo's (喬) grandson.
"Yuán Sōng" (袁崧)
should be
"Yuán Shānsōng" (袁山松).
Hùdú (滬瀆)
is now east of Wúxiàn (吳縣) in Píngjiāngfǔ (平江府).
Lù Guīmēng (陸龜蒙), in his description of fishing gear, said: "A row of bamboo in the seashore is called a 'hù' (滬)."
This waterway thus got its name.
The Wú Dū Jì (吳都記) states: "The Sōngjiāng (松江) flows east into the sea,
and is called Hùdú (扈瀆)."
The Yúdì Zhì (輿地志) states: "'Hù' (扈) is the name for fishing by coastal dwellers.
Bamboo is inserted in rows in the sea,
woven with ropes,
with two wings spread towards the shore.
When the tide comes in, it submerges;
when the tide recedes, it emerges.
Fish follow the sea tide,
are hindered by the bamboo and cannot leave.
This is called 'Hùdú' (扈瀆)."
Fàn Chéngdà's (范成大) Wújùn Zhì (吳郡志) states: "A row of bamboo on the seashore is called a 'hù' (滬),
and Wú's (吳) Hùdú (滬瀆) is this."
From Hùdú (滬瀆), going upstream along the Sōngjiāng (松江) to Wújùn (吳郡) Jiāngmén (將門).
Jiāngmén (將門) is now mistakenly called Jiàngmén (匠門).
Yuán Qiáo (袁喬)
is mentioned in volume 97, Mù Dì (穆帝), Yǒnghé (永和) second and third years.
The Kuàijī (會稽) heir apparent, Yuánxiǎn (元顯), sought to govern Xúzhōu (徐州).

An imperial edict appointed Yuánxiǎn (元顯) as Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī (開府儀同三司), Area Commander of the military affairs of sixteen prefectures, including Yáng (揚), Yù (豫), Xú (徐), Yǎn (兗), Qīng (青), Yōu (幽), Jì (冀), Bīng (幷), Jīng (荊), Jiāng (江), Sī (司), Yōng (雍), Liáng (梁), Yì (益), Jiāo (交), and Guǎng (廣), and Inspector of Xúzhōu (徐州).
His son Yànwěi (彥瑋) was enfeoffed
as Prince of Dōnghǎi (東海).
Qǐfú Gān'guī (乞伏乾歸) arrived at Cháng'ān (長安).
Qín (秦) King Xīng (興) appointed him Area Commander of Hénán (河南) military affairs, Inspector of Hézhōu (河州), and Marquis of Guīyì (歸義).
This Hénán (河南) refers to the south of Jīnchéng (金城) River.
After a long time,
Qǐfú Chìpán (乞伏熾磐) wanted to flee to Gān'guī (乾歸).
Wǔwēi (武威) King Lìlùgū (利鹿孤) pursued and captured him.
Lìlùgū (利鹿孤) was about to kill Chìpán (熾磐),
when Guǎngwǔ (廣武) Duke Rǔtán (傉檀) said:
"A son returning to his father is not something to be deeply blamed.
One should pardon him to show great magnanimity."
Lìlùgū (利鹿孤) followed this advice.
Tūfà Rǔtán (禿髮傉檀) advised his elder brother to pardon Chìpán (熾磐),
but eventually died by Chìpán's (熾磐) hand.
Was this not raising a tiger to bring trouble upon oneself?
Qín (秦) King Xīng (興) sent more than two hundred Jìn (晉) generals, including Liú Sōng (劉嵩), to surrender.
Liú Sōng (劉嵩) and others were likely captured by Qín (秦) due to the fall of Luòyáng (洛陽).
Jiāng (將)
is pronounced as 'jiàng'.
The Administrator of Jìnchāng (晉昌) in Běi Liáng (北涼), Táng Yáo (唐瑤), rebelled.
He issued a declaration to the six commanderies.
The six commanderies
were probably Dūnhuáng (敦煌), Jiǔquán (酒泉), Jìnchāng (晉昌), Liángxīng (涼興), Jiànkāng (建康), and Qílián (祁連).
Gǎo (暠) pardoned his territory
and changed the era name to Gēngzǐ (庚子).
The territory of Běi Liáng (北涼) was thus divided into Xī Liáng (西涼).
Guō Qiān (郭謙) was made Jūncí Jìjiǔ (軍諮祭酒),
Suǒ Xiān (索仙) was made Zuǒ Chángshǐ (左長史),
Zhāng Miǎo (張邈) was made Yòu Chángshǐ (右長史),
Yǐn Jiànxīng (尹建興) was made Zuǒ Sīmǎ (左司馬),
and Zhāng Tǐshùn (張體順) was made Yòu Sīmǎ (右司馬).
He sent the Attendant Zhonglang Sòng Yáo (宋繇) to campaign east against Liángxīng (涼興)
and also attack the cities west of Yùmén (玉門),
all of which surrendered.
The Administrator of Jiǔquán (酒泉), Wáng Dé (王德), also rebelled against Běi Liáng (北涼).
He proclaimed himself Inspector of Hézhōu (河州).
Běi Liáng (北涼) King Yè (業) ordered Jǔqú Méngxùn (沮渠蒙遜) to attack him.
Dé (德) burned the city
and led his troops to flee to Táng Yáo (唐瑤).
Méngxùn (蒙遜) pursued them to Shātóu (沙頭)
and thoroughly defeated them.
Shātóu (沙頭) county originally belonged to Jiǔquán (酒泉) Commandery.
Huì Dì (惠帝) divided it to belong to Jìnchāng (晉昌) Commandery.
Jǔ (沮)
is pronounced 'jǔ'.
Jiāng (將)
is pronounced 'jiàng'.
In the twelfth month,
on the day Wùyín (戊寅),
a comet appeared in Tiānjīn (天津).
The Tiānwén Zhì (天文志) states: "The nine stars of Tiānjīn (天津) lie across the river (Milky Way).
One is called Tiānhàn (天漢),
another Tiānjiāng (天江).
They govern the ferries and bridges of the four major rivers,
through which the divine power crosses the four directions."
Bèi (孛)
is pronounced 'bèi'.
He was again made Shàngshū Lìng (尚書令).
Lìbù Shàngshū (吏部尚書) Chē Yìn (車胤), seeing Yuánxiǎn's (元顯) arrogance and self-indulgence,
reported to Kuàijī (會稽) King Dàozǐ (道子),
requesting that he be restrained.
Yuánxiǎn (元顯) heard about it but had not yet verified it,
and asked Dàozǐ (道子):
"What did Chē Wǔzǐ (車武子) say in private?"
Chē Yìn (車胤),
courtesy name Wǔzǐ (武子).
Píng (屏)
is pronounced 'bǐng'.
He insisted on asking,
and Dàozǐ (道子) angrily said:
"You want to confine me,
and not let me speak with court officials!"
Yuánxiǎn (元顯) left
and said to his followers:
"Chē Yìn (車胤) is alienating my father and me."
He secretly sent men to accuse him.
Yìn (胤), in fear,
committed suicide.
On the day Rénchén (壬辰),
Yān (燕) Lord Shèng (盛) established Yāntái (燕臺)
to govern the various tribes of barbarians.
Since the two Zhào (趙) states,
all had established Shànyú Tái (單于臺) to govern the various barbarians,
and Shèng (盛) continued this practice.
The Grand Historian of Wèi (魏) repeatedly reported that the celestial phenomena were in disorder.
Wèi (魏) Lord Guī (珪) personally examined the divination books,
many of which spoke of changing kings and governments.
He then issued an imperial edict to admonish everyone,
stating that the succession of emperors and kings
was all by heaven's mandate,
and should not be rashly interfered with.
He also repeatedly changed official titles
to suppress disasters and anomalies.
The Yícáo Láng (儀曹郎) Dǒng Mì (董謐) presented a text on taking elixirs to become an immortal.
Guī (珪) established immortal doctors (Xiānrén Bóshì, 仙人博士)
and built immortal workshops (Xiānfāng, 仙坊),
where they brewed and refined various medicines.
He sealed Xīshān (西山) to provide firewood and kindling.
Xīshān (西山)
is the Xīshān (西山) of Píngchéng (平城).
Máo Huǎng (毛晃) said: "Rough wood is 'xīn' (薪), fine wood is 'zhēng' (蒸)."
He ordered those condemned to death to try the elixirs;
many died,
proving them ineffective,
but Guī (珪) still believed in them
and continued to seek them out.
Guī (珪) often considered Yān (燕) Lord Chuí's (垂) sons dividing and occupying strategic positions,
which led to the transfer of power downwards
and consequently to ruin,
and he strongly disapproved of this.
Bóshì (博士) Gōngsūn Biǎo (公孫表) tried to please him
by presenting Hán Fēi's (韓非) book,
advising Guī (珪) to use law to control his subordinates.
Zuǒ Jiāngjūn (左將軍) Lǐ Sù (李粟) was naturally careless and disrespectful,
"Sù" (粟)
is sometimes written as
coughing and spitting as he pleased.
Guī (珪) accumulated his past offenses
and then executed him.
Everyone was terrified.
The historian said that Wèi (魏) Lord Guī (珪) was cruel and tyrannical in his governance.
On the day Dīngyǒu (丁酉),
Yān (燕) King Shèng (盛) honored Empress Dīng (丁), consort of Xiànzhuāng (獻莊), as Empress Dowager.
He established Liáoxī (遼西) Duke Dìng (定) as Crown Prince.
There was a general amnesty.
In this year,
Nán Yān (南燕) King Dé (德) ascended the imperial throne at Guǎnggù (廣固).
Dé (德),
courtesy name Xuánmíng (玄明),
was the youngest son of Huǎng (皝).
He changed the era name to Jiànpíng (建平).
He changed his personal name to Bèidé (備德),
wanting to make it easier for officials and common people to avoid using his name.
He posthumously honored Yān (燕) Lord Wěi (暐) as Emperor Yōu (幽).
He appointed Běidì (北地) King Zhōng (鍾) as Sītú (司徒),
Mùyú Bá (慕輿拔) as Sīkōng (司空),
Fēng Fú (封孚) as Zuǒ Púyè (左僕射),
and Mùyú Hù (慕輿護) as Yòu Púyè (右僕射).
He established Lady Duàn (段) as Empress.

Long'an (隆安) fifth year (Xīnchǒu, 401 CE)
1 In spring,
in the first month,
Wǔwēi Wáng Lìlùgū (武威王利鹿孤) wanted to declare himself emperor.
All his ministers advised him to do so.
Ānguó Jiāngjūn Tōuwùlún (安國將軍鍮勿崙) said:
"Ānguó Jiāngjūn (安國將軍)
was a title conferred by Hàn Xiàndì (漢獻帝) upon Zhāng Yáng (張楊).
*Tōu* (鍮),
pronounced *tuō hóu* (託侯).
*Lún* (崙),
pronounced *lú kūn* (盧昆).
"Since the ancient past, our nation
has worn unbound hair and clothes fastened on the left,
without the adornment of caps and belts.
We have migrated with the availability of water and pastures,
without walled cities or fixed dwellings.
Thus, we have been able to dominate the desert
and contend with the Central Plains.
Now, to assume a great title
certainly accords with the will of the people.
However, establishing a capital and erecting cities
makes it difficult to avoid calamities, and
storing provisions in granaries
arouses the enemy's heart.
It is better to settle the Jìn (晉) people in walled cities,
encourage and supervise their farming and sericulture to provide resources and stores,
lead our own people to practice warfare and archery.
If a neighboring state is weak, we attack it;
if it is strong, we avoid it.
This is a long-term excellent strategy.
Since the Hàn (漢) dynasty,
no one has devised a better strategy for the barbarians
than this one.
*Chǔ* (處),
pronounced *chāng lǚ* (昌呂).
*Shuài* (帥),
read as *lǜ* (率).
What use is it to be mere targets for the world
to aim at?"
A *zhì* (質) receives an axe,
a *dì* (的) receives an arrow.
According to the *Shī Jīng* (詩經), 'They shoot at that *yǒu dì* (有的),'
Máo Chuán (毛傳) says: *dì* (的)
means *zhì* (質).
Zhèngyì (正義) says: Máo Shì (毛氏), concerning the matter of shooting at targets,
does not make the *zhèng gǔ* (正鵠) clear;
only in the *Yī Jiē Chuán* (猗嗟傳) does it say: a two-foot target is called *zhèng* (正),
but it does not state where the *zhèng* (正) is placed.
Zhōu Lǐ (周禮) with Zhèng Zhòng (鄭衆) and Mǎ Róng's (馬融) commentaries
all say: ten feet is a *hóu* (侯),
four feet is a *gǔ* (鵠),
two feet is a *zhèng* (正),
and four inches is a *zhì* (質);
thus, they consider all *hóu* (侯) to be one *zhàng* (丈),
and *gǔ* (鵠), *zhèng* (正), and *zhì* (質) form these grades within a single *hóu* (侯),
thus taking *zhì* (質) to be four inches.
Wáng Sù (王肅) quotes the *Ěryǎ* (爾雅) saying: archery,
a stretched hide is called *hóu* (侯),
the center of the *hóu* (侯) is called *gǔ* (鵠),
the center of the *gǔ* (鵠) is called *zhèng* (正),
the *zhèng* (正) is two feet square;
the center of the *zhèng* (正) is called *niè* (槷),
the *niè* (槷) is six inches square.
*Niè* (槷) is then *zhì* (質).
Previously, it was said to be four inches square;
now it says six inches square,
the *Ěryǎ* (爾雅) explanation
should be followed.
Wáng Sù's (王肅) intention was only to change *zhì* (質) to six inches,
the rest is the same as Zhèng (鄭) and Mǎ (馬).
Jiǎ Kuí's (賈逵) *Zhōu Lǐ* (周禮) commentary says: four feet is *zhèng* (正),
*zhèng* (正) has five layers,
*gǔ* (鵠) is inside it,
and it is two feet square to form *zhèng* (正),
*zhèng* (正) is larger than *gǔ* (鵠),
*gǔ* (鵠) is within *zhèng* (正);
although the inside and outside are different,
they are also both within one *hóu* (侯).
Zhèng (鄭), upon examining the *Zhōu Lǐ* (周禮) throughout,
concluded that for the *dà shè* (大射) (grand archery ceremony),
a hide *gǔ* (鵠) is made in the center of the *hóu* (侯);
for the *bīn shè* (賓射) (guest archery ceremony),
the center of the *hóu* (侯) is painted as a *zhèng* (正),
the *zhèng* (正) is as large as the *gǔ* (鵠),
both occupying one-third of the *hóu* (侯) center.
For the *yàn shè* (燕射) (banquet archery ceremony), they shoot at a beast-shaped *hóu* (侯),
with a beast form painted in the center of the *hóu* (侯),
which is similar to what is referred to as 'bear *hóu* (侯) and white *zhì* (質)' in the *Xiāng Shè Jì* (鄉射記).
The *Shè Yì* (射義) says: Confucius (孔子) said: 'To shoot by sound,
and not miss the *zhèng gǔ* (正鵠) when shooting,
is that not for the worthy!'
The *Shī Jīng* (詩經) says: 'They shoot at that *yǒu dì* (有的),
thereby praying for your noble title.'
Since *zhèng gǔ* (正鵠) is mentioned,
this *dì* (的) is quoted.
Thus, the poet's intention is to equate *dì* (的) with *zhèng gǔ* (正鵠).
The *Sī Qiú* (司裘) commentary describes the hide *hóu* (侯) saying: 'The sides are decorated with the hides of tigers, bears, leopards, and elks,
and then a square is made for the *zhì* (質),
called *gǔ* (鵠).'
This shows that Zhèng's (鄭) intention was that the place shot at in the *hóu* (侯) is the *zhì* (質).
This Máo Chuán (毛傳) only says: *dì* (的) is *zhì* (質).
"Ānguó's (安國) words are right."
So, he instead called himself Héxī Wáng (河西王),
and appointed Guǎngwǔ Gōng Rǔtán (廣武公傉檀) as Dūdū Zhōngwài Zhūjūnshì (都督中外諸軍事), Liángzhōu Mù (涼州牧), and Lù Shàngshū Shì (錄尚書事).
2 In the second month,
on the day of Bǐngzǐ (丙子),
Sūn Ēn (孫恩) attacked Xiákǒu (浹口).
*Xiá* (浹),
pronounced *yè* (叶).
He could not capture it.
Liú Láozhī (劉牢之) attacked him,
and Sūn Ēn (孫恩) fled back to sea.
3 Qín Wáng Xīng (秦王興) sent Qífú Gān’guī (乞伏乾歸) back to garrison Yuànchuān (苑川),
and gave him all his former troops.
This laid the foundation for the Qífú (乞伏) clan to become powerful again.
4 Liáng Wáng Zuǎn (涼王纂) was addicted to wine and fond of hunting.
Tàicháng Yáng Yǐng (太常楊穎) admonished him, saying:
"Your Majesty received the Mandate of Heaven,
and should govern with the Way.
Now, the territory is shrinking daily,
confined between two ridges.
Gūzāng (姑臧) has Hóngchí Lǐng (洪池嶺) to the south
and Dānlǐng (丹嶺) to the west.
One version writes
'Shāndānlǐng' (刪丹嶺).
Yet you are immersed in drinking and hunting,
not attending to affairs of state.
Your servant is secretly concerned."
Zuǎn (纂) humbly apologized,
but still did not reform.
Fānhé Tàishǒu Lǚ Chāo (番禾太守呂超) attacked Xiānbēi Sīpán (鮮卑思盤).
Fānhé (番禾) county,
during the Hàn (漢) dynasty, belonged to Zhāngyè (張掖) commandery,
abolished in the Later Hàn (後漢) and Jìn (晉) dynasties.
*Fān* (番),
pronounced *pán* (盤).
This commandery was probably established by the Lǚ (呂) clan.
Liú Xù (劉昫) says:
"Táng (唐) Liángzhōu (涼州) Tiānbǎo (天寶) county
was the territory of Hàn (漢) Fānhé (番禾) county."
*Quān* (悛),
pronounced *qī yuán* (七緣).
*Fān* (番),
pronounced *pán* (盤).
Zuǎn (纂) ordered both Chāo (超) and Sīpán (思盤) to come to court.
Chāo (超), feeling fearful,
arrived at Gūzāng (姑臧)
and deeply allied himself with Diànzhōng Jiān Dù Shàng (殿中監杜尚).
Zuǎn (纂) saw Chāo (超) and rebuked him, saying:
"You rely on your brothers' martial prowess,
Kǒng Ānguó (孔安國) says: *huánhuán* (桓桓) means martial appearance.
People today refer to outdoing each other as deceiving each other.
Only then will the world be settled!"
Today, people use *xiāng líng* (相陵) to mean *xiāng qī* (相欺).
Only then can the world be settled!"
Chāo (超) kowtowed and apologized.
Zuǎn (纂) originally intended to merely intimidate Chāo (超),
and had no real intention of killing him.
He then invited Chāo (超), Sīpán (思盤), and all his ministers to a banquet in the inner palace.
Chāo's (超) elder brother, Zhōnglǐngjūn Lóng (中領軍隆), repeatedly urged Zuǎn (纂) to drink.
Zuǎn (纂) became drunk,
and rode in a *bù wǎn chē* (步輓車).
A *bù wǎn chē* (步輓車) does not use oxen, horses, or sheep, etc.,
but requires people to pull it on foot.
In the *Wèi Shū Lǐ Zhì* (魏書禮志): a *bù wǎn chē* (步輓車) is for the emperor's minor carriage,
also served as a secondary carriage.
*Jiāng* (將),
as written.
The carriage could not pass.
Zuǎn's (纂) personal guards Dòu Chuān (竇川) and Luò Téng (駱騰) leaned their swords against the wall
and pushed the carriage through the gate.
Chāo (超) took a sword and struck Zuǎn (纂).
Zuǎn (纂) got out of the carriage to seize Chāo (超),
but Chāo (超) stabbed Zuǎn (纂), piercing his chest.
Chuān (川) and Téng (騰) fought with Chāo (超),
and Chāo (超) killed them.
Empress Yáng (楊氏) ordered the imperial guards to suppress Chāo (超).
Dù Shàng (杜尚) stopped them.
Chāo's (超) alliance with Shàng (尚)
likely involved a secret agreement.
Jiāngjūn Wèi Yìduō (將軍魏益多) entered
and took Zuǎn's (纂) head.
Yáng Shì (楊氏) said:
"The man is already dead,
like earth and stone,
knowing nothing more.
How can you bear to further mutilate his remains!"
Yìduō (益多) cursed her
and then took Zuǎn's (纂) head to display it, proclaiming:
"Zuǎn (纂) defied the orders of the former emperor,
killed the crown prince and enthroned himself.
Details can be found in the third year of the previous volume.
Fānhé Tàishǒu Chāo (番禾太守超), following the will of the people, eliminated him
to secure the imperial ancestral temple.
All you officers and commoners,
share in this joyful celebration!"
Zuǎn's paternal uncle, the Duke of Bāxī, Tuó,
and his younger brother, the Duke of Lǒngxī, Wěi, were both in the northern city.
Someone persuaded Wěi, saying:
"Chāo is committing rebellion.
As the Duke's younger brother,
Dù Yù said: 'Jiè'
means 'great'.
'Shuō'
is read 'shū ruì fān';
same below.
Jiāng Jì and Jiāo Biàn are in the southern city,
Yáng Huán and Tián Chéng are in the eastern park,
all are our partisans.
What concern is there that we will not succeed!"
Wěi prepared his troops, intending to join Tuó in attacking Chāo.
Tuó's wife, Lady Liáng, stopped him, saying:
"Wěi and Chāo are both sons of brothers.
Why abandon Chāo to assist Wěi,
and bring disaster upon ourselves?"
Tuó then said to Wěi:
"Chāo's undertaking is already complete.
He occupies the arsenal
and commands elite troops.
It would be very difficult to plan against him.
Moreover, I am old,
and incapable of doing anything."
Chāo's younger brother, Miǎo, was favored by Wěi.
He persuaded Wěi, saying:
"Zuǎn murdered his brothers,
meaning he killed Shào and also killed Hóng.
'Shuō'
is read 'shū ruì fān'.
He merely wishes to enthrone Your Illustrious Lord.
Currently, Your Illustrious Lord is the eldest son of the former emperor;
you should preside over the altars of soil and grain.
No one has any other aspirations.
What further doubt is there?"
Wěi believed him,
and thereupon allied with Lóng and Chāo.
He entered the city alone on horseback;
Chāo seized and killed him.
Chāo offered the throne to Lóng,
but Lóng showed signs of reluctance.
Chāo said:
"Now is like riding a dragon to ascend to heaven;
how can one stop halfway?"
Lóng then assumed the position of Heavenly King.
Lóng,
courtesy name Yǒngjī,
was the son of Guāng's younger brother, Bǎo.
He changed the era name to Shéndǐng.
Chāo had previously obtained a small tripod at Fānhé,
considering it a divine omen,
hence he named the era after it.
His wife, Lady Yáng, was made empress.
Chāo was appointed Grand Commander of All Military Affairs Inside and Outside, Auxiliary Grand General, and Overseer of the Affairs of the Department of State Affairs.
He was enfeoffed as the Duke of Āndìng.
Zuǎn was posthumously granted the title of Emperor Líng.
Empress Yáng, Zuǎn's empress, was about to leave the palace.
Chāo feared she might take precious treasures,
and ordered her searched.
Lady Yáng said:
"You brothers are unrighteous,
slaughtering each other with your own hands.
I am a person who will die any day now;
what use are treasures to me!"
Chāo then asked where the imperial seal was.
Lady Yáng said:
"It has already been destroyed."
The empress was beautiful;
Chāo intended to take her as his concubine.
He said to her father, the Right Director of the Department of State Affairs, Huán:
"If the empress kills herself,
disaster will befall your clan!"
Huán told Lady Yáng.
Lady Yáng said:
"My lord sold his daughter to the Dī for wealth and honor;
once is too much,
how can there be a second time!"
This quotes from the Zuǒ Zhuàn.
She was posthumously granted the title of Empress Mù.
Huán fled to Lìlùgū, the King of Héxī,
who made him Left Grand Marshal.
5 In the third month,
Sūn Ēn went north to Hǎiyán.
Hǎiyán County was originally Wǔyuán Township.
Qín made it Hǎiyán County.
Under Hàn, it belonged to Kuàijī Commandery.
Later Hàn and Jìn, it belonged to Wú Commandery.
It is now eighty *lǐ* southeast of Xiùzhōu.
'Qù'
is read 'qī yù fān'.
He built a city at the old seat of Hǎiyán.
Ēn attacked the city daily,
but Yù repeatedly defeated him,
beheading his general Yáo Shèng.
The city's forces were few and could not match him.
Yù concealed his flags and hid his troops at night,
then opened the gates the next morning,
sending a few weak and sick people to ascend the city wall.
The bandits asked from a distance where Liú Yù was.
They said,
"He fled last night."
The bandits believed them and
rushed into the city.
Yù fought fiercely and
severely defeated them.
Ēn knew the city could not be captured,
so he advanced towards Hùdú.
Yù again abandoned the city and pursued him.
Bāo Lòu, the Magistrate of Hǎiyán, sent his son Sìzhī to lead a thousand Wú soldiers,
requesting to be the vanguard.
Yù said:
"The bandit troops are very elite,
and the Wú people are not accustomed to fighting.
If the vanguard suffers a defeat,
it will certainly ruin our army.
You can be in the rear to make a show of force."
Sìzhī did not comply.
Yù then hid many flags and drums.
When the vanguard engaged,
all the hidden troops emerged.
Yù raised his flag and beat his drums,
making the bandits think there were armies on all four sides,
so they retreated.
Sìzhī pursued them and
was killed in battle.
Yù fought and retreated,
his remaining troops almost completely dead or wounded.
When he reached the previous battle site,
he ordered his attendants to strip clothes from the dead to show an appearance of leisure.
The bandits became suspicious
and dared not press on.
Yù shouted loudly and fought again,
and the bandits, fearing him, retreated.
Yù then led his troops back.
6 Lìlùgū, the King of Héxī, attacked Liáng,
fought with Lóng, the King of Liáng,
severely defeated him,
and relocated over two thousand households before returning.
7 In summer,
in the fourth month,
on the day Xīnmǎo,

The Wèi established the Yè Traveling Secretariat,

Wèi's Xiàngzhōu administered six commanderies: Wèi Commandery, Yángpíng, Guǎngpíng, Jí Commandery, Dùnqiū, and Qīnghé.

8 Qǐfú Gān'guī arrived at Yuànchuān.
