9 Yè, the King of Northern Liáng, feared Jǔqú Méngxùn's bravery and strategy
and wished to keep him at a distance.
Méngxùn also deeply concealed himself.
Yè replaced Méngxùn as Governor of Zhāngyè with Mǎ Quán, the Palace Gentleman.
Quán was always arrogant and outstanding,
highly favored and respected by Yè,
and he often slighted and insulted Méngxùn.
Méngxùn slandered him to Yè, saying:
"There is no need to worry about the empire;
one should only worry about Mǎ Quán."
Yè then killed Quán.
In my opinion,
Suǒ Sì and Mǎ Quán were both mediocre men.
Relying on their family wealth and status, they acted arrogantly,
but were incapable of achieving anything.
Méngxùn said to Jǔqú Nánchéng:
"Duke Duàn lacks the talent for discernment and decision.
'Jiàn'
means 'clear';
'duàn'
means 'decisive'.
'Duàn'
is read 'dīng luàn fān'.
Previously, the only ones we feared were Suǒ Sì and Mǎ Quán.
Now they are both dead.
Suǒ Sì's death is mentioned in the previous volume, 4th year.
What do you think?"
Nánchéng said:
"Yè was originally an isolated guest,
established by our family.
He relies on our brothers like a fish relies on water.
To plot against someone who trusts us,
is inauspicious."
Méngxùn then requested to be made Governor of Xī'ān.
Yè was pleased by his departure to an outer post
and granted his request.
Jǔqú Méngxùn and Nánchéng arranged to offer sacrifices together at Lánménshān,
but Méngxùn secretly sent Sīmǎ Xǔ Xián to inform Duàn Yè, saying:
“Nánchéng intends to use the holiday as an opportunity for rebellion.
If he seeks to sacrifice at Lánménshān,
my words will be proven true.”
When the appointed day arrived,
it was indeed so.
Duàn Yè arrested Nánchéng and granted him death.
Nánchéng said:
“Méngxùn first conspired with me to rebel.
Out of brotherly affection,
I kept silent.
Now, with me still alive,
he fears that his subordinates will not follow him,
so he arranged for me to sacrifice at the mountain and then falsely accused me.
His intention is for Your Majesty to kill me.
I beg Your Majesty to falsely announce my death,
exposing my alleged crimes.
Méngxùn will surely rebel,
and then I will obey Your Majesty's command and suppress him.
There will be no failure.”
Duàn Yè did not listen
and killed him.
Méngxùn wept and told the衆:
“Nánchéng was loyal to King Duàn,
but King Duàn wrongfully killed him without cause.
Can you gentlemen avenge him?
Moreover, we initially established King Duàn
merely to bring peace to the衆.
Now the province is in chaos,
which King Duàn cannot rectify.”
Nánchéng had always won the hearts of the衆,
so all the衆 were indignant, weeping and eager to fight.
By the time they reached Dīchí,
Dīchí County,
during the Hàn dynasty, belonged to Zhāngyè Commandery.
During the Jìn dynasty, it was abolished,
and its territory belonged to the region of Gānzhōu and Zhāngyè County in the Táng dynasty.
Bǐ,
pronounced bì mèi,
means “to reach.”
Dī,

assaulting Lìngzhī.
On the day Yǐchǒu,
Yàn's Zhōnglǐngjūn Yǔwén Bá rescued it.
On the day Rénwǔ,
Sù Dá Gān captured Lìngzhī and garrisoned it.
Lǚ Chāo attacked Jiāng Jì but failed to overcome him.
He then attacked Jiāo Lǎng.
Jiāng Jì at that time held Yànrán,
and Jiāo Lǎng held Wèi'ān.
Lì Lùgū dispatched Chēqí Jiāngjūn Nǔtán to assist them.
By the time Nǔtán arrived,
Lǚ Chāo had already retreated,
and Jiāo Lǎng had closed his gates and refused to admit them.
Nǔtán was angered
and intended to attack him.
Zhènběi Jiāngjūn Jù Yán admonished:
"Settling in one's native land and being reluctant to move
is a normal human sentiment.
Jiāo Lǎng's isolated city has no food;
if he does not surrender this year,
he will submit of his own accord the year after next.
Why must we kill many soldiers to attack him?
If we do not succeed,
he will certainly leave and follow another state.
Abandoning the common people in the prefectural borders to benefit a neighboring enemy
is not a good plan.
It is better to persuade him with kind words."
Nǔtán then made peace with Jiāo Lǎng
and subsequently displayed his forces at Gūzāng,
encamping at Húténg.
Húténg is west of Gūzāng.
Nǔtán knew that Lǚ Chāo would surely come to raid his camp,
and stockpiled fire to await him.
That night, Lǚ Chāo sent Zhōnglěi Jiāngjūn Wáng Jí to lead two thousand elite soldiers to raid Nǔtán's camp.
Nǔtán calmly made preparations but did not rise.
When Wáng Jí entered the stockade,
fires were lit both inside and outside,
illuminating the area as if it were day.
Nǔtán unleashed his soldiers to attack them,
beheading Wáng Jí and over three hundred armored heads.
Lǚ Lóng, in fear,
feigned goodwill with Nǔtán,
inviting him to form an alliance within the imperial park.
Nǔtán sent Jù Yán to enter the alliance.
Jù Yán suspected an ambush
and breached the park wall to enter.
Lǚ Chāo's hidden troops attacked him.
Jù Yán lost his horse and fled on foot.
Língjiāng Jiāngjūn Guō Zǔ fought bravely to resist them,
and only then did Jù Yán escape.
Nǔtán was enraged
and attacked Lǚ Lóng's Chāngsōng Administrator Mèng Yī at Xiǎnměi.
Chāngsōng and Xiǎnměi
were both counties belonging to Wǔwēi Prefecture during the Hàn and Jìn dynasties.
Lǚ Guāng changed Chāngsōng to Dōngzhāngyè Prefecture,
then later restored it to Chāngsōng Prefecture.
The Wǔdài Zhì states that
the Later Zhōu abolished Xiǎnměi and merged it into Gūzāng.
The character `禕`
is pronounced *yī*.
Ānguó and Níngyuǎn Jiāngjūn Shí Kě led five hundred cavalry to rescue him.
Ānguó and the others, intimidated by Nǔtán's strength,
fled back.
Huán Xuán memorialized for his elder brother Wěi to be Jiangzhou Inspector,
stationed at Xiàkǒu.
Sīmǎ Diāo Chàng was made Fǔguó Jiāngjūn and Inspector of military affairs of eight prefectures,
stationed at Xiāngyáng.
He sent his generals Huángfǔ Fū and Féng Gāi to garrison Pénhuá.
He moved two thousand households of the Jǔ and Zhāng barbarian tribes to the south of the river.
The Zuǒ Zhuàn states: The Jiāng, Hàn, Jǔ, and Zhāng rivers
were the hope of Chǔ.
The Shuǐ Jīng states: The Jǔ River originates in Fánglíng, Hánzhōng,
flows southeast past the border of Línjǔ,
then east past Zhījiāng County,
and enters the Jiāng to the south.
The Zhāng River originates in Jīngshān, east of Línjǔ County,
and flows south to the north of Zhījiāng County, entering the Jǔ.
Both rivers, upstream and downstream, were inhabited by barbarians.
The character `沮`
is pronounced *jǔ*.
The character `漳`
is pronounced *zhāng*.
He further recruited displaced people
and established Suí'ān Prefecture.
Suí'ān Prefecture
was governed from Chángníng County.
The Suí dynasty abolished Chángníng and merged it into Chánglín.
Huán Xuán kept them all and did not send them away.
Huán Xuán considered himself to possess two-thirds of the territory of the Jìn state.
He repeatedly sent people to present auspicious omens to himself,
intending to confuse the masses.
He also sent a letter to Kuàijī Wáng Dàozǐ saying:
"The bandits reached the near suburbs,
but the wind prevented them from advancing,
the rain prevented them from setting fires.
Their provisions ran out, so they departed;
it was not due to a lack of strength.
After Guóbǎo's death,
Wáng Gōng did not use this prestige to take control of court affairs,
which clearly shows that his intention was not to insult Your Highness,
yet he was called disloyal.
Among the current important and trusted officials,
who are the ones with pure and renowned reputations?
How can one say there are no excellent and outstanding individuals?
It is simply that they cannot be trusted!
The people of Jiāngdōng
whose positions were prominent at the time
were generally referred to as *jiāshèng* (excellent talents) and *míngshèng* (renowned talents).
This ultimately led to today's disaster.
*Ěrlái*
means 'since then.'
I, Xuán, hold a distant post,
and thus I write down the facts."
Yuánxiǎn saw this
and was greatly frightened.
Zhāng Fǎshùn said to Yuánxiǎn:
“Huán Xuán, relying on his family’s inherited resources,
has always possessed a heroic spirit.
Now that he has annexed Yīn and Yáng,
he solely possesses Jīng-Chǔ.
Yīn and Yáng
refer to Yīn Zhòngkān and Yáng Quánqī.
The matter of annexing Yīn and Yáng is detailed in the previous volume, Long’ān 3rd year.
‘Dì’ (第)
means ‘mansion’ or ‘residence’;
‘Dìxià’ (第下)
is akin to ‘Ménxià’ (門下) or ‘Géxià’ (閤下).
The eastern lands are devastated,
both public and private sectors are exhausted.
Xuán will certainly take advantage of this to unleash his treacherous cruelty,
which causes me deep worry.”
Yuánxiǎn said:
“What should we do about it?”
Fǎshùn said:
“When Xuán first obtained Jīngzhōu,
the people’s sentiments were not yet attached to him.
He is currently busy pacifying and comforting them,
and has no time for other schemes.
If we take advantage of this opportunity and make Liú Láozhī the vanguard,
and then Your Excellency follows up with a large army,
Xuán can be captured.”
Yuánxiǎn thought this was correct.
At that time, Yǔ Kǎi, the Administrator of Wǔchāng, fearing that Xuán’s conflict with the imperial court
would not succeed
and disaster would befall him,
Yǔ Kǎi’s submission to Huán Xuán is found in volume 110, Long’ān 2nd year.
said,
“Xuán has greatly lost popular support;
the masses will not serve him.
If the imperial court sends troops,
I will serve as an internal respondent.”
Yuánxiǎn was greatly pleased.
He dispatched Zhāng Fǎshùn to Jīngkǒu
to deliberate with Liú Láozhī;
Láozhī deemed it difficult.
Fǎshùn returned
and said to Yuánxiǎn:
“Judging by Láozhī’s words and demeanor,
he will surely betray us.
It would be better to summon and kill him;
otherwise,
he will ruin our great undertaking.”
Yuánxiǎn did not agree.
Thereupon, a large naval force was prepared,
troops were conscripted, and ships were outfitted
to plan the campaign against Xuán.
Yuánxīng 1st year (Rén-yín, 402 CE)
1 Spring,
1st month.
Gēngwǔ day (new moon).
In the 3rd month of this year,
Yuánxiǎn was defeated,
the Long’ān reign title was restored,
Huán Xuán subsequently changed it to Dàhēng,
and when Xuán usurped,
he again changed it to Yǒngshǐ.
The change to Yuánxīng 1st year occurred in the 1st month of this year.
From this year until the beginning of Yìxī,
the Zīzhì Tōngjiàn consistently uses Yuánxīng 1st year,
not altering it to acknowledge Huán Xuán’s usurpation,
in order to correct the chaotic era.

The President of the Department of State Affairs, Yuánxiǎn, was appointed General-in-Chief of Cavalry, Grand Commander of the Punitive Expedition, Overall Commander of Military Affairs of Eighteen Provinces, and granted the Yellow Axe.
At that time, the territory of Jìn comprised only the eighteen provinces of Yáng, Xú, Nánxú, Yǎn, Nányǎn, Yù, Nányù, Qīng, Jì, Sī, Jīng, Jiāng, Yōng, Liáng, Yì, Níng, Jiāo, and Guǎng.
Yuánxiǎn commanded all of them.
If he had successfully executed Huán Xuán,
he would certainly have overridden the emperor and usurped the throne.
'Piào' (驃),
pronounced 'piǎo' (pǐmiào).
pronounced 'qí' (qíjì).
The Prince of Qiáo, Shàngzhī, was appointed Commander of the Rear Guard.
Due to a general amnesty,
the reign title was changed,
and internal and external alerts were heightened.
The Prince of Kuàijī, Dàozǐ, was additionally appointed Grand Tutor.
Yuánxiǎn intended to execute all of the Huán clan.
The Central Protector-General, Huán Xiū,
was the nephew of Wáng Dàn, the Chief Clerk to the General-in-Chief of Cavalry.
Dàn was favored by Yuánxiǎn,
and on his behalf, he explained that Xiū and others held different aspirations from Xuán.
Yuánxiǎn then stopped.
Dàn
was the great-grandson of Dàozhī.
Zhāng Fǎshùn spoke to Yuánxiǎn, saying:
“Huán Qiān and his brothers are always spies for the upstream.
It is advisable to execute them to prevent their treacherous schemes.
Moreover, the success of the undertaking
depends on the vanguard,
but Láozhī is fickle.
Should there be any unexpected turn of events,
disaster and defeat would be immediate.
You could order Láozhī to kill Qiān and his brothers to demonstrate his loyalty.
If he does not obey the command,
we should preemptively act against him.”
“Preemptively act against him”
means to plan ahead before disaster strikes,
intending to kill Láozhī.
“Currently, without Láozhī,
there is no one to rival Xuán;
furthermore, to execute a grand general at the outset of the campaign
would unsettle public sentiment.”
He firmly refused a third time.
Fǎshùn spoke with Yuánxiǎn repeatedly,
but he ultimately deemed it unacceptable.
Huán Chōng had left behind a special benevolence,
and Qiān
was Chōng’s son.
Therefore, Qiān was appointed from Cavalry Sīmǎ to Overall Commander of Military Affairs of the four provinces of Jīng, Yì, Níng, and Liáng, and Governor of Jīngzhōu,
intending to win over the people of the west.
2 Dīngchǒu day,
Yàn’s Mùróng Bá attacked Wèi’s Lìngzhī outpost,
capturing it.
Sù Tádgān fled,
and Wèi’s Administrator of Liáoxī, Nàxié, was captured.
Yàn appointed Bá as Governor of Yōuzhōu,
garrisoned at Lìngzhī,
and appointed the Central Valiant General, Yáng Háo of Liáoxī, as Administrator of his home commandery.
Dīnghài day,
Yuān, the Duke of Zhāngwǔ, was appointed President of the Department of State Affairs;
Qián, the Duke of Bólíng, was appointed Left Assistant of the Department of State Affairs;
and Wáng Téng, a Secretary, was appointed Right Assistant.
3 Wùzǐ day,
Wèi’s Artisan-in-Chief, Hé Tū, attacked the various tribes of Chùfú and Sùgǔyán,
defeating them.
Previously,
Wèi’s lord Guī had sent Hè Dígān, the Northern Adult, to offer a thousand horses and seek marriage with Qín.
Qín’s king Xīng, hearing that Guī had already made Mùróng empress,
The matter of establishing Mùróng as empress is found in the previous volume, Long’ān 4th year.
Mòyìgān, Chùfú, and Sùgǔyán
were all tributary states of Qín,
but Wèi attacked them.
Consequently, Qín and Wèi had a rift.
Gēngyín day,
Guī conducted a grand review of his soldiers and horses,
and ordered the various commanderies of Bīngzhōu to store grain at Gānbì in Píngyáng in preparation for Qín.
According to the Wèi Shōu Dìxíng Zhì,
Píngyáng’s Qínchāng county
was the Běiqū of Hàn and Jìn,
and had Gānchéng.
The Suí dynasty merged Qínchāng into Xiānglíng.
Also, according to Yáo Xīng’s biography,
Gānbì is Gānchéng.
Rourán’s Shèlún was currently friendly with Qín,
and sent generals to rescue Chùfú and Sùgǔyán;
Xīnmǎo day,
Hé Tū met and attacked them,
greatly defeating them.
Shèlún led his tribes far away to the desert north,
seizing the land of Gāochē and settling there.
Húlü Lù Bù’s commander Bèihóulì attacked Shèlún,
and was greatly defeated by him.
Bèihóulì fled to Wèi.
Shèlún then attacked the remaining Xiongnu tribe of Rìbáyějī in the northwest,
greatly defeating them,
and subsequently annexed various tribes.
His soldiers and horses became numerous and powerful,
dominating the north.
His territory extended west to Yānqí,
east to Cháoxiǎn,
and south to the Great Desert.
The surrounding small states all became his dependencies;
he styled himself Dòudài Kèhán.
The Wèi Shū writes it as
“Qiūdòudài”,
which in Wèi language means 'to govern and expand'.
Hán (汗),
pronounced 'hán'.
Dù Yòu said: The title of Kèhán originated with Rourán’s Shèlún,
akin to calling oneself emperor.
However, the ancestors of the Tuòbá clan
are all referred to as Kèhán in the Zīzhì Tōngjiàn,
and this was also before Shèlún.
He organized a thousand men into a ‘jūn’ (軍),
with a general (jiàng) for each jūn;
a hundred men into a ‘chuáng’ (幢),
with a commander (shuài) for each chuáng.
The jūn generals and chuáng commanders
were both Wèi institutions,
which Shèlún presumably emulated.
Jiāng (將),
pronounced 'jiàng' (jiàng, lìang).
Chuáng (幢),
pronounced 'chuáng' (tázjiāng).
Shuài (帥),
pronounced 'shuài' (suǒlèi).
Those who were timid and cowardly were killed by having rocks thrown at their heads.
Rourán’s trouble for Wèi began from this point.
4 Tūfà Nǔtán conquered Xiǎnměi,
seized Mèng Yī and blamed him for not surrendering earlier.
Tūfà Nǔtán had attacked Xiǎnměi since last year,
and only now conquered it.
"Yī received great kindness from the Lǚ clan,
receiving a tally and guarding territory;
if your illustrious lord's grand army had just arrived,
and I had looked at your banner and submitted,
I fear I would have incurred guilt with my superiors."
Nǔtán released him and treated him with respect,
resettled over two thousand households, and returned,
appointing Yī as Zuǒ Sīmǎ.
Yī declined, saying:
"The Lǚ clan is about to perish,
and the Sacred Dynasty will surely take the region west of the Yellow River.
Everyone, intelligent or foolish, knows this.
But I, Yī, failed to fully defend the city I was guarding,
and now to again take a prominent position,
my heart secretly feels uneasy about this.
If I receive your illustrious lord's favor,
and am allowed to be executed in Gūzāng,
I shall die without regret."
Nǔtán respected his integrity and sent him back.
5 The eastern lands suffered from Sūn Ēn's rebellion,
and consequently from famine,
with grain transport cut off.
Huán Xuán blocked the Yangtze River route,
causing scarcity for both public and private sectors.
He fed his soldiers with acorns and oak nuts.
Xuán believed that the imperial court was currently plagued by many worries,
and would not yet have leisure to attack him,
so he could accumulate strength and observe opportunities.
When the grand army was about to set out,
his cousin Tàifù Chángshǐ Shí Shēng secretly informed him by letter;
Xuán was greatly alarmed,
and wanted to gather his forces in Jiānglíng.
Chángshǐ Biàn Fànzhī said:
"Your illustrious lord's heroic might shakes far and near.
Yuánxiǎn still has the smell of milk in his mouth,
and Liú Láozhī has greatly lost popular support.
If our troops approach the capital region,
and we demonstrate the consequences of good and ill fortune,
the collapse of the enemy can be awaited with anticipation.
Why would we allow the enemy to enter our borders,
and bring ourselves to a desperate situation?"
Xuán followed his advice,
left Huán Wěi to guard Jiānglíng,
sent up a memorial and issued a proclamation,
listing Yuánxiǎn's crimes,
and marched his army eastward.
When the proclamation arrived,
Yuánxiǎn was greatly afraid.
In the second month,
on the day Bǐngwǔ,
the Emperor saw Yuánxiǎn off at the West Pond;
Yuánxiǎn boarded the boat but did not depart.
Yuánxiǎn feared Huán Xuán internally,
thus he boarded the boat but did not depart.
6 On the day Guǐchǒu,
Wèi Chángshān Wáng Zūn and others arrived at Gāopíng.
In the twelfth month of last year,
Wèi sent Zūn and others to attack Gāopíng,
and they arrived at this time.
He led several thousand cavalry and fled with Liú Bóbó to Qínzhōu.
Qínzhōu was governed from Shàngguī.
Shuài,
read as shuài.
Qí,
read as qí jì fān.
They did not catch up and returned,
seizing all of their official treasuries and stored wealth,
over forty thousand horses,
and over ninety thousand miscellaneous livestock.
They resettled their people in the capital of Dài.
Wèi made Píngchéng the capital of Dài.
Píngyáng Tàishǒu Èr Chén again invaded Qín Hédōng.
Xìngpǔ: During the Spring and Autumn period, there were the two states of Èr and Zhěn.
Later, both became surnames.
The Èr of Èr Chén
is thus a barbarian surname.
Fù,
read as fú yòu fān.
The cities in Guānzhōng closed their gates during the day.
The Qín people selected soldiers and trained troops to plan an attack on Wèi.
7 Qín Wáng Xīng appointed his son Hóng as crown prince,
and issued a general amnesty.
Hóng was filial and friendly, broad-minded and harmonious,
fond of literature,
and skilled in conversation and poetry,
but he was weak and often ill;
Xīng wanted to make him his heir,
but was hesitant and indecisive,
only appointing him after a long time.
This foreshadows Yáo Hóng's weakness leading to the downfall of Qín.
8 Gūzāng suffered a great famine,
a dou of rice cost five thousand cash,
people ate each other,
and over a hundred thousand people starved to death.
City gates were closed during the day,
and the paths for gathering firewood were cut off.
Hundreds of people daily requested to leave the city to become slaves to the Hú barbarians.
Lǚ Lóng, displeased that they were demoralizing the populace,
buried them all alive,
with corpses piling up along the roads.
Júqú Méngxùn led his troops to attack Gūzāng.
Lóng sent an envoy to seek aid from Héxī Wáng Lìlùgū.
Lìlùgū sent Guǎngwǔ Gōng Nǔtán to lead ten thousand cavalry to rescue him;
before he arrived,
Lóng defeated Méngxùn's army.
Méngxùn requested to make an alliance with Lóng,
left over ten thousand hu of grain for him, and returned.
Nǔtán arrived at Chāngsōng,
heard that Méngxùn had already retreated,
then resettled over five hundred households of the Duàn family from Liángzé and returned.
Liángzé is the Zhūyě Zé of Yǔgòng,
east of Wǔwēi County,
also called Xiūtú Zé.
Huán,
read as cóng xuān fān.
Zhōng Sànjì Chángshì Zhāng Róng spoke to Lìlùgū, saying:
Sàn,
read as xī dǎn fān.
Qí,
read as qí jì fān.
"Jiāo Lǎng and his brothers hold Wèi'ān,
secretly communicating with the Yáo clan,
repeatedly being treacherous.
If we do not take them now,
they will surely become a concern for the imperial court later."
Lìlùgū sent Nǔtán to attack them,
and Lǎng came out with his hands bound and surrendered.
Jiāo Lǎng used Wèi'ān to attract Qín forces;
the matter is mentioned in May of last year.
Jiàng,
read as hù jiāng fān;
same below.
He resettled their people in Lèdū.
9 Huán Xuán departed from Jiānglíng,
fearing that his campaign might not succeed,
and constantly planned for a return to the west;
but when he passed Xúnyáng,
and saw no government troops,
he was very pleased,
and the morale of his generals and soldiers also rose.
Historians say that Huán Xuán was timid,
and Liú Láozhī and others were unable to rely on righteousness to defeat him.
Jiàng,
read as jí liàng fān;
same below.
Yǔ Kǎi's plot was discovered,
and Xuán imprisoned him.
On the day Dīngsì,
an imperial edict was issued, sending Qí Wáng Róuzhī with a Zōuyú banner to announce to Jīng and Jiāng provinces
to cease hostilities;
Xuán's vanguard killed him.
Róuzhī was the son of Zōngzhī.
In the tenth year of Xiàowǔ Tàiyuán,
Róuzhī inherited the title of Qí Wáng,
continuing the sacrifices to Yōu and Jiǒng;
Zōng was enfeoffed as Nándùn Wáng.
On the day Dīngmǎo,
Xuán arrived at Gūshú,
and ordered his general Féng Gāi and others to attack Lìyáng.
The Yùzhōu Cìshǐ was governed from Lìyáng.
Xuán's army cut off Dòngpǔ.
Dòngpǔ is Dòngkǒu,
where Wèi Cáoxīu defeated Lǚ Fàn.
Duàn,
read as dīng guǎn fān.
Yùzhōu Cìshǐ Qiáo Wáng Shàngzhī led nine thousand infantry to array themselves on the bank of the Pǔ,
and sent Wǔdū Tàishǒu Yáng Qiū to garrison Héngjiāng.
Qiū surrendered to Xuán's army.
Shàngzhī's forces disintegrated,
and he fled along the road to Tú.
Xuán captured him.
Tú,
same as Chú.
He abandoned the city and fled.
Liú Láozhī had long disliked Piàojì Dàjiāngjūn Yuánxiǎn,
fearing that once Huán Xuán was destroyed,
Yuánxiǎn would become even more arrogant and unrestrained,
and also fearing that his own accomplishments and fame would grow,
making him intolerable to Yuánxiǎn;
moreover, relying on his own talent and military prowess,
and commanding a strong army,
he wanted to use Xuán to remove the powerful officials,
and then await Xuán's weakness to seize power himself,
thus he was unwilling to attack Xuán.
Yuánxiǎn was drunk and muddled day and night,
appointing Láozhī as the vanguard.
Láozhī frequently visited his gate,
but could not be seen,
and when the Emperor went out to see Yuánxiǎn off,
he merely met him in a public setting.
Láo Zhī's army was stationed at Lìzhōu.
His staff officer, Liú Yù, requested to attack Xuán,
but Láo Zhī refused.
Xuán sent Láo Zhī's maternal uncle, Hé Mù, to persuade Láo Zhī, saying:
"From ancient times until now, of those who have held the might of the ruler,
wielding unrewarded merits, yet been able to preserve themselves,
who were they?
Wén Zhǒng of Yuè,
Bái Qǐ of Qín,
Hán Xìn of Hàn,
all served enlightened lords,
giving their utmost strength for them.
On the day their achievements were complete,
they still could not escape execution.
How much more so when employed by a savage and foolish person!
If you win the battle today, your clan will be overthrown;
if you lose, your family will be destroyed.
Where do you intend to return with this?
It would be better to change your plans decisively,
then you can long preserve wealth and nobility.
Ancient people who shot a belt hook or cut off a sleeve
were still not hindered from serving as assistants.
Qí Huán Gōng contended with Zǐ Jiū for the state,
and Guǎn Zhòng shot Huán Gōng, hitting his belt hook.
Zǐ Jiū died,
and Huán Gōng released Guǎn Zhòng from prison and made him his prime minister.
Jìn Xiàn Gōng sent the eunuch Pī to attack Gōngzǐ Chóng'ěr in Púchéng.
Chóng'ěr climbed over the wall and fled,
and Pī cut off his sleeve.
When Chóng'ěr returned to the state,
Pī repeatedly offered loyal advice."
*Shè*
and *yì fān*.
At this time, Qiáo Wáng Shàng Zhī had already been defeated,
and people's fears intensified.
Láo Zhī somewhat accepted Mù's words
and communicated with Xuán.
Hétú Zhōngwèi, Hé Wú Jì of Dōnghǎi,
who was Láo Zhī's nephew,
strongly advised against it with Liú Yù,
but Láo Zhī did not listen.
His son, Pàixí Cóngshì Zhōngláng Jìng Xuān, advised him, saying:
"Now the state is in decline and danger,
and the fate of the empire rests with you, my lord, and Xuán.
Xuán, relying on his father's and uncle's resources,
(Xuán's father was Wēn,
and his uncle was Chōng.)
carved out two-thirds of the state of Jìn.
If you let him dominate the court for a single day,
Xuán's prestige will be established,
and I fear he will be difficult to deal with.
The chaos of Dǒng Zhuó
will happen now."
(The affair of Dǒng Zhuó can be found in Volume 59, during the sixth year of Zhōngpíng of Emperor Líng of Hàn and the first year of Chūpíng of Emperor Xiàn.)
Láo Zhī said: "How could I not know!
Today, taking Xuán would be as easy as turning over one's hand;
but after pacifying Xuán,
what would I do about Pàixí?"
(Yuánxiǎn was Pàixí Jiāngjūn,
hence the reference.)
On the day *Yǐsì*,
Láo Zhī sent Jìng Xuān to Xuán to request surrender.
Xuán secretly intended to execute Láo Zhī,
so he feasted and drank with Jìng Xuān,
displaying famous calligraphy and paintings for them to admire together,
to soothe and please him.
Jìng Xuān did not realize this,
but none of Xuán's subordinate officials failed to look at each other and smile.
Xuán appointed Jìng Xuān as Cíyì Cānjūn.
(There was no imperial edict yet,
so he was given the appointment by a plaque.)
Yuánxiǎn was about to set out
when he heard that Xuán had already reached Xīntíng.
He abandoned his boats
and retreated to camp at the Guózǐxuě.
On the day *Xīnwèi*,
he deployed his forces outside Xuānyáng Mén.
There was a panic in the army,
with rumors that Xuán had reached Nánháng.
Yuánxiǎn led his troops, intending to return to the palace.
Xuán sent people to draw their swords and shout loudly from behind:
"Lay down your arms!"
The soldiers all scattered.
Yuánxiǎn rode his horse into Dōngfǔ,
with only Zhāng Fǎshùn following him on a single horse.
Yuánxiǎn asked Dàozǐ for a plan,
but Dàozǐ merely wept in response.
Xuán sent Tàifù Cóngshì Zhōngláng Máo Tài to arrest Yuánxiǎn and send him to Xīntíng.
He was tied to the front of a boat and reprimanded.
Yuánxiǎn said:
"I was misled by Wáng Dàn and Zhāng Fǎshùn."
On the day *Rénshēn*,
the title of the reign, Lóng'ān, was reinstated.
The Emperor sent Shìzhōng Wáng Mì to console Xuán at Ānlè Zhǔ.
Xuán entered the capital,
claiming an imperial edict to lift the emergency.
He appointed Xuán as overall commander of all affairs,
Superintendent of All Military Affairs Inside and Outside the Capital, Cíngxiàng, Lù Shàngshūshì, Yángzhōu Mù, and governor of the three provinces of Xú, Jīng, and Jiāng,
and granted him the Yellow Battle-axe.
(At this time, Jìn controlled all of Jīng, Jiāng, and Yáng provinces.
Xúzhōu mostly consisted of relocated commanderies,
but Jīngkǒu was an important strategic point.
Xuán took command of all of these,
thus fully controlling the state of Jìn.
Moreover, he intended to seize Liú Láo Zhī's troops,
hence he took command of Xúzhōu to control him.)
Huán Qiān was made Shàngshū Zuǒpúyè.
Huán Xiū was made governor of Xú and Yǎn provinces.
Huán Shíshēng was made governor of Jiāng province.
Biàn Fànzhī was made Dānyáng Yǐn.
(Biàn Fànzhī was Xuán's chief secretary
and his main strategist.
Dānyáng was
the capital district,
hence he was made its Yǐn.)
Initially,
when Xuán raised his army,
Shìzhōng Wáng Mì, bearing an imperial edict, went to Xuán,
and Xuán treated him with personal courtesy.
When Xuán became regent,
he made Mì Zhongshū Lìng.
(Mì was
the grandson of Dǎo.)
Yīn Zhòngwén, the Administrator of Xīn'ān,
who was the younger brother of Jì,
(Yīn Jì is mentioned in Volume 109, first year of Lóng'ān.
*Jì*
is pronounced *jì*.)
heard that Xuán had conquered the capital.
He abandoned his commandery and defected to Xuán,
and Xuán made him Cíyì Cānjūn.
Liú Mài went to see Xuán,
and Xuán said:
"Are you not afraid of death,
that you dare to come?"
Mài replied:
"Shooting a belt hook and cutting off a sleeve,
add me and there are three."
Xuán was pleased
and made him Cānjūn.
(Liú Mài's confrontation with Xuán is found in Volume 108, seventeenth year of Tàiyuán of Emperor Xiàowǔ.)
On the day *Guǐyǒu*,
the officials memorialized that Kuàijī Wáng Dàozǐ was dissolute and unfilial,
and should be executed in the market.
An edict ordered him to be exiled to Ānchéng commandery.
(In the second year of Bǎodǐng of Sūn Hào of Wú,
Ānchéng commandery was established by dividing Yùzhāng, Chángshā, and Lúlíng.
Ānfú county of Táng Jízhōu and the counties of Yuánzhōu
were all its territory.
Liú Xù said: Ānfú county was
the seat of Wú's Ānchéng commandery.)
Yànzhāng,
Yuánxiǎn's son,
in the early Lóng'ān period,
was made to succeed the Prince of Dōnghǎi.
Huán Xiū strongly pleaded for Wáng Dàn,
who was
exiled to Lǐngnán.
Xuán appointed Liú Láo Zhī as Kuàijī Nèishǐ.
Láo Zhī said:
"Right from the start,
he is taking away my troops.
Disaster is upon us."
Liú Jìng Xuān requested to return and persuade Láo Zhī to accept the appointment,
and Xuán sent him.
Jìng Xuān urged Láo Zhī to attack Xuán,
but Láo Zhī hesitated and was indecisive.
He moved his camp to Bāndú.
(Bāndú was southwest of Xīnzhōu.)
Láo Zhī said to Liú Yù: "Today, I should go north to Gāo Yǎzhī in Guǎnglíng
and raise an army to restore the state.
Can you follow me?"
Yù replied:
"General, with tens of thousands of elite soldiers,
you surrendered at the mere sight of him.
He has just achieved his ambition,
and his prestige shakes the world.
The hearts of the court and the people have all abandoned us.
How can we possibly reach Guǎnglíng?
I will return to Jīngkǒu and resume my former attire."
(*Fǎnfú*
means to return to one's original attire.
*Lísāo* says: 'Retire and mend my former attire.'
This means taking off military attire and wearing civilian clothes.)
Láo Zhī said: "Where shall I go?"
Yù replied:
"I believe Zhènběi will surely not escape.
(Láo Zhī was promoted to Zhènběi Jiāngjūn for his achievements in suppressing Sūn Ēn.)
If Huán Xuán adheres to the duties of a minister,
I will serve him with you;
otherwise,
I will plan against him with you."
(At this time, Liú Yù already had the intention of executing Xuán.)
At this, Láo Zhī
assembled his staff in full, and deliberated occupying the north of the Yangtze River to attack Xuán.
Staff officer Liú Xí said,
"Among impossible things, nothing is greater than rebellion.
Last year, the general rebelled against King Yǎnzhōu
(King Yǎnzhōu
refers to Wáng Gōng)
and Sīmǎ Lángjūn
(refers to Yuánxiǎn).
One man rebelling three times,
how can he establish himself?"
After speaking,
he hurried out,
and many officials and staff scattered and fled.
Láo Zhī was afraid,
and sent Jìng Xuān to Jīngkǒu to fetch his family,
but he was delayed and did not arrive.
Láo Zhī thought that the matter had been exposed
and that he would be killed by Xuán,
so he led his troops north,
and upon reaching Xīnzhōu,
he hanged himself.
When Jìng Xuān arrived,
he had no time to mourn,
and immediately crossed the river to flee to Guǎnglíng.
The generals and officers jointly embalmed and interred Láo Zhī,
and brought his remains back to Dāntú.
Xuán ordered his coffin to be chopped and his head to be cut off,
and his body to be exposed in the marketplace.
(Bào
is pronounced bùbǔ fān,
and also as written.)
10 There was a general amnesty,
and the reign title was changed to Dàhēng.
11 Huán Xuán declined the positions of Chancellor and governors of Jīng, Jiāng, and Xú prefectures.
(Since Xuán had already appointed his brothers to govern Jīng, Jiāng, and Xú prefectures,
and had already obtained Jiànkāng,
holding the imperial power,
he no longer considered the position of Chancellor important,
hence he declined all of them.)
He took charge of all government affairs;
he appointed Lángyá Wáng Déwén as Grand Tutor.
12 Sīmǎ Xiūzhī, Liú Jìngxuān, and Gāo Yázhī all fled to Luòyáng,
each offering their sons and younger brothers as hostages to Qín in exchange for aid.
King Qín Xīng gave them tallies and credentials,
and sent them to Guānzhōng
to recruit soldiers.
They obtained several thousand men,
and returned to garrison in the area of Péngchéng.
13 Sūn Ēn attacked Línhǎi.
Xīn Jǐng, the Administrator of Línhǎi, defeated him.
The men and women from Sānwú captured by Ēn
were almost all dead.
Fearing that he would be captured by the government forces, Ēn
threw himself into the sea and died.
His followers and concubines who died with him numbered in the hundreds;
they were called
"Water Immortals."
The remaining several thousand followers then acclaimed Lú Xún, Ēn's brother-in-law, as their leader.
(Xún
was the great-grandson of Chén.
Lú Chén
was the son of Lú Zhì.
He initially followed Liú Kūn.
After Kūn's death,
he served under the Duàn clan.
When Duàn Liáo was defeated,
he served Zhào.)
(Chén
is pronounced shìrén fān.)
He possessed considerable talent and artistic skill.
When he was young,
the Buddhist monk Huìyuǎn once told him,
"Although you appear to be refined and simple,
your ambition is to act contrary to rule,
how can this be?"
Grand Commandant Xuán wished to pacify the eastern territories,
so he appointed Xún as the Administrator of Yǒngjiā.
(In the first year of Tàiníng of Emperor Míng,
Yǒngjiā Commandery was established by separating it from Línhǎi,
which is modern-day Wēnzhōu.)
But the banditry and violence did not cease.
This is the beginning of Lú Xún's affairs.
14 On the day Jiǎxū,
Yān granted a general amnesty.
15 Héxī King Tūfà Lìlùgū became seriously ill
and left an edict entrusting the affairs of the state to his younger brother Nǔtán.
(Initially,
Tūfà Sīfùjiān greatly loved and valued Nǔtán.
(Jiān
is pronounced jūyán fān.)
He told his sons,
"Nǔtán's capacity and discernment
are beyond what you all can achieve."
Therefore, his elder brothers did not transmit the rule to their sons but to their younger brother.
Wú Shòumèng considered his youngest son Jìzhá to be worthy,
so his sons and brothers transmitted the rule among themselves,
intending to eventually transmit the state to Jìzhá,
but Jìzhá ultimately refused to accept it.
Tūfà Wūgū and Lìlùgū transmitted the state to Nǔtán,
which is similar to the accounts in the Wú annals.
How could they know that the state would perish in Nǔtán's hands?
It was merely a matter of folding hands.
(Chuígǒng
means to fold one's hands and do nothing.)
Lìlùgū died,
and Nǔtán succeeded to the throne,
changing his title to King of Liáng. From then on, history refers to the Tūfà clan as Southern Liáng.
He moved to Yuèdū
and gave Lìlùgū the posthumous title King Kāng.
16 In the summer,
in the fourth month,
Grand Commandant Xuán moved his garrison to Gūshú
and resigned from the position of Director of the Department of State Affairs.
An edict granted his request;
however, all major government affairs were still referred to him for consultation,
while minor matters were decided by the Director of the Department of State Affairs Huán Qiān and Biàn Fànzhī.
Since the Luóng’ān era,
people both within and outside the capital were weary of the calamities and chaos.
When Xuán first arrived,
he dismissed corrupt and treacherous officials and promoted outstanding and virtuous individuals,
which made the capital rejoice,
hoping for a little peace.
However, Xuán soon became extravagant and indulgent,
his decrees were inconsistent,
factions rose against each other,
he insulted and oppressed the imperial court,
and cut down on the supplies and provisions for the emperor's carriage and attendants,
so much so that the emperor nearly suffered from hunger and cold.
Consequently, people's hearts were disappointed.
The Sānwú region suffered a great famine,
the population was halved,
Kuàijī lost three or four tenths,
and Línhǎi and Yǒngjiā were almost entirely depopulated.
Wealthy households, though dressed in fine silk
and carrying gold and jade,
locked their doors and starved to death.
This was indeed caused by the misgovernance of those in power,
but the decline of people and depletion of resources
was also a great destiny ordained by Heaven and Earth.
"The remaining people of Zhōu,
none were left";
viewing it this way,
it is possible that such things happened.
(Yī
is pronounced yújì fān.)
17 Qǐfú Chìpán escaped from Xīpíng and returned to Yuànchuān.
(Qǐfú Gān'guī sent Chìpán to Xīpíng,
see Volume 28, the fourth year of Lóng'ān.)
Qǐfú Gān'guī sent Chìpán to pay homage to Qín.
Lord Qín Xīng appointed Chìpán as the Administrator of Xīngjìn.
18 In the fifth month,
Lú Xún entered Dōngyáng from Línhǎi.
Grand Commandant Xuán dispatched Liú Yù, Staff Officer for the Central Army under the Pacifying General, to lead troops to attack him.
Xún was defeated
and fled to Yǒngjiā.
19 Gāogōulí attacked Sùjūn.
(The city of Sùjūn was northeast of Lóngchéng.)
(Gōu
is pronounced as written,
and also gōu.)
(Lí
is pronounced lìzhī fān.)
The Inspector of Píng Prefecture of Northern Yān governed Sùjūn.
20 Lord Qín Xīng extensively mobilized all armies,
sending Duke Yìyáng Píng, Right Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs Dí Bózhī, and others to lead forty thousand infantry and cavalry to attack Wèi.
Xīng himself led the main army to follow,
appointing Director of the Department of State Affairs Yáo Huàng to assist Crown Prince Hóng in defending Cháng'ān,
Mòyì Gàn to temporarily garrison Shàngguī,
and Duke Guǎnglíng Qīn to temporarily garrison Luòyáng.
Píng attacked Wèi's Gānbì for over sixty days
and captured it.
In the autumn,
in the seventh month,
Lord Wèi Guī sent Pílíng Wáng Shùn and Yù Prefecture Inspector Zhǎngsūn Féi to lead sixty thousand cavalry as the vanguard,
and himself led the main army to set forth to attack them.
21 In the eighth month,
Grand Commandant Xuán subtly suggested to the imperial court that he be enfeoffed as Duke of Yùzhāng for his meritorious service in pacifying Yuánxiǎn,
and as Duke of Guìyáng for his meritorious service in pacifying Yīn and Yáng,
with his original fiefdom of Nánjùn remaining as before.
Xuán enfeoffed his son Shēng with Yùzhāng
and his elder brother's son Jùn with Guìyáng.
22 The Wèizhǔ Guī arrived at Yǒng'ān.
Yǒng'ān was originally Zhì Xiàn of the Hàn dynasty,
belonging to Hédōng Jùn.
Emperor Shùn renamed it Yǒng'ān.
During the Jìn dynasty, it belonged to Píngyáng Jùn.
Huòyì Xiàn of Jìnzhōu during the Suí and Táng dynasties was originally Yǒng'ān Xiàn.
Lì Dàoyuán said: Yǒng'ān
was the former capital of the Earl of Huò.
The county has Mount Huòtài.
Zhǎngsūn Féi met them and attacked,
capturing all of them.
Píng retreated,
and Guī pursued him.
On the day Yǐsì,
he caught up with him at Cháibì.
Píng fortified his position within the city,
and the Wèi army besieged it.
Qín Wáng Xīng led an army of forty-seven thousand to rescue him,
intending to occupy Tiāndù to transport grain to supply Píng.
Cháibì is east of the Fén River.
Tiāndù is probably the name of a ford on the Fén River,
on the west bank of the Fén River.
"The Art of War says: 'Those who are in high positions are vulnerable to the enemy,
and those who are in deep positions are imprisoned by the enemy.'
Now Qín has committed both.
It would be advisable, before Xīng arrives,
to send a detachment to first seize Tiāndù.
Then Cháibì can be taken without a fight."
Guī ordered the construction of a stronger double encirclement,
internally to prevent Píng from breaking out,
and externally to block Xīng's entry.
Guǎngwǔ Jiāngjūn Ān Tóng said:
"East of the Fén River there is Méngkēng,
extending over three hundred *lǐ* from east to west,
with impassable paths.
When Xīng comes,
he will surely come directly to Cháibì from west of the Fén River.
If this happens,
the enemy's forces will connect,
and although the double encirclement is strong,
it will not be able to control them.
It would be better to build a pontoon bridge,
cross to the west of the Fén River,
and build an encirclement to resist them.
When the enemy arrives,
they will have no way to exert their wisdom and strength."
Guī followed his advice.
When Xīng arrived at Púbǎn,
he feared the strength of Wèi
and only advanced his troops after a long delay.
On the day Jiǎzǐ,
Guī led thirty thousand infantry and cavalry to meet and attack Xīng south of Méngkēng,
beheading over a thousand.
Xīng retreated over forty *lǐ*.
Píng also dared not sally forth.
Guī then divided his troops to occupy strategic points,
preventing the Qín army from approaching Cháibì.
Xīng encamped west of the Fén River,
building a barricade relying on the ravines.
He bound cedar logs together and released them from the upper reaches of the Fén River,
intending to destroy the pontoon bridge.
The Wèi soldiers all hooked them out and used them as firewood.
Coarse wood is called *xīn*,
fine wood is called *zhēng*.
In winter,
in the tenth month,
Píng's provisions ran out and his arrows were exhausted.
At night,
he led all his troops to break out through the southwest encirclement.
Xīng arrayed his troops west of the Fén River,
raising beacon fires and shouting in response.
Xīng wanted Píng to fight hard and break free,
while Píng hoped Xīng would attack the encirclement and connect with him.
But they only called out and echoed each other,
none daring to approach the encirclement.
Píng could not break out.
At his wit's end,
he led his subordinates to plunge into the water and die.
Many generals followed Píng into the water.
Guī sent skilled swimmers to hook and catch them,
and none escaped.
They captured Dí Bózhī and Yuèqí Xiàowèi Táng Xiǎofāng and over forty others.
The remaining twenty thousand or so surrendered and were captured.
Xīng watched their plight helplessly,
powerless to save them.
His entire army wept bitterly,
their cries shaking the mountains and valleys.
He repeatedly sent envoys to seek peace with Wèi,
but Guī refused.
Taking advantage of his victory, he advanced to attack Púbǎn.
Qín Jìngōng Xù held firm and did not fight.
At this time, the Ròurán planned to attack Wèi.
When Guī heard of this,
on the day Wùshēn,
he withdrew his troops and returned.
Someone accused Tàishǐ Lìng Cháo Chóng and his younger brother, Huángmén Shìláng Yì, of secretly summoning Qín soldiers.
When Guī arrived at Jìnyáng,
he bestowed death upon Chóng and Yì.
23 Qín moved over ten thousand households of powerful and prominent families from Héxī to Cháng'ān.
24 Tàiwèi Xuán killed Wúxīng Tàishǒu Gāo Sù, Jiāngjūn Zhú Qiānzhī, as well as Qiānzhī's cousin Lángzhī, Liú Xí, and Xí's younger brother Jìwǔ.
They were all former generals of Liú Láozhī's Běifǔ army.
Xí's elder brother, Jìzhōu Cìshǐ Guǐ, invited Sīmǎ Xiūzhī, Liú Jìngxūan, Gāo Yǎzhī, and others to jointly occupy Shānyáng. Shěn Yuē said: Shānyáng
was originally a place name within Shèyáng Xiàn.
During the Yìxī *tǔduàn* reform,
Shānyáng Jùn and Shānyáng Xiàn were first separated from Guǎnglíng Jùn.
Chǔzhōu of the Táng dynasty was this area.
They intended to raise an army to attack Xuán,
but failed and fled.
Jiāngjūn Yuán Qiánzhī, Liú Shòu, Gāo Chángqìng, Guō Gōng, and others all went to join them,
intending to flee to Wèi.
When they reached south of Chénliú,
they split into two groups: Guǐ, Xiūzhī, and Jìngxūan fled to Nányàn;
Qiánzhī, Shòu, Chángqìng, and Gōng fled to Qín.
When Wèizhǔ Guī first heard that Xiūzhī and others were coming,
he was greatly pleased.
Later, he wondered why they had not arrived,
and ordered Yǎnzhōu to search for them. In the fifth year of Lóng'ān,
Wèi appointed Zhǎngsūn Féi as Yǎnzhōu Cìshǐ,
leading him to campaign south to seize territory,
though Wèi had not yet been able to fully possess Yǎnzhōu.
When he asked the reason,
they all said:
"The Wèi court's prestige has spread far and wide,
which is why Xiūzhī and the others all wished to submit.
But later they heard that Cuī Chěng had been killed."
The death of Cuī Chěng is mentioned in the third year of the previous volume.
Guī deeply regretted this,
and from then on, when educated people made mistakes,
he showed considerable leniency.
25 The Nánliáng King Rǔtán attacked Lǚ Lóng at Gūzàng.
26 The Yàn King Xī took two daughters of the former Zhōngshān Yǐn Fú Mó as his noble ladies.
At the beginning of Yàn King Bǎo's reign, Fú Mó was Zhōngshān Yǐn.
The younger one, named Xùnyīng,
was made a noble consort (Guìpín),
and the noble consort was especially favored.
Empress Dowager Dīng resented and was angry,
and plotted with her nephew, Shàngshū Xìn, to depose Xī and enthrone Zhāngwǔ Gōng Yuān.
When the plot was discovered,
Xī forced Empress Dowager Dīng to commit suicide.
She was buried with the rites of an empress
and posthumously titled Xiànyōu Huánghòu.
Empress Dowager Dīng had long had an affair with Xī.
This is mentioned in the previous year.
On the day Wùchén,
he killed Yuān and Xìn.
On the day Xīnwèi,
Xī went hunting in Běiyuán.
Běiyuán is north of Lóngchéng.
Shíchéng Xiàn,
in the Hàn dynasty, belonged to Běipíng Jùn,
and in the Yàn dynasty, belonged to Jiàndé Jùn.
Gāo Hé was originally the magistrate of Shíchéng,
and at that time had gathered in Lóngchéng for a grand funeral.
He killed Sīlì Xiàowèi Zhāng Xiǎn,
then plundered the palace,
took weapons from the arsenal,
coerced the military offices,
closed the gates, and defended the city walls.
Xī rushed back,
and the people on the city walls all threw down their weapons and opened the gates.
All the rebels were executed,
only Hé escaped.
On the day Jiǎxū,
a general amnesty was declared.
27 Wèi appointed Yǔ Yuè as Sīkōng.
28 In the twelfth month,
on the day Xīnhài,
Wèizhǔ Guī returned to Yúnzhōng.
Ròurán Kèhán Shèlún heard that Guī was attacking Qín,
and invaded Wèi from Cānhé Pō,
reaching Cháishān.
Cháishān is north of Shànwú Xiàn.
In the sixth year of Tiānxīng of Wèi, a palace was built here.
Lún,
pronounced like Lú Kūn.
Wèi Chángshān Wáng Zūn pursued him with ten thousand cavalry,
but failed to catch him and returned.
29 Tàiwèi Xuán ordered Yùshǐ Dù Lín to guard Huìjī Wénxiào Wáng Dàozǐ.
When Dàozǐ reached Ānchéng,
Lín, following Xuán's instructions,
poisoned Dàozǐ
and killed him.
30 Jǔqú Méngxùn's appointed Xījùn Tàishǒu Liáng Zhōngyōng rebelled
and fled to Xīliáng.
When Méngxùn heard of it,
he smiled and said:
"I treated Zhōngyōng
with kindness like flesh and blood,
but Zhōngyōng did not trust me.
He only overestimated himself.
How can I rely solely on this one person?"
So he returned all of Zhōngyōng's family.
Xīliáng Gōng Gǎo asked Zhōngróng,
"How do I compare to Suǒ Sì?"
Zhōngróng replied,
"It is not yet possible to measure."
Gǎo said,
"If Suǒ Sì's talent and measure were equal to mine,
how could I, from a thousand *lǐ* away, strangle him with a long rope?"
Suǒ Sì's death is mentioned in the previous volume, fourth year.
*Nú* (孥) rhymes with *nú* (奴).
*Gǎo* (暠),
read as *gǔ lǎo* (古老).
*Suǒ* (索),
read as *xī gè* (昔各).
*Liáng* (量),
pronounced *liáng*.
"Wisdom has its lengths and shortcomings;
fate has its successes and failures.
The principles of gain and loss
between Your Highness and Suǒ Sì
are truly something I have not yet been able to fully understand.
If death in battle is considered a defeat,
and calculating one's actions is considered a victory,
then how could Gōngsūn Zàn be more virtuous than Liú Yú?"
The affairs of Gōngsūn Zàn and Liú Yú are found in Volume 60, Hǎn Xiàndì Chūpíng, fourth year.
Yuán Qiánzhī and others arrived at Cháng'ān.
Qín Wáng Xīng asked,
"How does Huán Xuán's talent and strategy compare to his father's?
Will he ultimately succeed?"
Qiánzhī replied,
"Xuán took advantage of the Jìn dynasty's decline and chaos,
illicitly occupying the position of chancellor.
He is suspicious, cruel, and merciless,
and his rewards and punishments are unjust.
In my view,
he is far inferior to his father.
Xuán now holds great power,
and his ambition will inevitably lead him to usurpation.
He will merely clear the way for others."
Xīng approved of this
and appointed Qiánzhī as the Inspector of Guǎngzhōu.
Qín granting Guǎngzhōu to Yuán Qiánzhī
was merely to bestow upon him a prestigious position as a sign of favor.
In this year,
Qín Wáng Xīng established Zhāoyí Zhāng as empress,
and enfeoffed his sons Yī, Bì, Guāng, Xuān, Chén, Yīn, Pú, Zhì, Kuí, Yù, and Guó'ér, all as dukes.
He sent envoys to appoint Tūfà Nǔtán as General of Chariots and Cavalry and Duke of Guǎngwǔ,
Jūqú Méngxùn as General Who Guards the West, Inspector of Shāzhōu, and Marquis of Xīhǎi,
and Lǐ Gǎo as General Who Pacifies the West and Marquis of Gāochāng.
Qín's General Who Guards Afar, Zhào Yào, led an army of twenty thousand to garrison Jīnchéng in the west.
General Who Establishes Authority, Wáng Sōngcōng, led cavalry to assist Lǚ Lóng in defending Gūzāng.
When Sōngcōng reached Wèi'ān,
Nǔtán's younger brother Wénzhēn attacked and captured him.
Nǔtán was greatly enraged,
sent Sōngcōng back to Cháng'ān,
and made a profound apology.
The historian states that the various states of Hé and Huáng all feared the strength of Yáo Qín.
Niè Chóngqí punctuated, Wáng Chóngwǔ proofread.
Sīmǎ Guāng
Compiled by imperial order.
Later Learning. Tái.
Emperor Ān, year Wù.
Yuánxīng Second Year (Guǐmǎo, 403 CE).
1. Spring,
First month,
Lú Xún sent his commander Xú Dàofù to raid Dōngyáng.
Second month,
Xīchǒu day,
Jiànwǔ General Liú Yù attacked and defeated him.
Dàofù was
Lú Xún's brother-in-law.
2. Yǐmǎo day,
the Grand Commandant Huán Xuán was appointed Grand General.
The Grand General,
since the Hàn dynasty,
was a position of great honor and authority,
and those who held it usually controlled the court.
In the early Jìn, Sīmǎ Fú was appointed Grand Commandant.
He memorialized that the Grand General's position should be below the Grand Commandant.
Later, it reverted to the old system
and was above the Three Excellencies.
3. Dīngsì day,
Huán Xuán executed Sūn Wúzhōng, the Inspector of Jìzhōu.
Sūn Wúzhōng was also an old general of the Beǐfǔ (Northern Garrison).
4. Huán Xuán submitted a memorial requesting to lead all armies to pacify Guān and Luò.
Afterwards, he hinted to the imperial court to issue an edict denying his request,
then said,
"I halt upon imperial decree."
Huán Xuán initially intended to prepare his equipment,
first ordering light boats to be made
to carry his clothing, valuables, books, and paintings.
Someone asked him the reason.
Huán Xuán said,
"War is violent and dangerous.
Should there be any unforeseen circumstances,
they must be light and easy to transport."
Everyone laughed at him.
Huán Xuán's demeanor was always like this.
At the time, people mistakenly believed him to be heroic and feared him,
thus they were repeatedly defeated whenever they encountered him.
In the battle of Zhēngróngzhōu,
Liú Dàoguī and others, knowing his character, directly confronted him,
and he was defeated once, never to recover.
read as *yǐchǐ* (以豉).
5. Summer,
Fourth month,
Guǐsì day, the first day of the month,
there was a solar eclipse.
6. Zhào Róng, a former official of Nányàn Zhǔ Bèidé, came from Cháng'ān.
For the first time, Bèidé received news of the deaths of his mother and elder brother,
and he cried so loudly he vomited blood,
subsequently falling ill.
The Commandant of the Capital, Mùróng Dá, plotted rebellion,
sending his *yámén* (elite guard) Huáng Qiú to attack the Duānmén gate.
The palace commander Hóu Chìméi opened the gate to assist them.
The palace commander was like the three *dūdú* (military governors) of the palace in Jìn.
*Shuài* (帥),
read as *suǒlèi* (所類).
Duàn Hóng and others, hearing of the unrest in the palace,
mobilized troops and garrisoned the four gates.
These were the four gates of Guǎnggù city.
Chìméi and others were executed.
Mùróng Dá fled to Wèi.
Bèidé showed favor to the displaced people,
granting them a long period of exemption from corvée labor.
The people, due to this, successively sheltered each other,
some combining a hundred households into one,
or a thousand able-bodied men into one registry,
to avoid taxes and corvée.
The Grand Minister Hán Qǐng requested a thorough investigation.
Bèidé agreed
and sent him to tour the commanderies and counties,
uncovering fifty-eight thousand hidden households.
7. The bandit Wáng Shǐ from Tài Shān gathered tens of thousands of followers,
declared himself "Tàipíng Emperor,"
and appointed dukes and ministers.
Nányàn's Guìlín Wáng Zhèn attacked and captured him.
Before his execution,
someone asked about his father and brothers.
Wáng Shǐ said,
"The Grand Supreme Emperor is suffering outside,
and the General Who Conquers the East and the General Who Conquers the West were killed by rogue soldiers."
His wife angrily said to him,
"You are sitting here because of this mouth!
Why are you still like this?"
Wáng Shǐ said,
"Empress, you don't know:
since ancient times, has there ever been a nation that did not perish?
I will collapse,
but I will never change my title!"
The historian remarks that Wáng Shǐ presumptuously assumed a grand title,
and even in defeat and ruin, he showed no remorse.
8. Fifth month,
Yàn Wáng Xī constructed the Lóngténg Yuán (Dragon Ascent Park),
which was over ten *lǐ* square,
employing twenty thousand laborers.
He built Jǐngyún Shān (Scenic Cloud Mountain) within the park,
with a base five hundred paces wide
and a peak seventeen *zhàng* high.
9. Autumn,
Seventh month,
Wùzǐ day,
Wèi Zhǔ Guī toured the north,
building a detached palace on Cháishān mountain.
The Administrator of Píngyuán, Hé Báshē, was extravagant and loved fame.
Guī disliked this and had him killed,
sending his younger brother Pí and others to bid him farewell.
Báshē said,
"The land north of the Luǐ River is barren;
you can move south of the river and strive to make a living."
He also made them turn their backs to him,
saying,
"How can you bear to watch my death?"
Pí and others understood his intention,
pretended to be envoys,
and fled into Qín.
Guī was enraged
and exterminated their family.
The Central Camp General Dèng Yuān's younger cousin, the Grand Minister Huī, was good friends with Báshē.
Someone slandered him to Guī, saying,
"Huī was the one who helped Pí escape."
Guī suspected Yuān knew of the plot
and bestowed death upon Yuān.
10 Nánliáng King Núdàn and Jǔqú Méngxùn mutually sent troops to attack Lǚ Lóng.
Lóng was troubled by this.
Qín’s strategists said to Qín King Xìng:
“Lóng relies on his ancestors’ resources,
and unilaterally rules Héwài.
Although he is now in dire straits,
he can still sustain himself.
If in the future he becomes prosperous,
he will ultimately not belong to us.
Liángzhōu is strategically difficult to access,
and its land is fertile and abundant.
It would be better to seize it while it is in peril.”
Xìng then sent an envoy to summon Lǚ Chāo to attend him.
Lóng, considering that Gūzāng would ultimately be unable to sustain itself,
then, through Chāo, requested to be welcomed into Qín.

Xìng sent Grand Chancellor of the Palace Left Assistant Shàngshū Qí Nàn, General Who Guards the West Yáo Jié, Left Worthy King Qífú Gān’guī, and General Who Guards Afar Zhào Yào, leading forty thousand infantry and cavalry to welcome Lóng from Hexi.
Nánliáng King Núdàn consolidated the two garrisons of Chāngsōng and Wèi’ān to avoid them.
攝 (shè),
means to gather.
傉 (nǔ),
is pronounced nǔ wò fān.
When Qí Nàn and others arrived at Gūzāng,
Lóng, in a plain carriage and on a white horse, welcomed them by the roadside.
Lóng urged Nàn to attack Jǔqú Méngxùn.
Méngxùn sent Zāng Mòhái to resist them,
and defeated their vanguard.
Nàn then allied with Méngxùn.
Méngxùn sent his younger brother Ná to pay tribute to Qín.
Nàn appointed Supervisor of the Army Wáng Shàng as Inspector of Liángzhōu,
allocated three thousand troops to garrison Gūzāng,
and appointed General Yán Sōng as Administrator of Cāngsōng.
Cāngsōng,
is the Hàn Chāngsōng County.
They divided and garrisoned two cities,
and relocated Lóng’s clan, officials, and ten thousand households to Cháng'ān.
The Records state: From Guāng to Lóng, thirteen years passed until its destruction.
散 (sàn),
is pronounced xǐ dǎn fān.
騎 (qí),
is pronounced qí jì fān.
The remaining civil and military officials were promoted and arranged according to their talents.
Originally,
Guō Nún often said,
“One surnamed Wáng will replace Lǚ.”
Therefore, when he raised troops,
he first supported Wáng Xiáng,
and later supported Wáng Qǐjī.
The events are found in Volume 109, First Year.
黁 (nún),
is pronounced nú kūn fān.
Wáng Shàng ultimately replaced him.
Nún, having surrendered to Qín with Qífú Gān’guī,
believed that it would be Jìn who would destroy Qín,
and thus came to defect.
The Qín people pursued and captured him,
and killed him.
Guō Nún, confident in his divination arts,
hoped for chaos to seek good fortune,
but ultimately brought about his own death.
This is enough to show how difficult it is to know the Mandate of Heaven.
Jǔqú Méngxùn’s paternal uncle, the Middle Field Protector of the Army Qīn Xìn, and Administrator of Línsōng Kǒng Dǔ,
were both arrogant and tyrannical, causing distress to the people.
According to the Jìnshū, Méngxùn’s Biography,
the Middle Field Protector of the Army was established by Lǚ Guāng,
and was stationed in Línsōng.
[Méngxùn said,] “Those who disrupt my law
are my two paternal uncles.”
He then compelled them both to commit suicide.
Qín sent an envoy, Liáng Gòu, to Zhāngyè.
Méngxùn asked,
“Tūfà Núdàn is a duke, but I am a marquis.
Why is this?”
Qín had enfeoffed Núdàn as Duke of Guǎngwǔ,
and Méngxùn as Marquis of Xīhǎi.
The events are found in the previous volume, previous year.
[Gòu replied,] “Núdàn is fierce and cunning,
and his sincerity has not yet been proven.
Therefore, the imperial court restrains him with high titles and empty names.
Your Excellency’s loyalty penetrates the bright sun,
and you are destined to enter and assist the imperial house.
How could you be treated with distrust?
The sagely court’s titles are always commensurate with merit.
For example, Yǐn Wěi and Yáo Huàng,
ministers who aided in the founding of the dynasty, and Qí Nàn and Xú Luò,
brave generals of their time,
all have titles no higher than marquis or count.
How can Your Excellency precede them?”
[Gòu continued,] “In the past, Dòu Róng respectfully and firmly declined,
not wishing to be placed above the old officials.
The event is found in Volume 43, Hàn Guāngwǔ, Jiànwǔ 13th year.”
Méngxùn said,
“Why did the imperial court not simply enfeoff Zhāngyè, but instead grant the distant enfeoffment of Xīhǎi?”
Gòu replied,
“Zhāngyè,
Your Excellency already possesses.
The reason for granting the distant Xīhǎi is
to expand Your Excellency’s territory.”
Méngxùn was pleased,
and accepted the commission.
11 Jīngzhōu Inspector Huán Wěi died.
Grand General Xuán appointed Huán Xiū to replace him.
Assistant to the Commander Cáo Jìngzhī advised Xuán, saying,
“The brothers Qiān and Xiū exclusively control both internal and external affairs.
Their power is too great.”
Xuán then appointed Commander of Nánjùn Huán Shíkāng as Jīngzhōu Inspector.
Shíkāng
was the son of Huò.
Huán Huò
was Wēn’s second younger brother.
12 Liú Yù defeated Lú Xún at Yǒngjiā,
and pursued him to Jìn’ān.
During Emperor Wǔ’s Tàikāng 3rd year,
Jìn’ān Commandery was established by dividing Jiàn’ān.
Today’s Quánzhōu Nán’ān County is that place.
Sòng Bái said: When the Eastern Jìn moved south,
many noble families gathered here to seek peace,
and thus Jìn’ān Commandery was established.
In the Suí dynasty, it became Quánzhōu.
Xún fled south by sea.
Hé Wújì secretly went to Yù,
and advised Yù to raise troops in Shānyīn to attack Huán Xuán.
Yù consulted with the local magnate Kǒng Jìng.
Jìng said,
“Shānyīn is far from the capital.
Raising an army there would be difficult to succeed.
Moreover, Xuán has not yet usurped the throne.
It is better to wait until he has usurped it,
and then plan it from Jīngkǒu.”
Yù followed his advice.
Jìng
was the grandson of Yú.
Kǒng Yú served Emperors Yuán, Míng, and Chéng.
13 In the ninth month,
Wèi ruler Guī went to Nánpíngchéng.
In the first year of Emperor Mǐn’s Jiànxīng era,
Duke Yīlú built Shènglè as the Northern Capital,
and repaired the old Píngchéng as the Southern Capital.
Moving a hundred *li* further south,
at the sunny side of the Lěi River, at Huángguāduī, he built Xīnpíngchéng,
which is what is called Nánpíngchéng.
Southwest of Táng Shuòzhōu, there is a New City,
which is that place.
From the Lěi River south to Xiàwūshān,
all is the land south of Lěi.
度 (dù),
is pronounced tú luò fān.
灅 (lěi),
is pronounced lì shuǐ fān.
14 Attendant Chancellor Yīn Zhòngwén and Palace Attendant Biàn Fànzhī urged Grand General Xuán to quickly accept the imperial abdication,
and secretly drafted the Nine Marks of Favor document and the official mandate.
散 (sàn),
is pronounced xǐ dǎn fān.
騎 (qí),
is pronounced qí jì fān.
禪 (chán),
is pronounced shí zhàn fān.
撰 (zhuàn),
is pronounced shì miǎn fān.
Wáng Mì was appointed Supervising Secretary and concurrently Minister of Works.
Huán Yìn was appointed Minister of the Central Secretariat.
Huán Xiū was promoted to General Who Guards the Army.
Yìn
was the grandson of Chōng.
On the day *bǐngzǐ*,
Xuán was commissioned as Chancellor of State,
overseeing all government affairs,
enfeoffed with ten commanderies,
made King of Chǔ,
and granted the Nine Marks of Favor.
The state of Chǔ was to have officials from Prime Minister downwards.
Huán Qiān privately asked Administrator of Péngchéng Liú Yù,
“King of Chǔ’s achievements and virtues are greatly esteemed.
The sentiment of the imperial court
generally believes that he should be offered the throne by abdication.
What do you think?”
Yù replied,
“King of Chǔ
is the son of Xuānwǔ.
Huán Wēn
was posthumously given the epithet Yíwǔ.
The Jìn imperial house is weak,
and the people’s hopes have long shifted.
It is perfectly acceptable to seize the opportunity to receive the abdication of the throne.”
Qiān joyfully said,
“If you say it is acceptable, then it is acceptable.”
Liú Yù was a hero of his generation.
Huán Qiān asked him to decide whether it was acceptable or not.
Yù used deceptive words to comply with his wishes,
hence his joy.
Yú Zè of Xīnyě
was a partisan of Yīn Zhòngkān.
Xīnyě County
belonged to Nányáng Commandery during the Hàn dynasty.
During the Tàikāng reign of Emperor Wǔ of Jìn,
it was separated and assigned to Yìyáng Commandery.
Emperor Huì later again separated it and established Xīnyě Commandery.
Zè,
pronounced "zǔ lì" (inverted tone),
is from
"厂" (hǎn),
not from
"广" (guǎng).
Before Shí Kāng arrived,
he raised troops and attacked Fēng Gāi, the Inspector of Yōngzhōu, at Xiāngyáng,
driving him away.
Zè had seven thousand men.
He set up an altar
and sacrificed to the Seven Ancestral Temples,
declaring,
"I intend to punish Huán Xuán."
Jiānglíng was shaken.
Shí Kāng arrived at the prefecture
and dispatched troops to attack Xiāngyáng.
Zè was defeated
and fled to Qín.
Gāo Yǎzhī submitted a memorial to Mùróng Dé, the ruler of Southern Yàn,
requesting to attack Huán Xuán, saying:
"Even if we cannot clear the Wú and Kuàijī regions,
we can still take the lands north of the Jiāng River."
Hàn Fàn, the Attendant of the Central Secretariat, also submitted a memorial, saying:
"Now the Jìn court is in decline and chaos.
North and south of the Jiāng and Huái rivers,
the population is sparse,
and the cavalry is weak.
Furthermore, Huán Xuán is perverse and rebellious,
causing all, high and low, to be disunited.
With Your Majesty's divine military prowess,
if you dispatch ten thousand infantry and cavalry to approach them,
they will surely collapse and disintegrate,
and your troops will pass without resistance.
If we can acquire it,
Qín and Wèi will not be worthy adversaries.
Expanding territory and establishing achievements
is precisely now.
If we lose this opportunity and do not take it,
their local heroes will execute Huán Xuán
and restore virtuous governance.
Not only will Jiànkāng be unattainable,
but even the north of the Jiāng River will be beyond reach."
Mùróng Dé said:
"I believe that since our old state was overthrown,
I wish to first pacify the Central Plains,
then level Jīng and Yáng.
Therefore, I have not yet campaigned south.
Let the grandees debate this."
Consequently, he held a military drill west of the city,
with three hundred seventy thousand infantry,
fifty-three thousand cavalry,
and seventeen thousand chariots.
All the grandees believed that Huán Xuán had just achieved his ambition
and was not yet to be attacked,
so the plan was halted.
Mùróng Dé had taken Qīngzhōu
only five years earlier.
With such a large army,
he was unable to seize the opportune moment and utilize it,
judging himself to lack the talent to distinguish against Huán Xuán.
In winter,
in the tenth month,
Huán Xuán, the King of Chǔ, submitted a memorial requesting to return to his fief,
and had the Emperor issue a handwritten edict to firmly retain him.
He also falsely claimed that Línpíng Lake in Qiántáng had opened.
Línpíng Lake's reeds were always densely choked;
if it opened, it signified peace throughout the world.
He made all officials gather to congratulate him,
using it as a sign of his receiving the Mandate.
Furthermore, he observed that all previous eras had recluses,
and was ashamed that his own era alone lacked them.
He sought out Huángfǔ Xīzhī, the sixth-generation descendant of Huángfǔ Mì, a recluse from the Western Court in Āndìng.
When the Jìn clan moved east,
Luòyáng was referred to as the Western Court.
Huángfǔ Mì was invited to serve during the period between Wèi and Jìn but did not comply,
styling himself Master Xuányàn.
Cháo,
pronounced "zhí yáo" (inverted tone).
He made Xīzhī live in seclusion in the mountains and forests;
he then summoned him to be an Administrator of Writings.
He had Xīzhī firmly decline the appointment,
and only then issued an edict to commend and honor him,
styling him a "High Scholar."
People at the time called him
"Chōng Yǐn" (a placeholder recluse).
He was not a true recluse but was used to make up the numbers,
hence he was called a "Chōng Yǐn."
His enactments were diverse and confused,
his will was never firm,
and he frequently changed and reverted policies,
ultimately implementing nothing.
He was also greedy and mean.
If scholars possessed excellent calligraphy or fine paintings,
or beautiful gardens and residences,
he would certainly use gambling as a pretext to acquire them.
He especially loved pearls and jade,
never letting them leave his hands.
On the day Yǐmǎo,
Wèi Zhǔ Guī enfeoffed his son Sì as the Prince of Qí,
and promoted him to the rank of Chancellor;
Shào as the Prince of Qīnghé,
and promoted him to Commander-in-Chief of the Pacification of the South;
Xī as the Prince of Yángpíng;
and Yào as the Prince of Hénán.
On the day Dīngsì,
Wèi general Yī Wèi led twenty thousand cavalry to attack the remaining tribes of Gāochē, Yuán Hē and Wū Pín.
In the eleventh month,
on the day Gēngwǔ,
he decisively defeated them.
An edict was issued for Huán Xuán, the King of Chǔ, to observe the imperial rites and music,
for his consort to be queen,
and his heir apparent to be crown prince.
On the day Dīngchǒu,
Biàn Fànzhī drafted an abdication edict,
and compelled Emperor Ān to write it.
Bǎo
was the great-grandson of Xīzhī.
Wǔlíng Wáng Xī died during Huán Wēn's deposition and establishment of an emperor.
On the day Gēngchén,
the Emperor attended court,
and dispatched the concurrent Grand Preceptor and concurrently Minister of Works, Wáng Mì, to present the imperial seal and ribbon,
abdicating to Chǔ.
On the day Rénwǔ,
the Emperor left the palace to reside in the Yǒng'ān Palace.
On the day Guǐwèi,
the spirit tablets of the imperial ancestral temple were moved to Lángyá Commandery.
During the Yǒngjiā Disturbance,
over a thousand households from Lángyá Commandery followed Emperor Yuán across the river.
In the third year of Tàixīng,
Huáidé County was established.
Although Dānyáng had a Chancellor of Lángyá, it did not have the actual territory.
In the first year of Xiánkāng of Emperor Chéng,
Huán Wēn held the position of Grand Administrator of Lángyá,
garrisoned at Jīnchéng in Púzhōu, Jiāngchéng.
He requested to carve out territory from Jiāngchéng County to establish a commandery,
and only then did it have actual land.
All officials went to Gūshú to urge him to ascend the throne.
In the twelfth month,
on the first day, Gēngyín,
Huán Xuán built an altar north of Jiǔjǐngshān.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states that
Tàipíng Prefecture has Jiǔjǐngshān.
Today's Tàipíng Prefecture
is the ancient land of Gūshú.
There is a stream south of Wúhú County
still called Gūshú Creek.
The Běizhēng Jì states: Jiǔjǐngshān is south of Dānyáng.
On the day Rénchén,
he ascended the imperial throne.
His proclamation extensively disparaged the Jìn dynasty.
Some advised against it,
but Huán Xuán said:
"The language of courteous abdication
is only for presentation to the common people;
how can one deceive the Supreme Lord above?"
He issued a general amnesty
and changed the era name to Yǒngshǐ.
He demoted Empress Hé of Nánkāng's Pínggù County
(In the third year of Tàikāng of Emperor Wǔ,
Nánkāng Commandery was established with the Southern Commandant of Lúlíng.
Pínggù
was the Píngyáng County established by Wú.
In the first year of Tàikāng,
it was renamed Pínggù.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states that
Gàn County in Qiánzhōu has Pínggù Town.)
to the Lady of Línglíng County,
Wáng Déwén, the Prince of Lángyá, to the Duke of Shíyáng County,
and Zūn, the Prince of Wǔlíng, to the Marquis of Péngzé County.
He posthumously honored his father, Huán Wēn, as Emperor Xuānwǔ,
with the temple name Tàizǔ,
and Princess Nánkāng as Empress Xuān.
He enfeoffed his son Shēng as the Prince of Yùzhāng.
He appointed Wáng Yú, the Grand Administrator of Kuàijī, as Minister of Personnel,
and his son Wáng Suí, the Chief Clerk of the Chancellor's office, as Central Secretariat Director.
Suí
was Huán's nephew.
On the day Wùxū,
Huán Xuán entered the Jiànkāng Palace
and ascended the imperial throne, but the bed suddenly collapsed.
All the attendants turned pale.
Yīn Zhòngwén said:
"This must be because Your Sacred Virtue is so profound that the earth cannot bear it."
Huán Xuán was greatly pleased.
Kǒng Pú, a subject of Liáng Wáng Zhēnzhī, brought Zhēnzhī and fled to Shòuyáng.
Zhēnzhī
was Xīzhī's great-grandson.
Xī's son Jū
was adopted into the Liáng state and was Zhēnzhī's grandfather.
In the year Gēngshēn [of the 20th cycle] (400 CE),
Yān Wáng Xī honored Yān Zhǔ Chuí's esteemed consort, Lady Duàn, as Empress Dowager.
Lady Duàn
was Xī's biological mother.
On Jǐyǒu,
he established Consort Fú as Empress
and granted a general amnesty.
On Xīnhài [of the 21st cycle] (401 CE),
Huán Xuán moved the Emperor to Xúnyáng.
Xúnyáng Jùn was then governed from Cháisāng.
Yān appointed Wèi Wèi Yuè Zhēn as Qīngzhōu Cìshǐ,
garrisoning Xīnchéng;
Guānglù Dàfū Wèi Jū as Bīngzhōu Cìshǐ,
garrisoning Fánchéng.
On Guǐchǒu [of the 23rd cycle] (401 CE),
