constituted the Six Armies.
West of Jiànkāng was Xīlíng;
to its east was Dōnglíng.
Dōnglíng was northeast of Fùzhōushān.
Dàn,
pronounced tú lǎn fān.
Their combined forces amounted to twenty thousand.
On Jǐwèi,
Yù’s army, having finished eating,
abandoned all their remaining provisions
and advanced to the east of Fùzhōushān.
He sent the weak and infirm to climb the mountain,
displaying banners as a feint.
Several columns advanced simultaneously,
filling the valleys.
When Xuán’s scouts returned,
they reported:
“Yù’s army has surrounded us on all sides,
and their numbers are unknown.”
Xuán became even more anxious and fearful.
He dispatched Yú Zézhī, Wǔwèi Jiāngjūn, to lead elite troops as reinforcements for the various armies.
When Wèi Wéndì ascended the throne,
he established the Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn,
who commanded the Wǔxiào, Zhōnglěi, and Wǔwèi camps.
Later, generals were established for each.
Zé,
pronounced shì gé fān.
(Yú Zézhī) had always feared and submitted to Yù
and had no will to fight.
Yù and Liú Yì, dividing into several detachments,
charged and broke through Qiān’s formation.
Yù led the charge himself,
and his officers and men fought to the death,
each worth a hundred,
their shouts shaking heaven and earth.
At that time, a strong northeast wind was blowing,
so they set fires,
and the smoke and flames soared to the sky.
The sound of drums and shouts shook the capital,
and Qiān’s forces and others suffered a great defeat.
Although Xuán had sent troops to resist Yù,
his intention to flee was already decided.
He secretly ordered Yīn Zhòngwén, Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn, to prepare boats at Shítou.
Upon hearing of the defeat of Qiān and others,
he led several thousand of his trusted followers,
publicly declaring he was going to battle,
and then departed through Nányèmén with his son Shēng and nephew Jùn.
He met Hú Fān, former Xiàngguó Cānjūn,
who seized his horse’s reins and remonstrated:
“There are still eight hundred imperial archers (yǔlín shèshǒu),
all of whom are loyal.
The people from the west have received generations of kindness.
If you do not urge them to fight,
and suddenly abandon this place,
where do you intend to go?”
Xuán did not reply,
but merely raised his whip and pointed to the sky.
Xuán raising his whip and pointing to the sky
also conveys Xiàng Yǔ’s sentiment of "Heaven is destroying me."
He sped west to Shítou
and fled south across the river with Zhòngwén and others.
He had not eaten for a whole day.
When his attendants offered him coarse rice,
Xuán could not swallow it.
Shēng embraced his chest and consoled him.
Xuán was overwhelmed with grief.
When Yù entered Jiànkāng,
Wáng Zhòngdé, carrying Yuándé’s son Fānghuí, came out to greet Yù.
Yù, on horseback, embraced Fānghuí and wept with Zhòngdé.
He posthumously honored Yuándé as Gěishìzhōng
and appointed Zhòngdé as Zhōngbīng Cānjūn.
Yù stayed at Huán Qiān’s former camp
and sent Liú Zhōng to occupy the Eastern Palace (Dōngfǔ).
On Gēngshēn,
Yù garrisoned Shítou Chéng,
established the Liútái and its officials,
burned Huán Wēn’s spirit tablet outside Xuānyángmén,
created new spirit tablets for the Jìn dynasty,
and placed them in the Tàimiào.
When Huán Xuán first usurped the throne,
he moved the ancestral tablets of the Seven Temples to Lángxié Guó.
Subsequently, he moved the Emperor to Xúnyáng,
and the ancestral tablets (zōngmiào zhǔshí) all followed the Emperor west.
Therefore, new tablets were temporarily made.
Wáng Gǔ, Shàngshū, led the officials to welcome the imperial carriage
and executed those of Xuán’s clan who were in Jiànkāng.
Yù sent Zāng Xī into the palace
to collect books, records, and artifacts,
and sealed the storehouses.
There were gold-decorated musical instruments,
and Yù asked Xī:
“Do you not desire these?”
Xī, with a stern expression, replied:
“The Emperor is in dire straits
and displaced to an unsuitable location.
The General has initiated this great righteous cause,
toiling for the royal house.
Though I may be unworthy,
I truly have no inclination for music.”
Yù smiled and said:
“I was merely jesting with you.”
Xī was
Táo’s younger brother.
Liú Yù married into the Zāng clan.
On the day of Rénxū,
Xuán Sītú Wáng Mì and the assembly discussed and recommended Liú Yù to lead Yángzhōu.
Liú Yù firmly declined.
So Wáng Mì was appointed Shìzhōng, leader of Sītú, Yángzhōu Cìshǐ, and Lù Shàngshūshì.
Wáng Mì then recommended Liú Yù to be Shǐchíjié, Dūdū of the military affairs of the eight prefectures of Yáng, Xú, Yǎn, Yù, Qīng, Jì, Yōu, and Bīng, and Xúzhōu Cìshǐ.
Liú Yì was made Qīngzhōu Cìshǐ.
Hé Wújí was made Lángyá Nèishǐ.
Mèng Chǎng was made Dānyáng Yǐn.
Liú Dàoguī was made Yìchāng Tàishǒu.
According to the Sòng Yǒngchū Jùnguózhì,
Ānfēng had Yìchāng County.
It is likely that at the end of the Jìn dynasty, a commandery was established,
but at the beginning of the Sòng dynasty, it was abolished and became a county.
Liú Yù took the auspicious name of Yìchāng
and had Liú Dàoguī serve as its Tàishǒu.
When Liú Yù first arrived in Jiànkāng,
all major decisions were entrusted to Liú Mùzhī.
Matters were settled swiftly and decisively,
with nothing unsatisfactory.
Qiè
is pronounced kǔ yè.
Every action and movement was consulted with him.
Liú Mùzhī also dedicated himself with utmost sincerity and loyalty,
concealing nothing.
At that time, the Jìn government was lax and undisciplined,
with no proper order established.
Powerful clans were arrogant and unrestrained,
while the common people were impoverished and distressed.
Moreover, Sīmǎ Yuánxiǎn's policies were contradictory and flawed.
Although Huán Xuán wished to rectify and reorganize,
his regulations were excessively numerous and stringent,
and the populace did not follow them.
Liú Mùzhī considered the circumstances and acted appropriately,
rectifying matters as they arose.
Rúqū wéijiǎo.
It means to bend and twist things to bring them back to righteousness.
First, he used his authority to bring order to both internal and external affairs.
All officials scrupulously performed their duties.
In less than ten days,
the social customs were completely transformed.
The historian says Liú Yù possessed the talent to restore order from chaos.
Previously,
Zhūgě Chángmín arrived in Yùzhōu
behind schedule
and could not depart.
Diāo Kuí seized Zhūgě Chángmín
and sent him in a cage cart to Huán Xuán.
Upon reaching Dānglì, Huán Xuán was defeated.
Dānglì
is a place name.
They returned hastily to Lìyáng.
Diāo Kuí abandoned the city and fled,
but was captured by his subordinates
and executed at Shítóu.
All his sons and nephews, regardless of age, were killed,
except for his youngest brother, Jìshìzhōng Chěng, who was spared.
One of Diāo Kuí's former subordinates hid his nephew Diāo Yōng and sent him to Luòyáng.
Diāo Yōng later went from Qín to Wèi.
Yōng
is pronounced yú róng.
Liú Yù appointed Wèi Yǒngzhī as Yùzhōu Cìshǐ,
garrisoned at Lìyáng, and Zhūgě Chángmín as Xuānchéng Nèishǐ.
In the beginning,
Liú Yù was of low renown and humble position,
seen as cunning and lacking in conduct.
The prominent figures all refused to associate with him.
Only Wáng Mì particularly admired and valued him,
saying to Liú Yù,
"You shall be a hero of your generation."
Liú Yù once gambled at chú pú with Diāo Kuí,
and did not pay his debt on time.
Not winning at chú pú and not immediately paying the owed amount; this is also a common characteristic of reckless gamblers.
Wáng Mì saw this,
reprimanded Diāo Kuí and released Liú Yù,
paying the debt on his behalf.
Because of this, Liú Yù deeply resented Diāo Kuí and was grateful to Wáng Mì.
Xiāo Fāngděng said:
Xiāo Fāngděng was
the eldest legitimate son of Liáng Yuándì,
who compiled the Sānshí Guó Chūnqiū.
He was treated with disdain by small fish and shrimp.
Thus, Gāo of Hàn pardoned Yōng Chǐ,
and Wǔ of Wèi spared Liáng Hú.
The incident of Yōng Chǐ is found in volume 11, under the eleventh year of Gāo Dì of Hàn.
During the time of Líng Dì of Hàn,
Liáng Hú was Xuǎnbù Shàngshū.
Wǔ of Wèi wished to make him Luòyáng Lìng,
but Liáng Hú was made Běibù Wèi.
During Dǒng Zhuó's rebellion,
Liáng Hú fled to Liú Biǎo.
When Wǔ of Wèi defeated Jīngzhōu,
Liáng Hú, in fear, tied himself up and went to the gate.
He was kept in the secretariat,
and proved his worth through diligent writing.
Yōng
is pronounced yú yòng.
Now Wáng Mì is a Duke,
and Diāo Kuí's family is annihilated.
Repaying kindness and avenging grudges—
how narrow-minded this is!
The Shàngshū Zuǒpúyè Wáng Yú and his son, Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ Suī, conspired to attack Liú Yù.
The plot was discovered, and
their clan was executed.
Suī's nephew, Huìlóng, was hidden by Sēng Bīn
and thus escaped.
Huìlóng later fled to Qín,
and then from Qín to Wèi.
Wèi, seeing that the Central Plain was desolate,
issued an edict to abolish counties with fewer than a hundred households.
On the day of Dīngmǎo,
Liú Yù returned to garrison at Dōngfǔ.
Huán Xuán arrived at Xúnyáng,
and Guō Chǎngzhī supplied him with equipment and military forces.
On the day of Xīnwèi,
Huán Xuán forced the Emperor to move west.
Liú Yì, leading Hé Wújí, Liú Dàoguī, and other generals, pursued him.
Huán Xuán left Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn Hé Dànzhī and Qián Jiāngjūn Guō Quán, along with Guō Chǎngzhī, to guard Péngkǒu.
On the way, Huán Xuán personally wrote the Qǐjūzhù.
Dù Yòu's Tōngdiǎn states: The Zhōuguān had Zǔoyòu Shǐ,
which is likely the origin of today's Qǐjūzhù.
When there was movement, the Zuǒshǐ recorded it;
when there was speech, the Yòushǐ recorded it.
The Zuǒshǐ recorded words,
and the Yòushǐ recorded events.
Wǔ Dì of Hàn had a Jìnzhōng Qǐjūzhù.
Later, Empress Mǎ of Hàn compiled Míng Dì's Qǐjūzhù,
so the Hàn Qǐjūzhù seemed to be kept in the palace,
as a duty of female scribes.
Afterward, the Qǐjūzhù were all recorded by close attendants.
Throughout the dynasties, there was such a role but not a specific official position.
The Later Wèi dynasty first established the Qǐjū Lìshǐ.
Whenever there were imperial tours or banquets,
they would be by the emperor's side to record his words.
Later, a separate position for Xiū Qǐjūzhù was also established.
He claimed that his strategies were flawless,
and that the generals' disobedience to his commands
led to their defeat.
He concentrated deeply on his writing.
Tán
means deep
and extensive.
Sī
is pronounced xiāng lì.
Once the Qǐjūzhù was completed,
it was proclaimed far and wide.
On the day of Bǐngxū,
Liú Yù claimed to have received a secret imperial edict,
appointing Wǔlíng Wáng Zūn to act as regent and oversee all officials.
He was additionally granted the titles of Shìzhōng and Dàjiāngjūn.
Consequently, a general amnesty was declared,
but Huán Xuán's family alone was not pardoned.
Liú Jìngxuān and Gāo Yǎzhī colluded with the prominent families of Qīngzhōu and the Xianbei chieftains, planning to assassinate Nányàn Wáng Bèidé,
and to enthrone Sīmǎ Xiūzhī as their leader.
Bèidé had appointed Liú Guǐ as Sīkōng and trusted him greatly.
Gāo Yǎzhī wanted to invite Liú Guǐ to join the plot.
Liú Jìngxuān said,
"Duke Liú is old and frail,
and he has aspirations for a peaceful Qí,
so we cannot tell him."
Gāo Yǎzhī eventually told him,
but Liú Guǐ did not comply.
The plot was largely leaked,
and Liú Jìngxuān and others fled south.
The Nányàn people arrested Liú Guǐ
and killed him.
They pursued and caught Gāo Yǎzhī
and also killed him.
Liú Jìngxuān and Sīmǎ Xiūzhī reached the area between the Huái and Sì Rivers,
and upon hearing of Huán Xuán's defeat,
they came to surrender.
The story of Liú Jìngxuān and others fleeing to Nányàn is found in the previous volume, Yuánxīng first year.
The Nányàn ruler Bèidé, upon hearing of Huán Xuán's defeat,
ordered Běidì Wáng Zhōng and others to lead troops to conquer Jiāngnán.
However, Bèidé fell ill and halted the plan.
In the past, Duke Zhuāng of Lǔ attacked Qí
to install Zǐ Jiū, but Xiǎo Bái entered first from Jǔ,
which resulted in the defeat at Gānshí.
At this time,
Jiànkāng was already settled.
Had the army of Mùróng Zhōng and others indeed advanced,
Liú Yù would certainly have been ready to meet them.
Jiāng
is pronounced jì liàng.
11th year, Summer,
4th month,
on the Jǐchǒu day,
Wǔlíng Wáng Zūn entered and resided in the Eastern Palace.
Both inside and outside the court, all showed reverence.
Appointments and dismissals of officials were referred to as zhìshū (制書),
and decrees were referred to as lìngshū (令書).
Sīmǎ Xiūzhī was made Grand Administrator of military affairs of the six prefectures of Jīng, Yì, Liáng, Níng, Qín, and Yōng, and concurrently Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ.
As Liú Yì and others' troops had already advanced,
Xiūzhī was therefore proactively stationed in the southern border region.
監 (jiān),
read as gōng xián fān.
雍 (yōng),
read as yú yòng fān.
On the Gēngyín day,
Huán Xuán, escorting the Emperor, reached Jiānglíng,
and Huán Shíkāng received them.
Xuán again appointed and dismissed officials,
making Biàn Fànzhī Shàngshū Púyè.
Considering his previous defeat and flight,
he feared his authority and commands would not be obeyed,
so he further intensified punishments.
The populace grew increasingly resentful and disloyal.
Yīn Zhòngwén admonished him,
but Xuán angrily said:
"Now, because the generals lost the battle
and the celestial omens were unfavorable,
we have returned to the old capital of Chǔ.
But these petty people are making a fuss,
wantonly raising dissenting opinions.
They must be disciplined with severity;
leniency cannot yet be applied."
When the various commanderies in Jīng and Jiāng heard of Xuán's relocation,
some submitted memorials requesting to inquire about the Emperor's well-being.
Xuán did not accept any of them,
instead ordering each locality to congratulate him on moving to the new capital.
As the Táng people said,
"It is hard for one person's hand
to cover all the eyes under heaven" –
Huán Xuán was such a case.
Originally,
Wáng Mì was Xuán's chief minister in establishing his reign.
When Xuán received the abdication,
Mì personally unfastened the Emperor's imperial seal and ribbon.
When Xuán was defeated,
everyone thought Mì should be executed,
but Liú Yù particularly protected him.
Liú Yì once, during a court assembly,
asked Mì where the imperial seal and ribbon were.
Mì, feeling uneasy,
fled to Qǔ'ā.
Liú Xù said: Dānyáng County in Rùnzhōu during the Táng dynasty,
was the old Qǔ'ā County territory.
He was brought back and reinstated.
12Huán Xuán's nephew, Xīn, led the Dī chieftain Yáng Qiū to raid Lìyáng.
Wèi Yǒngzhī, leading Zhūgě Chángmín, Liú Jìngxuan, and Liú Zhōng, together attacked and defeated them,
beheading Yáng Qiū at Liàn Gù.
Liàn Gù is northwest of Lìyáng.
Xuán sent General of the Palace Guard Yǔ Zhìzǔ and Administrator of Jiāngxià Huán Dàogōng, leading several thousand men, to join Hé Dànzhī and others in defending Pénkǒu.
Hé Wújì and Liú Dàoguī reached Sāngluò Zhōu.
Sāngluò Zhōu is in the middle of the Great River northeast of Pénchéng.
Dù Yòu said: Sāngluò Zhōu is in Dūchāng County, Jiāngzhōu,
which was Péngzé County in the Hàn dynasty.
On the Gēngxū day,
Dànzhī and others led their naval forces to meet them in battle.
The boat Dànzhī usually rode
was grand with feathers, banners, and insignia.
Wújì said:
"The enemy commander will certainly not be in this one;
they intend to deceive us.
We should attack it quickly."
The crowd said:
"If Dànzhī is not in it,
capturing it will be useless."
Wújì said:
"Now our numbers are unequal,
and there is no absolute victory in battle.
Since Dànzhī is not in this boat,
the warriors must be weak.
If we attack it with strong troops,
we will surely capture it.
Once captured,
their morale will be dampened, and our spirit will double.
If we then press on,
we will surely defeat the enemy."
Dàoguī said:
"Excellent!"
So, they went and attacked it, capturing it.
Then they shouted:
"We've got Hé Dànzhī!"
Dànzhī's army was shocked and disorganized.
Wújì's troops also believed it to be true,
and, taking advantage of the victory, advanced to attack Dànzhī and others,
utterly defeating them.
Wújì and others captured Pénkǒu,
then advanced to occupy Xúnyáng,
and sent envoys to respectfully escort the ancestral tablets back to the capital.
Liú Yù was further appointed Grand Administrator of military affairs of Jiāngzhōu.
In the battle of Sāngluò,
Hú Fān's ship was burned by the government forces.
Fān, fully armored, entered the water,
swimming underwater for about thirty paces
before he was able to reach the shore.
At that time, the route to Jiānglíng was already cut off;
since the government forces had captured Xúnyáng,
the route to Jiānglíng was indeed cut off.
Liú Yù had long heard that Fān was a loyal and upright person,
so he invited him to participate in military affairs under the Commander-in-Chief.
13Huán Xuán gathered the Jīngzhōu troops;
in less than three decades,
he had an army of twenty thousand,
with many楼船 (lóuchuán) and much equipment.
On the Jiǎyín day,
Xuán again led his armies, escorting the Emperor, eastward.
He made Fú Hóng Liángzhōu Cìshǐ
to be the vanguard.
He also sent Mounted Regular Attendant Xú Fàng ahead
to persuade Liú Yù and others, saying:
"If you can withdraw your troops and disband your armor,
we will make a fresh start with you,
each assigning positions and responsibilities,
ensuring you do not lose your proper share."
Liú Yù made Zhūgě Chángmín Grand Administrator of military affairs of Huáiběi,
stationed at Shānyáng.
He made Liú Jìngxuan Jiāngzhōu Cìshǐ.
14Ruòrán Kèhán Shèlún's younger cousin, Yuè Dàidà Rǎn Èr, plotted to murder Shèlún,
but failed,
and fled to Wèi.
15Yàn Wáng Xī built the Xiāoyáo Palace in the Lóngténg Yuàn,
with hundreds of connected rooms.
He excavated the Qǔguāng Sea.
In midsummer,
soldiers could not rest,
and more than half died from heatstroke.
Last year, Xī built the Lóngténg Yuàn.
暍 (yē),
read as yú xiē fān.
Suffering from heatstroke.
16Xīliáng Shìzǐ Tán died.
17Liú Yì, Hé Wújì, Liú Dàoguī, and Administrator of Xiàpī, Mèng Huáiyù of Píngchāng, led their troops westward from Xúnyáng.
In the 5th month,
on the Guǐyǒu day,
they encountered Huán Xuán at Zhēngróng Zhōu.
Shuǐjīng Zhù: The Jiāng River flows east past Wǔkǒu,
then further east,
on the right it reaches Lǐ Mǔ Pǔ,
facing Zhēngróng Zhōu to the north.
The place where Liú Yì defeated Huán Xuán
is between present-day Huángzhōu and Shòuchāng Military Command.
Dù Yòu said: Zhēngróng Zhōu is in Wǔchāng County, Èzhōu.
崢 (zhēng),
read as shì gēng fān.
嶸 (róng),
read as hù méng fān.
However, Xuán had tens of thousands of warriors.
The crowd feared them
and wanted to retreat to Xúnyáng.
Dàoguī said:
"No!
They are numerous, we are few;
their strength and our weakness are unequal.
If we are cowardly and do not advance now,
we will surely be taken advantage of.
Even if we reach Xúnyáng,
how can we defend ourselves?
Although Xuán claims to be a heroic and powerful figure,
he is inwardly timid.
Moreover, having already suffered defeat and fled,
his troops have no firm resolve.
When deciding between two armies,
the one with the brave general wins,
not necessarily the one with more troops."
He then waved his troops forward,
and Yì and others followed him.
Xuán always kept a small boat beside his main ship in case of defeat and escape;
because of this, none of his troops had the will to fight.
Yì and others took advantage of the wind to set fires,
exerting their full strength to contend for victory first.
Xuán's army was utterly routed;
they burned their baggage train and fled during the night.
Guō Quán went to Yì and surrendered.
Xuán's former generals, Liú Tǒng, Féng Zhì, and others, gathered a party of four hundred men and attacked and captured Xúnyáng City.
Yì sent General of Establishing Awe Liú Huáisù to suppress and pacify them.
Huáisù
was Huáijìng's younger brother.
Liú Huáijìng is mentioned in Volume 111, Lóng'ān 3rd year.
Xuán, escorting the Emperor, fled westward in a single boat,
leaving Empress Yǒng'ān Hé and Empress Wáng at Bālíng.
Empress Yǒng'ān Hé
was Emperor Mù's Empress Zhāng.
Empress Wáng
was the current Emperor's empress.
They asked to leave their separate boat to gather scattered soldiers,
then rebelled against Xuán,
escorted the two empresses to Xiàkǒu,
and then returned to Jiànkāng.
On the *jǐmǎo* day,
Huán Xuán and the Emperor entered Jiānglíng.
Féng Gāi advised him to fight another battle,
but Xuán did not comply.
He wanted to flee to Hànzhōng to join Huán Xī,
who was then the Inspector of Liángzhōu.
His orders were no longer obeyed.
On the *gēngchén* day,
in the middle of the night,
he made arrangements to depart.
The city was already in chaos,
so he and more than a hundred of his close confidants rode out of the city, fleeing west.
When they reached the city gate,
his attendants, in the darkness, slashed at Xuán,
but missed.
His followers began killing each other,
in front and behind, in disarray.
Xuán barely managed to reach a boat,
his attendants scattered,
with only Biàn Fànzhī at his side.
On the *xīnsì* day,
Wáng Kāngchǎn, the Assistant Governor of Jīngzhōu, escorted the Emperor into the Nánjùn prefectural residence.
The Grand Administrator, Wáng Téngzhī, led civil and military officials to serve as his guards.
Xuán was about to go to Hànzhōng.
Máozhī, the Commandant of Cavalry,
a nephew of Qúzhī,
lured Xuán into Shǔ,
and Xuán followed him.
Máo Fán, the Inspector of Níngzhōu,
who was Qúzhī's younger brother,
died in office.
Qúzhī sent his elder brother's grandson, Yòuzhī, and the Army Advisor Fèi Tián, leading several hundred men, to escort Fán's coffin back to Jiānglíng.
On the *rénwǔ* day,
they encountered Xuán at Méihuízhōu.
The *Shuǐjīng Zhù* states: "The Jiāng River flows south of Jiānglíng County;
there is an islet called Méihuízhōu."
Arrows fell like rain.
Xuán's favorites, Dīng Xiānqī, Wàn Gài, and others, shielded Xuán with their bodies,
and all died.
Féng Qiān, the Supervisor of Yìzhōu and from Hánjiā, drew his sword,
intending to strike Xuán.
Xuán pulled the jade hair ornament from his head and gave it to him.
From the Wèi and Jìn dynasties onwards,
headwear (crowns and caps) had hairpins (*zān*)
and hair guides (*dǎo*).
The most revered used jade for them.
*Dǎo*
means "to guide";
it was used to guide the hair into the crown or cap.
"Who are you,"
(Xuán asked) "who dares to kill the Son of Heaven!"
Qiān replied:
"I am merely the bandit who killed the Son of Heaven!"
Thereupon, he beheaded him,
and also beheaded Huán Shíkāng, Huán Jùn, and Yǔ Zé
zhī.
He captured Huán Shēng and sent him to Jiānglíng,
where he was executed in the marketplace.
The imperial carriage returned to its rightful place in Jiānglíng.
Máozhī was appointed General of Gallant Cavalry.
On the *jiǎshēn* day,
a general amnesty was declared;
all who had been forced to join the rebellion were acquitted without question.
On the *wùyín* day,
the spirit tablets were enshrined in the Imperial Ancestral Temple.
This refers to receiving the spirit tablets of the ancestral temple that had been escorted from Xúnyáng.
(Huán Xuán's head was) displayed on the Great Bridge.
Yì and others, having won the battle,
believed that the great affair was settled,
and did not pursue urgently.
They also encountered headwinds,
and their boats could not advance.
Nearly ten days after Xuán's death,
the various armies had still not arrived.
At this time, Huán Qiān was hiding in Jūzhōng.
The area along the Jū River, both upstream and downstream, was called Jūzhōng;
Línjū and Shànghuáng counties were both part of it.
Jū is pronounced *zǐyú*.
Huáróng County had belonged to Nánjùn since the Hàn dynasty.
The *Shuǐjīng Zhù* states: "The Jiāng River's left branch forms Zhōngxiàkǒu,
while its right branch flows out as Zhōngláng Pǔ."
Huáróng County is now within the boundaries of Jiānlì County.
The *Jìnshū*, Biography of Zhèn, states: "He hid in the Yǒng River in Huáróng."
The *Zuǒ Zhuàn* states: "Yán Āo swam in the Yǒng and escaped."
Dù Yù's commentary says: "The Yǒng River is in Huáróng County, Nánjùn."
Yǒng
is pronounced *yǒng*.
(Qiān) sent someone to inform Zhèn, saying:
"Huán Xīn has already captured Jīngyì,
Féng Zhì has again captured Xúnyáng,
and Liú Yì's armies have all retreated in defeat midway."
Zhèn was greatly pleased,
gathered two hundred followers,
and attacked Jiānglíng.
Huán Qiān also gathered a crowd to support him.
In the intercalary month,
on the *jǐchǒu* day,
they again captured Jiānglíng,
and killed Wáng Kāngchǎn and Wáng Téngzhī.
Zhèn saw the Emperor at the temporary palace,
rode his horse, brandished his spear,
and went straight to the foot of the steps,
asking where Huán Shēng was.
Hearing that he was already dead,
he glared at the Emperor and said:
"What wrong has my family committed against the state,
that it should be massacred like this!"
Wáng Déwén, the Prince of Lángyé, got off his bed and said:
"How could this be my brothers' intention!"
Zhèn wanted to kill the Emperor,
but Qiān strenuously forbade it.
So he dismounted,
composed himself, bowed, and left.
On the *rénchén* day,
Zhèn mourned for Xuán,
established a mourning hall,
and posthumously titled him Emperor Wǔdào.
On the *guǐsì* day,
Qiān and others led the officials to present the imperial seals and ribbons to the Emperor, saying:
"Your Majesty followed Yáo in abdicating to Shùn;
now, the Chǔ dynasty's fortune is not enduring,
and the hearts of the people have returned to Jìn."
Wáng Déwén, the Prince of Lángyé, was appointed Inspector of Xúzhōu.
Zhèn was appointed General-in-Chief of Military Affairs of Eight Commanderies and Inspector of Jīngzhōu.
Qiān was reinstated as Attendant-in-Ordinary and General of the Guards,
and concurrently appointed Inspector of Jiāng and Yù provinces.
The Emperor's personal attendants
were all Zhèn's confidants.
Zhèn, being young, had little integrity.
Xuán did not treat him as a nephew.
At this point,
Zhèn sighed and said:
"Your Grace did not employ me early enough in the past,
thus leading to this defeat.
If Your Grace were still alive,
and I were the vanguard,
conquering the world would be nothing difficult.
Now, I am doing this alone,
where shall I go?"
Thereupon, he indulged in wine and women,
and freely carried out executions.
Qiān advised Zhèn to lead his troops to battle,
while he himself would defend Jiānglíng.
Zhèn had always disdained Qiān,
and did not follow his advice.
Liú Yì reached Bālíng,
and executed Wáng Zhìhuī.
Hé Wújì and Liú Dàoguī advanced to attack Huán Qiān at Mǎtóu.
The Mǎtóu bank is on the south bank of the Great River,
facing Jiāngjīnkǒu to the north.
The *Shuǐjīng Zhù* states: "East of Língxī, there is Lóngpó,
two hundred *bù* in circumference,
with very deep water.
A dragon was seen in it,
hence it is called Lóngpó."
Wèi was Mì's son.
Huán Mì is mentioned in volume 103, in the first year of Níngkāng, during Emperor Xiàowǔ's reign.
Wújì wanted to press on directly to Jiānglíng with his victorious momentum,
but Dàoguī said:
"In military strategy, there are times to advance and times to retreat;
one cannot just rush forward.
The various Huán clans have resided in Xīchǔ for generations;
all their subordinates will exert themselves to the utmost.
Zhèn's bravery surpasses all three armies;
it is difficult to contend with him.
It is better to rest our troops and conserve our strength,
then gradually wear him down with stratagems;
we need not worry about not defeating him."
Wújì did not listen.
Zhèn met them in battle at Língxī.
The *Shuǐjīng Zhù* states: "The Jiāng River flows south of Jiānglíng County,
then east past Yànwěizhōu,
and north to join the Língxī River."
At the confluence of the river and stream, there is the Língxī garrison,
backed by a hill and facing the river,
with Língxī to its west.
Wújì and others suffered a great defeat,
with over a thousand dead.
They retreated to Xúnyáng
and, together with Liú Yì and others, submitted a memorial begging for punishment.
Liú Yù put Yì in charge of directing the various armies,
and dismissed him from his post as Inspector of Qīngzhōu.
Huán Zhèn appointed Huán Wèi as Inspector of Yōngzhōu,
garrisoning Xiāngyáng.
Liǔ Yuēzhī, Luó Shù, and Zhēn Jìzhī heard of Huán Xuán's death,
and advanced their army from Báidì to Zhījiāng.
Zhījiāng County had belonged to Nánjùn since the Hàn dynasty.
Our dynasty abolished it as a county and made it a garrison,
belonging to Sōngzī County.
甄
is pronounced as "Rén" (之人).
They also led their troops to retreat.
Soon after, Shù and Jìzhī both fell ill.
Yuēzhī went to Huán Zhèn and feigned surrender,
intending to plot an attack on Zhèn.
The plot was leaked,
and Zhèn killed him.
Yuēzhī's Sīmǎ, Shí Yánzǔ,
Shí
is a surname.
held Fúlíng.
In the sixth month,
Máo Qú sent a general to attack Hànzhōng,
where Huán Xī was slain.
Qú personally took charge of Liángzhōu.
In the autumn of the 18th year [of Yuánxīng],
in the seventh month,
on the day Wùshēn,
Empress Yǒng'ān, Lady Hé, passed away.
Yàn's Fú Zhāoyí fell ill.
Wáng Róng, a man from Lóngchéng, claimed he could cure her.
When Zhāoyí died,
Yàn Wáng Xī had Róng executed at the Gōngchēmén [gate],
dismembered him, and burned him.
In the eighth month,
on the day Guǐyǒu,
Empress Mùzhāng was buried at Yǒngpínglíng.
Wèi established the Liùyè Guān (Six Reception Officials),
comparable to the ancient Liùqīng (Six Ministers).
In the ninth month,
Diāo Chěng plotted rebellion
and was executed,
thus ending the Diāo clan.
When Diāo Kuí was executed,
only Chěng was pardoned,
while Yōng managed to escape and fled north.
With Chěng's execution,
the Diāo clan of Jiāngnán was wiped out.
Their slaves and retainers ran rampant,
occupying mountains and marshes,
becoming a menace to Jīngkǒu.
Liú Yù distributed their wealth and provisions,
allowing the common people to take what they could according to their needs.
It took a full day to distribute it all.
At that time, the prefectures and commanderies were suffering from famine,
and the people relied on this to survive.
Qǐfú Gānkuī and Yáng Shèng fought at Zhúlǐng.
To the southwest of Shàngguī are Nánshān and Zhúlǐng.
Xīliáng Gōng Gǎo established his son Xīn as heir apparent.
Wèi Zhǔ Guī, at the Zhāoyáng Diàn, reorganized and appointed officials.
He summoned court officials, both civil and military,
personally selected them,
and assigned them positions according to their talents.
Ranks of nobility were divided into four grades: Wáng (kings) were enfeoffed with large commanderies,
Gōng (dukes) with small commanderies,
Hóu (marquises) with large counties,
and Bó (counts) with small counties.
Their ranks were from the first to the fourth grade.
Old officials who had rendered service but had no titles were posthumously granted enfeoffments.
Distant members of the imperial clan and those of other surnames who inherited titles had their ranks lowered by a specified degree.
He also established five grades of "loose" (sǎn) officials,
their ranks from the fifth to the ninth grade.
Sǎn
is pronounced "sǎndàn" (悉亶).
Their ranks were also comparable to the fifth to the ninth grade.
When there were vacancies among officials,
they were filled from these "loose" officials.
Many of these official titles did not follow the old Hàn and Wèi systems,
but imitated the ancient "dragon officials" and "bird officials."
The Zuǒ Zhuàn says: Tánzǐ said: "In ancient times, Tàihào Shì used dragons to chronicle,
hence he made dragon masters and named them after dragons."
"When my ancestor Shàohào Zhì was established,
phoenixes arrived,
hence he made bird masters and named them after birds: the Fèngniǎo Shì was the calendrical official;
the Xuánniǎo Shì was the director of divisions;
the Bóbǎo Shì was the director of solstices;
the Qīngniǎo Shì was the director of openings;
the Dānniǎo Shì was the director of closings;
the Zhùjiū Shì was the minister of education;
the [AS-FBED] Qǔjiū Shì was the minister of war;
the Shījiū Shì was the minister of works;
the Shuǎngjiū Shì was the minister of justice;
the Hújiū Shì was the minister of general affairs.
The five doves
were those who gathered the people.
The five pheasants were the five superintendents of crafts,
and the nine hoopoes were the nine superintendents of agriculture."
Dù Yù's commentary states: "Tàihào Shì had an auspicious dragon omen,
hence he named officials after dragons."
Yīng Shào says: "He used dragons to designate his chief officials: the Spring Official was the Green Dragon,
the Summer Official was the Red Dragon,
the Autumn Official was the White Dragon,
the Winter Official was the Black Dragon,
and the Central Official was the Yellow Dragon."
Zhāng Yàn says: "When Páoxī was about to rise,
a divine dragon arrived bearing a map,
and he accordingly named officials and masters after it."
The Wèi Shū Guānshì Zhì has
"various subordinate functionaries."
They called officials who patrolled and observed "White Egrets,"
taking their characteristic of stretching their necks to look far.
The rest were similar.
Lú Xún plundered Nánhǎi
and attacked Pānyú.
Púyáng Wú Yǐnzhī, the Cìshǐ of Guǎngzhōu, resisted for over a hundred days.
In winter,
in the tenth month,
on the day Rénxū,
Xún launched a night attack on the city and captured it.
He burned the government offices and civilian homes completely,
and captured Wú Yǐnzhī.
Xún proclaimed himself Píngnán Jiāngjūn (General Who Pacifies the South)
and acted as the administrator of Guǎngzhōu affairs.
He gathered the burned bones to form a collective tomb,
burying them on the islet,
recovering over thirty thousand skulls.
He also sent Xú Dàofù to attack Shǐxīng.
In the first year of Gānlù under Sūn Hào of Wú,
Shǐxīng Commandery was established by dividing the southern commandery of Guìyáng.
In the Táng dynasty, it was Sháozhōu.
Liú Yù was appointed Cìshǐ of Qīngzhōu.
Liú Yì was dismissed from Qīngzhōu,
and Yù personally took charge of it.
Liú Jìngxuan was in Xúnyáng,
gathering provisions and repairing ships, never without preparation.
Therefore, although Hé Wújí and others were defeated and retreated,
they relied on him to recover.
Huán Xuán's nephew, Liàng, proclaimed himself Cìshǐ of Jiāngzhōu
and raided Yùzhāng.
Jìngxuan attacked and defeated him.
Liú Yì, Hé Wújí, and Liú Dàoguī again advanced west from Xúnyáng,
reaching Xiàkǒu.
Huán Zhèn sent Zhèndōng Jiāngjūn Fény Gāi to defend the east bank,
Yángwǔ Jiāngjūn Mèng Shāntú to hold Lǔshān Chéng,
and Fúguó Jiāngjūn Huán Xiānkè to defend Yǎnyuè Lěi.
Their forces totaled ten thousand men,
with coordinated support by land and water.
Yì attacked Lǔshān Chéng,
Dàoguī attacked Yǎnyuè Lěi,
and Wújí blocked the middle of the river.
From Chén (7-9 AM) to Wǔ (11 AM-1 PM),
both cities fell.
The Hàn River joins the Jiāng at the southwest of Lǔshān.
To the left of the Hàn River is Quèyuè Chéng,
also called Yǎnyuè Lěi,
which was formerly Qǔlíng County,
later becoming the seat of Shāxiàn County.
Gāi fled to Shíchéng.
On the day Xīnsì,
Wèi granted a general amnesty
and changed the reign title to Tiāncì.
The Xīgōng was constructed.
In the eleventh month,
Wèi Zhǔ Guī went to the Xīgōng
and ordered that Zōngshī (clan masters) be established for the imperial clan,
Dàshī (grand masters) and Xiǎoshī (junior masters) for the eight kingdoms,
and masters also for each prefecture and commandery,
to identify clan members,
and recommend talents and conduct,
similar to the duties of the Zhōngzhèng in Wèi and Jìn.
The Wèi Shū Guānshì Zhì states: "As the clans and families of the eight kingdoms were difficult to distinguish,
Dàshī and Xiǎoshī were established in each kingdom
to identify their clan members
and recommend talented individuals.
Outside the eight kingdoms,
a master was established in each commandery,
whose duties were like those in the eight kingdoms,
comparable to today's Zhōngzhèng.
Zōngshī were established for the imperial clan,
also with duties like those in the prefectures, commanderies, and eight kingdoms."
Xíng
is pronounced as "xiàmèng" (下孟).
29 Yān Wáng Xī and Fú Hòu went on a hunting excursion.

When returning,

Yì’s orders were strict and orderly,

Liú Yù again appointed Yì as Yǎnzhōu Cìshǐ.

1 In spring,
in the first month,
Nányáng Tàishǒu, Fúfēng Lǔ Zōngzhī raised an army and attacked Xiāngyáng.
Huán Wèi fled to Jiānglíng.
On the day *jǐchǒu*,
Liú Yì and other armies arrived at Mǎtóu.

The Jiāngjīn post was in Jiānglíng,

Rìmò (日末),
pronounced Mò Gé (莫葛).

according to Máo Qú (毛璩)'s biography in the *Jìnshū* (晉書),
Lüèchéng (略城) was four hundred *lǐ* (里) from Chéngdū (成都) —
he fled back to Chéngdū (成都).
He dispatched Staff Officer Wáng Qióng (王瓊) to lead troops to suppress them,
but Qióng (瓊) was defeated by Zòng (縱)'s younger brother Míngzǐ (明子),
with eight or nine tenths of his men killed.
Lǐ Téng (李騰), a camp household from Yìzhōu (益州), opened the city gates and admitted Zòng (縱)'s troops.
A "camp household" was a commoner who had been displaced, fled, rebelled, and was assigned to a military camp.
His family was exterminated.
Zòng (縱) proclaimed himself King of Chéngdū (成都),
appointed his younger cousin Hóng (洪) as Inspector of Yìzhōu (益州),
and Míngzǐ (明子) as Inspector of Bāzhōu (巴州),
stationing him at Báidì (白帝).
Thereupon, Shǔ (蜀) fell into great disorder,
and Hànzhōng (漢中) became vacant.
The Dī (氐) king Yáng Shèng (楊盛) sent his nephew Fú (撫), the General Who Pacifies the South, to occupy it.
7 On the day *Guǐhài* (癸亥),
Emperor Guī (珪) of Wèi (魏) returned from Cháishān (豺山)
and abolished the thirty-six departments of the Secretariat.
The thirty-six departments of Wèi (魏) first appeared in Volume 109, during the first year of Lóng'ān (隆安).
8 In the third month,
Huán Zhèn (桓振) attacked Jiānglíng (江陵) from Yúnchéng (鄖城). [48)Dù Yù (杜預) said: "Southeast of Yúndù (雲杜) County in Jiāngxià (江夏) is Yúnchéng (鄖城),
the ancient state of Yúnzǐ (鄖子)."
Yún (鄖)
is pronounced like Yún (云).
Zhèn (振) had previously fled to Yǐnchuān (溳川);
Yúnchéng (鄖城) was probably in Yǐnchuān (溳川).
Yǐn (溳)
is pronounced like Yún (云).
He fled to Xiāngyáng (襄陽),
where Zhèn (振) styled himself Inspector of Jīngzhōu (荊州).
General Who Establishes Might Liú Huáisù (劉懷肅) led troops from Yúndù (雲杜) and rushed to the scene,
engaging Zhèn (振) in battle at Shāqiáo (沙橋);
Shāqiáo (沙橋) was north of Jiānglíng (江陵) city.
He personally beheaded Zhèn (振) in battle
and recaptured Jiānglíng (江陵).
On the day *Jiǎwǔ* (甲午),
the Emperor arrived in Jiànkāng (建康).
On the day *Yǐwèi* (乙未),
all officials went to the palace gate to request punishment,
but an imperial edict ordered their reinstatement.
Secretariat Director Yīn Zhòngwén (殷仲文), believing the court music was incomplete,
spoke to Liú Yù (劉裕),
requesting to manage it.
Yù (裕) said:
"Today, there is no time for it,
and besides, it's something I don't naturally understand."
Zhòngwén (仲文) said:
"If you like it, you will naturally understand it."
Yù (裕) replied:
"It is precisely because I would like it if I understood it
that I don't practice it."
On the day *Gēngzǐ* (庚子),
Wáng Déwén (王德文), the Prince of Lángxié (琅邪), was made Grand Marshal;
Zūn (遵), the Prince of Wǔlíng (武陵), was made Grand Tutor;
Liú Yù (劉裕) was made Palace Attendant, General of Chariots and Cavalry, and Commander of All Military Affairs Inside and Outside the Capital;
his positions as Inspector of Xú (徐) and Qīng (青) Commanderies remained as before.
Liú Yì (劉毅) was made Left General;
Hé Wújì (何無忌) was made Right General, Supervisor of Military Affairs for the five commanderies of Yùzhōu (豫州) and Yángzhōu (揚州), and Inspector of Yùzhōu (豫州);
Liú Dàoguī (劉道規) was made General Who Assists the State, Supervisor of All Military Affairs North of the Huái (淮), and Inspector of Bìngzhōu (幷州);
Wèi Yǒngzhī (魏詠之) was made General Who Quells Captives and Administrator of Wú County.
Yù (裕) firmly declined and did not accept;
he was further given the additional title of Recorder of Secretariat Affairs,
which he also refused,
repeatedly requesting to return to his fief.
To return to his fief
meant to return to Jīngkǒu (京口).
The Emperor personally visited his residence;
Yù (裕) was alarmed and fearful,
and again went to the palace gate to present his request,
whereupon he was allowed to return to his fief.
Wèi Yǒngzhī (魏詠之) was made Inspector of Jīngzhōu (荊州),
replacing Sīmǎ Xiūzhī (司馬休之).
Initially,
Liú Yì (劉毅) had once served as a Staff Officer to Liú Jìngxūn (劉敬宣), General Who Pacifies the North.
Liú Jìngxūn (劉敬宣) was General Who Pacifies the North,
and Yì (毅) was his Staff Officer.
Jìngxūn (敬宣) said:
"Indeed, extraordinary talents have their own demeanor;
how can one simply call this gentleman a hero?
This gentleman's nature
is outwardly generous but inwardly jealous,
self-aggrandizing yet looking up to others.
Should he ever meet with success,
he will surely bring disaster upon himself by overstepping his superiors."
Jìngxūn (敬宣)'s assessment of Yì (毅)
was indeed accurate,
yet he almost brought disaster upon himself by it;
the sages' comprehensive self-protection
is precisely for this reason.
When Jìngxūn (敬宣) was made Inspector of Jiāngzhōu (江州),
he declined, saying he had no merit
and should not be appointed before Yì (毅) and others,
but Yù (裕) did not permit it.
Yì (毅) sent someone to tell Yù (裕):
"Liú Jìngxūn (劉敬宣) did not participate in the righteous uprising.
Brave generals and diligent officials
are awaiting their rewards;
men like Jìngxūn (敬宣)
should be placed later.
If you do not forget your lifelong friendship (Yù (裕) served under Liú Láozhī (劉牢之)'s military command,
and Láozhī (牢之) and his son treated him with great respect,
hence this remark),
appointing him as Attendant-in-ordinary to the Palace (a position established at the end of Wèi (魏))
is truly excessive favor.
When Jìngxūn (敬宣) returned from the north,
Yù (裕) made him Administrator of Jìnling (晉陵).
It is particularly shocking and regrettable."
Jìngxūn (敬宣) felt increasingly uneasy
and submitted a memorial to resign his post;
he was then recalled and made Administrator of Xuānchéng (宣城).
9 In the summer,
the fourth month,
Liú Yù (劉裕) returned to his garrison at Jīngkǒu (京口).
He was reassigned as Commander of All Military Affairs of sixteen commanderies including Jīng (荊) and Sī (司),
and was additionally made Inspector of Yǎnzhōu (兗州).
10Lú Xún (盧循) sent an envoy to present tribute.
At this time, the court had just been settled,
and there was no leisure for military campaigns;
on the day *Rénshēn* (壬申),
Xún (循) was made Inspector of Guǎngzhōu (廣州),
and Xú Dàofù (徐道覆) was made Chancellor of Shǐxīng (始興).
Xún (循) sent Liú Yù (劉裕) *yìzhì zòngzi* (益智粽) (a type of rice dumpling said to improve intelligence);
Yù (裕) replied with *xùmìng tāng* (續命湯) (a decoction for prolonging life).
Xún (循) used the *yìzhì* (益智) to mock Yù (裕),
and Yù (裕) replied with *xùmìng* (續命);
although this seems trivial,
it was also a military stratagem.
Xún (循) appointed Wáng Dàn (王誕), the former Administrator of Lángxié (琅邪), as his Pacifying General of the South.
Dàn (誕) persuaded Xún (循), saying:
"I am not originally a military man,
and I am useless here.
I have always been held in high regard by General Liú (劉鎮軍);
if I can return north,
I will surely be entrusted with a post,
and with both public and private opportunities,
I can repay your great kindness."
Xún (循) was very much convinced.
Liú Yù (劉裕) wrote to Xún (循),
ordering him to send Wú Yǐnzhī (吳隱之) back,
but Xún (循) did not comply.
Dàn (誕) again persuaded Xún (循), saying:
"General, keeping Master Wú (吳公) now
is not a wise plan, neither publicly nor privately.
Did Sūn Bófú (孫伯符) not want to keep Huá Zǐyú (華子魚)?
It's just that one territory cannot accommodate two rulers."
Thereupon, Xún (循) sent Yǐnzhī (隱之) and Dàn (誕) back together.
In the first year of Yuánxīng (元興),
Huán Xuán (桓玄) exiled Wáng Dàn (王誕) to Língnán (嶺南).
In the second year,
Lú Xún (盧循) captured Guǎngzhōu (廣州),
took Wú Yǐnzhī (吳隱之) captive,
and Dàn (誕) also fell into Xún (循)'s hands.
In the fourth year of Jiàn'ān (建安) of Emperor Xiàn (獻帝) of Hàn (漢),
Huá Xīn (華歆) returned Yùzhāng (豫章) to Sūn Cè (孫策);
after Cè (策)'s death,
Cáo Cāo (曹操) memorialized to summon Xīn (歆),
and Sūn Quán (孫權) sent him back to Xǔ (許).
Huá (華)
is pronounced like Hù Huà (戶化).
Initially, Mùróng Bèidé (慕容備德), lord of Southern Yàn, served Qín as the Grand Administrator of Zhāngyè.
This event is detailed in Volume 102, under Hǎixī Gōng (海西公), Tàihé (太和) 5th year.
When Bèidé followed Qín King Fú Jiān (苻堅) to invade Huáinán,
the invasion of Huáinán is detailed in Volume 105, under Xiàowǔ Dì (孝武帝), Tàiyuán (太元) 8th year.
Bèidé and Yàn King Mùróng Chuí (慕容垂) raised troops in Shāndōng.
Fú Chāng (苻昌), the Grand Administrator of Zhāngyè, captured Bèidé's sons
and executed them all.
Gōngsūn Shì (公孫氏) was spared due to old age.
Bèidé's wife, Duàn Shì (段氏), whom Gōngsūn Shì had taken in, was pregnant
and her fate was undecided.
The prison official, Hūyán Píng (呼延平),
an former subordinate of Bèidé,
secretly helped Gōngsūn Shì and Duàn Shì escape to the Qiāng (羌) region.
Duàn Shì gave birth to a son, Chāo (超).
When Chāo was ten years old, Gōngsūn Shì fell ill.
Before his death,
he gave a golden knife to Chāo, saying:
"If you return east,
you should use this knife to return to your uncle."
Hūyán Píng then took Chāo and his mother to Liáng.
When Lǚ Lóng (呂隆) surrendered to Qín,
Chāo followed the people of Liángzhōu who were resettled in Cháng'ān.
The resettlement of Liángzhōu people by Qín is detailed in the previous volume, Yuánxīng (元興) 2nd year.
Duàn Shì married her daughter to Chāo.
Chāo feared he would be captured by the Qín people,
so he pretended to be mad and begged for alms.
The Qín people disdained him,
but Dōngpíng Gōng (東平公) Shào (紹) saw him and found him unusual.
He spoke to Qín King Yáo Xīng (姚興), saying:
"Mùróng Chāo (慕容超) has an imposing demeanor and presence,
he is probably not truly mad.
I wish you would subtly grant him an official title to secure him."
Xīng summoned him
and spoke with him.
Chāo deliberately gave absurd answers,
or did not respond when asked.
Xīng said to Shào:
"The proverb says 'a beautiful skin does not wrap foolish bones'
— that's just nonsense."
So he dismissed him.
Bèidé heard that Nà (納) had a posthumous son in Qín,
so he sent Wú Biàn (吳辯) from Jìyīn to see him.
Biàn found a fellow countryman, Zōngzhèng Qiān (宗正謙), who was selling divination services in Cháng'ān,
and informed Chāo.
Zōngzhèng
was a surname adopted from an official title.
Chāo secretly changed his name with Qiān and fled back to Southern Yàn.
When they reached Liángfù,
Yuè Shòu (悅壽), the Chief Clerk of Zhènnán, reported it to Mùróng Fǎ (慕容法), the Inspector of Yǎnzhōu.
Southern Yàn had appointed Fǎ as the Inspector of Yǎnzhōu,
stationed at Liángfù.
"In the past, there was a Han diviner who falsely claimed to be the Crown Prince Wèi (衛)."
This is detailed in Volume 23, under Hàn Zhāo Dì (漢昭帝), Shǐyuán (始元) 5th year.
Fǎ did not treat him with respect.
From this, Chāo and Fǎ developed animosity.
This laid the groundwork for Chāo's establishment and Fǎ's rebellion.
Bèidé was overjoyed upon hearing of Chāo's arrival,
and dispatched 300 cavalry to welcome him.
When Chāo arrived at Guǎnggù,
he presented the golden knife to Bèidé.
Bèidé wept bitterly,
overcome with grief.
He enfeoffed Chāo as King of Běihǎi,
and appointed him Attendant-in-ordinary, General of Agile Cavalry, Inspector of the Capital Region,
and granted him a residence and staff.
He carefully selected talented individuals of the time
to be his subordinates.
Bèidé had no sons,
and intended to make Chāo his heir.
When Chāo entered, he served with utmost joy;
when he went out, he humbled himself before scholars.
Because of this, his reputation and prestige both inside and outside the court unanimously inclined towards him.
12. In the 5th month,
Zhāngwǔ Wáng (章武王) Xiù (秀), the Grand Administrator of Guìyáng,
Yìyáng Wáng (義陽王) Wàng (望) had a son Hóng (洪), who had a son Wēi (威).
Wēi was enfeoffed as Zhāngwǔ and the title was passed down to his grandson.
When the grandson died without an heir,
Héjiān Wáng (河間王) Qīn (欽) adopted his son Fànzhī (範之) to succeed him.
Xiù
was Fànzhī's son.
He was executed.
Xiù's wife
was Huán Zhèn's (桓振) sister,
so he became suspicious of himself and rebelled.
13. Huán Xuán's (桓玄) remaining partisans, Huán Liàng (桓亮), Fú Hóng (苻宏), and others, gathered forces and raided several commanderies and counties.
Liú Yì (劉毅), Liú Dàoguī (劉道規), Tán Zhǐ (檀祗), and others divided their troops to suppress and eliminate them.
Jīng, Xiāng, Jiāng, and Yù regions were all pacified.
An edict appointed Yì as the Area Commander of the five commanderies including Huáinán, and Inspector of Yùzhōu.
The five commanderies were Huáinán, Lújiāng, Lìyáng, Jìnxī, and Ānfēng.
14. Liú Gāi (劉該), the Inspector of Northern Qīngzhōu, rebelled
and sought aid from Wèi.
In Lóng'ān (隆安) 5th year, Liú Gāi had previously surrendered to Wèi.
Shěn Yuē (沈約) said: In the Eastern Jìn, Qīngzhōu's seat was in Guǎnglíng.
In the 6th month,
Suǒ Dùzhēn (索度真), the Wèi Inspector of Yùzhōu, and the great general Húsī Lán (斛斯蘭)
Húsī
was also a Xiongnu surname.
besieged Péngchéng.
Liú Yù (劉裕) dispatched his younger brother, Liú Dàolián (劉道憐), the Administrator of Southern Péngchéng, and Mèng Lóngfú (孟龍符), the Administrator of Dōnghǎi, to lead troops to relieve it.
They beheaded Gāi and his entire family,
and the Wèi army was defeated and fled.
Lóngfú
was Huáiyù's (懷玉) younger brother.
15. Qín Lǒngxī Gōng (隴西公) Shuòdé (碩德) attacked Qiúchí,
repeatedly defeating Yáng Shèng's (楊盛) troops.
General Liǎn Jù (斂俱) attacked Hànzhōng.
Liǎn
was a Qiāng surname;
Jù
was his given name.
He resettled over 3,000 households of refugees in Guānzhōng.
In autumn,
the 7th month,
Yáng Shèng requested to surrender to Qín.
Qín appointed Shèng as the Area Commander of the two commanderies of Yì and Níng, General Who Conquers the South, and Governor of Yìzhōu.
16. Liú Yù sent an envoy to seek peace with Qín
and also requested the commanderies of Nánxiāng and others.
Qín King Yáo Xīng (姚興) granted it.
His various ministers all thought it was unacceptable,
but Xīng said:
"All good things in the world are one.
Liú Yù rose from humble origins,
was able to execute Huán Xuán,
restore the Jìn dynasty,
internally manage the common affairs,
and externally cultivate the borders.
Why should I begrudge a few commanderies and not complete his accomplishment!"
Thus, he ceded Nánxiāng, Shùnyáng, Xīnyě, Wǔyīn, and other twelve commanderies back to Jìn.
In Lóng'ān (隆安) 2nd year,
many areas north of the Huái and Hàn rivers surrendered to Qín;
these twelve commanderies were presumably all north of the Hàn River.
During Hàn Jiàn'ān (建安) era,
the right part of Nányáng was carved out to form Nánxiāng Commandery.
Jìn established Shùnyáng Commandery,
and made Nánxiāng a county.
Presumably, it was later re-divided to establish a commandery.
According to Jìn, Nánxiāng Commandery
was the land of Qín Hàn Yīn (漢陰) county and Zàn (酇) county,
now Guanghuà Jūn (光化軍).
Wǔyīn county belonged to Nányáng Commandery,
the beginning of its establishment as a commandery is unknown.
In the 8th month,
Shào Yán (邵顏), the Grand Administrator of Yàn Liáoxī, committed a crime
and fled to become a bandit.
In the 9th month,
Guō Zhòng (郭仲), the Palace Attendant, attacked and beheaded him.
17. The Ruǐ (汝) River dried up.
"Ruǐ"
should be written as
Guō Yuánshēng's (郭緣生) *Shù Zhēng Jì* (述征記) states: Qí Huán Gōng's (齊桓公) tomb is twenty *lǐ* south of Qí city,
and east of the tomb is the Nǚ River.
Some say: Qí Huán Gōng's daughter's tomb is above it,
hence the name of the river.
The Nǚ River flows northeast,
and is very divine.
When transformation flourishes, the water rises;
when governance is weak, the ford dries up.
The *Dìlǐ Zhì* (地理志) states: Mián Tóu Shān (葂頭山) is where the Nǚ River originates,
flowing northeast to Línzī and entering Jùdiàn (鉅淀).
Jùdiàn was the land of Hàn Jùdìng.
The *Jìn Shū Dìlǐ Zhì* (晉書地理志) states: The Nǚ River originates northeast of Dōng'ānpíng (東安平) county in Qí Commandery.
Soon after, Bèidé fell ill.
King of Běihǎi, Chāo, requested to pray for him.
Bèidé said:
"The lifespan of a ruler,
whether long or short, is determined by Heaven,
not by the Nǚ River."
Chāo insisted,
but was not permitted.
On the *wǔwǔ* (戊午) day,
Bèidé held an audience with his various ministers in the Dōngyáng (東陽) Palace
to discuss establishing Chāo as the Crown Prince.
Soon after, there was an earthquake.
The officials were frightened,
and Bèidé himself was uneasy,
so he returned to his palace.
That night,
his illness became critical,
and he closed his eyes, unable to speak.
Empress Duàn cried out loudly:
"If we now summon the Central Secretariat to draft an edict establishing Chāo,
is it permissible?"
Bèidé opened his eyes and nodded.
Thereupon, Chāo was established as the Crown Prince,
and a general amnesty was issued.
Bèidé soon died,
at the age of seventy.
That night,
his body was secretly taken out through the four gates
On the *Jǐwèi* day,
Mùróng Chāo ascended the imperial throne.
Mùróng Chāo,
courtesy name Zǔmíng,
was the son of Mùróng Dé's elder brother, Běihǎi Wáng Mùróng Nà.
He changed the era name to Tàishàng.
He honored Empress Duàn as the Empress Dowager.
He appointed Běidì Wáng Mùróng Zhōng as Grand Controller of all internal and external military affairs and acting director of the Department of State Affairs,
Mùróng Fǎ as Grand General of Conquering the South and Grand Controller of military affairs in the four provinces of Xú, Yǎn, Yáng, and Nányǎn,
and granted Mùróng Zhèn the title of *Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī*.
He made Shàngshū Lìng Fēng Fú the Grand Commandant,
and Qū
"Qū"
should be
"Jū".
Fēng Sōng the Left Executive Assistant of the Department of State Affairs.
On the *Guǐhài* day,
a mock burial was held for Mùróng Dé at Dōngyáng Líng,
with the posthumous title Xiànwǔ Huángdì,
and the temple name Shìzōng.
Mùróng Chāo appointed his trusted associate Gōngsūn Wǔlóu as his confidant.
Mùróng Dé's former grand ministers, such as Běidì Wáng Mùróng Zhōng and Duàn Hóng, all felt uneasy
and requested external appointments.
Mùróng Chāo made Mùróng Zhōng the Governor of Qīngzhōu,
and Duàn Hóng the Inspector of Xúzhōu.
Gōngsūn Wǔlóu was made General of the Martial Guard,
concurrently Commandant of Tunqi Cavalry,
and participated in internal political affairs.
Fēng Fú remonstrated, saying:
"Your servant has heard that close relatives should not be placed in external positions,
and those from outside the inner circle should not be placed in internal positions.
The *Zuǒ Zhuàn* records Shēn Wúyǔ remonstrating with Chǔ Língwáng, saying: 'Close relatives should not be outside,
and those from outside the inner circle should not be inside.'
Chǔ,
pronounced Chāng Lǚ.
Mùróng Zhōng is a minister of the imperial clan,
on whom the altars of soil and grain rely;
Duàn Hóng,
an esteemed member of the imperial consort clan,
is looked up to by the common people;
they should rightly assist in governing all affairs,
and should not be stationed far away in external regions.
Now Mùróng Zhōng and others are sent out to govern provinces,
and Gōngsūn Wǔlóu assists internally,
your servant secretly feels uneasy."
Mùróng Chāo did not heed him.
Mùróng Zhōng and Duàn Hóng were both displeased in their hearts
and said to each other,
"The skin of a yellow dog,
I fear, will ultimately be used to mend a fox fur robe."
The *Shǐ Jì* records: When Zōu Jì was Chancellor of Qí,
Chúnyú Kūn said to him,
"Although a fox fur robe is worn out,
it cannot be mended with the skin of a yellow dog."
Zōu Jì replied,
"I respectfully accept your command;
I shall carefully select gentlemen,
and not mix petty men among them."
Luó Xiū, the Magistrate of Jiānglíng, plotted to raise troops to attack Jiānglíng
and make Wáng Huìlóng their leader.
Liú Yù appointed Bìngzhōu Cìshǐ Liú Dàoguī as Grand Controller of military affairs in the six provinces of Jīng, Níng, etc., and Inspector of Jīngzhōu.
Luó Xiū did not carry out his plan,
and fled with Wáng Huìlóng to Qín.
Wáng Huìlóng was spared,
as seen in the previous volume, Yuánxīng 3rd year.
Qǐfú Gānzuī attacked Qiúchí
and was defeated by Yáng Shèng.
they appointed Zhāng Tǐshùn as Grand Administrator of Jiànkāng,
garrisoning Lèguàn.
The *Hàn Zhì* states that
Lèguàn County belonged to Jiǔquán Commandery;
the Zhāng clan divided it into Jiànkāng Commandery.
Guàn,
pronounced guān.
Lǐ Gǎo and his son, Dūnhuáng Tàishǒu Lǐ Ràng, garrisoned Dūnhuáng,
and then moved to Jiǔquán.
stating:
"Those who govern should be careful and prudent in rewards and punishments,
not acting on love or hatred,
drawing near to the loyal and upright,
and keeping away from sycophants,
not allowing those around them to usurp authority and power.
When praise or blame comes,
one should investigate its truthfulness;
when hearing lawsuits and judging cases,
one must maintain a pleasant demeanor and rely on reason,
being careful not to preemptively assume deceit or to make arbitrary predictions.
Zhū Zǐ said: *Nì* (逆),
means to meet it before it arrives.
*Zhà* (詐),
refers to people deceiving oneself.
means to anticipate it before seeing it.
means to expect it.
Yù,
