also known as Jìnkǒu City.
Liú Shǔ established the Administrator of Wǔxīng in Miányáng County, Hànzhōng.
During the Suí and Táng dynasties, it was Xīngzhōu.
Today's Miánzhōu City is the ancient Wǔxīng City.
濜 (jìn),
is pronounced 'xú rèn fān'.
In the nineteenth year of Tàiyuán of Xiàowǔ,
Yáng Shèng came to declare vassalage.
The reason he did not communicate with Jìn
was due to Huán Xuán's rebellion.
復 (fù),
is pronounced 'fú yòu fān'.
Shèng then appointed Xuān to act as Inspector of Liángzhōu.
The Zīzhì Tōngjiàn chronicles by Jìn's regnal years,
therefore it is unnecessary to write "Jìn" above Shèng as Grand Administrator.
The character "晉" (Jìn)
should be
the character "詔" (zhào).
In the fifth month,
on the day Bǐng
Xū,
Fú Jìn, the Minister of the Yàn Secretariat, plotted rebellion
and was executed.
Jìn
was Dìng's son.
In the eleventh year of Tàiyuán of Xiàowǔ, Fú Dìng surrendered to Yàn,
as seen in Volume 106.
8 Wèi ruler Guī made a northern tour and reached Rúyuán.
9 Wèi Chángshān Wáng Zūn was granted death for his crime.
10 Initially,
Wèi ruler Guī extinguished Liú Wèichén,
whose son Bóbó fled to Qín,
as seen in Volume 100, Tàiyuán sixteenth year of Xiàowǔ.
Bóbó was burly
and of handsome appearance,
with a clever and eloquent nature.
Qín King Xīng saw him and found him extraordinary,
discussing military and state affairs with him,
and his favor and treatment surpassed that of veteran officials.
Xīng's brother Yōng remonstrated, saying:
"Bóbó should not be kept close."
Xīng said:
"Bóbó possesses the talent to save the world;
I am about to pacify the empire with him,
why should I be so averse to him!"
So he appointed him General Pacifying the Far East,
and sent him to assist Mòyìgān in garrisoning Gāopíng,
granting him the Three Cities and the miscellaneous barbarians of Shuòfāng
(Wèi Shōu's Dìxíng Zhì states
that in the prefecture of Piānchéng Jùn, Guǎngwǔ County, there are Three Cities.
Táng Yánzhōu Fēnglín County was
the ancient land of Guǎngwǔ County)
to watch for魏's weaknesses.
Yōng firmly argued against it.
Xīng said:
"How do you know what kind of person he is?"
Yōng replied:
"Bóbó is disrespectful to his superiors and cruel to his subordinates,
greedy, treacherous, and unkind,
and changes allegiances lightly.
If you favor him excessively,
I fear he will ultimately become a border threat."
Xīng then stopped.
After a long time,
he eventually appointed Bóbó as General Pacifying the North and Duke of Wǔyuán,
assigning him the Xīanbéi of the Three Intersections and Five Tribes, and over 20,000 households of various barbarians,
to garrison Shuòfāng.
This laid the groundwork for Bóbó to later become a scourge to Qín,
and Xīng regretted not following Yōng's advice.
Wèi ruler Guī returned the captured Qín general Táng Xiǎofāng to Qín.
Qín King Xīng requested the return of Hè Dígān,
and also sent a thousand good horses to ransom Dí Bózhī.
Guī permitted it.
Qín's retention of Hè Dígān is seen in Volume 112, Yuánxīng first year.
Dí Bózhī and Táng Xiǎofāng being captured is also seen in the same year.
Bóbó was angered when he heard that Qín had re-established communication with Wèi,
and thus plotted to rebel against Qín.
The reason for Chǔ Bái Gōng Shèng's rebellion in Chǔ
was exactly like this.
He reached Dàchéng.
Dàchéng County in the Former Hàn belonged to Xīhé Commandery,
in the Later Hàn to Shuòfāng Commandery,
and was abolished during Wèi and Jìn.
崙 (lún),
is pronounced 'lú kūn fān'.
He gathered all his forces, over 30,000 men, and pretended to hunt in Gāopíng River.
Then he suddenly attacked and killed Mòyìgān,
and absorbed his forces.
Hūgē Bóbó (赫連勃勃) called himself a descendant of the Xiàhòu (夏后) clan.
The Shǐjì (史記) and the Hànshū (漢書) both state that the Xiongnú (匈奴) were descendants of Chúnwéi (淳維) of the Xiàhòu clan.
Bóbó
was a remnant of the Xiongnú,
hence this claim.
Xià (夏)
is pronounced `hù yǎ` (戶雅) in fanqie;
the same below.
He proclaimed himself the Great King of Xià (大夏天王)
and Great Chányú (大單于).
The Jìnshū (晉書) states: Bóbó,
courtesy name Qūjié (屈孑),
was a descendant of Qūbēi (去卑), the Right Worthy King of the Xiongnú,
a member of Liú Yuánhǎi's (劉元海) clan,
great-grandson of Liú Wǔ (劉武),
and son of Liú Wèichén (劉衞辰).
Liú Wǔ
was in fact Liú Hǔ (劉虎);
the Jìnshū, to avoid the taboo character of the Tang (唐) dynasty,
changed Hǔ (虎) to Wǔ (武).
Dān (單)
is pronounced `chán` (蟬).
He changed the era name to Lóngshēng (龍升)
and appointed officials.
He appointed his elder brother Yòudìdài (右地代) as Chancellor,
and enfeoffed him as Duke of Dài (代公);
Lìsìtí (力俟提) as Grand General,
enfeoffed as Duke of Wèi (魏公);
Chīyúālì (叱于阿利) as Grand Censor,
enfeoffed as Duke of Liáng (梁公);
his younger brother Ālìluóyǐn (阿利羅引) as Colonel-Director of Retainers;
Ruòmén (若門) as Minister of the Imperial Secretariat;
Chīyǐjiān (叱以鞬) as Left Assistant Director of the Imperial Secretariat;
and Yǐdǒu (乙斗) as Right Assistant Director of the Imperial Secretariat.
Hè Dīgān (賀狄干) had long been in Cháng'ān (長安),
always confined,
and thus accustomed himself to reading classics and histories,
behaving like a Confucian scholar.
When he returned,
Wèi Zhǔ Guī (魏主珪) saw that his speech and clothing were all like those of Qín (秦) people,
and believing he admired and imitated them,
became enraged,
and killed him along with his younger brother Guī (歸).
Qín Wáng Xīng (秦王興) appointed Crown Prince Hóng (泓) to oversee the affairs of the Imperial Secretariat.
In autumn,
seventh month,
on the *wùxū* (*戊戌*) day, the first day of the month,
there was a solar eclipse.
Rǔnán Wáng Zūnzhī (汝南王遵之) died due to an incident.
Zūnzhī
was the fifth-generation descendant of Liàngzhī (亮之).
Rǔnán Wáng Liàng (汝南王亮) died in the calamity caused by Chǔ Wáng Wěi (楚王瑋).
On the *guǐhài* (*癸亥*) day,
Yàn Wáng Xī (燕王熙) buried his empress Fú (苻) at Huīpínglíng (徽平陵).
The funeral carriage was tall and large,
requiring the destruction of the north gate to exit.
Xī walked twenty *li* (里) or more, with disheveled hair and bare feet, following the procession on foot.
On the *jiǎzǐ* (*甲子*) day,
a general amnesty was proclaimed.
Initially,
the Central Commander of the Guards Féng Bá (馮跋) and his younger brother, the Attendant Gentleman Sùfú (素弗), had both offended Xī.
Xī wanted to kill them,
so Bá fled
to the mountains and marshes to save his life.
Xī's levies and corvée were numerous and harsh,
and the people could not endure their plight.
Bá and Sùfú conspired with their cousin Wànní (萬泥), saying:
"We have no way to turn ourselves in.
Turning oneself in
means surrendering to beg for punishment.
Shǒu (首)
is pronounced `shì jiù` (式救) in fanqie.
If we together undertake a great enterprise,
we can establish the work of dukes and marquises;
if the endeavor does not succeed,
death will not come too late."
Thereupon, they got into a carriage together,
had a woman drive it,
and secretly entered Lóngchéng (龍城),
hiding in the home of Sūn Hù (孫護), the Northern Commander of Cavalry.
When Xī went out for the funeral,
Bá and his group, along with the Left Commander of the Guards Zhāng Xīng (張興) and the remaining partisans of Fú Jìn (苻進), rebelled.
Bá had always been on good terms with Mùróng Yún (慕容雲),
so he elevated Yún to be their leader.
Yún declined, citing illness.
Yún's claim of illness was mentioned in the previous year.
"Héjiān (河間) is dissolute and tyrannical;
heaven and men are both angered.
This is the time for his destruction by Heaven.
My lord,
you are from a prominent family, the Gāo (高) clan.
How can you be someone else's adopted son?"
The matter of being an adopted son is mentioned in Volume 109, Lóng'ān (隆安) first year.
They helped him up and went out.
Bá's younger brother Rǔchén (乳陳) and others led the masses to attack Hóngguāngmén (弘光門),
beating drums and shouting as they advanced.
All the imperial guards scattered and fled.
They then entered the palace, took up arms,
and closed the gates to defend themselves.
The Central Yellow Gate official Zhào Luòshēng (趙洛生) ran to report to Xī.
Xī said:
"What can these rat thieves do!
I will return and execute them."
He then placed the empress's coffin in the southern park,
gathered his hair, donned armor,
and galloped back to confront the rebellion.
That night,
he reached Lóngchéng,
attacked the north gate,
but could not breach it, and spent the night outside the gate.
On the *yǐchǒu* (*乙丑*) day,
Yún ascended to the throne of Heavenly King.
Yún,
courtesy name Zǐyǔ (子雨),
his grandfather Gāo Hé (高和),
was a collateral branch of the Gāogōulí (句麗),
and was adopted by Mùróng Bǎo (慕容寶) as his son.
He changed the era name to Zhèngshǐ (正始).
Xī retreated into Lóngténgyuàn (龍騰苑).
Chǔ Tóu (褚頭) of the Imperial Workshops' army scaled the wall and followed Xī,
claiming that the camp soldiers were of one mind and loyal,
only waiting for the army to arrive.
When Xī heard this,
he fled in a panic,
and none of his attendants dared to approach him.
Xī secretly absconded through a ditch.
After a long time,
his attendants wondered why he had not returned,
and searched for him together,
finding only his clothes and hat,
but not knowing where he had gone.
The Central Commander of the Guards Mùróng Bá (慕容拔) said to the Central Regular Attendant Guō Zhòng (郭仲):
"The great undertaking is on the verge of success,
yet the emperor inexplicably panicked.
This is truly strange.
However, those within the city are eagerly awaiting,
and success is certain upon arrival,
so we must not delay.
I will go ahead to the city;
you stay and wait for the emperor.
If you find the emperor,
come quickly.
If the emperor has not yet returned,
I will be able to pacify the city as desired,
and it will not be too late to welcome him later."
Thereupon, he divided his strong soldiers, over two thousand men, and ascended the north wall.
The officers and soldiers, thinking Xī had arrived,
all threw down their weapons and surrendered.
However, as Xī did not arrive for a long time,
Bá's troops had no reinforcements,
and their morale became doubtful and fearful.
They descended the wall again to the park,
and then all dispersed.
Bá was killed by people inside the city.
On the *bǐngyín* (*丙寅*) day,
Xī, in plain clothes, hid in the forest.
He was captured by someone,
and sent to Yún.
Yún enumerated his crimes and then killed him.
He was twenty-three years old.
Historians say that Mùróng Xī (慕容熙) was licentious and tyrannical,
that Heaven took away his spirit,
and that he died and his state was destroyed.
The Zàijì (載記) states: From Chúi (垂) to Xī, four generations,
a total of twenty-four years, and then it perished.
Shǔ (數)
is pronounced `suǒ jù` (所具) in fanqie.
Yún's original surname was Gāo (高).
Yōuzhōu Cìshǐ (幽州刺史) Shàngyōng Gōng Yì (上庸公懿) surrendered Lìngzhī (令支) to Wèi.
Wèi appointed Yì as Píngzhōu Mù (平州牧) and King of Chānglí (昌黎).
Yì
was the grandson of Píng (評).
The destruction of Former Yàn (前燕) was the fault of Mùróng Píng (慕容評).
Wèi Zhǔ Guī traveled west from Rúrén Yuán (濡源) to Cānhépō (參合陂),
and then returned to Píngchéng (平城).
Tūfà Nǔtán (禿髮傉檀) again defected to Qín.
He sent an envoy to invite Qífú Chìpán (乞伏熾磐).
Chìpán executed his envoy and sent his head to Cháng'ān.
This laid the groundwork for Qín to attack Nǔtán.
Shǐ (使)
is pronounced `shū lì` (疏吏) in fanqie;
the same below.
Chì (熾)
is pronounced `chāng zhì` (昌志) in fanqie.
17 The mother and wife of the ruler of Nányàn, Mùróng Chāo, were still in Qín.
Chāo dispatched Grandee Secretary Fēng Kǎi as an envoy to Qín to request their return.
Qín Wáng Yáo Xīng said:
"When the Fú clan was defeated,
all the musicians and dancers of the Grand Music Department entered Yàn.
When Cháng'ān fell,
the Grand Music Department musicians and dancers entered Xī Yàn;
when Xī Yàn perished,
Mùróng Chuí gathered them and returned to Zhōngshān;
when Zhōngshān fell,
they collectively fled to Yè,
which is how Nányàn obtained them.
伎 [jì],
read as Qú Qǐ.
Send the entertainers, or send a thousand Wú captives,
then what you request can be granted."
Chāo discussed this with his ministers.
Left Chief Minister Duàn Huī said:
"Your Majesty has inherited and maintained the ancestral altars and land;
it is not appropriate to lower your imperial title for the sake of private kin;
furthermore, the Grand Music Department contains the preserved sounds of previous dynasties,
which cannot be given away.
It is better to plunder Wú captives and give them."
Shàngshū Zhāng Huá said:
"Invading and plundering neighboring states leads to continuous warfare and mounting troubles.
If they can go there,
they can also come here;
this is not a blessing for the state.
Your Majesty's kind mother is in the hands of others;
how can you begrudge an empty title,
and not condescend for her sake!
Grandee Secretary of the Central Secretariat Hán Fàn once served as a palace attendant to Fú Shì's crown prince with Qín Wáng (Yáo Xīng).
If he is sent,
success is certain."
Chāo agreed with him,
and so sent Hán Fàn to Qín as an envoy,
declaring himself a vassal and presenting a memorial.
Mùróng Níng said to Yáo Xīng:
"If the King of Yàn gets his mother and wife back,
he will not submit again.
It is better to make him send the entertainers first."
Yáo Xīng then said to Hán Fàn:
"I will certainly return the Yàn King's family;
however, the weather is still hot now,
we should wait until autumn cools."
In the eighth month,
Qín sent Attendant Official, Cadet for the Imperial Retainers Wéi Zōng as an envoy to Yàn.
Chāo discussed the etiquette for meeting Wéi Zōng with his ministers.
Zhāng Huá said:
"Since Your Majesty previously presented a memorial,
you should now face north to receive the imperial edict."
Fēng Chěng said:
"The Great Yàn has seven sagely rulers whose radiance shines again,
from Mùróng Huì, Mùróng Huàng, Mùróng Jùn, Mùróng Wěi to Mùróng Chuí, Mùróng Dé, and Mùróng Chāo, a total of seven rulers."
重 [chóng],
read as Zhí Lóng.
Chāo said:
"I submit for the sake of the Empress Dowager;
I beg you, gentlemen, speak no more!"
He then faced north and received the imperial edict.
18 Máo Xiūzhī joined forces with the Administrator of Hàngjiā, Féng Qiān, to attack Yáng Chéngzǔ,
and decapitated him.
Máo Xiūzhī wanted to advance and attack Qiáo Zòng,
but the Inspector of Yìzhōu, Bào Lòu, disagreed.
Máo Xiūzhī submitted a memorial, stating:
"The reason people value life
is truly that there is a way to preserve it.
For me, in my situation,
the path to life has been exhausted.
My father Jǐn and paternal uncle Qú had their entire family annihilated by the people of Shǔ.
I wish to fight to the death to avenge them,
and no longer seek a path to life.
Morning dew quickly dries,
meaning life does not last long.
Now there have been several opportune moments,
but Bào Lòu has repeatedly missed the appointed time and failed to respond;
even if I die fighting the enemy,
if there is no rescue,
how can we succeed!"
Liú Yù then memorialized to appoint the Administrator of Xiāngchéng, Liú Jìngxūan, to lead five thousand troops to attack Shǔ.
When the Jìn dynasty moved south,
Xiāngchéng Commandery was established south of the Jiāngnán,
still governing Fánchāng and other counties.
Emperor Xiàowǔ abolished Xiāngchéng Commandery and made it Fánchāng County,
belonging to the migrant commanderies of Huáinán.
The Fánchāng County of present-day Tàipíng Zhōu is that very place.
Fánchāng was originally a county under Yǐngchuān Commandery in the Hàn dynasty,
and due to the establishment of migrant settlements, the name of this county was moved to south of the Jiāngnán.
This Xiāngchéng refers to Jìngxūan acting as Administrator of an old commandery's migrant settlement.
帥 [shuài],
read as 'lǜ' (率).
19 The Wèi ruler Tuòbá Guī went to Cáishān Palace.
An official from the surveillance office reported:
"Sīkōng Yú Yuè, his attire is splendid and luxurious;
his bearing and demeanor
emulate a ruler."
The surveillance official is mentioned in the previous volume, Yuánxīng Third Year.
He was killed.

20 The King of Běiyàn, Fēng Yún, appointed Fēng Bá as General Commander of All Military Affairs Inside and Outside the Capital, Grandee Minister with the Honors of the Three Ducal Ministers, and Overseer of the Imperial Secretariat.
Fēng Wànní was appointed Imperial Secretary.
Fēng Sùfú was appointed Governor of Chānglí.
Fēng Hóng was appointed General Who Conquers the East.
Sūn Hù was appointed Left Chief Minister of the Imperial Secretariat.
Zhāng Xīng was appointed General Who Guards the State.
Hóng [Hóng]
was Bá's younger brother.
21 In the ninth month,
Qiáo Zòng declared himself a vassal to Qín.
22 Tùfá Nǔtán led over fifty thousand men to attack Júqú Méngxùn.
Méngxùn engaged him in battle at Jūnshí,
and greatly defeated him.
Jūnshí is east of Zhāngyè,
west of Xī Shǎn,
presumably within Xī Commandery.
He surrendered.
Rìlè County
belonged to Zhāngyè Commandery in the Hàn dynasty.
Later, Xī Commandery was established,
with its seat at Rìlè.
Xián said: The old city of Rìlè
is southeast of present-day Gānzhōu Shāndān County.
23 In winter, the tenth month,
Qín's Inspector of Hézhōu, Péng Xīniàn, rebelled,
and surrendered to Tùfá Nǔtán.
Qín appointed Qǐfú Chìpán as acting Inspector of Hézhōu.

24 The ruler of Nányàn, Mùróng Chāo, sent Left Chief Minister Zhāng Huá and Palace Attendant Zōngzhèng Yuán Xiàn with one hundred and twenty musicians and dancers from the Grand Music Department to Qín.
Qín Wáng Yáo Xīng then returned Mùróng Chāo's mother and wife,
treating them generously and sending them off.
Mùróng Chāo personally led the imperial harem to welcome them at Mǎ'ěr Pass.
25 The Xià King Hèlián Bóbó defeated the three Xiānbēi tribes of Xuē Qiān and others.
"Xuē Qiān",
the Jìnshū Zàijì records it as
"Xuē Qiān",
the Shǔ edition has
"Xuē Gān".
He advanced to attack the various garrisons north of Qín's Sānchéng,
beheading Qín generals Yáng Pī, Yáo Shíshēng, and others.
All the generals said:
"Your Majesty wishes to manage Guānzhōng,
you should first secure your foundation,
so that people have something to rely on.
Gāopíng's mountains and rivers are rugged and strong,
and the land is fertile;
it can be made the capital."
Hèlián Bóbó said:
"You know one aspect,
but not the other.
My great enterprise is in its initial stage,
and my troops are not numerous;
Yáo Xīng is also a hero of his time,
and his generals are loyal;
Guānzhōng cannot yet be seized.
If I now secure one city,
he will certainly concentrate his forces against me.
My troops are no match for his,
and defeat would be imminent.
It is better to use swift cavalry, like the wind,
to strike unexpectedly.
If he saves the front, I will attack the rear;
if he saves the rear, I will attack the front,
causing him to be exhausted by constantly rushing to the rescue,
while I can roam and feed my troops at will.
In less than ten years,
Língběi and Hédōng will all be mine.
When Yáo Xīng dies,
and his heir is ignorant and weak,
I will slowly take Cháng'ān;
this is within my plan."
Thereupon, he plundered Língběi,
and the gates of all the cities in Língběi were not opened during the day.
Yáo Xīng then sighed:
"I did not heed Huáng'ér's words,
and it has come to this!"
Huáng'ér [Huáng'ér]
was the pet name of Yáo Xīng's younger brother, Yáo Yōng.
Gāojùlí sent envoys to pay tribute to Běi Yān,
and further recounted their family origins,
saying they were originally a branch of Gāojùlí.
Details can be found in Volume 109, Lóng'ān first year.
使 (envoy),
pronounced suō lì.
6. Summer.
In the fourth month,
Shàngshū Zuǒ Púshè Kǒng Ānguó died.
On the Jiǎwǔ day,
Lìbù Shàngshū Mèng Chǎng was appointed to replace him.
7. Běi Yān granted a general amnesty.
8. In the fifth month,
Běi Yān appointed Shàngshū Lìng Féng Wànní as the Mù of Yōu and Jì two Prefectures,
stationed at Féirú;
Zhōngjūn Jiāngjūn Féng Rǔchén as the Mù of Bìng Prefecture,
stationed at Báiláng.
The former Hàn dynasty’s Yòuběipíng Commandery had Báiláng County.
Shī Gǔ said: There was Báiláng Mountain,
hence the county was named after it.
The Later Hàn and Jìn dynasties abolished the county.
Wèi Shōu's Dìxíng Zhì says: Shìzǔ in the eighth year of Tàipíng Zhēnjūn established Jiàndé Commandery,
with its seat at Báiláng City.
Its territory belonged to the Liǔchéng County area of Táng’s Yíng Prefecture.
Sīlì Xiàowèi Wù Yíntí was appointed Shàngshū Lìng.
9. Qiáo Zòng sent envoys to declare himself a vassal of Qín,
and also secretly communicated with Lú Xún.
Zòng submitted a memorial requesting Huán Qiān from Qín,
intending to join him in attacking Liú Yù.
Qín Wáng Xīng asked Qiān about this,
and Qiān said:
"My family for generations
has been greatly benevolent in Jīng and Chǔ.
If I can rely on the resources of Bā and Shǔ,
and move downstream to the east,
the soldiers and people will surely respond enthusiastically."
Xīng said:
"A small stream cannot hold a giant fish.
If Zòng's talent and ability are sufficient to handle matters himself,
he does not need you as his 'scales and wings.'
You should seek your own good fortune."
So he sent him away.
When Qiān arrived in Chéngdū,
he openly welcomed scholars;
Zòng grew suspicious of him,
placed him at Lónggé,
and had people guard him.
Lónggé is probably the area of Lóngzhǎotān in Guǎngdū County, Chéngdū Prefecture today.
"Yáo Zhǔ’s words are indeed divine!"
10. Qín Zhǔ Xīng, knowing that Tūfà Nǔtán faced many internal and external difficulties—
at that time, Nǔtán’s Jūnzī Jìjiǔ Liáng Póu and Fǔguó Sīmǎ Biān Xiàn and others rebelled,
and Nǔtán executed all of them.
The Jìn Shū Zàijì states: Nǔtán suffered an external defeat at Yángwǔ,
and an internal rebellion by Biān and Liáng.
難 (difficulty),
pronounced nài dàn.
—sent Shàngshū Láng Wéi Zōng to observe him.
Nǔtán discussed the great strategies of the current era with Zōng,
conversing endlessly on all sides.
Zōng withdrew and
sighed, saying:
"Extraordinary talents and heroic capabilities
are not necessarily found in Huáxià;
intelligence and keen perception
are not necessarily acquired through reading.
Only now do I realize that beyond the Jiǔzhōu
and outside the Wǔjīng,
there are indeed other people of such caliber."
Nǔtán’s eloquence and talent,
sufficient internally to deceive his kinsmen,
and externally to deceive those who spied on his state,
ultimately led to his defeat and demise
because he used his troops lightly.
Judging by ancient standards,
he was of the same ilk as Zhì Bó Yáo,
but his talent and insight were not even equal to his.
復 (again),
pronounced fú yòu.
Zōng then spoke to Xīng, saying:
"Although Liángzhōu is weakened,
Nǔtán's cunning is extraordinary,
and he should not be attacked yet."
Xīng said:
"Liú Bóbó, with a ragtag army, could still defeat him;
how much more so when I deploy the troops of the whole empire against him!"
Zōng said:
"Not so.
Circumstances change, situations shift,
reversing in myriad ways.
The Shǔ edition reads
'返復' (repeatedly),
which should be followed.
Those who are wary and cautious are difficult to attack.
The reason Nǔtán was defeated by Bóbó
was that he underestimated him.
Now, if we approach him with a large army,
he will surely be fearful and seek to preserve himself.
I have secretly observed the talents and strategies of
Your Majesty's ministers, and none compare to Nǔtán.
Even if we approach him with heavenly might,
I dare not guarantee certain victory."
Xīng did not listen.
He sent his son, Zhōngjūn Jiāngjūn Guǎngpíng Gōng Bì, Hòujūn Jiāngjūn Liǎn Chéng, and Zhènyuǎn Jiāngjūn Qǐfú Gān Guī to lead 30,000 infantry and cavalry to attack Nǔtán,
and Zuǒ Púshè Qí Nán to lead 20,000 cavalry to campaign against Bóbó.
Lìbù Shàngshū Yǐn Zhāo remonstrated, saying:
"Nǔtán relies on his remote and dangerous location,
hence he dares to disobey and be insolent.
It would be better to issue an edict to Jǔqú Méngxùn and Lǐ Gǎo to attack him,
letting them exhaust and destroy each other,
without needing to trouble the troops of the central plains."
This also went unheeded.
Xīng sent a letter to Nǔtán, saying:
"Now I am sending Qí Nán to campaign against Bóbó.
Fearing that he might flee west,
I have ordered Bì and others to intercept him west of the river."
Nǔtán believed this to be true,
and thus made no preparations.
Bì crossed from Jīnchéng,
meaning he crossed the river from Jīnchéng.
"Now the royal army openly states it is attacking Bóbó,
and Nǔtán is hesitant, his defenses not yet strict.
I request 5,000 light cavalry
to surprise his city gates,
then the people of the mountains and marshes will all be ours,
and the isolated city, without aid,
can be taken easily."
Bì did not follow,
but advanced to Mòkǒu.
Mòkǒu is within Chāngsōng Commandery,
and is called Chāngsōng Mòkǒu.
Wèi Shōu's Dìxíng Zhì says:
Chāngsōng Commandery had Mòkǒu County.
Bì sent someone to persuade him to surrender,
and Bà said:
"You abandoned your sworn oath and attacked a friendly state.
I have only death awaiting me,
what is there to surrender for!"
Bì advanced to attack,
killed him,
and pressed on to Gūzāng.
Nǔtán fortified the city and held firm,
sending out surprise troops to attack Bì,
defeating him.
Bì retreated to Xīyuàn.
Within the city, Wáng Zhōng and others plotted an internal uprising.
The plot was exposed.
Nǔtán wanted to execute the ringleaders and pardon the rest.
Qiánjūn Jiāngjūn Yīlì Yánhóu said:
"Now strong bandits are outside,
and traitors are secretly rising within.
What could be more perilous?
If we do not bury them all,
how can we deter future incidents?"
Nǔtán agreed with him
and killed over 5,000 people.
He ordered the commanderies and counties to scatter cattle and sheep in the fields.
Liǎn Chéng let his troops plunder them.
Nǔtán sent Zhènběi Dàjiāngjūn Jù Yán and Zhènjūn Jiāngjūn Jìng Guī and others to attack them.
The Qín army suffered a great defeat,
with over 7,000 heads captured.
Nǔtán scattered cattle and sheep to bait the enemy,
and Liǎn Chéng plundered them,
so it was fitting that he was defeated.
Nǔtán attacked him,
but could not overcome him.
Autumn.
In the seventh month,
Xīng sent Wèi Dàjiāngjūn Chángshān Gōng Xiǎn to lead 20,000 cavalry as reinforcements for the various armies.
Arriving at Gāopíng,
he heard of Bì's defeat
and rushed to him by forced march.
Xiǎn sent skilled archers, Mèng Qīn and five others, to challenge at Liángfēngmén.
Before their arrows could be loosed,
Nǔtán's Cáiguān Jiāngjūn Sòng Yì and others met and attacked them,
killing them.
Xiǎn then blamed Liǎn Chéng,
sent an envoy to apologize to Nǔtán,
pacified the region beyond the river,
and withdrew his troops.
Nǔtán sent envoy Xú Sù to Qín to apologize.
Xià Wáng Bóbó, hearing that the Qín army was approaching,
retreated to defend Héqu.
Héqu is northeast of Shuòfāng;
the Yellow River takes a bend for a thousand li.
Nán let his troops plunder the countryside.
Bóbó secretly led his army to attack him,
capturing and killing over 7,000 people.
Nán led his troops in a retreat.
Bóbó pursued him to Mùchéng,
captured him,
and took 13,000 of his officers and soldiers prisoner.
At this, tens of thousands of the Yí and Xià north of the ridge pledged allegiance to Bóbó,
and Bóbó appointed governors and magistrates to govern them all.
With Yáo Bì's defeat,
Tūfà was not yet a threat to Qín.
With Qí Nán's defeat,
however, the trouble from Hèlián grew intense.
11 Sīmǎ Shúfán led an attack from Fānchéng on Zōushān.
The Administrator of Lǔjùn, Xú Yōng, abandoned the city and fled.
The Chief Clerk of the Chariots and Cavalry, Liú Zhōng, attacked and repulsed them.
12 Yān King Yún of Northern Yàn enfeoffed Mùróng Guī as the Duke of Liáodōng
and ordered him to preside over the Yàn ancestral sacrifices.
13 Liú Jìngxuan having entered the gorges,
which are known as the Three Gorges.
He personally led Bāo Lòu, the Inspector of Yìzhōu; Wén Chǔmào, the General Who Assists the State; and Shí Yánzǔ, the Dragon-Soaring General, to advance from Diànjiāng, fighting as they went.
Qiáo Zòng sought aid from Qín.
Qín King Xīng dispatched Yáo Shǎng, the General Who Pacifies the West, and Wáng Mǐn, the Inspector of Nánliángzhōu, leading twenty thousand troops to his aid.
Jìngxuan's army reached Huánghǔ,
five hundred *lǐ* from Chéngdū.
Huánghǔ is near Fúchéng.
They were locked in a stalemate for over sixty days;
Jìngxuan could not advance.
Their provisions ran out,
and sickness and plague broke out in the army,
with more than half dying.
He then withdrew his army.
Jìngxuan was dismissed from office
and had one-third of his enfeoffment reduced.
Liú Dàoguī, the Inspector of Jīngzhōu, had his supervisory title demoted to General Who Establishes Might.
This reflects the *Chūnqiū* principle of holding the commander responsible;
Dàoguī was then the Grand Commander for the expedition against Shǔ.
Liú Yù, considering Jìngxuan's defeat,
requested to resign his position.
An imperial edict demoted him to General of the Central Army,
but his office of *kāifǔ* remained as before.
Liú Yì wished to punish Jìngxuan severely with the law,
but Yù protected him.
Hé Wújì said to Yì:
"How can you let private resentment harm public justice!"
This private resentment is seen in the first year of his reign.
14 Qǐfú Chìpán, seeing that Qín's government was gradually weakening,
and also fearing Qín's attacks,
in winter,
the tenth month,
rallied over twenty thousand people from various tribes and built a city on Kāngliáoshān and occupied it.
Dīng Dù said: Kāngliáoshān is in Xīqiāng.
I assert that the Qǐfú clan occupied Yuànchuān,
its territory extending west to Báohǎn,
east to Lǒngdǐ,
bordered north by Hèlián,
and south by Tǔyùhún.
Kāngliáoshān must have been southwest of Yuànchuān.
In the Sòng dynasty, the western border ended at Qín and Wèi,
so Kāngliáoshān would have been within Xīqiāng.
嵻,
pronounced *qiū gāng*.
㟍,
pronounced *lú dāng*.
15 In the eleventh month,
Tūfà Nǔtán again proclaimed himself King of Liáng,
granted a great amnesty,
changed the era name to Jiāpíng,
and established all civil and military officials.
He made his consort, Lady Zhéjué, queen,
and his heir apparent, Wǔtái, crown prince,
overseeing the affairs of the Secretariat.
Wǔtái's
original name was Hǔtái.
When the Táng people compiled the *Jìnshū*,
to avoid the taboo name of the Táng ancestor,
they changed
"Hǔ"
to
"Wǔ,"
and the *Tōngjiàn* followed this.
Jù Yán, Marquis of Chāngsōng, was made Grand Tutor.
16 In Southern Yàn, the Ruǐ River dried up;
"汝" [Ruǐ],
should be
But the Miǎn River did not freeze.
The *Shuǐjīng Zhù* states: The Miǎn River originates east of Yíngchéng
and flows northwest into the Shí River.
Yíngchéng is Línbóchéng.
The Shí River is also commonly known as the Miǎn River,
or Shímǐan River.
The Shí River flows northeast into the Zī River,
and the Zī River further northeast joins the Zhuó River.
The Zhuó River flows northeast past the west of Guǎnggù City,
and the Zhuó River is also sometimes commonly called the Miǎn River.
Formerly, when Zhào attacked Guǎnggù,
the geomancers believed that with the Miǎn River surrounding the city, it could not be taken.
If the Wǔlóngkǒu were blocked,
the city would surely fall.
This refers to this river.
澠,
pronounced *shén líng*.
[Mùróng Chāo] questioned Lǐ Xuān,
who replied:
"The Miǎn River remaining unfrozen
is precisely because it is close to the imperial capital,
and thus close to the sun and moon."
Chāo was greatly pleased
and bestowed upon him a set of court robes.
17 In the twelfth month,
Qǐfú Chìpán attacked Péng Xīniàn at Báohǎn,
but was defeated by Xīniàn and returned.
18 In this year,
Wèi ruler Guī killed Mò Tí, Duke of Gāoyì.
Earlier,
when Tuòbá Kūdú attacked Guī,
(see Volume 106, Xiàowǔ Tàiyuán Eleventh Year), [Mò Tí] secretly sent an arrow to Kūdú, saying:
"How can a three-year-old calf bear a heavy load!"
Guī harbored resentment in his heart.
By this time,
someone reported that Tí's living arrangements were arrogant and that he emulated a sovereign.
Guī sent someone to show Tí the arrow and said to him:
"How does that three-year-old calf fare now?"
Tí and his son wept together.
The next morning,
they were arrested and beheaded.

Yìxī Fifth Year (Jǐyǒu, 409 CE)
1 In spring,
the first month,
on the *gēngyín* day, the first day of the lunar month,
Mùróng Chāo, ruler of Southern Yàn, held court with his officials.
He lamented the inadequacy of the grand music.
Three years prior,
Chāo had presented grand musical performers to Qín,
hence his lament about their inadequacy.
朝,
pronounced *zhāo*.
Hán Yuǎn, the General of the Leading Army, said:
Dīng Dù said: 員,
pronounced *zhú jué*.
"The late emperor, with the old capital overthrown,
gathered his forces in the Three Qí.
Zhōngshān fell,
and Mùróng Dé abandoned Yè,
securing Huátái.
Soon after, he lost Huátái again,
and then moved east to seize the Qí territory and occupy it.
These events are all mentioned previously.
戢,
pronounced *jí lì*.
[He waited] to seize a weakness in Wèi
and restore the former enterprise.
But instead, [Your Majesty] further invaded and plundered the southern neighbors to multiply your enemies.
Is this permissible!"
Chāo said:
"My plan is already settled;
I will not discuss it with you."
The history states that Mùróng Chāo's refusal to heed advice led to invasion and ruin.
伺,
pronounced *sì lì*.
2 On the *xīnmǎo* day,
a general amnesty was granted.
3 On the *gēngxū* day,
Liú Yì was made General of the Guard and was granted the privilege of establishing an office with the same honors as the Three Ducal Ministers.
Yì loved talent and esteemed scholars;
all the famous figures of the time flocked to him,
except for Zhāng Shào of Wú County, the Chief Clerk of Yángzhōu.
Someone asked him about it,
and Shào said:
"The Lord is an outstanding hero of his generation;
why bother asking too much?"
Liú Yù administered Yángzhōu,
hence the稱 "Lord."
4 Qín King Xīng dispatched his younger brother Chōng, the General Who Pacifies the North, and Dí Bózhī, the General Who Subdues the Barbarians, leading forty thousand cavalry
to attack Xià King Bóbó.
When Chōng reached Lǐngběi,
he conspired to return and attack Cháng'ān.
Bózhī refused to follow and stopped him,
whereupon Chōng poisoned and killed Bózhī to silence him.
5 Qín King Xīng sent an envoy to bow twice to Qiáo Zòng, appointing him Grand Commander, Chancellor, and King of Shǔ,
granting him the Nine Bestowals,
and authorizing him to confer titles and appointments,
all according to the rites of a king.
6 In the second month,
Nányàn generals Mùróng Xìngzōng, Húgǔtí, Gōngsūn Guī, and others led cavalry to raid Sùyù,
and captured it.
Sùyù city was north of the Huái River.
The emperor established Sùyù Commandery and Sùyù County.
Because Táng Dàizōng’s taboo name was Yù,
it was changed to Sùqiān County,
belonging to Xúzhōu.
Sòng Bái said: Sùyù city was 180 *lǐ* southeast of Xiàpī.
It was originally where the Sòng people relocated their encampment.
After the fall of Sòng,
it became a town.
During the Hàn dynasty, it was Qiúyóu County,
belonging to Línhuái Commandery.
During Jìn Āndì’s reign, Sùyù County was established.
The Táng dynasty changed it to Sùqiān County.
“Jiāng” (將)
is pronounced *liàng*.
Two thousand five hundred men and women were selected and handed over to the Grand Music Department to be taught.
Gōngsūn Guī
was the elder brother of Wǔlóu.
At this time,
Wǔlóu was a Shìzhōng, Shàngshū, and Leader of the Left Guard General,
presiding over all court affairs.
His relatives all occupied prominent positions,
and inside and outside the court, princes and dukes alike feared him.
Nányàn ruler Mùróng Chāo deliberated on the merits of Sùyù
and enfeoffed Húgǔtí and others as dukes of commanderies and counties.
Guìlín Wáng
Mùróng Zhèn remonstrated, saying:
“These several individuals,
exhausted the people and wasted troops,
and incurred enmity for the state.
What merit do they have to be enfeoffed?”
Chāo was enraged
and did not reply.
Shàngshū Dūlìngshǐ Wáng Yǎn flattered Wǔlóu.
During the Hàn dynasty, the Shàngshū had eighteen *lìngshǐ*;
later, they were increased to twenty-one;
thereafter, the number of personnel further increased,
and a Dūlìngshǐ was appointed to oversee them.
Wáng Yǎn rose to the office of Zuǒchéng.
The people of the state had a saying for him:
“If you want to become a marquis,
serve Wǔlóu.”
Chāo again sent Gōngsūn Guī and others to raid Jìnán,
capturing over a thousand men and women before leaving.
This Jìnán Commandery was also a relocated commandery established north of the Huái River.
“Jì” (濟)
is pronounced *zǐlǐ*.
The people all gathered in fortified strongholds to protect themselves.
An edict ordered Bìngzhōu Cìshǐ Liú Dàolián to garrison Huái’yīn to guard against them.
7 Qífú Chìpán entered to see Qín Tàiyuán Gōng Yáo Yì in Shàngguī.
Péng Xīniàn took advantage of the vulnerability to attack him.
Chìpán heard of this,
became enraged,
and returned without informing Yáo Yì.
He attacked Péng Xīniàn,
defeated him,
and then besieged Páohǎn.
Qífú Gān’guī followed Qín Wáng Yáo Xīng to Píngliáng.
Chìpán captured Páohǎn,
while Péng Xīniàn occupied Páohǎn.
“Páo” (枹)
is pronounced *fū*.
Qífú Gān’guī fled back to Yuànchuān.
Qífú Gān’guī was detained by Qín,
as seen in the third year of the previous volume.
Liú Jué, a man from Fèngyì, gathered several thousand people,
occupied Wànnián, and revolted.
Qín Wáng Yáo Xīng was in Píngliáng,
hence Jué took the opportunity to revolt.
Liú Jué was executed,
and his remaining followers were pardoned.
The generals requested a communiqué,
in their report greatly exaggerating the number of enemy heads.
Yáo Hóng did not permit it,
saying:
“The ruler entrusted me with the aftermath of affairs,
yet I could not stop the rebels and bandits.
I should blame myself and ask for punishment;
how dare I boast and claim credit for myself!”
Yáo Hóng was leisurely and literary.
From the perspective of a scholar,
he seemed to embody filial piety,
but he was not a talent for quelling chaos.
Qín Wáng Yáo Xīng went from Píngliáng to Cháonà.
He heard of Yáo Chōng’s plot,
believing he intended to return and attack Cháng’ān.
8 In the third month,
Liú Yù presented a memorial to attack Nányàn.
The court discussions all deemed it inadvisable.
Only Zuǒ Púyè Mèng Chǎng, Chēqí Sīmǎ Xiè Yù, and Cānjūn Zāng Xī believed it would certainly succeed,
and urged Yù to proceed.
Yù appointed Mèng Chǎng as Supervisor of the Central Army Resident Office.
He was the Supervisor of the Central Army General Resident Office.
“Chǎng” (昶)
is pronounced *chǒuliǎng*.
“Jiān” (監)
is pronounced *gǔxián*.
Mèng Chǎng was the grand-nephew of Xiè Ān.
Initially,
when the Fú clan was defeated,
Wáng Měng’s grandson Zhèn’è came to seek refuge
and was appointed Magistrate of Línlǐ.
Wǔdì Tàikāng’s fourth year established Línlǐ County,
belonging to Tiānmén Commandery.
During the Suí and Táng dynasties, it was merged into Lǐyáng County of Lǐzhōu.
“Lǐ” (澧)
is pronounced *lǐ*.
Wáng Zhèn’è was weak at drawing a bow,
but possessed strategy,
was decisive,
and enjoyed discussing military and state affairs.
Someone recommended Zhèn’è to Liú Yù.
Yù spoke with him
and was pleased,
so he kept him overnight.
The next morning,
he said to his advisors:
“I heard that a general’s household produces generals;
Zhèn’è is truly so.”
He immediately appointed him Cānjūn of the Central Army.
9 Héngshān collapsed.
10 In summer,
the fourth month,
Qífú Gān’guī went to Páohǎn,
leaving his heir Chìpán to garrison it.
He gathered his troops, obtaining twenty thousand,
and relocated his capital to Dùjiān Shān.
Dùjiān Shān
was where Qífú’s ancestor Sīfán resided.
11 Thunder struck the east wing of Wèi Tiān’ān Diàn.
Wèi Zhǔ Tuòbá Guī disliked this,
and ordered the Left School to use battering rams to attack the east and west wings,
destroying them all.
Initially,
Tuòbá Guī took *hánshísàn*.
Many Jìn people took *hánshísàn*;
the *Qiānjīnfāng* contains several prescriptions for it.
Sū Shì said: There are those in the world who eat stalactite and *wūhuì*, and indulge in alcohol and sex to seek longevity.
This probably began with Hé Yàn.
Hé Yàn was young and wealthy and noble,
so he took *hánshísàn* to satisfy his desires.
All who take it
suffer from carbuncles on the back and vomiting blood in succession.
When the medicine took effect,
his temperament became mostly agitated and restless,
and his anger was unpredictable;
by this time, it worsened progressively.
Moreover, numerous ominous signs appeared,
and diviners mostly said that a sudden change would arise close at hand.
Tuòbá Guī was anxious and uneasy,
sometimes not eating for several days,
or not sleeping until dawn,
recounting his successes and failures, gains and losses throughout his life,
and talking to himself incessantly.
He suspected that all his close ministers and attendants were untrustworthy.
Whenever officials presented memorials before him,
he would recall their old misdeeds,
and immediately kill them.
As for the others, if their expressions changed,
or their breathing was uneven –
a breath is one exhalation and one inhalation –
or their words were mistaken,
he would assume they harbored evil in their hearts,
which manifested outwardly,
and often personally struck and killed them.
Historians say that Wèi Zhǔ Tuòbá Guī’s death was approaching.
People in the court could not feel safe.
Officials merely sought to avoid trouble,
and none supervised each other.
Bandits openly roamed.
In the residential areas,
people became few.
Tuòbá Guī also knew this,
saying:
“I deliberately allowed it to be so.
Once the year of disaster passes,
I will clean it up again.”
At this time,
ministers feared punishment
and mostly dared not seek closeness.
Only Zuòzuòláng Cuī Hào remained diligent and tireless,
sometimes not returning home all day.
Cuī Hào
was the son of Lìbù Shàngshū Cuī Hóng.
Cuī Hóng never defied orders,
nor did he flatter,
thus Cuī Hóng and his son alone were not reprimanded.
12 Xià Wáng Hèlián Bóbó led twenty thousand cavalry to attack Qín,
plundering over seven thousand households of various Hu people from Píngliáng,
and then advanced to station at Yīlìchuān.
The *Wèi Shōu Dìxíng Zhì* states: Píngliáng city was on the border of Hàn Āndìng Qúnyīn.
During the Táng dynasty, it was the land of Yuánzhōu.
Yīlìchuān should also be to its southeast.
On the 13th day of the Jǐsì month,
Liú Yù set out from Jiànkāng,
leading a naval force from the Huái River into the Sì River.
In the fifth month,
he reached Xiàpī.
He left his boats, ships, and heavy baggage there,
and advanced on foot to Lángyá.
Wherever they passed, they built cities
and left soldiers to guard them.
He feared that Southern Yàn might cut off his rear with surprise troops.
"If the Yàn people block the strategic pass of Dàxiàn,"
The commentary to the Shuǐ Jīng says: The Shù River originates from the mountain northwest of Dōngguǎn County in Lángyá.
It flows southeast,
joining the Xiàn River on the right.
The river comes out of Dàxiàn Mountain to the north.
There is now Dàxiàn Pass.
Wèi Shōu's records state
that Pányáng County in Qí Prefecture has Dàxiàn Mountain.
The Wǔdài records state
that Línqú County has Dàxiàn Mountain.
Dù Yòu says: Dàxiàn is north of Yíshuǐ County in Yí Prefecture.
Sè,
pronounced like 'sì' (悉則翻).
Xiàn,
pronounced like 'diǎn' (戶典翻).
"and our large army penetrates deep,
not only will we achieve nothing,
but we will not be able to return.
What should we do?"
Yù replied:
"I have considered this thoroughly.
The Xiānbēi are greedy
and lack foresight.
When they advance, they profit from plunder;
when they retreat, they regret losing their crops.
They will assume that my isolated army has penetrated far
and cannot last long.
They will do no more than advance to occupy Línqú.
Wèi Shōu's records say: Línqú was the former Qú County of the Hàn dynasty,
belonging to Dōnghǎi Commandery;
during the Jìn dynasty, it was called Línqú,
belonging to Dōngguǎn Commandery.
Sòng Bái says: It was named after Línqú Mountain.
Qú,
pronounced like 'qú' (音劬).
They will certainly not be able to hold the pass and clear the fields.
I dare to guarantee this to all of you."
The ruler of Southern Yàn, Chāo, heard there was a Jìn army,
and summoned his ministers to a conference.
General Zhēnglǔ Gōngsūn Wǔlóu said:
"The Wú soldiers are light and swift,
and their advantage lies in quick battles.
We should not contend with them directly.
We should occupy Dàxiàn,
preventing them from entering,
dragging out the days and delaying their advance,
thereby dampening their morale.
Then, we can slowly select two thousand elite cavalry,
follow the coast southward,
and cut off their supply lines.
Separately, we can order Duàn Huī to lead the forces of Yǎn Prefecture
to descend along the mountains to the east.
Southern Yàn's Yǎn Prefecture administration was in Liángfù;
meaning, to descend eastwards along the mountains of Liángfù.
Qí,
pronounced like 'jì' (奇寄翻).
Shuài,
pronounced 'shuài' (讀曰率).
This is the best strategy.
Each governor and administrator should be ordered to fortify themselves along the strategic passes.
Apart from their essential stores,
everything else should be burned and destroyed,
and the crops mown down,
so that the enemy has nothing to rely on.
With their foreign army having no food,
and unable to force a battle,
within a month or so,
we can control them without effort.
This is the middle strategy.

Bá (跋) offered the position to his younger brother, the Duke of Fànyáng (范陽), Sùfú (素弗).
Sùfú (素弗) declined.
Bá (跋) then ascended to the position of Heavenly King in Chānglí (昌黎).
The Annals record: Fēng Bá (馮跋),
courtesy name Wénqǐ (文起),
was a native of Xìndū (信都) in Chánglè (長樂).
His ancestors were descendants of Bì Wàn (畢萬).
Among Wàn's (萬) descendants, some were granted a fief in Fēngxiāng (馮鄉),
and thus adopted the surname.
A decree stated:
"The Chén (陳) clan replaced the Jiāng (姜) clan,
but did not change the state's name, Qí (齊).
The Zhou (周) Grand Tutor Shàngfù (尚父) was first enfeoffed in Qí (齊),
and his surname was Jiāng (姜).
During the Warring States period,
Qí Tàigōng Tián Hé (齊太公田和),
a descendant of Chén Jìngzhòng (陳敬仲),
usurped the descendants of the Jiāng (姜) clan and took their state,
yet still called it Qí (齊)."
He changed the era name to Tàipíng (太平),
and gave Yún (雲) the posthumous title of Huìyì Huángdì (惠懿皇帝).
Bá (跋) honored his mother, Lady Zhāng (張), as Empress Dowager.
He established his wife, Lady Sūn (孫), as Queen.
His son Yǒng (永) was made Crown Prince.
He appointed Fànyáng Gōng Sùfú (范陽公素弗) as Grand General of Cavalry and Supervisor of the Secretariat.
Sūn Hù (孫護) was made Director of the Imperial Secretariat.
Zhāng Xīng (張興) was made Left Assistant Director.
Jí Jùn Gōng Hóng (汲郡公弘) was made Right Assistant Director.
Guǎngchuān Gōng Wànní (廣川公萬泥) was made Governor of Yōu (幽) and Píng (平) Prefectures.
Shànggǔ Gōng Rǔchén (上谷公乳陳) was made Governor of Bīng (幷) and Qīng (青) Prefectures.
In his youth, Sùfú (素弗) was chivalrous and unrestrained.
He once sought a marriage alliance from Hán Yè (韓業), the Left Aide to the Imperial Secretariat.
Yè (業) refused him.
When he became a chief minister,
he treated Yè (業) with particular generosity.
He liked to promote old families.
Humble, respectful, frugal, and modest,
he led by example.
All officials held him in awe.
Commentators praised him for having the demeanor of a prime minister.
Wēn Gōng (溫公) in his Zīzhì Tōngjiàn (資治通鑑),
even when discussing minor states,
if there was any good deed,
would certainly highlight it based on old histories,
to illustrate the difficulty of assisting a ruler.
22 Wèi Zhǔ Guī (魏主珪) was about to establish Qí Wáng Sì (齊王嗣) as Crown Prince.
According to Wèi (魏) custom,
whenever a successor was established, his mother was first put to death.
So, Sì's (嗣) mother, Lady Liú Guìrén (劉貴人), was granted death.
Guī (珪) summoned Sì (嗣) and instructed him, saying:
"Emperor Wǔ of Hàn (漢武帝) killed Lady Gōuyì (鉤弋夫人)
to prevent the empress dowager from interfering in politics
and her family from causing chaos.
The event is recorded in Volume 22, in the first year of Hòu Yuán (後元) of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn (漢武帝).
I, therefore, follow the example of the ancients."
The Shǔ (蜀) version reads
"故吾 (gù wú)".
Sì (嗣) was filial by nature,
and wept uncontrollably in sorrow.
Guī (珪) was angered by this.
Sì (嗣) returned to his residence and
cried day and night. Guī (珪) learned of this and summoned him again.
His attendants said:
"The Emperor is extremely angry.
If you enter, the consequences will be unpredictable.
It would be better to avoid him for now,
and enter after his anger subsides."
Sì (嗣) then escaped and hid outside.
Only Chēlùtóu (車路頭) and
Chē Kūn Shì (車焜氏) of Dàirén (代人), who were his personal attendants,
distant relatives of the Tuòbá (拓跋) clan,
later changed their surname to Chē (車) during Emperor Xiàowén (孝文) of Later Wèi (魏).
Initially,
Guī (珪) went to the Hèlán (賀蘭) tribe and
saw that the sister of Xiànmíng Hè Tàihòu (獻明賀太后) was beautiful.
Guī's (珪) father, Shí (寔),
was the legitimate son of Wèi Zhāochéngdì Shíyìjiān (魏昭成帝什翼犍).
He died before Zhāochéng (昭成) and was posthumously honored as Xiànmíng Huángdì (獻明皇帝).
Empress Dowager Hè (賀) received the posthumous title from her husband.
He requested to marry her.
Empress Dowager Hè (賀) said:
"No.
She is excessively beautiful;
there will certainly be something inauspicious."
The Zuǒ Zhuàn (左傳) records: Jìn Shūxiàng (晉叔向) wanted to marry a woman from the Shēn Gōng Wū Chén (申公巫臣) clan,
but his mother stopped him, saying:
"What is extremely beautiful will surely have something extremely evil."
This saying is similar.
"She must not be taken."
Guī (珪) secretly ordered someone to kill her husband and then married her,
giving birth to Qīnghé Wáng Shào (清河王紹).
Shào (紹) was brutal, cunning, and lawless,
fond of wandering through streets and alleys,
robbing and stripping travelers for pleasure.
Guī (珪) was angry with him,
and once hung him upside down in a well.
When he was on the verge of death,
he was taken out.
Qí Wáng Sì (齊王嗣) repeatedly admonished and reprimanded him.
Shào (紹) was therefore at odds with Sì (嗣).
On the day Wùchén (戊辰),
Guī (珪) reprimanded Lady Hè (賀),
imprisoned her,
and was about to kill her.
It was already dusk,
and the decision had not yet been made.
The lady secretly sent a message to Shào (紹), saying:
"How can you save me?"
The attendants, knowing Guī (珪) was cruel and ruthless,
were all fearful.
Shào (紹), sixteen years old,
at night,
conspired with several of his attendants and palace eunuchs and maids.
He climbed over the wall into the palace,
reaching the Tiān'ān Diàn (天安殿).
The attendants cried out:
"Thieves are here!"
Guī (珪) was startled and rose,
but could not find his bow or sword.
He was then murdered.
He was thirty-nine years old.
In the second year of Yǒngxīng (永興) of Emperor Míngyuán (明元帝),
he was given the posthumous title Xuānwǔ Huángdì (宣武皇帝),
and the temple name Lièzǔ (烈祖).
In the fifth year of Tàicháng (泰常),
the posthumous title was changed to Dàowǔ (道武).
On the day Jǐsì (己巳), the palace gates remained unopened until noon.
Shào (紹) falsely claimed to have an imperial edict
and gathered all officials in front of the Duānmén (端門).
The main south gate of the palace was called Duānmén (端門).
Punctuation mark.
Fēi (扉)
means a door leaf.
He said: "I have an uncle,
and also an elder brother.
Whom do you dukes and ministers wish to follow?"
The crowd was astonished and turned pale,
no one dared to reply.
After a long while,
Nánpíng Gōng Chángsūn Sōng (南平公長孫嵩) said:
"Follow the King."
Only then did the multitude realize that the Emperor had passed away,
but they did not know the reason,
and no one dared to speak.
Only Yīnpíng Gōng Liè (陰平公烈) wept loudly and departed.
Liè (烈) was Yí's (儀) younger brother.
When Wèi (魏) conquered Yàn (燕),
Yí (儀) had rendered meritorious service.
He was granted death in the eighth month of that year.
People harbored different intentions.
Féirú Hóu Hè Hù (肥如侯賀護) lit a beacon north of Ānyángchéng (安陽城).
Ānyángchéng (安陽城)
was the county seat of Dōng'ānyáng (東安陽) in Hàn (漢) era's commandery.
The Wèi Shōu Dìxíng Zhì (魏收地形志) records: In the middle of Yǒngxī (永熙),
Gāoliǔ Jùn (高柳郡) was established,
with its seat in Ānyáng (安陽).
The other tribes also gathered and fortified themselves.
Shào (紹) heard that the people were uneasy,
so he generously distributed cloth and silk to the kings, dukes, and others below them.
Only Cuī Hóng (崔宏) refused to accept.
Historians say that Cuī Hóng (崔宏) was discerning.
Qí Wáng Sì (齊王嗣) heard of the disturbance,
so he returned from outside.
During the day, he hid in the mountains,
and at night, he lodged at Wáng Luò'ér's (王洛兒) house.
Luò'ér's (洛兒) neighbor, Lǐ Dàoqián (李道潛), provided Sì (嗣) with provisions.
The common people knew about this to some extent,
and they were happy to tell each other.
Shào (紹) heard about it,
arrested Dàoqián (道潛),
and executed him.
Shào (紹) recruited people to search for Sì (嗣),
intending to kill him.
The Hunter Commander Shúnsūn Jùn (叔孫俊)
The Tuòbá (拓跋) clan originated in Dàiběi (代北).
Their custom was to value hunting,
so they established the position of Hunter Commander,
appointing talented and brave children of powerful families to it.
This was similar to the Hàn (漢) Dynasty's Qímén Láng (期門郎) and Yǔlín Láng (羽林郎).

According to the Wèi Shū Guānshì Zhì (魏書官氏志), in the first year of Tiāncì (天賜), positions such as Sǎnqí Láng (散騎郎), Lièláng (獵郎), Zhūshěng Lìshǐ (諸省令史), Shěngshì (省事), and Diǎnqiān (典籤) were established.
Later, Wèi Xiàowén (魏孝文) changed the Yǐzhān (乙旃) clan, descendants of Emperor Xiàndì's (獻帝) paternal uncle, to the Shúsūn (叔孫) clan.
Móhún (磨渾)
was the son of Qū (屈), the Marquis of Yuánchéng (元城).
Shào (紹) sent two of his personal guards to go with them.
Jùn (俊) and Móhún (磨渾) managed to get out,
then immediately seized the personal guards and went to Sì (嗣),
executing them.
Jùn (俊)
was the son of Jiàn (建).
Wáng Luò'ér (王洛兒) traveled to and from Píngchéng (平城) for Sì (嗣),
communicating with high officials.
At night,
he informed Ānyuǎn Jiāngjūn (安遠將軍) Ān Tóng (安同) and others.
When the multitude heard this,
they all responded in unison,
vying to come out and welcome him.
When Sì (嗣) arrived at the west side of the city,
the guards seized Shào (紹) and delivered him.
Sì (嗣) killed Shào (紹) and his mother, Hè (賀) clan.
He also executed Shào's (紹) personal guards and more than ten eunuchs and palace women who had acted as internal collaborators.
Those who had first assaulted the imperial carriage
were all torn apart and eaten by his subjects.
On the day of Rénshēn (壬申),
Sì (嗣) ascended the imperial throne.
Sì (嗣)
was the eldest son of Dàowǔ Huángdì (道武皇帝).
Xiāo Zǐxiǎn (蕭子顯) said: Sì (嗣),
courtesy name Mùmò (木末).
He changed the reign title to Yǒngxīng (永興).
He posthumously honored Liú Guìrén (劉貴人) as Xuānmù Huánghòu (宣穆皇后).
The ducal ministers who had previously been dismissed and returned to their residences, not participating in court affairs,
were all recalled and employed.
He issued an edict to Zhǎngsūn Sōng (長孫嵩), Ān Tóng (安同), Marquis of Běixīn (北新), Xī Jīn (奚斤), Marquis of Shānyáng (山陽),
Later, Wèi Xiàowén (魏孝文) changed the Dáxī (達奚) clan, descendants of Emperor Xiàndì's (獻帝) third elder brother,
and soon after changed it to the Xī (奚) clan.
When subjects and sons reached the palace gate, they all dismounted their carriages and entered,
hence it was called Zhǐchēmén (止車門) (Car-Stopping Gate).
People at the time called them the Eight Dukes.
Qū (屈)
was Móhún's (磨渾) father.
Sì (嗣) considered Shàngshū Yān Fèng (尚書燕鳳) to have served Shíyìjiān (什翼犍)
Shíyìjiān (什翼犍) was the King of Dài (代),
and he appointed Fèng (鳳) as Zuǒ Zhǎngshǐ (左長史).
Jiān (犍),
pronounced jū yán.
Wèi (魏) referred to the Shàngshū Dūshěng (尚書都省) as Shàngshū Dūzuò (尚書都坐).
Dūzuò Dàguān (都坐大官) was probably the head of the Shàngshū (尚書).
Zuò (坐),
pronounced cú wò.
to discuss political affairs.
He appointed Wáng Luò'ér (王洛兒) and Chē Lùtóu (車路頭) as Sǎnqí Chángshì (散騎常侍),
and Shúsūn Jùn (叔孫俊) as Wèi Jiāngjūn (衞將軍).
Sǎn (散),
pronounced xǐ dàn.
Qí (騎),
pronounced qí jì.
All were bestowed with titles of duke of commanderies and counties.
Sì (嗣) asked his old officials who among them had been most trusted by the late emperor.
Wáng Luò'ér (王洛兒) named Lǐ Xiān (李先).
Xiān (先)
was Mùróng Yǒng's (慕容永) chief strategist.
When Yǒng (永) was destroyed,
Xiān (先) was relocated to Zhōngshān (中山).
When Wèi (魏) attacked Yān (燕),
Xiān (先) surrendered to Wèi (魏),
and Dàowǔ (道武) deeply trusted him.
"By what talent or merit did you become known to the late emperor?"
He replied:
"I have no talent or merit;
it is only by my loyalty and straightforwardness that I was known to the late emperor."
An edict appointed Xiān (先) as Āndōng Jiāngjūn (安東將軍),
to constantly reside inside the palace
to be available for consultation.
Yuè (悅), King of Zhūtí (朱提),
was the son of Qián (虔).
For Tuòbá Qián (拓跋虔), see Volume 108, Tàiyuán (太元) 21st year of Xiàowǔ (孝武).
Zhūtí (朱提),
pronounced zhū shí.
felt self-doubt and fear.
In the intercalary eleventh month,
on the day of Dīnghài (丁亥),
Yuè (悅) entered the imperial presence, concealing a dagger,
intending to cause trouble.
Shúsūn Jùn (叔孫俊) noticed his unusual demeanor,
extended his hand to seize him,
searched his bosom,
found the dagger,
and then killed him.
23 In the twelfth month,
on the day of Yǐsì (乙巳),
Venus trespassed upon Xū (虛) and Wēi (危) constellations.
Xū (虛) has two stars,
Wēi (危) has three stars.
According to the Jìn Tiānwén Zhì (晉天文志), from 8 degrees of Xūnǚ (須女) to 15 degrees of Wēi (危) is Xuánxiāo (玄枵),
the field of Qí (齊),
belonging to Qīngzhōu (青州).
Chāo (超) personally killed him.
24 The Ròurán (柔然) invaded Wèi (魏).
1 In spring,
the first month,
on Jiǎyín (甲寅) the first day of the month,
Nányān (南燕) ruler Chāo (超) ascended Tiānmén (天門).
Tiānmén (天門)
was the south gate of Guǎnggù's (廣固) inner city.
On Yǐmǎo (乙卯),
Chāo (超) and his favorite concubine, Madame Wèi (魏夫人), ascended the city wall,
saw the might of the Jìn (晉) army,
and held hands and wept together.
Hán Jiàn (韓諫) said:
"Your Majesty has encountered a time of difficulty and adversity.
You should be striving to strengthen yourself to bolster the morale of your soldiers and people,
yet you weep like a child! "
Chāo (超) wiped his eyes and apologized.
Shàngshū Lìng (尚書令) Dǒng Shēn (董詵) urged Chāo (超) to surrender.
Chāo (超) was enraged and
imprisoned him.
2 Wèi (魏) Zhǎngsūn Sōng (長孫嵩) led troops to attack the Ròurán (柔然).
3 Wèi (魏) ruler Sì (嗣) observed that many powerful local gentry in the commanderies and counties were causing trouble for the people,
so he summoned them all with generous edicts.
The people were attached to their land and were unhappy about being moved inland.
The chief officials forced them to move,
whereupon unruly youths fled and gathered,
and banditry erupted everywhere.
Sì (嗣) summoned the Eight Dukes to discuss it, saying:
"I wish to remove pests for the people,
but the governors and magistrates cannot pacify and comfort them, causing such disorder.
Now that the offenders are numerous,
they cannot all be executed.
I wish to grant a great amnesty to pacify them.
What do you think? "
Qū (屈), Marquis of Yuánchéng (元城), said:
"The people have fled and become bandits.
To pardon them without punishing them
would be for those above to seek from those below.
It would be better to execute the ringleaders
and pardon the rest of the followers."
Cuī Hóng (崔宏) said:
"A sagely ruler's governance of the people
focuses solely on pacifying them,
not on competing for victory or defeat with them.
Although amnesty is not always the correct policy,
it can be used as an expedient.
Qū (屈) wishes to execute first and then pardon,
which ultimately means he cannot avoid both.
'Cannot avoid both'
means he cannot avoid execution first,
and then cannot avoid amnesty later.
Qù (去),
pronounced qiāng lǚ.
If they are pardoned and do not comply,
it will not be too late to execute them then."
Sì (嗣) followed his advice.
In the second month,
on Guǐwèi (癸未) the first day of the month,
he dispatched General Yú Lìdī (于栗磾) with ten thousand cavalry to suppress those who did not obey.
All places he went were pacified.
The historian says that Wèi (魏) had wise strategists,
which is why the rebellion was quelled.
Dī (磾),
pronounced dīng xī.
Jiāng (將),
pronounced jí liàng.
Qí (騎),
pronounced qí jì;
same below.
4 Nányàn's Hèlàilú and Gōngsūn Wǔlóu made a tunnel to launch a surprise attack on the Jìn forces,
but could not repel them.
The city had been closed for a long time,
and more than half of the men and women in the city suffered from foot weakness,
with those surrendering following one after another.
Mùróng Chāo was carried in a palanquin to ascend the city wall.
Shàngshū Yuè Shòu advised Mùróng Chāo, saying:
"Today, Heaven is helping the invaders commit atrocities.
Our warriors are withered and exhausted.
We are alone in defending this desolate city,
cut off from external aid.
The timing and human affairs are already clear.
If a dynasty's mandate has an end,
even Yáo and Shùn yielded their positions.
How can Your Majesty not consider a flexible strategy?"
Mùróng Chāo sighed, saying:
"Rise and fall [of a state]
is fate.
I would rather wield my sword and die
than live by offering a jade disk!"
On the day of Dīnghài,
Liú Yù led his entire army to attack the city.
Someone said:
"Today is a 'wǎngwáng' day,
unfavorable for military expeditions."
According to the almanac, the fourteenth day after the 'Jīngzhé' solar term in the second month is a 'wǎngwáng' day.
Liú Yù replied, "We go (wǎng), they perish (wáng).
How can it be unfavorable!"
They attacked from all four sides.
Yuè Shòu opened the gate to let the Jìn army in.
Mùróng Chāo, with several tens of cavalrymen, scaled the city wall and broke through the encirclement to escape,
but was pursued and captured.
Liú Yù repeatedly interrogated him about the crime of not surrendering.
Mùróng Chāo remained composed,
saying nothing,
except to entrust his mother to Liú Jìngxuan.
Liú Jìngxuan had previously defected to Yàn,
which is why Mùróng Chāo entrusted his mother to him.
There is no greater filial piety than bringing peace to one's parents.
For his mother's sake, Mùróng Chāo compromised his principles to serve Qín,
exhausting his musical and artistic skills to entertain Fú Jiān.
Then, he plundered Jìn people to increase his entertainers.
This brought about invasion,
leading to both mother and son becoming captives.
Yet, he still wanted to entrust his mother to Liú Jìngxuan.
How shallow-minded!
Liú Yù was enraged that Guǎnggù had not fallen for so long,
and wanted to bury all its inhabitants alive,
rewarding his officers and soldiers with their wives and daughters.
Hán Fàn remonstrated, saying:
"When the Jìn court moved south,
the Central Plains were in turmoil.
Scholars and common people were without support,
so they attached themselves to the strong.
Once they became sovereign and subject,
they naturally had to exert themselves fully for their lord.
These are all old families of the literati,
and the surviving people of the former emperor.
Now, if the royal army, sent to punish and pacify, were to bury them all alive,
where would they go for refuge!
I fear that the people of the northwest will no longer have any hope of revival."
When Tāng campaigned against the feudal lords,
he campaigned in the east, and the western barbarians resented it.
He campaigned in the south, and the northern barbarians resented it,
saying:
"Why does he leave us last?"
Wherever he went,
the people, their households filled with joy,
said:
"We await our sovereign;
when our sovereign comes, we shall revive."
Nevertheless, Liú Yù executed three thousand people, from princes and dukes downwards,
confiscated over ten thousand households,
razed their city walls,
sent Mùróng Chāo to Jiànkāng,
and beheaded him.
In the second year of Lóng'ān,
Mùróng Dé founded his state,
named Nányàn.
It had two rulers,
and perished after thirteen years.
Your servant Sīmǎ Guāng says: Since Jìn crossed the Jiāng River,
its awe-inspiring power has not been strong.
Barbarian tribes have rampaged,
like tigers devouring the Central Plains.
Liú Yù first used the royal army to conquer and pacify the eastern regions.
If, at this time, he had not commended and honored the worthy and outstanding,
comforted and settled the exhausted populace,
promoted the spirit of benevolence and kindness,
and cleansed the corrupt administration,
making all scholars turn towards him,
and the remaining people eagerly await him,
but instead indulged in slaughter to satisfy his anger,
then his actions and policies
were even inferior to those of Fú Jiān and Yáo Xìng.
It is no wonder that he could not unify the four seas
and achieve a great and beautiful enterprise.
Was this not because, though he possessed wisdom and courage,
he lacked benevolence and righteousness?
5 Initially,
Xú Dàofù, hearing that Liú Yù was campaigning in the north,
advised Lú Xún to take advantage of the void and attack Jiànkāng.
Lú Xún did not comply.
Xú Dàofù then went to Pānyú
himself and persuaded Lú Xún, saying:
"Our initial reason for living outside the Lingnan region
was not to establish ourselves permanently here
and pass it on to our descendants, was it?
It was precisely because Liú Yù was difficult to contend with.
Now, Liú Yù's troops are bogged down beneath a fortified city,
with no return date in sight.
If we take these death-defying warriors who long to return home
(Sūn Tàī's followers were originally from the Three Wú region,
and those plundered by Sūn Ēn were also from the Three Wú region;
having been at sea for a long time,
they all yearned for their homeland and desired to return),
it will be as easy as turning over a hand.
He and Liu (
referring to Hé Wújì and Liú Yì)
are always considered a grave internal threat by the court.
If Liú Yù, after pacifying Qí,
rests his troops for more than a year,
and the imperial edict summons you,
Liú Yù himself will lead troops to garrison Yùzhāng,
and dispatch his generals with elite forces to cross the Lingnan mountains.
Even with your general's divine prowess,
I fear you will certainly be unable to resist them.
Today's opportunity
must not be missed.
If we first capture Jiànkāng,
overturning their foundation,
even if Liú Yù returns south,
he will be powerless.
If you do not agree,
I will lead the forces of Shǐxīng directly to Xúnyáng."
In the third year of Yuánxīng,
Lú Xún sent Xú Dàofù to attack and capture Shǐxīng,
and then made him guard it.
Lú Xún had no way to counter his plan,
so he followed it.
Earlier,
Xú Dàofù had sent people to fell timber for boats in Nánkāng Mountain.
Nánkāng Mountain
is the mountain of Nánkāng County.
Wú established Ānnán County at Meǐlíng in Yùzhāng of Hàn.
In the first year of Tàikāng of Emperor Wǔ, it was renamed Nánkāng.
The so-called Meǐlíng
is today's Dàyǔ Mountain.
Nánkāng Mountain
is the Dàyǔ Mountains,
all within the current Nán'ān Commandery.
They sold the timber cheaply,
from Nánkāng west to Shǐxīng is four hundred li.
A large quantity of timber was piled up, but no one suspected anything.
By this time, all of it was taken to outfit ships,
and it was ready in ten days.
Lú Xún himself, from Shǐxīng, raided Chángshā.
Xú Dàofù raided Nánkāng, Lúlíng, and Yùzhāng.
All the defending officials abandoned their posts and fled.
Xú Dàofù floated downstream
(floating downstream along the Gànshí River).
At this time, the news of the capture of Yàn had not yet arrived.
The imperial court urgently summoned Liú Yù.
Liú Yù was then planning to garrison Xiàpī
and manage Sī and Yōng.
When he received the imperial edict,
he appointed Hán Fàn as the Grand Administrator of Yàn Commandery, overseeing military affairs of eight commanderies
(Qīngzhōu previously oversaw the eight commanderies of Qí, Jìnán, Lè'ān, Chéngyáng, Dōnglái, Chángguǎng, Píngchāng, and Gāomì;
and the so-called Yàn Commandery
was probably where Nányàn had established the Yàndū Magistrate in Guǎnggù, and now it was renamed Yàn Commandery Administrator).
Tán Sháo was made Grand Administrator of Lángyá.
On the day of Wùshēn,
he led his troops back.
Tán Sháo
was the elder brother of Tán Zhī.
After a long time,
Liú Mùzhī accused Hán Fàn and the others of plotting rebellion,
and had them all executed.
Hán Fàn and the other two were former officials of Yàn.
Liú Mùzhī feared they would cause trouble,
so he killed them.
6. Hé Wú-Jì (何無忌), Duke Zhōngsù (忠肅公) of Ānchéng (安成), led troops from Xúnyáng (尋陽) to resist Lú Xún (盧循).
According to the rules for posthumous titles: "To endanger one's person in service of the sovereign is called Zhōng (忠);
to possess unyielding virtue and achieve it is called Sù (肅)."
"The safety or danger of the state
rests on this one action.
I hear that Lú Xún’s (盧循) fleet is very large,
and holds the upper stream.
It is advisable to breach Nántáng (南塘),
and hold the two cities to await them."
The Gàn-shuǐ (贛水) originates from Nièdū-shān (聶都山) in Nányě-xiàn (南壄縣) of Yùzhāng (豫章) Commandery in the Hàn (漢) dynasty;
Nányě (南壄) of the Hàn (漢) dynasty
was Nánkāng (南康) territory in the Jìn (晉) dynasty.
The Gàn-shuǐ (贛水) reaches Nánchāng-xiàn (南昌縣),
passing Nántáng (南塘);
Nántáng (南塘) is west of Xú Rú-zǐ’s (徐孺子) residence.
The two cities
refer to Yùzhāng (豫章) and Xúnyáng (尋陽).
The Shuǐjīng-zhù (水經註) states: "East of Yùzhāng (豫章) city is a large lake,
ten *lǐ* and two hundred and twenty-six *bù* long,
its north side level with the city.
Its southern edge winds around to Nántáng (南塘).
It originally connected to the Gàn-jiāng (贛江),
its water level rising and falling with the river.
During the Yǒngyuán (永元) era of the Hàn (漢) dynasty,
the Grand Administrator Zhāng Gōng (張躬) built a dike to open the southern road
and also to block this water."
"If Nántáng (南塘) is breached,
Lú Xún's (盧循) naval forces will be useless.
We can then hold firm and await their exhaustion.
Conserve strength and nurture spirit,
wait until they are weary and old,
and then strike them.
This is the most secure plan.
To decide success or failure in a single battle now,
if by some chance we suffer a defeat,
regret will be of no avail."
Cānjūn (參軍) Yīn Chǎn (殷闡) said:
"The forces Lú Xún (盧循) leads are all old bandits from Sān Wú (三吳),
veterans of a hundred battles with residual courage.
The Xī-zǐ (溪子) of Shǐxīng (始興)
are agile and skilled in combat.
They are not to be taken lightly."
"The Xī-zǐ (溪子) of Shǐxīng (始興)
refers to the Shǐxīng (始興) troops commanded by Xú Dào-fù (徐道覆)."
The Shī (詩) says: "Without strength, without courage."
The Máo-zhuàn (毛傳) says: "Quán (拳)
means strength."
Jiāng (將)
is pronounced like liàng (亮).
Yì (易)
is pronounced like gǔ (鼓).
"Conscripting troops in the affiliated commanderies and engaging in battle when they arrive
would not be too late;
if we rashly advance with these forces,
there will most likely be regret."
Wú-Jì (無忌) did not listen.
In the third month,
on the day Rénshēn (壬申),
he met Xú Dào-fù (徐道覆) at Yùzhāng (豫章).
The rebels ordered several hundred powerful crossbowmen to ascend a small hill on the west bank to intercept and shoot at them.
At that time, a west wind suddenly became violent,
blowing the small vessel Wú-Jì (無忌) was on towards the east bank.
The rebels took advantage of the wind to press in with their large vessels,
and his forces consequently broke and fled.
Wú-Jì (無忌) shouted loudly:
"Bring me my Sū Wǔ (蘇武) ensign!"
When the ensign arrived,
he held it to direct the battle.
The rebels gathered like clouds.
Wú-Jì’s (無忌) expression and words showed no yielding;
he grasped the ensign and died.
Thereupon, the interior and exterior of the court were shocked and terrified,
and the imperial council wished to escort the imperial carriage north
to join Liú Yù (劉裕).
But later they learned the rebels had not yet arrived,
so they stopped.
7. Qín (秦) King Gān-Guī (乾歸) of Western Qín (西秦) attacked Jīnchéng (金城) Commandery of Qín (秦),
and captured it.
8. Xià (夏) King Bó-Bó (勃勃) sent Shàngshū (尚書) Hú Jīn-zuǎn (胡金纂) to attack Píngliáng (平涼).
Qín (秦) King Xìng (興) rescued Píngliáng (平涼),
attacked Jīn-zuǎn (金纂),
and killed him.
Bó-Bó (勃勃) again sent his nephew, Zuǒ Jiāngjūn (左將軍) Luó Tí (羅提), to attack and capture Dìngyáng (定陽).
The Wèi-shōu Dìxíng-zhì (魏收地形志) states that Fūchéng (敷城) Commandery has Dìngyáng-xiàn (定陽縣);
it is now within the boundaries of Fūchéng-xiàn (鄜城縣) in Fūzhōu (鄜州).
Qín (秦) generals Cáo Chì (曹熾), Cáo Yún (曹雲), Wáng Sì-fó (王肆佛) and others each led several thousand households to move inwards,
and Xìng (興) settled them at Huángshān (湟山) and Chéncāng (陳倉).
According to the Zàijì (載記),
Huángshān (湟山)
is a lake name.
Chǔ (處)
is pronounced like chāng-lǚ (昌呂).
He broke Báiyá-bǎo (白崖堡),
and then headed for Qīngshuǐ (清水).
Qīngshuǐ-xiàn (清水縣),
in the Former Hàn (前漢) belonged to Tiānshuǐ (天水) Commandery,
was abolished in the Later Hàn (後漢),
and in the Jìn (晉) was divided and belonged to Lüèyáng (略陽) Commandery.
The Yuánfēng Jiǔyù-zhì (元豐九域志) says: Qīngshuǐ-xiàn (清水縣) is ninety *lǐ* east of Qínzhōu (秦州);
it has Báishā-zhèn (白沙鎮),
and west of the county there is also Báishí-bǎo (白石堡).
Qù (趣)
is pronounced like qī-yù (七喻).
Bó-Bó (勃勃) moved sixteen thousand of its households to Dàchéng (大城).
Xìng (興) pursued him from Āndìng (安定),
reaching Shòuqú-chuān (壽渠川),
but did not overtake him and returned.
9. Previously,
Southern Liáng (南涼) King Rǔtán (傉檀) sent Zuǒ Jiāngjūn (左將軍) Kū-mù (枯木) and others to attack Jūqú Méng-xùn (沮渠蒙遜),
plundering over a thousand households from Línsōng (臨松) before returning.
Zhāng Tiān-xī (張天錫) divided Zhāngyè (張掖) to establish Línsōng (臨松) Commandery.
The Wǔdài-zhì (五代志) says: Gānzhōu (甘州) Zhāngyè-xiàn (張掖縣),
in the Later Zhōu (後周) merged Línsōng (臨松) into it.
Rǔ (傉)
is pronounced like nú-wò (奴沃).
Jū (沮)
is pronounced like zǐ-yú (子余).
Huán (還)
is pronounced like cóng-xuān (從宣),
or as written;
the same below.
Upon arriving at Xiǎnměi (顯美),
he moved several thousand households and left.
Xiǎnměi-xiàn (顯美縣),
in the Former Hàn (前漢) belonged to Zhāngyè (張掖) Commandery,
in the Later Hàn (後漢) and Jìn (晉) belonged to Wǔwēi (武威) Commandery.
The Wǔdài-zhì (五代志) says: In the Later Zhōu (後周) Xiǎnměi (顯美) was abolished and merged into Gūzāng-xiàn (姑臧縣).
He was utterly defeated and returned.
That month,
Rǔtán (傉檀) personally led fifty thousand cavalry to attack Méng-xùn (蒙遜).
They battled at Qióngquán (窮泉),
and Rǔtán (傉檀) was utterly defeated,
fleeing back on a single horse.
Méng-xùn (蒙遜) took advantage of the victory to advance and besiege Gūzāng (姑臧).
The people of Gūzāng (姑臧), having been punished by Wáng Zhōng (王鍾)’s execution,
all panicked and scattered.
Wáng Zhōng’s (王鍾) execution is seen in the fourth year of the previous volume.
Rǔtán (傉檀) was afraid,
and sent Sīlì Xiàowèi (司隸校尉) Jìng Guī (敬歸) and his son Tuó (佗) as hostages to Méng-xùn (蒙遜) to request peace.
Hé Chéng-tiān’s (何承天) Xìngyuàn (姓苑) says: The Jìng (敬) surname
is descended from Jìng Kāng (敬康), grandson of the Yellow Emperor;
the Fēngsú-tōng (風俗通) says: it is descended from Chén Jìng-zhòng (陳敬仲).
Zhì (質)
has the sound of zhì (致).
Guī (歸) reached Húkēng (胡阬)
and escaped back.
Tuó (佗) was captured by the pursuing soldiers.
Méng-xùn (蒙遜) moved over eight thousand of their households and departed.
Yòuwèi Jiāngjūn (右衞將軍) Zhéjué Qí-zhèn (折掘奇鎮) occupied Shílǘ-shān (石驢山) and rebelled.
Shílǘ-shān (石驢山) is southwest of Gūzāng (姑臧), northwest of Chángníng-chuān (長寧川),
belonging to Jìnchāng (晉昌) Commandery.
Zhāng Shí (張寔) attacked Cáo Qū (曹袪) at Jìnchāng (晉昌),
crossing Shílǘ (石驢) from west of Gūzāng (姑臧)
to occupy Chángníng (長寧).
Zhé (折)
is pronounced like ér-shè (而設).
Jué (掘)
is pronounced like qí-yuè (其月).
Fearing that the area south of the ridge would be occupied by Qí-zhèn (奇鎮),
Rǔtán (傉檀) then moved to Lèdū (樂都),
leaving Dàsīnóng (大司農) Chéng Gōng-xù (成公緒) to guard Gūzāng (姑臧).
As soon as Rǔtán (傉檀) left the city,
Hóu Chén (侯諶) and others from Wèi’ān (魏安)
(the Jìn-shū Zàijì (晉書載記) records them as
"Jiāo Chén (焦諶), Wáng Hóu (王侯) and others")
Chén (諶)
is pronounced like shì-rén (氏壬).
gathered over three thousand households,
occupied the southern city,
and proclaimed Jiāo Lǎng (焦朗) as Dà Dūdū (大都督), Lóngxiáng Dà Jiāngjūn (龍驤大將軍).
Chén (諶) declared himself Cǐshǐ (刺史) of Liángzhōu (涼州),
and surrendered to Méng-xùn (蒙遜).
After Rǔtán (傉檀) seized Gūzāng (姑臧),
he engaged in battle with his four neighbors,
and was defeated in every encounter.
Not only did he lose Gūzāng (姑臧),
but he could not even hold Lèdū (樂都).
The Shī (詩) says:
"Do not plow the broad field,
for weeds will grow proudly.
Do not think of distant people,
your heart will be distressed and anxious."
This is exactly what is meant here.
10 Liú Yù (劉裕) reached Xiàpī (下邳).
He transported supplies by boat,
while he himself led elite infantry on foot.
Arriving at Shānyáng (山陽),
he heard that Hé Wújì (何無忌) had been defeated and killed.
Fearing that the capital might fall,
he marched day and night,
and with several tens of men, reached the Huái (淮) River.
Lǐ Yánshòu’s (李延壽) Nánshǐ (南史) writes
“the Jiāng (江) River,”
which should be followed,
as Yù (裕) had already crossed the Huái (淮) when he reached Shānyáng (山陽).
Travelers said:
“The rebels have not yet arrived.
If Duke Liú (劉) returns,
there will be nothing to worry about.”
Yù (裕) was greatly pleased.
As he was about to cross the Jiāng (江) River,
the wind was strong,
and everyone found it difficult.
Yù (裕) said:
“If Heaven’s mandate assists the state,
the wind will cease by itself;
if not,
what harm is there in perishing by drowning!”
He immediately ordered them to board the boat,
and as the boat moved, the wind stopped.
After crossing the river,
and arriving at Jīngkǒu (京口),
the populace finally felt greatly relieved.
In summer,
in the fourth month,
on the Guǐwèi (癸未) day,
Yù (裕) arrived at Jiànkāng (建康).
As Jiāngzhōu (江州) had been lost,
he submitted a memorial offering to return his official sash and seal,
but an imperial edict disallowed it.
Zhūgě Chángmín (諸葛長民), the Cìshǐ (刺史) of Qīngzhōu (青州), Liú Fān (劉藩), the Cìshǐ (刺史) of Yǎnzhōu (兗州), and Liú Dàolián (劉道憐), the Cìshǐ (刺史) of Bīngzhōu (幷州), each led troops to defend Jiànkāng (建康).
Qīngzhōu (青州), Yǎnzhōu (兗州), and Bīngzhōu (幷州) were
at that time all provisional administrations located between the Jiāng (江) and Huái (淮) rivers.
Jiāng (將) [meaning 'to lead'],
is pronounced like liàng (亮);
same below.
Yùzhōu (豫州) Cìshǐ (刺史) [Liú] Yì (毅) was his younger cousin.
Yì (毅) heard that Lú Xún (盧循) had invaded,
and was about to resist him when he fell ill;
after recovering,
he was about to set out.
Liú Yù (劉裕) sent a letter to Yì (毅) saying:
“I have previously practiced attacking demon rebels.
Sūn Tài (孫泰) misled the masses with heterodox ways,
and Sūn Ēn (孫恩) and Lú Xún (盧循) are both his followers,
hence they are called demon rebels.
Yí (遺),
is pronounced like Jì (季).
Yāo (妖),
is pronounced like jiāo (嬌).
The rebels have recently gained ill-gotten profits,
and their vanguard cannot be taken lightly.
Now that the repair of our boats is almost complete,
I should undertake this endeavor with you, my brother.
On the day we achieve victory and peace,
the responsibility for the upper reaches of the river
will all be entrusted to you.”
He also dispatched Liú Fān (劉藩) to
persuade and stop him.
Yì (毅) was enraged,
and said to Fān (藩):
“In the past, I deferred to him due to his temporary achievement,
but do you really think I am truly inferior to Liú Yù (劉裕)! ”
He threw the letter to the ground,
and led a naval force of 20,000 from Gūshú (姑孰).
At that time, Yì (毅) was stationed in Gūshú (姑孰) as the Cìshǐ (刺史) of Yùzhōu (豫州).
Shuài (帥),
is read as Shuài (率).
When Xún (循) first invaded,
he sent Xú Dàofù (徐道覆) towards Xúnyáng (尋陽),
while Xún (循) himself attacked the various commanderies in Xiāngzhōng (湘中).
The various commanderies in Xiāngzhōng (湘中) were the territory of Hàn’s (漢) Chángshā (長沙), Líng (零), and Guì (桂).
He was defeated at Chángshā (長沙).
Xún (循) advanced to Bālíng (巴陵),
intending to head towards Jiānglíng (江陵).
Xú Dàofù (徐道覆) heard that Yì (毅) was approaching,
and urgently sent a messenger to report to Xún (循), saying:
“Yì’s (毅) troops are very numerous,
and the success or failure of this matter
depends on this encounter.
We should combine our forces to crush him;
if we achieve victory here,
Jiānglíng (江陵) will be nothing to worry about.”
Xún (循) immediately departed from Bālíng (巴陵) that very day,
