flows north past the west of Cháng'ān city,
and merges with the water of Kūnmíng Chí.
Its tributary flows northeast,
past the south of Dèng Ài Cí,
then divides into two streams to the east.
One stream enters Xiāoyáoyuán.
Zhèn'è sailed upstream on the Wèi River,
using *méngchōng* (covered assault boats) and small warships.
All the boatmen were inside the warships.
When the Qín people saw the warships advancing without any boatmen,
they were all astonished, thinking it was divine.
At dawn on the day of Rénxū,
Zhèn'è arrived at Wèiqiáo.
He ordered his soldiers to finish eating,
then all to hold their weapons and disembark.
Those who disembarked later would be beheaded.
After the multitude had disembarked,
the Wèi River was swift,
and all the warships were carried away by the current,
disappearing without a trace.
At that time, Hóng still commanded tens of thousands of men.
Zhèn'è instructed his soldiers, saying:
"We are all from Jiāngnán.
This is the northern gate of Cháng'ān,
ten thousand *lǐ* from home.
Our boats, clothes, and provisions have all been swept away by the current.
Now, if we advance and win,
both fame and achievement will be manifest.
If we do not win,
our bones will not return,
and there is no other path."
*Qí*
means a divergent path.
Then he personally led the charge,
and the multitude surged forward,
greatly defeating Yáo Pī at Wèiqiáo.
Hóng led troops to rescue him,
but was trampled by Pī's fleeing soldiers,
and disintegrated without a fight.
Yáo Chén and others all died,
and Hóng returned to his palace on a single horse.
Zhèn'è entered through Píngshuòmén.
The Hàn dynasty had no Píngshuòmén.
It was presumably a northern gate of Cháng'ān city,
whose name was changed by later generations.
Prince of Dōngpíng, Zàn, heard of Hóng's defeat
and led his troops to reinforce him,
but all his men dispersed.
Hú Yìdù surrendered to Grand Commandant Yù.
As Hóng was about to surrender,
his son, Fóniàn,
who was eleven years old,
said to Hóng:
"The Jìn people will indulge their desires.
Even if we surrender, we will not escape.
It is better to end our lives."
Hóng was disheartened and did not respond.
Fóniàn climbed the palace wall and threw himself down to his death.
Although Yáo Fóniàn was not as prominent as Liú Chén,
for a child of his age to possess such fierce spirit
is also worthy of admiration.
On the day of Guǐhài,
Hóng led his wife and children and his retainers to Zhèn'è's camp gate to surrender.
Zhèn'è handed them over to his subordinates.
There were over sixty thousand barbarian and Jìn households in the city.
Zhèn'è pacified them with the state's benevolence,
and his orders were strict,
so the people lived in peace.
In the ninth month,
Grand Commandant Yù arrived at Cháng'ān.
Zhèn'è welcomed him at Bàshàng.
Yù praised him, saying:
"It is you, Sir, who has achieved my hegemony!"
Zhèn'è bowed twice in thanks, saying:
"It is due to your Excellency's might
and the strength of all the generals.
What merit do I, Zhèn'è, have?"
Yù smiled and said:
"Do you wish to emulate Féng Yì?"
He meant that Féng Yì was humble and unboastful,
yet was able to pacify Guānzhōng.
The Qín treasury was full of accumulated wealth,
and Zhèn'è's thefts were innumerable.
Yù, considering his great merits,
did not question him.
Someone slandered him to Yù, saying:
"Zhèn'è has hidden Yáo Hóng's fake imperial carriage
and harbors ulterior motives."
Yù sent someone to observe him.
Zhèn'è had stripped the gold and silver from it
and discarded the carriage by the wall.
Yù's mind was then put at ease.
Yù collected Qin's *yíqì*, armillary sphere, *tǔguī*, odometer carriage, and south-pointing chariot and sent them to Jiànkāng.
*Zuǒzhuàn*: Zhù Tuó said: "King Chéng divided for Duke Lǔ official posts and *yíqì*."
Dù Yù's commentary: *Yíqì* are
commonly used instruments.
During Emperor Wǔ's reign,
Luòxià Hóng, Xiānyú Wàngrén, and Gěng Shòuchāng constructed a celestial sphere to calculate calendar degrees.
During Emperor Hé's reign,
Jiǎ Kuí added the ecliptic.
During Emperor Shùn's reign,
Zhāng Héng further created a *húnxiàng*,
which included inner and outer circles, the ecliptic and equator, the north and south poles,
and listed the twenty-four solar terms, twenty-eight lunar mansions, inner and outer star officials, as well as the sun, moon, and five planets.
It was rotated by dripping water in a chamber on a palace hall,
with stars appearing and disappearing,
corresponding to the heavens.
Afterwards,
Wú's Lù Jì created a *húnxiàng*,
and Wáng Fán made an armillary sphere.
The old *húnxiàng* used two parts for one degree,
with a total circumference of seven *chǐ* three *cùn* and a half.
Zhāng Héng reformed its construction,
using four parts for one degree,
with a total circumference of one *zhàng* four *chǐ* six *cùn*.
Wáng Fán, finding the ancient system too small,
with stars too dense,
and Héng's instrument too large,
making it difficult to move,
redesigned the *húnxiàng*,
using three parts for one degree,
with a total circumference of one *zhàng* nine *cùn* and three-fifths of a *fēn*.
*Zhōulǐ*: The Grand Minister of Education used the method of the *tǔguī* to measure the depth of the earth,
correct the sundial shadow,
and thereby find the center of the earth.
If the sun is south, the shadow is short and there is much heat;
if the sun is north, the shadow is long and there is much cold;
if the sun is east, the evening shadow indicates much wind;
if the sun is west, the morning shadow indicates much cloudiness.
The shadow at the solstice,
being one *chǐ* five *cùn*,
is called the center of the earth.
The commentary says: "The *tǔguī* is used to determine the shadows of the four seasons, sun, and moon."
Zhèng Sīnóng said: "Measuring the depth of the earth
refers to the depth in the north, south, east, and west directions."
"Sun south"
means the measuring post is too far south,
close to the sun.
"Sun north"
means the measuring post is too far north,
far from the sun.
"Evening shadow"
means the shadow is centered only after the sun has passed its zenith,
the measuring post is too far east,
close to the sun.
"Morning shadow"
means the shadow is centered before the sun has passed its zenith,
the measuring post is too far west,
far from the sun.
Xuán says: "Place the *tǔguī* at the halfway point of the daytime clepsydra,
indicating yin and yang,
and determining its north and south.
If the shadow is shorter than the *tǔguī*,
it is called 'sun south,'
meaning this location is relatively south of the sun.
If the shadow is longer than the *tǔguī*,
it is called 'sun north,'
meaning this location is relatively north of the sun.
East of the *tǔguī* is called 'sun east,'
meaning this location is relatively east of the sun.
West of the *tǔguī* is called 'sun west,'
meaning this location is relatively west of the sun.
If this is the case,
then cold, heat, cloudy skies, and wind will be unbalanced and disharmonious,
which means the desired location has not been found."
Generally, the sun's shadow changes by one *cùn* for every thousand *lǐ* on the ground.
Zhèng Sīnóng also said: "The length of the *tǔguī* is one *chǐ* five *cùn*.
On the day of the summer solstice, erect an eight-*chǐ* gnomon,
and if its shadow is exactly equal to the *tǔguī*,
it is called the center of the earth.
Today, the land in Yǐngchuān, Yángchéng, is such."
*Jìn Yúfú Zhì*: The odometer carriage
is drawn by four horses, and its construction is like that of the south-pointing chariot.
Cuī Bào's *Gǔjīn Zhù* says: "The Dàzhāng carriage, which is used to mark distances,
originated in the Western Capital;
it is also called the *jìlǐ* carriage.
The carriage has two layers,
both with wooden figures.
After one *lǐ* of travel,
the lower layer strikes a drum;
after ten *lǐ* of travel,
the upper layer strikes a bell.
Huángdì created the south-pointing chariot.
*Jìn Yúfú Zhì*: The Sīnán chariot,
also called the south-pointing chariot,
is drawn by four horses.
Its lower structure is like a multi-storied building,
with three tiers and four corners,
golden dragons holding feathered banners in their mouths.
Wooden immortals are carved,
wearing feathered garments,
standing on the chariot;
even when the chariot turns,
their hands always point south.
When the emperor travels,
it serves as the vanguard vehicle.
Xiāo Zǐxiǎn said: "The south-pointing chariot
has a roof over its four side panels.
The south-pointing figure wears a skirt, jacket, and celestial robe inside the panels.
All four upper corners are adorned with dragon finials,
with a variegated color scheme;
it has true peacock feathers,
a black cloth covering,
lacquered wheels,
is drawn by oxen,
and all fittings are made of bronze.
The odometer carriage is constructed like the south-pointing one,
with an ornate canopy on top,
its garments are of silk and lacquered,
and its drum mechanism is all inside."
Hún,
pronounced *hùběn*.
All were bestowed upon generals and soldiers.
Qín's Prince of Píngyuán Pú and Jìngzhōu Inspector Yǐn Zhāo surrendered with Púbǎn.
The Duke of Dōngpíng Zàn led his clan of over a hundred people to surrender to Yù.
Yù killed them all.
Yáo Hóng was sent to Jiànkāng
and executed in the marketplace.
In the ninth year of Tài Yuán of Emperor Xiàowǔ,
Yáo Cháng founded his state,
changed the era name to Báiquè,
in the *jiǎshēn* year.
It passed through three rulers
and perished after thirty-four years.
Yù appointed Xuē Biàn as Prefect of Píngyáng,
ordering him to guard the northern road.
Yù proposed moving the capital to Luòyáng.
His Advisory Military Counselor Wáng Zhòngdé said:
"Extraordinary matters
are certainly not within the grasp of ordinary people
and will inevitably cause alarm.
Now, the army has been exposed for a long time,
and the soldiers long to return home.
The plan to move the capital
cannot be discussed yet."
So Yù stopped.
Over ten thousand Qiāng people fled west to Lǒngshàng.
Shěn Línzǐ pursued and attacked them as far as Huáilǐ,
capturing tens of thousands.
The Yáo clan
were Qiāng;
since the Yáo clan was destroyed,
the Qiāng masses fled west.
Héxī King Méngxùn heard that Grand Commandant Yù had destroyed Qín
and was extremely angry.
Attendant Clerk Liú Xiáng entered to report on matters.
Since Cáo Cāo and Sūn Quán established *jiàoshì* to observe officials,
they were called *jiàoláng*;
later this name was adopted.
Méngxùn established various *cáo jiàoláng*,
such as the Attendant Clerk and Central Army Clerk.
Méngxùn said:
"You heard that Liú Yù entered the pass,
yet dared to be so arrogant!"
Thereupon he executed him.
Earlier,
Xià King Bóbó heard that Grand Commandant Yù was attacking Qín,
and said to his officials:
"Yáo Hóng is no match for Yù.
Moreover, his brothers have rebelled internally,
how can he resist others!
Yù will certainly take Guānzhōng.
However, Yù cannot stay long
and will surely return south;
he will leave his sons, nephews, and various generals to guard it,
and I will take it as easily as picking up mustard seeds."
Thereupon he fed his horses and sharpened his weapons,
trained his soldiers,
advanced to occupy Āndìng,
and all the commanderies, counties, towns, and garrisons north of Qínlíng surrendered to him.
Yù sent an envoy with a letter to Bóbó,
proposing brotherhood.
Bóbó ordered Secretary of the Central Secretariat Huángfǔ Huī to draft a reply and secretly recite it,
then dictated it to a scribe in front of Yù's envoy.
Yù read the text
and sighed,
"I am not as good as he!"
Historians say barbarian leaders often possess stratagems.
16 Guǎngzhōu Inspector Xiè Xīn died;
Xú Dàoqí of Dōnghǎi gathered a crowd and captured the provincial capital,
then attacked Shǐxīng.
Shǐxīng Administrator Liú Qiānzhī of Péngchéng suppressed and executed him.
An imperial edict appointed Qiānzhī as Guǎngzhōu Inspector.
In the 17th year, Guǐyǒu,

Sīmǎ Xiūzhī, Sīmǎ Wénsī, Sīmǎ Guóyán, Sīmǎ Dàocì, Lǔ Guǐ, Hán Yánzhī, Diāo Yōng, Wáng Huìlóng, and Huán Wēn's grandsons Dàodù and Dàozǐ, along with clan members Huán Mì, Huán Suì, Yuán Shì of Chénjùn, and others, all went to Northern Wèi's Zhǎngsūn Sōng and surrendered.
As the Later Qín had already been destroyed,
Sīmǎ Xiūzhī and the others feared being executed by Yù,
and so they all surrendered to Wèi.
Yán,
pronounced fú yuán fān.
Yōng,
pronounced yú róng fān.
Suì,
pronounced suì.
Jiàng,
pronounced hù jiāng fān.
Wèi's ruler, Sì, issued an edict stating that anyone in the populace who captured and brought a son or younger brother of the Yáo clan to Píngchéng would be rewarded.
In winter,
10th month,
Jǐyǒu,
Sì summoned Zhǎngsūn Sōng and others to return.
Sīmǎ Xiūzhī soon died in Wèi.
Wèi granted Sīmǎ Guóyán the title of Duke of Huáinán, Dàocì the title of Viscount of Chíyáng, and Lǔ Guǐ the title of Duke of Xiāngyáng.
Diāo Yōng submitted a memorial requesting to demonstrate his loyalty in the southern borderlands.
Sì appointed Yōng as Jiànyì Jiāngjūn.
The title Jiànyì Jiāngjūn
was bestowed upon Diāo Yōng by Wèi to honor him,
meaning to allow him to raise a righteous army to avenge his father and elder brother.
He agitated Xú and Yǎn;
Grand Commandant Yù sent troops to suppress him,
but they were unsuccessful.
Yōng advanced and garrisoned Gùshān,
his forces reaching 20,000.
An edict was issued promoting the Duke of Sòng's peerage to King,
and increasing his fief by ten commanderies;
he declined to accept.
The King of Western Qín, Chìpán, dispatched Left Chancellor Tándá and others to attack Yáo Ài, a former general of Qín.
Ài
was the garrison commander of Shàngguī in Qín.
Jiāng,
pronounced jí liàng fān.
Chìpán appointed Ài as Grand General Who Conquers the East and Shepherd of Qínzhōu.
Wáng Sōngshòu was summoned to be Minister of the Left.
In the twelfth year,
Chìpán sent Sōngshòu to garrison Mǎtóu to threaten Qín's Shàngguī;
Shàngguī surrendered,
so he was recalled.
In the 11th month,
Wèi's Shūsūn Jiàn and others attacked the Dīnglíng Zhái Shǔ Luòzhī and others in the Western Mountains,
and pacified them.
The Western Mountains
were the Western Mountains of Wèi's Ānzhōu.
Xīnwèi,
Liú Mùzhī died.
Grand Commandant Yù, upon hearing of it,
was shocked, grieved, and lamented for several days.
Initially,
Yù wanted to remain in Cháng'ān to manage the northwest,
but his generals and advisors, having served for a long time, desired to return,
and many did not wish to stay.
When Mùzhī died,
Yù, feeling that his foundation had no one to rely on,
then decided to return east.
When Mùzhī died,
the imperial court was fearful
and wanted to issue an edict
appointing Grand Commandant Left Sīmǎ Xú Xiànzhī to replace him.
Zhāng Shào, Central Army Consultative Adjutant, said:
"Though this is an urgent matter,
the responsibility ultimately rests with Xú;
however, the heir apparent cannot issue commands unilaterally,
so it is advisable to consult with him."
Yù wished to appoint Wáng Hóng to replace Mùzhī.
Xiè Huì, Cóngshì Zhōngláng, said:
"Xiūyuán is too light-hearted;
he is not as good as Xiànzhī."
Wáng Hóng's courtesy name was Xiūyuán.
Yì,
pronounced yǐ chì fān.
Dài guǎn liúrèn.
Consequently, all important court matters that used to be decided by Mùzhī
were now
all consulted with the north.
Yù appointed his second son, Guìyánggōng Yìzhēn, as Grand Commander of Military Affairs of Yōng, Liáng, and Qínzhōu, General Who Guards the West, and Governor of Yōng and Eastern Qínzhōu.
Yìzhēn was then twelve years old.
He appointed Wáng Xiū of Jīngzhào, Consultative Adjutant to the Grand Commandant, as Chief Clerk;
Wáng Zhèn'è as Sīmǎ and concurrently Administrator of Fēngyì;
Shěn Tiánzǐ and Máo Dézǔ both as Central Army Adjutants,
with Tiánzǐ concurrently Administrator of Shǐpíng,
and Dézǔ concurrently Governor of Qínzhōu and Administrator of Tiānshuǐ;
Fù Hóngzhī as Yōngzhōu Zhìzhōng Cóngshìshǐ.
Previously,
displaced households from Lǒngshàng who had taken refuge in Guānzhōng
hoped to regain their homeland through military might;
and when Eastern Qínzhōu was established—
at that time Yù had not yet secured Tiānshuǐ,
and Eastern Qínzhōu was administered by Máo Dézǔ—
some said
that Yù established Eastern Qínzhōu
and had Yìzhēn concurrently administer it.
Xiān,
pronounced xī jiàn fān.
All sighed in disappointment.
The people of Guānzhōng had always esteemed Wáng Měng.
When Yù conquered Cháng'ān,
Wáng Zhèn'è's contributions were numerous,
which caused the southerners to be wary of him.
Shěn Tiánzǐ, considering his swift victory at Yáoliǔ,
competed with Zhèn'è for credit and felt unfairly treated.
When Yù was about to return,
Tiánzǐ and Fù Hóngzhī repeatedly spoke to Yù, saying:
"Zhèn'è's family is in Guānzhōng;
he cannot be trusted."
Yù said:
"I am leaving behind for you ten thousand elite soldiers, civil and military officers.
If he intends to do evil,
it will only lead to his own destruction.
Do not speak further."
Yù privately told Tiánzǐ:
"Zhōng Huì failed to carry out his rebellion
because of Wèi Guàn.
The matter of Huì and Guàn can be found in Volume 78, Wèi Yuándì Xiánxī first year.
You and more than ten others,
why fear Wáng Zhèn'è!"
This was setting the stage for Shěn Tiánzǐ to kill Wáng Zhèn'è.
Your servant Guāng says: The ancients had a saying:
"If in doubt, do not appoint;
if appointed, do not doubt."
Since Yù had entrusted Guānzhōng to Zhèn'è,
yet again spoke behind his back with Tiánzǐ,
this was inciting them to rebellion.
Alas,
a century-old enemy,
a thousand li of land,
gained with difficulty,
lost in an instant,
causing the capitals of Fēng and Hào to fall into enemy hands again.
Xúnzǐ said:
"Unification is easy to achieve,
but consolidation is difficult."
Indeed!
The elders of the Three Qín, hearing that Yù was about to return,
came to his gate, weeping and pleading:
"Our suffering people have not been blessed by royal civilizing influence
for a hundred years now.
Only now do we see the proper attire and manners, and everyone congratulates each other.
The ten mausoleums in Cháng'ān are the imperial family's tombs,
and the palaces in Xiányáng are the imperial family's residences.
Hàn Gāodì's Chánglíng, Huìdì's Ānlíng, Wéndì's Bālíng, Jǐngdì's Yánglíng, Wǔdì's Màolíng, Zhāodì's Pínglíng, Xuāndì's Dùlíng, Yuándì's Wèilíng, Chéngdì's Yánlíng, Āidì's Yìlíng, Píngdì's Kānglíng,
are all in Guānzhōng,
totaling eleven mausoleums;
saying ten
is using a round number.
Cháng'ān and Xiányáng palaces are all former Hàn sites.
Yù
was a descendant of the Liú clan,
hence the elders used this as a reason to ask him to stay.
Yù was moved by this
and comforted them, saying:
"I have received orders from the imperial court
and cannot remain here.
I truly appreciate your patriotic sentiments.
Now I will let my next son
next son
means second son.
stay and live with you."
In the 12th month,
Gēngzǐ,
Yù departed Cháng'ān,
entered the Yellow River from Luò,
opened the Biàn Canal, and returned.
The Dī chieftains Xú Hàinú and Qí Yuánzǐ and others,
leading a tribe of 30,000, were in Yōng
and sent envoys to request surrender to Wèi.
Wèi's ruler Sì dispatched General Wáng Luòshēng, Administrator of Hénèi Yáng Shēng, and others to travel west to respond to them.
In the intercalary month,
Rénshēn,
Wèi's ruler Sì visited Dàníng Chángchuān.
Over a thousand households from Qín and Yōng
chose Kòu Zàn of Shànggǔ, the Magistrate of Xiāngyì, as their leader and surrendered to Wèi.
Zàn was Qín's Magistrate of Xiāngyì.
After a long time,
the Qín and Yōng people who migrated into Wèi's Hénán, Xíngyáng, and Hénèi
numbered tens of thousands of households.
Sì then established Southern Yōngzhōu,
appointed Zàn as its Governor,
enfeoffed him as Duke of Hénán,
and governed from Luòyáng;
he established prefectures and counties in Yōngzhōu to pacify them.
Zàn was good at attracting and winning over people,
and the number of displaced people who returned to him
tripled from the initial number.
26 King Bóbó of Xià, hearing that Grand Commandant Liú Yù had returned east,
was greatly pleased.
Those skilled in using troops observe the opportune moment and then act.
"I wish to take Guānzhōng.
Please tell me your strategy for this."
Mǎi Dé said:
"Guānzhōng is a strategically important place,
yet Yù has left his young son to guard it,
and returned in disarray,
precisely because he wishes to hastily complete his usurpation,
and has no time to be concerned with the Central Plains again.
Liú Yù's intentions
were known to Cuī Hào and Wáng Mǎi Dé.
(Fù,
pronounced fú yòu fān.)
This opportunity must not be missed.
Qīngní and Shàngluò are
vital strategic points in the north and south,
and an expeditionary force should first be dispatched to cut them off;
block Tóngguān to the east,
severing its land and water routes;
then send a summons to Sānfǔ,
applying both might and virtue.
Then Yìzhēn will be caught in a net,
and can easily be captured."
Bóbó defeated Yìzhēn and took Guānzhōng,
exactly as Mǎi Dé had planned.
(Gǔ,
pronounced gǔ.)
He led twenty thousand cavalry towards Cháng'ān,
with former general Chāng stationed at Tóngguān,
and Mǎi Dé as Fǔjūn Yòuchángshǐ,
stationed at Qīngní.
Liú Yù gained Luòyáng but could not prevent Kòu Zàn from lurking nearby,
and left Yìzhēn to guard Guānzhōng but could not prevent the Xià army from cutting off Tóngguān and Qīngní.
He returned south to Péngchéng,
and before his mat was warm, Yìzhēn was defeated.
Having abandoned the empire,
before his meat was cold, the four garrisons were lost,
which was fitting.
27 In this year,
Fēng Yì, Marquis of Zhāng'ān, a high official of the Wèi capital, passed away.
1 In spring,
the first month,
on the dìnyǒu day of the new moon,
Emperor Sī of Wèi arrived at Píngchéng.
He ordered Hù Gāochē Zhōnglángjiàng Xuē Fán to lead the Gāochē and Dīnglíng to raid north,
reaching Ruòshuǐ before returning.
Wèi imitated Hàn in establishing the office of Hù Gāochē Zhōnglángjiàng, similar to the position of Xiōngnú Zhōnglángjiàng.
(Shuài,
read shuài.)
2 On the xīnsì day,
a general amnesty was declared.
3 In summer,
Hèlián Guī arrived at Wèiyáng.
The people of Guānzhōng who surrendered to him filled the roads.
Longxiáng General Shěn Tiánzǐ led troops to resist him,
but fearing their numerous strength,
retreated to Liúhuíbǎo,
and sent an envoy to report back to Wáng Zhèn'è.
Zhèn'è said to Wáng Xiū:
"The Duke entrusted a ten-year-old child to us.
We should all think of exerting our utmost strength;
but you are holding back troops and not advancing,
how can the barbarians be pacified then!"
The envoy returned
and reported this to Tiánzǐ.
Tiánzǐ and Zhèn'è had long harbored intentions to harm each other,
which made Tiánzǐ even more furious and fearful.
(Soon after,
Zhèn'è and Tiánzǐ both went out to Běidì to resist the Xià army.
Hèlián Guī had already reached Wèiyáng,
how could Wáng and Shěn go out to Běidì?
This mention of Běidì
refers to the area north of Cháng'ān.)
(Jī,
pronounced jū qǐ fān.)
"Zhèn'è wishes to kill all southerners,
send Yìzhēn back south with just a few dozen men,
and then seize Guānzhōng and rebel."
On the xīnhài day,
Tiánzǐ invited Zhèn'è to Fù Hóngzhī's camp to discuss matters;
Tiánzǐ asked for the attendants to be dismissed,
then had his kinsman Shěn Jìngrén kill him under the tent,
falsely claiming to have received the Grand Commandant's order to execute him.
Hóngzhī hurried to inform Liú Yìzhēn.
Yìzhēn and Wáng Xiū donned armor and ascended Héngmén to observe the situation.
(Héngmén is the first gate at the eastern end of the northern side of Cháng'ān city.)
(Bèi,
pronounced pí yì fān.)
(Héng,
pronounced guāng.)
Xiū, claiming Zhèn'è had rebelled,
seized Tiánzǐ,
enumerated his crime of unauthorized execution,
and beheaded him;
he replaced Zhèn'è with Guānwèi Jiāngjūn Máo Xiūzhī as Ānxī Sīmǎ.
Fù Hóngzhī greatly defeated Hèlián Guī at Chíyáng,
and again defeated him at Guǎfù Dù.
(According to Sòng Bái's Xù Tōngdiǎn,
there is a Guǎfù Mountain fifteen li north of present-day Qìngzhōu,
from which a river originates,
and its lower course is Guǎfù Dù.)
The Xià army then retreated.
On the rénxū day,
Grand Commandant Yù arrived at Péngchéng and
lifted the emergency.
Wáng Déwén, Prince of Lángxié, had already returned to Jiànkāng.
Yù, hearing of Wáng Zhèn'è's death,
submitted a memorial stating
that "Shěn Tiánzǐ suddenly became deranged,
and unexpectedly harmed a loyal and meritorious official."
(Kuángyì refers to becoming mentally ill and changing one's normal state of mind.)
(Yì,
as written.)
He appointed Liú Zūnkǎo, Intendant of Péngchéng, as Bìngzhōu Cìshǐ and concurrent Administrator of Hédōng,
stationed at Púbǎn;
and summoned Liú Dàolián, Governor of Jīngzhōu, to be Governor of Xú and Yǎn prefectures.
Yù wished to station his heir apparent Yìfú in Jīngzhōu,
and appoint Liú Yìlóng, Governor of Xúzhōu, as Sīzhōu Cìshǐ,
stationed at Luòyáng.
Zhōngjūn Zīyì Zhāng Shào remonstrated, saying:
(Zīyì refers to Zīyì Cānjūn.)
"The heir apparent holds a weighty position,
on which the fate of the four seas depends,
and should not be stationed externally."
So he instead appointed Yìlóng as Dūdū Jīng‧Yì‧Níng‧Yōng‧Liáng‧Qín Liùzhōu Zhūjūnshì, Xīzhōnglángjiàng, and Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ,
appointed Dào Yànzhī, Administrator of Nánjùn, as Nánmán Xiàowèi,
Zhāng Shào as Sīmǎ and concurrent Nánjùn Xiàng,
Guànjūn Gōngcáo Wáng Tánshǒu as Chángshǐ,
and Běixúzhōu Cóngshì Wáng Huá as Xīzhōngláng Zhǔbù.
(Jìn established Nánxúzhōu at Jīngkǒu,
and Běixúzhōu still had its seat at Péngchéng.)
Dào Yànzhī, Wáng Tánshǒu, and Wáng Huá assisted Yìlóng in establishing his administration,
and subsequently held positions of generals and prime ministers.
Yìlóng was still young,
and all matters of the government were decided by Shào.
(Tánshǒu was Hóngzhī's younger brother.)
Yù said to Yìlóng:
"Wáng Tánshǒu is profound, resolute, and possesses great capacity;
he is a talent for a prime minister.
You should consult him on every matter."
He appointed Liú Yìqìng, Duke of Nánjùn, as Yùzhōu Cìshǐ.
(Yìqìng was Dàolián's son.)
Yù relinquished the governorship of Sīzhōu,
and concurrently held the governorships of Xú and Jì prefectures.
4 King Chìpán of Qín appointed Qǐfú Mùyìgān as Shāzhōu Cìshǐ,
stationed at Lèdū.
5 In the second month,
Yǐfú Wūdìyán led two thousand households to surrender to Qín.
6 In the third month,
envoys were sent to pay respects to Wèi.
7 In summer,
the fourth month,
on the jǐsì day,
Wèi moved the Túhé people from Jì, Dìng, and Yōu prefectures to the capital of Dài.
(In the second year of Huángshǐ under Emperor Guī of Wèi, Zhōngshān was conquered,
Ānzhōu was established,
and a Xíngtái was also set up to govern and pacify its people;
in the third year of Tiānxīng, it was renamed Dìngzhōu,
administering Zhōngshān, Chángshān, Jùlù, Bólíng, Běipíng, Héjiān, Gāoyáng, and Zhàojùn.)
(Sòng Bái said: Initially, Ānzhōu was established,
soon renamed Dìngzhōu,
named to mean "pacifying and stabilizing the world.")
(Túhé likely refers to the people of Túhé who followed Mùróng into China and remained in the three prefectures,
whom the Wèi people then called Túhé.)
Initially, in Hélóng, a red aura filled the four directions and obscured the sun.
From the *yín* to the *shēn* hour,
Zhāng Mù, the Grand Astrologer of Yān, said to Yān Wáng Bà:
"This is an aura of war.
Now Wèi is strong and prosperous,
and you have detained their envoy,
saying he was held at Shímén.
The event is recorded in Volume 116, Yìxī 10th year.
Your servant is secretly fearful."
Bà said:
"I am pondering it."
In the fifth month,
Wèi Zhǔ Sì made an eastern tour,
reaching Rúyuán and Gānsōng.
He dispatched General Zhēngdōng Chángsūn Dàoshēng, General Āndōng Lǐ Xiān, and Palace Attendants Huángmén Shìláng Xī Guān, leading twenty thousand elite cavalry to attack Yān.
He also ordered General Xiāoqí Yán Pǔ and Yōuzhōu Cìshǐ Wèi Nuò to lead troops from Yōuzhōu towards Liáoxī,
to create a show of force.
*Wèishū Guānshì Zhì* states that
the Yán family, among the various families that entered the court, became the Yán氏.
Xiāo
is pronounced *jiāoráo fān*.
The Wèichí family in the west
later changed to the Wèi氏.
Wèi
is pronounced *yù*.
Dàoshēng and the others captured Yǐlián City
and advanced to attack Hélóng.
They battled against Gǔ Ní, the right assistant to the Chányú of Yān,
and defeated him.
In Yìxī 7th year,
Bà appointed four assistants to the Chányú.
Chán
is pronounced *chán*.
Yān Wáng Bà defended himself within the city walls.
The Wèi people attacked,
but could not overcome it.
They plundered over ten thousand households of its people and returned.
9 In the sixth month,
Tàiwèi Yù finally accepted the appointments of Xiàngguó, Sòng Gōng, and the Nine Emblems.
The order was issued in the twelfth year,
but he accepted it only now.
He posthumously honored his stepmother, Lady Xiāo of Lánlíng, as Tàifūrén.
He appointed Tàiwèi Jūnzī Jìjiǔ Kǒng Jìng as Sòng Guó Shàngshū Lìng,
Zuǒ Chángshǐ Wáng Hóng as Púyè,
overseeing selections.
Cóngshì Zhōngláng Fù Liàng and Cài Kuò were both appointed Shìzhōng.
Xiè Huì was appointed Yòuwèi Jiāngjūn.
Yòu Chángshǐ Zhèng Xiānzhī was appointed Fèngcháng.
Xíng Cānjūn Yīn Jǐngrén was appointed Mìshū Láng.
As for the other hundred officials,
all followed the regulations of the imperial court.
Jìng declined the appointment.
Liàng
was the grandson of Xián.
Fù Xián served during the reigns of Wǔ and Huì,
and was renowned for his straightforwardness.
(Kǒng Jìng was) the great-grandson of Mó.
Cài Mó served through three reigns—Chéng, Kāng, and Mù—
serving both locally and as a central minister,
achieving renown and success in both.
(Zhèng Xiānzhī was) the great-great-grandson of Hún.
For Zhèng Hún, see Volume 66, Hàn Xiàndì, Jiàn'ān 17th year.
(Yīn Jǐngrén was) the great-grandson of Róng.
For Yīn Róng, see Volume 94, Chéngdì, Xiánhé 3rd year.
He was intelligent and thoughtful;
he did not speak of righteousness but
deeply understood principles;
as for national codes, court rituals, old statutes, and records,
he compiled and recorded them all.
Those who knew him recognized his ambition for the current age.
10 The Wèi Tiānbù Dàrén, Báimǎ Wénzhēn Gōng Cuī Hóng, was gravely ill.
Last year,
Wèi established six Dàrén for heaven, earth, and the four directions.
He would frequently turn over during the night.
When he died,
an imperial edict commanded all ministers and leaders of allied states to attend the funeral.
Qú
means 'great'.
Zú
is pronounced *zǐxù fān*.
Shuài
is pronounced *suǒlèi fān*.
11 In autumn,
the seventh month,
on the *wùwǔ* day,
Wèi Zhǔ Sì arrived at Píngchéng.
12 In the ninth month,
on the *jiǎyín* day,
the Wèi people ordered all prefectures to levy grain taxes from the people:
fifty *shí* per household,
to be stored in Dìng, Xiàng, and Jì three prefectures.
In Tiānxīng 4th year of Wèi Zhǔ Guī,
Xiàngzhōu was established at Yè,
governing Wèi, Yángpíng, Guǎngpíng, Jí Jùn, Dōng Jùn, Dùnqiū, Púyáng, Qīnghé, and other commanderies.
Jìzhōu only governed Chánglè, Bóhǎi, Wǔyì, Zhāngwǔ, and Lèlíng.
Diào
is pronounced *túdiào fān*.
Xiàng
is pronounced *xīliàng fān*.
13 Héxī Wáng Méngxùn again led his troops to attack Liáng.
Liáng Gōng Xīn was about to resist him,
but his Zuǒ Chángshǐ Zhāng Tǐshùn strongly advised against it,
so he stopped.
Méngxùn reaped their autumn crops and returned.
Xīn sent an envoy to announce his accession to the throne.
In winter,
the tenth month,
Xīn was appointed Dūdū Qī Jùn Zhūjūn Shì, Zhènxī Dà Jiāngjūn, and Jiǔquán Gōng.
He was to command Dūnhuáng, Jiǔquán, JìnXīng, Jiànkāng, Liángxīng, and Huìjī and Guǎngxià, which Xīn's father Gǎo had established—
a total of seven commanderies.
14 Yáo Ài rebelled against Qín
and surrendered to Héxī Wáng Méngxùn.
Yáo Ài had pledged allegiance to Qǐfú,
as recorded in the previous year.
Jiàng
is pronounced *hùjiāng fān*.
Ài's uncle, Jùn, said to the assembled people:
"Qín Wáng is benevolent and magnanimous;
we can surely live in peace and serve him.
Why should we follow Héxī Wáng and move west?"
Everyone agreed,
so they jointly drove out Ài,
acclaimed Jùn as their leader,

"When you arrive,"

Yìzhēn did not follow this advice.
Soon, the Xià troops arrived in great numbers.

Upon reaching Qīngní,

(He) was also captured by the Xià army.

Between Wèi and Jìn,
all sons referred to their fathers as "jiāgōng,"

Wěn (刎),
read "fúfěn" in fanqie.
"We share life and death;
your humble servant cannot bear to."
Thereupon, he tied Yìzhēn to his back

Yìzhēn said to Hóng:
"Today's events

Bóbó, the King of Xià, wanted Fù Hóngzhī to surrender,

Bóbó stripped him naked,
and Hóngzhī cursed and died.
Bóbó piled up human heads into a Jingguān,

The people of Cháng'ān pursued Zhū Língshí.
Língshí burned his palaces and halls,

Since Yìzhēn had plundered Cháng'ān greatly before returning,

Língshí, acting on the command of Sòng Gōng, should have returned with Yìzhēn.
Why did he foolishly stay in Cháng'ān to await being driven out?
What was he thinking?
He feasted his generals and soldiers,
raised his cup, and said to Wáng Mǎidé:
"Your words from back then
have been proven true within a single cycle;
it can be said that your calculations leave no strategy unforeseen.
To whom should this cup be offered,

He appointed Mǎidé as Dūguān Shàngshū
and enfeoffed him as Héyáng Hóu.
Wáng Jìngxiān, the Lóngxiáng General, was garrisoned at Cáogōnglěi.
Cáogōnglěi was at Tóngguān,
built by Cáo Cāo when he attacked Hán and Mǎ.
Xiáng (驤),
read "sījiāng" in fanqie.
Zhū Chāoshí arrived at Púbǎn.
Hearing of Língshí's whereabouts,

Hèlián Chāng attacked Jìngxiān's fortress,

The troops suffered from thirst
and could not fight.
As the city was about to fall,

Chāoshí held his brother and wept, saying:

Thereupon, he, Jìngxiān, and Liú Qīnzhī, the Yòujūn Cānjūn, were all captured and sent to Cháng'ān,
where Bóbó killed them.
Qīnzhī's younger brother, Xiùzhī, wept sadly and did not enjoy banquets for ten years.
Qīnzhī
was Mùzhī's cousin's son.
Sòng Gōng Yù heard of the defeat at Qīngní,
and did not know if Yìzhēn was alive or dead.
He set a date for a northern expedition.
If Yù was able to resume his northern expedition,
then upon hearing of the defeat at Qīngní, he should have risen immediately,
why wait to set a date?
The actions of heroes
are indeed beyond the comprehension of ordinary people.
"The soldiers are exhausted;
please wait for another year."
He did not agree.
Huì asked to wait for another year;
this was also what Yù called 'one who understands changes in circumstances'.
Zhèng Xiānzhī's words, however, differed from this.
He believed:
"The barbarians, hearing of Your Highness's personal campaign,
will surely
concentrate their forces to defend Tóngguān.

I fear it may not be easily overcome.
If the imperial carriage halts at Luòyáng,

Furthermore, although the barbarians have had their way,
they dare not press their advantage beyond Shǎn,
still being awed by Your great might,

If we reach Luòyáng and turn back,
the barbarians will surely entertain further conjectures,

Moreover, a large army far from home
entails many future perils.
In past years, during the Western Expedition,
Liú and Zhōng were in distress;
refers to when bandits attacked Yětíng in the eleventh year.
Guǎngzhōu was overthrown;
refers to Xú Dàoqī's capture of Guǎngzhōu.
These are lessons from the past.
Now, the various prefectures are flooded,
the people's food is scarce,
and the Three Wú regions are plagued by bandits attacking and occupying various counties,
all due to being exhausted by military levies.
The gentry and commoners south of the Yangtze
eagerly crane their necks
to await Your Highness's return.
Hearing of another northern expedition,
without knowing the depth of the plan
or the timing of return,
I fear that the worries about what is behind us will increase in the very heartland."
If you worry that the Western barbarians will again cause trouble for Hé and Luò,
it would be advisable to establish good relations with the Northern barbarians.
If the Northern barbarians are friendly, then Hénán will be peaceful.
The Northern barbarians
refer to Wèi.
Hǎo (好),
read "hūdào" in fanqie.
Upon receiving Duàn Hóng's report,

merely ascending the city wall, looking north,

He demoted Yìzhēn to Jiànwēi General and Sīzhōu Cìshǐ.
He appointed Duàn Hóng as Sòngtái Huángménláng and concurrently Tàizǐ Yòuwèi Shuài.
Yù appointed Máo Dézǔ, the Tīanshǔ Tàishǒu, as Hédōng Tàishǒu,

Although Yù knew Dézǔ was good at defense and used him,

making it appropriate that he could not hold it firm.
This sets the stage for Dézǔ's abandonment of Púbǎn.

18 A comet appeared in Tiānjīn
and entered Tàiwēi.

and circled the Zǐwēi.

are also called Tiānjīn,

are located north of the Běidǒu.
彗 (huì) is read as "xiáng suì fān."
Wèi Zhǔ Sì again summoned various scholars

All of you speak frankly,

The assembly urged Cuī Hào to respond.

"The emergence of omens and anomalies

Afterwards, there was indeed the disaster of Wáng Mǎng usurping the state.
The people have no different aspirations.
The Jìn dynasty is declining,
and its demise is not far off;
this comet as an anomaly,

courtesy name Déwén,

"Honoring the worthy and valuing righteousness,"

9. The Xìa ruler, Hèlián Bóbó, summoned the recluse Wéi Zǔsī from Jīngzhào.
When Zǔsī arrived,
he was excessively reverent and fearful.
Bóbó angrily said:
"I summoned you as a national worthy,
yet you treat me as if I am not of your kind!
You did not bow to Yáo Xīng in the past,
why do you bow to me alone now?
While I am alive,
you still do not consider me an emperor;
when I die,
and you scribblers wield your pens,
where will you place me then!"
He then killed him.
Bóbó's killing of Zǔsī
was tyrannical.
However, Zǔsī's excessive reverence and fear,
which Bóbó took as a slight and killed him for,
shows that Bóbó had insight,
while Zǔsī had no firm principles.
All the ministers requested to make Cháng'ān the capital.
Bóbó said:
"How can I not know that Cháng'ān has been the capital of emperors for generations,
fertile and strategically strong!
However, the Jìn people are far away,
and ultimately cannot be a threat to us.
Wèi and I have roughly similar customs,
and our territories are adjacent.
From Tǒngwàn to the Wèi border is barely a hundred *lǐ*.
If I am in Cháng'ān,
Tǒngwàn will certainly be in danger;
if I am in Tǒngwàn,
Wèi will certainly not dare to cross the river to the west.
You, my lords, simply haven't seen this yet."
They all said:
"We did not consider this."
If Bóbó were to live forever,
it might be acceptable;
but when Bóbó dies,
Tǒngwàn will belong to Wèi.
The way ancient people left things for their descendants
indeed has its principles.
Hèlián Guī was appointed Grand General, Governor of Yōngzhōu, and concurrently Supervising Secretary of the Southern Bureau.
Bóbó returned to Tǒngwàn,
issued a general amnesty,

Bóbó was by nature arrogant and cruel,

He often stayed on the city wall,
with a bow and sword at his side.
If he harbored any suspicion or resentment,

Those of his ministers who looked at him askance had their eyes gouged out.
Suǒyǐn states: *Wǔ* means

*Wǔ* (迕) is pronounced 'wǔ gù fān'.

(*Cóng* is pronounced 'cái yòng fān'.)

When Wáng Zhèn'è died,

Yù appointed him as *Xiàngguó Xíng Cānjūn*.
(According to the Jìn system: all ducal residences established various staff officers (*cānjūn*) for departments,

At that time, Cháng'ān could not be held.

He led three thousand men from Dōngyuán to garrison west of the city.

Sīmǎ Chǔzhī garrisoned at Bǎigǔ Wù.
Wèi's Hénèi Zhenjiāng, Yú Lìdī's, cavalry were on Máng Shān,

Píngděng and all others scattered and fled.

fourth month,

without a fixed month.
Also, to the west of Báidēng, at the place where Tàizǔ used to roam,
temples for Zhāochéng, Xiànmíng, and Tàizǔ were built.
Sacrifices were personally offered there at the turn of the ninth and tenth months.
Thus, the Eastern Temple was
the temple on Báidēng Shān.
Since there was also a temple west of the mountains,
this one was called the Eastern Temple.)
On the *xīnsì* day,
he went south on an inspection tour and reached Yànmén.
Fifth month,
on the first day of the month, *gēngyín*,
Wèi ruler Sī observed fishing at the Lěishuǐ.
On the *jǐhài* day,
he returned to Píngchéng.
13 Láng Gōng Xīn 歆 used severe punishments.
He also liked to construct palaces and chambers.
Zhāng Xiǎn 張顯, the Zhongláng of Engagements, submitted a memorial,
believing:
"The land of Liáng is divided into three parts,
referring to the Lǐ 李 clan, the Jǔqú 沮渠, and the Qǐfú 乞伏.
The basis for unification
lies in promoting agriculture;
the strategy for attracting distant peoples
is none other than leniency and simplicity.
Now, since the beginning of the year,
yin and yang are out of order,
and wind and rain are disharmonious.
Thus, it is appropriate to reduce meals and remove musical instruments.
In ancient times,
the Son of Heaven's meals included six kinds of sacrificial animals,
namely horse, ox, sheep, dog, pig, and chicken.
Feudal lords' meals included three kinds of sacrificial animals.
Xuán 懸 refers to
the musical instruments hung in a frame.
The Son of Heaven had gōngxuán 宮懸 (instruments hung on four sides),
while feudal lords had xuānxuán 軒懸 (instruments hung on three sides).
In times of great famine
or great pestilence,
when Heaven and Earth suffer calamities,
or the state faces major disasters,
then meals are reduced and music is removed.
The Gǔliáng Zhuàn 穀梁傳 says: 'When the five grains do not rise (fail to grow), it is called 'heavenly famine'.
When one grain fails to rise, it is called qiǎn 嗛;
when two grains fail to rise, it is called jī 饑;
when three grains fail to rise, it is called jǐn 饉;
when four grains fail to rise, it is called kāng 康;
when five grains fail to rise, it is called dàqīn 大侵.'
In the rites of dàqīn,
the ruler does not eat dishes of multiple flavors,
platforms and pavilions are not plastered,
the imperial courtyard roads are not cleaned,
all officials are dispatched but no sacrifices are made,
and prayers are offered to spirits and gods but no offerings are made.
The Báihǔ Tōng 白虎通 says: 'When one grain fails to rise, quails and sparrows are removed;
when two grains fail to rise, ducks and geese are removed;
when three grains fail to rise, pheasants and rabbits are removed;
when four grains fail to rise, the animals in the hunting park are reduced;
when five grains fail to rise, the three kinds of sacrificial animals are not fully prepared.'
Yet, Your Highness instead makes punishments more severe and laws harsher,
and construction never ceases.
This is probably not the way to achieve prosperity.
In the past, Wén Wáng 文王 rose from a hundred-li territory,
while Èr Shì 二世 perished despite possessing all within the four seas.
Zhōu Wén Wáng 周文王 rose in Qízhōu 岐周,
an area of a hundred li.
Qín Èr Shì 秦二世 succeeded Shǐ Huáng 始皇,
encompassed all within the four seas,
but ultimately perished.
The successes and failures are clear.
Tàizǔ 太祖, with his divine and sagely demeanor,
was supported by the Western Xià,
taking Jiǔquán 酒泉 on the left,
and opening up the Western Regions on the right.
Lǐ Hào 李暠's temple name was Tàizǔ.
'Supported by the Western Xià'
is recorded in volume 112, in the 4th year of Āndì's 安帝 Lóng'ān 隆安 reign;
'taking Jiǔquán'
is recorded in the 5th year;
'opening up the Western Regions'
is also recorded in the 4th year.
Xià 夏
is pronounced Hù Yǎ Hùyǎ (戶雅).
He unified the land of Liáng,
equaling Zhāng Hòu 張后's achievements.
Zhāng Hòu refers to
Zhāng Guǐ 張軌 and his sons and grandsons.
Jǔqú Méngxùn 沮渠蒙遜, a hero among the Hu-Yí 胡夷,
internally cultivates governance,
and externally treats the wise and virtuous with courtesy.
During battles,
he personally shares the same hardships as his soldiers;
the common people cherish him,
and are happy to serve him.
Your servant believes that Your Highness not only cannot pacify and eliminate Méngxùn,
but also fears that Méngxùn will become a source of trouble for the state."
Xīn 歆 read it,
and was displeased.
The Master of Records, Fàn Chēng, submitted a memorial remonstrating:
"Heaven's love for the human ruler
is most earnest.
Therefore, if the government is not reformed,
it sends down calamities and anomalies to warn and admonish him.
Those who change, though in peril, will surely prosper;
those who do not change, though secure, will surely perish.
In the first year (of the Yuánxǐ [元熙] era),
in the third month,
on the guǐmǎo [癸卯] day,
the Qiāndétáng [謙德堂] in Dūnhuáng [敦煌] collapsed.
Zhāng Jùn [張駿] occupied Hexī [河西]
and built the Qiānguāngdiàn [謙光殿] in Gūzāng [姑臧].
He called himself the sole ruler of one region,
yet he served the Jìn [晉] dynasty without altering his vassal status,
hence the 'humility' (qiān [謙]) and 'light' (guāng [光]).
Lǐ Hào [李暠] obtained Dūnhuáng,
also declared himself a vassal to Jìn,
and built the Qiāndétáng;
his ambition was still like that of the Zhāng [張] clan.
Dūnhuáng:
dúmén fān [徒門翻].
The land in Xiàogǔ [效穀] cracked.
In the second year,
on New Year's Day,
a dense fog covered all four directions.
In the fourth month,
the sun was red and had no light;
it only recovered after twenty days.
In the eleventh month,
a fox ascended the southern gate.
This year, in spring and summer,
the earth frequently quaked five times.
In the sixth month,
a meteor fell in Jiànkāng [建康].
Although my learning does not delve into antiquity,
I am fifty-nine years old;
please allow me, Your Highness, to briefly speak of what I have seen and heard,
and I can no longer discuss matters from ancient books and chronicles from afar.
Recently, at the beginning of the Xián'ān [咸安] era,
the ground in Xīpíng [西平] cracked,
and a fox entered in front of the Qiānguāngdiàn;
soon after, the Qín [秦] army suddenly arrived,
and the capital city could not be defended.
Xián'ān was the reign title of Emperor Jiǎnwén [簡文帝].
Liáng [涼] territory took Gūzāng as its capital city.
In the first year of Emperor Xiàowǔ's [孝武] Tàiyuán [太元] era,
Qín [秦] entered Gūzāng.
The ground cracking and the fox entering occurred at the beginning of Xián'ān,
but its consequence appeared at the beginning of Tàiyuán.
Not caring for the common people,
but focusing solely on accumulating wealth,
in the nineteenth year of Jiànyuán [建元],
the southern gate of Gūzāng collapsed,
and a meteorite fell into Xiányùtáng [閑豫堂];
the following year, he was killed by Lǚ Guāng [呂光].
The first year of Tàiyuán [太元] was the twelfth year of Qín [秦] ruler Jiān's [堅] Jiànyuán [建元] era.
Jiān had Liáng Xī [梁熙] stationed in Liángzhōu [涼州].
The nineteenth year of Jiànyuán was the eighth year of Jìn [晉] Tàiyuán, when Jiān was defeated at Huáinán [淮南].
The following year,
Lǚ Guāng killed Liáng Xī.
Within three years,
there were more than fifty earthquakes;
soon after, the former king rose gloriously in Guāzhōu [瓜州].
Guāzhōu was Dūnhuáng Commandery.
Consulting the Jìnzhì [晉志],
the Zhāng [張] clan established Shāzhōu [沙州] in Dūnhuáng,
but never Guāzhōu.
Also consulting the Tángzhì [唐志],
Shāzhōu Dūnhuáng Commandery
was originally Guāzhōu.
In the fifth year of Wǔdé [武德], it was called Xīshāzhōu [西沙州];
in the seventh year of Zhēnguān [貞觀], it was called Shāzhōu.
Guāzhōu Jìnchāng [晉昌] Commandery
was established in the fifth year of Wǔdé by separating Chánglè [常樂] from Shāzhōu.
Lǐ Hào rose in Dūnhuáng
and called himself the pastor of Qín [秦] and Liáng [涼] two prefectures;
afterwards, he moved to Jiǔquán [酒泉]
and made Dūnhuáng Guāzhōu.
Until the Táng [唐] dynasty, Dūnhuáng was again made Shāzhōu,
and Jìnchāng was made Guāzhōu,
so Guāzhōu was divided into two prefectures.
These are all established facts before your eyes,
which Your Highness clearly knows.
Xiàogǔ was the place where the former king gradually advanced.
Hào [暠], starting as the magistrate of Xiàogǔ, obtained Dūnhuáng
and then possessed seven commanderies;
hence it is said thus.
The 'great advance' (hóngjiàn [鴻漸]) mentioned in the Yì [易]
refers to the wild goose (hóng [鴻]),
a water bird,
which gradually advances from water to dry land,
then gradually to a flat rock,
then gradually to the land,
and then gradually to a tree:
advancing from below,
gradually rising and ascending.
The chamber of the exalted
sinking and the ground cracking
is a sign of great misfortune.
The sun (rì [日])
is the essence of the great yang,
and the symbol of the central state;
red and without light
means the central state will decline.
The proverb says:
'When wild beasts enter a house,
the master will soon depart.'
A fox ascending the southern gate
is also a great anomaly.
Now the barbarians are increasingly prosperous,
and the central state is increasingly weak.
I pray Your Highness to immediately cease the construction of palaces,
stop the pleasure of hunting,
treat outstanding talents with respect,
and love and nurture the common people,
in order to respond to the celestial changes and prevent unforeseen events."
Xīn [歆] did not comply.
In the autumn of the 14th year,
in the seventh month,
Sòng Gōng [宋公] Yù [裕] first received the order to be promoted in rank.
In the eighth month,
he moved his garrison to Shòuyáng [壽陽],
and appointed the Minister of Revenue, Liú Huáishèn [劉懷慎], as the Supervisor of all military affairs north of the Huái [淮] and the Inspector of Xúzhōu [徐州],
garrisoned at Péngchéng [彭城].
Emperor Wén [文帝] of Cáo Wèi [曹魏] established the Minister of Revenue,
in charge of military and state expenditures;
Jìn [晉] followed this.
The character dù [度] is pronounced túluò fān [徒洛翻].
On the xīnwèi [辛未] day,
Wèi [魏] ruler Sì [嗣] went on an eastern tour;
on the jiǎshēn [甲申] day,
he returned to Píngchéng [平城].
In the ninth month,
Sòng Wáng [宋王] Yù [裕] voluntarily resigned as Inspector of Yángzhōu [揚州].
Qín [秦] Left General of the Guard Pǐ Dá [匹達] and others led troops to attack Péng Lìhé [彭利和] in Qiángchuān [漒川],
utterly defeating him.
Lìhé [利和] fled alone on horseback to Qiúchí [仇池];
his wife and children were captured.
Three thousand households of Qiāng [羌] magnates were relocated to Fāohǎn [枹罕],
and more than thirty thousand households of Qiāng in Qiángchuān were all settled as before.
In winter,
in the tenth month,
Wáng Sōngshòu [王松壽], the Minister of Personnel and Right Vice Director, was appointed Inspector of Yìzhōu [益州],
garrisoned at Qiángchuān.
Sòng Wáng Yù, seeing the desolation in Hénán [河南],
on the yǐyǒu [乙酉] day,
transferred Inspector of Sīzhōu [司州] Yìzhēn [義真] to be Inspector of Yángzhōu,
garrisoned at Shítou [石頭].
Xiāo Tài [蕭太] said to Yù:
"Dàolián [道憐] is your brother from humble origins;
he should be appointed to Yángzhōu."
Yù replied:
"How could Jìnú [寄奴] begrudge Dàolián anything!
Yù's childhood name was Jìnú.
Dàolián was born of Xiāo Tài.
Affairs are too numerous,
and Dàolián is not capable of handling them."
Tài said:
"Dàolián is over fifty years old;
how could he be inferior to your ten-year-old son?"
Yù replied:
"Although Yìzhēn is an Inspector,
all matters, big or small,
are handled by Jìnú.
Dàolián is older,
and does not personally attend to affairs;
this is insufficient for public observation and expectation."
Tīngwàng [聽望] means 'observation' or 'public expectation'.
The character zhǎng [長] is pronounced zhīliǎng fān [知兩翻].
Dàolián's nature was foolish, vulgar, greedy, and undisciplined;
therefore, Yù was unwilling to employ him.
In the eleventh month,
on the dīnghài [丁亥] day, the first day of the month,
there was a solar eclipse.
In the twelfth month,
on the guǐhài [癸亥] day,
Wèi ruler Sì toured west to Yúnzhōng [雲中],
crossed the river west at Jūnzǐjīn [君子津],
and had a great hunt at Xuēlínshān [薛林山].
According to the Dìjì [帝紀] in the Wèishū [魏書]: Xuēlínshān is west of Wūdòuchéng [屋竇城].
On the xīnmǎo [辛卯] day,
Sòng Wáng Yù was granted special honors,
his mother Wáng [王] was promoted to Empress Dowager,
and his heir-apparent was made Crown Prince.
